According to Josephus they held that man has free will and that the soul is not immortal, with no rewards or penalties after death. They denied the resurrection of the dead, a point Paul of Tarsus used to divide them from the Pharisees in the Acts of the Apostles. Many of their disputes with the Pharisees concerned ritual purity.

After the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE the Sadducees appear only in a few references in the Talmud and some Christian texts, and the group became extinct sometime afterwards. In the early days of Karaite Judaism the followers of Anan ben David were called Sadducees and claimed historical continuity with them. The gospels name them mainly among the opponents of Jesus, and the Mishnah, the Dead Sea Scrolls and later rabbinic literature all treat them with hostility.
sadeh: The name means hundred in Persian and refers to the hundred days and nights left until the beginning of spring. The festival dates back to the Achaemenid Empire. According to legend it was founded by King Hushang, the second king of the mythological Pishdadian dynasty, who threw a stone at a snake on a mountain; the stone struck another flint, fire broke out, and Hushang praised God for revealing the secret of fire and declared it a light from God.

Two different days were once observed: one 50 days before the spring new year and another a hundred days before the religious new year. Why different regions kept different dates is unclear; many Zoroastrian holy days were kept twice, most likely because of a calendar reform in the 3rd century.

For Zoroastrians the chief preparation was gathering wood the day before. Teenage boys went with a few men to the mountains to collect camel thorn and brought it to the temples, a step that resembled a rite of passage. The fires were set near water and temples, to help revive the sun and to drive off the demons of frost that turned water to ice and killed the roots of plants. The fire burned all night; next morning women took a portion of it home, and what remained was kept at the temple until the following year. The festivities lasted three days, with food from slaughtered lambs given to the poor.

The fullest account after the Muslim conquest comes from the 10th century, under Mardavij of the Ziyarid dynasty at Isfahan: bonfires in metal holders on both banks of the Zayandeh River, hundreds of birds released, fireworks, music and feasts.

Sadeh is still kept much as before in Kerman and Yazd, in the Kushke Varjavand gardens at Karaj, and at the Chak-Chak Fire Temple near Yazd, where the last Zoroastrian princess is believed to have sheltered in 640. Zoroastrians in Iran and abroad celebrate it on 30 January. For most Iranians it has no religious meaning beyond lighting fires at sunset. Tajikistan has officially recognised it since 2017, and on 30 January 2023, after the Mahsa Amini protests, people lit fires for it in many Iranian cities.
sadeq-khan-zand: Sadeq Khan, also called Mohammad Sadeq, belonged to the Zand, a small tribe of Laks, a branch of the Lurs, who lived around Pari and Kamazan in the Malayer district and roamed the central Zagros. He was a son of Inaq Khan Zand. In 1732 Nader Qoli Beg, the future Nader Shah, killed the Zand chief Mehdi Khan and 400 of his kinsmen and deported the survivors under Inaq Khan to Abivard and Dargaz in Khorasan, where their able men were taken into his army.

Under his brother Karim Khan Zand, war with the Ottomans broke out in 1775 over the meddling of Omar Pasha, the Mamluk governor of Iraq, in the Baban principality, his seizure of the property of Iranian pilgrims who had died of plague and his charges on pilgrims to Najaf and Karbala. Basra was also a rich port that had drawn the East India Company's trade away from Bushehr. While other Zand forces held the Pasha's troops in Kurdistan, Sadeq Khan besieged Basra in April 1775 with an army of 30,000, helped by boats and supplies from the Banu Ka'b and the Arabs of Bushehr.

The fort's commander, Suleiman Agha, resisted for more than a year. A ship of the East India Company under Henry Moore attacked Sadeq Khan's supply boats, and in October ships from Oman brought aid before withdrawing to Muscat for the winter. A relief force from Baghdad was driven off by the Khaza'il, a Shia Arab tribe allied with the Zands. By spring 1776 the defenders were near famine and many had deserted, and Suleiman Agha surrendered on 16 April 1776.

Karim Khan died on 1 March 1779, and Sadeq Khan's forces left Basra soon afterwards. A power struggle followed: Karim Khan's sons Mohammad Ali Khan and Abol-Fath Khan were proclaimed co-rulers while their uncle Zaki Khan held real power until he was murdered. Supported by the Nizari imam Abū-l-Ḥasan ʻAlī, Sadeq Khan raised an army in Kerman and entered Shiraz against little resistance, and on 22 August 1779 he became the fourth Shah of the Zand dynasty. His reign ended on 14 March 1781, and his nephew Ali-Morad Khan Zand succeeded him.
sadiya: Sadiya stands on a grassy plain, almost surrounded by forested Himalayan mountains, on the right bank of the Lohit River, which is locally but wrongly taken to be the main stream of the Brahmaputra. Its name is believed to be a corrupted form of Sadhayapura, the name copper inscriptions give to the land between the Lohit and the Dibang. Three routes led from here to Tibet, through the valleys of the Dihang, the Dibang and the Lohit, the last reaching Zayul; a trade route also ran by way of the Shan state of Mongkawng to Yunnan.

Inscriptions suggest Sadiya was the capital of the Chutiya king Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa in the early 15th century, and ruins of the Chutia period survive in the region, among them the Tamreswari temple, whose wall inscription is dated Saka 1364 (1442 CE). In 1524 the Mongkawng king Phukloimung attacked Sadiya and was driven back. After Suhungmung Dihingia Roja annexed the Chutia kingdom, the Sadiya-khowa Gohain governed the frontier from Kaicheng and kept relations with the Adi, Mishmi and other hill peoples. A great earthquake devastated Sadiya in 1697.

In 1799 the Khamtis and their allies rose and were harshly suppressed by Purnananda Burhagohain. In 1810-11 the Khamtis and Singphos ousted the last Ahom governor, Govinda Gohain, and Khamti chiefs held the post until the British annexed the tract in 1839. Sadiya became the extreme north-east frontier station of British India, garrisoned by native infantry and military police, with a bazaar where Mishmis, Abors and Khamtis bartered rubber, wax, ivory and musk for cloth, salt and metal goods. In 1943-44 the United States Army Air Force had a field there.

Sadiya is one of the three sub-divisions of Tinsukia district, with its centre at Chapakhowa, and lies at an average elevation of 123 metres. It is the only part of Assam where the Mishmi Hills hoolock gibbon is found. The Tamreswari temple was submerged under silt in the floods of 1959.
sadri-maqsudi: He was born Sadreddīn Nizāmeddin al-Maqsūdī in 1878 in the village of Taşsu near Kazan. After graduating from the Teacher's Institute in Kazan in 1900 he spent some time in Istanbul, and two years later went to study at the Sorbonne, where he took a master's degree in law. In the Duma he used the Russified form Sadrutdin Nisamutdinovich Maksudov, and from 1935 in Turkey he added the surname Arsal, becoming Sadri Maksudi Arsal. He is counted among the leading figures of the national awakening of the Tatars of Russia in the early 1900s.

On his return to Russia he joined the Islamic Constitutional Party and represented the District of Kazan in the second Duma in 1907 and the third in 1908. In 1917 he chaired a national assembly at Ufa concerned with the proposed state, and he was later elected president of the short-lived Idel-Ural State.

In 1918, after the rise of Bolshevism and the break-up of his party, he escaped through Saint Petersburg to Finland, where he stayed in Tampere at the home of a Finnish Tatar, Imad Samaletdin. The next year he went on to Paris and at the Peace Conference spoke for the political rights of the peoples of the Idel-Ural region, without result. In 1922 he returned briefly to Finland, where his family had fled from the Soviet Union, and settled with them in Berlin, turning to historical study and keeping out of politics.

He then lectured on Turkish history at the Slavic Faculty of the Sorbonne in Paris. In 1925 he moved to Turkey, where he became professor of legal history and philosophy at the universities of Ankara and Istanbul and received an honorary title. He also served as a delegate to the League of Nations and studied the Turkic languages.

Among his writings, Türk dili için traced the development of the Turkish language and proposed ways to improve it, among them removing foreign influences. He was elected to the Turkish Parliament for three legislative periods and died in Istanbul on 20 February 1957.
sadriddin-ayni: Sadriddin Ayni was born on 15 April 1878 into a peasant family in the village of Sāktare in the Emirate of Bukhara, now in Gʻijduvon District. He became an orphan at twelve and moved to Bukhara to join his older brother. There he attended the Mir-i Arab madrasa and learned to write in Arabic, working as a janitor and cook while he studied. He knew prominent Bukhara intellectuals and took part in the Jadid movement of enlighteners. From September 1915 to April 1916 he worked at the cotton-ginning plant at Kızıltepe station, where he met the workers who became the heroes of his first novels.

In April 1917 reactionary forces of the Emirate, mostly clergy, staged a demonstration of loyalty in front of the Emir's residence in Bukhara. Ayni refused to take part. Seized at home, he was publicly beaten with 75 blows of sticks and thrown into the Obhona prison, from which Bolsheviks rescued him. In the early 1920s he helped to spread the Russian Revolution in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and in 1934 he attended the first Soviet Congress of Writers as the Tajik representative. He sat in the Supreme Soviet of Tajikistan for 20 years, received the Order of Lenin three times, and was the first president of the Academy of Sciences of the Tajik SSR.

By stressing national identity in his writing, he escaped the Soviet censors who silenced many intellectuals in Central Asia. His early poems were about love and nature, but after the national awakening in Tajikistan he wrote of the dawn of the new age and of the working class.

His writings often criticised the Amir of Bukhara. Two well-known works are The Slave and The Bukhara Executioners. In 1927 he wrote Dokhunda, the first Tajikistani novel in the Tajik language. Lev Kuleshov worked in Tajikistan in 1934 and 1935 on a film of it, but the authorities suspected it might excite Tajik nationalism and stopped the project. A film of the book was approved in 1956. His four-volume Memoirs, completed in 1949–54, are widely read.

Ayni died in Dushanbe on 15 July 1954 and is buried in a mausoleum in his honour. Tajiks regard him as the national poet, and after 1992 his writing helped to bind together a sense of Tajik nationalism that survived the collapse of the Soviet Union.
sadyattes: Sadyattes was the grandson of Gyges of Lydia, and he came to the throne during a severe crisis caused by repeated invasions of the Cimmerians, a nomadic people from the Eurasian Steppe. Gyges had repelled their earlier attacks, but in 644 BCE the Cimmerians under their king Lygdamis invaded for the third time, defeated the Lydians, sacked Sardis and killed Gyges, who was succeeded by Ardys.

In 637 BCE, in the seventh year of Ardys, the Thracian Treres, who had crossed the Thracian Bosporus under their king Kobos, attacked Lydia in alliance with the Cimmerians and the Lycians. They defeated the Lydians and sacked Sardis a second time, all but its citadel. Ardys was probably killed in this attack, or else deposed for failing to protect the kingdom.

Sadyattes reigned only briefly, from 637 to about 635 BCE. Little is known of it beyond the war he began against the Ionian Greek maritime city of Miletus. It ended in 635 BCE. He may, like his grandfather, have died fighting the Cimmerians, or he may have been deposed for failing to protect Lydia from them. His son Alyattes succeeded him, continued the war against Miletus and went on to make Lydia a powerful empire.

Soon after 635 BCE the Scythians under their king Madyes, with Assyrian approval and in alliance with the Lydians, entered Anatolia, drove the Treres out of Asia Minor and defeated the Cimmerians so that they were no longer a threat. Strabo credits Madyes with expelling the Treres and Cimmerians, while Herodotus and Polyaenus credit Alyattes with their final defeat. The Scythians then extended their rule into Central Anatolia until the Medes expelled them from Western Asia in the 600s BCE.
saeberht-of-essex: The genealogies and regnal lists agree that Sæberht was the son of King Sledd, who may have been regarded as the founder of the East Saxon dynasty, and Bede names his mother as Ricula, a sister of King Æthelberht of Kent. The main source for his reign is Bede's Historia Ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum of the early 8th century, whose account of the mission of Mellitus came from Abbot Albinus of Canterbury through the London priest Nothhelm; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and later genealogies add a little.

In 604 Augustine consecrated Mellitus bishop in the province of the East Saxons, whose capital was London, making him the first Saxon Bishop of London. Bede tells that Sæberht was converted and baptised by Mellitus, while his three sons stayed pagan. The episcopal church built in London was probably founded by Æthelberht rather than Sæberht, and a charter claiming to record a grant of lands from Æthelberht to Mellitus is a forgery.

Æthelberht and Sæberht both died in 616, leaving the Gregorian mission without strong patrons. Bede says that Sæberht's sons, two of whom a genealogy names as Sexred and Sæward, drove Mellitus from London after he refused them a taste of the sacramental bread.

Later medieval legend made Sæberht and his wife Ethelgoda the founders of a monastery of St Peter on the site of Westminster Abbey. During Henry III's rebuilding their supposed remains were moved to a tomb in the Chapter House, and in 1308 reportedly to a marble tomb in the south ambulatory, though modern scholars doubt the bones were ever his. A local tradition places his home and burial at Great Burstead in Essex.

The Prittlewell burial found in 2003, whose gold foil crosses mark an early Christian, was at first thought most likely to be his. Carbon dating later placed the tomb between 575 and 605, and in 2019 specialists of the Museum of London Archaeology suggested it could be that of Seaxa, Sæberht's brother.
saeima: The Saeima traces its origins to the Sejm of the Kingdom of Poland, which led to the Sejm of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later that of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Polish Livonia, part of the Commonwealth, was introduced to the Sejm system. The Warsaw Sejm of 1677 settled the status of what remained of it, Latgale, naming it a voivodeship and a duchy with the right to name three senators, and it sent six deputies to the Sejm. The rest of Latvia belonged to the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia, governed by its dukes and the Landtag of Courland.

The word sejm comes from a Slavic verb meaning to get together. In the 19th century Juris Alunāns of the Young Latvians claimed saeims as a purely Latvian word that he had invented, from the archaic eima, meaning to go. He could not explain the added s- prefix.

In pre-war Latvia the Saeima was elected for three-year terms. The first met from 7 November 1922 to 2 November 1925, the second from 3 November 1925 to 5 November 1928, the third from 6 November 1928 to 2 November 1931, and the fourth from 3 November 1931 until the Latvian coup d'état of 15 May 1934. Its rules of procedure were adopted on 23 March 1923 and amended in 1929 and 1994. Today the term is four years. On 28 May 2011 President Valdis Zatlers initiated the dissolution of the Saeima, which a referendum approved, and it was dissolved on 23 July 2011.

The Saeima is unicameral, with 100 members elected by proportional representation from five constituencies: Kurzeme (11 deputies), Latgale (12), Riga (38), Vidzeme (26) and Zemgale (13). Overseas votes count for Riga. Seats go to parties that win at least 5% of the national vote, by the Webster/Sainte-Laguë method. Voters may mark a candidate FOR or AGAINST, so that a candidate's total is the list's votes plus positive votes minus negative ones. No party has usually won more than 30%, so coalitions have always been necessary.

All citizens over 18 may vote, and candidates must be over 21. Former employees of the USSR and Latvian SSR security and intelligence services are barred. If the President proposes dissolution, a national referendum must confirm it, and if it fails the President is removed from office. A petition of one-tenth of the electorate can also force a referendum. The Communist Party of Latvia is the only banned party.
safavid-empire: The realm's common and official name was the Guarded Domains of Iran, which remained the country's official title under later rulers until 1924. Safavid history begins with the Zahediyeh Sufi order, founded in Gilan by Zahed Gilani. Having no male heir, he married his daughter to his favourite disciple, Safi al-Din Ardabili, who succeeded him in 1301 and made the order a great influence in the city of Ardabil. The order gradually became known as the Safaviyya after him.

From their base in Ardabil the Safavids established control over parts of Greater Iran. The Qizilbash, Turkoman tribes whose name means red-heads, made up the bulk of the army, while ethnic Iranians held the posts in the bureaucracy and in cultural affairs. Ismail I took the title King of Iran, with the idea of an Iranian state stretching from Khorasan to the Euphrates.

The state rested on a division between the Turkic-speaking military and the Persian-speaking administrative elite. Shah Tahmasp began in 1540 to build a third force of ethnic Circassians, Georgians and Armenians, a process widened under Abbas I, in order to restrict the power of the Qizilbash. The shah held total power, legitimised by his descent as a sayyid. Every office had a deputy or superintendent who kept records and reported to him. Local governors were mostly Qizilbash generals, and Abbas I brought some provinces under direct royal control as Crown Provinces. The empire's population is estimated at eight to ten million in 1650.

The Safavids were not the first Shi'i rulers in Iran, but they played a crucial role in forcing Shi'a Islam on the whole country as the official religion. The Silk Road through northern Iran was revived in the 16th century, and Abbas I supported direct trade with Europe, particularly England and the Netherlands, which sought carpets, silk and textiles. In 1602 he drove the Portuguese out of Bahrain, and with help from the English East India Company he later expelled them from the Strait of Hormuz.

Abbas I recognised the commercial value of the arts, and tile making, pottery, textiles, miniature painting, bookbinding and calligraphy advanced in his time. In the 16th century carpet weaving grew from a nomadic and peasant craft into an industry centred on Tabriz, and the carpets of Ardabil were commissioned to commemorate the dynasty. Islamic philosophy flourished in the School of Isfahan, founded by Mir Damad and reaching its height with Mulla Sadra.

The Safavids made Iran the spiritual bastion of Shi'ism and the repository of Persian cultural traditions and of a sense of Iranian identity, acting as a bridge to modern Iran. They also spread Shia Islam in parts of Central Asia, the Caucasus, Anatolia, the Persian Gulf and Mesopotamia.
safaviyya: Safi al-Din Ardabili, who lived from 1252 to 1334 and led the order from 1301, followed the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islam. His standing is attested in two letters of the vizier Rashid al-Din Hamadani, one pledging him a yearly gift of foodstuffs and the other telling Rashid al-Din's son, the governor of Ardabil, to treat the mystic with proper respect. After his death the leadership passed from father to son, first to Sadr al-Din Musa, then to Khavjeh Ali and Shaykh Ibrahim.

From the early 1300s the order's leaders showed that they sought political power as well as religious authority, which made the rulers of western Iran and Iraq first uneasy and then hostile. By the mid-15th century, under Shaykh Junayd and Shaykh Haydar, it had turned to a ghulat form of Twelver Shi'ism, declared jihad against the Christians of Georgia and adopted messianic beliefs about its leaders. Three leaders in a row died in battle: Junayd in 1460, Haydar in 1488 and Ali Mirza in 1494. The order survived under Haydar's son Isma'il.

Isma'il, Junayd's grandson, founded the Safavid empire in 1501, proclaimed Twelver Shi'ism the religion of the state and brought Twelver Shia scholars, largely from Lebanon and Syria, to turn the order into a Shi'i dynasty. The Safavid kings rested their authority on three claims: that they were divinely appointed to rule Iran, that they represented on earth Muhammad al-Mahdi, the Twelfth Imam whose return Twelver Shi'is await, and that they were the moršed-e kāmel, the perfect spiritual guide of the order. In the years just before 1501 the order's propaganda, its da'va, went further, presenting its leader as the Mahdi himself or even a divine incarnation.
safdar-jang: Safdar Jang was a descendant of Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu confederation. He received the rank of sipahsalar in 1735, and on 19 March 1739 he succeeded his maternal uncle and father-in-law, Burhan-ul-Mulk Saadat Khan, as ruler of Awadh. The Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah gave him the title Safdar Jang, by which he is known.

He kept firm control of Awadh while giving valuable help to Muhammad Shah, received the governorship of Kashmir and became a central figure at the Delhi court, gaining control of the whole imperial administration in the emperor's later years. When Ahmad Shah Bahadur came to the throne in 1748, Safdar Jang became his wazir, governor of Ajmer and faujdar of Narnaul.

That year his rival Javed Khan invited Nasir Jung, the new Nizam of Hyderabad, into an alliance against him; Safdar Jang turned to the Marathas, and Balaji Baji Rao sent the Scindia and Holkar chiefs to keep Nasir Jung's forces from Delhi. In 1752 he put down a rebellion of the Rohillas of the Doab, again with Maratha help.

His army included 20,000 Mughaliya cavalry, many of them Shia men from the Jadibal district of Srinagar who dressed like the Qizilbash and spoke Persian. Kashmiri Shias migrated to Awadh to escape persecution and find patronage, looking to him as the sword-arm of the Shias in India.

Dismissed from court, Safdar Jang returned to Awadh in December 1753 and chose Faizabad as his military headquarters and administrative capital. He intervened for Madho Singh of Jaipur in his conflict with the Marathas, who left with an apology and some compensation. He died at Sultanpur near Faizabad in October 1754, aged 46. All later Nawabs of Awadh descended from him in the male line, and his tomb stands on Safdar Jang Road in New Delhi, near the airport and hospital that bear his name.
safed: Safed stands at an elevation of up to 937 metres, making it the highest city in the Galilee and in Israel, 40 km east of Acre and 20 km north of Tiberias. It lies above the Dead Sea Transform, which makes it one of the Israeli cities most at risk from earthquakes. It has been identified with Sepph, a fortified town of the Upper Galilee mentioned by the historian Josephus, and the Jerusalem Talmud names it as one of five elevated places where fires were lit to announce the new moon and festivals in the Second Temple period. Legend holds that a son of Noah founded it.

Little is known of Safed before the Crusaders took the area in 1101-1102, though a Cairo Geniza document shows Jews living beside Muslims there in the 11th century. The Crusaders built a large fortress in 1168. Saladin conquered it 20 years later, and his grandnephew al-Mu'azzam Isa demolished it in 1219. After a treaty with the Crusaders in 1240 a larger fortress was built. The Mamluk sultan Baybars captured it in July 1266 after a six-week siege and had nearly the whole garrison killed. He spared the fortress, unlike the coastal ones, repaired and enlarged it in 1268 and made Safed the capital of a new province spanning the Galilee. By the end of his reign it was a prosperous town.

The Ottomans conquered Mamluk Syria in 1516-1517, and Safed became the capital of the Safed Sanjak. The stability that followed brought nearly a century of growth, in which Jewish immigrants from across Europe made the city a centre of wool and textile production and of the mystical Kabbalah movement; it became known as one of the Four Holy Cities of Judaism. It declined in the 17th and 18th centuries. Druze and Muslim locals raided the Jewish community in 1834 and 1838, and many Jews died in the earthquake of 1837; Moses Montefiore's philanthropy helped rebuild synagogues and homes. Towards the end of the 19th century the population reached 24,000, divided roughly equally between Jews and Muslims, with a small Christian community.

Safed became part of the State of Israel in 1948 and now has an almost entirely Jewish population of 38,687 in 2024, including a large Haredi community. It remains a centre of Jewish religious studies. Its old Jewish quarter holds 32 synagogues, among them those named for Abuhav, Alsheich, Karo and Isaac Luria. The ruins of the Crusader and Mamluk castle still stand on Citadel Hill, and Mamluk buildings include the Red Mosque, completed in 1275. In the 1950s and 1960s the city was known as Israel's art capital, and its Artists' Quarter still holds galleries. Its mild summers and scenic views make it a holiday resort.
saffarid-dynasty: The Saffarid dynasty was a culturally Persianate dynasty of eastern Iranian origin that ruled parts of Persia, Khorasan and eastern Makran from 861 to 1002, and was one of the first indigenous Persian dynasties to emerge after the Islamic conquest. Its founder, Ya'qub ibn al-Layth al-Saffar, was born in 840 at Karnin, east of Zaranj and west of Bost, in what is now Afghanistan. A native of Sistan and a local ayyar, he worked as a coppersmith before becoming a warlord. He moved to Zaranj, left his trade and gained the power to act as an independent ruler.

From his capital Zaranj, Ya'qub moved east into Arachosia, Zamindawar and Kabul; by 865 he had vanquished the Zunbils and forced the Hindu Shahis to move to Udabhanda. He then invaded Bamyan, Balkh, Badghis and Ghor, territories ruled mostly by Buddhist tribal chiefs, taking vast plunder and slaves. The Tahirid city of Herat fell in 870, and the Saffarids annexed Khorasan in 873. They turned west to Khuzestan, Kerman and Fars, and in 876 came within a few days' march of Baghdad before the Abbasid army turned them back. Silver mines in the Panjshir Valley let them mint silver coins. The Abbasids recognised Ya'qub as governor of Sistan, Fars and Kerman, but he had no concept of centralised government.

Ya'qub's brother and successor Amr ibn al-Layth was defeated at Balkh by Ismail Samani and lost Khorasan, leaving the Saffarids Fars, Kerman and Sistan. Under Tahir ibn Muhammad (901–908) they fought the Abbasids for Fars, but a civil war broke out in 908 and the governor of Fars defected to the Abbasids. In 912 the Samanids expelled them from Sistan, which they later regained under Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Muhammad, though only as a minor power. In 1002 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Sistan and dethroned Khalaf ibn Ahmad, ending the dynasty.

The Saffarids patronised Persian in court poetry and gave impetus to a renaissance of New Persian literature. After Ya'qub's conquest of Herat, when some poets praised the victory in Arabic, he asked his secretary Muhammad ibn Wasif al-Sistani to compose the verses in Persian.

The religion of Ya'qub is debated, since most sources are hostile and contradict one another: Ibn Khallikan calls him a Kharijite, Nizam al-Mulk an Isma'ili, and the Abbasid caliph's propaganda even claimed he was a Christian. The only contemporary source, al-Ya'qubi, called him a righteous holy warrior fighting on the caliph's command. D. G. Tor argues that Ya'qub was a pious Sunni holy warrior in the tradition of the volunteer frontier fighters, supported by leading hadith scholars, an argument A. C. S. Peacock has called convincing.
saffron-revolution: Before the protests, unease about the economy had been growing. Late in 2006 the price of rice, eggs and cooking oil rose by 30 to 40 per cent, and the United Nations counted Myanmar among the 20 poorest countries. Many, the United Nations among them, blamed the military government for the situation, pointing to the share of national income spent on the armed forces. Small demonstrations over prices, health and education took place in Yangon in February and April 2007, and some demonstrators were detained.

On 15 August 2007 the government, the only seller of fuel, removed its subsidies without warning. Diesel and petrol prices rose by 66 to 100 per cent, and the price of compressed natural gas for buses by 500 per cent within a week. Protests began on 19 August, and the authorities arrested 13 prominent dissidents, among them Min Ko Naing and Ko Ko Gyi. On 5 September troops broke up a demonstration at Pakokku and injured three monks. Younger monks held officials briefly hostage, demanded an apology and, when the military refused, withdrew religious services from the military and began marching.

On 22 September about two thousand monks marched through Yangon and ten thousand through Mandalay. In Yangon they chanted the Metta Sutta past the house of Aung San Suu Kyi, who was under house arrest and appeared at her gate to accept their blessings. On 26 September troops barricaded the Shwedagon Pagoda and attacked some 700 protesters with batons and tear gas, yet monks went on marching in the following days. The government tried to block websites and email, but bloggers in Yangon still got photographs and video out.

The number of dead is not known. The official toll was 13, among them the Japanese photojournalist Kenji Nagai, and the United Nations envoy Paulo Sérgio Pinheiro confirmed 31. Pinheiro also reported independent sources who counted 30 to 40 monks and 50 to 70 civilians killed, while the Democratic Voice of Burma gave 138. State media said 2,100 people had been arrested by 11 October, but foreign sources put the number held above 6,000. In November 2008 a court sentenced 14 members of the 88 Generation Students Group to 65 years in prison. The United States, the European Union and Canada imposed sanctions, while China and India held to non-interference.
safi-al-din-ardabili: Safi al-Din Ishaq Ardabili was born in 1252/3 in the town of Ardabil, in Azerbaijan, then under Mongol rule. It was a commercial centre in a mountainous area near the Caspian Sea. His father was Amin al-Din Jibrail and his mother Dawlati. The family was of Kurdish origin and spoke Persian. His father's life is obscure: Ibn Bazzaz says he died when Safi was six, while Hayati Tabrizi gives his years as 1216 to 1287.

The earliest known record of his lineage, the Safwat al-Safa by Ibn Bazzaz, traces his genealogy to Fehruz, a Kurd from Sanjan. Vladimir Minorsky refers to Safi's claim to descend from Ali ibn Abu Talib but is uncertain of it. The Safavids later fabricated a genealogy making him a descendant of the Seventh Twelver Shia Imam.

According to hagiographical chronicles Safi saw visions of angels as a child. Unable to find a spiritual guide who satisfied him, he left for Shiraz at 20, in 1271/2, intending to meet Shaykh Najib al-Din Buzghush, who died before he arrived. He continued his search in the Caspian region and in 1276/7 met Zahed Gilani at the village of Hilya Karin. He became Zahed's disciple and married his daughter Bibi Fatima, while Zahed's son Hajji Shams al-Din Muhammad married Safi's daughter.

Zahed named Safi his successor, and Safi led the order from 1301, when Zahed died, though Zahed's family and some followers resented it. He renamed the Zahediyeh the Safaviyya and reformed it from a local order into a religious movement whose propaganda reached Iran, Syria, Asia Minor and even Sri Lanka. He gained considerable political influence and named his son Sadr al-Din Musa his heir, which shows his resolve to keep leadership in his family. He wrote poems in Old Azeri and Persian, of which only a few double verses, called Dobaytis, survive.

Safi died on 12 September 1334 and was buried. He was the eponymous ancestor of the Safavid dynasty, which ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736. His poems are of linguistic importance, since B. V. Miller concluded that the dialect of the quatrains was the language of the ancestors of the modern Talysh.
safi-of-persia: Safi was born Sam Mirza, the son of Mohammad Baqer Mirza, the eldest son of Shah Abbas I, and Dilaram Khanum, a Georgian wife. In 1615 Abbas had Mohammad Baqer killed, fearing a plot against his life. Over the next few years the suspicious Abbas killed or blinded his other sons, which left his grandson Safi as heir to the throne.

Safi was crowned on 28 January 1629 at the age of eighteen. He eliminated anyone he regarded as a threat, executing almost all the Safavid royal princes as well as leading courtiers and generals. On the night of 20 February 1632, known as the Bloody Ma'bas, he had forty women of the imperial harem put to death. He paid little attention to government, had never learned to read or write properly and preferred wine and opium. He excluded the Qizilbash from the bureaucracy and let a coalition of concubines, eunuchs and ghulams hold power in the last decade of his reign.

The leading political figure was Saru Taqi, a ghulam and eunuch, who became grand vizier in 1634 after Safi had his predecessor Mirza Taleb Khan Ordubadi killed. He raised revenue, passed the province of Fars to the crown domain and placed his brother as governor of Mazandaran.

Iran's enemies exploited the shah's perceived weakness. The Ottomans under Sultan Murad IV began incursions within a year of his accession, briefly occupied Yerevan and Tabriz in 1634 and recaptured Baghdad and other parts of Mesopotamia in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab of 1639 ended the wars between the two empires. In 1638 Iran also lost Kandahar to the Mughals after its governor, Ali Mardan Khan, was dismissed. In 1636 Safi received a trade delegation from Frederick III, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, which included Adam Olearius, who published a book about the visit in 1647.

Safi died on 12 May 1642, related to heavy drinking, and was buried in Qom. His son Abbas II succeeded him. According to one account, in Archangelo Lamberti's Relation de la Colchide ou Mengrellie (1654), he died in a drinking contest with a Georgian named Shedan Chiladze. He left a country smaller than the one he inherited. Later writers saw in his reign problems that afflicted the Safavid empire in decline, among them his failure to prepare the crown prince for rule.
saga-prefecture: Saga Prefecture occupies the north-western corner of Kyushu, an isthmus-like area between the Genkai Sea and the Tsushima Strait to the north and the Ariake Sea to the south. It borders Fukuoka Prefecture to the northeast and Nagasaki Prefecture to the southwest and covers about 2,439 square kilometres. Its nearness to mainland Asia made it an important gateway for the transmission of culture and trade throughout Japanese history. Outside the cities of Saga and Karatsu it is largely rural, and agricultural and forested land makes up over 68 per cent of its area.

In ancient times the area of Saga and Nagasaki prefectures was called Hizen Province, and the present name dates from the Meiji Restoration. Rice farming has flourished here since ancient times, and its traces survive at the ruins of Nabatake in Karatsu and at the Yoshinogari site, where villages flourished in the middle of the Yayoi period. The Mongol invasions of Japan began here with the Battle of Bun'ei in 1274 and the Battle of Kōan in 1281, and in 1591 Nagoya Castle was built for the Japanese invasions of Korea.

In the Sengoku period the Ryūzōji clan extended its control over all of Hizen and Chikugo and parts of Higo and Chikuzen. After the death of Ryūzōji Takanobu, Nabeshima Naoshige took control, and by 1607 the whole Ryūzōji domain was in Nabeshima hands. In the Edo period the Saga Domain, with its three sub-domains, remained under the Nabeshima and was politically stable, though the cost of defending Nagasaki and disasters such as the Kyōhō famine and the Siebold Typhoon of 1828 strained its finances. Land reclaimed from the Ariake Sea roughly doubled its yield in koku over two centuries.

Nabeshima Naomasa reformed the domain's finances in the middle of the 19th century and encouraged Arita porcelain, green tea and coal. Technologies such as the reverberatory furnace and models of steam locomotives arrived through the nearby port of Nagasaki. Many people from the domain assisted the Meiji Restoration. After the han system was abolished in 1871 the area was merged into Imari Prefecture, renamed Saga Prefecture in 1872, absorbed into Nagasaki Prefecture in 1876 and set up again as a separate prefecture in 1883. The Saga Rebellion took place in February 1874.

The prefecture has a population of roughly 780,000. Saga is its capital and largest city, and other major cities include Karatsu, Tosu and Imari. Its western region is known for ceramics and porcelain, particularly in Karatsu, Imari and Arita. All of its coal mines closed in 1972 with the closing of the Nishiki mine, and the Yoshinogari History Park opened to the public in 1992.
sagala: Sagala stood in the northwestern Indian subcontinent and is known in the sources as Śākala or Sangala, and to the Greeks as Euthydemia. It was the capital of the Madra kingdom. It is probably the city of Śākala named in the Mahabharata, the Sanskrit epic, which places it in much the same area as the Greek accounts do. The epic noted the region for the women who lived in its woods, whom it called loose and Bacchanalian.

The Roman-Greek historian Arrian, in his Anabasis of Alexander, records that Alexander the Great took a city he calls Sagala and Sangala from the Cathaeans, who had entrenched themselves there with their neighbours, and that Porus joined him with elephants and some five thousand troops. The city, said to have held 80,000 residents, was razed as a warning to other cities that might resist. After overthrowing the Mauryan Empire, Pushyamitra Shunga extended the Shunga Empire northwest as far as Sagala. The Ashokavadana says he persecuted Buddhists and at Sakala offered a hundred dinara for the head of each Buddhist monk.

Menander, who reigned between 160 and 135 BCE, made the city his capital. Under his rule it prospered as a trading centre known for its silk, and literary accounts suggest that Greeks and the local population lived in relative harmony, some Greeks converting to Buddhism. According to the Milinda Panha, Menander embraced Buddhism there after long debates with the monk Nagasena, and the city became a centre of Buddhist thought. The text describes its parks and lakes, its towers and gates, a white-walled royal citadel, and bazaars selling Benares muslin, jewels and perfumes.

Ptolemy recorded the city in his Geography in the 1st century CE under the name Euthymedia. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who visited it in the 7th century, described it as the old capital of the Alchon Hun king Mihirakula, by then lying in the kingdom of Takka.

Sagala is generally identified as the predecessor of present-day Sialkot, in the Pakistani province of Punjab. Evidence of its Indo-Greek age has been found nearby: a hoard containing numerous coins of Menander I, together with shards of Hellenistic pottery, was unearthed at Siranwali village near Sialkot.
sagar-madhya-pradesh: Sagar lies in central India on a spur of the Vindhya Range, 536 metres above sea level and about 182 kilometres northeast of the state capital, Bhopal, with a lake in the middle of the city. It is the administrative headquarters of Sagar district and of Sagar division, which has six districts: Sagar, Damoh, Chhatarpur, Tikamgarh, Panna and Niwari. The dominant spoken language is Hindi, in its dialect Bundeli, and a large Sindhi community lives in the city.

The ancient kingdom of Chedi had its capital at Suktimati, which is placed at Sagar in the present day. The history of the district before 1022 is generally unknown. It was ruled by Ahir rajas, whose capital was at Garhpehra, and in 1660 Udenshah founded the present town. After 1735 the city came under the Peshwas: when Chhatrasal gave a region to Bajirao, Govindpant Kher was appointed its administrator and made the city, beside Sagar Lake, his capital.

In 1818 Peshwa Baji Rao II ceded a large part of the district to the British East India Company. In 1820 the area, as the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories, was placed under an agent to the governor-general. It fell under the North-Western Province after 1835, and was affected by the Bundela rising of 1842. In 1861 the territories and the Nagpur state formed the Central Provinces.

The 2011 census counted 274,556 people within the municipal corporation. The city is known for the headquarters of the Mahar Regiment and for the Jawaharlal Nehru Police Academy. Dr. Hari Singh Gour University, the first and oldest university of Madhya Pradesh, was founded on 18 July 1946 by Sir Harisingh Gaur and became a central university in 2008. At Garhpehra, six miles north of the city, stand a fort and a Shish Mahal, and the Aabchand caves, about 35 kilometres east, hold rock paintings of hunters, animals and dancers. Excavations at Eran, which has a colossal Varaha statue about 10 feet high, show that it formed the northernmost limit of the Chalcolithic culture in Madhya Pradesh.
sagunto: Sagunto lies about 30 km north of the centre of Valencia, on the Costa de Valencia on the Mediterranean, in the fertile comarca of Camp de Morvedre. The municipality has three urban nuclei: the old town, Ciutat Vella, Grau Vell and Puerto de Sagunto, and over half its population lives in the coastal settlement of Puerto de Sagunto. The old town climbs the hill that carries the castle, above the plain.

In the 5th century BCE the Iberians built a walled settlement on the hill, known as Arse; a stretch of cyclopean limestone slabs from the former Temple of Diana survives near the church of Santa Maria. The city traded with coastal colonies such as Carthage and minted its own coins. By 219 BCE Saguntum was a large, prosperous town that sided with Rome against Carthage, and Hannibal besieged it first; after eight months of stiff resistance it fell, and the siege triggered the Second Punic War.

The Romans retook it seven years later, and in 214 BCE it became a municipium. They built a great circus and a theatre seating 8,000, and texts suggest an amphitheatre and about 50,000 inhabitants. Its Catholic patron saint was Bishop Sacerdos, who died about 560.

After the Arab conquest in the early 8th century the town was called Morvedre, from the Latin muri veteres, "ancient walls". El Cid conquered it in 1098, but the Muslims soon recovered it, and James I of Aragon took it in 1238. During the Peninsular War a Spanish attempt to relieve the French siege of the castle failed at the Battle of Saguntum on 25 October 1811, and much of the Roman theatre was dismantled for stone to restore the walls.

A Jewish community lived in the town under Muslim rule; after the massacre of 1391 it was the only surviving community in Valencia, and about 500 Jews left at the expulsion of 1492. A steel industry grew up in the late 19th century, and the last steel oven closed in April 1984.

The remains of Sagunto Castle, with ramparts of Roman and Moorish origin, crown the hill. The Roman theatre on its northern slope, partly restored in the late 20th century, was the first official National Monument declared in Spain, in 1896. The town also has the Gothic church of Santa Maria, the neoclassical Palau Municipal, one of the best-preserved Jewish quarters in Spain and a history museum in the Jewish quarter, whose largest collection is from the Ibero-Roman period.
sahara: The Sahara covers about 9,200,000 square kilometres, 31 per cent of the African continent, and is the largest hot desert in the world. It stretches from the Red Sea in the east and the Mediterranean in the north to the Atlantic, and excludes the fertile Mediterranean coast, the Atlas Mountains of the Maghreb and the Nile Valley. To the south it is bounded by the Sahel, a belt of semi-arid tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic ṣaḥrāʾ, meaning desert.

Its landscape includes hamada, or rocky plateaus, ergs, or sand seas whose dunes often rise over 180 metres, gravel plains, dry valleys called wadis, and salt flats. Mountain massifs rise from it, among them the Ahaggar, the Tibesti and the Aïr, and Emi Koussi in the Tibesti is its highest peak. The central Sahara is hyperarid and may go years without rain, and the Libyan Desert is among the driest and sunniest places on Earth. Trees and taller shrubs grow in the wadis and oases, and the vegetation at the margins is sparse grassland and desert shrub.

For several hundred thousand years the Sahara has alternated between desert and savanna grassland in a cycle of about 20,000 years, caused by the precession of Earth's axis, which shifts the North African monsoon. Scientists have identified more than 230 humid periods in North Africa over the past eight million years. The Green Sahara of the most recent humid period was home to Epipaleolithic, Mesolithic and pastoral peoples, whose rock art survives. The remains of a child at Uan Muhuggiag and of another at Tin Hanakaten have been examined in modern laboratories.

From around 7,500 years ago, populations associated with European Neolithic farmers moved into north-western Africa from the Iberian Peninsula, and pastoralists from the Levant also reached the region. The proto-Berber tribes evolved from these prehistoric communities during the late Bronze and early Iron Ages. Archaeological evidence shows that Nilo-Saharan speaking groups lived in the central and southern Sahara before Berber and Arabic speakers, who now largely populate it, arrived around 1,500 years ago.

The Sahara covers large parts of Algeria, Chad, Egypt, Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Niger, Western Sahara and Sudan, and parts of southern Morocco and Tunisia. Its peoples include the Amazigh, among them the Tuareg, the Hassaniya-speaking Sahrawis, the Toubou, Nubians, Zaghawa, Kanuri, Hausa, Songhai, Beja and Fulani. The Haratins are believed to descend largely from ancient black populations of the desert. Arabic dialects are the most widely spoken languages, followed by Berber languages and Beja, all of the Afro-Asiatic family. The Richat Structure in Mauritania is among its unusual landforms.
sahel: The Sahel is a biogeographical region of Africa, the transition zone between the more humid Sudanian savannas to the south and the drier Sahara to the north. It spans 5,900 kilometres from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, in a belt several hundred to a thousand kilometres wide, and has a hot semi-arid climate. The name comes from the Arabic word sāḥil, coast or shore, explained as a figurative reference to the southern edge of the Sahara. Rainfall varies from around 100 to 200 millimetres a year in the north to 700 to 1,000 in the south.

Around 4000 BCE the climate of the Sahara and the Sahel began to dry at great speed. Lakes and rivers shrank and the land became more desert, and farming communities migrated to the more humid climate of West Africa. For hundreds of years the region has had frequent droughts; one megadrought lasted 250 years, from 1450 to 1700. The larger Sahelian kingdoms emerged from 750 CE and founded several large cities in the Niger valley, among them Timbuktu, Gao and Djenné.

In the eastern Sahel the Christian Nubian kingdom of Alodia was first mentioned in 569 and reached its zenith from the 9th to the 12th century; its capital Soba, near present-day Khartoum, was described as a city of extensive dwellings and churches.

With the forest-savanna mosaic to their south, the Sahelian states could not expand into the forest, because mounted warriors were ineffective there and horses and camels were susceptible to the humidity and diseases of the tropics. The western Sahel fell to France in the late 19th century as part of French West Africa, and Chad was added in 1900 as part of French Equatorial Africa. The French territories were decolonised in 1960. The eastern Sahel was conquered by Muhammad Ali of Egypt in the 1820s, came under British rule by 1899 and was granted independence in 1956.

Traditionally most people of the Sahel have been semi-nomads who farm and raise livestock in a system of transhumance, grazing herds in the drier north during the wet season and trekking hundreds of kilometres south in the dry period. Its peoples include the Fulani, Tuareg, Hausa, Dogon, Songhai, Mande, Kanuri and Arabs. Trans-Saharan trade routes and the spread of Islam created strong historical connections between many Sahelian peoples and Arab communities, which influenced language, religion and social customs.
sahib-i-giray: Sahib I Giray was a son of the Crimean khan Meñli I Giray and a grandson of Hacı I Giray, founder of the Giray dynasty. His brothers included Mehmed I Giray, Saadet I Giray and Mubarak. In 1510–11 he accompanied his stepmother Nur Sultan to Moscow and Kazan, and during Mehmed's reign he was imprisoned for a long time. Khans had by custom to be descended from Genghis Khan, as Sahib was.

The khanate of Kazan was unstable and alternated between pro- and anti-Russian khans. After the death of Mohammad Amin, the Russians imposed their vassal Shahgali, but in the spring of 1521 the anti-Russian faction invited Sahib and he entered Kazan. His brother Mehmed, then khan of Crimea, had placed him there, and in the summer of 1521 the two raided Muscovy together, Sahib reaching Nizhny Novgorod and Vladimir and Mehmed the outskirts of Moscow. His request to Saadet for cannon, muskets and Janissaries was refused. In spring 1524 he declared himself an Ottoman vassal, but a large Russian army under Ivan Belsky forced him to flee.

In Crimea Saadet imprisoned him, then freed him, and he served as Saadet's deputy, or kalga. In May 1532 Saadet gave up the throne and the Ottoman sultan appointed Sahib khan. He arrived with Turkish troops and was recognised by the Crimean nobles. He faced revolts by his nephew İslâm I Giray, whom he drove out of Perekop in 1537. He founded the new capital of Bakhchisarai, expanded the harbour of Gozlev, tried to weaken the great nobles by raising lesser ones and tried to settle the Nogais. He campaigned in the North Caucasus, joined Suleiman against Petru Rareș in 1538, and in 1546 his artillery and musket fire defeated 10,000 Nogais near Perekop.

In 1551 Suleiman ordered Sahib to march against Persia, much farther east than the Crimeans had ever gone. Sahib replied that his warriors were poorly equipped, and the sultan, doubting his loyalty, decided to replace him with his nephew Devlet. While Sahib was in the Taman peninsula, Devlet landed with 1,000 Janissaries and 60 cannon and took Bakhchisarai. Sahib's army deserted and his son Emin was killed. Sahib was imprisoned at Taman and killed on Devlet's orders. All his children and grandchildren were put to death, and Devlet I Giray became khan.
sahin-giray: Şahin Giray was born in 1745 in Edirne, the son of Ahmed Giray and grandson of Devlet II Giray. After his father's early death he was educated under his mother's care; the family lived briefly in Thessaloniki and then settled in the Republic of Venice, where he received a Western-style education. He reputedly spoke Crimean Tatar, Ottoman Turkish, Italian and Greek.

At 20 he was recalled to Crimea by his uncle, Khan Qırım Giray, and made commander of the Nogai Horde. When Selim Giray refused an alliance with Russia against the Turks in 1770 and Russia attacked, Şahin went with the envoys sent to Saint Petersburg to seek peace. Catherine II wrote that he was the most gentle Tatar she had ever seen, talented and good-looking, a writer of poetry who wanted to learn everything.

As khan he set out to modernise the state: he opened factories, moved the capital from Bakhchisaray to the trade city of Caffa, restructured taxation and tried to bring Jewish and Christian minorities into the Muslim-majority army. The Nogai nobility and local aristocracy saw the reforms as a threat to their privileges and as anti-Muslim, and many common people thought them contrary to the laws of Islam.

A rebellion broke out in 1777, and he regained control in 1778 only with the help of Catherine II's army. The turmoil grew into civil war, and under heavy Russian pressure, facing certain defeat, he accepted the annexation of the khanate.

Şahin Giray was then sent to live under house arrest in Saint Petersburg. Despite Catherine's warnings, he asked to move to Edirne, and in 1787 Russia and the Ottoman Empire allowed it. Sultan Abdul Hamid I, who regarded him as a traitor for surrendering Crimea and as a possible challenger for the throne, had him taken under arrest to Constantinople and then Rhodes. After a failed attempt to find asylum at the French consulate there, he was executed. His head was sent to the sultan and his body buried in an undisclosed place; his property was returned to his family in Edirne, who later lived on Burgazada.
sahl-smbatean: The Albanian history of Movses Kaghankatvatsi calls him Sahl-i Smbatean Eranshahik and makes him a descendant of Zarmihr, the last survivor of the Aranshahiks, the first known royal dynasty of Caucasian Albania. Charles Dowsett thought this genealogy might have been assumed by Sahl or invented to support his claim to the Albanian throne; Cyril Toumanoff suggested mixed Bagratid and Aranshahik descent, and Alison Vacca argues he was a Mihranid. Sahl seems to be an Arabic name he adopted: Michael the Syrian calls him Isaac, and Bagrat Ulubabyan takes Sahl as a corruption of Sahak.

Scholars also differ on his lands. Vladimir Minorsky, following Tovma Artsruni, held that Shaki north of the Kura was his first holding and that by 835 he had taken Arran, while Ulubabyan and Aleksan Hakobyan limit him to Khachen and its surroundings. Robert H. Hewsen made him a Syunid prince who seized Gegharkunik after the death of Vasak II in 821.

Armenian sources remember Sahl and his brothers for their battles against invaders in the mountains of Artsakh. In 822-823 he defeated an Arab force from Barda that had destroyed Amaras and invaded Metsarank. Arab rule was weakened by the revolt of Babak Khorramdin, and Minorsky thought Sahl's interests and Babak's may at first have coincided. After Afshin, general of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutasim, arrived in 835, Sahl ambushed and defeated an Arab army. When Babak fled to him in 837, Sahl at first received him with honour. According to al-Masudi, his reward for surrendering Babak was a royal robe, a crown, a horse and exemption from tribute, which Dowsett reads as an official investiture as ruler of Albania.

According to Tovma Artsruni, in 854 Bugha al-Kabir, commander for the caliph al-Mutawakkil, captured Sahl and other Armenian princes and sent them to Samarra; Tabari says it was his son Mu'awiya who was deported. Sahl's fate is unknown, but he died after 855. Movses Kaghankatvatsi calls Atrnerseh, ruler of Khachen, his son, and Ulubabyan and Hewsen accept this, while Minorsky held that Atrnerseh's father was a different man.
sahnun: His full name was Abu Said Abd al-Salam ibn Said ibn Habib al-Tanukhi; the nickname Sahnun, the name of a sharp bird, was given for the quickness of his mind. He came of an Arab family of the tribe of Tanukh that originated in Syria, and his father was a soldier from Homs. In his youth he studied under the scholars of Qayrawan and Tunis, above all the Tripolitanian scholar Ali bin Ziyad, who had learned from Imam Malik himself.

In 178 AH Sahnun travelled to Egypt to study under other pupils of Malik, who had died before Sahnun could afford to reach him. He went on to Medina to study with prominent scholars and returned to North Africa in 191 AH. On accepting appointment as a judge he is said to have told his daughter Khadija that her father had that day been slain without a knife. He was known as scrupulous and courteous to litigants, but strict with the men around the emir: he would not let them send representatives to court, and he refused the emir's request not to interfere in their illegal ventures.

Sahnun was known for a strict orthodoxy, to the point of refusing to pray behind a Mu'tazilite imam. Until his time scholars of every tendency had spoken freely in the Great Mosque of Kairouan; the Encyclopedia of Islam describes how he purged its circles, dispersing the Ibadi, Mu'tazilites and other sects, parading their leaders in disgrace and forcing some to recant in public. It counts him among the chief architects of the exclusive supremacy of Sunnism in its Maliki form throughout the Muslim West. His son Muhammad ibn Sahnun, who died in 256 AH (870), was also a noted jurist.
sahure: Sahure, whose name means He who is close to Re, was a pharaoh of the Old Kingdom. Excavations at his pyramid at Abusir, directed by Miroslav Verner and Tarek El-Awady in the early 2000s, show from reliefs on the causeway that his mother was Queen Neferhetepes II, wife of Userkaf and bearer of the title king's mother. This makes Userkaf, in all likelihood, his father, and Sahure's cartouche in Userkaf's mortuary temple at Saqqara indicates that he finished a structure his father began.

He was succeeded by Neferirkare Kakai, who until 2005 was believed to be his brother. A relief found that year shows Sahure seated before two sons, Ranefer and Netjerirenre, with the name Neferirkare Kakai added beside Ranefer, so the next king was his son.

Contacts with foreign lands were numerous under Sahure and seem to have been economic rather than military. Reliefs from his pyramid complex show the return of a naval expedition to Lebanon with ships laden with cedar trunks, and others carrying Asiatics, either slaves or merchants, who greet the king. Another relief shows Syrian brown bears, which Karin Sowada and William Stevenson Smith take to be tribute.

He ordered the earliest attested expedition to Punt, which brought back myrrh, malachite and electrum, and a relief in his mortuary temple shows him tending a myrrh tree in his palace garden, the only relief in Egyptian art showing a king gardening. He also sent expeditions to the turquoise and copper mines of Sinai and military campaigns against Libyan chieftains in the Western Desert, which brought back livestock.

The Palermo Stone records mostly religious acts, including a journey to the Elephantine fortress, the fashioning of six statues of the king, the appointment of 200 priests and fixed daily offerings to Ra, Hathor, Nekhbet and Wadjet.

Sahure left the royal necropolises of Saqqara and Giza for Abusir, possibly because Userkaf's sun temple was there. His pyramid, named Khaba Sahura, was 47 m high and much smaller than those of the Fourth Dynasty, with a core of roughly hewn stones in mud mortar that has left it largely ruined. Its mortuary temple and the 235 m causeway carried an estimated 10,000 square metres of polychrome reliefs, which Miroslav Bárta calls the largest collection known from the third millennium BCE. The complex introduced palmiform columns, and the layout of the temple became the standard for the rest of the Old Kingdom.

The state cult of Sahure, supplied by at least 22 agricultural estates, lasted to the end of the Old Kingdom. In the New Kingdom he was equated, for unknown reasons, with a form of the goddess Sekhmet, and this cult continued until the end of the Ptolemaic period, nearly 2,500 years after his death.
saicho: Saichō was born in 767 in Ōmi, in present-day Shiga Prefecture, with the given name Hirono. Family tradition traced his ancestors to emperors of Eastern Han China, for which no positive evidence exists, though the region had a large Chinese immigrant population. At thirteen he became a disciple of the monk Gyōhyō, took tonsure at fourteen and received the name Saichō. By twenty he had received the full precepts at Tōdai-ji. A few months later he abruptly retreated to Mount Hiei, for a reason that is unknown, and wrote his Ganmon, a prayer of vows not to leave the mountain or take part in worldly affairs until he had attained wisdom.

Monks from Nara and elsewhere gathered round him, and the community grew into Enryaku-ji. The capital moved to Kyoto in 795, and because Hiei lay to its north-east, a direction thought dangerous in Chinese geomancy, his presence there was believed to protect the city and brought him to the court's notice.

Emperor Kanmu granted his petition to study Tiantai doctrine in China. Because he could read Chinese but not speak it, he took the disciple Gishin. The four-ship diplomatic mission of 803 was turned back by winds, and on the second attempt two ships sank, but his reached Ningbo in 804. At Tiantai Mountain Daosui, the seventh Tiantai patriarch, was his chief teacher for about 135 days. Saichō copied texts and, at Yuezhou, received esoteric initiation, though it is unclear which transmission he received.

He returned to Tsushima in 805 after about eight months, and in the first month of 806 the court recognised his school and allowed two annual ordinands, one on the esoteric course and one on the Tiantai course based on Zhiyi's Mohe Zhiguan.

He had met Kūkai, who had gone to China on a longer mission, and the two cooperated for a time. Saichō helped Kūkai to give the esoteric initiation at court and supported the gift of Takaosan-ji to him. Their relationship later deteriorated over Kūkai's secretive approach to esoteric practice. Saichō also debated the Yogācāra scholar Tokuitsu over whether all beings can attain Buddhahood, and defended the view that they can.

In 822 Saichō asked that Hiei monks be ordained under the Bodhisattva Precepts of the Brahma Net Sutra instead of the traditional Vinaya, a petition the Nara establishment protested. He wrote the Kenkairon in defence. He died on 26 June 822 at fifty-six, and the court granted the request seven days later, with the ordination platform built in 827. His ordination model became standard in many schools that grew out of Tendai, among them Jōdo-shū, Rinzai and Sōtō Zen.
said-bin-sultan: Said bin Sultan was born on 5 June 1791, the son of Sultan bin Ahmad, who ruled Oman until his death in 1804 on an expedition to Basra. Sultan bin Ahmad had appointed Mohammed bin Nasir bin Mohammed al-Jabry as regent and guardian of his two sons, Salim bin Sultan and Said. Sultan's brother Qais bin Ahmad, the ruler of Sohar, besieged Muscat in 1805, but Badr bin Saif, called in by the regent, forced him back to Sohar. Badr then became the effective ruler, allied himself with the Wahhabis and grew unpopular.

To remove the two brothers from the capital, Badr made Salim governor of al Maṣna'ah and Said governor of Barka. In 1806 Said lured Badr to Barka and had him killed nearby. Accounts differ, but it seems clear that Said struck the first blow and his supporters finished the work. He was acclaimed as a liberator from the Wahhabis, who left the country.

In 1820 Said launched an expedition against the Bani Bu Ali with the help of the East India Company. It was defeated, but a larger Company force returned the next year and defeated the tribe. He signed the Moresby Treaty in 1822, which restricted the Zanzibar slave trade, and in 1845 the Hamerton Treaty, which restricted it further. In 1835 he ratified a treaty with the United States negotiated at Muscat by Edmund Roberts on 21 September 1833.

In 1837 he conquered Mombasa, and in 1840 he moved his capital from Muscat to Stone Town in Zanzibar, where Richard Waters was American Consul. In 1843 he named a nominal representative in Mogadishu and was obliged to pay tribute to Sultan Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim of the Sultanate of the Geledi.

On his death in 1856 his realm was divided. His third son, Thuwaini bin Said, became Sultan of Muscat and Oman, and his sixth son, Majid bin Said, became Sultan of Zanzibar. Said had 36 children, and several sons later ruled in Zanzibar, among them Barghash bin Said from 1870. A daughter, Salme bint Said (1844–1924), later became known as Emily Ruete. He is regarded as one of the most important Omani sultans, and Zanzibar was his capital while the Omani Empire reached the height of its power and wealth.
said-bin-taimur: Said bin Taimur was born in 1910 into the Al Bu Said dynasty. His father, Sultan Taimur bin Feisal, was strongly against his learning Western ways or English, and once ordered the books of Said and his brother Nadir burned after finding an English primer. Said nonetheless attended Mayo College at Ajmer in India from 1922 to 1927 and mastered English and Urdu. His father feared that Beirut would expose him to Christianity, so he was sent instead to Baghdad for a year to study Arabic literature and history. On his return he joined the government and in August 1929 became president of the Council of Ministers.

In February 1932, at 21, Said became sultan after his father abdicated for financial reasons. He inherited an administration in debt to Britain and British India, and from 1933 he controlled the state budget. With British help he regained control of the tribal interior, bringing Muscat and Oman together, and then lived in a coastal town in Dhofar. Britain recognised Oman's independence in 1951. In 1938 he visited the United States at the invitation of President Franklin Roosevelt, and in the Second World War he cooperated with Britain, allowing Royal Air Force landing fields to be built between Salalah and Muscat.

He faced opposition from Imam Ghalib bin Ali, whose revolt in Jebel Akhdar was suppressed in 1955 with British help. Saudi Arabia supported the Imam, and Egypt disliked British involvement; both backed a renewed revolt in 1957, which was suppressed by 1959. On 8 September 1958 Said handed Gwadar over to Pakistan. In 1965 he made concessions to export oil to Iraq, Iran and Britain, and the same year Dhofar revolted, with support from the People's Republic of China and some nationalist Arab states. After an assassination attempt in 1966 his rule became more erratic: smoking in public, football and sunglasses were forbidden. At the end of his reign there were three schools, a literacy rate of 5% and 10 kilometres of paved roads.

His son Qaboos, back from the Royal Military Academy and a year in the British Army, was kept under house arrest at Al Hosn Palace in Salalah, and Said did not speak to him for the last 14 months before the coup. On 23 July 1970 Qaboos deposed him at the palace in Salalah with British help and his uncle's, and sent him into exile in the United Kingdom. Said spent his last two years at the Dorchester Hotel in London and died on 19 October 1972. He was first buried at Brookwood Cemetery in England, and his remains were later taken to Oman and buried in the royal cemetery in Muscat.
saidu-sharif: Saidu Sharif, also known as Saidu Baba or simply Saidu, lies in the Swat valley, on the road that joins it to Mingora. It has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate: the average annual temperature is 19.3 °C and about 894 mm of rain falls in a year. June is the hottest month, with an average of 29.2 °C, and January the coldest, at 7.5 °C. August is the wettest month and November the driest.

The place was once called Baligram. In 1835 the Akhund of Swat, a Sufi saint and a Gujjar commonly known as Saidu Baba, settled there, and the town took the name Saidu Sharif after him. His mausoleum still stands in the town, as does the residential palace of the former Wali-e-Swat, the ruler of the state of Swat.

The site is far older than its name. Near the museum stands one of the most important Buddhist monuments of Swat, a stupa that may have been built by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka to hold some of the ashes of the Buddha. Over the following centuries it was enlarged five times, each time by encasing the existing structure in a new shell. Italian excavators working in 1955 exposed these successive layers, each of which shows a stage in the development of building techniques. The remains of the Butkara Buddhist Stupa are among the town's archaeological sites.

Saidu Sharif is the capital of Swat District and of the Malakand Division, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and a ward of Babuzai tehsil. The Swat Museum holds Gandharan statuettes and friezes of the life of the Buddha, seals and reliquaries, mostly from Butkara No 1 and Odigram, together with pre-Buddhist objects and a gallery of carved Swati furniture, jewellery and embroidery. Jahanzeb College was built in 1952 and Saidu Medical College in 1998, and the district's first university was founded there on 7 July 2010.
saif-bin-sultan: Saif bin Sultan was the son of the second Yaruba Imam, Sultan bin Saif, and a member of the Ibadi sect. When his father died, his brother Bil'arab bin Sultan became Imam in 1679. Saif later fell out with his brother, built up his own forces and besieged Bil'arab in Jabrin, and after Bil'arab died there he became the fourth Imam of the dynasty.

Saif built aflaj in many parts of the interior and planted date palms in the Al Batinah Region to draw Arabs from the interior to settle on the coast. He also built new schools, and he made the castle of Rustaq his residence, adding the Burj al Riah wind tower.

He continued the struggle against the Portuguese in East Africa. In 1696 his forces attacked Mombasa, besieging 2,500 people who had taken refuge in Fort Jesus; the siege ended after 33 months, when the thirteen survivors of famine and smallpox surrendered. The Omanis soon took Pemba Island, Kilwa and Zanzibar, which saw the first large-scale settlement of Omani migrants. Saif appointed Arab governors to the coastal city states, many of which later came under Muhammed bin Uthman al-Mazrui, governor of Mombasa, and his Mazrui descendants, who acknowledged Oman's suzerainty only in name. He also encouraged piracy against the merchant shipping of India, Persia and Europe.

Saif bin Sultan died on 4 October 1711 and was succeeded by his son Sultan bin Saif II. His tomb in the castle of Rustaq was later destroyed by a Wahhabi general. At his death his wealth was said to include 28 ships, 700 male slaves and a third of Oman's date trees, and he earned the title the chain of the Earth for the benefits he had brought. Samuel Barrett Miles wrote that Oman was never so powerful or prosperous as under him, judged him as unscrupulous as he was capable, and held that under him Omani commerce greatly extended.
saifuddin-azizi: Saifuddin Azizi was born on 12 March 1915 into an influential Uyghur trading family originally from Artush. In 1935 he moved to the Soviet Union, joined the Communist Party of the Soviet Union and studied at the Central Asia Political Institute in Tashkent. Returning to Xinjiang as a Soviet agent, he helped instigate a Soviet-backed rebellion against the Kuomintang in 1937, and the warlord Sheng Shicai exiled him to Tacheng as a radical young man. During the Second Sino-Japanese War he called for resistance to Japan and was for a time imprisoned by the Kuomintang.

In 1944 he joined the Ili Rebellion against Kuomintang rule in the districts of Ili, Tacheng and Altay. In the Second East Turkestan Republic he was education minister from 1945 to 1946 and led the Kashgar contingent of the East Turkestan National Army. A leader of the East Turkestan Revolutionary Party, he was a delegate to the peace talks that formed the Coalition Government of Xinjiang Province in 1946, in which he directed the education department.

He attended the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference in September 1949, applied to join the CCP on Mao Zedong's recommendation and was admitted on 27 December, becoming vice chairman of Xinjiang's provincial government. He went with Mao and Zhou Enlai to Moscow for the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, and in December 1950 with Wang Zhen to choose sites for the military reclamation units that grew into the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps.

In 1955 he was made a Lieutenant General of the PLA. He objected to Mao against naming the region the Xinjiang Autonomous Region, arguing that autonomy is given not to mountains and rivers but to particular nationalities, and the Central Committee adopted the name Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region. He promoted land reform and schools, and founded a flight school that trained Xinjiang's first ethnic-minority pilots.

From February 1978 he worked in Beijing as a vice chairman of the Standing Committee of the fifth, sixth and seventh National People's Congresses. He died in Beijing on 24 November 2003 and was buried at the Ürümqi Revolutionary Martyrs Cemetery according to Uyghur custom. In 2017 Radio Free Asia reported that the Xinjiang authorities had told bookstores to remove his books, among them his memoir The Epics of Life.
saigo-takamori: Saigō Takamori was born in Kagoshima, the castle town of Satsuma Domain, on 23 January 1828, into a low-ranking samurai family that faced financial hardship. His father was a division chief in the domain's exchequer. At sixteen he began work in a county office, inspecting farm villages and collecting taxes, which made him aware of the peasants' hardships. In 1854 he became an attendant of the daimyō Shimazu Nariakira, a progressive leader keen on Western learning, and relayed his secret messages as his Edo gardener. Nariakira's sudden death in July 1858 left him exposed.

Facing arrest in the Ansei Purge, Saigō attempted suicide in November 1858 by throwing himself into Kagoshima Bay with the monk Gesshō, who drowned. Satsuma declared him dead and exiled him to Amami Ōshima, and after a quarrel with Shimazu Hisamitsu in 1862 he was sent to the harsher island of Okinoerabujima. Recalled in 1864, he was persuaded by Katsu Kaishū that the shogunate was doomed and worked towards the Satchō Alliance of 1866, brokered by Sakamoto Ryōma.

The Boshin War began in January 1868 at Toba–Fushimi. Saigō commanded the imperial forces and in April negotiated with Katsu Kaishū the bloodless surrender of Edo Castle. In the new government he helped create the Imperial Guard, which backed the abolition of the han system in July 1871. In 1873 he proposed to go to Korea as envoy, expecting his uncompromising stance, or his killing, to give Japan a cause for war. Ōkubo Toshimichi and Iwakura Tomomi opposed it; when the plan was rejected in October 1873 he resigned and went home to Kagoshima.

In Kagoshima Saigō founded private schools in 1874 that became centres of anti-government feeling. In January 1877 the government tried to remove munitions from the arsenal, and students of the schools seized it. Saigō reluctantly led them and set out on 15 February 1877. The siege of Kumamoto Castle lasted 54 days, and the rebels were defeated at Tabaruzaka. On 24 September 1877, wounded at Shiroyama, he was beheaded by his associate Beppu Shinsuke; the usual account says by his own request after seppuku, though an autopsy found no abdominal wound.
His death made him a tragic hero. On 22 February 1889 he was posthumously pardoned and his court rank restored, and a bronze statue of him with his dog was unveiled in Ueno Park, Tokyo, in 1898.
sail: A sail provides propulsive force through a combination of lift and drag, depending on its angle with respect to the apparent wind, the air velocity felt on the moving craft. A sail may be attached to a mast, boom or other spar and is typically raised by a line called a halyard, while its angle to the wind is controlled by a line called a sheet. Sailing craft use two types of rig: the square rig, with the main sails on horizontal yards set square to the keel, and the fore-and-aft rig, with sails set along the line of the keel.

The invention of the sail has been judged by some to be as important as the wheel, or as the Neolithic way of life, but it is not known when or where it took place. Early water transport is believed to have developed in two nursery areas, Island Southeast Asia and the Mediterranean, where warm waters and intervisible islands encouraged travel. The Nile, which flows north against a prevailing wind, offered a way to drift in one direction and sail in the other. Many do not consider sails to have been used before the 5th millennium BCE, while others place their invention much earlier.

Sails from ancient Egypt are depicted around 3200 BCE, and the Sumerians used square-rigged boats at about the same time and are believed to have established sea trading routes as far as the Indus valley. Greeks and Phoenicians began trading by ship by around 1200 BCE.

Lateen sails emerged in the Mediterranean by around the 2nd century CE and became common in the 5th century, probably as a cost-saving simplification of the square rig. Maritime historians have often wrongly presumed that the lateen sailed far better; analysis of voyages and replica vessels shows the two performed very similarly. The popularity of the caravel in Northern European waters from about 1440 made lateen sails familiar there, and they were used as mizzens on early three-masted ships as balancing sails.

The Austronesian peoples developed catamarans, outriggers and the bi-sparred triangular crab claw sail, which let them cross open ocean. From Taiwan they settled the islands of Maritime Southeast Asia and later Micronesia, Island Melanesia, Polynesia and Madagascar. Their sails were woven from salt-resistant leaves, usually pandan, and the proto-Austronesian word for sail dates to about 3000 BCE. In western Island Southeast Asia the tanja and junk rigs later evolved from the crab claw sail.
sailendra-dynasty: The name Shailendra, from Sanskrit words meaning king of the mountain, appears clearly in the Kalasan inscription of 778 from central Java, which commemorates a Buddhist shrine to the goddess Tara. It also occurs in the Ligor inscription of 775 on the Malay peninsula, the Kelurak inscription of 782, the Karangtengah inscription of 824 and the Nalanda inscription of about 860 in India. The inscriptions use Old Javanese, Old Malay and Sanskrit, and the Old Malay has led to speculation about a Sumatran origin.

Their origin is debated. A Sumatran origin rested on the Sojomerto inscription, which names Dapunta Selendra, but later analysis found that the name is unlikely to be a spelling of Shailendra. An older theory of Ramesh Chandra Majumdar placed the family in Kalinga, in Odisha. The latest studies favour a native Javanese origin, and one theory holds that the Sanjaya dynasty was itself a branch of the Shailendras.

The Shailendras covered the Kedu Plain of central Java with Buddhist monuments, among them the stupa of Borobudur. They are regarded as a maritime power, though they also relied on intensive rice cultivation.
