They kept cordial relations and marriage alliances with Srivijaya in Sumatra: Samaragrawira married Dewi Tara, daughter of the Srivijayan king Dharmasetu. The Karangtengah inscription of 824 names King Samaratungga and his daughter Pramodhawardhani, who inaugurated a Buddhist sanctuary.

The older account holds that the Shailendras existed beside the Sanjaya dynasty, with peaceful cooperation until the middle of the 9th century, when around 852 the Sanjaya ruler Pikatan defeated Balaputra. Balaputra withdrew to Sumatra, where he became the paramount ruler. The Nalanda inscription says that King Devapaladeva of Bengal granted Balaputra, king of Suvarnadvipa, the revenues of five villages for a monastery near Bodh Gaya.

From Sumatra the Shailendras kept ties with the Chola kingdom of southern India. Hostilities broke out in 1025, when Rajendra Chola I invaded Srivijaya and took the last Shailendra king, Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman, hostage; this marked the end of the family as rulers in Sumatra. A charter of 1090 for an old Buddhist sanctuary is the last known inscription to mention the Shailendras. Traditionally their period was placed in the 8th and 9th centuries in central Java, but recent interpretation extends it to the early 11th century, with the family at times ruling both Mataram and Srivijaya.
saint-barthelemy: Saint Barthélemy lies about 30 kilometres southeast of Saint Martin, northeast of Saba and Sint Eustatius and north of Saint Kitts and Nevis. It is a volcanic island, encircled by shallow reefs, with an area of 25 square kilometres. Its highest peak is Morne de Vitet, at 286 metres. The climate is essentially arid, and the hills have poor soil that supports mostly cacti and succulent plants. Its capital and main harbour is Gustavia, built in a U-shaped cove on the west coast.

Before European contact the island was possibly visited by Taíno and Arawak people, but it was probably not permanently inhabited because it lacked fresh water. Christopher Columbus was the first European to encounter it, in 1493, and named it in honour of his younger brother Bartholomew Columbus and Bartholomew the Apostle. By 1648 French settlers had arrived, encouraged by Phillippe de Longvilliers de Poincy of the French West India Company, and they began cultivating cacao. Caribs attacked the settlement in 1656 and it was briefly abandoned.

The island proved economically unsuccessful and was troubled by pirates. British forces captured it in 1744 and it returned to French control in 1764. In 1784 King Louis XVI, deeming it of little worth, traded it to Sweden in return for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes declared Gustavia, named after Gustav III, a free port, which brought prosperity from trade, and built three forts. British forces occupied the island in March 1801, and the outnumbered Swedes surrendered without resistance. It remained a Swedish colony for nearly a century and returned to French rule after a referendum.

On 19 March 1946 the people of the island became French citizens with full rights. For many years it was a commune forming part of Guadeloupe, and in 2003 its voters chose to separate. It became a separate overseas collectivity of France in February 2007. The Three Crowns of the Swedish arms appear in its coat of arms. The language, cuisine and culture are French Caribbean, the euro is the currency, and the economy rests on tourism and duty-free retail.
saint-basils-cathedral: The site was a busy marketplace between the gate of the Moscow Kremlin and the outlying settlement. Its centre was marked by the Trinity Church, built of white stone. Ivan IV marked each victory of the Russo-Kazan War by building a wooden memorial church beside Trinity Church, and by the end of his Astrakhan campaign it was surrounded by seven wooden churches. In the autumn of 1554, according to Nikon's Chronicle, he ordered a wooden Church of the Intercession on the moat, and a year later a new stone cathedral on the site of Trinity Church to commemorate his campaigns. Dedicating a church to a military victory was a major innovation in Muscovy.

The building was consecrated on 12 July 1561 as Trinity Church, after its easternmost sanctuary. Its popular name Jerusalem arose in the late 16th century, and the name of Vasily the Blessed, who died during construction and was buried on the site, was attached to it at the beginning of the 17th century.

Ivan's architects chose a symmetrical plan with eight side churches around a central core. The core and the four larger churches on the compass points are octagonal, and the four smaller churches between them are cuboid. The central Church of the Intercession is 46 metres tall inside but has a floor area of only 64 square metres. The foundations are of white stone and the churches of red brick, then a relatively new material, and restorers in 1954–1955 found that the brick walls conceal a wooden frame, built as a life-size model of the cathedral and gradually enclosed in masonry.

The building has no analogue in earlier or later Muscovite architecture, and the sources that inspired its builders Barma and Postnik are disputed. Nineteenth-century Russian writers, starting with Ivan Zabelin, stressed the vernacular wooden churches of the Russian North, while a modern hypothesis sees it as a recreation of the Qolşärif Mosque at Kazan. A chapel over the grave of Vasily was added in 1588, and in 1680–1683 arcades and galleries joined the nine churches into one monolithic building.

In the 16th and 17th centuries the church was perceived as the earthly symbol of the Heavenly City, and it served as an allegory of the Jerusalem Temple in the Palm Sunday parade, in which the tsar led the patriarch of Moscow on a donkey. Under the Soviet Union's antireligious campaigns it was confiscated from the Russian Orthodox community and has been part of the State Historical Museum since 1928. It became part of the Moscow Kremlin and Red Square UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1990, and weekly liturgical celebrations have been restored since 1997. The Russian historian Dmitry Shvidkovsky wrote that it is like no other Russian building.
saint-boniface: The earliest life of Boniface does not give his place of birth. It says that as a boy he attended a monastery ruled by Abbot Wulfhard in a place called escancastre, which seems to denote Exeter. Later tradition places his birth at Crediton, but the earliest mention of Crediton in this connection dates from the early fourteenth century. His English name is recorded as Winfrid or Winfred. Before leaving for the continent he wrote a grammatical treatise, the Ars Bonifacii, and a collection of twenty acrostic riddles, the Enigmata.

Boniface first left for the continent in 716 and went to Utrecht, where Willibrord had worked among the Frisians since the 690s. Their preaching was frustrated by the war between Charles Martel and Radbod, King of the Frisians, and he returned to Nursling. The next year he went straight to Rome, where Pope Gregory II renamed him Boniface after a fourth-century martyr and appointed him missionary bishop for Germania, a bishop without a diocese in a region that lacked any church organisation. He never returned to England but kept up a correspondence with his countrymen and kinsfolk.

The support of the Frankish mayors of the palace and later the Carolingians was essential; he was under the protection of Charles Martel from 723. The Frankish leaders wished to defeat the pagan Saxons and incorporate their lands, and his destruction of pagan sites may have helped them. Pope Gregory III made him Archbishop of Mainz. Through his efforts to reorganise and regulate the Frankish church he helped shape the Latin Church in Europe, and many of the dioceses he proposed remain.

According to the vitae, Boniface never gave up hope of converting the Frisians, and in 754 he set out for Frisia with a retinue. He baptised many and summoned a meeting for confirmation near Dokkum, but armed robbers appeared instead and killed the aged archbishop along with 52 others. His remains were returned to Fulda, where veneration began at once; a decorative tomb followed about ten years after his burial, and in 819 his relics were moved to a new apse of the rebuilt abbey church. His feast day is 5 June.

His life became widely known through several vitae, notably the near-contemporary life by Willibald, and through about 150 letters of the Bonifatian correspondence, assembled by order of his successor at Mainz, Lullus. Anniversaries have been marked in Germany since 1805, and Pope John Paul II prayed at his grave in 1980. Tradition credits him with inventing the Christmas tree.
saint-cadoc: Most of what is told of Cadoc comes from the Vita Cadoci written shortly before 1086 by Lifris of Llancarfan to honour that house and confirm its endowments, so it is of limited historical value. In it his father, Gwynllyw the Bearded, elopes with Gwladys, daughter of King Brychan of Brycheiniog, and Cadoc is born in Monmouthshire around 497. After Gwynllyw stole a cow from the Irish monk Tathyw of Caerwent, he sent the boy to be educated at Tathyw's monastery there, where Cadoc learned basic Latin.

Refusing to lead his father's army, Cadoc founded his first monastery at Llancarfan on land given by his uncle, King Pawl of Penychen. He went to Ireland to study for three years, then studied with Bachan, a teacher of rhetoric from Italy. Tradition says that on his return he found the monastery in ruins and set the monks to rebuild it, helped by two stags, which is why the stream there is called the Nant Carfan. Illtud spent the first period of his religious life under Cadoc's tutelage.

About 528 Cadoc is said to have built a monastery in Scotland, probably at Kilmadock north-west of Stirling, and his Scottish followers were known as Gille Dog. In Brittany he settled on an island in the Etel river, now L'Ile de Cado, built an oratory and founded a monastery; his name lies behind some thirty Breton place-names.

Cadoc is known as Cattwg Ddoeth, the Wise, and a large collection of maxims credited to him was printed in the Myvyrian Archaiology. His Life is one of seven saints' lives that mention Arthur independently of Geoffrey of Monmouth: Cadoc shelters a man who killed three of Arthur's soldiers, and the cattle paid in compensation turn into bundles of ferns. Later Welsh Triads name him with Illtud and Peredur as a keeper of the Holy Grail. The 2004 Roman Martyrology lists him under 21 September; Cardiff has kept his day on 25 September, and elsewhere his feast is 24 January.
saint-catherines-monastery: The oldest record of monastic life at Mount Sinai is the Itinerarium Egeriae, the travel journal of a Christian pilgrim named Egeria, written about 381/2 to 386. The monastery itself was built between 548 and 565 by order of Justinian I, around a Chapel of the Burning Bush attributed to Empress Helena, mother of Constantine I, at the place where Moses is said to have seen the burning bush. It also encloses the Well of Moses, where Moses is said to have met his future wife Zipporah.

Centuries later the body of Catherine of Alexandria was said to have been found in a cave nearby; her relics made it a pilgrimage site, and it was renamed after her. Its king post truss is the oldest known surviving roof truss in the world.

In the seventh century the isolated anchorites of Sinai were eliminated and only the fortified monastery remained. Until the twentieth century access was through a door high in its walls. During the Fatimid Caliphate a chapel was converted into a mosque, and a Fatimid mosque of 1106 is preserved. In the Middle Ages the community was multiethnic, with Arab, Greek, Syrian, Slavonic and Georgian monks; in the Ottoman period it became almost entirely Greek Orthodox.

During the Crusades both Byzantine emperors and the rulers of the Kingdom of Jerusalem patronised it. From the 1480s Wallachian princes sent alms. In the mid-14th century there were several hundred monks, and a century later only several dozen, as Bedouins harassed the community.

The monastery and its dependencies form the Church of Sinai, headed by an archbishop who is also abbot. Its administrative status is ambiguous: the church itself regards it as autocephalous, others as autonomous under the Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem.

The library, founded between 527 and 565, holds manuscripts in Greek, Syriac, Georgian, Arabic, Armenian, Church Slavonic and other languages. Constantin von Tischendorf found the Codex Sinaiticus there in 1844 and 1859. It left for Russia, was sold by Stalin to the British Museum in 1933, and is now in the British Library. In 1892 Agnes Smith Lewis found the Syriac Sinaiticus, which remains at the monastery.

Since 2011 the Sinai Palimpsests Project has imaged the palimpsests, among them those found in 1975, recovering over 6,800 pages by June 2018. The icon collection begins with a few from the 5th and 6th centuries and holds over 120 icons in the hybrid style of Crusader art. UNESCO made the monastery a World Heritage Site in 2002.
saint-cloud: Saint-Cloud lies in the western suburbs of Paris, about 10 kilometres from the centre, on the Seine. According to the account of its name, Clodoald, a grandson of Clovis, sought refuge in a hamlet on the river then called Novigentum, one of many newly founded mercantile settlements outside the traditional towns. After Clodoald was canonised, the village where his tomb stood took the name Sanctus Clodoaldus.

The Château de Saint-Cloud was built in 1572. It was the residence of several French rulers and served as the main country residence of the cadet Orléans line until the French Revolution. Henri III of France was assassinated at Saint-Cloud in 1589, and Henrietta of England lived and died in the château in 1670. Philippe d'Orléans lived there from 1658 until his death in 1701. The palace was also the site of the coup d'état led by Napoleon Bonaparte that overthrew the French Directory in 1799, and Napoleon lived there as ruler. The château was destroyed by fire in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War.

The town was also known for Saint-Cloud porcelain, produced there from 1693 to 1766. Its Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1874. The headquarters of the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) stood at 22 Rue Armengaud from 1966 until 1989, when it moved to Lyon.

The main landmarks are the park of the demolished château and the Pavillon de Breteuil, which houses the International Bureau of Weights and Measures. The Saint-Cloud Racecourse was built by Edmond Blanc in 1901 and hosts the annual Grand Prix de Saint-Cloud. On the Avenue de Longchamp a bronze statue of Icarus, inaugurated on 19 October 1913, honours the Brazilian aviation pioneer Alberto Santos-Dumont, who made his experiments near the old Aerostation of Saint-Cloud and built the world's first hangar. The original hangar was destroyed for its bronze during the German occupation, and a replica has stood on its site since 1952.
saint-comgall: According to the Irish annals, Comgall was born in Dál nAraidi in Ulster, near the place now called Magheramorne in County Antrim; his father was Setna. He served as a soldier in his youth, then studied under Fintan of Clonenagh, Finnian of Movilla, Mobhí Clárainech at Glasnevin and Ciarán of Clonmacnoise. Bishop Lugidius ordained him deacon and priest, at Clonmacnoise or Connor. For a time he lived with a few companions on an island in Lough Erne under so harsh a rule that seven of them died of cold and hunger.

Comgall meant to go to Britain, but Lugidius persuaded him to stay and spread the monastic life in Ireland. He founded Bangor on the southern shore of Belfast Lough, opposite Carrickfergus, and is said to have governed over four thousand monks there and in other houses, all of them set to tillage or other manual work. The rule was severe: one meal a day, taken in the evening, of herbs, water and bread, with milk counted an indulgence; confession was made in public, silence kept at meals, and fasting was frequent and long.

Adamnan's Life of Columba shows a close connection between Comgall and Columba, though not, it seems, that Comgall was his disciple. He was a friend of Cormac, Brendan and Canice, and among the monks believed to have been trained at Bangor were Columbanus and Saint Moluag. Comgall belonged to the Second Order of Irish Saints, who founded the great monastic schools of 6th-century Ireland.

After a period of great suffering Comgall received the Eucharist from Saint Fiacre and died at Bangor. His relics, kept there, were scattered in Viking raids in 822. The seventh-century Antiphonary of Bangor called him strict, holy and constant, and a Rule of Saint Comgall in Irish survives. Jonas's Life of Columbanus names him as the superior under whom Columbanus studied. His feast day is 10 May, and he is commemorated in the Felire of Óengus of Tallaght, the Stowe Missal and the Martyrology of Tallaght.
saint-corentin: Corentin, also Corentinus and in Breton Kaourintin, is counted among the Seven Saints who evangelised Brittany, with Tugdual de Tréguier, Paterne de Vannes, Samson of Dol, Pol de Léon, Malo and Brieuc. Tradition holds that these monks came from Wales and Cornwall, brought Christianity to Armorica and founded its first bishoprics in the 5th and 6th centuries; the pilgrimage of the Tro Breiz, the tour of Brittany, joins their cities. According to Albert le Grand, Corentin was born in Cornouaille and became a hermit at Plomodiern, beside Ménez-Hom, where he lived on herbs and roots from the forest besides the fish of the legend.

When King Gradlon decided to create the diocese of Quimper, the tradition continues, he asked Corentin to be its first bishop and sent him to Tours to be consecrated by Martin of Tours. He travelled with his disciples Guénolé, the founder of Landévennec Abbey, and Tudy. Gradlon gave him a palace on the site where Quimper Cathedral now stands, and after his death he was buried before its altar.

In the Breton legend of the city of Ys, Corentin is the saint who warned Gradlon of the sin of his daughter Dahut, also called Ahes. In the common plot of the tales, king and princess escape the flood on horseback and are met by Corentin, or in some versions by Guénolé, who denounces Dahut, so that she falls into the water and becomes a morgen, or siren. The lost king later finds Corentin's hermitage and is given a morsel of the fish, which the tales take as a figure of the gift of Christianity.

His life is told in a Vita written around 1220–1235, revised after the discovery of The Ancient Life of Saint Corentin, and the song of Aiquin also tells of him. In 1201 King Philippe Auguste dedicated an abbey near Mantes to him, and in Cornwall St. Corentine's Church at Cury bears his name. He is the patron saint of Cornouaille and of seafood, and his feast falls on 12 December. Images show him holding a whole or half fish, or with one at his feet, sometimes beside a fountain.
saint-croix: Saint Croix is the largest island of the United States Virgin Islands, with a land area of 214.66 square kilometres. Its highest point is Mount Eagle, at 355 metres. A fairly even plain slopes from the north-side hills to the south coast and was cultivated as the island's prime sugar land. It has two towns, Frederiksted on the west and Christiansted on the north-east, which give it the nickname Twin City.

The Taíno name was Ay Ay, meaning the river, and the Carib name Cibuquiera, the stony land. The present name comes from the French Sainte-Croix, a translation of the Spanish Isla de la Santa Cruz, given by Christopher Columbus in 1493.

Igneri pottery shows human presence from 1 to 700 CE, followed by the Taíno from 700 to 1425, before the Caribs encroached, and by 1590 the island was uninhabited. Columbus landed on 14 November 1493 and was at once attacked by the Kalinago at Salt River, the first recorded fight between the Spanish and a native population of the New World, and he named the place Cabo de la Flecha, Cape of the Arrow. The Spanish never colonised the island.

Dutch and English settlers landed in 1625. The English expelled the Dutch and French before a Spanish invasion from Puerto Rico evicted them in August 1650. About 1650 a French force established a colony of 300. The Knights of Malta ruled the island in the name of Louis XIV from 1651, and it then passed to the French West India Company. The colony was evacuated to Saint-Domingue in 1695, during the War of the Grand Alliance, and the island lay abandoned for another 38 years.

Sugarcane, cotton and tobacco, planted and processed by enslaved Africans, were its main exports, and sugar led in the 18th and 19th centuries, with more than 150 sugar mills. Slavery was abolished in 1848, and a labour riot shook the island in 1878. In 1916 Denmark sold Saint Croix, Saint Thomas and Saint John to the United States for $25 million in gold, and 64.2% of Danish voters approved. The formal transfer took place on 1 April 1917.

Saint Croix belongs to the United States Virgin Islands, an unincorporated territory of the United States, and 41,004 people lived there at the 2020 census. English has been the dominant language since the 1700s and the official one since 1917, when it replaced Danish. Frederiksted keeps its Victorian architecture and its design of seven streets by seven, and the Christiansted National Historic Site is among its protected areas. Alexander Hamilton lived on the island from the age of 10 or 11 to 17.
saint-cuthbert: Cuthbert was born in the mid-630s, perhaps into a noble family, in or near Dunbar, then in Anglo-Saxon Northumbria and now in East Lothian. The kingdom had been Christian only since the conversion of King Edwin in 627, and Irish monks from Iona had founded Lindisfarne at about the time of Cuthbert's birth. According to his early biographies, he was a shepherd boy who saw the soul of Aidan carried to heaven by angels on the night Aidan died, in 651, and then decided to become a monk. He seems to have served as a soldier first. He joined the new monastery at Melrose under the prior Boisil and later succeeded him as prior.

Cuthbert served for a time as guest master at the new monastery of Ripon, but returned to Melrose with Eata when Wilfrid was given Ripon. Educated in the Celtic tradition, he accepted the Roman customs after the Synod of Whitby in 664 and introduced them at Lindisfarne as prior. He travelled as a preacher as far as Galloway, and gained the name Wonder Worker of Britain for gifts of healing and insight. In 676 he withdrew to a hermit's life, and later to Inner Farne, where he lived austerely and eventually received visitors only through a window.

In 684 he was elected bishop of Hexham, but he accepted only after a visit from a large group including King Ecgfrith, and exchanged sees with Eata to become bishop of Lindisfarne. Archbishop Theodore consecrated him at York on 26 March 685. After Christmas 686 he returned to his cell on Inner Farne and died there on 20 March 687. He was buried at Lindisfarne the same day.

When his coffin was opened eleven years after his death, Bede reports, the body was found incorrupt, and his cult grew until he became the most popular saint of northern England. In 875 the monks fled from Danish attack, carrying his body to places including Melrose before it came to rest at Chester-le-Street, and in 995 another Danish invasion led to its removal. The community settled at Durham, where a new church was built and the relics were enshrined in 999.

A small copy of the Gospel of John, the Saint Cuthbert Gospel, was found in his tomb in 1104, and King Æthelstan gave vestments to the shrine. By the later 11th century the bishops of Durham held the semi-autonomous Liberty of Durham, and the saint became a symbol of its autonomy; his banner was carried in battle against the Scots until the Reformation. Henry VIII's commissioners stripped the shrine in the Dissolution of the Monasteries, but his relics remain at the cathedral.
saint-david: David, Dewi Sant in Welsh, is traditionally believed to be the son of Non and the grandson of Ceredig ap Cunedda, king of Ceredigion. His birth date is uncertain, with suggestions ranging from 462 to 512. Many traditional tales survive in the Buchedd Dewi, a life written by Rhygyfarch around 1090 and said by him to rest on documents in the cathedral archives. Modern historians doubt some of its claims, since one of Rhygyfarch's aims was to win some independence for the Welsh church, which had refused the Roman rite until the 8th century. The tradition that David was born at Henfynyw in Ceredigion is not improbable.

David became known as a teacher and preacher and founded monastic settlements and churches in Wales, Dumnonia and Brittany. St David's Cathedral stands on the site of the monastery he founded in the Glyn Rhosyn valley of Pembrokeshire. Around 550 he attended the Synod of Brefi, where his eloquence in opposing Pelagianism caused his fellow monks to elect him primate of the region, and he presided over the synod of Caerleon around 569. According to Rhygyfarch, the ground rose beneath him at Brefi to form a small hill, where Llanddewi Brefi now stands, and a white dove settled on his shoulder.

His Monastic Rule prescribed that monks pull the plough themselves without draught animals, eat only bread with salt and herbs and drink only water, which earned them the name 'watermen'. No personal possessions were allowed: even to say 'my book' was an offence.

Tradition holds that David died on 1 March, now Saint David's Day, and that the monastery was filled with angels as Christ received his soul. His last sermon urged his followers to do the little things they had seen him do.

He was buried at St David's, where his shrine was a place of pilgrimage throughout the Middle Ages. Vikings raided the cathedral in the 10th and 11th centuries and stripped the shrine, a new shrine was built in 1275, and Edward I prayed there in 1284. Pope Callixtus II recognised David in 1120. The first explicit reference to him is in the Irish Martyrology of Tallaght in the early ninth century, and the poem Armes Prydein of about 930 foretold that the Welsh would unite behind his banner. His emblems are the dove and the leek.
saint-deiniol: According to a Latin Life of Deiniol, preserved in Peniarth MS226 and transcribed in 1602 by Sir Thomas Williams of Trefriw, he was the son of Abbot Dunod Fawr, son of Pabo Post Prydain. The family had lost their land in the North of England and were given land by Cyngen Glodrydd, king of Powys. Deiniol took up the religious life and is said to have studied under Cadoc of Llancarfan. Sir David Trevor describes him as one of seven blessed cousins who spent part of his early life as a hermit in Pembrokeshire and was called to be a bishop despite gaps in his formal education.

Deiniol left Powys for Gwynedd, where he founded the monastery of Bangor under the patronage of Maelgwn Gwynedd. The king endowed it with lands and privileges and later raised it to the seat of a bishop, its boundary shared with the principality of Gwynedd. Deiniol is said to have been consecrated to the see by Dubricius in 516, and he spent the rest of his life at Bangor as abbot and bishop. He attended the Synod of Llanddewi Brefi with Saint David around 545, when rules for penance were discussed.

According to the Annales Cambriae Deiniol was buried on Bardsey Island. His cult was widespread in North Wales, where churches dedicated to him include those of Worthenbury near Wrexham, Hawarden and Marchwiel. Others stand at Llanfor, Llanuwchllyn and Eyton, at Itton in Monmouthshire and at Llangarron in Herefordshire, and near Cardigan Bay lies the village of Llanddeiniol, the parish of St Deiniol. In Brittany he is venerated as Saint Denoual, and in English and Latin his name is sometimes given as Daniel.

In 1896 William Ewart Gladstone dedicated St Deiniol's Library, a residential library in Hawarden, to him. The Roman Catholic calendar for Wales and the Anglican Church in Wales commemorate him on the traditional date of 11 September, and the hymn tune St. Denio may take its name from him.
saint-domingue: Christopher Columbus claimed Hispaniola for Spain in 1492. In 1605 Philip III of Spain ordered Governor Antonio de Osorio to depopulate the western, central and northern parts of the island to stop smuggling with French, English and Dutch traders. French, English and Dutch pirates instead set up bases on the abandoned coasts. French buccaneers settled on Tortuga in 1625, and the settlement was officially established in 1659 under a commission from Louis XIV.

Plantation agriculture based on slavery began in 1665. Bertrand d'Ogeron encouraged tobacco planting, and after a tobacco crisis around 1670 indigo and cane sugar were introduced; the first sugar windmill was built in 1685. Spain tacitly recognised the French presence in the western third of the island in the Peace of Ryswick of 1697.

After the Seven Years' War the colony expanded rapidly. By the 1780s it produced about 40 percent of the sugar and 60 percent of the coffee consumed in Europe, from about 8,000 plantations by 1789. Between 1681 and 1791 an estimated 790,000 or 860,000 enslaved people provided the labour, a third of the entire Atlantic slave trade in 1783 to 1791. Disease and harsh conditions prevented natural increase, so most of the enslaved were African-born.

Estimates for 1789 give 40,000 to 45,000 whites, 28,000 to 32,000 free people of color and between 406,000 and 465,000 enslaved people. The gens de couleur libres were the largest and wealthiest such group in the Caribbean.

The French Revolution was at first welcomed on the island. In 1791 an uprising of the enslaved in the north burned 280 sugar plantations within two months. Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines took charge of the revolt, and slavery was abolished in 1793. The last French troops left the western part of the island in late 1803, and the colony declared independence the following year as Haiti. More than 25,000 colonists fled between 1791 and 1810, many to Louisiana.

On 17 April 1825 Charles X issued a decree recognising Haitian independence in return for 150 million francs, to compensate former colonists. On 11 July 1825 President Jean-Pierre Boyer signed, with a French naval squadron present. Researchers have linked the resulting debt to later underfunding of education, health care and public works in Haiti.
saint-dominic: Dominic was born in Caleruega in Old Castile and named after Dominic of Silos, whose Benedictine abbey lies a few miles to the north. At fourteen he was sent to the Premonstratensian monastery of Santa María de La Vid and then to the schools of Palencia, where he spent six years on the arts and four on theology. In 1191, in a famine, he is reported to have sold his clothes, furniture and manuscripts to feed the hungry. Ordained at twenty-four, he joined the canonry of the Cathedral of Osma, and in 1198 Bishop Martin de Bazan made him subprior of the chapter.

Around 1203 or 1204 he accompanied Bishop Diego de Acebo on a diplomatic mission for Alfonso VIII of Castile to Denmark. On the way home they met Cistercian monks sent by Pope Innocent III to preach against the Cathars, and concluded that the monks failed because their pomp contrasted with Cathar asceticism. Dominic and Diego adopted a more ascetic life and began preaching in the south of France. In late 1206 they settled at Prouille, where Dominic gave the Rule of St. Augustine to a house partly meant for women who had lived in Cathar religious houses. After Diego died in December 1207, Dominic continued alone. Dominican tradition says that in 1208 he saw a vision of Mary at Prouille who gave him a rosary.

In 1215 Dominic and six followers moved into a house given by Peter Seila of Toulouse, and Bishop Foulques gave them authority to preach. Honorius III granted written approval for the Order of Preachers in December 1216. In 1218 Dominic reached Bologna, where the order held its first two General Chapters, and in 1220 the friars took up residence at Santa Sabina in Rome.

Dominic died on 6 August 1221 at Bologna, aged fifty-one, and was canonized in 1234 under Gregory IX. His remains were moved in 1233 and in 1267 to a shrine by Nicola Pisano and his workshop. He is commonly but wrongly associated with the Inquisition: sources of his own time say nothing of it, and it was established only in 1231 in Lombardy and 1234 in Languedoc, though his order later became closely associated with it. The legend grew through a painting for the Spanish Inquisition and Protestant polemic. Dominic is the patron saint of astronomers and natural scientists, and the Dominican Republic and Santo Domingo are named after him.
saint-elie: Saint-Élie is a commune of French Guiana, an overseas department and region of France in South America. It covers 5,680 square kilometres, a third of the territory of the arrondissement of Cayenne, yet holds only about 0.09% of the arrondissement's residents. The commune lies in primary tropical rain forest, and the village of Saint-Nazaire is among its settlements.

Gold was discovered at Saint-Élie in 1873. The mines lay in the middle of the rain forest with no river connection to the outside world. In 1884 construction began on a Decauville railway line to Gare Tigre, near Saint-Nazaire, to reach the Sinnamary River. The line needed frequent repairs and had over 100 bridges. In 1930 Saint-Élie became capital of the Inini territory. From 1953 the commune was called Centre, and in 1969 it was renamed Saint-Élie.

The railway was abandoned in 1990, when a road opened. The roads end near Saint-Nazaire, and a 45-minute ferry to the Petit-Saut Dam is needed to reach the outside world. Construction of the dam began in 1989, to produce hydroelectric power, and finished in 1994. In 1996 the La Trinité National Nature Reserve was founded; it covers 76,903 hectares of primary rain forest in the heart of the Guyana plateau forest.

Gold remains the backbone of the local economy. The commune had 138 inhabitants in 1982 and 123 in 1990, then 239 in 1999. The population peaked at an estimated 450 in 2007 and fell to 95 in 2015, then rose to an official estimate of 159 in 2023, a density of 0.02799 inhabitants per square kilometre.
saint-emeric-of-hungary: Emeric, known in Hungarian as Imre, was the son of King Stephen I of Hungary and Giselle of Bavaria. He is believed to have been Stephen's second son and was the only one of Stephen's sons to survive into adulthood. He was named after his maternal uncle, Emperor Henry II, and his Hungarian name derives from the Latin Henricus, which means "ruler of the home".

Emeric was educated in a strict and ascetic spirit by Benedictine monks from Venice, among them Gerard, from the age of 15 to 23. He was intended to be the next monarch of Hungary, and his father wrote the Admonitions to prepare him for the task. Stephen also tried to make him co-heir during his own lifetime. Emeric married in 1022, but the identity of his wife is disputed. Some name Irene Monomachina, a relative of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, or a woman of the Argyros family of Emperor Romanos III Argyros. Others name Patricissa of Croatia, daughter of Krešimir III of Croatia, or Adelaide (Rixa) of Poland or one of her unnamed sisters.

Stephen's succession plans could not be fulfilled: on 2 September 1031, at the age of 24, Emeric was killed by a boar while hunting. It is assumed that this happened at Hegyközszentimre, now Sântimreu in Romania. He was buried in the Székesfehérvár Basilica. Several healings and conversions were reported at his grave, and on 5 November 1083 King Ladislaus I unearthed his bones in a large ceremony.

Pope Gregory VII canonised Emeric for his pious life and purity, together with his father and Bishop Gerard of Csanád. He is most commonly depicted wearing knight's armour and a crown and holding a lily. Some claim that the explorer Amerigo Vespucci, after whom the Americas are named, was named in his honour, but there is no definitive evidence for this.
saint-emmeram: The main account of his life is the Vita Sancti Emmerami, written by Arbeo of Freising in 750, about a century after his death. It makes him a man of noble family from Aquitaine, born in Poitiers. Alban Butler and others say he became Bishop of Poitiers, though this cannot be verified; some suggest he held the see briefly between the death of Dido and the accession of Ansoaldus.

Hearing of idolatry in Bavaria, he set out some time after 649 for Ratisbon, as Regensburg was then called, and the court of Theodo I, Duke of Bavaria. He is said to have travelled up the Loire, crossed the Black Forest and followed the Danube. The duke welcomed him, and he spent three years as a missionary there, gaining a name for piety and founding the monastery that later bore his name.

Setting out on a pilgrimage to Rome, he was attacked five days into the journey at the place now called Kleinhelfendorf, south of Munich, by the duke's son Lantpert of Bavaria, who tortured him. He died soon afterwards at Aschheim, about fifteen miles away. The cause of the attack and the circumstances of his death are not known.

Arbeo's legend explains the attack: the duke's daughter Uta, pregnant by Sigipaldus of her father's court, named Emmeram as the father on his advice to spare her shame, and Lantpert pursued him, tied him to a ladder and tortured him. Later critics judged these details and the wonders said to have attended his death to be pious additions to the facts.

He was first buried at Aschheim. Tradition holds that it then rained for forty days, and that his body, set on a raft in the Isar, floated up the Danube to Regensburg, where it was laid in the church of St. George. The later church dedicated to him burned in 1642; his bones were found under the altar in 1645 and moved to St. Emmeram's Abbey, now a basilica minor, where his leg bones rest in a silver reliquary. A chapel was built in 1842 where he is said to have died, and his feast day is 22 September.
saint-gall: Gall, in Latin Gallus, is known through lives written long after his death. The fragmentary oldest Life was recast in the 9th century by two monks of Reichenau, enlarged between 816 and 824 by Wettinus, and again by Walafrid Strabo. According to these biographers he came from Ireland and studied under Comgall at Bangor Abbey, where Columbanus was a fellow student. His origin is disputed: Hilty proposed in 2001 that he more probably came from the Vosges or Alsace, and Schär suggested in 2010 that he may have been of Irish descent but born and raised in Alsace.

Gall and his companions settled first at Luxeuil in Gaul. In 610 Columbanus was exiled and fled with Gall to Alemannia, travelling up the Rhine to Bregenz. When Columbanus went on to Italy in 612, Gall was ill and stayed behind, nursed at Arbon. He lived as a hermit with several companions in the forests southwest of Lake Constance, near the source of the Steinach. Cells were soon added for twelve monks whom he instructed, and he became known in Switzerland as a powerful preacher.

When the see of Constance fell vacant, the assembled clergy unanimously favoured Gall, but he refused, pleading that electing a stranger would be contrary to church law. In 625 monks of Luxeuil asked him to take over their monastery after the death of its abbot Eustasius, and he again refused to leave his solitude. He died at the age of ninety-five, around the middle of the 7th century, in Arbon.

After his death his disciples remained in his cell and followed the rule of Columbanus. In 719 Otmar, the brotherhood's first abbot, extended the cell into the Abbey of St. Gall, which became the nucleus of the canton of St. Gallen. The abbey followed the rule of Benedict of Nursia from 747. It regained its independence from the bishop of Constance in the 9th century, when Emperor Louis the Pious made it a royal monastery. Its scriptorium, evidenced from 760, played a major part in intellectual history until the abbey was secularised in 1798.

Later legend told that a bear Gall had rebuked gathered firewood for him, and he is usually shown standing with a bear. His feast is on 16 October. In Bohemia he was known as Havel, and Wenceslas I built a church in his honour in Prague after his coronation in 1230.
saint-helena: Saint Helena is a volcanic tropical island in the South Atlantic Ocean, measuring about 16 by 8 kilometres. It lies some 1,860 kilometres west of Angola and 3,280 kilometres east of Brazil, which makes it one of the most remote major islands in the world. Its climate is mild, tempered by the Benguela Current and almost continuous trade winds. The island is named after Helena of Constantinople.

By long tradition the island was sighted on 21 May 1502 by the four ships of the 3rd Portuguese Armada under João da Nova. A paper of 2022 observed that the only primary sources are Portuguese chronicles written at least fifty years later, none of which gives a precise date. The Portuguese found it uninhabited, with many trees and fresh water, brought livestock and fruit trees, and built a chapel, but formed no permanent settlement. It became a source of food for ships on the Cape Route from Asia to Europe, and sick mariners were left there to recover.

The East India Company received a charter from Oliver Cromwell to govern the island and decided to fortify it and settle it with planters. In 1815 the British government chose Saint Helena as the place of exile for Napoleon Bonaparte after Waterloo. He arrived in October 1815, lived at the Briars pavilion until Longwood House was ready in December, and died at Longwood on 5 May 1821. The Company then resumed control until the India Act of 1833 made the island a crown colony. Dinuzulu, the Zulu king, was exiled there from 1890 to 1897.

Royal Navy ships also brought liberated Africans to the island after rescuing them from slave ships. The remains of some 325 of them, disinterred during airport construction, were stored in Jamestown awaiting reburial.

Saint Helena is one of the three parts of the British overseas territory of Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha, with 4,439 inhabitants at the 2021 census. The island is known for its many endemic birds and plants, over 500 endemic species in all, most of them in the highland cloud forest.
saint-helier: St Helier is the most populous of the twelve parishes of Jersey, and the town, the island's only town, lies on the south coast at the eastern end of St Aubin's Bay. The land on which it stands was once a low-lying basin of marsh and sand dunes, with dunes to the west and low hills on the other sides. There is very little evidence of prehistoric settlement in the basin; the one archaeological site was an Iron Age dolmen that stood on Mont de la Ville, the present site of Fort Regent, and was moved to a former Governor's house at Henley-on-Thames in the 1780s. The site is thought to have been settled in the time of Roman control of Gaul.

The town takes its name from Helier, a 6th-century ascetic hermit from Belgium. Tradition dates his martyrdom to 555, and the parish arms of two crossed gold axes on blue refer to his death at the hands of Saxon pirates. His feast day, 16 July, is marked by an annual municipal and ecumenical pilgrimage to the Hermitage. Medieval accounts of his life suggest a small fishing village on the dunes between the marshy land behind and the high-water mark. Evidence of settlement exists from the 13th century, and the town's growth since has been described as spasmodic, reflecting waves of migration to the island.

In 1700 the cattle market moved from Broad Street to a site on the beach, and around 1800 the market was moved to a new building at its present site. Military roads linking coastal defences with St Helier harbour let farmers use fast sailing ships and then steamships to reach the markets of London and Paris first, which began Jersey's agricultural prosperity in the 19th century. By the turn of the century the open spaces around the town were mostly built over. After the First World War ribbon development spread along the coast and into neighbouring parishes, and in the 1930s the States built Jersey's first public housing estate, at Wellington Park.

St Helier is the de facto capital of Jersey. The States Assembly meets in the States Chamber next to the Royal Court, both in the Royal Square. The Town Church, the oldest building in the town, predates the Battle of Hastings; after the Reformation it became a Huguenot temple, and eight successive Rectors were French Huguenot ministers. Elizabeth Castle, a 16th-century castle on a tidal island, was built to supplement the defence provided by Mont Orgeuil. Fort Regent was built as a barracks at the end of the Napoleonic Wars, and the Central Market opened in 1882.
saint-jean-pied-de-port: The name means foot of the pass in Pyrenean French; in Basque the town is Donibane Garazi. It lies on the river Nive in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department of south-western France, 8 km from the Spanish border and about 75 kilometres by road from Pamplona, the capital of Upper Navarre. The region around it is called the Pays de Cize, or Garazi in Basque. The town's layout is essentially one main street, encircled by sandstone walls.

The original town at nearby Saint-Jean-le-Vieux was razed in 1177 by the troops of Richard the Lionheart after a siege. The Kings of Navarre refounded the town on its present site shortly afterwards. It then belonged to the Kingdom of Navarre and was the seat of the sheriff of the district of Lower Navarre, the merindad of Ultrapuertos or Deça-Ports.

It remained the seat until the period of the Spanish conquest (1512-1528), when King Henry II of Navarre transferred the seat of the royal institutions to Saint Palais (Donapaleu) on safety grounds. The citadel above the town was remodelled by Vauban in the 17th century, and the Porte St-Jacques, the city gate, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1998 as part of the sites along the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France.

The town stands at the base of the Roncevaux Pass, and the routes from Paris, Vézelay and Le Puy-en-Velay meet there. It was the pilgrims' last stop before the mountain crossing and is the second most popular starting point of the French Way of the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela.

The cobbled rue de la Citadelle runs from the fifteenth century Porte St-Jacques to the Porte d'Espagne by the bridge, past old houses of pink and grey schist. Nearby stands the 14th-century red schist Gothic church of Notre-Dame-du-Bout-du-Pont, the original of which was built by Sancho the Strong of Navarre to commemorate the 1212 Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa. The town is a member of the association of the Most Beautiful Villages of France. Its notable people include Bernard Etxepare, writer of the first printed book in Basque, and the physician Juan Huarte de San Juan (c. 1530-1592).
saint-john-u-s-virgin-islands: Saint John is the smallest of the three main US Virgin Islands, about 50 square kilometres in area. It lies about four miles east of Saint Thomas, the site of the territory's capital, Charlotte Amalie, and about four miles southwest of Tortola in the British Virgin Islands. Its largest settlement is Cruz Bay. Its nickname is Love City.

Petroglyphs and artifacts found at Cinnamon Bay indicate a Taíno presence from about 700 to the late fifteenth century. Christopher Columbus sailed past in 1493 on his second voyage without coming ashore. Britain claimed the island as part of the Leeward Islands in 1684, but it was uninhabited when 20 Danish planters came from Saint Thomas in 1717, and Denmark claimed it again in 1718. The planters grew sugar cane and cotton, and by 1733 there were 109 plantations, 21 of them producing sugar. The Annaberg sugar plantation was built in 1731. Britain relinquished its claims to the island in 1762.

In 1733 enslaved people, led by those formerly from Akwamu, entered Fort Frederiksvaern on Fortsberg Hill in Coral Bay with cane bills hidden in bundles of wood, and killed five of the six soldiers. Firing the fort's cannon gave the signal for a revolt that lasted six months and ended only when French troops were brought from Martinique. More than a dozen men and women, including the leader Breffu, shot themselves rather than submit to captivity.

The enslaved population peaked at 2,604 in 1804. Denmark emancipated the enslaved in 1848, and by 1850 many plantations were abandoned. The last sugar factory ceased operation in 1908. Between 1845 and 1945 the population declined by 70%. In 1917, during the First World War, the United States bought the Virgin Islands from Denmark for $25 million to establish a naval base and prevent German expansion into the Western Hemisphere.

Saint John is a district of the United States Virgin Islands, an organised, unincorporated territory of the United States. The population was 3,881 at the 2020 census. In 1956 Laurance Rockefeller donated his lands on the island to the National Park Service on condition that they be protected, and Virgin Islands National Park now covers about 60% of the island, with the Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument added in 2001. The economy depends almost entirely on tourism.
saint-kentigern: Kentigern (Welsh Cyndeyrn) probably bore a British name meaning hound-lord, while Mungo is a pet name, possibly from the Cumbric for my dear one. According to the medieval accounts, his mother Teneu was a daughter of King Lleuddun, who ruled around what is now Lothian, and his father was Owain mab Urien of Rheged; the British Library manuscript says Teneu was raped, while other accounts tell of a love affair. Her furious father had her thrown from Traprain Law, and she drifted in a coracle across the Firth of Forth to Culross in Fife, where Mungo was born and raised by Saint Serf.

At the age of twenty-five, the Life relates, he began missionary work on the Clyde, building his church beside the Molendinar Burn where the medieval cathedral of Glasgow now stands, and lived austerely there for some thirteen years. Driven out by an anti-Christian movement under a King Morken, he went to Wales, staying with Saint David and founding a church at Llanelwy (St Asaph), though S. Mundahl-Harris has shown his links with St Asaph to be a Norman invention. Invited back by the new king of Strathclyde, Riderch Hael, he set his seat at Hoddom and preached in Galloway; excavations at Hoddom have found a late 6th-century stone baptistery.

Mungo later returned to Glasgow, where a large community gathered around him, and at Kilmacolm he is said to have met Saint Columba and exchanged pastoral staffs with him. Historians see little reason to doubt that he was one of the first evangelists of Strathclyde and probably the first Bishop of Glasgow. Jocelin of Furness, who wrote his Life in about 1185, seems to have added episodes such as a pilgrimage to Rome to promote the bishopric of Glasgow.

In old age Mungo grew very feeble, and he is said to have died in his bath on Sunday 13 January; David McRoberts has argued that this garbles a collapse during a baptismal service. His shrine in Glasgow Cathedral was a great centre of pilgrimage until the Scottish Reformation. The four miracles of his Life, the bird, the tree, the bell and the fish, appear on the city's coat of arms, and its motto Let Glasgow flourish comes from his call. His feast is kept on 13 January.
saint-kitts: Saint Kitts lies in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles, with its west side on the Caribbean Sea and its east coast facing the Atlantic. It is about 168 square kilometres in area and 29 kilometres long. Nevis lies 3 kilometres to the south across a shallow channel called The Narrows. The island is named for Saint Christopher, Kit being a formerly common short form of Christopher.

It has three groups of volcanic peaks, and the highest point is the dormant volcano Mount Liamuiga, formerly Mount Misery, at about 1,156 metres. The interior is too steep for habitation, and a ring road runs round the coast.

During the last ice age Saint Kitts, Nevis, Saba and Sint Eustatius were one island. The first settlers were Archaic people who came south from Florida. Around 100 BCE the farming Saladoid people arrived from the Orinoco, and around 800 CE the Arawakan-speaking Igneri replaced them. About 1300 CE the Kalinago dispersed the Igneri and named the island Liamuiga, fertile island. Columbus claimed it for Spain in 1493.

The first English colony was founded in 1623, followed by a French one in 1625. The colonists united to forestall a Kalinago ambush, massacred the Kalinago, and then partitioned the island, the English taking the middle and the French each end. A Spanish force seized the island in 1629, and the English settlement was rebuilt after the peace of 1630. Through the 17th and 18th centuries the island passed repeatedly between English, later British, and French control.

Tobacco was the first crop, but farmers switched to sugarcane in 1640, and the labour-intensive cultivation led to large-scale importation of enslaved Africans. Parliament outlawed the purchase of enslaved people in 1807 and abolished slavery with effect from 1 August 1834, followed by four years of apprenticeship, against which the nominally freed people revolted until martial law was declared. Saint Kitts and Nevis became independent on 19 September 1983.

Saint Kitts and Nevis form one country, the Federation of Saint Kitts and Nevis, whose capital and largest port is Basseterre on Saint Kitts. English is the main language. Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, is the largest fortress ever built in the Eastern Caribbean.
saint-louis-senegal: The heart of the old colonial city stands on a narrow island in the Senegal River, a little more than 2 km long and about 400 m wide, 25 km north of the river's mouth. A sand spit 300 m wide, the Langue de Barbarie, separates it from the Atlantic; the seaside neighbourhoods of Ndar Toute and Guet Ndar lie on it, and the older settlement of Sor stands on the east bank. The city lies in the Sahel and is nearly surrounded by tidal marshes, 320 km north of Dakar.

A Wolof settlement at Guet Ndar dates from around 1450 and was a meeting and departure point for Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Portuguese, Dutch and English traders visited over the next two centuries. The French built a fort on Bocos Island in 1638 and, because of repeated flooding, moved it in 1659 to the island the Wolof called Ndar. It was uninhabited, supposedly because local people thought spirits haunted it. The Diagne of Sor, the local leader, allowed the French to settle there for annual payments of cloth, iron bars and eau de vie.

The trading post exported slaves, gold, hides, beeswax, ambergris and later gum arabic. British forces took Senegal in 1758 and the French recaptured Saint-Louis in February 1779. Between 1659 and 1779 nine chartered companies in turn administered it.

A Franco-African Creole merchant community, the Métis, grew up in the 17th and 18th centuries, known for its signares, women entrepreneurs; it controlled most of the river trade and financed the main Catholic institutions. After the Atlantic slave trade declined from 1790, gum arabic became the main trade. Britain held the city again in the Napoleonic Wars and returned it in 1817.

Louis Faidherbe, governor from 1854, built bridges, supplied fresh water and began a telegraph line to Dakar. Saint-Louis was capital of the federation of French West Africa from 1895 until 1902, when Dakar took the role. The railway from Dakar, completed in 1885, let up-country trade bypass its port. From 1920 to 1957 it was also capital of Mauritania. Its population was 10,000 in 1826, 23,000 in 1914 and 39,000 in 1955.

The island was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000 for its colonial architecture, regular town plan and quays. The city had 254,171 inhabitants in 2023 and is the capital of Senegal's Saint-Louis Region. After independence, when Dakar became the sole capital, it declined economically. Its economy now rests on tourism, fishing, sugar production and trade. Gaston Berger University was created there in 1990, and the Saint-Louis Jazz Festival has been held since 1993. Fanals, night processions of giant paper lanterns, take place at Christmas.
saint-lucia-labour-party: The party was backed by the Saint Lucia Workers Cooperative Union. Led by its founder George Charles, it won five of the eight seats in the first elections held under universal suffrage, in 1951. It kept all five in 1954 and enlarged its majority to seven of eight seats in 1957 and nine of ten in 1961.

The party lost an election for the first time in 1964, when the United Workers Party won six of the ten seats and Labour was reduced to two. The UWP had grown out of a split within Labour led by John Compton and the merger of the breakaway faction with the People's Progressive Party. Labour gained a seat in 1969 and rose to seven in 1974, but the UWP stayed in power as the House grew to 17 seats.

Labour won 12 of 17 seats in the elections of 1979, the first after independence from the United Kingdom on 22 February 1979. Allan Louisy led the government until he was replaced as prime minister by Winston Cenac, who was in turn replaced by Michael Pilgrim. In 1982 the party fell to two seats, while George Odlum's breakaway Progressive Labour Party took one, and it stayed in opposition after the two elections of April 1987 and in 1992.

Under Kenny Anthony, a minister of the 1979-1982 government, Labour took 16 of the 17 seats in 1997 and 14 in 2001. It lost in 2006 to the UWP under the returning John Compton, won the general election of 28 November 2011 with 11 seats, and lost in 2016 by 11 seats to 6, after which Anthony resigned. Philip J. Pierre, a former deputy prime minister, was confirmed as leader on 18 June 2016, and the party won the general elections of 2021 and 2025 under him.
saint-lucian-creole: Saint Lucia was settled by Amerindian peoples, most recently the Caribs, and then fought over by the French and the British, who exchanged control of the island fourteen times. A British attempt at settlement in 1605 ended with the colonists killed or driven out by the Caribs, and by 1745 French settlers had established working administrative settlements. Like other varieties of Antillean Creole, the language arose as a means of communication among the enslaved African population of the plantations. A form of Creole brought by French settlers from Martinique was taken up as a vernacular by the black population of small, remote mountain settlements.

After the British gained full control in 1803, English became the official language, but Kwéyòl remained the only language of most of the population. Speaking Kwéyòl alone became less common as schooling in English reached more people from the mid-1960s. In the mid-19th century the language was carried to Panama, where it is known as San Miguel Creole French and is now moribund.

Kwéyòl combines vocabulary drawn mainly from French with syntax of African origin, with some recorded Carib influence and many English loanwords. Its grammar and vocabulary are virtually identical to those of Martinican Creole, and speakers understand the creoles of Dominica, Guadeloupe, Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago almost completely, and Haitian Creole as well, though not Standard French. Nouns have no gender and do not change for number; verbs are not conjugated, tense being shown by particles such as ka for the present. Its alphabet of 24 letters, shared with Dominica, represents 32 phonemes and uses no q or x.

Kwéyòl remains the everyday language of Saint Lucia, spoken across the island beside English. It is not an official language, but the government and the media present information in it alongside English, and movements from the 1980s onward have widened its use in media, education and government. Many Saint Lucians have come to view the language more positively and support making it official.
saint-malo: The walled city stands on the English Channel coast. It was originally a rocky granite island joined to the mainland only by a narrow sand spit and tidal mudflats called le Sillon. Stonework and a basic road were first laid along this sandbar in 1509, and over the centuries, particularly in the 19th century, the structure was widened and raised to form the modern dyke, La Digue du Sillon, which permanently connects the old town to the coast.

The site was founded by Gauls in the 1st century BCE and was known in Roman times as Reginca or Aletum. By the late 4th century CE a Saxon Shore fort in the Saint-Servan district protected the Rance estuary from seaborne raiders. In the 5th and 6th centuries Armorica received many Celtic Britons fleeing instability across the Channel, and the modern city traces its origins to a monastic settlement founded early in the sixth century.

The city asserted its autonomy in dealings with both the French and the local Breton authorities. From 1590 to 1594 it declared itself an independent republic and functioned as a de facto city-state, which gave it the motto "Ni Français, ni Breton, Malouin suis". It became notorious as the home of corsairs, French privateers and sometimes pirates, who forced English ships passing up the Channel to pay tribute and brought wealth from further afield. Jacques Cartier lived in and sailed from Saint-Malo to the Saint Lawrence River. The explorer Louis-Antoine de Bougainville named the Falkland Islands the Îles Malouines in 1764 after the people of Saint-Malo, his point of departure. The writer François-René de Chateaubriand was born in the city in 1768.

In August 1944 American shelling and bombing almost totally destroyed the walled city during the fight against a German garrison of more than twelve thousand troops in the area. The German commander, Colonel Andreas von Aulock, refused to surrender. The last holdout in the citadel gave up on 17 August, and the island of Cézembre surrendered on 2 September. More than ten thousand prisoners were taken.

Saint-Malo was rebuilt over twelve years, from 1948 to 1960, and in 1967 it merged with Saint-Servan and Paramé, more than doubling its population. It is a subprefecture of Ille-et-Vilaine and has a ferry terminal serving Jersey, Guernsey, Portsmouth and Poole. Its inhabitants are called Malouins. The Route du Rhum, a single-handed transatlantic yacht race to Pointe-à-Pitre in Guadeloupe, starts here every four years.
saint-marinus: Marinus is a Christian saint who, according to hagiographical accounts recorded centuries after his lifetime, founded a chapel and monastery in 301 from whose first community the state of San Marino later grew. Tradition holds that he was a stonemason by trade from the island of Arba, today Rab, across the Adriatic in what is now Croatia and was then part of the Roman Empire, and that he fled the persecution of Christians under Diocletian. He is known only by the single name Marinus, literally 'of the sea'.

He was ordained a deacon by Gaudentius of Rimini. In one account he was recognised and accused by an insane woman of being her estranged husband, and he quickly fled to Monte Titano to build a chapel-monastery and live as a hermit. Another version says that, hearing that Rimini was being rebuilt, he went there and found among the workmen many Christians of formerly high position who had been sentenced to hard labour for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, and he tried to comfort them. In his old age he withdrew to a hermitage on Mount Titano. As his reputation for holiness grew, others followed him, until a lady from Rimini and the owner of the mountain gave it to him as a gift.

According to legend he died in the winter of 366, and his last words were 'Relinquo vos liberos ab utroque homine', 'I leave you free from both men'. The phrase most likely refers to the Emperor and the Pope, and this affirmation of freedom, first of all from taxation, though a legend, has always inspired the republic. His feast day, 3 September, commemorates the day in 301 when he founded what became San Marino, and it is the state's national holiday. He is venerated in the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.

The American historian William Miller called the accounts of Marinus and the origin of San Marino a mixture of fables and miracles that perhaps contain some grains of fact. The earliest historical evidence of a monastic community there dates to the 5th or 6th century, when a monk named Eugippus recorded that another monk had lived in a monastery in the area.
saint-martin-island: Saint Martin is an island in the Leeward Islands of the Lesser Antilles, in the north-eastern Caribbean, about 300 km east of Puerto Rico. Its area is 87 square kilometres, divided between France in the north and the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the south. It is the only land border shared by France and the Netherlands. The main towns are Marigot on the French side and Philipsburg on the Dutch side, and the highest hill is Pic Paradis, at 424 metres, in the French part. There are no rivers, only dry gullies, and dry forest covers the hilltops and slopes. The island's pre-colonial names include Oualichi, an Arawakan name meaning the island of women, and Soualiga, a Kalinago name meaning the island of salt.

It is commonly believed that Christopher Columbus named the island in honour of Saint Martin of Tours on his second voyage. In fact he applied the name to the island now called Nevis when he anchored offshore on 11 November 1493, the feast day of Saint Martin. Because the small islands of the Leeward group were poorly charted, the name was accidentally transferred to the island now called Saint-Martin or Sint Maarten.

After jointly reclaiming the island, the Kingdom of France and the Dutch Republic agreed on 23 March 1648 to divide it between them, and the Treaty of Concordia created a formal border. The treaty was signed on the hill on the border between Marigot and Philipsburg, known as Mount Concordia. Later conflicts brought 16 border changes over the years, but the border has been stable since 1816. The treaty is one of the oldest still in effect, and it allows freedom of movement between the two parts of the island. A Unity Flag, representing the people of both halves, was adopted on 31 August 1990 at a conference in Philipsburg.

The northern French part is the Collectivity of Saint Martin, an overseas collectivity of France, and the southern Dutch part is Sint Maarten, which since 2010 has been one of four constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Official languages are French in the French part, and Dutch and English in the Dutch part; an English-based creole is the main local vernacular. The island's population comes from more than 70 countries, and tourism is its main industry. Princess Juliana International Airport on the Dutch side is its main airport. Hurricane Irma struck on 6 September 2017 and caused widespread damage.
saint-meinhard: As a canon of Segeberg Abbey in Holstein, Meinhard was possibly inspired by the missionary work of Vicelinus among the Slavs. In the 1170s or early 1180s he travelled to Livonia with merchants from Lübeck, who were probably trading in costly furs, to convert the pagan Semigallians, Latgalians and Livonians. He settled on the Daugava River at Ikšķile, in German Üxküll, southeast of present-day Riga, and in 1184 built a stone church there dedicated to Our Lady.

After an attack by Lithuanian raiders looking to carry off slaves, Meinhard brought stonemasons from Gotland to build a fortress. These were the first known stone buildings among the Baltic tribes. A second stone castle at Salaspils, in German Holm, was a gift to newly converted pagans, but its people rebelled and tried to drive him out of Livonia. Meinhard first sought converts by peaceful means; faced with resistance and apostasy, he turned to the idea of a crusade.

On a brief return to Germany in 1186 he was consecrated by Hartwig of Uthlede, Archbishop of Bremen. Pope Clement III confirmed the new bishopric in September 1188 and in 1190 allowed any monk to join the mission. In April 1193 Pope Celestine III authorised active recruitment, relaxed the rules on monks' food and clothing and granted indulgences to those who joined. Among the recruits was Theodorich of Loccum Abbey, who began a mission at Turaida, in German Treyden.

Meinhard died in 1196, on either 14 August or 11 October, and his life is told in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry. His successors, Berthold of Hanover and Albert of Riga, began the Livonian Crusade and founded the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, a crusading military order, in Riga. His remains were moved to Riga in 1226 and rest in Riga Cathedral, now Lutheran.

On 8 September 1993 Pope John Paul II, visiting the Baltic states, proclaimed that the veneration of Saint Meinhard would be restored on 14 August each year, an act considered equivalent to canonisation. Remains of his church at Ikšķile survive. When the Riga Hydroelectric Power Plant was built in the 1970s, an artificial island was raised to keep the water from flooding the ruins, which were covered with metal in 2002.
saint-nicholas: Little is known about the historical Nicholas. The earliest accounts of his life were written centuries after his death and probably contain elaborations, and no contemporary chronicler mentions him. Tradition says he was born at the Anatolian seaport of Patara, in Lycia, to wealthy Greek Christian parents. Shortly after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land he is said to have become bishop of Myra, chosen because he was the first priest to enter the church one morning.

He is said to have been imprisoned in Diocletian's persecution and released on Constantine's orders, but this is not attested in the earliest sources and is unlikely to be historical. A list of attendees at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 includes him, yet neither Athanasius of Alexandria nor Eusebius, who were there, mentions him.

His best-known story, first attested in Michael the Archimandrite's Life of Saint Nicholas, tells of a once-wealthy man who could not afford dowries for his three daughters. Nicholas, too modest to help in public, threw bags of gold coins through the window of the house at night. His secret gift-giving gave rise to the folklore of Santa Claus through Sinterklaas. Other stories tell of him calming a storm at sea and saving three innocent soldiers from execution.

He is patron of sailors, merchants, children, students and many others. In Greek folklore he was the Lord of the Sea, and he is patron saint of Greece and the Hellenic Navy. The Eastern Orthodox Church commemorates his death on 6 December, and icons show him as an elderly bishop with a short white beard holding a Gospel Book.

Less than 200 years after his death the Emperor Theodosius II ordered a church built at Myra over the site where Nicholas had served, and his remains were moved to a sarcophagus there. In 1087, after the Battle of Manzikert had put Myra under Seljuk rule, sailors from Bari seized the main bones over the objections of the Greek Orthodox monks and took them to Bari, where they are enshrined in the Basilica di San Nicola. According to one chronicle, a Venetian fleet took the remaining fragments in 1100. Small bones soon spread across western Europe.

In the late 1950s, when the crypt in Bari was restored, the anatomist Luigi Martino examined the bones. He concluded that the man died at over seventy and had severe arthritis of the spine and pelvis. Two investigations found the relics in Bari and Venice anatomically compatible and possibly from one person.
saint-nino: The oldest surviving account of Nino is the Latin one by Rufinus in his Historia ecclesiastica, composed around 403, which rests on what a Georgian prince named Bacurius told him in Palestine. Later writers include Socrates of Constantinople, Sozomen and Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and the 10th-century Georgian Conversion of Kartli largely repeats them. Her ethnic background is not clearly known. According to tradition she was born in Cappadocia into a Greek-speaking Roman family, and her father was the commander Zabulon and her mother Susanna. Georgian church tradition also makes her a relative of Saint George.

At twelve she went with her parents to Jerusalem, where her parents entered religious life and she was entrusted to a devout woman, Sarah Miafore. According to tradition she later fled the persecution of Emperor Diocletian with a group of women who were martyred in Armenia, and only she escaped. In a vision the Virgin Mary gave her a grapevine cross.

Nino crossed the Javakheti mountains into the Kingdom of Kartli and stayed a month in Urbnisi among the Jewish community to learn local customs. She learned Georgian and began to preach, gaining followers such as Salome of Ujarma. Her missionary work was accompanied by miraculous healings, among them that of Queen Nana, who converted to Christianity. King Mirian III at first persecuted the new faith. According to legend he was struck blind while hunting and, praying to the God of Nino, found light and his way back to his palace at Mtskheta. He was baptised as the first Christian king of Iberia and, in about 326, made Christianity the state religion.

Mirian then petitioned the emperor Constantine I to send clergy for the baptism of the population. Under Nino's guidance crosses were erected in the mountains where idols had stood, and churches were built at Svetitskhoveli and Nekresi among other places.

In her final years Nino lived at Bodbe in Kakheti, where she died, and Mirian soon began a monastery there. Her tomb is still venerated at the Bodbe Monastery. She is one of the most venerated saints of the Georgian Orthodox Church, her main commemoration is on 14 January, and her grapevine cross is a symbol of Georgian Christianity. Nino and its variants remain the most popular name for girls and women in Georgia.
saint-odile: Odile, also called Odilia and Ottilia, was the daughter of Etichon, Duke of Alsace, founder of the Etichonid family, and of his wife Bethswinda. What is told of her life comes mostly from her medieval Life, which retells her legend and cannot be considered to have much historical value. According to it, her father did not want a blind daughter, and her mother sent her to Palma, perhaps Baume-les-Dames in Burgundy, where peasants raised her. At twelve she entered a nearby monastery, where the itinerant bishop Erhard of Regensburg, led by an angel it was said, baptised her and she recovered her sight.

In the legend her younger brother Hughes brought her home, and Etichon in his rage accidentally killed him; Odile revived him and left again, fleeing across the Rhine to a cave in the Musbach valley near Freiburg im Breisgau or at Arlesheim near Basel, according to different sources. When her father fell ill she returned to nurse him, and he gave up his resistance. She became abbess of Hohenburg in the Hochwald, where Etichon was later buried. After a vision of St. John the Baptist she founded a second monastery with a hospital at Niedermünster, at the foot of the mountain. She died there around 720 and was buried at Ste. Odile; her niece, Saint Eugenia of Alsace, succeeded her as abbess.

Her cult spread quickly into Germany, and she was named in the litanies of Freising, Utrecht and Ratisbon from at least the 9th century. Emperors from Charlemagne onwards made pilgrimages to her; Charlemagne granted the convent immunity, which Louis the Pious confirmed on 9 March 837. By the 14th century her relics had been divided among Corbie, Prague and Einsiedeln. Pope Pius VII made her patronage of Alsace and of eye patients official in 1807. She is often shown with a pair of eyes on a book, and her feast falls on 13 December, on 14 December in Alsace.
saint-othmar: Othmar, also called Audomar, was of Alemannic descent and was educated at the cathedral school of Chur in Rhaetia. After his ordination as a priest he presided for a time over a church of St. Florinus in Rhaetia, probably the church of St. Peter at Remus, where Florinus had laboured as a priest and was buried.

Waltram of Thurgau appointed Othmar superior over the cell of St. Gall and custodian of the relics of Gall. Othmar united the monks living around the cell into a monastery under the Rule of St. Columban and became their first abbot. He added a hospital and a school, which became the foundation on which the monastery library, the Stiftsbibliothek, was built. In 747, as part of a reform of church institutions in Alamannia, he introduced the Benedictine Rule, which remained in force until the monastery was secularised and closed in 1805.

Othmar also provided for the surrounding community, building an almshouse and the first leprosarium in what is now Switzerland. When Carloman renounced his throne in 747, he visited Othmar at St. Gall and gave him a letter to his brother Pepin recommending Othmar and his monastery to the king's generosity. Othmar carried the letter to Pepin himself and was kindly received.

In 759 Counts Warin and Ruodhart tried to take possession of property belonging to St. Gall, and Othmar resisted their demands. They seized him on a journey to Constance and held him prisoner, first at the castle of Bodmann and then on the island of Werd in the Rhine, where he died after six months of imprisonment and was buried. In 769 his body was taken to St. Gall. Legend says that on the hot crossing of the lake the rowers' only barrel of wine never ran dry, and the barrel became his attribute in art.

His cult spread soon after his death and was officially recognised in 864 by Solomon I, Bishop of Constance; in 867 he was entombed in the new church of St. Othmar at St. Gall. His feast is kept on 16 November. Next to Maurice and Gall he is one of the most popular saints in Switzerland. St. Gallen Cathedral is dedicated to Gall and Othmar, and a chapel in his memory was built on Werd in the 10th century.
saint-padarn: The main source for Padarn is the Vita Sancti Paterni, perhaps an epitome of a longer work. It makes him Armorican by race, the son of Petran and Guean, who dedicated themselves to Christ before Petran left Letavia, modern Brittany, for Ireland. Canon G. H. Doble held that this Breton origin can no longer be maintained and favoured a Welsh one, while Bowen thought Padarn was later confused with Breton saints of the same name. Around 524, the Life says, he went to join his father in Ireland and travelled to Britain with his cousin Saint Cadvan.

Padarn studied at Cor Tewdws, the school of Illtud, and then founded the monastery of Llanbadarn Fawr, which became the seat of a new diocese with him as its first bishop. In the Life, Maelgwn Gwynedd tries to cheat the monastery of its property, is struck blind and sick, and is cured only when he begs forgiveness and grants the community land from the mouth of the river Rheidiol to the Clarach. Padarn also travels to Jerusalem with Saint David and Saint Teilo to be ordained bishop by the patriarch, and returns with a crozier and a finely woven tunic.

Finally he goes back to Letavia, builds a monastery at Vannes and joins the six bishops of Armorica as the seventh, which is why he is counted among the seven founding saints of Brittany. He appears to be the same person as the first bishop of Braga and as Saint Paternus of Avranches in Normandy.
