According to tradition its founder was Teucer, son of Telamon, king of the Greek island of Salamis, who could not return home after the Trojan War because he had failed to avenge his brother Ajax. There is little direct evidence for this myth, and some evidence that the area was occupied long before, with the town developing as a replacement when Enkomi was cut off from the sea.

Children's burials in Canaanite jars indicate a Phoenician presence, and Assyrian inscriptions name the town among the kingdoms of Iadnana, as Cyprus was called. In 708 BCE the city-kings of Cyprus paid homage to Sargon II of Assyria, but they kept relative independence as long as they paid tribute, which let them gather wealth and power. The royal tombs of Salamis hold chariots and rich grave goods, much of it from the Levant or Egypt, and burial customs such as the sacrifice of horses echo Homeric rites. The first coins were minted in the 6th century BCE.

In 450 BCE Salamis was the site of a simultaneous land and sea battle between the Delian League and the Persian Empire. It was later besieged and conquered by Artaxerxes III. Under King Evagoras I (411–374 BCE) Greek culture and art flourished. In 306 BCE Demetrius I of Macedon defeated the fleet of Ptolemy I of Egypt off Salamis and captured the island. Rome annexed Cyprus in 58 BCE, and the governor's seat moved to Nea Paphos, though Salamis kept its wealth and the Emperors Trajan and Hadrian restored its public buildings.

Paul the Apostle and Barnabas landed at Salamis on their first journey, and tradition holds that Barnabas was stoned to death there around 61 CE. Earthquakes destroyed the town early in the 4th century. Constantius II rebuilt it as Constantia, and it became an episcopal seat, its best-known occupant being Saint Epiphanius. The silting of the harbour led to a gradual decline, and the city was finally abandoned during the Arab invasions of the 7th century.

The ruins are very extensive, with a gymnasium, theatre, amphitheatre, stadium and public baths; the theatre could seat up to 15,000. The necropolis covers around 7 km2 to the west of the town. Excavations began in the late nineteenth century under the Cyprus Exploration Fund, and finds from them are in the British Museum in London.
salamis-island: Salamis lies about two kilometres from the coast of Piraeus, Athens' port, and about 16 km west of the centre of Athens. It has an area of 93 square kilometres, and a significant part of it is rocky and mountainous; the highest point is Mavrovouni at 404 metres. The chief city, Salamina, stands on Salamis Bay, and the main port, Paloukia, on the eastern side connects the island with Perama by ferry.

The traditional etymology derives the name from the nymph Salamis, mother of Cychreus, the first king of the island in tradition. A more modern theory connects it with a root meaning salt and a suffix meaning middle, so that Salamis would be the place amid salt water. From at least the 13th century until the 19th the island was called Koulouri, after its round shape, and the ancient name was then revived.

Salamis was probably first colonised by Aegina and later occupied by Megara, and it became an Athenian possession after a war between Athens and Megara. According to Homer's Iliad it sent twelve ships to the Trojan War under Ajax, who is said to have been born on the island, as was the playwright Euripides, whose birth is popularly placed on the day of the battle. In 480 BCE the allied Greek fleet led by Athens and by Themistocles won its decisive naval victory over the Persian Empire off the island. In the north of the Kynosoura peninsula lie the remains of an ancient tumulus thought to be the burial site of Greek warriors of that battle.

The ancient capital lay in the south according to Strabo, in classical times on the Kamatero Peninsula overlooking the strait, and in modern times lies in the west. The oldest known counting board, of marble and about 150 by 75 centimetres, was found on the island in 1899 and is thought to have been used by Babylonians about 300 BCE. Arvanites were recorded among the inhabitants in 1688. On 23 April 1941, during the German invasion of Greece, the Luftwaffe bombed the harbour and sank the Greek battleships Kilkis and Lemnos.

Since the local government reform of 2011 the island has been administered as one municipality in the Islands regional unit of Attica. About 31,000 people live there permanently, many working in fishing, ferries and shipyards or commuting to Athens, and the number rises sharply in the holiday season. Salamis Naval Base, a major base of the Hellenic Navy, stands beside Paloukia. A festival called Salaminia commemorates the naval battle each year, and the island has a Museum of Folklore Art and History.
salamiyah: Salamiyah lies in a fertile plain on the edge of the Syrian steppe, 33 kilometres south-east of Hama and 45 kilometres north-east of Homs, at an average elevation of about 460 metres. It is administratively part of the Hama Governorate. In the Byzantine period it was a flourishing town called Salaminias or Salamias, linked by roads to Emesa (Homs), Chalcis and Resafa. Its bishop Julian attended the consecration of Patriarch Severus of Antioch in 512, and one dated inscription records the building of a church of the Theotokos in 604.

Muslim Arabs conquered Salamiyah in 636. Not long after the Abbasids came to power in 750, the dynast Salih ibn Ali and his descendants settled it, and his son Abdallah built its irrigation networks. In the early 9th century the great-grandson of Ja'far al-Sadiq, also named Abdallah, settled there concealing his identity as a merchant, and his palace became the seat of the Ismaili da'wa.

Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah was born in Salamiyah in 873 or 874, and his reforms led to a break with Hamdan Qarmat. The Qarmatians razed the town in 903 and massacred its inhabitants; al-Mahdi had left the year before and went on to found the Fatimid Caliphate.

Salamiyah then declined. It was captured by a Fatimid general in 1009, passed in 1092 to Tutush, brother of the Seljuk sultan Malikshah, and to Saladin in 1174–1175, and was incorporated into the Mamluk empire after 1263. The Mamluk army was defeated by the Mongols under Ghazan there in 1299.

Under early Ottoman rule, from 1517, it was a large ruin held by Bedouin emirs, and in the 1830s it was still uninhabited. In July 1849 Isma'il ibn Muhammad, the Ismaili emir of Qadmus, obtained a firman from Sultan Abdülmecid I to settle the site with his followers, who called it Mecidabad. Many Ismailis followed from the Jabal Ansariya, and by the end of the 19th century about 6,000 people lived there.

Salamiyah had 66,724 inhabitants at the 2004 census, and a little more than half of its residents are Ismaili. It is the largest population centre of Ismailis in the Arab world and holds the headquarters of the Ismaili Higher Council of Syria. The mausoleum of the Ismaili imam Abdallah, rebuilt in 1088 according to an inscription, still stands, and the poet Muhammad al-Maghut was born there in 1934. The city is an agricultural centre.
salammbo: After the legal troubles that followed Madame Bovary, for which he was tried and acquitted on a charge of immorality, Flaubert looked for a less controversial subject. His principal source was Book I of the Histories of the Greek historian Polybius. In 1857 he wrote to the archaeologist Félicien de Saulcy about his plans, and from 12 April to 5 June 1858 he travelled in Tunisia to see the places of the novel, though little survived from ancient times. He changed the name of the Carthaginian general Hannibal, whom the mercenaries executed, to Hanno, so as not to confuse him with the Hannibal of the Second Punic War.

After the First Punic War, Carthage cannot pay its army of mercenaries and comes under attack. The fictional title character, a priestess of the goddess Tanit and the daughter of the general Hamilcar Barca, is the object of the obsessive desire of Matho, a Libyan leader of the mercenaries. With the help of the freed slave Spendius, Matho steals the Zaïmph, the sacred veil of Carthage, which kills anyone who touches it. Salammbô goes into the mercenaries' camp to retrieve it, and Matho and she make love in his tent.

Hamilcar then defeats the mercenaries, many of whom starve in a defile. The novel's fifteen chapters include the sacrifice of Carthaginian children to Moloch, and it ends with Matho's torture and execution, at the sight of which Salammbô dies.

The novel was a bestseller on publication in 1862, though its violence and sensuality bore little resemblance to Madame Bovary. Readers praised its style and story, its descriptions of Carthaginian dress influenced fashion, and its picture of Roman North Africa stirred interest in archaeological exploration there. Eleanor Marx made the first English translation in 1886. The book renewed interest in the conflict between Rome and Carthage and inspired operas by Ernest Reyer in 1890 and Josef Matthias Hauer in 1929, as well as silent films, among them Pierre Marodon's of 1925.
salar-jung-i: Mir Turab Ali Khan was born in Bijapur on 21 January 1829 into a family that had held office under the Adil Shahi dynasty of Bijapur, then under the Mughal Empire and finally under the Nizams. His father was Muhammad Ali Khan, eldest son of Mir Alam, and he was educated privately. In 1847 he served for eight months as talukdar of Medak, and in 1853 he succeeded his uncle Siraj-ul-Mulk as prime minister.

He took over a government with no separate departments, in which everything lay in the minister's hands. He set up courts of justice in Hyderabad, organised a police force, repaired irrigation works and founded schools, among them Dar-ul-Ulum in 1854. In 1867 the state was divided into five divisions, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur, Aurangabad and Hyderabad, and seventeen districts. He also set up a central mint, abolished the district mints and made the Hali Sikka rupee the standard currency.

During the rebellion of 1857 he warned the British of a planned attack on the Residency, which was repulsed, and used the government's preoccupation with the rising to push his reforms further. In 1868 he survived an attempt on his life on the day of Eid ul-Fitr. When Asaf Jah V died on 26 February 1869, he shared the regency for the two-year-old Mir Mahbub Ali Khan with Shams-ul-Umara, and became sole regent on the latter's death in 1881.

He was made G.C.S.I. on 28 May 1870, and in 1876 he visited England in an unsuccessful attempt to recover Berar, receiving an honorary D.C.L. from the University of Oxford on 21 June 1876. On his travels he bought the double sculpture Mephistopheles and Margaretta in France and the marble Veiled Rebecca in Rome; the collections of Salar Jung I, II and III later went to the Salar Jung Museum.

He died of cholera at Hyderabad on 8 February 1883 and was buried at the Daira Mir Momin, and three days of mourning were declared across the state. His son Salar Jung II succeeded him as prime minister. Through his daughter Amat-uz-Zehra, who married Asaf Jah VI, he was the maternal grandfather of the last Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan.
salar-jung-museum: The museum began as the private art collection of the Salar Jung family of Hyderabad. Nawab Mir Yousuf Ali Khan, Salar Jung III (1889–1949), served as Prime Minister of Hyderabad under the Nizam and spent a substantial part of his income over thirty-five years collecting artefacts from across the world. The collections of Salar Jung I and II also ended up in the museum. Salar Jung I bought the double sculpture Mephistopheles and Margaretta on a trip to France in 1876 and a marble statue, Veiled Rebecca, in Rome.

After the Nawab died in 1949 the collection remained in his ancestral palace, Diwan Devdi, where it was shown as a private museum and inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru on 16 December 1951. The state then decided to move it to a new building designed by Mohammed Fayazuddin, chosen after a design competition. Nehru laid the foundation stone in 1963, and in 1968 the museum moved to its present site at Dar-ul-Shifa on the southern bank of the Musi River. It is run by a board of trustees under the Salar Jung Museum Act of 1961. Some pieces were lost or stolen during the move.

Salar Jung III collected about 43,000 artefacts and 50,000 books and manuscripts, of which only a part is displayed. The collection includes sculpture, paintings, carvings, textiles, manuscripts, ceramics, metalwork, carpets, clocks and furniture from Japan, China, Burma, Nepal, India, Persia, Egypt, Europe and North America. It is organised into Indian, Middle Eastern, Far Eastern and European art, a children's section and a gallery devoted to the Salar Jung family.

The Indian holdings include miniature paintings of the Mughal, Rajasthani, Thanjavur, Malwa and Deccan schools, an ivory chair given to Tipu Sultan by Louis XVI, and jade daggers associated with Jahangir, Nur Jahan and Shah Jahan. Its jade collection numbered 984 objects according to a publication of 1979. European works include pieces by Canaletto, William-Adolphe Bouguereau and Francesco Hayez. There are also many clocks, about 600 coins, and a Quran collection that includes copies written in gold and silver.

The Indian Parliament has declared the museum an Institution of National Importance, and it is counted among the National Museums of India. The building is semicircular, with 38 galleries on two floors, and shows only part of the original collection. In 2003 the museum signed a memorandum of understanding with the National Mission for Manuscripts and became a manuscript conservation centre. A fire in an auditorium in 2006 was quickly put out and no artefact was damaged; fire safety was upgraded afterwards. Plans exist for a new Islamic Gallery for manuscripts of the Qur'an and other Islamic works.
sale: Salé lies in northwestern Morocco on the right bank of the Bou Regreg river, opposite the national capital Rabat, which it serves as a commuter town. Rabat and Salé together form a single metropolitan area. The Phoenicians established a settlement called Sala on the south side of the estuary, later the site of a Roman colony, Sala Colonia. The town of Salé proper was probably founded in the 11th century by families from al-Andalus, most importantly the Banu 'Ashara, who included learned jurists and judges and became the city's de facto rulers.

The Banu 'Ashara reportedly hosted Ibn Tumart, the founder of the Almohad movement, in 1121. They resisted his successor 'Abd al-Mu'min, who destroyed the city walls, eliminated the family and seized their palace. In the 12th century the Almohad caliph Yaqub al-Mansur founded Ribat al-Fath, present-day Rabat, across the river, and Salé remained important as a residence of the Almohad caliphs.

He ordered the Great Mosque built in 1196. In September 1260 warriors sent by Alfonso X of Castile raided and occupied Salé, and the Marinid sultan Abu Yusuf Yaqub reconquered it and helped rebuild the walls, including the gate of Bab el-Mrisa. The Marinids also built a protected harbour and the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan.

In the 17th century Salé became a haven for Barbary pirates, among them Moriscos expelled from Spain after Philip III's decree of 1609. About 2,000 refugees from Hornachos settled around Salé and occupied the kasbah, and thousands more joined them. Rabat and Salé united to form the Republic of Bou Regreg in 1627.

The corsairs captured ships and sold their crews and sometimes passengers into slavery, although their ships were based across the river in Rabat. Spain bombarded Salé in May 1628, and the French admiral Isaac de Razilly did so on 20 July 1629, destroying three corsair ships. Salé was later incorporated into Alawi Morocco.

Salé's historic medina occupies a large area near the mouth of the Bou Regreg and is enclosed by walls, of which Bab el-Mrisa, dating to the 1270s, is the most notable gate. The Great Mosque is the religious centre, beside the Madrasa of Abu al-Hasan, dating to 1342. The Sufi Ibn 'Ashir, who moved to Salé in the 14th century, became the city's patron saint, and his mausoleum dominates the seaside cemetery. Salé was a stronghold of the Moroccan national movement before independence, and many of its activists signed the Manifesto of Independence of Morocco on 11 January 1944.
salem-baden-wurttemberg: Salem lies in the Linzgau, about 9 km north of Lake Constance, mainly in the valley of the Linzer Aach. It is about nine kilometres east of Überlingen and ten kilometres north-east of Meersburg, and has a population of 11,100. The municipality consists of eleven member locations, of which Salem Stefansfeld is the chief town, and covers about 6,270 hectares. The district of Oberstenweiler lies on a side peak of the Gehrenberg, rising to about 600 metres.

The area has been settled since at least the Bronze Age. From the 3rd century the Alemanni and later the Franks established several villages, among them the small settlement of Salemanneswilare, later Salmannsweiler. Salem Abbey was founded here in 1134, when the knight Guntram von Adelsreute donated land to the Cistercians, and it quickly attained the rank of an imperial abbey. It had its own scriptorium in the 12th century and held one of the most important monastery libraries in Europe.

The High Gothic minster was built from about 1285 to 1425. In the 17th century the monastery suffered serious setbacks, including the Thirty Years' War. In 1697 a fire destroyed most of the buildings and many art treasures, and the Baroque buildings now on the site were then raised under the master builder Franz Beer of Vorarlberg. In 1749 Abbot Anselm II Schwab founded an Orphans' Fund, considered the first savings bank in Germany, and he also had the pilgrimage church of Birnau built on the shore of Lake Constance. The abbey's heyday ended with the German mediatization of 1803, when it was secularized and its territory fell to the Margraviate of Baden.

The abbey complex covers 17 hectares. Its grounds house the middle school campus of Schule Schloss Salem, a boarding school founded in 1920 by Kurt Hahn and Prince Max of Baden. The Gothic minster, the former abbey church, and a Baroque chapel remain among the main sights. The Rococo plasterer and sculptor Joseph Anton Feuchtmayer (1696–1770) is among the notable people associated with the town, as is Johann Baptist von Keller (1774–1845), Bishop of Rottenburg.
salem-massachusetts: Salem lies on Massachusetts Bay, between Salem Harbor, which divides it from Marblehead, and Beverly Harbor. Between the two harbors lie Salem Neck and Winter Island. The city has a total area of 18.1 square miles, of which 8.1 square miles is land and the rest water. The peninsula was known as Naumkeag to the Native people who lived there in the early 1600s, the Naumkeag people, whose settlement controlled territory from the Merrimack to the Mystic rivers.

Colonists settled in Naumkeag in 1626, when a company of fishermen from Cape Ann arrived under Roger Conant. The Massachusetts Bay Company replaced him with John Endecott, and Conant received 200 acres in compensation. To mark this peaceful change of government the settlement was renamed Salem, a form of Shalem, the royal city of Melchizedek, which is identified with Jerusalem. Early musters of militia on Salem Common laid a foundation for what became the Army National Guard. On 26 February 1775 patriots raised the drawbridge at the North River and stopped Colonel Alexander Leslie and 300 troops of the 64th Regiment of Foot from seizing stores hidden in North Salem; an agreement ended the standoff without bloodshed.

The Salem witch trials began in 1692 after girls including Abigail Williams and Betty Parris played with an egg and a glass to learn their future husbands' trades. Nineteen people were hanged, and Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to plead. After the American Revolution, Salem's owners of large privateers turned to distant trade. In 1795 Captain Jonathan Carnes brought home a bulk cargo of pepper from Sumatra, the first imported into the country, sold at a profit of seven hundred per cent. Elias Hasket Derby owned the Grand Turk, the first New England vessel to trade with China.

Salem is a residential and tourist city of 44,480 people at the 2020 census. It was one of two county seats of Essex County until county governments in Massachusetts were dissolved in 1999. The Salem Maritime National Historic Site, the House of the Seven Gables (1668), the Peabody Essex Museum and the Chestnut Street District preserve its maritime and colonial past. The site of the 1692 executions was identified in 2016 as Proctor's Ledge, now a memorial. Salem State University, founded in 1854 as the Salem Normal School, is in the city.
salem-new-jersey: Salem is the county seat of Salem County, the most rural county in New Jersey, and lies along the Salem River. It is part of the Philadelphia metropolitan area. The name of both city and county is derived from the Hebrew word shalom, meaning peace. The Port of Salem was designated by the British Crown in 1682 as a port of entry on the Salem River, reached from the Delaware River.

The town and colony were laid out in 1675 by John Fenwick, a Quaker. Fenwick had a financial dispute with another Quaker, Edward Byllynge, who had bought a share of New Jersey from Lord John Berkeley, then went bankrupt and had the property transferred to Fenwick to hold in trust. William Penn was asked to adjudicate and awarded 90 per cent of the claim to Byllynge and 10 per cent to Fenwick, but Fenwick refused the decision. He sailed to Delaware Bay with settlers and governed the Fifth Tenth near the abandoned Swedish settlement of Fort Nya Elfsborg, issuing land patents in defiance of Byllynge and Penn. The court of Dominion Governor Andros upheld his claim, and he governed the Salem tenth by 1689.

In October 1693 the community was given permission to choose its own officers. On 18 March 1778, during the American Revolutionary War, British forces under Lieutenant-Colonel Charles Mawhood raided Salem and defeated American militia at a nearby bridge. Three days later Major John Graves Simcoe led a surprise attack on Hancock House, where between 20 and 30 militiamen were killed, some reportedly while trying to surrender; the Loyalist judge William Hancock Jr. was fatally injured. After the war, treason trials were held at the county courthouse, and four men sentenced to death were pardoned by Governor William Livingston and exiled. Salem was incorporated as a township on 21 February 1798 and reincorporated as Salem City on 25 February 1858.

The Old Salem County Courthouse, built in 1735 of locally made bricks, is the oldest courthouse in New Jersey still in active use and the second-oldest in continuous use in the United States. A legend holds that Colonel Robert Gibbon Johnson proved the tomato safe to eat on its steps in 1820; it did not appear in print until 1948, and modern scholars question it. At the 2020 census the city had 5,296 inhabitants.
salem-witch-trials: Witch trials were fading across much of Europe by the middle of the seventeenth century but continued on its fringes and in the American colonies. Witchcraft had been a capital offence in the Massachusetts Body of Liberties since 1641, although the provision was repealed in 1684. The Puritans who settled New England would have been familiar with witch trials in England. The 1629 royal charter of the Massachusetts Bay Colony was vacated in 1684, and the colony passed through constitutional turmoil. Salem Village, now Danvers, was known for a fractious population that quarrelled over property lines, grazing rights and church privileges.

In February 1692 Betty Parris, aged nine, and her cousin Abigail Williams, aged eleven, the daughter and niece of the Reverend Samuel Parris, began to have fits. Local women were accused of causing the girls harm by witchcraft, and when Sarah Cloyce and Elizabeth Proctor were arrested in April they were examined by the magistrates John Hathorne and Jonathan Corwin. A Court of Oyer and Terminer convened in Salem Town on 2 June 1692 under William Stoughton, and Bridget Bishop was the first case brought to the grand jury.

Much of the evidence was spectral evidence, the testimony of the afflicted that they saw the apparition of the accused. The court held that the Devil could not use a person's shape without that person's permission, so such testimony was taken as proof of complicity. On 19 September 1692 Giles Corey refused to plead and was killed by peine forte et dure, a form of torture in which the subject is pressed beneath stones. A new Superior Court of Judicature convened in January 1693 and did not allow spectral evidence; of the cases it heard, three people were found guilty, one of them Elizabeth Johnson Jr.

In 1702 the General Court of Massachusetts declared the trials unlawful, and in 1711 the colonial legislature annulled the convictions. Several accusers, mostly teenage girls, later admitted that they had fabricated their charges. The historian George Lincoln Burr wrote that the Salem witchcraft was the rock on which the New England theocracy shattered.

Acts of 1957 and 2001 absolved victims. The executions took place at Proctor's Ledge, at the foot of Gallows Hill. Researchers have proposed medical explanations for the fits, among them convulsive ergotism from infected rye, while some historians prefer motives such as jealousy and a need for attention.
salento: Salento is a cultural, historical and geographic region at the southern end of Apulia, a sub-peninsula of the Italian Peninsula. It encompasses the entire Province of Lecce, most of the Province of Brindisi and the south-eastern part of the Province of Taranto, though not Taranto itself. The peninsula is composed of limestone and divides the Gulf of Taranto in the west from the Strait of Otranto in the east, with the Adriatic Sea to the north and the Ionian Sea to the south. A depression called the Messapic threshold, running along the Taranto-Ostuni line, separates it from the Murge. The climate is Mediterranean, suited to olives, citrus fruits and palm trees.

In ancient times the peninsula was called Sallentina or Messapia, and the Iapygians are said to have migrated to it from the Illyrian coast in the eleventh century BCE. The Romans took control in 272 BCE. Under Roman rule it was known as Calabria and had a flourishing agricultural economy of wheat and olive oil. The name Calabria later moved to the region now called by it: from 580 the Calabrian province was gradually expanded westward, and by the 10th century the term had shifted.

Justinian I's reconquest of Italy, the Gothic War of 535 to 554, brought Byzantine rule, which strengthened Greek influence, shown in the use of the Greek language and the Byzantine rite. The Lombards tried to conquer the region from 569 and were pushed back.

The Saracens occupied Taranto and other places in 847 and destroyed Ugento in 870, deporting its inhabitants to Africa. The Normans arrived in southern Italy in 1016, and Robert Guiscard governed Apulia from 1059, beginning a period of prosperity. In 1480 the Ottomans under Gedik Ahmed Pasha besieged and sacked Otranto; they killed hundreds of men who refused to convert to Islam, and neighbouring towns were fortified. The Venetians briefly controlled Salento between 1482 and 1484, and in 1534 Charles V restored several castles, among them that of Lecce. The coastal towers, mostly of the 15th and 16th centuries, were watchtowers against maritime attack by the Saracens.

The Salentino dialect of Extreme Southern Italian is predominantly spoken, although an old Hellenic dialect, Griko, is also spoken in a few inland towns. Typical dishes include orecchiette, parmigiana di melanzane, pitta di patate and fried honey cookies called purciaddruzzi. The nearest international airports are those of Brindisi and Bari, and the main railway line ends at Lecce. Its sagre, communal food festivals, show off local cooking traditions.
salghurids: The dynasty was of Salur Turkoman origin. Its founder, Sunqur ibn Mawdud, profited from the rebellions of the reign of the Seljuq sultan Mas'ud ibn Muhammad to establish himself in Fars, and during his reign a cathedral mosque was built in Shiraz. His successors strengthened their position in southern Persia, campaigning against the Kurds and intervening in the succession of the Kirman Seljuqs, where they held Mahmud, son of Sultan Malik-Shah III, as a possible claimant to the Seljuq throne.

Sunqur was followed by his brother Zangi ibn Mawdud in 1161, and Zangi by his son Tekele, who first had to eliminate Sunqur's son Toghril. The Salghurids briefly occupied Isfahan in 1203–4. Under Sa'd I ibn Zangi Fars enjoyed considerable prosperity, though he acknowledged the Khwarazm Shahs as his overlords. In 1235 the dynasty took Bahrain from the Uyunid dynasty.

In the last years of Abu Bakr ibn Sa'd and his son Sa'd II, Fars came under the Mongol Empire and then the Ilkhanate of Hulegu, and the Mongols gave Abu Bakr the title of Qutlugh Khan. The later atabegs were powerless figureheads until Sa'd II's daughter Abish Khatun received the atabegate of Fars. She ruled alone for one year and then married Mengu Temur, eleventh son of Hulegu; after their deaths Fars was ruled directly by the Ilkhanate.

In the 13th century the Salghurid court supported a circle of scholars and writers that included Qadi Baydawi, Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi, the poet Saadi Shirazi and the historian Wassaf. The dynasty deliberately presented itself as both Iranian and Islamic, in part through its links with the ruins of the pre-Islamic Achaemenid Empire, and under its rule Shiraz became a centre of Persian culture.
salian-franks: The Salians are named in the sources only in connection with the campaign of Julian, then Caesar in Gaul under his cousin the emperor Constantius II, around 358 CE. Ammianus Marcellinus calls them Franks whom custom calls the Salii. Zosimus, writing around 500 CE, says they had been driven out by the Saxons and settled on the island of Batavia in the Rhine delta. Some modern scholars think they descended from Frankish groups that the Romans allowed to remain there around 293 to 294 and in Texandria in 342. The origin of the name is uncertain; proposals include a Germanic word related to German Geselle, meaning companion, and a word for island dwellers.

Julian's campaign was partly prompted by the Roman need to bring grain from Britain safely up the Rhine. The praetorian prefect Florentius had promised the peoples of the delta two thousand pounds of silver for passage, and Julian refused to pay it and marched against the Salians and the Chamavi. In the winter of 357 to 358 a Salian deputation came to Tongeren. Ammianus writes that Julian sent his general Severus along the Maas to attack them suddenly, after which the Salians surrendered. Julian let them keep the land they had settled and took them into Roman service. The Notitia Dignitatum lists units such as the Salii seniores in Gaul.

In the first half of the fifth century Franks under a king named Chlodio took Tournai and Cambrai, probably in the period 445 to 450. Chlodio is called only Frankish in the sources. Childeric I and his son Clovis I, who gained control of Roman Gaul, were said to be related to him. Clovis made Paris his capital and was baptised in 496, beginning the alliance of the Franks with the Catholic Church.

Until the 1950s it was assumed that the Salians expanded south under that name and formed one of two great divisions of the Franks, the other being the Ribuarian Franks. This rests on the names of two law codes, the Salic law and the Lex Ripuaria of about 630. Scholars now doubt that the term Salic referred to a specific tribe by the fifth century. The Salic law applied between the Loire and the Silva Carbonaria and was the earliest known code of the Merovingian kingdom. The Salian language is presumed ancestral to the Low Franconian dialects, which include Dutch dialects and Afrikaans.
salic-law: The original edition was commissioned by Clovis I, the first king of all the Franks, and published sometime between 507 and 511. He appointed four commissioners to research customary law that had until then been kept only in the minds of designated elders, who met in council when their knowledge was needed. The code therefore reflects ancient usages, and a written text let monarchs and their administrations govern more effectively. It is written in Late Latin and contains some of the earliest known instances of Old Dutch.

For about 300 years the code was copied by hand and amended, and each of the several dozen surviving manuscripts has its own errors, corrections and organisation. The edition called the Lex Salica Emendata dates from about 798, late in the reign of Charlemagne. It added laws taken from the codes of the Ripuarian Franks, the Alamanni and the Suebi, so that all the Franks of Francia lived under one code.

The criminal law set damages and fines for injuries to persons, damage to goods, theft and unprovoked insults, and one third of each fine paid the court costs. A person who belonged to no family was legally unprotected, and land was divided equally among all living male heirs rather than passing by primogeniture. Another title required the unanimous consent of a village for any newcomer to settle there, and a migrant's tenure became secure only if no one objected within twelve months.

On inheritance the code said that of Salic land no portion would come to a woman, but all would come to the male sex. This applied only to ancestral Salic land, not to other property, and about 570, under Chilperic I, the law was amended to allow a daughter to inherit land if a man had no surviving sons.

In France, when Louis X died in 1316 without a son, his brother became Philip V, and the Estates-General of 1317 declared that women do not succeed in the kingdom of France; the Salic law was not yet invoked. In 1328 the claim of Edward III of England through his mother Isabella of France was rejected with the argument that women cannot transmit a right they do not possess. The monk Richard Lescot invoked the Salic law in 1358 against Charles II of Navarre, and jurists later echoed him in defence of the Valois dynasty.

The principle of agnatic succession spread beyond France. The Carlist Wars in Spain arose over whether the heir should be female or male, and the thrones of Britain and Hanover separated in 1837 and those of the Netherlands and Luxembourg in 1890. Shakespeare uses the Salic law as a plot device in Henry V.
salih-ibn-mirdas: The year of Salih's birth is not known. Both his parents came from princely households of the Banu Kilab: his father, Mirdas ibn Idris, from the Rabi'a ibn Ka'b line, and his mother, Rabab al-Zawqaliyya, from the Zawqal clan of the country around Aleppo. The family controlled Qinnasrin, south-west of Aleppo, and like most Aleppine Muslims of the time the Kilab followed Twelver Shia Islam. He first appears in 1008, when he backed Ibn Mihkan's seizure of al-Rahba on the Euphrates and later took the town himself.

In 1012 Mansur ibn Lu'lu', emir of Aleppo, lured Kilabi chiefs to a feast and imprisoned them; many died in his dungeons, and Salih was tortured and forced to divorce his wife Tarud. He escaped in 1014, defeated Mansur outside Aleppo and freed him for a ransom of 50,000 gold dinars and half the emirate's revenues, becoming supreme emir of the Kilab. He went on to take Manbij and Balis and, by 1022, Raqqa and al-Rafiqah.

In 1023 he joined the Banu Tayy and the Banu Kalb in a pact to divide Syria among three Bedouin states, with the Kilab holding Aleppo and the north. Late in 1024 he besieged Aleppo; after more than fifty days of fighting a gate was opened to him by Salim ibn al-Mustafad, while the citadel held out for months more. He also took Baalbek, Homs, Rafaniyya, Sidon and Hisn Ibn Akkar, giving his emirate an outlet to the sea.

Salih paid formal allegiance to the Fatimid caliph az-Zahir, who recognised his emirate. He entrusted finance to a Christian vizier, Tadhrus ibn al-Hasan, justice to a Shia qadi and policing to the urban militia under Ibn Mustafad, and granted fiefs to other Kilabi emirs. He appeared in the dress of a Bedouin chief and preferred his tribal camp outside the city.

When the Fatimid general Anushtakin al-Dizbari moved against the Tayy, Salih went to their aid. At al-Uqhuwana, on the eastern shore of Lake Tiberias, the Tayy fled during the battle, and Salih, his youngest son and his vizier were killed. His head was displayed in Cairo and his body nailed to the gate of Sidon. His sons Nasr and Thimal held Aleppo, and with interruptions his descendants ruled it until 1080.
salih-ibn-tarif: Salih ibn Tarif is remembered as the second king of the Berghouata, the prophet of a new Abrahamic religion and the eponymous ancestor of the Oulad Salah tribe of Morocco. The eleventh-century Andalusian scholar Al-Bakri reports that he was a Judean (Yahūd) who claimed descent from Simeon, son of Jacob, son of Isaac. According to some sources he regarded himself as a successor to Muhammad, had ten disciples (Ṣahāba) and many wives, and claimed to be able to speak with the dead and heal the sick.

He is said to have claimed to be the final Mahdi, with Isa (Jesus) as his companion who would pray behind him. He proclaimed that his name was Ṣāliḥ in Arabic, Mālik in Syriac, Rūbyā in Hebrew and Werba in Berber, and that no prophet would come after him.

Arabic writers such as Ibn Hazm and Ibn Khaldun describe tenets that set his religion apart from Islam: capital punishment for theft, no limit on the number of wives, fasting in the month of Rajab instead of Ramadan, ten obligatory daily prayers instead of five, different ways of performing ablution and prayer, and a ban on marriage between cousins.

At the age of 47 he left the kingdom for the east, promising to return in the reign of its seventh king. He told his son Ilyās to support the Umayyads of al-Andalus and to profess Islam in public, revealing his own religion only once he was strong enough; it was his grandson Yūnus who did so.

Islamic literature treats his belief as heretical. Its political motive was presumably to secure the Berghouata's independence from the Umayyads, in a manner compared with Kharijism and the earlier Donatism, by giving the state an ideology of its own. Some modern Berber activists regard him as a Berber hero for resisting the Umayyad-Arab conquest and founding the Berghouata state.
salim-rubaya-ali: Salim Rubaya Ali, commonly known by the nickname Salemin, led the left-wing faction of the National Front for the Liberation of South Yemen (NLF). The NLF forced the British to withdraw from southern Yemen on 29 November 1967, and its radical Marxist wing then gained the upper hand over the more moderate elements of President Qahtan al-Shaabi. This allowed Rubaya Ali to take power on 22 June 1969 as the second head of state of South Yemen.

He kept the title of Chairman of the Presidential Council throughout his time in power, even after the NLF renamed the country from the People's Republic of South Yemen to the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970. His first prime minister, Muhammad Ali Haitham, served until August 1971, when Ali Nasir Muhammad replaced him. All rival parties had been outlawed, and in 1975 the National Front joined with other groups to form the United Political Organisation NF. Rubaya Ali opposed the creation of the Yemeni Socialist Party (YSP), which Abdul Fattah Ismail championed.

His government became increasingly drawn into the politics of the Horn of Africa. Early in 1977 he hosted a summit in Aden with Fidel Castro and the leaders of Ethiopia and Somalia, in an attempt to bring about a socialist-aligned regional federation. When these efforts failed, South Yemen sent about 2,000 troops to support the Ethiopian government in the Ogaden War of 1977–1978, a marked widening of its military commitments abroad. On 26 June 1978 the collective leadership of the YSP, led by Abdul Fattah Ismail, overthrew and executed Rubaya Ali.
salima-machamba: Salima Machamba was born on 1 November 1874 in Fomboni on the island of Mohéli, also called Mwali. Her mother was Jumbe Fatima bint Abderremane, Queen (Sultan) of Mohéli, and her father was Emile Fleuriot de Langle, a great-grandson of Paul Antoine Fleuriot de Langle. She was born out of wedlock, but she officially bore the name of her mother's husband and was recognised as Salima Machamba bint Saidi Hamadi Makadara. Through her family she was a relative of Ranavalona I, Queen of Madagascar.

She held the title of sultan of Mohéli from 1888 to 1909. The French, who made the Comoros a protectorate, chose her as a puppet queen of the island. On 28 August 1901 she married Camille Paule, a French gendarme with whom she had fallen in love, at Saint Denis on Réunion. Her rule ended in 1909, the year in which France annexed the Comoros.

Salima Machamba and her family were taken to France. Her three children, Henriette, Louis Camille and Camille Fernand, were born between 1902 and 1917 at Cléry in Côte-d'Or, and were styled princess and princes of Mohéli. The French government paid her a yearly allowance of 3,000 gold francs, and she lived as a simple farmer in Haute-Saône. She died at Pesmes on 7 August 1964 and was buried at the church of Saint-Hilaire in Pesmes on 10 August 1964.

Her daughter Henriette died at Dijon in 1989, her son Louis Camille at Dole in the Jura in 1983, and her youngest son Camille Fernand at Dijon in 2007. Her granddaughter Anne Etter, the daughter of Louis Camille, born in 1941, came to represent the royal family of Mohéli in the Comoros as president of the Association Développement des Iles Comores.
salinisation: Soil salinity is the salt content of the soil, and salinization is the process by which it increases. Salts occur naturally in soils and water, and the ions responsible are sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and chloride. Where rainfall or irrigation is sufficient, salts released as soil minerals weather are flushed out by drainage water. Under intense evaporation in dry periods they may instead rise through capillarity and collect near the surface, which leads to naturally saline soils in dry regions, as in large parts of Australia.

Salinization can arise from natural processes such as mineral weathering or the gradual withdrawal of an ocean, and from artificial ones such as irrigation and road salt. Almost all water, even natural rainfall, contains dissolved salts. When plants use irrigation water the salts are left behind in the root zone and begin to accumulate, and the problem is much greater where drainage is poor or saline water is used.

Disrupting natural drainage can also cause it. After the Aswan High Dam was built in Egypt in 1970, the continuous high level of the water table led to the salinization of arable land. Clearing trees for farming has the same effect in some dry regions, since deep tree roots are replaced by the shallow roots of annual crops.

Salinity harms plant growth and yield, damages roads, bricks and pipes, lowers water quality and can in the end cause erosion when vegetation cover collapses. It is an important land degradation problem. Sensitive crops lose vigour even in slightly saline soils, while only salt-resistant crops thrive in severely saline ones. Salinity can be reduced by leaching salts out with good-quality irrigation water, together with control of the water table and drainage, and gypsum is the most common compound used to reclaim sodic soil, where sodium predominates.
salins-les-bains: Salins-les-Bains, usually called Salins, is a commune in the Jura department of the Bourgogne-Franche-Comte region, on the border with Doubs and 34.8 km south-south-west of Besancon. It lies in the narrow valley of the Furieuse between two fortified hills, Fort Belin and Fort Saint-Andre, with Mont Poupet (851 metres) rising to the north. The town owes its name to its saline waters, for the bedrock contains salt and gypsum deposits.

Salins was an important city in Celtic times and became a Roman oppidum known as Salinae Sequanorum. In the 10th century its territory was enfeoffed by the Abbey of Saint Maurice-en-Valais to the counts of Macon, whose descendants held it until 1175. Maurette de Salins, heiress of the dynasty, brought the lordship to the house of Vienne, and her granddaughter sold it in 1225 to Duke Hugh IV of Burgundy, who ceded it in 1237 to John, Count of Chalon, in exchange for the county of Chalon. John's heirs, counts and dukes of Burgundy, emperors and kings of the House of Austria, bore the title of sire de Salins.

In 1477 the French took Salins, and King Louis XI temporarily made it the seat of the parlement of Franche-Comte. The French retook the town in 1668 and 1674, and it remained in their power from then on. In 1825 the town was almost destroyed by fire, and in 1871 it successfully resisted German troops in the Franco-Prussian War. Until the early 20th century vines covered the slopes round the town, but they were almost entirely abandoned after the phylloxera crisis of the mid-19th century.

Salt was extracted at Salins in the Middle Ages at the latest, and by 1115 there were two saltworks at wells around the town. Because of this production Salins was the largest town in Franche-Comte after Besancon in medieval times. Deforestation in the 17th and 18th centuries led to the creation of the Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans, nearer a large forest, but Salins brine was still channelled to it, 21 km away, for processing. The Great Saltworks of Salins ceased all production in 1962.

In 2009 the historic saltworks of Salins were added to the UNESCO World Heritage Site that includes the Royal Saltworks at Arc-et-Senans, inscribed in 1982. The town has a well-restored Romanesque church, St-Anatoile, an 18th-century town hall and a 17th-century Jesuit chapel that holds a library, founded in 1593, and a museum.
sallust: Sallust was probably born at Amiternum in the country of the Sabines, though Eduard Schwartz held that he was born in Rome. His family, the Sallustii, were provincial nobles of Sabine origin who belonged to the equestrian order and had full Roman citizenship, but not to Rome's ruling class. During the Social War his parents hid in Rome, so he may have been raised there, and he received a very good education. After an ill-spent youth he entered public life as a novus homo, serving as a military tribune in the 60s BCE.

His earliest certain office is plebeian tribune in 52 BCE, the year in which Milo's followers killed Clodius. He supported the prosecution of Milo and organised street demonstrations to pressure Cicero, who defended Milo. In 50 BCE the censor Appius Claudius Pulcher expelled him from the senate on grounds of immorality, probably a pretext for his opposition to Milo, and he joined Julius Caesar. In the civil war he commanded at least one legion in Illyricum in 49 BCE, an unsuccessful campaign. In late summer 47 BCE he was sent with other senators to persuade mutinous soldiers near Rome, but the rebels killed two senators and he narrowly escaped.

In 46 BCE he was praetor and accompanied Caesar to Africa, where he organised supplies through the Kerkennah Islands before the victory at Thapsus. He was then appointed governor of Africa Nova. As governor he made a fortune and was so corrupt that only Caesar's influence saved him from conviction for extortion. He bought and laid out the Gardens of Sallust on the Quirinal, later inherited by the emperors. Without prospects of advancement, he turned to writing history.

Sallust is the earliest known Latin historian with surviving works. His Conspiracy of Catiline, probably written about 42 BCE, tells of Lucius Sergius Catilina's attempt to overthrow the Republic in 63 BCE. The Jugurthine War, written about 41–40 BCE, covers the war in Numidia from 112 to 106 BCE and introduces the rivalry of Marius and Sulla. His Histories began in 78 BCE; only fragments survive. Two letters to Caesar and an attack on Cicero attributed to him are thought by modern scholars to be by a later rhetorician.

His theme is moral and political decline, which he traced to the wealth that flowed in after the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. He was influenced by Thucydides, and his style is brief and abrupt, with archaic words, unlike the flowing periods of Cicero. Historians since the 19th century have noted his bias and some errors of geography and dating, and many reject moral failure as the cause of the Republic's collapse.
salmas: Salmas is the capital of Salmas County and of its Central District in West Azerbaijan province. It lies in the historic Azerbaijan region. Its original name was Dilman, which is probably related to the Daylamites, who sometimes controlled the region, and in the 20th century it was known as Shapur. Archaeological remains dating back to the Urartian kingdom (860 to 590 BCE) attest to long habitation. Salmas has a cold semi-arid climate, typical of north-western Iran.

In late antiquity Salmas belonged to the Armenian province of Nor Shirakan, also called Persarmenia. A rock relief at Khan-Takhti village near the city, made in the reign of the Sasanian king Ardashir I (r. 224 to 242), shows a standing man receiving a ring from a horseman. The horsemen are usually taken to be Ardashir and his son Shapur I; scholars differ on what the scene commemorates, and one suggests a peace between Ardashir and the Kingdom of Armenia. When the Arsacid house of Armenia was abolished in 428, Nor Shirakan was incorporated into the Sasanian province of Adurbadagan. The sites of Haftan Tepe and Qazun Basi near Salmas show Sasanian-era occupation.

The 9th-century historian al-Baladhuri reported that Salmas's taxes had long gone to Mosul. In the 10th century it came under the Daylamite Sallarid ruler Marzuban ibn Muhammad, and by 975 apparently under the Rawadid dynasty. Geographers of that century describe a small walled town inhabited by Kurds. The Seljuks took it in 1070. After standing in ruins in the time of Yaqut al-Hamawi (d. 1229), it was thriving again in the mid-14th century, its wall having been rebuilt under the Ilkhanate ruler Ghazan (r. 1295 to 1304). On 17 and 18 September 1429 the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh defeated the Kara Koyunlu at the Battle of Salmas, though they retook the area in 1447.

From about 1910 Russian infantry and Cossacks were stationed in Salmas, withdrawing at Enver Pasha's offensive and returning in early 1916. In March 1915 Cevdet Bey ordered 800 Assyrians of Salmas killed, and in March 1918 the Kurdish chieftain Simko Shikak murdered Mar Shimun, patriarch of the Church of the East, in the town.

Its population is mainly Azerbaijanis and Kurds, with some Armenians, Assyrians and Jews. The city had 79,560 people at the census of 2006 and 127,864 at that of 2019. Its notable natives include the Armenian novelist Raffi (1835 to 1888), the Chaldean Catholic priest and orientalist Paul Bedjan (1838 to 1920) and the boxer Emmanuel Agassi (1930 to 2021).
salo: Salò is a town in the Province of Brescia, in Lombardy, on the banks of Lake Garda, on which it has the longest promenade. Its Latin name was Salodium. The area around the lake is a seismic zone: a meteorological observatory was established in the town in 1877 and a seismic station in 1889, which became an important research centre after the earthquake of 1901.

Legend gives Salò Etruscan origins, but recorded history begins with the Roman colony of Pagus Salodium, whose ruins include the Lugone necropolis. Its autonomy from Brescia dates to about the end of the 13th century, and from 1334 until 1797 it belonged to a federation of town councils along the western shore of the lake, later called the Riviera di Salò. After a short protectorate under Venice, from 1336 to 1349, Salò became a stronghold of the Milanese Visconti, and in 1377 Beatrice della Scala, wife of Bernabò Visconti, had it made capital of the area, with walls and a castle.

On 13 May 1426 the towns of the western shore joined the Venetian Republic, where they remained for three centuries. Venice gave the area great autonomy, and it was styled the Magnifica Patria. Its general council stayed at Salò, though Venice sent a governor with the title of Provveditore, and the linen industry developed. The end of the Venetian republic in 1797 ended Salò's position as capital of the riviera; it joined the Cisalpine Republic and then the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy, and from 1815 to 1859 it was part of the Austrian Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia. Garibaldi entered the town on 18 June 1859, and in 1866 it was headquarters of the Italian navy during the war with Austria.

From 1943 to 1945 it was the de facto capital of Benito Mussolini's Nazi-backed Italian Social Republic. Villa Castagna housed the police headquarters, Villa Amedei the Ministry of Popular Culture and Villa Simonini the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The cathedral of Santa Maria Annunziata, rebuilt in late Gothic style in the 15th century, has a Renaissance portal. The 16th-century Palazzo della Magnifica Patria houses a historical museum with documents on Renaissance history, Italy's colonial wars, the Spanish Civil War and the Resistance, and the Communal Palace holds the Civic Archaeological Museum with finds from ancient Salodium. A column with the Lion of St Mark, symbol of Venice, still stands in the main square.
salomon-gessner: Gessner was born on 1 April 1730, the son of the Zürich printer, publisher and bookseller Hans Konrad Gessner, who sat on the city's High Council. In 1749 he began an apprenticeship at a bookshop in Berlin but stayed only a year, having decided to devote himself to landscape painting and etching. In Hamburg he came across the poetry of Karl Wilhelm Ramler and Friedrich von Hagedorn and developed an interest in poetry. Back in Zürich he joined a group of young men called the Dienstags-Compagnie, who imagined themselves to be ancient shepherds.

His first published poem was Lied eines Schweizers an sein bewaffnetes Mädchen, and his first painting, Die Nacht, dates from 1753. Daphnis followed in 1754, and the first edition of the Idyllen appeared in 1756, with collected works in 1762. From then until 1772 he concentrated on painting. An English translation, New Idylles, was published in London in 1776, and his collected works were issued in Zürich in 1777 and 1778 and translated into French and Italian.

He co-founded the Helvetic Society in 1760, and in 1763 became a partner and artistic director of the porcelain manufactory at Kilchberg-Schooren. He sat on the Zürich High Council from 1765, three years later became an Obervogt, and from 1780 published and edited the Zürcher Zeitung, which became the Neue Zürcher Zeitung in 1821. From 1781 he was Sihlherr, responsible for supplying firewood to Zürich.

Gessner died on 2 March 1788. A monument designed by Alexander Trippel was put up in the Platzspitz park in 1792 and 1793, one of the first patriotic monuments in Switzerland. Another, at Bad Dürkheim, was destroyed by the French in 1794. A plaque marks his lifelong home, and streets and a bridge in Zürich bear his name.
salomon-of-brittany: Salomon, Salaün in Breton, was the son of Riwallon III of Poher, an elder brother of Nominoe. After Charles the Bald's defeat at the Battle of Jengland in 851, the Frankish king made peace with Salomon's cousin Erispoe, son of Nominoe. In 852 Salomon swore an oath to Charles as his fidelis and received Rennes, Nantes and Retz, a third of Brittany, to hold from the king. He was the most powerful noble at Erispoe's court.

Probably fearing the loss of his benefices if Louis the Stammerer became king at Le Mans, Salomon conspired with the otherwise unknown Almarchus to kill Erispoe and took the Breton throne in 857. He was behind the great revolt of the Frankish nobles of Neustria against Charles in 858, and a synod at Savonnières in 859 ordered him in vain to keep his oath and resume Brittany's tribute. In 862 he hired Vikings against Robert the Strong. Charles marched on Brittany in 863 but made peace near Entrammes, recognising western Anjou as Breton and granting Salomon the lay abbacy of Saint-Aubin in Angers in return for tribute.

War resumed in 865, when Vikings and Bretons ravaged the land around Le Mans, and in 866 Robert was killed at the Battle of Brissarthe. In August 867 Salomon's son-in-law Pascweten made peace with Charles at Compiègne, and the peace held for the rest of Salomon's life. In 868 Charles sent him regalia, among them a golden jewelled crown, and probably stood godfather to his son Wigo. Salomon also tried to persuade Pope Nicholas I to send the pallium to the Bishop of Dol, which would have given the Breton sees an archbishop of their own instead of the Archdiocese of Tours.

In 874 Pascweten, Wrhwant and Wigo, son of Riwallon, Count of Cornouaille, conspired against Salomon and killed him. The conspirators soon fell out, and a civil war followed until 876. Popular tradition in Brittany later venerated him as Saint Salomon and a martyr, and the Catholic Church honours him on 25 June.
saloninus: Saloninus was the son of the emperor Gallienus and Cornelia Salonina, a Greek from Bithynia. His grandfather was the emperor Valerian I. In 258 his father appointed him Caesar, as he had his older brother Valerian II, who died around that year. Saloninus was sent to Gaul to make sure his father's authority was respected there, and his main seat was Cologne. Like Valerian II, who was made the ward of Ingenuus, governor of the Illyrian provinces, he was placed under the protection of the praetorian prefect Silvanus, who is also named Albanus.

The historian Bray conjectures that the appointment was made at the instigation of Valerian I, who as senior Augustus and head of the Licinian family exercised authority over all its members, and that his aim was to secure the succession and establish a lasting dynasty. It is not known how Valerian expected his grandson to work with the existing governors and commanders of the Gallic provinces. Silvanus seems to have believed that as guardian he should exercise real authority in Gaul.

In 260, probably in July, Silvanus ordered the general Postumus to hand over booty that his troops had taken from a German warband returning home from a raid into Gaul. Postumus's men reacted violently, turned on Saloninus and Silvanus, and drove them to Cologne with some loyal troops. It was probably then that Postumus was acclaimed emperor by his army, and he besieged Cologne.

Gallienus, probably campaigning on the middle Danube, could do nothing to save his son, and Valerian was probably already a captive of the Persian king Shapur I. In their desperation, Saloninus's troops proclaimed him Augustus, perhaps hoping that Postumus's army would desert to them. It did not, and about a month later the citizens of Colonia Agrippina handed Saloninus and Silvanus over to Postumus. He may have been unable to prevent his army from killing them, though it seems unlikely that he tried seriously to do so. The deaths of Valerian II and then Saloninus seem to have ended Gallienus's interest in a dynastic scheme, and he made no attempt to raise his third son, Egnatius Marinianus, to the purple.
salote-tupou-iii: Sālote was born on 13 March 1900, the eldest daughter and heir of King George Tupou II and his first wife, Queen Lavinia Veiongo. Her mother died of tuberculosis in 1902. Because Tongan tradition allowed offspring of previous marriages to be killed, the king sent her to Auckland in December 1909 for her protection, where she lived with the Kronfeld family and kept the connection all her life. She was educated for five years in New Zealand, including two years at the Anglican Diocesan School for Girls in Epsom.

The king's later marriage produced no son, and under the Constitution of 1875 she became heir presumptive after her fifteenth birthday. In 1917 she married Viliami Tungī Mailefihi, a noble thirteen years older and a direct descendant of the Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua, so that their children would combine the blood of Tonga's three great royal dynasties.

She was proclaimed queen on 6 April 1918, the day after her father died of tuberculosis. In 1920–1921 she gave the Bernice P. Bishop Museum's Bayard Dominick Expedition access to sites and information for its mapping of Tongan archaeology. She also wrote dance songs and love poems, published in 2004. From 1924 to 1946 the Australian missionary Rodger Page advised her and helped to reunify the Free Wesleyan Church of Tonga, of which she was a member; the historian Sione Lātūkefu called him a power behind the throne.

Tonga declared war on Germany in 1940 and on Japan in 1941, and she put its resources at Britain's disposal; Tongan troops fought in the Solomon Islands campaign, including on Guadalcanal. In 1953 she attended the coronation of Elizabeth II in London, her only visit to Europe. When rain began, she refused a hood on her carriage, since Tongan etiquette forbids imitating the person one honours, and rode in an open carriage through the downpour with Sultan Ibrahim of Kelantan, which endeared her to spectators.

Diabetic for years, she was treated in Auckland, where a second cancer was found in 1965. She took part in a festival marking her record reign at a festival in July 1965, and she died in hospital in Auckland on 16 December 1965. Fifty thousand people attended her funeral on 23 December. She is known as the longest-reigning Tongan monarch, nearly 48 years, and her rule has been called a golden age for Tonga.
salt-lake-valley: The Salt Lake Valley, also known as the Jordan Valley, covers about 500 square miles (1,300 km2) of Salt Lake County in north-central Utah. Steep mountains, rising at points 7,100 feet (2,200 m) above the valley floor, surround it on every side except the northwest. The Wasatch Mountains lie to the east, the Oquirrh Mountains to the west and Traverse Ridge to the south, while the Great Salt Lake lies to the northwest, with the peaks of Antelope Island in view.

Every way into the valley is narrow. Point of the Mountain leads in from the south through the Jordan Narrows, a gap in the Traverse Mountains; narrow passages lie between the Great Salt Lake and the Oquirrh Mountains to the northwest and between the lake and the Wasatch Mountains to the north; and several canyons open to the east, among them Parley's Canyon and Emigration Canyon. The Jordan River flows north from Utah Lake in Utah Valley through the gap in the Traverse Mountains, divides the valley and empties into the Great Salt Lake. With mountain streams and reservoirs, it supplies the valley's irrigation water.

Brigham Young and his fellow Mormon settlers moved into the valley after being driven out of several states, and Young is reported to have said, "this is the right place". The valley they settled now holds Salt Lake City and many of its suburbs, among them Murray, Sandy, South Jordan, West Jordan and West Valley City.

The valley held 1,029,655 people in 2010. Interstate 15 runs north to south through it and Interstate 80 east to west across its northern quarter from Parley's Canyon towards Tooele County, with the Interstate 215 belt route and several state highways besides. The Utah Transit Authority runs buses and three TRAX light rail lines in the valley, and the FrontRunner commuter railway links it with Pleasant View in Weber County to the north and Provo in Utah County to the south.
salt-march: The Indian National Congress issued the Declaration of Sovereignty and Self-rule, or Purna Swaraj, on 26 January 1930, and the declaration included readiness to withhold taxes. Gandhi chose as his target the Salt Act of 1882, which gave the British a monopoly on the manufacture and collection of salt and levied a tax on it. Violating the act was a criminal offence, although salt was freely available to people on the coast by evaporating sea water.

His choice was at first met with incredulity by the Congress Working Committee. Lord Irwin, the Viceroy, wrote that a salt campaign did not keep him awake at night. 2 percent of the Raj's revenue and hurt the poorest most, and that next to air and water salt was among the necessities of life.

Gandhi set out on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati Ashram with 78 volunteers who came from almost every region, caste and religion of India, and walked to the coastal village of Dandi in Navsari district. In the villages volunteers collected donations and registered new satyagrahis, and village officials resigned. Gandhi called the salt tax inhuman and the campaign a poor man's struggle. At 8:30 in the morning of 6 April 1930 he broke the salt law at Dandi.

Millions then broke the salt laws by making salt or buying illegal salt, and the British arrested over sixty thousand people by the end of the month. The campaign grew into a boycott of British cloth and goods and the defiance of forest laws. In Peshawar a crowd of Khudai Khidmatgar led by Ghaffar Khan was fired on at the Qissa Kahani Bazaar on 23 April, and an estimated 200 to 250 people were killed. Gandhi was arrested on the night of 4 and 5 May, just days before the planned action at the Dharasana Salt Works.

The Salt Satyagraha did not produce immediate concessions or self-rule, and Congress ended satyagraha as official policy in 1934. It drew worldwide attention to the Indian independence movement through newspaper and newsreel coverage and showed the effect of civil disobedience, and the Civil Disobedience Movement it began continued until 1934 in Gujarat. Nehru considered it the high-water mark of his association with Gandhi. Its methods influenced American activists in the civil rights movement of the 1960s, among them Martin Luther King Jr. The National Salt Satyagraha Memorial in Dandi opened on 30 January 2019.
salta: In early 1536 the large expedition of Diego de Almagro, on its way to Chile, passed through the plains of Chicoana west of the present city and fought skirmishes with local tribesmen while foraging. Hernando de Lerma founded Salta on 16 April 1582, intending the settlement to be an outpost between Lima in Peru and Buenos Aires. The origin of the name is a matter of conjecture, and several theories have been advanced.

During the war of independence the city was a commercial and military strategic point between Peru and the Argentine cities. From 1816 to 1821 it was led by the local military leader General Martín Miguel de Güemes, who under the command of General José de San Martín defended the city and the surrounding area from Spanish forces coming from the north. Salta emerged from the war politically in disarray and financially bankrupt, a condition that lasted through much of the 19th century. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Italian, Spanish, British and Arab immigrants, particularly Syrians and Lebanese, revived trade and agriculture in the area and added to the city's multicultural character.

Salta is the capital and largest city of Salta Province and the cultural and economic centre of the Valle de Lerma Metropolitan Area. It stands at an altitude of 1,200 metres and has a subtropical highland climate, with over 80 per cent of its rainfall between December and March. Around the Ninth of July Square stand the neoclassical Cathedral Shrine, the Cabildo, once the town hall and now a historical museum, a museum of contemporary art and the Museum of High Altitude Archaeology, which houses artefacts from the Inca civilisation, among them the mummies of three Inca children. San Bernardo Hill rises in the east. The local culture blends Spanish and gaucho traditions, and the April Culture Festival lasts the whole month.
saltsjobaden-agreement: Since the Swedish General Strike of 1909 the labour market had been marked by unregulated conflict, with the Swedish Trade Union Confederation (LO) and the Swedish Employers Association (SAF) as the main actors. A restrictive legal framework was discussed, but both sides criticised it, and after the Social Democratic government's bill was rejected in parliament in 1935 the two organisations began to negotiate directly. The chapters on industrial action drew largely on the earlier proposals.

The agreement's rules on industrial action came to be regarded almost as general legal principles for conflicts in the labour market. To carry it out, the LO changed its statutes. Its secretariat could suspend conflict aid to a member union that rejected the secretariat's proposed settlement, and could forbid a strike covering more than three percent of a union's members or threatening to grow that large through a lockout. Member unions had to give the confederation's board power to decide on contracts and industrial action even against their members' wishes.

Reception was mixed. The Swedish Transport Workers' Union, an LO affiliate, commented that "in fear of death, one commits suicide" and called the fourth chapter, on industrial action by unions, repugnant. Even so, the agreement opened an era of consensus and cooperation known as the Saltsjöbaden spirit, which shaped Swedish labour policy at least until the late 1960s, when the LKAB industrial conflict began a period of confrontation.

In the early 1980s the parties again sought consensus, which led to the Development Agreement between the LO, the SAF and the PTK. Nils Elvander has pointed to the Industry Agreement of 1997 in manufacturing as a modern equivalent, restoring regulation by the parties themselves after the confrontations of the 1970s. The Saltsjöbaden Agreement was last amended in 2022.
salur: The Salur, also written Salyr or Salgur, were a sub-branch of the Üçok tribal federation of the Oghuz. Rashid al-Din Hamadani, historian and statesman of the Ilkhanate, wrote in the Oghuzname of his Jami' al-tawarikh that the name means wherever you go, you fight with a sword and a club. Abu al-Ghazi Bahadur, khan of Khiva and historian, took it in his Shajara-i Tarākima to mean armed with a saber. The Turkologist Peter B. Golden derives it from a root meaning to put into violent motion, a name expressing military force.

Versions of the Oghuzname give the Salyr an important place in the Oghuz Yabgu State until the beginning of the Seljuk movement, with many of its khans drawn from them. Rashid al-Din wrote that royal dignity long stayed in the Salyr branch. In the 11th and 12th centuries much of the tribe moved west with other Oghuz-Turkmen tribes. The Salghurid dynasty that ruled Fars from 1148 to 1282 was of Salur origin, and the Karamanid principality of Anatolia belonged to the tribe's Karaman branch. Part of the tribe went to Crimea, and some scholars derive the name of the river Salgir from it.

In the 14th to 16th centuries the Salyr led an alliance of five Turkmen tribes, the Salyr, Arsary, Tekke, Yomud and Saryk, which lasted until the Amu Darya stopped flowing along the Uzboy watercourse. Between the 16th and 19th centuries the Salyr lived on the Mangyshlak peninsula and around the Northern Balkan mountains, then in the Khiva Khanate, on the middle Amu Darya and in the Murghab oasis, and finally in Serakhs, where they settled in 1884.

Salur Kazan, one of the heroes of Dede Korkut's epic tales, is a Salur. Matthew Arnold's poem Sohrab and Rustum mentions the lances of Salore among the Tartar army fighting the Persians. The patriarchs of the modern Salyr tribe of the Turkmen in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran claim descent from the original Oghuz Salur, and Salurs still live in the Middle East and Central Asia.
salvador-allende: Salvador Guillermo Allende Gossens was born on 26 June 1908 in Santiago. His family belonged to the Chilean upper middle class and had a long tradition of involvement in progressive and liberal causes. His grandfather was a prominent physician and social reformer who founded one of the first secular schools in Chile. Allende was of Basque and Belgian descent. In 1938 he directed the campaign of the Popular Front headed by Pedro Aguirre Cerda, and as Minister of Health in the following government he passed safety laws for factory workers, higher pensions for widows, maternity care and free lunches for schoolchildren.

Allende was a committed member of the Socialist Party, which he helped found, and over nearly forty years was a senator, a deputy and a cabinet minister. He ran unsuccessfully for the presidency in 1952, 1958 and 1964. In 1970 he won a close three-way race as the Popular Unity candidate and was confirmed in a run-off by Congress. As president he pursued what he called the Chilean Path to Socialism, representing the more moderate faction of his party, while its left wing under Carlos Altamirano sought a more radical course.

In the first year his economy minister Pedro Vuskovic's policy brought 12% industrial growth, but by 1972 inflation of the escudo reached 140%. His government returned land to the Mapuche and in 1971 re-established relations with Cuba. A 24-day strike began in October 1972, and on 29 June 1973 Colonel Roberto Souper's tank regiment surrounded La Moneda in a failed coup known as the Tanquetazo. On 22 August 1973 the Chamber of Deputies voted 81 to 47 to accuse the government of breaching the Constitution.

In early September 1973 Allende considered resolving the crisis with a plebiscite, to be announced on 11 September. That day the military under Augusto Pinochet staged the coup. As troops surrounded La Moneda he spoke to Chileans on live radio, refused an offer of safe passage and died in his office, by suicide, though the exact circumstances are disputed. The junta that followed dissolved Congress, and at least 3,095 civilians disappeared or were killed. Allende is buried in the general cemetery of Santiago, and many socialists revere him as a hero and martyr.
salvadoran-civil-war: El Salvador has long been marked by extreme inequality. Coffee became its main cash crop in the late 19th century, and the divide between rich and poor widened through the 1920s and after the fall in coffee prices that followed the crash of 1929. In 1932 the Central American Socialist Party led an uprising of peasants and Indigenous people, and in La Matanza the armed forces killed approximately 30,000 civilians. Military dictatorships then monopolised political power while protecting the landowning elite, and opposition grew among middle-class, working-class and poor Salvadorans through the 20th century. The later guerrilla coalition took its name from Farabundo Martí, a leader of the 1932 uprising.

On 15 October 1979 a civil-military junta deposed President Romero in a coup, and killings of anti-coup protesters by the government are widely seen as the start of the war. The United States feared a communist revolution like those in Nicaragua and Cuba and backed the new government, with economic aid and with training and equipment for the army; the FMLN was backed by Cuba, Nicaragua and the Soviet Union. On 24 March 1980 Archbishop Óscar Romero, who had written to President Carter asking him to suspend military aid, was assassinated while celebrating Mass. On 2 December 1980 members of the National Guard were suspected of raping and murdering four American church women.

The army adopted a scorched-earth strategy of draining the sea, aimed at the civilian population in the countryside. In March 1981 troops swept through Cabañas Department, and the air force bombed and strafed fleeing civilians at the Río Lempa. On 11 December 1981 the Atlácatl Battalion massacred at least 733, possibly up to 1,000, unarmed civilians at El Mozote, including 146 children. José Napoleón Duarte won the 1984 presidential election, held under military rule, with 54 per cent of the vote. On 11 November 1989 the FMLN launched its final offensive, bringing the fighting into the wealthy suburbs of San Salvador.

The Chapultepec Peace Accords were signed in Mexico City on 16 January 1992. The United Nations reports that the war killed more than 75,000 people and left about 8,000 disappeared, and it estimated that the FMLN was responsible for 5 per cent of atrocities and the security forces for 85 per cent. The accords reduced the army from a wartime high of 63,000 to 32,000 by 1993, abolished the National Guard and Treasury Police, and created a National Civil Police, which deployed its first officers in March 1993. A 1993 amnesty law hindered accountability until the Supreme Court of Justice ruled it unconstitutional in 2016.
salve-regina: The text is traditionally ascribed to the eleventh-century German monk Hermann of Reichenau, and also to Bernard of Clairvaux, Peter of Compostela and Adhemar of Le Puy, among others, but most musicologists regard it as anonymous. It was set down in largely its present form at the Abbey of Cluny in the 12th century, where it served as a processional hymn on Marian feasts. The current text is almost exactly that of the original: the word Mater in the first line seems to have been added in the 16th century, and Virgo in the final line in the 13th.

Marian antiphons have been sung at the close of Compline, the last Office of the day, since the thirteenth century, and the Salve Regina is the best known of the four. Its use there is likely to go back to the monastic practice of intoning it in chapel and chanting it on the way to the sleeping quarters. The Cistercians chanted it daily from 1218. It was popular at medieval universities as an evening song, and it came to form part of the ritual for the blessing of a ship; it was especially dear to sailors.

In the 1220s or 1230s the Dominican friars in Bologna adopted a nightly Salve procession at Compline, and the practice spread through their whole order. Pope Gregory IX, on the advice of the Dominican Raymond of Penyafort, instituted it for the diocese of Rome on Fridays at Compline, and many dioceses and religious orders adopted it in some form during the 13th century. Pope Leo XIII added it to the prayers said at the end of Low Mass. It is also the final prayer of the Rosary and is traditionally sung at the end of a priest's funeral Mass.

In the 18th century Alphonsus Liguori used the Salve Regina as the outline of his book The Glories of Mary, whose first part explains how God gave Mary to mankind as the Gate of Heaven. As an essential part of Compline, the hymn was set to music by many composers, among them Victoria, Palestrina, Josquin and Lassus, and later Pergolesi, Vivaldi, Handel and Liszt. Schubert composed no fewer than seven versions, Francis Poulenc one in 1941 and Arvo Pärt another, first performed in Essen Cathedral in 2002.

A separate hymn grew from it. The German priest Johann Georg Seidenbusch published "Gegrüßet seist du, Königin" in 1687, drawing its salutations mostly from the Salve Regina. Its modern melody first appeared in the 1736 hymnal Geistliche Spiel- und Weckuhr, and the English version "Hail, Holy Queen enthroned above" first appeared in The Roman Missal in 1884.
salween: The Salween is about 3,289 kilometres long. It rises in the Tanggula Mountains of the central Tibetan Plateau, passes through Cona Lake, and flows through Tibet and Yunnan, where it is called the Nu Jiang, then through Shan, Karenni, Karen and Mon states of Myanmar, where it is the Thanlwin. A short section forms the Myanmar–Thailand border. Its basin is long and narrow, between the Irrawaddy and Brahmaputra systems on the west and the Mekong on the east, and about 89 per cent of the annual flow comes in the monsoon season.
