Only the last 90 kilometres, at the estuary and delta at Mawlamyine, are navigable. The spelling Salween is an anglicisation of the Burmese name from 19th-century maps.

Human presence along the upper river dates to at least 31,000 to 39,000 years ago. The Mon migrated south from China around 3000 BCE, the ancestors of the Karen from about 1000 BCE, and Tai peoples, ancestors of the Shan, entered the Shan Hills from Yunnan from about 1000 CE. Martaban was a major port on the Maritime Silk Road as early as 200 BCE, and from 738 to 902 CE the Salween formed the south-western boundary of Nanzhao with the Pyu city-states.

In the 1060s Anawrahta of Pagan conquered Thaton and the Mon kingdoms of the delta, and in the late 1100s Narapatisithu brought most of the Shan States under Burmese rule. For almost 500 years the lower Salween defined the frontier between Burma and Ayutthaya.

After the First Anglo-Burmese War of 1824 the Konbaung dynasty ceded the Tenasserim coast south of the river to the British Empire, and Mawlamyine was capital of British Burma from 1826 until 1852. Teak logs were floated down the Salween to the port. In 1935–36 the British geographer Ronald Kaulback walked the length of the river and produced some of the first comprehensive maps of its course.

The Salween is one of the least fragmented large river systems in Asia, with only a few small dams on its headwaters and tributaries. Along with the Lancang and Jinsha rivers it flows through the Three Parallel Rivers World Heritage Site in Yunnan. Its delta is a major rice-growing area and its estuary a rich fishery. The basin is home to many minority peoples, including the Karen, Shan, Mon and Nu.
salzburg: Salzburg stands on both banks of the River Salzach at the northern edge of the Alps. The mountains lie to the south and rolling plains to the north; the nearest alpine peak, the Untersberg at 1,972 metres, is less than 16 kilometres from the centre. The old town is flanked by two smaller hills, the Mönchsberg and the Kapuzinerberg, and dominated by the Hohensalzburg Fortress. The city lies about 150 kilometres east of Munich and 300 kilometres west of Vienna.

The area has been inhabited continuously since the Neolithic. In the La Tène period it was an administrative centre of the Celtic Taurisci in the Kingdom of Noricum. After the Roman invasion of 15 BCE the settlements on the surrounding hills were abandoned for a Roman city, which received the status of a municipium in 45 CE and became one of the most important cities of the province of Noricum.

When Noricum collapsed in 488, part of the Romano-Celtic population remained, and in the sixth century it came under the Baiuvarii. The Life of Saint Rupert credits Rupert with the city's rebirth: Duke Theodo II of Bavaria gave him the remains of the Roman town and an upper castle on the Nonnberg Terrace, and in return he was to evangelise the east and south-east of Bavaria.

Independence from Bavaria was secured in the late fourteenth century, and the archbishopric became a prince-bishopric of the Holy Roman Empire. During the German Peasants' War the archbishop fled to the fortress, which was besieged for three months in 1525. On 31 October 1731 Archbishop Count Leopold Anton von Firmian signed an Edict of Expulsion ordering all Protestant citizens to recant; 21,475 citizens refused and were expelled, and most of them accepted an offer from King Friedrich Wilhelm I of Prussia to settle in East Prussia. Napoleon secularised the archbishopric in 1803. Salzburg passed to Austria in 1805, to Bavaria in 1809 and finally back to Austria under the Treaty of Munich of 1816.

Salzburg's historic centre was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996 and is one of the best-preserved city centres north of the Alps. Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau began to rebuild the medieval town on late Renaissance lines, and Santino Solari's cathedral was the first early Baroque church in the city. The Franziskanerkirche dates from 1208, and the Großes Festspielhaus, opened in 1960, was built for the annual Salzburg Festival. The city has three universities, among them the Mozarteum University for music and drama.
salzkammergut: The Salzkammergut is a resort area in Austria stretching from the city of Salzburg eastwards along the Alpine Foreland and the Northern Limestone Alps to the peaks of the Dachstein Mountains. Its main river is the Traun, a right tributary of the Danube. The land along the Traun comprises numerous glacial lakes and raised bogs, the Totes Gebirge and the Upper Austrian Prealps. The name means salt demesne. The region is not an official administrative division and has no clear borders.

Archaeological finds date back to the Neolithic, especially the stilt houses of the Mondsee group, who settled the region from about 3800 BCE. The salt mines had been in use at least since the Celtic Hallstatt culture, and the Romans continued the work after the area was incorporated into the province of Noricum in 15 BCE. From about 530 Bavarian tribes settled the region from the west, and salt trade along the Traun is documented again from 900.

In 1278 King Rudolph I of Germany, of the House of Habsburg, seized the duchies from King Ottokar II of Bohemia. Emperor Maximilian I added the estates of Mondsee Abbey in 1506. The surrounding estates were designated a Kammergut, first documented in a deed of 1656, and the mines were administered from the salt chamber in Gmunden. A decree of Empress Maria Theresia of 22 May 1745 made it the Salzoberamt, and the term Salzkammergut dates to this period. Emperor Franz Joseph I transformed the office in 1850 into a salt and forest directorate.

Under Franz Joseph I the area was a hub of cultured life. The emperor spent his summer holidays in Bad Ischl in the Kaiservilla, where he signed the declaration of war on Serbia that began World War I. Salt mining is now a minor part of the local economy, and forestry is more important.

UNESCO designated the Hallstatt–Dachstein/Salzkammergut Cultural Landscape a World Heritage Site in 1997. Its description notes that salt deposits were exploited as early as the 2nd millennium BCE and that this resource was the basis of the area's prosperity up to the middle of the 20th century. The site covers 284 square kilometres, and its core includes Hallstatt, Obertraun, Gosau and Bad Goisern.
salzwedel: Salzwedel lies on the river Jeetzel in the north-western part of the Altmark, between Hamburg and Magdeburg, and is the capital of the district of Altmarkkreis Salzwedel. It stands on the German Timber-Frame Road. Test drillings in 1968 revealed a significant reservoir of natural gas near the town.

The castle of Salzwedel was first documented in 1112. As part of the Margraviate of Brandenburg the settlement was first mentioned as a town in 1233, and a new town began to develop to the north-east of the old town in 1247. Salzwedel belonged to the Hanseatic League from 1263 to 1518, and in religious matters to the Diocese of Verden until 1648. It became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701, the old and new towns were united in 1713, it joined the Prussian Province of Saxony in 1815 after the Napoleonic Wars, and it received a railway connection in 1870.

Under Nazi rule the town's Jewish residents were systematically deprived of their rights and then expelled. A forced labour camp for some 1,000 women was converted in mid-1944 into a subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, which held over 1,500 female prisoners, mostly Jewish. When the US Army liberated it on 14 April 1945, it found more than ninety women dead of typhus, dysentery and malaria. Five air raids between 1942 and 1945 killed more than 300 people.

The US Army handed the town to the Soviet Red Army, and it became part of the German Democratic Republic. The border crossing near Salzwedel opened on 9 November 1989, and in 1990 the town received its first democratically elected government. Its official name became Hansestadt Salzwedel on 1 April 2008, recalling its Hanseatic past.

The medieval part of the town remains its commercial and administrative centre. It is enclosed by the historic city wall and town gates, among them the Neuperver Gate, built 1460–1470, the Stonegate of around 1530, the Hungerturm tower and the Kluhs, a storehouse of 1490 built on the wall. The brick Gothic churches of St Marien, St Katharina and St Lorenz stand in the old town, and the birth house of Jenny von Westphalen, later the wife of Karl Marx, is also preserved. Local specialities include Baumkuchen, the layered tree cake, Salzwedel wedding soup and Tiegelbraten, a mutton dish.
sam-bellamy: Bellamy may have been born in 1689 in the parish of Hittisleigh on Dartmoor in Devon, the youngest of six known children of Stephen and Elizabeth Bellamy. Alternatively, a sailor he captured testified in 1716 that Bellamy declared himself an Englishman born in London. He became a sailor young and in his late teens joined the Royal Navy, where he fought in several battles.

Around 1715 he travelled to Cape Cod, allegedly to seek relatives. In early 1716 he left the Cape with a group of men to seek the treasure of the 1715 Spanish Treasure Fleet, which had been wrecked in a hurricane off the east coast of Florida. The jeweller Palgraves Williams, son of the Rhode Island attorney general John Williams, joined him and funded the expedition.

The treasure hunters met with little success and turned to piracy in the crew of Benjamin Hornigold, who commanded the Marianne with his first mate, Edward Teach, later known as Blackbeard. In the summer of 1716 the crew grew irritated by Hornigold's unwillingness to attack English ships. By majority vote he was deposed, and he left with his loyal followers, Teach among them. The remaining crew of 90 elected Bellamy captain. After capturing a second ship, the Sultana, Bellamy took it as his own and gave Williams command of the Marianne.

In the spring of 1717 Bellamy sighted the Whydah Gally in the Windward Passage between Hispaniola and Cuba. Built in England in 1715, she was a 300-ton slave ship with 18 guns, on her maiden voyage, carrying gold, indigo, ivory and other goods. After a chase of three days and a single shot, Captain Lawrence Prince surrendered. Bellamy gave him the Sultana in exchange, raised the Whydah's guns to 28 and sailed north. His known career as a captain lasted little more than a year, and he and his crew captured at least 53 ships.

At midnight on 26 April 1717 the Whydah was caught in a nor'easter off Cape Cod and driven onto shoals about 500 feet from the coast of what is now Wellfleet. Her masts snapped and she capsized, drowning Bellamy and all but two of her 146 crew. Nine survivors of the Whydah and the Marianne were prosecuted in Boston, and six were convicted on 22 October 1717 and hanged on 15 November.

The wreck was announced in July 1984 and became the first authenticated pirate shipwreck found in North America. The diving crew was led by Barry Clifford, who in 1985 recovered a bell marked THE WHYDAH GALLY 1716.
sam-houston: Samuel Houston was born on 2 March 1793 in Rockbridge County, Virginia, into a slave-owning family, and he owned enslaved people throughout his life. After his father died in 1807 he ran away at 16 to live with a Cherokee group led by Chief John Jolly on Hiwassee Island, learned the Cherokee language and customs, and was known as Raven. He enlisted in the army on 24 March 1813 for the War of 1812, served under General Andrew Jackson and was badly wounded at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend.

After studying law he became district attorney for Nashville in 1819. With Jackson's support he was elected to the House of Representatives in 1823 and governor of Tennessee in 1827. His marriage to Eliza Allen in January 1829 lasted eleven weeks, and he resigned and went to live again with the Cherokee.

Houston crossed into Mexican Texas in December 1832. The Texas Revolution began in October 1835 with the Battle of Gonzales, and Houston led the Texian Army to victory at San Jacinto in 1836. He won the 1836 presidential election and took office on 22 October 1836 after the interim president, David G. Burnet, resigned. He sought normal relations with Mexico, arranged the release of Santa Anna, and urged an end to the importation of enslaved people. Term limits ended his presidency in 1838, and he won another term in 1841.

After annexation in 1845 the Texas legislature elected him one of its first two senators in February 1846. He voted for the Compromise of 1850 but against the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, which he believed would raise tensions over slavery, and he left the Democratic Party over it. He was elected governor in 1859 and campaigned against secession. He was the only Southern governor to refuse an oath of allegiance to the Confederacy and was forced out of office in 1861.

Houston died at Huntsville, Texas, on 26 July 1863, aged 70, of what is believed to have been pneumonia. His record on slavery was complicated: he held enslaved people and governed Texas as a slave state, yet voted several times against extending slavery into the West and put the Union above dividing it over slavery. The city of Houston was founded in his name in 1836, and Sam Houston State University and Fort Sam Houston also commemorate him.
sam-nujoma: Samuel Shafiishuna Daniel Nujoma was born on 12 May 1929 at Etunda, a village in Ongandjera, near Okahao, Ovamboland, in South West Africa. He was the eldest of eleven children, and his mother, Helvi Mpingana Kondombolo, was a Uukwambi princess by descent. He tended the family's cattle, attended a Finnish missionary school at Okahao from the age of ten and completed Standard Six, the highest level open to black pupils at the time.

In 1946 he moved to Walvis Bay, where he worked in a general store and later at a whaling station. In 1949 he went to Windhoek, working as a cleaner for South African Railways while attending night school. He became involved in politics in the early 1950s through trade unions, shaped by his experience of the contract labour system, and was dismissed from the railways in 1957.

In 1959 Nujoma co-founded the Ovamboland People's Organization and was elected its first president. After the Old Location Massacre in December 1959 he was arrested for organising the resistance, and in February 1960 he went into exile to lobby the United Nations. The organisation was reconstituted as the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO) in New York on 19 April 1960, with Nujoma elected president in absentia. He built its headquarters in Dar es Salaam with the help of Julius Nyerere, and in 1962 SWAPO founded an armed wing, later the People's Liberation Army of Namibia.

The first armed clash with South African forces took place on 26 August 1966 at Omugulugwombashe and began the Namibian War of Independence. Nujoma's role in the army has been questioned following allegations of torture and imprisonment of fighters in the Lubango dungeons in Angola, where about 1,000 SWAPO members were held for over nine years. He led SWAPO's negotiators over the proposals that became United Nations Security Council Resolution 435 in 1978, and a ceasefire with South Africa was signed on 19 March 1989. After 29 years in exile he returned in September 1989.

The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1989 chose Nujoma as Namibia's first president, and he was sworn in on 21 March 1990. He proclaimed a policy of national reconciliation to improve relations among the country's racial and ethnic groups, and began a land reform programme in 1990. He was re-elected in 1994, and the constitution was changed so that he could stand for a third term in 1999. His successor, Hifikepunye Pohamba, took office on 21 March 2005, and Pohamba also succeeded him as SWAPO president in 2007. Parliament conferred on him the title Founding Father of the Namibian Nation in December 2005. He published his autobiography, Where Others Wavered, in 2001, and died in Windhoek on 8 February 2025, aged 95.
samanid-empire: The dynasty descended from Saman Khuda, a dehqan of Iranian origin from the village of Saman in Balkh province. Some sources say the Samanids claimed descent from the House of Mihran of Bahram Chobin; a few medieval sources made them Oghuz Turks, which is considered unlikely, and others have given them a Sogdian or Hephthalite princely background. In 819 four brothers, Nuh, Ahmad, Yahya and Ilyas, were made governors of territories under Abbasid suzerainty. Nuh seized Isfijab from the nomadic pagan Turks of the steppe, and by 855 Ahmad ruled most of Transoxiana.

In 892 Ismail Samani, son of Ahmad, united the Samanids under his rule and moved the capital from Samarkand to Bukhara. In the spring of 900 he defeated the Saffarid emir Amr ibn al-Layth near Balkh and took him captive. The caliph then recognised him as ruler of all Khorasan and Transoxiana and gave him the investiture of Tabaristan, Ray and Isfahan. Ahmad, who succeeded him in 907, took Sistan by 911 but was murdered by some of his slaves in 914, and his eight-year-old son Nasr II (r. 914 to 943) followed him.

By 945 the government had fallen under the de facto control of the Turkic military slave faction. In 962 the commander Alp Tigin seized Ghazna, and his successor Sabuktigin took all the provinces south of the Oxus and founded the Ghaznavid Empire. The Karakhanids conquered Bukhara in 999, ending the dynasty. Ismail Muntasir, the youngest son of Nuh II, escaped, retook Bukhara and Samarkand and held Nishapur for a time, but Karakhanid and Ghaznavid armies forced him to flee, and his attempt ended in 1005.

The state was modelled on the Abbasid system, itself modelled on the Sasanian. The ruler was the amir; provinces were governed by appointed governors or local vassal rulers, who collected taxes and supplied troops. The bureaucracy used Arabic for diplomacy. Khorasan was the most important province, and its governor was normally the commander-in-chief.

The Samanids patronised the poets Rudaki, Bal'ami and Daqiqi, and Ferdowsi lived under their rule. Scholars gathered at Bukhara, where a library called Siwan al-Hikma was assembled. They propagated Sunni Islam and repressed Ismaili Shiism, while being more tolerant of Twelver Shiism. Arabic remained the language of science and religion. Most of their subjects were Iranian peoples, Sogdians, Bactrians, Khwarazmians and others. Persian gradually replaced the eastern Iranian languages, of which only Yaghnobi survives. Samanid pottery from Nishapur, with Arabic proverbs or figural decoration, is held in collections worldwide.
samaria: Samaria is a historical and biblical name for the central region of the Land of Israel, bordered by Judea to the south, Galilee to the north, the Jordan River to the east and the Mediterranean Sea to the west. Its hills lie between the Jezreel Valley, the Jordan Rift Valley, the Sharon plain and the Jerusalem mountains, and include Mount Carmel, Mount Gilboa, Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim. Mount Ebal, at 935 metres, is the highest peak.

The Hebrew name Shomron is linked in the Hebrew Bible to Shemer, from whom King Omri bought the hill on which he built his capital. Assyrian inscriptions first call the place Bet Ḥumri, the house of Omri, and later Samirin. The name for the whole region is first documented after the Neo-Assyrian conquest, when the land became the province of Samerina.

Settlement grew in the Iron Age II, from about 950 BCE: archaeologists estimate 400 sites, up from 300 in the Iron Age I. After the Assyrian conquest, Sargon II claimed to have deported 27,280 people, mainly to Guzana and to the cities of the Medes, while people from other parts of the empire were settled in Samerina. This resettlement is the basis of the narrative of the Ten Lost Tribes.

The region then passed to the Neo-Babylonian and Achaemenid Persian empires. Many scholars hold that a Samaritan temple was built on Mount Gerizim in the first half of the 5th century BCE. After Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE, Samaria was ruled by the Ptolemies and the Seleucids; around 110 BCE the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the cities of Samaria and Shechem and the temple on Mount Gerizim. In 6 CE it became part of the Roman province of Iudaea.

Samaritan revolts against the Byzantine Empire, mostly in 525 and 555 CE, were suppressed with death, displacement and conversion to Christianity, and the Samaritan population fell sharply. Muslim rule followed from the 7th century, then the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Ayyubids, the Mamluks and, from 1516 to 1917, the Ottomans.

The ancient site of Samaria-Sebaste covers a hillside above the village of Sebastia and holds Canaanite, Israelite, Hellenistic, Roman and Byzantine remains. Roman-era finds include a colonnaded street, a temple-lined acropolis and a lower city, where John the Baptist is believed to have been buried. The Harvard excavation, begun in 1908 under George Andrew Reisner, was followed in 1931–35 by a joint British-American-Hebrew University dig under John Winter Crowfoot. Their finds include inscriptions, coins and a large collection of ivory carvings from the early first millennium BCE.
samaritans: The Samaritans identify as descendants of the Israelite tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh and of the priestly tribe of Levi, and hold that they preserve the most authentic form of the Mosaic covenant. Their own tradition, recorded in the Kitab al-Ta'rikh compiled by Abu'l-Fath in 1355, traces the split from the southern Israelites to the priest Eli, who is said to have usurped the high priesthood and set up a rival shrine at Shiloh.

In contemporary scholarship the community is generally understood to have emerged in Samaria from populations of the former northern Kingdom of Israel together with people of Mesopotamian origin, its distinctive identity taking shape in the Persian and Hellenistic periods. Josephus, a key source, is considered a prejudiced witness hostile to them.

In 331 BCE the Samaritans rose against Macedonian rule and killed the prefect Andromachus, and the army carried out a brutal reprisal. A Samaritan diaspora is documented in the Hellenistic period, including inscriptions on Delos. Under the Roman Empire Samaria became part of the province of Judaea, and Samaritans appear in the Christian gospels, notably in the account of the Samaritan woman at the well and the parable of the Good Samaritan.

Their numbers were drastically reduced by failed revolts and severe Byzantine repression in the 5th and 6th centuries CE. According to Samaritan sources the emperor Zeno persecuted them, appropriated Mount Gerizim and built a tomb for his son there, and by 484 they revolted, burning five churches in Neapolis and electing a king, Justa, who was killed by the Byzantine commander.

Christianisation under the Byzantines and gradual conversion to Islam after the Muslim conquest reduced them further. In the 12th century Benjamin of Tudela estimated about 1,900 remained in Palestine and Syria. Ottoman censuses of 1525-1526 recorded 25 Samaritan families in Gaza and 29 in Nablus, and the community reached a low of around 100 in 1786. Their situation improved under the British Mandate.

Samaritans recognise only the Samaritan Pentateuch as scripture, which they believe to be the original version of the Torah given to Moses, and it differs from the Masoretic text in some 6,000 places. They hold that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, is God's chosen sanctuary, and that Abraham was commanded there to offer Isaac. Their religion centres on a hereditary high priesthood, strict observance of biblical law and festivals, and the Passover sacrifice on Gerizim.

Many believe that at the end of days the dead will be resurrected by the Taheb, a restorer. They use Samaritan Hebrew and Samaritan Aramaic for liturgy, written in the Samaritan script. The community comprises four families or houses, Cohen, Tsedakah, Danafi and Marhiv, and lives mainly at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus and in Holon.
samarkand: Samarkand is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Central Asia and prospered from its place on the trade route between China, Persia and Europe. There is no direct evidence of when it was founded; researchers at the Institute of Archaeology of Samarkand date it to around 700 BCE. It was the central city of the Sogdian civilisation. It was known as Marakanda when Alexander the Great conquered it in 329 BCE. According to some sources the present name comes from the Sogdian samar, stone, and kand, fort or town, though this cannot be proven.

The Persian Sasanians conquered Samarkand around 260 CE, and under their rule the region became an essential site for Manichaeism. Nomadic Xionites took it between 350 and 375, and the Hephthalites controlled it until the Göktürks, allied with the Sasanians, won it around 560. The armies of the Umayyad Caliphate under Qutayba ibn Muslim captured the city around 712. It was the capital of the Samanid Empire in the 9th century, when New Persian gradually replaced Sogdian, and from 1040 to 1212 it was the capital of the Western Qarakhanid Khaganate.

The Mongols under Genghis Khan conquered the city in 1220. According to the historian Juvayni, Genghis killed all who had taken refuge in the citadel and the mosque, pillaged the city completely and conscripted 30,000 young men and 30,000 craftsmen. Samarkand remained in the Chagatai Khanate until 1370. Timur ruled from 1370 to 1405 and made it the capital of the Timurid Empire. Between 1417 and 1420 his grandson Ulugh Beg built a madrasah that became the first building of the Registan ensemble, and in 1428 he built an observatory whose chief instrument was a wall quadrant with a radius of 40 metres.

Muhammad Shaybani of the Uzbek Shaybanid dynasty took the city in 1501, and it became the capital of the new Bukhara Khanate. Russian forces under General Konstantin Petrovich von Kaufman took the citadel in 1868, and the Russian section of the city was built to the west of the old city. Samarkand was the first capital of the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic, from 1925 to 1930.

Samarkand is the second-largest city of Uzbekistan and capital of the Samarkand Region. The Timurid and Uzbek Khanate periods gave it the Registan Square, the Gur-i Amir Mausoleum, the Bibi-Khanym Mosque and the Shah-i-Zinda Necropolis, known for their tilework in cobalt and turquoise. UNESCO added the city to its World Heritage List in 2001 as Samarkand, Crossroads of Cultures.
samarra: Samarra stands on the east bank of the Tigris in the Saladin Governorate, 125 kilometres north of Baghdad. Its earliest remains were first excavated between 1911 and 1914 by the German archaeologists Ernst Herzfeld and Friedrich Sarre, and Samarra became the type site of the Samarra culture, which flourished alongside the Ubaid period as one of the first town states in the Near East. A Neo-Assyrian city, Sur-marrati, refounded by Sennacherib in 690 BCE, is insecurely identified with a fortified site opposite the modern city.

In 836 CE the caliph al-Mu'tasim founded a new capital on the Tigris. He built extensive palace complexes surrounded by garrison settlements for his guards, drawn mostly from Central Asia and Iran, chiefly the Turks, or from North Africa. Although often called Mamluk slave soldiers, their status was quite elevated, and some of their commanders bore Sogdian titles of nobility. Earlier, Harun al-Rashid had dug a canal here and laid out the octagonal city of al-Mubarak, abandoned unfinished in 796.

Caliph al-Mutawakkil sponsored lavish palaces, such as al-Mutawakkiliyya, and the Great Mosque of Samarra with its spiral minaret, the Malwiya, built in 847. The Nestorian patriarch Sargis moved the seat of the Church of the East from Baghdad to Samarra to be close to the seat of power. Samarra remained the caliph's residence until 892, when al-Mu'tadid returned the capital to Baghdad. The city was looted around this time, and its population probably fell, though it remained an important market centre. Later the river's course shifted to the east, the main road from Baghdad to Mosul moved to the west bank, and Samarra lost its importance as a trading town.

From the tenth century the city became a pilgrimage site. In the 1730–1735 Ottoman–Persian War the Battle of Samarra cost over 50,000 Ottoman and Persian casualties and decided the fate of Ottoman Iraq, which stayed under Istanbul's suzerainty until the First World War. In the 1950s the Samarra Barrage created Lake Tharthar to prevent the flooding of Baghdad.

Samarra is a holy site in Shia Islam because of the al-Askari Shrine, which holds the tombs of the tenth and eleventh Imams, Ali al-Hadi and Hasan al-Askari, and of Hakimah and Narjis, female relatives of the Prophet and the Imams. The archaeological site preserves much of the historic city's plan, architecture and artistic relics, and UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2007. A story of an appointment with Death at Samarra, from the Babylonian Talmud, was retold by W. Somerset Maugham and gave John O'Hara's novel its title.
samatata: Inscriptions, Chinese writings and archaeology place Samatata in the trans-Meghna part of the Bengal delta, along the Meghna River and its tributaries. At its widest it took in much of present-day eastern and southern Bangladesh, including the districts of Sylhet, Dhaka, Comilla, Noakhali, Barisal and Chittagong, the islands of Hatia, Sandwip and Bhola, and the undivided 24 Parganas in southern West Bengal, with parts of Tripura and northern Arakan. Its neighbours were Vanga, Pundravardhana and Kamarupa. In Sanskrit sama means equal and tata means shore.

Punch-marked coins from the Wari-Bateshwar ruins suggest that the region was probably a province of the Mauryan Empire. The archaeologist Sufi Mostafizur Rahman identifies the fortified riverside site there with Sounagoura, a trading post Ptolemy placed on the old course of the Brahmaputra, and Dilip Kumar Chakrabarti argues that Wari-Bateshwar, occupied from the mid-fifth century BCE, was probably Samatata's ancient capital. Alexander Cunningham held that Jessore was the capital.

Between the 6th and 11th centuries the Gauda, Khadga, Deva, Chandra and Varman dynasties made Samatata a leading region of Bengal, and its rulers also held parts of Arakan, Tripura and Kamarupa. The Khadgas came from Vanga, and a Chinese account places the capital of their king Rajabhatta at Karmanta-vasaka, identified with Barakamata village near Comilla. The Devas ruled from Devaparvata at Mainamati, where they built the Shalban, Ananda and Bhoj viharas. The Chandras, strong enough to hold off the Pala Empire, had ports linked with present-day Myanmar, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam, and may have helped spread Mahayana Buddhism in Southeast Asia.

Xuanzang, who called the kingdom San-mo-ta-ch'a, found 30 monasteries and 2,000 monks there; the later traveller Yijing counted 4,000 monks and nuns. During the Muslim conquest of Bengal in the 13th century Samatata was the last refuge of the Sena kings, and the forces of the Delhi Sultanate eventually absorbed it. Its decline coincided with the decline of Buddhism in India.
samaveda: The Samaveda, from the Sanskrit saman, "song", and veda, "knowledge", is the Veda of melodies and chants. It is a liturgical text of 1,875 verses, all but 75 of them taken from the Rigveda. Its earliest parts are believed to date from as early as the Rigvedic period, but the existing samhita belongs to the post-Rigvedic Mantra period. Michael Witzel, who notes that there is no absolute dating for the Vedic texts, estimates it at 1200 to 1000 BCE, roughly contemporary with the Atharvaveda and the Yajurveda.

The text has several layers: the Samhita, the oldest, then Brahmana texts and finally the Upanishads, likely composed around the 6th century BCE. Three recensions survive. The Kauthuma is current in Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal, the Ranayaniya in Maharashtra and Karnataka among other regions, and the Jaiminiya in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Kerala. The Jaiminiya preserves the oldest surviving tradition of Samavedic chanting.

The Samaveda has two major parts: four collections of melodies and three books of verses. The Gramageya melodies were for public recitation, and the Aranyageya for personal meditative use, as in the solitude of a forest. The verse books divide into the Purvarcika, with 585 single-stanza verses arranged by deity, and the Uttararcika, arranged by ritual. In all there are 1,549 unique verses. The purpose of the text was liturgical, and it was the repertoire of the udgatar, or singer, priests.

The text is not meant to be read: like a musical score, it must be heard. It contains notated melodies, probably the oldest that survive anywhere. Frits Staal argued that the melodies likely existed before the verses, since some early words fit them well and later ones do not, and that stobha, embellishing syllables, were used to fit words to the music. The Chandogya Upanishad and the Kena Upanishad are embedded in the Samaveda; the Chandogya was cited 810 times by Adi Shankara in his commentary on the Vedanta Sutra.

Theodor Benfey published a German edition in 1848, Satyavrata Samashrami a Sanskrit one in 1873, Filipp Fortunatov a Russian translation in 1875 and Ralph Griffith an English translation in 1893. The Samaveda has received less attention than the Rigveda, since all but 75 of its verses derive from it. In the Bhagavad Gita Krishna says, "Among the Vedas I am the Samaveda." Guy Beck holds that Indian classical music and dance are rooted in its sonic and musical dimensions, and musicologists widely acknowledge its chant theory as a root of Indian music.
samawah: Samawah is built on both sides of the Euphrates, 280 kilometres (174 mi) southeast of Baghdad and midway between Baghdad and Basra. It is the capital of the Al Muthanna Governorate, which was established in 1975; before that date the area formed a single province with Qadissiya (Diwaniya) and Najaf. Hundreds of palm groves surround the city, and they inspired the Iraqi folk song The Palm of Samawah. About 25 km to the north lies Sawa Lake, a salt lake with no obvious source, whose water stands above ground level behind natural levees.

The city was settled by the Arab tribe of Banu Quda'a around the 3rd century CE. Its commercial heart and old town lie on the west bank, including the covered market Suq Al Masgoof, which dates to the Ottoman period, and the Jewish quarter. The Saray on the east bank, also from Ottoman times, was the seat of authority and the focus of popular uprisings over the following century, among them one in 1991 when prisoners were freed by the townspeople. The ruins of Uruk, the Sumerian city dating to about 4000 BCE, lie nearby; the oldest written script found there dates to about 3300 BCE.

The terrorisation of the Jewish minority by Arab nationalists in the 1940s and after drove most of its members into exile, and the Torat Synagogue has stood abandoned since. Al Muthanna province holds Nigret Al Salman, a desert prison camp in use since the monarchy (1921–1958), which housed the surviving prisoners of the Dujail Massacre and, during the Anfal campaign against the Kurds, older men and women. In 1979–81 Shia Iraqis deemed to be of Persian origin were deported by the Baathist government. In 2003 U.S. forces took the town in the Battle of Samawah, a running battle with Baathist forces in the days after the invasion of Iraq.

The population is primarily Shiite, with a small Sunni community. The surrounding land produces dates, wheat, barley, citrus fruits and tomatoes, and the Bahr al Milh, or Salt Sea, 20 km to the southwest, is a main source of industrial salt in Iraq. Cement plants built in the 1970s once made Samawah home to the largest cement works in the Middle East, and its rail yard overhauls locomotives and rolling stock on the Baghdad–Basra line.
sambandar: What is known of Sambandar comes mainly from the Periya Puranam, the 11th-century Tamil book on the Nayanars, and from the earlier Tiruttondartokai of Sundarar and Nambiyandar Nambi's Tiru Tondar Tiruvandadi; a Sanskrit life, the Brahmapureesa Charitam, is lost. According to these texts he was born in Sirkazhi to Sivapada Hrudiyar and his wife Bhagavathiar, who were Shaivite Brahmins. He was a contemporary of Appar, another Shaiva poet-saint.

Tradition holds that when he was three his parents took him to the Shiva temple, where Shiva and Parvati appeared to him. Seeing drops of milk on the child's mouth, his father asked who had fed him, and the boy pointed to the sky and sang Todudaya Seviyan, the first verse of the Tevaram, which praises Shiva as the lord who dwells at Piramapuram. At the same age he is said to have mastered the Vedas.

Tradition credits him with a vast output in complex metres, of which 383 or 384 hymns survive, preserved in the first three volumes of the Tirumurai, the canon of Tamil Shaiva Siddhanta. They express intense loving devotion, bhakti, to Shiva. John Cort reads his praise of the namah sivaya mantra as turning the essence of the Vedas into a direct, personal bond with Shiva that did not pass through Brahmin priests. His hymns also carry a bitter polemic against Jain monks, which Richard Davis reads as a symbolic contest of ideas and patronage.

Tradition says he merged with the divine light at his own wedding, together with all who attended, in the Tamil month of Vaikasi, at the age of sixteen. An inscription of Rajaraja Chola I at Tiruvarur names him beside Appar, Sundarar and Sundarar's wife Nangai Paravaiyar, and Chola records show singers of the hymns maintained in the temples. His image, a child or youth pointing upwards, stands in almost every Shiva temple of Tamil Nadu, and Odhuvars still sing the Tevaram after the daily rites. Francis Kingsbury and Godfrey Phillips translated 24 of his hymns into English in 1921.
sambhar-salt-lake: The lake surrounds the historic town of Sambhar and straddles the Nagaur and Jaipur districts, bordering Ajmer district, with the Aravali hills all around. It is a playa, a seasonal lake with a flat bottom, and the largest in the Thar Desert. Fed mainly by four seasonal streams, the Rupangarh, Mendha, Kharian and Khandel, it drains a catchment of 5,700 square kilometres. Its water is three to four times as salty as the sea, and its depth varies from about 60 centimetres in the dry season to about 3 metres after the monsoon, when it covers up to 230 square kilometres.

Small excavations in 1884 found terracotta pieces, coins, seals and a clay stupa, and the sculpture of Sambhar appears to show the influence of Buddhism. A larger excavation around 1934 yielded many terracotta figurines, stoneware and decorated discs, some of them now in the Albert Hall Museum. The Mahabharata and the Bhagavata Purana name Sambhar as the capital of the demon king Vrishparva, where his priest Shukracharya lived and his daughter Devayani married the emperor Yayati; a temple near the lake is dedicated to her.

Believers hold that the goddess Shakambhari, a form of Durga and the tutelary goddess of the Chauhan Rajputs, created the lake: in one legend she turned a forest into a plain of precious jewels and then, fearing strife over them, into salt. The name Sambhar comes from a form of Shakambhari that arose around the 6th century. The Mughal dynasty managed its salt, and afterwards the princely states of Jaipur and Jodhpur shared it. A sandstone dam 5.1 km long divides the basin, and east of it salt has been farmed in evaporation ponds for a thousand years.

The lake supplies most of Rajasthan's salt, much of it produced by the state-owned company Sambhar Salts Ltd. It was designated a Ramsar wetland in 1990 and is a wintering ground for Greater and Lesser Flamingos. In 2019 thousands of migratory birds died there of avian botulism.
sambia-peninsula: Sambia is a peninsula bounded by the Curonian Lagoon to the north-east, the Vistula Lagoon to the south-west, the Pregolya River to the south and the Deyma River to the east. It is named after the Sambians, an extinct tribe of Old Prussians. The landscape is hilly in the west, with coastal bluffs and beaches, and low and flat in the east; its highest point, Galtgarben, rises to 111 metres. Gvardeysk lies at its south-eastern end and Polessk at the north-eastern end, and the coast holds the port of Baltiysk and the seaside resorts of Zelenogradsk and Svetlogorsk.

Amber has been found here for over two thousand years, and the ancient Amber Road led south from Old Prussian settlements such as Kaup in Sambia. In imperial Germany the right to collect it was restricted to the Hohenzollern dynasty, and from the 19th century it was mined on an industrial scale, by Germans before 1945 and by Soviets and Russians afterwards, at Yantarny. The Greek traveller Pytheas is thought to refer to the area as an amber island called Abalus.

The Teutonic Knights conquered Sambia in the 13th century and the Bishopric of Samland was established in 1243. Settlers from the Holy Roman Empire arrived and the Sambians were gradually assimilated; the peninsula was the last area where Old Prussian was spoken, until the language died out at the beginning of the 18th century. After the Thirteen Years' War it was held from 1466 as part of Poland, as a fief of the Teutonic Order, and from 1525 it belonged to the Duchy of Prussia, which became the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 and part of the Province of East Prussia in 1773.

It entered the German Empire in 1871. In 1945 the Soviet Union annexed northern East Prussia, including Sambia, and expelled its German inhabitants under the Potsdam Agreement. It became part of the Kaliningrad Oblast, was repopulated with Russians and Belarusians, and until 1991 was largely a closed military area.
sambor-prei-kuk: Sambor Prei Kuk lies in Kampong Thom Province, 30 km north of the provincial capital, 176 km east of Angkor and 206 km north of Phnom Penh, on the eastern bank of the Tonle Sap lake close to the Steung Saen River. It stands amid mature sub-tropical forest with limited undergrowth. The complex is made of three clusters, called North, South and Central, each with a square layout surrounded by a brick wall, and the whole is enclosed by a double wall around about 1,000 acres in which 150 Hindu temples stood, mostly now in ruins.

Isanavarman I reigned over the Chenla Kingdom from 616 to 637 and took Isanapura as his capital. He is argued to have built the main temple, Prasat Sambor in the North group, which was dedicated to a form of Shiva called Gambhireshvara; an inscription on the site attributed to his reign is dated 13 September 627. He sent his first embassy to the Sui court in China in 616–617, and an inscription of his reign calls him king of kings, ruling over Suvarnabhumi.

The South group, Prasat Yeah Puon, has 22 sanctuaries dated to 600–635 and dedicated to Shiva, while the Central group, with its lion sculptures that gave the name Prasat Tao, the Lions' Temple, is the newest, from the 9th century. The last important king at Isanapura was Jayavarman I, whose death caused turmoil at the start of the 8th century; the kingdom broke into principalities, opening the way to Angkor. The site is also claimed as an early capital of Jayavarman II.

The buildings are characteristic of the pre-Angkorian period, with simple external plans and brick as the main material, with sandstone for some structures. Features include prasats, octagonal towers, lingams and yonis, ponds, reservoirs and lion sculptures. After the coup of 1970, US aircraft bombed positions inside the site and left craters near the temples, and guerrillas laid mines that were cleared only in 2008. Sambor Prei Kuk was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list on 8 July 2017.
sambre: The Sambre is a river in northern France and in Wallonia, Belgium, and a left-bank tributary of the Meuse, which it joins at Namur, the Walloon capital. Its source lies near Le Nouvion-en-Thiérache, in the Aisne department. In France it passes Landrecies, Aulnoye-Aymeries, Hautmont and Maubeuge in the Nord department, and in Belgium Thuin, Montigny-le-Tilleul, Charleroi, Floreffe and Namur.
Its main tributaries include the Helpe Mineure, the Helpe Majeure, the Eau d'Heure, which gives its name to the Eau d'Heure lakes, the Piéton, which joins in Charleroi, and the Orneau.

The river runs through the Franco-Belgian coal basin, formerly an important industrial district. It lies at the western end of the sillon industriel, which remains the backbone of Wallonia's industry even though all coal mining has ceased and the steel industry has declined.

Navigation begins at Landrecies, where the Canal de la Sambre à l'Oise joins the river and links it with the central French waterway network, until navigation was interrupted in 2006 following structural failures. The French stretch runs 54 km with nine locks down to the border at Jeumont. Beyond the border the river is canalised in two sections over 88 km with 17 locks. The Haute-Sambre is 39 km long, with ten locks, down to Charleroi, and the rest of the Belgian river was upgraded to European Class IV dimensions, for barges of 1,350 tonnes, in the years after World War II.

Fleurus, a suburb of Charleroi on the north bank, saw three important battles: the Thirty Years' War Battle of Fleurus in 1622, the Nine Years' War Battle of Fleurus in 1690 and, on 26 June 1794, the Battle of Fleurus, the most significant battle of the Flanders Campaign in the French Revolutionary Wars. The last was fought on both banks of the river after a campaign of many crossings and re-crossings. Heavy fighting also occurred along the river in World War I, at the siege of Namur in 1914, during the Battle of Charleroi, and in the Battle of the Sambre in 1918.
samguk-sagi: The Samguk sagi was the first book compiled by a Korean government. King Injong of Goryeo, who reigned from 1122 to 1146, ordered its compilation, and a government official and historian, Kim Busik, undertook it with a team of junior scholars. It was completed in 1145 and is written in Classical Chinese, the written language of the literati. The motives were ideological and political. In his preface Kim Busik complained that scholars and high officials could discuss the Five Classics and the histories of Qin and Han in detail but were utterly ignorant of the events of their own country from beginning to end.

It was based on the Old History of the Three Kingdoms and on earlier records such as the Annals of Hwarang, most of which no longer survive. For external material Kim Busik drew generously on Chinese dynastic chronicles and even unofficial Chinese records, among them the Records of the Three Kingdoms, the Book of Wei, the Book of Jin, the Old and New Books of Tang and the Zizhi Tongjian. He cites no Japanese chronicle such as the Kojiki or the Nihon Shoki, and he may have been ignorant of them or scorned to quote them.

The work has 50 books, each originally a scroll. Twelve scrolls hold the annals of Silla, ten those of Goguryeo and six those of Baekje. Three scrolls of chronological tables follow, then nine monographs on rites and music, vehicles, clothing and dwellings, the geography of the three kingdoms and the offices of the Silla government, and ten scrolls of biographies.

The biographies begin with three books on Kim Yusin, and the later ones cover generals such as Ŭlchi Mundŏk and Gyebaek, scholars including Ch'oe Ch'iwŏn, hwarang warriors, and the figures of Book 49, Ch'ang Chori and Yŏn Kaesomun. The last book concerns the later kings Kung Ye and Kyŏn Hwŏn. The translation tables in Books 35 and 36 have been used for a tentative reconstruction of the Goguryeo language.

The Samguk sagi is critical to the study of Korea in the Three Kingdoms and Unified Silla periods. Together with its Buddhist counterpart, the Samguk yusa, it is the only surviving Korean source for the era, and it holds a large amount of detail. It is well known in Korea as the oldest surviving chronicle of Korean history. The National Institute of Korean History has digitized it and offers it online with a modern Korean translation in Hangul.
samguk-yusa: The Samguk yusa was written in Classical Chinese in the late Goryeo dynasty. Its compiler, the Buddhist monk Il-yeon (1206–1289), became a monk at the age of eight in 1214 and served as abbot of various temples. The Mongols first invaded Korea in 1231 and destroyed valuable cultural properties, records and literature, which motivated Il-yeon to preserve the folklore and stories handed down. The earliest version is believed to have been compiled in the 1280s, and the earliest extant printing dates from 1512.

Il-yeon's name appears in the fifth fascicle, and most modern scholars accept him as the main compiler, though his disciple Muguk (1250–1322) and others probably expanded it. The word yusa means a text supplementary to an earlier work, here the Samguk sagi.

The work has five volumes in nine parts. Wangnyeok is a brief chronology, and Gii holds records from Gojoseon to the late Three Kingdoms. Heungbeop treats the rise of Buddhism, Tapsang pagodas and Buddhist images, Uihae the lives of noted monks, and the remaining parts miracles, devotion, solitary heroes and filial piety. It begins with Dangun Wanggeom, the mythological ancestor who founded Gojoseon. It includes the tale of Lady Suro, whom a dragon drags into the sea, and Choshin's Dream, in which a monk lives a long hard life that turns out to have been a dream. Buddhist stories make up nearly half of the text.

Samguk yusa is National Treasure No. 306 and a key source for ancient Korean history, religion and language. Its fourteen hyangga, ancient Korean songs, are important to the study of early Korean literature. Il-yeon quoted the Tangun legend from the Wei-shu and the Tangun Kogi, texts that are no longer accessible. Historians question its reliability because of its myths and because it was written about six centuries after the Three Kingdoms, and most of its stories concern Silla and its upper class. It is often compared with the Samguk sagi of the Confucian statesman Kim Pusik, and the two works are regarded as complementary.
sami-people: The Sámi are the traditionally Sámi-speaking indigenous people of Sápmi, formerly called Lapland. In English they were long known as Lapps, a term some Sámi regard as offensive. Their languages form a branch of the Uralic family. The groups that reached the Finnish Lakeland between 1600 and 1500 BCE later became the Sámi, who arrived in Sápmi during the Bronze Age or early Iron Age.

The first probable mention is by Tacitus, about 98 CE, who called them Fenni. Norse speakers used Finn for the Sámi, as in the Icelandic Eddas and sagas of the eleventh to fourteenth centuries. The word Lapp appears in Saxo Grammaticus's twelfth-century Gesta Danorum, and Johannes Schefferus's Lapponia of 1673 made it standard.

For centuries the Sámi and the Scandinavians had little contact. The Sámi lived mainly in the inland north, while Scandinavians gradually settled the Norwegian coast. Until the bubonic plague reached northern Norway in 1349 the two peoples occupied separate economic niches, the Sámi herding reindeer or fishing along the fjords. How far south the Sámi settled has long been debated: Yngvar Nielsen, commissioned by the Norwegian government in 1889, concluded they had lived no farther south than Lierne until about 1500, but later archaeological finds suggest a presence in southern Norway in the Middle Ages.

From the eighteenth and especially the nineteenth century the governments of Norway and Sweden asserted sovereignty more aggressively in the north and pursued forced assimilation. Generations of Sámi children were taken to missionary or state-run boarding schools, and laws denied the Sámi rights to their beliefs, language, land and livelihoods. In the 1970s the idea of Sápmi as a Sámi nation gained acceptance, and a flag, an anthem and a national day followed in the 1980s and 1990s.

Traditional livelihoods include coastal fishing, fur trapping and sheep herding, and the best known is semi-nomadic reindeer herding. Herders traditionally lived in groups of several families called siidat. About 10 percent of Sámi are connected to herding, which in some regions of the Nordic countries is legally reserved for them.

There are ten distinct Sámi languages, closely related but not mutually intelligible. Many Sámi kept their ancestral religion until the eighteenth century, and most now belong to the Lutheran churches of Norway, Sweden and Finland. The joik, a song-chant sung a cappella, is characteristic of the music, and the craft duodji makes useful objects from wood, bone, antler and leather. The Laponian Area in Swedish Lappland became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
samnite-wars: The Samnites were a confederation of four tribes living in the mountains east of Campania. Rome and the Samnites made a treaty in 354 BCE whose terms are not recorded; modern historians have proposed that it made the River Liris the boundary between their spheres. Livy, the only continuous source for the first war, says it began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini and then the Campanians, and Capua surrendered itself to Rome. Modern historians doubt his three Roman victories of 343 BCE. The war ended in 341 BCE in a negotiated peace: Rome accepted that the Sidicini lay in the Samnite sphere but kept its alliance with the Campanians.

The second war grew out of Roman moves in Campania: a colony founded at Fregellae in 328 BCE and the taking of Naples in 326 BCE. In 321 BCE the consuls Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius Albinus were trapped by the Samnite commander Gaius Pontius in the Caudine Forks and surrendered; their soldiers passed unarmed under the yoke and six hundred equites were given as hostages. Livy says Rome rejected the agreement and avenged it, a claim some modern scholars doubt. Fighting resumed in 316 BCE, and in 304 BCE, after the fall of Bovianum, the Samnites sought peace; Livy says the old treaty was restored.

The third war began in 298 BCE, when the Lucanians asked for Roman protection against Samnite invasion. In 295 BCE Rome faced a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senone Gauls. At Sentinum the consul Publius Decius Mus devoted himself, charging into the enemy line to his death, and Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus won the battle; Livy gives 8,700 Roman dead and 20,000 of the enemy. Livy's surviving narrative ends in 293 BCE, and the last campaigns to 290 BCE are known only in outline.

The Samnites were forced to become allies of Rome, on terms that must have been unequal, and a colony was planted at Venusia in south-eastern Samnia. Gaius Pontius was captured, paraded in a triumph and beheaded. Around Samnia Rome had already bound the Marsi, Marrucini, Paeligni and Frentani by alliance in 304 BCE and the Vestini in 302 BCE, and it annexed the Hernici and the Sabines by giving them citizenship without the vote. The allies supplied soldiers at their own expense and shared the spoils, which greatly enlarged the manpower Rome could call on.
samo: Almost everything known of Samo comes from the Chronicle of Fredegar, written about 660, the only contemporary source; later accounts all derive from it. Fredegar calls him a Frank by birth from the pago Senonago, which could be Soignies in Belgium or Sens in France. A text written at Salzburg in the ninth century, the Conversio Bagoariorum et Carantanorum, makes him a Carantanian merchant instead, and Slavic nationalist accounts have often preferred a Slavic origin. According to Fredegar, the Wends had long been subjects of the Avars, who wintered among them, took their wives and daughters and demanded levies.

Samo went to the Slavs as a merchant, perhaps one of those who supplied them with arms for their frequent revolts. When the Wends rose against the Avars, he accompanied their army, and a great many Avars fell to Wendish swords. His victories led to his election as king. The date is uncertain. Fredegar places his arrival in the fortieth year of Chlothar II, 623 to 624, but many scholars think the rising followed the Avar defeat at the siege of Constantinople in 626. Samo secured his throne by marrying into the major Wendish families, with at least twelve wives, twenty-two sons and fifteen daughters.

His realm probably lay in southern Moravia, Lower Austria and western Slovakia, and is generally thought to have included Bohemia, Silesia and Lusatia. Whether it also took in Carantania is disputed. After the Franks invaded in 630 over banditry against Frankish merchants, Samo's forces routed the army of King Dagobert I near Wogastisburg in 631, and the Franks lost most of the besieging armies. Samo then raided Thuringia, and the Sorbian duke Dervan, until then subject to the Franks, joined him. In 641 the rebellious Radulf of Thuringia sought an alliance with Samo against King Sigebert III.

Samo ruled, by Fredegar's count, for thirty-five years, and died in 658 or 659. His title did not pass to his sons, and little is known of his union afterwards, though it is generally assumed to have ended. The Avars returned to their earlier lands, and the Moravian and Nitravian principalities of the late 8th century are the first firm trace of these Slavs. Great Moravia is viewed as a continuation or successor of his realm, which is often called the first Slavic state.
samoan-islands: The archipelago covers 3,030 km2 in the central South Pacific and has 18 islands spread from west to east. It lies between 13° and 14° south latitude, about 800 km from Fiji, 530 km from Tonga, 2,900 km from New Zealand and 4,000 km from Hawaii. The larger islands are volcanic, mountainous and covered in tropical moist forest, while some of the smaller ones are coral atolls with black sand beaches.

In the west, Upolu (1,718 km2) is the most populous island and Savaiʻi (1,125 km2) the largest and highest, with Mt Silisili at 1,858 m. The small islands of Manono, Apolima and Nuʻulopa lie in the Apolima Strait between them, and the four Aleipata Islands lie off the east of Upolu. In the east, Tutuila is the largest island of American Samoa, and the Manuʻa group comprises Ofu, Olosega and Taʻū. The islands may have been formed by the Samoa hotspot, though some evidence long seemed inconsistent with that theory until submarine samples gathered in 2005 gave older ages.

The oldest known evidence of human activity dates to around 1050 BCE, from a Lapita site at Mulifanua wharf on Upolu. The inhabitants share the Samoan language, a culture called faʻa Samoa and an indigenous form of governance called faʻamatai. In 1768 the French explorer Bougainville visited the eastern islands and named them the Navigator Islands, a name that missionaries used until about 1845 and official European dispatches until about 1870.

In the late 19th century the United States, Germany and the United Kingdom competed for control of the islands. In 1892 the ruler Malietoa Laupepa proclaimed that Monday 4 July would occur twice, moving the islands to the eastern side of the International Date Line, probably because of increasing trade with Americans. The Tripartite Convention of December 1899 partitioned the archipelago into German Samoa in the west and American Samoa in the east. New Zealand began occupying the western islands in World War I and governed them under a League of Nations Class C Mandate from 1920 to 1946 and as a United Nations Trust Territory from 1946 to 1962. The Mau movement, popular across the area, led to independence in 1962.

The archipelago comprises all of the Independent State of Samoa, whose capital is Apia, and most of American Samoa, an unincorporated territory of the United States whose capital is Pago Pago. The two jurisdictions are separated by 64 km of ocean at their closest points. Together they have approximately 250,000 inhabitants, and Samoans are one of the largest Polynesian populations in the world. Independent Samoa was known as Western Samoa until 1997. It moved back to the western side of the date line by skipping Friday 30 December 2011.
samogitia: Samogitia, in Lithuanian Žemaitija, is one of the five cultural regions of Lithuania and was formerly one of the two core administrative divisions of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, alongside Lithuania proper. Its capital is Telšiai and its largest city is Šiauliai. The Lithuanian name comes from žemas, low, and žemė, land, and means lowlands. Its people speak Samogitian, a variety of Lithuanian with a broken intonation similar to that of Latvian. The region is predominantly Roman Catholic, with Lutheran minorities in the south.

The territory of ancient Samogitia was much larger than the present region and embraced central and western Lithuania. The original Samogitian culture, known from flat burial grounds in the central lowlands, formed as early as the 5th and 6th centuries. The western part, inhabited before the 12th and 13th centuries by southern Semigallians and southern Curonians, became ethnically Lithuanian between the 13th and 16th centuries.

From the 13th to the 16th centuries the Teutonic Order and the Livonian Order bordered Samogitia, and the land was offered to them or exchanged in peace treaties several times, Lithuania regaining it in later conflicts. Invasions began in 1229, and battles included Saule in 1236, Skuodas in 1259, Durbe in 1260 and Lielvārde in 1262. Between 1345 and 1382 the Teutonic Knights attacked from Prussia some 70 times and the Livonian Knights about 30. Fortresses were attacked, farms and crops burned, women and children enslaved and men killed.

The Samogitians held their lands until the Battle of Grunwald in 1410, where united Polish-Lithuanian forces defeated the Order. In the 15th century Samogitia was the last region of core Europe to be converted to Christianity, and until the 18th century it was the Duchy or Eldership of Samogitia, an autonomous unit of the Grand Duchy. After the partitions of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth it passed to the Russian Empire, and in the 19th century it was the main source of the Lithuanian cultural revival and a focal point for smuggling Lithuanian books, which were banned. After the First World War it became part of the re-established Lithuanian state.

Samogitia corresponds to no present administrative division of Lithuania. Its landmarks include the Hill of Crosses, Tauragė Castle and Plungė Manor, and Palanga and Žemaičių Kalvarija are visited by tourists and pilgrims. Its coat of arms shows a black bear with silver claws on a red shield, and the Lithuanian government recognised it and the region's flag on 21 July 1994.
samora-machel: Samora Moisés Machel was born on 29 September 1933 in the village of Madragoa, now Chilembene, in Gaza Province, to a family of farmers. Under Portuguese rule his father was classified as an "indígena", a native, and had to accept lower prices than white farmers, grow labour-intensive cotton and refrain from branding his cattle; even so he owned four ploughs and 400 head of cattle by 1940. Machel attended mission schools run by Catholic missionaries, finishing the fourth grade, and trained as a nurse.

He began his political activity at the Miguel Bombarda hospital in Lourenço Marques, protesting that black nurses were paid less than white ones. Warned that the Portuguese political police were watching him, he left the country and made his way to Dar es Salaam to join FRELIMO, travelling through Swaziland, South Africa and Botswana.

He was one of the second group of FRELIMO guerrillas sent for training in Algeria and then ran the movement's camp at Kongwa. When FRELIMO began the war of independence on 25 September 1964 he became a key commander, notably in Niassa, and became head of its army after the death of Filipe Samuel Magaia in October 1966.

After the change of government in Lisbon, Machel rejected General António de Spínola's plan for a referendum on independence, saying that one does not ask a slave if he wants to be free. Talks in Lusaka in June 1974 produced nothing, and FRELIMO turned to the military movement then holding power in Portugal. Machel became the first President of independent Mozambique in 1975.

He supported nationalist movements in Rhodesia, whose guerrillas operated from FRELIMO-held areas in Tete province, and sent Mozambican units to fight alongside ZANU guerrillas. In 1977 RENAMO, backed first by Rhodesia and later by South Africa, began a rebellion that plunged the country into civil war. On 30 June 1981 South African commandos attacked houses in Matola, killing 12 members of the African National Congress.

On 19 October 1986 Machel attended a summit at Mbala in Zambia. Although invited to stay overnight, he insisted on returning to Maputo, and his plane crashed that night into a hillside at Mbuzini, just inside South Africa. Machel and 33 others died; nine passengers at the back survived. The Margo Commission concluded that pilot error caused the crash, but the Mozambican and Soviet governments rejected its report, and the Soviet minority report suggested the aircraft was lured off course by a decoy beacon. Speculation continues.

His state funeral was held in Maputo on 28 October 1986, and he was buried in a star-shaped crypt at Mozambican Heroes' Square. Streets in many countries bear his name, and a memorial at the crash site was inaugurated on 19 January 1999 by Nelson Mandela.
samori-ture: Samori Ture was born around 1830 in Manyambaladugu, the son of Kemo Lanfia Ture, a Dyula weaver and merchant, and Sokhona Camara. His father set him to trading kola nuts from the coast for cloth. In 1853 the Cissé clan raided Sanankoro and captured his mother. Samori went to Madina to exchange himself for her and served seven years as a warrior for the Cissé, learning to handle firearms and converting to Islam. After 1859 he and his mother were freed, and he then joined a war band of the Manding region, took control of another, and from 1866 to 1873 built up his following.

In 1873 Samori defeated the pagan king Nantenin Famoudou Kourouma by bribing one of his lieutenants to switch sides. In 1875 he allied with the Bate Empire of the Kaba dynasty of Kankan, and by 1878 he was strong enough to proclaim himself Faama of his Wassoulou Empire. He imported breech-loading rifles through Freetown. In 1884 a council proclaimed Islam the state religion and he took the title of Almamy. When his forces forced conversion and destroyed sacred sites in 1885, the population rebelled, and the rebellion was put down brutally. The siege of Sikasso, capital of Kenedougou, lasted 15 months from April 1887 and failed.

Samori first fought the French in 1882, sacking Kiniéran on 21 February and fighting at Samaya on the 26th, where he turned to guerrilla tactics. He signed the Treaty of Kenieba Koura on 28 March 1886 and the treaty of Bissandougou on 23 March 1887. In March 1891 Colonel Louis Archinard took Kankan, and Samori answered with a war of manoeuvre and scorched earth and moved east, founding a second empire around Kong.
After Sikasso fell on 1 May 1898 he marched towards Liberia. Thousands died of starvation on the way, and Captain Henri Gouraud captured him at Guelemou on 29 September 1898.

Condemned to exile on 22 December 1898, Samori was deported to Gabon in February 1899 and held on the island of Missanga in the Ogooué River, a camp known as the dry guillotine for its death rate. He died there of pneumonia on 2 June 1900. In the interwar period African intellectuals began to rehabilitate his memory, and he is generally remembered as a hero and martyr of African resistance to colonialism, though some communities in southern Mali that suffered brutal repression under his rule remember him as a tyrant. His great-grandson Ahmed Sékou Touré became the first president of Guinea.
samos: The island covers 477.395 square kilometres and is 43 kilometres long and 13 kilometres wide. It is largely mountainous, with several relatively large and fertile plains. Two mountains dominate its relief: the Ampelos massif in the centre, rising to 1,095 metres, and Mount Kerkis, smaller in area but taller, whose summit at 1,434 metres is the island's highest point. Both are a continuation of the Mycale range on the Anatolian mainland. A great part of the island is covered with vineyards from which Muscat wine is made, and the capital is Vathy, in the north-east.

In antiquity Samos was a centre of Ionian culture and one of the twelve members of the Ionian League. By the 7th century BCE it was one of the leading commercial centres of Greece, trading with the Black Sea, Egypt, Cyrene, Corinth and Chalcis, and it founded colonies, mostly in the 6th century BCE. Its rivalry with Miletus broke into open war in the Lelantine War. About 535 BCE the tyrant Polycrates overturned the oligarchy, and Samos reached the height of its prosperity, with a navy that ruled the Aegean. After his death the Persian Empire conquered and partly depopulated the island.
In 440 BCE Samos seceded from the Delian League and, after a long siege, was forced to surrender to an Athenian fleet led by Pericles, and was ordered to pay 1,300 talents in instalments.

The Romans transferred the island in 189 BCE to the kingdom of Pergamon. Under the Byzantine Empire it became part of the Samos theme, and from 1346 to 1566 it was the property of the Genoese Giustiniani family. It came under Ottoman rule in 1475 or about 1479–80, when it was practically abandoned because of piracy and plague. In 1572/3 it was granted to the Ottoman admiral Kilic Ali Pasha, who attracted settlers with tax exemptions and considerable local autonomy. On 18 April 1821, under Lykourgos Logothetis, Samos joined the Greek War of Independence and repulsed three Ottoman attempts to retake it. Great Power pressure made it an autonomous, tributary principality under the Sultan. Greek troops landed in March 1913, and the Ottoman garrison withdrew.

Samos is a separate regional unit of the North Aegean region. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture and tourism, with grapes, honey, olives, olive oil and figs among its products. The town of Tigani was renamed Pythagoreio in 1955 in honour of Pythagoras.
samothrace: Samothrace is 17 km long and 178 square kilometres in size. It is one of the most rugged Greek islands, with Mount Saos and its highest peak, Fengari, rising to 1,611 metres. It never became a state of political significance in ancient Greece, since it lacks natural harbours and most of it is too mountainous for cultivation. The ancient city, whose ruins are called Palaeopolis, stood on the north coast, and considerable remains survive of its walls, built in massive Cyclopean style.

The Sanctuary of the Great Gods was the site of important Hellenic and pre-Hellenic religious ceremonies, the Samothracian Mysteries, which like the Eleusinian Mysteries were open to slaves and free people. Visitors initiated there included Lysander of Sparta, Philip II of Macedon and Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, father-in-law of Julius Caesar. The traditional account is that the island was first inhabited by Pelasgians and Carians and later by Thracians, while the archaeological evidence points to Greek settlement in the 6th century BCE.

Samothrace came under Persian occupation in 508 BCE, followed by a period of Athenian control, and it joined the Delian League in the 5th century BCE. It was under Macedonian suzerainty from Philip II until 168 BCE, was then independent, and was absorbed into the Roman Empire by Vespasian in 70 CE. In the imperial period pilgrims flocked to the sanctuary from all over the Roman world. The Byzantines ruled until 1204, when Venetians took their place, and a Genoese family, the Gattilusi, dislodged them in 1355. The Ottoman Empire conquered the island in 1457. It came under Greek rule after the Balkan Wars and was occupied by Bulgaria from 1941 to 1944.

The best-known find from the sanctuary is the 2.5-metre marble statue of Nike, now known as the Winged Victory of Samothrace, which dates from about 190 BCE. The French archaeologist Charles Champoiseau found it in pieces on the island in 1863, and it is now displayed, headless, at the Louvre in Paris. It appears on the island's municipal seal, and the Archaeological Museum of Samothrace stands by the sanctuary. The island's population was 2,596 at the 2021 census, and its main industries are fishing and tourism. The port town of Kamariotissa provides ferry links to northern Greece.
sampot: In Khmer art the deities of the pre-Angkor era wear skirt cloths, sampot samluy, knotted at the waist; from about the 900s this style is shown only on women. By the Baphuon period in the 11th century pleats were popular, and floral patterns were fashionable in depictions of the 12th and 13th centuries. The Indian scholar Ramanlal Nagarji Mehta has suggested that the Khmer textile word sampat-hol goes back to the Sanskrit sam-patola, meaning like a Patola.

The sampot chong kben is a unisex garment wrapped round the waist and twisted into a knot that is pulled between the legs and held by a belt; it was adopted in Thailand and Laos as the chong kraben. The sampot samloy hangs free as a wraparound or tube skirt, the sampot sup adds darts and a waistband, and the sampot bot is secured by a long flat fold along the side, a method said to come from Western influence.

Cloths are also named by their weaving. Hol is a weft ikat silk woven in uneven twill, so that one side is brighter than the other. Phamuong is a single-coloured, shimmering silk worn for formal events. Charobab, brocaded with silver and gold thread, is worn by dancers of Khmer classical dance, by royalty and at weddings, while the sampot soeng, with a patterned lower hem, spread from Laos in the 1980s.

In 1856 the Siamese King Mongkut and his Second King Phra Pin Klao presented to the US President Franklin Pierce three pairs of Khmer silk sampot chong kben of the hol kind. Henri Mouhot, the French naturalist who met the Cambodian king between 1858 and 1860, saw him in a langouti of yellow silk held by a gold belt set with precious stones.

Cambodians kept the sampot under the French, despite some westernisation. In the run-up to the 1993 general election Son Sann even called for a sampot test of whether women were truly Khmer. Rural and poorer Cambodians wear printed batik-patterned cloth imported from Indonesia rather than hand-woven silk, and the sampot is regarded as the national garment.
samsam-al-dawla: Abu Kalijar Marzuban was born in 963, the son of Adud al-Dawla and Sayyida bint Siyahgil, a daughter of the Gilite ruler Siyahgil, which made him a distant relation of the Ziyarid dynasty. In his father's lifetime he governed Buyid Oman and Khuzestan. Although Shirdil was the eldest son, Marzuban was considered the heir, but Adud al-Dawla never settled the question. Marzuban was in Baghdad when his father died and kept the death secret to secure his succession; on announcing it he took the title Samsam al-Dawla, Cutting Sword of the Dynasty, which the Abbasids recognised.

The disputed succession broke up the Buyid lands. Shirdil invaded Fars from Kerman as Sharaf al-Dawla, two other brothers set up rule in Basra and Khuzestan, and the Kurd Badh ibn Hasanwaih forced Samsam al-Dawla to confirm him in Diyar Bakr. In 983 the Turkic soldiers of Iraq went over to Sharaf, until Ziyar ibn Shahrakawayh, a maternal relative, persuaded most of them to stay. Samsam al-Dawla defeated the Dailamite rebel Saffar ibn Quddawiyah in 985 and took Basra and Khuzestan early in 986.

Sharaf al-Dawla then broke a peace between them, took Ahwaz and Wasit, and a revolt in Samsam's own army forced him to surrender. After Sharaf's death Samsam al-Dawla left prison and, aided by Sharaf's former vizier Ala ibn Hasan, took Fars, Kerman and Khuzestan from his brother Baha' al-Dawla. Threatened by their uncle Fakhr al-Dawla, the two brothers allied as equals, each taking the title of king, Samsam keeping Arrajan, Fars and Kerman. When Baha' al-Dawla attacked in 991, he was defeated, and Samsam al-Dawla regained Khuzestan and the Buyid lands in Oman.

To strengthen his position Samsam al-Dawla recognised Fakhr al-Dawla as senior amir. Fakhr's death in 997, and growing trouble within Samsam's realm, left Baha' al-Dawla the strongest of the Buyid princes. With the support of the Kurdish ruler Badr ibn Hasanwaih he invaded in December 998. Fleeing from Shiraz, Samsam al-Dawla was murdered near Isfahan by one of the sons of 'Izz al-Dawla. Baha' al-Dawla took Shiraz and reunited Iraq, Fars and Kerman. Historians judge that Samsam al-Dawla lacked his father's qualities and never gained a firm grip on the affairs of his state.
samsat: Samosata was founded some time before 245 BCE on the earlier Neo-Hittite site of Kummuh by Sames I, the Orontid king of Sophene, perhaps to assert his claim over the area. It became one of the Orontid kings' most important royal residences, built in a Persian architectural style, and its architecture shifted when the Orontids of Commagene drew closer to the Greco-Roman world. Antiochus I Theos, who reigned from 70 to 31 BCE, founded sanctuaries here with inscriptions about his cult and reliefs of his handshake with Apollo-Mithras. In 73 CE Samosata and the rest of Commagene were incorporated into the Roman Empire, and under Hadrian it was given the status of metropolis, together with Damascus and Tyre.

In 260 it was the first city sacked by the Sasanian emperor Shapur I after he captured the Roman emperor Valerian. Julian II had ships built here for his campaign against Shapur II. Lucian (c. 120–192) and Paul of Samosata, active around 260, were born here. The Arabs took Commagene from the Byzantines in 640, and in June 966 the town hosted an exchange of prisoners between Nikephoros II Phokas and Sayf al-Dawla.

In the early 12th century it was sold to Baldwin of Boulogne and joined the county of Edessa. Warfare devastated it in the 13th century: the Anatolian Seljuks took it in 1203, the Anushtegins looted it in 1237 and Hülagü Khan conquered it in 1240. Bayezid I briefly absorbed it into the Ottoman Empire in 1392, Timur destroyed it in 1401, and Selim I recaptured it in 1516 and renamed it Samsat.

The town was evacuated on 5 March 1988 and the old settlement was submerged in 1989 by the Atatürk Reservoir; a new town was built beside the new waterline. An earthquake destroyed it on 2 March 2017, and it was largely rebuilt. Its population was 3,790 in 2022. The tell, Samsat Höyük, was excavated from 1978 to 1987 under Ankara University and yielded evidence of settlement from the Halaf period to the Ottoman period; it now lies under the reservoir, and the old town below it was never excavated.
samsenthai: The king, whose name is written Samsenethai or Sam Saen Thai, was known before he took that name as Oun Hueun or Un Heuan. He was the son of Fa Ngum, whom he succeeded as king of Lan Xang in Laos, and of Queen Keo Kang Ya, who came from the Khmer Empire and died in 1368, five years before her son came to the throne.

Three temples, Wat Manorom, Wat Oubôsôt and Wat Xiang Kham, were built during his reign. In 1377 he married Queen Buvana Dhanipaya, also called Bua Then Fa, a daughter of his uncle. Among his other consorts was Nang Nawiangsari, or Noi On Sor, a daughter of the King of Lan Na. In 1393 he married his cousin Queen Keava Rudhi Fa, or Nang Keo Lot Fa, who was his father's widow and a daughter of King Ramadipati of Ayudhaya.
