He also took as consorts Princess Nang Keava Sridha, or Chao Nang Keo Sida, a daughter of Chao Sidhakama, the Hsenwifa of Muang Lü (Chieng Hung), and his cousin Princess Nang Keava Yudhi Fa, or Nang Keo Yot Fa, a daughter of King Intharacha of Ayutthaya. His wives thus came from his own family and from the ruling houses of Lan Na, Ayutthaya and Muang Lü. One daughter, Princess Mahakani, died before 1408 at the age of five.

Many of the kings who followed him were his sons. He was succeeded by Lan Kham Deng, his son by Bua Then Fa, who reigned from 1416 to 1428. After him the throne passed among other sons of Samsenethai within a few years: Konekham reigned from 1430 to 1432, Kham Tam Sa in 1432 and Thao Lue-Sai from 1432 to 1433. Kham Keul, his son by a slave, was king from 1436 to 1438. Another son, Vong Buri, also called Sai Tia Kaphut, reigned far longer, from 1442 to 1480. Other children named in the royal genealogy include Thao Somphon and the princesses Anocha, Manora and Supatthat.
samshvilde: The ruins lie on a rocky promontory at the confluence of the Khrami and Chivchavi rivers, 4 km south of the town of Tetritsqaro, beside a modern village of the same name. They stretch for 2.5 km and are 400 metres wide. The 10th-century Armenian chronicler Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi explained the name as three arrows, but it is formed from mshvildi, bow, and means a place of the bow. Excavations in 1968–1970 found two layers of the early Bronze Age Kura–Araxes culture, with a settlement, a burial ground and a circular cult building.

The medieval Georgian Chronicles call the place Orbi, ascribe its founding to Kartlos and say that Alexander the Great took it in his alleged campaign in the Georgian lands. From the 3rd century BCE it was the seat of an eristavi, or duke, under the kings of Kartli, and King Archil (c. 411–435) gave it to his son Mihrdat. In the 7th century Anania Shirakatsi named it with Tbilisi and Mtskheta as the three main towns of Iberia. Smbat I of Armenia occupied it around 888, and Kiurike II surrendered it to King Bagrat IV of Georgia in 1064.

The Seljuks under Malik-Shah I held it until 1110, when Bishop George of Chqondidi took it for King David IV, who granted it to Ivane Orbeli in 1123. George III stormed it in 1178 after the Orbeli revolt. In March 1440 Jahan Shah of the Qara Qoyunlu sacked the city; the historian Thomas of Metsoph wrote that he massacred its people and built a minaret of 1,664 severed heads at the gate. The city never recovered.

Taken by Lala Mustafa Pasha in 1578 and recovered by Simon I of Kartli in 1583, it remained a peripheral fortress. In 1747 the Muslim Georgian prince Abdullah Beg fortified it against Teimuraz II, whose son Heraclius stormed it in 1749. By the end of the 18th century it was in ruins.

The site is listed in the National Heritage of Georgia as the City-Site of Samshvilde. The citadel stands on the east of the promontory and the city proper on the west, with the walled fortress between. The domed Sioni church is dated to c. 759–777 by an inscription naming the Byzantine emperors Constantine V and Leo IV, though tradition credits Queen Sagdukht. Other remains include a basalt basilica, a church with an inscription naming David IV, palaces, cisterns, baths and a bridge.
samsi: Šamši came to power as a vassal of Assyria when the former queen Zabibe abdicated in her favour. On taking the throne she renewed Zabibe's oath of allegiance, swearing by the sun, the god of Arabia, to be loyal to Assyria, and Tiglath-Pileser III, son of Ashur-nirari V, formally recognised her accession. He was the first foreign ruler to bring the Arabs under his control. Like the queens before and after her, Šamši led embassies and caravans carrying spices and incense from the Arabian Peninsula to the Near East and Syria.

Assyrian chronicles describe her as a powerful ruler, bold enough to face the Assyrian kings in the 730s and 720s. She broke her oath by joining the alliance of Rezin of Damascus against Tiglath-Pileser. The Assyrian army, having recently subdued Edom, turned on the anti-Assyrian forces of Arabia and the Levant and defeated her near Mount Sa-qu-ur-ri, a place not identified. According to the Assyrian records the victors took many prisoners, 30,000 camels and more than 20,000 oxen; an inscription adds that 9,400 of her soldiers were killed and that 5,000 bags of spices, the altars of her gods, arms including an ornamental staff of her goddess, and her estates were seized.

The chroniclers wrote that she fled the battlefield like a wild she-ass of the desert, and Tiglath-Pileser burned the tents left behind. She was soon captured, or by another account escaped to the land of Bazu and then surrendered.

The Assyrians restored her because they needed a pliable Arab ruler to keep open the profitable trade route running north and south from Assyrian territory across Arabia. Tiglath-Pileser set a qepu, or governor, over her and her 10,000 soldiers, and she paid a tribute of gold, silver, camels and spices. Seven other kingdoms of the Arabian trade, among them Massa, Tyma and Saba, also had to pay tribute and guard the incense trade. Šamši ruled for over 20 years, and Queen Iatie succeeded her in about 700 BCE.
samson: Samson is described in the Book of Judges, chapters 13 to 16, as the last of the judges of the Israelites and one of the last leaders who judged the twelve tribes before the monarchy. According to the account, he lived at a time of repeated conflict between Israel and Philistia, when God was disciplining the Israelites by giving them into the hand of the Philistines.

His father Manoah, a Danite from Zorah, and his wife had no child until the Angel of the Lord told the wife that she would bear a son who would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. The boy was to be a Nazirite from birth, never shaving or cutting his hair, and his mother was to abstain from alcohol and unclean foods.

As a young man Samson fell in love with a Philistine woman from Timnah and decided to marry her despite his parents' objections; the account presents the marriage as part of God's plan to strike at the Philistines. Seized repeatedly by the Spirit of the Lord, he was given immense strength. On the way to ask for her hand he tore apart a lion with his bare hands, and he later killed a Philistine army with a donkey's jawbone. At Gaza he tore the city gate from its frame and carried it to the hill in front of Hebron.

He then fell in love with Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and Philistine leaders offered her 1,100 pieces of silver to learn the secret of his strength. He misled her three times, saying fresh bowstrings, new ropes or weaving his hair into a loom would bind him, and each time he broke free. According to the account she finally learned that cutting his hair would end his strength, had it cut while he slept and handed him to the Philistines, who gouged out his eyes and made him mill grain at Gaza.

The Philistine rulers gathered in the temple of Dagon, about 3,000 people in all, to celebrate Samson's capture. Samson's hair had begun to grow again in prison. He asked to lean against the pillars, prayed, recovered his strength and broke them, so that the temple collapsed and killed him and the people inside. Rabbinic literature identifies him with Bedan, a judge named in 1 Samuel 12:11, and Caesarius of Arles read his death as prefiguring the crucifixion. John Milton wrote the closet drama Samson Agonistes about him, and his emblem in Lungau, Austria, is carried in parades first documented in 1635.
samsu-iluna: Samsu-iluna was the seventh king of the founding Amorite dynasty of Babylon and the son and successor of Hammurabi. His name is Amorite and means "The Sun is our god". When Hammurabi died he had conquered Sumer, Eshnunna and Mari, reduced Assyria to vassal status and weakened Elam, so that Babylon was master of Mesopotamia. These states were weakened but not destroyed. Within a few years of Hammurabi's death Elam and Assyria had left Babylon's orbit and revolts had begun in the conquered territories. Dealing with them fell to Samsu-iluna.

In his ninth year a man calling himself Rim-Sin, known as Rim-Sin II and perhaps a nephew of the Rim-Sin who had opposed Hammurabi, raised a rebellion at Larsa that spread to some 26 cities, among them Uruk, Ur, Isin, Kisurra and Eshnunna. Samsu-iluna dealt the coalition a blow within a year, and the king of Eshnunna, Ilūni, was taken to Babylon and executed by strangulation. After four years of fighting along the borderlands he pulled down the walls of Ur and sacked it, did the same at Uruk and Isin, and defeated Larsa, where Rim-Sin II was killed.

A few years later a pretender named Ilum-ma-ili, claiming descent from the last king of Isin, led another revolt in Sumer. One battle was indecisive and a second went his way, and he founded the First Dynasty of Sea-Land, which held Sumer for some 300 years. By Samsu-iluna's death Nippur recognised Ilum-ma-ili as king. Kuturnahunte I of Elam entered the wall-less Uruk and plundered it, taking a statue of Inanna that was returned only under Ashurbanipal, eleven centuries later. Assyria also regained its independence under a native dynasty.

Samsu-iluna turned back a Kassite army in his ninth year, the earliest known mention of the Kassites. He also destroyed Apum, killed its king Yakun-ashar, and built the fortress of Dur-samsuiluna to hold Eshnunna after a second rebellion. He rebuilt the walls of Kish, Nippur and Sippar, restored temples and ziggurats, and promoted the cult of Marduk as his father had. Some scholars speculate that he introduced the Standard Babylonian calendar. Records at Ur and Uruk largely stop after his tenth year, and the archaeological evidence points to long abandonment of these southern cities.
samsung: According to its founder, the name Samsung means three stars: the three stands for something big, numerous and powerful, and the stars for something everlasting. In 1938, in the Japanese era, Lee Byung-chul, a member of a large landowning family, moved to nearby Taikyu and founded the Mitsuboshi Trading Company, in Korean Samsung Sanghoe. It began as a small trading company of forty employees, dealing in dried fish, locally grown groceries and noodles. It prospered, and Lee moved its head office to Seoul in 1947. When the Korean War broke out he was forced to leave Seoul and started a sugar refinery in Pusan named Cheil Jedang.

In 1954 Lee founded the textiles company Cheil Mojik and built its first plant in Taegu, the largest woollen mill in the country at the time. Over the next decades the group diversified into food processing, textiles, insurance, securities and retail. It entered the electronics industry in the late 1960s, and the construction and shipbuilding sectors in the mid-1970s. In 1980 it acquired Hanguk Jeonja Tongsin, based in Kumi, and entered telecommunications hardware, with switchboards as its early products; in the 1980s the company grouped its electronics under Samsung Electronics. After Lee died in 1987 the group was divided into five business groups: Samsung Group, Shinsegae Group, CJ Group, Hansol Group and JoongAng Group.

Samsung Group is a South Korean conglomerate headquartered in Samsung Town in Seoul. It is a chaebol, a family-controlled conglomerate, and comprises around 80 companies in fields such as construction, consumer electronics, financial services, shipbuilding and medical services. Key affiliates include Samsung Electronics, Samsung Heavy Industries, Samsung Engineering, Samsung C&T Corporation and Samsung Life Insurance. The group has had a powerful influence on South Korea's economic development, politics, media and culture, and has been a major driving force behind the Miracle on the Han River. Its logo is blue, said to symbolise stability, reliability and corporate social responsibility. The smartphone platform was launched with the Samsung Solstice line in 2008, later developed into the Galaxy line.
samudera-pasai-sultanate: The sultanate is also known as Samudera, Pasai, Samudera Darussalam or Pacem. Little evidence survives for its study. Tradition, preserved in the 14th-century chronicle Hikayat Raja-raja Pasai, credits its foundation to Merah Silu, who later converted to Islam and took the name Malik ul Salih. The chronicle derives Samudera from a word for a very large ant that he is said to have found while hunting, and Pasai from the name of his hunting dog, Si-Pasai, which he buried there.

Arab and Indian Muslims had traded in Indonesia and China for many centuries, but substantial evidence of Islam in Indonesia begins only in northern Sumatra at the end of the 13th century, where two small Muslim trading kingdoms, Pasai and Peureulak or Perlak, existed. A royal tomb at Samudra, dated to 1297, is inscribed entirely in Arabic. The rise of such harbour kingdoms was probably commercial. With the collapse of Srivijayan power, traders were drawn to the northern Sumatran shores of the Bay of Bengal, safe from the pirate lairs at the southern end of the Strait of Malacca.

The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta visited Samudra Pasai in 1345 on his way to China and stayed about two weeks in its wooden-walled town as the sultan's guest. He noted that the ruler was a pious Muslim who followed the school of Imam al-Shafi'i, and that no territory east of Pasai was ruled by a Muslim. The sultan sent him on to China aboard one of his own junks.

By the end of the 14th century Samudra Pasai was a wealthy commercial centre. Northern Sumatra had a hinterland rich in gold and forest produce, and pepper was being cultivated at the start of the 15th century. Majapahit attacked and looted the place in the middle of the 14th century, and in the early 15th century the better protected harbour of Malacca overtook it. The Portuguese occupied Pasai in 1521, ten years after taking Malacca. Their garrison left in 1524, and Ali Mughayat Syah, the first Sultan of Aceh, annexed the territory.

Historians have taken the tomb of Sultan Malik as-Saleh as a sign that Islam had entered the Archipelago by the 13th century, although some think it may have come earlier. The stories of the Pasai kings are full of myths and legends, but they have helped to uncover the history of the kingdom. Its name lives on in Lhokseumawe, where the University of Malikussaleh is named after the founder.
samudragupta: Samudragupta was a son of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta I and Queen Kumaradevi, who came from the Licchavi clan. His fragmentary Eran stone inscription says that his father chose him as successor for his devotion, righteous conduct and valour. The Allahabad Pillar inscription adds that when Chandragupta I appointed him, the faces of other people of equal birth bore a melancholy look. One interpretation takes these people to be neighbouring kings, so that the succession was uncontested; another takes them to be Gupta princes with a rival claim.

The Allahabad Pillar inscription, a eulogy composed by his minister and military officer Harishena, gives the most detailed account of his conquests, in geographical and partly chronological order. It says that he fought a hundred battles and earned the title Prakrama, the valorous. It records that he forcibly uprooted eight kings of Aryavarta, northern India, whose territories seem to have been annexed to his empire.

In the south the inscription lists twelve kings of Dakshinapatha, among them Vishnugopa of Kanchi and Hastivarman of Vengi, whom he captured and then released and favoured. Most scholars take this to mean that he restored them as tributaries. Rulers of frontier kingdoms such as Samatata, Kamarupa and Nepala, and tribes such as the Malavas and Yaudheyas, paid tribute. Since the inscription is a royal eulogy, its claims are to be treated with caution.

Samudragupta performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice to prove imperial sovereignty and issued gold coins to mark it. The Eran inscription records the installation of a Vishnu image in a temple, and two disputed inscriptions call him a devotee of Vishnu. He was also tolerant of Buddhism and allowed the king Meghavarna of Anuradhapura to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

His coinage was derived from that of the Kushan Empire, from which the Guptas took the name dinara and the weight standard; his standard type shows a sacrificial scene over an altar, and an archer type shows him with a bow. The inscription calls him king of poets and says that his music put Tumburu and Narada to shame, and coins show him playing the veena. Vincent Smith called him the Indian Napoleon. Chandragupta II, his son by Dattadevi, succeeded him.
samuel-aba: Samuel came from the Aba family, which held extensive domains in the region of the Mátra Hills. The Gesta Hungarorum and later Hungarian chronicles stress its non-Hungarian origin, calling it Cuman or Khwarezmian, and modern historians write that the Abas headed the Kabar tribes, a people of Khazar origin who joined the Hungarians in the 9th century. Gyula Kristó argues that both Samuel's Khazar origin and his first name suggest a family that adhered to Judaism. Samuel founded an abbey at Abasár, and Stephen I, the first King of Hungary, made him the first palatine of Hungary.

Stephen died on 15 August 1038, and his nephew Peter Orseolo of Venice, who preferred his German and Italian courtiers, set Samuel aside. In 1041 discontented Hungarian nobles expelled Peter and elected Samuel king. The Hungarian chronicles agree that he favoured commoners over nobles, and Hermann of Reichenau called him the tyrant of Hungary. He abolished the laws of Peter and had many of his supporters killed or tortured. In 1042 he stormed Austria, which provoked an invasion by the German king Henry III the following year. Samuel gave up the territories west of the Leitha and Morava and agreed to pay tribute, funded by taxes on the clergy and seizure of Church estates. Bishop Gerard of Csanád refused to perform the Easter crown-wearing ceremony.

Henry III invaded again in 1044 to restore Peter. The decisive battle was fought at Ménfő near Győr, where Henry routed Samuel's army, the larger of the two. Samuel's fate is uncertain: nearly contemporary German sources say he was soon captured and executed on Peter's order, while 14th-century Hungarian chronicles say he fled up the Tisza and was killed by locals, and was buried in a nearby church and later moved to his family's monastery at Abasár. No report on his widow and children survives, but historians suppose that the later Aba family descended from him.
samuel-ajayi-crowther: Ajayi was born in Osogun, in present-day Oyo State, Nigeria, and was a grandson of King Abiodun through his mother, Afala. In March 1821, when he was about twelve, Fulani slave raiders captured him with his family and his whole village during the Yoruba civil wars, and he was sold to Portuguese slave traders. His father, Ayemi, was most likely killed in the raid. Before the ship left port it was boarded by a Royal Navy crew under Captain Henry Leeke, and the captives were taken to Freetown, Sierra Leone.

In Freetown the Church Missionary Society taught him to read and write English. He was baptised on 11 December 1825, taking the name of Samuel Crowther, vicar of Christ Church, Newgate. After a year at the school of St Mary's Church in Islington he returned in 1827 and became the first student of Fourah Bay College, where he studied Latin, Greek and Temne and later taught.

In 1841 Crowther accompanied the missionary James Schön on the Niger expedition, which aimed to stimulate commerce, encourage Christianity and help end the slave trade. Recalled to England, he was ordained by the Bishop of London, and with Henry Townsend he opened a mission at Abeokuta, in today's Ogun State. His Yoruba grammar was published in 1843, and A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language, with many local proverbs, appeared in London in 1852. After the expeditions of 1854 and 1857 he published an Igbo primer in 1857, a Nupe primer in 1860 and a full Nupe grammar and vocabulary in 1864.

He was consecrated bishop by Charles Longley, Archbishop of Canterbury, at Canterbury Cathedral on St Peter's day in 1864, and later received the degree of Doctor of Divinity from Oxford. In Lagos he and Captain James Pinson Labulo Davies founded The Academy on 24 October 1866.

Crowther continued to supervise the translation of the Yoruba Bible, completed in the mid-1880s. He married Asano, baptised Susan, who had also been freed from a Portuguese slave ship; their son Dandeson Coates Crowther became archdeacon of the Niger Delta, and their grandson Herbert Macaulay was one of the first Nigerian nationalists. Crowther died of a stroke in Lagos on 31 December 1891 and was buried at Ajele Cemetery. His remains were reburied in 1976, and a cenotaph stands at the Cathedral Church of Christ, Lagos. Some Anglican churches, including the Church of Nigeria, keep his feast on 31 December.
samuel-baker: Samuel White Baker was born on 8 June 1821 in London into a wealthy commercial family; his father was a sugar merchant, banker and shipowner. He completed his studies in Frankfurt in 1841. As a civil engineer he later planned railways and bridges across the Dobruja, from the Danube to the Black Sea. In 1846 he went to Ceylon, where the next year he founded an agricultural settlement at Nuwara Eliya. His first wife, Henrietta, died of typhoid fever in 1855. In the Balkans in 1858 and 1859 he met Florence, who became his wife and followed him on all his travels; the Acholi called her Anyadwe, Daughter of the Moon.

In March 1861 Baker began his first tour of central Africa, in his own words to discover the sources of the Nile. After a year on the Sudan–Ethiopian frontier he reached Khartoum and in December 1862 set out up the White Nile. At Gondokoro he met John Speke and James Grant, who gave him information that allowed him to make the first European visit to Lake Albert, which he first sighted on 14 March 1864. He showed that the Nile flowed through the lake, though he overestimated its contribution to the river's flow. He and Florence were also the first Europeans to see a substantial waterfall on the Victoria Nile, which he named Murchison Falls after Sir Roderick Murchison.

He returned to England in October 1865, received the Patron's Medal of the Royal Geographical Society and was knighted in August 1866. In 1869, at the request of the khedive Ismail, he led a military expedition of 1,700 Egyptian troops to the equatorial Nile to suppress the slave trade and open the way to commerce. He was made a pasha and major-general and governor of the new territory of Equatoria for four years. He met the blocking of the river in the Sudd, hostility from officials who profited from the slave trade and armed opposition, and Charles George Gordon succeeded him.

Baker published his narrative of the expedition as Ismailia in 1874. He bought the Sandford Orleigh estate in Devon that year and died there of a heart attack on 30 December 1893. He never received quite the same acclaim as other British explorers of Africa, in part because of the circumstances of his marriage and a scandal involving his brother Valentine. Baker's Falls in Sri Lanka and Mount Baker in the Rwenzori Mountains bear his name.
samuel-de-champlain: Champlain's exact birth date and place are debated. He was the son of Antoine Champlain and Marguerite Le Roy, probably born in Brouage or La Rochelle in Aunis, into a family of mariners. His education was practical, in navigation, cartography and drafting, and did not include Greek or Latin. He served in Henry IV's army in Brittany from 1594 or 1595 to 1598 and by 1597 commanded a company near Quimper. He then sailed on a two-year voyage with his uncle-in-law François Gravé Du Pont, a navigator, and wrote an illustrated secret report on the Spanish holdings he saw from the Caribbean to Mexico City, for which King Henry gave him a pension.

Champlain began exploring North America in 1603 under Du Pont and took part from 1604 to 1607 in establishing Port Royal in Acadia, the first permanent European settlement north of Florida. In spring 1608 Dugua sent him with three ships from Honfleur to found a colony and fur trading centre on the St. Lawrence. He reached Quebec on 3 July 1608 and chose the point of Quebec, covered with nut-trees, for the settlement. In 1609 he allied with the Wendat, Algonquin, Montagnais and Etchemin against the Haudenosaunee, and on an expedition along the Richelieu River became the first European to map Lake Champlain.

On 29 July 1609 he killed two Haudenosaunee chiefs with a single arquebus shot. In 1615 he joined a campaign by the Wendat and their allies against the Haudenosaunee that failed after the attack began prematurely; he was wounded twice in the leg by arrows. In 1613 he travelled up the Ottawa River, writing its first description. Louis XIII ordered him in 1620 to focus on administration. He built Fort Saint-Louis on Cape Diamond and was one of the 100 investors in Richelieu's Compagnie des Cent-Associés, formed in 1627.

Champlain returned to Quebec on 22 May 1633 after four years away, with a commission from Richelieu as Lieutenant General of New France, not governor. Many colonists nonetheless called him their governor. He suffered a severe stroke in October 1635 and died on 25 December, leaving no immediate heirs. His exact burial site is unknown despite research since about 1850, but it is thought to lie near Notre-Dame de Québec Cathedral. His maps of the eastern coast and the Great Lakes combined his own observation with information from Indigenous peoples, and his published works include Des Sauvages (1604) and Voyages de la Nouvelle-France (1632). Lake Champlain bears his name.
samuel-doe: Samuel Kanyon Doe was born on 6 May 1951 in Tuzon, a small inland village in Grand Gedeh County, into the Krahn people, an important minority group in the area. He finished elementary school at sixteen and enrolled at a Baptist junior high school in Zwedru. Two years later he enlisted in the Armed Forces of Liberia, hoping to obtain a scholarship, but was assigned to military duties instead. Over the next ten years he served at various stations, attended a military school, commanded garrisons and prisons in Monrovia and finished high school by correspondence. On 11 October 1979 he was promoted to master sergeant.

On 12 April 1980 Doe led a group of Krahn soldiers in an attack on the Executive Mansion, killing President William Tolbert; his forces killed 26 of Tolbert's supporters in the fighting, and thirteen cabinet members were publicly executed ten days later. Doe assumed the rank of general, suspended the constitution and set up the People's Redemption Council of himself and 14 other low-ranking officers. The coup ended 133 years of Americo-Liberian political domination, and many welcomed it as a shift towards the majority of the population, who had been largely excluded from government. He broke relations with the Soviet Union and supported United States Cold War policy, and the two countries agreed staging rights for the American Rapid Deployment Force.

A new constitution was approved by referendum in 1984, and in the election of 15 October 1985 Doe won 51% of the vote by official figures. Foreign observers declared the election fraudulent and suggested that Jackson Doe of the Liberian Action Party had won. He was sworn in on 6 January 1986. On 12 November 1985 General Thomas Quiwonkpa, a leader of the 1980 coup, attempted to seize power and was killed. Afterwards Doe's government shut down newspapers, banned political activity and mistreated the Dan and Mano peoples, since Quiwonkpa was a Dan, causing violence among groups that had coexisted peacefully.

Charles Taylor crossed into Liberia from Ivory Coast on 24 December 1989 and began the First Liberian Civil War; by June 1990 rebel factions held most of the country. On 29 July 1990 about 600 civilians, mostly Dan and Mano, were killed in a church in the Sinkor section of Monrovia by about 30 government soldiers of Doe's Krahn people. On 9 September 1990 Doe went to the headquarters of the ECOMOG peacekeepers, where forces of Prince Johnson's Independent National Patriotic Front of Liberia disarmed his escort and captured him. After about 12 hours of torture he was killed, and his body was exhibited in the streets of Monrovia.
samuel-fritz: Fritz was born at Trautenau in Bohemia on 9 April 1654. After a year at the Charles University in Prague he entered the Society of Jesus as a novice in 1673 and studied mathematics, geodesy and surveying. He taught at the Jesuit seminaries in Uherské Hradiště and Březnice and became deputy rector at Brno, where he also conducted the student orchestra. Ordained on 4 February 1683, he was sent to Quito in September 1684, landing at Cartagena and travelling overland, and in 1686 was assigned to the Upper Marañón.

Among the Omagua, who had asked for protection from Portuguese slavers, he wrote a catechism in their language, visited their thirty-eight villages over about three years and later gathered people into Jesuit reductions. In 1689, gravely ill, he travelled more than 6,000 kilometres down the Amazon to Pará, where the governor, Artur de Sá Meneses, held him for eighteen months as a supposed Spanish spy. Released in 1691 on the King of Portugal's order, he went on to Lima, where the viceroy, the Conde de la Monclova, gave him two thousand silver pesos for his churches.

From 1693 he moved the Omagua from their islands to defensible settlements on the riverbanks, but slave raids from Pará grew worse, and in 1697 Portuguese soldiers and Carmelites demanded that he withdraw upstream. In 1701 the cacique Payoreva led a rising that burned the mission and killed some Jesuits; many of his followers, and Payoreva himself in 1704, were later enslaved by the Portuguese. In 1704 Fritz became Jesuit Superior. Portuguese raids from 1709 and a smallpox epidemic from April 1710 left the Upper Solimões uninhabited. Replaced as Superior in 1712, he worked at Limpia Concepción de Jeberos from 1714.

The last entry in his diaries, kept from 1689, is dated November 1723, and he died in a mission village of the Jivaro, attended by a priest named Wilhelm de Tres. His map, drawn with few instruments, set the source of the Amazon in the Marañón, rising at Lake Lauricocha near Huánuco, a view generally held into the 20th century. Its copy for Madrid was intercepted by the English, who published it in 1712, and French versions followed in 1717 and 1781. Its chief error was Lake Parime, which Fritz knew only by hearsay and later explorers found to be a myth.
samuel-gompers: Gompers was born Samuel Gumpertz on 27 January 1850 in Spitalfields, in London's East End, into a Jewish family from Amsterdam; his father, Solomon Gumpertz, was a cigar maker. He went to the Jewish Free School at six and was apprenticed as a cigar maker three months after his tenth birthday, while studying Hebrew and the Talmud at night school. In New York he helped his father make cigars at home and formed a debating club, where he met Peter J. McGuire, later important in the AFL.

Elected president of Local 144 of the Cigar Makers' International Union in 1875, Gompers and his friend Adolph Strasser rebuilt the union after the crisis of 1873–77 with high dues and out-of-work, sickness and death benefits. He helped found the Federation of Organized Trades and Labor Unions in 1881, which reorganised in 1886 as the American Federation of Labor. The AFL grew as the Knights of Labor faded, almost vanishing by 1900; Gompers edited The American Federationist from 1894 and spoke for the unions at the National Civic Federation.

He opposed unions taking political action and mostly backed Democrats. He led the opposition to immigration from China, writing with Herman Gutstadt the 1902 pamphlet Meat vs. Rice. He supported the war with Spain in 1898 but joined the Anti-Imperialist League against annexing the Philippines, a stance the historian Mandel attributes to fear of low-paid workers and a sense of racial superiority. In the First World War he and the AFL backed the war effort and opposed the Industrial Workers of the World; afterwards he supported amnesty for political prisoners convicted under wartime laws.

From 1919 Gompers was going blind, as his father had, and kept it secret. Influenza in February 1923 and then bronchitis weakened him, and by June 1924 he was suffering from diabetes, heart failure and uremia. He collapsed in Mexico City on 6 December 1924 at a meeting of the Pan-American Federation of Labor, asked to die on American soil, and was carried by special train towards the border; he died in San Antonio, Texas. He is buried at Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, New York, near Andrew Carnegie. George Meany later praised him as an immigrant who pioneered a distinctly American unionism.
samuel-gottlieb-gmelin: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin was born at Tübingen on 4 July 1744 into a well-known family of naturalists. His father, Johann Conrad Gmelin, was an apothecary and surgeon. His uncle Johann Georg Gmelin was also uncle to Johann Friedrich Gmelin, the naturalist who published the Systema Naturae of Carolus Linnaeus. Samuel earned his medical degree at the University of Leiden in 1763, at the age of 18. While living in the Dutch Republic he developed a keen interest in marine algae.

In 1766 Gmelin was appointed professor of botany at St Petersburg. He was then sent on an expedition to study the natural history of the Russian Empire, exploring the rivers Don and Volga and the western and eastern coasts of the Caspian Sea. In 1772 he married Anna von Chappuzeau, granddaughter of the naval captain Jacob Chappuzeau (Iakov Shapizo), who commanded the Raphail at the battle of Osel Island in 1719.

While travelling in the Caucasus Gmelin was taken hostage by Usmey Khan of Khaïtakes and died of ill treatment in captivity at Akhmedkent in Dagestan on 27 July 1774, at the age of 30. His death led to a Russian punitive expedition, which briefly conquered Derbent.

Gmelin wrote Historia Fucorum (1768), the first work dedicated to marine biology that dealt exclusively with algae and the first to use the binomial system of nomenclature. It contains elaborate illustrations of seaweed and marine algae on folded leaves, though the algal specimens he used are thought no longer to exist. The results of his travels appeared as Reise durch Russland zur Untersuchung der drey Natur-Reiche, in four volumes between 1770 and 1784. The last volume was to be completed by Güldenstädt but was edited by Peter Simon Pallas after Güldenstädt's death.
samuel-ibn-naghrela: Samuel came from a wealthy Jewish family and was raised in Córdoba, where he studied Jewish law, astronomy, logic and biblical exegesis under Hanoch ben Moses, head of the rabbinical community of the Caliphate of Córdoba. He was fluent in Hebrew, Arabic, Latin and a Berber language. He was about twenty when the caliphate fell in the Fitna of al-Andalus. He left Córdoba, settled in the port of Málaga as a spice merchant or grocer, and devoted his leisure to Talmudic and literary study.

According to the 12th-century Sefer ha-Qabbalah, his shop stood near the palace of Abu al-Kasim ibn al-Arif, vizier of Granada, whose maidservant asked him to write letters for her. He became tax collector, then secretary and assistant vizier to King Habbus al-Muzaffar. In 1027 he was named Nagid, leader of the Jewish community, the first in al-Andalus to hold that title. When Habbus died, Samuel ensured that his second son, Badis ibn Habus, succeeded rather than the firstborn Bulukkin, and Badis made him vizier and top general. For a dhimmi to hold such office was very rare.

He led Granada's forces against Seville, Carmona and Christian mercenaries, and on 8 September 1047 he defeated the allied armies of Seville, Malaga and the Berbers at Ronda. He supported Jewish academies in Babylonia and North Africa, founded a yeshiva in Granada and was patron to Solomon Ibn Gabirol. He died in 1056, reportedly of exhaustion after a campaign.

His poetry fills three collections: Ben Tehillim, of secular and war poetry; Ben Mishlei, of rhymed proverbs; and Ben Qohelet, of philosophical and didactic verse, titles that recall books attributed to King David. Abba Eban wrote that he created a new style by applying Arabic poetry to biblical Hebrew. He also wrote the halakhic work Hilkhata Gabrata, of which fragments survive. His son Joseph succeeded him as vizier but was assassinated on 30 December 1066, when most of Granada's Jews were killed in a massacre.
samuel-johnson: Samuel Johnson was born on 18 September 1709 in Lichfield, Staffordshire, above the bookshop of his father Michael Johnson. His mother Sarah was 40, an unusually late age for a first birth, and the infant did not cry, so the family feared for his life and had him baptised at once. He attended Pembroke College, Oxford, until lack of money forced him to leave. His father fell deeply into debt and died in December 1731, when Johnson was twenty-two. Johnson was turned down for a post as usher at Stourbridge Grammar School because he had no degree. After working as a teacher he moved to London and began writing for The Gentleman's Magazine.

His early works include the poem London (1738), the Life of Mr Richard Savage (1744) and the poem The Vanity of Human Wishes (1749). In 1746 a group of publishers approached him to make an authoritative dictionary, and a contract with William Strahan and associates, worth 1,500 guineas, was signed on 18 June. Johnson said the work would take three years, remarking that the Académie Française had used forty scholars for forty years. A Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755. Critics included Thomas Babington Macaulay, who called Johnson a wretched etymologist, while the biographer Walter Jackson Bate called it one of the most notable single achievements of scholarship.

Johnson then wrote the novella The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759) and edited The Plays of William Shakespeare (1765). In 1763 he befriended James Boswell, and in August 1773 the two set out on a journey to Scotland, which Johnson described in A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland (1775). There he entered the dispute over James Macpherson's Ossian poems, arguing that they could not be translations of ancient Gaelic writing because nothing had been written in that language in those times. Near the end of his life he wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1779–1781), biographies and critical appraisals of 52 poets.

Johnson suffered from scrofula, gout, deafness in one ear and blindness in one eye, and from long periods of depression. His tics and gestures, closely recorded by Boswell, have led to a posthumous diagnosis of Tourette syndrome. He died on the evening of 13 December 1784, aged 75, and is buried in Westminster Abbey. In his criticism he preferred contemporary language and was suspicious of Milton's blank verse and obscure allusions. His Dictionary was pre-eminent until the Oxford English Dictionary appeared some 150 years later, and he changed the course of biography; Boswell's Life of Samuel Johnson (1791) is described by Bate as the best-known single work of biographical art in the whole of literature.
samuel-maharero: Samuel Maharero was a son of Maharero, an important Herero warrior and cattle raider. He was baptised in 1869 and attended the local Lutheran schools, where he was seen as a possible future priest. When his father died in 1890 he gained the chieftainship in the area of Okahandja, but under Herero inheritance customs he received little of his father's wealth and cattle.

At first he kept fairly good relations with the German colonial administration under Theodor Leutwein. Attacks by German farmers, economic difficulties, pests and the use of Herero land for railways strained them. Settlers and officials treated the Herero as cheap labour for cotton and other export crops. Maharero secretly planned a revolt with the other chiefs, and in a letter to the Nama chief Hendrik Witbooi he sought an alliance, writing "Let us die fighting!"

The rising began on 12 January 1904. Its first attacks killed 123 people, mostly German landowners; Maharero had ordered his forces to spare Boers, the English, missionaries and other whites who were not German, and he let missionaries with a small number of German women and children pass to Okahandja. Herero raiders destroyed the Waldau and Waterberg post offices, killed the garrison of the Waterberg military station, besieged Gobabis on 16 January and ambushed a German company near Otjiwarongo.

Leutwein was then replaced as military commander by Lothar von Trotha, who brought 15,000 troops and put a bounty of 5,000 marks on Maharero. At the Battle of Waterberg on 11 August 1904 the Herero were defeated by colonial forces with breech-loading artillery and 14 Maxim machine guns. The survivors, women, children and the elderly among them, were driven into the Omaheke desert, where tens of thousands died of thirst, starvation or disease; those who tried to surrender were shot. After Berlin countermanded the extermination order, captured survivors were sent to a concentration camp on Shark Island.

Maharero led around 1,000 of his people into the British Bechuanaland Protectorate, remained leader of the exiled Herero and became a vassal of Sekgathôlê a Letsholathêbê, a chief in northern Bechuanaland. He died there in March 1923. On 23 August 1923 his body was brought back to Okahandja and reburied beside his ancestors, an occasion the Herero still mark on Herero Day. He is one of the nine national heroes of Namibia named at the inauguration of Heroes' Acre near Windhoek in 2002, where a granite tombstone bears his name and portrait.
samuel-pepys: Samuel Pepys was born in Salisbury Court, Fleet Street, London, on 23 February 1633, the son of John Pepys, a tailor, and Margaret Pepys. He was the fifth of 11 children and was soon the eldest survivor. He attended Huntingdon Grammar School and then St Paul's School, and in 1649 he watched the execution of Charles I. In 1650 he went to Magdalene College, Cambridge, as a sizar, and took his Bachelor of Arts degree in 1654.

He suffered from bladder stones from a young age. On 26 March 1658 the surgeon Thomas Hollier removed the stone in a bedroom of the house of Pepys's cousin Jane Turner, an operation known to be painful and hazardous. Pepys marked the anniversary for several years. He then worked as a teller in the Exchequer under George Downing.

In 1660, through his cousin Sir Edward Montagu, Pepys became Clerk of the Acts to the Navy Board. He had no maritime experience, learned arithmetic from a tutor and used models of ships, but proved more able and efficient than colleagues in higher positions. He joined the Tangier committee in 1662 and became its treasurer in 1665. When the Second Anglo-Dutch War began in 1665 he proposed a centralised approach to supplying the fleet and was made surveyor-general of victualling in October 1665.

In 1673 he became Secretary of the Admiralty Commission and was elected Member of Parliament for Castle Rising; he later sat for Harwich. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1665 and was its President from 1 December 1684 to 30 November 1686, and the imprimatur of Isaac Newton's Principia is signed by him in that role. He was imprisoned on suspicion of Jacobitism from May to July 1689 and again in June 1690, without any charge succeeding, and then retired from public life. He moved to Clapham in 1701 and died on 26 May 1703.

On 1 January 1660 Pepys began a diary, which he kept for almost ten years. It runs to one and a quarter million words and names over 3,000 people. He wrote of the court and theatre, his household, his finances and what he ate, and gave eyewitness accounts of the Second Anglo-Dutch War, the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of London in 1666. It was written in the shorthand called tachygraphy, devised by Thomas Shelton. Fear for his eyesight made him end it on 31 May 1669.

He had the diary bound into six volumes and kept it in his large library of more than 3,000 volumes, which survives as one of the most important private libraries of the 17th century. John Smith transcribed the diary between 1819 and 1822, and the first edition, by Lord Braybrooke, appeared in 1825.
samuel-richardson: Samuel Richardson was baptised on 19 August 1689 and was probably born in Mackworth, Derbyshire, one of nine children. He always concealed the exact location of his birth. His father was a joiner who, by Richardson's own account, had come to the notice of James Scott, 1st Duke of Monmouth, and was forced to give up his London business after the failure of the Monmouth Rebellion. The family later returned to London, and Richardson was probably educated at Christ's Hospital, although accounts of his schooling conflict.

His father could not afford to train him as a clergyman, so he chose printing. In 1706, at the age of 17, he was bound in a seven-year apprenticeship to the printer John Wilde in Aldersgate Street, a master said to grudge every hour that did not serve his profit. Richardson later married Wilde's daughter Martha. All six of their children died in infancy or childbirth, and Martha died in childbirth in 1731. In 1733 he married Elizabeth Leake, the daughter of the printer John Leake, and four of their six children, all daughters, reached adulthood.

Richardson's printing business prospered. He printed the Daily Journal between 1736 and 1737 and the Daily Gazetteer in 1738, and in all printed almost 500 works, working periodically with the bookseller Andrew Millar. In 1739 the booksellers Charles Rivington and John Osborn asked him for a volume of model letters for country readers who could not write for themselves. While writing it he was inspired to attempt a story, and on 6 November 1740 he published Pamela; or, Virtue Rewarded, his first novel, at the age of 51. It was sometimes regarded as the first novel in English.

Pamela was followed by sequels, and then by Clarissa; or, The History of a Young Lady, which was not complete to his satisfaction until October 1746. Readers whom he asked to help shorten it wanted it kept entire. His third and last novel, The History of Sir Charles Grandison, appeared in 1753. Richardson became Master of the Stationers' Company and counted Samuel Johnson, Sarah Fielding, the physician George Cheyne and the theologian William Law among his acquaintances.

All three novels are epistolary, told in letters. Richardson was a tireless letter writer and had faith that letters could portray character accurately. The form let him give distinct characters a voice directly to the reader and offered multiple perspectives. He hoped, however, to lead readers to interpret the text in the ways he chose, towards moral regeneration, and Susan Whyman writes that his goal was to reform reading practices and lives as well. His one major later work was a collection of the moral sentiments of his three novels. He died in July 1761 after an attack of apoplexy.
samuel-sharpe: Sharpe was born into slavery in the parish of St James, on a plantation owned by Samuel and Batty Sharpe. The Slave Return of 1832 that recorded his death named him Archer, also called Samuel Sharpe, the son of Eve, and a return of 1817 lists Archer on the plantation with his mother Juda Bligom and his siblings Joe and Eliza. He was allowed an education, which earned him respect among the enslaved.

He became a preacher and a deacon of the Burchell Baptist Church in Montego Bay, whose pastor was Thomas Burchell, a missionary from England, and travelled between parishes teaching the enslaved a Christianity that he believed promised freedom. In the mistaken belief that emancipation had already been granted, he organised a strike across many estates during the sugar harvest, when the planters most needed labour.

The rebellion began on 27 December 1831 at the Kensington Estate. After reprisals by the planters the rebels burned crops, and the protest became Jamaica's largest slave rebellion, mobilising as many as 60,000 enslaved people. Colonial troops and Maroon warriors suppressed it within two weeks. Some 14 whites were killed, while troops killed more than 200 of the enslaved, and between 310 and 340 people were executed after trials, many for property offences such as stealing livestock.

In jail Sharpe met the missionary Henry Bleby, who reported him saying: "I would rather die upon yonder gallows than live my life in slavery." The rebellion and its repression led to two parliamentary inquiries and are believed to have helped bring about the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 and the end of slavery across the British Empire in 1838. Jamaica proclaimed him a National Hero on 31 March 1982, with the posthumous title Rt. Excellent Samuel Sharpe.

Sam Sharpe Teachers' College in Granville, a suburb of Montego Bay, was founded in his honour in 1975. His portrait appeared on the Jamaican $50 note and, from 2023, on the new $500 note. The saxophonist Courtney Pine recorded a tribute, Samuel Sharpe, on his 2012 album House of Legends.
samuel-von-brukenthal: Samuel von Brukenthal was born on 26 July 1721 in Leschkirch (Nocrich), between Hermannstadt (Sibiu) and Agnetheln (Agnita). His grandfather and father had been royal judges. The family's original name was Brekner: his father, Michael Brekner, was ennobled in 1724 and received the noble name von Brukenthal. His mother, Susanna, belonged to the aristocratic family of Conrad von Heydendorff.

Brukenthal served as Habsburg governor of the Grand Principality of Transylvania from 6 July 1774 to 9 January 1787 and was a personal adviser to Empress Maria Theresa. As governor he began building a town palace in Hermannstadt. Inside the medieval town the building had to keep to two demolished plots beside the Jesuit church and seminary, so, unlike palaces set in parks, it was bounded by the lots it stood on.

The palace has a rectangular plan enclosing an inner courtyard, entered through a portal on the axis of its narrow side facing the street. It is counted among the Baroque buildings of Central Europe, and from the start it was meant as a setting for the conservation of his art collection and antiquities. He died in Sibiu on 9 April 1803.

The collections he gathered formed the core of the Brukenthal National Museum, which grew from a public exhibition first opened in his palace in 1817. A summer palace and park at Freck (Avrig) bear his name. At Sâmbăta de Jos he built a Baroque residence in 1750–1760, where Count Johannes von Brukenthal later founded a Lipizzaner stud farm in 1874.

The Samuel von Brukenthal Gymnasium, across from the Protestant Cathedral of Sibiu, is also named after him. First mentioned in 1380, it is the oldest German school in Romania; its present building dates from the 18th century, and it still teaches in German, the language of the German minority, with Romanian taught as the official language. Since the exodus of the Transylvanian Saxons in the twentieth century most of its pupils have been Romanians.
samurai: Until the late 8th century Japan had a national conscript army, which the imperial court dismantled, ending it by 792. Conscripts were seen as unreliable, and in the war against the Emishi, who relied on mounted warriors, professional mounted archers from wealthy families decided most battles. The government recruited men who already had those skills, acquired through private training funded by their families. The word samurai is thought to come from saburau, to serve, and so means a retainer or vassal; the proper term for a professional warrior is bushi, and the daimyo and the shogun were bushi but were not called samurai.

The Minamoto and Taira clans, both with court positions, became rivals. Taira no Kiyomori became the first bushi given a senior court rank, as chief minister in 1167. After the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled through a military government in Kamakura and was appointed shogun, and in 1192 he created the gokenin class of warrior vassals, who owed the shogun military service in exchange for privileges. The Ōnin War, which began in 1467, brought down the Ashikaga shogunate and led to the Sengoku period, in which daimyo fought each other.

After the Battle of Sekigahara Tokugawa Ieyasu was declared shogun in 1603, and after the siege of Osaka in 1615 there was a period of peace for 250 years. Under the Tokugawa the samurai first became a truly hereditary class, a process begun by Hideyoshi with the Sword Hunt of 1588 and the Separation Edict of 1591. With no warfare they gradually lost their military function; many served as officials, police, teachers or domain administrators, while keeping stipends and the right to bear arms.

After the Meiji Restoration the abolition of the domains, conscription, the ending of hereditary stipends and the removal of privileges such as wearing swords dismantled the basis of samurai status. Former feudal lords became kazoku, nobility, and most former warriors became shizoku, classes that remained legally recognised until 1947.

The samurai class was highly stratified, by the rank of one's lord and the size of one's stipend. Below the daimyo came the hatamoto, who had the right of audience with the shogun, and then the gokenin. Samurai trained from a young age in swordsmanship, archery and horsemanship. Confucianism, Buddhism and, to a lesser extent, Shinto influenced their culture, and the works Hagakure and Gorin no Sho, written in the Edo period, contributed to the development of bushidō.
samye: Samye Monastery was built during the reign of King Trisong Detsen and is counted as the first Tibetan Buddhist and Nyingma monastery. The Testament of Ba gives the earliest dates for its construction, a foundation in a hare year and the consecration of the main shrine in a sheep year, each of which can be read in two ways. All accounts agree that the king was the patron. The first Tibetan monks were ordained there in 779.

According to the Testament of Ba and later accounts, the Indian scholar Khenpo Śāntarakṣita began the work after accepting the king's invitation to Tibet. The building kept collapsing, and the workers believed that a demon or obstructive spirit in a nearby river was responsible. On his advice the king invited Padmasambhava, who subdued the obstacles. The 5th Dalai Lama described a Vajrakilaya dance and a rite of namkha, followed by the raising of four Vajrakilaya stupas at the cardinal points.

The plan follows a mandala of the Buddhist cosmos. A main temple stands in the middle, representing Mount Meru, enclosed by four stupas of different colours and by a circular wall with four openings at the cardinal points. The three-storeyed main building was designed with its first floor in Indian style, the second in Chinese style and the third in Khotanese style. Like the Tōdai-ji in Japan, the temple is dedicated to Vairocana. A stone pillar of the eighth century records the building of Samye and the oaths of the king, ministers and nobles to protect its endowments, and a bronze bell at the entrance was made by Queen Rgyal mo brtsan.

After the death of Śāntarakṣita a dispute among his followers grew into a debate hosted by Trisong Detsen in the early 790s. Kamalaśīla spoke for Indian Buddhist theory and Moheyan, a teacher of the East Mountain tradition of Chan, for the Chinese view. The king judged that Kamalaśīla had won.

The original buildings have long disappeared. Civil war in the 11th century, fires in the mid 17th century and in 1826, an earthquake in 1816 and the Cultural Revolution all damaged the site, and each time it was rebuilt. After 1986 the 10th Panchen Lama, Choekyi Gyaltsen, was the main force behind the latest rebuilding. The Puning Temple at Chengde, built in the 18th century by the Qianlong Emperor, was modelled on Samye.
san-antonio: San Antonio lies in the southern part of Texas, on the Balcones Escarpment at about 202 m above sea level, with the Texas Hill Country reaching into its far north. It is roughly 75 miles south-west of Austin and 150 miles north of the Mexican border. Its gently rolling terrain is dotted with oak trees, mesquite and cacti, and its climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot summers and mild winters. It is the county seat of Bexar County.

When the Spanish arrived, the Payaya people lived near the San Antonio River valley in the San Pedro Springs area and called it Yanaguana, meaning refreshing waters. On 13 June 1691, the feast day of Saint Anthony of Padua, Spanish explorers and missionaries came upon the river and the Payaya settlement and named the place and the river San Antonio in his honour. A Spanish mission and colonial outpost was founded there in 1718, and in 1731 San Antonio became the first chartered civil settlement in present-day Texas.

The city belonged to the Spanish Empire until 1821, to the Mexican Republic from 1821 to 1836, and to the Republic of Texas from 1836 until annexation by the United States, of which it was part from 1846. It was in the Confederate States from 1861 to 1865. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of San Antonio traces its origin to 27 August 1784 and was raised to an archdiocese in 1926. The San Antonio Express-News has served the area since 1865. The city is a key military centre, with Fort Sam Houston and nearby Lackland and Randolph Air Force Bases.

San Antonio had 1,434,625 residents at the 2020 census and is the second most populous city in Texas after Houston. Five 18th-century Spanish frontier missions, among them the Alamo and those in San Antonio Missions National Historical Park, were designated UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2015. Because of the Alamo Mission the city is often called Alamo City. About 64% of its residents identify as Hispanic, and Roman Catholicism is the largest religious group, a legacy in part of its Spanish and Mexican heritage.
san-carlos-pangasinan: San Carlos is a component city in the province of Pangasinan, Philippines, about 20 km from the provincial capital Lingayen and about 203 km from Manila. It is divided into 87 barangays and has a population of 208,330 according to the 2024 census. Pangasinan is its main language. It is known as the Mango-Bamboo Capital of the Philippines, and its economy rests on mango growing and a bamboocraft industry, along with livestock, crops, inland fishing, pottery, food processing and flour-making.

The place was formerly called Binalatongan, and its people spoke the original Pangasinan dialect. They were known for staunch adherence to their own beliefs and practices, which led to frequent conflicts with Augustinian friars and forced the Augustinians to abandon the area. The Dominicans later succeeded in establishing a Christian community there. Two leaders of uprisings are particularly remembered: Andrés Malong, who led the first significant revolt in 1660, and Juan de la Cruz Palaris, whose real name was Pantaleon Perez and who earned his nickname through his skill in native fencing. Palaris led a revolt against Spanish authority from 1762 that lasted two years and spread across Pangasinan, resisting excessive tribute and forced labour, and set up an independent government based at Binalatongan.

During a minor uprising led by Juan Caragay in 1718 the church and convent were set on fire and the town centre was moved east of the San Juan River. The church of Saint Dominic was burned again during Palaris's revolt. King Charles III of Spain then decreed that the site be moved and the town renamed San Carlos after him, a punishment that also set a new order. Until 1764 the town centre and church were moved several times within the present boundaries. In 1965 a smaller part became the Municipality of Basista, and in 1966 the larger part became San Carlos City by Republic Act No. 4487.

Sites in the city include the Minor Basilica of Saint Dominic, the Binalatongan Ruins in San Juan, the Speaker Eugenio Perez Memorial Park and the Quadricentennial Arch in Bolingit. On 26 April 2011 the city's barangays baked a mango pie of 100 square metres, recorded as the largest of its kind, during its Mango-Bamboo Festival.
san-diego: San Diego is a city on the Pacific coast of Southern California, next to the Mexican border. Its bay is the surface expression of a north-south nested graben, and the Rose Canyon and Point Loma fault zones are part of the San Andreas Fault system. About 40 miles east of the bay are the Laguna Mountains. The city is known for a mild Mediterranean climate, beaches and parks, and its long association with the United States Navy.

The area is historically home to the Kumeyaay people, whose town on the site was called Kosa'aay, "drying out place". The San Dieguito complex was established in the area at least 9,000 years ago, and the Kumeyaay may have developed from it or arrived around 1000 CE, a question on which scholars differ. The first European to visit was Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo, who claimed the bay for the Spanish Empire in 1542 and named it San Miguel. In November 1602 Sebastián Vizcaíno surveyed the harbour, Mission Bay and Point Loma, and named the area San Diego de Alcalá after Saint Didacus.
The Presidio and Mission San Diego de Alcalá, founded in 1769, formed the first European settlement in what is now California, and the city has been called the Birthplace of California.

In 1821 Mexico won its independence from Spain, and San Diego became part of the Mexican territory of Alta California. The fort on Presidio Hill was gradually abandoned and the town grew on the level land below it. The Mexican government secularized the mission in 1834 and granted most of its lands to former soldiers. The 432 residents of the town petitioned to form a pueblo, and Juan María Osuna was elected its first alcalde.

California was ceded to the United States in 1848 after the Mexican-American War and admitted as a state in 1850. That year San Diego was made the seat of the new County of San Diego and incorporated as a city, with Joshua H. Bean, the last alcalde, as first mayor. Two years later it was bankrupt, and the legislature revoked its charter and placed it under a board of trustees until 1889.

San Diego is the seat of San Diego County and the second most populous city in California, with over 1.4 million residents. Its economy rests largely on military and defence activities, tourism, international trade, research and manufacturing. The San Ysidro Port of Entry connects it with Tijuana, and the city's present charter was adopted in 1931.
san-fernando-pampanga: San Fernando is the capital of Pampanga and a regional centre of Central Luzon. It lies 66 kilometres north of Manila and 17 kilometres south of Clark Air Base in Angeles City, in the urban core of Metro Clark. It is named after King Ferdinand VI of Spain and placed under the patronage of Saint Ferdinand III of Castile and León, whose feast falls on 30 May.

The town was founded in 1754 from Bacolor and Mexico, and its first church, of wood and nipa, was built in 1755. In 1892 its railway station opened on the Manila–Dagupan line and earned more than any other provincial station. On 26 June 1898 representatives of the Pampanga towns, except Macabebe, gathered there to swear allegiance to General Maximino Hizon, the representative of Emilio Aguinaldo. In 1899 General Antonio Luna's troops burned the municipal hall, the church and several houses to deny them to the approaching Americans, and Aguinaldo led Filipino forces in the Battle for San Fernando on 16 June, which failed to retake the town. The provincial government moved from Bacolor on 15 August 1904.

Pedro Abad Santos founded the Socialist Party of the Philippines in 1932, and his compound became the focal point of the peasant movement. President Manuel Quezon proclaimed his social justice programme to farmers there on 14 February 1939. After the Japanese occupation began, thousands of Filipino and American prisoners walked from Bataan to the San Fernando station in what became known as the Bataan Death March. American forces retook the town on 29 January 1945, and after martial law was declared in September 1972 Camp Olivas housed detainees, some documented as tortured.

Lahar from Mount Pinatubo, after its eruption, and from Typhoon Sibyl in 1995 damaged several barangays, and a dike and then the Pampanga Megadike were built. San Fernando became a city on 4 February 2001 after a plebiscite ratified Republic Act 8990.

San Fernando had 377,534 inhabitants at the 2024 census and has 35 barangays. About 80% of residents are Roman Catholic, and it is the seat of the Archdiocese of San Fernando. It is called the Christmas Capital of the Philippines, where barangays compete each December in the Giant Lantern Festival. José Abad Santos, chief justice and briefly acting president of the Commonwealth during the Second World War, was born there.
san-francisco: San Francisco lies on the West Coast of the United States, at the north end of the San Francisco Peninsula, and its boundaries take in stretches of the Pacific Ocean and San Francisco Bay. Alcatraz, Treasure Island and the adjacent Yerba Buena Island belong to the city, as do the uninhabited Farallon Islands, 43 kilometres offshore. The mainland within the city limits forms roughly what residents call the seven-by-seven-mile square, and the total area, including water, is nearly 600 square kilometres.

The name, Spanish for 'Saint Francis', comes from Mission San Francisco de Asís, founded in 1776 under Padre Francisco Palóu and named for Francis of Assisi. The first civilian pueblo was called Yerba Buena, 'good herb', and the city has officially been San Francisco since 1847, when its alcalde, Washington Allon Bartlett, renamed it.

The earliest evidence of human habitation dates to 3000 BCE. The Ohlone name for the place was Ahwaste, 'place at the bay', and the Yelamu group of the Ramaytush people lived in small villages there. The Portolá expedition, led by Gaspar de Portolá and Juan Crespí, reached the bay on 2 November 1769, the first documented European visit, and noted the strategic value of its large natural harbour. Settlers from New Spain founded the Presidio of San Francisco at the Golden Gate and the Mission San Francisco de Asís on 29 June 1776. The Mission system marked the beginning of the assimilation of the Ramaytush and the decline of their language and culture.

The California gold rush of 1849 brought rapid growth and made San Francisco the largest city on the West Coast. In 1856 it became a consolidated city-county. The earthquake and fire of 1906 destroyed three-quarters of the city, which was quickly rebuilt and hosted the Panama–Pacific International Exposition nine years later. In the Second World War it was a major port of embarkation for naval personnel bound for the Pacific. After the war returning servicemen, immigration, liberalizing attitudes, the beatnik and hippie countercultures and opposition to the Vietnam War led to the Summer of Love and the gay rights movement, which made the city a centre of liberal activism.

San Francisco is a city on the Pacific coast of California whose boundaries are the same as those of its county; the 2020 census counted 873,965 people. It is known for its steep hills, Chinatown and the Mission District, and for landmarks including the Golden Gate Bridge, cable cars and Alcatraz. The Presidio, the former Spanish military base, is now one of the city's largest parks and the site of museums and institutions.
san-giorgio-dei-greci: The confraternity founded by the Greek community in 1498 was the Scuola de San Nicolò dei Greci, which aided members of that community; the permission of 1539 to build a church came only after protracted negotiations. Construction was begun by Sante Lombardo and continued from 1548 by Giannantonio Chiona. Inside, Baldassarre Longhena made a monument to Gabriele Seviros in 1619. A similar church of the period, Santi Pietro e Paolo dei Greci, served the Greeks of Naples.

The priesthood of the painter Emmanuel Tzanes at the church, from 1655 to 1690, was one of the most important periods in its history. His brothers, the painter Konstantinos Tzanes and the poet Marinos Tzanes, also lived in Venice and were affiliated with the church, as were the painters Ioannis Moskos, Leos Moskos and Philotheos Skoufos.

Giovanni Kyprios frescoed the Last Judgement in the dome in 1589–93. Other painters who worked for the church included Markos Bathas, Thomas Bathas, Venediktos Emporios and Emmanuel Tzanfournaris, while Emanuele Tzane-Buniales, a priest and hagiographer from Crete, painted the ascetic hermits Saints Simeon and Alypios on top of the pilasters.

Michael Damaskinos worked for the church between 1560 and 1583. Twenty of his paintings belong to it, eighteen of them icons of the iconostasis, among them one of the Archangel Michael and nine of the Great Feasts of the Eastern Orthodox Church; two more stand behind the iconostasis in the sanctuary. Four of Tzanes' paintings belong to the church, including an icon of Alypius, Abraham and Melchizedek on the royal doors and a Crucifixion.

Anna Notaras, daughter of Loukas Notaras, the last megas doux of the Byzantine Empire, gave her three icons to the Scuola in trust until a church of the Greek Orthodox faith could be built. They show Christ in glory with the symbols of the four Evangelists and the twelve Apostles, Christ Pantokrator, and the Virgin Hodegetria.

Near the church stands the Flanginian School, once a Greek teachers' school, which now houses the Hellenic Institute of Byzantine and Post-Byzantine Studies in Venice. Its museum, established by Sophia Antoniadis, keeps four further works by Damaskinos and thirteen by Tzanes.
san-jorge-river: The San Jorge begins in the Paramillo National Park, which spans the departments of Antioquia and Córdoba, and runs between the mountains of San Geronimo and Ayapel before it flows into the Cauca River in Sucre Department. Its basin takes in the waters of the Ayapel swamp and reaches the Mompox region through the Caribbean departments of Córdoba, Sucre and Bolívar. Its tributaries include the San Pedro and Ure rivers. Its flow ranges from a minimum of 24 cubic metres per second to a maximum of 697. The river is still rich in fish, but it has been badly polluted and degraded, largely by fishing with explosives and by the recovery of alluvial gold with mercury.

The Spanish conquistador Alonso de Heredia came upon the river in the 1530s while seeking contact with the Zenú. It was then known as the Xegú or Jegu, and many villages stood on its banks, among them Yape, now Ayapel in Córdoba, and Tacasuán, now San Benito Abad. Heredia named it after Saint George, the Christian saint who fought a dragon.

In 1966 an American aviator noticed an extensive network of canals and artificial ridges along the river and saw that the pattern was not natural but the work of human engineering. In 1986 the Colombian archaeologists Clemencia Plazas and Anna Maria Falchetti showed that these ridges and channels were built by the pre-Columbian Zenú, and the pottery and jewellery found along the banks point to a technically skilled society.

The limited evidence suggests that the hydraulic works were built by a people who lived in the area between the first and fourth centuries. Because the land stays flooded for several months each year, a drainage system was needed before people could settle there for good, and the canals and ridges rank among the largest such networks in Hispanic America.
san-jose-california: San Jose lies in the Santa Clara Valley, in the southern part of the San Francisco Bay Area, and is the county seat of Santa Clara County. Its northernmost part touches San Francisco Bay at Alviso. The Guadalupe River runs north from the Santa Cruz Mountains through the city. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. The city takes its name from the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, its predecessor.

The Tamien nation of the Ohlone people has lived in San Jose and most of the Santa Clara Valley since around 4,000 BCE. California was claimed for the Spanish Empire in 1542, but for nearly 200 years it remained a distant frontier largely controlled by the Native nations. British gains after the Treaty of Paris of 1763 and Russian colonisation in the north-west led the Spanish authorities to sponsor the Portolá Expedition of 1769. San Jose was founded on 29 November 1777 as the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe, the first city founded in the Californias.

It became part of the First Mexican Empire in 1821, and in 1833 Mexico secularised the California missions. The United States completed its conquest of California by the end of 1847, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 formally ceded it. On 15 December 1849 San Jose became capital of the territory of California, and on California's admission to the Union on 9 September 1850 it became the state's first capital.

After the Second World War the city grew rapidly: under the City Manager Dutch Hamann, in office from 1950 to 1969, it annexed property 1,389 times and grew from 17 to 149 square miles. The nickname Silicon Valley was coined in 1971, and in 1988 Mayor Tom McEnery adopted the motto Capital of Silicon Valley. The 1990 census showed that San Jose had surpassed San Francisco in population.

San Jose is the most populous city in the San Francisco Bay Area and in Northern California, with 1,013,240 residents at the 2020 census. San José State University, founded in 1862 as the California State Normal School, has been in downtown San Jose since 1870. The city has historic ethnic districts such as Japantown and Little Portugal, a large Vietnamese population and the largest Sikh gurdwara outside India. Alum Rock Park, established in 1872, is the oldest municipal park in California.
san-jose-costa-rica: San José stands in the middle of Costa Rica, in the mid-west of the Central Valley. It is the seat of national government, the focus of political and economic activity and the country's chief transport hub. Together with the neighbouring cantons of Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago it forms the Greater Metropolitan Area. The city is named in honour of Joseph of Nazareth. Its climate is tropical wet and dry, with average temperatures that vary little through the year.

San José was founded in 1736 by order of the Cabildo de León, to gather the scattered inhabitants of the Aserrí Valley. A chapel was completed a year later with help from the church of Cartago, and St Joseph was chosen as parish patron, which gave the town its name. Unlike Cartago, it was not founded by formal decree and so lacked a city government until the Constitution of Cádiz was enacted in 1812. On 18 October 1813 the presbyter Florencio del Castillo defined it as a city, but the title was lost in 1814 when Ferdinand VII annulled the proceedings of the courts. It was restored in 1820, and in 1823 San José became the capital of Costa Rica.

The installation of the Tobacco Factory in 1782 spurred growth, and capital from tobacco plantations let the city surpass neighbouring provinces economically. In the late 19th century the French coffee entrepreneur Monsieur Amon created the first modern urban neighbourhood, Barrio Amon, in Belle Époque style; it and the National Theater remain symbols of the Costa Rican coffee golden age. The University of Santo Tomas, the country's first university, was established in San José in 1843 and closed in 1888.

San José is the capital and largest city of Costa Rica, with an estimated 352,381 people in its canton in 2022. It holds the National Museum of Costa Rica and the National Theater, considered the finest historic building in the capital; El Teatro Variedades, built in 1892, is its oldest theatre. The Museum of Pre-Columbian Gold and the Museum of Jade are also in the city. The University for Peace, established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1980, is located in San José.
san-jose-mogote: The site lies in the fertile bottomlands of the Etla arm of the valley, about 12.1 kilometres north-west of the city of Oaxaca. It is considered the oldest permanent farming village of the Valley of Oaxaca and probably the first there to use pottery, and it was supported by smaller settlements such as San Pablo Huitzo, Santa Marta Etla, Tomaltepec and Tierras Largas. Kent Flannery and Joyce Marcus investigated it over two decades of the late 20th century.

Between 1500 and 1150 BCE it grew from a few houses into the largest of some 25 villages in the valley and the only one with public buildings. Households stored maize in bell-shaped pits, placed figurines with burials and obtained obsidian from outside the valley, while irrigation ditches and pot irrigation from shallow wells may have raised harvests. The site has produced Mexico's oldest known defensive palisades and ceremonial buildings, of about 1300 BCE, and a men's house oriented eight degrees west of north, as at La Venta.

Between 900 and 600 BCE about half the valley's people lived there. Only San José Mogote made mirrors of polished magnetite, traded to the Olmec Gulf Coast some 400 kilometres away, and it also obtained turtle-shell drums, conch-shell trumpets and stingray spines. John E. Clark judges that by the end of the San José phase it was a chiefdom. Monument 3, set as the doorstep of a ceremonial building, bears the earliest known Zapotec glyphs, and Mound 1 was raised on a hill augmented to 15 metres.

When Monte Albán rose as the main city of the valley, San José Mogote became a lesser community under its control, and the public buildings on Mound 1 were rebuilt as the residence of a high-ranking family.

The ruins are surrounded by the present-day village of San José Mogote in the Mexican state of Oaxaca, and the site is studied as an early centre of Zapotec culture and a forerunner of Monte Albán. Artefacts from the excavations are shown in the village's Community Museum, housed in the El Cacique Hacienda.
san-juan-de-ulua: The island in the Gulf of Mexico was named by the expedition of Juan de Grijalva in 1518, and there, on 30 March 1519, Hernán Cortés met Tendile and Pitalpitoque, envoys of Moctezuma II of the Aztec Empire. The Spanish authorities began the fort in 1535, and building went on until 1769 as its bounds were repeatedly enlarged. In the 1580s the engineer Battista Antonelli redesigned it during a stop on his way to the Gulf of Fonseca.

In 1568 the garrison trapped a privateer fleet under John Hawkins, whose commanders included his young cousin Francis Drake, in the harbour. Both escaped on their ships, but many sailors were killed by Spanish cannon fire and several ships were sunk or scuttled. The sailors left behind went inland and settled among the local population. The episode is credited with Drake's lasting hatred of the Spanish and of Catholicism.

Spanish troops held the fortress after independence in 1821, the last place of the former New Spain in Spanish hands, until they surrendered it to General Miguel Barragán in November 1825. It became a symbol of Mexican resistance to foreign attack. The French bombarded it in 1838 during the Pastry War, the United States besieged it in the Mexican–American War, and the French occupied Veracruz in 1863 while installing Maximilian I as emperor.

For much of the 19th century it was a prison, above all for political opponents of the government, and it remained one under Porfirio Díaz.
