Part of it served at times as a presidential palace, housing Benito Juárez and Venustiano Carranza. In 1914, after the Tampico Affair, American forces took Veracruz and the fortress and held them for seven months.

The fortress was decommissioned when it proved too impractical for a modern naval base and, after years of decay, was restored from the late 20th century. A museum opened there in 1984, and the prison and fortress are open to visitors, apart from the former presidential palace, which suffered severe decay.
san-juan-province-argentina: San Juan lies in the western part of Argentina and borders Chile to the west, with La Rioja, San Luis and Mendoza as its neighbours. It covers 89,651 square kilometres of mountainous country with scarce vegetation, fertile oases and turbulent rivers. It belongs to the semi-desert Cuyo region: arid plains in the east rise through a few low hills to peaks of 6,000 metres in the west, and both areas are subject to the Zonda, a dry hot foehn wind. The Jáchal and San Juan rivers feed the fertile valleys that are the centre of the province's economy.

Before the Spanish conquest the area was inhabited by the Huarpes, Diaguitas, Capazanes, Olongastas and Yacampis, who were strongly influenced by the Inca Empire. The city of San Juan de la Frontera was founded by Juan Jufré y Montesa in 1562 and moved 2 kilometres south in 1593 because the San Juan River flooded so often.

In 1776 it was annexed to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata as one of the cities of the Province of Cuyo, and in the same year the first recorded earthquake caused massive damage. José de San Martín was appointed Governor of the Province of Cuyo in 1814 and began from there his crossing of the Andes; San Juan, then a small town, supplied the expedition with gold, men and mules. In 1820 it was granted autonomy from Cuyo, and the rest of Cuyo became Mendoza Province.

After the more liberal government of 1853, exiled intellectuals returned to San Juan, among them the military officer and novelist Domingo Sarmiento. Elected governor in 1862, he made public investments and passed Argentina's first law for compulsory education, at a time when about 80 per cent of adults lacked any education; when he became president in 1868 the policy became national law. In 1944 an earthquake near the capital destroyed most of the city and killed 10,000 people. A stronger earthquake in 1977 did little damage because of the new building codes, though the Cathedral of San Juan was destroyed and a modernist church was opened in its place in 1979.

Agriculture is a leading activity, especially wine and olive oil, with fruit and vegetables grown in valleys irrigated by artificial channels. The Ullum Dam and Reservoir, inaugurated in 1980, expanded irrigated crops such as olives, figs and above all wine grapes. The National University of San Juan opened in 1973. The province also has mining and oil production and a number of paleontological sites.
san-juan-puerto-rico: San Juan lies on the north-eastern coast of Puerto Rico in the Northern Plains region, facing the Atlantic Ocean. The municipality covers 199.2 square kilometres, of which about a third is water. Its main bodies of water are San Juan Bay and two natural lagoons, the Condado and San José. The old city stands on the Islet of San Juan, and all the city's beaches face the Atlantic.

The Taíno were the original inhabitants before Europeans reached the island in 1493. The site of San Juan marked the boundary between two Taíno territories, Guaynabo and Haimanio, led by the chiefs Mabo and Yuisa. In 1508 Juan Ponce de León founded the settlement of Caparra, named for a Roman town in the Spanish province of Cáceres, the birthplace of Nicolás de Ovando, then governor of Spain's Caribbean territories. The settlement was later moved to a site then called Puerto Rico, Spanish for rich port.

San Juan was the first stopover in the Americas for ships sailing from Spain. A network of fortifications was built to protect the transports of gold and silver from the New World to Europe, and the rich cargoes made the port a target of foreign powers. The Puerta de San Juan, built in 1635, is the main preserved gate of the colonial walls.

On 8 May 1898 United States Navy ships under Rear Admiral William T. Sampson arrived at San Juan Bay during the Spanish–American War. On 10 May Captain Ángel Rivero Méndez, commanding the Spanish forces in the fortress of San Cristóbal, ordered his men to fire on USS Yale, the first attack against the Americans on the island.

San Juan is the capital and most populous municipality of Puerto Rico, an unincorporated territory of the United States. It is the second oldest European-established capital in the Americas, after Santo Domingo. The historic district of Old San Juan, with the former defensive walls, Fort San Felipe del Morro, Fort San Cristóbal and La Fortaleza, the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.
san-julian-de-los-prados: The church, also known as Santullano, is a work of the Pre-Ramirense phase of Asturian art and dates from the beginning of the 9th century. Its building was ordered by Alfonso II of Asturias, and it was built by the court architect Tioda around 830. It is dedicated to the martyred Egyptian saints Julian and Basilissa. Although it appears more a monastic church than a royal one, a gallery for the king was set aside in the transept.

The church is a basilica with a nave and two aisles, separated by square piers that carry semicircular arches, and a transept of great height. The iconostasis that divides the sanctuary from the rest of the building closely resembles a triumphal arch. In its size and originality the church differs from the works of Visigothic art. Of its three original entrances, two have been filled in.

The only sculpture to survive is on the marble capitals beneath the arches, together with two marble flagstones in the central chapel carved with hexagonal geometric figures and floral motifs. The chief feature is the painted decoration: aniconic frescoes, finely executed in stucco and painted in three layers with architectural designs of clear Roman inspiration. In its extent, its state of preservation and the variety of its designs it is among the most important painted decoration of its time in Western Europe.

San Julián de los Prados is counted among the principal works of Asturian art. The Spanish Ministry of Culture declared it a Historical-Artistic Monument in June 1917, and on 2 December 1998 UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site. It stands in Oviedo, the capital city of the Principality of Asturias in Spain.
san-lorenzo-tenochtitlan: The three sites lie on what was an island in the swamps and marshes west of the Coatzacoalcos River. San Lorenzo proper occupies the slopes and summit of the plateau; Tenochtitlán lies within the modern village of that name at the island's northern end, and Potrero Nuevo on a hill east of the plateau. Unlike the swampy surroundings of La Venta, San Lorenzo stood amid a large farming area. Michael Coe and Richard Diehl calculated that the 77 square kilometres they studied could yield about 500 metric tons of maize a year, and residents also ate dog, fish such as snook and tarpon, and turtles.

Farmers had lived in the area for centuries before San Lorenzo became a regional centre, and it was the first Olmec site to show state-level complexity. Its core of 55 hectares was raised and levelled with, by one estimate, 500,000 to 2,000,000 cubic metres of earth carried by the basketload, and buried lines of U-shaped drain stones carried water to the edges of the plateau.

The elite lived on low clay platforms among thrones and colossal heads of basalt brought from the Cerro Cintepec volcano in the Tuxtla mountains; one residence, the Red Palace, had roof columns of basalt 4 metres tall. Commoners lived in wattle-and-daub houses on terraces down the slopes. The ceremonial centre may have housed 5,500 people and the whole area 13,000.

Pottery and figurines from San Lorenzo reached distant parts of Mesoamerica: over 5,000 objects in the early Olmec style were found at Canton Corralito in coastal Chiapas. The city's decline in the 10th century BCE, and its replacement by La Venta, remain unexplained; warfare, environmental change, economic decline and rival centres have all been proposed, and the region's rivers changed course at the time. By 800 BCE the plateau was nearly empty, though it was resettled from 600 to 400 BCE and again around 800 to 1000 CE.

The original Olmec name is unknown; Matthew Stirling coined the name San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán in 1955 from the nearby villages. Up to 124 stone sculptures have been found, and many more are thought to remain buried. The sites are open to visitors.
san-luis-potosi: San Luis Potosí, officially the Free and Sovereign State of San Luis Potosí, is one of the 32 federal entities of Mexico and takes its name from its capital. It lies in eastern and central Mexico and is divided into 59 municipalities. It borders Nuevo León, Tamaulipas, Veracruz, Hidalgo, Querétaro, Guanajuato and Zacatecas. The state lies mostly on the Mexican Plateau, at a mean elevation of about 1,800 metres, while the Sierra Madre Oriental separates the plateau from the Gulf Coastal Plain to the east. The eastern quarter is the Huasteca potosina, part of a region along the Gulf of Mexico historically associated with the Huastec people.

In pre-Columbian times the territory contained parts of the cultural areas of Mesoamerica and Aridoamerica. The Otomi and Chichimeca, nomadic hunter-gatherers, lived in the north and the west-central parts. Many indigenous people died during Spanish colonisation, but Huasteco groups still live in the state, together with Pame and Nahua peoples.

The discovery of gold and silver in 1592 led to the founding of the first town, known as San Luis de Mezquitique, at the site of the present capital, and Juan de Oñate was appointed first mayor. The name San Luis honours Louis IX of France, and Potosí compares the wealth of the place with the rich silver mines of Potosí in Bolivia, a rivalry the settlers hoped for but never fully achieved. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Franciscans, Augustinians and Jesuits built churches and other buildings, many still standing.

In mid-1821, after Mexican independence, General José Antonio Echávarri pressed the mayor and city council to surrender the city to the Army of the Three Guarantees, and independence was proclaimed in San Luis Potosí. The first state constitution was written on 16 October 1826 and remained in effect until 1835, when Congress proclaimed a centralist system. The state's part in the Mexican–American War of 1846–1847 earned it the name San Luis de la Patria. During the French Intervention in 1863 President Benito Juárez made the city of San Luis Potosí the capital of the country. In 1866 a telegraph line opened between San Luis Potosí and Mexico City, which helped begin the industrialisation of the state.

Besides the capital, major cities include Ciudad Valles, Matehuala, Rioverde and Tamazunchale. The area around Real de Catorce has some of the richest silver mines in the country, and Guadalcázar's ores yield gold, copper, zinc and bismuth as well as silver. Nahuatl is the most widely spoken indigenous language, followed by Huasteco. The state's coat of arms shows Louis IX of France on a hill at Cerro de San Pedro, where the metals were found.
san-michele-maggiore-pavia: Ostrogothic silverware found at the site in 1968 suggests that an early Christian basilica may have stood there in the 5th century; the plates, spoon and cup fragment, hidden beneath a later tomb, are now in the Pavia Civic Museums. Between 662 and 671 King Grimoald had a church dedicated to St Michael built on the site of the Lombard Palace chapel. It burned in 1004, and only the lower part of its bell tower survives. Work on the present crypt, choir and transept began in the late 11th century and was finished by 1130.

The basilica, a well-preserved example of the Lombard Romanesque style, served as the model for other Pavia churches such as San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro and San Teodoro, but differs from them in its use of sandstone instead of brick. It has a Latin cross plan with a nave, two aisles and a transept 38 m long, against 55 m for the whole church, with a façade of its own. Over the crossing rises a 30 m octagonal dome on squinches, reportedly the earliest of its form in Lombardy. The nave vaults were rebuilt between 1488 and 1491 by Iacopo da Candia and his son Agostino.

Inside are fragments of a pavement mosaic with the Labours of the Months, a silver-clad crucifix two metres high commissioned in the 10th century by the abbess Raingarda, the high altar of 1383 holding the remains of Sts Ennodius and Eleucadius, and a Nativity carved by Baldino da Surso in 1473.

The church was the seat of royal coronations, among them those of Berengar I in 888, Arduin in 1002 and Henry II in 1004. Its two portals and monumental transept, a plan common in German imperial churches but absent elsewhere in northern Italy, served the ceremony. The procession entered by the northern portal, which originally connected the basilica to the Royal Palace, the throne was set on stones in the nave, and the procession left by the southern Porta Speciosa. In February 1397 Gian Galeazzo Visconti held a ceremony there modelled on the early medieval coronations, and he ordered that his heart be kept in the basilica.
san-miguel-bulacan: San Miguel lies in the north of Bulacan, bounded by Nueva Ecija Province to the north and Pampanga Province to the west, about 53 kilometres from Malolos and 76 kilometres from Manila. Its land ranges from plain farmland to hills, caves, springs, rivers and waterfalls. The town was once named Mayumo, from the Kapampangan word for sweets; Augustinian missionaries added the name of its patron, Michael the Archangel. Another account derives the name Miguel de Mayumo from Miguel Pineda, the first gobernadorcillo.

San Miguel de Mayumo was founded in 1763 by Carlos Agustin Maniquiz, his wife Maria Juana Puno and Miguel Pineda, a native of Angat who had settled in the barrio of San Bartolome and allied himself with Mariano Puno of the nearby village of Santo Rosario. The town was separated from Candaba and belonged to Pampanga until 1848, when it was added to Bulacan, which explains its Kapampangan culture.

In 1897 Governor-General Fernando Primo de Rivera set out to crush Emilio Aguinaldo's forces in Cavite. Aguinaldo withdrew to Batangas, where he joined General Miguel Malvar, then through Morong to Biak-na-Bato, where he made the mountain caves his headquarters. Manuel L. Quezon declared Biak-na-Bato a national park on 16 November 1937. Between 1903 and 1906 the poorer neighbouring town of San Ildefonso was joined to San Miguel. Japanese troops occupied the town in 1942, and soldiers of the Philippine Commonwealth Army and Philippine Constabulary withdrew to the mountains as guerrillas. San Miguel was the largest town of Bulacan until 13 September 1977, when Doña Remedios Trinidad was created from part of it.

San Miguel has 49 barangays and had 179,792 people at the 2024 census. Most residents speak Tagalog and some Kapampangan, and the area is a homeland of the Alta Kabulowan, the first inhabitants of Bulacan, whose language is endangered. The town keeps its Holy Week processions of about 60 carrozas and, at the parish of San Jose, the rite of Los Desposorios, the Betrothal of Mary and Joseph.
san-miguel-de-lillo: The church, in Asturian Samiguel de Lliño, stands on the Naranco mount near the Church of Santa María del Naranco. It was completed in 842 and consecrated in 848 by Ramiro I of Asturias and his wife Paterna. It was first dedicated to St. Mary, but in the 12th century that dedication passed to the nearby palace, leaving the church dedicated to Saint Michael.

The church originally had a basilica plan of three aisles with barrel vaults, probably about five bays long. The building collapsed in the 12th or 13th century, and only its western part survives, a royal westwork in the Frankish style. Though narrow, it is tall, thanks to the buttressing outside. It keeps the carved jambs of its vestibule and the plate tracery of its windows, each window sculpted from a single slab of stone by perforating it.

On the west facade, paired openings on columns are topped, above a slender lintel, by a roundel or half-roundel with a four-light opening beneath, and the transept has three-light windows with elaborate geometric tracery. The entrance projects slightly from the three-part front. Above the low barrel-vaulted vestibule, an upper gallery or choir is reached by stairs on both flanks. The walls were once covered with murals like those of Santuyano, of which only fragments remain. The lost apse may have mirrored the west facade, as at the neighbouring Church of St. Mary.

In the 16th century the historian Ambrosio de Morales described the church in his Viaje Santo and the Crónica general. He praised its good proportions seen from outside and, within, the harmonious arrangement of transept, dome, main chapel, gallery, stairs and bell tower, and he noted the marbles, fine jasper and porphyry of its transept and main chapel. Morales compared it with the Cámara Santa in Oviedo. Since 1985 the church has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Monuments of Oviedo and the Kingdom of the Asturias.
san-miguel-de-tucuman: San Miguel de Tucumán lies in northern Argentina, 1,311 kilometres from Buenos Aires, on the slopes of the Aconquija mountains, the easternmost range before the large Chaco-Pampean flats. It is the commercial centre of an irrigated area producing sugarcane, rice, tobacco and fruit, which gave the province its nickname, the Garden of the Republic. The climate is humid subtropical, with most of the year's rain falling in the summer months.

Diego de Villarroel founded the city on 31 May 1565, as San Miguel de Tucumán y Nueva Tierra de Promisión, in the Campos de Ibatín, about 60 kilometres south-west of its present site, during an expedition from present-day Peru. In 1685 it moved to La Toma, where the old town stands, because of the poor quality of the water at Ibatín. On 24 September 1812 the Battle of Tucumán was fought near the city. Manuel Belgrano, who had been ordered to fall back to Córdoba but was called on by the inhabitants to resist, attacked the Spanish army from behind with tired troops and local gauchos and defeated it. Belgrano then built a circular fortress, La Ciudadela.

Because the city had patriot barracks and lay between the Río de la Plata and Upper Peru, it was chosen as the seat of the Congress of Independence. On 9 July 1816 the congress declared the independence of Argentina, not only from Spain but from any other foreign domination, and signed the act at the Casa de Tucumán. After the national government broke down in 1820 the town was capital of the short-lived Republic of Tucumán. The first railway arrived around 1870, and immigrants, mostly Spanish, Arab, Jewish and Italian, changed the colonial architecture towards neoclassical and eclectic styles. By 1930 the population had doubled.

The city is the capital of Tucumán Province. The Casa de Tucumán, where independence was declared, was acquired by the national government in 1874, demolished almost completely in 1903 except for the room of the declaration, and rebuilt in 1942 from the original plans and an 1869 photograph by Angel Paganelli. It is a national monument. Other landmarks include the cathedral, the Basílica de San Francisco and the Government House, built in Art Nouveau style at the end of the 19th century. The National University of Tucumán was founded in 1914.
san-millan-de-la-cogolla: San Millán de la Cogolla is a sparsely populated municipality in La Rioja, Spain. It had 293 inhabitants registered in 2009, and its population fell significantly during the twentieth century. In a papal bull of 1199 granting privileges to its monasteries the place appears as Coculla, from the Latin cuculla, a small hill or hilltop, a word typically used for high sites of a defensive nature from the time of the Reconquista. The other part of the name comes from a saint of the sixth century, Saint Emilianus or San Millán, who lived there.

The village has a claim to be the birthplace of the Spanish language. Its monasteries were the home of a medieval manuscript containing the Glosas Emilianenses, examples of writing in an early Romance language that was a forerunner of Spanish. The claim is reinforced by the nearness of Berceo, associated with Gonzalo de Berceo, the first Spanish poet known by name. The Glosas give evidence that Basque was spoken alongside an early form of Spanish in medieval times.

In medieval times the monastery had a large estate, documented in its cartulary, the Becerro Galicano, and it benefited from lying on one of the variants of the Camino de Santiago. A number of its abbots held episcopal titles between 1025 and 1065. The monastery and its surroundings suffered in the civil war between Peter of Castile and Henry II of Castile, which brought a major battle nearby, the Battle of Nájera in April 1367. Peter was killed by Henry in 1369. The small Jewish community of San Millán was affected as well, and in 1369 Henry ordered that the Christian and Moorish population discharge their debts to its members promptly so that they could pay their taxes.

The twin monasteries of San Millán de Yuso and San Millán de Suso were declared a World Heritage Site in 1997. Both stand in the municipality, which had 293 registered inhabitants in 2009. The area is now Spanish-speaking, though some local place-names are of Basque origin, and the population has fallen sharply since the twentieth century.
san-pedro-sula: San Pedro Sula lies in the northwest corner of Honduras, in the Sula Valley, about 50 km south of Puerto Cortés on the Caribbean Sea, and is the capital of Cortés Department. Like most cities built in the Spanish colonial period it is divided into quadrants: First Street and First Avenue mark the centre, avenues run north to south and streets east to west. The climate is tropical, with a dry season from January to May and a wet season for the remaining months, and the city is prone to hurricanes and tropical storms.

Before the Spanish arrived the Sula Valley was home to about 50,000 native inhabitants, and the site served as a local trade hub. The Spanish conquest brought a demographic collapse from which the native population never recovered. On 27 June 1536 Pedro de Alvarado founded a Spanish town beside the Indian settlement of Choloma, calling it Villa de Señor San Pedro de Puerto Caballos. It had 35 Spanish citizens, and Alvarado allocated 200 of his slaves to build the town and work the fields. He cancelled the encomienda rights granted under Andres de Cerezeda and reassigned the villages to the town's citizens.

The settlement barely survived the colonial period. In 1601 the Spanish government made Santo Tomás the official port for the Central American colonies, which diverted exports from Puerto Cortés and began an economic decline that lasted through the 17th century, while pirates and French, Dutch and English mercenaries raided the town. After the Spanish built the Fortaleza de San Fernando at Omoa in the mid-18th century, trade increased and the population rose from 70 in 1714 to 357 in 1789. After independence it remained an impoverished village, living from trade between Omoa and the interior; in 1875 an American consul reported 1,200 inhabitants.

The city grew with the banana trade of the 1870s and 1880s, with the Interoceanic Railroad built between 1869 and 1874 to connect it to the coast at Puerto Cortés, and through close ties between local elites and Samuel Zemurray's Cuyamel Fruit Company. The central urban area had 701,200 inhabitants in 2023 and the metropolitan area 1,445,598. It is the main industrial centre of Honduras and its second city after Tegucigalpa, with a large apparel manufacturing industry, the maquila.
san-people: The San are the members of the indigenous hunter-gatherer cultures of southern Africa, which are the oldest surviving cultures of the region. They speak, or their ancestors spoke, languages of the Khoe, Tuu and Kxʼa families. Their recent ancestral territories span Botswana, Namibia, Angola, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Lesotho and South Africa.

Some 10,000 years ago their ancestors were spread from Tanzania, Zambia and Angola down to Cape Agulhas. A set of tools almost identical to those of the modern San, dated to 42,000 BCE, was found at Border Cave in KwaZulu-Natal in 2012. Some interpretations of genetic analysis suggest a divergence from other humans as early as 100,000 to 200,000 years ago.

During the Bantu expansion the San met herder groups, who later became the Khoekhoe, and herder-farmers. They were partly driven off their lands or incorporated by Bantu speaking groups. Other societies often turned to San shamans for rainmaking, as at Mapungubwe, and one writer claims they were involved in the early foundations of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and of later states such as Great Zimbabwe.

After the Dutch settled at the Cape under Jan van Riebeeck in 1652, the Cape San population was estimated at 30 000 to 50 000. From about 1714 the Dutch East India Company's loan farm system gave stock farmers grazing rights in the dry interior, and Trekboers occupied waterholes, shot the game on which the San lived and overgrazed the land.

The San resisted by raiding stock, and the Trekboers answered with militia units called commandos. From the 1770s to the late 1790s this violence became general along the frontier of the Dutch Cape Colony. Two scholars write that tens of thousands of Khoekhoe and San lost their lives to genocide, murder, mistreatment and disease, and that some commandos hunted San.

Traditionally the San lived in small mobile foraging bands. Women gather fruit, berries, tubers and bush onions and sometimes hunt, and may lead family groups, make decisions and claim ownership of waterholes and foraging areas. Ostrich eggshells serve as water containers, and insects provide perhaps 10 percent of animal protein.

Early spring is the hardest season, and meat matters most in the dry months. Leisure is important at every age, with much time given to conversation, music and sacred dances. In kinship, the older of two people decides what to call the younger, and each child is named after a grandparent or other relative, never a parent.

From the 1950s to the 1990s government modernisation programmes pushed San communities towards farming. San and Bushmen are both exonyms; San comes from a Khoekhoe word for foragers without cattle, and in 2003 San representatives said they preferred to be called by their respective nations.
san-remo-conference: The conference followed the London Conference of February 1920, where the Allies discussed the partition of the Ottoman Empire and the agreements that became the Treaty of Sèvres. On 30 September 1918 supporters of the Arab Revolt in Damascus had declared a government loyal to Sharif Hussein. On 6 January 1920 his son Prince Faisal initialled an agreement with the French prime minister Georges Clemenceau acknowledging the right of the Syrians to unite and govern themselves as an independent nation, and on 8 March 1920 a Pan-Syrian Congress in Damascus proclaimed an independent Arab Kingdom of Syria with Faisal as head of state.

The conference met at Castle Devachan in Sanremo from 19 to 26 April 1920. The Principal Allied Powers were represented by the prime ministers of Britain, David Lloyd George, France, Alexandre Millerand, and Italy, Francesco Nitti, and by Japan's ambassador Keishirō Matsui. The United States sent observers. The agenda covered the peace treaty with Turkey, mandates in the Middle East, Germany's obligations under the Treaty of Versailles and the Allies' position on Soviet Russia.

On 25 April the San Remo Resolution established Class A mandates under Article 22 of the Covenant of the League of Nations for Syria, Mesopotamia and Palestine. Syria and Mesopotamia were to be provisionally recognised as independent states receiving administrative advice from a mandatory until they could stand alone, with boundaries and mandatories chosen by the Principal Allied Powers. Palestine was entrusted to a mandatory responsible for putting into effect the Balfour Declaration of 1917, on the understanding that nothing should prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities. France received Syria and Britain Mesopotamia and Palestine. The Italian delegation reserved its approval until Italian interests in Turkey were settled.

Britain and France also signed the San Remo Oil Agreement, giving France a 25 percent share of the oil production from Mosul. The draft peace agreement with Turkey became the basis of the Treaty of Sèvres. The Balfour Declaration and Article 22 were the basic documents on which the British Mandate for Palestine was built.

The resolution left the boundaries open, and the status of areas such as Transjordan unclear. In July 1920 France issued an ultimatum and defeated the Arab government at the Battle of Maysalun, and Faisal was removed from Damascus in August. On 31 August 1920 the French proclaimed Greater Lebanon and other component states of their mandate. Britain decided to associate Transjordan with the mandated area of Palestine without applying the provisions for a Jewish national home to it. In 1920 Britain appointed Herbert Samuel as high commissioner, and the mandatory government in Palestine remained in power until 1948.
san-salvador: San Salvador lies in the Salvadoran highlands at an average height of 658 metres, surrounded by volcanoes. The Boquerón Volcano rises to 1,893 metres above the metropolitan area. The city has a tropical wet and dry climate, with a dry season from November to April and a rainy season from May to October, when thunderstorms come almost daily.

The conquistador Gonzalo de Alvarado founded a mission he named San Salvador in 1525. The name probably refers to the feast of the Transfiguration, called Divino Salvador in Spanish, held on 6 August, the day on which in 1456 Pope Callixtus III commemorated the Christian victory at the Siege of Belgrade. Names such as San Salvador became a popular choice for churches and places, and Christopher Columbus had given it to the island of Guanahani in 1492. The city was part of the Kingdom of Spain until 1821, and then of the Mexican Empire in 1822 and 1823 and of Central America until 1841.

The city has suffered from many severe earthquakes, of which the most disastrous came in 1854. When the San Salvador volcano erupted in 1917, three major earthquakes damaged the city so badly that the government temporarily moved the capital to Santa Tecla. On 10 October 1986 another earthquake killed between 1,000 and 1,500 people and left 200,000 homeless. Colonial buildings, cathedrals above all, have been destroyed over time, and the few notable buildings of the historic downtown that survive date from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

San Salvador is the capital and largest city of El Salvador, with 525,990 inhabitants in the municipality. It is the seat of the Legislative Assembly and the Supreme Court. The National Theatre, built in 1917, is the oldest theatre in Central America, and the National Palace dates from 1905.
san-salvador-de-jujuy: Jujuy lies near the southern end of the Humahuaca Canyon, where wooded hills meet the lowlands, at the junction of the Xibi Xibi River and the Río Grande de Jujuy, 1,238 metres above sea level. National Route 9 passes through it, linking La Quiaca and Salta, and it is 1,525 km from Buenos Aires. It is the capital and largest city of Jujuy Province and the seat of the Doctor Manuel Belgrano Department, and the provincial administrative offices that serve petroleum, sugar, tobacco, steel and fruit production are located there.

In late 1535 a party from Diego de Almagro's expedition to Chile clashed with local indigenous men at Jujuy, and Almagro sent a punitive force of 80 men that dislodged them from a fortified pucará. After attempts in 1565 and 1592, the present city was founded as San Salvador de Velazco en el Valle de Jujuy on 19 April 1593 by Francisco de Argañarás y Murguía. It developed as a strategic site on the mule trade route between San Miguel de Tucumán and the silver mines of Potosí.

The city reached its peak importance in the colonial period and declined to a remote provincial capital after the Argentine Declaration of Independence in 1816. It became the capital of Jujuy Province when the province separated from Salta in 1834, and the earthquake of 1863 levelled the town. Growth began again with the arrival of the Northern Central Railway in 1900, and the National University of Jujuy was created in 1973 from the Economic Sciences Institute of 1959.

The colonial city centre includes the Cabildo, the cathedral and the colourful Andean carnivals. The 2001 census counted 237,751 inhabitants, rising to around 300,000 with the suburbs. Winters are dry and cold and summers humid, and temperatures vary widely between day and night. The city is the provincial government, financial and cultural centre.
sanaa: Sanaa stands at about 2,300 metres above sea level, on a plain of the same name, the Haql Sanaa, between the mountains of Jabal An-Nabi Shu'ayb and Jabal Tiyal. The plain is roughly 50 to 60 km long from north to south and about 25 km wide, bordered by cliffs and mountains from which wadis descend. The Old City is known for its tower houses of stone and fired brick, which can rise to eight storeys. Their ground floors were traditionally used for grain and animals, and the top room, the mafraj, serves as a second reception room.

The city was a secondary capital of the Kingdom of Saba, whose main capital was the oasis of Marib. Its name is probably derived from a Sabaic root meaning well-fortified. From the time of Muhammad, around 622 CE, Sanaa was the governing seat of Yemen until independent sub-states appeared, and all of Yemen's states competed to control it.

The Ottoman Empire entered Yemen in 1538, under Suleiman, and conquered Sanaa in 1547 under Özdemir Pasha. In 1602 the local Zaydi imams, led by Imam al-Mu'ayyad, reasserted their control, and Ottoman troops were forced out in 1629. In 1904, as Ottoman influence waned, Imam Yahya took power in Sanaa and followed a policy of isolation that left the city with little new infrastructure. Before the revolution of 1962 society was divided into five ranked groups, headed by the sayyids and the qadis. The Jewish community, present in Yemen since the 5th century BCE, was expelled in 1679 and returned in 1680 to a quarter outside the walls. After 1948 about 49,000 of an estimated 51,000 Yemenite Jews were airlifted to Israel.

Sanaa is the capital and largest city of Yemen, with a population of about 3,300,000 in 2023. It grew rapidly from the 1960s, when it became the capital of the republic and a new city spread beyond the old one. The Old City, enclosed by clay walls 9 to 14 metres high and holding more than 100 mosques, 12 hammams and 6,500 houses, was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The Great Mosque is more than 1,400 years old. The sung tradition al-Ghina al-San'ani, which dates to the 14th century, was designated UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2003.
sanaag: Sanaag has a long coastline facing the Gulf of Aden to the north and is bordered by the regions of Sahil to the west, Sool to the south and Bari to the east. Its capital is Erigavo. It is the largest region of Somaliland, accounting for 35 per cent of that territory's land area. The region is divided into five districts: El Afweyn, Erigavo, Garadag, Badhan and Dhahar. Its people are mainly Somali, principally the Habr Yunis and Habar Jeclo sub-clans of the Isaaq and the Dhulbahante and Warsangali sub-divisions of the Harti Darod.

From 1944 to 1974 the area was one of three districts of the Burao region, with Burao and Las Anod. Sanaag was carved out of the Togdheer region and established as a separate region on 23 June 1973, with the three districts of Erigavo, Las Qorey and Garadag.

The region holds many archaeological sites, with rock art, ancient ruins, buildings and cairns at places such as Gudmo Biyo Cas, Heis, Maydh, Haylan, Qa'ableh, Qombo'ul, Gelweita and El Ayo. Many of these structures have not been properly explored. Near El Afweyn stands the ruined Islamic city of Maduna, the most substantial and most accessible ruin of its type in Somaliland. Its large rectangular mosque has walls 3 metres high that still stand, with a mihrab and possibly several smaller arched niches. The Swedish-Somali archaeologist Sada Mire dates the city to the 15th to 17th centuries.

The region is disputed between Somaliland and Puntland. Somaliland claims all of Sanaag on the basis of the British Somaliland boundaries, while Puntland claims only the parts inhabited by the Harti. Somaliland effectively controls the western and central parts, and Puntland the east, including Badhan. The economy rested on livestock, frankincense and leather exports, and after the civil war its markets and infrastructure collapsed. Livestock rearing is now its main activity, and a ban on Somali livestock imposed by Gulf countries, once Sanaag's largest market, hit it hard. The Siilaanyo road links the region to Burao and the rest of the country.
sanahin-monastery: The name Sanahin means in Armenian this one is older than that one, presumably a claim to be older than the neighbouring Haghpat Monastery, about 3 kilometres to the east, with which it forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 966 King Ashot III and Queen Khosrovanuysh built the church of the Holy Savior, Surb Amenaprkich. Their sons Kyurike and Smbat founded a congregation and a high school and invited clergymen, scholars and writers. The founding abbot was Polycarp, followed by the scholar Hovhannes, and in 979 King Smbat II made the monastery the seat of a new bishopric of the Kyurikian kingdom.

In the middle of the 11th century Dioscoros Sanahnetsi led the monastery, and its school became a large educational centre teaching theology, philosophy, rhetoric, music, medicine and calendars. The library and the chapel of Saint Gregory were built in 1063. The monastery suffered under the Seljuk invasions and after the fall of the Kyurikian kingdom in 1113, but from the end of the 12th century, under the Zakarid princes, it recovered, with new vestibules, a bell tower and many khachkars. The Mongol invasions of the 1230s interrupted its life again.

In the 14th and 15th centuries writing revived, and 35 manuscripts written there are kept in the Matenadaran. In the middle of the 17th century Archbishop Sargis Arghutyan renovated buildings damaged by earthquakes. The monastery's activity ceased at the start of the 20th century. Under Soviet rule it was a protected monument, and in 1998 the government of Armenia handed it to the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin.

The complex took about three centuries to form. Its main material is local light grey polished basalt, and its forms are simple and monumental. The church of the Holy Mother of God is one of the earliest examples of the cruciform dome type. On the east front of the Holy Savior is a relief of Kyurike and Smbat holding a model of a church, which set a precedent for similar sculptures at Haghpat and Ani. Some 50 khachkars survive nearby, with about 190 inscriptions from the 10th to the 19th centuries. The complex belongs to the Armenian Apostolic Church.
sanai: Hakim Abul-Majd Majdud ibn Adam Sanai Ghaznavi, known as Sanai, lived in the late 11th and early 12th century and was associated with the city of Ghazni. He was connected with the court of Bahram Shah. The details of his personal life are not well documented, and much of what is told of it rests on later sources. His surviving poetry is the main source for understanding his literary and religious ideas.

Sanai wrote a very large quantity of mystical verse. His master work is The Walled Garden of Truth, or Hadiqat al-Haqiqa, dedicated to Bahram Shah, which is the first Persian mystical epic of Sufism. It sets out the poet's ideas on God, love, philosophy and reason. For almost 900 years it has been read as a classic and used as a Sufi textbook. John Stephenson wrote that Sanai's fame has always rested on the Hadiqa, and that through it he stands as one of the great trio of Sufi teachers with Attar and Rumi. His other great work is the Divan.

Sanai taught that lust, greed and emotional excitement stand between humankind and divine knowledge, which alone is true reality, called haqq. For him love, or ishq, and a social conscience are the foundation of religion. He saw mankind as asleep, living in a desolate world, and treated common religion as only habit and ritual. His poetry stresses the possibility of an awakening, to be reached by surrender to God, and it attacks human hypocrisy and folly.

Sanai is considered the first poet to use the qasidah (ode), the ghazal (lyric) and the masnavi (rhymed couplet) to express the philosophical, mystical and ethical ideas of Sufism. His poetry had a great influence on Persian literature. Rumi acknowledged Sanai and Attar as his two great inspirations, saying that Attar was the soul and Sanai its two eyes, and that he came after them. The Walled Garden of Truth was also a model for Nizami's Makhzan al-Asrar, the Treasury of Secrets.
sanandaj: The name Sinna first appears in records from the 14th century CE. Before that the main city of the region was Sisar, also called Sisar of Sadkhaniya, or Sisar of the hundred springs, whose exact location is unknown; it has been proposed that Sinna is a contracted form of Sadkhaniya.

The name Sisar disappears in the 14th century, and Sinna replaces it in the works of Hamdallah Mustawfi, who refers to a mountain and a pass of that name. The Kurdish historian Sharaf al-Din Bitlisi mentions that in 1580 an Ardalan ruler named Timur Khan held a land grant that included Sinna and the earlier Ardalan capital of Hasanabad.

The local historian Ali-Akbar Munshi Waqayi-Nigar wrote in 1892/3 that Sinna was founded by the Ardalan ruler Soleyman Khan on the site of an earlier settlement, giving a chronogram that corresponds to 1046 AH, or 1636-7 CE. The town grew greatly under Aman Allah the Great, who reigned from 1797 to 1825. In the 19th century it was a lively commercial centre, exporting oak galls, tragacanth, furs and carpets.

Sanandaj is the capital of Kurdistan province in western Iran, and of its county and district. It lies between the Qishlaq river, a tributary of the Diyala, and Mount Awidar, which separates it from Hasanabad. Its people are mainly Kurdish, most follow the Shafi'i branch of Sunni Islam, and Central Kurdish is the vernacular of daily life while Persian is the language of education and government. It is regarded as a historic centre of Kurdish cultural and intellectual life, with traditions of music, poetry and carpet weaving. Carpet making is the biggest industry.

In the 19th century its population was mostly Kurdish, with a significant Jewish minority and smaller numbers of Armenian and Assyrian Christians, mostly Chaldean Catholic. Until 1979 the city had a small Aramaic-speaking Jewish community of about 4,000 people, and its Assyrian community spoke a dialect of Aramaic called Senaya.
sanation: The name comes from the Latin sanatio, healing. The movement drew mainly on former military officers who were dissatisfied with what they saw as corruption in Polish politics, and it joined rightists, leftists and centrists around the aims of fighting corruption and curbing inflation. Józef Piłsudski, once leader of the Polish Socialist Party, had come to distrust political parties as serving themselves rather than the state, so Sanation never became a party. In 1928 its members formed instead the Nonpartisan Bloc for Cooperation with the Government (BBWR).

After the coup Piłsudski approved every government informally before the President confirmed it, beginning with Kazimierz Bartel's. Eugeniusz Kwiatkowski's economic reforms addressed stagnation, while the regime acted against the communist parties and split the support of the opposition. Press, speech and parties were never legally abolished, and opponents were often dealt with by unidentified perpetrators rather than by the courts.

The 1928 election was relatively free but left the BBWR without a majority. In 1930 the government dissolved parliament, and leaders of the Centrolew alliance, among them Wincenty Witos and Wojciech Korfanty, were arrested without warrants; in the Brest election that November the BBWR won over 46 percent of the vote. At the Brest trial, which ended in January 1932, ten were sentenced to up to three years.

The April Constitution of 1935 had been written with Piłsudski in mind, and after his death the movement split into the Colonels around Walery Sławek, the Castle around President Ignacy Mościcki, and a group around Edward Śmigły-Rydz, who was made Marshal of Poland in November 1936 and through the Camp of National Unity set the movement's nationalist course from 1937.

During the invasion of 1939 many Sanationists fled through Romania and Hungary to France and later Britain, keeping influence in exile though France tried to keep them out of the Polish Government in Exile. In occupied Poland they founded resistance groups such as the Polish Fighting Movement of 1942, which came under the Home Army in 1943. Poland's Soviet-installed communist government treated them as enemies of the state, and many were executed or driven into exile.
sancai: Sancai is lead-glazed earthenware with a body of white clay, fired at about 800 degrees Celsius. Lead oxide was the main flux, often mixed with quartz in a proportion of three to one, and metal oxides gave the colours: copper turned green, iron brownish yellow, and less often manganese and cobalt were used, the imported cobalt for a costly blue. Though it needed two firings, it was cheaper to make than porcelain or celadon and suited to large figures, which were cast in sections in moulds and joined with clay slip.

Except on the carefully painted offering-trays, the colours were usually applied loosely, splashed or spotted, and ran into each other at their edges. Dealers called such wares egg-and-spinach. The vessels, none very large and found almost only in burials, often borrow shapes from metalwork, including the amphora and the oinochoe with a spout shaped like a bird's or phoenix's head; they may have been cheaper copies of silver vessels for the dead.

Green and brown glazes were known under the Han, though rarely mixed in one piece, and then almost disappear for about four hundred years, leaving only a tenuous tradition linking Han to Sui and Tang. Northern Qi tombs of 550 to 577 have yielded forerunners with splashed green designs. The full three-colour combination appeared shortly before the end of the 7th century and is called Tang sancai; because it was first unearthed and is most often found at Luoyang, it is also known as Luoyang Tang sancai. After about 70 years the making of tomb figures almost ceased with the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 and a Tibetan invasion of 763, though vessels went on for fifty years or more.

Sancai was made again from the late Tang and under the Liao dynasty, often for temples, such as the life-size Yixian glazed pottery luohans built around iron bars. Along the Silk Road it influenced Syrian, Cypriot and Italian pottery from the 13th to the mid-15th century, and Japanese wares such as Nagayo ware. Qing emperors with antiquarian tastes had it revived in Jingdezhen porcelain. In the 1980s and early 1990s reproductions served as Chinese state gifts to foreign leaders, and more than 3,000 small workshops around Luoyang produced copies.
sancha-of-leon: Sancha was a daughter of Alfonso V of León by his first wife, Elvira Menéndez. She became a secular abbess of the Monastery of San Pelayo. In 1029 a political marriage was arranged between her and Count García Sánchez of Castile, but García was assassinated by a group of disgruntled vassals after travelling to León for the wedding. In 1032 she was married to García's nephew and successor, Ferdinand I of Castile, who was then 11 years old.

At the Battle of Tamarón in 1037 Ferdinand killed Sancha's brother Bermudo III of León, which made Sancha the heir and allowed Ferdinand to be crowned king of León. Her own position as queen is unclear and contradictory in the sources. She succeeded as her brother's heir, in her own right, yet she is not clearly called a queen regnant, and after her husband's death the throne passed to her son although she was still alive. With Ferdinand she commissioned the Crucifix of Ferdinand and Sancha as a gift for the Basilica of San Isidoro. She had five children: Urraca of Zamora, Sancho II, Elvira of Toro, Alfonso VI and García II of Galicia.

After Ferdinand's death in 1065 and the division of his kingdom among their sons, she is said to have played the futile role of peacemaker among them. She died in León and was buried in the Royal Pantheon of the Basilica of San Isidoro, with her parents, her brother, her husband and her children Elvira, Urraca and García. The inscription on her tomb calls her queen of all Spain, wife of the great king Ferdinand and daughter of King Alfonso, who repopulated León after its destruction by Almanzor.
sancho-garces-i-of-pamplona: Sancho Garcés was born around 860, the son of García Jiménez and his second wife Dadildis de Pallars. Around the time of King García Íñiguez's death he ruled the Onsella valley in the west of the kingdom. With the help of Alfonso III of Asturias and the Count of Pallars he took control of the city of Pamplona while Fortún Garcés was still king. Together with the Pamplonese nobility they plotted to remove the king's children from the succession, which passed to the king's granddaughter Toda, who was married to Sancho Garcés. He proclaimed himself king in 905.

Throughout his reign Sancho involved himself in the quarrels of the Muslim lords to the south. In 907 he turned on his former ally Lubb ibn Muhammad and killed him in battle. Four years later Galindo Aznárez, with his brother-in-law Muhammad al-Tawil and Abd Allah ibn Lubb al-Qasawi, attacked him and was defeated; the power of the Banu Qasi was severely damaged, and Galindo became Sancho's vassal, which led to the County of Aragon being incorporated into the kingdom.

In 918 Sancho joined Ordoño II of León against the Upper March. They failed to occupy Nájera but took Calahorra, Arnedo and Viguera from the Banu Qasi, and burned the mosque at Valtierra. Two years later he allied with Bernard I of Ribagorza and Amrus ibn Muhammed to attack Monzón. His successes let him add Lower Navarre to his dominions and extend his territory as far as Nájera. As a thanksgiving for his victories he founded the monastery of San Martín de Albelda in 924.

Sancho died near Resa, close to the Ebro, on 10 December 925, and was buried in Villamayor de Monjardín. His son García was only seven years old, so his brother Jimeno Garcés succeeded him. He had married Toda Aznárez; according to the Códice de Roda they had a son and five daughters, and the daughters married kings of León or counts, among them Onneca Sánchez, wife of Alfonso IV of León, and Urraca Sánchez, wife of Ramiro II of León.

His son became García Sánchez I, king until 970. The byname Abarca seems to have been Sancho's originally, though it came to be applied to his grandson Sancho II. His dynasty ruled several Iberian kingdoms, the last until the 13th century, and Al-Andalus scholars called it the Banu Sanyo or Banu Abarca.
sancho-garcia-of-castile: Sancho was the son of Count García Fernández and Ava of Ribagorza, daughter of Raymond I, Count of Pallars and Ribagorza. With the support of Almanzor of Córdoba he rebelled against his father, and the county was divided between them until his father's death five years later, when Sancho became count of Castile and Álava.

Sancho then turned against Almanzor, together with García Gómez and their cousin García Sánchez II of Pamplona. He led the coalition defeated at the Battle of Cervera in July 1000, but early that September he turned back the Córdoban invasion of his county. Almanzor's death in 1002 left the Caliphate of Córdoba in crisis. In 1010 Sancho intervened in Ribagorza, ending Muslim domination there; his aunt Countess Toda abdicated and the county was divided between William Isarn, who had been educated in Castile, and Raymond Sunyer of Pallars, husband of Sancho's sister Mayor.
His name el de los Buenos Fueros comes from the rights and charters he granted to various towns. In 1011 he founded the Monastery of San Salvador de Oña for his daughter Tigridia to direct as abbess.

Sancho died on 5 February 1017 and was buried at Oña. He married Urraca, who is identified, from the name the couple gave a daughter, as a sister of García Gómez and daughter of Count Gómez Díaz of Saldaña. Their son García, born in November 1009, succeeded him. Their daughter Sancha was betrothed at Zaragoza in 1016 to Berenguer Ramon I, Count of Barcelona, and married him by 1021, and the eldest, Muniadona, married Sancho III of Pamplona, through whom the right to the county eventually passed.
sancho-i-of-leon: Sancho was the son of Ramiro II of León and his second wife, Queen Urraca Sánchez of Pamplona, and a grandson of Sancho I of Pamplona and Toda Aznárez. Ramiro II was succeeded by Sancho's elder brother Ordoño III in 951, and at first the younger Sancho disputed the throne with him. When Ordoño died in 956 Sancho took the vacant throne with the support of part of the nobility, his grandmother, and Fernán González, Count of Castile, who was Ordoño's brother-in-law.

Within two years Sancho was deposed by nobles led by Fernán González because of his extreme obesity, and Ordoño the Wicked, later numbered Ordoño IV, replaced him from 958 to 960. Sancho had also refused to respect the peace that Ordoño III had agreed with the Cordovans, who sent an army against him and defeated him in 957.

That defeat added to his discredit. He turned to his grandmother Toda of Pamplona for help, and in 958 Toda, Sancho and his wife Teresa Ansúrez travelled to Córdoba, where a deal was signed with the caliph Abderramán III to help him recover his throne in exchange for some territory on the banks of the Duero.

During his stay in Córdoba, according to the historian Dozy, Sancho managed to lose some of his weight under the treatment of the court physician Hasdai ibn Shaprut, who allowed him only infusions for forty days. A Muslim-Pamplonian army took Zamora in the spring of 959 and León in the second half of 960, and Ordoño IV fled to Asturias.

Sancho soon forgot his agreement with the caliph, who then supported Ordoño IV, though their confrontation went no further than a few punitive raids. The last years of the reign were marked by the growing independence of the Castilian and Galician nobility. In 966 Sancho founded the monastery of San Pelayo in León.

Sancho was poisoned and died in 966, not yet 35 years old. According to the chronicle of Sampiro, the rebel count Gonzalo Menéndez gave him a poisoned apple at the Galician monastery of Castrelo de Miño, though not all historians accept that identification, since another count named Gonzalo Muñoz lived at the time. His death fell between 15 November, the date of the last diploma in which he appears, and 19 December, the date of the first diploma of his son Ramiro III, who succeeded him. He was buried at Castrelo de Miño and later moved to León, to the church of San Salvador de Palat del Rey.
sancho-ii-of-castile: Sancho II, called the Strong, was born at Zamora, the eldest son of Ferdinand the Great and Sancha of León. Ferdinand had defeated and killed his wife's brother in battle and been crowned king of León and Castile, taking the title Imperator totius Hispaniae, Emperor of all of Spain. Sancho married a woman named Alberta, known only from her appearance as his wife in contemporary charters. When Ferdinand died in 1065 the kingdom was divided: Sancho received Castile, his brother Alfonso León and his youngest brother García the re-established Kingdom of Galicia.

Each brother was assigned a sphere of influence among the taifa states, and Sancho was to receive the parias, or tributary payments, of the Taifa of Zaragoza. Ferdinand also gave his daughters Urraca the city of Zamora and Elvira the city of Toro, both within Alfonso's León. In 1068 Sancho defeated his cousins Sancho IV of Navarre and Sancho of Aragon in the War of the Three Sanchos, and added the lands of Bureba, Alta Rioja and Álava to Castile. The same year he defeated Alfonso at the Battle of Llantada, after Alfonso invaded the Taifa of Badajoz, a client of García's Galicia.

In 1071 Sancho joined Alfonso in conquering García's northern lands, and García fled to exile in the Taifa of Seville. Sancho then turned on Alfonso. In 1072, with the help of his alférez El Cid, he defeated Alfonso at the Battle of Golpejera, and Alfonso fled to the Taifa of Toledo. Sancho was crowned king of León on 12 January 1072, holding all three crowns his father had divided. Toro fell easily, but he stalled in a siege of Urraca's better-defended Zamora.

A Zamoran noble, Vellido Adolfo, entered Sancho's camp pretending to be a deserter and killed him. El Cid chased him back to Zamora, but he escaped through a gate afterwards called the Portillo del Traidor, the Traitor's Gate. Sancho was buried at San Salvador de Oña and succeeded by Alfonso, the brother he had deposed. Alfonso deceived García, who had been induced to return from exile, and imprisoned him for life, then held the reunited lands of their father and later took his father's title of emperor of all Spain.
sancho-ii-of-pamplona: Sancho Garcés was born about 938, the eldest son of García Sánchez I of Pamplona and Andregoto Galíndez, daughter of Galindo Aznárez II, Count of Aragon. Her father left no legitimate sons, so the rights to the county passed to her and then to Sancho, who became Count of Aragon in 948 while still under age, at first under the guardianship of Count Fortún Jiménez. After his father's death in 970 he became king of Pamplona. In 987, in a donation to the monastery of San Juan de la Peña, he called himself king of Navarre, the first to use the title, though the title did not come into common use until much later.

Pamplona was linked by family ties to the Kingdom of León and the County of Castile, and the realms often acted together, the Navarrese monarchy supporting the young Ramiro III of León. Sancho founded the monastery of San Andrés de Cirueña in 972, and in 976 the Codex Vigilanus was completed at Albelda, the cultural centre of his kingdom: an illuminated manuscript containing the canons of the Councils of Toledo and the first Western representation of the Arabic numerals.

After the death of the Caliph al-Hakam II in 976, the troops of Almanzor, who had taught the new caliph Hisham II, defeated the Christians at Torrevicente and Taracueña. Sancho was beaten at San Esteban de Gormaz in 975, and it has been suggested that he was captured at Estercuel that year.

After another defeat at Rueda in 981, he went to Córdoba as ambassador, with many gifts, made a pact with Almanzor and agreed to give him his daughter. She was known in Arabic as Abda, converted to Islam and bore Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo. Almanzor raided again in 989, 991 and 992, the last leading to a second submission at Córdoba, and the next year Sancho sent his son Gonzalo on an embassy there. A caliphate army invaded once more in 994.

Sancho died in 994 and was buried at San Esteban de Monjardín, later being moved to San Juan de la Peña. He had married Urraca Fernández, daughter of Count Fernán González of Castile, and they had four children. His son García Sánchez succeeded him as king of Pamplona and Count of Aragon and ruled until 1000.
sancho-iii-of-castile: Sancho was the son of King Alfonso VII of León and Castile and Berengaria of Barcelona. His nickname, the Desired (el Deseado), arose because he was the first child of his parents, born after eight years of childless marriage. In 1152 he was endowed with the Kingdom of Nájera, although, according to Carolina Carl, he never appears in documents as king of Nájera. He also succeeded Urraca the Asturian in ruling the Kingdom of Artajona. In 1151 he married Blanche of Navarre, daughter of García Ramírez of Navarre.

Under the will of his father, the kingdom was partitioned between his two sons: Sancho inherited Castile and Toledo, and his brother Ferdinand inherited León. Sancho ruled for one year, from 1157 to 1158, as king of Castile and Toledo.

During his reign the castle of Calatrava-la-Vieja was conceded to Abbot Raymond Serrat of Fitero, who proposed using the lay brothers of his monastery as knights to defend it. These knights gave rise to the Order of Calatrava, which was confirmed in 1164 by Pope Alexander III.

In May 1158 the brothers agreed the Treaty of Sahagún, which outlined the spheres of conquest of Leonese and Castilian forces against al-Andalus. A possible division of the Portuguese kingdom between the two sons of Alfonso VII was also considered.

Sancho died suddenly in the summer of 1158, shortly after the two brothers had signed their treaty, and was buried at Toledo. His death was premature, and the proposed division of the Portuguese kingdom came to nothing. He was succeeded by his son Alfonso VIII of Castile. A second child, the infante García, died at birth in 1156, which apparently also caused the death of Queen Blanche.
sancho-iii-of-navarre: Sancho was the eldest son of García Sánchez II, called the Tremulous, and Jimena Fernández, daughter of Fernando Bermúdez, count of Cea on the Leonese frontier. The year of his birth is not known, but it falls between 992 and 996. He was raised in the monastery of Leyre and is first found as king in 1004. Because his father last appears in 1000, there has been speculation about an interregnum. On his succession he ruled at first under a council of regency led by the bishops, his mother and his grandmother Urraca Fernández.

Sancho aspired to unify the Christian principalities as Muslim Spain fragmented into taifa kingdoms. About 1010 he married Muniadona of Castile, daughter of Sancho García of Castile, and in 1015 began to expand. He took the county of Sobrarbe from Muslim control, and in 1018 he claimed part of Ribagorza after William Isarn was killed. In 1025 Raymond III of Pallars Jussà submitted to him as a vassal.

In 1017 he became protector of the young García Sánchez of Castile. After the count was assassinated at León in 1027, Sancho occupied the county and named his younger son Ferdinand its count. He then fought Bermudo III of León, and by March 1033 he was king from Zamora to the borders of Barcelona. In 1034 León itself fell and he had himself crowned there again. In Gascony he extended his authority to the Garonne after 1032. He died on 18 October 1035 and was buried at San Salvador de Oña.

Before his death Sancho divided his possessions among his sons: García received Navarre, Gonzalo Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, Ferdinand Castile, and the eldest but illegitimate Ramiro lands in Aragon. The division created the enduring kingdoms of Castile and Aragon, all held by one dynasty, the Jiménez.

He moved his residence to Nájera, patronised the road to Santiago de Compostela, and brought French ideas of vassalage and ecclesiastical reform into Iberia, so that he has been called the first Europeaniser of Iberia. He also began the Navarrese coinage. The abbot Oliva acknowledged him only as king of Navarre and of Iberia, while he called the kings of León emperor.
sancho-iv-of-castile: Sancho was born on 12 May 1258, the second son of Alfonso X and Yolanda, daughter of James I of Aragon. His elder brother, Ferdinand de la Cerda, died in November 1275, leaving a son, Alfonso. In 1282 Sancho assembled a coalition of nobles to declare for him against that son, and when Alfonso X died in 1284 he took control of the kingdom, against his father's wishes. He was crowned in Toledo, with the support of most of the nobility and the cities, though a sizable minority opposed him throughout his reign.

One leader of the opposition was Sancho's brother John of Castile, who won over Lope Díaz III de Haro, lord of Biscay. Sancho executed the lord of Biscay and imprisoned his brother. According to the chroniclers, he secured his power by executing 4,000 followers of the Infante Alfonso at Badajoz, 400 more at Talavera and others at Ávila and Toledo. He later pardoned John, who soon revolted again in the conflict over Tarifa. John called in the Marinids of Morocco and besieged Guzmán the Good in his castle in 1291, where Guzmán's son died in an act of heroism often remembered. Tarifa held until Sancho could rescue it, and the Marinids withdrew to the Maghreb.

When James II became King of Aragon he sought to bind the two crowns more closely and unite the Christian forces to reconquer the Iberian peninsula from Islam, as his predecessors had tried to do. In 1282 Sancho married María de Molina, though the marriage at first lacked a papal dispensation because they were cousins once removed and he had been betrothed in infancy to a Catalan heiress, Guillerma Moncada.

Sancho fell ill with what may have been tuberculosis, and just before he died he named his wife regent for their nine-year-old son, Ferdinand IV. He died in Toledo on 25 April 1295. The couple had seven children, among them Isabella, who married James II of Aragon, and Beatrice, who married Afonso IV of Portugal.
sancho-iv-of-navarre: Sancho Garcés IV, born about 1039, was the eldest son and heir of García Sánchez III and his wife Stephanie. His father was killed at the Battle of Atapuerca on 1 September 1054, during a war with the Kingdom of León. Sancho, then fourteen years old, was proclaimed king by the army in the camp by the battlefield, with the consent of King Ferdinand I of León, who was his uncle. His mother acted as regent until her death on 25 May 1058, continuing her husband's policies and her support for the monastery of Santa María la Real of Nájera.

Soon after his accession many lords in the west of the kingdom went over to the Leonese; only Íñigo López, lord of Biscay, and Sancho Fortúnez, lord of Pancorbo, stayed loyal. On 29 December 1062 Sancho and Ferdinand signed a treaty fixing their border, which recognised Ferdinand as king of all Castile and Sancho's authority in the Rioja, Álava, Biscay and implicitly Guipúzcoa. His other uncle, King Ramiro I of Aragon, supported him and received Lerda, Undués and the castle of Sangüesa in gratitude. From 1060 Sancho pressed al-Muqtadir, king of Zaragoza, for annual tribute payments called parias.

From 1065 he was in conflict with Castile, which had been raised to a kingdom for Ferdinand's son Sancho II of Castile, ending in the War of the Three Sanchos of 1067–1068. Sancho of Pamplona asked for help from Sancho of Aragon, but their forces were beaten by Sancho of Castile and his commander El Cid, and he lost Bureba, Alta Rioja and Álava. In 1068 he married Placencia, a French woman, and they had two children.

Sancho was assassinated at Peñalén, near Funes, on 4 June 1076, by a conspiracy headed by his brother Ramón and his sister Ermesinda: during a hunt, his siblings forced him off a cliff, which gave him his nickname. The kingdom was then invaded and partitioned between Sancho of Aragon and Alfonso VI of León and Castile. Alfonso occupied La Rioja and Sancho was proclaimed king in Pamplona. The older of his sons named García Sánchez was removed from the line of succession.
sancho-ramirez: Sancho Ramírez was the eldest son of Ramiro I and Ermesinda of Bigorre. His father was the first king of Aragon and an illegitimate son of Sancho III of Pamplona. Sancho Ramírez succeeded him as second king of Aragon in 1063. Like his father, he did not use the royal title early in his reign, even though his state had become fully independent. Between 1067 and 1068 the War of the Three Sanchos set him against his first cousins Sancho IV of Navarre and Sancho II of Castile, who defeated the two allies and retook Bureba, Alta Rioja and Álava.

In 1076 Sancho IV of Navarre was murdered by his own siblings, which began a succession crisis in the neighbouring kingdom. Alfonso VI recognised the murdered king's young son García as titular king, while Sancho Ramírez gathered Navarrese nobles who resented Alfonso's influence. The crisis ended in partition: Sancho Ramírez was elected king of Navarre and ceded the contested western provinces to Alfonso. From then he styled himself king of both Aragon and Navarre.

He conquered Barbastro in 1064, Graus in 1083 and Monzón in 1089. El Cid, who was raiding his lands and those of his Muslim allies, defeated him at the Battle of Morella, probably in 1084. Sancho died in 1094 at Huesca.

Sancho married first Isabella, daughter of Count Armengol III of Urgel, a marriage dissolved in 1071, and then Felicia, daughter of Hilduin IV, Count of Montdidier. His son Peter by Isabella succeeded him, followed by Alfonso and Ramiro, his sons by Felicia, so that three of his sons reigned in turn after him.
sancho-vi-of-navarre: Sancho Garcés VI was born on 21 April 1132, the eldest son of García Ramírez, the Restorer, and Margaret of L'Aigle. He became king in 1150 and was the first monarch to drop officially the title of king of Pamplona in favour of king of Navarre, changing the designation of his kingdom. He is credited with bringing Navarre into the political orbit of Europe.

Sancho inherited a debilitated kingdom, subject to frequent raids by Castile under Alfonso VII and by the County of Barcelona under Ramon Berenguer IV, also king of Aragon. In 1140 these two had agreed on the partition of Navarre in the Treaty of Carrión. In his early reign Sancho was forced to sign the Treaties of Tudején and Carrión, which reduced his borders, and by the Accord of Soria Castile was finally confirmed in its conquests. He tried to repair the borders, and the Kingdom of Artajona was returned to him by Sancho III of Castile in 1157.

Facing a possible Castilian takeover of western Navarrese territory, he reasserted royal authority in 1181 by founding several towns, among them San Sebastián, Vitoria and Treviño. He was hostile to Ramon Berenguer IV, but Raymond's son Alfonso II of Aragon divided with him the lands taken from Murcia in the treaty of Sangüesa in 1168. In 1190 the two neighbours signed a pact at Borja of mutual protection against Castilian expansion.

On 20 July 1153 Sancho married Sancha of Castile, daughter of Alfonso VII, and they had six children. Berengaria married Richard I of England in 1191 and became queen consort of England. Sancho the Strong succeeded his father and ruled from 1194 to 1234. Blanche married Theobald III, Count of Champagne, and her son Theobald later became king of Navarre after the death of his uncle. Sancho VI died in Pamplona on 27 June 1194 and is buried there.
sancho-vii-of-navarre: Sancho was probably the eldest child of Sancho VI and Sancha, daughter of Alfonso VII of León, born soon after their marriage, probably in Tudela. His younger sister Berengaria married Richard I of England in 1191 on Cyprus, on the way to the Third Crusade, and Sancho and Richard were reputed to be good friends and close allies. In 1194 his knights were besieging the castle of Loches for Richard when news came of his father's death, and he returned to Navarre and was crowned in Pamplona on 15 August.

Sancho arrived late at the Battle of Alarcos in 1195 and spoiled his relations with Alfonso VIII of Castile; he devastated Soria and Almazán, and the two made the Peace of Tarazona. Between 1198 and 1200 he campaigned in Africa, probably in the service of the Almohads. While he was away Alfonso VIII and Peter II of Aragon invaded Navarre, which lost Álava, Guipúzcoa and Biscay to Castile, losses confirmed by the Treaty of Guadalajara in 1207.

At the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 the forces of Sancho, Alfonso VIII, Afonso II of Portugal and Peter II of Aragon defeated the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir. Sancho led a charge that broke through the bodyguard around the caliph's tent, and the chains in the arms of Navarre are said to commemorate this, the guards supposedly having been slaves chained together. In 1231 he signed a treaty with James I of Aragon under which the survivor would inherit the other's kingdom; it was never carried out. He continued the building of the new cathedral at Pamplona, begun by his father.

Sancho married Constance, daughter of Raymond VI of Toulouse, in 1195 and repudiated her a few years later; the identity of his second wife is disputed. He had no known children. Suffering from a varicose ulcer on his right leg and ashamed of it and of his obesity, he withdrew to Tudela, where his sister Blanche administered the kingdom until she died in 1229.

He died at Tudela in 1234, probably of complications from the ulcer, and was recognised as succeeded by his nephew Theobald IV of Champagne, Blanche's son. He was first buried at San Nicolás and later moved to Roncesvalles. Examination of his remains measured him at 2.20 metres tall, probably the basis for the epithet the Strong. Alberic de Trois-Fontaines said he left a large library, though the figure of 1.7 million books is probably exaggerated.
sanchuniathon: All that is known of Sanchuniathon comes from the Praeparatio Evangelica of Eusebius, which quotes Philo of Byblos. His name probably means "Sakkun has given" in Phoenician, and he was also called Sanchoniatho the Berytian. Eusebius cites the neo-Platonist writer Porphyry, who said that Sanchuniathon of Berytus (Beirut) wrote the truest history because he had records from Hierombalus, priest of Ieuo, and that he dedicated it to Abibalus, king of Berytus, who approved it. Porphyry placed the work before the Trojan War, near the time of Moses, "when Semiramis was queen of the Assyrians."

Sanchuniathon is said to have drawn on secret writings of the Ammouneis found in the shrines and on inscriptions on temple pillars. These, in the account, revealed that the gods had been human beings worshipped after death, and that the Phoenicians had given their kings' names to the sun, moon, stars and forces of nature, a reading akin to euhemerism. Eusebius used this to discredit pagan religion.

The fragments begin with a cosmogony traced to Taautus, whom Philo identifies with the Egyptian Thoth: from Erebus and Wind came Desire, then Môt, and creatures called Zophasemin formed together as an egg. A line of mortal culture heroes follows, among them Genus and Genea, who prayed to the sun as Beelsamen, lord of heaven. In the history of the gods El, or Cronus, overthrows and castrates his father Uranus and founds Byblos, the first city of Phoenicia. Eusebius also names a treatise by him On the Phoenician Alphabet.

The euhemerist slant and the weight given to Beirut, a city of little importance in early times, suggest that the work is not nearly as old as it claims. Some think Philo forged it or gathered various traditions under an ancient name; the Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition said he belonged "more to legend than to history." Not all readers took so critical a view: Squier Payne defended him in 1720 in a preface to Richard Cumberland's translation.

In 1952 Otto Eissfeldt showed that the work holds genuine Phoenician elements that match the Ugaritic texts excavated at Ras Shamra since 1929. The modern consensus is that Philo offered a Hellenistic view of Phoenician material written between Alexander the Great and the first century BCE, if he did not invent it.
sanctuary-of-artemis-orthia: The cult of Orthia was shared by the four villages that first made up Sparta: Limnae, where the sanctuary lies, Pitane, Cynosura and Mesoa. Historians believe it probably came after the cult of Athena Polioukhos, protectress of the city. Pottery fragments from the late Greek Dark Ages suggest that worship began in the 10th century BCE, and the first temple is believed to date from about 700 BCE. After a flood in the 6th century BCE the ground was raised on a bed of river sand, and around 570 BCE a second temple and altar of limestone were built a little to the north.

The second temple was rebuilt in the 2nd century BCE, except for the altar. In the 3rd century CE the Romans built a theatre around the temple and altar to hold the visitors who came to watch the flogging of youths. Worship continued into the 4th century CE, when non-Christian cults were banned in the late Roman Empire.

The cult centred on a wooden effigy, a xoanon, which according to Euripides was the image stolen by Orestes and Iphigenia from Tauride. Pausanias tells that after quarrels at the altar an oracle demanded human blood, and that Lycurgus replaced human sacrifice with the scourging of youths, while a priestess held the image. In the diamastigosis cheeses were piled on the altar and guarded by men with whips, and the youths tried to seize them. Plutarch saw the rite as a reenactment of an episode of the Greco-Persian Wars. The cult also included dances by young men, whose prize was a sickle, and by choruses of girls.

The British School at Athens brought the site to light in its digs in Laconia of 1906–10, led by R. M. Dawkins. Before the dig it seemed to be only a ruined Roman theatre, plundered after the foundation of modern Sparta in 1834 and close to falling into the river. The excavators found a long sequence of strata, with the richest deposits beneath the altar, including the bones of animals burned as offerings. Carved ivories of a winged goddess holding animals were found, made locally, as half-finished pieces show. Over 100,000 lead offerings are now in the Liverpool collections, and others are in the British Museum.
sandakan: Sandakan is the capital of the Sandakan District in Sabah, Malaysia, on the Sandakan Peninsula and the east coast of the state, facing the Sulu Sea. It lies about 319 kilometres east of Kota Kinabalu and 28 km from the international border with the Philippines. It is one of the main ports for oil, tobacco, coffee, sago and timber exports, and other activities include fishing, shipbuilding and eco-tourism. Nearby are the Turtle Islands and the Sepilok Orang Utan Sanctuary. The climate is tropical rainforest, hot and wet, with the wettest months from October to February.

Like most of Borneo, the area was under the Bruneian Empire in the 15th century, and was later ceded to the Sultanate of Sulu as a gift for helping Brunei in a civil war. By 1864 Spain had blockaded the Sultanate's possessions in the Sulu Archipelago. The Sultanate awarded a former German consular official a piece of land in Sandakan Bay, and in 1878 sold north-eastern Borneo to an Austro-Hungarian consul, who left the territory to a British merchant. A protocol among the British, German and Spanish recognised Spanish sovereignty over the Sulu Archipelago in return for Spain not intervening in British affairs in northern Borneo.
