The first European settlement was built by a Scottish arms smuggler, William Clark Cowie, who named it Sandakan, which in the Suluk language means the place that was pawned. It was soon called Kampong German because of German bases there. After a fire, a new settlement was built and named Elopura, meaning beautiful town, by the British North Borneo Company, though local people kept the old name. Sandakan began to prosper when the company started a new settlement in 1879, making it a commercial and trading centre and the main administrative centre of North Borneo, and encouraged Chinese migration from Hong Kong, which gave the town the nickname Little Hong Kong.

Prosperity halted when the Japanese occupied the area, and Allied bombing from 1944 destroyed the town totally. Unable to fund reconstruction, the company handed the administration of North Borneo to the Crown Colony government, and the administrative capital moved to Jesselton. Under the Colonial Office's Reconstruction and Development Plan of 1948 to 1955 the colonial government developed the fishing industry. Fishing is now in decline because the bay is silting up.

The 2020 census counted a municipal population of 439,050. In 2010 the largest group in the municipal area was non-Malaysian citizens, mostly from the southern Philippines, followed by other Bumiputras, Chinese, Bajau and Suluk. The Chinese are mostly Cantonese and Hakka, the latter partly descended from refugees of the Taiping Rebellion. Attractions include the Sandakan Heritage Museum, the Sandakan War Memorial, the Gomantong Caves and the Sandakan Cultural Festival.
sandinista-national-liberation-front: The Sandinistas took their name from Augusto César Sandino (1895-1934), who led Nicaragua's nationalist rebellion against the United States occupation of the country in the early 20th century. Sandino was assassinated on 21 February 1934 by the National Guard, the US-equipped force of Anastasio Somoza García, whose family ruled the country from 1936 until the Sandinistas overthrew it in 1979.

The movement grew out of opposition and student groups of the late 1950s and early 1960s, with the universities of Léon and the National Autonomous University in Managua as principal centres. Inspired by the Cuban Revolution and the FLN in Algeria, it was founded in 1961 by Carlos Fonseca, Silvio Mayorga, Tomás Borge, Casimiro Sotelo and others as the National Liberation Front. Only Borge lived to see the victory of 1979.

After a defeat at Pancasán in 1967 the Front adopted the doctrine of the Prolonged Popular War. The earthquake of 23 December 1972 destroyed much of Managua, and Anastasio Somoza Debayle's National Guard embezzled much of the aid. The killing of the newspaper editor Pedro Joaquín Chamorro on 10 January 1978 set off riots and a general strike. By mid-April 1979 five guerrilla fronts operated under the Front's joint command, and the Somoza regime fell in the Nicaraguan Revolution of that year.

The Sandinistas inherited a debt of US$1.6 billion, an estimated 30,000 to 50,000 war dead and 600,000 homeless. They first governed through a five-member Junta of National Reconstruction, and took exclusive power in March 1981. The United States, under President Ronald Reagan, authorised the CIA to finance, arm and train the Contras, mostly remnants of Somoza's National Guard, and imposed a trade embargo in May 1985. Elections were held in 1984, and the war continued until 1989. After the Esquipulas II treaty of 1987, the Sandinistas lost the election of 26 February 1990 to Violeta Barrios de Chamorro and passed power peacefully.

In government the Front carried out a literacy campaign, with Cuban teachers, that lowered illiteracy from 50% to 12%, a land reform affecting half of the country's arable land and a Ministry of Culture led by the poet and priest Ernesto Cardenal. Cuba also sent advisers, who numbered over 2,500. Critics reported detentions, censorship of the newspaper La Prensa and abuses against the Miskito people, while supporters and church delegations disputed some allegations as political. Its flag, red above black with the letters F S L N, is a modified version of Sandino's. Daniel Ortega was elected president in 2006, and held the office from 1985 to 1990 and again from 2007.
sandor-garbai: Sándor Garbai was born on 27 March 1879 into the family of a Protestant bricklayer. He took part in the labour movement from a young age and joined the Social Democratic Party of Hungary in 1901, rising quickly through its ranks. From 1908 he was chairman of the Workers' Insurance Fund, and during the First Hungarian Republic he headed the All National Housing Council.

Garbai favoured the merger of the Social Democratic Party with the Hungarian Communist Party, which took place on 21 March 1919 and led to the foundation of the Hungarian Soviet Republic. He became Chairman of the Central Executive Council, which made him both head of state and prime minister. He remained titular leader for the better part of the republic's existence, but the de facto leader was the Communist foreign minister Béla Kun.

After the fall of the Soviet Republic he was arrested by the Romanian military. Fearing reprisals, he escaped from captivity in Cluj and fled to Czechoslovakia, settling first in Bratislava and then moving to Vienna, where he became a leader of the centrist Marxist movement among Hungarian political refugees.

In Vienna Garbai and his family opened a restaurant that hosted former communist and other socialist leaders. It soon went bankrupt, and he suffered heavy financial losses and lived in poverty for the rest of his life. He left Austria in 1934 after the victory of the right-wing Fatherland Front and settled in Bratislava, and in 1938 he moved to Paris.

During the German occupation of France he did not take part in the French Resistance, although the underground tried to recruit him, and the German occupiers did not trouble him. After the liberation of Hungary he and his family wished to return home, but their request was rejected. He remained in Paris and died there on 7 November 1947.
sandro-botticelli: Alessandro di Mariano di Vanni Filipepi, known as Botticelli, was born in Florence in a house on the Borgo Ognissanti and lived in the same area all his life. He was the youngest of the four surviving children of the tanner Mariano di Vanni d'Amedeo Filipepi and his wife Smeralda. His birth date is unknown, but his father's tax returns, which give his age as two in 1447 and thirteen in 1458, show that he was born between 1444 and 1446. Giorgio Vasari reported that Botticelli was first trained as a goldsmith. From about 1461 or 1462 he was apprenticed to Fra Filippo Lippi, from whom he learned intimate compositions with melancholic figures drawn in clear contours.

Botticelli was an independent master throughout the 1470s, and his reputation rose. His only significant time away from Florence was spent painting in Pisa in 1474 and, in 1481 to 1482, in the Sistine Chapel in Rome, where Pope Sixtus IV summoned him and other Florentine and Umbrian painters to fresco the walls. He received patronage from members of the Medici family, including Lorenzo de' Medici and his circle.

The 1480s were his most successful decade. Primavera of about 1482 and The Birth of Venus of about 1485, both now in the Uffizi, depicted classical mythology on a very large scale, which was virtually unprecedented in Western art since antiquity. In the same decade he painted many Madonnas and altarpieces, among them the Bardi Altarpiece, finished by February 1485, and the San Marco Altarpiece, his largest. By the 1490s his style became more personal and to some extent mannered, and his last works moved in a direction opposite to that of Leonardo da Vinci and the painters of the High Renaissance, towards a style many have called more Gothic or archaic.
He painted dozens of Madonnas, many of them in the round tondo shape, as well as portraits, although fewer than have been attributed to him. He had a lifelong interest in Dante.

According to Vasari, Botticelli became a follower of the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola, who preached in Florence from 1490 until his execution in 1498, gave up painting and fell into poverty. Botticelli died on 17 May 1510 and was buried in the church of Ognissanti. His reputation was then eclipsed longer than that of any other major European artist, until the Pre-Raphaelites rediscovered him in the late 19th century.
sandzak: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps. In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.
sanford-b-dole: Sanford Ballard Dole was born in Honolulu on 23 April 1844 to Protestant missionaries from Maine. His father, Daniel Dole, was principal of Oahu College, and his mother, Emily Hoyt Ballard, died within days of his birth. The family moved to Kōloa on Kauaʻi in 1855, where they ran another school that Sanford attended. He studied at Oahu College and at Williams College in 1866–1867, and read law in a Boston office. Elected to the legislature of the Hawaiian Kingdom for Kauaʻi in 1884 and 1886, he served until 1887 and was active in securing the constitution of 1887, which he and other lawyers of American descent drafted.

The 1887 constitution, called the Bayonet Constitution, limited voting to literate males of Hawaiian, European and American descent and set income and wealth requirements for voting for the House of Nobles. King Kalākaua appointed Dole to the Supreme Court in December 1887, and Queen Liliʻuokalani to her Privy Council in 1891. After the coup that ended the monarchy on 17 January 1893 he helped draft the Committee of Safety's declaration, though he did not join it, and became president of the Provisional Government, which was recognised within 48 hours by all nations with diplomatic ties to the kingdom.

President Grover Cleveland's commissioner James Henderson Blount reported in July 1893 that the Committee of Safety had conspired with the US ambassador John L. Stevens to land marines and remove the queen. The Morgan Report of February 1894 concluded instead that the overthrow was locally based and that the troops had only protected American property and citizens. The Republic of Hawaii was proclaimed on 4 July 1894, and Dole, elected its first and only elected president, served until 1898. Voting rights were restricted, which kept power with residents of American and European descent. He put down the counter-rebellion of January 1895 led by Robert William Wilcox, and commuted the death sentences of its leaders.

In January and February 1898 he visited Washington to urge annexation. Congress passed the Newlands Resolution on 4 July 1898, effective 12 August, and the transfer was marked that day at ʻIolani Palace. In June 1900 he became the first governor of the Territory of Hawaii, resigning in November 1903 to serve as a federal district judge until his retirement on 16 December 1915.
Dole died on 9 June 1926 after a series of strokes, and his ashes were placed in the cemetery of Kawaiahaʻo Church. Dole Middle School in Kalihi Valley was named after him in 1956.
sang-nila-utama: In the Malay Annals Sang Nila Utama is a prince of Palembang, son of King Sang Sapurba, the supposed descendant of Rajendra I through his Islamic guise as Iskandar Zulkarnain and the half-mythical ancestor of many rulers of the Malay world. He married Princess Wan Sri Bini, daughter of Permaisuri Iskandar Syah, queen of Bentan on Bintan Island, and received a jewelled golden crown and a royal signet ring. His title at his coronation, Sri Tri Buana, means Lord of Three Worlds: perhaps the heavens, the human world and the underworld, or Java, Sumatra and Temasek.

The Annals tell that while hunting on Bintan he chased a stag up a hill, climbed a great rock and saw across the sea an island with a white beach, which his chief minister named as Temasek. On the crossing a storm nearly sank his ship until, on the captain's advice, he threw his crown into the sea. Hunting near the river mouth on the open ground now called the Padang, he saw a beast with a red body, black head and white breast, which his chief minister Demang Lebar Daun called a lion. Taking it as a good omen, he founded a city there and named it Singapura.

He had two sons with Wan Sri Bini. The elder, Raja Kechil-Besar, succeeded him as Sri Wikrama Wira, and the younger became his prime minister. Sang Nila Utama was buried on Bukit Larangan, now Fort Canning Hill, though the site of his grave is unknown.

Scholars debate how far the Annals record real events, and some hold that he may be a mythical figure, though Singapore's 14th-century settlement is no longer in doubt: the Yuan traveller Wang Dayuan described Long Ya Men and Ban Zu under local rulers. The tale is highly symbolic. Casting away the crown may stand for the shift of power from Palembang to Singapura, and since lions never lived in Singapore the beast has been read as a Malayan tiger or the janggi of Minangkabau legend. Some suggest the figure was a literary device to cover the story of Parameswara, the founder of Melaka, whose life in the Suma Oriental of Tomé Pires is strikingly similar.
sangam-literature: Sangam literature is also called the Poetry of the Noble Ones. Tamil tradition links it to three traditional gatherings, or sangams, around Madurai and Kapāṭapuram, said to have lasted over 4,440, 3,700 and 1,850 years. Scholars regard this chronology as mythical, and David Shulman writes that there is not the slightest shred of evidence that such academies ever existed, though Pandya inscriptions mention an academy of scholars. Kamil Zvelebil holds that a kernel of reality lies in the myth and that such an academy probably existed at Madurai at the beginning of the Christian era.

Most scholars place the historical Sangam period from about 300 BCE to 300 CE, while Zvelebil considers 100 BCE to 250 CE the most acceptable range. In those centuries Tamilakam, the ancient Tamil-speaking land, was ruled by the three dynasties of Pandya, Chola and Chera and by a few independent chieftains, the Velir. The poems were made by 473 poets, some 102 of them anonymous, who included members of royal families, merchants and farmers and at least 27 women.

The surviving collection holds 2,381 poems of between 3 and 782 lines. Sixteen poets account for about half of them, and Kapilar alone for nearly a tenth. The Tolkappiyam, the oldest surviving Tamil grammar, is counted with the corpus, together with the Ettuttokai (Eight Anthologies) and the Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls). Poetry is classed as akam, concerned with love and inner feeling, which makes up about three quarters, and puram, concerned with war, kings and public life, which makes up about a quarter.

Each is arranged by landscape, among them mountains, pastoral forest, farmland, coast and arid land. Akam poems use imagery and never name persons or places, while puram poems name both. Early poems follow the akaval and vanci metres. Paripatal, in contrast, praises Vishnu, Durga and Murugan. The Pattinappalai describes the Chola capital and its harbour, with ships and trade, bards and dancers.

The poems were forgotten for most of the second millennium and rediscovered by scholars of the later 19th century. Arumuka Navalar printed the first Sangam text, the Tirumurukarruppatai, in 1851. C. W. Damodaram Pillai published the Kalittokai in 1887 and other works. U. V. Swaminatha Aiyar found major collections of palm-leaf manuscripts in 1883 at the Thiruvavaduthurai monastery and published the Ten Idylls in 1889. Zvelebil argues that the term Sangam literature is a misnomer and that classical literature is better.
sangama-dynasty: The dynasty's founders, Harihara I, also called Vira Harihara or Hakka Raya, and Bukka Raya I, were the sons of Bhavana Sangama, who had been taken prisoner in 1327 by Muhammad bin Tughluq. The brothers founded Vijayanagara in 1336. Harihara I reigned from 1336 to 1356 and Bukka Raya I, also counted a founder of the empire, from 1356 to 1377.

Bukka's successor, Harihara II, who reigned from 1377 to 1404, carried on his campaigns across southern India. He took control of coastal Andhra between Nellore and Kalinga, conquered the Addanki and Srisailam areas and most of the lands of the peninsula south of the Krishna River, and won the ports of Goa, Chaul and Dabhol. His death brought a contest for the throne between Virupaksha Raya, Bukka Raya II and Deva Raya, which Deva Raya won; he reigned from 1406 to 1422 and kept firm control of the empire's many territories.

His immediate successors, Ramachandra Raya in 1422 and Vira Vijaya Bukka Raya from 1422 to 1424, achieved little of note. Deva Raya II, who reigned from 1424 to 1446, brought the dynasty to its height. He completed the conquest of southern India, taking Kondavidu and defeating the ruler of Quilon and other chieftains, so that the empire reached from Odisha to Malabar and from Ceylon to Gulbarga, and he took over many of the major Indian ports.

After Deva Raya II the dynasty declined under weaker kings, Mallikarjuna Raya from 1446 to 1465 and Virupaksha Raya II from 1465 to 1485, while the Bahamani kingdoms took much of Vijayanagara's territory. Praudha Raya held the throne briefly in 1485, the year in which the house of Sangama came to an end.
sangha: In Buddhism the term refers to the monastic communities of bhikkhu (monks) and bhikkhuni (nuns), traditionally called the bhikkhu-sangha and the bhikkhuni-sangha. As a separate category, Buddhists who have attained any of the four stages of enlightenment, whether or not they belong to the monastic community, are called the āryasaṅgha, the noble Sangha. A glossary by Richard Robinson and others gives two levels of meaning: an ideal level, covering all the Buddha's followers, lay or ordained, who have reached at least the level of srotāpanna, and a conventional level, covering the orders of monks and nuns. The two overlap but are not identical, since some members of the ideal Sangha are not ordained.

Usage differs between schools. Mahayana practitioners may use the word for all Buddhists, whereas the Pāli Canon uses parisā, the assembly, for the larger community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen who have taken the Three Refuges. The Sangha is the third of those refuges, and in the Theravada tradition its qualities are chanted daily or on Uposatha days.

The Sangha was established by Gautama Buddha in the fifth century BCE for those who wished to practise full-time, free from the responsibilities of household life. It has also preserved the Buddha's teachings, given spiritual support to the lay community, and taken responsibility for the integrity of the doctrine and for its translation and propagation. Its key feature is adherence to the vinaya, which contains 227 main rules of conduct, known as the Patimokkha in Pāli, including complete chastity and eating only before noon. Transgressions carry penalties from confession to permanent expulsion.

The words bhikkhu and bhikkhuni mean one who lives by alms, and early monastics went on daily alms rounds. The vinaya did not allow the sangha to farm, but in East Asia monastic communities came to engage in agriculture, an emphasis attributed to the Chan master Baizhang Huaihai. In Japan Saichō, the founder of Tendai, reduced the rules to about 60, based on the Bodhisattva Precepts.

In its political sense the word denoted a governing assembly in a republic or a kingdom, and some Buddhists have called the sangha humanity's oldest surviving democratic institution. Nichiren Shōshū holds that the sangha is the priesthood of its head temple Taisekiji, while the Soka Gakkai, expelled from it in December 1991, understands the sangha to include all who practise Buddhism in its way, lay or clerical.
sanghamitta: According to Sri Lankan tradition Sanghamitta was a daughter of Emperor Ashoka and his first wife, Devi, a Buddhist, and was born in Ujjain. Her brother Mahinda was her elder. She was married at fourteen to Agribrahma, a nephew of Ashoka, and had a son, the novice Sumana. At eighteen she was ordained into the Theravada order, at the same time as her brother, and in time she became an arahant and lived at Pataliputra. Ashoka meanwhile took Buddhism to nine regions, after a Third Buddhist Council presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa had agreed to send delegations.

Mahinda led the mission to Sri Lanka, where he met King Devanampiya Tissa and the king's sister-in-law Princess Anula at the Mahamegha Garden. Anula and many other women wished to be ordained as nuns, but Mahinda said that this had to be done by a nun. He advised the king to ask Ashoka to send Sanghamitta, and to ask for a sapling of the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya. Ashoka was at first reluctant to send his daughter, but she urged that so many women in Lanka were to be ordained that she must go. She sailed with ten other nuns, carrying the sapling in a golden vase, and landed at Jambukola, where King Tissa received her and escorted her to Anuradhapura.

The sapling was planted by the king in the Mahamegha Grove. A legend says that serpent spirits, or Nagas, encircled the tree and that Sanghamitta drove them off by taking the form of a Garuda. She ordained Anula, who became the first Sri Lankan woman to be a bhikkhuni, and more than a thousand companions. The chronicle Dipavamsa records that women of every age and rank joined the new order and became learned in the rules of discipline.

Sanghamitta died in 203 BCE, aged 79, in the ninth year of King Uttiya, who performed her last rites. She was cremated east of the Thuparama, in front of the Bodhi tree, and a stupa was raised over her ashes. The order of nuns she founded flourished for over a thousand years and disappeared in 1017, an end attributed to the Chola invasion. The Bodhi tree still grows at Anuradhapura inside a compound wall. Theravada Buddhists in Sri Lanka keep Unduvapa Poya, the December full moon, as Sanghamitta Day.
sangju: Sangju lies on the north-western border of North Gyeongsang Province, touching North Chungcheong Province. All of it lies in the valley of the Nakdong River, which several tributaries join, among them the Yeong, which rises in Mungyeong. The land slopes down from the Sobaek Mountains in the east to the river basin, and the highest point is the top of Songnisan, 1,058 metres above sea level. The terrain is hilly, with few flat areas along the rivers, and 67 per cent of the land is classed as vacant. The city spans about 49 kilometres from north to south and 43.3 kilometres from east to west.

Sangju first emerged after Silla conquered the area and subjugated small states such as Goryeong Gaya and Sabeol-guk. The dates are debated, but the area was under firm Silla control by 505. Under Silla the fortress of Sangju was one of the nine ju, or provincial units, near Gyeongju, and it regulated traffic along the east-west route linking the Han River valley, which Silla acquired in 553, with the Gyeongju area. Buddhist missionaries from Goguryeo travelling down from Haneuljae Pass in the 6th century would have reached it as their first major city.

In the late 9th century, as Unified Silla declined, rebellions broke out at Sangju. Ajagae seized the fortress and declared himself a general, then surrendered to Wang Kŏn in 918. The Silla noble Bak Eon-chang founded a kingdom of Sabeol-guk until the Later Baekje leader Kyŏn Hwŏn overthrew him in 927. Sangju became a county in 1895 and absorbed Hamchang County in 1914. Under Japanese rule the railway was completed in 1924, and an agricultural training institution that became Sangju National University was founded. The city and county were reunited on 1 January 1995.

Sangju is traditionally agricultural, and about 40 per cent of its residents farm. It has the most farming households of any district in South Korea. Silk production has been known here since Silla times, and rice is the chief crop, with grapes, apples, pears, cucumbers and dried persimmons also grown. The city's nickname, Sam Baek or Three Whites, refers to rice, silkworm cocoons and dried persimmons. The Gyeongbuk Line railway and the Jungbu Naeryuk Expressway pass through it. In 2002 the first Carthusian monastery in Asia, the Charterhouse Our Lady of Korea, was founded in the city.
sangkum-reastr-niyum: Prince Norodom Sihanouk set up the Sangkum on 22 March 1955, after stepping down from the throne in favour of his father, Norodom Suramarit. It grew out of four small monarchist and rightist parties, among them the Victorious Northeast party of Dap Chhuon and the Khmer Renovation party of Lon Nol, broadened to fight the 1955 parliamentary election, the first after independence. It called itself a movement rather than a party, and members had to give up membership of any other political group. Its sweeping victory was followed by allegations of massive electoral fraud and of intimidation of the Democratic Party and the socialist Krom Pracheachon.

Its Buddhist or Khmer socialism had little to do with Marxist or welfare socialism. It joined socialist slogans to monarchism, nationalism and Theravada Buddhist teaching, urging the wealthy to give to the poor to gain merit rather than abolishing private property, and it was defined above all by Sihanouk's personal popularity. In practice state enterprises such as OROC, the Office royale de coopération, were run by members of the Sangkum elite, often for their own gain. A youth wing, the Royal Khmer Socialist Youth, followed in 1957.

Sihanouk alternately attacked opponents and offered them posts, which stifled dissent and drew much of the opposition into the regime. The Democratic Party was absorbed in 1957, and communists such as Hu Nim and Khieu Samphan took posts. Outside stood the hardline communists and Son Ngoc Thanh's Khmer Serei, whose captured leaders were executed: Preap In's execution in 1963 was shown in cinemas across the country.

Sihanouk was made Head of State for life in 1963. After rightist candidates swept the 1966 elections he created a left-wing Counter-Government as a check. Repression of the left, led by Lon Nol and the army in Sihanouk's name, grew increasingly violent, above all after a rebellion in Battambang Province from early 1967; captured communists were reported killed, some disembowelled or thrown from cliffs. Khieu Samphan, Hou Yuon and Hu Nim fled to the forests in 1967-8. In 1970 Lon Nol and the rightists led by In Tam and Prince Sisowath Sirik Matak deposed Sihanouk. Opinion on the Sangkum remains divided between those who see an authoritarian, conservative movement and those who stress the wider participation it brought.
sangrur: Sangrur lies at an average elevation of 237 metres and is the headquarters of Sangrur district. At the 2011 census the Sangrur Municipal Council had a population of 88,043, of whom 46,931 were males and 41,112 females, with an overall literacy rate of 83.54 per cent. It has a satellite centre of the PGIMER and the Homi Bhabha Cancer Hospital, set up by the Tata Memorial Centre with the Government of Punjab. The Sangrur parliamentary constituency is one of the 13 Lok Sabha seats of Punjab.

The rulers of Jind State used to spend their summers in the buildings around the Banasar Bagh, the city's garden, whose twelve-doored marble baradari stands in a pond reached by a small bridge. The Durbar Hall in the complex, built in or around 1865, has been turned into the Jind State Memorial Museum by the Punjab Government's Department of Culture and holds objects used by the Jind royals and a collection of arms and armour. A Maha Kali Devi temple, with shrines of several Hindu deities, was built in 1867 on Patiala Gate Market Road, and the clock tower near the courts complex was built in 1885 by order of Maharaja Raghubir Singh, from the Canal Foundry at Roorkee.

Outside the Nabha Gate stands the Shahi Samadhan, the tombs of the rulers of the former Jind State. Of its 16 samadhis, 14 were built over 125 years ago of brick and lime-surkhi and two about 60–65 years ago in marble. They include those of Maharaja Gajpat Singh, the maternal grandfather of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and of his maternal uncle Maharaja Bhag Singh, and those of Maharaja Fateh Singh, Maharaja Sangat Singh, Maharaja Sarup Singh, Maharaja Ranbir Singh and Maharaja Rajbir Singh.
sangye-gyatso: Sangye Gyatso, whose name is also written Sangye Gyamtso, was born near Lhasa in September 1653. Some accounts held him to be a son of the Fifth Dalai Lama, though the Dalai Lama had then been away on his journey to China for the preceding sixteen months. He became regent, or Kalon, of the Ganden Phodrang government in 1679 at the age of 26, the sixth regent of the Fifth Dalai Lama.

From 1679 to 1684 the Ganden Phodrang fought the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War against the Namgyal dynasty of Ladakh, which Sangye Gyatso and King Delek Namgyal ended with the Treaty of Tingmosgang in 1684. To counter the Khoshut Mongols, protectors of Tibet since 1642, he kept close contact with Galdan Boshugtu Khan of the Dzungar Khanate. The reincarnation of the Fifth Dalai Lama, born in 1683, was found two years later in southern Tibet and educated in secret at Nankhartse. When the fifteen-year-old Tsangyang Gyatso was installed as Sixth Dalai Lama in 1697, the Kangxi Emperor, who had not been told, was greatly angered.

In 1694, under a commission of the Fifth Dalai Lama, Sangye Gyatso founded the Chagpori College of Medicine, a school of Tibetan medicine for monks; in 1916 it was refounded under the 13th Dalai Lama as the Men-Tsee-Khang, with departments of astrology and astronomy. He wrote the Blue Beryl medical treatise and had a series of nearly 100 paintings made to illustrate medical theory and practice, which were copied for other monasteries. A set made in 1920 and kept in Ulan Ude was published in facsimile with a translation of the treatise in 1992.

In 1702 the Sixth Dalai Lama renounced his monastic vows, and the next year Sangye Gyatso passed the title of regent to his son Ngawang Rinchen while keeping his executive powers. At the Monlam Prayer Festival in Lhasa in 1705 he proposed to seize and execute the Khoshut ruler Lhazang Khan, but the cleric Jamyang Zhépa opposed it. Lhazang feigned departure, gathered his tribesmen at the Nagchu River and marched on Lhasa in three columns, one led by his wife Tsering Tashi. Sangye Gyatso was defeated with the loss of 400 men and surrendered on condition that his life was spared, but Tsering Tashi had him taken to the Tölung Valley, where he was killed, probably on 6 September 1705.
sanin-region: The San'in region is the northern part of the Chūgoku region of Honshū, a long coastline on the Sea of Japan that sweeps south to the Chūgoku Mountains. It is primarily mountainous with few plains. Its climate is less harsh than that of the Hokuriku region to the north, but its winters bring the heavy snow and rainfall typical of the Japan Sea coast. The northern areas of Hyōgo and Kyōto prefectures are sometimes counted as part of it as well.

The region has numerous Paleolithic and Jōmon remains, and the Mukibanda Yayoi remains in the foothills of Mount Daisen, in the cities of Daisen and Yonago, are the largest in Japan; though only partly excavated, they indicate that the San'in was then a regional centre of power. Much of the mythology of Shinto is set in the Izumo area, home to Izumo-taisha, one of the oldest and most important Shinto shrines, and eastern Shimane had early ties with the Asian mainland.

In the Asuka period the region became the San'indō, one of the five provinces and seven circuits of the Ritsuryō legal system. The name meant both the area, the provinces of Tanba, Tango, Tajima, Inaba, Hōki, Izumo, Iwami and Oki, and the main road that linked it to the capital at Kyoto. The road carried goods and served armies, and it was most important in the Edo period, when the Tokugawa shogunate fixed its route and shukuba post stations and the daimyō used it for their sankin-kōtai journeys to Edo.

The San'in has no administrative authority. Japan Route 9, the San'in Expressway and the JR West San'in Main Line follow the old San'indō, along which remains of the post stations survive. The cities of more than 100,000 people are the prefectural capitals Tottori and Matsue, with Yonago and Izumo, and the region's coasts and mountains are protected as national, prefectural and municipal parks.
sanjak-of-smederevo: The Sanjak of Smederevo was formed after the fall of the Serbian Despotate in 1459, with its administrative seat at Smederevo, then defended by the imposing Smederevo Fortress. It belonged to Rumelia Eyalet at first, later to Budin Eyalet from 1541 to 1686, and for periods to Temeșvar Eyalet. In the 1470s, fighting with the Hungarians left many areas of northern Serbia deserted, and Ottoman sources note a migration of Vlach pastoralists into the sanjak, who were settled as a military element. In 1476 there were 7,600 Vlach households and 15,000 peasant households. Tax registrations of 1476 and 1516 show that about 17 per cent of villages had been abandoned.

After the Ottoman conquest of Belgrade in 1521 the seat moved to that city, though the name stayed the same. Habsburg forces took Belgrade in 1688 during the Great Turkish War, but the Ottomans recaptured it in 1690. Austria occupied the sanjak again in 1717 and received it in 1718 by the Treaty of Požarevac, holding it for twenty years as the Kingdom of Serbia until the Ottomans retook it by the Treaty of Belgrade. Austrian forces held Belgrade once more from 1788 to 1791.

In 1793 and 1796 Sultan Selim III issued firmans that gave Serbs more rights, including tax collection by the obor-knez, and freedom of trade and religion. Hadji Mustafa Pasha governed from 1793 to 1801 and was seen as a trusted ally of the sultan. Janissaries whom Selim III wished to remove found refuge with Osman Pazvantoğlu, a rebel in the Sanjak of Vidin, whose raids caused fear in the region. By 1799 the janissaries had returned under a pardon and suspended Serbian autonomy, raised taxes and imposed martial law.

On 15 December 1801 Hadji Mustafa Pasha was murdered by Kučuk Alija, one of the four leading dahije, janissary commanders who opposed the sultan's reforms. The sanjak was then ruled by these renegade janissaries independently of the Ottoman government. On 4 February 1804 several district chiefs were killed in the Slaughter of the Knezes, which sparked the First Serbian Uprising (1804–13), the first phase of the Serbian Revolution. The uprising was suppressed in 1813, but the Second Serbian Uprising, led by Duke Miloš Obrenović, produced the semi-independent Principality of Serbia. Serbia gained full independence in 1878 and became a kingdom in 1882.
sanjaya-of-mataram: Sanjaya's name, Sanskrit for conquest or victory, is carved in the Canggal inscription, found at the Gunung Wukir temple on Wukir or Ukir hill, about 340 m high, on the southern Kedu Plain of Central Java. The inscription tells that the island of Yawadwipa (Java), rich in rice and gold, had long been ruled by the wise king Sanna but fell into disunity after his death. Sanjaya, the son of Princess Sannaha, Sanna's sister, then took the throne as his legitimate successor.

The inscription praises Sanjaya's mastery of the holy scriptures and of martial arts, and says that after he conquered neighbouring areas his reign was peaceful and prosperous. By raising a lingam of Shiva on the hill of Kunjarakunja he marked the founding of a new centre of power, a court or kraton. His accession was proclaimed in the Ukir inscription, which reads as a warning to vassal states and defeated kings and suggests that Ukir hill was the first centre of the kingdom. A Chinese annal records that the kraton was moved between 742 and 755, by Sanjaya or by his successor.

Later kings counted their years from him: inscriptions of Daksha, the successor of King Balitung, used an era beginning with Sanjaya's accession, which L.C. Damais calculated as 638 Śaka, or 716. The Balitung charter and the Wanua Tengah III inscription also record his line.

Historians disagree over the dynasty he founded. Bosch proposed that two dynasties ruled Central Java, the Buddhist Sailendra and the Shivaist Sanjaya, and an old Chinese report that names Sanjaya as Chi-Yen tells of a rival forced to move eastward by him. Poerbatjaraka argued instead that there was only one kingdom, Mataram with its capital in the Poh Pitu area, and one dynasty, the Shailendra, whose members were at first Shivaists and turned to Mahayana Buddhism after the conversion of Rakai Panangkaran. A much later Sundanese manuscript, the Carita Parahyangan, portrays a King Sanjaya as the Sundanese king and hero of Galuh.
sankin-kotai: Sankin-kōtai, meaning alternate attendance, was a policy of the Tokugawa shogunate for most of the Edo period, created to control the daimyo and keep them from trying to overthrow the regime. Earlier practices prepared the way. Toyotomi Hideyoshi had required his lords to keep their wives and heirs at Osaka Castle or nearby as hostages. After the Battle of Sekigahara and the founding of the Tokugawa shogunate the practice continued at Edo as a custom. It became compulsory for the tozama daimyo in 1635 and for the fudai daimyo from 1642. Apart from an eight-year interval under Tokugawa Yoshimune, the law stayed in force until 1862.

Kamakura-period gokenin had owed guard duty at Kyoto and Kamakura and attendance at the shogun's court, and sons of local officials sometimes served there as hostages. The philosopher Kumazawa Banzan described detailed rules of alternate attendance in the Kamakura shogunate, which modern scholars cannot confirm.

In general each daimyo of a domain moved between Edo and his fief, typically spending alternate years in each, while his wife and heir remained in Edo as hostages. Some fudai daimyo near Edo alternated every six months, and illness or other grave circumstances brought temporary exceptions. In principle the system was a military service to the shogun, and each daimyo had to furnish samurai in proportion to the kokudaka assessment of his domain, who accompanied him on the journeys.
Hundreds of daimyo entered or left Edo each year, so processions were almost daily sights in the capital. They followed the main routes, the kaido, and stayed at special lodgings called honjin.

Maintaining lavish residences in both places and paying for the journeys cost daimyo dearly. Expenses of the system regularly made up 70 to 80 percent of their yearly spending. Because their income depended on rice, which was limited by what a domain could produce, incomes failed to keep up and the daimyo fell into debt. Economic programmes, efforts to raise production and special taxes gave no lasting solution. By the Genroku period practically every daimyo was deep in debt, and even the Maeda clan of Kaga, the wealthiest, ran into difficulties.

The frequent travel also encouraged road building and the construction of inns along the routes, which stimulated economic activity. Louis XIV of France later had a similar practice, requiring nobles to spend six months of each year at Versailles.
sankore-madrasah: The Sankoré mosque stands in the Sankoré quarter of Timbuktu, where most of the town's Berbers and Arabs lived. It was built in the 14th or early 15th century with the financial backing of a Tuareg woman of the Aghlal tribe, and its Sudano-Sahelian architecture differs from that of the mosques of North Africa and Andalusia. Timbuktu grew as a commercial centre in the 14th century as Walata declined. Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1352, said nothing of Islamic learning there, but a century later the Aqit clan of the Massufa Berbers settled in the town with a deep tradition of Islamic law.

Between 1578 and 1582 the Chief Qadi of Timbuktu, Imam Al-Aqib ibn Mahmud ibn Umar, demolished the sanctuary and had it rebuilt with the dimensions of the Kaaba in Mecca. Classes were held in its open courtyard, built of clay and wood beams.

The name University of Sankoré has sometimes been used, but there is no evidence of a central teaching body as in medieval European universities. The madrasa had no central administration, student registers or set course of study. It consisted of individual scholars, each with private students, who usually studied with one teacher for up to ten years. Lessons took place at the teacher's house or at the mosque, and students paid their own way with money or goods rather than from waqf endowments.

Study began at Qur'anic schools, which taught writing and the memorisation of the Qur'an; by the 16th century Timbuktu had as many as 150 to 180 of them, with an estimated 4,000 to 9,000 pupils. Higher study covered Arabic grammar, jurisprudence, mathematics, astronomy and history, and graduates at each level received a turban. Around 200 to 300 people from wealthy families reached the rank of scholar. When Leo Africanus visited in 1526 he noted that manuscripts brought from North Africa sold for more than any other merchandise.

The madrasa flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries under the Askia dynasty of the Songhai Empire, drawing scholars from as far as Egypt and Syria. Ahmad Baba, its last chancellor, wrote over forty books, among them the biographical dictionary Nayl al-ibtihaj. After Ahmad al-Mansur of Morocco defeated the Songhai at the Battle of Tondibi in 1591, Moroccan troops arrested many Sankoré scholars in 1594 on charges of sedition and deported them to Morocco with their manuscripts. Ahmad Baba lost a library of 1,600 books.

The madrasa and its scholars left a lasting mark on the Sudanic Muslim world. The building has since been threatened by urban growth and flood damage, and restoration committees and a planned buffer zone have aimed to protect it.
sankt-goar: Sankt Goar lies in the Rhine Gorge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2002, in the district of Rhein-Hunsrück in Rhineland-Palatinate. Above the town stand the ruins of Burg Rheinfels, and across the river, about 250 m wide at this point, lies its sister town of Sankt Goarshausen, with the castles Katz and Maus. The Loreley Ferry links the two towns. The nearest major towns are Koblenz, some 24 km to the north, and Bingen am Rhein, some 25 km to the south-east. Besides the main centre on the Rhine the town includes Biebernheim and Werlau on the heights and Fellen on the river.

The area was settled in Roman times, and in the early Middle Ages the place was called Wochara after a brook that enters the Rhine there. The present name comes from Goar of Aquitaine, a monk who lived as a hermit in a cave on the Rhine in the reign of the Merovingian king Childebert I, worked as a missionary with leave from the Bishop of Trier and was known for hospitality to Rhine boatmen. He built a hospice and a chapel, and his grave became a pilgrimage site. In 765 Pepin the Younger transferred the hospice and chapel to the Abbot of Prüm, and from this grew the Sankt Goar Canonical Foundation.

From 1190 the town was under the protection and jurisdiction of the Counts of Katzenelnbogen, and Count Diether V built Burg Rheinfels in 1245. When the last count died in 1479 the town passed to the Landgraviate of Hesse. Adam Krafft began to introduce the Reformation on 1 November 1527. The plague killed 175 people in 1580 and 142 in 1598. Between 1626 and 1647 the town belonged to Hesse-Darmstadt, and in 1648 it was ceded to Hesse-Kassel. French revolutionary troops took the castle in 1794 and blew up great parts of it in 1796 and 1797. In 1815 it passed to Prussia, and Sankt Goar became a district seat.

Burg Rheinfels is one of the biggest castle ruins on the Rhine. The Evangelical Collegiate Church is a late Gothic hall church on a Romanesque crypt, and a Catholic parish church of Saint Goar and Saint Elizabeth was built in 1887 to 1891. Parts of the town wall survive on the side towards the mountains. Since 1946 Sankt Goar has been part of Rhineland-Palatinate, and in 1969 the district of Sankt Goar was dissolved and the town joined the Rhein-Hunsrück district.
sanliurfa: Urfa, officially Şanlıurfa, lies on a plain about 80 km east of the Euphrates, at the border between the foothills of the Taurus Mountains and the Mesopotamian plain. The earliest name recorded for the city is Admaʾ, found in Assyrian cuneiform of the Old Assyrian period. About 12 km to the north-east is the Neolithic site of Göbekli Tepe, founded in the tenth millennium BCE, and the area was part of a network of the first settlements where agriculture arose. Because of its place in Jewish, Christian and Islamic history, and a legend that it was Abraham's hometown, Urfa is nicknamed the City of Prophets.

The Seleucid king Seleucus I Nicator founded the city as Edessa in 302 or 303 BCE, naming it after the ancient capital of Macedonia. It surrendered to the Rashidun general Iyad ibn Ghanm in 639 without resistance, and the terms guaranteed that the city's Christians would keep their cathedral. The Numayrid emir Waththab ibn Sabiq annexed it after declaring independence in 990.

Urfa was the capital of the crusader County of Edessa for about half a century from 1098, ruling subjects who were a mix of Armenians and Syrians, among whom the Armenians were dominant in the city itself. Nur ad-Din's nephew Sayf al-Din Ghazi II captured it after Nur ad-Din's death in 1174. The city submitted to the troops of Hulagu in 1260 and its inhabitants were spared, though it was left desolate.

The Mamluks gained control in the early fourteenth century and renovated the ruined citadel, but the city attracted few inhabitants because merchant traffic took another route. It was likely incorporated into the Ottoman Empire under Selim I around 1517, and an Ottoman tax register of 1518 documented 1,082 families, 700 of them Muslim and 382 Christian.

During the First World War Urfa was a site of the Armenian and Assyrian genocides from 1915. Armenians were deported and killed; about 400 were taken to the edge of town and killed in four days from 15 to 19 August, and another massacre on 23 September killed 300.

Urfa is the capital of Şanlıurfa Province. The citadel stands on rocky heights south of the old centre, and its first known fortification dates from the early sixth century under the emperor Justinian. The old city walls date from an Abbasid rebuilding in 812. According to legend, the pool of Balıklıgöl was formed when Abraham was thrown into a fire by Nimrod and the flames turned to water. The Şanlıurfa Museum houses some 10,000 artefacts from the Paleolithic through Islamic times, including finds from Göbekli Tepe, and the Haleplibahçe Mosaic Museum displays the oldest known mosaic depicting the Amazons.
sanmenxia: Sanmenxia is the westernmost prefecture-level city of Henan. It borders Luoyang to the east, Nanyang to the southeast, Shaanxi to the west and Shanxi to the north, and lies on the south bank of the Yellow River at the point where the river cuts through the Loess Plateau on its way to the North China Plain. Mountains surround it on three sides. The name means the Gorge of Three Gateways and comes from two islands that split the river into three channels. According to Chinese mythology Yu the Great cut the ridge three times with a divine axe to prevent flooding, and the gates were named the Gateway of Man, the Gateway of Gods and the Gateway of Devils.

In the Western Zhou period the area belonged to the State of Western Guo, ruled by relatives of the Ji family of Zhou. Guo moved its capital from the area of modern Baoji to Shangyang, next to Sanmenxia, and the territory was later annexed by the State of Jin. Archaeological finds near the city between 1956 and 1991 revealed mass chariot graves and bronzeware of the Western Guo rulers.

In the Western Han and Tang periods, when the capital lay at Chang'an, the grain tribute passed upstream through the gorge. The rapids were dangerous, with losses of 20 to 50 per cent in the Tang dynasty, which was one reason for moving the capital to Luoyang. Several projects to bypass the rapids with canals or by removing boulders failed, and from 150 CE gallery roads were built for towpaths. The Sanmenxia Dam, built in the late 1950s, began to flood the ancient passes, and archaeologists studied them intensely before they were submerged.

The city administers two districts, two county-level cities and two counties. The excavated Shihao Section of the Xiaohan Ancient Road, near Sanmenxia, forms part of the World Heritage Site Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor.
sannyasa: The Sanskrit word saṃnyāsa is formed from saṃ, meaning together or all, ni, meaning down, and āsa, from a root meaning to throw or put, so that it means to put down everything. The term appears in the Samhitas, Aranyakas and Brahmanas, the earliest layers of Vedic literature, but rarely, and it is not found in ancient Buddhist or Jain vocabulary.

Jamison and Witzel state that the early Vedic texts do not mention sannyasa or the ashrama system, although the Rig Veda mentions munis, long-haired holy men in soil-coloured garments given to meditation, whose way of life probably influenced the concept. The three-stage idea emerged after about the 7th century BCE, when sages such as Yājñavalkya left their homes to wander as recluses, and the explicit four-stage scheme appeared a few centuries later.

Hinduism sets no formal requirement on the discipline, method or deity a sannyasi or sannyasini must follow, so lives differ widely. Common themes are a simple, detached and itinerant life without possessions, a walking stick, a book and a vessel for food and drink, and clothes of yellow, saffron, orange or ochre. Most ascetics adopt celibacy, though the Shaiva Tantra school is an exception.

Some live as solitary anchorites, others as cenobites in groups, sometimes in a matha or ashrama. The goal is moksha, liberation, understood differently in each tradition: in the Bhakti traditions as service to the Divine, in Yoga as the highest samadhi and in Advaita as jivanmukti, awareness of Brahman in this life. Sannyasa abandons the ritual customs of the social world rather than society itself.

The Dharmasutras and later law texts place growing emphasis on all four stages, but renunciation was never mandatory and only a small percentage chose it. The Baudhayana Dharmasutra allows anyone who has finished student life to become an ascetic at once, and generally recommends sannyasa after the age of 70 once children are settled.

From the 12th century CE, after the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate, part of the Shaiva and Vaishnava ascetics formed military orders, the akharas, which developed martial arts. The Nath Siddhas may have been the earliest. These warrior ascetics were a political force through the Mughal period and the early British Raj, including the Sannyasi rebellion of 1763 to 1800, and their importance fell away as British rule was consolidated in the late 19th century.
sans-souci-palace: The palace stands in the commune of Milot, about five kilometres northeast of the Citadelle Laferrière. Before it was built Milot was a French plantation, which Christophe had managed for a time during the Haitian Revolution. Its name, French for carefree, is shared with Jean-Baptiste Sans Souci, a rebel leader who stayed loyal to the revolutionary cause when Christophe and others went over to the French in 1802, and who scorned Christophe. In 1803 Christophe invited him to the neighbouring Grand Pré plantation, where his guards bayoneted Sans Souci and his escort to death. The palace was built a few yards away from that spot, or perhaps over it.

The palace housed the king, Queen Marie-Louise, their children and the royal staff of advisors, and was the most important of the nine palaces Christophe commissioned. It had immense gardens, artificial springs and a system of waterworks, and was the scene of feasts and dances. It is not known how many labourers died building it.

Some scholars have linked it with Frederick the Great's Sanssouci at Potsdam or with Germain Boffrand's designs for the Château de la Malgrange, but the Haitian historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot calls the Potsdam link unfounded, and Vergniaud Leconte showed that Christophe's military engineer, Henri Barre, designed it. Christophe's adviser Baron Valentin de Vastey said that the palace and its church, erected by descendants of Africans, showed they had not lost the architectural genius of their ancestors.

Christophe was crippled by a stroke on 15 August 1820, and amid rebellion he shot himself with a silver bullet on the palace grounds. He was buried in the Citadelle, and his heir, Jacques-Victor Henry, was bayoneted to death ten days later. The southern republic took over the kingdom, and the palace was stripped of its valuables and abandoned. The earthquake of 1842 that devastated Cap-Haïtien destroyed much of it, and it was never rebuilt. The neighbouring Church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception was rebuilt and served until a fire destroyed it in 2020. Many in Haiti see the ruins as a symbol of resistance, freedom and national pride. UNESCO inscribed the palace and the Citadelle as World Heritage Sites in 1982.
sansepolcro: According to tradition the town arose from two 9th-century pilgrims to the Holy Land, Arcanus and Giles. They returned, built a chapel dedicated to Saint Leonard and began a monastic life there. They had brought a stone from the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, which was installed in the monastery and gave the place its name, Santo Sepolcro.

It became a popular pilgrimage site, and the church was raised to the rank of Benedictine abbey, the Badia, and declared an abbey nullius. The first historical mentions date to 1012 and refer to the building of the monastery, around which a commune began to develop. The Emperor Conrad II declared the settlement a market town, and in the following century the abbey affiliated with the Camaldolese Order.

During the conflicts of Guelfs and Ghibellines the town's factions were led by local families, among them the Pichi, Bercordati, Graziani and Bacci. In the 13th century, because of its position on local trade routes, control of the town passed between Uguccione della Faggiola, Lord of Pisa, Guido Tarlati, Bishop of Arezzo, and his brother Pier Saccone Tarlati di Pietramala.

In 1367 Pope Urban V gave it to the Malatesta family, whose heirs ruled it until the Republic of Florence took control in the 15th century with the approval of Pope Eugene IV. Pope Leo X raised it to the rank of a city a century later.

Sansepolcro stands on the upper Tiber in the province of Arezzo, in eastern Tuscany. Its Cathedral of St. John the Evangelist, in Gothic-Romanesque style, was built in 1012-49. It was the birthplace of the painters Piero della Francesca, Raffaellino del Colle, Matteo di Giovanni, Santi di Tito and Angiolo Tricca, and of the mathematician Luca Pacioli. In the World War II the town was saved from destruction when a British officer, Tony Clarke, halted an Allied artillery attack to protect Piero della Francesca's fresco of the Resurrection. That painting is now in the Museo Civico.
sanskrit: Sanskrit is a classical language of the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European family. It arose in South Asia after its predecessor languages had spread there from the northwest in the late Bronze Age, and it is one of the three earliest documented languages descended from Proto-Indo-European. Its closest ancient relatives are the Nuristani languages of the Hindu Kush and the Iranian languages Avestan and Old Persian.

The oldest form is Vedic Sanskrit, found in the Rigveda, a collection of 1,028 hymns composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE by Indo-Aryan tribes moving east into northwestern India. The Dravidian languages influenced its sounds and syntax. Classical Sanskrit, refined and standardised from the mid-first millennium BCE, was codified in Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī. The epics, the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa, were composed in Epic Sanskrit, used in northern India between 400 BCE and 300 CE.

The word saṃskṛta means well prepared, perfected or polished. The Rigveda was passed on orally by methods of memorisation of exceptional rigour, as a single text with no variant readings, which makes its archaic forms important for reconstructing Proto-Indo-European. Sanskrit has no native script: from around the turn of the first millennium CE it has been written in various Brahmic scripts, most commonly today in Devanagari. The earliest known inscriptions date from the first century BCE.

For nearly 2,000 years Sanskrit was the language of a cultural order that reached across South Asia, Inner Asia and Southeast Asia, and to some extent East Asia. Inscriptions and manuscripts have been found from Nepal and Tibet to Cambodia, Indonesia, Mongolia, Korea and Japan. Classical Sanskrit covers epics, drama, law, grammar, medicine, astronomy and mathematics; the dramatist Kālidāsa wrote in it, and the foundations of modern arithmetic were first described in it. Its surviving manuscripts number over 30 million.

Sanskrit later stopped being learned as a first language and ceased developing as a living one. It remains the sacred language of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions and is used in worship. It is one of the languages of the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India, and the oldest Sanskrit college, the Benares Sanskrit College, was founded in 1791 under East India Company rule.
sanskritisation: M. N. Srinivas chose the word Sanskritisation in preference to Brahminisation, because certain Vedic rites were confined to the Brahmins and the two other twice-born castes. He defined it as the process by which a low or middle Hindu caste, or a tribal or other group, changes its customs, ritual, ideology and way of life in the direction of a high and frequently twice-born caste, usually followed by a claim to a higher rank than the local community had conceded.

The idea was older than the name. The scholar Jaffrelot notes that Ambedkar described something similar in 1916 and 1917, and that colonial administrators such as E. T. Atkinson in his Himalayan Gazetteer and Alfred Lyall had described the process before him.

In a broader sense the term covers the way local deities, rituals and literary genres came to be identified with the great tradition of Sanskrit and Brahmanical culture. It is seen as part of Brahmanisation, through which local traditions were absorbed into the Hindu synthesis. Srinivas held that it brought new ideas as well as habits: karma, dharma, papa, maya, samsara and moksha entered the everyday speech of Sanskritised groups. Anthropologists sometimes speak instead of Kshatriyisation or Rajputisation.

Claims usually aimed at Brahmin or Kshatriya status. Tillers such as the Kurmi, Koeri and Murao pressed such claims through caste organisations from the late 19th century, the Kalwar, traditionally distillers and sellers of liquor, sought to recast their image around the start of the 20th century, and the Hindu Jat of rural North India did so with the help of the Arya Samaj. Srinivas contrasted the success of the Lingayat caste in Karnataka with the Vishwakarma, whose claim to Brahmin status, despite adopting the sacred thread, is not generally accepted outside the community.

Srinivas argued that the process was not limited to Hindu castes: semi-tribal groups such as the Pahadis of the Himalayas, the Gonds and Oraons of central India and the Bhils of western India also underwent it and then claimed to be castes and so Hindus. It has been observed in Nepal among the Khas, Magar, Newar and Tharu. Yogendra Singh objected that the theory neglects non-Sanskritic traditions and that Sanskritic rites were often added to older ones without replacing them.
sansoen-phra-barami: In 1851 two former British officers, Captain Impey and Lieutenant Thomas George Knox, trained the troops of King Mongkut and the Second King Pinklao, and adopted God Save the King as honour music for the king of Siam. Phraya Srisunthonwohan later wrote Thai words for it, named Chom Rat Chong Charoen, meaning long live the great king. After King Chulalongkorn visited Singapore and Batavia in 1871, Siam needed a tune of its own, since it was using the same anthem as Britain. Court musicians chose Bulan Loi Luean, a royal composition of King Rama II, and Chulalongkorn ordered the Dutch bandmaster Christopher Hewetson to arrange it for military band.

In 1888 a sheet music of the Siamese national anthem, arranged by the Russian composer Pyotr Schurovsky, was printed in Russia, with the main melody of the present anthem. According to Sugree Charoensook, Schurovsky composed its music.

Prince Narisara Nuvadtivong wrote various lyrics for the tune, for the army, for schools and for traditional music bands, and Prince Abhakara Kiartivongse wrote a version for the navy. The current words were written by Narisara in 1886 and revised by King Vajiravudh in 1914, when he set aside all the earlier versions. They were first used by the Wild Tiger Corps and Siamese scouts on 22 January 1914 at Ban Bo Suphan, and the Ministry of Education adopted them in schools nationwide on 1 March of that year.

The anthem was the de facto national anthem of Siam from 1888 until 1932, when it was replaced by Phleng Chat Siam after the Siamese Revolution. It remained the royal anthem, played to honour the king. In 1935 the melodies of the royal and national anthems were shortened for ceremonial honours in Western style. In 1940 the government of Plaek Phibunsongkhram issued the eighth cultural mandate, shortening the words and replacing Siam with Thai; after the Second World War these versions were quietly abandoned as unpopular, and the version of 1914 returned.

The anthem is performed on state occasions and when a high-ranking member of the royal family is present, and it is played before films in cinemas and before many live performances in Thailand. It was first recorded on an Edison wax cylinder by the ethnomusicologist Carl Stumpf in 1900, performed by a Siamese theatre group visiting Berlin.
sant-climent-de-taull: The church stands in Taüll, in the municipality of the Valley of Boí in the province of Lleida. The date of its building is unknown, but it was consecrated on 10 December 1123 by Guillem Ramon, Bishop of Roda-Barbastro, who consecrated the nearby church of Santa Maria de Taüll the next day. An inscription recording the consecration, painted in white letters on a red and black ground, was found on the first column on the north side near the apse; it is now in the National Art Museum of Catalonia.

The church follows a basilica plan with three naves, each ending in an apse, divided by cylindrical columns of amalgamated stone and covered by a roof of wooden beams. Its facades are plain, but the apses carry simple Lombard decoration, the central one with groups of four arches separated by half columns and the side apses with groups of three. In the south corner rises a slim square bell tower of a base and six floors, whose windows grow larger towards the top. The walls, apses and columns were once covered with painting.

The painter of the murals is unknown and is called the Master of Taüll. In the central apse Christ in Majesty sits in a mandorla, his feet on a hemisphere, above the Virgin Mary and five saints. On the arches appear the Agnus Dei with seven eyes, Lazarus at the rich man's door with a dog licking his wounds, and saints among whom Peter, Clement and Cornelius can be identified. The wooden altar frontal, 1.36 m by 0.98 m and repainted in 1579, shows Christ enthroned among the twelve apostles.

In the early twentieth century the National Art Museum of Catalonia in Barcelona removed the murals to protect them. Horsehide glue was applied to the paintings and, once hard, peeled away, carrying the pigments with it. An exact replica now fills the central apse, while the painting of the northern apse can be seen only in the museum. Holes caused by damp in the central apse painting have been left unrestored. When the altar frontal reached Barcelona a later coat of paint was removed from it.
sant-joan-de-caselles: The church stands on a rock above the road that connects Canillo to France, and it is registered as a heritage property in the Cultural Heritage of Andorra. Its layout is typical of the Romanesque: a rectangular nave under a wooden roof, a semi-circular apse and a square bell tower in the Lombardy style. The two simple porches were probably added in the 16th and 17th centuries, and inside there is a Baroque wooden choir.

The main work inside is a large stucco image of Christ in Majesty. Beside it is a mural with 12th-century frescoes of the Calvary, showing Saint Longinus and Stephaton with the Sun and Moon half hidden.

The retable, dated 1575 and attributed to the Master of Canillo, is considered of exceptional quality. Influenced by the Italian and Germanic Renaissance, it shows scenes from the life and martyrdom of Saint John the apostle, the author of the book of Revelation and the patron saint of the church, and in particular his visions on Patmos.

The church was built in the 11th and 12th centuries and has been restored twice in modern times. The architect Cèsar Martinell restored it between 1934 and 1935; his work affected the roof of the apse, the bell tower and the porch of the main facade. A further restoration followed in 1962 and 1963, when the altarpiece, the nave and the stucco Christ were treated.
sant-julia-de-loria: Sant Julià de Lòria lies in the Eastern Pyrenees on the banks of the Gran Valira, the largest river in Andorra. The parish covers an area of 60 square kilometres and is bordered by the capital Andorra la Vella to the north, by Escaldes-Engordany to the northeast and by the Spanish region of Catalonia on the other sides. The town of the same name is the seat of the parish and is headed by a mayor.

The parish has five quarts and eleven villages: Bixessarri, Aixàs, Aixovall, Certers, Llumeneres, Nagol, Aixirivall, Auvinyà, Juberri, Fontaneda and Canòlic. The Naturlandia park occupies about 100 hectares of hill slopes at altitudes between 1,600 and 2,000 metres.

The University of Andorra, the only university in the country, stands in the parish. In the 20th century the region was a major centre of tobacco processing, and the Tobacco Museum occupies the old tobacco factory, which functioned until 1957. Large shopping malls stand close to the Spanish border. The Sant Serni de Nagol Church was built in the 11th century.

Roads connect the parish with the rest of Andorra and with Spain, and buses run to Barcelona, Vic, Tarragona, Lleida, Girona and Toulouse. Andorra has no airport of its own; the Andorra–La Seu d'Urgell Airport in Catalonia lies about 12 km away. The region has more than 20 km of alpine skiing trails, and Naturlandia has a 5,300 metre alpine toboggan course. The parish counts among its notable people Carme Travesset (1925–2022), the first woman to hold political office in Andorra, and Òscar Ribas Reig (1936–2020), the country's first prime minister in 1982.
santa-cruz-massacre: In October 1991 a delegation of members of the Assembly of the Republic of Portugal and twelve journalists was planned to coincide with a visit by the UN Special Rapporteur on Torture, Pieter Kooijmans. The Indonesian government objected to the Australian journalist Jill Jolliffe, whom it regarded as a supporter of Fretilin, and Portugal cancelled the visit, to the dismay of independence activists. On 28 October Indonesian troops found resistance members in Dili's Motael Church; in the clash that followed the independence supporter Sebastião Gomes was taken out and shot by troops, and the integration activist Afonso Henriques was stabbed to death.

On 12 November several thousand men, women and children walked from the Motael Church to the Santa Cruz cemetery after a memorial service for Gomes, raising banners and East Timorese flags. By most accounts the crowd was loud but peaceful; it was the largest demonstration against the occupation since 1975. In a brief confrontation on the way some protesters and a major, Geerhan Lantara, were stabbed. At the cemetery about 200 more soldiers advanced with weapons drawn and opened fire on hundreds of unarmed civilians. Among the dead was Kamal Bamadhaj, a New Zealand student and human rights activist.

The American journalists Amy Goodman and Allan Nairn tried to shield the Timorese and were beaten, Nairn's skull being fractured. The British cameraman Max Stahl, filming undercover for Yorkshire Television, recorded the killings, and the footage was smuggled to Australia and shown in the ITV documentary In Cold Blood: The Massacre of East Timor in January 1992. Indonesian authorities called the event a spontaneous reaction or a misunderstanding, but two days later the armed forces' commander, Try Sutrisno, said that such agitators must be shot.

The pictures embarrassed the Indonesian government and, circulated back into Indonesia, encouraged student groups to discuss East Timor and the New Order openly. Solidarity groups formed abroad, among them the East Timor Action Network in the United States, and the US Congress cut funding for IMET training of the Indonesian military. Portugal stepped up its diplomatic campaign. The Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans called the killings an aberration rather than state policy. In Timor-Leste, 12 November is now a public holiday honouring the young people who fought for independence.
santa-fe-argentina: Santa Fe de la Vera Cruz, meaning Holy Faith of the True Cross, stands in north-eastern Argentina near the junction of the Paraná and Salado rivers. It lies 170 kilometres north of Rosario and about 340 kilometres east of Córdoba, and is linked by the Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel to the city of Paraná. A canal connects it with the port of Colastiné on the Paraná. Its climate is humid subtropical, with hot and humid summers and mild winters.

The conquistador Juan de Garay founded the city in 1573 at the nearby site of Cayastá, during an expedition from Asunción to the Paraná River. Constant flooding of the Cayastá River led to the move to the present site in 1653. Cayastá now has a historical park containing the grave of Hernandarias, the first American-born governor in South America. Santa Fe became the provincial capital in 1814, when the province of Santa Fe was separated from the province of Buenos Aires. In 1853 the National Constituent Assembly met in the city. This history of the Argentine Constitution led lawmakers to choose it for Constitutional Conventions in 1949, 1957 and 1994.

Santa Fe is the capital of its province and the commercial and transport centre of a rich agricultural area producing grain, vegetable oils and meat. The National University of the Littoral began as the Provincial University in 1889 and took its present name in 1919. The Salado has flooded the city repeatedly. A catastrophic flood on 29 April 2003 forced at least 100,000 people to be evacuated. The Santa Fe Belgrano railway station, built in 1891 and named Cultural Heritage, was reopened as a convention centre.
santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico: The name means Holy Faith of New Mexico. It did not come from the independent nation of Mexico: as early as 1561 Spanish explorers used el Nuevo México for Cíbola, cities of wealth said to lie far north of the conquered Aztec Empire, and the Crónica Mexicayotl of 1609 identifies it with Aztlán, the Mexica homeland. The province centred on the upper Rio Grande valley and took in most of the present state of New Mexico with parts of Texas, Colorado, Kansas and the Oklahoma panhandle. Spanish settlement reached from Taos pueblo in the north to Albuquerque in the south.

The Coronado Expedition of 1540–1542 fought the Pueblo peoples in the Tiguex War before withdrawing. In 1598 the All Pueblo Council allowed Juan de Oñate's expedition of 500 men, which he financed himself, to settle the Rio Grande Valley, and on 12 July 1598 he founded the colony at San Juan de los Caballeros beside Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo. His rule was marked by great cruelty, and the king removed him; he was found guilty of cruelty, immorality and false reporting. His successor, Pedro de Peralta, founded Santa Fe in 1610.

Franciscan missionaries baptized thousands, mostly Pueblo people, in the 1600s, while destroying religious objects, banning ceremonies and persecuting holy men. Twelve years after the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, the Spanish returned at the invitation of some Pueblo elders, and Diego de Vargas reoccupied Santa Fe. Under Mexico the 1824 constitution made it the federally administered Territory of New Mexico. Antonio Armijo's expedition of 1829 opened a trade route west, and his scout Raphael Rivera found Las Vegas Springs. Mestizo and Pueblo inhabitants rose against the Centralist Republic in the Río Arriba Rebellion of 1837, and in 1841 New Mexican troops under Governor Manuel Armijo captured the Texan Santa Fe Expedition. The U.S. Army under Stephen Kearny occupied the territory in 1846.

The name New Mexico, the capital at Santa Fe and the governor's seat at the Palace of the Governors passed to the New Mexico Territory and to the state of New Mexico, admitted in 1912. Its Hispano and Pueblo inhabitants became United States citizens under the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, but the Navajo, Apache and Comanche peoples were denied citizenship until 1924.
santa-fe-new-mexico: Santa Fe lies at the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and is the highest state capital in the United States. Its climate is cold semi-arid, with cool, dry winters and hot summers. The name is Spanish for Holy Faith and is a shortened form of the original La Villa Real de la Santa Fe de San Francisco de Asís. The Tewa call the place P'oegeh, water place, a name that predates European colonisation.

The area was originally occupied by Tanoan peoples who lived in Pueblo villages along the Rio Grande. Tewa built a cluster of homes around the site of today's Plaza sometime after 900 CE, but the Pueblo peoples had abandoned the site for at least 200 years by the time the Spanish arrived in the early 17th century. Juan de Oñate led the first Spanish effort to colonise the region in 1598; the Spanish banished him after his rule was judged cruel to the indigenous population.

Santa Fe was founded in 1610 as the capital of Nuevo México, a province of New Spain, and is the oldest state capital in the United States. The Spanish laid it out by the Laws of the Indies of 1573, around a central plaza with the Palace of the Governors on its north side. It prospered on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro and the Santa Fe Trail. In 1846 General Stephen W. Kearny led some 1,700 soldiers into the city, and by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848 the United States gained New Mexico. Santa Fe became the capital of the territory in 1851 and of the state in 1912.

Santa Fe is the fourth most populous city in New Mexico and the county seat of Santa Fe County. It blends indigenous, Spanish and American influences and has been a UNESCO Creative City in Crafts and Folk Art since 2005. The Plaza and the Palace of the Governors remain at its centre, and its adobe-style Pueblo Revival and Territorial Revival architecture is largely preserved. The city has been associated with science since 1943, when it served as the gateway to Los Alamos National Laboratory.
santa-hermandad: Because the medieval kings of León, Castile and Aragon were often unable to keep the peace, municipal leagues began to form in the 12th century against bandits and rural criminals and against the lawless nobility, or to support a claimant to the crown. The first recorded hermandad united the towns and peasantry of the north to police the pilgrim road to Santiago de Compostela against robber knights. Among the most powerful was the Hermandad de las Marismas, a league of northern Castilian and Basque ports including Santander, Laredo, Bermeo and San Sebastian.

Hermandades also formed in Andalusia from 1265, in towns defending their interests against Islamic rebels, and may have been inspired by an earlier Islamic police force, the shurṭa. Besides policing and defence they came to collect taxes and act as judges, with jurisdiction over crimes on roads or in unpopulated areas, rape, blasphemy and the passing of false money. At times they were used against royal authority, at others to enforce it.

Ferdinand and Isabella adapted the old form into a centrally organised police force with themselves at its head, under officials they appointed, with large powers of summary jurisdiction even in capital cases. By 1476 the league was incorporated into Isabella's government as the Santa Hermandad, and it was used to consolidate her authority and silence those who objected to her reign. It was paid for by taxes and by wartime grants, servicios, allowed by a papal bull as a crusading indulgence, which it could collect by force from resistant towns.
