He then governed through tribal leaders, without whose leave no tribesman could meet him.

He held back from the United Arab Emirates in December 1971 over the dispute with Iran about the Gulf islands, and agreed to join once Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi and Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum of Dubai promised federal support for Ras Al Khaimah's claim. He made education compulsory for both sexes, built modern schools and four hospitals, and created the emirate's first proper government administration. Ras Al Khaimah Airport opened in 1976 and Saqr Port in 1977, and companies such as RAK Rock and Julphar Pharmaceuticals were founded.

He named his eldest son, Khalid bin Saqr Al Qasimi, crown prince in 1974, but on 28 April 2003 replaced him with another son, Saud bin Saqr Al Qasimi, while UAE troops and tanks guarded key sites; Khalid went into exile in Muscat. Saqr died on 27 October 2010 after several months of illness. Khalid proclaimed himself ruler in a web video, but the Federal Supreme Council quickly backed Saud's succession.
sara-people: The Sara, sometimes called the Kaba, also live along the southern border of South Sudan. In Chad they are concentrated in the Moyen-Chari, Logone Oriental and Logone Occidental regions and parts of Tandjile, and make up roughly 30% of the population; in the Central African Republic, where they live in the north-west, they are about ten percent and the fourth largest group. Their society is made up of several patrilineal clans that were once united in a single polity with a common language, identity and religion. A genetic study by Excoffier and colleagues in 1987 found them most closely related to the Kunama of Eritrea.

The Muslim peoples of the region called the Sara Kirdi, a word for non-Muslims, and the conflict between the Kirdi and the raiders known as Bagirmi went on through the 19th century. In the early 20th century the Sara became part of French Equatorial Africa, in the area the French called le Tchad utile. French schooling changed their society, as did forced labour and conscription into the French army in the World Wars. In the 1920s and 30s thousands of Sara workers were forced to travel far to the south to build the Congo-Ocean Railway, where they suffered abuse and high death rates.

At independence in 1960 the southerners were more closely tied to French institutions than the northerners, which gave them political dominance in the new state. The Sara were drawn into the civil war against populations of the north and centre. Sara figures include Noël Milarew Odingar, who overthrew Tombalbaye in the coup of 1975, and Ange-Félix Patassé, President of the Central African Republic from 1993 to 2003.

The Sara live chiefly by hoe farming, with taro, yams and sweet potatoes as their staples, and raise cattle, sheep, goats, chickens and small horses. Most are Christian or follow their ethnic religion, with a Muslim minority. They speak the Sara languages, part of the Central Sudanic branch of the Nilo-Saharan family.
sarah-forbes-bonetta: Oke-Odan had been founded by Egbado refugees during the collapse of the Oyo Empire, which disintegrated by 1836 after Dahomey under King Gezo threw off its overlordship and the Sokoto Caliphate's jihads weakened it. Dahomey then expanded east into former Oyo lands, taking towns and enslaving their people. When its army captured Oke-Odan, Aina's parents were beheaded and other inhabitants were killed or sold into the Atlantic slave trade. Gezo, whose kingdom profited greatly from the export of slaves, resisted British efforts to end it.

Forbes came to Abomey in July 1850 with Consul John Beecroft and witnessed the Annual Customs, at which captives were sometimes executed. At its end Gezo gave each envoy a girl, and Forbes wrote that refusing would have signed her death warrant. He had her baptised at St Mary's Church, Winkfield; British newspapers called her an African princess, though her ancestry is unknown and Forbes may have claimed high birth for her to further his career. Rather than the Queen's goddaughter, as she is often called, she was in effect indentured to Victoria as a Liberated African under the anti-slave-trade laws.

She was schooled at the Church Missionary Society's Female Institution in Kissy, Sierra Leone, and from 1855 lived with the clergyman Frederick Schön and his wife Elizabeth at Palm Cottage in Gillingham, where Dorugu helped him compile the first Hausa-English dictionary. In January 1858 she attended the wedding of Princess Alice; her visits to Windsor were short and sporadic.

She married Davies at St Nicholas' Church in Brighton in August 1862, having been pressed into the match, and they moved to Lagos, where they had four children and she worked as a teacher. She travelled to England four times in all and wrote many letters. After her death her husband raised a granite obelisk to her at Ijon. The biography Becoming Sarah Forbes Bonetta by Henry Lovejoy, published in 2026, corrected the claims that she was a princess or a goddaughter of the Queen.
sarajevo: Sarajevo lies near the geometric centre of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Sarajevo valley in the middle of the Dinaric Alps, along the Miljacka River, 518 metres above sea level. Forested hills and five major mountains surround it: Treskavica, Bjelašnica, Jahorina, Trebević and Igman. The last four are known as the Olympic Mountains of Sarajevo, because venues for the 1984 Winter Olympics were built on them. The name comes from the Turkish saray, meaning palace or mansion, and scholars disagree on the origin of the ending evo. The official name under Ottoman rule was Saraybosna, the Palace of Bosnia.

One of the earliest settlements in the area is that of the Neolithic Butmir culture, discovered in 1893 at Ilidža by Austro-Hungarian authorities building an agricultural school. The area's flint attracted settlers, and the Butmir people developed distinctive ceramics. The modern city arose in the fifteenth century as an Ottoman stronghold, when the Ottoman Empire extended into Europe. Isa-Beg Ishaković called the town he was going to construct Šeher, Turkish for city. Gazi Husrev-beg established a school of Sufi philosophy in 1537, the first institution that can be classed as tertiary education.

Ottoman rule lasted until 1878 de facto and 1908 de jure, and Austria-Hungary then governed to 1918. Muslims, Orthodox Christians, Roman Catholics and Sephardi Jews shared the city under Ottoman rule while keeping distinct identities, and by 1909 about 50 per cent of its people were Muslim, 25 per cent Catholic, 15 per cent Orthodox and 10 per cent Jewish. In 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a local Young Bosnia activist, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, a murder that sparked the First World War. Austro-Hungarian rule ended and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was created.

After the Second World War the city became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, and grew rapidly. It hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics. During the Bosnian War it endured the longest siege of a capital city in modern history, 1,425 days from April 1992 to February 1996. The 1991 census recorded 527,049 people in the city's ten municipalities, 49.2 per cent of them Bosniaks, 29.8 per cent Serbs and 6.6 per cent Croats. The war displaced hundreds of thousands, most of whom have not returned.

Sarajevo is the capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the de jure capital of Republika Srpska. All national institutions are there. It is one of the few major European cities with a mosque, a Catholic church, an Orthodox church and a synagogue in the same neighbourhood, and has been called the Jerusalem of Europe. The Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque and the Sarajevo cathedral are among its landmarks.
sarala-das: Sarala Dasa was born Siddheswara Parida, of the Chasa community, at a village called Kanakavati Patana, known as Kanakapura, at Tentuliapada in what is now Jagatsinghpur district. The date of his birth cannot be fixed, and little is known of his early life. He had no organised schooling, and what he learnt by himself was attributed to the grace of Sarala, goddess of devotion and inspiration; the name Sarala Dasa means servant of Sarala. A story like those told of Kalidasa relates that as a boy ploughing his father's field he sang so sweetly that the goddess stopped to listen and gave him the gift of poetry.

Several passages of his Mahabharata suggest that he served as a soldier in the army of the Gajapati king of Odisha, and the battles, places and events he knew from that service went into his writing. He spent his last years at Bila Sarala; a religious house called Munigoswain at his birthplace marks the traditional spot where he composed his works.

Besides the Sarala Mahabharata, the Vilanka Ramayana and the Chandi Purana, he wrote the Laxmi Narayana Vachanika. His Mahabharata opens with an invocation to Lord Jagannatha of Puri which shows that he began it under Kapilendra Deva (1435–67). It keeps the outline of the Sanskrit epic but adds many stories of his own, so that it reads as a new creation. The Chandi Purana retells Durga's killing of the buffalo demon Mahishasura with its own departures, and his earliest work, the Vilanka Ramayana, tells of Rama's fight with the thousand-headed Ravana.

He wrote in dandi chand, a metre in which the number of letters in a verse is not fixed, and the two lines of a couplet rhyme without being of equal length, as in the Odia folk songs of dances such as the Ghoda-nacha and Sakhinacha. His verse is plain and musical, uses colloquial words and avoids Sanskritisation. War rather than love is its main mood, and he said he wrote for the benefit of ordinary people, so that religious books could be read in a language all understood.
saramaka: The ancestors of the Saramaka were Africans of many peoples, among them the Akan, Bakongo and Fon, sold to plantations in Suriname, who escaped into the rainforest alone, in small groups and in great collective rebellions, and fought there for their independence for nearly a hundred years. Their language, Saramaccan, which they share with the Matawai, is a creole related to Sranan Tongo: about half its words come from West and Central African languages, a fifth each from English and Portuguese, and the rest from Amerindian languages and Dutch.

After their treaty the Saramaka lived almost as a state within a state until the mid-20th century. From the 1960s about 6,000 of them were moved to transmigration villages on the Lower Suriname River when around half their territory was flooded for a hydroelectric project supplying an aluminium smelter. The civil war of the late 1980s between Maroons and the military government brought great hardship, and by mid-1989 about 3,000 Saramaka were refugees in French Guiana, where an accord of 1883 between the governor and the Saramaka Granman already allowed them to live.

After the war the government granted timber and mining concessions in Saramaka territory to foreign companies without consulting the Saramaka authorities. The Association of Saramaka Authorities complained to the Inter-American Commission of Human Rights in the mid-1990s, and in November 2007 the Inter-American Court for Human Rights granted the Saramaka collective rights to the lands of their ancestors, a say over timber and gold, and compensation for earlier timber grants, paid into a development fund that they manage.

Saramaka society rests on matrilineal clans, lo, each descended from an original band of escaped slaves and holding land claimed in the early 18th century, and on lineages, bee, of 50 to 150 people. Villages of 100 to 200 people stand by rivers. Women do most of the farming of hill rice, cassava and other crops once men have cleared the fields, while men hunt, fish and spend years working for wages on the coast.

A paramount chief, the gaamá, headmen, kabiteni, and assistant headmen, basiá, hold offices that belong to the clans. Problems are settled in council meetings, kuútu, and through divination, by which village deities, ancestors, forest spirits and snake gods are consulted in every part of life. About a quarter of the Saramaka are nominal Christians, mainly Moravian.
saraswati: Saraswati is one of the earliest river goddesses of the Indian tradition. In the Rigveda, dated about 1500 to 1000 BCE, she is primarily a deified river embodying abundance, power and fertility. Hymn 6.61 is dedicated entirely to her, and with Ila and Bharati she forms a triad of sacrificial goddesses invoked in Vedic rituals. Her association with inspired thought, linked to sacrifice performed on the banks of the river, already points toward her later role.

In the Brahmanas she is increasingly identified with Vac, the Vedic goddess of speech, and the two merge into the single goddess of later tradition. Her connection to the river then fades, while her association with speech, poetry, music and culture grows. The name is Sanskrit, from saras, meaning pooling water or sometimes speech, and vati, she who possesses.

In classical and medieval Hinduism Saraswati is the goddess of learning, the arts and poetic inspiration, and the inventor of the Sanskrit language. She is linked to the creator god Brahma, as his creation or consort, and in some Vaishnava traditions she is one of Vishnu's consorts. With Lakshmi and Parvati she forms the Tridevi. In Shaktism she is venerated as the creative aspect of the Supreme Goddess, and she is also worshipped as a celibate goddess without a consort.

She is shown as a serene woman in white, the colour of sattva, or goodness, usually seated on a white lotus. She has four arms, holding a book, a rosary, a water pot and the veena, and her mount is a hamsa, a white goose or swan, or a peacock.

Saraswati is worshipped across India, above all on Vasant Panchami, the fifth day of spring, when students honour her as patron of knowledge. Traditionally the day is marked by helping young children learn to write the letters of the alphabet. In Kerala and Tamil Nadu the last three days of Navaratri are Saraswati Puja. Sharada Peeth in Kashmir, dated from the sixth to the twelfth century CE, is one of the earliest known shrines.

In Buddhism she is venerated in many forms, including the East Asian Benzaiten, the Tibetan Yangchenma and the Burmese Thurathadi, and she is the consort of Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom. In Jainism she is the goddess of knowledge, responsible for spreading the Tirthankaras' sermons, and the Jain Saraswati from Mathura, dated 132 CE, is the earliest sculpture of her in any tradition.
saraswati-mahal-library: The library began as a royal collection for the private learning of the Nayak kings of Thanjavur and their families, who ruled from 1535 until 1676. The Maratha rulers who took Thanjavur in 1675 promoted local culture and went on enlarging the palace library until 1855. The most notable of them was Serfoji II, who reigned from 1798 to 1832. Taught in his youth under the influence of the German missionary Christian Friedrich Schwartz, he learned English, French, Italian and Latin among other languages, and employed many pandits to collect, buy and copy works from the centres of Sanskrit learning in northern India and further afield.

The collection holds well over 49,000 volumes, of which only a small part is on display. Most of the manuscripts, 39,300, are in Tamil and Sanskrit. There are 3,076 Marathi manuscripts of the 17th to 19th centuries, mostly on paper, among them works of the Ramadasi and Dattatreya monastic orders; 846 Telugu manuscripts, mostly on palm leaf; and 22 Persian and Urdu manuscripts, mostly of the 19th century. The Dhanvantari section keeps the records of Ayurveda scholars, including case studies of patients.

The library also has 1,342 bundles of records of the Maratha kingdom, written in the Modi script of Marathi, on the politics, culture and administration of the Maratha kings of Thanjavur. Among its printed rarities are Samuel Johnson's dictionary in an edition of 1784, a pictorial Bible printed in Amsterdam in 1791, the Madras Almanac of 1807, Lavoisier's Elements of Chemistry, old maps of the world and town-planning documents of Thanjavur's drainage and water supply.

The library, within the palace grounds, was opened to the public in 1918. In 1965 Indira Gandhi, then Minister of Information and Broadcasting, sanctioned funds to microfilm and catalogue the collection. Computers were installed in 1998 to catalogue the holdings, and the library is a Manuscript Conservation Centre of the National Mission for Manuscripts, set up in 2003.
sarcophagus-of-the-spouses: The lid shows a man and a woman lying on a klinē, a dining couch with cushions that prop them up. It was made of terracotta in four pieces, fired separately and then assembled, and was once brightly painted. In the Archaic manner the bodies are elongated; the woman wears a soft cap with braids over her shoulders, the man's braids fan out over his back, and both smile with almond-shaped eyes. The busts are in high relief while the legs are flattened to fit the lid, a typically Etruscan contrast, and the man is barefoot while the woman wears pointed shoes.

Cremation was the main Etruscan funerary practice, and the ashes and bones of the dead were placed in urns; since Etruscan hut urns have held the remains of both men and women, the sarcophagus is presumed to have held cremated remains too. Its banquet scene matches the frescoes of the Monterozzi necropolis at Tarquinia, where couples recline side by side on couches, served by attendants and entertained by musicians and dancers. The Etruscans buried parts of the funeral meal with the dead, with dishes and utensils, and the scene has been read as an eternal family dinner shared in the afterlife.

At Banditaccia itself, rock-carved funerary beds marked the sex of the dead: a bed on the left of a tomb was for a man, one on the right, with a gabled end like a roof, for a woman. Smaller sarcophagi found near the women's beds are presumed to have been for children.

The sarcophagus is counted among the masterpieces of Etruscan art. Because men and women share the couch in the same proportions and poses, it is cited alongside other evidence that women of the Etruscan upper class held the same status as men, were often buried more lavishly and could be literate. A second sarcophagus of the same name and probably the same workshop, also from the Banditaccia necropolis, is in the Louvre in Paris, its male figure missing a hand. A smaller urn from Monte Abatone in Caere, showing a single woman pouring liquid into her hand, may come from the same studio.
sardar: Sardar, from Persian sardār, literally commander, chief or leader, is a title of royalty and nobility that was originally used for Muslim princes, noblemen, kings and other aristocrats. It has also been used for the chief of a Muslim tribe, and it serves as a Persian synonym of the Arabic title Sheikh. The term and its cognates have been used across Persia, the Ottoman Empire and Turkey (as Serdar), Afghanistan, Pakistan, Mesopotamia, Syria, Central Asia (as Sardor in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan), the Caucasus, the Balkans and Egypt (as Sirdar).

The title took different forms in each region. In Afghanistan a member of the royal Mohammadzai clan was a Sardar in the sense of nobleman, and Sardar-i-Salar meant a field marshal or general of the army. King Amanullah founded the Nishan-i-Sardari, the Order of the Leader, in 1923; its recipients took the titles Sardar-i-Ala or Sardar-i-Ali and received grants of land. The order was disbanded in 1929 and later revived by King Muhammad Zahir Shah. In Persia, Sardar-i-Bozorg was the title of Hossein Khan Sardar and his brother Hasan Khan Qajar, and Sardar i-Azam was occasionally used for the head of government.

In Ottoman Turkey Serdar, or Serdar-i-Ekrem, was the title of the commander-in-chief in several campaigns, and it was also a rank in the Bosnia Eyalet. The Principality of Montenegro and the Principality of Serbia used it as an honorary title below that of Vojvoda; these were not noble titles, since neither country had a nobility. Janko Vukotić, a military leader and former prime minister of Montenegro, was a Serdar. Sirdar was the official title of the British commander-in-chief of the Anglo-Egyptian army.

In Punjab, tribal chiefs, military commanders and wealthy, influential notables were called Sardars, and the title is used by both Muslims and Sikhs. The Sikh Empire used it for important political, tribal, military and religious ranks. In Pakistan it marks the chief of a tribe, and several tribes in Hazara, Poonch, Sudhanoti and the Attock area use it as a sign of noble status. The Sardars of Bengal are hereditary village chiefs, and under the Nawabs of Dhaka a Sardari system was introduced in the old city.

In the Maratha Empire the Sirdar-Bahadur was a governor general or chief minister of a remote province, comparable in rank to a Mughal subahdar or a British viceroy. In the Kingdom of Nepal and the Gorkha Kingdom, Sardars were chiefs of administration and the military in the provinces, and the rulers of Kapurthala State were styled Sardar. In Iran the word is used to address senior officers of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
sardinia: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea after Sicily, with an area of 24,100 square kilometres. It lies 200 kilometres west of the Italian Peninsula, 200 kilometres north of Tunisia and 16.5 kilometres south of Corsica. Its mountains, woods, plains, rocky coasts and sandy beaches have led to its description as a micro-continent. The name is pre-Latin. It appears as ŠRDN on the Phoenician Nora Stone, and some have speculated that the Nuragic Sards were the Sherden, one of the Sea Peoples.

Humans have lived on the island since the end of the Paleolithic, although authors disagree whether the evidence from Corbeddu Cave, about 20,000 years old, is solid or whether occupation is secure only from about 10,000 years ago. The Nuragic civilization flourished from the 18th century BCE to either 238 BCE or, in some parts, the 2nd century CE, and in Barbagia to the 6th century. The Phoenicians began visiting from about the 9th century BCE, using ports such as Caralis, Nora, Bithia, Sulci and Tharros. In the 6th century BCE the Carthaginians planned to annex it, and a first invasion led by Malchus was foiled by Nuragic resistance, but from 510 BCE the southern and west-central part came under Carthaginian rule.

The Vandals conquered the island in 456, and their rule lasted 78 years. In 530 the Vandal governor Godas declared Sardinia independent of Carthage and negotiated with Emperor Justinian I. When Gelimer sent the bulk of his army and navy to subdue him in 533, Justinian's general Belisarius took Carthage, and Sardinia returned to Byzantine rule, which lasted about 300 years apart from a short period after the Ostrogoths invaded in 551.

In 1297 Pope Boniface VIII created a Kingdom of Sardinia and Corsica and offered it to James II of Aragon. Spanish rule followed, and in 1708 the Austrians occupied the island, although in 1717 Cardinal Giulio Alberoni reoccupied it for Philip V of Spain. In 1861 the parliament of the Kingdom of Sardinia renamed the state the Kingdom of Italy. Italy became a republic in 1946, and Sardinia has been governed since 1948 under a special statute of autonomy.

Sardinia is one of the twenty regions of Italy and one of five with statutory autonomy. Cagliari is its capital and largest city, followed by Sassari. The Sardinian language and the Algherese dialect of Catalan are recognised as protected minority languages. Thousands of nuraghe, Bronze Age buildings, still characterise the prehistoric landscape, alongside tombs, megalithic circles and well temples, and the Phoenicians and Punics left traces on the coasts.
sardis: Sardis, in Lydian Sfar and in Old Persian Sparda, stood in the middle of the Hermus River valley, about 4 kilometres south of the river. Its citadel was built on a steep spur of Mount Tmolus, and a lower town extended to the Pactolus stream, where archaeologists have found installations for processing alluvial metals. The site was occupied for at least 3,500 years, fluctuating between a wealthy city of international importance and a collection of modest hamlets.

Sardis was settled before 1500 BCE. In the 7th century BCE it became the capital of Lydia, whose kings, such as Croesus, ruled an empire reaching the Halys River. The city covered 108 hectares and was protected by walls twenty metres thick, and three enormous burial tumuli at Bin Tepe marked it from a distance. Its artisans specialised in seals and jewellery, and its pottery blended Aegean and Anatolian styles.

After defeating Croesus at the battles of Pteria and Thymbra, Cyrus the Great's Persians followed his army back to Sardis and sacked it after a brief siege. The destruction is vivid in the archaeological record: the fortifications burned in a great fire, and arrowheads and household tools lie in the debris, suggesting that civilians joined the fighting. Sardis was rebuilt and, though never again the capital of an independent state, served as the capital of the Persian satrapy of Sparda and as the end station of the Royal Road. Ionian forces burned it in 499 BCE during the Ionian Revolt.

Alexander the Great received its surrender in 334 BCE. Under Hellenistic rulers the city took on a strongly Greek character, with a gymnasium, theatre, hippodrome and the great Temple of Artemis, and Antiochos III settled Jews there. It passed to Rome in 129 BCE, was one of the seven churches of Asia, and declined from the 600s after being sacked in 615. It was lost to the Seljuk Turks in 1078, retaken in 1097, and probably destroyed by Timur in 1402; by the 1700s only two small hamlets stood there.

The site lies near the village of Sart, near Salihli in Manisa Province, Turkey. Princeton University excavated it from 1910 to 1914, and the Archaeological Exploration of Sardis, founded in 1958, has since uncovered the Roman bath-gymnasium complex, a synagogue in use from the 4th to the 6th century, Byzantine shops and a Lydian area for refining electrum. It was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025, for its significance as the home of coinage.
sare-jahan-se-accha: Iqbal was a lecturer at Government College, Lahore, when the student Lala Har Dayal invited him to preside over a function in 1905. Instead of giving a speech he sang the poem, which quickly became an anthem of opposition to the British Raj. At 27 Iqbal saw the future society of the subcontinent as a plural, composite Hindu-Muslim culture. Later that year he left for three years in Europe, which turned him into an Islamic philosopher. The poem was later included in his Urdu collection Bang-i-Dara of 1924.

The poem is an ode to Hindustan, the land of present-day Bangladesh, India and Pakistan. Its singers call themselves the nightingales of a garden, guarded by the highest mountain and watered by thousands of rivers; it recalls the day the caravan first reached the banks of the Ganges, and notes that ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome have vanished while Hindustan endures. Its sixth stanza, often quoted as proof of Iqbal's secular outlook, says that religion does not teach ill-will among ourselves, for we are of Hind and our homeland is Hindustan.

In 1910 Iqbal wrote another song for children, Tarana-e-Milli, in the same metre and rhyme, whose first stanza claims Central Asia, Arabia and Hindustan and names the whole world as the homeland of Muslims. In 1930, addressing the Muslim League at Allahabad, he supported a separate state in the Muslim-majority areas, an idea that inspired the creation of Pakistan.

The song has remained popular in India only. Mahatma Gandhi is said to have sung it more than a hundred times while held in Yerawada Jail in Pune in the 1930s. Ravi Shankar, finding the slow tune of those years too sad, set it in 1945 to the stronger tune sung today, and Antsher Lobo arranged that version as the quick march of the Indian Armed Forces. Four stanzas became an unofficial national song. In 1984 the astronaut Rakesh Sharma used its first line to describe India from space to Indira Gandhi.
sarekat-islam: Its forerunner was the Sarekat Dagang Islam (Islamic Trade Association), which grew from a movement begun in Batavia in 1909 and Buitenzorg in 1910 by the journalist Tirto Adhi Soerjo, a member of the priyayi nobility. He meant it to unite small indigenous and Arab traders, bound by their common faith, against the large Chinese-Indonesian traders, and it was also a reaction to the work of Christian missionaries. In 1911 Samanhudi, a batik trader of Surakarta, founded the association there with Tirto's help. After a brief suspension by the colonial government following anti-Chinese riots, it took the name Sarekat Islam at Surabaya on 19 September 1912.

At the first congress, in Surabaya on 26 January 1913, Oemar Said Tjokroaminoto rose to lead it; hailed by followers as a messianic Ratu Adil, he spread it across Java and the outer islands. Its leaders professed loyalty to the Dutch and sought self-government by constitutional means, but in the villages it became a vehicle of protest, and 1913–1914 saw violence against Chinese-Indonesians, priyayi officials and the colonial regime. Its Semarang branch under the union activist Semaun turned to communism through the Indies Social Democratic Association of Henk Sneevliet.

After the Garut shooting of June 1919 the government arrested leaders, Tjokroaminoto among them, and membership fell sharply. The Islamist wing of Agus Salim and the communist wing of Semaun drew apart, and in 1921 Salim had dual membership forbidden, expelling the communists, who formed the Sarekat Islam Merah, later the Sarekat Rakjat, the mass organisation of the Communist Party of Indonesia (PKI).

In February 1923 the movement became the Islamic Association Party, renamed the Indonesian Islamic Union Party (PSII) in 1929, by which time it was a secondary party; by 1930 it had about 19,000 members. Tjokroaminoto died in 1934, and in 1937 Salim and Mohammad Roem were expelled. The Japanese banned the party in 1942. Revived in 1947 under Tjokroaminoto's sons, it won 2.9% of the vote in the 1955 election and was merged into the United Development Party (PPP) by the Suharto regime in 1973.
sargon-ii: Nothing is known of Sargon II's life before he became king. He was probably born about 770 BCE and cannot have been born later than about 760 BCE. He is generally believed to have taken the throne by overthrowing Shalmaneser V, most likely his brother and a son of Tiglath-Pileser III, and is typically regarded as the founder of the Sargonid dynasty, though he was probably a scion of the incumbent Adaside dynasty. He grew up when rebellion and plague had reduced Assyria's prestige, a decline that Tiglath-Pileser reversed.

The name Šarru-kīn means the faithful king or the legitimate king. Sargon was the first king in more than a thousand years to bear it, and it was probably an assumed regnal name, chosen because of Sargon of Akkad, the conqueror of large parts of Mesopotamia. Late Assyrian texts spell the two names alike, and Sargon II is sometimes called the second Sargon.

His reign began with large-scale resistance in Assyria's heartland, and several peripheral regions regained independence. In early 721 BCE the Chaldean warlord Marduk-apla-iddina II captured Babylon and allied with Elam. Sargon intervened in Mannaea in 718, and in 715 he restored its king Ullusunu against Rusa I of Urartu, whose army had been weakened by the Cimmerians. He also annexed Quwê after its king Urik turned to Midas of Phrygia.

From 717 to 707 BCE he built a new capital, Dur-Sharrukin, about 16 kilometres north-east of Nineveh, at a site with no earlier buildings, which he conceived as an ideal city with proportions based on mathematical harmony; he made it his residence in 706. In 710 he set out to reconquer Babylonia, declaring that Marduk had commanded him to liberate the south, and he won over cities and tribes by diplomacy. The citizens of Babylon proclaimed him king, and he spent three years there while his son Sennacherib oversaw Assyria.

In early summer 705 BCE Sargon led a campaign against Tabal in Anatolia and was killed in battle. The Assyrian army could not recover his body, so he could not be buried, and by Mesopotamian belief he was doomed to wander as a restless ghost. Sennacherib believed his father must have committed some grave sin and distanced himself from him, and Sargon was barely mentioned in later ancient literature.

Sargon called himself a guardian of justice, put conquered peoples on the same footing as native Assyrians, and is not known to have committed atrocities against civilians. He was nearly forgotten until Paul-Émile Botta learned of Dur-Sharrukin in 1843 and excavated its palace; Assyriology did not fully accept him as a real king until the 1860s.
sargon-of-akkad: Sargon's reign is poorly understood, since few commemorative inscriptions can be reliably dated to it, most of them known from later copies, and few archives survive from his time. Like the other kings of his dynasty he does not name his father in his inscriptions; the Sumerian Sargon Legend, written long after his death, calls his father La'ipum. He rose as ruler of the small city of Akkad in central Mesopotamia, which lay in the shadow of its powerful neighbour Kish, though the circumstances of his rise remain unclear. His daughter Enheduanna was a high priestess of the moon god at Ur who composed hymns, among them the Exaltation of Inanna, that were used for centuries.

Sargon's reign began in the last phase of the Early Dynastic period, when Lower Mesopotamia was divided among several city-states and the idea of unifying it was emerging. Lugal-zage-si of Uruk had brought the south, the land of Sumer, under his control. According to datable sources it took Sargon three battles to defeat Lugal-zage-si and his allies and take Uruk, whose walls were razed. The captured king was led to the sanctuary of Enlil at Nippur. The date of the conquest is debated, and it is placed around 2300 BCE.

Sargon also led expeditions beyond Lower Mesopotamia, east towards Elam and west towards Mari, though he did not incorporate those lands. Their purpose seems to have been glory, riches, control of trade routes and the restraint of rival powers. His inscriptions summarise his successes as 34 battles. One mentions that he fed 5,400 men at his table each day, usually understood as soldiers bound personally to him, and it names the nine regiments of Akkad. The former kingdoms became provinces under governors, and Akkad remained the capital. His scribes began to write inscriptions in Akkadian as well as Sumerian, and the image of the king changed from a cultic and administrative official to a war hero.

The dates of Sargon's reign are uncertain; they are often estimated at 2334 to 2279 BCE, and other proposals exist. After his death his sons Rimush and Manishtushu succeeded him, in an order that is unknown, and Rimush suppressed revolts in the southern cities. Naram-Sin followed, and then Shar-kali-sharri, whose reign ended in the first half of the 22nd century BCE with the decline of the Akkadian Empire.

Sargon became the archetype of the conquering ruler. Stories of his birth, rise and campaigns were still being composed in the 8th century BCE, and Assyrian and Babylonian kings saw themselves as heirs of his empire. The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus excavated the palaces of Sargon and his successors.
sari-gelin: The song's names reflect its languages. In Armenian, Sari Aghjik joins sari, of the mountain, and aghjik, girl, to mean a girl or bride from the mountains. In Azerbaijani and Turkish, sarı means yellow and gelin a bride, so that Sarı Gelin can mean a golden, blond or fair-skinned bride. The Azerbaijani version was arranged by the composer Asaf Zeynally (1909–1932), and its Azerbaijani text was published in Baku in 1982, edited by Hamid Arasly, and again in 2001 by Rafik Babayev.

In each version a young man laments an unattainable girl he loves. In the Armenian Sari Aghjik she has chosen someone else; in the Persian Dāman Kešān she is unkind and flees. In Azerbaijan the song is tied to a legend of love between a Muslim Azerbaijani and a Christian Armenian girl who are kept apart. The verses belong to the bayati genre, popular across much of the Middle East, usually lines of seven syllables in a simple rhythm.

The Armenian, Azerbaijani and Turkish versions share much: the girl is from the mountains (in the Turkish one the young man meets her in the market of Erzurum and places her on Palandöken mountain), she is blond and tall, the lovers are kept apart, and he cries aman, an Arabic word of lasting pain. The Turkish and Armenian versions also call her Leyli, after Layla, the beloved of Persian tradition.

Versions exist in Sorani Kurdish, sung by Mohammad Mamle of Mahabad, and in Greek, with lyrics by Christos C. Papadopoulos. The Armenian-Soviet opera singer Pavel Lisitsian sang his own version, the Iranian singer Viguen performed the Persian one, and Kardeş Türküler recorded it in Turkey in 1997. Djivan Gasparyan and Hossein Alizadeh included it on Endless Vision (2006), nominated for a Grammy Award. The poet Huseyn Javid retold the story in his play Sheikh Sanan, and Yaver Rzayev's film Sari Gelin (1999) is about Azerbaijan's fight with Armenia. In Turkey a documentary of the same title, distributed in schools, denies the Armenian Genocide and drew criticism.
sari-iran: Sari lies in the north of Iran, between the northern slopes of the Alborz Mountains and the southern coast of the Caspian, here called the Mazandaran Sea. Excavations in the Hutto cave show settlements around Sari as far back as the 7th millennium BCE. The climate is humid subtropical, with cool, rainy winters and hot, humid summers, and the surrounding land is known for its gardens and citrus groves. Sari is the largest city of Mazandaran.

The Muslim historian Hamdollah Mostowfi attributed the foundation of Sari to the king Tahmoures Divband of the Pishdadian dynasty, and Ferdowsi names the city in the Shahnameh. Local folklore says it was settled when the blacksmith Kaveh, a native of the city, revolted against the tyrant Zahak, and that Fereydun chose to live near him. The city may be the Zadracarta of Greek sources of the Achaemenid era, though other sources place Zadracarta at or near Gorgan. According to Arrian it was the largest city of Hyrcania. It was again a regional capital in the Sasanian era.

In the seventh century Farrukhan the Great of the Dabuyid dynasty rebuilt the city and named it after his son Saruyeh, and Sari again became the capital of Tabaristan, which Amol had been before. After invasions it lost its high standing and was periodically burnt. Shah Abbas the Great settled large numbers of Georgians, Circassians, Armenians and other peoples of the Caucasus in Mazandaran, and made Farahabad his alternate capital to the north of the city. Under Reza Shah in the Pahlavi era the face of the town changed drastically, and the railway station and most of the streets and government buildings date from then.

Sari is the capital of Mazandaran province and of its county and district. Most of its people speak the Mazandarani language, with Persian as the lingua franca. Zoroastrians from Sari who fled to India in the 10th century founded a town called Navu Sari, now Navsari, still a centre of the Parsi community. The clock tower in the Clock Square, built in 1930, is a local landmark, and the tomb towers include the Imamzadeh Abbas. The economy rests on food production, citrus fruit, paper and wood, and Mazandaran Wood and Paper Industries has its works there.
sarissa: A sarissa had two main parts, a long wooden shaft and a metal tip; some may also have had a metal butt at the other end, with which the weapon could be stood in the ground without damage to the shaft. Ash, which is long, flexible and light, and cornel wood, which is shorter but stronger, are the likeliest woods. It replaced the considerably shorter dory.

Ancient writers agree that its length set it apart, but not on the figure: Theophrastus, a contemporary of Alexander the Great, puts the longest at 12 cubits, and Polybius gives 16 cubits in the original design, reduced in practice to 14. In modern units this suggests about 5.8 m in Alexander's time and perhaps 6.3 m later.

The weapon needed both hands, so the phalangite carried only a smaller shield, the pelta, perhaps hung from a neck strap. On the march the sarissas were held upright; levelled for battle, fully five rows of points projected in front of the first rank, while the rear ranks held theirs angled upward, which also deflected arrows. A phalanx so formed was considered practically invulnerable from the front, but it turned with difficulty, and a soldier out of formation had to fall back on a sword or dagger.

Sarissa-armed phalanxes were vital in the early battles of Alexander, including the Battle of Gaugamela, though in his later campaigns he gradually reduced their importance. The surest way to beat such a phalanx was to break its formation or outflank it, as the Romans did at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE. A light cavalry unit of Alexander's army, the sarissophoroi, carried somewhat shorter versions; Nicholas Victor Sekunda argues that the Macedonian cavalry spear is better classed as a xyston.

A leaf-shaped spearhead 51 cm long, found by Manolis Andronikos in a Macedonian tomb at Vergina, shaped much scholarship between 1970 and 2000, but more recent work doubts that it belonged to a sarissa; Sekunda favours a small diamond-shaped iron tip of about 13.5 cm. Earlier estimates put the weight at 5.5 to 6.5 kg, yet Peter Connolly reconstructed a pike 5.8 m long in cherry wood that weighed only 4.05 kg. Scholars also draw on later pikemen, such as the Swiss and the German Landsknecht: preserved English pikes are 5.6 to 5.9 m long, which suggests that the lengths reported for the Macedonian weapon were workable.
sarkel: Sarkel, which means 'white house' in the Khazar language, was a large fortress of limestone and brick on a hill on the left bank of the lower Don River, in what is now Rostov Oblast of Russia. It took its name from the white limestone bricks used in its construction. The left bank was much lower than the right. On the higher right bank, across the river, stood another large Khazar fortress of roughly the same age, known as the Pravoberezhnoye Tsimlyanskoye site; its ancient name is unknown.

The Khazars built Sarkel to protect the north-western border of their state. According to Constantine Porphyrogenitus in De Administrando Imperio, they asked the Byzantine emperor Theophilus for a fortress, and he sent his chief engineer Petronas Kamateros. In return the khagan ceded Chersonesos and some other Crimean dependencies to Byzantium.

Historians have been unable to determine why so strong a fortress was needed. They generally suppose that its costly construction answered the rise of a strong regional power. Alexander Vasiliev and George Vernadsky, among others, argue that it defended a vital portage between the Don and the Volga against the Rus' Khaganate, although other historians place that polity many hundred miles to the north. Constantine's record connects the fortress with the Hungarians, and the Persian explorer and geographer Ahmad ibn Rustah wrote in the 10th century that the Khazars had entrenched themselves against Hungarian attacks.

The city was a busy commercial centre because it controlled the portage between the Volga and the Don, which the Rus used to cross from the Black Sea to the Volga and on to the Caspian and the Baltic. The route was known as the Khazarian Way. The garrison included Oghuz and Pecheneg mercenaries. Kievan Rus', under Sviatoslav I, captured the fortress and city in 965. It was renamed Belaya Vezha, Slavic for White Tower or White Fortress, and was settled by Slavs. It remained Slavic until the 12th century, when the district was taken over by the Kipchaks.

Mikhail Artamonov excavated the site in the 1930s, the most ambitious excavation of a Khazar site ever undertaken. Among many Khazar and Rus items he found Byzantine columns that had been used in building Sarkel. The site now lies submerged under the Tsimlyansk Reservoir, completed in 1952, so that no further excavation is possible.
sarmatism: The idea of a Sarmatian ancestry was set out by the chronicler Jan Długosz in the 15th century and continued by writers such as Marcin Kromer and Maciej Miechowita, whose Tractatus de Duabus Sarmatiis became a widely used reference work abroad. It arose from the humanists' admiration for Antiquity. According to Ptolemy's Geography, Sarmatia covered the lands of Poland, Lithuania and Tartary. The Sarmatians themselves were a confederacy of mostly Iranian tribes north of the Black Sea, whom Herodotus called descendants of the Scythians and Amazons. Some writers held that the Sarmatians descended from Japheth, son of Noah.

Poles were not alone in claiming an ancient people as ancestors: the Dutch took the Batavians, the French the Gauls and the Hungarians the Huns. Modern scholarship has found that the Alans, a late Sarmatian people, did invade Slavic lands before the sixth century and formed a ruling class that was gradually absorbed into the Slavic population, though a direct tie to Poland remains uncertain.

Sarmatism stressed equality among all nobles, horsemanship, village life and hospitality, and a culture of honour in which scars were prized. Nobles wore the żupan, the kontusz with its sash, and a curved sabre, dress derived from Ottoman models, and kept moustaches rather than beards. Latin was widely spoken, if superficially. Funerals were elaborate, with a castrum doloris and portraits fixed to the coffin, an art form not found elsewhere in Europe.

Politically it prized the Golden Liberty. Only nobles held the vote in the Sejm and the sejmiki, the king was elected and his power limited, and from Siciński's veto each deputy could block a measure by the liberum veto. Adherents regarded Poland as the bulwark of Christendom. Religious freedom was recognised in the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, but the Counter-Reformation brought intolerance: Arians were banished in 1658 and conversion from Catholicism was outlawed ten years later. Sarmatism also drew Lithuanian and Ruthenian nobles into a common identity.

By the late 18th century the word carried negative associations. Publications such as Monitor mocked it as a name for unenlightened ideas, and Franciszek Zabłocki's play Sarmatyzm appeared in 1785. After the partitions of Poland between 1772 and 1795, Romanticism rehabilitated the old traditions, notably in Adam Mickiewicz's Pan Tadeusz of 1834 and Henryk Sienkiewicz's Trilogy of 1884 to 1888. In modern Polish, Sarmata is an ironic self-description.
sarmizegetusa-regia: Sarmizegetusa Regia was the capital and the most important military, religious and political centre of the Dacians before their wars with the Roman Empire. It stood on top of a mountain 1,200 metres high, in the Orăștie Mountains in present-day Romania, and its remains lie in the village of Grădiștea de Munte in Hunedoara County. It should not be confused with Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, the Roman capital of Dacia built by Trajan about 40 kilometres away.

The fortress was the core of a defensive system of six Dacian fortresses in the Orăștie Mountains: Sarmizegetusa, Costești-Blidaru, Piatra Roșie, Costești-Cetățuie, Căpâlna and Bănița. All six are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The citadel was built on five terraces, on an area of almost 30,000 square metres, of massive stone blocks in the style called murus dacicus.

Towards the end of his reign, Burebista moved the Geto-Dacian capital from Argedava to Sarmizegetusa. It served as the Dacian capital for at least a century and a half and reached its peak under King Decebalus, whom the Romans defeated in the reign of Emperor Trajan. Finds from the site include a medical kit in a brass-bound wooden box, containing a scalpel, tweezers, powdered pumice and miniature pots for medicines, a huge vase with an inscription in the Roman alphabet, DECEBAL PER SCORILO, meaning Decebalus, son of Scorilus.

The Romans dismantled the walls in part at the end of the First Dacian War in 102 and rebuilt them as Roman fortifications. These were later destroyed, possibly by the Dacians, and rebuilt again after the successful Roman siege of 105-6. The Romans then built a new capital, Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa, 40 kilometres away. Emperor Hadrian wanted it seen as the successor to the Dacian one, and so added the name Sarmizegetusa.

The sacred zone lies about 100 metres east of the citadel gate, on a terrace joined to it by a paved road. It includes some of the largest circular and rectangular Dacian sanctuaries. The bases of the columns of the rectangular temples are still visible in regular rows. The large circular sanctuary was a setting of timber posts shaped like a D inside a timber circle and a low stone kerb, and its layout resembles Stonehenge. In 2011 workers building a car park for visitors, paid for by the Hunedoara County Council and done without archaeologists' approval, destroyed part of the site and endangered about 30 metres of the citadel wall.
sarnath: Sarnath lies eight kilometres northeast of Varanasi, near the confluence of the Ganges and the Varuna. It is also known as the Deer Park, Isipatana and Migadaya. The name comes from Sāranganātha, Lord of the Deer, which refers to a Buddhist legend in which the Buddha, in an earlier life as a deer, offered his life in exchange for that of a doe a king meant to kill; the king was so moved that he made the park a deer sanctuary.

Here, around 528 BCE according to the tradition, the Buddha gave his first teaching to his five original disciples, Kaundinya, Assaji, Bhaddiya, Vappa and Mahanama, the First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta he named Sarnath as one of four places of pilgrimage, with Lumbini, Bodh Gaya and Kushinagar.

Buddhism flourished at Sarnath from about 600 to 200 BCE, helped by the patronage of kings and wealthy merchants of Varanasi. The Chinese monk Faxian, who travelled in northern India from 400 to 411, saw four large towers and two viharas there. Around 640 Xuanzang reported hundreds of small shrines and votive stupas, a vihara about 61 metres high holding a large Buddha statue, and about 1,500 monks of the Sammatiya school. Under the Pala rulers pilgrims and monks came from all over Asia, and the Gahadavala kings, though Hindu, also supported the monasteries.

The site was plundered in 1194, when Qutb ud-Din Aibak led his men to Varanasi and Sarnath. Some scholars now dispute that Muslim invasions were the main cause of its destruction, arguing that Brahmanical hostility toward Buddhists was responsible. In 1794 workmen of Jagat Singh dismantled a stupa and its relics were thrown into the Ganges. Alexander Cunningham carried out the first systematic excavations in 1835 and 1836 and identified Sarnath as the site of the first sermon. Friedrich Oertel's excavations of 1904 and 1905 uncovered parts of the Ashokan pillar with its lion capital.

The Dhamek Stupa, 39 metres high and 28 metres across, marks the place of the first teaching. The Ashokan pillar was broken in the 12th century, but the Lion Capital of Ashoka, which is in the Sarnath Archaeological Museum, is the State Emblem of India, and the wheel of dharma that topped it appears on the Indian flag. The modern Mulagandha Kuty Vihara was opened in 1931 by the Maha Bodhi Society, with frescoes by the Japanese artist Kosetsu Nosu.

Sarnath is also a pilgrimage site for Jains: the village of Singhpur is believed to be the birthplace of Shreyansanatha, the eleventh tirthankara, and a temple dedicated to him was built in 1824. Several Buddhist countries have built temples and monasteries here.
sarnen: Sarnen lies at an altitude of 471 metres on the northern shore of Lake Sarnen, along the outflow of the Sarner Aa, 20 km south of Lucerne. The lake covers about 7.5 square kilometres. The town is surrounded by chains of mountains, and a protected bog lies nearby; the best-known peak in the neighbourhood is Mount Pilatus, at 2,132 metres. The municipality covers 73.12 square kilometres, of which about 39 per cent is agricultural land and 50.7 per cent forest. It is made up of five sections: Sarnen, Stalden, Wilen, Kägiswil and Ramersberg.

Stone Age and Bronze Age finds show that the Sarnen valley was inhabited from the earliest times. Over the years Sarnen developed into an important trading centre. Ten sites in the municipality are Swiss heritage sites of national significance. Three are religious buildings: the Ossuary of St Michael, the parish church of St Peter and Paul and the Church of St Martin. Others are the double house am Grund and Grundacher, the Hexenturm, the Cantonal Rathaus, the musical collection of the Frauenkloster, the Landenberg armory and the State Archives of Obwalden. The whole small city, the hamlet of Ramersberg and the Kirchhofen area belong to the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites.

Sarnen is the capital of the canton of Obwalden and a small regional centre with 10,514 inhabitants in December 2020. Most speak German, and about three quarters of the population belongs to the Roman Catholic Church. The town has grown steadily and is attractive to commuters because of its closeness to Lucerne, which they reach by motorway or railway. Sarnen station is on the Brünig line, a narrow-gauge railway from Interlaken to Lucerne. Companies active in the town include SIKA, a maker of specialty chemicals, and Leister Technologies, which makes heated-air tools.
sarolt: Sarolt was born around 950, a date reckoned from the birth years of her children. Her father, the gyula of Transylvania, was the second-highest-ranking leader in the Hungarian tribal federation after the Grand Prince; his name is given as Zombor or Gyula II, and he was a grandson of Tétény, one of the seven chieftains who led the Hungarian tribes into the Carpathian Basin. He reportedly converted to Byzantine Christianity in Constantinople after 950 and established the first Christian mission in Hungary, so his household, Sarolt included, was probably baptised in the Byzantine rite.
Her name is of Turkic origin, Šar-oldu, and means white stoat. According to the Gesta Hungarorum she had a sister named Karold and a brother, who can be identified as Gyula III.

Sarolt married Géza, a great-grandson of Árpád, around 970, which was likely also the start of his rule as Grand Prince of the Hungarians. She exerted a powerful influence on her husband and through him on his government, and Catholic missionaries watched her with suspicion. The chronicles accused her of drinking without limit and even of manslaughter. She and Géza received baptism late in life and raised their son as a Christian, changing his name from Vajk to Stephen as a sign of their faith.

When Géza died in 997, his distant cousin Koppány claimed the leadership of the Magyars against Stephen and, appealing to Hungarian tradition, sought to marry Sarolt. Koppány was defeated, and shortly afterwards her son was crowned the first King of Hungary.

Her children married into several ruling houses. Her daughter Judith became the wife of the future King Bolesław I of Poland, Margaret married the future Tsar Gavril Radomir of Bulgaria, and Grimelda married Otto Orseolo, Doge of Venice. Another daughter, possibly also named Sarolt, may have been the wife of the future King Samuel Aba of Hungary. Her son Stephen I ruled until his death on 15 August 1038.
saronic-gulf: The Saronic Gulf, in Greek Saronikos kolpos, forms part of the Aegean Sea between the peninsulas of Attica and Argolis. It marks the eastern side of the isthmus of Corinth and is the eastern end of the Corinth Canal, which cuts across the isthmus. The Gulf of Megara makes up its northern end. Besides Aegina, Salamis and Poros, it includes the smaller islands of Patroklos and Fleves, and the urban area of Athens lies on its north and east coasts, with the port of Piraeus on the north-eastern edge. Bays in the gulf include Phaleron Bay, Elefsina Bay in the north, Kechries Bay in the north-west and Sofiko Bay in the east.

The volcanic centre of Methana lies to the south-west and forms the north-western end of the Cycladic arch of active volcanoes that includes Milos, Santorini and Nisyros. Hot sulphurous water still rises there and is used by a hydropathic institute. The most recent eruption, of a submarine volcano north of Methana, was in the seventeenth century.

The name is said to come from the mythological king Saron, who drowned at the Psiphaea lake, now Psifta. The Saronic Islands have played a pivotal part in the history of Greece. The Battle of Salamis, fought in 480 BCE in the gulf near modern Piraeus, was a major naval engagement in which the Athenian-led Greek fleet defeated the much larger Persian forces of Xerxes I. The victory was a turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars and contributed to Athens' rise as a dominant power in the classical Greek world. The ancient port of Cenchreae also stood on the gulf.

Beaches line much of the coast, and sailing is popular, as the Attic mainland partly shelters the gulf from the summer meltemi wind. Two notable archaeological sites lie on its shores: the ancient theatre at Epidaurus with its nearby asclepieion, and the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina. The gulf is also a gathering area for short-beaked common dolphins.
sarreguemines: Sarreguemines lies at the confluence of the Blies and the Saar, 79 km east of Metz, in north-eastern France. Its name is a French spelling of the local Lorraine-German Saargemin, meaning "confluence into the Saar". It has railway connections to Strasbourg, Saarbrücken and Metz. Traditionally it was the head of river navigation on the Saar, a depot where boats were unloaded. It is the seat of an arrondissement and a canton, and its inhabitants are called Sarregueminois.

Sarreguemines was originally a Roman settlement and obtained civic rights early in the 13th century. In 1297 the count of Saarbrücken ceded it to the Duke of Lorraine, and it passed with Lorraine to France in 1766. Under French rule its industries developed further, including the production of plush velvet, leather, faience, porcelain and papier-mâché boxes, mainly used as snuffboxes, and the town became known for its artisanal craftsmanship.

The Treaty of Frankfurt, which followed the Franco-Prussian War, transferred it to Germany in 1871, and until 1918 it formed part of the German imperial province of Alsace-Lorraine, still making plush velvet, leather, faience and porcelain. It returned to France after World War I. On 21 to 23 December 1944 the 44th Infantry Division of the United States threw back three German attempts to cross the Blies River, and the defence of the Sarreguemines area continued through February and most of March 1945.
sarsa-dengel: Sarsa Dengel, a member of the Solomonic dynasty, was the son of Emperor Menas and Empress Admas Mogasa. He was barely fourteen when the Shewan commanders of the army and the Dowager Empress elected him king, and he took the throne name Malak Sagad I. On coming of age he had to put down revolts by his cousins, first Hamalmal, defeated at the Battle of Endagabatan, and then Fasil. During his rule he moved the centre of the empire from Shewa to Begemder.

In the 1570s Oromo groups were moving north. In 1572 he fought off a Borana raid near Lake Zway, and in 1574 he gathered an army at Gind Beret and drove the Oromo out of Wej and Maya. When the Adal Sultan Muhammad ibn Nasir declared a jihad and campaigned in Hadiya, Sarsa Dengel defeated him at the Battle of Webi River. When the local ruler, Bahr Negus Yeshaq, allied with the Ottomans at Debarwa, the emperor defeated them at the Battle of Addi Qarro in Tigray, where Yeshaq and the Ottoman commander Ahmad Pasha were killed. The garrison of Debarwa surrendered, and he had its mosque and fort destroyed.

After a coronation at Aksum he campaigned from 1580 against the Beta Israel in Semien, declining to turn back when the Borana raided Shewa, Waj and Damot, to the frustration of his officials. In 1586 the Borana invaded Gojjam, and he then forced the Dawé Oromo in Wej to flee south. In 1587 the Ottomans advanced from Hirgigo and retook Debarwa; he drove them back, raided the fort at Hirgigo and killed its commander, Kadawert Pasha, after which they withdrew and handed the port to a local Balaw chief.

According to his chronicle, monks warned him on his last campaign, against the Oromo in Damot, not to eat fish from a certain river; he ate it, fell sick and died. He was buried in the Medhane Alem church on Rema Island. Historians differ over his reign. J. Spencer Trimingham hails him as one of the great warrior-kings of the Ethiopian Empire and Franz Dombrowski credits him with ending the Ottoman threat, while Mordechai Abir and Richard Pankhurst argue that his northern campaigns left the south open to the Oromo migration, which Abir calls a turning point towards the empire's decline.
sarsina: Sarsina lies in the Tuscan-Romagnolo Apennines, in the province of Forlì-Cesena. Its ancient name was Sarsina or Sassina, and it stood in the valley of the Savio River. It was the centre of a pasture district, and its milk is frequently mentioned in ancient sources. Inscriptions preserved in the local museum show that the town had strategic importance.

In 266 BCE Roman consuls held a triumph over the Sassinates. In 225 BCE the Umbri and Sassinates are named together as Roman allies providing 20,000 men between them. The town gave a number of recruits to the Praetorian Guard, and the playwright Plautus was a native of Sassina. Devastation towards the end of the 3rd century, perhaps by barbarian tribes, left signs of fire on the floors of some houses, and the Visigoths and the Heruli made further incursions between 409 and 470.

Saint Vicinius of Sarsina was the first bishop, from around 303 to his death in 330. In the 10th century the bishops obtained temporal sovereignty over the city and its district, which became a prince-bishopric, and work on the cathedral began around the year 1000.

From 1327 until 1400 the Ordelaffi of Forlì, the popes and the bishops disputed it. In the fifteenth century it passed to the Malatesta of Cesena and then of Rimini, and Cesare Borgia took it from them, and after his death the Venetians captured it. In 1518 it was enfeoffed to the Pio di Meldola and later passed to the Aldobrandini. In a reprisal in 1944 the German Wehrmacht killed or injured many people and burned public buildings and houses.

Remains of the Roman forum and necropolis can still be seen, along with what was probably a public bath, and an archaeological museum holds finds from the Roman era. The Romanesque cathedral dates from around the year 1000, and beside it stands the Sanctuary of San Vicinio. Besides agriculture and cattle breeding, the sulphur and manganese industries have been principal employments.
sarts: The word is attested in 11th-century Turkic works, among them Mahmud al-Kashgari's Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk and Yusuf Balasaguni's Kutadgu Bilig, meaning merchant or trader. It is traced to the Sanskrit sārthavāha, caravan leader, through Iranian and Uyghur forms; John R. Perry takes the Iranian form to be probably Parthian sartvā. Because Persians controlled the trade routes towards the nomads, Mongols and Turks called them Sarts, and the name spread to all settled Muslims; 13th-century Mongols used sartaq and sartaul for Tajiks and Muslims.

After the Mongols, Sart became a synonym of Tajik, set against Turk for the nomads, and the nomadic Uzbeks who conquered Central Asia in the 16th century called the whole settled population they ruled Sarts, whatever its language. In the Khanate of Khiva, according to Yuri Bregel, the Sarts descended from the ancient settled people of Khwarazm, lived mainly in the south and formed the tax-paying estate, while the Uzbeks were warriors; the Sarts used the name for themselves until 1917.

Russian officials met the term after taking the Khanate of Kokand. The 1867 statute of the Turkestan Governor-Generalship divided the native population into two nationalities, the settled Sarts and the nomadic Kirghiz, each with its own self-government, courts, land rules and taxes. Grammars of a Sart language were published, and the Turkestan Native Newspaper appeared in Tashkent in Old Uzbek (Sart) and Old Kyrgyz. Scholars argued whether Sarts were Tajiks, a separate people or simply townspeople; Leonid N. Sobolev wrote in 1874 that a Sart was not a separate tribe but an Uzbek or Tajik who lived in a city and traded.

In 1920 Lenin asked for a map dividing Turkestan into Uzbekia, Kirghizia and Turkmenia, with no place for the Sarts, and in the 1926 census enumerators were told to record people who called themselves Sarts as Uzbeks. The word survives as a derogatory term for Uzbeks, notably in southern Kyrgyzstan. Since 1991 scholars of the new states have revived the question, some calling the Sarts Tajiks, others a distinct people or a social rather than an ethnic group.
saruj: Suruç lies on a plain near the Syrian border, 46 kilometres south-west of Urfa, in a fertile district well suited to fruit and grapevines. It sits between the Euphrates on the west and Urfa and Harran on the east, about a day's journey from both cities by pre-industrial transport, and this traffic brought it a measure of commercial prosperity. It was also a post station between Raqqa and Sumaysat. The town itself was mainly agricultural: in the 12th century Ibn Jubayr described orchards and irrigation channels within it.

The region was held successively by Hurrians, Mitanni, Hittites and Assyrians in the Bronze Age. In the Roman and Byzantine periods the town was called Batnae. Constantine the Great, who reigned from 306 to 337, placed it under the control of Edessa, and in 363 Emperor Julian visited it on his march from Antioch to the Euphrates. Batnae became a suffragan bishopric of Edessa. Its best-known bishop, the Syriac hymnographer Jacob of Serugh, was born around 451, became bishop at the age of 67 and died around 521; he wrote hymns, 760 homilies and a Syriac translation of Evagrius, and both Chalcedonian and non-Chalcedonian Christians claim him.

The Arabic name Saruj became prominent after the Islamic conquests of the 7th century, and the town surrendered in 639 to Iyad ibn Ghanm. In the 900s it came under the Hamdanid dynasty and was later taken by the Byzantines. In the late 1090s a civil war between the Seljuk princes of Damascus and Aleppo let the Artuqid prince Sökmen set up a short-lived principality there. Baldwin I of Jerusalem captured it in 1101, and for almost half a century it belonged to the crusader County of Edessa. The poet al-Hariri made the hero of his maqamat, Abu Zayd al-Saruji, a native of Saruj driven out by the Christians. Imad ad-Din Zangi took the town in January 1145.

Abu'l-Fida described the town as lying in ruins in the 1300s, and Selim I brought the area into the Ottoman Empire in 1517. In late Ottoman times Suruç was the seat of a kaymakam. The visitor Evliya Çelebi wrote that the plain was first inhabited by Arabs and Turkomans, but found it in the 17th century mainly settled by Kurds and Turkomans. Suruç is now a municipality and district of Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey, inhabited mostly by Kurds and Turks.
sarvastivada: The Sarvastivada was one of the early Buddhist schools, established in the time of Emperor Ashoka. Its name is a Sanskrit term glossed as 'the theory of all that exists'. According to K. L. Dhammajoti, the school and its rival, the Vibhajyavada lineage, were both present in Ashoka's reign, so that it was already a distinct school.

According to some accounts, the Sarvastivadins emerged from the Sthavira Nikaya, a small group of conservatives, and were expelled from Magadha, after which they moved to north-western India. Charles Prebish observes that a great deal of mystery surrounds the school's rise and early development. Its beginnings have also been linked to Ashoka's sending of Majjhantika on a mission to Gandhara, and a community of Sarvastivadin monks was said to have been established at Mathura by the patriarch Upagupta.

The central doctrine held that all dharmas, the elementary components of experience, exist in the past, present and future. It was justified partly from the Buddha's teaching on karma: since good or bad actions ripen into fruit, the dharmas involved must still exist when the fruit appears, even though the cause lies in the past.

The school also taught momentariness, causal simultaneity, conditionality and its own account of the spiritual path. The Vaibhasikas, the orthodox Kashmiri branch, held that only present dharmas have efficacy, and that each dharma has a constant essence, its svabhava, through all three times.

The school had a distinct Abhidharma literature of seven canonical texts, among them the Jnanaprasthana, together with the Mahavibhasa, a great commentary compiled in Kashmir around the reign of the Kushan emperor Kanishka. All were translated into Chinese. Not every Sarvastivadin accepted the new orthodoxy: masters of Gandhara and Bactria, and the Sautrantikas who relied on the sutras, disagreed with it.

Sarvastivadins flourished in north India, Kashmir and Central Asia until the 7th century CE. When the pilgrim Xuanzang visited Kucha in 630 CE he found about one hundred convents and more than five thousand disciples of the school. The Sautrantika Vasubandhu wrote the Abhidharmakosa, which became the standard Abhidharma text in Indo-Tibetan and East Asian Buddhism, and he later turned to the Yogacara school of Mahayana. Saṃghabhadra answered him for the Vaibhasikas.

The Mulasarvastivada Vinaya, whose relation to the school is uncertain, remains the monastic rule of Indo-Tibetan Buddhism. In China the Sarvastivada Vinaya was once the commonest, until an imperial edict of Emperor Zhongzong of Tang in the early 8th century required the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya for ordination.
sasak-people: The Sasak live mainly on the island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara Province, Indonesia, and number around 3.6 million, which is 85% of the island's population. They are related to the Balinese in language and in ancestry, and to other ethnic groups on the neighbouring island of Sumbawa. The Bayan people are a distinct part of the Sasak and are the oldest group on Lombok.

The name Sasak was first mentioned in the Pujungan Inscription of the 11th century, found in Tabanan Regency on Bali. Its origin is uncertain. It may come from sak-sak, meaning boat or one by one, and the 14th-century Nagarakṛtāgama pairs Sasak with Lombok in the Kawi phrase Lombok Sasak Mirah Adhi. Local tradition derives it from sa'-saq, 'the one'. Another theory links it to the word for weaving, since the sound of the loom resembles sak-sak.

Little is known about early Sasak history. Lombok was brought under direct rule by the Mahapatih Gajah Mada by the 14th century. Before Islam became widespread the island was primarily Hindu, and many ancient Hindu temples, among them Gunung Pengsong, Lingsar, Meru and Suranadi, still stand.

Islam reached the area around the 15th century, and the Sasak converted between the late 16th and early 17th centuries. This is attributed to Pangeran Prapen, son of Raden Paku (Sunan Giri), or alternatively to Sunan Giri himself and the Muslim Makassarese, who frequently mixed basic Islamic belief with animism and so created the Wetu Telu religion. Balinese kingdoms also conquered Lombok, bringing a large Balinese population, about 300,000 people or 10 to 15 percent of the island's inhabitants, and strongly influencing Wetu Telu.

The Sasak language, Base Sasaq, is an Austronesian language of the Malayo-Sumbawan branch, closely related to the languages of Java and Bali. It has several dialects, including Kutó-Kuté and Bayan-Sasak in the north, Menó-Mené in the centre, Meriaq-Meriku, Ngenó-Ngené and Nggetó-Nggeté.

Most Sasak follow Lima Waktu ('Five Times') Islam, with the five daily prayers that orthodox teachers prescribe, while followers of Wetu Telu ('Three Times') pray three times a day. Large Wetu Telu communities remain, especially in Bayan, where the religion originated. Weaving is an important part of Sasak culture, and the Gandrung and Gendang beleq dances are among their performing arts.
sasanian-conquest-of-jerusalem: Jews and Samaritans had long been persecuted under Byzantine rule, and a pogrom at Antioch in 608 was followed by Jewish revolts in 610 that were crushed. Since the Bar Kokhba revolt Jews had been barred from Jerusalem, apart from a yearly visit on Tisha B'Av. In 613 Khosrow II sent Shahrbaraz into the Byzantine Diocese of the East; he took Antioch and Caesarea Maritima, gaining access to the Mediterranean, and Nehemiah ben Hushiel and Benjamin of Tiberias raised Jewish rebels in Galilee, between 20,000 and 26,000 of whom joined the advance on Jerusalem.

Sebeos, an Armenian bishop and historian, writes that the city first submitted, and its rule was handed to Nehemiah ben Hushiel, who began preparing to build a Third Temple. After a few months a Christian revolt killed him and his council of sixteen, along with many other Jews, and the survivors fled to Shahrbaraz at Caesarea. The Persians then besieged the city for 19, 20 or 21 days, depending on the source, and broke the walls, by undermining according to Sebeos and with ballistae according to the monk Antiochus Strategos.

Accounts of the killing that followed differ widely: Sebeos gives 17,000 Christian dead, versions of Antiochus up to 66,509, and the 9th-century Dionysius of Tel Mahre a doubtful 90,000. Antiochus accuses the Jews of massacring captives at the Mamilla reservoir, where a mass grave was found in 1989; 35,000 to 37,000 people, the patriarch Zacharias among them, are said to have been deported. Clergy were reportedly tortured in the search for the True Cross.

Modestos was set over the city, and by the first half of 616 churches including the Holy Sepulchre were being rebuilt. By 617 the Persians had turned to favour the Christians, and further Jewish settlement was banned. Excavations show no destruction layer from the conquest and continuous habitation, as the archaeologist Gideon Avni notes. After Kavadh II made peace in 628, Shahrbaraz returned the city, and on 21 March 630 Heraclius entered Jerusalem with the True Cross; Jews were then expelled and massacred. The Qur'an's Sūrat ar-Rūm mentions the Persian victory and foretells their defeat.
sasanian-empire: The Sasanian Empire, officially Ērānšahr, the Empire of the Iranians, was founded and ruled by the House of Sasan from 224 to 651. Ardashir I rose as Arsacid influence declined in the face of internal and external strife, and after defeating Artabanus IV of Parthia at the Battle of Hormozdgan in 224 the dynasty set out to restore the legacy of the Achaemenid Empire. The details of the fall of the Parthians and the rise of the Sasanians are shrouded in conflicting accounts.

Ctesiphon was the capital for all but the first two years, when Istakhr briefly served. At its height the empire controlled all of present-day Iran and Iraq and parts of Arabia, the Caucasus, the Levant, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent.

The Sasanians competed with Rome more zealously than the Arsacids had, opening a new phase of the Roman–Iranian Wars. Shapur I extended his authority into the north-west of the Indian subcontinent and made the Kushans accept his suzerainty. After the division of the Roman Empire in 395, the Byzantine Empire was Persia's principal western enemy. A largely peaceful period followed the death of Shapur II, with only two brief wars with the Romans, in 421–422 and in 440.

Under Kavad I the empire took Amida on the Tigris in 503 and made peace with the Romans in 506. Khosrow I patronised letters, and had the works of Plato and Aristotle translated into Pahlavi. In the early seventh century Khosrow II's campaign was successful from 602 to 622, but it exhausted the army and treasury, and he overtaxed the population. Between 622 and 627 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius counter-attacked in Anatolia and the Caucasus and sacked the Zoroastrian temple at Ganzak. Weakened by that war, the empire fell to the early Muslim conquests.

The ruler took the title shahanshah, king of kings, and guarded the sacred fire of the national religion, which appears on the reverse of Sasanian coins. Historians believe society had four classes: priests, warriors, commoners and artisans, with the royal princes, petty rulers, great landlords and priests forming a privileged group of grandees. The Azatan, a low aristocracy living on small estates, provided the cavalry backbone of the army.

An orthodox Zoroastrianism was revived. Christians, mainly of the Church of the East, were recognised as an allowable faith by Yazdegerd I in 409, and a large Jewish community flourished, in whose academies the Babylonian Talmud was composed between the third and sixth centuries. Mani spent most of his life within the empire. The economy rested on farming, above all in Khuzestan and Iraq, with the Nahrawan Canal among its irrigation works, and Sasanian merchants came to dominate Indian Ocean trade. Chinese records mention sixteen embassies from Persia between 455 and 555.
saskatchewan: Saskatchewan is bordered by Alberta to the west, the Northwest Territories to the north, Manitoba to the east and Montana and North Dakota to the south. With Alberta it is one of only two landlocked provinces of Canada, and it is the only province without a natural border, since its borders follow the 49th and 60th parallels and the 110th meridian. The overwhelming majority of the population lives in the southern third. The name comes from the Saskatchewan River, which in Cree is kisiskāciwani-sīpiy, swift flowing river.

Indigenous peoples, among them the Cree, Saulteaux, Assiniboine and Sioux, have lived in the region for thousands of years. The first known European to enter it was Henry Kelsey of England in 1690, who travelled up the Saskatchewan River to trade for fur. The first permanent European settlement was the Hudson's Bay Company post at Cumberland House, founded by Samuel Hearne in 1774. Most of the province lay in Rupert's Land, controlled by the Hudson's Bay Company, and in the late 1850s and early 1860s expeditions led by John Palliser and Henry Youle Hind explored the prairie.

Saskatchewan became a province on 1 September 1905, carved out of the North-West Territories. In 1901 there were 19,200 families, and 150,300 only fifteen years later, and women's labour was critical to the survival of family farms and the wheat economy. In the early 20th century the province became a stronghold of Canadian social democracy, and the 1944 provincial election brought North America's first socialist government to office. In 1992 the federal and provincial governments signed a land claim agreement with First Nations in the province.
