Regina is the capital and Saskatoon the largest city of Saskatchewan, and roughly half the people live in the two. The economy is based on agriculture, mining and energy. Wheat has long been the best-known crop, and canola production surpassed it in 2017.
sasol: South Africa has large deposits of coal whose high fly ash content gave it little commercial value, and from the 1920s South African scientists studied turning it into liquid fuels. P. N. Lategan of the Transvaal Coal Owners Association pioneered the work, and a government white paper of 1927 described the oil-from-coal processes used overseas. After the Second World War Anglovaal bought the rights to a Fischer–Tropsch method patented by M. W. Kellogg Limited, and in 1950 the company was incorporated as the South African Coal, Oil and Gas Corporation, whose Afrikaans name gives the abbreviation Sasol. Etienne Rousseau, a scientist trained at the University of Stellenbosch, was its first managing director.

Commissioning of the Sasol 1 plant began in 1954. Its first reactor of 1955, a circulating fluidised bed with a capacity of about 1,500 barrels a day, was improved to about 6,500, and later fixed fluidised bed and slurry phase reactors raised capacities further. Sasol 2 was completed in 1980 and Sasol 3 came on stream in 1982. The Sigma mine in Sasolburg began with two million tons of coal a year, and its output peaked at 7.4 million tons in 1991.

To lessen its exposure to the oil price, Sasol moved into chemicals made in the Fischer–Tropsch process: ammonia, styrene and butadiene in the 1960s, nitrogen fertilisers by 1964, phosphate and potassium fertilisers in the 1980s. The Natref refinery at Sasolburg, a joint venture commissioned in 1971, received 70% of its oil from Iran by 1979, before the Iranian Revolution. Abroad, the Oryx gas-to-liquids plant in Qatar opened in 2007 with QatarEnergy, and a cracker complex was built at Lake Charles, Louisiana, whose overrun of $4 billion led the joint chief executives to resign in October 2019.

Its coal-to-liquids process gives some of the highest greenhouse gas emissions per unit of product in the world: in 2020 the Secunda plant was the largest single point source of greenhouse gas, at 56.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. In 2008 the European Commission fined Sasol €318 million for taking part in a paraffin wax cartel. The company is listed on the Johannesburg and New York stock exchanges and is based in Sandton.
satake-yoshinobu: Yoshinobu was born at Ota Castle in Hitachi Province, the eldest son of Satake Yoshishige; his mother was a daughter of Date Harumune, which made him a cousin of Date Masamune. His youth was spent in constant war. As a condition of peace with the Nasu clan to the north he was engaged at the age of three to a daughter of the Nasu, and he fought his first battle at Hitotoribashi in 1586. His father retired in 1589 and left him head of the clan, its 19th.

Pressed by Date Masamune in the north and Hōjō Ujinao in the south, Yoshinobu kept his lands by pledging allegiance to Toyotomi Hideyoshi during the Siege of Odawara in 1590, when he also defeated Hōjō supporters and won nearly all of Hitachi. He moved his seat to Mito Castle, sent troops to Hideyoshi's subjugation of the Tohoku region and a smaller force to the invasion of Korea, though he himself stayed in Japan, and his income rose to 545,765 koku.

Bound to Ishida Mitsunari by long friendship and to the Uesugi clan by a secret treaty, he hesitated when Tokugawa Ieyasu called him against Uesugi Kagekatsu, although his father and many of his samurai favoured the Eastern Army. Apart from a few horsemen sent to Tokugawa Hidetada, he stayed in Mito. After the Tokugawa victory his income was cut to 180,000 koku. Ieyasu also distrusted the Satake as direct descendants of the Minamoto, with a better hereditary claim to the title of shōgun than his own.

In his new domain he quickly put down a rising of rōnin loyal to its former lord, Onodera Yoshimichi, and he later won favour with the shogunate by fighting at the Siege of Osaka, where he met the Toyotomi commanders Kimura Shigenari and Gotō Matabei at the Battle of Imafuku. His sons died in infancy; his adopted son Satake Yoshinao was disinherited for falling asleep at a performance in Edo Castle, and Satake Yoshitaka succeeded him. He died at the domain's Edo residence in Kanda in 1633.
satake-yoshishige: Satake Yoshishige was born on 7 March 1547, the eldest son of Satake Yoshiaki, and held Ota Castle in Hitachi Province. He was the eighteenth head of the Satake clan. His father, whose health was failing, handed him the leadership in 1562 and died three years later. Known for his ferocity in battle, Yoshishige carried the nickname Oni Yoshishige, the Ogre or Devil Yoshishige.

An aggressive lord, Yoshishige tightened the Satake hold on Hitachi and fought local houses such as the Ashina, Oda and Naya, and he took Shirakawa Castle from the Yûki. He organised his followers into four groups: ichimon, fudai, tozama and kakushō-shu. His main concern was the Hôjô, who were pushing into southern Hitachi, and in 1567 he allied with the Satomi and Utsunomiya against them. At the Battle of Numajiri 20,000 men under Yoshishige met 80,000 Hôjô troops, and the Satake won, partly through the use of over 8,600 matchlock guns.

In the mid-1580s he joined the Ashina and Sôma, both former rivals, against Date Masamune of Mutsu, and Satake troops fought at Hitotoribashi in 1586, in the Kōriyama campaign of 1588 and at Suriagehara in 1589. He formally gave control of the clan to his son Yoshinobu in 1589 but remained in effective command. In 1590 the Satake submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi and sent forces to the Odawara campaign.

In 1600 Yoshinobu wavered between Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ishida Mitsunari. After Sekigahara Yoshishige interceded for his son, and the clan was only moved to Akita in 1602, its income cut from 545,000 koku to about 200,000. Yoshishige lived afterwards at Rokugo Castle. It is said that he slept on a thin campaign mat rather than a futon, and could not get comfortable on the futon his son sent him there. He died on 19 May 1612.
sati-beg: Sati Beg was the daughter of the Il-Khan Öljaitü and his Khongirad wife Eltuzmish Khatun. When her brother Abu Sa'id came to the throne in 1316 she was betrothed to the amir Chupan, one of the most powerful men at the Ilkhanid court, and they married on 6 September 1319. Their son was Surgan. When Chupan and Abu Sa'id fell out in 1327, Sati Beg was returned to her brother, and Chupan was executed that year at the Il-Khan's insistence, while she and Surgan were spared.

After Abu Sa'id's death in 1335 the Ilkhanate began to break apart. By 1336 Sati Beg and Surgan had sided with Arpa Ke'un, whom she married. After his death they joined Hasan Buzurg, founder of the Jalayirid dynasty, and when he took control of western Persia Surgan was made governor of Karabakh, where mother and son settled. In July 1338, when Chupan's grandson Hasan Kuchak defeated Hasan Buzurg, they changed sides to his camp.

Using her family ties, Hasan Kuchak raised Sati Beg to the Ilkhanid throne in July or August 1338. Her viziers came from leading families in Iran and she struck coins with the title sultan or sultana, but her authority was nominal and reached only the Chobanid lands of north-western Persia. Early in 1339 Togha Temur, a rival claimant backed by Hasan Buzurg, invaded. Hasan Kuchak offered him Sati Beg's hand as a ruse to split him from the Jalayirids, and Togha Temur withdrew without her. Growing suspicious of Sati Beg and her son, Hasan Kuchak then deposed her and made her marry his new candidate, Suleiman Khan.

After Hasan Kuchak was murdered late in 1343, Surgan fought his brother Malek Ashraf and his uncle Yagi Basti for the Chobanid lands. Defeated, he joined his mother and Suleiman, and when Hasan Buzurg withdrew his promised support the three fled to Diyarbakir and, after another defeat in 1345, to Anatolia. Coins in her name from Hesn Kayfa and Arzan, the latest dated 1345, are the last trace of her. Surgan was later executed by Hasan Buzurg in Baghdad; whether Sati Beg shared his fate is unknown.
satna-district: Satna district lies in the north-east of Madhya Pradesh, in central India, and covers 7,502 square kilometres. The city of Satna is its headquarters. It borders Uttar Pradesh to the north, Rewa to the east, Shahdol to the south-west, Umaria and Katni to the south and Panna to the west, and it belongs to Rewa Division. Its eight tehsils are Nagod, Unchehara, Raghuraj Nagar, Majhgawan, Kotar, Birsinghpur, Rampur Baghelan and Kothi.

The district forms part of Baghelkhand, most of which was ruled by Singrauli and Rewa. A small western portion was held under the British by feudatory chiefs, in eleven states: Baroundha, a saluted state, Maihar, Nagod, Sohawal, Kothi and Jaso, and the five Chaube jagirs of Chanpurwa, Pahra, Taraon, Bhaisunda and Kamta-Rajaula. The Haihaya, Kalchuri or Chedi clan gained importance in the region in the 3rd century CE and based itself on the fort of Kalinjar, just beyond the district's border.

In the 4th and 5th centuries the Gupta dynasty held sway, while the feudatory chiefs of Uchchhakalpa and the Parivrajakas of Kot held their own. The Chandel chief Yashovarmma seized Kalinjar and its surroundings (925-55), although the Kalchuris kept most of their possessions until the 12th century.

The chiefs of Rewa were Baghel Rajputs descended from the Solanki clan. About the middle of the 13th century Vyaghra Deo, brother of the ruler of Gujarat, came into northern India, and his son Karandeo received the fort of Bandhogarh as a dowry. It was the Baghel capital until Akbar captured it after a siege of eight months and dismantled it in 1597, after which Rewa grew in importance.

Raja Jaisingh of Rewa accepted British protection by treaty in 1812. Rewa State, with an area of 33,670 square kilometres, was the biggest princely state of Baghelkhand, and most of Raghuraj Nagar tehsil and all of Amarpatan tehsil lay in it before the formation of Vindhya Pradesh.

The 2011 census counted 2,228,935 people in the district. Hindi was the first language of 76.10 per cent, Bagheli of 21.37 per cent and Bundeli of 1.10 per cent. Bagheli has a lexical similarity of 72 to 91 per cent with Hindi. Places visited include Chitrakoot Dham, Tulsi Peeth, Madhavgarh Fort and the Shiv temple at Birsinghpur.
satpura-range: The Satpura Range, formerly also known as the Seeonee Hills, rises in eastern Gujarat, runs east along the border of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh and ends in Chhattisgarh. It parallels the Vindhya Range to the north, and the two east-west ranges divide the Indian subcontinent into the Indo-Gangetic Plain of the north and the Deccan Plateau of the south. The Satpura is a horst mountain, flanked by the Narmada Graben in the north and the smaller Tapi Graben in the south. At its eastern end it meets the hills of the Chotanagpur Plateau.

The Narmada River rises at Amarkantak at the north-eastern end of the range and runs west in the depression between the Satpura and the Vindhya to the Arabian Sea. The Tapti rises at Multai in the east-central part of the range, crosses it and runs west along its southern slopes to meet the sea at Surat. The Godavari and its tributaries drain the Deccan Plateau south of the range, and the Mahanadi drains its easternmost part. The eastern part of the range receives more rainfall than the western, which is seasonally dry.

Most of the range was heavily forested, and although it has been gradually deforested, significant stands remain. They shelter at-risk species such as the Bengal tiger, barasingha, gaur, dhole, sloth bear and blackbuck. The range is known for its tiger reserves and protected areas, among them the Kanha, Pench, Gugamal and Satpura National Parks, the Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve and the Melghat Tiger Reserve. The Bori Reserve Forest, established in 1865 along the Tawa River, is described as India's oldest forest preserve. Kanha National Park was created on 1 June 1955, and its forests helped shape the setting of Rudyard Kipling's Jungle Book, which was set in the Seeonee Hills, partly preserved in the Pench Tiger Reserve.

The highest point of the range, Dhupgarh, lies at the hill station of Pachmarhi, known as the Queen of Satpura. Amarkantak, where the Narmada rises, is a pilgrim town in which the 15th-century mystic and poet Kabir is said to have meditated, and Multai, where the Tapti rises, has temples to the river goddess Tapti, the daughter of Surya. Muktagiri, on the border of Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, is a Jain pilgrimage centre with 52 temples around a waterfall, and Toranmal draws pilgrims to a Shiva temple at Mahashivratri. The range's forests are the subject of conservation work that continues to face pressure from development, logging and poaching.
satrapy: The word satrap comes through Latin from Greek satrápes, borrowed from an Old Iranian form. In Old Persian it is recorded as xšaçapavan, literally protector of the province, and its Sanskrit cognate is kṣatrapa. Provincial organisation began in the Median era, from at least 648 BCE, and the first large-scale use of satrapies came with the Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great, from around 530 BCE. Before the conquest of Media, emperors had ruled conquered lands through client kings and governors. The twenty-six satraps Cyrus established were never kings but viceroys ruling in the king's name, and Darius the Great gave the satrapies a definitive organisation, raising their number to thirty-six and fixing their annual tribute.

A satrap served as viceroy to the king, with considerable autonomy. He collected taxes, controlled local officials and subject tribes and cities, was supreme judge of the province, and was responsible for the safety of the roads and for putting down brigands and rebels. He had a court that was all but royal and a council of Persians, and he was allowed troops of his own. There were checks on him: his secretary, his chief financial official and the general of the regular army and fortresses were independent of him and reported directly to the king, and the king's emissary, the eye of the king, inspected each year.

When central authority weakened, satraps often enjoyed practical independence, particularly when they were also made generals of the army district, contrary to the original rule. Satrapal rebellions became frequent from the middle of the 5th century BCE, and under Artaxerxes II much of Asia Minor and Syria was at times in open rebellion in the Revolt of the Satraps. The last great rebellions were put down by Artaxerxes III.

Alexander the Great kept the satrapic administration and title, even for Greco-Macedonian officials, and so did his successors, especially in the Seleucid Empire, where provinces were much smaller than under the Persians. In the Sasanian Empire centrally appointed governors called shahrabs ruled royal cities and their districts. The Western Satraps or Kshatrapas, Saka rulers in western India from 35 to 405 CE, bore the title too. The word later came to suggest tyranny or ostentatious splendour, and in modern use it is a pejorative for a subordinate or local ruler.
satsuma-domain: The Satsuma Domain was a han of the Tokugawa shogunate from 1600 to 1871. It was based at Kagoshima Castle in Satsuma Province, in the south of Kyushu, and covered territory in the provinces of Satsuma, Osumi and Hyuga. The Shimazu clan, who had ruled the Kagoshima area since the 1200s, governed it throughout as tozama daimyo. At Sekigahara in 1600 they fought on the losing side, yet they remained among the most powerful clans in the archipelago. The domain's assessed value peaked at 770,000 koku, the second highest in Japan after the Kaga Domain.

In 1609 Shimazu Iehisa asked the shogunate for permission to invade the Ryukyu Kingdom. After a three-month war against stiff resistance, Satsuma captured the capital Shuri and King Sho Nei. In the peace that followed it annexed the Amami and Tokara Islands, demanded tribute and made the king pledge loyalty to its daimyo.

Satsuma's wealth came from its size and productivity, from its great distance from Edo and from its hold over Ryukyu, whose tributary status with China let it trade in Chinese goods when strict maritime prohibitions began in the 1630s. The Shimazu won exceptions from the shogunate: they were allowed more than one castle, giving castles to their vassals and running the domain somewhat like a mini-shogunate, and they travelled to Edo for sankin-kotai only once every two years. The ban on Christianity was enforced there perhaps more strictly and brutally than anywhere else in Japan.

The killing of an Englishman by Satsuma retainers in the Namamugi Incident of 1862 led to the Royal Navy's bombardment of Kagoshima in 1863. Satsuma withstood the attack, but it showed the need to import Western technology. When the shogunate moved to defeat Choshu in a second expedition, Saigo Takamori and Okubo Toshimichi switched sides, and the Satcho Alliance with Choshu was brokered by Sakamoto Ryoma of Tosa. The expedition ended in disaster for the shogunate, which was defeated again at Toba-Fushimi in 1868.

The Boshin War ended in 1869. In 1871 the Meiji government abolished the domains, and Kagoshima-han became Kagoshima Prefecture. The new government was largely dominated by politicians from Satsuma and Choshu, and figures from the two areas dominated Japanese government until roughly the First World War. Former samurai, discontented as their authority withered, rose under Saigo Takamori in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.
satsuma-rebellion: Satsuma had been one of the key players in the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War, and many of its men had risen to influential posts, yet dissatisfaction grew. Modernisation abolished the privileged status of the samurai and undermined their finances. Saigō Takamori, a senior leader of the Satsuma clan, was concerned about political corruption and had strongly supported war with Korea in the Seikanron debate of 1873. When the plan was rejected he resigned all his government positions and returned to Kagoshima, as did many other Satsuma ex-samurai. In 1874 he founded a private academy in Kagoshima, the Shi-gakkō, with 132 branches in the prefecture. By the end of 1876 Satsuma had effectively seceded from the central government.

In December 1876 the government sent a police officer, Nakahara Hisao, and 57 other men to investigate unrest in Satsuma. They were captured and, under torture, confessed to having been sent to assassinate Saigō; Nakahara later repudiated the confession, but it was widely believed.

On 30 January 1877 the government sent a warship to remove weapons from the Kagoshima arsenal, and students from Saigō's academy raided arsenals in reply. Saigō was reluctantly persuaded to lead the rebellion, and on 12 February he announced that he would march to Tokyo to ask questions of the government. His army besieged Kumamoto Castle. The main Imperial Army reached Kumamoto on 12 April and put the besiegers to flight. The eight-day Battle of Tabaruzaka left each side with more than 4,000 killed or wounded.

Saigō retreated, and by 17 August his army had been reduced to 3,000 combatants. With about 500 men he reached Kagoshima on 1 September and seized Shiroyama, where General Yamagata Aritomo's troops, which outnumbered the rebels 60 to 1, built ditches and walls around them. The final assault came on 24 September 1877. Saigō was severely wounded, and by the most widely accepted accounts he committed seppuku with his associate Beppu Shinsuke as his second. An autopsy found no abdominal wounds consistent with seppuku, which suggests he was beheaded to prevent capture.

Crushing the rebellion cost the government ¥420,000,000, forced Japan off the gold standard and led it to print paper currency. The rebellion effectively ended the samurai class, because the new army of conscripts had proved itself in battle. The historian Mark Ravina argues that the name War of the Southwest suits the conflict better than Satsuma Rebellion, as it was closer to a civil war.
sattar-khan: Sattar Khan was born in Sardar Kandy, of Iranian Azerbaijani origin, the third son of Haj Hasan Bazzaz of the Qaradagh. In his childhood his eldest brother, a highway robber, was executed. After the family moved to Tabriz he was jailed for two years in the Narin Qalʿa prison for trying to hide two Caucasian fugitives whom his father had sheltered, and he was later imprisoned again for robbery. He also served in the gendarmerie on the road between Khoy and Marand, rode in the armed escort of the crown prince Mozaffar-al-Din Mirza, and led an auxiliary troop against Turkmen robbers near Mashhad.

Close to the Social Democratic Party, he rose from obscurity to lead the Constitutionalist fighters of the Amirkhiz district of Tabriz, and by 1907 he was a favoured leader of the rebels. After Mohammad Ali Shah shelled the Majles, 40 thousand of the Shah's soldiers were ordered against Tabriz. In June 1908 a High Military Council was set up with Sattar Khan as commander-in-chief and Bagher Khan as his deputy. By October 1908 most cities of Azarbaijan province had been cleared of royalist forces, and the Shah allowed the Majles to reopen.

The defence of Tabriz cost the rebels many fighters. The Assembly gave Sattar Khan the title Sardar-e Melli and Bagher Khan the title Salar-e Melli. Committees named after Sattar Khan sprang up in Tehran, Rasht, Qazvin, Isfahan and other cities, and his fame helped bring the Bakhtiyari tribal leaders over to the rebels' side.

In March 1910 Sattar Khan and Bagher Khan set out for Tehran with 300 soldiers and were welcomed by crowds on 3 April. Camped in Atabek Park, they refused the order to disarm, and on the night of 7 August 1910 government troops and police under Yeprem Khan surrounded and disarmed them; about 30 fighters were killed and Sattar Khan was wounded in the leg, which left him disabled for the rest of his life. He was buried in the Shah-Abdol-Azim shrine cemetery at Shahr-e Ray, and he is remembered in Iran in poems and songs as a hero of the revolution.
saturn-mythology: Saturn was described as a god of time, generation, dissolution, abundance, wealth, agriculture, periodic renewal and liberation. The Romans kept the memory of a remote time in which Saturn and Janus reigned on the site of the city before its foundation, and the Capitol was called mons Saturnius. After the Roman conquest of Greece he was conflated with the Greek Titan Cronus, whose myths were adapted for Latin literature, and as early as the 3rd century BCE Jupiter was called his son. His consort Ops, equivalent to Rhea, was a later association, since the goddess was originally paired with Consus; earlier was his link with Lua, a goddess of destruction and loosening who received the bloodied weapons of enemies killed in war.

Ancient writers offered several explanations of the name. Varro derived it from satus, sowing, and Cicero's Balbus from satis, because Time is satiated by the years; a modern alternative connects it with the Etruscan god Satre.

In Roman legend Saturn arrived in Italy dethroned and fugitive after his son Jupiter usurped him, was received by Janus and brought agriculture and civilisation. Virgil describes his reign as a golden age of peace under which he gathered the unruly fauns and nymphs and gave them laws. The temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitoline Hill was consecrated in 497 BCE and housed the state treasury throughout Roman history; a row of columns from its last rebuilding still stands. His statue was filled with oil and had its feet bound with wool, which was removed only during the Saturnalia.

The Saturnalia, held from 17 to 23 December, marked the harvest and sowing. Social restrictions of Rome were relaxed, and its revels were meant to recall the lost golden age before Saturn's rule was overthrown. Sacrifices to him were made in the Greek rite with the head uncovered, unlike those of other major deities, a custom ancient commentators linked to the god's own veiled image. In the 3rd century CE and later, gladiatorial munera were given near the festival, which Christian writers criticised as a form of human sacrifice.

Little evidence exists for his cult in Italy outside Rome. The Romans equated him with the Carthaginian god Baal Hammon, to whom children were sacrificed, and the poet Tibullus called the Sabbath Saturni dies, from which Saturday derives. The identification with Baal Hammon gave rise to the African Saturn, a cult that was popular until the 4th century and had the character of a mystery religion.
satyrus-i: Satyrus built on the expansive policy of his father, Spartocus I. He took Nymphaion from Gylon, and perhaps Kimmerikon, and was drawn into the affairs of the neighbouring Sindike kingdom. He also came into conflict with the Greek cities of Heraclea Pontica and Theodosia, a serious commercial rival because of its ice-free port and its nearness to the grain fields of eastern Crimea. Ties with Athens grew closer under him, and a statue may have been raised to him in that city.

One episode shows the workings of his court. He allowed the son of his powerful minister Sopaeus to sail to Athens with two ships of wheat, and there the young man settled his affairs with the banker Pasion. Satyrus then came to believe that Sopaeus was plotting against his life, had him arrested and ordered the Bosporans in Athens to seize the son's property and send him home. Later he acquitted Sopaeus and agreed to the marriage of Sopaeus's daughter, Theodosia, to his own son Leucon.

According to Polyaenus, his troubles with the Sindi began when he offered his daughter to Hecactaeus, king of the Sindi, on condition that Hecactaeus kill his wife Tirgatao. Instead the king shut her in a tower, from which she escaped to her own people, the Ixomatae. She married her father's successor and roused many tribes against Satyrus, who, unable to win, gave his son Metrodorus as a hostage and asked for peace.

After an attempt on her life, probably arranged by Satyrus, Tirgatao had Metrodorus killed and went to war again; that war was ended only after his death by his sons Leucon and Gorgippus, who went on to build the Bosporan Kingdom into a powerful state. Satyrus died at the age of 81 during the unsuccessful siege of Theodosia.
saudi-aramco: The company's origins trace to the oil shortages of the First World War and to the exclusion of American companies from Mesopotamia by the United Kingdom and France under the San Remo Petroleum Agreement of 1920. The United States administration had popular support for an Open Door policy, which Herbert Hoover, secretary of commerce, initiated in 1921. Standard Oil of California was among the American companies seeking new sources of oil abroad. In 1932 its wholly owned subsidiary, the Bahrain Petroleum Company, discovered the first oil field in the Persian Gulf outside Iran.

In 1973, after the United States supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War, the Saudi government acquired a one-quarter participation interest in Aramco's assets and raised it to sixty per cent in 1974. Aramco continued to operate the former assets on the government's behalf until November 1988, when a royal decree created a new company, the Saudi Arabian Oil Company, to take control of them and of the management of the kingdom's oil and gas fields. In 1989 and 1990 high-quality oil and gas were discovered in three areas south of Riyadh.

After the start of the Persian Gulf War in September 1990, Aramco was expected to replace much of the oil lost to the embargo of Iraq and occupied Kuwait. It recommissioned 146 wells at Harmaliyah, Khurais and Ghawar that had been mothballed during the oil price collapse of the 1980s, and daily production rose from 5.4 million barrels in July to 8.5 million in December 1990. From 1990 the company expanded its crude sales in Asia, with agreements with South Korea, the Philippines and China.

In 2001 Saudi Arabia announced a Gas Initiative proposing joint ventures with international companies for gas exploration, and in 2005 Aramco began a five-year plan to spend US$50 billion to raise its daily capacity to 12.5 million barrels. On 15 August 2012 a virus known as Shamoon attacked some 30,000 of its workstations. Its shares began trading on the Saudi Exchange on 11 December 2019.

Saudi Aramco is headquartered in Dhahran, and its operations include exploration, production, refining, chemicals, distribution and marketing. It manages over a hundred oil and gas fields in Saudi Arabia. In the Eastern Province it operates the Ghawar Field, the world's largest onshore oil field, and the Safaniya Field, the world's largest offshore oil field, and it runs the Master Gas System, the world's largest single hydrocarbon network. A significant part of its workforce consists of geophysicists and geologists, who work mostly at the EXPEC Advanced Research Center. The Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources and the Supreme Council for Petroleum and Minerals oversee its activities.
sauerland: The Sauerland is a rural, hilly area across most of the south-east of North Rhine-Westphalia and a small north-western part of Hesse, heavily forested in parts and, apart from the major valleys, sparsely inhabited. Its major rivers are the Ruhr and the Lenne, and its highest point is the Langenberg, 843 metres, near Olsberg, just above the better known Kahler Asten, 842 metres, near Winterberg; both belong to the Rothaargebirge. Its bedrock is mostly slates, sandstones and greywackes from the Devonian, when the area lay under a shallow sea, with karstified limestones and caves, the biggest at Attendorn and Balve. The name first appears as Suderland in a document of 1266, and probably means the southern country.

Before 1800 the western Sauerland belonged to the County of the Mark, based in Altena, while the eastern part adhered to the County of Arnsberg, later known as the Duchy of Westphalia, which was owned by the Archbishops and Electorate of Cologne. The Duchy of Limburg covered a very small area in the lower Lenne valley. After the Napoleonic Wars the area passed to Prussia and was joined to the new province of Westphalia, which after the Second World War was merged into North Rhine-Westphalia.

Parts of the region, especially the major north-western valleys, are an old industrial area. Iron ore, wood and water allowed iron production long before the Ruhr's industrialisation. Lead, zinc and silver ores supported a mining industry centred on Meggen until the second half of the 20th century, and wire production is still important in Altena.

The largest town is Iserlohn, followed by Lüdenscheid and Arnsberg. Today the Sauerland is the largest tourist region of North Rhine-Westphalia, with more than 30,000 km of marked hiking trails, the winter sports of Winterberg and Willingen, and six reservoir lakes created to store water for the Ruhr area, the biggest being the Möhne and the Bigge. Balve Cave is among the largest prehistoric caves in Europe.
saul: According to the Hebrew Bible, Saul was the son of Kish, of the family of the Matrites, and came from Gibeah. He married Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, and had at least five sons, among them Jonathan and Ish-bosheth, and two daughters, Merab and Michal. The Books of Samuel give three accounts of his rise. In one he is sent to look for his father's strayed donkeys and is anointed in private by the seer Samuel at Ramah. In another Samuel assembles the people at Mizpah and uses the Urim and Thummim to choose the tribe of Benjamin, the clan of Matri and then Saul. In a third he leads an army to relieve Jabesh-Gilead from the Ammonite king Nahash and is crowned at Gilgal.

After relieving Jabesh-Gilead, Saul is said to have fought the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, the kings of Zobah, the Philistines and the Amalekites. With Jonathan he defeated a large Philistine force at the pass of Michmash, though his rash oath that the army should fast nearly cost Jonathan his life. Samuel then rebuked him for offering sacrifice himself, and later told him that God had rejected him as king after he spared the Amalekite king Agag and the best livestock in a war meant to destroy Amalek completely.

From then on the narrative turns largely on his troubled relationship with David, the son of Jesse whom Samuel anointed. Saul, troubled by an evil spirit, took David to play the harp for him, and David became his armour bearer. Scholars note that the text portrays Saul positively before David appears and negatively afterwards, and suggest that the David story came from a source loyal to David's house. The reign length in the Hebrew text, two years, is regarded as faulty; a reign of 20 or 22 years is thought more probable.

Before the Philistine battle at Mount Gilboa, Saul consulted a spirit medium at Endor, and the spirit that appeared as Samuel told him he would lose the battle and his life. First Samuel says he asked his armour bearer to kill him and, when refused, fell on his own sword; Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua died with him. A conflicting account in 2 Samuel has an Amalekite claiming to have killed him. Ish-bosheth succeeded him for two years before being murdered. The historicity of Saul's kingdom is debated, since the evidence is mostly biblical. In the Qur'an Talut is traditionally identified with Saul, a divinely appointed king chosen by a prophet.
saulteaux: The Saulteaux are also called the Anihšināpē (Anishinaabe), and their name is written in several forms, among them Salteaux and Saulteau. The French word means people of the rapids or waterfalls and refers to their former home around Sault Ste. Marie, on the St. Marys River between Lake Superior and Lake Huron. They lived chiefly by hunting and fishing and traded widely with the French, the British and later the Americans at that post. Their historic lands lay around Lake Superior and Lake Winnipeg, chiefly about Sault Ste. Marie and northern Michigan.

Pressure from European Canadians and Americans gradually pushed them west. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, as partners of the Cree in the fur trade, Saulteaux groups moved north-west into the Swan River and Cumberland districts of west-central Manitoba, and into Saskatchewan along the Assiniboine River as far as its confluence with the Souris River. There they took on cultural traits of their allies, the Plains Cree and Assiniboine, forming a mixed culture of woodland and plains customs. Because they were moved to land ill-suited to European crops, they kept much of the territory assigned to them as reserves. Among the numbered treaties, Saulteaux First Nations signed Treaty 1, Treaty 2, Treaty 3, Treaty 4, Treaty 6 and Treaty 8.

The Saulteaux have three main divisions. The Ontario or Eastern Saulteaux live around Rainy Lake and Lake of the Woods, speak a form of Anishinaabemowin sometimes called the Northwestern Ojibwa language, and keep a culture descended from that of the Eastern Woodlands. The Manitoba or Central Saulteaux, in eastern and southern Manitoba, have a culture between woodland and plains; they and their Métis population have been called Bungi, from bangii, a little bit.

The Western Saulteaux, centred in Saskatchewan and reaching into Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia, call themselves Nakawē, while the Plains Cree call them Nahkawiyiniw. Their language, Nakawēmowin or Western Ojibwa, is Algonquian, and their culture is that of the Plains. Together the Manitoba and Western Saulteaux are sometimes called the Plains Ojibwe. Today English is the first language of many Saulteaux. Their communities include Cote First Nation at Kamsack, Peguis in Manitoba and the Saulteau First Nations at Moberly Lake.
saur-revolution: Mohammad Daoud Khan took power in the 1973 coup that overthrew the monarchy of his first cousin, King Mohammad Zahir Shah, with the help of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA), and founded the first Republic of Afghanistan. Coup attempts against him followed in 1973, 1974 and 1976. The PDPA was split between two factions, Parcham and Khalq. On 17 April 1978 a prominent Parchamite, Mir Akbar Khyber, was assassinated; Nur Muhammad Taraki blamed the government, and large protests broke out in Kabul on 19 April. Daoud ordered the protesters and the party leadership suppressed, and most PDPA leaders, including Babrak Karmal, were arrested.

Hafizullah Amin, under house arrest, instructed the party's Khalqist army officers to act. On 27 April tanks that had been placed around the Arg, the presidential palace, turned their guns on it, and the 4th and 15th Tank Brigades began firing. Fighter aircraft attacked the palace with rockets, and in the evening Radio Afghanistan announced that the Khalq were overthrowing the government. Fighting spread through Kabul, and a column of tanks attacked the Air Force headquarters. In the night armoured units were sent to Jalalabad against loyalist officers of the 11th Division, with a death toll said to be near 1,000.

On 28 April soldiers entered the palace to arrest Daoud, who fired a pistol at them and was killed with his brother Naim. Most of his family, women and children included, were killed there too, as were the defence minister, the interior minister and the vice-president. The deaths of as many as 2,000 military personnel and civilians have been reported, though a former Afghan officer claimed only about 40. Soviet advisers had been told of the coup some hours before it began, but there is no convincing evidence that the Soviet Union planned it.

A civilian government under Nur Muhammad Taraki, with Karmal and Amin in its cabinet, was formed, but the Khalq and Parcham alliance was brief: by July most Parchamites had been removed, and in September 1979 Amin overthrew and executed Taraki. From late October 1978 the party launched drastic reforms, including a new red flag, a ban on usury and land redistribution, and it declared the equality of the sexes. Its repression, which Barnett Rubin compared in scale to that of Abdur Rahman Khan, included mass arrests, torture and executions; more than 27,000 are reported to have been killed in Pul-e-Charkhi prison alone.

The first anti-government revolts began in Kunar Province in October 1978, and an uprising at Herat in 1979 left most provinces under guerrilla control. The Soviet Union invaded in December 1979, and insurgents fought Soviet troops and the PDPA government until the Soviet withdrawal in 1989.
sauromates-ii: Inscriptions name Sauromates as the son of the Bosporan king Rhoemetalces, and his predecessor, Eupator, may have been his uncle. His epithets Philocaesar, Philoromaios and Eusebes mean friend of Caesar, friend of Rome and pious one. The name Sauromates points to claimed Sarmatian ancestry through marriages to Sarmatian princesses, though it need not mean the family was Sarmatian.

His dynasty went back to Tiberius Julius Aspurgus and his son Mithridates in the 1st century, son and grandson of the Bosporan ruler Asander and his queen Dynamis. They were related to the ruling house of Thrace and descended both from Mithridates VI Eupator of Pontus and from the Roman triumvir Mark Antony, through Antonia Tryphaena and her mother Pythodorida of Pontus.

Sauromates succeeded Eupator in the early 170s and was a contemporary of the emperors from Marcus Aurelius to Caracalla. His coins, which name him King Sauromates in Greek, suggest devotion to the cult of Aphrodite. An inscription found at Tanais celebrates his victory over the Scythians and the Sirachi in 193, at the end of a campaign that may have begun in 186.

That campaign may have brought on a financial crisis, and from 186 he reformed the coinage over a decade, gradually reducing the weight of the bronze coins while putting more gold staters into circulation. In the last decade of the 2nd century his coins often carried the portrait of Septimius Severus; whether at the emperor's command or by his own choice is not known. His wife's name has not survived, but their son Rhescuporis III succeeded him in 210 or 211.
sava: The Sava is the longest tributary of the Danube and the largest by volume of water. Its headwater, the Sava Dolinka, rises in the Zelenci Pools in the Upper Carniola region of Slovenia, at 833 metres above sea level, and meets the Sava Bohinjka near Radovljica. The river then crosses the Ljubljana Basin, flows into Croatia and passes Zagreb. Below the confluence of the Una it forms the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, then turns north-east after the Drina joins and reaches Serbia.

It discharges into the Danube at the Great War Island in Belgrade. Its basin covers 97,713 square kilometres and drains much of the Dinaric Alps through tributaries such as the Drina, Bosna, Kupa, Una and Vrbas. The river's course is sometimes used to describe the northern boundary of the Balkans and the southern border of Central Europe. Before the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1991 it was the longest river lying completely within that country.

The name is believed to derive from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to press or take liquid, so that it means that which waters the ground. The ancient Greeks called the river Saos, Strabo wrote of the Saüs, and the Romans used the name Savus. Worship of river gods in the area dates to the Late Bronze Age, when the first settlements were founded along the river. The Taurisci associated their river goddess Adsullata with the Savus, and altars or inscriptions to the river god Savus have been found at several places, among them the Zelenci Pools, Emona, Andautonia and Siscia.

The Romans built settlements and forts along the Via Pannonia, the road from Aquileia to the Danube. Upstream of the Kupa confluence these included Emona, Andautonia and Siscia, near modern Ljubljana, Velika Gorica and Sisak. Downstream stood Marsonia, built over a prehistoric settlement, then Cibalae, Sirmium and Singidunum, on the sites of Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci, Sremska Mitrovica and Belgrade.

About 8,176,000 people live in the Sava basin, and Ljubljana, Zagreb and Belgrade stand on the river, with Sarajevo in the basin. The river is navigable to larger vessels for 593.8 kilometres between Belgrade and Sisak, and its valley carries road and rail routes, among them Pan-European Corridor X. In Zagreb in 1964 the most destructive flood of the river put one third of the city under water and killed 17 people, after which a flood-relief canal to the Odra plain was built. The basin holds large alluvial wetlands, and six areas of it are protected under the Ramsar Convention.
savaii: Savaiʻi is the largest and highest island both in Samoa and in the Samoan Islands chain, and the sixth largest in Polynesia. Its classical Samoan name, used in formal oratory and prose, is Salafai. It lies north-west of Upolu, from which it is separated by the Apolima Strait, about 13 km wide, with the small inhabited islands of Manono and Apolima between them. The island is mountainous and fertile and is surrounded by coral reefs, rising to 1,858 metres at Mt Silisili, the highest peak in the country.

Savaiʻi is the largest shield volcano in the South Pacific, and only 3% of it is above water. Its central region holds the Central Savaiʻi Rainforest, about 72,699 hectares, the largest continuous rainforest in Polynesia, dotted with more than 100 volcanic craters. The name is cognate with Hawaiʻi and with Hawaiki in Māori, and shares a root with the original homeland of Polynesian folklore, although Samoans themselves preserve no tradition of having originated elsewhere. The island has been called the Cradle of Polynesia.

Archaeology has uncovered prehistoric settlements inland, including sites at Sapapaliʻi and Vailoa, and star mounds, fortifications and pyramids such as the Pulemelei Mound in Palauli district. In prehistory the village of Safotu was a settlement for Tongans. The missionary John Williams (1796-1839) arrived at Sapapaliʻi in 1830, a village that was also a base for the Malietoa title on Savaiʻi. In October 1839 the island was surveyed by the United States Exploring Expedition under Charles Wilkes.

The Matavanu eruptions of 1905 to 1911 sent lava over the central north coast and destroyed villages including Saleaula. Resistance to colonial rule began on Savaiʻi: the Mau a Pule movement, led by the exiled orator Lauaki Namulauulu Mamoe (died 1915) of Safotulafai, was the beginning of the Mau, Samoa's non-violent movement for political independence.

The island is home to 43,958 people (2016 census), 24% of the population of Samoa, and is divided into six political districts. Its only township and ferry terminal is Salelologa. Faʻa Sāmoa, the traditional way of life based on extended family, chiefly titles (matai) and obligations, remains strong there, and the term Pule is applied to traditional authority. Samoa became independent from New Zealand on 1 January 1962. Falealupo, at the westernmost point, lies just 32 km from the dateline, and the 1926 documentary Moana was filmed at Safune.
savak: After the 1953 Iranian coup d'état removed Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, Mohammad Reza Shah set up an intelligence service with police powers, intending to place political opponents under surveillance and repress dissident movements. A United States Army colonel working for the CIA assembled its nucleus in 1953 and 1954 with General Teymur Bakhtiar, and in September 1954 the service destroyed a large communist Tudeh Party network in the armed forces. SAVAK was established in Tehran in 1957 by national security law; the French service SDECE helped train it, and a declassified CIA memo credits the CIA with providing funding and training. It was reorganised and given its name in 1965.

SAVAK had the power to censor the media and to screen applicants for government jobs. After 1963 the Shah expanded his security organisations, and SAVAK grew to over 5,300 full-time agents and an unknown number of part-time informers. Estimates of its size vary widely among historians, from 6,000 to 60,000. It ran its own detention centres, such as Evin Prison, and watched Iranians abroad, especially students on government stipends. Its first director, Teymur Bakhtiar, was dismissed in 1961 and assassinated by its agents in 1970. Hassan Pakravan directed it from 1961 to 1965, and Nematollah Nassiri from 1965.

A turning point in its reputation for brutality was reportedly the attack of February 1971 by armed Marxists on a gendarmerie post at Siahkal. According to the historian Ervand Abrahamian, SAVAK and other forces killed 368 guerrillas between 1971 and 1977 and executed up to 100 political prisoners between 1971 and 1979. Its methods included the bastinado, sleep deprivation, solitary confinement and electric shocks. By the end of 1975 twenty-two prominent writers, professors and film makers were in jail for criticising the regime. Scrutiny from foreign newspapers and from United States President Jimmy Carter's raising of human rights softened the repression.

Time magazine wrote in February 1979 that SAVAK had long been Iran's most hated and feared institution. It ceased to exist in 1979 as the monarchy fell, but according to Charles Kurzman it was never dismantled and instead changed its name and leadership, with a relatively unchanged staff. It was replaced by the much larger SAVAMA, the Ministry of Intelligence and National Security of Iran. A museum named Ebrat, in the former Towhid Prison in central Tehran, displays the documented abuses of SAVAK.
savang-vatthana: Savang Vatthana was born on 13 November 1907, the son of Sisavang Vong, and was a cousin of Prince Souvanna Phouma. At ten he was sent to France, where he attended a lycée in Montpellier and then the École Libre des Sciences Politiques in Paris. After a decade abroad he is said to have been unable to speak Lao. He married a cousin, Khamphoui, and unlike his polygamous father took only one wife; they had five children. Under an arrangement made with the French in 1941 he became chairman of the King's Council, and after Japan overthrew the French administration in March 1945 he protested against the Japanese actions at their headquarters in Saigon.

He succeeded his father in 1959 but was never formally crowned, postponing the ceremony until the end of the war. He was devoted to Buddhism and guarded a sacred Buddha image, believing that as long as it was in his hands the country was safe. Time wrote in 1961 that his most striking political characteristic was a profound lethargy.

After a coup by Captain Kong Le in August 1960, rival governments claimed office, and after the 1962 Geneva agreements on neutrality Souvanna Phouma headed a coalition. In February 1963 the king visited the United States and met President John F. Kennedy. A reviewer of Christopher Kremmer's history of the dynasty wrote that in the 1960s he allowed the United States to bomb guerrilla-held territory in the northeast.

On 29 November 1975 Souvanna Phouma and Prince Souphanouvong persuaded the king to abdicate, and the Lao People's Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 2 December, with the former king as supreme adviser to the president. In 1977 he, the queen and the crown prince were moved to Camp 01 in Houaphan province. The government confirmed his death only in December 1989, and accounts of the date differ; one account, drawn on a former prisoner's memoir, places it about two months after the crown prince's death. The royal palace in Luang Prabang was preserved largely as he had left it.
savannah: The word derives from the Spanish sabana, itself a loanword from Taíno, where it meant treeless grassland in the West Indies. It entered English as Zauana in a description of the islands of the kings of Spayne from 1555, in which Peter Martyr reported it as the local name for the plain around Comagre, the court of the cacique Carlos in present-day Panama.

The English explorer William Dampier, in his volumes of A New Voyage Round the World published between 1697 and 1705, used the spelling savannah with a final h, which became the British English form. He applied it to dry, sandy ground with tufted grass and palmetto trees on an island in the Bay of Campeche, and to similar country in Sumatra and the Philippines.

A savanna is a mixed woodland and grassland biome in which the trees are spaced widely enough that the canopy does not close. The light reaching the ground supports an unbroken layer of grasses. Four forms are distinguished: savanna woodland, tree savanna, shrub savanna and grass savanna. Savannas are marked by seasonal water, with most rain falling in one season, and by yearly variations in rainfall and dry-season wildfires. Annual rainfall ranges from about 500 to 1,270 millimetres. Savanna covers roughly 20 percent of the Earth's land area, mostly in warm to hot climates in Africa, Australia, South America and India, unlike the prairies of North America and the steppes of Eurasia, which have cold winters.

In East Africa, acacias, baobabs and Combretum are common trees, and the African savanna's animals include giraffe, elephant, buffalo, zebra, hippopotamus and rhinoceros. In Australia kangaroos and wallabies predominate. Ecoregions include the Serengeti, the Brazilian Cerrado, the Pantanal and the Sudd.

The ecosystem appears to be in large part the result of human use of fire. Fire-stick farming seems to have been responsible for the widespread savanna of tropical Australia and New Guinea, savannas in India are a result of human fire use, and Native Americans created woodlands in pre-Columbian North America by periodic burning. Controlled burns kill or suppress tree seedlings, preventing a continuous canopy that would shade out the grass.

The open structure that allows grass to grow also suits grazing, and much of the world's savanna has been changed by sheep, goats and cattle. Large areas of Australian and South American savanna have been cleared of trees to improve pasture, which can raise pasture production two to fourfold. Early pastoralists felled and girdled trees. In the 1950s arboricides for stem injection were developed, and war-surplus heavy machinery was used to push or pull timber.
saverne: Saverne is a commune in the Bas-Rhin department of north-eastern France, 45 kilometres north-west of Strasbourg. It lies on the river Zorn at the foot of a pass over the Vosges Mountains, and the Marne–Rhine Canal and the Paris–Strasbourg railway cross it. Its Latin name was Tres Tabernae Caesaris, Caesar's three taverns, from the three inns that once stood on the way to the Lorraine plateau, where oxen were changed because of the steep climb.

Saverne was an important place in Roman times and, after being destroyed by the Alemanni, was rebuilt by the emperor Julian. After the settlement of the Alemanni it became part of the Germanosphere, and after 870 it belonged to East Francia, which became the Holy Roman Empire. In 1525, during the German Peasants' War, insurgents occupied the town and were driven out by Duke Anton of Lorraine. It suffered heavily in the Thirty Years' War, and its episcopal palace, destroyed then, was later rebuilt. The French annexed the town after 1680.

In 1852 Louis Napoleon converted the episcopal palace into a residence for widows of knights of the Legion of Honour. Saverne was conquered by Imperial Germany after the Franco-Prussian War and returned to France after the First World War. In 1913 it was the scene of the Saverne Affair, which gave rise to the term Zabernism, from the German name Zabern, meaning abuse of military authority or unwarranted aggression.

The town's emblem is a unicorn. Legend says a unicorn's horn was found in one of the ruined castles nearby, though it was more likely a narwhal's tooth. Its principal building is the Château des Rohan, the former residence of the bishops of Strasbourg, rebuilt by Cardinal de Rohan in 1779 and used by the Germans as barracks; it now houses the town museum with its Roman and Celtic collection. Other sights include the 15th-century Château vieux, the parish church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Nativité, a former Franciscan monastery with a cloister decorated with 17th-century frescoes, and the decorated Maison Katz. The ruined castles of Haut-Barr, Grand Geroldseck, Ochsenstein and Greifenstein lie nearby.
saverne-affair: Two battalions of the Prussian 99th (2nd Upper Rhenish) Infantry Regiment were garrisoned in Zabern, now Saverne, in Alsace-Lorraine. On 28 October 1913 the twenty-year-old Second Lieutenant Günter Freiherr von Forstner told recruits that he would give ten marks to any of them who stabbed a Wackes, a derogatory word for native Alsatians that military regulations prohibited. The local newspapers, the Elsässer and the Zaberner Anzeiger, reported the remark on 6 November. The Statthalter of Alsace-Lorraine, Count Karl von Wedel, urged that Forstner be transferred, but the army held this inconsistent with its honour, and he received six days of house arrest, which was not made public.

Protests continued, and on 28 November Colonel Adolf von Reuter had Second Lieutenant Schadt disperse a crowd before the barracks. Soldiers arrested many people without legal basis, among them the president, two judges and a prosecuting attorney of the Saverne court, and twenty-six were held overnight in a coal cellar. Emperor Wilhelm II, hunting at Donaueschingen, held six days of talks with the Prussian War Minister Erich von Falkenhayn and General Berthold von Deimling and approved the officers' conduct. On 2 December Forstner struck the journeyman shoemaker Karl Blank with his sabre, causing severe head injuries.

In the Reichstag, deputies of the Centre Party, the Social Democratic Party and the Progressive People's Party opened a debate on 3 December. The next day the house used the censure vote, available to it since 1912, for the first time in the history of the Empire, by 293 votes to 54, all the opposing votes coming from the conservatives. Chancellor Theobald von Bethmann Hollweg refused to resign, answering that he depended only on the confidence of the Kaiser, as article 15 of the Constitution provided. Social democrats then rallied in 17 cities.

In January a military court in Strasbourg acquitted Reuter and Schadt, citing a Prussian cabinet order of 1820 under which the senior officer of a town had to take authority if the civil power failed to keep order, and Wilhelm II decorated Reuter. A regulation the Kaiser issued on 19 March forbade the army to intervene in civilian matters unless the civilian authorities asked for troops; it stood until the Nazis abolished it on 17 January 1936.

Wedel resigned on 18 April and was replaced by the Prussian Minister of the Interior, Johann von Dallwitz, to the disappointment of the Alsatians. Heinrich Mann drew on the affair in his novel Der Untertan, and the word zabernism entered English for the abuse of military authority. Forstner was killed in combat at Kobryn on the Eastern Front in 1915.
savitsky-museum: Igor Savitsky, a Russian painter, archaeologist and collector, first came to Karakalpakstan in 1950 with the Khorezm Archaeological and Ethnographic Expedition. He settled in Nukus, the capital, collected Karakalpak jewellery, carpets, coins, clothing and other artefacts, and persuaded the Karakalpak authorities to establish a state museum, of which he became the first curator. It first showed archaeological finds, among them material from the Khorezm fortresses, copies of classical antiquities and Karakalpak folk art, most of it collected by Savitsky himself.

To inspire young Karakalpak artists, Savitsky also bought works by modern Central Asian painters and by Russian artists who had worked in or been influenced by Central Asia, including works of Constructivism, Cubism, Futurism and Neo-Primitivism banned by Stalin in the 1930s. Many of these artists were persecuted: Kurzin was imprisoned and exiled for anti-Soviet propaganda, and Lysenko was confined to a mental asylum for much of his life because of his art. The Karakalpak authorities had some awareness of what Savitsky acquired but did not restrict him.

Most of the works were never put on show. Marinika Babanazarova succeeded Savitsky as curator in 1984, and only with Perestroika in 1985, a year after his death, and Uzbek independence in 1991 did the extent and importance of the collection become known. A new building opened in 2003, later joined by two more with exhibition space and an archive and storage centre. Babanazarova was dismissed in 2015, and in 2019 Tigran Mkrtychev, a Russian archaeologist and art historian who had known Savitsky, was appointed director.

The museum holds more than 82,000 items, among them around 10,000 avant-garde works, a collection second in size only to that of the Russian Museum in Saint Petersburg. It has about 100 paintings by Alexander Volkov, considered the father of the Uzbek avant-garde, more than any other museum, 1,000 works by Tarasov, and the only known surviving works of Vladimir Lysenko, whose painting The Bull is its emblem. The Guardian called it the Louvre of Uzbekistan.
savoie: Savoie lies in the French Alps and borders the departments of Haute-Savoie, Ain, Isère and Hautes-Alpes, as well as Italy's Aosta Valley and the Metropolitan City of Turin. Much of it is mountainous, with the Mont Blanc, Vanoise, Beaufortain and Belledonne massifs among its ranges. The Isère river has its source at the Iseran pass, and the department's two main lakes are Lac du Bourget, the largest and deepest lake entirely in France, and Lac d'Aiguebelette.

The other main Alpine valley is the Maurienne, one of the longest intra-alpine valleys in the Alps, which two passes connect to the Tarentaise valley. The col de l'Iseran is the highest pass in Europe, and the col du Mont Cenis was the major commercial route between France and Italy.

The name is widely accepted to come from the Latin Sapaudia or Sabaudia, meaning land covered in fir trees. Savoie was long part of the states of Savoy, though from the sixteenth century France occupied it several times. It was part of the Mont-Blanc department from 1792 to 1815, and partly of the Léman department from 1798 to 1814. France annexed the former Duchy of Savoy in 1860, following the Treaty of Turin, and it became the two departments of Savoie and Haute-Savoie. Moûtiers, the capital of the former province of the Tarentaise, ceased to be a subprefecture under a law that took effect on 10 September 1926.

Chambéry is the prefecture and the most populous commune. Savoie belongs to the region of Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, created on 1 January 2016, and was previously part of Rhône-Alpes. Tourism began to develop towards the end of the nineteenth century, at first mostly in summer, and the popularity of skiing in the twentieth century made Savoie home to the largest number of ski resorts in France, among them Val-d'Isère, Courchevel and Méribel. The department hosted the 1992 Winter Olympics, based in Albertville. Spa treatment has been practised in the region since antiquity, and Aix-les-Bains is one of four places where it continues. The area is known for cheeses such as Beaufort and Reblochon and for dishes such as fondue savoyarde.
savona: Savona is a seaport and municipality in the west of the Italian region of Liguria and the capital of the Province of Savona. It faces the Ligurian Sea, between the sea and the Ligurian Alps, 40 kilometres west of Genoa, and is the main city of the western section of the Italian Riviera. The navigator Christopher Columbus is associated with the town. A cottage in the Savona hills is called Columbus's house, and a house in the neighbourhood is documented as the property of his father Domenico Colombo, where the family lived for many years.

Ligurian tribes lived here in ancient times, and the city, which had been allied to Carthage in the Punic Wars, came under Roman influence about 180 BCE. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it passed under Lombard rule in 641, being destroyed in the attack. It recovered as a county seat in the Carolingian Empire. In the tenth century its bishops were counts of Savona, and the countship passed to the Marquesses of Montferrat in 981 and to the Marquesses Del Vasto in 1084.

After a long struggle against the Saracens, Savona became independent in the eleventh century as a free commune allied with the Holy Roman Emperor, and its freedom declaration was signed in 1191 in the Torre del Brandale. Two monasteries, one Dominican and one Franciscan, made it a centre of religious culture from the thirteenth to the sixteenth century. It then fought the Republic of Genoa and was definitively conquered in 1528. The Genoese destroyed the upper town and buried the port, and in 1542 they built the Priamar fortress on the site of the old cathedral and old city. Savona shared the fortunes of Genoa until Napoleonic times.

Austrian forces besieged the city between April and mid-May 1800 while a small British naval force blockaded it, and the fortress surrendered on 15 May. From 1809 the city held Pope Pius VII, a prisoner of Napoleon Bonaparte, for a few years. Savona was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia-Piedmont in 1815 and later became part of the unified Kingdom of Italy. In 1830 and 1831 Giuseppe Mazzini was imprisoned in the Priamar. In the twentieth century Savona became a regional industrial hub.

The Cappella Sistina beside the Cathedral of the Assumption was built from 1480 to 1483 and holds the mausoleum that Pope Sixtus IV of the Della Rovere family erected for his parents. Cardinal Giulio della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II, built the Palazzo Della Rovere, designed by Giuliano da Sangallo as a university. The Torre Leon Pancaldo, built in the fourteenth century, is the symbol of the town. The Priamar now holds the Museum Centre of Priamar.
savva-morozov: Savva Morozov was the son of Timofei Savvich Morozov and Maria Feodorovna Morozova. The family fortune had been founded by Savva Vasilyevich Morozov (1770–1862), and the family held the hereditary rank of honorary citizens, which freed its members from conscription, corporal punishment and the poll tax. He grew up in the Morozov house on Trehsvyatitelskaya Lane on Ivanovo Hill in the White City of Moscow, the most expensive home in the city, whose gardens were frequented by Sergey Aksakov, Dostoevsky, Ostrovsky, Tolstoy and Tchaikovsky.

He attended the gymnasium at Pokrovsky Gates. At Moscow University he wrote a study on dye and met Mendeleev. In January 1885 workers at the Morozov factories in Bogorodsk, especially Orekhovo-Zuyevo, went on strike for several weeks in what became known as the Morozov strike. In England he studied the structure of the textile industry in Great Britain, above all in Manchester.

Morozov married Zinaida Grigorievna, née Zimin, the former wife of his second cousin. The couple held lavish parties and balls attended by Savva Mamontov, Feodor Chaliapin, Maxim Gorky, Anton Chekhov, Konstantin Stanislavski and others; the actress Olga Knipper recalled never having seen such luxury and wealth.

The improvements he paid for on Kamergersky Lane were Schechtel's and included Anna Golubkina's plaster high relief The Wave above the right entrance. In 1903 the theatre gained its own power station and a second small stage, separate from the main building, so that full rehearsals could go on during performances. The new hall seated 1,200, a third more than before, and Morozov paid all its costs for the 1902–1904 seasons. When the rent rose for 1904–1905 he stopped paying the lease and running costs. After Stanislavski and Nemirovich-Danchenko received Gorky's play Summerfolk poorly, Gorky left the theatre and Morozov followed him.

With his relative Nikolai Pavlovich Schmidt, Morozov was a significant financial contributor to the Bolshevik faction of the Russian Social Democratic Workers Party. According to the author Suzanne Massie, he proposed to his mother, the family's matriarch, that the factories share their profits with the workers, one of the first industrialists to suggest the idea. In her account his mother angrily removed him from the family business, and a month later the apparently despondent Morozov shot himself in the south of France. He died at Cannes on 26 May 1905.
sawad: Sawad means black land or arable land, a name drawn from the contrast between the alluvial plain of Mesopotamia and the Arabian Desert. In Arabic the word could mean the cultivated land of any district, and in Iraq it came to name the farmland around a city: the Sawad of Baghdad, Basra, Kufa or Wasit. Under the Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates it was also an official province covering most of modern Iraq except the Syrian Desert and Upper Mesopotamia. It replaced the earlier and narrower name Rādhān.

Farming depended almost wholly on irrigation, since dry farming needs 200 mm of rain a year and Basra gets 60. Most canals ran west to east from the Euphrates to the Tigris, whose water level was lower. Too much water raised the water table and brought salt to the surface, too little left the salt in the soil; the historian Robert M. Adams suggested that over-irrigation made much of the lower Nahrawan region too saline to farm.

Southern Mesopotamia had supported an urban civilisation built on irrigation since the late fourth millennium BCE. Settlement reached its peak in the late Sasanian period, when the canal network grew so large that only the state could maintain it. The Islamic conquest brought a steep decline, but the Muslims soon restored much of the Sasanian system.

From the mid-800s instability in the Abbasid Caliphate led to neglect of the countryside and harsher exploitation of the peasants. Revenues from the Sawad fell from 100 million dirhams under Harun al-Rashid to 20 million by the early 10th century. The siege of Baghdad in 865, the Zanj rebellion, put down in 883, and the Qaramita movement after it shrank the area under state control, and by the early 10th century 62 per cent of the settlements around Baghdad had been abandoned. The Mongol conquest dealt the final blow to the old pattern of settlement.

Early Abbasid revenue lists show the Sawad yielding four times the tax of Egypt, the next richest province. In 105 AH the caliph Yazid II had Umar Ibn Hubayra survey its land to centralise taxation. In the 9th century it was divided into 12 districts and 60 sub-districts, many with Sasanian names. Wheat and barley grew in every district, and most of the kharaj tax was paid in them. One estimate puts its rural population at about 4 million around 800.
sawlu: Saw Lu, also known as Min Lulin, the Boy King, was born on 19 April 1049 to King Anawrahta and Queen Agga Mahethi, Queen of the Southern Palace. The Burmese chronicles disagree on the dates of his life and on whether he or Kyansittha, Anawrahta's son by a minor queen, was the elder. Anawrahta made Saw Lu heir presumptive. He was brought up by a Mon lady of noble birth and grew up with his wet nurse's son Yamankan, who became his close friend. He took no interest in government, never joined his father's campaigns, and viewed his popular half-brother Kyansittha, a general of the Pagan army, with suspicion.

Saw Lu came to the throne on 11 April 1077, after Anawrahta died in mysterious circumstances, and took the regnal title Śrīvájrabharaṇatribupati. He married his father's Mon queen Manisanda, also called Khin U, and made her chief queen. He gave his childhood friend Yamankan, an ethnic Mon, charge of the Mon-speaking territories of the south. At the urging of the primate Shin Arahan he reluctantly recalled Kyansittha, whom Anawrahta had exiled for an affair with Manisanda, but soon banished him again, to Dala near Yangon, when the affair was renewed.

As governor of Pegu, Yamankan knew the king's inexperience well and decided to rebel. The chronicles tell of a game of dice in which Saw Lu taunted the winning Yamankan to rebel if he was so clever. In late 1082 Yamankan sailed up the Irrawaddy with his army. Saw Lu recalled Kyansittha to command, but against his warning attacked Yamankan's prepared positions near Thayet; his army was routed and he was taken prisoner.

Kyansittha tried to rescue him, but Saw Lu refused, believing that Kyansittha would kill him for the throne while his friend would not. Yamankan killed him to prevent further attempts, and scholars place his death in about April 1084. Yamankan was later killed by a bow-shot from Nga Sin the hunter, and Kyansittha became the third king of the Pagan Empire.
saxe-merseburg: In his will of 20 July 1652 Elector John George I of Saxony laid down that his three younger sons should receive secundogeniture principalities of the House of Wettin. After his death on 8 October 1656 the brothers concluded a treaty at Dresden on 22 April 1657, and a further treaty of 1663 fixed their territories and sovereign rights. Christian, the third son, received the estates of the secularised Bishopric of Merseburg, including Merseburg, Delitzsch, Bad Lauchstädt, Schkeuditz, Lützen, Bitterfeld and Zörbig, the County of Brehna and the Margraviate of Lower Lusatia with Lübben, Doberlug, Finsterwalde, Forst and Guben.

The duchy reached the western edge of Leipzig, with its customs station in what is now the Leipzig district of Lindenau. Christian I ruled until his death in 1691, and his son Christian II only until 1694. Christian II's son Christian III Maurice died in November 1694, a few days after his fourteenth birthday, and his brother Maurice Wilhelm, then six, ruled until 1712 under the regency of Elector Frederick August I of Saxony and the guardianship of his mother, Erdmuthe Dorothea of Saxe-Zeitz.

Christian I had given his younger sons apanages of their own, Saxe-Merseburg-Zörbig for August, Saxe-Merseburg-Lauchstädt for Philipp and Saxe-Merseburg-Spremberg for Heinrich, named after their residences and with very limited sovereignty. None of the three left surviving male heirs, so each ended with its first duke. Philipp died at Fleurus in 1690 and August in 1715. When Maurice Wilhelm died in 1731, his uncle Heinrich of Spremberg inherited the whole duchy. Heinrich died at Doberlug on 28 July 1738, the last male of the line.
saxe-weissenfels: John George I of Wettin, Saxon prince-elector from 1611 to 1656, laid down in his will that his eldest son, John George II, would succeed him as elector, while his younger sons were to receive secundogeniture duchies as appanages. On his death the duchies of Saxe-Zeitz, Saxe-Merseburg and Saxe-Weissenfels were formed, the last going to his second son Augustus. Augustus had served since 1638 as the Protestant administrator of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg and resided at Halle. From about 1660 he had the Baroque residence of Neu-Augustusburg built at Weissenfels.

Besides Weissenfels, the duchy comprised the ämter of Freyburg, Sachsenburg (present-day Oldisleben), Sangerhausen, Eckartsberga, Weißensee and Langensalza. Augustus added several lordships once held by the archbishops of Magdeburg and awarded to Saxony by the Peace of Prague of 1635, among them the immediate lordship of Querfurt and the exclaves of Jüterbog, Dahme and Burg. Through Querfurt the ducal line gained the status of an Imperial State, at times called Saxe-Querfurt, and membership of the Upper Saxon Circle, though without a vote in the Reichstag.

In 1659 Augustus acquired the County of Barby, which on his death in 1680 passed to his younger son Heinrich, who built a new Baroque castle at Barby from 1687. His eldest son and successor, Duke Johann Adolf I, sold Burg to Brandenburg in 1687. On the extinction of this cadet branch of the Albertine House of Wettin, the duchy fell back to the electoral line.

The court had links with two leading composers. From 1657 Georg Händel, father of George Frideric Handel, served as physician to Duke Augustus, and the composer was born at Halle, the former ducal residence. According to legend, Duke Johann Adolf I heard the young Handel play the organ of Neu-Augustusburg Castle and promoted his career. In 1713 Johann Sebastian Bach dedicated his cantata Was mir behagt, ist nur die muntre Jagd, BWV 208, to Duke Christian of Saxe-Weissenfels for his 31st birthday; it was first performed at the ducal Neuenburg Castle at Freyburg.
saxo-grammaticus: Saxo is thought to have been born in Zealand, on the evidence of the Jutland Chronicle, which first gives him the name Grammaticus, meaning the learned. The Sjælland Chronicle calls him Saxo cognomine Longus, with the byname the tall. Sven Aggesen, a Danish nobleman who wrote a slightly earlier history of Denmark, describes him as his contubernalis, or tent-comrade, which suggests that both may have served in the royal guard, the Hird. Saxo writes that he comes from a warrior family: he follows the ancient right of hereditary service, and his father and grandfather frequented the war camp of Valdemar I. Whether he was a layman or a cleric is uncertain, but either way he was well educated.

Saxo was in the retinue of Absalon, Archbishop of Lund and the foremost adviser to Valdemar I, and received his patronage. In his will Absalon forgives his clerk Saxo a small debt of two and a half marks of silver and tells him to return two borrowed books to the monastery of Sorø. In the preface to his history Saxo writes that Absalon had encouraged him to write a heroic history of the Danes, to glorify the fatherland on the model of Virgil's Aeneid. The work is thought to have been begun about 1185. Saxo wrote the preface last, under Anders Sunesen, who replaced Absalon as archbishop, and in it he warmly praised both archbishops and the reigning king, Valdemar II.

The Gesta Danorum begins with the founders of the Danish people, Dan I of Denmark and Angul, and extends to about the year 1187. The first four books treat the Danes before Christ, the next four their history after Christ, books 9 to 12 Christian Denmark, and books 13 to 16 promote Lund and exploits before and during Saxo's own lifetime. His sources were of questionable historical value: oral tales of the Icelanders, ancient volumes, letters carved on rocks and stone, and the statements of Absalon.

Saxo's world has very warlike values, and he glorifies heroes who made their names in battle far more than those who made peace. His gods are not always good characters. Odin teaches Harald, in Saxo's tale a king of the Danes, the ways of war and then betrays and kills him. Erasmus praised Saxo's Latin, and early in the sixteenth century Christiern Pedersen of Lund printed the work with Jodocus Badius Ascensius.
saxon-wars: The Saxons were divided into four groups in four regions. Westphalia lay nearest the Frankish kingdom of Austrasia and Eastphalia farthest, with Engria (or Engern) between them and Nordalbingia to the north, at the base of the Jutland peninsula. The first war began in January 772, when a Saxon expedition sacked and burned the church of Deventer. Charlemagne then invaded Saxon territory, subjugated the Engrians and destroyed their sacred symbol, the Irminsul, near Paderborn. Irminsul may have been a hollow tree trunk representing the pillar that supported the skies.

In all, 18 campaigns were fought, mostly in what is now northern Germany. Charlemagne's campaigns in 775 and 776 brought all of Saxony except Nordalbingia under his control, but rebellions destroyed his fortress at Eresburg and the Saxon leader Widukind fled to the Danes. In 777 a diet at Paderborn set out to bring Saxony into the Frankish kingdom. Many Saxons were baptised and missionaries, mainly Anglo-Saxons, were recruited. Charlemagne issued decrees that imposed capital punishment for observing heathen practices, which earned him the title butcher of the Saxons. His adviser Alcuin of York urged leniency.

In 782 Widukind returned and led a revolt, and the Saxons won the Battle of Süntel. In response Charlemagne ordered the beheading of 4,500 Saxons at the Massacre of Verden. Warfare was constant in 783–785, and in 785 Widukind was baptised and swore fealty. Revolts continued sporadically.

Westphalians rose in 792 against forcible recruitment for the wars against the Avars, and Eastphalians and Nordalbingians joined in 793, but it was put down by 794. In 798 the Obotrites under Thrasco defeated the Nordalbingian Saxons at Bornhöved, killing between 2,800 and 4,000. In 804 Charlemagne deported 10,000 Nordalbingians to Neustria and gave their lands to the king of the Obotrites.

Einhard, Charlemagne's biographer, said the war ended when the Saxons accepted terms: they renounced their religious customs, accepted the sacraments of the Christian faith and united with the Franks as one people. The capitulary of 785, the Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, had prescribed death for any Saxon who remained unbaptised and pagan, and a poet of the Paderborn Epic praised terror as a means of conversion.

Alcuin argued that faith is a free act of the will and that people could be forced to be baptised but not to believe. Charlemagne abolished the death penalty for paganism in 797 and in 802 Saxon common law was codified as the Lex Saxonum. Bishoprics were founded at Paderborn, Münster, Bremen, Minden, Verden and Osnabrück. A last Saxon uprising, the Stellinga, took place between 841 and 845.
saxons: The earliest possible record of the Saxons is a reference in Ptolemy's Geographia to a tribe north of the lower Elbe, but the manuscripts differ, some reading Saxones and others Axones, and its interpretation is disputed.
