The school also produced the Antidotarium Nicolai, a pharmacopeia of the Middle Ages, and the Latin verse Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum, a collection of rules of hygiene whose author gave it a Salernitan origin, in the 12th or 13th century, to advertise it.

With the rise of the University of Naples, and of Montpellier, Padua and Bologna, the school lost importance. Gioacchino Murat abolished it on 29 November 1811 in his reorganisation of public education in the Kingdom of Naples, and its remaining doctors of medicine and law worked in Salerno's Convitto Tasso until 1861, when Francesco De Sanctis closed them. Because it also taught philosophy, theology and law, some consider it the first university.
scholar-officials: The Chinese term, shi dafu, joins two ranks that were once distinct. In the order ascribed to the Duke of Zhou under the Western Zhou dynasty, the dafu were aristocrats who served as officers, and the shi stood between them and the ordinary people and could hold only low offices. During the Warring States period, as states annexed one another and bureaucracies grew, talented shi gave valuable service to their lords and gained influence, while dafu became an office and ceased to be a hereditary rank. The two merged. In the scheme of the Four Occupations the scholar-officials stood first, above farmers, artisans and merchants.

From the Han dynasty to the end of the Northern and Southern dynasties, officials were chosen through the recommendatory and nine-rank systems, and came mostly from prominent clans such as the Wang clan of Langya and the Cui clan of Qinghe, which supplied officials for generations and intermarried with one another and with the imperial family. The civil service examination was officially established in 587 under the Sui dynasty. In the early Tang dynasty Empress Wu Zetian reformed it by instituting a metropolitan examination, whose graduates were called jinshi; candidates were tested on poems and essays.

The Song dynasty is described as the golden age of the class. Examination had become the main path to office and the bureaucracy replaced the aristocracy. The Song was also the only dynasty to grant scholar-officials a judicial privilege: one who committed a crime faced internal impeachment in place of the ordinary courts, and for a lesser offence only a reprimand. Under the Yuan, Ming and Qing dynasties the fixed form of the eight-legged essay dominated the examinations, and the political climate left officials less free to speak and write. The Qing government abolished the examinations in 1905, and the class gradually disappeared.

Only a few degree-holders became court or local officials. Most stayed in their villages and towns as social leaders: they taught in private schools, organised welfare, helped settle minor disputes, supervised community projects, kept local order, conducted Confucian ceremonies and assisted in collecting taxes. The district magistrate, who was barred from serving in his home district, depended on them for advice, which gave them power to benefit themselves and their clients. In Confucian theory ministers were not mere subordinates and might oppose an unfit ruler. The system offered a path of upward mobility but had no formal safeguard against corruption beyond the moral teaching it examined.
scholasticism: The words scholastic and scholasticism come from the Latin scholasticus, the Latin form of the Greek scholastikos, meaning of or pertaining to schools, so that the scholastics were roughly schoolmen. Its foundations were laid by Boethius through his logical and theological essays. The Carolingian Renaissance brought the first significant renewal of learning in the West: Charlemagne drew scholars from England and Ireland and by a decree of 787 established schools at every abbey in his empire. Among them was Johannes Scotus Eriugena (815–877), who knew Greek and translated works into Latin. Lanfranc and Anselm of Canterbury in the 11th century and Peter Abelard in France are counted among its founders.

Scholasticism was a method of learning more than a philosophy or a theology, with a strong emphasis on dialectical reasoning to extend knowledge by inference and to resolve contradictions. A teacher would choose a book by an established authority and read it with the class. Points where sources disagreed were written down as sententiae, and the two sides were then reconciled by philological analysis, which showed that words could have several meanings, or by logical analysis.

Instruction had several parts. In the lectio a teacher read an authoritative text followed by a commentary, with no questions allowed. The meditatio let students reflect on the text, and in the quaestio they could ask the questions that had occurred to them. Disputations were arranged to resolve controversial questions: each side of an either/or question was argued in turn and the arguments against the chosen position were refuted.

The 13th and early 14th centuries are generally seen as the high period of scholasticism. Universities grew in the large cities, and the Franciscans, founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209, and the Dominicans, founded by St Dominic in 1215, competed for control of them. The Franciscan Bonaventure held that reason can discover truth only when it is illuminated by faith. The Dominicans Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas made more use of Aristotle. Aquinas's Summa Theologica (1265–1274) is considered the pinnacle of scholastic philosophy.

Scholastic methods outlasted the Middle Ages. After the Reformation Calvinists largely adopted the scholastic method of theology, while differing about sources of authority and its content. A revival of medieval scholastic philosophy, sometimes called neo-Thomism, began in the second half of the 19th century.
schollenen-gorge: The gorge, formed by the upper Reuss and enclosed by sheer granite walls, gives access to the Alpine valley of Urseren and so to the St Gotthard Pass to the south, the Furka Pass to the west and the Oberalp Pass to the east. At the Urnerloch the river enters the granite of the Aar massif, and the gorge is an exemplary late alpine water gap. Its name comes from the Rumantsch scalinae, stairs or steps, recorded in German as Schellenden in 1420, presumably for steps hewn into the rock.

Before the 12th century the gorge marked the upper limit of Alemannic settlement and the border between the bishoprics of Constance and Raetia Curensis, and by the mid-12th century a difficult footpath climbed around it. The first bridle path used a wooden ledge fixed to the rock wall, the Twärrenbrücke, whose technique is attributed to the Walser, and a wooden bridge recorded in 1306 as the stiebende Brugge, the spray bridge. Opening the Gotthard Pass, it had consequences for the Italian politics of the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1595 a stone bridge replaced the wooden one; the name Devil's Bridge is first recorded in 1587. A legend told by Johann Jakob Scheuchzer in 1716 has the people of Uri promise the Devil the first soul to cross, then send a dog over instead. In 1608 Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, lost gold in the torrent here, and in 1707/08 Pietro Morettini cut the Urnerloch, a tunnel about 60 metres long and the first road tunnel in the Alps.

In September 1799 the bridge was one of the sites of the battles at the Saint-Gotthard during Suvorov's Italian and Swiss expedition. The retreating French badly damaged it, and the route's trade with Italy shifted to the Splügenpass. In the 1890s the Russian Empire commissioned the Suvorov monument just south of the bridge.

A new cut-stone bridge by the cantonal engineer Karl Emanuel Müller was completed in 1830, and the bridge of 1595 collapsed in 1888. The Schöllenenbahn rack railway has run through the gorge since 1917, and the present road bridge and tunnel date from 1958. Since the Gotthard Road Tunnel opened in 1980 the road through the gorge has been of regional importance only.
schonborn-family: The family first appears in the Rheingau with H. von Sconenburne in 1275, its original seat being Schönborn in the County of Katzenelnbogen. By the end of the 14th century it had split into branches, one serving as Burgmann at the castle of Burgschwalbach and the other as vassals in the Westerwald. In the 16th century so many younger sons became cathedral canons that both branches died out, except a side line holding the fiefs of Freienfels and Eschbach. From it came Johann Philipp von Schönborn, son of a minor nobleman in the service of the Lutheran counts of Wied, who became a Catholic priest during the Thirty Years' War.

Johann Philipp was elected prince-bishop of Würzburg in 1642 and Archbishop of Mainz in 1647, which made him an elector and archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire. He suppressed Lutheranism in his lands and helped mediate the peace of 1648. His brother Philip Erwein acquired castles and estates and became a baron in 1663, and from his twelve children the later lines descend. Philip Erwein's son Lothar Franz became prince-bishop of Bamberg in 1693 and Elector of Mainz in 1695. In 1726 Emperor Charles VI granted him Palanok Castle and Mukacheve with 200 villages in Hungary, one of the largest estates in Eastern Europe.

Through the marriage of Rudolf Franz to Eleonore von Hatzfeld in 1701 the family gained Wiesentheid and, for the first time, imperial immediacy. Its counties were divided in 1717 and mediatised in 1806. In 1743 members of the family ruled Bamberg, Würzburg, Konstanz, Speyer, Worms and Trier. Their rise rested on elections by cathedral chapters across generations, backed by advantageous marriages; the family never gained hereditary princely rank. At the end of the 18th century three brothers founded the Austrian, Franconian and Bohemian branches that still exist.

The Schönborn prelates were among the main builders of Southern German baroque, employing Johann Dientzenhofer, Maximilian von Welsch and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt as well as Balthasar Neumann. More than 100 churches were built under their rule, among them the Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers. The years 1642 to 1756 are called the Schönbornzeit, a name now given to a style of Rhenish and Franconian baroque. Weissenstein Palace at Pommersfelden, still owned by the family, holds the largest private baroque art collection in Germany.
school-of-salamanca: The School of Salamanca takes its name from the University of Salamanca, founded in 1218. Most properly the term covers the intellectual movement of the early 16th century led there by Francisco de Vitoria. It began in 1526, when Vitoria, a Dominican who had studied in Paris during a Thomist revival, was elected to the Prime chair of Theology, which he held until his death in 1546. Against the university's statutes, he made Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae the main textbook and turned scholastic method to the problems raised by the Spanish conquest of the Americas, the growth of long-distance commerce and the Protestant Reformation.
The early phase was dominated by Dominican Thomists, notably Domingo de Soto and Melchor Cano. Soto served as confessor to Charles V and took part in the Council of Trent.

Many members were jurists as well as theologians and worked on natural law. The school separated the civil realm from the supernatural, so that a king had no jurisdiction over souls and the pope no temporal power. Vitoria extended his ideas of legitimate power to relations between nations, arguing that the common good of the world stands above that of each state. He has been called, with Grotius, the 'father of international law'. Francisco Suárez distinguished ius inter gentes, close to modern international law, from ius intra gentes, the civil law of each nation.

On the conquest of America, Vitoria rejected illegitimate titles of conquest. He questioned whether the Bulls of Donation of Alexander VI gave dominion over the new lands. The indigenous peoples, he held, were free people by nature with legitimate property rights. In just war theory he required legitimate authority, a just cause and proportional means, and opposed wars waged for religious conversion or territorial gain.

The school also developed economic thought. Martín de Azpilcueta, observing how American silver and gold lowered the value of metal and raised prices in Spain, set out a first form of the quantity theory of money. Joseph Schumpeter's History of Economic Analysis (1954) drew much attention to this work, and he argued that the school most deserved to be seen as the founders of economics as a science. Its work was not continued until the end of the 17th century, and many contributions were forgotten and rediscovered later.
school-of-the-americas: In 1946 the United States Army founded the Latin American Training Center-Ground Division at Fort Amador in the Panama Canal Zone, to centralise the training of the growing number of Latin Americans attending American service schools there. It taught Latin American personnel to use artillery and advanced weapons bought from the United States and gave instruction in nation-building. Renamed the Latin American Ground School, it was divided into departments of engineering, communications, and weapons and tactics. Enrolment was low at first, as Latin American officials preferred training in the continental United States, and from 1947 officers and lower ranks were taught in separate classes.

In February 1949 the army moved the school to Fort Gulick and named it the U.S. Army Caribbean School; that year it graduated 743 American and 251 Latin American students from ten countries. By 1954 its pupils were overwhelmingly Latin American, and in 1956 Spanish became its only language of instruction. In 1963 it was renamed the U.S. Army School of the Americas. During the mid-1960s it was one of the places where the army trained soldiers in jungle warfare, among them men of the 1st Cavalry Division bound for Vietnam.

By the time Congress withdrew the Secretary of the Army's authority to run it in 2000, the school had graduated 60,428 officers, cadets, police and defence officials from 22 Latin American countries and the United States. Renamed the following year, it came under a Board of Visitors of 14 members, among them representatives of human rights, religious, academic and business communities. Venezuela stopped sending soldiers in 2004, Argentina on 28 March 2006, Bolivia in 2008 and Ecuador in 2012.

From the early 1980s Latin American critics accused the school of teaching techniques of repression. Since 1990 the organisation School of the Americas Watch has held a yearly protest at Fort Benning, which drew 19,000 people in 2005. It marks the killing on 16 November 1989 of six Jesuit priests, their housekeeper Elba Ramos and her daughter Celia Marisela Ramos by the Atlácatl Battalion in San Salvador; a United Nations panel concluded that nineteen of the 27 killers were graduates. The school denied teaching torture, and Major Joseph Blair, a former instructor, said in 2002 that only the name had changed.
schutterij: Members trained on grounds called the Doelen, usually beside a large hall where they met and where their group portraits hung; in bad weather they might train inside a church. Archers and kloveniers, musket bearers, formed separate guilds, many under Saint Sebastian, Saint Anthony, Saint George or Adrian of Nicomedia, whose altars stood in local churches where the dues were paid. The ideal was three guardsmen for every hundred inhabitants. Two men guarded each district at night in shifts from 22:00 to 02:00 and from 02:00 to 06:00, and the company paraded once a month.

Not everyone served. Mennonites were excluded from the 16th to the 18th century and paid a double tax instead, and Roman Catholics were allowed only in the lower ranks. City servants such as the minister, physician, teacher and sexton, and the city's Jews, were exempt, while the beer and peat bearers served as the town's firefighters. A few years as an officer were often a step towards other public posts in the town.

After the Reformation the altars were removed and dues were paid at the city hall; in Haarlem the guilds of St. Adriaen and St. Joris kept their old rules, with banquets and collections for sick members and widows. From 1581 the schutterijen were officially barred from influencing city politics. In 1748 the Doelisten asked stadtholder William IV, Prince of Orange, to let the middle class appoint the officers, and he refused. In 1783 the Patriots tried to revive the guards or to found free corps open to all, with elected officers. The system outlasted the Batavian Revolution and French rule until William I of the Netherlands set up professional police forces.

Group portraits were usually painted when a leading officer died, retired or moved away, each sitter paying according to his place in the picture, which could cause quarrels. Frans Hals, Hendrik Gerritsz Pot and Caesar van Everdingen were members of the guilds that commissioned them, and Bartholomeus van der Helst launched his career with his first such commission in 1639. Many Amsterdam works are in the Amsterdams Historisch Museum, many from Haarlem in the Frans Hals Museum.

Ceremonial schutterijen that keep the old traditions survive in the Netherlands, many of them in the Catholic regions. More than 160 from Belgian and Dutch Limburg compete each year at the Oud Limburgs Schuttersfeest, whose winner organises the next festival.
scinawa: Ścinawa was first documented as a possession of the newly established Trzebnica Abbey in a deed of Pope Innocent III dating to 1202, when it was part of fragmented Poland. Town privileges were first granted between 1248 and 1259 by Konrad I, Duke of Głogów. After his sons partitioned the Duchy of Głogów in 1273, Ścinawa became the capital of a duchy of its own under Konrad II the Hunchback. It was reunited with Głogów under Duke Henry III in 1290. His son John, sole ruler at Ścinawa from 1317, titled himself heir of the Kingdom of Poland, but paid homage to King John the Blind in 1329, after which the duchy became a fiefdom of Bohemia.

The Polish king Casimir III the Great renounced his claims to Silesia in the 1335 Treaty of Trencin, yet campaigned in Silesia and set Ścinawa on fire in 1343. The conflict was settled in 1348 by the Treaty of Namysłów. In 1358 John sold half of Ścinawa to Duke Bolko II the Small of Świdnica, whose half was annexed by Emperor Charles IV on Bolko's death in 1368. The other half passed to Duke Henry V of Iron at Żagań in 1365 and was acquired in 1397 by Duke Konrad II the Gray of Oleśnica. The town was a centre of linen and cloth production.

From 1526 Ścinawa belonged to the Habsburg monarchy with the Lands of the Bohemian Crown, and in 1528 it became part of the united duchies of Wołów and Brzeg under Duke Frederick II of Legnica. It was heavily devastated in the Thirty Years' War, and in October 1633 Albrecht von Wallenstein's troops routed a Swedish corps under Jindřich Matyáš Thurn nearby. When the last Piast duke, George William, died in 1675, his lands fell to the House of Habsburg as reverted fiefs, and many craftsmen emigrated during the Counter-Reformation. Prussia annexed it with most of Silesia in 1742, and it became part of the German Empire in 1871. Rail links to Głogów and Wrocław opened in 1874.

In the Second World War the Germans set up forced labour camps there for French and Soviet prisoners of war and turned the town into a fortress. The Red Army captured it on 30–31 January 1945, after fierce fighting that destroyed about 75 per cent of the buildings. The German population was expelled in accordance with the Potsdam Conference, and the first Poles displaced from Soviet-annexed eastern Poland arrived in May and June 1945. The town lies on the Oder in Lubin County, and its sights include the Gothic church of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, a 19th-century town hall tower and part of the medieval city walls.
scindias: The family's ancestors held the hereditary post of Patil, or village head, of Kanherkhed in the Satara region of the Deccan, and in the 15th and 16th centuries had served as shiledars, cavalrymen, of the Bahmani Sultanate. Members of the family joined the Maratha army under Shivaji and his sons Sambhaji and Rajaram. Under Maratha rule the name was spelled Shinde; Scindia, also written Sindhia, is the Indo-Persian form of Sendrak. The house was founded by Ranoji Scindia, who rose from bodyguard to commander under Peshwa Bajirao I, one of several young men without hereditary rights, Malhar Rao Holkar among them, whom Bajirao promoted.

Ranoji led the Maratha conquests in Malwa in 1726 and made Ujjain his capital in 1731. The Scindias held sway over many of the Rajput states and became a major power in northern India in the later 18th century, collecting chauth, a share of revenue, from neighbouring rulers. Under Mahadji Scindia (1768–1794) their territory stretched from Lahore to Ahmednagar and from Bharuch to the border of Prayagraj, and he defeated the British at Wadgaon in the First Anglo-Maratha War. His successor Daulat Rao Scindia fought the British in the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War of 1818 the family accepted a subsidiary alliance with the British, gave up Ajmer and moved its base from Ujjain to Gwalior, which became a princely state. After Daulat Rao's death Baiza Bai ruled until the adopted Jankoji Rao took charge; when Jankoji died in 1843 his widow Tarabai Raje Scindia adopted Jayajirao. On 29 December 1843 East India Company forces defeated the Scindia armies at Maharajpur and Punniar, and a treaty of 31 December arranged the occupation of Gwalior fort.

The Scindias ruled Gwalior until India's independence in 1947, when Maharaja Jivajirao Scindia acceded to the Government of India. Gwalior was merged into the new state of Madhya Bharat, which he served as rajpramukh, or appointed governor, from 28 May 1948 to 31 October 1956, when it became part of Madhya Pradesh. The monarchy was abolished in 1971. The family's career in electoral politics began in 1962, when his widow Vijayraje Scindia was elected to the Lok Sabha, and several of her descendants have since sat in parliament and state assemblies. Maharaja Madho Rao Scindia founded two orders of chivalry, the Order of the Snake and the Gwalior Medal, in 1900 and 1907.
scipio-aemilianus: Scipio Aemilianus was the second son of Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus, the victor of the Third Macedonian War, and his first wife, Papiria Masonis. He was adopted by his first cousin Publius Cornelius Scipio, a son of Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus, who had defeated Hannibal. At seventeen he took part in his father's campaign in Greece. Plutarch relates that when he was missing after the Battle of Pydna the whole army searched for him, and that he returned late, covered with the blood of the enemies he had slain.

In 151 BCE, when Roman recruitment for the war in Hispania had collapsed, he asked the Senate to send him there as a military tribune or legate, and his example led others to volunteer. In the Third Punic War he was a military tribune who repeatedly saved Roman forces from disaster. In 147 BCE he was elected consul although under the legal age and was assigned to Africa without the usual drawing of lots. After a year of fighting he took Carthage and made about 50,000 survivors prisoner, roughly one tenth of the city's population. On the Senate's orders he had the city burnt and razed. It was formerly believed that he also salted the ground, but modern scholars have found no evidence of that.

Elected consul again in 134 BCE, he took command in the Numantine War, restored discipline in a demoralized army and besieged Numantia with a circuit of fortifications nine kilometres long. The Numantines were starved into surrender, and Scipio sold the survivors into slavery and destroyed the city. He served as censor in 142 BCE. A patron of writers and philosophers, he gathered the Scipionic circle, which included Polybius, Panaetius, Lucilius and Terence.

Scipio disliked the land reforms of his brother-in-law Tiberius Gracchus, and he became unpopular when he took the side of Rome's Italian allies against the commission applying the land law of Gracchus. He died at home in 129 BCE, and rumours of murder circulated, naming Cornelia, Sempronia, Fulvius Flaccus, Gaius Gracchus and Gaius Papirius Carbo. Modern historians see no strong evidence for any cause but natural death. According to Polybius, Scipio wept at the burning of Carthage and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy, saying he feared the same fate for Rome.
scipio-africanus: Publius Cornelius Scipio was born in 236 BCE into the patrician Cornelii Scipiones, one of the major families of Rome. His father, also called Publius, was consul in 218 BCE. He followed his father to the war against Carthage that began that year. Polybius claims that at the river Ticinus the son saved his father's life, though other sources credit an unnamed Ligurian slave. He survived the Roman disaster at Cannae.

In 211 BCE his father and uncle, who commanded Rome's armies in Spain, divided their forces against three Carthaginian armies and fell in separate battles. In 210 BCE Scipio, though he had never held consular office, was elected to command in Hispania. His campaign led to victory at Ilipa in 206 BCE against Hannibal's brother Mago Barca and to the Roman conquest of Carthaginian Iberia. He was elected consul for 205 BCE, at 31 still technically too young, and demanded the province of Africa. Despite the opposition of Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, the senate gave him Sicily with permission to cross into Africa. It assigned him no additional soldiers, so he recruited volunteers.

His invasion of the Carthaginian homeland forced the recall of Hannibal. After failed negotiations Scipio routed Hannibal's army at Zama in 202 BCE, forcing Carthage to sue for peace and ending the Second Punic War. He earned the epithet Africanus. He was censor in 199 BCE and consul again in 194 BCE.

Scipio had many political opponents, among them Cato the Elder. In 187 BCE he and his brother Lucius were tried for bribes they were said to have received from the Seleucid king Antiochus III. He retired to his estate at Liternum on the coast of Campania, where he died. Sources give different dates, but most modern ones, such as the Oxford Classical Dictionary, prefer 183 BCE.

His memoirs, written in Greek, are lost, so accounts of his life rest on Polybius, Livy, Appian and Cassius Dio. He was the first Roman general to expand Roman territory outside Italy and the nearby islands, and his victory at Zama paved the way for the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE. His interest in Greek culture influenced the Roman elite. Petrarch made him the hero of his Latin epic Africa, and the Continence of Scipio, in which he returns a captive woman to her fiancé, was painted by artists from Mantegna to Poussin.
scorpion-macehead: The Scorpion Macehead, also called the Major Scorpion Macehead, is a pear-shaped limestone object 25 centimetres long. It was found by the British archaeologists James E. Quibell and Frederick W. Green in what they called the main deposit of the temple of Horus at Hierakonpolis. It is attributed to the ruler Scorpion because of the glyph of a scorpion carved near the image of a king. Its carving follows the conventions of Egyptian depiction: figures shown with the head and legs in profile and the torso from the front, a more distant scene placed above a nearer one, and the king drawn larger than those around him.

The king, wearing a bull's tail as well as the White Crown, stands by a body of water, probably a canal, holding a hoe. A scorpion and a rosette appear close to his head, and two fan bearers follow him. Facing him are a man holding a basket and men carrying standards, while others work along the banks of the canal. Behind the king's retinue are plants, a group of women clapping their hands and a few people who face away from him. The top register shows a row of nome standards, from each of which a bird hangs strung up by its neck.

A second, smaller fragment, known as the Minor Scorpion Macehead, shows little of its imagery. It depicts a king wearing the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, seated on a throne beneath a canopy and holding a flail, with a scorpion and a rosette beside his head. A falcon facing him may hold the end of a rope in one claw, a motif also found on the Narmer Palette. Together the two maceheads show the same ruler with the crowns of both Upper and Lower Egypt.
scoti: Where the word Scoti came from is unclear. It is not a Latin derivation and matches no known name the Gaels used for themselves as a whole or for any of their groups, and none of the proposed origins has won general acceptance. In the 19th century Aonghas MacCoinnich derived it from the Gaelic sgaothaich, crowd or horde. Charles Oman in 1910 suggested scuit, someone cut off, and saw the Scots as bands of outcast raiders. Philip Freeman in 2001 pointed to an Indo-European root *skot, as in the Greek skotos, darkness, and the linguist Kim McCone in 2013 derived it from the Old Irish scoth, the pick of the population.

An early use of the name appears in the Nomina Provinciarum Omnium, a short list of the provinces of the Roman Empire dating to about 312, which ends with tribes seen as a growing threat; among them were the Scoti, a new term for the Irish. Prosper's chronicle for 431 records Pope Celestine sending Palladius to Ireland to preach to the Scots who believed in Christ. The Latin writers Pacatus, Ammianus Marcellinus and Claudian and the Chronica Gallica of 452 report raids, and Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis, named them in Greek in the 370s.

The raids seem to have grown from the early 360s to the barbarian conspiracy of 367–368 and continued beyond the end of Roman rule around 410, though where and how often they struck, and which Gaelic groups took part, remain unclear.

By the 5th century the Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata had arisen in what is now Argyll. The Pictish kingdom under Angus I subjugated it in the 8th century, but Pictish and Gaelic speech converged over the following centuries, and in the early 10th century the English called Pictland under Constantine II Scottish, a usage first attested in 920. From the 12th century, with the arrival of Norman-French knights and the southward spread of Scotland's borders under David I, the words Scot, Scottish and Scotland came into common use among the country's own people.
scotland: The mainland of Scotland makes up the northern third of the island of Great Britain, with a total area of 30,977 square miles (80,231 km2). Its only land border, with England, runs for 96 miles (154 km) between the basin of the River Tweed and the Solway Firth. The mainland is divided into the Highlands, a mountainous region in the north and north-west, the Lowlands, a flatter plain across the centre, and the Southern Uplands along the border. Ben Nevis, at 4,413 feet (1,345 m), is the highest peak of the British Isles.

The earliest known evidence of people in Scotland is stone tools of the Hamburgian culture, made by hunter-gatherers who arrived around 14,500 to 14,000 years ago, soon after the ice sheet retreated. Neolithic farmers came about 6000 years ago. Skara Brae on Orkney, the Callanish Stones on Lewis and Maes Howe on Orkney belong to this period, the stone monuments of the third millennium BCE. The Greek sailor Pytheas made the first written reference in 320 BCE, calling the northern tip of Britain Orcas.

The Roman governor Agricola invaded in 79 CE and defeated a Caledonian army at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 83 CE, but within three years the Roman armies had withdrawn to the Southern Uplands. Under Trajan, who reigned from 98 to 117, Roman control had lapsed to the south of a line between the River Tyne and the Solway Firth, where Hadrian later built his wall. The Kingdom of Scotland emerged as a sovereign state in the 9th century and kept its independence from England partly through an alliance with France.

Its extent was largely fixed by the Treaty of York of 1237 with England and the Treaty of Perth of 1266 with Norway. Orkney and Shetland were acquired from Norway in 1472, and Berwick-upon-Tweed was ceded to England in 1482. James VI succeeded to the English and Irish thrones in 1603, and on 1 May 1707 Scotland and England combined as the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Scotland is a country within the United Kingdom, with Edinburgh as its capital and Glasgow as its largest city. The census of 2022 counted 5,436,600 people. A Scottish Parliament was re-established in 1999 with devolved authority over many areas of domestic policy. Scotland keeps its own legal system, education system and religious history. English and Scots are the most widely spoken languages, while Scottish Gaelic is spoken natively mainly in the Hebrides. Its seven World Heritage Sites include St Kilda, the Old Town and New Town of Edinburgh, New Lanark and the Antonine Wall.
scottish-enlightenment: The Scottish Enlightenment was the period in the 18th and early 19th centuries in Scotland marked by an outpouring of intellectual and scientific work. By the eighteenth century Scotland had a network of parish schools in the Lowlands and five universities: St Andrews, Glasgow, Edinburgh, King's College and Marischal College. The union with England in 1707 ended the Scottish Parliament and drew politicians to London, but Scots law, the Church of Scotland, the universities and the medical establishment stayed in Scotland. Their lawyers, ministers, professors, doctors and architects formed a new middle-class elite that dominated urban Scotland and made the Enlightenment possible. Glasgow's trade with the Americas, especially in tobacco, brought wealth, and banking grew.

Intellectual life centred on books and on clubs, beginning in Edinburgh in the 1710s with the Easy Club. Others included the Select Society, formed by the painter Allan Ramsay the younger with David Hume and Adam Smith, and the Poker Club, formed in 1762 and named by Adam Ferguson. Glasgow had a Political Economy Club to link academics and merchants.

Its thinkers shared the rational outlook of the wider Enlightenment, asserting the importance of reason and rejecting authority that reason could not justify. In Scotland it was marked by a thorough empiricism and practicality, whose chief values were improvement, virtue and practical benefit. Francis Hutcheson, professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow from 1729 to 1746, was its first major philosopher. David Hume's Treatise of Human Nature (1738) helped set out philosophical empiricism and scepticism, while Thomas Reid, in An Inquiry into the Human Mind (1764), formulated Common Sense Realism. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, is the starting point of modern economics.

Its influence reached far beyond Scotland, carried by the Scottish diaspora and by foreign students at its universities. The new Encyclopædia Britannica was designed in Edinburgh and first published in three volumes between 1768 and 1771. The architect Robert Adam influenced building in Britain, Western Europe, North America and Russia. The political ideas had an impact on the Founding Fathers of the United States, and Common Sense Realism was influential in nineteenth-century American thought. The movement was long linked with abolitionism, but the academic John Stewart argues that many of its members supported slavery and scientific racism, a result of Scotland's large part in the Atlantic slave trade.
scottish-highlands: The Highlands are the northernmost mountain ranges of Great Britain, divided by the Great Glen between the Grampian Mountains to the south-east and the Northwest Highlands. The name also covers the area north and west of the Highland Boundary Fault, which runs from Arran to Stonehaven, though the exact boundary is not clearly defined, particularly in the east. The region lies on ancient Cambrian and Precambrian rocks uplifted in the Caledonian Orogeny, with Lewisian gneiss up to 3 billion years old, and includes Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the British Isles. The Highlands are the only area in the British Isles with a boreal forest biome, with remnants of the Caledonian Forest.

The region was home to the Caledonians or Picts and became the mainland stronghold of the Hebridean Gaels, whose Gaelic language succeeded that of their neighbours. The cultural distinction between Highlander and Lowlander was first noted towards the end of the 14th century. The clan was the main social unit, and James VI saw clans as a challenge to royal authority. The Statutes of Iona in 1609 began integrating clan leaders into Scottish society. After the Jacobite rising of 1745 the British government banned the bearing of arms and the wearing of tartan, laws mostly repealed by the end of the 18th century. The Black Watch, raised in 1739, was the first Highland regiment of the British Army.

Between about 1760 and 1850 agricultural improvement brought the Highland clearances, in which many tenants were evicted to make way for large-scale sheep farms; in the west and north they were resettled in crofting communities and worked in kelping and fishing. Famine recurred, and potato blight arrived in 1846. The population, around 300,000 in the 18th and early 19th centuries, then declined through emigration, mostly to Canada, the United States, Australia and New Zealand. Crofters, many in the Free Church after 1843, challenged landlords through the Highland Land League in the 1880s, and the Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act 1886 reduced rents and guaranteed fixity of tenure.

Inverness is regarded as the capital of the Highlands, and the Highland Council has its administrative centre there. The area is among the most sparsely populated in Europe. Scottish Gaelic, once the language of the region, is now largely confined to the Hebrides, and a Highland form of Scottish English predominates. Tartan and the kilt were adopted by elites in the 1820s after the Ossian cycle and Walter Scott's staging of George IV's visit in 1822, and tartan became a major symbol of Scottish identity.
scottish-norwegian-war: Norwegian influence over the Hebrides and the Isle of Man went back to the reign of King Harald Fairhair. It was formalised in 1098, when Edgar, King of Scotland, signed the islands over to King Magnus III of Norway after a swift campaign in which Magnus had imposed direct royal control on the Hebrides, Orkney and Man at the expense of their Norse-Gaelic leaders. In Norwegian terms the islands were the Suðreyjar, the Southern Isles.

From the 1240s Alexander II of Scotland repeatedly asked Haakon IV to sell him the islands, without success, and the talks lapsed after Alexander II died. In 1262 his son Alexander III sent Haakon a final request, warning that if the islands were not sold the Scots would take them by force.

Haakon answered by gathering a fleet of more than 120 leidang warships and sailing in July 1263 to defend the isles. He halted at the Isle of Arran, where negotiations began. Knowing that Haakon needed a decisive victory before winter, Alexander drew out the talks until the autumn storms arrived. In October 1263 several Norwegian ships were driven ashore at Largs; when a party landed to salvage them, Scottish forces attacked, and the skirmish that followed, the only major battle of the war, ended indecisively.

The next morning the fleet sailed back to Orkney for the winter, and Haakon died there in December. The rest of the conflict consisted mainly of skirmishes and feuds. His successor, King Magnus the Lawmender, faced problems at home and lacked the money for a new expedition.

Alexander III took the Hebrides in 1264 and pressed a formal claim to the islands. Under the Treaty of Perth they were bought from Norway for 4,000 marks and 100 marks a year thereafter, and the Scots in turn recognised Norwegian rule over Shetland and Orkney.
scramble-for-africa: By 1841 European businessmen had set up small trading posts along the African coasts, but they seldom moved inland, and large parts of the continent were close to uninhabitable for Europeans because of tropical diseases such as malaria. As late as the 1870s Europeans controlled about 10 per cent of Africa, all of it near the coasts, chiefly Angola and Mozambique, held by Portugal, the Cape Colony, held by the United Kingdom, and Algeria, held by France. Steamships, railways, telegraphs and quinine made the interior far more accessible.

During the Long Depression of 1873–1896 Africa offered European states an open market and raw materials such as ivory, rubber, palm oil, cocoa, diamonds, tea and tin. Britain also wished to secure the route to India and the Suez Canal, completed in 1869, and navies needed coaling stations and bases.

Seven Western European powers took part: Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the United Kingdom. In the Congo, Henry Morton Stanley made treaties with chiefs on behalf of Leopold II of Belgium, and by 1882 these gave a base for the Congo Free State. In 1881 Pierre de Brazza raised the French flag over the newly founded Brazzaville. Portugal, which claimed the area under old treaties with the Kingdom of Kongo, made a treaty with Britain on 26 February 1884 to block Leopold's access to the Atlantic. The Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 regulated European colonisation and trade and is seen as emblematic of the scramble.

The later years of the century saw a move from informal imperialism, meaning military influence and economic dominance, to direct rule. Many regimes claimed to be suppressing slavery and the slave trade, the central theme of the Brussels Anti-Slavery Conference of 1889–1890.

By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained outside European control, and Ethiopia was occupied by Italy in 1936. Between 1885 and 1914 Britain took nearly 30 per cent of Africa's population under its control, France 15 per cent, Portugal 11, Germany 9, Belgium 7 and Italy 1. After the First World War Germany's possessions were divided among Britain, France and Belgium. Rivalries among the imperial powers contributed to the crises that led to the outbreak of the First World War in August 1914.

Most African colonies became independent during the Cold War. At the conference of the Organisation of African Unity in 1964 the new states decided to keep their colonial borders, out of fear of civil wars and regional instability.
screw: Most screws are tightened by clockwise rotation, which is called a right-hand thread. Left-hand threads are used in exceptional cases, such as the left pedal of a bicycle, where the twisting force would tend to loosen a right-hand screw. The head of a screw is usually larger than the body, which gives a bearing surface and stops the screw from being driven deeper than its length. The cylindrical part below the head is the shank, and the distance between threads is the pitch. Screws are normally made from wire in three steps: cold heading, thread rolling and a coating such as zinc to prevent corrosion.

Fasteners such as dowels, pins, wedges, mortises and tenons, dovetails and nails were widespread before the screw. The screw was one of the last of the simple machines to be invented. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws were in common use around the Mediterranean in presses for olive oil and for grape juice. Metal screws used as fasteners were rare in Europe before the 15th century, if known at all, and did not become common until machine tools for mass production developed toward the end of the 18th century. The first documented screwdriver appears in the Housebook of Wolfegg Castle, written between 1475 and 1490, but screwdrivers probably did not become widespread until after 1800.

Standard thread forms came late. The English engineer Sir Joseph Whitworth created the first standard in about 1841, and the British Standard Fine thread was added in 1908 because his thread was too coarse for some uses. The British Association thread was devised in 1884 and standardised in 1903, and its sizes were defined in metric terms. In the United States the Unified Thread Standard is most common, while in much of the world the ISO metric screw thread has displaced the older systems. Whitworth threads are still used in UK scaffolding and on photographic tripods, and BA threads in railway signalling and in clocks and moving-coil meters.
scrovegni-chapel: The chapel stands in Padua beside the Augustinian monastery of the Eremitani. It is called the Arena Chapel because the banker Enrico Scrovegni built it on land that abutted the site of a Roman arena, which he bought from Manfredo Dalesmanini, with a palace beside it. The chapel was meant as the family's private oratory and as a funerary monument for himself and his wife, Jacopina d'Este. The land was bought on 6 February 1300. It was dedicated to Santa Maria della Carità on 25 March 1303, the Feast of the Annunciation, and received its definitive consecration on 25 March 1305. Giotto's work falls between those two dates.

Giotto was then about 36 to 38 years old and had a team of about 40 collaborators. They calculated that 625 working days were needed, a working day being the portion of fresco that could be painted before the plaster dried. In January 1305 the friars of the Eremitani complained to the bishop that Scrovegni was turning his oratory into a church with a bell tower, in competition with them.

Giotto covered every interior surface. The nave is 20.88 metres long, 8.41 wide and 12.65 high. The cycle runs in tiers. At the top are the stories of Joachim and Anne on the south wall and of Mary on the north, then the Life of Christ in the middle tier, and the Passion and Resurrection below, ending with Pentecost. The Annunciation and the Visitation stand on the triumphal arch, and the Last Judgement fills the entrance wall. Along the bottom run fourteen grisaille personifications, the Vices on the north wall and the Virtues on the south.

The vault is painted as a blue sky studded with eight-pointed stars. Its tondos hold the seven great prophets of the Old Testament and John the Baptist, with two suns showing God and the Madonna and Child.

The frescoes are regarded as an important masterpiece of Western art and as the beginning of a revolution in mural painting that influenced technique, style and content for a century. Giotto's innovation lies in the monumentality of his forms and the clarity of his compositions. In 2021 the chapel became part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the 14th-century fresco cycles of Padua. Marcel Proust refers to Giotto's Charity in his novel, and Stanley Spencer based the scale and narrative sequence of the Sandham Memorial Chapel at Burghclere on it.

The palace was demolished in 1827, and Padua bought the chapel in 1881. A full restoration began in June 2001, and the chapel reopened in March 2002. Visitors now wait fifteen minutes in a technological chamber that lowers their humidity and filters dust.
scupi: The site lies between the hill of Zajčev Rid and the Vardar River, several kilometres from the centre of Skopje. According to the archaeologist Ivan Mikulčić, Scupi was once twice the size of Stobi, five times larger than Heraclea near Bitola and nine times larger than Bargala near Štip, the largest known Roman settlement in the region. Archaeologists distinguish four building periods, from a military camp of the second century BCE to the early Christian town that ended in 518.

The Dardanians had stayed independent after the Roman conquest of Macedonia because they had supported the Romans, and they most likely lost their independence in 28 BCE. Scupi grew as a colony of legionaries, mainly veterans of the Legio VII Claudia, in the time of Domitian, and became the chief centre from which Dardania was romanized. It belonged to Moesia Superior after that province was formed and from 272 to the province of Dardania. The Goths ravaged it in 269 and the Huns in the 5th century.

Its theatre is thought to date from the 2nd century, as the seats bear the name Colonia Scupi Aelia, and may have been built for a visit of the emperor Hadrian. After the earthquake of 518 life in Scupi stopped; its people are assumed to have moved to Kale, a hill in the centre of Skopje, and much of the theatre's stone was probably carried there. Some scholars connect this move with Justiniana Prima, the city Justinian I founded near his birthplace, though the identification rests on assumptions.

Excavation began between the two World Wars, when Radoslav Gruić found the early Christian basilica in 1925 and Nikola Vulić the theatre. The Museum of the City of Skopje has worked on the site since 1966, and in July 2008 a statue of Venus 1.7 metres tall was found there. In 2016 Scupi was designated a cultural heritage site of exceptional significance; a restoration project begun that year was halted in 2017.
scythians: The Scythians, also called the Pontic Scythians, were an Eastern Iranic equestrian nomadic people. They migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe, in present-day Ukraine and southern Russia, during the ninth and eighth centuries BCE, and remained there until the third century BCE. They already practised goldsmithing and bronze-casting, as gold pieces from the eighth-century BCE Aržan-1 kurgan show. Their name comes from the endonym *Skuδa, meaning archers.

Skilled in mounted warfare, they displaced the Agathyrsi and the Cimmerians as the dominant power on the western steppe in the eighth century BCE. From about 750 BCE they settled in the Ciscaucasian Steppe, concentrated in the Kuban valley, where their capital stood until the end of the seventh century BCE. In the seventh century BCE they crossed the Caucasus and often raided West Asia with the Cimmerians.

The sources are Akkadian cuneiform texts, which deal with early Scythian history from the seventh century BCE, and Graeco-Roman writers, above all Herodotus, who cover the whole history but mix in folk tales. Scythian raids destabilised the balance among Assyria, Urartu and Phrygia and spread steppe military technology in West Asia.

In the late sixth century BCE the Scythians left Ciscaucasia and Sauromatian incomers arrived on the Pontic Steppe, giving rise to the Classical Scythian period, with a rise in monumental burials. The Sarmatians later invaded and the Pontic kingdom collapsed, leaving the Scythians in fortified settlements along the rivers and in the two regions called Little Scythia. By the third century CE the remnants were overwhelmed by the Goths, and the last Scythians were absorbed by later populations.

Clan groups formed the basis of society, and clan elders could depose kings. The king came from the dominant tribe, the Royal Scythians. Their herds were about 40 percent horses, 40 percent cattle and 18 percent sheep, with no pigs, and mares' milk was an important food. Trade with the Greek colonies on the Black Sea brought exports of grain, iron, furs, slaves and mounted archers, and by the third century BCE many had become settled farmers.

Mounted archery was their main form of warfare, with the recurved composite bow, and they invented the saddle in the seventh century BCE. Their remains include kurgans, the royal ones holding weapons, horse harness and gold objects in Scythian animal style.
sea-of-azov: The Sea of Azov is a shelf sea about 360 kilometres long and 180 kilometres wide, with an area of 39,000 square kilometres. It joins the Black Sea through the narrow Strait of Kerch, about 4 kilometres wide, and is sometimes regarded as a northern extension of the Black Sea. The Don and Kuban rivers bring sand, silt and shells, which build bays, limans and long narrow spits; the Arabat Spit stretches over 112 kilometres. The inflow keeps the salinity low, almost fresh in places, and the sea is the shallowest in the world, between 0.9 and 14 metres deep. The name Azov probably derives from a settlement whose name comes from the Kipchak Turkish asak or azaq, meaning lowlands.

Traces of Neolithic settlement lie in the area now covered by the sea. In antiquity it was known as the Maeotis Swamp, from the Maeotians who lived by fishing and farming near its northeastern marshes; it remains unclear whether the sea took its name from them or they from it. The marshes around the mouth of the Tanais, today's Don, served as a check on the migration of nomadic peoples from the steppe. Ancient geographers had only a vague idea of its extent: Herodotus judged it as large as the Black Sea, Pseudo-Scylax about half as large, and it was long believed to connect directly with the Arctic Ocean.

The sea was often a theatre of conflict between Russia, seeking naval expansion to the south, and the Ottoman power. In 1695–96 Peter I led two campaigns to take the Turkish fortress of Azov, defended by a garrison of 7,000. The first, in 1695, brought an army of 31 thousand men and 170 cannon to the fortress; after two failed assaults on 5 August and 25 September the siege was lifted. During the Crimean War, British and French forces took Kerch on 12 May 1855 and then besieged Taganrog, which withstood them despite their great superiority in numbers, and their army withdrew around August 1855.

The sea has long been an important waterway, and navigation grew after the Volga–Don Canal was built in 1952, linking it with the Volga. The major ports are Taganrog, Mariupol, Yeysk and Berdyansk. Fishing has long been a major activity, with sturgeon, pike-perch and bream among the valuable species. Dams, over-fishing and pollution have reduced the catch, and the anchovy fisheries have collapsed.
sea-of-galilee: The Sea of Galilee, also called Lake Tiberias or Kinneret, lies in northeast Israel between the Golan Heights and the Galilee region, in the Jordan Rift Valley, formed by the relative motion of the African and Arabian plates. It is the lowest freshwater lake on Earth, with its surface between 215 and 209 metres below sea level depending on rainfall. Its main source is the Jordan River, which flows through it from north to south. The area is subject to earthquakes and had volcanic activity in the past, shown by abundant basalt. The lake in its present form was created less than 20,000 years ago.

The Hebrew name Kinneret appears in the Hebrew Bible; scholars derive it from the Bronze and Iron Age city of Kinneret rather than from the Hebrew kinnor, harp. After Tiberias was founded on its western shore in 16 CE, it came to be called the Sea of Tiberias.

A village of the late Natufian period at Nahal Ein Gev is considered one of the first permanent human settlements in the world. The lake lies on the ancient Via Maris, which linked Egypt with the northern empires. Greeks, Hasmoneans and Romans founded towns on its shores, including Hippos and Tiberias. Flavius Josephus reports a thriving fishing industry, with 230 boats regularly working the lake. After the Romans put down Bar Kokhba's revolt in 135 CE, the centre of Jewish learning shifted to Galilee, particularly Tiberias, where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled.

In 1187 Sultan Saladin defeated the armies of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem at the Battle of Hattin, largely because he was able to cut the Crusaders off from the fresh water of the lake. The border between Mandatory Palestine and the French Mandate of Syria was fixed in 1923 so that the whole lake lay in Palestine. The National Water Carrier, completed in 1964, linked it to Israel's water infrastructure.

Tourism is important around the lake. Christian pilgrims visit places where, according to the New Testament, Jesus performed miracles, and the Jesus Trail ends at Capernaum on its shore. The lake has supported a commercial fishery for more than two millennia.
sea-of-japan: The Sea of Japan is almost completely enclosed. The Japanese archipelago separates it from the Pacific Ocean, and like the Mediterranean it has almost no tides. It has a surface area of about 1,050,000 square kilometres, a mean depth of 1,752 metres and a maximum depth of 4,568 metres. It is joined to neighbouring seas by five straits: the Strait of Tartary, La Pérouse Strait, the Tsugaru Strait, the Kanmon Straits and the Korea Strait. All are shallow, which isolates its water and life from the Pacific. The sea has no large islands, bays or capes. Few rivers flow into it, though the four largest rivers of Japan, the Shinano, Ishikari, Agano and Mogami, do.

Its geological history is long. The Japan Sea began to open in the Early Miocene, and the northern and southern parts of the Japanese archipelago separated. The straits formed in recent geological periods, and the Tsugaru and Tsushima straits, the oldest, interrupted the migration of elephants into the Japanese islands about 2.6 million years ago.

For centuries the sea protected Japan from land invasions, particularly by the Mongols. Asian ships had long crossed it, and from the 18th century European ships did too. Russian expeditions of 1733–1743 mapped Sakhalin and the Japanese islands. In the 1780s the Frenchman Jean-François de Galaup, comte de Lapérouse, sailed north across the sea through the strait later named for him. In 1796 the British naval officer William Robert Broughton explored the Strait of Tartary and the coasts of the Russian Far East and the Korean Peninsula. In 1849 the Russian explorer Gennady Nevelskoy found the strait between the mainland and Sakhalin.

American, Canadian and French whaleships hunted in the sea between 1847 and 1892, chiefly for right whales, and then humpbacks. In the peak years of 1848 and 1849 over 170 vessels cruised there in all. The Chinese name for the sea was once the Sea of Whales. Japanese scientific study of the sea began only in 1915 and became systematic from the 1920s.

Several names are in use: Nihonkai in Japan, Donghae, the East Sea, in South Korea, and Yaponskoye more in Russia. Japan holds that the name Sea of Japan has been the internationally accepted term since the early 19th century, while South Korea says that the East Sea was in use before Japanese colonial rule and asks that it be used alongside the other. The International Hydrographic Organization has used the name Japan Sea in its publication on the limits of seas since 1928. Fishing is the dominant economic activity, and Vladivostok, the terminus of the Trans-Siberian Railway, is a major port.
sea-of-marmara: The Sea of Marmara lies entirely within Turkey and links the Black Sea and the Aegean Sea by way of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, separating the country's European and Asian sides. It covers 11,350 square kilometres, measures roughly 280 by 80 kilometres, and is considered the smallest sea in the world. Its maximum depth is 1,370 metres. The south coast is heavily indented and has the Gulf of İzmit, the Gulf of Gemlik, the Gulf of Bandırma and the Gulf of Erdek.

The surface water averages about 22 parts per thousand of salt, slightly more than the Black Sea and about two-thirds that of most oceans. At the bottom it is much more saline, averaging about 38 parts per thousand, like the Mediterranean, and this dense water does not rise to the surface.

The sea is named after Marmara Island, the largest island on its south side, which is rich in marble, mármaron in Greek. In classical antiquity it was called the Propontis, from the Greek pro, in front of, and pontos, sea, because the ancient Greeks sailed through it to reach the Black Sea. In Greek mythology a storm on the Propontis brought the Argonauts back to an island they had left, which led to a battle in which either Jason or Heracles killed King Cyzicus, who had mistaken them for his Pelasgian enemies.

Two groups of islands lie in the sea. To the north are the Princes' Islands, made up of the inhabited islands Kınaliada, Burgazada, Heybeliada, Büyükada and Sedef Adası, and several uninhabited ones. They are reached by ferry from both shores of Istanbul and form part of its conurbation. To the south are the Marmara Islands, with Marmara Island, Avşa, Paşalimanı and Ekinlik inhabited and 17 largely uninhabited islands, among them the prison island of Imralı. They lie within Balıkesir Province and are reached from Tekirdağ or from Erdek.

The North Anatolian Fault runs under the sea. It has caused several major earthquakes, among them those of İzmit in August 1999 and Düzce in November 1999. The August earthquake is commonly called the Marmara Earthquake, since its epicentre lay under the sea and the places worst affected, by the shaking and a tsunami, lay along its shores. About one third of Turkey's population lives in the basin, and Istanbul, the largest city of the country, stands on the sea.
sea-of-okhotsk: The Sea of Okhotsk covers 1,583,000 square kilometres, with a mean depth of 859 metres and a maximum depth of 3,372 metres. It connects to the Sea of Japan on either side of Sakhalin, through the Gulf of Tartary and through the La Pérouse Strait. It is the coldest sea in East Asia and the southernmost sea in the Northern Hemisphere that freezes over seasonally.

Cold Siberian air forms sea ice over the north-western shelf, where fresh water from the Amur River lowers the salinity of the surface and so raises its freezing point. In a typical winter 50 to 70 percent of the surface is covered, with ice present from about December until early summer. The circulation is cyclonic, and the sea is among the most biologically productive in the world, with walleye pollock, herring, salmon, squid and king crab among its catches.

The Okhotsk culture and the later Ainu people, coastal fishing and hunting peoples, lived on the lands around the sea and in northern Japan. Russian explorers Vassili Poyarkov in 1639 and Ivan Moskvitin in 1645 were the first Europeans to visit it. The Dutch captain Maarten Gerritsz Vries entered from the south-east in 1643 and charted parts of the Sakhalin coast and the Kuril Islands, but did not realise that Sakhalin and Hokkaido were islands. The sea was sometimes called the Sea of Kamchatka.

The port of Okhotsk was the first and foremost Russian settlement on the shore; it gave up commercial supremacy to Ayan in the 1840s. The Second Kamchatka Expedition under Vitus Bering began mapping the whole coast in 1733, and the Russian-American Company almost monopolised commercial navigation in the first half of the nineteenth century. Mamiya Rinzō and Gennady Nevelskoy showed that Sakhalin was an island. American whalers took bowhead whales from 1847, and from 1854 to 1856 an average of over 160 vessels a year cruised the sea.

Japan administered South Sakhalin as Karafuto Prefecture from 1907 to 1949 and held the Kuril Islands until 1945, after which the Soviet Union occupied them. During the Cold War the sea was a base for Soviet ballistic missile submarines and the scene of the Soviet attack on Korean Air Lines Flight 007 in 1983.

With the exception of Hokkaido, the sea is surrounded by territory administered by the Russian Federation. Japan claims the southern Kuril Islands, which it calls the Northern Territories. Its main ports include Magadan in Russia and Abashiri, Monbetsu and Wakkanai on Hokkaido.
sea-peoples: The Sea Peoples are known mainly from Egyptian inscriptions, and the name is a modern coinage, often regarded as a misnomer since most of them appear to have travelled by land. The concept was proposed in 1855 by Emmanuel de Rougé, who read the battles of Ramesses III on the second pylon at Medinet Habu as a conflict with peoples of the sea, and Gaston Maspero developed it in 1895–96 into a theory of seaborne migrations. Scholars have questioned it since the early 1990s. Early scholarship saw the Sea Peoples as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse, but recent work tends to see them as refugees fleeing a crisis that was already under way.

Raiders called Sherden attacked the Nile Delta in the second year of Ramesses II and were captured, and some then served in his army at the Battle of Kadesh. In the reign of Merneptah the chief of Libya fell upon Egypt's western border with a force that included Sherden, Shekelesh, Ekwesh, Lukka and Teresh, and was defeated at Perire.

The best-recorded campaign is that of Ramesses III in his eighth year. The Medinet Habu inscription says that no land could stand before the invaders from Hatti and Carchemish, and it names the Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh. The reliefs show the Peleset and Tjeker accompanied by women and children in ox-carts, so these were movements of whole populations by land and sea. Ramesses ambushed their fleet at the mouths of the Nile and routed their land army.

Contemporary texts from Ugarit, whose last king was Ammurapi, record the approach of enemy ships, and the destruction of Hatti, Ugarit, Ascalon and Hazor falls around this time. The Onomasticon of Amenope, dated to about 1100 BCE, lists the Sherden, Tjeker and Peleset after place names in Philistia, which suggests that some were settled in Canaan.

Some groups are well identified. The Lukka lived in the later Lycia, never formed a unified kingdom and were described as raiders and pirates. Historians generally identify the Peleset with the later Philistines, and Philistine Bichrome ware and genetic evidence suggest that newcomers from the Aegean world settled at sites such as Ashkalon and quickly intermarried with local people. The Ekwesh and Denyen have been tentatively identified with the Greek names Achai(w)oí and Danaoí, which occur in the Homeric epics, and some archaeologists connect the Sherden with the Nuragic civilisation of Sardinia. The Weshesh are the most sparsely attested.
sebastian-hurtado-de-corcuera: Hurtado de Corcuera was born on 25 March 1587 at Bergüenda in the mountains of Álava and became a knight of the Order of Alcántara. He served for many years in Flanders, where he was one of the Spanish commanders at the Siege of Breda and a member of the Council of War, then became master-of-camp at Callao in Peru and captain general of its cavalry. From 1632 to 1634 he governed Panama, then part of the Viceroyalty of Peru.

He reached Manila on 25 June 1635 with reinforcements from Peru and Panama, replacing the interim governor Juan Cerezo de Salamanca. His quarrel with Archbishop Hernando Guerrero came to a head when the artilleryman Francisco de Nava killed an enslaved woman, María, and took sanctuary in an Augustinian church; the governor had him seized, tried and hanged before the church on 6 September 1635, and the archbishop laid an interdict. In May 1636 Guerrero was exiled to Marivales Island, returning within a month under humiliating conditions.

In March 1637 he sailed from Zamboanga with about 800 Peruvian soldiers, landed at Lamitan and defeated the forces of Sultan Qudarat, who narrowly escaped; the victory inspired the Moro-Moro, a play that became part of Filipino festivals. In January 1638 he attacked Jolo with 500 Peruvians and 1,000 native allies. In the second Chinese insurrection of 1639 to 1640, which began among labourers he had forced to farm rice at Calamba, some 24,000 Chinese were killed, and in 1642 the Dutch took the lightly garrisoned Spanish fort on Formosa.

When his successor Diego Fajardo Chacón arrived in 1644, his enemies, above all among the clergy, brought him to court; he was heavily fined and spent five years in prison until a royal order freed him. He declined a second term in Panama in 1651, served as mayor of Córdoba and commander of the armed forces of Asturias, and in 1659 became governor and captain general of the Canary Islands, dying at Tenerife on 12 August 1660.
sebastian-lerdo-de-tejada: Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada was born in Xalapa, Veracruz, on 24 April 1823, into a middle-class Criollo family, the younger brother of Miguel Lerdo de Tejada. He studied theology on a scholarship at the Palafoxiano Seminary in Puebla but decided against the priesthood. He took a law degree at the Colegio de San Ildefonso in Mexico City in 1851 and directed the college from 1852 to 1863. He became known as a Liberal leader, was foreign minister for three months in 1857 under Ignacio Comonfort, and presided over the Chamber of Deputies in 1861, 1862 and 1863.

When the Republican government left Mexico City on 31 May 1863, Lerdo de Tejada remained loyal to it. On 12 September 1863 at San Luis Potosí he became Juárez's minister of foreign affairs and was the president's closest ally throughout the French occupation. He came third in the presidential election of 1871, behind Juárez and Porfirio Díaz. Juárez died of a heart attack in July 1872, and Lerdo de Tejada, as president of the Supreme Court, was his constitutional successor and won election in his own right in November.

He kept Juárez's cabinet almost unchanged. He pacified the country, using federal troops to end the regional rule of Manuel Lozada of Tepic. In January 1873 he inaugurated the railway from Veracruz to Mexico City, begun under Juárez. The Laws of the Reform were incorporated into the constitution on 25 September 1873, and the Sisters of Charity were expelled from the country.

Lerdo de Tejada ran again in 1876, which gave opponents grounds under the principle of no re-election. Díaz issued the Plan of Tuxtepec before the election of 24 July 1876, which Lerdo won, though some charged fraud. Díaz defeated Lerdo's forces at Tecoac on 16 November 1876 and took the presidency on 28 November. Lerdo went into exile in New York, where he died on 21 April 1889. Díaz had his body returned for burial with full honours in the Rotonda of Illustrious Men. His overthrow marks the end of the Restored Republic and the start of the Porfiriato. A statue of him stands outside the Mexican Congress, and Toluca de Lerdo bears his name.
sebastian-of-portugal: Sebastian was born on 20 January 1554, the feast of Saint Sebastian, whose name he was given. He was the only child of João Manuel, Prince of Portugal, and Joanna of Austria, and was born two weeks after his father's death, so he was heir apparent from birth. His mother left him soon afterwards to serve as regent of Spain and never saw him again. He succeeded his grandfather, King John III, at the age of three, and a regency followed, first under his grandmother Catherine of Austria and then under his great-uncle Cardinal Henry of Évora.

He grew up under heavy Jesuit influence and became extremely devout, carrying a copy of Thomas Aquinas at his belt. He did not marry, and a plan of Catherine de' Medici to marry him to her daughter Margaret of Valois failed.

During his short personal reign, which began when he attained his majority in 1568, Sebastian strengthened ties with the Holy Roman Empire, England and France and restructured much of the kingdom's administrative, judicial and military life. In 1569 Duarte Nunes de Leão compiled the laws in the Código Sebastiânico, and in 1570 the king ordered that Brazilian Indians should not be used as slaves. During the plague of Lisbon in 1569 he brought doctors from Seville and created two hospitals.

Sebastian dreamed of a great crusade against Morocco, where several Portuguese way stations on the route to India had been lost. His chance came in 1576 when Abu Abdallah Mohammed II Saadi lost his throne and fled to Portugal. In June 1578 an army of 17,000 men, including foreign mercenaries and almost all the country's nobility, sailed from Lisbon.

At the Battle of Alcácer Quibir, also called the Battle of the Three Kings, the Portuguese army was routed by Abd al-Malik at the head of more than 60,000 men. Sebastian was last seen riding headlong into the enemy lines. Philip II claimed to have received his remains and buried them in the Jerónimos Monastery in Lisbon after 1580, but the body could not be identified. His great-uncle Henry succeeded him. The belief that he would return, called Sebastianism, led to four pretenders during the Iberian Union of 1580 to 1640, and he came to be known as the Desired and the Hidden. His reputation in Morocco remained positive as a symbol of chivalry.
sebastian-pinera: Miguel Juan Sebastián Piñera Echenique was born in Santiago on 1 December 1949, the third child of José Piñera Carvallo and Magdalena Echenique Rozas. He studied business administration at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile and economics at Harvard University. From 1971 to 1988 he lectured in economics at the University of Chile, the Pontifical Catholic University and Adolfo Ibáñez University. He married Cecilia Morel in 1973, and they had four children. He was general manager of the Banco de Talca, and in 1982 a warrant was issued for his arrest over unpaid loans, but the Supreme Court acquitted him.

A member of the party National Renewal, he was senator for Eastern Santiago from 1990 to 1998. In 1998 he opposed the arrest of Augusto Pinochet in London, calling it an attack on Chile's sovereignty and dignity. He announced a candidacy in the 2005 presidential election, which he lost to Michelle Bachelet. In 2010 he won the first round of the election with 44.05 per cent of the vote and the run-off on 17 January with 51.61 per cent against Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle. He was the first conservative president democratically elected in Chile since 1958. He offered to sell his shares in major corporations before taking office and put US$400 million in blind trusts.

Piñera was sworn in as the 34th president on 11 March 2010, during a 6.9 magnitude earthquake and its aftershocks. His first term, to 2014, included the reconstruction after the 2010 earthquake, the rescue of 33 trapped miners and the student protests of 2011. After leaving office he founded the think tank Fundación Avanza Chile. He won the presidency again and took office for a second term on 11 March 2018. He died on 6 February 2024, aged 74, when the helicopter he was piloting crashed into Lake Ranco.
sebinkarahisar: Şebinkarahisar is a town in the Black Sea region of north-eastern Turkey and the administrative seat of Şebinkarahisar District. It stands about 40 kilometres from the provincial city of Giresun, on the north side of the valley of the river Avutmuş in the Giresun Mountains. The town is hard to reach, since the road along the riverbank is winding and narrow. In the 11th century the town kept the name Koloneia while the fortress above it was called Mavrokastron, Greek for Black Fortress; the Turkish name Karahisar, first recorded in the 14th century, translates it, and the place has been known as Şebinkarahisar since the 19th century.

Its recorded history begins with the Third Mithridatic War, after which Pompey strengthened the fortifications and founded a Roman colony. Theodore Gabras defended it against the Seljuks after the Battle of Manzikert, and after his death in 1099 it fell to them. In 1201 or 1202 the Mengujekids, vassals of the Seljuks of Rum, took over. After the Mongol invasion the Eretnids held it, and Uzun Hasan of the Ak Koyunlu took it in 1459. Mehmed II took the town for the Ottomans in 1461 and consolidated his rule in 1473, after defeating Uzun Hasan at the Battle of Otluk Beli.

In 1915 Şebinkarahisar was one of the few places where Armenians actively resisted the Armenian genocide. After 300 Armenians, mostly wealthy merchants, were arrested on 15 June, fighting broke out and barricades went up in the Armenian districts. About 5,000 Armenians, 75% of them women and children, retreated into the medieval fortress and were surrounded by Turkish troops with heavy artillery. On the night of 11 July they tried to leave secretly; those who left were killed. The fortress surrendered on 12 July, and all Armenian men were then killed. Official Turkish records claim that the rebels killed 403 Turkish villagers.

Şebinkarahisar had a population of 10,695 in 2022. Its sights include the castle, Atatürk's House Museum, the Seljuk Behramşah Mosque and an Ottoman stone caravanserai at the castle entrance. The Şebin walnut is a local variety grown on the valley sides.
second-anglo-afghan-war: The war was part of the Great Game between the British and Russian empires. Tension between them in Europe ended with the Congress of Berlin in June 1878, and Russia then turned to Central Asia. It sent an uninvited mission to Kabul, which arrived on 22 July 1878, and Sher Ali Khan tried unsuccessfully to keep it out. On 14 August the British demanded that he accept a British mission as well. The viceroy of India, Lord Lytton, sent one in September 1878, but it was turned back at the eastern entrance of the Khyber Pass, and a deadline of 20 November was set.

The first campaign began in November 1878, when about 50,000 British fighting men, mostly Indians, entered Afghanistan in three columns. Victories at Ali Masjid and Peiwar Kotal left the way to Kabul virtually undefended. Sher Ali left for Mazar-i-Sharif, was refused entry to Russian territory and died there on 21 February 1879. His son Yaqub Khan signed the Treaty of Gandamak on 26 May 1879, giving up control of Afghan foreign affairs, ceding Quetta and areas of the North-West Frontier, and receiving an annual subsidy of 600,000 rupees. On 3 September 1879 an uprising in Kabul killed the British envoy Sir Louis Cavagnari with his guards and staff.

Major General Sir Frederick Roberts defeated the Afghan army at Charasiab on 6 October and occupied Kabul two days later. Yaqub Khan, suspected of complicity, abdicated, and an uprising besieged the Sherpur Cantonment in December before collapsing on 23 December. Meanwhile Abdur Rahman Khan, long in exile in Turkestan, was allowed by the Russians to re-enter Afghanistan, took Badakhshan and Afghan Turkestan, and in July 1880 was told that the British would recognise him as ruler. That month Ayub Khan, governor of Herat, rebelled, defeated a British detachment at the Battle of Maiwand and besieged Kandahar. Roberts defeated him on 1 September 1880 at the Battle of Kandahar.

With Ayub Khan beaten, Abdur Rahman Khan ruled as emir and was seen as the real victor. The British returned Kandahar, gave up the plan of a resident in Kabul, and handled Afghanistan's foreign policy in return for a subsidy and protection, while the Afghans kept internal rule and a buffer against Russia. The war cost Britain some 17 million pounds, about three times the estimate, and about 19.5 million by the withdrawal in March 1881. Abdur Rahman governed autocratically and became known as the Iron Amir. In 1893 Mortimer Durand reached the Durand Line Agreement with him on 12 November, fixing the limits of their spheres of influence.
second-anglo-burmese-war: The Second Anglo-Burmese War, fought between 5 April 1852 and 20 January 1853, was the second of three wars between the Burmese and British empires in the 19th century. It followed Lord Dalhousie's dispatch of Commodore George Lambert to Burma over a number of minor issues related to the Treaty of Yandabo. The Burmese made immediate concessions, including the removal of a governor whom the Company made its casus belli. Lambert, whom Dalhousie privately called the 'combustible commodore', then blockaded the port of Rangoon and seized King Pagan's royal ship, provoking a naval confrontation in questionable circumstances.

Richard Cobden attacked Dalhousie's conduct in the pamphlet How Wars are Got Up In India. He criticised the sending of a naval officer to negotiate and the raising of the initial compensation demand from £1000 to £100,000, and he held that the nature of the dispute had been misrepresented to Parliament. Dalhousie denied that Lambert caused the outbreak of hostilities.
