The Company took the port of Martaban on 5 April 1852 and occupied Rangoon on 12 April. The Shwedagon Pagoda was bombarded and taken on 14 April, and the Burmese army retired northwards after heavy fighting. Bassein fell on 19 May, and Pegu on 3 June after sharp fighting round the Shwemawdaw Pagoda.

During the rainy season the Company's court of directors and the British government approved the annexation of the lower Irrawaddy valley, including Prome. Dalhousie visited Rangoon in July and August and decided against marching on the capital unless complete annexation was intended, which was judged unachievable for the time being. Major-General Godwin occupied Prome on 9 October against slight resistance. In December Dalhousie informed King Pagan that the province of Pegu would form part of the Company's dominions.

The annexation was proclaimed on 20 January 1853, and the war ended without any treaty. In Amarapura, still called the Court of Ava, Pagan Min was overthrown by his half-brother Mindon Min. Mindon sued for peace at once, but the two Italian priests he sent found the British 50 miles (80 km) farther north at Myedè, with a rich belt of Ningyan teak forest already claimed as fact. No treaty was ever signed, although trade resumed between Company Burma and the Kingdom of Ava until fresh hostilities broke out in 1885–1886.
second-anglo-dutch-war: The Second Anglo-Dutch War began on 4 March 1665 and ended with the Treaty of Breda on 31 July 1667. It followed the First Anglo-Dutch War of 1652 to 1654, whose treaty had not settled the issues behind it, among them Dutch opposition to the Navigation Acts and English objections to Dutch trading monopolies. Charles II renewed the Acts in August 1660 and strengthened them in 1663.

In 1660 he and his brother James founded the Royal African Company to challenge Dutch dominance of the Atlantic slave trade. In August 1664 the English occupied New Amsterdam, renamed New York, and took Dutch slaving posts in Guinea, which Michiel de Ruyter recaptured in early 1665. After English attacks on convoys, the Dutch declared war.

At the Battle of Lowestoft on 13 June 1665 the Dutch lost some sixteen ships and over 30 per cent of their personnel, among them their commander Jacob van Wassenaer. De Ruyter then became commander in chief. France declared war on England on 16 January 1666 and Denmark-Norway followed in February. The Four Days' Battle, fought from 11 to 15 June 1666, cost the English ten ships and the Dutch four. The English won the St. James's Day Battle of 4 and 5 August, but on 19 August up to 150 Dutch merchantmen were destroyed at the Vlie estuary in Holmes's Bonfire.

English finances then collapsed. The Great Plague of London and the Fire of London in September 1666 turned opinion against the war. By early 1667 much of the Royal Navy lay laid up at Chatham, and peace talks opened at Breda in March. In June De Ruyter led the Dutch raid on the Medway, broke the chain guarding it and attacked the fleet on 13 June. Three major warships were burnt and HMS Royal Charles was taken to the Netherlands. In the Caribbean Abraham Crijnssen captured Suriname in February 1667.

Under the Treaty of Breda England kept New Netherland, while the Dutch kept Pulau Run, Fort Cormantin and Suriname and regained Tobago, Sint Eustatius and their West African posts. The Navigation Act was modified in the Dutch favour, and England accepted the principle of Free Ship, Free Goods. The Dutch regarded the peace as a personal triumph for Johan de Witt. Fear of France and its invasion of the Spanish Netherlands made both sides prefer a quick end, and in 1668 the Triple Alliance joined the Dutch Republic, England and Sweden. Charles II's wish to avenge the Medway setback led to the Third Anglo-Dutch War in 1672.
second-anglo-maratha-war: The British had supported the Peshwa Raghunathrao in the First Anglo-Maratha War and continued their support for his son, Baji Rao II. He provoked the enmity of Yashwant Rao Holkar by having one of Holkar's relatives killed. The Maratha Empire was then a confederacy of five major chiefs: the Peshwa at Poona, the Gaekwad of Baroda, the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore and the Bhonsle of Nagpur, who quarrelled among themselves. Lord Mornington, the Governor-General of British India, had repeatedly offered a subsidiary treaty to the Peshwa and Scindia, but Nana Fadnavis strongly refused.

In October 1802 the combined armies of Baji Rao II and Scindia were defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar at the Battle of Poona. Baji Rao fled to British protection and in December concluded the Treaty of Bassein with the East India Company, ceding territory to maintain a subsidiary force and agreeing to make treaties with no other power. The treaty has been called the death knell of the Maratha Empire.

The Scindia and Bhonsle rulers contested the agreement. The British planned for Major General Arthur Wellesley to secure the Deccan Plateau and for Lt. Gen. Gerard Lake to take the Doab and then Delhi, with other columns sent to Bundelkhand, Badoch and Bihar, and over 53,000 men available. Wellesley attacked on 8 August 1803, taking the pettah of Ahmednagar the same day, and the fort surrendered on 12 August. In September 1803 Scindia forces lost to Lake at Delhi and to Wellesley at Assaye. British forces took the pettah of Asirgarh on 18 October and its garrison surrendered on the 21st. In November Lake defeated another Scindia force at Laswari, and Wellesley defeated Bhonsle forces at Argaon on 29 November 1803.

On 17 December 1803 Raghoji II Bhonsale signed the Treaty of Deogaon and gave up the province of Cuttack. On 30 December Daulat Scindia signed the Treaty of Surji-Anjangaon, ceding Hisar, Panipat, Rohtak, Rewari, Gurgaon, the Ganges-Jamuna Doab, the Delhi-Agra region, parts of Bundelkhand, Broach, some districts of Gujarat and the fort of Ahmadnagar.

The British began hostilities against Yashwantrao Holkar on 6 April 1804. He had some success by guerrilla warfare, but received no help from Scindia, who had already signed with the British, and Ranjit Singh in the Punjab refused it. Lack of resources forced him to terms, and the Treaty of Rajghat of 24 December 1805 made him give up Tonk, Rampura and Bundi.
second-anglo-mysore-war: Hyder Ali, who ruled Mysore without the title of king, held that the British had broken faith with him during an earlier war against the Marathas and allied himself with France. When France declared war on Britain in 1778, the British East India Company set out to take the remaining French enclaves in India, capturing Pondicherry in 1778 and the port of Mahé on the Malabar Coast in 1779. Mahé mattered to Hyder, who received French arms through it and had placed it under his protection. He formed a confederacy against the British with the Marathas and the Nizam of Hyderabad.

In July 1780 Hyder entered the Carnatic with an army of 80,000, burning villages as he came down the Eastern Ghats. On 10 September his son Tipu Sultan caught Colonel William Baillie's column near Pollilur; of 3,820 men, 336 were killed and Baillie surrendered, and Colonel Hector Munro fell back on Madras. Hyder took Arcot on 3 November instead of pressing on, which let Sir Eyre Coote bring reinforcements; Coote then beat Hyder at Porto Novo and Sholinghur. The British took the Dutch post of Negapatam in November 1781, and Tipu destroyed Colonel Braithwaite's force at Annagudi on 18 February 1782.

Hyder died of cancer while Tipu was campaigning in the Malabar. General Richard Matthews crossed the Western Ghats and took Bednore, but Tipu besieged him there and forced him to capitulate; Matthews and seventeen officers died in captivity at Gopal Drooge, apparently poisoned. On the east coast French troops joined Mysore at Cuddalore, where General James Stuart's siege ended when news came of a preliminary peace between France and Britain in 1783. Tipu then retook Mangalore, whose garrison surrendered on 30 January.

Ordered by London to make peace, the company signed the Treaty of Mangalore with Tipu on 11 March 1784, on terms Warren Hastings and others thought very unfavourable. It was the last time an Indian power dictated terms to the company. In Britain, Pitt's India Act gave the government control of the company's political affairs. The war was the second of four Anglo-Mysore Wars, which ended with British control over most of southern India.
second-anglo-sikh-war: Maharaja Ranjit Singh consolidated the Sikh misls of the Punjab into an empire and expanded it in the early nineteenth century. After his death in 1839 it fell into disorder, with short-lived rulers at the Lahore Durbar and rising tension between the court and the Sikh army. The First Anglo-Sikh War ended in defeat, and the empire ceded the Jullundur Doab to the East India Company. A British Resident, Sir Henry Lawrence, took up office at Lahore with authority over every department of the state, while the boy Maharaja Duleep Singh kept his throne.

Early in 1848 Lawrence went on leave, and Lord Dalhousie appointed Sir Frederick Currie, a legalist unfamiliar with the Punjab, in his place. Currie refused to act on James Abbott's reports that Sardar Chattar Singh Attariwalla was plotting rebellion.

Dewan Mulraj, the governor of Multan, had grown independent and tried to hand his post to his son when the Durbar demanded more revenue. Currie sent Sardar Kahan Singh Mann to replace him, with the British agent Lieutenant Patrick Vans Agnew. On 18 April 1848 Mulraj's troops and a mob attacked the party, and Vans Agnew and Lieutenant William Anderson were murdered the next day. Sikh soldiers deserted in large numbers.

Lieutenant Herbert Edwardes defeated Mulraj's forces at Kinyeri and Suddusain with Bhawalpuri allies, and besieged Multan. Gough and Dalhousie delayed the main army until the cold weather. Sher Singh Attariwalla's contingent went over at Multan on 14 September, and the siege was lifted.

In the cold weather Hugh Gough met Sher Singh on the Chenab, where the Sikhs repelled a British cavalry attack at Ramnagar on 22 November. The Battle of Chillianwala on 13 January 1849 cost Gough heavy losses, and he claimed a victory that Dalhousie called perhaps poetical. Whish took Multan, and Mulraj surrendered the citadel on 22 January. On 21 February Gough won the Battle of Gujrat after a three-hour bombardment from almost 100 guns; Sikh losses were put at 3,000 to 5,000 men. Chattar Singh and Sher Singh surrendered near Rawalpindi on 12 March.

Dalhousie proclaimed the annexation of the Punjab on 2 April 1849, and Duleep Singh signed the document at the Lahore Fort. The British also gained control of the Khyber Pass, which became the westernmost boundary of the British Raj. Many people from the communities of the Punjab were recruited into the Punjab Irregular Force and fought for the Company in the Indian Rebellion of 1857.
second-balkan-war: In the First Balkan War, which began in October 1912, the Balkan League of Bulgaria, Serbia, Montenegro and Greece drove the Ottoman Empire out of most of its European provinces. The Treaty of London, signed on 30 May 1913, acknowledged the allies' gains west of the Enos–Midia line and created an independent Albania. Bulgaria was unhappy with the division of Macedonia. Serbia and Greece signed an alliance and drew up a military plan against Bulgaria, while on the Bulgarian side General Mihail Savov drafted plans on 31 May for a war with both of them.

After General Savov's ultimatum to the government expired, Tsar Ferdinand authorised a limited military demonstration, which was not meant to grow into a real war. Fighting began on 29–30 June 1913 between the Bulgarian 4th Army and the Serbian 1st and 3rd Armies, first on the Zletovska and then on the Bregalnica river. Internal confusion brought heavy Bulgarian losses on 1–3 July, and by 8 July the Bulgarian army had been severely defeated. In the south the Greek army under King Constantine I also repelled the attack and advanced.

Romania mobilised on 5 July and declared war on 10 July, invading Southern Dobruja and then crossing the Danube on the night of 14–15 July. Its advance met almost no organised resistance and halted before Sofia. The Ottoman Empire, encouraged by the lack of resistance, crossed the Enos–Midia line on 20 July and recovered Adrianople, held by only 4,000 men. Bulgaria asked for peace and its delegation went to Bucharest on 24 July.

By the Treaty of Bucharest Bulgaria gave up Southern Dobruja to Romania and most of Macedonia to Serbia and Greece, keeping only the town of Štip and the port of Dedeagac. Greece obtained Kavala, with support from Germany and France. Adrianople returned to the Ottoman Empire by a separate treaty signed at Constantinople. Serbia grew from 18,650 to 33,891 square miles and gained more than one and a half million people, but the inhabitants of the new lands were denied voting rights, and British vice-consuls reported intimidation, beatings and massacres there.

Atrocities against civilians were widespread on every side. Retreating Bulgarian forces killed Greek civilians at Doxato and Serres, Greek and Serbian troops retaliated against Bulgarian villages, and Ottoman forces in Eastern Thrace killed civilians of the Bulgarian population, with up to 60,000 deaths estimated. Over 100,000 Bulgarians fled to Bulgaria. The war made Serbia the strongest military power south of the Danube and sharpened its rivalry with Austria-Hungary, while Bulgaria, weakened by defeat, later aligned with the Central Powers in the First World War.
second-battle-of-dongola: Relations between Makuria and Rashidun Egypt had begun badly with the first battle of Dongola in 642. After their defeat the Arabs withdrew from Nubia, and something of a peace was in place by 645. According to the 14th-century Arab-Egyptian historian al-Maqrizi, Makuria then broke the truce, and Abdallah ibn Sa'd, successor of the first governor of Arab Egypt, invaded to bring the Makurians to heel. Northern and central Nubia were at that time united under the Makurian king Qalidurut.

Archaeology shows that Dongola was well fortified in the seventh century, with walls of mudbrick faced with stone at least 6 metres high and 4 metres wide at the base, and round corner towers projecting 8 metres from the wall. The towers may have been added after the siege, perhaps in response to it.

Abdallah marched on Dongola with 5,000 men, heavy cavalry and a catapult, or manjaniq, probably a traction trebuchet, which al-Maqrizi says the Makurians had never seen before. His cavalry faced the task of storming a walled city held by the Nubian archers. Catapult fire damaged the town's cathedral; a damaged church of the mid-seventh century has been found outside the remains of the walls.

The siege ended in a pitched battle in which Abdallah's forces suffered heavy casualties, and Qalidurut did not sue for peace. The 9th-century Egyptian historian Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam wrote that Abdallah made terms because he was unable to defeat them, and the 10th-century Shiite historian Ahmad al-Kufi wrote that the Muslims had never before suffered such a loss.

Abdallah called off the siege in exchange for a negotiated pact, the baqt. It set up trade between Muslim Egypt and Christian Nubia, in which Egypt sent wheat, barley, wine, horses and linen and Nubia sent 360 slaves a year. The baqt had no precedent in the early history of Islam, and Nubia's status as a land free from conquest was equally new; its rulers dealt with Muslim rulers on equal terms until the 12th century, when Nubian power began to wane.

In later centuries Muslim historians recast the siege as a victory, al-Maqrizi describing Qalidurut coming out submissively to seek terms, a version that may stem from confusing the events of 652 with the conflicts between Nubia and the Mamluks in the late 13th century.
second-battle-of-el-alamein: The battle was fought from 23 October to 4 November 1942 near the Egyptian railway halt of El Alamein. The Axis Panzer Army Africa had advanced into Egypt after its success at the Battle of Gazala in May and June, threatening British control of the Suez Canal, the Middle East and its oil. General Claude Auchinleck withdrew the Eighth Army to within 50 miles of Alexandria, where the Qattara Depression, impassable and 40 miles south of El Alamein, meant that any attack had to be frontal. The Axis attacks of the First Battle of El Alamein in July were defeated. In August Winston Churchill replaced Auchinleck with General Harold Alexander, and Lieutenant-General Bernard Montgomery took command of the Eighth Army.

Montgomery planned a battle of three stages, the break-in, the dogfight and the final breaking of the enemy, and expected it to last twelve days. At 21:40 on 23 October, Operation Lightfoot opened with a barrage of about 1,000 guns, and infantry advanced while engineers cleared lanes through the deep Axis minefields for the tanks, a task not completed because of the depth of the mines. Rommel was ill and absent. His replacement, Georg Stumme, suffered a heart attack and died on 24 October, and Hitler ordered Rommel back.

Montgomery then tried to crumble the Axis defences by attrition, with heavy artillery and air support. Rommel moved much of his armour north to meet the main attack, but a fuel shortage prevented him from reversing the move. On 2 November Operation Supercharge began, with the objective of destroying enemy armour. Rommel signalled that his army could offer no effective opposition to another break-through, and Hitler replied that he must stand fast.

The Axis forces were forced back from Egypt and Libya to the borders of Tunisia, and the battle ended the Axis threat to the Middle East and Iran. It revived the morale of the western Allies as their first large success against the Axis since late 1941, and its end coincided with the Allied landing in French North Africa on 8 November. On 10 November Churchill said that it was not the end, nor the beginning of the end, but perhaps the end of the beginning. The Allies had a comprehensive superiority, with Sherman tanks, 6-pounder anti-tank guns and Spitfires. Axis losses were heavy and the figures differ between sources, but the number of Axis prisoners had risen to 30,000 by 11 November.
second-battle-of-panipat: Humayun had been driven out of India by Sher Shah Suri, who founded the Sur Empire in 1540, and recovered Delhi and Agra on 23 July 1555 when the Mughals defeated Sikandar Shah Suri. The Sur realm was by then divided by a succession struggle after the death of Islam Shah Suri in 1554, and the ruler Adil Shah Suri left government largely to Hemchandra, a Hindu from Rewari who was both his chief minister and general of the Suri army. When Humayun died on 27 January 1556, Hemchandra marched rapidly from Bengal, drove the Mughals out of a series of towns and took Delhi on 7 October 1556 after defeating the governor Tardi Beg Khan. He assumed the title of Vikramaditya.

Akbar, then 13, and his guardian Bairam Khan set out for Delhi. Ali Quli Khan Shaibani, sent ahead with 10,000 cavalry, came upon Hemchandra's artillery under weak guard and captured all of it, a costly loss. On 5 November 1556 the armies met at Panipat, and Akbar and Bairam Khan stayed eight miles in the rear. Hemchandra had a numerically superior force, including 30,000 Afghan cavalry and 500 armoured war elephants, and had won 22 battles from Bengal to Punjab, but he had no artillery. He led the attack himself on the elephant Hawai, and the Mughal wings drew his elephants into a ravine, where they could not reach their opponents, while Mughal cavalry attacked the flanks and rear.

The battle seemed to turn in Hemchandra's favour until an arrow struck him in the eye and he collapsed unconscious. His army panicked and fled. Some 5,000 died on the field, and many more were killed in flight.

Hemchandra's elephant was captured with him unconscious and almost dead. Muhammad Arif Qandhari recorded that Akbar followed Bairam Khan's advice and beheaded him, taking the title Ghazi, whereas Akbar's later courtier Abu'l-Fazl said he refused to strike a dead man, an account that is probably a later invention. Hemchandra's head was sent to Kabul and his body displayed at Delhi. Adil Shah was defeated and killed in April 1557. The spoils included 120 of Hemchandra's war elephants, whose rampages impressed the Mughals and made elephants an integral part of their military strategy.
second-battle-of-tarain: Prithviraj Chauhan's forces had defeated the Ghurids on the same field at the First Battle of Tarain in 1191, after which Mu'izz al-Din, seriously injured, returned to Ghazni and prepared to avenge his defeat. The size of the armies is uncertain. The 16th–17th-century writer Firishta gave the Chauhan army 3,000 elephants and 300,000 cavalry and infantry, figures that modern historians such as Satish Chandra and Kaushik Roy regard as exaggerated, while Minhaj-i-Siraj credits Mu'izz al-Din with 120,000 armoured men. The Hammir Mahakavya and Prithviraj Raso say that only part of Prithviraj's army was on the field.

According to Hasan Nizami's Taj-ul ma asir, Prithviraj advised Muhammad Ghuri to return home, and Ghuri replied that he would ask his brother, the reigning ruler, to approve a peace in which the Ghurids would take Tarhind, Punjab and Multan. Nizami and Firishta make clear that this was a deception, which Prithviraj accepted as a genuine truce. The Ghurids, formed into five units, attacked before sunrise while the Chahamana army had passed the night in slumber and merry-making.

Minhaj describes 10,000 mounted archers in four divisions sent to surround the enemy on four sides, with orders not to engage when attacked but to fall back and wear out the elephants, horses and infantry. A fifth unit feigned retreat, drawing the Chahamana troops into a charge that a fresh unit of 12,000 cavalry then repelled. When the remaining Ghurid forces attacked, the Chahamana troops fled in panic.

Prithviraj left his elephant, fled on horseback and was captured near Sursuti. Most medieval sources say he was taken to Ajmer, where Muhammad planned to reinstate him as a vassal, and was killed for treason after rebelling. The Ghurids subjugated the whole Chahamana territory and placed his son Govindaraja IV on the throne of Ajmer. Prithviraj's younger brother Hariraja dethroned Govindaraja and recaptured part of the kingdom, but was defeated by the Ghurid general Qutb al-Din Aibak, and the Ghurids went on to defeat Jayachandra of the Gahadavala dynasty at the Battle of Chandawar and conquer northern India as far as Bengal.
second-boer-war: Britain occupied the Cape permanently after the Battle of Blaauwberg in 1806, and many Boers, itinerant farmers on the colony's frontiers, were dissatisfied with British administration, in particular the abolition of slavery in 1834. Britain annexed the bankrupt Transvaal in 1877, and the Boers regained their independence after the First Boer War of 1880 to 1881. The discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand in June 1884 brought thousands of prospectors, mostly British, who were allowed to vote only after 14 years' residence. In 1895 Leander Starr Jameson led a column of 600 armed men from Bechuanaland towards Johannesburg in the Jameson Raid. President Kruger re-equipped the Transvaal army with 37,000 Mauser rifles. The conference at Bloemfontein, which began on 30 May 1899, broke down.

War was declared on 11 October 1899 with a Boer offensive into Natal and the Cape Colony, and the Boers besieged Ladysmith, Mafeking and Kimberley. Under General Sir Redvers Buller the British suffered defeats at Stormberg, Magersfontein, Colenso and Spion Kop. Lord Roberts replaced Buller, with Lord Kitchener as chief of staff, and by January 1900 Britain had sent 180,000 men, the largest force it had ever sent overseas. Kimberley was relieved on 15 February 1900, Johannesburg was captured on 31 May and Pretoria on 5 June. Roberts declared the war over on 3 September 1900, and the South African Republic was annexed.

The Boers then turned to guerrilla war, raiding railways and supply targets. The British built over 8,000 blockhouses and adopted a scorched earth policy, destroying crops, poisoning wells and burning farms, and interning Boer and African civilians in concentration camps. Over 100,000 Boer civilians were relocated, and 26,000 died of starvation and disease. About 20,000 interned Africans also died. Many British soldiers died of disease, and few combatants were killed in action.

Eager to see Boers released from the camps, most Boer commanders accepted Kitchener's terms in the Treaty of Vereeniging and surrendered in May 1902. The former republics became the British colonies of the Transvaal and Orange River, and in 1910 they joined the Natal and Cape Colonies in the Union of South Africa, a self-governing colony within the British Empire. International opinion was sympathetic to the Boers, and volunteers came from Germany, the United States, Russia, Australia and Ireland. Opposition to the war was significant within the United Kingdom itself. Some consider that the war's surprising duration and unforeseen losses began the questioning of British dominance.
second-continental-congress: The Second Continental Congress met in Philadelphia on 10 May 1775, with representatives of 12 of the 13 colonies, after the first battles of the Revolutionary War at Lexington and Concord on 19 April. It succeeded the First Continental Congress of September and October 1774, which had sent entreaties to King George III against the Intolerable Acts and created the Continental Association to boycott British goods. Many delegates had attended the first Congress. They elected Peyton Randolph president and Charles Thomson secretary, and Benjamin Franklin and John Hancock were notable arrivals. Randolph was soon recalled to Virginia, Hancock succeeded him and Thomas Jefferson joined the Virginia delegation. Georgia endorsed the Congress in July 1775.

At first the Congress acted as the de facto government. On 14 June 1775 it voted to create the Continental Army from the militia units around Boston, and the next day it unanimously named George Washington of Virginia its commanding general. On 6 July it approved the Declaration of Causes for taking up arms, and two days later delegates signed the Olive Branch Petition to George III. The king, who had already proclaimed on 23 August a state of open and avowed rebellion, refused to receive it.

The Congress had no legal authority from Britain but appointed ambassadors, signed treaties, raised armies, borrowed in Europe and issued paper money called Continentals. It could not levy taxes and had to ask the states for funds, supplies and troops, which they often ignored.

In May 1776 it recommended that colonies without governments inclined to independence form new ones. On 7 June Richard Henry Lee offered the resolution declaring the colonies independent, and the Congress created three committees to draft a declaration, a model treaty and the Articles of Confederation. It approved the resolution of independence on 2 July 1776 and the Declaration of Independence on 4 July. In the winter of 1776 to 1777 it moved to Baltimore, and from late September 1777 to York, Pennsylvania, when British troops took Philadelphia.

The Congress passed the Articles of Confederation on 15 November 1777, and Virginia ratified first, on 16 December 1777. Each state was given one vote, and western land claims remained with the states. Maryland, the last holdout, ratified on 2 February 1781, after Virginia gave up its claims north of the Ohio River. On 1 March 1781 the body became what is often called the Confederation Congress. During its years as provisional government it managed the war effort, secured diplomatic recognition and support from foreign nations and resolved state land claims west of the Appalachian Mountains.
second-crusade: After the First Crusade three Crusader states stood in the east, the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Edessa, with the County of Tripoli added in 1109. Edessa was the most northerly, weakest and least populated, and was exposed to attack from Artuqid, Danishmendid and Seljuk neighbours. Zengi, atabeg of Mosul, took Aleppo in 1128. News of Edessa's fall reached Europe in 1145, and Pope Eugene III issued the bull Quantum praedecessores on 1 December. It met a poor response and was reissued on 1 March 1146. Bernard of Clairvaux preached the crusade at Vézelay on 31 March 1146, where Louis VII and Eleanor of Aquitaine took the cross, and then in Germany, where Conrad III received it at Speyer.

The German army of about 20,000 men left in May 1147 and the French in June, both going overland through Hungary and Byzantine territory. Emperor Manuel I Komnenos feared an attack and posted troops, and the Germans, after a clash at Constantinople, crossed into Anatolia quickly. Later sources, notably Odo of Deuil, accuse Manuel of having the Turks attack the Crusaders, but this is likely an invention of Odo. Both armies were separately defeated by the Seljuks. Louis reached Antioch on 19 March 1148 but refused Raymond of Poitiers's request to attack Aleppo, preferring to finish his pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

On 24 June 1148 the High Court of Jerusalem and the Crusaders met at Palmarea near Acre and chose to attack Damascus, a former ally of Jerusalem. Historians have long called this inexplicable folly, though David Nicolle defends it, arguing that Damascus was the most powerful Muslim state in southern Syria. The Crusaders arrived at Darayya on 23 July 1148 and were pushed back from the orchards by the defenders and Nur ad-Din. They moved to a less defended eastern plain with little food and water. The local lords refused to continue, and the army retreated on 28 July, harassed by Turkish archers all the way.

In the east each side felt betrayed by the other, and the distrust lingered for a generation, to the ruin of the Christian kingdoms. In Iberia the crusade was successful: crusaders from England landed at Porto in June 1147 and helped Afonso I of Portugal take Lisbon after a siege from 1 July to 25 October, and they also helped conquer Sintra, Almada, Palmela and Setúbal. Louis left Jerusalem in 1149, and he and Eleanor, barely speaking, boarded separate ships in April 1149. Bernard of Clairvaux, humiliated, wrote an apology to the pope attributing the failure to the sins of the Crusaders.
second-dynasty-of-egypt: The Second Dynasty is the latter of the two dynasties of the Egyptian Archaic Period, when the seat of government was centred at Thinis. It is best known for its last ruler, Khasekhemwy, and is otherwise one of the most obscure periods of Egyptian history. Archaeological evidence is very scant, but contrasting data from the First and Third Dynasties indicates important institutional and economic developments during these years.

Manetho states that Thinis was the capital, as in the First Dynasty, but the first three kings were buried at Saqqara, which suggests that the centre of power had moved to Memphis. For the first three pharaohs the sources are fairly close in agreement, and their order is supported by an inscription on the statuette of Hetepdief, who served in the mortuary cults of these kings. The identity of the next few rulers is unclear: surviving sources may give a Horus name, a Nebty name or a birth name, or may name entirely different individuals or names with no firm historical basis.

It has been theorised that after the reign of Nynetjer the country was split and ruled by two successors, because the administration of the whole of Egypt had become overly complex. The annual records on the Palermo stone survive only to the end of the reign of Nebra and for parts of that of Nynetjer, so little can be said of events.

The dynasty saw the advent of the first known complete sentences in Egyptian hieroglyphs. Probably the first is a seal impression from the tomb of Peribsen, dating to about 2660 to 2650 BCE, which relates to the unification of Egypt: He of Ombos has joined the Two Lands for his son, the Dual King Peribsen.

The base of a statue of Khasekhemwy shows slain enemies on its four sides, recording a campaign against the northern rebels, the inhabitants of the Nile Delta. The number of dead is given as 47,209. The scene seems to record his victory over a northern population led by its ruler, Besh, a name that may be a variant of Peribsen or that of a Libyan tribe near the Fayum. The unification of Upper and Lower Egypt might have occurred under Khasekhemwy, since many Egyptologists read his name as the Two Powers arise. The king crushing enemies at his feet remained a central theme of royal iconography for three millennia.
second-fitna: The roots of the war lay in the First Fitna, which followed the killing of the caliph Uthman in 656. Mu'awiya I became sole ruler after the killing of Ali in 661 and the abdication of Ali's son Hasan, and in 676 he announced the nomination of his son Yazid as successor. With no precedent in Islamic history, hereditary succession aroused opposition, and it was regarded as turning the caliphate into a monarchy. The sons of several prominent companions of Muhammad, including Husayn ibn Ali and Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, objected, but Mu'awiya's threats and the general recognition of Yazid silenced them until Mu'awiya died in 680.

The war brought three challenges to Umayyad rule: Husayn and the pro-Alid movements, Ibn al-Zubayr, and the Kharijites. Husayn, invited by supporters in Kufa, was intercepted at Karbala and killed in October 680. Yazid's Syrian army suppressed a rebellion in Medina in August 683 and besieged Mecca, where Ibn al-Zubayr had established himself, but the siege was abandoned after Yazid died in November. Most provinces then recognised Ibn al-Zubayr, while in parts of Syria Marwan I was proclaimed caliph. The Penitents under Sulayman ibn Surad were crushed at Ayn al-Warda in January 685.

Mukhtar al-Thaqafi took Kufa in October 685, drawing support from non-Arab converts, the mawali, and his forces routed an Umayyad army at the Battle of Khazir in August 686, but he and his followers were killed by the Zubayrids in April 687.

Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan reconquered Iraq by defeating the Zubayrids at the Battle of Maskin in 691, and Ibn al-Zubayr was killed in the second siege of Mecca in 692. The Kharijites had split into the moderate Najdat in central Arabia and the extremist Azariqa, who sanctioned killing the women and children of their opponents. Organised Kharijite resistance collapsed by 692, with al-Muhallab's long campaigns in Persia eliminating the Azariqa.

The victory restored Umayyad authority and secured hereditary rule, and Abd al-Malik and his descendants held the caliphate for another fifty-eight years, until the Abbasid revolution of 750. He centralised caliphal power, restructured the military and carried out policies of Arabization and Islamization in the bureaucracy. The war also deepened the rivalry between the Qays and the Yaman among the Arab tribes. The death of Husayn is commemorated every year by Shi'a Muslims on the Day of Ashura, and the events of the war intensified sectarian tendencies from which the Sunni and Shi'a denominations later developed.
second-franco-dahomean-war: In 1890 the Kingdom of Dahomey and France had fought the First Franco-Dahomean War over rights to territory in the Ouémé Valley. After two defeats the Fon signed a treaty conceding all French demands, but Dahomey remained a strong power in the region and re-armed. Before the second war it stockpiled between 4,000 and 6,000 rifles, among them Mannlicher and Winchester carbines bought from German merchants through the port of Whydah, and King Béhanzin also bought some machine guns and Krupp cannons, though it is unlikely these were ever used.

When the Fon resumed raids in the valley, Victor Ballot, the French Resident at Porto-Novo, went upriver by gunboat to investigate; his ship was attacked and five men were wounded. Béhanzin rejected French complaints, and France declared war. Colonel Alfred-Amédée Dodds of the Troupes de marine brought Foreign Legionnaires, marines, engineers, artillery, Senegalese spahis and tirailleurs, and the French protectorate kingdom of Porto-Novo supplied some 2,600 porters.

French gunboats fired the first shots on 4 July 1892, shelling villages along the lower Ouémé, and the column moved inland in mid-August. At Dogba on 19 September the Fon attacked for three to four hours, leaving hundreds dead to five French dead. At Poguessa on 4 October Béhanzin led the attack himself and lost some 200 soldiers against 42 French casualties. At Adégon on 6 October the Fon lost 86 regulars and 417 Amazons, and the royal court lost hope.

The Fon then turned to guerrilla tactics, fighting from foxholes and trenches, and the French took a month to cover the 40 kilometres to Cana. By early November Béhanzin's army numbered no more than 1,500, including slaves and pardoned convicts, and it was overrun after fighting at Cana and the palace village of Diokoué.

A truce mission sent on 5 November failed. When the French entered Abomey, the tricolour was hoisted over the Singboji palace, which survived the fire and still stands in modern Benin. Béhanzin fled to Atcheribé, 48 kilometres north, and tried to rebuild his army and its Amazon corps until the French chose his brother Goutchili as the new king.
second-french-empire: On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, elected President of the Republic in 1848, dissolved the National Assembly without the constitutional right to do so and restored universal male suffrage. A referendum later that month, which reported 92 percent support, approved a new constitution that made him president for ten years. A second referendum in November 1852 reported 97 percent, though most of the yes votes were manufactured. The Senate re-established the empire on 2 December 1852, and the constitution changed little beyond replacing the word president with emperor and making the post hereditary.

The constitution of 1852 entrusted all executive power to the emperor. The legislative body was elected by universal suffrage but could not propose laws or vote the budget in detail, and the press worked under caution money and official warnings. Napoleon III consolidated three dozen small railway lines into six major companies centred on Paris, and with Georges-Eugène Haussmann rebuilt the capital.

After a general amnesty on 16 August 1859 the regime moved towards a liberal, and later parliamentary, empire. A senatus-consulte of 8 September 1869 replaced personal government with a parliamentary monarchy, and Émile Ollivier headed a ministry from 2 January 1870. A plebiscite on 8 May 1870 brought seven and a half million votes in favour and one and a half million against.

Abroad, the Crimean War ended in 1856 with a peace that excluded Russia from the Black Sea. Napoleon III doubled the area of the overseas empire, with New Caledonia, Cochinchina and a protectorate over Cambodia in 1863. The intervention in Mexico, meant to set up the Second Mexican Empire under Maximilian, ended when the United States demanded French withdrawal; Maximilian stayed and was executed.

France declared war on Prussia on 15 July 1870 and found itself without allies. The French army surrendered at the Battle of Sedan, Napoleon III was taken prisoner, and the Third French Republic was proclaimed on 4 September 1870. France gave up Alsace and Lorraine, and the German Empire was created.

Napoleon III and the Empress Eugénie went into exile in England; their bodies lie in a mausoleum at Farnborough, today St Michael's Abbey. Historians of the 1930s and 1940s disparaged the regime as a precursor of fascism, but later writers have treated it as a modernising one, judging its foreign policy a failure and its domestic legacy more favourably.
second-french-intervention-in-mexico: Some Mexican conservatives hoped to restore a monarchy, as at the First Mexican Empire of Agustín I in 1821. Through his wife Eugénie de Montijo, Napoleon III met the monarchist exiles José María Gutiérrez de Estrada and José Manuel Hidalgo y Esnaurrízar, who had long sought a European prince for a Mexican throne. He was at first uninterested, expecting opposition from the United States, but the American Civil War offered an opportunity. The conservatives had been defeated by Juárez's liberal government in the three-year Reform War, and the Catholic Church, much of the upper class and some indigenous communities welcomed the French.

In July 1861 Juárez placed a moratorium on foreign debt payments and expelled all Spanish diplomats. Spain, France and a reluctant United Kingdom agreed to the Convention of London. On 14 December Spanish general Juan Prim occupied Veracruz with 6,200 soldiers, and French and British forces joined him on 7 January 1862.

Britain and Spain withdrew, leaving the French. Their army aimed to take Mexico City quickly, but Mexican republican forces defeated it at the Battle of Puebla on 5 May 1862, delaying the advance for a year. Juárez evacuated the capital and moved the government to San Luis Potosí. French and imperial forces captured much of the country, including Tampico on 11 August 1862 and by 26 September 1864 every major Gulf port, though republican guerrillas remained active and Juárez never left the national territory. At its peak in 1863 the French expeditionary force counted 38,493 men, and 6,654 French died, 4,830 of them from disease. Maximilian's Black Decree created liberal martyrs and deepened opposition to the empire.

After the Union victory in April 1865 the United States began supporting the republicans, and demobilised veterans went south to volunteer. Invoking the Monroe Doctrine, the American government said it would not tolerate a lasting French presence. Facing financial strain, discontent at home and the Prussian threat, Napoleon III announced a withdrawal in January 1866, in phases from November 1866 to November 1867.

Without French support the Second Mexican Empire collapsed. Maximilian and the conservative generals Miguel Miramón and Tomás Mejía were executed by firing squad on 19 June 1867. The republican victory consolidated liberal hegemony. The Conservative Party, discredited by its alliance with the French, became effectively defunct, and the Liberal Party was almost unchallenged in the first years of the Restored Republic. In 1871 Juárez was elected for another term despite a constitutional ban on re-election.
second-helvetic-confession: Heinrich Bullinger, the Swiss Reformed theologian who had also helped draw up the First Helvetic Confession at Basel in 1536, wrote the Second Helvetic Confession in 1562 and revised it in 1564 as a private exercise. It came to the notice of Frederick III, Elector Palatine, who had it translated into German and published. Some Reformed leaders welcomed it as a corrective to what they saw as the overly Lutheran statements of the Strasbourg Consensus.

Early in 1566 an attempt was made to have all the churches of Switzerland sign it as a common statement of faith. The Swiss churches, which had found the First Confession too short and too Lutheran, received it well, although the Basel clergy declined to sign, preferring to keep their own Basel Confession of 1534. On the strength of this near-universal approval Frederick presented it to the Diet of Augsburg of 1566 as an authoritative statement of the international Reformed faith.

The confession opens with Scripture as the sole infallible authority, its own interpreter, against which all other human writings are judged. It confesses the Trinity and accepts the Apostles' Creed, condemns images of God or Christ and rejects the invocation of saints while honouring them as examples of faith.

Its chapter on predestination has been read as moderate Calvinism or Augustinianism. It rejects confession to a priest and the doctrines of penance and indulgences, teaches an invisible Church known only to God, and holds that presbyter and bishop were one office in the apostolic Church. It counts two sacraments, condemns Eucharistic adoration of the Mass, and treats the civil magistrate as God's servant, condemning the Anabaptists, who held that a Christian should not hold civil office.

Reformed churches adopted the confession throughout Switzerland and in Scotland in 1566, Hungary in 1567, France in 1571 and Poland in 1578. According to Dezső Buzogány, in 17th- and 18th-century Hungary it was central to the training of future clergy, while the Heidelberg Catechism taught congregations and children. In 1791 the Hungarian Reformed Synod of Buda ordered schools to teach it as part of the official curriculum. In 1967 it was included in the Book of Confessions of the United Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A., and it remains in that of the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.).
second-intermediate-period: The Second Intermediate Period is the time when ancient Egypt was divided into smaller dynasties for the second time, dated from 1782 to 1550 BCE, between the end of the Middle Kingdom and the start of the New Kingdom. Egyptologists do not agree on how to define it. It is best known as the period when the Hyksos, a people of West Asia, established the 15th Dynasty and ruled from Avaris. Manetho's Aegyptiaca says the dynasty was founded by a king named Salitis and presents the Hyksos as invaders of an obscure race who conquered Egypt with brutality, although their settling may have occurred peacefully.
The primary source for its chronology is the Turin King List, from the time of Ramesses II, together with the study of scarabs, beetle-shaped amulets often inscribed with the names of rulers.

The 12th Dynasty ended in the late 19th century BCE with the death of Queen Sobekneferu, who left no heirs, and the weaker 13th Dynasty followed, ruling for most of its existence from Itjtawy. It moved to Thebes, possibly in the reign of Merneferre Ay, and after it withdrew its southern garrisons the rising Nubian state of Kush reoccupied the forts. A provincial family in the Nile Delta broke away to form the 14th Dynasty, and in the north the Hyksos took Lower Egypt.

The Hyksos kings of the 15th Dynasty ruled Lower Egypt from Avaris for about a hundred years, and Avaris may have been the largest city in the world from 1670 to 1557 BCE. Whether the Hyksos came as an army or as a mass migration from Palestine is still debated. In Upper Egypt the 16th Dynasty ruled the Theban region and was eventually subsumed around 1580 BCE. A short-lived Abydos Dynasty may have ruled part of Upper Egypt in the meantime. The Thebans then founded the 17th Dynasty, which made a short peace with the Hyksos.

The peace ended in the reign of Seqenenre, who began a series of wars against the Hyksos and died in battle. His successor Kamose continued the war, and his brother Ahmose I dealt the final blow, expelled the Hyksos, united Upper and Lower Egypt and became the first king of the 18th Dynasty and the New Kingdom.

Advances of the period were adopted by the early New Kingdom, among them the horse and chariot, the composite bow and the khopesh sickle sword, although the credit given to Avaris for the chariot is contested. The Hyksos adopted Egyptian royal titles and hieroglyphic inscriptions and worshipped the Egyptian pantheon, taking Set as their patron god. A strontium isotope analysis favoured a migration model over an invasion.
second-international: By the 1880s rapid industrialisation, especially in Germany, had created a new urban proletariat, and the extension of the vote made mass parliamentary parties of the working class possible. The strongest was the Social Democratic Party of Germany, founded in 1875 at Gotha by a merger of Marxist and Lassallean groups and led by Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel. French socialism was more divided, among several factions.

The demand for an eight-hour day was taken up by French socialists, and the centenary of the French Revolution in 1889 offered an occasion for a congress. Because of the French divisions two rival congresses met in Paris: the Possibilists, with the British Trades Union Congress, in the Rue de Lancry, and the Marxists, led by Jules Guesde and supported by the SPD, in the Salle Petrelle.

The early congresses were absorbed by the struggle against the anarchists. After their exclusion the International had to face the question of revolution or reform. Eduard Bernstein argued from 1896 that Marx's predictions of collapse had proved wrong and that the movement should embrace gradual reform. In France, the socialist Alexandre Millerand joined the government of Pierre Waldeck-Rousseau in June 1899, causing a great controversy. At Amsterdam in 1904 Jean Jaurès and August Bebel debated, and the congress condemned revisionism and ministerialism.

After the Russo-Japanese War and the Russian Revolution of 1905, preventing war became its central task, and the congresses of Stuttgart (1907), Copenhagen (1910) and Basel (1912) passed ever more urgent resolutions. The containment of the Balkan Wars brought optimism, and by 1913 many leaders believed the threat of war had receded. The International was caught off guard by the crisis of July 1914. Jaurès was assassinated, and the major parties supported their governments in the war, a split between pro-war majorities and an anti-war minority that prefigured the later division between social democracy and communism.

The Second International was a loose federation of autonomous national parties and trade unions, with no executive machinery in its first decade; the London Congress of 1896 affirmed the autonomy of national groups. The Paris Congress of 1900 created the International Socialist Bureau in Brussels, which grew in authority under its secretary Camille Huysmans after 1905 but remained an organ of correlation, not direction.

The conference at Bern in February 1919 failed to revive it, and it was succeeded by the Communist International in 1919 and the Labour and Socialist International in 1923. Lenin called its collapse a betrayal by opportunist leaders; Georges Haupt argued that it came from the International's long-standing contradictions, among them parties with no means of enforcing joint action.
second-intifada: Under the Oslo Accords, signed in 1993 and 1995, Israel committed to a phased withdrawal of its forces from parts of the Gaza Strip and West Bank and affirmed Palestinian self-government there through a Palestinian Authority. The Palestine Liberation Organization formally recognised Israel and took on responsibility for internal security in the evacuated areas. Self-rule was to last five years while a permanent agreement was negotiated, but both sides were deeply disappointed with the process and blamed each other for its failure.

From 11 to 25 July 2000 the Camp David summit brought together US President Bill Clinton, Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat. The talks failed, each side blaming the other.

On 28 September 2000 the Israeli opposition leader Ariel Sharon visited the Temple Mount, also known as the Haram al-Sharif, with a Likud delegation guarded by hundreds of riot police. He said that it was the holiest site in Judaism and the right of every Jew to visit it. Palestinians saw the visit as provocative, and protests and riots followed, which Israeli forces dispersed with tear gas, rubber bullets and live ammunition. In the first five days Israeli forces killed 47 Palestinians, and Palestinians killed five Israelis.

Unlike the First Intifada of 1987 to 1993, which was a civil uprising of mass protests and strikes, the Second Intifada rapidly became an armed conflict. Palestinian groups including Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and the al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades carried out shootings, rocket attacks and about 138 suicide bombings after March 2001, mostly aimed at Israeli civilians. The Israel Defense Forces responded with incursions into the West Bank and Gaza Strip, airstrikes and targeted killings.

The violence is estimated to have killed about 3,000 Palestinians, 1,000 Israelis and 64 foreign nationals. The uprising ended with the Sharm el-Sheikh summit of 2005, where the Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas and Prime Minister Sharon agreed to de-escalate and reaffirmed the roadmap for peace proposed by the Quartet in 2003. Israel's disengagement from the Gaza Strip was completed in August 2005. The ending date is disputed, since no single event closed it; some place it in late 2004, after Arafat's death. Israeli public support for the Oslo Accords fell, according to surveys, from 39% in May 2000 to 26% in May 2004.
second-italian-war-of-independence: After Piedmont's defeat by Austria in the First Italian War of Independence, Prime Minister Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, looked for allies, partly by taking Piedmont into the Crimean War. Britain and France were sympathetic but would not act against Austria. On 14 January 1858 Felice Orsini led an attempt on the life of Napoleon III, which brought sympathy for Italian unity and left the emperor determined to help Piedmont.

After a covert meeting at Plombières on 21 July 1858, Napoleon III and Cavour signed a secret alliance against Austria on 28 January 1859. France would help Sardinia if it were attacked, in return for Nice and Savoy. Cavour provoked Vienna with military manoeuvres near the border; Sardinia mobilised on 9 March 1859, Austria on 9 April, and an Austrian ultimatum of 23 April demanding demobilisation led to war on 26 April.

The French army, about 170,000 strong under Napoleon III, moved into Piedmont in the first massive military use of railways. The Austrian commander, Count Gyulai, was cautious, and heavy rain, together with rice fields flooded by the Piedmontese, slowed his advance. Napoleon III arrived at Alessandria on 14 May and took command. After the Battle of Montebello on 20 May and the Battle of Turbigo, the allies entered Lombardy and defeated the Austrians at the Battle of Magenta. Gyulai was relieved, and Emperor Franz Josef took command himself.

The two armies met by accident around Solferino on 24 June, and after a day of confused fighting the French broke through and the Austrians withdrew into the fortresses of the Quadrilateral. Giuseppe Garibaldi's Hunters of the Alps meanwhile defeated the Austrians at Varese and Como. A ceasefire was agreed on 8 July, and the two emperors met at Villafranca di Verona on 11 July; the armistice was signed the next day.

Napoleon III made peace partly because the Quadrilateral would be costly to attack, France was exposed in his absence, his actions were criticised at home and he feared involvement of the German states. Under the armistice Lombardy, apart from Mantua and Legnago, passed from Austria to France and then to Sardinia. Cavour resigned in protest at a deal made behind Sardinia's back. The terms never took effect, since Piedmont occupied the central Italian states and would not restore their rulers.

On 22 March 1860 the United Provinces of Central Italy were annexed by Sardinia, and France received Savoy and Nice. Garibaldi, a native of Nice, opposed the cession, which led to his expedition to Sicily. Austria's influence in Italy was severely weakened. Prussia mobilised 132,000 men but never fought, and the weaknesses it found led to military reforms that underlay its victories over Austria in 1866 and France in 1870-71.
second-italo-ethiopian-war: Italy began to seek colonies in the Horn of Africa in the 1880s. That phase ended with the defeat of Italian forces at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896 by the army of Negus Menelik II. Afterwards Italy kept only Italian Eritrea and Italian Somaliland, and for decades its economic and diplomatic relations with Ethiopia stayed relatively stable.

In 1930 Italy built a fort at the Walwal oasis in the Ogaden, garrisoned by Somali dubats under Italian officers, well beyond the border set by the Italo-Ethiopian Treaty of 1928. Britain and France, preferring Italy as an ally against Germany, did little to discourage the Italian build-up. In April 1935 mobilisation began, and between February 1935 and January 1936 six army divisions were sent to Eritrea and one to Somalia.

On 3 October 1935 Marshal Emilio De Bono led some two hundred thousand soldiers across the Mareb River from Eritrea without a declaration of war, while a smaller force under General Rodolfo Graziani attacked from Somalia. Adwa fell on 6 October, and Aksum on 15 October, where its obelisk was taken down and sent to Rome. Benito Mussolini, impatient at De Bono's caution, replaced him with General Pietro Badoglio on 14 November.

An Ethiopian counterattack in December 1935 halted the advance for a time. Mussolini had authorised gas in an order of 27 October 1935, and the Regia Aeronautica dropped about 330 tons of mustard gas over the following months, against the 1925 Geneva Protocol. The Italians resumed the offensive in February 1936 and defeated the Ethiopian armies at Amba Aradam, Tembien and Shire, then won at Maychew on 31 March, ending organised resistance. Haile Selassie went into exile on 2 May, Badoglio entered Addis Ababa on 5 May, and Mussolini announced the annexation on 9 May, forming Italian East Africa.

Hundreds of thousands of Ethiopian civilians died in the invasion, which some historians have described as genocide. After an attempt on Graziani's life on 19 February 1937, Italian reprisals in Addis Ababa killed thousands; estimates range from a few hundred in Italian sources to 30,000 in Ethiopian ones. Resistance continued until Haile Selassie returned with British and Ethiopian forces in 1941 and entered Addis Ababa on 5 May.

The war was a propaganda success for the Fascist regime, but it strained Italy's budget. It ended the Stresa Front with the Western powers and led Italy towards Nazi Germany, while the failure of the League of Nations to stop the invasion discredited that body in the years before the Second World War.
second-macedonian-war: In 204 BCE King Ptolemy IV Philopator of Egypt died, leaving the throne to his six-year-old son Ptolemy V. Philip V of Macedon and Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire made a secret pact on spheres of interest, which opened the Fifth Syrian War. Philip's capture of cities in Thrace and near the Dardanelles alarmed Rhodes and King Attalus I of Pergamon, who appealed to Rome, which had just won the Second Punic War.

Athens also broke with Philip after two Acarnanians who entered the Temple of Demeter during the Eleusinian Mysteries were put to death in 201 BCE. On 15 March 200 BCE the consul Publius Sulpicius Galba took office. The Comitia centuriata first rejected his proposed war almost unanimously, an unprecedented act attributed to war weariness, but a second session voted for it.

Sulpicius crossed the Adriatic in the autumn of 200 BCE and based himself on the Seman river in Illyria. The Illyrians, Dardanians and Athamanians joined the Roman side, and in 199 BCE he campaigned in Upper Macedonia in indecisive clashes. Philip ravaged the sanctuaries of Attica, damage that marked the permanent end of their use.

Titus Quinctius Flamininus took command in 198 BCE, not yet thirty and a self-proclaimed Philhellene. He demanded that Philip make reparations and withdraw his garrisons from every city outside Macedonia, including Thessaly. When Philip refused, Flamininus won the Battle of the Aous after being shown a pass that let him attack from the rear. Talks at Nicaea in Locris in November 198 BCE failed; Polybius and Plutarch say Flamininus drew them out until he learnt that his command had been extended. In June 197 BCE his legions defeated Philip's phalanx at Cynoscephalae.

The final peace of spring 196 BCE required Philip to remove his garrisons from Greek cities in Europe and Asia, pay an indemnity of 1,000 talents and surrender his navy except his flagship. His army was limited to 5,000 men, without elephants, and could not leave his borders without the Senate's permission. At the Isthmian Games of May 196 BCE Flamininus proclaimed the freedom of the Greeks, to general rejoicing. The Romans nevertheless kept garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, and the legions were not fully withdrawn until 194 BCE.

The Aetolians, who had wanted harsher terms, claimed that Rome meant to replace Macedon as overlord of Greece, and the quarrel led to the Aetolian War. Antiochus III advanced into the Asia Minor communities that Philip had given up, which led to the Roman-Seleucid War. The war marked a significant stage in the decline of Macedon and in Rome's growing involvement in the eastern Mediterranean.
second-messenian-war: In the First Messenian War, fought from 743 to 724 BCE, Sparta conquered the south-western Peloponnese after two decades of struggle, and the Messenians were made helots, serfs of the Spartan state. Tradition held that the first war began when Messenian men carried off Spartan women praying at a temple and refused to return them. The second war is usually dated c. 660-650 BCE, some forty years after the first, though some scholars place its start in 668 BCE and see Sparta's defeat at the First Battle of Hysiae as a possible spur to the rising.

The war began as a revolt of the helots of Messenia, backed by the Argives and the Arcadians, and the Messenians invaded Laconia. In the traditional account Aristomenes fought so well at the Battle of Deres, before the allies arrived, that his people made him king. He crossed into Sparta and set a shield in the temple of Athena to frighten the Spartans, who consulted Delphi and were told to take a leader from Athens. Aristomenes then defeated them at Boar's Grave.

Sparta gained the upper hand at the Battle of the Great Foss by bribing Aristocrates, king of the allied Arcadians, to retreat through the Messenian lines as the Spartans advanced. The Messenians withdrew to a fortified town at Eira and raided the surrounding towns from it, Aristomenes leading some of the raids himself. He was once captured but escaped before he could be executed. The Messenians held Eira for more than ten years.

Before Eira fell the Spartans let the women and children go, with Aristomenes, who went to Rhodes, died there and was honoured as a hero. Most of those who escaped fled to Italy, and those who stayed were made helots again. Local resistance may have lasted to the end of the century. To hold down the helots and prevent further risings, Sparta became a strongly militarised society. The Messenians broke free of Spartan rule only in 371 BCE, with Theban help.
second-mithridatic-war: At the end of the First Mithridatic War, Lucius Cornelius Sulla had made a hasty peace with Mithridates VI because he needed to return to Rome to face his enemies. Mithridates kept the Kingdom of Pontus but gave up his claims in Asia Minor and returned to the pre-war borders. Murena, Sulla's legate, was left in Asia with the two legions formerly under Gaius Flavius Fimbria. Mithridates was then fitting out a fleet and raising an army against a rebellion of the Colchians and the tribes around the Cimmerian Bosphorus. The scale of these preparations, and his failure to return the whole of Cappadocia to its king, the Roman ally Ariobarzanes I, aroused Roman suspicion.

According to Appian, Murena marched through Cappadocia and attacked Comana, a town of Mithridates. When envoys invoked the peace, he replied that he saw no treaty, since Sulla had never put it in writing. In 82 BCE he seized 400 villages belonging to Mithridates, who did not resist while he waited for his ambassadors to return from Rome. A messenger told Murena that the senate wished Mithridates left alone, but he brought no decree and was seen speaking with Murena in private.

When Murena invaded again, Mithridates took it as Rome's will and sent his commander Gordius to raid Roman villages. In the hard battle that followed Murena was defeated and fled to Phrygia, and many states of Asia Minor went over to Mithridates, who drove the Roman garrisons out of Cappadocia. Another ancient account tells a different story, in which Murena founded the city of Licinia near the border and a battle near Sinope ended even.

Sulla disapproved of the war, since Mithridates had not broken the treaty, and sent Aulus Gabinius to make Murena obey. Gabinius brought Mithridates and Ariobarzanes together; Mithridates betrothed his four-year-old daughter to Ariobarzanes, who kept the part of Cappadocia he held and received another. Murena was recalled to Rome. The Third Mithridatic War followed.
second-northern-war: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 confirmed Sweden as a major power and replaced Denmark-Norway as the leading state in the Baltic. Sweden remained at war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, though a truce had been renewed since 1630. The Commonwealth was weakened by rebellions such as the Khmelnytsky Uprising and by conflict between King John II Casimir Vasa and the Sejm.

When Russian troops invaded in the Russo-Polish War (1654-67) and neared the Baltic coast, Charles X Gustav of Sweden intervened, claiming to protect Polish Protestants. Talks in Lübeck ended in February 1655 without result because John II Casimir would not drop his claims to the Swedish crown, and Sweden decided on a preemptive attack.

Swedish forces entered the Commonwealth in July 1655 from Swedish Pomerania and Livonia. The nobles of Greater Poland surrendered at Ujście, and by the Treaty of Kėdainiai Prince Janusz Radziwiłł placed Lithuania under Swedish protection. Charles X Gustav occupied Warsaw on 8 September, won at Żarnów and Wojnicz, and Kraków surrendered on 19 October. John II Casimir went into exile in Silesia. The rapid occupation became known in Poland as the deluge.

Resistance grew after Swedes looted Catholic churches and mistreated clergy. The monastery of Jasna Góra in Częstochowa withstood a siege from November 1655 to January 1656, and John II Casimir returned on 1 January 1656. Russia declared war on Sweden in May 1656. Brandenburg, allied with Sweden, took the Duchy of Prussia as a fief in the Treaty of Königsberg of 17 January 1656 and later full sovereignty in the Treaty of Labiau. In 1657 it changed sides, winning Polish withdrawal of claims in the treaties of Wehlau and Bromberg.

When Denmark declared war in 1657, Charles X Gustav marched on Jutland. In February 1658 a Swedish army crossed the frozen Belts, and Frederick III of Denmark signed the Treaty of Roskilde on 26 February 1658, yielding Scania, Halland, Blekinge, Bornholm and Trøndelag. Sweden attacked Denmark again in August 1658, but Copenhagen did not surrender.

Charles X Gustav died on 23 February 1660, and the Treaty of Oliva was signed on 23 April. Sweden was accepted as sovereign in Swedish Livonia, Brandenburg in Ducal Prussia, and John II Casimir withdrew his claims to the Swedish throne. Occupied territories were restored to their earlier sovereigns. The Treaty of Copenhagen returned Bornholm and Trøndelag to Denmark, and the borders it set among Denmark, Sweden and Norway have lasted to the present day. Russia settled with Sweden in the Treaty of Cardis in 1661. Historians are split on whether Sweden or the Commonwealth emerged the victor.
second-partition-of-poland: By 1790 the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth had fallen into such a helpless condition that it was forced into an alliance with Prussia, signed as the Polish-Prussian Pact of 1790. The Constitution of 3 May 1791 enfranchised the bourgeoisie and separated the three branches of government. These reforms prompted aggressive actions by neighbours wary of a revival of the Commonwealth. Empress Catherine II, arguing that Poland had fallen prey to the Jacobinism then at its height in France, sent Russian forces into the Commonwealth in 1792. They were invited by the Targowica Confederation, an alliance of pro-Russian Polish magnates who believed the Russians would help them restore their Golden Liberty.

Polish forces under Prince Józef Poniatowski fought a defensive war with some success in the Polish–Russian War of 1792, but they were ordered to abandon the effort by King Stanisław August Poniatowski, who joined the Targowica Confederation as the Russians demanded. Russia had no overt aim of another partition, but Frederick William II of Prussia asked to be compensated, preferably with Polish land, for abandoning Poland as an ally and for taking part in the War of the First Coalition against France. Russia accepted. On 23 January 1793 the two states signed a treaty that revoked the Polish reforms and shared broad areas of the Commonwealth between them.

Russia annexed 250,000 square kilometres, including the Kiev Voivodeship, Bracław Voivodeship, Podole Voivodeship and Minsk Voivodeship, while Prussia took 58,000 square kilometres, including Gdańsk, Toruń and the voivodeships of Gniezno and Poznań, and organised them as South Prussia. The Commonwealth lost about 307,000 square kilometres and about 5 million people, leaving some 215,000 square kilometres and about 4 million people.

The Grodno Sejm, the last of the Commonwealth, accepted the demands in the presence of Russian forces; it became infamous because its deputies had been bribed and coerced. Russia accepted its gains on 22 July. What remained was a small buffer state with a puppet king and Russian garrisons watching a reduced army. The Targowica confederates and the king lost prestige, while the reformers gained support. In March 1794 the Kościuszko Uprising began, and its defeat in November led to the Third Partition, which ended the Commonwealth.
second-peace-of-thorn: The Thirteen Years' War, the longest of the Polish–Teutonic Wars, began in February 1454 when the Prussian Confederation, led by the cities of Danzig (Gdańsk), Elbing (Elbląg), Kulm (Chełmno) and Toruń together with the Prussian gentry, rose against the rule of the Teutonic Knights in order to join the Kingdom of Poland. In the end both sides had exhausted their money and sought a negotiated peace. Talks opened at Nieszawa on 23 September 1466 and moved to Toruń for their last stages. The treaty was signed by King Casimir IV Jagiellon and the Order in the Artus Court on 19 October, followed by a mass in the Franciscan Church of the Assumption.

The Order renounced Gdańsk Pomerania and Chełmno Land, and recognised the region of Elbing and Marienburg (Malbork) and the Bishopric of Warmia as Polish. The Diocese of Chełmno became a suffragan of the Archdiocese of Gniezno. Each Grand Master had to swear allegiance to the Polish king within six months of taking office and became a prince and counsellor of the king.

Any lands the Order gained, even outside Prussia, would belong to Poland; Poles were to be admitted to the Order; the knights had to help Poland in war and could not fight Catholics without the king's consent. Prisoners were released. Both sides agreed to seek confirmation from Pope Paul II and Emperor Frederick III, but the treaty ruled out any revision by a foreign authority.

The lands held directly by Poland formed the province of Royal Prussia, made up of the Chełmno, Pomeranian and Malbork voivodeships and the Prince-Bishopric of Warmia. It kept its own coinage, Diet, military and use of German in administration, and a dispute over the choice of bishops in Warmia led to the War of the Priests (1467–1479). Royal Prussia kept distinctive features until the partitions of Poland. In 1525 Grand Master Albert Hohenzollern adopted Lutheranism and became hereditary duke under Polish overlordship in the Prussian Homage, creating the Duchy of Prussia.
second-persian-invasion-of-greece: Athens and Eretria had supported the unsuccessful Ionian Revolt against Darius I in 499-494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish them. His first invasion ended in defeat at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE. After his death his son Xerxes spent about four years preparing a second, full-scale invasion: pontoon bridges were built across the Hellespont, a canal was dug across the isthmus of Mount Athos, and five food depots were stocked along the route. Herodotus names 46 nations from which troops were drafted and claimed 2.5 million soldiers; modern scholars reject such figures, and the consensus revolves around 200,000 or 300,000-500,000.

In Athens the politician Themistocles had persuaded the city in 482 BCE to build a large fleet of triremes. About a tenth of the Greek city-states joined the alliance led by Athens and Sparta; most stayed neutral or submitted.

The Persian army crossed into Europe in April 480 BCE and took about three months to march unopposed to Therme. After Thermopylae, Boeotia fell and Thespiae and Plataea were razed. The people of Athens were evacuated to Salamis, and in September the Persians took the Acropolis and burned the city, destroying the Older Parthenon and the Old Temple of Athena. Themistocles lured the Persian navy into the narrow straits of Salamis, where it was beaten, and Xerxes withdrew to Asia, leaving Mardonius with the elite of the army.

Over the winter the Persian general Artabazus besieged Potidaea for three months without success and massacred the defenders of Olynthus. In 479 BCE the Athenians rejected Mardonius's offer of peace, and he burned Athens again. The allies then formed the largest hoplite army ever assembled and defeated him at the Battle of Plataea, where he was killed, while their navy destroyed the remnants of the Persian fleet at the Battle of Mycale.

After Mycale the Athenians besieged and took Sestos, where Herodotus ends his history. The Greeks under the Delian League went on the offensive and drove the Persians from Greece, the Aegean islands and Ionia, and the wider conflict ended with the Peace of Callias in 449 BCE. The campaign confirmed the lesson of Marathon, the superiority of the hoplite at close quarters, and the Persian empire later came to rely on Greek mercenaries. Many historians hold that a Persian conquest would have prevented the development of the Greek culture on which Western civilisation rests, though this may be an exaggeration.
second-punic-war: The First Punic War had ended in a Roman victory in 241 BCE after 23 years and enormous losses on both sides. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, then expanded its holdings in Iberia. In 219 BCE a Carthaginian army under Hannibal besieged, captured and sacked the pro-Roman city of Saguntum, and in spring 218 BCE Rome declared war.

Hannibal marched overland from Iberia through Gaul and over the Alps into Cisalpine Gaul. With Gallic allies he defeated the Romans at Ticinus and the Trebia in 218 BCE and at Lake Trasimene in 217 BCE. At Cannae in 216 BCE he destroyed the largest army the Romans had ever assembled. More than 120,000 Roman troops died or were captured in less than three years, and Capua and other Italian allies defected. Syracuse and Macedon joined Carthage, and Philip V began the First Macedonian War. The Romans enrolled slaves and criminals and slowly recaptured most of the Italian cities.

In Iberia Publius Cornelius Scipio captured New Carthage in 209 BCE and ended the Carthaginian presence at Ilipa in 206 BCE. Hasdrubal Barca crossed the Alps in 207 BCE to join Hannibal but was defeated at the Battle of the Metaurus. In 204 BCE Scipio landed in Africa, joined by the Numidian prince Masinissa, and Hannibal was recalled from Italy.

Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE. The treaty, accepted in spring 201 BCE, stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some African ones, imposed an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents over 50 years, and limited its fleet to ten warships. Carthage was forbidden to wage war outside Africa, and within Africa only with Rome's permission, so it was now politically subordinate. Scipio received a triumph and the name Africanus. Rome used Carthaginian action against the Numidians as a pretext for the Third Punic War in 149 BCE, which ended in 146 BCE with the sack and demolition of the city.
second-sacred-war: In 458 or 457 BCE the Phocians captured three towns in Doris, the region the Spartans regarded as their mother country. A Spartan army marched north, defeated the Phocians and restored Dorian rule. On its way back to the Peloponnese an Athenian force attacked it but was repelled, and the Spartans returned home. After the Five Years' Truce between the two powers, Sparta set out to check what historians have called Athens' imperialistic ambitions in Central Greece, where the Phocians were allies of Athens.

The war turned on who should hold the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, seat of the Pythia. The Phocians, backed by Athens, had control of the sanctuary. A Spartan expedition quickly removed them and returned its stewardship to the Delphians, restoring their self-government. Once the Spartans had gone home, an Athenian army led by Pericles took the city and installed Phocian rule again.

The chronology is disputed. One group of historians, among them Karl Julius Beloch, Benjamin Dean Meritt, Theodore Wade-Gery and Malcolm Francis McGregor, followed the Greek historian Philochorus and placed the Spartan march in 449 BCE, with the Athenian return some time later. Another group, led by Arnold Wycombe Gomme and Felix Jacoby, rejected Philochorus' dates and placed both marches on Delphi in 448 BCE.

Scholars have found no evidence that these changes in the governance of Delphi had any effect on the pilgrims who came to consult the Pythia. The episode is one of only two conflicts that writers of classical antiquity themselves called a sacred war, the other being the Third Sacred War of 356–346 BCE. This struggle over Delphi also formed one episode in the wider contest between Athens and Sparta for influence in Central Greece in the years after the Five Years' Truce.
second-schleswig-war: Denmark received its first liberal constitution in 1848, and the movement of the large German majority in Holstein and southern Schleswig to form a united, independent state was suppressed in the First Schleswig War. Holstein was ethnically German and had been a German fief before 1806; Schleswig was a Danish fief with a mixed population speaking Low German, Danish and North Frisian. Two systems of government existed within one state, constitutional monarchy in Denmark and absolutism in the duchies, under one cabinet, which produced deadlock.

On 18 November 1863 King Christian IX signed the November Constitution, which established a shared law of succession and a common parliament for Schleswig and Denmark. The German Confederation saw this as a breach of the London Protocol of 1852. In December Saxon and Hanoverian troops entered Holstein for the Confederation.

Otto von Bismarck had been under great pressure since the constitutional crisis of 1862 over army taxes, and hoped to win Prussian liberals by the liberation of Schleswig. Prussia and Austria alone decided to invade Schleswig rather than only occupy Holstein. On 16 January 1864 Bismarck issued an ultimatum demanding that the November Constitution be abolished within 48 hours, which Denmark rejected, and on 1 February Prussian and Austrian forces crossed the border.

The Danish army numbered about 38,000 men, of whom about 36,000 defended the Danevirke, a task said to need 50,000. Political pressure led to a frontal defence of Jutland at the Danevirke.
