In a hard winter the waters and marshes at both ends froze and let the Germans bypass the line; an attempt near Missunde failed, but when they appeared in force in its rear the Danish high command ordered it abandoned. The war ended on 30 October 1864 with the Treaty of Vienna.

Denmark ceded Schleswig, except the island of Ærø, together with Holstein and Saxe-Lauenburg to Prussia and Austria, and about 200,000 Danes came under German rule. The Peace of Prague of 1866 promised a plebiscite in north Schleswig, set aside by Prussia and Austria in 1878. After the German defeat in 1918 a plebiscite returned North Schleswig to Denmark.

The war is generally considered a national trauma for Denmark. Sweden-Norway, despite a promise of troops, did not help. Many Danes in the ceded lands were later conscripted into the German army in the First World War. In Prussia the victory led liberals to cease opposing Bismarck, and the Landtag retroactively legalised the taxes he had collected without its consent.
second-seminole-war: In the 18th century bands of Alabamas, Choctaw, Yamasees, Yuchis and Muscogees had moved into Florida. The Spanish in St. Augustine called the Alachua Muscogees cimarrones, roughly wild ones or runaways, the probable origin of the name Seminole, though the groups still saw themselves as separate tribes. Most European Americans regarded them as Creeks recently arrived, while the Seminoles claimed Florida as their home. In the spring of 1832 the Treaty of Payne's Landing called for them to move west and join the Creek reservation, and the fighting began with Dade's massacre in 1835.

The regular army had fewer than 7,500 men at 53 posts, and Generals Edmund P. Gaines and Winfield Scott both failed to defeat the Seminoles. In April 1836 the Seminoles attacked several forts, and on 23 July 1836 they burned the Cape Florida lighthouse. Thomas Jesup then wore the Seminoles down with more than 9,000 men, captured King Phillip of the Mikasukis on 10 September 1837, and swept the peninsula with several columns, while Colonel Zachary Taylor led one between the Kissimmee and Peace rivers.

On 7 August 1840 a party of Spanish Indians raided Indian Key, killing Dr. Henry Perrine. In December Colonel William S. Harney led ninety men into the Everglades, killed the chief Chakaika and hanged several captives. From May 1841 Colonel William Jenkins Worth cut costs, released nearly 1,000 civilian employees of the army and drove the Seminoles from the Cove of the Withlacoochee with summer raids. Early in 1842 he recommended leaving the remaining bands in peace in southern Florida, and he declared the war over on 14 August 1842 without any peace treaty.

The war has been called the longest and most costly of the Indian conflicts of the United States. Estimates cited by the historian Mahon put its cost at 30 to 40 million dollars, and 10,169 regulars and about 30,000 militiamen and volunteers served in Florida. The remaining Seminoles stayed on an informal reservation in southwestern Florida, but renewed pressure to remove them led to the Third Seminole War of 1855–1858.
second-serbian-uprising: The First Serbian Uprising (1804–1813) freed the country from the Ottoman Empire for the first time in three centuries, until its failure in 1813. Most commanders, including its leader Karađorđe Petrović, escaped to the Habsburg Monarchy. Miloš Obrenović and Stanoje Glavaš stayed. Obrenović surrendered to the Ottomans and received the title of obor-knez of his home district of Rudnik, while Glavaš, made a supervisor of a road, was killed by the Turks, who had become suspicious of him.

In mid-September 1814 the veteran Hadži-Prodan raised a rebellion in the Požega nahija. Obrenović felt the time was not right and helped capture the rebels, and the revolt soon failed. Afterwards the Ottomans inflicted more persecution, including high taxation, forced labour and rape, and in March 1815 the Serbs decided on a new revolt.

A meeting at Takovo proclaimed open revolt on 23 April 1815 and chose Miloš Obrenović as leader. He is said to have declared: "Here I am, here you are. War to the Turks!" The Ottomans sentenced all the leaders to death. The Serbs fought battles at Rudnik, Ljubić, Palež, Valjevo, Čačak, Karanovac, Požarevac, Kragujevac, Jagodina and Dublje, and drove the Ottomans out of the Pashalik of Belgrade.

In mid-1815 Obrenović began negotiations with the Ottoman governor Marashli Ali Pasha and obtained a form of partial autonomy. In 1816 the Porte signed several documents normalising relations between Serbs and Turks, and Obrenović received the title of Prince of Serbia. In 1817 he forced Marashli Ali Pasha to agree an unwritten settlement, which effectively ended the uprising. In the same year Karađorđe returned to Serbia and was assassinated on Obrenović's orders.

The principality paid a yearly tax to the Porte and had an Ottoman garrison in Belgrade until 1867, but in most other matters it was effectively independent. A ferman of 1830 reaffirmed its semi-independence, and in 1835 one of the first constitutions in the Balkans was written there. It introduced a regular parliament and made the Obrenović dynasty heirs to the throne, and it described Serbia as an independent parliamentary principality, which outraged the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy. Formal independence came in 1878 under the Treaty of Berlin, in the time of Milan, a grandson of Miloš's brother.
second-silesian-war: By the Treaty of Berlin of July 1742 Austria ceded most of Silesia to Prussia in return for its neutrality, and then recovered its losses against Bavaria and France. In September 1743 Austria, Britain-Hanover and Savoy-Sardinia allied under the Treaty of Worms, which made no mention of Britain's earlier guarantee of Prussian Silesia. Fearing an anti-Prussian coalition, Frederick II formed the League of Frankfurt with Bavaria, Sweden, Hesse-Kassel and the Electoral Palatinate on 22 May 1744, ostensibly to restore the territories of Emperor Charles VII, and concluded a treaty with France on 5 June. On 7 August Prussia declared its intervention.

About 70,000 Prussians entered Bohemia in three columns on 15 August 1744, and Prague surrendered on 16 September. The French failed to hinder the return of Prince Charles Alexander of Lorraine's army from Alsace, and Otto Ferdinand von Traun avoided battle while harassing Prussian supply lines, so the Prussians abandoned Bohemia in November. In January 1745 Austria, Britain-Hanover, Saxony and the Dutch Republic formed a Quadruple Alliance, and Charles VII died on 20 January. After the Battle of Pfaffenhofen on 15 April, Bavaria made peace by the Treaty of Füssen.

Frederick routed the Austrian-Saxon army at Hohenfriedberg on 4 June, and on 29 September he held off a surprise attack at Soor. Francis Stephen of Lorraine was elected emperor as Francis I on 13 September. When Austria and Saxony struck toward Brandenburg, Frederick scattered Prince Charles's army at Hennersdorf on 23 November, Leopold I of Anhalt-Dessau destroyed Frederick Augustus Rutowsky's Saxons at Kesselsdorf on 15 December, and the Prussians occupied Dresden on 18 December.

The Treaty of Dresden of 25 December 1745 confirmed Prussian Silesia and Glatz; Frederick recognised Francis I as emperor and accepted the Pragmatic Sanction, and Saxony paid one million rixdollars in reparations. The victories of 1745 won Frederick acclaim as a commander, and he began to be called Frederick the Great. The war marked the start of Prussia's rise toward great-power status and made Austria and Prussia lasting enemies. Maria Theresa refused to sign the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 because it guaranteed Prussian Silesia, and she reformed her army and diplomacy to recover it, leading to the Third Silesian War in 1756.
second-sino-japanese-war: The war followed a long period of Japanese expansion on the Chinese mainland. After defeating China in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895, Japan gained Taiwan under the Treaty of Shimonoseki, and after the Russo-Japanese War of 1905 it held the South Manchuria Railway Zone and the Kwantung Leased Territory. On 18 September 1931 Japanese officers staged the Mukden incident, a false flag event used to justify the invasion of Manchuria and the creation of the puppet state of Manchukuo.

Inside China, Nationalist forces under Chiang Kai-shek and Communist forces under Mao Zedong had been fighting each other since 1927. Chiang's policy was first internal pacification, then external resistance, and his encirclement campaigns drove the Communists onto the Long March. As a Japanese invasion became imminent, Chiang formed a United Front with the Communists in 1936, a process hastened by the Xi'an Incident.

The war is dated from the night of 7 July 1937, when Chinese and Japanese troops exchanged fire near the Marco Polo Bridge, about 16 km from Beijing. The skirmishing grew into full-scale invasion. After the long Battle of Shanghai, Japanese forces took the capital Nanjing in 1937 and committed the Nanjing Massacre. China had little military-industrial strength and no mechanised divisions. The Nationalist government withdrew into the interior and made Chongqing their wartime seat, trading space for time, while Communist forces waged guerrilla warfare in the north.

By 1939 the war had reached a stalemate, with Japanese supply lines stretched deep into China. After Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941 the conflict merged with the wider Second World War, and the United States became China's main financial and military supporter. Supplies came over the Burma Road and, once it was cut, by air over the Himalayas. In 1944 Japan launched Operation Ichi-Go, its largest campaign of the war, which mobilised 500,000 troops and cost Chinese armies about 300,000 casualties. In 1945 Chinese forces retook Hunan and Guangxi.

Japan formally surrendered on 2 September 1945, after the atomic bombings and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, and the surrender in China was signed at Nanjing on 9 September. Estimates of Chinese deaths range from 10 million to 20 million, with a common figure of 15 to 16 million, most of them civilians. Japan used chemical weapons and carried out large biological warfare attacks, and its scorched earth policies in North and Central China killed millions of civilians. The war produced about 95 million refugees.

China emerged as one of the Allied great powers, regained Taiwan and became a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council. It was also economically weak, with ruined farmland, inflation and famine, and it was on the verge of renewed civil war between the two sides.
second-swedish-crusade: Sweden had held a foothold in Finland Proper since the First Swedish Crusade. Swedish missionaries, possibly led by Bishop Thomas, were active in Tavastia around 1230, and the Tavastian uprising of 1236–1237 gave the Swedes a reason to invade, with Pope Gregory IX calling on them to attack the Tavastians. Although Erik's Chronicle presents the expedition as a war of conquest, historians tend to see it as an unusually bloody phase in the longer incorporation of Finland into the Swedish state, in which Finnish chieftains who joined the Swedes gained power and prestige.

The chronicle gives no year, placing the expedition only before King Erik's death in 1250. In the 16th century Mikael Agricola dated it to 1248, and Paulus Juusten gave 1249, which became the traditional date. In the 19th century Peter Andreas Munch argued from the Saga of Haakon Haakonarson, written in 1264–1265, that a Swedish-Norwegian crisis kept Birger near the Norwegian border until the summer of 1249.

In 1946 Jarl Gallén held that the chronicle's chronology could not be trusted and proposed 1238–39, after the papal call and before the Swedish defeat by Alexander Nevsky at the Neva; Dick Harrison also finds the early date most probable. Rolf Pipping in 1926 and Igor Pavlovich Shaskol'skii defended the later dating, and Seppo Suvanto and Mauno Jokipii noted that Birger became jarl only in 1248.

In August 1249 Pope Innocent IV took Finland under his special protection without mentioning Sweden. Bero, who came from the Swedish court, became bishop in 1248 or 1249, and in 1249 the first monastery in Finland, a Dominican convent, was founded beside the bishop's fortification at Koroinen. From 1249 sources generally treat Finland Proper and Tavastia as part of Sweden, and the diocese first appears among the Swedish dioceses in 1253.

According to the chronicle the expedition cost Birger the crown: he was away when King Erik died in 1250, and the lords led by Joar Blå chose his young son Valdemar as king. Few records of the following decades survive, as Novgorodian forces burned Turku in 1318. The last Swedish crusade to Finland, against the Karelians, came in 1293.
second-temple-of-hera-paestum: The temple, a building of Magna Graecia in Campania, stands just north of the first Hera Temple, which dates from around 550–525 BCE. It measures 24.46 by 59.98 metres, with six columns on its shorter sides and fourteen on its longer sides, counting the corner columns twice. The columns are 8.88 metres high and taper from nearly 7 feet across at the base to about 5 feet at the top, a ratio of height to lower diameter of 4.25:1 that is unusually low for the period.

It was built of a very porous local limestone, originally hidden under a stucco of powdered marble. The large outer columns have 24 flutes instead of the 20 normal for Doric columns at that date, the smaller lower columns of the cella 20 and the still smaller upper ones 16. Wide columns set close together and a strong entasis, the curve of the shaft, give it a heavy visual presence.

The name Temple of Neptune is an 18th-century misnomer; the temple is now thought to have been dedicated to Hera, though Poseidon, the Roman Neptune, may also have been honoured there, and some offertory statues found around the larger altar are thought to show this. Zeus and another deity whose identity is unknown were also worshipped. On the east side are the remains of two altars. The smaller is a Roman addition, built when a road to a Roman forum was cut through the larger one. The temple is aligned with a double-peaked mountain that the Greeks considered sacred.

A. W. Lawrence called it the best preserved of all Greek temples, and with the other temples of Paestum it is among the best preserved early Greek temples. It resembles the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, built in the same period, and it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
second-triumvirate: The Second Triumvirate was an extraordinary commission and magistracy created at the end of the Roman republic for Mark Antony, Lepidus and Octavian. The name is a modern misnomer, derived from the branding of the alliance of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar as the First Triumvirate, and it first appears in the late 17th century. After Julius Caesar was assassinated on 15 March 44 BCE, the liberatores and the remaining supporters of Caesar reached a settlement, but Antony pushed through legislation assigning himself the provinces of Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul.

Octavian reached Rome on 19 August 43 BCE and secured election as consul. At the urging of the soldiers he reconciled with Antony under the protection of Lepidus, and the three established themselves for five years. The lex Titia confirmed this on 27 November 43 BCE, giving them power to issue binding edicts, to act without appeal and to appoint magistrates and provincial governors.

The triumvirs issued a death list of proscribed men. Ancient sources differ on the number: Plutarch gives figures of 200, a bit more than 200 and 300, Livy 130 senators, and Florus 140. François Hinard believes about 300 men were proscribed, split roughly evenly between senators and equestrians. In 42 BCE Antony and Octavian crossed to Macedonia with some forty legions, and at Philippi the forces of Brutus and Cassius were defeated. Antony then reorganised the eastern provinces, while Octavian settled veterans in Italy and faced Sextus Pompey in Sicily.

Unrest over land for veterans led to the Perusine War, in which Lucius Antonius was besieged at Perusia; Octavian sacked the town and burnt it. The Treaty of Brundisium in September 40 BCE confirmed Antony as master of the east and Octavian in the west, with Lepidus keeping Africa. The triumvirate was renewed in 37 BCE, and in 36 BCE Octavian forced Lepidus out.

The triumvirate was formally constituted for five years, renewed in 37 BCE and expired in 32 BCE. Its powers exceeded those of ordinary consuls, and the Capitoline Fasti listed the triumvirs above the consuls. After Lepidus fell, Octavian prepared for a showdown with Antony and worked to link him with Cleopatra, whose relationship with Antony was unpopular in Italy. Relations between the two broke down, and they fought a final war, from which Octavian emerged the victor.
second-united-front: From late 1935 Chiang Kai-shek secretly sought Soviet aid against Japan, and the Soviet Union made a ceasefire with the CCP a condition. Meanwhile the CCP signed secret ceasefires with the Nationalist generals besieging them in the north-west, Zhang Xueliang of the Northeastern Army and Yang Hucheng of the Northwestern Army, who resented Chiang's preference for civil war over resistance to Japan.

Chiang still hoped for a military victory, encouraged when Hui cavalry allied with him cut up two Red Army corps in the Ningxia campaign in October 1936. But at the Battle of Shanchengbao the Northeastern Army held back most of its forces, and the Red Army nearly wiped out a regiment of Hu Zongnan's army. On 12 December 1936 Zhang and Yang seized Chiang to force a truce with the CCP.

The CCP accepted Chiang's leadership and some financial support from the central government. Its leaders, among them Mao Zedong, sat in the new People's Political Council, intellectuals such as Guo Moruo joined the Political Department of the Military Affairs Commission, and in August 1937 Zhou Enlai and Shao Lizi agreed that the Xinhua Daily could be published in Nationalist areas. The two sides fought together at the Battle of Taiyuan, and their cooperation reached its height at the Battle of Wuhan in 1938.

In practice the front worked more as a non-aggression pact than an alliance: Communist forces acted independently, and coordination was minimal. Within the CCP, Mao wanted autonomy while his rival Wang Ming favoured doing everything through the united front. By late 1938 the alliance was breaking down as both sides competed for territory in Free China; in June 1939, according to Chiang's diary, Red Army troops under He Long destroyed a Chinese militia brigade in Hebei.

After the New Fourth Army Incident the two parties fought each other behind Japanese lines, the CCP destroying or absorbing Nationalist partisan forces or driving them into the collaborationist army. The CCP built influence through rural mass organisations and land and tax reforms favouring poor peasants, while many Nationalist divisions were tied down blockading their areas. Peace talks between Chiang and Mao after the war failed; by 1946 civil war was general, and in October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China as Chiang retreated to Taiwan.
second-vatican-council: John XXIII, elected in 1958 at the age of seventy-six and widely expected to preside over a brief pontificate, announced the council on 25 January 1959, less than three months into his papacy, and described its purpose with the Italian word aggiornamento, bringing up to date. He framed its aims as renewing the internal life of the church, advancing Christian unity and enabling the church to speak more effectively to contemporary social and political problems. Pius XII's 1943 encyclical Divino afflante Spiritu had encouraged Catholic scholars to use the original Hebrew and Greek texts of scripture, and informed the council's later teaching on revelation.

Preparation took nearly three years, and the council was formally convoked by the apostolic constitution Humanae Salutis on 25 December 1961. John XXIII opened it on 11 October 1962 with the address Gaudet Mater Ecclesia, in which he distanced himself from prophets of doom and urged the bishops to favour the medicine of mercy over condemnation. About 2,900 bishops and heads of male religious orders were entitled to attend, and nearly 2,500 did so at some point, along with non-Catholic observers and, from the second session, a small number of lay auditors. The council met in four annual sessions and closed on 8 December 1965. Paul VI presided over the last three sessions and promulgated all its documents.

It approved four constitutions, nine decrees and three declarations. Sacrosanctum Concilium on the liturgy, approved on 4 December 1963, made the full, conscious and active participation of the laity in worship its central demand. Lumen gentium, promulgated on 21 November 1964, described the church as mystery, sacrament, the People of God and a hierarchical communion. Dei verbum, on revelation, followed on 18 November 1965, and Gaudium et spes, the longest, on 7 December 1965, addressed to the whole of humanity.

The council reshaped the Roman Rite, permitting vernacular languages in a liturgy conducted almost entirely in Latin for centuries. Sacrosanctum Concilium permitted but did not require the vernacular, and said nothing about the priest facing the congregation or removing altar rails, which became widespread through implementing decisions in the next two years. The council also set in motion changes in the church's relations with other Christian communities, with Judaism and with the modern secular state. Catholic scholars disagree on how to read it: some treat it chiefly as a body of texts to be read against continuous tradition, while others, following Joseph Komonchak, see Vatican II as a historical event whose meaning continued to be worked out afterwards.
second-viennese-school: The principal members besides Arnold Schoenberg were Alban Berg and Anton Webern, among his first composition pupils. Both had already written much music in a late Romantic idiom but felt they gained new direction and discipline from his teaching. Other members of this generation included Ernst Krenek, Heinrich Jalowetz, Erwin Stein and Egon Wellesz, and somewhat later Eduard Steuermann, Hanns Eisler, Rudolf Kolisch, Viktor Ullmann and others. Schoenberg's brother-in-law Alexander Zemlinsky is sometimes included, though he was never Schoenberg's pupil and never renounced a traditional conception of tonality. Several later disciples, among them Winfried Zillig and the Greek Nikos Skalkottas, studied in Schoenberg's masterclass in Berlin, not in Vienna.

The music was at first marked by late-Romantic expanded tonality, then by a totally chromatic expressionism without a firm tonal centre, often called atonality, and later by Schoenberg's serial twelve-tone technique, in which all twelve tones of the chromatic scale form a melody called the prime series. Berg and Webern each adopted the method soon after Schoenberg did, in their own ways, though not all the others followed, or they waited a considerable time. The school's development followed neither a common timeline nor a cooperative path. It did not result directly from Schoenberg's teaching, which his textbooks show to have been highly traditional and conservative, but from the influence of his creative example.

The impression of cohesion was strengthened by members' writings. Wellesz wrote the first book on Schoenberg, Josef Rufer and Leopold Spinner wrote on twelve-tone technique, and René Leibowitz's study Schoenberg et son école helped establish the image of a school in France and elsewhere after the Second World War. Teachers such as Jalowetz and Rufer, and performers such as Kolisch, Rankl, Stein, Steuermann and Zillig, spread the group's ideas and repertoire.

Perhaps the culmination came at Darmstadt, at the Internationale Ferienkurse für Neue Musik, almost immediately after the Second World War. Schoenberg, invited but too ill to travel, was ultimately supplanted in musical ideology by his pupil Webern, as members of the school converged there with the new serialists, among them Pierre Boulez and Luigi Nono. Boulez and others extended serialisation beyond pitch to rhythm, articulation and dynamics. Theodor Adorno called the mature twelve-tone method a message in a bottle addressed to an unknown future. Membership is not generally extended to Schoenberg's pupils in the United States from 1933, such as John Cage and Leon Kirchner.
second-war-of-scottish-independence: The First War of Scottish Independence had ended with the Treaty of Northampton of 1328, by which the regents of the young Edward III recognised Robert Bruce as king of an independent Scotland. In 1331 the disinherited Scottish nobles, led by Edward Balliol, son of the former king John Balliol, and Henry Beaumont, Earl of Buchan, gathered in Yorkshire to plot an invasion. Edward III officially forbade it but let their forces sail from Yorkshire ports on 31 July 1332. The guardian of Scotland, Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, had died ten days before.

At Dupplin Moor Balliol's force defeated a Scottish army ten times its size, and he was crowned, but within three months the supporters of the eight-year-old David II had driven him out. Edward III invaded in 1333, besieged Berwick and crushed a relieving army at Halidon Hill. In May 1334 David took refuge in France, and on 19 June Balliol did homage to Edward for Scotland after ceding the eight counties of the south-east. Balliol's allies then fell out, and by late 1334 he had lost most of the country again. In 1335 Edward led more than 13,000 men north, the largest force he ever brought against the Scots.

In August 1336 Philip VI of France pledged full military support to David's party, and from 1337 the war became a side theatre of the Hundred Years' War. With French help the Scots retook Perth in 1339; David returned in 1341, and by 1342 the English had been cleared from north of the border. In 1346, answering Philip's appeals while Edward campaigned in France, David invaded England and was defeated and captured at Neville's Cross. His nephew and heir Stewart, the future Robert II, governed as guardian. Late in 1355 the Scots broke a truce, ravaged Northumberland and took Berwick, and Edward's invasion of early 1356 devastated Lothian before storms scattered his supply ships.

The French defeat at Poitiers in September 1356 ended Scottish hopes of French help. Under the Treaty of Berwick the ransom of 100,000 marks (£67,000) was to be paid each 24 June over ten years, with 23 Scottish nobles held as surety. The English dropped their claim of suzerainty, while the Scots acknowledged a vague English overlordship. Edward had achieved little and the Scots kept their independence. The treaty was a truce, not a peace, and although intermittent fighting continued it was broadly observed for four decades, until Henry IV of England led an army into Lothian in 1400.
second-white-terror: The terror followed the defeat of Napoleon at the Battle of Waterloo on 18 June 1815 and the return of Louis XVIII as King of France after the Hundred Days. Its victims were suspected sympathizers of the French Revolution, among them former Jacobins, together with Republicans, Bonapartists and, to a lesser degree, Protestants. The period takes its name from the First White Terror of the Thermidorian Reaction in 1794–1795, when people associated with Robespierre's Reign of Terror were harassed and killed. The historian John B. Wolf argues that the ultra-royalists, many of them just back from exile, were staging a counter-revolution against both the French Revolution and Napoleon's revolution.

The purge fell first on a civilian administration that had turned almost entirely against the Bourbon monarchy: about 70,000 officials were dismissed. The remnants of the Napoleonic army were disbanded and its senior officers cashiered. Approximately 6,000 people who had rallied to Napoleon were brought to trial. Throughout the Midi, in Provence, Avignon and Languedoc, royalists hunted down those they saw as traitors, while the government was powerless or unwilling to intervene. There were about 300 mob lynchings in the south, notably in Marseille, where many of Napoleon's Mamelukes were massacred in their barracks, and General Jean-Pierre Ramel was assassinated in Toulouse. Several hundred people in all were killed by mobs or executed after quick trials by drumhead court-martial.

The violence frightened many liberal and moderate electors, 48,000 of the 72,000 entitled to vote, into supporting the ultra-royalists in the elections of August 1815. Of 402 deputies, 350 were ultra-royalists, a chamber more royalist than the king, which Louis XVIII called the Chambre introuvable. The Chamber of Peers sentenced Marshal Michel Ney and the Comte Charles de la Bédoyère to death for treason, 250 people received prison sentences, and Joseph Fouché, Lazare Carnot and Cambacérès were among those exiled, as were the surviving regicides who had voted for the death of Louis XVI. The terror in the political sphere ended when Louis XVIII dissolved the Chambre introuvable in 1816, fearing that it would provoke a new revolution.
second-world-war: The causes of the war included unresolved tensions after the First World War and the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Under the Treaty of Versailles Germany lost around 13 per cent of its home territory and all its overseas possessions, and had reparations imposed and its armed forces limited. Benito Mussolini's fascist movement seized power in Italy between 1922 and 1925, and Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933. Earlier events included Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia from October 1935, the Spanish Civil War, in which Germany and Italy backed General Francisco Franco's Nationalists, and the Second Sino-Japanese War from July 1937.

The war began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded Poland, and the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. The Soviet Union invaded Poland on 17 September, and the two states partitioned it. In 1940 Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and France fell in June. In June 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. In December 1941 Japan attacked American and British territories, including Pearl Harbor, and the United States entered the war. Japan's advance was halted at the Battle of Midway in June 1942.

In early 1943 the Axis were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad. In 1944 the Western Allies landed in Normandy while the Soviet Union advanced into Central Europe. Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May 1945. The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August, and Japan signed a surrender document on 2 September 1945.

An estimated 60 million to more than 75 million people died, a majority of them civilians. About 6 million Jews were killed in the Holocaust, together with millions of Slavs and over 130,000 Romani. Germany lost a quarter of its pre-war territory and nine million Germans were expelled from the eastern provinces. German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes. The United Nations came into being on 24 October 1945, and the Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War. The weakened great powers of Europe saw the decolonisation of Africa and Asia follow, and Italy lost its monarchy and colonial empire.
secret-history-of-the-mongols: The Secret History of the Mongols is the oldest surviving literary work in the Mongolic languages. It was written for the Mongol royal family some time after the death of Genghis Khan in 1227, and it recounts his life and conquests and partially the reign of his successor Ögedei Khan. The author is unknown and wrote in Middle Mongol in the Mongolian script. A colophon says the book was finished in the Year of the Rat on the banks of the Kherlen River, which scholars have conjectured to be 1228, 1229, 1240, 1252 or 1264.

The work begins with a semi-mythical genealogy of Genghis Khan, born Temüjin. According to legend a blue-grey wolf and a fallow doe begat the first Mongol, Batachiqan. Eleven generations later a widow named Alan Gua bore three sons to a supernatural glowing man, and the youngest, Bodonchar, founded the Borjigin. The account of Temüjin's life begins with his father Yesügei's kidnapping of his mother Hoelun, then covers his birth around 1160, the hard years after his father's murder, and the wars and plots before he took the title Genghis Khan in 1206. The later parts deal with the conquests of Genghis and his third son Ögedei, and the text ends with Ögedei's reflections on what he did well and what he did wrong.

The full Mongolian text survives only through a version made around the 15th century, at the start of the Ming dynasty, in which the pronunciation was transcribed into Chinese characters as a tool for interpreters. It has a transcription, an interlinear Chinese gloss and an often abridged Chinese translation, in 12 parts and 282 sections, and it was folded into the Yongle Encyclopedia in 1408. About two-thirds of the text also appear in the Altan Tobchi, written in 1651 by the monk Lubsang-Danzin and discovered in 1926.

Scholars value the work for its information on Mongol language and culture and its vivid portrayal of tribal life in the 12th and 13th centuries. Its worth as a historical source is disputed: René Grousset judges it positively, Igor de Rachewiltz values chiefly its faithful description of tribal life, and Arthur Waley thought its historical value almost nil. It has been translated into more than 40 languages.
secret-society: The exact qualifications for calling a group a secret society are disputed. Definitions generally rely on how far the organization insists on secrecy, and may involve the keeping and passing on of secret knowledge, the denial of membership or knowledge of the group, bonds between members and the use of secret rites. The term usually excludes covert groups such as intelligence agencies or guerrilla insurgencies, which hide their activities and members but keep a public presence. Anthropologists and historians have linked secret societies closely to the Männerbund, the all-male warrior-band of pre-modern cultures.

Alan Axelrod, author of the International Encyclopedia of Secret Societies and Fraternal Orders, defines one as an organization that is exclusive, claims to own special secrets and shows a strong inclination to favour its members. The historian Richard B. Spence offers a similar definition: the group's existence is usually not secret, but some beliefs or practices are hidden and require an oath of secrecy and loyalty; it promises members superior status or knowledge; and its membership is restricted, for example by sex, religion or invitation.

Societies of this kind have existed in many regions. In Africa sources list, among others, Poro and Sande in Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone and the Ivory Coast, Ekpe in Cameroon and Nigeria, Ogboni and Nze na Ozo in Nigeria, Simo in Ghana and Mali, and Nyau in Zimbabwe. Abakuá is recorded in Cuba. In Europe the list includes Freemasonry, Rosicrucianism, the Carbonari in France, Italy and Portugal, and the Irish Republican Brotherhood.

In China, secret societies played a major role in affairs for centuries and were a key part of anti-Qing sentiment. Examples include the White Lotus, the Tiandihui and the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists. After the Qing collapse they collaborated with the Nationalist government, and the People's Republic targeted them in campaigns in the 1950s.

Because some secret societies have political aims, they are illegal in several countries; the constitutions of Italy and Poland, for example, ban secret political parties and organizations. The historian Jasper Ridley calls Freemasonry the world's most powerful secret society. The Catholic Church strongly opposed secret societies, especially the Freemasons, although in the United States it allowed membership in labour unions and the Knights of Columbus.

Student societies have also been called secret societies. Skull and Bones at Yale University is a notable example, and the Cambridge Apostles, founded in 1820 as an essay and debating society, is a British example.
secretary-general-of-the-united-nations: The role of the secretary-general and of the Secretariat is laid out in Chapter XV, Articles 97 to 101, of the United Nations Charter. The Charter calls the secretary-general the chief administrative officer of the organisation and gives the power to make employment decisions about Secretariat staff. It also empowers the secretary-general to inform the Security Council of any matter which in his opinion may threaten the maintenance of international peace and security. The qualifications, selection process and tenure of the office are open to interpretation and have been established by custom. The secretary-general also chairs the Chief Executives Board for Coordination, which brings together the heads of all UN funds, programmes and specialized agencies.

Appointment is by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council, so any of its five permanent members can veto a nomination. By precedent the appointee may not be a citizen of a permanent member, and most secretaries-general have been compromise candidates from middle powers with little prior fame. The length of the term is discretionary, but every secretary-general since 1971 has been appointed to a five-year term, and every one since 1961 was chosen for a second term except Boutros Boutros-Ghali, vetoed by the United States in 1996. Incumbents have avoided seeking a third term since 1981, when China cast sixteen vetoes against a third term for Kurt Waldheim.

Many powers are informal, and some holders have taken activist roles while others have been more administrative. Much depends on the use of their good offices, steps taken in public and in private to prevent international disputes from arising, escalating or spreading. Examples include Dag Hammarskjöld's promotion of an armistice between the warring parties of the Arab-Israel conflict, U Thant's role in de-escalating the Cuban Missile Crisis and Javier Pérez de Cuéllar's negotiation of a ceasefire in the Iran-Iraq War. Hammarskjöld is the only holder to have died in office.

Observers have variously called the office the world's most visible bully pulpit or the world's moderator. The official residence, a townhouse at 3 Sutton Place in Manhattan built for Anne Morgan in 1921, was given to the United Nations by Arthur A. Houghton Jr. in 1972; before that, secretaries-general chose where to live.
secunderabad: Secunderabad lies on the northern part of the Deccan Plateau, north of Hyderabad, from which it is separated by the lake of Hussain Sagar, built under the Qutb Shahi dynasty in the 16th century. Most of the area is rocky and some of it hilly, at an average elevation of 543 metres. The two cities are joined by roads across the Tank Bund, and Secunderabad Junction railway station, established in 1874, became the headquarters of the South Central Railway zone.

The area came under the Delhi Sultanate in 1310 after the capture of Warangal, and Hyderabad was founded in 1592 by the Golconda Sultanate under Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah. By the 18th century the land around Secunderabad belonged to the Nizam's Hyderabad.

After the Nizam Asaf Jah II was defeated by the British East India Company, he signed the Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance in 1798 to obtain British troops, who camped at the village of Ulwul. In 1803 Sikandar Jah, the third Nizam, renamed Ulwul Secunderabad after himself, and in 1806 an order allotted the land north of Hussain Sagar for a British cantonment. Unlike Hyderabad, Secunderabad used English as its official language and was exempt from customs duty on imported goods, which made trade profitable; markets such as the Regimental Bazaar and the General Bazaar grew up. A seven-metre wall was begun at Trimulgherry after 1857 and completed in 1867.

A municipality was formed in 1945 and became a municipal corporation in 1950. In 1960 it was merged with the Hyderabad corporation. Winston Churchill was posted there as a subaltern in the 1890s, and Ronald Ross carried out early research on the cause of malaria in the city.

Secunderabad is no longer a separate municipal unit and forms part of Greater Hyderabad in Telangana, India. It remains one of the largest cantonments in India, with a large presence of army and air force personnel, and houses the Rashtrapati Nilayam, the winter office of the president of India. The Residency House, built in 1860 for the British Resident at Hyderabad, is now the Rashtrapati Nilayam. Ramoji Film City is also in the city.
seediq-people: The Seediq live mainly in Nantou County and Hualien County, and their language is also called Seediq. Conflict with Japan began after 1897, when a Japanese road-building programme pushed into Indigenous territory, which the people saw as an invasion. Clashes followed and some Indigenous people were killed. In 1901 Indigenous fighters defeated 670 Japanese soldiers, and in 1902 the Japanese isolated Wushe. At Renzhiguan in 1902 Japanese troops shot Tgdaya people who resisted them, and in 1903 the Japanese mounted a punitive expedition, the Zimeiyuan incident, to avenge their loss there. In the Xincheng events, after Japanese soldiers raped Indigenous women, two leaders and 20 men killed 13 Japanese soldiers.

In 1914, after eight years of surveying, the Japanese invaded the lands of the Truku group. Two thousand Indigenous people resisted an army of 10,000 soldiers with 200 machine guns, and the Governor-General Sakuma Samata suffered wounds in the war that led to his death. Between 1914 and 1917 a pacification campaign killed many who resisted. Mona Rudao, leader of Mahebo, twice planned resistance but was betrayed when his plans became known; at his third attempt he brought seven of the twelve groups into the fight.

The Wushe Incident began in October 1930 and was the last major uprising against Japanese rule in Taiwan. After long oppression, Seediq of Wushe attacked the village and killed over 130 Japanese, and the Japanese counter-attack killed over 600 Seediq. The authorities' handling of the incident was strongly criticised and led to many changes in policy toward Indigenous peoples.

Mona Rudao came to be regarded as a national hero of Taiwan. The uprising has been shown on screen several times: in the 1957 film Qing Shan bi xue, in the 2003 television drama Dana Sakura and in the 2011 film Seediq Bale, which also depicts the Renzhiguan and Zimeiyuan incidents. The band Chthonic retold the experiences of the Seediq in fictional form on its albums Seediq Bale (2007) and Takasago Army (2011). Long classed with the Atayal, together with the closely related Taroko, the Seediq were recognised as Taiwan's 14th Indigenous group on 23 April 2008.
sees: Sées lies on the river Orne, five kilometres from its source and about twenty kilometres north-north-east of Alençon, within the Normandie-Maine Regional Natural Park and the forest of Écouves. It is classed as a Petite Cité de Caractère. The commune covers just over 40 square kilometres, most of it arable land, with meadows and a little forest. The name comes from the Latin civitas Sagiensis, the city of the Sagii, a Gaulish tribe that made it their capital. The traditional spelling, Séez, is kept by the Church, whose diocese is headed by the Bishop of Séez.

Its line of bishops goes back to late antiquity, and Saint Lain is placed about the fourth century. In the ninth century it was a fortified town and fell prey to the Normans. It then had two parts on the Orne, the bishop's borough to the north and the new count's borough to the south. The counts of Alençon took control in 1356. The town was captured and recaptured in the wars between Henry II of England and his sons, and in the Hundred Years' War it was one of the first towns of Normandy to fall to the English, in 1418.

Pillaged by Protestants during the Wars of Religion, Sées attached itself to the Catholic League in 1589, but voluntarily surrendered to Henry IV of France in 1590. The civil authorities adopted the spelling Sées after Napoleon's Italian campaign of 1796-97, which brought another, Savoyan Séez into France.

Sées Cathedral occupies the site of three earlier churches and dates from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its west front carries two open-work spires about 70 metres high, the nave was finished towards the end of the thirteenth century, and the choir is notable for the lightness of its construction. It was declared a monument historique in 1875. Nine other buildings and areas are listed, among them the bishop's palace of 1778, the former abbey of Saint-Martin, and an eleventh-century castle mound. A museum of religious art, opened in 1969 in the old chapter house, holds over 2,000 pieces.
seewoosagur-ramgoolam: Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, often known as SSR or Chacha, 'uncle', was born on 18 September 1900 at Belle Rive, a sugar-estate village in the Flacq district of Mauritius, into a poor Hindu family. His father died when he was seven, and by the age of nine he had lost both parents. In 1921 he left for Britain to study medicine, one of the first young Mauritian Hindus at a British university. In London he joined the Fabian Society and Indian nationalist circles and met Mahatma Gandhi.

After returning in 1935 he became a leader of the Indo-Mauritian community, co-founded the newspaper Advance in 1940 and was elected to the Legislative Council in 1948. By 1958 he led the Labour Party.

Ramgoolam became chief minister in 1961 and premier in 1964. At the Lancaster House conference of 1965 he led the parties that sought independence. After being told that Britain could separate the islands without Mauritian consent, he agreed to the detachment of the Chagos Archipelago, which Britain made into the British Indian Ocean Territory. The inhabitants were expelled between 1967 and 1973, a decision taken by the United Kingdom and the United States. Opponents and some of the displaced Chagossians long accused him of trading the islands for independence.

British records later showed Britain was prepared to detach them regardless, and in 2019 the International Court of Justice found that the detachment had not been based on the free and genuine will of the people of Mauritius. His Independence Party won the 1967 election, and Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968.

As the first prime minister, from 1968 to 1982, he governed through coalitions, including one formed on 1 December 1969 with his former opponents in the Parti Mauricien Social Démocrate. His governments built a welfare state, introduced free secondary education and promoted export processing zones. They ruled under a state of emergency from 1971 to 1976 to contain strikes led by the Mauritian Militant Movement. He signed the Lomé Convention, which guaranteed a European market for Mauritian sugar, and chaired the Organisation of African Unity in 1976-1977.

After losing his seat in the 1982 election he became governor-general in 1983 and died in office on 15 December 1985. He is widely known in Mauritius as the Father of the Nation. The main airport and the botanic garden at Pamplemousses are named after him, and his likeness appears on Mauritian coins and banknotes.
sefidrud: The Sefid-Rud, meaning White River, is about 670 kilometres long, rising in the Alborz mountains of north-western Iran and flowing generally north-east to empty into the Caspian Sea at Kiashahr. Its other transcriptions include Sepidrud and Sefidrood. It has cut a water gap through the Alborz, the Manjil gap, where it captures its two headwater tributaries, the Qizil Üzan and the Shahrood, and then widens the valley between the Talesh Hills and the main range. The gap provides a major route between Tehran and Gīlān Province and its Caspian lowlands. In the wide valley before the sea a number of transport and irrigation canals have been cut, the two biggest being the Khomam and the Now.

In antiquity the river was known as the Mardos or Amardos in Greek and the Mardus or Amardus in Latin, and William Smith equated it with that river. In the Hellenistic period the Cadusii, a mountain tribe, occupied the north side of the river, then called the Mardus. It has long been known for its abundant fish, especially the Caspian trout.

The river was dammed in 1962 by the Shahbanu Farah Dam, later renamed the Manjil Dam, which created a reservoir of 1.86 cubic kilometres and allowed the irrigation of a further 2,380 square kilometres. The reservoir reduces some flooding and greatly increased rice production in the delta, and its hydroelectric plant generates 87,000 kilowatts. The dam had a harmful effect on the river's fisheries through reduced flow, higher water temperature and less food, above all for sturgeon but also for the Caspian trout.
segestes: Segestes belonged to the Cherusci, a Germanic people caught up in the Roman attempts to conquer northern Germany under Augustus and then Tiberius. His name is believed to come from Germanic roots meaning master of victory, *segaz, victory, and the Old Frankish gastes, master. He favoured Roman overlordship, and the marriage of his daughter Thusnelda to the Cheruscan noble and war leader Arminius, made against his will, left him with a lasting grudge against his son-in-law.

His warning to the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus was not believed, and Varus and his three legions perished in the three-day Battle of the Teutoburg Forest, ambushed by several allied Germanic tribes under Arminius. Segestes turned openly against Arminius when Germanicus invaded northern Germany in 15 to renew the attempt at Roman rule. Besieged in his stronghold by his own countrymen, he appealed to Germanicus, whose forces relieved the siege, and he then handed over his pregnant daughter to Germanicus as a prisoner.

Thusnelda was displayed with her brother Segimundus in Germanicus' victory parade in Rome in 17, with her father watching as an honoured spectator, and she never returned to her homeland. Her son Thumelicus, born in captivity, was trained as a gladiator at Ravenna and is thought to have died in a fight before the age of 20. In 21 Segestes and other members of his family killed Arminius. Germanicus gave Segestes a residence in a Roman province west of the Rhine.
segobriga: The town stood on the hill of Cabeza de Griego, and the Cigüela river is thought to have served as a moat for an early Celtiberian fortress commanding the basin to the north. Its name joins two Celtiberian words, sego-, victory, and -briga, city or fortress, so that it may be rendered Victory City. Pliny the Elder called it the head of Celtiberia, and it seems to have lain on the boundary between the Celtiberians and the Carpetani.

A Bronze Age burial cave, found nearby in 1888, and a fragment of 5th-century BCE Attic pottery show early settlement. Frontinus describes how the Lusitanian leader Viriathus ambushed the Segobrigenses, allies of Rome, in 146 BCE, and Strabo mentions fighting around Segóbriga in the Wars of Sertorius. After those wars it controlled a large part of the Meseta Central, and around 12 BCE it became a municipium, beginning a building programme completed in Flavian times with the theatre, amphitheatre and walls.

Elites still lived there in the 3rd century, but by the 4th the main monuments had been abandoned. Under the Visigoths it remained important, with basilicas and a large cemetery, and its bishops attended the Third Council of Toledo in 589 and the Sixteenth in 693. After the Muslim conquest its bishops and elites fled north and a fortification was built on the summit. After the Reconquista the people moved 3 kilometres north to Saelices, and stone from the ruins went into the convent-fortress of Uclés.

The site was declared a National Monument on 3 June 1931 and is protected as a Bien de Interés Cultural within an archaeological park. Besides the Roman buildings it preserves the North Gate, the aqueduct, the quarries, a rock sanctuary of Diana and the basilica of Cabeza de Griego; the circus, built over a cemetery, was apparently never finished.
segontium: The fort probably takes its name from the Afon Seiont, or from an earlier British settlement named after the river; the name is a Latinised form of the Brythonic *seg-ontio, which may be translated as strong place. There is no evidence of any link with the Segontiaci, a British tribe noted by Julius Caesar. Unlike the medieval Caernarfon Castle, built beside the Seiont estuary more than a thousand years later, the fort stood on higher ground to the east, with a good view of the Menai Strait.

Agricola founded Segontium in 77 or 78 CE. It was the main Roman fort in the north of Roman Wales, built for about a thousand auxiliary infantry and linked by road to the legionary base at Chester, Deva Victrix. In the first half of the 2nd century its timber defences were rebuilt in stone and a large courtyard house with its own small bathhouse was put up inside, perhaps for an official in charge of regional mineral extraction. Archaeology shows that the garrison had been reduced by 120. An aqueduct inscription of the time of Septimius Severus records 500 men of the Cohors I Sunicorum, first raised among the Sunici of Gallia Belgica.

The fort shrank further in the 3rd and 4th centuries, when its main task was to defend the north Wales coast against Irish raiders and pirates, and coins show it was still occupied in 394. The History of the Britons ascribed to Nennius is generally thought to list it among the 28 cities of Britain as Cair Segeint, and claims that the emperor Constantius died there, though Constantius Chlorus died at York. In the 11th century the Normans built a motte nearby, the nucleus of present-day Caernarfon, replaced by Caernarfon Castle after the Edwardian conquest of the 13th century.

The A4085 to Beddgelert cuts through the site, but most of the fort's foundations are preserved. Traces of a civilian settlement, a temple of Mithras known as the Caernarfon Mithraeum, and a cemetery have been found around the fort. In the Mabinogion tale Breuddwyd Macsen Wledig, the emperor Macsen dreams of Saint Elen at the fort at the mouth of the Seiont.
segou: Ségou lies on the right bank of the Niger in south-central Mali, 235 kilometres north-east of Bamako, and is the capital of the Ségou Region. In the middle of the 19th century four villages called Ségou stood along about 12 kilometres of the bank: Ségou-Koro, Ségou-Bougou, Ségou-Koura and Ségou-Sikoro. The present town is on the site of Ségou-Sikoro.

Its origins are contested. Some derive the name from Sikoro, meaning at the foot of a shea butter tree, others from Cheikou, a marabout said to have founded the city, and others hold that Bozo fishermen coming from the north in the 4th century founded villages along the river. The 11th century brought an influx of Soninke people escaping the collapse of the Ghana Empire, followed by Mandinka.

Around 1650 Kaladian Coulibaly overthrew the ruling Koita dynasty and established a powerful if short-lived kingdom with Ségou-Koro as its capital. His great-grandson Mamary Coulibaly, known as Bitòn, became chief of his tòn, an association of men, after 1700. By 1712 he had used his military strength to displace local elders, and he extended the Bambara Empire over regional commercial centres such as Macina and Djenné; Timbuktu became a tributary. A distinct urban architecture, including mosques, began to emerge at Ségou-Koro.

After Bitòn's death in 1755 the capital moved repeatedly. In 1766 Ngolo Diarra, a former slave and warrior, took control of the empire and moved the capital to Ségou-Sikoro. The Diarra dynasty ruled until the mid-19th century. When Mungo Park passed through in 1797 he described the city, its many canoes on the river, its crowded population and cultivated countryside, as a prospect of civilization and magnificence he had not expected to find in Africa.

On 10 March 1861 the Muslim Toucouleur leader El Hadj Oumar Tall conquered the town, and the military architect Samba Ndiaye rebuilt some of its defences. Oumar died in 1864 and his son Ahmadu Tall succeeded him, facing repeated rebellions and challenges from his brothers. French forces led by Colonel Louis Archinard entered Ségou on 6 April 1890. France at first ruled indirectly, and on 13 March 1893 made the town the capital of a local cercle.

Ségou remains a regional commercial centre, known for its market, its fishing and its pottery; Kalabougou, across the river, is a large pottery district. Bogolan cloth, weaving and sculpture are also among its crafts. Its people include Bambara, Bozo, Malinke, Soninke, Fulani and Toucouleur, and in 2009 it had 130,690 inhabitants. The Office du Niger, which administers a large irrigation scheme in the region, has its headquarters there, and Maryse Condé's novel Segu tells the city's history from 1797 to its defeat by the army of El Hajj Oumar Tall.
segovia: Segovia is the capital and most populated municipality of the Province of Segovia, in Castile and León. It lies on the Inner Plateau of the Iberian Peninsula, near the northern slopes of the Sistema Central, with its housing set on a bend of the Eresma river. The main route of the Camino de Santiago de Madrid passes through it. Its name is of Celtiberian origin and is mentioned by Livy in the context of the Sertorian War.

The first recorded settlement on the site was a Celtic possession, which later passed to the Romans. The city is a possible site of the battle of 75 BCE in which Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius defeated Quintus Sertorius and Hirtuleius. After Alfonso VI of León and Castile conquered Toledo, Segovia was resettled with Christians from the north of the peninsula and from beyond the Pyrenees.

Its position on trade routes made it an important centre of the wool and textile trade, and the end of the Middle Ages was something of a golden age, with a growing Jewish population. Isabella I was proclaimed queen of Castile in Segovia on 13 December 1474. The city joined the Revolt of the Comuneros under Juan Bravo, and its population rose to 27,000 in 1594, then fell to only 8,000 by 1694 as Castilian cities declined. The Royal School of Artillery, the first military academy in Spain, opened in 1764. French troops sacked the city in 1808.

The old city and its aqueduct were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 1985. The Roman aqueduct, dating from the late 1st or early 2nd century, consists of about 25,000 granite blocks held together without mortar and spans 818 metres with more than 170 arches. The Alcázar, a royal palace on a stone peninsula between the Eresma and Clamores, is first documented in 1122 and was rebuilt after a fire in 1862. The cathedral, consecrated in 1768, is the last Gothic cathedral built in Spain. The walls, enlarged by Alfonso VI, encircle the historic quarter.
segura-river: The Segura is a medium-sized river of south-eastern Spain, known in Latin as the Thader and in Arabic as Shaqūrah or Wādī l-Abyaḍ. It begins at Santiago Pontones in the province of Jaén and passes Calasparra, Cieza, Blanca, Murcia, Beniaján, Orihuela and Rojales before flowing into the Mediterranean near Guardamar del Segura in the province of Alicante. Its tributaries include the Mundo, the Alhárabe, the Mula and the Guadalentín.

Its alluvial plain, the Vega del Segura, is a very productive agricultural region growing a wide variety of fruit, vegetables and flowers. The vegas are divided into three areas, the Alta, Media and Baja, the upper, middle and lower plain.

By the 1990s the Segura had become one of the most polluted rivers in Europe, because of the canning industry and urban and agricultural waste from the densely populated middle and lower basin. Low flows made the pollution worse, since agricultural use and summer drought could reduce the mean discharge in Murcia to 2 or 3 cubic metres a second.

Public protest peaked in 2001 with a demonstration of 40,000 people, and a comprehensive action plan, the Segura River Project, followed. Between 2001 and 2010 some 100 water treatment plants and 350 kilometres of wastewater collection systems were built, financed in part by a levy on the principle that the polluter pays. Water quality began to improve by 2003, and otters and eels, which are sensitive to pollution, had returned to long stretches of the river by 2013.

The river is usually in a state of semi-permanent drought, but torrential autumn and spring rains cause floods roughly once every six to nine years. Significant floods occurred in 1946, 1948, 1973, 1982, 1987 and 1989. Since 1990 the lower reaches have been canalized, removing meanders to carry flood water away more quickly.
sei-shonagon: Little is known of Sei Shōnagon's life except what can be found in her own writing. Her given name is unknown. It was the custom to call a court lady by a nickname taken from a court office held by her father or husband. Sei is the Sino-Japanese reading of Kiyohara, her father's family name, and Shōnagon means lesser councilor of state, a post that neither her father nor either of her two husbands held. Her grandfather Kiyohara no Fukayabu was also a waka poet, and the family of middle-ranking courtiers had financial difficulties, possibly because they were not granted a revenue-producing office.

She married Tachibana no Norimitsu, a government official, at 16 and gave birth to a son, Norinaga. In 993, at 27, she began to serve Empress Teishi, consort of Emperor Ichijō, and may by then have been divorced.

The Pillow Book is a collection of lists, gossip, poetry, observations and complaints written during her years at court, in the miscellaneous genre known as zuihitsu. It describes the daily experiences and customs of the Imperial Court in Kyoto from a unique point of view, and circulated at court in handwritten manuscripts for several hundred years before it was first printed in the 17th century. Four main variants are known, and the Sankanbon and Nōinbon texts are considered the most complete and accurate. She writes with apparent lightheartedness about Teishi's court, omitting harsh realities such as the empress's death in childbirth, since to have written more passionately would have been considered unstylish.

Courtiers regarded her as having an excellent memory, and she was adept at quoting a classic poem to suit the occasion. The book includes advice on conversation, preaching and letter writing, with particular attention to the morning-after letters that followed a night together. One of her waka is included in the Ogura Hyakunin Isshu as number 62. Her contemporary Murasaki Shikibu, author of The Tale of Genji and a court lady of Empress Shoshi, wrote of her in her diary somewhat scathingly while conceding her literary gifts.

There are no details about Shōnagon's life after 1017, and very few records of her after the death of Empress Teishi. According to one tradition she lived out her twilight years in poverty as a Buddhist nun. Another has her marrying Fujiwara no Muneyo, governor of Settsu province, and having a daughter, Koma no Myobu. The Pillow Book is thought to have been finished sometime between 1001 and 1010, while she was in retirement.
seikilos-epitaph: The Seikilos epitaph is an inscription on a marble column found at the ancient Greek town of Tralles, now Aydın. The column bears two texts: an elegiac distich at the top, and below it a short song with vocal notation signs written above the words. The song is a Hellenistic Ionic piece, either in the Phrygian octave species or in the Ionian tonos.

It is generally understood to be an epitaph created by a man named Seikilos and possibly dedicated to a woman named Euterpe. The scholar Armand D'Angour holds instead that it does not mark a tomb but was a monument Seikilos set up to commemorate his own musical and poetic skill. The date is debated: one authority argues from letter forms for the first century, another equally firmly for the second, comparing it with inscriptions of 127/128 and 149/150.

In the distich the stone speaks in the first person. Landels translates: "I, the stone, am an image and Seikilos places me here (to be) a long-lasting monument to immortal memory." D'Angour prefers "and" to "the" and reads "I am an image and a stone." The song reads, in Rohland's translation: "As long as you're alive, shine, don't be sad at all; life is short, time asks for its due."

Before its last line was cut away, the dedication read "Seikilos Euter...", with the verb zei, "is alive", a convention showing that the dedicator had outlived the person commemorated. It has been reconstructed as "Seikilos to Euterpe", or alternatively as "Seikilos, son of Euterpes". In 1893 the German scholar Otto Crusius observed that the melody tends to follow the pitch of the word accents, and the publication of the two Delphic hymns that year confirmed this tendency.

The British engineer Edward Purser found the column around 1883 while a railway was being built at Aydın. William Mitchell Ramsay described it that year in the Bulletin de correspondance hellénique, and the French archaeologist Théodore Reinach published a rubbing in 1894. Purser had the foot of the column sawn flat so that his wife could use it as a stand for flowerpots, which destroyed a line of text known only from the earlier rubbing.

It passed to the collection of De Jongh, Purser's son-in-law, at Buca, and during the burning of Smyrna in 1922 the Dutch consul in İzmir protected it. It was taken to The Hague and remained there until 1966. Presumed lost, it was acquired by the National Museum of Denmark in Copenhagen and revealed in December of the following year, and it is still displayed there.
seille-moselle: The Seille, in German the Selle, is a right tributary of the Moselle, also called the Seille lorraine or Grande Seille to tell it from a small Seille that flows into the Saône. It rises near Azoudange in the department of Moselle, leaves the Lindre lake, skirts Dieuze and passes Vic-sur-Seille and Nomeny before reaching the Moselle at Metz. Its basin covers 1348 square kilometres. Most of its course lies in Moselle, and from Chambrey to Aulnois-sur-Seille it forms the border with Meurthe-et-Moselle.

The upper river crosses the Saulnois, a region in the south of Moselle, through a broad valley of marl and clay, part of the Regional Natural Park of Lorraine. Since the Middle Ages the river has been worked on, straightened to make it navigable, its marshes drained and its floods held back, which left a straight course with bare banks that now suffer from erosion. Salt water rising in the valley supports plants usually found only on coasts, such as glasswort, aster tripolium and sea-spurreys.

Downstream the river winds along the border of the department and takes in few tributaries, among them the Osson at Ajoncourt. In Metz it passes the Porte des Allemands, a 13th-century castle whose name means Gate of the Germans, before joining the Moselle. Many places carry the river's name with the suffix sur-Seille, among them Aulnois-sur-Seille, Moncel-sur-Seille, Port-sur-Seille and Vic-sur-Seille.

The upper tributaries include the Spin and the Verbach at Dieuze, the Nard at Marsal and the Petite Seille at Salonnes. The river holds a wide variety of fish and is home to otters and herons, though it suffers from eutrophication.
seimas: The word Seimas is of Slavic origin, derived from the Polish sejm through the Ruthenian sejmъ. Traces of large meetings of the nobility appear in the negotiations for the Treaty of Salynas in 1398, but the first Seimas is considered to have met at Hrodna in 1445, during talks between Casimir IV Jagiellon and the Council of Lords. As the Muscovite–Lithuanian Wars raged, the Grand Duke needed more tax revenue to finance the army and called the Seimas more often. In exchange for taxation the nobility demanded privileges, including a stronger Seimas.

At first it had no legislative power. It debated foreign and domestic affairs, taxes, wars and the treasury. By the beginning of the 16th century it had gained some legislative powers and could petition the Grand Duke to pass certain laws, which he usually granted in return for the nobility's support in taxation and war.

The first widely elected body in Lithuania after the declaration of independence on 16 February 1918 was the Constituent Assembly, elected on 14–15 April 1920 with a turnout of about 90 per cent. It adopted the Constitution on 1 August 1922, and a land reform. The constitution gave broad powers to the Seimas, elected to a three-year term, which would select the Cabinet and elect the President.

The First Seimas, elected on 10–11 October 1922, could not form a sustainable coalition and was dissolved on 12 March 1923. The Second Seimas, elected in May 1923, was the only regular interwar Seimas to complete its full term. With a slim Christian Democrat majority it continued the land reform, expanded primary and secondary schools and introduced social support, but it saw several short-lived governments.

On 11 March 1990 the Supreme Council of the Lithuanian SSR proclaimed independence from the Soviet Union and renamed itself the Supreme Council of the Republic of Lithuania, regarded as the Fifth Seimas. The present Constitution was approved by referendum on 25 October 1992. The first election under it, on 25 October 1992, was won by the Democratic Labor Party, which took 73 of the 141 seats in the Sixth Seimas.

The Seimas is the unicameral legislature of Lithuania. It enacts laws and amendments to the Constitution, passes the budget, confirms the Prime Minister and the Government and ratifies international treaties. Of its 141 members, 71 are elected in single-seat constituencies and 70 by proportional representation, for four years. The Act of the Re-Establishment of the State of Lithuania was proclaimed on 11 March 1990 in the main hall of its building.
seine: The Seine rises at Source-Seine, about 30 kilometres north-west of Dijon on the Langres plateau, and flows through Paris into the English Channel at Le Havre. Its drainage basin lies in the Paris Basin and covers most of northern France. The river is divided into five parts: the Petite Seine from the sources to Montereau-Fault-Yonne, the Haute Seine to Paris, the Paris waterway, the Basse Seine from Paris to Rouen, and the Seine maritime from Rouen to the sea. Ocean-going vessels can reach Rouen, 120 kilometres from the sea. Because the river is only 24 metres above sea level 446 kilometres from its mouth, it flows slowly and is easily navigated.

The name comes from the Gaulish Sēquana, the Celtic Gallo-Roman goddess of the river, to whom offerings were found at the source. The buried remains of a Gallo-Roman temple lie at the same site, and small statues of the goddess Sequana and other ex-votos found there are now in the Dijon archaeological museum. The source has belonged to the city of Paris since 1864.

On 28 or 29 March 845 an army of Vikings led by a chieftain named Reginherus, possibly another name for Ragnar Lothbrok, sailed up the Seine with siege towers and sacked Paris. On 25 November 885 another Viking expedition, led by Rollo, travelled up the river to attack Paris again. In March 1314 King Philip IV of France had Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Knights Templar, burned on a scaffold on an island in the river in front of Notre Dame de Paris. After the burning of Joan of Arc in 1431 her ashes were thrown into the Seine from the Mathilde Bridge at Rouen, though counter-claims persist without support.

On 9 August 1803 the American engineer Robert Fulton made the first successful test of his steamboat on the Seine beside the Tuileries Garden. The Seine flooded Paris severely in January 1910. In 1944 reaching the Seine was one of the original objectives of Operation Overlord, and the Allies met it within 90 days of D-Day. At the 1900 Summer Olympics the river hosted the rowing, swimming and water polo events.

The Seine is 777 kilometres (483 miles) long, and Paris has 37 bridges across it, among them the Pont Alexandre III and the Pont Neuf. In 1991 UNESCO added the banks of the Seine in Paris to its list of World Heritage Sites. Four large storage reservoirs built since 1950 on the Seine and its tributaries help to keep the river level constant through the city. The river inspired many artists of the 19th and 20th centuries, among them Claude Monet, Camille Pissarro, Georges Seurat and Alfred Sisley.
seismoscope: A seismoscope merely indicates that ground motion has occurred, perhaps with some simple measure of how large it was. It differs from a seismometer or seismograph, which gives a continuous record of ground motion. The word seismometer comes from the Greek seismós, a shaking or quake, and métron, to measure, and was coined by David Milne-Home in 1841 for an instrument designed by the Scottish physicist James David Forbes.

Zhang Heng of China's Han dynasty is said to have invented the first seismoscope in 132 CE. It was called Houfeng Didong Yi, translated as instrument for measuring the seasonal winds and the movements of the Earth. The description in the History of the Later Han Dynasty says it was a large bronze vessel about 2 metres in diameter, with dragon's heads at eight points around the top holding bronze balls. In an earthquake one dragon's mouth would open and drop its ball into a bronze toad at the base, making a sound and supposedly showing the direction.

On at least one occasion, probably during a large earthquake in Gansu in 143 CE, it indicated an earthquake that was not felt. The text says a central column could move along eight tracks, thought to refer to a pendulum, though it is not known how this was linked to a mechanism that opened only one mouth. The first earthquake it recorded was supposedly somewhere in the east, and days later a rider from the east reported it. Some secondary sources mention unverified claims of an earlier device in ancient Egypt, but no reliable sources confirm one.

By the 13th century seismographic devices existed at the Maragheh observatory in Persia, founded in 1259, though it is unclear whether they were independent of the first seismoscope. The French physicist and priest Jean de Hautefeuille described a seismoscope in 1703, a bowl of mercury that would spill into one of eight receivers, although there is no evidence he built it. Atanasio Cavalli built a mercury seismoscope in 1784 or 1785. Pendulum devices developed at the same time: Nicola Cirillo set up a network of pendulum detectors after the 1731 Puglia earthquake, and Andrea Bina in 1751 had a pendulum trace marks in sand. The first seismographs, which recorded continuously, were developed in the 1870s and 1880s, and the modern seismometer descends from them.
seiyun: Seiyun lies in the middle of the Hadhramaut Valley, 12 km from Shibam and 35 km from Tarim, on a flat plain of the Wadi Hadramaut between mountain ranges that lead up to the northern and southern plateaus. The district covers about 804 square kilometres. Summers are hot and winters mild, and rain is rare. Villages around the town include Madurah, Burr, Hazkir and Houta Sultana. Tradition says the place began as a resting point for travellers, named after a woman called Seiyun who kept a café there.

Seiyun is first mentioned at the beginning of the 4th century, under King Dhamar, who ruled the Hadhramaut Valley. In the Islamic period it emerged as a village in the era of the Rashidun Caliphate and was administratively part of Tarim, and from 708 part of Shibam. It became the capital of the valley under Sultan Badr Abu Tuwairq (1501-1556), who built a wall around it, ruled a sultanate that reached from Ain Ba to west of Dhofar and made the Kathiri palace his residence, adding a mosque.

In the 18th century the Yafa took over much of Seiyun. In 1852 it became the capital of the Kathiri State, which lay within the British Aden Protectorate, and the sultanate's postage stamps were sometimes inscribed Kathiri State of Seiyun. Ghalib bin Muhsin Al Kathiri made the town his capital and the palace his seat, and his son Mansour bin Ghalib enlarged it with a new entrance and a large hall. After independence Seiyun became the capital of the southern district of the fifth province.

Seiyun is a city of Hadhramaut Governorate, served by Seiyun Airport. Part of the mud-brick Kathiri Palace, also called the Dawil Palace, has been a museum since 1983, with finds from sites in the Wadi Hadhramaut, including Ribat, and documents of the Kathiri Sultanate. The town's Friday mosques include the Al-Jami Mosque, the oldest, and the Taha, Al-Qarn and Basalam mosques, and the hill fortresses of Qarat Al-Ar and Hisn Al-Fals stand within it.
sejm: The word is an ancient Proto-Lechitic one meaning gathering or meeting. The Sejm traces its roots to the King's Councils, the wiece, which gained authority during the fragmentation of Poland between 1146 and 1295. The Sejm of 1180 at Łęczyca, known as the first Polish parliament, was the most notable, since it established laws constraining the ruler. These early assemblies met only at the king's behest.

After the Sejm of 1493 in Piotrków it became a regularly convening body, to which indirect elections were held every two years. It had two chambers: the Senate, of 81 bishops and other dignitaries, and the Chamber of Deputies, of 54 envoys elected by the local assemblies of landed nobility, the sejmiki, in each province. The nobility made up around 10% of the population, the highest share in Europe, and with the development of the Golden Liberty the powers of the Sejm increased dramatically.

The Union of Lublin in 1569 joined the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania into the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and the Sejm gained envoys from the Lithuanian nobility. The Sejm, Senate and King formed the three estates and the supreme deliberating body. Early in the 16th century the Senate had precedence, but from the middle of the century the Sejm became a very powerful representative body of the szlachta. It held final decisions in legislation, taxation, the budget, military funding, foreign policy and the confirmation of nobility.

Until the end of the 16th century unanimity was not required and majority voting was common. Later, as the magnates grew in power, unanimity returned with the right of liberum veto, the free veto. If the envoys did not reach a unanimous decision within the six weeks of a session, its deliberations were void and all its acts annulled. From the mid-17th century any objection by an envoy or senator rejected the other resolutions as well, since a session's resolutions formed one constituent act. From the second half of that century the liberum veto was used to paralyse the Sejm and brought the Commonwealth to the brink of collapse.

The Constitution of 3 May 1791 abolished the liberum veto, although the Sejm needed four years to adopt it. Its acceptance is arguably the reason Habsburg Austria, Russia and Prussia decided to partition the Commonwealth, ending over 300 years of Polish parliamentary continuity.
