Between 1493 and 1793 a Sejm is estimated to have been held 240 times, with a total debate time of 44 years. Since 1918 the name has referred only to the lower house of parliament.
sejo-of-joseon: Sejo, personal name Yi Yu, was born on 11 November 1417, the second son of the future King Sejong. He showed great ability at archery, horse riding and martial arts, and had a musical talent that delighted his father. In 1445 his title became Grand Prince Suyang, by which he is commonly known. After Sejong died in 1450 his brother took the throne as King Munjong and died two years later, and the crown passed to Munjong's 12-year-old son, the future King Danjong. Government was controlled by Hwangbo In and General Kim Chongsŏ, and as Kim's faction extended the power of court officials against the royal family, tension with Suyang grew.

In 1453 Suyang killed Kim Chongsŏ and his faction and took power, and had his younger brother, Grand Prince Anpyeong, exiled and then sentenced to death. In 1455 he forced the powerless king to abdicate. When his younger brother Grand Prince Geumsung and six scholars, among them Sŏng Sammun, plotted to restore Danjong, he demoted Danjong to Prince Nosan and later ordered him to take poison.

He continued Taejong's policy of strengthening the monarchy, weakening the State Council and bringing officials under the king's direct control. His administrative system let the government count the population and mobilise troops, which caused Yi Si-ae's Rebellion, which he suppressed. He attacked the Jurchens in 1460 and 1467, revised the land ordinance and encouraged the publication of books. He used his father's ritual music, which conservative officials had blocked, for the royal ancestral rituals, and it is now inscribed as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage.

Sejo died in 1468, and the throne passed to his third son, King Yejong. His State Code, the Kyŏngguk Taejŏn, became the cornerstone of dynastic administration and the first written constitutional law in Korea. Historians count him one of Korea's ablest rulers, yet his killing of rivals, including his brothers, and his overly generous treatment of old supporters have been blamed for weakening royal power and opening the way for the rise of royal in-laws and for political instability lasting to the late 17th century.
sejong-the-great: Sejong was born as Yi To in 1397 at Hanyang, now Seoul, the third son of Grand Prince Chŏngan, the future King Taejong, and Princess Chŏngnyŏng. His grandfather Taejo was the founder of Joseon. By 1406 Taejong, wishing to abdicate in his lifetime, had designated his eldest son, Grand Prince Yangnyŏng, as heir. In mid-1418 Yangnyŏng was deposed and Yi To, then Prince Ch'ungnyŏng, was made crown prince. Taejong abdicated on the 10th day of the 8th month of 1418, and the 21-year-old Sejong took the throne at Gyeongbokgung. Taejong remained king emeritus until 1422.

Sejong's reign saw major developments in science, medicine, agriculture and the arts. In 1420 he re-established the Hall of Worthies, a government research body. After a solar eclipse in 1432 came two days later than predicted, he commissioned astronomical instruments, and an armillary sphere was made in 1433 and a water clock designed by Chang Yŏngsil in 1434. In 1441 a rain gauge, the ch'ŭgugi, was invented under the supervision of the crown prince. The farming treatise Nongsa chiksŏl, completed in 1429, was meant to suit Korean agriculture more directly than Chinese works. In 1434 the court cast more than 200,000 copper kabin movable types, twice as efficient as the earlier kyŏngja types.

In 1419 Sejong launched an expedition against Tsushima, followed by decades of peace and trade with Japan. He extended Korea's northern borders to roughly their present extent through campaigns against the raiding Jurchens. He reformed taxation, allowing peasants in 1421 to report their own crop assessments, and tried with limited success to raise the status of marginalised groups. His government restricted Buddhist institutions and promoted Confucianism, although Sejong was privately Buddhist. Hangul, the Korean alphabet, is associated with him; scholars debate how far he created it personally, though most think he was significantly involved.

Sejong suffered from recurring and worsening health problems, including back pain and poor eyesight. From 1445 the crown prince, the future Munjong, handled daily government. Sejong died in 1450 at the age of 52 and was buried at Yeongneung. Historians have often described his reign as a golden age, and his name appears more than 2000 times in the Veritable Records. Hangul Day, a national holiday on 9 October, marks the alphabet.
seku-amadu: Seku Amadu was raised by his father's younger brother, Hamman Lobbo, and studied under the Qadiriyya Sufi teacher Sidi Mukhtar al-Kunti. In the Inner Niger Delta, Fulbe traders ruled towns such as Djenné while the non-Muslim Bambara controlled the river, and the Fulbe chiefs paid tribute to the Bambara of Ségou. He may have served in the Sokoto jihad. His teaching drew a large following but led to his expulsion, first from a village under Djenné and then from Sebera, under Massina.

Usman dan Fodio authorised him to wage jihad and sent him a flag as a sign of his authority. Seku Amadu's conflict with his local Fulani chief, who called on the Bambara king of Segu, turned into a general uprising, aimed first at Fulbe rulers he accused of idolatry and then at the Bambara. He defeated the Segu army, took Djenné, whose scholars welcomed him, and in 1819 founded his capital, Hamdullahi, north-east of Djenné. One estimate puts the deaths of the jihad at 10,000.

He governed through provincial governors, mostly relatives, a central council of forty elders and qadis who applied the Maliki school of law strictly. He settled nomadic herders, banned alcohol, tobacco, music and dancing, ordered six hundred madrasas and provided for widows, orphans and the poor, and his pastoral code regulated the use of the delta by herders and farmers. His rigour and his title of Commander of the Faithful alienated the leaders of Timbuktu and Sokoto; Timbuktu's ruler marched against Hamdullahi in 1833 and was defeated.

Seku Amadu died on 20 April 1845 and was succeeded by his son, Amadu II. Under his heirs the Niger bend was stable and trade flourished, until the jihad of El Hadj Umar Tall overthrew his grandson, Amadu III, in 1862 and threw the region into chaos.
selbach-mac-ferchair: Selbach's existence is well attested, for the Irish annals mention him repeatedly. He had two known sons, Dúngal and Feredach. He is first named after the death of Fiannamail ua Dúnchado in 700, but it seems likely that he had deposed his brother Ainbcellach in 698. He ruled the Cenél Loairn from around then until 723, though he may have been undisputed king of all Dál Riata only in his last years.

Whether his destruction of Dún Olaigh in 701 was part of a war against Ainbcellach, against a king of the Cenél nGabráin or against other enemies is unknown. The annals record a defeat for Dál Riata in Glen Lemnae in 704 and victories over the Britons at Lorg Ecclet in 711 and at the rock called Minuirc in 717, without naming Selbach. In 712 he besieged Aberte, Dunaverty near Southend in Kintyre, in the lands of the Cenél nGabráin, and in 714 he rebuilt Dún Olaigh.

In September 719 he fought Ainbcellach at Finnglen, perhaps near Loch Fyne, and his brother was killed. A month later he met the Cenél nGabráin under their king Dúnchad Bec, also called king of Cenn Tíre (Kintyre), at sea off Ard Nesbi, and was defeated. Dúnchad Bec died in 721, which may have left Selbach unchallenged.

When he abdicated and withdrew to a monastery in 723, one annalist called him lord of Dál Riada. He was probably succeeded by his son Dúngal, whom Eochaid mac Echdach replaced in 726, and in 727 Selbach was fighting Eochaid's supporters at Irros Foichnae. He died in 730. The Duan Albanach, a praise poem, lists his father, brother, son and nephew among the forebears of Máel Coluim mac Donnchada (Malcolm III) of Scotland, but leaves Selbach out, perhaps a form of damnatio memoriae.
selenga-river: The Selenga, or Selenge, is formed by the meeting of the Ider, which rises in the Hangyn Mountains of central Mongolia, and the Delger mörön, which comes from the Sangilen Mountains on the border of Mongolia and Tyva. It flows north-east, joins the Orkhon at Suhbaatar and continues north into Russia, turns east towards Ulan-Ude, the capital of Buryatia, and enters Lake Baikal through a lobate delta about 40 km wide. It carries almost half of the river water that flows into the lake.

Its basin is semi-arid, the largest in Mongolia, with harsh winters and warm summers, and the river is frozen from November to April. The name comes from the Mongolian seleh, "to swim", though one view derives it from the Evenki sele, "iron"; Mongolia's Selenge Province is named after it.

Evidence of Paleolithic culture was found in the basin at the end of the 19th century. G. P. Sosnovskii directed a Stone Age study of the valley near Kiakhta in 1928 and 1929, and from 1947 to 1958 an expedition under A. P. Okladnikov found 30 new sites in the Trans-Baikal region. One of them, Ust-Kyakhta-3, was excavated in 1976 and 1978 and yielded more than 40,000 stone artifacts and abundant animal remains; further work there in 2012 found two human tooth fragments, one of which later helped establish a link between Native Americans and their ancestors in East Asia.

The river floods every summer, and twenty-six floods are documented between 1730 and 1900, of which three were catastrophic, in 1830, 1869 and 1897. The first to be recorded in some detail began on 1 August 1830, when the Selenga and its tributaries burst their banks. On 16 August Verkhneudinsk, now Ulan-Ude, was flooded to a depth of 420 centimetres. The flood destroyed fifty-four buildings in Selenginsk, and the town was afterwards moved to higher ground on the left bank. There were heavy losses of pasture and hayfields.

The wetlands of the delta, in Buryatia, are a Ramsar site and an Important Bird Area, habitat of the Siberian Baikal sturgeon, which breeds in the river, and of over 170 species of birds. The Irkutsk Hydroelectric Power Station, built on the Angara between 1950 and 1956 to raise the level of Lake Baikal by 1.5 metres, has made part of the delta waterlogged. The Selenge-Orkhon forest steppe, an ecoregion of scattered forests and mountain ranges, takes in the basins of the Orkhon and the Selenga.
seleucia: Seleucia stood on the west bank of the Tigris, at the confluence of the river with a major canal from the Euphrates, in what is now the Baghdad Governorate of Iraq. This position let it receive traffic from both great waterways. It was the largest and most important of the many cities named for Seleucus I Nicator, and it is distinguished from the others as Seleucia-on-Tigris. Church of the East texts call it Salīq, and the Persian name Veh-Ardashir belongs to a new eastern city that Italian excavations showed to be separate from Seleucia and Ctesiphon.

Seleucus I, one of the Diadochi who divided Alexander the Great's empire, enlarged an earlier settlement and made it his capital around 305 BCE; other scholars propose foundation dates of 312 and 306 BCE. He soon moved his main capital to Antioch, but Seleucia stayed an important centre of trade, Hellenistic culture and regional government. To fill it, he forced almost all the inhabitants of Babylon, except temple priests and workers, to move there. In the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE it was one of the great Hellenistic cities, comparable to Alexandria and larger than Syrian Antioch. Its walls enclosed at least 550 hectares.

The Parthians under Mithridates I conquered it in 141 BCE, and it became the western capital of the Parthian Empire. Tacitus described it as fully Hellenistic even then, and ancient texts claim 600,000 inhabitants and a senate of 300. In 41 BCE about 5,000 Babylonian Jewish refugees were massacred there. Trajan burned the city in 117 CE, Hadrian ceded it back to the Parthians, and it was rebuilt in the Parthian style. The Roman general Avidius Cassius destroyed it completely in 165.

Archaeologists rediscovered the site in the 1920s, while looking for Opis. University of Michigan teams excavated from 1927, and an Italian mission from the University of Turin worked there from 1964 to 1968 and from 1985 to 1989. It found a Seleucid archive building with about 30,000 seal impressions, all in a fully Greek style. The city faded into obscurity, probably abandoned after the Tigris shifted its course.
seleucid-empire: Alexander the Great died in 323 BCE without an adult heir, and at the Partition of Babylon his generals became satraps of his vast realm. Seleucus received Babylonia after the Partition of Triparadisus in 320 BCE, but Antigonus forced him out of Babylon around 315 BCE and he fled to Egypt. After Ptolemy I Soter and Seleucus defeated Demetrius at Gaza in 312 BCE, Seleucus returned, and in August 311 BCE his army took the citadel of Babylon. Seleucus then declared himself strategos autokrater of Asia, and the Seleucid state dates its founding to 312 BCE.

In 305 BCE Seleucus marched to the Indus against Chandragupta Maurya. The war ended in an understanding sealed by a marriage relationship, and Alexander's conquests along the Indus passed to the Maurya Empire. After he and Lysimachus defeated Antigonus at Ipsus in 301 BCE, Seleucus took eastern Anatolia and northern Syria, and founded Antioch on the Orontes and Seleucia on the Tigris. The empire reached its largest extent after he defeated Lysimachus at Corupedion in 281 BCE; he was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus as he landed in Europe.

His successors faced repeated wars with Ptolemy II and a Celtic invasion of Asia Minor, and under Antiochus II Theos provinces broke away: Bactria and Sogdiana under Diodotus, Cappadocia, and Parthia, where the Parni of Arsaces killed the satrap Andragoras. Antiochus III the Great, who took the throne in 223 BCE, lost at Raphia in 217 BCE but then restored Parthia and Bactria to at least nominal obedience on his anabasis through the east. His war with Rome ended at the Battle of Magnesia, after which the Seleucids paid reparations and gave up claims west of the Taurus Mountains.

Later civil wars weakened the crown. The Maccabees established independence by 143 BCE, Demetrius II was captured by the Parthians in 139 BCE, and by then the whole Iranian Plateau was lost. By 100 BCE little remained beyond Antioch and some Syrian cities. Tigranes the Great of Armenia invaded Syria in 83 BCE, and Pompey ended the dynasty in 63 BCE.

The empire held Greeks, Assyrians, Armenians, Persians, Medes, Jews and many others. Its kings tolerated local customs while controlling local elites, and they founded Greek cities and settlements that drew migrants from Greece. These settlers, a small minority of the population, served in the army and government and seem to have rarely married non-Greeks. The army fought in the Greco-Macedonian style, with a phalanx of pikemen supplemented by native and mercenary troops. Most of the population worked in agriculture on land held by temples, cities and royal estates, much of it inherited from the Achaemenid system.
seleucid-era: The Seleucid era, also called Anno Graecorum (year of the Greeks) and sometimes the Year of Alexander, was a system of numbering years used by the Seleucid Empire and other Hellenistic civilisations, and later by the Parthians. It dates from the reconquest of Babylon by Seleucus I Nicator in 312/311 BCE, after his exile in Ptolemaic Egypt, an event that Seleucus and his court considered to mark the founding of the Seleucid Empire.

Two versions of the Seleucid years existed, differing in when the year began. The natives of the empire used the Babylonian calendar, whose new year falls on 1 Nisanu (3 April in 311 BCE), so that year 1 corresponds roughly to April 311 BCE to March 310 BCE. Coele-Syria followed it, notably the Jews, who call it the Era of Contracts. The Macedonian court adopted the Babylonian calendar with Macedonian month names but reckoned the new year from autumn, on an unknown date, so that year 1 ran from autumn 312 BCE to summer 311 BCE. By the 7th century CE the west Syrian Christians settled on 1 October to 30 September, and Jews reckon each year from the lunar month Tishri.

Dates between spring and autumn therefore differ by one. The Jewish book 1 Maccabees generally uses the Babylonian and Judean count, while 2 Maccabees uses the Macedonian version, probably because it was written in Cyprus or Egypt. Elias Bickerman gave the restoration of the Temple of Jerusalem by Judas Maccabaeus, about 15 December 164 BCE, as an example: year 148 by Jewish and Babylonian reckoning, year 149 for the court.

The era remained in use long after the dynasty. It appears in the Zabad inscription in Syria, dated the 24th of Gorpiaios, 823 (24 September 512 CE), and in the writings of John of Ephesus. Syriac chroniclers used it until Michael the Syrian in the 12th century CE, and it has been found on Central Asian tombstones of Christians of the Church of the East as late as the 14th century.

Yemenite Jews used the count of contracts in their legal deeds and contracts until modern times, a practice derived from an ancient teaching in the Talmud that required Diaspora Jews to uphold it. It is mentioned in 1 Maccabees and by the historian Josephus. Most Jewish communities abandoned it after Rabbi David ben Zimra, as Chief Rabbi of Egypt, cancelled the practice.
seleucid-mauryan-war: After Alexander the Great's Indian campaign, Chandragupta Maurya led a revolt from north-western India against the Nanda dynasty of the Gangetic Plain, took its capital Pataliputra and made himself Emperor of Magadha around 321 BCE. The Persian provinces of what is now Afghanistan, the kingdom of Gandhara and the states of the Indus Valley had submitted to Alexander, and when the Wars of the Diadochi split his empire, Seleucus I Nicator took control in the east. The Roman historian Appian lists his conquests as far as the Indus, while Justin says that India had killed Alexander's prefects under Chandragupta's leadership.

Seleucus crossed the Indus into the former Indian satrapies, which Chandragupta had conquered. Only a few passages in Strabo, Appian, Plutarch and Justin mention the conflict, and no Indian source records it. Appian says that Seleucus waged war with Sandrocottus, king of the Indians, until the two came to an understanding and contracted a marriage relationship. Whether a pitched battle was fought is unknown. Many authors read the Greek sources as describing a Mauryan victory, but the historian Jansari notes that none of the ancient writers names a clear victor, and Wheatley and Heckel suggest the hostilities were probably neither prolonged nor grievous.

The sources record three terms. Seleucus ceded territory to Chandragupta; Strabo says he gave lands along the Indus that Alexander had taken from the Arians, on terms of intermarriage and in exchange for five hundred elephants. A marriage alliance joined the two kings, most likely with Chandragupta marrying a female relative of Seleucus. Which lands changed hands is disputed: Kosmin counts Gandhara, the Paropamisadae and eastern Gedrosia as certain and Arachosia and Aria as far as Herat as possible, V.A. Smith argued for a large cession, and Tarn limited it to the Indus Valley.

The border between the two empires stayed stable for generations, and friendly relations are reflected in the ambassador Megasthenes and in the envoys later sent west by Chandragupta's grandson Ashoka. With the elephants Seleucus defeated his rival Antigonus and his allies at the Battle of Ipsus, while Chandragupta went on to extend his rule southward into the Deccan.
seleucus-i-nicator: Seleucus was the son of Antiochus, who may have belonged to an upper Macedonian noble family, and was born at Europus in northern Macedonia. His year of birth is unclear. Ancient writers give his age at the Battle of Corupedium as 77, 73 or 75, which would place his birth in 358, 354 or 356 BCE; the last date would make him the same age as Alexander the Great, which is most likely propaganda on his part. In spring 334 BCE, aged about twenty-three, he accompanied Alexander into Asia, and by the Indian campaigns he commanded the elite infantry corps of the Hypaspistai, and fought against the elephants of King Porus at the Hydaspes in 326 BCE.

After Alexander died in Babylon on 10 June 323 BCE, Seleucus was made commander of the Companion cavalry and chiliarch under the regent Perdiccas. Perdiccas was assassinated in a conspiracy that included Seleucus, though his participation has not been established, and at Triparadisus in 321 BCE Seleucus received the satrapy of Babylon. In about 315 BCE he quarrelled with Antigonus and fled to Egypt, where he served Ptolemy as an admiral. He returned to Babylon in 312 BCE with Ptolemy's support, defeated Nicanor, the satrap of Media, and over the following years brought the eastern part of Alexander's empire as far as the Jaxartes and Indus rivers under his authority.

In 306 BCE he took the title of king, as did Antigonus, Ptolemy, Lysimachus and Cassander. His war against Chandragupta Maurya in 305 to 303 BCE ended in a treaty by which the Maurya Empire annexed the eastern satrapies, and Seleucus received 500 war elephants. They decided the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, where he, Cassander and Lysimachus defeated Antigonus, and Syria passed to Seleucus. He founded Antioch in 300 BCE and Seleucia on the Tigris, which overshadowed Babylon. In 281 BCE he defeated Lysimachus at Corupedium and added Asia Minor to his empire.

Seleucus then crossed into Europe to take Thrace and Macedon, intending to leave Asia to his son Antiochus I, whom he had named co-ruler in 292 BCE. Near Lysimachia in September 281 BCE he was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus, who had taken refuge at his court. Antiochus succeeded him and founded a cult of his father, and Seleucus was later worshipped as a son of Zeus Nikator. The Seleucid Empire remained one of the major powers of the Hellenistic world until the Roman Republic and the Parthian Empire overcame it in the late second and early first centuries BCE.
seleucus-ii-callinicus: After the death of his father Antiochus II in July 246 BCE, Seleucus was proclaimed king at Ephesos by his mother Laodice, while his father's second wife Berenice declared her own son king at Antioch. Berenice was murdered by partisans of Seleucus and Laodice before her brother Ptolemy III of Egypt could support her, and the feud opened the Third Syrian War. Ptolemy accepted the surrender of Syria and Cilicia and marched as far as the Tigris or beyond. Seleucus appointed his brother Antiochus Hierax viceroy in Asia Minor, took back Antioch by 244 BCE and regained northern Syria by 242 BCE.

In 241 BCE a treaty recognised Seleucus as king and kept the Eleutheros river as the boundary in Syria, but Ptolemy kept Seleucia Pieria, Ephesus and conquests in Thrace. The loss of Seleucia Pieria, which held the tomb of the dynasty's founder Seleucus I, helped cause the Fourth Syrian War in 219 BCE. Meanwhile Antiochus Hierax rebelled with the support of their mother. About 237 BCE he defeated Seleucus at the Battle of Ancyra, aided by Mithridates II of Pontus and the Galatians, and Seleucus barely escaped with his life.

In the east the satrap Andragoras had begun minting his own coins in 245 BCE, and he was killed by 238 BCE by Arsaces I, chieftain of the nomadic Parni, whose people became the Parthians. Diodotus I in Bactria likewise gained de facto independence, and his son Diodotus II declared himself king of Bactria in 235 BCE. An expedition by Seleucus to recover Parthia came to nothing. In Asia Minor Attalus I of Pergamon defeated Antiochus Hierax, the Galatians and Seleucus in turn, and Antiochus Hierax was killed by robbers in Thrace about 226 BCE.

Seleucus also faced a rebellion at Antioch led by his aunt Stratonice, which he put down by siege; she was captured and executed. He spent his later years rebuilding his domains, expanding Antioch and suppressing unrest in Babylon, and by 227 BCE was planning a new offensive against Attalus. He died unexpectedly in 225 BCE after a fall from his horse. He was succeeded by his eldest son, who took the name Seleucus III, and then by a younger son, Antiochus III the Great, in 222 BCE, under whom the empire was restored.
self-strengthening-movement: The phrase self-strengthening comes from the ancient Yijing, and the Qianlong Emperor had used it of warding off foreign ambitions. Defeat in the Second Opium War and the successes of the Taiping Rebellion forced the court to acknowledge a crisis in 1860. In 1861 Prince Gong and Grand Councilor Wenxiang proposed an office to direct foreign affairs, and Prince Gong became head of the new Zongli Yamen. The same year the scholar Feng Guifen, impressed by Western weapons in Shanghai, presented essays on self-strengthening to Zeng Guofan.

Historians divide the movement into three phases. From 1861 to 1872 it centred on Western firearms, machines and the training of technical and diplomatic staff: the Tongwen Guan opened in 1862 to teach English, French, Russian and German. Zeng Guofan, with Yung Wing, set up the Shanghai arsenal, Li Hongzhang built the Nanjing and Tianjin arsenals and Zuo Zongtang the Fuzhou Dockyard, with foreign advisers such as Prosper Giquel. Regional leaders acted largely on their own, with little coordination from Beijing.

After the Tianjin riots of 1870, Li Hongzhang emerged as the movement's leading figure, and over 90 percent of its projects were launched under him. Government-supervised merchant undertakings followed, among them the China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company in 1872 and the Kaiping Mines in 1877. Cadets were sent to France and Britain, laying the ground for the Beiyang Fleet. In the third phase, from 1885, a Navy Board was created and textiles were promoted, though by then the conservative faction at court had overwhelmed Prince Gong.

Output was considerable but limited: the Jiangnan Arsenal made 65,000 rifles, 742 cannons and 15 ships between 1867 and 1895, too few to arm the Qing bannermen. Opponents at court argued that westernized officials might not stay loyal and that railways would carry foreign armies inland. Historians such as Michael Gasster and Kwang-Ching Liu see a programme doomed by its conservative ideology, while Luke S. K. Kwong argued that as an adaptive reform it succeeded in spreading Western ideas.
selim-i: Selim was born in Amasya on 10 October 1470, the son of Şehzade Bayezid, later Bayezid II, and Gülbahar Hatun, a Pontic Greek concubine. In 1487 his father sent him to Trabzon as governor. There he faced the Safavids on the eastern frontier. In 1505 a Safavid prince, Ebrahim Mirza, marched on Trabzon with 3,000 men, and Selim repelled him with an expeditionary force of 450 and chased him to Erzincan. In 1507 Selim attacked Erzincan and Bayburt and defeated a Safavid army of 10,000, at a time when his father had not answered Shah Ismail I's violations of Ottoman sovereignty.

Selim's early reign was dominated by tension with Shah Ismail I, who had made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Persia and by 1510 held Iran, Azerbaijan, Mesopotamia and eastern Anatolia. In 1511 Ismail supported the Şahkulu Rebellion in Anatolia, and Selim's mufti issued a fatwa of takfir against him and his followers. Selim had Shiites aged 7 to 70 listed in central Anatolian cities including Tokat, Sivas and Amasya, and his forces executed those they found, most by beheading, in what was the largest massacre in Ottoman history until the end of the 19th century. During the advance of 1514 his troops suffered from Ismail's scorched-earth tactics.

In 1516 Selim attacked the Mamluk Sultanate and defeated it at Marj Dabiq on 24 August 1516 and at Ridaniya on 22 January 1517. He annexed Syria, Palestine, the Hejaz and Egypt, and with them the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He took the title Servant of the Two Holy Cities. The last Abbasid caliph, al-Mutawakkil III, was sent to Istanbul. An account of a formal transfer of the caliphate to Selim emerged in the eighteenth century, but it was a later invention, and Selim himself made no claim to the office. The conquest ended the Portuguese–Mamluk naval war, and the Ottomans took over attempts to check Portuguese expansion in the Indian Ocean.

Selim was planning a campaign westward when he fell ill and died on 22 September 1520, aged 49. The official cause was a mistreated carbuncle, though some historians suggest cancer or poison, and others note that plague was then present in the empire. He was buried in what became known as the Yavuz Selim Mosque, commissioned by his son Suleiman I.

He was bilingual in Turkish and Persian and wrote poetry in both under the pen name Selimi. He had a fiery temper, and a popular Ottoman curse wished that one might be a vizier of Selim's. Many historians hold that he prepared the empire for its height under Suleiman I.
selim-ii: Selim was born on 28 May 1524 in the Topkapı Palace, Constantinople, the second surviving son of Suleiman and Hürrem Sultan. In 1542 he became governor of Karaman, with Konya as his seat, and after the death of his brother Şehzade Mehmed in November 1543 he was appointed governor of Saruhan, residing in Manisa. The execution of his elder half-brother Şehzade Mustafa on Suleiman's order in September 1553 left Selim and his brother Bayezid as the main contenders for the throne. Their rivalry ended when Bayezid marched on Konya in 1559 and Selim, with troops sent by Sokollu Mehmed Pasha, won the engagement.

Selim took the throne on 29 September 1566. Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept Suleiman's death secret until Selim reached the army at Belgrade, where the allegiance ceremony was held. The soldiers, refused an accession payment, revolted in Istanbul until Selim's sister Mihrimah Sultan paid the Janissaries from her own fortune. Sokollu, grand vizier from 1565 until his assassination in 1579, persuaded Selim to make peace with the Habsburgs, and the Treaty of Edirne of 1568 had Maximilian II recognise Ottoman conquests in Hungary and keep paying tribute. Sokollu opposed the Cyprus campaign, but Selim ordered it.

Elsewhere the reign met mixed fortunes. In 1567 the Zaydi imam al-Mutahhar ibn Yahya Sharaf al-Din rose in Yemen and took Sana'a and Ta'izz; Ottoman forces recovered Aden, Ta'izz and much of the highlands, and a peace at Kawkaban in May 1570 brought recognition of Ottoman suzerainty. A fleet intended for Aceh, which had asked for help against the Portuguese, was diverted to Yemen, and only two ships with cannon and gunsmiths arrived. An attempt on Astrakhan in 1569 failed, and a canal between the Don and Volga was left unfinished. The Ottomans also pressed for Henry of Valois's election in Poland in 1573. Venice ceded Cyprus in a peace of 7 March 1573 and agreed to pay 300,000 ducats.

Selim died on 15 December 1574. His wife Nurbanu Sultan kept the death hidden for several days so that her son Murad could arrive and claim the throne unopposed. Murad III later had five of Selim's young sons executed. Selim was buried in Hagia Sophia. He wrote poetry under the pen name Selimi, supported poets, and restored the stipend of Mahidevran, mother of Mustafa. The Selimiye Mosque in Edirne, built by Sinan between 1569 and 1575, is the largest of all Ottoman mosques, and Sinan also renovated Hagia Sophia between 1572 and 1574.
selim-iii: Selim III was the son of Sultan Mustafa III and his wife Mihrişah Sultan, who was ethnically Georgian. Mustafa III believed in the necessity of reform and had tried to build a professional army in peacetime, partly from fear of a Russian invasion. He died in 1774, and Selim's uncle Abdul Hamid I took the throne, looked after Selim and emphasised his education. Selim succeeded him on 7 April 1789, aged 27. He was fond of literature, calligraphy and music, and wrote poetry under the pen name İlhami.

Contemporaries saw Selim as capable and energetic, and his accession raised expectations of reform. Austria and Russia left him little room for anything but defence until the Peace of Iaşi in 1792. He then abolished the military tenure of fiefs, changed the fiscal administration, and in 1797 formed the Nizam-i Cedid, or New Order, from Turkish peasant youths of Anatolia, trained by foreign officers and equipped with modern weapons. By 1806 it numbered around 23,000 troops, but Selim never integrated it with the regular army. He also pushed for permanent embassies in European courts, and resident embassies were set up in Britain, France, Prussia and Austria.

French forces under Napoleon Bonaparte landed in Egypt on 1 July 1798, and Selim declared war on France; peace came in June 1802. Provincial notables such as Osman Pazvantoğlu defied the sultan, and in Serbia the Janissaries returned and murdered his governor. The Janissaries had viewed the reforms as a threat from the start. The Derebeys were alarmed by the confiscation of timars to pay for the new troops, and the ulama objected to European models. In 1806 an armed confrontation at Edirne between the New Order and a coalition of Balkan magnates and Janissary garrisons ended with the imperial forces retreating to Istanbul and Anatolia.

The Janissaries rose again, obtained a fatwa against the reforms from the Sheikh ul-Islam, and placed Selim's cousin on the throne as Mustafa IV on 29 May 1807. The European embassies were dismantled and the New Order troops dispersed. Alemdar Mustafa Pasha marched on Constantinople with an army to restore Selim but arrived too late, and Selim was killed on 28 July 1808. He was buried in the Laleli Mosque. Mahmud II then took the throne. Selim was also a composer who created fourteen makams, and sixty-four of his compositions are known.
selim-iii-giray: Selim III Giray, whose name is also written Gerai or Geray, was a member of the Giray dynasty, the son of Khan Fetih II Giray and a grandson of Devlet II Giray. Under Khan Arslan Giray, who reigned from 1748 to 1756, he held the post of kalgi. His reigns brought about major changes in the life of the khanate.

In his first reign Selim III persuaded the Ottoman sultan of the need to make peace with Austria so that the two could confront Russia together, but he was soon deprived of the khan's rank. He then appointed his brothers Mehmed Gerai and Kyrim Gerai as kalga and nureddin. In his second reign he again made his brother Mehmed Geray kalga, and named as nureddin Kyrym Geray, a son of Khan Halim Geray.

By the time he returned to the throne, the Ottoman Empire was already at war with Russia and could not protect its possessions north of the Black Sea. The local Nogais, seeing Russia's military superiority, abandoned their obedience to the khan and to the Ottoman Empire and sided with Russia. Proposals for Crimea to leave Ottoman vassalage came from St. Petersburg and from within Crimea, but Selim III refused them and broke off the negotiations. In June 1771 a Russian army under Prince V. Dolgorukov invaded the peninsula, defeated the khan's army of 70,000, took Perekop, and two weeks later defeated a second Tatar army of 95,000 at the battle of Kafa. Russian troops occupied Arabat, Kerch, Yenikale and Balaklava.

A pro-Russian party had already arisen among the Crimean beys and even among the khan's relatives, and together with his own unsuccessful command this let the enemy occupy the country very quickly. The assembly of the beys signed an alliance with Russia and resolved to elect the khan independently, which meant leaving Ottoman rule. Selim III at first went along with the beys, hoping the situation would change, but realising his powerlessness he gave up the throne and withdrew to the Ottoman lands. He was remembered as a brave man but reproached for inaction and indecision, and he died in 1786.
selma-to-montgomery-marches: At the turn of the 20th century Alabama adopted a constitution whose poll tax and literacy test shut most black citizens out of politics. In 1961 Dallas County, whose seat is Selma, was 57% black, yet only 130 of its 15,000 black adults of voting age were registered. A registration drive begun in 1963 by the Dallas County Voters League and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee met arrests and harassment, and local activists known as the Courageous Eight invited Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The campaign opened on 2 January 1965 at Brown Chapel A.M.E. Church, and 3,000 people had been arrested by the end of February.

On 18 February a state trooper, James Bonard Fowler, shot Jimmie Lee Jackson during a march in Marion, and Jackson died eight days later. James Bevel, directing the SCLC's Selma movement, called for a march to Montgomery to confront Governor George Wallace.

The first march was led by John Lewis of SNCC and Hosea Williams of the SCLC. Sheriff Jim Clark had ordered the white men of the county to be deputised, and after the commanding officer, John Cloud, told the marchers to disband, troopers beat them with nightsticks, fired tear gas and charged on horseback; Amelia Boynton was beaten unconscious.

On 9 March King led a second march but turned it back while a restraining order by Judge Frank Minis Johnson stood, and that night segregationists murdered James Reeb, a Unitarian Universalist minister from Boston. On 17 March Judge Johnson ruled that the right to march could not be abridged. The third march set out on 21 March under the Alabama National Guard, the FBI and federal marshals, and the marchers covered about 10 miles a day along U.S. Route 80.

On 15 March President Lyndon B. Johnson asked a joint session of Congress, in a nationally televised speech, to pass a voting rights bill, ending with the words "we shall overcome". He signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965. In 1996 the route was designated the Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail, preserved by the National Park Service, and in 2016 Congressional Gold Medals were awarded to the foot soldiers of the campaign, accepted by John Lewis and Frederick Reese. The crossing is commemorated each year in the Selma Bridge Crossing Jubilee.
selsey: Selsey lies about eight miles (13 km) south of Chichester, at the southernmost point of the Manhood Peninsula, almost cut off from the rest of Sussex by the sea. Bracklesham Bay bounds it on the west, Broad Rife on the north and Pagham Harbour on the east, and it ends at Selsey Bill. The Owers and Mixon rocks lie under the sea off its coasts. Bede described the name as the Isle of Sea Calves, meaning seals; others have suggested Holy Island, from the link with Saint Wilfrid.

Stone implements show people living in the area from the Palaeolithic. Late in the first century BCE the Atrebates had three oppida, one of them in the Chichester and Selsey area, and coins of their rulers were found on Selsey beach in 1877. The archaeologist Barry Cunliffe wrote that the Romans used the area as a base for supplies in their conquest of south-west Britain before moving to Chichester. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that Ælle and his sons landed near Selsey to found Sussex.

Stephen of Ripon and Bede say that Wilfrid arrived about 680 and converted the Kingdom of the South Saxons. Selsey was the seat of the diocese until the Council of London ordered the see moved to Chichester in 1075; there had been twenty-two Bishops of Selsey over 370 years. The manor stayed with the bishops of Chichester until the crown took it in 1561. In the eighteenth century its people took part in smuggling and in the illegal export of wool known as owling, and in 1749 members of the Hawkhurst Gang were tried at Chichester for the murder of a customs officer and a shoemaker.

A light railway linked Selsey to Chichester from 1897 to 1935. In the Second World War the shore off East Beach was used for secret work on the Mulberry harbours towed to Normandy, and RAF Selsey, an advanced landing ground, supported D-Day. Sea defences have been repeatedly rebuilt against erosion and flooding, most recently a managed realignment scheme completed in 2013. The parish church of St Peter dates from the 13th century. The parish had 10,737 people in 2011.
semarang: Semarang lies on the northern coast of Java, bounded by the Java Sea to the north and by Kendal, Demak and Semarang regencies to the west, east and south. Its coastline is 13.6 kilometres long, and its elevation ranges from 0.75 to 348 metres above sea level. It is the capital and largest city of Central Java province, and its population is predominantly Javanese with a significant Chinese presence.

The history of the place goes back to the 9th century, when it was known as Bergota. At the end of the 15th century the Demak Sultanate appointed an Islamic scholar, Ki Ageng Pandan Arang, to build an Islamic school in this fishing village. On 2 May 1547 Sultan Hadiwijaya of Pajang declared him the first bupati of Semarang, which created the city administratively and politically. In 1678 Sunan Amangkurat II promised control of Semarang to the Dutch East India Company as a debt payment, and on 5 October 1705 Susuhunan Pakubuwono I gave the company extensive trade rights in return for wiping out Mataram's debt, making it officially a company city.

The early Dutch settlement was a pentagonal fortress with five towers, beside a Muslim quarter called Kauman and a Chinese quarter; only the Dutch quarter counted as the city. The Great Mail Road of 1847 connected the northern coastal cities of Central and East Java, and railways followed at the end of the 19th century. The mail and railway projects brought an economic boom in the 1870s, but the Javanese kampongs reached as many as 1,000 inhabitants per hectare, and cholera, tuberculosis, dysentery, typhoid and malaria were rife. The city doctor Willem T. de Vogel and the councilman Hendrik Tillema campaigned to extend the city into the healthier hills to the south. By the 1920s the city had doubled in size.

In 1918 the Indonesian People's Hall was established by Sarekat Rakyat as a centre for political and social activity; the Dutch closed it in 1927. Japan occupied the city in 1942. After the Proclamation of Indonesian Independence reached Semarang on 17 August 1945, a local government under the Republic was set up, and the Five Days Battle between Indonesian forces and Japanese soldiers followed in October 1945.

Semarang was designated a city on 1 March 1906. It is a municipality of 16 districts, covers 373.78 square kilometres, and remains an important regional centre and port. It had a population of 1,653,524 at the 2020 census.
semey: Semey lies on the Irtysh River in north-eastern Kazakhstan, near the border with Russia, about 1,000 km north of Almaty and 700 km south-east of the Russian city of Omsk. It has a cold semi-arid climate with warm summers and very cold winters, and low rainfall throughout the year. It stands on the Turkestan-Siberia Railway, which links it with Almaty, Barnaul and Novosibirsk.

The first Russian settlement dates from 1718, when a fort was built beside the Irtysh near the ruins of an ancient Buddhist monastery with seven buildings. The fort and later the city took the name Semipalatinsk, Russian for Seven-Chambered City, from the monastery. The fort suffered frequent flooding from snowmelt, and in 1778 it was moved 18 km upstream to higher ground. A small city grew around it and served the river trade between the nomadic peoples of Central Asia and the growing Russian Empire. On 19 May 1854 it became the capital of Semipalatinsk Oblast, and the Turkestan-Siberia Railway of the early 20th century made it a major point of transit between Central Asia and Siberia.

The city was one of the main centres for publishing books by the Kazakh intelligentsia. Between 1917 and 1920 it was the capital, under the name Alash-qala, of the largely unrecognised Alash Autonomy, set up after the outbreak of the October Revolution. Red Army forces loyal to Petrograd took control in 1920. From October 1941 to July 1942 a Polish diplomatic post connected with the formation of Anders' Army stood in the city.

In 1949 the Soviet atomic bomb programme chose a site on the steppe 180 km west of the city for weapons testing. The Semipalatinsk Test Site operated until 1989, with 456 nuclear tests, of which 340 were underground and 116 atmospheric. Fallout and the uncontrolled exposure of workers led to high rates of cancer, childhood leukaemia and birth defects among residents of neighbouring villages.

In 2007 the city council voted unanimously to change the name from Semipalatinsk to Semey, because the old name had negative associations with the atomic testing. Semey became the administrative centre of the new Abai Region in 2022. It is a university town, home to Semey Medical University. The city has a museum to the poet Abai Qunanbayuli, and a museum of Fyodor Dostoevsky, who is listed among its notable residents, which opened in 1971 and is the only one of seven Dostoevsky museums outside Russia.
semigallians: The Semigallians, in Latvian Zemgaļi, lived in the south central part of present-day Latvia and northern Lithuania, in the lower parts of the Mūša and Lielupe river valleys. Their name probably means 'people of the northern borderlands' or 'people of the low borderlands'. They had close linguistic and cultural ties with the Samogitians. In the Viking Age they fought Swedish Vikings for control of the lower Daugava waterway. In 1106 they defeated an invading army from Polotsk led by Prince Rogvolod Vseslavich, and Russian chronicles claim that 9,000 Russian soldiers were killed. At the start of the German conquests their land was divided into chieftaincies, among them Upmale, Dobele, Spārnene, Rakte, Silene and Tērvete.

According to the Livonian Chronicle of Henry, the Semigallians allied with Bishop Albert of Riga against rebellious Livonians before 1203. In 1219 a crusader invasion ended this alliance, and Duke Viestards allied with the Lithuanians and Curonians. In 1228 Semigallians and Curonians attacked the Daugavgrīva monastery, the main crusader stronghold on the Daugava. In 1236 Semigallians attacked crusaders retreating to Riga after the Battle of Saule and killed many. The Livonian Order partly subdued them in 1254.

In 1270 Grand Duke Traidenis of Lithuania and the Semigallians attacked Livonia, and at the Battle of Karuse on the frozen Gulf of Riga defeated the Order and killed its master, Otto von Lutterberg. In 1279, after the Battle of Aizkraukle, Traidenis supported a Semigallian revolt led by Duke Nameisis. At the Battle of Garoza in 1287 more than 40 knights died, among them the master of the Livonian Order, Willekin von Endorp. It was the last Semigallian victory.

In the 1280s the Order burned Semigallian fields and caused a famine. The Semigallians held out until 1290, when they burned their last castle at Sidrabene, and a large number, which the Rhymed Chronicle puts at 100,000, migrated to Lithuania and went on fighting the Germans there.

Semigallian archaeological sites are known in many districts of Latvia and Lithuania, among them hillforts at Tērvete, Dobele and Mežotne in Latvia and at Ąžuolpamūšė and Papilė in Lithuania. There is an unconfirmed theory that the Semigallians were among the first Baltic tribes to establish a monarchy, a weak one compared with the power of the Semigallian nobles. Viestards is regarded as one of their most notable leaders: after he united hostile clans into one state he allied with the crusaders, and after they broke the treaty he allied with the Lithuanians, which led to the near annihilation of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword at Saule in 1236.
semiramis: The historical Shammuramat, the Akkadian form of the name, was the Assyrian wife of Shamshi-Adad V, who ruled from 824 to 811 BCE. She ruled the Neo-Assyrian Empire as regent for five years, until her son Adad-nirari III came of age. She governed at a time of political uncertainty after a destructive civil war, which may partly explain why Assyrians accepted rule by a woman. In the city of Aššur she had a stele inscribed naming her as queen of Shamshi-Adad, mother of Adad-nirari and daughter-in-law of Shalmaneser. It has been speculated that her achievements were retold over generations until she became a figure of legend.

According to Diodorus Siculus, who drew mainly on Ctesias of Cnidus, Semiramis was the daughter of the fish-goddess Derketo of Ascalon and a mortal. Doves fed her until the royal shepherd Simmas adopted her. She married Onnes, a general under King Ninus, and advised the king, and at the Siege of Bactra she led soldiers to seize a key defensive point.

Ninus fell in love with her and Onnes hanged himself. After Ninus died of an arrow wound she disguised herself as their son Ninyas, and Diodorus says she reigned 42 years, restored Babylon with a high brick wall and built palaces including Ecbatana. She attacked King Stabrobates of India with false elephants made of buffalo skins over camels, but was wounded and her army mostly destroyed.

About 80 ancient writers recorded legends of her. Herodotus ascribed to her the banks that confined the Euphrates, and her name was applied to monuments whose origins were forgotten, even the Behistun Inscription of Darius. In Armenian tradition, which portrays her negatively, she asked the handsome King Ara to marry her, and when he refused she marched against Armenia, where Ara was slain despite her orders to capture him alive. She is credited with founding Van, called Shamiramagerd.

Semiramis was generally viewed positively before the rise of Christianity. In the Middle Ages she became associated with lust, and a story from Pompeius Trogus, later spread by Orosius, claims an incestuous relationship with her son. Dante places her among the lustful in the Second Circle of Hell, while Christine de Pizan included her in The Book of the City of Ladies, and she was commonly found on the Nine Worthies list for women.

She appears in plays by Voltaire and Calderón and in an opera by Rossini, and Margaret I of Denmark and Catherine the Great were called the Semiramis of the North. In 1853 Alexander Hislop's The Two Babylons made her a figure in a claimed conspiracy, a view that scholars such as Lester Grabbe have rejected. Armenians and Assyrians still use Shamiram as a girl's name.
semitic-languages: The Semitic languages are a branch of the Afroasiatic language family. They occur in written form from a very early date: Akkadian, also known as Assyrian and Babylonian, and Eblaite texts, written in a script adapted from Sumerian cuneiform, appear from about 2600 BCE in Mesopotamia and the north-eastern Levant respectively. Egyptian, from about 3000 BCE, is a sister branch of Afroasiatic, related to Semitic but not part of it. Amorite appeared about 2100 BCE, followed during the 2nd millennium BCE by the Canaanite languages, including Hebrew and Phoenician, by Aramaic, and by Ugaritic. Where Semitic-speaking peoples originated is still debated: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Ethiopia, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa have all been proposed.

The Semitic languages are notable for their nonconcatenative morphology. Word roots are sets of consonants, usually three, and words are formed by filling in vowels between them. In Arabic the root k-t-b, dealing with writing, gives kitāb, book, and kataba, he wrote; Hebrew uses the same root in katav, he wrote, and michtav, letter. Most Semitic scripts are abjads, which omit some or all vowels. The Geʽez script of Ethiopia and Eritrea is technically an abugida, and Maltese is the only Semitic language written in the Latin script. The reconstructed word order of Proto-Semitic is verb–subject–object, which Classical Arabic and Biblical Hebrew keep.

Scholars have accepted the similarity of Hebrew, Arabic and Aramaic since medieval times. Guillaume Postel published a comparison of them in Latin in 1538, but did not name the group. The term Semitic was created by the Göttingen school of history, first by August Ludwig von Schlözer in 1781, from Shem, one of Noah's three sons in the Book of Genesis, and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn popularised it in 1795. Classical Syriac, an Aramaic dialect of about 200 CE, became a literary language of early Christianity. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, and Maltese descends from the extinct Siculo-Arabic of Sicily.
semmering-railway: The Semmering Railway, which starts at Gloggnitz and leads over the Semmering to Mürzzuschlag, was the first mountain railway in Europe built with standard gauge track. It was constructed between 1848 and 1854 by some 20,000 workers under the project's designer and director, Carl von Ghega. The works include 14 tunnels, among them the 1,431 m summit tunnel, 16 viaducts, several of them two-storey, and over 100 stone arch bridges and 11 small iron bridges.

Over a track length of 41 km the line overcomes an altitude difference of 460 m. On 60% of its length the gradient is 2.0–2.5%, equivalent to a rise of one metre in 40, and 16% has a curve radius of only 190 m. This was an entirely new technical dimension of railway construction, and new instruments and methods of surveying had to be developed.

A competition in 1851, the Semmering trials, decided which locomotives to buy. One stretch had gradients of 1 in 40 and curves with a minimum radius of 190 metres, and entrants had to hold a speed of 11.5 kilometres per hour with a maximum axle loading of 14 tonnes. Four entrants met the conditions but did not prove reliable in practice.

The railway itself used the Engerth design, in which the tender is articulated with the main locomotive frame so that part of the fuel and water weight rests on the driving wheels to improve adhesion, while the locomotive can still take relatively sharp curves. Sixteen Engerth locomotives were supplied between November 1853 and May 1854, and could climb a 1 in 40 gradient at 19 kilometres per hour.

Even while it was being built, the railway was seen as a form of landscape gardening, an attempt to combine technology and nature harmoniously. The travel experience it offered contributed greatly to opening the Semmering region to tourism, and numerous hotels and mansions date from that epoch. The line remains part of the Southern Railway, operated by the Austrian Federal Railways. In 1998 it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list.
semna: Semna lies about 15 miles south of Wadi Halfa, where rocks cross the Nile and narrow its flow at the Semna Cataract. The Semna gorge was the narrowest part of the Nile valley and the southern edge of ancient Egypt, in the Batn-El-Hajar, the Belly of the Rock, a land of bare granite ridges and wind-blown sand with only a thin layer of fertile soil. Pharaohs of the Twelfth Dynasty built a cluster of four mud-brick fortresses here: Semna West, Kumma or Semna East across the river, Semna South about a kilometre upstream, and Uronarti.

The forts were among 17 Middle Kingdom strongholds in Nubia that guarded the river and the flow of southern goods into Egypt, such as ebony, ivory, pelts, incense, ostrich feathers and enslaved people. Their mud-brick walls were reinforced with logs, which made them more vulnerable to fire, and they had doubly fortified gates and a protected corridor down to the Nile. A great wall found in the 1960s joined Semna South to Semna West, a sign of the pressure from the south recorded in the Semna Stela and the Semna Dispatches. In the New Kingdom, when the region had become part of an Egyptian empire, Semna and Kumma held temples, houses and cemeteries.

George Reisner investigated the forts in 1924 and 1928. Semna South was excavated by Jean Vercoutter and Sayed Thabit Hassan Thabit for the Sudan Antiquities Service in 1956 and 1957, and by the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute under Louis Vico Žabkar from 1966 to 1968, before the flooding. Seal impressions in a Twelfth Dynasty dump gave the fort's Egyptian name, Subduer of the Setiu-Nubians. A cemetery of about 560 graves held more than 800 people of the Meroitic, X-Group and Christian periods, and a small church probably dates from the ninth to the early eleventh century. Lake Nasser has covered the forts since 1971.
semnones: The Semnones were a Suebian people. Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century geographer, placed them between the Elbe and a river he called the Suebos, which modern scholars take to be the Oder. Their own name appears to be related to, or even the same as, the one Roman authors recorded as Suebi; Julius Caesar mentions the Suebi but not the Semnones, as a powerful group with 100 cantons.

Under Augustus, Velleius Paterculus reported that the future emperor Tiberius reached the Elbe, which flowed through the lands of the Semnones and Hermunduri. In the Res Gestae Divi Augusti, Augustus records that after his fleet sailed to present-day Denmark the Cimbri, Charydes and Semnones sent envoys to seek his friendship and that of the Roman people.

They worshipped a supreme god, the regnator omnium deus, at a sacred grove. Tacitus wrote that at a set time all the tribes of their group sent representatives to the grove, which no one entered unless bound with a chain, as an inferior before the god; anyone who fell had to crawl out along the ground. The Semnones believed that their people had begun there. They occupied, he said, a hundred pagi, and their numbers made them see themselves as the head of the Suebi.

Cassius Dio records that Masyas, king of the Semnones, and his priestess Ganna came to Rome under Domitian, between 92 and 96. In 177/178–180, in the last phase of the Marcomannic Wars, the Quadi tried to migrate to the Semnones through the mountain passes to their north but were blocked by the Romans, which scholars take as a sign of continuing contact among the Suebi and perhaps of a move southwards.

The Augsburg Victory Altar, found in 1992, calls the Juthungi of the 3rd century the barbarian people of the Semnones, or more precisely the Juthungi. It is the first surviving record of the Juthungi, whose name, meaning descendants or offspring, probably referred to Semnonic ancestry. They lived north of the Danube near present-day northern Bavaria and appear in Roman records until about 430, when the Roman general Aëtius defeated them.
semyon-dezhnev: Dezhnev was a Pomor Russian, probably born in 1605, possibly at Veliky Ustyug or the village of Pinega. According to the anthropologist Lydia T. Black he was recruited for Siberian service in 1630. He served for eight years at Tobolsk and Yeniseisk and went to Yakutia in 1639 or earlier, where he married a Yakut captive and spent three years collecting yasak, the fur tribute. In 1641 he moved north-east under Mikhail Stadukhin, and in 1643 he, Stadukhin and Yarilo Zyrian built a fort on the Kolyma River, then the easternmost Russian frontier. The Kolyma soon proved one of the richest areas of eastern Siberia.

From about 1642 Russians heard of a Pogycha River to the east, rich in sable, walrus ivory and silver ore. A first attempt to reach it in 1646 failed, and in 1647 an expedition organised by Fedot Alekseyev, agent of a Moscow merchant, was turned back by drift ice. In 1648 they tried again, in koch vessels, with between 89 and 121 people. They set out on 20 June (old style). Four of the seven vessels were lost before the strait, and Gerasim Ankudinov's koch was wrecked near it. A storm then separated the rest; Alekseyev's koch disappeared, and Dezhnev's was wrecked somewhere south of the Anadyr River.

His 25 survivors wandered for ten weeks until they reached the mouth of the Anadyr. In 1649 the twelve who were left built boats from driftwood and went upriver, where they built winter quarters and subjected the local Yukaghirs to tribute. Dezhnev found a walrus rookery at the Anadyr's mouth and accumulated over two tons of ivory. In 1664 he reached Moscow, where he sold 4.6 tons of tusks, and he died there.

Dezhnev deposited his reports at Yakutsk, but the sea route was of little commercial use, and they stayed in the local archives. In 1728 Vitus Bering entered the strait, and in 1736 Gerhardt Friedrich Müller found the reports, which he published in 1758. Some people have doubted the story since 1777, because the documents are poor and no one repeated the route until Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld in 1878. Most scholars agree that the account is basically correct. Cape Dezhnev, the easternmost cape of Eurasia, a mountain ridge in Chukotka and a bay of the Bering Sea bear his name.
sen-no-rikyu: Sen no Rikyū was born in Sakai, now in Osaka Prefecture. His father was a warehouse owner named Tanaka Yohei, who later also used the family name Sen. As a young man he studied tea under the Sakai townsman Kitamuki Dōchin, and at nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, he began to study under Takeno Jō'ō, who is also associated with the development of the wabi aesthetic. He is believed to have received the Buddhist name Sōeki from the Rinzai Zen priest Dairin Sōtō of Nanshū-ji in Sakai. He married around the age of 21 and trained in Zen at Daitoku-ji in Kyoto. Little is known about his middle years.

In 1579, at the age of 58, Rikyū became tea master to Oda Nobunaga, and after Nobunaga's death in 1582 he served Toyotomi Hideyoshi. He entered Hideyoshi's circle of confidants and became the most influential figure in the world of chanoyu. In 1585 he needed extra credentials to enter the Imperial Palace to help at a tea gathering Hideyoshi gave for Emperor Ōgimachi, and the emperor bestowed on him the lay name and title Rikyū Koji. He also played a central role in the Grand Kitano Tea Ceremony of 1587.

In his later years he began to use very small rustic tea rooms called sō-an, 'grass hermitage'. The two-tatami room Tai-an at Myōki-an temple in Yamazaki, credited to his design, is a National Treasure. Raku ware tea bowls originated in his collaboration with a tile-maker named Raku Chōjirō. He preferred simple, local wares to the costly Chinese items then fashionable. Though he did not invent the philosophy of wabi-sabi, he is among those most responsible for popularising it and bringing it into the tea ceremony. His style became known as sōan-cha or wabi-cha.

Hideyoshi ordered Rikyū to commit ritual suicide, apparently because of crucial differences of opinion and because Rikyū was too independent. One year earlier Hideyoshi had had Rikyū's disciple Yamanoue Sōji tortured and beheaded. Hideyoshi's reason may never be known for certain. Rikyū committed seppuku at his residence in Hideyoshi's Jurakudai palace in Kyoto on 21 April 1591, at the age of seventy. Okakura Kakuzō wrote that his last act was to hold a tea ceremony and that he left a death poem. Three houses of tea, the Omotesenke, Urasenke and Mushakōjisenke, descend directly from him. His grave is at the Jukō-in sub-temple in the Daitoku-ji compound.
sena-dynasty: The Sena dynasty was a Hindu dynasty that succeeded the Pala Empire and ruled much of the eastern Indian subcontinent from Bengal. Its rulers traced their origin to the south. The Deopara Prashasti describes the founder, Samanta Sena, as a migrant Brahmaksatriya from Karnataka, a term suggesting Brahmins who took up arms and became Kshatriyas. According to the historian P. N. Chopra the Sena kings were probably Baidyas. A copper plate suggests the Senas settled in western Bengal before Samanta Sena's birth and entered Pala service as sāmantas in Rāḍha.

After Samanta Sena came Hemanta Sena, who usurped power and styled himself king in 1095. His successor Vijaya Sena (r. 1096–1159) laid the foundations of the dynasty in a reign of over sixty years, and by its end its territory included Vaṅga and part of Varendra. The Palas were ousted entirely sometime after 1165. Ballala Sena conquered Gaur from the Pala, ruled the Bengal delta and made Nadia a capital as well. He married Ramadevi, a princess of the Western Chalukya Empire. Lakshmana Sena succeeded him in 1179 and expanded the dynasty to Odisha, possibly up to Varanasi.

In 1203–1204 Muhammad Bin Bakhtiyar Khalji, a general of the Ghurid Empire, captured Nadia, and Lakshmana Sena retreated to the south-east of Bengal. His sons Vishvarupa Sena and Keshava Sena kept their independence in southern and eastern Bengal, probably until at least 1230, and the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri suggests that his descendants ruled there until at least 1245 or 1260.

The Senas built Hindu temples and monasteries, and Ballala Sena is credited with the Dhakeshwari Temple in Dhaka. They patronised literature, and Govardhana, Sarana, Jayadeva, Umapati and Dhoyi were poets at the court of Lakshmana Sena. Later genealogies say Ballala Sena introduced Kulinism, which conferred titles of nobility on Brahmanas, Kayasthas and Vaidyas, but most scholars regard those accounts as unhistorical. Later dynasties in Nepal, Suket and Mandi claimed descent from the Senas.
sena-gallica: Senigallia is a resort town and comune on Italy's Adriatic coast, in the province of Ancona in the region of Marche, about 30 kilometres north-west of Ancona. Its small port lies at the mouth of the River Misa. The town is one of the endpoints of the Massa–Senigallia Line, an important dividing line, or isogloss, in the classification of the Romance languages. The name Sena is probably a corrupted form of Senones, and Gallica, meaning Gaulish, distinguished the place from Sena, the present Siena, in Etruria.

The Gallic Senone tribe first settled the place in the 4th century BCE. In 284 BCE the Romans took over the area and the settlement and established the colony of Sena Gallica to control the region they called the Ager Gallicus. In 207 BCE, in the prelude to the Battle of the Metaurus between Romans and Carthaginians, Sena Gallica was the southernmost point of the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal Barca's invasion of Italy.

Alaric ravaged the town as the Roman Empire declined, and it was fortified when it became part of the Byzantine Empire. The Lombards laid it waste in the 8th century and the Saracens in the 9th. It was one of the five cities of the medieval Adriatic duchy of Pentapolis.

The diocese and bishopric were long established, and around the 13th century the town saw economic development, including the Magdalena Fair, visited by merchants from Europe and the Levant. In the 15th century the town was captured and recaptured many times in the Guelph and Ghibelline conflict. Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta of Rimini fortified it in 1450–1455, and Pope Sixtus IV later assigned the lordship to the Della Rovere family. In 1503 Cesare Borgia ordered a series of executions there as revenge for the Magione conspiracy, in which princes who had been his military allies plotted to remove him.

In 1516 Pope Leo X transferred the lordship to Lorenzo II de' Medici, and the Della Rovere took it again, until in 1624 the town was annexed to the Papal States' legation of Urbino. Giovanni Maria Mastai Ferretti, later Pope Pius IX, was born there in 1792.

In the First World War the town and its port were devastated by shelling from Austro-Hungarian naval units led by the battleship SMS Zrínyi. A strong earthquake damaged it in 1930, and it suffered again in the Second World War, so that much of the present city is modern. Its sights include the Rocca Roveresca, a castle of Gothic origins restored by Baccio Pontelli in 1492, the 17th-century Palazzo Comunale and the church of Santa Maria delle Grazie.
senat-conservateur: The Constitution of 22 frimaire year VIII (13 December 1799), drawn up under the direct influence of First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte after the Coup of 18 Brumaire, was the first to recreate a senate in France. Charged with watching over the survival of the constitution, the Sénat sat beside the Tribunat and the Corps législatif as one of the three major assemblies of the Consulate, though it did not exercise ordinary legislative powers.

It was to have 60 permanent members aged at least 40, with two more added each year for ten years. There were no elections. Sieyès and Roger Ducos, the outgoing consuls, became members by right and, with the new consuls Cambacérès and Lebrun, chose 29 others; this majority picked the rest. Thereafter the Senate filled vacancies itself from three candidates put forward by the First Consul, the Tribunat and the Corps législatif. It met, not in public, at the Luxembourg Palace, and its first members included Monge, Lagrange, Berthollet, Cabanis, the explorer Bougainville and the painter Vien.

A revision of the constitution in year X (1802) let the Senate rule by acts with the force of law, the sénatus-consultes, in matters the constitution had not foreseen; one, on 2 August 1802, proclaimed Napoleon First Consul for life. Its membership rose to 120, and Bonaparte directly controlled its activity and composition. From January 1803 the sénatoreries ensured its docility: from June 1804, 36 senators received a residence for life and annual revenues of 20,000 to 25,000 francs, so that Berthollet, for example, held the sénatorerie of Montpellier and lived in the bishop's palace at Narbonne.

The Constitution of the Year XII (1804) proclaimed the First French Empire and made the Senate still more dependent on Napoleon. On 1 January 1806 he gave the senators 54 enemy flags, and Marshal Catherine-Dominique de Pérignon proposed a triumphal arch to his glory. Despite these favours the senators proclaimed his fall in 1814 and summoned Louis XVIII, who abolished the senate.
senchus-fer-n-alban: The Senchus survives in several manuscripts. The most important, Ms. H.2.7 of Trinity College Dublin, once belonged to Dubhaltach Mac Fhirbhisigh and then to Edward Lhuyd. It was compiled in the 14th century by Lúcás Ó Dalláin, probably working with Seán Mór Ó Dubhagáin (died 1372), chief poet and historian of the Uí Maine; the idea that it formed part of the Book of Uí Maine is no longer considered plausible. Other copies are in the Book of Ballymote, the Book of Lecan and Mac Fhirbhisigh's 17th-century genealogical compilations. The text may derive from earlier documents presumed to have been written in Latin.

It is a short document of around 70 or 80 lines of type, depending on the version. Appended to it is the Genelaig Albanensium, with genealogies of the kings of Alba Máel Coluim mac Cináeda and Causantín mac Cuilén and of Ainbcellach mac Ferchair and other kings of Dál Riata. Most versions follow the late origin myth of Dál Riata and begin with Eochaid Muinremar and the sons of Erc, Fergus Mór among them. Mac Fhirbhisigh's own version traces the kingdom instead to the Síl Conairi and Cairpre Riata, who may be the Reuda of Bede's Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum.

The census apparently dates from a time when the Cenél Comgaill were still part of the Cenél nGabráin. It lists no kindreds or military duties for any Irish lands Dál Riata may have held, and it curiously places Airgíalla, perhaps settlers from Ireland or simply people called additional clients, among the Cenél Loairn.

Its historical value lies mainly in its later sections, which name historical kings: myth may give way to history in the reign of Conall mac Comgaill in the middle of the 6th century, and the last king identifiable in the genealogies proper is Conall Crandomna, who died around 660. The divisions it describes need not be very old, and its lists have problems. It also holds what is believed to be the oldest reference to a naval battle in the British Isles, a brief record of a fight between rival groups of Dál Riata in 719.
sendai: Sendai stretches from the Pacific Ocean to the Ōu Mountains, which form the east and west borders of Miyagi Prefecture. Its eastern part is a plain, its centre hilly and its west mountainous, and the highest point is Mount Funagata at 1,500 metres. Unusually for a large Japanese coastal city, the city core stands on a terrace 40 to 60 metres above sea level. The area was inhabited as early as 20,000 years ago, though the history of Sendai as a city begins with Date Masamune. It became a designated city in 1989 and has five wards, whose names deliberately avoid directions.

Date Masamune was unhappy with his previous stronghold at Iwadeyama, in the north of his territories and hard to reach from Edo. Sendai lay in the centre of his newly defined lands on the major road from Edo, and Tokugawa Ieyasu gave him permission to build a new castle on Aobayama after the Battle of Sekigahara. The name had been written with characters meaning a thousand generations, and Masamune changed it to characters meaning a hermit and a platform. The characters come from a Chinese poem praising a palace of the Han emperor Wen, and tradition says Masamune chose them so that the castle would prosper like a mountain inhabited by an immortal hermit.

In 1613 Masamune built a galleon to send an embassy headed by Hasekura Tsunenaga to the Pope in Rome. The embassy established relations with the Holy See, but the suppression of Christianity in Japan frustrated Masamune's plans. The first railway between Sendai and Tokyo, now the Tōhoku Main Line, opened in 1887 and put the area within a day's travel of Tokyo. Tohoku Imperial University was founded in 1907 and became the first Japanese university to admit women in 1913. After the Second World War the city was rebuilt as a transport and logistics hub for the region.

Sendai is the capital of Miyagi Prefecture and the largest city of the Tōhoku region. It is known as the City of Trees, because of the zelkova trees along Jōzenji Street and Aoba Street, and its Tanabata Festival is the largest in Japan. The ruins of Sendai Castle stand on Aobayama, and the Zuihōden is the tomb of Date Masamune. The Ōsaki Hachimangū shaden, built by Masamune in 1607, is a National Treasure. On 11 March 2011 coastal areas of the city suffered severe damage from a magnitude 9.0 offshore earthquake and the tsunami it caused.
sendai-castle: The castle stands on a plateau above Sendai, across the Hirose river, which partly surrounds the hill to the north and east; cliffs guard the south and east and a forest the west. That forest was strictly guarded in the Edo period and is a rare survivor of the original virgin forests of Honshū, now a botanical garden of Tohoku University. The honmaru, or inner bailey, about 115 metres high and 250 metres long, was ringed by stone walls up to 15 metres high. Only the base of a main keep was ever built, and four three-storey yagura protected it instead.

Mount Aoba had earlier held a fortified residence of a branch of the Shimazu clan and was later controlled by the Kokubun clan, whom the Date destroyed. After the Battle of Sekigahara, Tokugawa Ieyasu visited the area, and Date Masamune began the castle; Date Tadamune completed the works in 1637. The daimyō's residence was built in the Momoyama style, and contemporaries compared it with Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Jurakudai Palace in Kyoto. Earthquakes and fires damaged it in 1616, 1648, 1668 and 1710.

In the Boshin War the castle was a centre of the Ōuetsu Reppan Dōmei, the pro-Tokugawa alliance led by Date Yoshikuni. The Meiji government took it over after Sendai's surrender, partly dismantled it in the 1870s and gave the grounds to the Imperial Japanese Army as the base of the Sendai Garrison, later the 2nd Division. A fire in 1882 destroyed many of the remaining buildings. The omotemon gate and the wakiyagura tower, made National Treasures in 1931, were destroyed with everything else on 10 July 1945 in the Bombing of Sendai.

The United States Army razed the remaining Edo-period structures during the occupation and returned the site in 1957. The Sendai City Museum was built on the san-no-maru enclosure in 1961, and the stone base, some walls and wooden buildings have since been rebuilt. The ruins were designated a National Historic Site in 2003.
senebkay: Senebkay's full name was Woseribre Senebkay, and his tomb names him king of Upper and Lower Egypt, Woseribre, the son of Re, Senebkay. Nothing is known of his reign except that it may have been short and held at Abydos in a time of turmoil after the late 13th Dynasty. The discovery of his tomb supports the existence of an independent Abydos Dynasty, contemporary with the Fifteenth and Sixteenth Dynasties, which Detlef Franke first proposed and Kim Ryholt developed in 1997. The Turin King List preserves parts of two prenomens beginning Woser, and it has been suggested that Woseribre Senebkay fits there. His name may mean Seneb, son of Kay.

His skeleton shows a man about 1.78 metres tall who died aged 35 to 40. Eighteen wounds on his lower back, feet and ankles were struck from below, perhaps while he was on a chariot or on horseback, and several blows to the skull, whose curved cuts match battle axes of the period, killed him. His head had once been covered with a mummy mask.

Josef W. Wegner of the University of Pennsylvania and a team of Egyptian archaeologists found the tomb, known as CS9, at South Abydos in January 2014. It has four chambers and a decorated limestone burial chamber, most of whose blocks were taken from older structures such as the stela of Idudju-iker. Its walls show the two Wadjet-eyes, a winged sun disc, the goddesses Neith and Nut and texts naming Duamutef, Qebehsenuf, Amset and Hapi, with the king's name in a cartouche. Few funerary goods remained, and the tomb may have been robbed in antiquity. The wooden canopic box was made from a coffin inscribed for a king Sobekhotep, probably from the nearby tomb S10, now believed to be that of Sobekhotep IV.
seneca-falls-convention: In the decades before 1848 a small number of women pushed against the limits placed on them. Charles Grandison Finney allowed women to pray aloud in mixed gatherings from 1831, and from 1832 William Lloyd Garrison's anti-slavery associations encouraged women's full participation. The Grimké sisters and Abby Kelley spoke to mixed audiences against slavery, and Ernestine Rose lectured from 1836 on the enfranchisement of women. Under state statutes and common law women could not inherit property, sign contracts, serve on juries or vote, and they were paid about half of what men earned for the same work. On 7 April 1848 the New York State Assembly passed the Married Woman's Property Act.

The convention was planned on 9 July 1848 over tea at the Waterloo home of the Quaker Jane Hunt, where Lucretia Mott, Mary Ann M'Clintock, Martha Coffin Wright, Jane Hunt and Elizabeth Cady Stanton, the only non-Quaker, agreed to call a meeting while the Motts were in the area. The notice in the Seneca County Courier appeared on 11 July, giving eight days' warning. At the M'Clintock home on 16 July the women drafted ten resolutions and the Declaration of Sentiments, which Stanton adapted from the Declaration of Independence, adding the phrase "and women" to "all men … are created equal". Stanton added an eleventh resolution, on women's suffrage.

On 19 July the chapel doors were found locked, and Stanton's young nephew was lifted through a window to open them. About 40 men came although the first day had been announced for women only, and they were asked to stay silent. Stanton and Mott spoke, the declaration was read and amended, and Mott gave an evening address to a large audience. On the second day James Mott chaired the morning meeting, since a woman chairing before men and women was still thought too radical.
