Facing the Ottomans after the Battle of Maritsa, the two churches agreed in 1375 to revoke the act and recognise the patriarchate, on condition that the contested southern eparchies returned to Constantinople. The Ottomans took the monastery of Peć in 1455, and after Patriarch Arsenije II died in 1463 the office fell vacant, while the Archbishopric of Ohrid took over its eparchies. Metropolitan Pavle of Smederevo briefly seized the throne of Peć, but his movement was crushed and he went into exile after 1541.

The patriarchate was restored in 1557, when Makarije, a cousin of the Ottoman statesman Mehmed Sokolović, was elected patriarch. It grew to more than 40 eparchies, from Skopje to Buda. Patriarch Arsenije III sided with the Austrians in 1689 during the Great Turkish War, and Ottoman reprisals led to the Great Migration of the Serbs; Arsenije IV likewise backed the Habsburgs in the war of 1737–1739. The Ottomans then favoured Greek bishops, beginning with Joannicius III in 1739, and after 1752 Serbian and Greek claimants fought over the throne until Sultan Mustafa III abolished it and placed its eleven remaining eparchies under Constantinople.

For Serbs under Ottoman rule the restored patriarchate was a religious and ethnic symbol that stood in for their lost state. The historian Frederick Anscombe has argued that its offices had no ethnic monopoly in the Ottoman era, yet most of the patriarchs were Serbs who kept the title of successors of Saint Sava.
serbo-bulgarian-war: On 18 September 1885 Bulgaria and the semi-autonomous Ottoman province of Eastern Rumelia declared their unification at Plovdiv. Eastern Rumelia, whose population was mostly ethnic Bulgarian, had been created by the Congress of Berlin seven years earlier. The unification went against the will of the Great Powers, including Russia, and Austria-Hungary strongly opposed it. Serbia feared a loss of its own position in the Balkans, and its ruler, Milan I, resented the asylum that Bulgaria had given to pro-Russian opposition leaders such as Nikola Pašić after the Timok Rebellion. Encouraged by Austro-Hungarian promises of support and territorial gains, Milan declared war on 14 November 1885, using the Bregovo dispute over a border guardhouse as a pretext.

Russia had withdrawn its officers from the Bulgarian army when unification was declared, so the remaining officers, mostly captains, had no experience of commanding units larger than platoons, and the conflict was called the War of the Captains. Bulgaria's main forces stood on the Ottoman border, and it took five to six days to bring them west. Serbia's rifles were modern, but its artillery was old, and Milan, who took command himself, called up only the first class of infantry, about half of the available men. Bulgarian artillery, made by Krupp, was better than the Serbian guns.

Prince Alexander arrived on 16 November at Slivnitsa, where Major Guchev held a ridge with nine battalions, about 2,000 volunteers and 32 guns. From 17 to 19 November the Serbian attacks failed, with some 1,200 casualties in the first day's assault on the centre, and on 19 November Alexander ordered a counterattack. Slivnitsa was the decisive battle, and by 24 November the Serbs were back in Serbia. The Bulgarian army then converged on Pirot, and on 27 November, with Alexander leading the final attack, the Serbs abandoned the town.

On 28 November the Austro-Hungarian ambassador, Count Rudolf of Khevenhüller-Metsch, visited the Bulgarian headquarters and demanded an end to the fighting, threatening that otherwise the Bulgarians would face Austro-Hungarian troops. A ceasefire was signed that day. The peace was signed at Bucharest on 3 March 1886 and made no change to the border. The war strengthened Bulgaria's international position and largely preserved the unification, while it damaged the Serbian army's reputation and the trust between the two countries. Serbian historians generally blame King Milan's leadership, and the Serbian army afterwards carried out ambitious reforms.
serbs: The origin of the name Serb is unclear. The most prominent theory holds that it is of Proto-Slavic origin, meaning family kinship or alliance, and ultimately rooted in a word for sipping or breast-feeding, so that it carries the idea of milk kinship and brotherhood. Early Slavs, especially the Sclaveni and Antae, including the White Serbs, invaded and settled Southeastern Europe in the 6th and 7th centuries. Until the late 560s they mainly raided across the Danube, but large-scale settlement overwhelmed the Danube and Sava frontier in the late 6th and early 7th centuries. The region of Raška was the centre of Serb settlement, and Serb tribes also occupied most of modern Herzegovina and Montenegro.

The first Serb states, Serbia (c. 780–960) and Duklja (10th century to 1186/9), were formed chiefly under the Vlastimirović and Vojislavljević dynasties. As Duklja declined in the late 11th century, Raška gained independence and became the most powerful Serbian state. Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja, (r. 1166–96), founded the Nemanjić dynasty, which ruled Serbia until the 14th century. His son Stefan Nemanjić became the first recognised king, and his younger son Rastko founded the Serbian Orthodox Church in 1219 and became known as Saint Sava.

Under the Ottomans, the devshirme took Christian boys from the Balkans, many of them Serbs, from their families, converted them by force to Islam and trained them for the Janissary corps. Some Serbs who converted rose to the highest ranks, among them the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha. The Serbian Revolution (1804–1817) began with the First Serbian Uprising under Karađorđe Petrović, which created an independent state for almost a decade until the Ottomans crushed it in 1813. The Second Uprising under Miloš Obrenović won substantial autonomy in 1815–1816, the last Ottoman troops withdrew in 1867, and full international recognition of independence came at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

Serbs are predominantly Eastern Orthodox Christians, traditionally affiliated with the Serbian Orthodox Church. During the centuries of Ottoman rule it remained the only permitted Serb institution, and through its monasteries and clergy it preserved the Serbian language, literacy and national consciousness. When the Principality of Serbia became independent, Orthodoxy became crucial in defining national identity, since language was shared with other South Slavs.

Serbs are noted for icon painting, frescoes, literature, music and medieval architecture, shaped by Byzantine tradition. The gusle, a bowed single-stringed instrument, accompanies a centuries-old oral tradition of epic songs, most of which centre on the Ottoman occupation and the struggle for liberation. The Kosovo Myth is a central national myth that symbolises martyrdom and the defence of the homeland against the Ottomans.
serdica: The earliest mention of the city is an Athenian inscription of the 1st century BCE naming it the city of the Serdi. A local inscription and Dio Cassius record that the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi and beheaded the captives, and around 29 BCE the Romans conquered Serdica. Under Emperor Trajan (98–117) it became a municipium, the centre of an administrative region, and was renamed Ulpia Serdica.

The Costoboci burned it in 170, and it was rebuilt with its first defensive walls between 176 and 180 under Marcus Aurelius, as inscriptions above the gates show. Public baths, administrative and cult buildings, a civic basilica and a large theatre followed. A Gothic raid of 268 burned parts of the city, including the theatre, over whose remains an amphitheatre was later built under Diocletian and Constantine the Great. The emperors Aurelian and Galerius were born in Serdica.

In 311 Galerius issued the Edict of Serdica there, ending the Diocletianic persecution and granting Christianity conditional toleration two years before the Edict of Milan. The city was capital of the Diocese of Dacia from 337 to 602.

For Constantine, Sardica mea Roma est, Serdica is my Rome, and he considered making it his capital instead of Constantinople. Eight horrea, or warehouses, of the early 4th century show that it was a supply centre for the army on the Danube, linked to the river by the valley of the Iskur. The Huns destroyed the city in 447, and Emperor Justinian rebuilt it in the 6th century under the name Triaditsa.

Much of the ancient city has been excavated and is on public display in Sofia, including the complex of Ancient Serdica, the eastern and western gates, the city walls, thermal baths, a Roman bridge, the 4th-century Rotunda of St. George, the amphitheatre and the tombs and basilicas beneath the basilica of St. Sophia. The name lives on in the Serdica Fortress in the centre of Sofia and the city's administrative subdivision of Serdika. Serdica is a titular see of the Roman Catholic Church.
serengeti: The Serengeti spans the Mara and Arusha Regions of Tanzania and extends into south-western Kenya. Its protected area covers about 30,000 square kilometres and includes Serengeti National Park and several game reserves. Habitats range from riverine forests, swamps, kopjes and grasslands to woodlands, supporting about 70 large mammal species and some 500 bird species. Altitudes run from 920 to 1,850 metres, and rain falls in two seasons, from March to May and in October and November. The name is often said to come from the Maa word seringit, meaning endless plains, but this does not appear in Maa dictionaries.

The great migration is a circular movement of wildebeest, driven by the availability of grazing. It begins in the Ngorongoro Conservation Area in the south and loops clockwise through the national park towards the Maasai Mara in Kenya. Calving takes place in February on the short-grass plains of the south-east, when about 500,000 calves are born in two or three weeks. The herds move north-west as the rains end in May, cross the Grumeti and Mara rivers from July, reach Kenya in late July or August and return south from early November. About 250,000 wildebeest die each year on the journey, from thirst, hunger, exhaustion or predation.

The plains were sparsely inhabited by people until nomadic Maasai pastoralists began to migrate there in the early 1800s. They were struck by drought and disease: thousands died in a cholera epidemic in the 1880s and in a smallpox outbreak in 1892, and rinderpest wiped out their cattle. Later in the 20th century the Tanzanian government resettled the Maasai around the Ngorongoro Crater. With human-set fires gone, and with poaching, dense woodland and thicket developed over the next 30 to 50 years, and tsetse flies prevented any significant human settlement. By the mid-1970s wildebeest and Cape buffalo had recovered and were cropping the grass, which reduced the fuel for fires and let acacia become established again.

Tanzania and Kenya maintain national parks, conservation areas and game reserves that give legal protection to over 80 per cent of the Serengeti, though the ecosystem has shrunk to about 60 per cent of its original size through human encroachment. It lies beside the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, which contains the Ngorongoro Crater and Olduvai Gorge, where some of the oldest hominin fossils have been found.
seretse-khama: Seretse Khama was born in 1921 in Serowe, in the Bechuanaland Protectorate, the son of Queen Tebogo and Sekgoma Khama II, paramount chief of the Bamangwato, and the grandson of Khama III. His name means the clay that binds, chosen to celebrate the reconciliation of his father and grandfather. At the age of four he became kgosi, with his uncle Tshekedi Khama as regent. He studied at Fort Hare University College, graduating in 1944, then at Balliol College, Oxford, and the Inner Temple in London.

In June 1947 he met Ruth Williams, an English clerk at Lloyd's of London, and they married in September 1948. The marriage alarmed South Africa, which had banned interracial marriage in 1949 under apartheid, and it angered the Bamangwato elders. After a series of kgotla meetings in 1949 the elders reaffirmed him as kgosi. Britain, fearing the loss of South African gold and uranium supplies, announced on 8 March 1950 that he could not return to Bechuanaland for at least five years, and exiled him and his wife in 1951. A judicial enquiry found him fit to rule but its report was suppressed for thirty years.

In 1956 Khama and his wife were allowed to return as private citizens, after he renounced the chieftainship. He was elected secretary of the tribal council in 1957 and founded the Botswana Democratic Party, which swept the 1965 elections. As prime minister he pressed for independence, and Botswana became independent on 30 September 1966, with Khama as its first president.

At independence the country had only 12 kilometres of paved roads and few graduates. Khama set out to build an export economy on beef, copper and diamonds, helped by the discovery of diamonds at Orapa in 1967. His government renegotiated the diamond mining agreement in 1975 to secure 50 per cent of the revenues, and spent them on infrastructure, health and education. The Botswana pula replaced the South African rand in 1976. His party won the elections of 1969, 1974 and 1979.

Khama had heart and kidney ailments and was diagnosed with diabetes in 1960. In June 1980 he was found to have terminal pancreatic cancer, and he died in his sleep on 13 July 1980. Vice President Quett Masire succeeded him. Forty thousand people paid their respects as he lay in state, and he was buried in the Royal Cemetery on a hill in Serowe. Sir Seretse Khama International Airport, opened in 1984, bears his name, and the film A United Kingdom, released in 2016, told the story of his marriage.
serfdom: Institutions similar to serfdom existed in antiquity; the status of the helots of Sparta resembled that of medieval serfs. By the 3rd century CE the Roman Empire faced a labour shortage, and large landowners relied increasingly on free tenant farmers, later called coloni, instead of slaves. Diocletian's tax system assessed both land and its inhabitants, so it became administratively inconvenient for peasants to leave the land where they were counted. Medieval serfdom really began with the breakup of the Carolingian Empire around the 10th century, when powerful lords encouraged it as a source of agricultural labour. The word serf comes from Middle French, from Latin servus, and serfdom was coined only in 1850.

A serf lived on and worked a parcel of land within the manor of a lord, who owed protection and justice in return. Unlike a slave, a serf could not be sold individually, although serfs passed with the land when it was sold. A serf could not leave without permission and had no saleable title to the land. A freeman usually became a serf through force or necessity, sometimes in a ceremony of bondage, and children inherited the status.

Serfs paid dues mainly in seasonally appropriate labour on the lord's demesne and in produce, and Easter eggs or a Christmas goose might be owed on top. They had rights in land and could take their disputes to the manorial court. A well-off serf might buy his freedom, and in England one who reached a chartered borough and lived there a year and a day became free.

Serfdom varied greatly in time and place. In Poland the labour owed was commonly a few days a year per household in the 13th century, one day a week in the 14th, four in the 17th and six in the 18th. Serfdom began to disappear west of the Rhine in the later Middle Ages while it spread through eastern Europe, becoming dominant there around the 15th century. The decline in the west has sometimes been attributed to the Black Death. In Russia it became the dominant relation between peasants and nobility in the 17th century.

Abolition came by stages. France abolished serfdom in Crown lands in 1779 and formally on 4 August 1789. Joseph II issued the Serfdom Patent for the Habsburg monarchy in 1781, though dues and unpaid labour continued until the revolutions of 1848. Prussia abolished it in 1807, and Alexander II freed Russia's privately held serfs in 1861, with owners compensated through taxes on the freed serfs. The United Nations 1956 Supplementary Convention on the Abolition of Slavery prohibits serfdom.
serfdom-in-russia: Forms of dependency go back to the 12th century, when the Russkaya Pravda distinguished several degrees of it; the zakups who worked arable land and the smerds owing corvée came closest to later serfdom. In the mid-15th century some peasants could leave their master only in the week before and after Yuri's Day, 26 November, and the Sudebnik of 1497 also fixed a departure fee, the pozhiloye, which the Sudebnik of 1550 raised. Decrees of 1597 under Boris Godunov took away the right to move at Yuri's Day, and in 1658 flight became a criminal offence.

By the censuses of 1678 and 1719 about four-fifths of Russian peasants were serfs; free peasants remained only in the north and north-east. Landowners could transfer a serf without land to another owner but had no right to kill him. A separate form of slavery, kholopstvo, was ended by Peter I in 1723.

The work a serf did for the landowner on the lord's part of the estate was called barshchina, often translated as corvée; a decree of Paul I in 1797 described three days a week as normal. Others paid a quit-rent, obrok: in the black-earth region 70% to 77% of serfs did labour service, while in the seven central provinces in 1860 67.7% were on obrok. Landowners sought to keep their workers: before 1812 serfs could not marry serfs of other estates, and church rules left most weddings to January, February, October and November.

The state also set limits. Edicts from 1718 to 1767 obliged landlords to feed their peasants in famine, and in 1775 Catherine II provided for prosecuting owners who treated serfs cruelly. Those who returned from captivity and retired soldiers were declared free, and graduates of the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts could not be enserfed. Alexander I freed the serfs of Estonia and Livonia in 1816 and of Courland in 1817.

Scholars explain the emancipation of 1861 by fear of a large serf revolt, the government's financial needs, changing cultural sensibilities and the army's need for soldiers. A 2018 study in the American Economic Review found substantial increases in agricultural productivity, industrial output and peasants' nutrition as a result. Serfdom also gave a backdrop and dramatic tension to the works of Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky.
sergei-eisenstein: Sergei Mikhailovich Eisenstein was born on 22 January 1898 in Riga, then in the Russian Empire, to a middle-class family. His father, the architect Mikhail Osipovich Eisenstein, came from a Jewish family but had converted to the Russian Orthodox Church before his marriage in 1897. His mother took Sergei to Saint Petersburg in 1905. He was raised an Orthodox Christian and later became an atheist. At the Petrograd Institute of Civil Engineering he studied architecture and engineering, but in 1918 he left to join the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. In Minsk in 1920 he saw Kabuki theatre and studied Japanese, learning about 300 kanji characters, which he cited as an influence on his pictorial development.

In 1920 Eisenstein moved to Moscow and worked in the theatre for Proletkult, an experimental institution that aimed at a revolutionary working-class aesthetic. In 1923 he began as a theorist with the essay The Montage of Attractions. His first full-length film was Strike in 1925, followed in the same year by Battleship Potemkin, which was acclaimed around the world, and by October: Ten Days That Shook the World, made for the tenth anniversary of the Revolution. His attention to camera angles, crowd movements and montage drew criticism in the Soviet film community and led to self-criticism and promises to conform to socialist realism.

In 1930 Paramount Pictures gave him a short contract in Hollywood, but his projects failed to impress the studio and it ended by mutual consent. He then made a film in Mexico, Que viva Mexico, financed by the author Upton Sinclair and other investors. It ran far beyond the three or four months agreed, and Sinclair shut down production, leaving the footage in the United States, where others edited it into films that Eisenstein never saw. Alexander Nevsky, made in 1938 with music by Sergei Prokofiev, was received well in the Soviet Union and the West and won him the Order of Lenin and the Stalin Prize.

During the war he worked on the film about Tsar Ivan IV, with Prokofiev scoring it. Ivan the Terrible, Part I won a Stalin Prize. Part II was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958, and the footage of the unfinished Part III was confiscated and mostly destroyed.

Eisenstein suffered a heart attack on 2 February 1946 and died of a second on 11 February 1948, aged 50. His ashes were buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow. He was a pioneer in the theory and practice of montage.
sergei-prokofiev: Sergei Sergeyevich Prokofiev was born on 27 April 1891 (15 April in the old style) on the rural estate of Sontsovka, in what is now Ukraine. His father was an agronomist and his mother came from a family of former serfs. In 1902 she met Sergei Taneyev, the director of the Moscow Conservatory, who arranged for Reinhold Glière to teach the boy at Sontsovka that summer. At eleven Prokofiev tried to write a symphony. Later he complained that Glière had given him conventional phrase structure that he had to unlearn, and he began experimenting with dissonant harmony in short piano pieces.

Prokofiev studied at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory and in 1914 won its competition for the best piano students by playing his own Piano Concerto No. 1. In London he met the impresario Sergei Diaghilev, who rejected his first ballet as non-Russian and commissioned Chout instead. In the summer of 1917 he wrote the Classical Symphony, in the style he said Joseph Haydn would have used had he lived then. After the Revolution he left with the approval of the commissar Anatoly Lunacharsky and reached San Francisco in August 1918. His opera The Love for Three Oranges was delayed by the illness and death of the Chicago Opera's director, and in 1920 he left for Paris.

He toured the Soviet Union in 1927 and settled in Moscow with his family in 1936, after four years of moving between Moscow and Paris. That year he wrote Peter and the Wolf for Natalya Sats's Central Children's Theatre. His Cantata for the 20th Anniversary of the October Revolution was effectively blocked and was not performed until 1966. The German invasion of 22 June 1941 led him to begin War and Peace, for which Mira Mendelson, who became his second wife, co-wrote the libretto. He was evacuated to Tbilisi, where he wrote the first version.

On 10 February 1948, the day before the decree of the Zhdanov Doctrine was published, Prokofiev was honoured at the Kremlin as a People's Artist of the RSFSR. He was then attacked for anti-democratic formalism, but he kept the support of younger performers, among them Sviatoslav Richter, for whom he wrote his Ninth Piano Sonata. He died on 5 March 1953 at the age of 61, the same day as Joseph Stalin. Crowds mourning Stalin made it impossible to hold the funeral service at the Composers' Union headquarters, and his coffin was carried by hand through back streets. About thirty people attended, Dmitri Shostakovich among them. He is buried in the Novodevichy Cemetery in Moscow.
sergei-witte: Sergei Yulyevich Witte was born on 29 June 1849. His father, from a Lutheran Baltic German family, converted to Russian Orthodoxy on marrying Yekaterina Fadeyeva, and Sergei was raised on the estate of his mother's parents. He studied at Novorossiysk University in Odessa, graduating at the top of his class in 1870. He had planned an academic career in mathematics, but his relatives thought it unsuitable for a noble, and he was persuaded to enter the railways.

After six months of training on the Odessa Railways he became chief of the traffic office. A wreck in late 1875 cost many lives and led to a four-month prison sentence, but in the Russo-Turkish War he directed the Odessa Railways and attracted the notice of Grand Duke Nicholas Nikolaevich, who commuted the sentence to two weeks.

From 1889 to 1891 Witte was Director of Railway Affairs in the Finance Ministry, expanding the railways under state control and assigning staff by merit rather than patronage. Appointed Minister of Finance in August 1892, he held the post for eleven years and nearly doubled the empire's revenues. He accelerated the construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway, established a state alcohol monopoly in 1895 and, in 1896, placed the ruble on the gold standard, which increased investment and the inflow of foreign capital. In 1896 he concluded the Li-Lobanov Treaty with Li Hongzhang, which gave Russia the right to build the Chinese Eastern Railway.

Under pressure from the landed gentry and his enemies at court, he was moved in August 1903 to the chairmanship of the Committee of Ministers, a post with no real power. In 1905 the tsar sent him to the United States to negotiate the end of the Russo-Japanese War at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where he is credited with negotiating well for Russia, and he was made a count.

On 9 October 1905 Witte told Nicholas II that the country faced a catastrophic revolution and offered two choices: a military dictator or broad reforms. He framed the October Manifesto, and on 20 October 1905 he was appointed the first chairman of the Council of Ministers, effectively prime minister. With his Council he designed Russia's first constitution, but within months court opposition discredited him as a reformer, and he resigned before the First Duma met on 10 May 1906. He remained a member of the State Council but never again held an administrative post. Witte died in St Petersburg in 1915. His memoirs, completed in 1912, were published in translation in 1921.
sergio-osmena: Sergio Osmeña was born on 9 September 1878 in Cebu. His mother, Juana Osmeña y Suico, was about twenty; his biological father, Antonio Sanson, a wealthy Chinese mestizo businessman and landowner, was already married, so the boy was treated as illegitimate and took his mother's surname. A Y-DNA test in 2023 identified Sanson, where earlier records had also suggested Pedro Lee Gotiaoco. Osmeña studied in Manila, where he met his classmate Manuel L. Quezon, and placed second in the bar examinations of 1903. He had served on General Emilio Aguinaldo's war staff as a courier and journalist, and in 1900 founded the Cebu newspaper El Nuevo Día.

Osmeña was elected governor of Cebu in 1906. In 1907 he won a seat in the first Philippine Assembly and became its first speaker at the age of 29. With Quezon he set up the Nacionalista Party as a counterweight to the Manila-based Partido Federalista. Bills to repeal the sedition law and the flag law, and to give local governments more power, were rejected by the Philippine Commission, but the assembly won a Council of State and a Board of Control that let the legislature share some executive powers with the governor-general. He resigned as speaker in 1922 after a political crisis.

Elected to the Senate in 1922, he served as president pro tempore. In 1933 he went to the United States to secure the Hare–Hawes–Cutting Independence Bill, which was superseded by the Tydings–McDuffie Act of March 1934. He supported the bill and Quezon opposed it, and Osmeña's faction was defeated in the 1934 elections.

Osmeña was inaugurated vice-president beside Quezon on 15 November 1935 and was re-elected in 1941. He remained in office through the Japanese occupation, when the government was in exile. He became president of the Commonwealth on Quezon's death in 1944 and was sworn in on 1 August in Washington. On 20 October 1944 he landed at Leyte with General Douglas MacArthur, who transferred authority to him, and on 27 February 1945 MacArthur handed the government over at Malacañang Palace.

Osmeña reorganised the government, restored the courts and sent a delegation under Carlos P. Romulo to the founding of the United Nations in 1945. The Nacionalista Party split, and Manuel Roxas of its Liberal wing defeated him in the election of 23 April 1946. Osmeña retired to Cebu City and died on 19 October 1961, aged 83, receiving a state funeral.
sergipe: Sergipe covers 21,910 square kilometres and borders Bahia to the south and west and Alagoas to the north. The São Francisco River forms its northern boundary. Inland the state is almost entirely savanna, called caatinga, while the coastline has mangroves, swamps and sandy beaches. The rivers that drain the southern half into the Atlantic are obstructed by sandbars at their mouths, so there are no good ports on the coast. The name comes from an Old Tupi word meaning in the river of the siri, a species of crab.

The region was home to numerous Indigenous peoples, including the Kanindé, the Aratus and the Tupi. Gaspar de Lemos briefly landed there in 1501, and the Portuguese Crown declared it part of the Captaincy of Bahia. It was one of the last coastal regions of Brazil whose Indigenous population resisted Portuguese rule, and it was fully brought under it after about two decades of warfare, during which thousands of Indigenous people were killed and thousands more enslaved to work on sugar plantations. The first Portuguese settlement was at São Cristóvão, then called Sergipe D'El-Rey.

Sergipe was invaded several times by the Dutch and often raided by French buccaneers, who were drawn by its king-wood, a prized commodity. The territory belonged to Dutch-controlled Brazil until the Portuguese regained control in 1645. By 1723 Sergipe, still part of Bahia, produced a third of Bahia's sugar. Land unsuitable for sugarcane was used for livestock, and Sergipe supplied draft animals to farms in Bahia and Pernambuco.

John VI of Portugal signed a decree separating Sergipe from Bahia on 8 July 1820. It kept its separation after the independence of Brazil in 1822, first as a captaincy and then as a province. On 17 March 1855 the provincial president moved the capital from São Cristóvão, inland, to Aracaju on the coast. Sergipe became a state when the Republic of Brazil was proclaimed in 1892.

Sergipe is the smallest Brazilian state by area, larger only than the Federal District, with Aracaju as its capital and largest city. São Cristóvão, the fourth oldest town in the country and the state capital until 1855, has a main square, São Francisco Square, that became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
sergius-i-of-naples: Before he became duke, Sergius was the dux of Cumae, a Neapolitan dependency. In 840, with the Franks trying to take Naples, its people elected him duke, or magister militum. The election was a move towards complete independence from the Byzantine Empire, which was incapable of defending the Ducatus Neapolitanus against the Lombards. His line, often called the Sergi, held Naples until the death of his namesake Sergius VII in 1137.

Sergius at first kept the alliance the Neapolitans had made with the Saracens of Palermo, and helped them take Bari from the Byzantines in 841 and Messina in 842. The Saracens soon became too dangerous as friends, and Naples allied with Amalfi, Gaeta and Sorrento, its practically independent underlings, to make war on them. The Christians drove the Muslims out of Ponza and defended Rome in 846, although the Vatican was sacked, and in 849 the Neapolitan fleet fought alongside those of Gaeta and the Vatican in the victory at the Battle of Ostia.

Turning away from the Byzantines towards the papacy and the Franks, Sergius allied himself with the emperors Lothair I and Louis II. In 847 he and Guy I of Spoleto were charged with establishing peace between the Lombard princes Siconulf of Salerno and Radelchis I of Benevento. In 850 he appointed his eldest son, Gregory, co-duke, a successful step towards making the duchy hereditary, and he began to mint his own coins bearing his own effigy.

In 859 Sergius made war on Capua. He married his daughter to Landulf, gastald of Suessola and son of Lando I of Capua, and with the gastald he sent two of his sons, Gregory among them, to sack New Capua; they failed. Two other sons held high church office: Athanasius became bishop of Naples, an imperial familiaris and a papal legate close to the Roman curia, and Stephen held the bishopric of Sorrento.

Before he died in 864, Sergius bade Gregory to follow the counsel of his brother the bishop. Gregory succeeded him, and with that succession the hereditary, independent dukedom of Naples was born. His alliances with the papacy and the Franks also opened the way for the expulsion of the Muslims from Campania.
sergius-iv-of-naples: Sergius succeeded his father, John IV, and like him was nominally a Byzantine vassal. In 1024, when Pilgrim, Archbishop of Cologne, was besieging Capua on behalf of Emperor Henry II, Sergius submitted to him, although his own duchy was not threatened. By this he acquired a reputation for weakness in the eyes of Prince Pandulf IV of Capua, whom Pilgrim had defeated.

In 1026 Pandulf, returned from captivity, besieged his old capital, then ruled by Pandulf V, the count of Teano. Basil Boioannes, the Greek catapan of Italy, negotiated a surrender and gave Pandulf V safe conduct to Naples, where Sergius offered him asylum and so earned Pandulf IV's enmity. In 1027, after Boioannes had been recalled, Pandulf IV attacked Naples and quickly captured it, by treachery according to some. Pandulf V fled to Rome and Sergius went into hiding.

Fortune turned in 1029, when the Norman Rainulf Drengot abandoned Pandulf. Sergius and his nephew, Duke John V of Gaeta, sent an embassy asking for Rainulf's help, and with it Pandulf was chased from Naples and Sergius reinstated. Early in 1030 Sergius gave Rainulf the county of Aversa as a fief, the first Norman principality in the region, and his own sister in marriage. These grants made Sergius one of the prime catalysts in the growth of Norman power in the Mezzogiorno.

In 1034 Pandulf IV instigated a revolt in Sorrento and annexed it to Capua. In the same year Sergius' sister died and Rainulf returned to Pandulf's side. Broken in spirit, Sergius retired to the monastery of the Holy Saviour in insula maris, and was succeeded by his son, John V.

When John went to Constantinople to seek aid from the Byzantines, Sergius came out of retirement for a time to act as regent, and on John's return he went back to his monastery. He was still living there as late as June 1036 and probably died shortly afterwards. His two retirements explain why Amatus of Montecassino refers to him twice becoming a monk.
sergius-of-radonezh: His medieval biography says Sergius was born to Kiril and Maria, a boyar family, near Rostov Veliky, and was given the baptismal name Bartholomew. The year of his birth is unclear. When Rostov fell into the hands of Ivan I of Moscow his parents became poor and moved with their three sons to the village of Radonezh. The biography tells that the boy found learning to read very hard until an elder gave him a piece of holy bread; Orthodox Christians interpret the incident as an angelic visit.

After his parents died Bartholomew joined his older brother Stefan, a monk at Khotkovo near Moscow, and persuaded him to seek a more secluded place. In the forest at Makovets Hill they built a small cell and a church dedicated to the Trinity, the beginning of the Trinity-St. Sergius Lavra. Bartholomew was tonsured and named Sergius, and lived more than a year alone as a hermit. Other monks came, and they persuaded him to become their abbot. He was ordained a priest and required every monk to live by his own labour. The town of Sergiev Posad grew beside the monastery.

His disciples spread his teaching across central and northern Russia, settling in the most inaccessible places, and founded about 40 monasteries, among them Borisoglebsky, Ferapontov, Kirillo-Belozersky and Vysotsky. Metropolitan Alexius asked him to be his successor, but Sergius declined, preferring to remain a simple monk. He stayed out of politics, though he blessed Dmitry Donskoy before the Battle of Kulikovo, after making sure that Dmitry had tried every peaceful means to settle the dispute.

Sergius died on 25 September 1392, and his incorrupt relics were found in 1422 and placed in the new cathedral of the Lavra. His canonization by the Russian Orthodox Church dates to 1452 or 1448. He is remembered on 25 September and on 5 July, the day his relics were uncovered, and is also commemorated in the Catholic Church and the Church of England. Much of what is known of him comes from a life written in the 15th century by the hagiographer Pachomius the Serb. The historian Serge Zenkovsky counted him, with Epiphanius the Wise, Stephen of Perm and the painter Andrei Rublev, among the figures of the Russian spiritual and cultural revival of the late fourteenth and early fifteenth century.
sergius-vii-of-naples: Sergius succeeded his father, John VI, in 1122 as the thirty-ninth duke, or magister militum, of Naples, at a time when Roger II of Sicily was rising rapidly in power. Roger became duke of Apulia in 1127 and was crowned king in 1130, and from then on the fate of Naples hinged on Sergius' relations with the Sicilian court.

In 1131 Roger demanded from the citizens of Amalfi the defences of their city and the keys to their castle. When they refused, Sergius prepared to aid them with a fleet, but Admiral George of Antioch blockaded the port with a larger fleet and Sergius submitted to Roger. The chronicler Alexander of Telese remarked that Naples, which since Roman times had hardly ever been conquered by the sword, now submitted on the strength of a mere report.

In 1134 Sergius supported the rebellion of Robert II of Capua and Ranulf II of Alife, but avoided any direct confrontation with Roger and did homage to the king after the fall of Capua. On 24 April 1135 a Pisan fleet under the exiled Robert anchored at Naples carrying 8,000 reinforcements, and a full-scale revolt began again. Sergius had to welcome Ranulf, who like him was in revolt against a king to whom he had recently sworn fealty.

Robert, Ranulf and Sergius were then besieged in Naples, where many people died of starvation. According to Falco of Benevento, a historian sympathetic to the rebels, the Neapolitans preferred to die of hunger rather than submit. The naval blockade had gaps, and Sergius and Robert each slipped out to Pisa for supplies. When a relief army under Emperor Lothair II came to the city's rescue, Roger lifted the siege.

Lothair left soon after conquering nearly the whole of the Mezzogiorno, and Roger retook his lost possessions. Sergius again did homage, hoping to spare his city another siege, was forgiven, and accompanied Roger on an expedition against his former ally Ranulf, now duke of Apulia. At the Battle of Rignano on 30 October 1137 Roger and his son were defeated, and Sergius died on the field.

Sergius died without an heir, and the nobility of Naples could not agree on a successor. Roger's defeat at Rignano thus opened the way to his conquest of the city itself. He absorbed the Duchy of Naples into his kingdom in 1139, when Pope Innocent II and the Neapolitan nobility acknowledged the young Alfonso of Hauteville as duke.
sergo-ordzhonikidze: Sergo Ordzhonikidze was born Grigol Ordzhonikidze on 24 October 1886 in Ghoresha, a village in the Kutais Governorate of the Russian Empire, now in the Imereti region of Georgia. His father Konstantine belonged to an impoverished noble family and his mother Eupraxia was a peasant; she died six weeks after his birth. He was raised by an uncle and aunt, and his father died when he was ten. He trained as a medical orderly and briefly worked as a medical assistant.

He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1903, at 17, and worked in an underground printshop for the Bolshevik faction. He was first arrested in December 1905 for transporting arms, worked in Baku, and was imprisoned several times by the Russian police. He was in Siberian exile when the February Revolution began in 1917, then returned and took part in the October Revolution.

During the Civil War he was the leading Bolshevik in the Caucasus. In 1918 he persuaded Chechen and Ingush leaders that the soviet system resembled the Islamic order they favoured, and with Ingush help the Bolsheviks retook Vladikavkaz. After Lenin ordered him on 17 March 1920 to prepare an invasion of Azerbaijan, he oversaw the invasions of Azerbaijan, Armenia and Georgia. As head of the Kavbiuro he clashed with the Georgian Bolsheviks, especially Budu Mdivani, whose advice he ignored. He backed their union in the Transcaucasian Socialist Federative Soviet Republic and was its First Secretary until 1926. Colleagues called him authoritarian; Lenin explained that he shouted because he was deaf in one ear.

In 1926 Stalin made him head of the Workers' and Peasants' Inspectorate and the Central Control Commission. In 1930 he took over Vesenkha, reorganised in 1932 as the People's Commissariat of Heavy Industry, and became a full member of the Politburo. He argued Stalin down to a yearly industrial growth target of 13 to 14 per cent for the second five-year plan and helped launch the Stakhanovite movement in 1935. He tried to protect his officials from the hunt for wreckers and saboteurs and had prosecutors barred from factories, which strained his friendship with Stalin.

Ordzhonikidze died on 18 February 1937, a few days before a Central Committee plenum at which he was expected to speak on wrecking in his commissariat. Rumours spread at once that Stalin had ordered his death or driven him to suicide. The historian Oleg Khlevniuk thinks suicide likely, and the cause remains contested. His brother Papulia was shot in November 1937, and other relatives and colleagues were arrested. Vladikavkaz was renamed Ordzhonikidze in 1931 and bore the name again from 1954 to 1990.
seri-menanti: Seri Menanti lies in Kuala Pilah District in central Negeri Sembilan, 33 kilometres east of the state capital Seremban and 14 kilometres southwest of Kuala Pilah, in a valley among the hills of the Titiwangsa range. The area is known as the Adat Circle, and Seri Menanti also governs the surrounding chiefdoms, or luak, of Terachi, Gunung Pasir, Ulu Muar, Jempol and Ineh, together called Luak Tanah Mengandung. Much of its land is Malay Reserve and Malay Customary Land, and a few houses in the Minangkabau Rumah Gadang style still stand in the villages.

The Minangkabau people came to the wider area of Negeri Sembilan in the 14th century through the custom of merantau, and around the 17th century some moved inland from Rembau to the site of the town. According to legend, the explorer Datuk Puteh of Pagar Ruyung found three stalks of fresh green paddy and named the place Padi Menanti, awaiting paddy, which later became Seri Menanti; the word seri is believed to recall the Javanese rice goddess Sri. Raja Melewar, who arrived in 1773, was proclaimed the first Yamtuan Besar at Kampung Penajis in Rembau and later moved his palace to Seri Menanti.

The old wooden palace, the Istana Lama, replaced the Istana Pulih, which British soldiers had burned. It was built under Tuanku Muhammad Shah ibni Almarhum Tuanku Antah, who reigned from 1888 to 1933, from designs by the local craftsmen Kahar and Taib, in chengal and belian wood held with wooden pegs. Six years in the building, it rises five levels to 67 feet on 99 columns. The ruler used it until 1932, when he moved to the new Istana Besar.

Seri Menanti remains the royal capital of Negeri Sembilan, and the Istana Besar complex holds the Main Palace, the Throne Room and the Royal Banquet Hall. The Istana Lama became a Royal Museum in 1992 and was gazetted in 2009 among ten national heritage structures of Malaysia. The town also has the Seri Menanti Royal Mausoleum.
seria: Seria lies about 65 kilometres west of Bandar Seri Begawan, within a mangrove swamp and surrounded by its oilfield. It takes its name from the river near which oil was first found; the area between the Bera and Seria rivers was once called Padang Berawa, a name translated as Wild Pigeon's Field. Its coast of mudflats, mangroves and beach forest is an Important Bird Area recognised by BirdLife International, home to species such as the Bornean crestless fireback and the lesser adjutant.

The first commercial well was completed on the west bank of the Seria River in 1929; production began in 1931 and exports in 1932, and by 1935 Seria's royalties made up 47% of the state's revenue. Seria became a town in 1936. Japanese troops of the Kawaguchi Detachment landed on 16 December 1941, after the British had destroyed the oilfield; Australian forces liberated the town on 29 June 1945, and production resumed in November. Between 1932 and 1959 the government earned $340 million in royalties from the field.

In the 1950s the oil company ran Seria almost as a state within a state, and the British watched its workers for signs of unrest. A. M. Azahari organised among the oil workers, and in the Brunei revolt Seria was a main target of the rebels. Its security forces held out, British troops of the 1/2nd Gurkha Rifles and the Queen's Own Highlanders retook the town on 11 December, and hostages held at the Panaga police station were freed the next day. Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III then accepted a Gurkha garrison at Seria to guard the oil installations.

Seria is the centre of Brunei's oil and gas industry, with the country's only refinery and the headquarters of Brunei Shell Petroleum at nearby Panaga. British Forces Brunei have had their headquarters there since 1963. The Billionth Barrel Monument of 1991 marks the field's billionth barrel of crude oil.
sericulture: Sericulture, or silk farming, is the cultivation of silkworms to produce silk. The caterpillar of the domestic silkmoth is the species most widely used and intensively studied. It is no longer found in the wild, because selective breeding has left most of these moths flightless and without defence against predators. Silk is believed to have first been produced in China as early as the Neolithic period.

According to a Confucian text the discovery of silk production dates to about 2700 BCE, while archaeological records point to silk cultivation as early as the Yangshao period, 5000 to 3000 BCE. A ceramic piece made to look like a silkworm, found in 1977 at Nancun in Hebei and 5,400 to 5,500 years old, is the earliest known evidence. Silk fibre found on Indus Civilization sites dating to 2450 to 2000 BCE suggests that silk was used over a wide region of South Asia.

By about the first half of the 1st century CE the practice had reached ancient Khotan through a series of interactions along the Silk Road, and by 140 CE it was established in India. In the 6th century CE the smuggling of silkworm eggs into the Byzantine Empire led to its establishment in the Mediterranean, where it remained a monopoly of the Byzantine Empire for centuries.

In 1147, during the Second Crusade, Roger II of Sicily attacked Corinth and Thebes, two important centres of Byzantine silk production. He captured the weavers and their equipment and set up his own silkworks in Palermo and Calabria, which eventually spread the industry to Western Europe.

The silkworms are fed with mulberry leaves, and after the fourth moult they climb a twig and spin their cocoons. The silk is a continuous filament of fibroin protein, secreted from two salivary glands in the head of each worm, held together by a gum called sericin. Placing the cocoons in hot water removes the sericin, a step known as degumming, and frees the filaments for reeling. The hot water also kills the pupa inside.

One cocoon holds approximately 1,000 yards of filament, and about 2,500 silkworms are needed to produce a pound of raw silk. Mahatma Gandhi criticised silk production on the philosophy of ahimsa, not to hurt any living thing, and promoted silk made without boiling the pupa and wild silk from the cocoons of wild and semiwild moths.
sermon-on-law-and-grace: The sermon is one of the earliest Slavonic texts, written several decades before the Primary Chronicle, and its date was worked out by matching it against events that the chronicle records. It was most likely composed for the Christian elite of Kievan Rus' and delivered at the St. Sophia Cathedral in Kiev. The Russian philologist Aleksander Uzhankov holds that it was spoken on the evening of 25 March 1038 in the Church of the Annunciation at the Golden Gate, while some scholars think its two parts were given on different occasions and joined later.

Its full title sets out its themes: the Law given by Moses and the Grace and Truth that came by Jesus Christ, how Grace and Faith spread to all nations even to the Rus', an encomium to the kagan Volodimer by whom they were baptised, and a prayer to God from all the land.

In the first part Hilarion retells the story of Hagar and Sarah, likening Isaac, the free son of a free mother, to the followers of Christianity and Ishmael to the Jews: as Ishmael came before Isaac, so the Law came before Grace, and now the Gospel spreads over the earth while the lake of the Law has dried up. The second part is a eulogy of Vladimir, grand prince of Kiev, in a highly rhetorical panegyric style, possibly meant to present him as a candidate for canonisation.

Hilarion was regarded as a writer worthy of imitation, and the sermon strongly influenced both the style and the content of the literature that followed in Kievan Rus'. Its delivery was itself an event thought important enough to be mentioned in the Primary Chronicle.
serpent-column: The Greek states that had fought the Persians dedicated the monument to Apollo at Delphi from the spoils of the victory at Plataea. Herodotus records that they set apart a tithe for the god, and from it was made the tripod that rested on the bronze three-headed serpent, nearest to the altar. The golden tripod and cauldron, made from Persian weapons, are long lost. The bronze column of three intertwined snakes is about 8 metres (26 ft) high. Herodotus also records dedications to Zeus at Olympia and to Poseidon at the Isthmus.

Pausanias, regent of Sparta and commander at Plataea, had a dedication engraved on it that ascribed the victory to himself alone. Thucydides cites the affair among the grounds for Spartan suspicion that he was ready to go over to the Persians. The Spartans removed the inscription and engraved the names of the cities that had taken part. Pseudo-Demosthenes gives a different account, in which the Plataeans brought a suit against Sparta before the Amphictyonic council. Diodorus Siculus says a couplet by the poet Simonides replaced the dedication.

The travel writer Pausanias saw the bronze part at Delphi in the second century CE. The gold had been taken in 354 BCE by the Phocian general Philomelus to pay mercenaries in the Third Sacred War. Constantine the Great moved the column to Constantinople in 324 to decorate the spina of the Hippodrome. Later it was made into a fountain with three mouths, and travellers described it from 1422. Ahmed Bican wrote that the citizens regarded it as a talisman against snake bites.

One serpent's lower jaw went missing in the decades after the Ottoman conquest. The accepted version says Mehmed II shattered it, and Edward Gibbon tells it so, though other Ottoman writers named Selim II, Suleiman II or Murad IV. Petrus Gyllius in 1550 and Pietro Della Valle in 1614 mention no damage. According to the chronicler Silahdar Findiklili Mehmed Aga, in the Nusretname, the heads fell off on the night of 20 October 1700. An upper jaw is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums.

The ground was raised in 1630 and hid the inscribed part. Charles Thomas Newton supervised the excavation of the base in 1855, which uncovered the inscription from the 13th coil to the 3rd. It was deciphered by C. Frick in 1856 and by Ernst Fabricius in 1886. The 13th coil reads 'Those who fought the war', and coils 12 to 3 give the names of 31 city-states, eight of them not named by Herodotus as present at Plataea. The list suggests that the monument relates to the whole Persian war, not only to that battle. A bronze copy was set up at Delphi in 2015.
serres: Serres stands on a fertile plain at an elevation of about 70 metres, some 24 kilometres north-east of the Strymon river and 69 kilometres north-east of Thessaloniki. The ancient city was built on a high, steep hill known as Koulas, just north of the modern one, and controlled the land road that followed the Strymon valley from the Strymonian Gulf to the Danubian countries. Herodotus mentions it as Siris in the 5th century BCE; Livy later calls it Sirae, and the name has stayed plural since.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Bryges and Strymonians, followed by the Paeonian tribes of the Siropaiones and Odomantes. In the Roman period the city, called Sirra, was an important city of the province of Macedonia and the seat of a federation of five cities, the Pentapolis. It flourished under the Pax Romana, declined in the crisis of 235 to 284 CE and recovered under Diocletian. Its first attested bishop took part in the Second Council of Ephesus in 449.

In about 803 Emperor Nikephoros I rebuilt the town and installed a garrison against the Slavic tribes. It was pillaged by Bulgarians in the 10th century and taken by Ivan Asen I's forces after the Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Serres in the late 12th century. After the Fourth Crusade it passed to Boniface of Montferrat and then to Kaloyan of Bulgaria, who according to George Akropolites reduced it to a small settlement around the citadel.

The Nicaean Empire took it in 1246, and by the 14th century Nikephoros Gregoras called it large and marvellous. The Serbs took it on 25 September 1345, and after Stefan Dušan's death in 1355 it became the Principality of Serres, ruled first by the Empress-dowager Helena and from 1365 by the Despot Jovan Uglješa, whose administration worked in Greek.

The Ottoman Empire took Serres definitively on 19 September 1383, and it became a fief of Evrenos Beg. In the 17th century Evliya Çelebi recorded a prosperous town with 2,000 shops in its market. A fire in 1849 destroyed most of its churches. A Bulgarian army took the city on 6 November 1912, and Greek forces entered it on 11 July 1913; the retreating Bulgarians set fire to it. In 1943 its Jewish population was deported to the Treblinka death camp.

Serres is the capital of the Serres regional unit and the second largest city of Central Macedonia after Thessaloniki. Its municipal population was 70,703 in 2021. It is a trade centre for tobacco, grain and livestock, and it hosts a campus of the International Hellenic University and a department of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki. The Archaeological Museum is housed in an Ottoman bezesten.
sertorian-war: During Sulla's civil war Quintus Sertorius fought for the Marian-Cinnan faction, which sent him to govern Hispania in 83 BCE. When his side lost in Italy, a Sullan army drove him out in 81 BCE. In Tingis in North Africa, where he helped the inhabitants depose the pro-Sullan tyrant Ascalis, he received an embassy of Lusitanians asking him to lead them against Sulla's government, which had remembered his mild rule. Philip Spann argues that the Lusitanians hoped for a regime in Rome sympathetic to them rather than independence, and that Sertorius accepted because he could expect no amnesty.

Sertorius landed at Baelo in 80 BCE, defeated Fufidius at the Baetis and, with his legate Lucius Hirtuleius, won control of both Hispanian provinces by 77 BCE, wearing down Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius with guerrilla tactics. Marcus Perperna joined him in 76 BCE with fifty-three cohorts, the remnant of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus's army. The Senate sent Pompey, who had never held a magistracy, with 30,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, but Sertorius defeated him at the Battle of Lauron in 76 BCE.

The year 75 BCE turned the war. Pompey defeated Perperna and Gaius Herennius at Valentia, where Herennius died among 10,000 casualties, and Metellus beat Hirtuleius at Italica, where Hirtuleius lost 20,000 men. Sertorius fought Pompey to a draw at the Sucro and the combined Sullan armies at Saguntum, then withdrew to Clunia and rebuilt his army. Reinforced from Rome, Metellus and Pompey waged a war of attrition from 74 BCE. Metellus offered a hundred silver talents and twenty thousand acres to any Roman who betrayed Sertorius, and when Sertorius replaced his Roman bodyguard with Iberians, Roman officers began to plot against him.

Perperna invited Sertorius to a feast celebrating a supposed victory and had him murdered there, usually dated 72 BCE, though there are strong arguments for 73. Many Iberian allies made peace with Pompey or Metellus or went home, and Pompey soon defeated Perperna by a feigned retreat and ambush at the Battle of Osca. In the view of the historian Scullard, Pompey treated Hispania humanely by the Roman standard for rebels: many supporters received citizenship, and a group of determined opponents was resettled at Lugdunum Convenarum in southern Gaul. The war is remembered for Sertorius's use of guerrilla warfare.
seru-epenisa-cakobau: Seru Epenisa Cakobau was born around 1815 on Nairai, the son of Ratu Tanoa Visawaqa and one of his nine wives, Adi Savusavu. For nearly a century the Vunivalu, the war chief, and the Roko Tui Bau, the sacred chief, had struggled for power in Bau. Tanoa was exiled in 1832 after killing the Roko Tui Bau. Seru married two sisters, daughters of the Roko Tui Bau. He was called Cikinovu, the Centipede, because he moved silently and struck painfully, and later Cakobau, destroyer of Bau, though he also built a new Bau.

Cakobau succeeded as Vunivalu of Bau on 8 December 1852. The missionary James Calvert converted him to Christianity, and he renounced cannibalism in 1854, taking the added name Epenisa, or Ebenezer. He claimed that Bau ruled the rest of Fiji, but other chiefs regarded him at best as first among equals, and he fought almost constantly for nearly nineteen years to unify the islands. He crushed the last brief rebellion at the Battle of Kaba with the aid of the King of Tonga, and on the battlefield he pardoned the captives, who under pagan custom would have been humiliated, killed and eaten.

On 8 May 1865 a Confederacy of Independent Kingdoms of Viti was founded, with Cakobau as chairman of its General Assembly. Two years later it split into the Kingdom of Bau and the Confederation of Lau. With the support of foreign settlers he created a united Fijian kingdom in 1871 with its capital at Levuka, and the first legislative assembly met in November.

The United States had recognised his claim to the kingship long before other chiefs did, but the American government held him responsible for an arson attack in 1849 on the Nukulau Island home of its consul, and demanded 44,000 dollars. Unable to pay and fearing American annexation, Cakobau decided to cede the islands to the United Kingdom. He gave his war club to Queen Victoria on 10 October 1874, when the Deed of Cession was signed. He kept the title Vunivalu of Bau and lived quietly until his death on 1 February 1883. His descendants include Ratu Sir George Cakobau, Fiji's first native-born governor-general, and Ratu Sir Kamisese Mara, its first prime minister.
servian-wall: The wall takes its name from Servius Tullius, the sixth Roman king. The literary tradition that some kind of defensive wall or earthwork encircled Rome in the 6th century BCE has been found to be false, and the main extent of the wall was built in the early 4th century BCE, under the Roman Republic. It was up to 10 metres high in places, 3.6 metres wide at its base and about 11 kilometres long, and enclosed an area of 246 hectares. It is believed to have had 16 main gates, of which only one or two survive.

The first wall was built of large blocks of Cappellaccio tuff, a volcanic rock quarried from the Alban Hills. By the late 390s BCE it was partly damaged and needed restoration, either because it was disintegrating quickly or because of damage in the Sack of Rome in 390 BCE. The repairs used a better stone, Grotta Oscura tuff, which became available after the Romans defeated Veii in the 390s and which was quarried by the defeated Veientines. Livy dates the completion of this second wall to 378 BCE.

Some sections had a deep ditch, a fossa, in front of the wall, which effectively raised its height. Along part of the weaker northern perimeter an agger, a ramp of earth, was built up along the inside. It thickened the wall and gave defenders a place to stand when repelling an attack. The wall was also fitted with defensive war engines, including catapults. Hannibal camped his army within sight of the Porta Collina, the northernmost gate, in 211 BCE when he considered besieging Rome, and that stretch had the agger.

The wall was maintained to the end of the Late Republic and into the Roman Empire, but Rome had already begun to outgrow it. Protected by the field armies of the Republic and then the Empire, the city was essentially without a border wall for the first three centuries of imperial rule, and new houses simply took sections of the old wall into their foundations, as in the Auditorium of Maecenas. When German tribes made further incursions along the frontier in the 3rd century CE, Emperor Aurelian had the larger Aurelian Walls built to protect the city.

Several sections are still visible in Rome. The largest is preserved outside Termini Station, the main railway station. The Porta Esquilina on the Esquiline Hill still stands and incorporates the later arch of the emperor Gallienus. A section on the Aventine Hill incorporates an arch that was supposedly made for a catapult, and the Arch of Dolabella and Silanus, built in 10 CE, may preserve the Porta Caelimontana.
servius-tullius: Most Roman sources name the mother of Servius Tullius as Ocrisia, a young noblewoman taken at the Roman siege of Corniculum and given to Tanaquil, wife of King Tarquinius Priscus. Several traditions describe his father as divine, either the household Lar or Vulcan. Livy tells how members of the royal household saw a ring of fire about the head of the sleeping boy, a sign of divine favour, after which he became a protégé of the royal family and married their daughter. Livy argues that no slave could have been granted so great an honour. The Emperor Claudius offered a different account, based on Etruscan tradition, in which Servius was an Etruscan mercenary named Mastarna who fought for Caelius Vibenna.

According to Livy, the sons of Ancus Marcius had Tarquinius Priscus wounded by assassins, and Tanaquil announced from a palace window that he had named Servius regent. When the king's death became known, the senate elected Servius, the first time the people were not involved in choosing a king. He fought Veii and the Etruscans.

The so-called Servian reforms extended voting rights to commoners and defined the fiscal and military obligations of all citizens. Tradition holds that Servius held the first Roman census and formed the comitia centuriata, which displaced the comitia curiata as the central legislative body. The census grouped male citizens in classes by wealth, each divided into centuries, and the wealthiest centuries voted first. Modern scholars think the reforms were a long, piecemeal process that extended beyond his reign. He is also said to have extended the city, protected it with a rampart, moat and wall, built a temple of Diana on the Aventine and founded or reformed the Compitalia.

In Livy's account Servius gave his two daughters to the sons of Tarquinius Priscus. The younger Tullia and her husband Lucius Tarquinius Superbus had their siblings murdered and conspired against the king. Tarquinius went to the senate house with armed men and threw Servius down the steps, and Servius was killed in the street. Livy calls this a tragic crime and makes it the just cause for the end of the monarchy.

Servius is described as Rome's second founder and as a kind of proto-Republican magistrate. Claudius's identification with Mastarna draws some support from the François Tomb at Vulci, whose paintings show a Macstrna among the allies of the Vibenna brothers.
ses-s-a: SES was formed in 1985 on the initiative and with the support of the Luxembourgish government, as the Société Européenne des Satellites. In December 1988, as Europe's first private satellite operator, it launched its first satellite, Astra 1A, to the 19.2° East orbital position. Rupert Murdoch's Sky TV and the German broadcasters Pro7, Sat.1 and RTL were among Astra's first major customers. By 1990 Astra was broadcasting to 14 million cable and direct-to-home viewers. SES pioneered co-location, in which several satellites share one orbital position to provide mutual backup and more channels for a fixed receiving dish, creating a 'satellite neighbourhood'. Rapid growth in Germany, its largest European market, was helped by the German government's decision to liberalise the installation of dishes in 1991.

From 1999 SES expanded beyond Europe and beyond television into telecommunications services for businesses and governments, and broadband access. In 1999 it acquired a 34.13% stake in the Hong Kong operator AsiaSat, and in 2000 it took 50% of Nordic Satellite AB and 19.99% of Brazil's Star One. In 2001 it bought GE Americom, which gave it a presence in North America, and formed SES Global with two operating companies, SES Astra and SES Americom. It then operated 41 geostationary satellites, the largest fleet in the world. The company has been called simply SES since 2006.

In April 2024 SES announced the acquisition of Intelsat for €2.8 billion in cash. The UK Competition and Markets Authority cleared it in May 2025, the European Commission in June 2025 and the US Federal Communications Commission in July 2025, and the acquisition was completed on 17 July 2025.

SES provides services through two units, SES Media for video distribution and services, and SES Networks for data connectivity to telecommunications, aviation, maritime, government and other customers. It operates satellites in geostationary and medium Earth orbit, including the O3b and O3b mPOWER systems. Its innovations include co-location, digital broadcasting, high-definition and Ultra HD television, and it broadcast the first live Ultra HD satellite programme in November 2014. The company is based at Betzdorf in Luxembourg.
sesame: Sesame, Sesamum indicum, is a plant also called benne. Most of the other species of its genus are wild and native to sub-Saharan Africa, while the cultivated type originated in India. It was described by Carl Linnaeus in 1753, and its epithet means of India. The seeds, which are white or black and grow in pods, have one of the highest oil contents of any seed. The plant tolerates drought and heat and will grow where other crops fail, so subsistence farmers at the edge of deserts have grown it. The word sesame comes through Latin and Greek from ancient Semitic languages such as the Akkadian šamaššamu.

Sesame is considered the oldest oilseed crop known to humanity. Charred remains dated to about 3500 to 3050 BCE show that it was domesticated in the Indian subcontinent at least 5,500 years ago. The archaeobotanist Dorian Q. Fuller states that sesame was traded between Mesopotamia and the Indian subcontinent by 2000 BCE, and the Indus Valley civilization may have exported sesame oil to Mesopotamia, where it was called ilu in Sumerian and ellu in Akkadian. Some believe it may instead have originated in Ethiopia.

Egyptians called it sesemt, and it appears in the list of medicinal drugs of the Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BCE. Baskets of sesame were found among the grave goods of King Tutankhamen, which suggests it was present in Egypt by 1350 BCE. It was grown and pressed for oil at least by 750 BCE in the empire of Urartu.

The seeds are a common ingredient in many cuisines, made into tahini paste and halva in the Middle East and a part of the spice mixture za'atar. Enslaved West Africans brought sesame to colonial America in the 17th century and grew it as a subsistence crop. In Southern Italian cuisine sesame sweets such as giurgiulena remain from the Arabic period. In the early twentieth century sesame oil was a compulsory ingredient of margarine in Europe, because its presence made it simple to detect margarine used to adulterate butter. Around 1920 Burma exported about 197,400 tons of the oil a year.
sese-islands: The Ssese Islands lie in two main groups separated by the Koome Channel. The south-western Bugala Group is named after Bugala Island, which holds more than half of the archipelago's land and is over 40 kilometres long; it includes Bubeke, Bubembe, Bufumira, Bugaba, Bukasa, Buyova, Funve and Serinya. The north-eastern Koome Group includes Damba, Koome and Luwaji. About half the islands are inhabited, and the largest town, Kalangala on Bugala, lies about 51 kilometres across the water south-west of Entebbe. Kalangala District has no territory on the mainland.

Little is known of the earliest inhabitants. Some oral traditions of the founding of Buganda say that its founder Kintu came from the islands, or reached Buganda by way of them. The Baganda revere Ssese as the Islands of the Gods, and before colonial times the kings of Buganda used to visit them and pay tribute to the balubaale, the spirits whose main shrines stood there: Musisi, the spirit of earthquakes, and Wanema, of physical handicaps, on Bukasa Island, and Mukasa, the spirit of the lake, on Bubembe. Henry Morton Stanley described the islanders as the principal canoe builders and most of the sailors of Mtesa's empire.

The islands are home to the Bantu-speaking Bassese, closely related to the Baganda and the Basoga, whose language is similar but distinct. Fishing for Nile perch is the main industry, much of the catch exported, alongside farming, forestry and tourism, and a large palm oil plantation on the islands has generated electricity since 2010. The forests shelter vervet monkeys, bushbuck and black-and-white colobus, and Bugala has an endemic creek rat and three endemic butterflies.
sessho-and-kampaku: In earlier times only members of the imperial family could act as sesshō. The Kojiki reports that Emperor Ōjin was assisted by his mother, Empress Jingū, though it is doubtful whether this is historical; the first historical sesshō was Prince Shōtoku, who assisted Empress Suiko. The regents of the Heian court came from the Fujiwara Hokke, the northern branch of the Fujiwara clan, to which Fujiwara no Yoshifusa belonged. Fujiwara no Mototsune, the first kampaku, was his nephew and adopted son.

The regents carried to the emperor the policies drawn up by the Sadaijin, the Minister of the Left, and other senior officials of the Daijō-kan, the Council of State, and carried the emperor's decisions back to them. They sometimes decided on the emperor's behalf, yet their offices were not defined by law and carried no specific political authority. Like imperial princes and princesses, both were styled denka, Highness. Power under the Fujiwara reached its height in the time of Fujiwara no Michinaga and Fujiwara no Yorimichi.

The five regent houses, the Konoe, Kujō, Ichijō, Takatsukasa and Nijō families, descended from Yorimichi; the Konoe and Kujō through Fujiwara no Tadamichi, the others from those two. Until 1868 they held the titles alone, with two exceptions. Toyotomi Hideyoshi became the first kampaku not noble by birth, by having himself adopted into the Konoe family, and his nephew Toyotomi Hidetsugu followed him. A retired kampaku was called Taikō, a title that came to mean Hideyoshi himself.

Although the old offices were abolished in the Meiji Restoration, the office of sesshō was set down again in the Imperial Household Law of 1889 and in the new law of 1948, both of which restrict it to members of the imperial family. Crown Prince Hirohito, later Emperor Shōwa, served as sesshō from 1921 to 1926 for Emperor Taishō and was called sesshō-no-miya, the Prince-Regent. The Taikō district of Nagoya, with its main street Taikō-dōri, takes its name from Hideyoshi's title.
sesshu-toyo: Sesshū was born into the samurai Oda family at Akahama, now part of Sōja in Okayama Prefecture, in the Muromachi period. As a child he entered the Buddhist community at the Hofukuji temple. A well-known tale says that when his instructor tied him to a temple post as discipline, he drew a mouse on the floor with his tears, and the mouse came to life and gnawed through the ropes. At twelve or thirteen he entered Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto as an acolyte under the head priest Shunrin Shuto and became a Zen monk.

At Shōkoku-ji Sesshū was a pupil of Tenshō Shūbun, often regarded as Japan's first great master of ink landscape painting, and worked under him for twenty years. He then left Kyoto for a small provincial Zen temple in western Japan, where he was free of monastic and political duties and could focus on painting. In 1467, funded by a wealthy warrior clan that traded with Ming China, he travelled to China with a Japanese envoy and stayed three years. He explored Chan monasteries and landscapes and studied the paintings of professional artists rather than literati masters.

In his last years he visited Masuda to study Zen and made gardens known as Sesshū's gardens. He died in 1506 at the Tokoji temple, and his remains were cremated at Ikoji temple, later known as Sesshū temple. His pupil Shutoku inherited his studio, Unkoku-an.

Sesshū's paintings are mostly suibokuga, water and ink paintings, in diluted greys and black sumi ink on paper or silk. They show flattened space, emphatic outlines and angular brushstrokes, and carry Zen ideas of simplicity. Winter Landscape, from the 1470s, shows a single figure climbing a steep path towards a barren temple, in flat overlapping mountains drawn with short, expressive strokes. His Four Landscape Scrolls of the Seasons show the Chinese influence of his travels most clearly in the Autumn scroll. Another work is Haboku Sansui, a splashed-ink scroll of 1495. His emphasis on Zen, personal interpretation and economical expression was the basis of his legacy for later Japanese artists, and many schools of art appointed him their founder.
seth: Set was the son of Geb, the Earth, and Nut, the Sky, and his siblings were Osiris, Isis and Nephthys; he married Nephthys. In art he is usually shown as an animal that Egyptologists call the Set animal, which has not been identified with any known species. It has a downward curving snout, long ears with squared-off ends and a thin, forked tail. Proposed identities include the Saluki, aardvark, hyena, donkey and giraffe. The earliest certain Set animal appears on a ceremonial macehead of Scorpion II, a ruler of the Naqada III phase. The meaning of his name is unknown.

Set was lord of the Red Land, the desert, balancing Horus as lord of the Black Land, the fertile land. In the Osiris myth he murders and mutilates his brother Osiris. Isis reassembles the body, and Osiris lives long enough to father Horus, who seeks revenge. The conflict appears as early as the Pyramid Texts, where the two gods are sometimes uncle and nephew and sometimes brothers. In the account called Contendings, the gods race in boats and fight as hippopotami before an assembly of deities, and the dispute lasts eighty years, largely because the judge favours Set. Horus loses an eye to Set, and the restored eye represents the return of the moon to full brightness and of kingship to Horus.

Set also stood on the prow of Ra's barge and helped overcome the serpent Apep. In the Second Intermediate Period (1650 to 1550 BCE) the Hyksos, who ruled the Nile Delta from Avaris, took him as patron, identifying him with their own god Hadad. After Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos, the cult at Avaris continued. Ramesses I came from a military family from Avaris with ties to Set's priesthood, and several Ramesside kings took names from the god, among them Seti I and Setnakht. Ramesses II set up the Year 400 Stela at Pi-Ramesses for the cult's 400th anniversary.

Egyptologist Herman te Velde holds that Set was demonised after foreign conquests in the Third Intermediate and Late Periods, when the god of foreigners became linked with the Kushite and Persian rulers. His murder of Osiris was emphasised and his defeat by Horus welcomed. The Greeks later associated him with Typhon. Even so, in outlying places such as Kharga and Dakhla he remained a chief deity, called Lord of the Oasis, and he was worshipped at Ombos, Oxyrhynchus and parts of the Faiyum. Today he is honoured in Kemetism, a revival of ancient Egyptian religion, and in the Temple of Set, founded in 1975.
setif: Sétif lies in north-eastern Algeria, about 270 kilometres east of Algiers and about 132 kilometres west of Constantine, in the Hautes Plaines region. It stands at an altitude of roughly 1,100 metres, which makes it the second-highest provincial capital in Algeria. The city sits between the Tellian Atlas to the north and the Aurès mountains to the south, on sedimentary rock of sandstones, marls and limestones.

Its streams, the Boussalem and El Kébir wadis, flow irregularly. The climate is continental with a strong Mediterranean influence, with warm dry summers and cold, very rainy winters. The name comes from the Latin Sitifis, which is drawn from a Berber word Zdif, meaning black lands, a reference to the fertility of the soil.

The city is of Numidian origin and was part of the kingdom of the Massaesyli in 225 BCE; it was small under the Numidian kings. Near Sétif the Numidian king Jugurtha campaigned and lost against Marius in 105 BCE. Under Rome it became the capital of Mauretania Sitifensis. The first Muslim expedition to Africa took place in 647, and by 700 the area had been conquered and converted to Islam. Little is known of the early Islamic town, but by the 10th century the area outside the fortress was again filled with houses, and over a dozen with large courtyards were excavated on the site of the Roman baths.

A column of the French colonial army took the city in 1838, as part of the operations against Constantine. At first the occupation was military, but civilians soon arrived. A first urban plan was set up by decree in 1843, a European city was laid out in 1846, and on 11 February 1847 a royal decree created it with an endowment of 2,509 hectares of land.

From 1850 it was a centre of colonial settlement, drawn by the farming potential of the region. The protests and massacre of 8 May 1945 began in the city and were a crucial factor in the start of the Algerian War. The municipality was created at the start of independence, on 5 July 1962.

Sétif is the capital of Sétif Province and is regarded as one of the most important trading and industrial cities of Algeria. Agriculture in the region rests on grain and livestock, and local wheat is turned into semolina, couscous and noodles. One of its main historical monuments is the Ain El Fouara fountain, a sculpture by the French sculptor Francis de Saint-Vidal that was brought to the city at the end of the 19th century and was classified as national heritage on 3 November 1999.
