The local cuisine includes the couscous dish Berboucha, and a music genre called Staifi, based on the zendali rhythm, is popular across the Maghreb.
setif-and-guelma-massacre: Anti-colonial movements in Algeria began to organise before World War II under Messali Hadj and Ferhat Abbas, and Algeria's part in the war hastened the rise of nationalism. Algiers was the capital of Free France from 1943, which raised hopes of independence. In 1943 Ferhat Abbas published a manifesto claiming a constitution and a state associated with France, and the lack of a French response led to the Amis du Manifeste et de la Liberté. Drought and famine in rural Constantine Province added to the tension. In April 1945 a senior French official proposed an armed settler militia at Guelma, where 4,000 settlers lived beside 16,500 Muslim Algerians.

On the morning of 8 May 1945 about 5,000 Muslims paraded in Sétif to celebrate the German surrender, some carrying banners attacking colonial rule. Gendarmes tried to seize the banners and clashes followed. It is uncertain who fired first, but both protesters and police were shot. Armed groups using farm tools, blades and hunting rifles then attacked settlers in the countryside at Kherrata and Chevreul, killing 102 people in all, including about 90 around Sétif and 12 near Guelma, until 12 May.

On instructions from Paris, the army, which included the Foreign Legion and Moroccan and Senegalese troops, carried out summary executions in rural communities. French aircraft bombed villages between 9 and 19 May, dropping 41 tons of bombs, and the cruiser Duguay-Trouin shelled Aokas. Settler vigilantes lynched prisoners. At Guelma the sous-préfet André Achiari set up a Comité de Salut Public that encouraged settler violence against nationalist activists, and attacks lasted until 26 June. Victims were buried in mass graves, and later officials had corpses dug up and burned.

Estimates of the Algerian dead vary widely. French authorities gave 1,020 in the Tubert report, historians range from 3,000 to 30,000, and the present Algerian government cites 45,000. The French administration arrested 4,560 Muslims, 99 of whom were sentenced to death, and twenty-two of the sentences were carried out. General Raymond Duval warned in a secret report that he had secured peace for ten years and that without reforms the events would recur in worse form. A general uprising began nine years later and Algeria became independent in March 1962 with the Évian Accords. The massacre was censored in France until 1960. In February 2005 the French ambassador Hubert Colin de Verdière called it an 'inexcusable tragedy'.
seton-lloyd: Seton Howard Frederick Lloyd was born on 30 May 1902 in Birmingham. He was educated at Uppingham School and studied at the Architectural Association in London, qualifying as an architect in 1926. He gained his first archaeological experience at Tel el Amarna, which Henri Frankfort was excavating for the Egypt Exploration Society, and in 1930 Frankfort invited him to join his next excavation, a series of sites in the Diyala valley dug from 1930 to 1937 under the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago.

From 1937 to 1939 Lloyd excavated with John Garstang at Mersin, in southern Turkey, for the University of Liverpool. In 1939 he was appointed Archaeological Adviser to the Directorate of Antiquities in Iraq, where he helped to establish the Iraq Museum and to reorganise the Gertrude Bell Museum. He trained Iraqi archaeologists and took part with Iraqi colleagues in several major excavations, notably at 'Uqair and Eridu, at Assyrian Khorsabad and at the Aqueduct of Sennacherib at Jerwan. He later succeeded Max Mallowan as President of the British School of Archaeology in Iraq.

In 1948 Lloyd became Director of the British Institute of Archaeology at Ankara. With James Mellaart, one of the first scholars at the Ankara school, he excavated the mound at Beycesultan in western Anatolia, and he also conducted excavations at Polatli, Haran, Sultantepe and other Anatolian sites. Michael Gough succeeded him as Director at Ankara. From 1962 to 1969 Lloyd was Professor of Western Asiatic Archaeology at the Institute of Archaeology of the University of London. He died at Faringdon on 7 January 1996.

Lloyd published excavation reports with his colleagues, among them Sennacherib's Aqueduct at Jerwan with Thorkild Jacobsen (1935), Pre-Sargonid Temples in the Diyala Region with Pinhas Delougaz (1942), the volumes on Beycesultan with Mellaart (1962-1965) and Private Houses and Graves in the Diyala Region (1967).

He also wrote general accounts of the ancient Near East for a wider readership: Ruined Cities of Iraq (1942), Twin Rivers: A Brief History of Iraq from the Earliest Times to the Present Day (1943), Foundations in the Dust: A Story of Mesopotamian Exploration (1947, revised in 1980), Early Anatolia (1956), Mounds of the Ancient Near East (1963), Early Highland Peoples of Anatolia (1967) and The Archaeology of Mesopotamia from the Old Stone Age to the Persian Conquest (1978). The Interval appeared in 1986 and Ancient Turkey: A Traveller's History of Anatolia in 1989.
setthathirath: Setthathirath was born on 24 January 1534, the son of King Photisarath of Lan Xang and Princess Yotkhamtip, daughter of King Ketklao of Lan Na. When Ketklao died without a male heir, the high officials and Buddhist monks of Lan Na agreed in 1546 to give the throne to the young prince, known there as Chao Upayo. He took the Emerald Buddha as his personal palladium. On his father's death his half-brothers Prince Tha Heua and Prince Lanchang began to divide Lan Xang, and he hurried home with the sacred images, leaving Chiang Mai under Queen Chiraprapha.

He subdued his rivals and pardoned Lanchang, but the nobles of Lan Na, feeling he had stayed away too long, chose the Shan prince Mekuti in 1551, and his attempts to retake the kingdom in 1553 and 1555 won back only Chiang Saen. In 1556 Bayinnaung of Burma took Chiang Mai. Setthathirath strengthened Vientiane's defences, built a great palace and renovated That Luang before formally making it the capital in 1560, a role it kept for some two hundred and fifty years; Wat Xieng Thong rose in Luang Prabang.

An alliance with Ayutthaya, to be sealed by his marriage to Princess Thepkasattri, failed when Maha Thammaracha seized her on the way to Lan Xang in 1564. When the Burmese took Vientiane, he harassed them with guerrilla raids until disease and hunger drove Bayinnaung back in 1565, leaving Lan Xang the only independent Tai kingdom. He joined an Ayutthayan rising in 1567, killing five pursuing Burmese generals in an ambush, but in 1569 was trapped near Phetchabun. After a second Burmese occupation of Vientiane, his counterattack in 1570 took more than 30,000 prisoners, 100 elephants and 2,300 pieces of ivory. He then campaigned against the Longvek Kingdom of the Khmer.

His heir, Noi Hno Muang Keo Koumane, was a toddler, and the boy's maternal grandfather Sen Soulintha declared himself king. Years of unsteady rule followed until Bayinnaung conquered the country in 1574 and took the child to Burma. The prince returned to be crowned in Vientiane in 1591. Setthathirath is counted among the great leaders of Lao history, and Wat Xieng Thong, the Haw Phra Kaew, Wat Ong Teu Mahawihan and Pha That Luang remain among his works.
setthathirath-ii: Setthathirath II, also written Jyesthadhiraj and called Triều Phúc in Vietnamese records, was the son of Prince Som Phou of the royal house of Lan Xang. When the nobles made Som Phou's younger brother Suliyavongsa king, Som Phou fled to Vietnam, and his son spent most of his early years in exile at Huế. Some references make Setthathirath a grandson of Suliyavongsa, but the timeline does not allow it. After Suliyavongsa's death the kingdom passed through years of turmoil: a noble named Tian Thala took the throne and was deposed within six months.

With the help of Vietnamese forces Setthathirath ousted King Nan Tharat and took Vientiane, the capital, and he declared himself king under the name Setthathirath II. He moved the Prabang Buddha, the sacred statue and symbol of royalty, from Luang Prabang to Vientiane. He then sent his brother to take Luang Prabang from his cousin Prince Kitsarat, a grandson of Suliyavongsa, who refused to recognise his authority. Kitsarat asked the Siamese king for help and was granted independence, founding the Kingdom of Luang Phrabang, while the realm left to Setthathirath became the Kingdom of Vientiane. In 1713 Prince Nokasat broke away in the south and, also with Siam's grant, formed the Kingdom of Champasak, dividing the Lao lands further.

Accounts of these years differ. Some sources claim that Ong Long was Setthathirath's son, or the same person; the History of Laos by Sila Viravong makes Ong Long a grandson of Suliyavongsa, deposed by Setthathirath's brother Chao Nantharath, whom Setthathirath then had killed.

Setthathirath II had three sons and a daughter. His son Bunya succeeded him as king of Vientiane, and another son, Guangnaya, was appointed viceroy in 1730. His daughter Kalyani married in 1699 King Suriyenthrathibodi of Ayudhya, son of King Phetracha.
setubal: Setúbal stands on the northern bank of the Sado estuary, about 50 km by road from central Lisbon, and belongs to the Lisbon metropolitan area. The Arrábida hills begin at its western beaches, and the Tróia peninsula lies across the river. In the time of Al-Andalus it was called Shaṭūbar in Andalusian Arabic, after the older pre-Roman name Caetobriga. English traders of the 17th century called the port Saint Ubes.

Remains of human occupation in the municipality date from the Neolithic onwards. Phoenicians, Greeks and Carthaginians came to Iberia in search of salt and tin, and in Roman times the settlement developed fish-salting factories and pottery kilns. No records survive for the period between the 6th and 12th centuries. After the Christians took Alcácer do Sal in 1217, Setúbal came under the Order of Santiago, which granted it a municipal charter in March 1249. In 1343 an agreement settled its territory against its neighbours Palmela and Alcácer do Sal, and a wall was built.

In the 15th century shipbuilding and maritime trade brought wealth, and in 1458 Afonso V sailed from its port to conquer Ksar es-Seghir. The Convent of Jesus, designed by Master Diogo Boitaca, was built in the late 15th and early 16th centuries. John III granted the title of notable town in 1525. In 1580 the town supported Dom António, Prior of Crato, against Philip II of Spain and was besieged by Spanish troops under the Duke of Alba; Philip later ordered the Fort of São Filipe, the work of Filippo Terzi. Salt made the 17th century the town's most prosperous age, and new walls were built after 1640. The earthquake of 1755 interrupted this prosperity.

The railway arrived in 1860, the year Pedro V made Setúbal a city, and sardine canning, oranges and muscatel wine made it known in the 19th century. It became the seat of a district in 1926 and of a diocese in 1975.

The municipality had 123,496 inhabitants at the census of 2021. Its main historical monument is the Monastery of Jesus, a church of the 15th and 16th centuries that is one of the first buildings in the Manueline style. The cathedral of Our Lady of Grace has a Mannerist façade, and the Fort of São Filipe overlooking the city is now a hotel. The port and its industries, among them paper, cement, fertilisers and shipbuilding, still tie the city to the sea.
seuthes-i: Seuthes was the son of Sparatocos (Sparadocus), the first Odrysian monarch known to have left coins, and a grandson of Teres I. Before his accession he was already described as Sitalces' highest official. In 429 BCE, as part of a peace settlement between his uncle and the king of Macedon, he married the sister of Perdiccas II, and the prospect of the marriage and its dowry is said to have led him to counsel Sitalces to withdraw from Macedon.

The contemporary Thucydides says only that Sitalces died during an unsuccessful campaign against the Triballi and was succeeded by his nephew. Some scholars have seen a conspiracy in this, pointing to the later charge of Philip II of Macedon that the Athenians, on Sitalces' death, at once allied with his murderer. Others suggest that the Odrysians followed the principle of tanistry, under which Seuthes, as son of Sitalces' apparently older brother, may have had a prior claim over Sitalces' sons.

As king, Seuthes raised the tribute due to his treasury. Perhaps because of his alliance with Perdiccas, who sided with Sparta, he did not support the Athenians in their contest with Sparta for Amphipolis in 425–423 BCE, nor against Perdiccas in 418–415 BCE. Whether this came from loyalty, prudent neutrality, a preference for peace or a weakening hold on subject peoples is unclear.

He appears to have died after 411 BCE, as Thucydides records neither his death nor a successor. Before the Battle of Aegospotami in 405 BCE the exiled Athenian commander Alcibiades boasted of his friendship with the Thracian kings Medocus and Seuthes; some scholars take this as a last reference to Seuthes I, others as one to Seuthes II, in which case Amadocus I had succeeded by 405. Seuthes I is thought the probable father of the later kings Hebryzelmis and Cotys I, though Cotys is often given as a son of Seuthes II.
seuthes-ii: Seuthes II was the son of Maesades and a descendant of Teres I. Maesades had ruled as a paradynast, a subordinate regional ruler, over the Melanditi, Thyni and Tranipsi of southeastern Thrace west of Byzantium, but was expelled in unclear circumstances. The young Seuthes became the ward of Medocus, also called Amadocus I, who later restored him to part of his father's lands, including Bisanthe, while other parts stayed with another paradynast, Teres II. Both were ruling by 405 BCE, when the exiled Athenian commander Alcibiades boasted of his friendship with them.

Xenophon describes Seuthes as the subordinate of Amadocus I, and most scholars hold that he was a paradynast and later a claimant to the kingship, never the supreme king of the Odrysian state. With the mercenaries he hired, remnants of the army that had followed Cyrus the Younger into Persia, he waged a brief campaign that removed local opposition to his rule in eastern Thrace, and he offered Xenophon a daughter in marriage. The mercenaries then passed into Spartan service in Asia Minor, and Seuthes sent the Spartan commander Dercylidas 200 horsemen and 300 peltasts for Bithynia.

As Spartan fortunes declined, Seuthes turned to an alliance with Athens and Persia by 394 BCE. By 391 BCE he had attacked his overlord, and the Athenian general Thrasybulus reconciled the two and renewed their alliance with Athens in 390/389 BCE; Seuthes possibly offered him a daughter as well. He may have quarrelled again with Amadocus II or Hebryzelmis and was rescued from unnamed foes by the Athenian commander Iphicrates. He is last mentioned in 387 BCE among the allies of Athens at the King's Peace. He is often named as the father of Cotys I, but that king's parentage is unclear.
seuthes-iii: After the campaigns of Philip II of Macedon in 347–342 BCE, a large part of Thrace became subject to Macedon, which governed it through military governors such as Memnon and Zopyrion. Some Thracian tribes revolted against Alexander the Great after Philip's death in 336 BCE, while other Thracians sent troops to his army. The origins of Seuthes III are unclear. Scholars have proposed that he was a son or a brother of Cersobleptes, a descendant of the earlier king Seuthes I, or a son or near kinsman of Teres III, which would place him in a junior line of the Odrysian royal dynasty.

Seuthes revolted against Macedon in about 325 BCE, after Zopyrion was killed in battle against the Getae. After Alexander died in 323 BCE he opposed the new governor Lysimachus, and in 322 BCE he mustered some 8,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry; the two sides fought to a draw and withdrew. He came to acknowledge the authority of Lysimachus, and perhaps around 320 BCE he established his residence at Seuthopolis, which he built and named after himself in imitation of Philip and Alexander.

In 313 BCE Seuthes supported the revolt of Callatis against Lysimachus, allying with other towns and tribes and occupying the passes of Mount Haemus. Lysimachus defeated the allies but had to abandon the siege of Callatis to meet Pausanias, a commander sent by Antigonus I. Seuthes seems to have kept his autonomy and made peace. An inscription from Seuthopolis names his wife Berenice, apparently a Macedonian, and their sons Hebryzelmis, Teres, Satocus and Sadalas. He ruled only part of Thrace, sharing it with Lysimachus and other Thracian rulers, and his succession is unknown.

His tomb, a mound 1 km south of the town of Shipka, was discovered in 2004 by the Bulgarian archaeologist Georgi Kitov. It has a corridor, an anteroom, a round chamber with a high tholos ceiling and a rectangular chamber made from two monolith blocks, one weighing more than 60 tons. A two-winged marble door bearing images of the god Dionysus closes the round chamber. The finds include a golden wreath, a golden kylix, greaves and a helmet, now in the historical museum of Kazanlăk.

The name of Seuthes is written on two silver vessels and on the helmet. After the burial the ruler's horse was sacrificed and the corridor was ritually set on fire. The tomb belongs to the Valley of the Thracian Kings, which also includes the Kazanlăk Tomb, which is recognised as part of the UNESCO world heritage.
seuthopolis: Seuthopolis was a Hellenistic city near Kazanlak, in Stara Zagora Province, founded by the Thracian king Seuthes III as the capital of the Odrysian kingdom. Several kilometres to the north lies the Valley of the Thracian Rulers, where many Thracian royal tombs are found. The city's cemetery included brick tholos tombs, some under tumuli, in which members of the upper class were buried, sometimes with their horses, while the less affluent were cremated with modest grave goods.

Seuthopolis was not a true polis but the seat of Seuthes and his court, and most of the space inside the walls held official buildings rather than homes; most people lived outside. Its population was both Thracian and Greek. The palace was also a sanctuary of the Cabeiri, the gods of Samothrace, which suggests that Seuthes was a priest-king, the high priest of the Cabeiri among the Odrysian Thracians. A sanctuary of Dionysius or Sabazios stood on the square. The Great Inscription, found in the palace-citadel in 1953, is written in Greek, showing that the Thracians were already hellenised in the 3rd century BCE. Celts sacked the city in 281 BCE.

Bulgarian archaeologists discovered the ruins in 1948 while the Georgi Dimitrov Reservoir, later renamed Koprinka, was being built, and the government gave them six years to study and preserve what they could before the valley was flooded. The ruins now lie at the bottom of the reservoir. In 2005 the architect Zheko Tilev proposed surrounding them with a round wall 420 metres across so that the city could be uncovered and visited. Sevtopolis Peak on Greenwich Island in the South Shetland Islands is named after the city.
sevastopol: Sevastopol lies at the south-western tip of the Crimean Peninsula, on the Heracles Peninsula, on the coast of the Black Sea. Much of the city is gathered around the long Bay of Sevastopol, and its navigable harbours made it an important port and naval base throughout its history. Its name joins the Greek sebastós, venerable, and pólis, city, and probably honours Empress Catherine II, who founded it. In the west of the city stand the well-preserved ruins of the ancient Greek port of Chersonesos, founded in the 5th century BCE by settlers from Heraclea Pontica.

Sevastopol was founded in June 1783, in the area of the ruined Greek city of Chersonesus, as a base for a naval squadron under the name Akhtiar, White Cliff, by Rear Admiral Thomas MacKenzie, a Scot in Russian service. In February 1784 Catherine the Great ordered Grigory Potyomkin to build a fortress and call it Sevastopol, and Captain Fyodor Ushakov, commander of the port from 1788, carried out the plans. The name Sevastopol was restored on 29 April (10 May) 1826.

In the Crimean War the allies chose Sevastopol as Russia's main Black Sea naval base. They landed in September 1854 and settled into a siege marked by brutal conditions on both sides. The city fell after eleven months, and the Treaty of Paris of 30 March 1856 forbade Russia to base warships in the Black Sea. In the Second World War it withstood intensive German bombardment in 1941-42, in which the Germans used the 80-cm railway gun Schwerer Gustav, and after 250 days of fierce fighting fell to Axis forces in July 1942. The Red Army liberated it on 9 May 1944.

In the Soviet era it was a closed city. In 1954 Sevastopol and the rest of Crimea were transferred from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR. Russia annexed Crimea, with Sevastopol, in March 2014; the annexation is not recognised internationally.

Sevastopol is the largest city of Crimea and a major Black Sea port, with a population mostly of ethnic Russians and a substantial minority of Ukrainians. Because of its military history most of its streets are named after Russian and Soviet military heroes, and hundreds of monuments and plaques recall its military past.
seven-branched-sword: The sword is 74.9 cm long, with a blade of 65.5 cm and a tang of 9.4 cm that has no hole for fixing a hilt; it is broken at the top of the tang. Research by Tsutomu Suzuki and replicas made by the swordsmith Kunihira Kawachi indicate that it was cast rather than forged. The branches are too delicate for combat, so the sword probably had a ceremonial use. Its design, with the tip counted as the seventh branch, recalls Korean tree motifs such as those of the Paekche and Silla crowns. The Nihon Shoki tells of a seven-branched sword brought to Empress Jingū with a seven-little-one mirror.

A gold-inlaid inscription runs along both sides. The first side records that the sword was made of 100 times hardened steel on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of the fourth year of an era whose name is partly illegible, and that it repels 100 enemy soldiers. The second side says that no such blade had existed before and that it was made in Paekche for the King of Wa, to be handed down to later generations. Some scholars read three characters as crown prince, identifying the giver with the future King Geungusu, but the reading is uncertain.

The inscription, hidden by rust, was rediscovered in the 1870s by Masatomo Kan, a Shinto priest of Isonokami Shrine. X-ray pictures were published in 1996, and CT scans have since shown the name Paekche clearly. The traditional date rests on reading the era as Taihe of the Eastern Jin, but that name was written with a different character, and Hong Sung-Hwa argues from the calendar for 408. Scholars also dispute the relationship it shows: Kim Sok Hyong reads it as treating the Wa king as a vassal, most Japanese scholars take the term as an honorific, and Kōsaku Hamada proposes a Jin original copied for Wa.
seven-sages-of-greece: The Seven Sages, or Seven Wise Men, were an honorary title given to seven philosophers, statesmen and lawgivers of the 7th and 6th centuries BCE who were especially noted for their wisdom. The oldest explicit mention of a standard list of seven is in Plato's Protagoras. There Socrates names Thales of Miletus, Pittacus of Mytilene, Bias of Priene, Solon of Athens, Cleobulus of Lindos, Myson of Chenae and Chilon of Sparta. He says they emulated Spartan education and made the brief remarks Know thyself and Nothing too much their joint first fruits of wisdom to Apollo at Delphi. The passage is elaborately ironical, so it is unclear which parts are meant seriously.

Diogenes Laertius reports that seven men were held in high esteem for wisdom well before Plato. According to Demetrius Phalereus, they first became known as the wise men in the archonship of Damasias, 582/81 BCE, with Thales the first so acknowledged.

The members were various. Thales is the first well-known Greek philosopher, mathematician and astronomer. Pittacus governed Mytilene on Lesbos with the support of the common people. Solon framed laws that shaped Athenian democracy. Cleobulus was tyrant of Lindos, and Chilon was a Spartan politician credited with the militarisation of Spartan society.

Diogenes Laertius points out that his sources disagreed greatly about who belonged. Periander of Corinth or Anacharsis the Scythian was often put in the place of Myson. Plutarch says some counted Epimenides the seventh if they would not admit Periander. Dicaearchus gave ten names, Hippobotus twelve and Hermippus seventeen, from which people chose seven. Aesop was also a popular contender.

Later tradition ascribed a pithy saying to each sage, though ancient and modern scholars have doubted this. A collection of 147 maxims inscribed at Delphi was preserved by Stobaeus as Sayings of the Seven Sages, but they were most likely popular proverbs later attributed to individuals. Stories told of a golden tripod, or a bowl or cup, to be given to the wisest, which passed from sage to sage until Thales or Solon, depending on the version, dedicated it to Apollo. Diogenes Laertius also records that the maxims were thought sceptical and the sages precursors of Pyrrho's scepticism, and that Dicaearchus held the seven to be merely shrewd men who had studied legislation.
seven-sages-of-the-bamboo-grove: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, also called the Seven Worthies, were a group of Chinese scholars, writers and musicians of the third century CE. They were Ji Kang, Liu Ling, Ruan Ji, Ruan Xian, Xiang Xiu, Wang Rong and Shan Tao. Although each of them existed, their interconnection is not entirely certain. Several were linked with the Qingtan school of Daoism as it existed in the state of Cao Wei. As traditionally depicted, the group wished to escape the intrigues, corruption and stifling atmosphere of court life during the politically fraught Three Kingdoms period, and gathered in a bamboo grove near Ji Kang's house in Shanyang, now in Henan province.

The sages found their lives in danger when the avowedly Confucian Jin dynasty of the Sima clan came to power. Some of them wrote poems criticising the court and the administration, and wrote literature influenced by Daoism. They did not all hold similar views. Some negotiated the difficult political situation by adopting the roles of alcohol-fuelled pranksters and eccentrics who avoided government control, as Liu Ling did, while others ended by joining the Jin dynasty, as Wang Rong did. Ji Kang's refusal to work for the new regime of Sima Zhao eventually led to his execution.

In the grove, as tradition has it, they enjoyed and praised in their works a simple rustic life, and they stressed alcoholic drink, cold-food powder, personal freedom, spontaneity and the celebration of nature. Ji Kang was especially close to Ruan Ji, whose bond was described as stronger than metal and fragrant as orchids.

Whether or not they took part in witty conversation or debates, the sages themselves became subjects of it in A New Account of the Tales of the World. Their rural life became a common theme in art, and they inspired other artists who wished to retreat during times of political upheaval. Rong Qiqi, who lived much earlier, is associated with them in some apocryphal art from the fourth century CE, in a tomb near Nanjing. The sages, or the symbol they became, have been remarked on as influential in Chinese poetry, music, art and culture generally.
seven-wonders-of-the-ancient-world: After the conquests of Alexander the Great in the 4th century BCE, Hellenistic travellers gained access to the civilizations of the Egyptians, Persians and Babylonians, and began to list the landmarks that impressed them. The ancient Greeks spoke not of wonders but of theamata, meaning sights or things to be seen, so the list was the ancient counterpart of a travel guidebook. Later the word for wonder, thaumata, was used instead.

The first known list of seven dates to the 2nd to 1st century BCE, and at least eight full lists and ten partial lists are known. Diodorus Siculus mentioned only the Walls of Babylon and the Pyramids. The epigrammist Antipater of Sidon, who lived around or before 100 BCE, listed six of the present wonders and put the walls of Babylon where the Lighthouse of Alexandria now stands. Lists by Herodotus and by the poet Callimachus of Cyrene survive only as references.

The seven names now generally given are the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, the Statue of Zeus at Olympia, the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, the Colossus of Rhodes and the Lighthouse of Alexandria. This canonical list was first established in the 1572 publication Octo Mundi Miracula from a combination of historical sources. Two wonders stood in Greece, two in Turkey, two in Egypt and one in Iraq. Five of the seven celebrate Greek construction; the exceptions are the pyramids and the Hanging Gardens.

Only the Great Pyramid survives, and it lost its white stone facing around 1300 when local communities removed it for building. The Colossus, finished after 280 BCE, fell to an earthquake in 226 or 225 BCE, so all seven stood together for less than sixty years. The Temple of Artemis and the statue of Zeus were destroyed by fire, and the Lighthouse and the tomb of Mausolus by earthquakes.

Sculptures from the tomb and the temple are in the British Museum. Scholars debate the nature of the Hanging Gardens and whether they existed. Later lists added Roman and Christian sites, and Gregory of Tours named the Temple of Solomon and Noah's Ark. Wilhelm Heinrich Roscher found 22 distinct places across 18 classical lists in 1906.
seven-years-war: In North America the boundary between British and French possessions was largely unsettled in the 1750s. France claimed the entire Mississippi River basin, which Britain disputed, and in the early 1750s the French began building a chain of forts in the Ohio River Valley. British settlers resented French troops near their western borders and wanted the fertile Ohio land for newcomers. In Europe, Frederick II of Prussia had seized the province of Silesia from Austria in the War of the Austrian Succession. Empress Maria Theresa signed the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 to gain time to rebuild her forces and find new allies.

The result was a strategic realignment known as the Diplomatic Revolution, which ended the long rivalry between Austria and France. The two powers signed the Treaty of Versailles in 1756, and a second agreement in 1757 brought Prussia into the war on the side of Britain. Britain's allies included Hanover and several small German states, which together supplied nearly 50,000 troops.

In 1756 the French attacked Menorca, and a British relief attempt failed at the Battle of Menorca; Admiral Byng was court-martialled and executed. In 1757 Frederick marched into Bohemia and won the Battle of Prague on 6 May, but then suffered his first defeat at Kolín and withdrew from Bohemia. In 1759 he lost half his army at Kunersdorf, the worst defeat of his career, which drove him to the brink of abdication. William Pitt the Elder, head of the British government from 1756 to 1761, committed Britain to seizing the French Empire, especially in North America and India, using the Royal Navy and subsidies to European allies that tied down the French army.

Outside Europe, Robert Clive recaptured Calcutta in India and ousted the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, a French ally, at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. In 1758 the British took the French settlement at Saint-Louis in Senegal. Spain became a French ally in 1762, invaded Portugal unsuccessfully and lost Havana and Manila to Britain. In 1762 Russia withdrew after the death of Peter III, and when Catherine II took power she ended the alliance with Prussia. By 1763 the war in central Europe was essentially a stalemate between Prussia and Austria.

The Treaty of Hubertusburg, signed in 1763, confirmed Prussian occupation of Silesia and Prussia's status as a great power, challenging Austria for dominance within Germany. The Treaty of Paris, also of 1763, ended the hostilities between Britain and France. France ceded Louisiana to Spain and the rest of New France to Britain, and Britain returned the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon to assist French fishing rights. Havana and Manila were returned to Spain. France lost its possessions in North America, and Britain established its commercial dominance in India.
seventh-crusade: The Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Ayyubid dynasty were both weakened by internal strife in the years after the Barons' Crusade. On 17 and 18 October 1244 a Crusader army and a Damascene army met the Egyptian and Khwarezmian armies at Hirbiya, the Battle of La Forbie or Gaza. About 5,000 Crusaders died and 800 were taken prisoner, and Jerusalem had already been lost. At the end of 1244 Louis IX of France fell gravely ill with malaria and vowed to go on crusade if he recovered. He took the cross from William of Auvergne, bishop of Paris, without papal authorisation. Pope Innocent IV, in exile at Lyons, directed a new crusade under Louis at the First Council of Lyon in 1245.

The preparations took three years. The costs came to over 1.5 million livres tournois, six times his annual revenues, partly raised by taxing towns and by expelling Jewish moneylenders from the kingdom and confiscating their property. The crusade formally began on 12 August 1248, when Louis left Paris. He reached Cyprus on 17 September 1248, where disease killed many men during the long wait, and the army landed at Damietta the following year.

The Frankish army set out for Mansurah on 20 November 1249. After weeks facing the Egyptians across a canal, the Crusaders crossed a ford on 8 February 1250. Robert I of Artois attacked the Egyptian camp against orders, and the attack on Mansurah ended in an Ayyubid victory on 11 February 1250. During the retreat Louis and most of his army were captured. The sultan estimated his prisoners at 30,000, certainly an exaggeration, and the infirm were executed. Louis ransomed himself by surrendering Damietta and his army by a payment of a million bezants, later reduced to 800,000.

Louis sailed to Acre and decided on 3 July 1250 to stay, remaining four years as de facto ruler of the kingdom. He resolved the succession crisis at Antioch, negotiated with the Assassins and sent William of Rubruck to the Mongol prince Sartaq, but no alliance followed. A popular Shepherds' Crusade in 1251 set out to rescue him and ended in disaster. After his mother's death on 27 November 1252 and unrest in France, he sailed from Acre on 24 April 1254 and landed at Hyères in July.

The crusade cost the Kingdom of Jerusalem a manpower it never recovered. Jean de Joinville's Life of Saint Louis is the most detailed personal account of any crusade. Troubadours such as Austorc d'Aorlhac wrote poems on the defeat.
seventh-day-adventist-church: The church is the largest of several Adventist groups that arose from the Millerite movement of the 1840s in upstate New York, a phase of the Second Great Awakening. William Miller predicted from Daniel 8:14 to 16 and the day-year principle that Jesus Christ would return between the spring of 1843 and the spring of 1844. His followers came to expect the return on 22 October 1844, and the failure of the prediction became known as the Great Disappointment.

As the early Adventists consolidated their beliefs, the question of the day of rest arose. Its foremost advocate was Joseph Bates, who had learned of the Sabbath doctrine from a tract by the Millerite preacher Thomas M. Preble. The periodical The Present Truth took up the subject in July 1849. For about twenty years the movement was a small, loosely knit group, whose leading figures were Joseph Bates, James White and Ellen G. White. Ellen White's visions and leadership convinced her fellow Adventists that she had the gift of prophecy.

The church first published its beliefs at Battle Creek, Michigan, in 1872 in a brief statement, "A Synopsis of Our Faith". Conservative evangelicals at first regarded it as a cult. Adventist scholars credit the writings of Ellen White with moving it towards Trinitarian theology, which the church adopted early in the 20th century. It then began dialogue with other Protestants and gained wide recognition as a Protestant church.

Members keep Saturday as the Sabbath, preparing on Friday and attending worship the next day, which begins with Sabbath School, a structured period of small-group Bible study. The church advocates a vegetarian diet and the avoidance of pork, shellfish and other foods held unclean in Leviticus 11, and it discourages alcohol and tobacco. It is governed by a General Conference through unions, local conferences and local churches, a representative system resembling Presbyterian church government.

Adventist mission work began in the late 19th century. Until J. N. Andrews was sent to Switzerland in 1874, global efforts had consisted entirely of posting tracts. The church has a presence in over 200 countries and territories, and much of its membership lives outside the United States, in Africa, Asia and Latin America. It runs more than 7,500 schools, colleges and universities and a network of hospitals, clinics and sanitariums. The Adventist Development and Relief Agency provides non-sectarian relief.
severan-dynasty: The dynasty is sometimes called the Septimian dynasty. Lucius Septimius Severus was born in Leptis Magna, in the province of Africa Proconsularis, into an equestrian family of Libyan-Punic and Italic origin, and rose through military service to consular rank. In 187 he married the Syrian Arab noblewoman Julia Domna, and they had two sons, Caracalla and Geta. His legionaries proclaimed him emperor in 193 in Noricum, in the unrest after the death of Commodus. He secured sole rule in early 197 by defeating Clodius Albinus at the Battle of Lugdunum.

Severus fought the Parthians in late 197 and campaigned in Britain between 208 and 210, rebuilding Hadrian's Wall. His relations with the Senate were poor, but he was popular with the commoners and the soldiers, whose pay he raised. He died of natural causes in early 211 in Britain. His sons were hostile to each other, and Caracalla had Geta murdered in their mother's apartments in 211. Caracalla bestowed Roman citizenship on all non-slaves in the empire, for reasons that are not entirely clear, and the Baths of Caracalla in Rome are the most lasting monument of his rule. He was killed near Carrhae in April 217 on the order of the praetorian prefect Macrinus.

Macrinus, the first emperor not of senatorial family, ruled briefly with his son Diadumenian. In May 218 troops near Elesa hailed Julia Domna's grandnephew Elagabalus, who defeated him near Antioch. Elagabalus, a priest of the Syrian sun god Elagabal, was emperor at about the age of 14. Inscriptions and coins confirm that he replaced Jupiter with Elagabal in late 220 and married a Vestal Virgin. He was murdered in 222, and his cousin Severus Alexander was hailed emperor.

The dynasty's women, Julia Domna and her sister Julia Maesa, and Maesa's daughters Julia Soaemias and Julia Mamaea, were powerful augustae who helped win the throne for their male relatives. Severus Alexander ruled from the age of 14 under the influence of his mother. In 231 he led an expedition against Parthia and kept control of Mesopotamia against the rising Sasanian Empire. His own troops murdered him and his mother in early 235 in Germany, and he was deified in 238.

His death began the Crisis of the Third Century. Maximinus Thrax, the first of a series of weak emperors, succeeded him, and the series ended some fifty years later with the Tetrarchy under Diocletian.
severia: Severia is a historical region of south-western Russia, northern Ukraine and eastern Belarus, its largest part lying in modern Russia and its central part around the city of Chernihiv in Ukraine. It took its name from the Severians, an East Slavic tribe of the late first millennium whose name means Northerners. Their main settlements included Kursk, Rylsk, Starodub, Trubchevsk, Sevsk, Bryansk and Belgorod in modern Russia, and Liubech, Novhorod-Siverskyi, Chernihiv, Putyvl and Hlukhiv in modern Ukraine.

According to the Primary Chronicle the Severians paid tribute to the Khazars. Prince Oleg of Novgorod (reigned 879–912) conquered them and added their lands to the new principality of Kievan Rus'. By the time of Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054) they had lost most of their distinctness, and the upper Desna came under Chernihiv. In 1096 Oleg I of Chernigov created a large Severian Principality, reaching the upper Oka, which served until the end of the century as a buffer against Cuman attacks. Its ruler Prince Igor is the subject of in the 12th-century epic The Tale of Igor's Campaign.

After the Mongol invasion the principality was largely ruined, though it survived repeated Tatar invasions, and little is recorded of it in the 13th century. By the mid-14th century it was an appanage duchy of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, whose Gediminid princes, Ruthenian-speaking and Orthodox, made their capitals at Novhorod-Siverskyi, Starodub and Trubchevsk. After the Lithuanian defeat at the Battle of Vedrosha the principality passed to Muscovy. Prince Vasiliy Shemiachich held it for Moscow until he was imprisoned there in 1523, after which Muscovite voivodes governed it. In the 18th century the Hetmans of the Ukrainian Cossacks resided at Baturyn, Hlukhiv and Pochep, and Hlukhiv grew into a capital of 18th-century Ukraine.

After the October Revolution the Severian lands, populated by a mixture of Ukrainians and Russians, were divided between the Ukrainian and Russian Soviet republics. A distinctive Severian style of icon painting formed from the 16th and 17th centuries, marked by restraint and asceticism under conservative Byzantine influence, and a collection of such icons is kept in the Museum of Ukrainian home icons in Radomysl Castle.
severus-alexander: Severus Alexander was born on 1 October 208 at Arca Caesarea in Phoenicia. He and his cousin Elagabalus were grandsons of Julia Maesa, the sister of the empress Julia Domna. When Elagabalus became unpopular, Maesa had him adopt the young Alexander and arranged his murder. The army hailed Alexander as emperor on 13 March 222 and the Senate ratified the acclamation the next day. At about 13 he was the youngest sole emperor of the united empire, and he relied on the guidance of Maesa, until her death in 224, and of his mother Julia Mamaea.

Under Mamaea's influence the court's extravagance was reduced and jurists such as Ulpian were employed to oversee justice. Alexander restored the Baths of Nero and built the Nymphaeum of Alexander at the end of the Aqua Claudia. He lightened taxes, set up loan offices that lent at moderate interest, and confirmed the rights of soldiers to make wills and to keep property gained in service. Military discipline nevertheless broke down: in 228 the Praetorian Guard murdered its prefect Ulpian in the emperor's presence, and soldiers fought the people of Rome for three days.

In 231 Ardashir I of the Sassanid Empire invaded the eastern provinces. In 233 Alexander launched a threefold invasion from Antioch. The northern army had some success, but the southern army was destroyed by Ardashir's horse-archers, and Alexander retreated after an indecisive campaign, though Mesopotamia was retaken. He held a triumph at Rome in 233. In 234 Germanic tribes crossed the Rhine and Danube, and he went north, hoping to win time by buying them off on the advice of his mother.

Many soldiers saw the bribery as dishonourable, and the legions turned to Maximinus Thrax, a Thracian soldier with a high reputation. In early March 235 the Legio XXII Primigenia mutinied at Moguntiacum, the modern Mainz, and killed Alexander and his mother during a meeting. Ancient accounts differ about the details. Maximinus succeeded him. Alexander was deified after the death of Maximinus in 238.

His death ended the Severan dynasty and was the first overthrow of an emperor by military discontent on a wide scale. His economic policies were discarded and the currency was devalued. Historians treat it as the opening of the Crisis of the Third Century, which brought nearly fifty years of civil war, foreign invasion and the collapse of the monetary economy.
seville: Seville lies on the lower reaches of the River Guadalquivir in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula, in a fertile valley, at an average height of 7 metres above sea level. Its port, about 80 kilometres from the Atlantic, is the only river harbour in Spain. The summers are very hot and dry.

The city is about 2,200 years old. The original core dates to the 8th century BCE, when the site was on an island in the Guadalquivir, and the Phoenicians and the Tartessians called it Hisbaal. It was founded as the Roman city of Hispalis, and after the Islamic conquest of 711 was called Ishbiliyah. It was the seat of the Wali of Al-Andalus until 716, when the capital moved to Córdoba. After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in the early 11th century it became the centre of the independent Taifa of Seville, and it was later ruled by the Almoravids and the Almohads, who built its main mosque in the 12th century. It was incorporated into the Crown of Castile in 1248.

Following the voyages of Columbus, Seville was chosen in 1503 as the headquarters of the Casa de Contratación, which made it the gateway to the Indies, though ships had to sail about 80 kilometres up the Guadalquivir to reach it. In the 16th century it was one of the largest cities in Western Europe. Worsening drought in the river gradually moved the trade away to the Bay of Cádiz, which received the fleets of the Indies in 1680 and the Casa de Contratación in 1717.

Seville is the capital of Andalusia and of the province of Seville. Its old town contains a UNESCO World Heritage Site made up of three buildings: the Alcázar, the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies. Its motto, NO8DO, is popularly read as a rebus for the Spanish No me ha dejado, She has not abandoned me.
sewing-needle: A sewing needle for hand-sewing is a long slender tool with a point at one end and an eye to hold the thread. The earliest were made of bone or wood, and modern ones are made of high-carbon steel wire, plated with nickel or gold against corrosion. Needles have come in many kinds for their uses: sharps for general sewing, embroidery needles with longer eyes, quilting needles, tapestry needles with blunt tips for loose weaves, leather needles with a triangular point, and long upholstery needles that may be straight or curved. Sizes are not standardised, and within a class a higher number means a shorter, thinner needle.

The first sewing was probably the tying together of animal skins, with shards of bone as needles and sinew or plant material as thread. The early limit was making an eye small enough not to damage the material. Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000 to 70,000 years ago, and a point that may come from a bone needle, found in Sibudu Cave, to 61,000 years ago.

Later needles are better dated. A bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia belongs to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Ivory needles about 30,000 years old come from Kostenki in Russia, and 8,600-year-old needles from Ekşi Höyük in western Anatolia. Flinders Petrie found copper needles at Naqada in Egypt from 4400 to 3000 BCE, and iron needles from the third century BCE were found at the oppidum of Manching. Needles apply the wire-making technology that appeared in the second millennium BCE.

Native Americans used needles from natural sources. The agave leaf, soaked until only long fibres and a sharp tip remained, gave both needle and thread. Steel-making from China reached Spain in the tenth century in the form of the Catalan furnace and later Germany and France. England began making needles in 1639 at Redditch, with the drawn-wire technique still in common use, and about 1655 a Guild of Needlemakers was established in London. In Japan the Festival of Broken Needles, Hari-Kuyo, dates back to the 1600s.
sexagesimal: According to Otto Neugebauer, the origins of sexagesimal are not as simple, consistent or singular in time as they are often portrayed. Throughout its centuries of use, sexagesimal notation has always contained a strong undercurrent of decimal notation, and it has always been applied inconsistently, even within a single text. The strongest driver of a fully consistent use was its advantage for writing and calculating fractions, which is why it appears most uniformly in mathematical tables.

The number 60 has twelve divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30 and 60. With so many factors, many fractions simplify. An hour divides evenly into sections of 30, 20, 15, 12, 10, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1 minutes, and 60 is the smallest number divisible by every number from 1 to 6. Any fraction whose denominator has only 2, 3 and 5 as prime factors can be written exactly, so that one third is 0;20 and one eighth is 0;7,30.

In Mesopotamia the system was not a pure base-60 system with sixty distinct digit symbols. Cuneiform digits used ten as a sub-base: narrow wedges for units up to nine and wide wedges for up to five tens. Numbers above 59 were written in blocks in place value notation. With no symbol for zero, the signs for 1 and 60 were identical and a value sometimes had to be judged from context. Later Babylonian texts used a placeholder for zero, but only in the middle of a number, not at its right-hand end.

The Old Babylonian Period (1900–1650 BCE) approximated the square root of 2 in sexagesimal. Ptolemy's Almagest, written in the 2nd century CE, expressed fractions in base 60, and its table of chords was the only extensive trigonometric table for more than a millennium. Al-Biruni first divided the hour into minutes, seconds, thirds and fourths in 1000, and the Parisian version of the Alfonsine tables of about 1320 recorded fractions of a day in base 60. European astronomers still used it for calculation as late as 1671; Jost Bürgi, in a work presented to Emperor Rudolf II in 1592, used sexagesimal multiplication tables to calculate sines.

The system survives in a modified form in the 60 minutes of an hour, the 60 seconds of a minute, the 360 degrees of a circle and in geographic coordinates. The modern signs for degrees, minutes and seconds descend from the notation John Wallis generalized in the 17th century.
sextus-julius-frontinus: No honorary or funerary inscription survives for Frontinus, so there is no outline of his life, and the names of his parents and his wife are unknown. Some details can be inferred from chance mentions. He is thought to have been of Narbonese origin and originally of the equestrian class. The name of Publius Calvisius Ruso Julius Frontinus, consul about 84, suggests that Frontinus had a sister who was that man's mother. He had at least one daughter, who married Quintus Sosius Senecio and was the mother of Sosia Polla.

In 70 CE Frontinus took part in the suppression of the Rhineland revolt, and he later recorded that he received the surrender of 70,000 Lingones. He was appointed suffect consul before being sent to Britain to succeed Quintus Petillius Cerialis as governor. There he subjugated the Silures of South Wales and is thought to have campaigned against the Brigantes as well. His successor was Gnaeus Julius Agricola, the father-in-law of the historian Tacitus. An inscription at Hieropolis in Phrygia and coins of Smyrna attest that he was proconsul of Asia in 86.

In 97 the emperor Nerva appointed him curator aquarum, supervisor of the aqueducts, an office given only to men of very high standing. The next year he held a second consulship as suffect, with Trajan as his colleague, and two years later he was consul ordinarius with Trajan, an honour that the historian Birley takes as a sign of the high regard in which he was held. He was also a member of the College of Augurs, and Pliny the Younger wrote that he was elected to fill the vacancy Frontinus' death had created.

His chief work, De aquaeductu, is an official report to the emperor in two books. It gives the history, sizes and discharge rates of the nine aqueducts of Rome in his day and sets out the laws governing their use and maintenance. As water commissioner he first had maps of the system prepared in order to judge its condition. He found that many channels were neglected and was concerned by farmers and tradesmen who tapped the supply with pipes; lead pipe stamps bearing the owner's name were used against such theft. He also separated the waters of different systems rather than mixing them, and warned that tree roots could damage the masonry.

He also wrote a treatise on military science, which is lost. His surviving military work, the Stratagems, collects examples of stratagems from Greek and Roman history for the use of generals. It draws on his own experience as a general in Germania under Domitian, though similarities with Valerius Maximus and Livy suggest he relied mainly on literary sources. The authenticity of its fourth book has been challenged.
sextus-pompey: Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius was the son of Pompey by his third wife, Mucia Tertia, with an elder brother, Gnaeus Pompeius, and a sister, Pompeia. When Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BCE, Gnaeus followed their father to the East while Sextus stayed in Rome in the care of his stepmother, Cornelia Metella. After the defeat at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE the two met Pompey on Lesbos and fled with him to Egypt, where Sextus watched his father killed by treachery on 29 September of that year.

He then joined the resistance to Caesar in the African provinces alongside Metellus Scipio, Cato the Younger and his brother. Caesar defeated the Pompeius brothers at the Battle of Munda in Hispania in 45 BCE. Gnaeus died soon afterwards in a last stand at Lauro; Sextus escaped and raised another army in Spain.

After Caesar's death Mark Antony moved that Sextus be recalled, paid 50 million Attic drachmas for his father's confiscated property and given command of the whole Roman navy. He accepted, but went no further than Massilia before returning to Sicily. When the Second Triumvirate began its proscriptions, many of the proscribed fled to him, and after the battles of Philippi in 42 BCE survivors of the party of Brutus and Cassius did the same. With the whole island as his base he built an army and a strong navy.

In 40 BCE his admiral, the freedman Menas, seized Sardinia from Octavian's governor Marcus Lurius. By the Pact of Misenum in 39 BCE the triumvirs recognised his control of Sicily and Sardinia in exchange for keeping the grain supply to Rome open and his pirates in check. The peace was short. Each side accused the other of breaking it, and Menas betrayed Sardinia to Octavian. Sextus defeated Octavian at sea off Messina in 37 BCE.

Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa spent a winter building and training a fleet near Lake Avernus. He fought Sextus at Mylae in August 36 BCE, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Titus Statilius Taurus invaded Sicily, and after Naulochus Sextus fled to Asia Minor. Captured in 35 BCE, he was put to death without trial at Miletus by Marcus Titius, whom he had once spared, either on Titius's own initiative or possibly on the orders of Antony or Plancus. Plutarch gives him a minor role in the fall of the Republic; Appian treats him as a central figure who might even have emerged as the final victor.
seychelles: Seychelles is an archipelago of 115 islands in the Indian Ocean, with its capital and largest city, Victoria, about 1,500 kilometres east of mainland Africa. The islands lie northeast of Madagascar. The inner islands, 42 granitic and 2 coralline, occupy the shallow Seychelles Bank and hold 54% of the land area. The granitic islands rest on a submerged granite block, the Seychelles microcontinent, which lay between Madagascar and India before the breakup of Gondwanaland. Alfred Wegener cited this granite as evidence of continental drift.

The islands were uninhabited before sustained outside contact. Arab sailors knew of them through Indian Ocean trade routes, and scholars identify them with the Zarin islands described by al-Mahri. Europeans learnt of them in the early 16th century. The first sighting was made on 15 March 1503 by Thomé Lopes, during Vasco da Gama's fourth Portuguese India Armada. The earliest recorded landing was in January 1609, by the crew of the Ascension under Captain Alexander Sharpeigh, on a voyage of the British East India Company.

France began to take control in 1756, when Captain Corneille Nicholas Morphey laid a Stone of Possession on Mahé. The islands were named after the French politician Jean Moreau de Séchelles and formed part of the colony of Isle de France. In August 1770 the ship Thélémaque landed 15 white settlers and 13 African and Indian slaves on Ste. Anne Island. Enslaved Africans were then brought to work the plantations.

In 1794 the senior administrator, Jean-Baptiste Quéau de Quinssy, negotiated with the British frigate HMS Orpheus and kept the islands under French control as neutral territory. Britain took control after invading Isle de France in December 1810, formalised by the Treaty of Paris of 1814. Slavery was prohibited in 1835, and indentured labourers from India were later employed. Seychelles became a separate crown colony from Mauritius in 1903. It gained independence as a republic in 1976, and a coup in 1977 ousted its first president, James Mancham.

Seychelles is a republic whose president is both head of state and head of government. French, English and Seychellois Creole are official languages, and the Creole, a French-based language, is the most widely spoken. The population was estimated at 100,600 in 2022, making it the smallest African country by area and the least populated sovereign African state. Most people descend from African, French, Indian and Chinese immigrants. It belongs to the United Nations, the African Union and the Commonwealth of Nations.
seymour-martin-lipset: Lipset grew up in the Bronx among Irish, Italian and Jewish youth. He recalled an atmosphere of political talk in which the question was never Democrats or Republicans but communists, socialists, Trotskyists or anarchists. From an early age he was active in the Young People's Socialist League, a Trotskyist youth organisation that he later headed. He graduated from the City College of New York as an anti-Stalinist leftist, and before taking his doctorate at Columbia University in 1949 he taught at the University of Toronto.

Lipset held the Caroline S.G. Munro chair of political science and sociology at Stanford University and was a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution. He then became George D. Markham Professor of Government and Sociology at Harvard University, and also taught at Columbia, the University of California, Berkeley, Toronto and George Mason University. He was the only person to serve as president of both the American Political Science Association (1979–1980) and the American Sociological Association (1992–1993), and led several other bodies, including the World Association for Public Opinion Research. He won the MacIver Prize for Political Man and, in 1970, the Gunnar Myrdal Prize for The Politics of Unreason. His book The First New Nation was a finalist for the National Book Award.

His article "Some Social Requisites of Democracy" (1959) set out the Lipset hypothesis that economic development leads to democracy, a proposition that became central to modernisation theory and was later challenged by Guillermo O'Donnell, Adam Przeworski and Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson. Political Man (1960) analysed the social bases of democracy, fascism and communism, which Lipset called working-class authoritarianism, and argued that each major social stratum has both democratic and extremist expressions. It sold more than 400,000 copies and was translated into 20 languages.

With Stein Rokkan he published an influential study of party systems and voter alignments in 1967, and in The Democratic Century (2004) he traced the divergence of North and Latin America to their patterns of colonisation.
Lipset left the Socialist Party in 1960 and later described himself as a centrist. He was considered one of the first neoconservatives but did not call himself one. He died on 31 December 2006.
sfatul-tarii: After the February Revolution, teachers and intellectuals set up committees in almost every village of Bessarabia, and congresses of peasants, teachers, cooperators and clergy followed. In April 1917 the First Congress of Cooperatives of Bessarabia, meeting in Chișinău, demanded autonomy and a legislative assembly called Sfatul Țării. The National Moldavian Party, formed the same month under the boyar Vasile Stroescu, pressed for autonomy too, while Moldavian soldiers organised a Central Soldiers' Committee for All of Bessarabia. When the Ukrainian Central Rada claimed the province, the Commissar Constantin Mimi gathered delegates to reject the claim.

In November 1917 the soldiers' council proclaimed the autonomy of Bessarabia and called elections. The soldiers' councils chose 44 deputies, the Peasants' Congress 36, and county and communal commissions with professional and ethnic associations the remaining 70. The diet had first been planned with 120 seats, 70 per cent for Moldavians to match estimates of the population, and was enlarged to 135 and then 150. About 70 per cent of its members were Romanians and the rest Russians, Bulgarians, Jews and others. Ion Inculeț, sent by Alexander Kerensky, became president of the republic it proclaimed.

Sfatul Țării opened on 21 November 1917 (O.S.) as the first parliament of autonomous Bessarabia, and Vladimir Lenin is said to have told a delegation that visited him to go home and organise. As Bolshevik detachments spread disorder, they occupied Chișinău on 18 January 1918; members fled, some were arrested, and a secret session asked Romania for help. On 26 January the Romanian 11th Infantry Division under General Ernest Broșteanu entered Chișinău, and the pro-Soviet troops withdrew beyond the Dniester after a battle at Tighina.

On 6 February 1918 the council voted unanimously for the independence of the Moldavian Democratic Republic, and a Ministry Council under Daniel Ciugureanu replaced the Directory Council. In the vote on union with Romania, 86 members voted for it, 3 against, 36 abstained and 13 failed to appear; the vote did not divide clearly by ethnic group. The act of union listed special privileges for Bessarabia, among them its own democratically elected diet and an agrarian reform, and King Ferdinand I sanctioned it by decree in Iași the same evening.
sfax: Sfax lies about 270 km south-east of Tunis on a low coastal strip about 15 km wide, with an average altitude of 20 m. The rivers of the region are shallow and rarely reach the sea. The climate is hot and semi-arid, and because the city is sheltered from the winter storms of the Mediterranean it receives about half the rainfall of Tunis.

The present city was founded by the Aghlabids in 849 on the site of the town of Taparura. By the end of the 10th century it was an independent city-state. In the 12th century the geographer al-Idrisi described a thriving city with a stone wall, lively markets and a harbour, whose olive oil was of a quality found nowhere else. Roger II of Sicily conquered it in 1148; it was liberated by a revolt in 1156 and taken by the Almohads. Venice mounted an unsuccessful invasion in 1185, as Sfax had become a base of Barbary piracy.

The city returned to Hafsid rule around 1370. In 1534 the privateer Barberousse entered Tunis and reunited the towns of the coast, Sfax among them. Under the Husseinid dynasty the ramparts were restored, the Great Mosque was enlarged and in 1776 the Frankish quarter was built to the south for Jews and Christians. Venetian ships bombarded the city four times in 1785–86.

After the Bardo Treaty of 1881 made Tunisia a French protectorate, an insurrection broke out in Sfax; French ironclads bombarded it and troops took it on 16 July after hard fighting. The Axis powers used it as a major base in the Second World War until British forces took it on 10 April 1943.

Sfax is the second most populous city in Tunisia, with 341,999 inhabitants at the census of 2022. It is the country's largest fishing port and a centre of olive and nut processing, phosphate shipping and trade. Its medina, home to about 113,000 residents, is dominated by the Great Mosque and enclosed by walls 2,750 m long and seven to eleven metres high. The kasbah in its south-western corner, once an Aghlabid control tower and later army barracks, is now a museum of traditional architecture.
shaanxi: Shaanxi covers more than 205,000 square kilometres and borders Inner Mongolia to the north, Shanxi and Henan to the east, Hubei, Chongqing and Sichuan to the south, and Gansu and Ningxia to the west. It is divided into northern Shaanxi on the Loess Plateau, central Shaanxi or Guanzhong, where most of the population lives, and the mountainous south beyond the Qinling Mountains. The Wei River valley between them is a cradle of early Chinese civilisation. The name means west of Shan and is attested around 1000 BCE, when the dukes of Shao and Zhou marked their borders along the Shan plateau.

Thirteen dynasties established their capitals in Shaanxi over more than 1,100 years, from the Zhou to the Tang. Fossils of Lantian Man, a subspecies of Homo erectus about a million years old, were found near Xi'an. After the fall of the Qin the region was briefly governed as the Three Qins, which is the origin of one of its two abbreviations, Qin, the other being Shaan. Under the Han the Northern Silk Road connected Xi'an westward to Kashgar. The Ming founded the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission in 1376, which also covered Gansu and Ningxia. On 23 January 1556 an earthquake near Hua Shan killed an estimated 100,000 people.

From late 1935 to early 1947 Yan'an, at the end of the Long March, was the base of the Chinese Communist Revolution, and the Communists formed the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region in parts of Shaanxi. The People's Government of Shaanxi was established in Xi'an on 10 January 1950.

The capital and largest city, Xi'an, includes the sites of the former capitals Fenghao and Chang'an. It is the oldest of China's Four Ancient Capitals and the eastern terminus of the Silk Road. Xianyang, capital of the Qin dynasty from 221 to 206 BCE, lies just north across the Wei River. The population is about 37 million, and the vast majority are Han Chinese, with Hui, Manchu and Mongol minorities. Mandarin is the main language.
shabaka: Neferkare Shabaka, also written Shabako or Sabaco, was the third Kushite pharaoh of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty of Egypt. The Greek sources, among them Herodotus and Manetho, call him Sabakon or, more likely, Sebikhos. He ruled from the city of Napata, deep in Nubia, in what is now Sudan, and took as his throne name that of the Sixth Dynasty ruler Pepi II Neferkare.

He is thought to have been a son of King Kashta and Pebatjma, although a text from the time of Taharqa could be read to make him a son of Piye. His queen was Qalhata, a sister of Taharqa according to Assyrian records, and they were the parents of King Tantamani. His son Haremakhet became High Priest of Amun and is known from a statue found at Karnak.

Shabaka's reign consolidated Kushite control over all of Egypt, from Nubia down to the Delta. It saw a great deal of building throughout Egypt, especially at Thebes. At Karnak he set up a pink granite statue of himself wearing the twin crowns of Egypt. He is credited with preserving Egypt's independence from outside powers, above all the Neo-Assyrian Empire of Sargon II.

The best-known object from his reign is the Shabaka Stone, which records several Old Kingdom documents that the king ordered preserved. A large stone door, the Shabaka Gate, unearthed in 2011, is believed to have guarded the room where his treasures were kept. Shabaka and his family were immensely interested in Egypt's past, and the art of the period looked back to earlier periods.

Shabaka is assumed to have died in his fifteenth regnal year, since a cube statue (BM 24429) is dated to Year 15 of his reign. He was buried in a pyramid at el-Kurru, whose fully tunnelled burial chamber was an architectural improvement followed by Taharqa and later kings, and Taharqa succeeded him.

The succeeding 26th Dynasty ruler Psamtik I made no effort to destroy the monuments of the Nubian kings, whom the Assyrians had expelled. This changed under Psamtik II, who mutilated their monuments and in his third year campaigned into Nubia and sacked Napata. Even so, Shabaka's memory survived: the Egyptians gave a street his name in Late Period Memphis, his inscriptions were restored in the Ptolemaic period, and Greek historians spoke of him highly.
shabankara: The Buyid Shahanshah ʿAdud al-Dawla (r. 949–983) had deported the Shabankara to eastern Fars from Isfahan and Syria. The tribe was made up of the Ismāʿīlī, Rāmānī, Karzuwī, Masʿūdī and Shakānī, all herders and warriors. Their capital was Ij (Ig), and their land was divided into six districts, among them Zarkān, Iṣṭabānān, Nayriz and Darabjird.

The Ramanid branch rose under Fadluya, son of the chief Ali bin al-Hassan, who served in the Buyid army under Sahib-i Adil, vizier of the Buyid king of Fars. When the last Buyid of Fars, Abu Mansur Fulad Sutun, had the vizier put to death, Fadluya rebelled. As ruler of Fars he soon clashed with the Seljuk Turks: he submitted to Qawurd, brother of Sultan Alp Arslan, then revolted, and was captured and executed in 1071 by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

The Shabankara remained a force in Kerman and Fars. In 1099, with Qawurd's son Iran Shah, they defeated Amir Unar, the governor of Fars, and they revolted again under the Seljuk sultan Mahmud II (1117–1131). Abu Tahir ibn Muhammad, founder of the Hazaraspid dynasty, won great prestige by defeating them. The chief Kutb al-Din Mubariz and his brother Nizam al-Din Mahmud took Kerman from the Oghuz Turks in 1200 but lost it, and the atabeg of Fars Sad ibn Zengi finally defeated them.

In 1260 the Mongol Hulegu destroyed Ig and killed the chief Muzaffar al-Din Muhammad ibn al-Mubariz. Under the Ilkhans the Shabankara ruled a province centred at Darabgird, and they rebelled in vain in 1312. In 1355 the chief Ardashir refused the orders of Mubariz al-Din, who sent his son Mahmud against him, defeated him and took his country. The Shabankara may have kept some local power until 1424.

At their court the Shabankara combined strict Sunni orthodoxy with ancient Persian customs. They claimed descent from the mythical Iranian king Manuchehr and from Ardashir I (r. 224–242), founder of the pre-Islamic Sasanian Empire, and through him from the hero-king Faridun. A Kurdish tribe named Shabankara lives today in Kermanshah province.
shaduf: One theory holds that the shadoof was invented in Mesopotamia as early as the time of Sargon of Akkad, around the 24th and 23rd centuries BCE. The Minoans are believed to have adopted it next, with evidence of its use from around 2100–1600 BCE. Its appearance in Upper Egypt is placed most likely in the 18th Dynasty. Some historians believe instead that the Egyptians invented it along the Nile, citing tomb drawings of shadoofs at Thebes from 1250 BCE. A third theory places its origin in India at about the same time as in Mesopotamia, because it was so widespread there, but little other evidence supports it.

The pole is hung on its frame about one-fifth of its length from one end. The vessel on the long arm may be a bucket, a skin bag or a reed basket coated with bitumen, and some have an uneven base or a tie at the top so that the water runs out at once. The operator pushes the vessel down with his own weight, and the counterweight raises it full without effort. The water is emptied into runnels that carry it along irrigation ditches. The frame may be one post or a pair, and the vessel may hang from a rope or from a thinner stick.

The device lifts water from 1 to 6 metres, and its efficiency has been calculated at 60 per cent. A study in Nigeria, which measured effort by heart rate, found that suitable adjustments reduced the energy the operator spent from about 109 to 71 watts.

In ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia shadoofs set in tiers, one above another, raised water to higher levels by the work of several people. In Egypt under the Middle and New Kingdoms, pleasure gardens watered by shadoof became a mark of luxury residences and a symbol of status. Women have often worked it, since it is easy to use.

The name comes from the Arabic šādūf; in English it is also called a well sweep or swape. The ancient Greeks knew it as the kēlōn or kēlōneion, the Chinese call it jiégāo, and its Hungarian name, gémeskút, means heron well. Today it is very common in rural India and Pakistan, and in Europe in Ukraine, Belarus, Poland and Germany. On the Great Hungarian Plain it is considered a symbol of the region.
shafii-school: The school belongs to the Ahl al-Hadith tradition and takes its name from the jurist and traditionist al-Shafi'i, who lived from about 767 to 820 CE. He visited most of the great centres of Islamic jurisprudence in the Middle East and gathered a comprehensive knowledge of different legal theories. He was a student of Malik ibn Anas, the founder of the Maliki school, and of Muhammad Shaybani, a Hanafi scholar of Baghdad. His students first spread his thought in Cairo and Baghdad, and by the 10th century Mecca, Medina and Syria had also become chief centres of it.

Al-Shafi'i was the first jurist to insist that hadith were the decisive source of law over the traditional doctrines of earlier thinkers. In order of priority the sources are the Quran, the Sunnah, defined by him as the sayings, acts and tacit acquiescence of Muhammad as related in solidly established traditions, then analogical reasoning, qiyas, and finally ijma, the consensus of scholars, which was accepted but not stressed. The school rejected dependence on local community practice as a source of precedent and rebuffed personal opinion and juristic discretion. The groundwork text is al-Shafi'i's al-Risala, composed in Egypt. A first version, produced during his stay in Baghdad, is lost.

The school later held the judgeships exclusively in Syria, Kirman, Bukhara and Khorasan, and it flourished in northern Mesopotamia and Daylam. The Ghurids endorsed it in the 11th and 12th centuries. Under Salah al-Din it again became the paramount school in Egypt, after a period of Shia influence, and it was the official school of the Ayyubid dynasty and remained prominent in the Mamluk period. The rise of the Ottomans in the 16th century replaced Shafi'i judges with Hanafi scholars, and after the start of Safavid rule its presence in Iran was limited to the western regions.

Traders and merchants spread it across the Indian Ocean as far as India and Southeast Asia. It is predominant in the Horn of Africa, Lower Egypt, Yemen, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, and among most Kurdish Muslims. It is the third-largest Sunni school, after the Hanafi and Maliki.
shaftesbury: Shaftesbury is a town in Dorset, England, on the A30 road, 20 miles west of Salisbury, near the border with Wiltshire. It is the only significant hilltop settlement in Dorset, built about 215 metres above sea level on a greensand hill on the edge of Cranborne Chase. The old centre sits on a westward-pointing promontory, and below it to the west lies the Blackmore Vale, part of the River Stour basin. Its names have included the Celtic Caer Palladour, the probably Roman Melezo, the Domesday Book's Sceptesberie and the local Shaston, which Thomas Hardy used in his novels.

The town's recorded history begins in Anglo-Saxon times. By the early 8th century there was an important minster church, and in 880 Alfred the Great founded a fortified burgh as a defence against the Danish invaders. The Burghal Hidage lists it as one of only three burghs in the county. In 888 Alfred founded Shaftesbury Abbey, a Benedictine nunnery by the east gate, and appointed his daughter Ethelgifu its first abbess. Æthelstan founded two royal mints, and the abbey became the wealthiest Benedictine nunnery in England. On 20 February 981 the relics of Edward the Martyr were brought from Wareham and received at the abbey, making Shaftesbury a major pilgrimage site for healing miracles. King Canute died here in 1035 but was buried at Winchester.

In 1086 the Domesday Book recorded 177 houses, down from 257 before the Norman conquest, though Shaftesbury was still the largest town in Dorset. In the Middle Ages the abbey was the focus of the town, and a saying held that if the abbot of Glastonbury could marry the abbess of Shaftesbury their heir would hold more land than the king of England. A market charter was granted in 1260. In 1539 the last abbess, Elizabeth Zouche, signed a deed of surrender, and the abbey was demolished and its lands sold, which led to a temporary decline. Sir Thomas Arundell bought the abbey and much of the town in 1540, and the lands later passed through Pembroke and the Earl of Shaftesbury to the Grosvenors.

The town returned two members to Parliament from 1296 until the Reform Act of 1832. Cloth, swanskin, buttons and beer shaped its economy in the 17th and 18th centuries. Railways bypassed the town, and in 1918 Lord Stalbridge sold a large part of it at auction.

The civil parish had 9,160 inhabitants at the 2021 census. Few buildings predate the 18th century, since the Saxon and most medieval buildings have not survived. The abbey ruins now hold a museum, and next to them Gold Hill, a steep cobbled street, became nationally known through a 1970s television advertisement for Hovis bread directed by Ridley Scott. Shaftesbury has never had a direct railway connection.
shaghab: Shaghab first belonged to Umm Qasim, a daughter of Muhammad ibn Abdallah ibn Tahir, the Tahirid governor of Baghdad from 851 to 867. It is not recorded how she entered al-Mu'tadid's harem. Her original name, Na'ima, gentle, was changed to Shaghab, turbulent, a common practice meant to draw attention from a girl's beauty or to ward off jealousy and misfortune. Al-Mu'tadid's first wife, Qatr al-Nada, once threatened to cut off her nose.

She promoted her sister Khatif, her nephew Harun and her brother Gharib al-Khal, who until his death in 917 was among the leading commanders and provincial governors of the state. Under Caliph al-Muktafi her son was the target of palace intrigues, but she could rely on the loyalty of al-Mu'tadid's old ghilman. According to Miskawayh, the officials who chose her son as heir in 908 wanted a weak and pliable ruler.

Her secretaries handled civil and military business, and when her katib Ahmad al-Khasibi became vizier in 925 through her influence and her sister's, he regretted it, finding his post with her more profitable. Her first stewardess, Fatima, drowned in the Tigris.
