Umm Musa, who followed, was blamed for the fall of the vizier Ali ibn Isa al-Jarrah in 917 and was arrested in 922/3, accused of plotting to put a relative on the throne. Thumal, who replaced her, tortured her family until they revealed treasure reportedly worth a million gold dinars.

Shaghab had the qadi Ahmad ibn Yaqub executed when he refused to recognise her son because of his age, and she put Thumal in charge of the mazalim courts over the objections of the qadis. According to al-Tabari, Thumal's reforms, which lowered the cost of bringing a case, made her popular. In 918 Shaghab even rode a horse in public, though she spent most of her life in the harem.

Medieval writers made her influence a central charge against her son's reign. The contemporary historian al-Mas'udi complained that power lay with women and servants, the 13th-century chronicler Ibn al-Tiqtaqa called al-Muqtadir a squanderer whose reign was run by women and servants, and Ibn Hazm counted Thumal's appointment among the scandals of the age.
shah-abdul-latif-bhittai: Bhittai was born in Hala Haweli, near modern Hala, to Shah Habib, a great-grandson of the Sufi poet Shah Abdul Karim Bulri, in a Sayyid family whose ancestors had come to Sindh from Herat in the late 14th century. The family moved to nearby Kotri Mughal. Local tradition holds that he was illiterate, but his use of Arabic and Persian and the influence of Rumi show that he was well educated. Most of what is told of his life was passed down orally and written down in the late 19th century by Mirza Qalich Beg and Mir Abd al-Husayn Sangi.

At about twenty he left home and travelled for three years through Sindh and beyond, to Thatta, Kalachi (Karachi), Hinglaj in Balochistan with a band of Jogis, Lasbela, Dwarka, Junagadh, Nagarparkar and Jaisalmer. After the killing of the Arghun nobleman Mirza Mughal Beg in 1713 he married his daughter Saida Begum, who died a few years later; he did not remarry and had no children.

His verses were not written down in his lifetime but sung and memorised by his disciples at his musical sessions, and compiled after his death as the Shah Jo Risalo. The German philologist Ernest Trumpp first published it in 1866. It has thirty chapters, each called a Sur and tied to a musical mode; the most widely accepted version holds some 3,000 abyat and 200 wa'is. Some Surs retell Sassui Punhun, Sohni Mehar, Umar Marui and Lilan Chanesar; Sur Kedaro laments Husayn ibn Ali at Karbala. He kept the Qur'an and the Mathnawi of Rumi with him, and his poems sometimes translate Rumi's verses. Though Sindh passed from Mughal rule to the local Kalhora dynasty in his lifetime, his poetry never mentions politics.

His following reportedly earned him the hostility of nobles and of Noor Mohammad Kalhoro, ruler of Sindh, who is said to have tried to poison him before becoming his disciple. Some ten years before his death he settled on a sandhill near Hala Haweli, later called Bhit Shah. He died there on 21 December 1752, and Mian Ghulam Shah Kalhoro built a tomb over his grave in 1754 or 1765. His poetry is sung there every Thursday evening, and his three-day Urs falls on 14 Safar. Sindhi Hindus revere him too: he visited the Hinglaj Mata temple, and his Sur Ramkali was composed in reverence to Hinglaj Mata and the jogis who came there.
shah-jahan: Shah Jahan was born Khurram on 5 January 1592 in Lahore, the third son of Prince Salim, later Emperor Jahangir. His grandfather Emperor Akbar chose the name and, thinking the child auspicious, had him raised in his own household under the care of Ruqaiya Sultan Begum. In 1607 he became engaged to Arjumand Banu Begum, later known as Mumtaz Mahal, and they married five years later. Her aunt became the Empress Nur Jahan, who married Jahangir in 1611 and came to hold great power at court. Khurram first proved himself in the campaign against Mewar, whose ruler Rana Amar Singh I surrendered after a year of war and became a Mughal vassal.

Khurram was in constant conflict with Nur Jahan, who favoured her son-in-law Shahryar Mirza for the succession. He rebelled against his father in 1622 and failed. After Jahangir's death in 1627, Khurram won the struggle with Shahryar and became the fifth Mughal emperor.

Shah Jahan executed most of his rival claimants, and Nur Jahan was placed under house arrest. A famine in 1630–1632 in the Deccan, Gujarat and Khandesh followed crop failures; two million people are reported to have died, and he set up free kitchens for the victims. His armies captured Daulatabad and imprisoned Husein Shah of the Nizam Shahi Kingdom of Ahmednagar; Golconda submitted in 1635 and Bijapur in 1636. Mughal forces took Kandahar from the Safavids in 1638, but Abbas II recaptured it in 1649. An invasion of Central Asia in 1646–1647 temporarily occupied Balkh and Badakhshan.

Under his rule nobles and their contingents multiplied almost fourfold, as did the demands for revenue. He was one of the foremost patrons of Mughal architecture and commissioned the Red Fort, the Shah Jahan Mosque and the Taj Mahal, where Mumtaz Mahal is entombed.

When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1658, his eldest son Dara Shikoh assumed the regency, which incurred the animosity of his brothers. Aurangzeb defeated Dara at the Battle of Samugarh. Shah Jahan recovered, but Aurangzeb declared him unfit to rule and confined him in the Agra Fort. He died on 22 January 1666 and was buried next to his wife in the Taj Mahal. Historians describe his reign as the zenith of Mughal architectural and cultural achievement.
shah-murad: Shah Murad was born in 1749 at Kermine, the eldest of eleven children of Daniyal Biy, a member of the Uzbek aristocracy who held the post of ataliq. His mother came from the Uzbek Qongirat tribe. His father, who loved him dearly, called him Beg-i Jan, and Bukharan historians also gave him the titles Amir al-Mu'minin, Commander of the Faithful, Amir Ma'sum Ghazi and Padishah Ghazi. Drawn to Sufism from his youth, he spent his days praying in khanaqahs and mosques, and he refused the wealth he inherited, asking that it be shared among the common people.

His political career began in his father's lifetime, as governor of Kermine and then of Qarshi. In 1780 to 1781 he was made ruler of Samarkand and worked to restore the city: he built 24 districts and settled many families there from the eastern regions of the country, so that the city grew more populous and its economy and culture improved. A street of Samarkand bears his name. For his modest way of life people called him Amir Ma'sum, the sinless emir.

Coming to power after his father's death in 1785, he launched that year a campaign against the Qajar principality of Merv, meaning to use it as a base for raids on Iran. He killed its governor, Bayram 'Ali Khan Qajar, conquered the region fully in 1788, and built the town of Islamabad near Merv. He abolished the luxurious court and set up instead a courtroom of forty judges under his direct supervision, which anyone summoned could attend, high officials and slaves alike; each judge held books written by Shah Murad, which have not survived.

According to the writer Malcolm, the reverence of the Uzbeks allowed him many successful campaigns with an army mainly of cavalry, which he led himself in the plain clothes of a man of religion. He kept diplomatic relations with the Ottoman Empire and the Russian Empire. The historian Ahmad Donish counted him among the renovators of their century in Central Asia. His son Haydar succeeded him.
shah-nimatullah-wali: Ni'matullah traced his descent from the sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, in both a poem and an epistle that his biographers 'Abd al-Razzāq Kirmānī and 'Abd al-'Azīz Wā'iẓ reproduced. As a young man he travelled widely through the Muslim world, learning from many masters without finding one to whom he could commit himself, and he studied the writings of the Sufi philosopher Ibn ʿArabī. In Mecca he met Abdollah Yafe'i of the Suhrawardiyya and became his disciple, studying with him intensely for seven years.

He was then sent out on a second round of travels, now as a teacher in his own right. For a time he lived near Samarkand on the Central Asian Silk Road, where he met the conqueror Tamerlane, but he soon left to avoid conflict and settled in the region of Kerman. By the time he died his fame had spread through Persia and India, and it is said that he initiated hundreds of thousands of followers into the path that bears his name.

He left a collected diwan of Persian poetry with qasidas, ghazals, tarjī‘āt, mathnawis, do-baytīs and rubāʿiyāt. An ode attributed to him, with the rhyme Mey Beenum, has been published in several editions; Maulwi Firozuddin, who died in 1949, built his book Qaseeda Zuhoor-e-Mehdi around what he took to be its most authentic text and added an Urdu translation. His prose includes the Sharḥ-e Lama‘āt, a commentary on the Lama‘āt of Fakhr al-Din Ibrahim Iraqi, and a collection of 97 treatises.

Around 1430 Sultan Ahmed Shah Al Wali Bahamani of Bidar invited him to the Deccan. Pleading his great age, he sent his son Shah Khalilullah, who became the next qutb, or master, of the order; Shah Khalilullah's own son Shah Nurullah had already come to Bidar and married the sultan's daughter. The order's lineage settled at Ashtoor outside Bidar, and it returned to Iran in 1194 AH, near the end of the Zand dynasty, when Reza Ali Shah Deccani sent his disciple Ali Shah Deccani to Shiraz.

A shrine was raised over his grave at Mahan in 1436 and became a place of pilgrimage. Successive rulers added to it, and the complex has four courtyards, a reflecting pool, a mosque and twin minarets covered in turquoise tiles. Sunni Islam reveres him as a saint, and the Ni'matullahi order, which publicly declared itself Shia not long after the Safavid state was founded, honours him as its founder.
shah-rukh: Shah Rukh was born on 20 August 1377, the youngest of Timur's four sons. Some sources name his mother as Saray Mulk Khanum, a Chaghatai princess and Timur's chief consort, while the historian Khwandamir names a woman of the Qara Khitai. He was raised by Saray Mulk alongside Timur's grandson Khalil Sultan. In 1397 Timur appointed him governor of Khorasan with Herat as his capital, and he was never promoted beyond that post in his father's lifetime. Sources give no explanation; suggestions include his mother's status, his reputation for modesty and piety and his rejection of the laws of Genghis Khan. In 1402 he commanded the left wing at the Battle of Ankara.

Timur died in 1405 without a clearly appointed heir. Khalil Sultan proclaimed himself emperor at Tashkent and seized the treasury and Samarqand, and the succession war lasted years. Khalil Sultan lost support among his emirs, and Shah Rukh took Samarqand unopposed. Khalil Sultan submitted and died in 1411. Shah Rukh held court in Herat, not Samarqand, and made his eldest son Ulugh Beg governor of Transoxiana.

He recovered Fars in 1414 and Kirman two years later. In the west the Qara Qoyunlu held Azerbaijan and Mesopotamia, and Shah Rukh led three campaigns against them, in 1420, 1429 and 1434. The last brought stability for the rest of his reign under the Turkoman ruler Jahan Shah. He repeatedly put down rebellions by relatives. In 1426 an attacker, Ahmed Lur, stabbed him outside a mosque; he recovered, and an investigation linked Lur to the Hurufis, a Sufi sect, leading to purges that reached intellectuals in Herat.

He ruled as an Islamic sultan rather than a Turco-Mongol conqueror. In 1411 he abolished the Mongol yarghu tribunals in favour of Sharia courts and took the titles Sultan and Padshah. His empress Gawhar Shad built the Gawhar Shad Mosque in Mashhad and the Gawhar Shad Mosque and madrasa in Herat. Embassies passed between Herat and the Ming court in 1414-1420, and Shah Rukh asserted his independence of China.

Shah Rukh died at Rayy on 13 March 1447, after putting down the revolt of his grandson Sultan Muhammad. Chaos broke out in the camp, and his grandson Abdal-Latif took the body and Gawhar Shad hostage before another grandson, Ala al-Dawla, freed them and buried him in Herat. Ulugh Beg later had the body reburied with Timur's in the Gur-e-Amir at Samarqand. Struggles among his descendants followed, and after civil wars control of the Timurid Empire passed out of his line.
shah-shuja-durrani: Shuja Shah Durrani was born on 4 November 1785, a son of Timur Shah Durrani and of the Sadozai lineage of the Durrani clan of Pashtuns. He was governor of Herat and Peshawar from 1798 to 1801. In October 1801 he proclaimed himself king after the deposition of his brother Zaman Shah, whom his step-brother Mahmud Shah had blinded, since by tradition a blind man cannot be ruler. He ascended the throne properly on 13 July 1803.

After coming to power in 1803 Shuja ended the blood feud with the Barakzai family, forgave them and married their sister Wafa Begum to make an alliance. In 1809 he allied Afghanistan with British India as a defence against a feared invasion, and a British mission under Mountstuart Elphinstone visited him. In June 1809 Mahmud Shah overthrew him at the battle of Nimla. He was captured in the Punjab, held at Attock in 1811 and 1812, taken to Kashmir and then went to Lahore, where Ranjit Singh took from him the Koh-i-Noor and other diamonds. He escaped to Ludhiana and from 1818 drew a pension from the East India Company.

In exile the American Josiah Harlan, who visited his court, recorded that Shuja had the courtiers and slaves who displeased him mutilated, and he later judged him a tyrant. In 1833 Shuja agreed with Ranjit Singh to march through Punjab and cede Peshawar to the Sikhs if they took it, but the following year he was defeated at Kandahar, in July, by the Qandahar Sardars and Dost Mohammad Khan. In 1838 he won the support of the British and Ranjit Singh. The British restored him on 7 August 1839, thirty years after his deposition. By then most Afghans, it is said, remembered him as cruel, and he shut himself in the Bala Hissar and took revenge on those he felt had betrayed him.

Under religious pressure Shuja mustered an army near Kabul on 4 April 1842, ostensibly to attack the British. The next day his godson Shujah ud-Daula, who had been passed over for a command, led a gang that ambushed and killed him. He died on 5 April 1842.
shah-shuja-muzaffarid: Shah Shoja was born on 10 March 1333, the son of Mubariz al-Din Muhammad and of the Khitan princess Makhdum Shah, daughter of Qutb al-Din Shah Jahan of the Qutlugh-Khanids. After conquering Kerman in 1341 his father married him to the daughter of a chieftain of one of the non-Muslim Mongol tribes of Kerman, the Avḡāni and Jormāʾi, who were important allies; the marriage produced three princes and the princess Pādšāh Solṭān. Shah Shoja later prevented his father from demolishing the tomb of the poet Saadi Shirazi, whose verse Mubariz al-Din Muhammad had condemned.

Less of a tyrant than his father, he was constantly at war with his brothers. Around 1362 he had his vizier Qavam al-Din Hasan executed and replaced by Kamal al-Din Husayn Rashidi. In 1363 he marched against his brother Shah Mahmud, who held Isfahan, and a peace was soon brokered, but in 1364 Shah Mahmud, backed by his father-in-law Shaikh Awais Jalayir, invaded Fars and captured Shiraz, which Shah Shoja did not retake until 1366. Shah Mahmud's death soon after a short occupation of Tabriz let Shah Shoja take Isfahan.

He then held Azerbaijan and Arran for four months, until trouble in Fars forced him back: his nephew Shah Yahya, son of his brother Shah Muzaffar, had risen in Isfahan. The Jalayirid ruler Shaikh Hussain Jalayir refused his offer to marry his son Zain al-Abidin to Shaikh Hussain's sister and invaded, but Shah Shoja kept the Jalayirids from advancing beyond Soltaniyeh.

In 1383, while drunk, he had his son Sultan Shebli blinded, and regretted it the next day. His mother and his nephew Shah Hossein died soon after, and his own heavy drinking brought on a fatal illness. That year he wrote to Timur, then campaigning in Azerbaijan, entrusting his sons to him; Timur asked for a marriage alliance, and a granddaughter of Shah Shoja married Timur's grandson Pir Muhammad at Balkh in 1384. Before he died he named Zain al-Abidin his successor and his brother Imad al-Din Ahmad governor of Kerman.

Contemporary and later historians portray him as a sophisticated but at times harsh prince, learned in the scholarly and theological sciences, a poet himself and a patron of learning who took part in scholarly debates. Hafez spent much of his career as a poet under his rule and alluded to him 39 times. In the 18th century the Zand ruler Karim Khan Zand had his burial place renovated.
shahaji-bhonsle: Shahaji was born on 15 March 1594 to Maloji Bhosale, a Maratha nobleman who held the jagirs of Pune and Supe and other lands from Sultan Murtuza Nizamshah of Ahmadnagar. As a child he was betrothed to Jijabai, daughter of Lakhuji Jadhav, the Deshmukh of Sindkhed. He served in the army of Malik Ambar, prime minister of the Ahmadnagar Sultanate, and was a minor commander when his father died in 1622. By 1625 he held the rank of Sar Lashkar, major general.

In the wars between Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and the Mughal Empire Shahaji changed sides several times: to Bijapur in 1625, back to Ahmadnagar in 1628 and to the Mughals in 1630, after his in-laws were murdered in the factional politics of the Ahmadnagar court. In 1632 the Mughals gave his jagir to Malik Ambar's son Fatah Khan, and Shahaji left them. When the Mughals captured Daulatabad that year he held a war-torn area between Nashik, Pune and Ahmadnagar, set up the young Murtaza as king with himself as chief minister, and raised an army that at its height numbered 12,000.

Defeated at Parenda in 1634 and driven back when Shah Jahan came to the Deccan in person, he surrendered Mahuli and Junnar in October 1636 under the Mughal-Bijapur treaty. Barred from living in his Pune jagir, which his son Shivaji held in name under the manager Dadoji Kondadev, Shahaji served Bijapur in the south. Bijapur's forces took Bangalore in December 1638 and gave it to him as a jagir, and he ruled the region almost independently, building gardens and a palace called Gowri Mahal.

His relations with Bijapur's government rose and fell. In 1648, while Bijapur and Golconda besieged Jinjee, he was arrested for dealing on his own with the Nayakas, brought to Bijapur in chains and made to give up Kondana and Bangalore, but he was pardoned within a year. Most historians believe he did not support Shivaji's rising. Between 1659 and 1662 he went to Pune as a mediator, meeting his son for the first time in 12 years. He died in a hunting accident and is buried at Hodigere, near Channagiri in Karnataka.
shahnameh: Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh in 977 and completed it on 8 March 1010. It is a poetic recasting of what he, his contemporaries and his predecessors regarded as the account of Iran's ancient history, and many such accounts already existed in prose, among them the Shahnameh of Abu-Mansur. Traditional Iranian historiography holds that Ferdowsi grieved at the fall of the Sasanian Empire and wrote to preserve the memory of Persia's golden days, though some scholars have challenged this view. Josef Markwart and Theodor Nöldeke argued that much of the epic's world reshaped Parthian history, and that Rostam had Parthian origins.

The mythical age is short, about 2,100 verses or four per cent of the whole. After an opening in praise of God and Wisdom it gives the creation of the world as the Sasanians believed it, then the first man and king, Keyumars, and Hushang, who accidentally discovered fire. Almost two thirds of the poem belong to the heroic age, from Manuchehr's reign to the conquest of Alexander the Great, in which myth and legend are combined; its stories include Zal and Rudaba, Rostam and Sohrab, and Rostam and Esfandyar.

A brief mention of the Arsacid dynasty leads to Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian Empire, and from there Sasanian history is told with a good deal of accuracy, while the Arab conquest is narrated romantically.

Later works in Persian followed the Shahnameh in style and method, but none matched its fame, and some experts hold that Modern Persian remains much the same language as in Ferdowsi's day because of works like it. The Shirvanshah dynasty took many of its names from the poem, and the Qarakhanid dynasty called itself the family of Afrasiab.

Illustrated copies are among the most sumptuous examples of Persian miniature painting. The Baysonghori Shahnameh, made in 1430, is preserved at Golestan Palace and was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2007. Turner Macan published the first complete edition in 1829, and Arthur and Edmond Warner translated the whole work into English in nine volumes between 1905 and 1925.
shahrbaraz: Shahrbaraz is a title, meaning "the Boar of the Empire", since the boar was the animal of the Zoroastrian Yazata Vahram, the epitome of victory. According to al-Tabari his real name was Farrukhān. He belonged to the House of Mihran, one of the Seven Parthian clans, and was the son of a certain Ardashir. He rose in the Sasanian army and was appointed spahbed of Nēmrōz. He married Mirhran, a sister of Khosrow II, and had a son, Shapur-i Shahrvaraz, and another son, Niketas the Persian.

Shahrbaraz is first mentioned when Khosrow II began the last and most devastating Byzantine-Sasanian war, which lasted 26 years. Khosrow handed operations to his best generals, Shahrbaraz among them. When Heraclius, who had become emperor in 610, attacked near Antioch in 613, Shahrbaraz defeated him decisively and took the city, giving the Sasanians naval access to the Mediterranean. He then took Damascus, defeated a Byzantine army near Adhri'at, and led the army to Palaestina, where a bloody siege captured Jerusalem, and the Holy Cross was carried away. Ordered to invade Egypt in 618, he held Alexandria by 619 and the province by 621.

Heraclius turned the war. Shahrbaraz was defeated by him in Anatolia in 622 and barely escaped, naked and alone, from a night attack on his camp in February 625. Later his army stood at Chalcedon across the Bosphorus while the Avars besieged Constantinople, but the Byzantine fleet held the strait and the attack failed. Khosrow II then ordered his second-in-command Kardarigan to kill him. The letter was intercepted, and Shahrbaraz, shown it by Heraclius, changed sides in effect, altering the letter so that the army stayed loyal to him.

In 627 Shahrbaraz refused Khosrow's order to bring his army to Ctesiphon. In 628 the nobles freed Khosrow's son, who took the throne as Kavadh II and had his father executed. After Kavadh's death from plague, Shahrbaraz besieged Ctesiphon on 27 April 630 with 6,000 men, and with the help of Piruz Khosrow and Namdar Gushnasp he took it and executed Ardashir III.

He ruled for forty days. On 9 June 630 Farrukh Hormizd killed him with a javelin during a ceremony and helped Boran, Khosrow's daughter, to the throne. His son Shapur-i Shahrvaraz deposed Boran but was soon deposed, and Niketas served the Byzantines at the Battle of Yarmouk. A saga about Shahrbaraz later entered the One Thousand and One Nights.
shahrisabz: Shahrisabz lies about 80 km south of Samarkand at an elevation of 622 m, in Qashqadaryo Region. Historically it was called Kesh or Kish, meaning heart-pleasing, and has been known as Shahrisabz since the Timurid era. It is one of the most ancient cities of Central Asia and was founded more than 2,700 years ago. It has been tentatively identified with the ancient Nautaca, and excavated hills near the village of Kumyrtepa in the Kitab district are held to be parts of that city: a citadel, the town and a Zoroastrian temple, among the oldest religious structures in Central Asia.

Kesh was part of the Achaemenid Empire from the 6th to the 4th century BCE and an important urban centre of Sogdiana. Alexander the Great spent winters in the area and met his wife Roxanna there around 328 to 327 BCE. From the 6th to the 8th century Kesh belonged to the Turkic and Western Turkic khaganates.

The Arabs conquered it in the 8th century, and the Kashkadarya valley became the centre of a revolt led by al-Muqanna, known as the Revolt of the Men in White Clothes. The Karakhanid Ibrahim ibn Nasr conquered Kesh in 1040, and under the Khwarazmshahs in the early 13th century it was first enclosed by defensive walls.

Timur was born at Kesh into a family of the Barlas, and in the early years of the Timurid dynasty the city enjoyed his patronage. He regarded it as his home town and meant it to hold his tomb, but under his reign the centre of activity shifted to Samarkand.

Work on the Ak-Saray palace began in 1380, with artisans deported from Khwarezm; only parts of its 65 m gate-towers survive. Ulugh Beg built the Kok Gumbaz Mosque in 1437 in honour of his father Shah Rukh. The Dorus-Saodat complex holds the tomb of Timur's eldest son Jehangir. A stone casket intended for Timur was found in a crypt in 1943, although he was buried in Samarkand. The historic centre was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2000, and the city's population was 152,700 in 2026.
shahrizor: The plain lies in the Silêmanî Governorate, west of Hewraman, and is watered by tributaries of the Tanjaro river, which flows to the Diyala and the Tigris. Its name is probably Iranian, from shah, king, and razur, forest, so a royal forest; the scholar Herzfeld suggested white forest instead and linked it to Avestan legends. Adherents of the Yarsan religion hold the plain sacred as the place where God descends for the Last Judgement. The 12th-century geographer Yaqut al-Hamawi derived the name from a son of Zahhak, whom he named as founder of the city.

The Shahrizor Survey Project has shown that the valley was inhabited in the Late Neolithic and Chalcolithic, with Halaf and Ubaid remains at sites such as Bakr Awa, Tell Begum and Bestansur, which is on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List. Bakr Awa was also occupied in the Akkadian period. In the 3rd millennium BCE the plain belonged to the kingdom of Lullubi, and in the Iron Age it was the centre of Zamua, which the Neo-Assyrian king Assurnasirbal II had to subdue.

Sharazor and its king Yazdan Kurd appear in the Karnamag of Ardashir I and in the inscription of Narseh, and under the Sassanids the region was one of five provinces of the satrapy of the Medes. In the 4th century the Sassanids persecuted inhabitants who had converted to Christianity, killing Bishop Shahdost Shahrazori and 128 of his followers. From the 11th century to the 16th it belonged to the Ardalan Principality, whose first capital it was, and it later passed to the Baban Principality.

In the medieval era the area was ruled by the Annazid, Aishanid and Ayyubid dynasties, all of Kurdish origin, and in 1190 Saladin granted it with Erbil as a fief to the emir Gökböri. Yaqut described the region as stretching between Erbil and Hamadan, with inhabitants who were entirely Kurds and defended themselves against the Sultan.
shahrokh-shah: Shahrokh Mirza was born in March 1734, the son of Reza Qoli Mirza Afshar and his Safavid wife Fatemeh Soltan Begom, a sister of the Safavid shah Tahmasp II. His grandfather Nader Shah named him after Shah Rukh, the son and heir of Timur, to present himself as a conqueror on the level of Timur. His half-Safavid descent helped bolster Nader Shah's legitimacy, and Nader appointed him ruler of Herat. In 1740 coins were minted in his name there. In 1747, as Nader Shah grew increasingly paranoid, he had Shahrokh sent to the fortress of Kalat.

After Nader Shah was murdered on 21 June 1747, his nephew Ali-qoli Khan took the throne at Mashhad as Adel Shah and had sixteen descendants of Nader Shah massacred. Shahrokh, then 14, was spared in case his Safavid lineage proved useful, and was kept prisoner at Kalat. In 1748, while Adel Shah fought his rebellious brother Ebrahim Mirza, a party of Turkic, Kurdish and Arab tribal leaders declared Shahrokh shah at Mashhad on 1 October. Adel Shah was executed at Shahrokh's request. Shahrokh won followers by his generosity and presented himself, unlike his grandfather, as a champion of Twelver Shi'ism.

Real power stayed with the tribal leaders. On 14 January 1750 dissident nobles led by Mir Alam Khan imprisoned Shahrokh and installed Mir Sayyed Mohammad as Suleiman II, and Shahrokh was blinded soon after. Suleiman II was in turn deposed under the leadership of Yusuf Ali Khan Jalayir, and on 20 March 1750 the tribal leaders restored Shahrokh anyway, though he was blind. Ahmad Shah Durrani invaded Khorasan and took Herat, and after a second campaign he restored Shahrokh as king on 9 May 1755.

After Ahmad Shah Durrani died in 1772, Shahrokh was a pawn of the chieftains who controlled the towns around Mashhad. When Agha Mohammad Shah Qajar reached Mashhad in his conquest of Khorasan, Shahrokh went to the Qajar camp. Agha Mohammad Shah had Nader Shah's corpse dug up and sent to Tehran, and demanded the riches that had belonged to Nader. Shahrokh said he had no more, but was disbelieved and tortured severely until he revealed the hiding places of the last gems. He was sent to Mazandaran with his family, and died at Damghan of the injuries he had suffered. He was the last Afsharid ruler of Khorasan.
shahsevan: Where the Shahsevan came from is still unknown, and the ancestors of several tribes were of other origins, such as Kurdish, though Turkic identity and culture predominate. Between the 16th and the 18th century several tribal confederacies merged to form them. In the Safavid chronicle of Iskandar Beg Munshi, the expression shāhī-sēvan was used for an appeal to the faithful to rally round the shah, as Shah Mohammad Khodabandeh did during the uprisings of 1581 and 1584. Accounts recorded by 19th-century Russian officials made Anatolia their homeland and traced the chiefs to a leader called Yunsur Pasha, stories the chiefs probably told to justify their rule and their pastures.

In the 1720s, with the swift collapse of the Safavid dynasty to the Afghans and Ottoman and Russian incursions, Mughan and Ardabil became a main field of conflict. In 1732 Nader Shah restored Iranian control, deported several tribes to Khorasan and seems to have united those that remained under his general Badr Khan Shahsevan. The Russo-Iranian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828 were fought over their land and cost them most of their winter quarters. In late 1909 most chiefs joined a tribal alliance against the Constitution and pillaged Ardabil, but nationalist forces under Yeprem Khan soon defeated them.

During the Iranian Revolution of 1978–1979 some former chieftains were killed and others fled abroad. The new regime renamed the tribes Elsevan, those who love the people, but the name was not widely taken up and had fallen out of use by 1992. The anthropologist Richard Tapper judged that by the end of the century their pastoral nomadism did not seem likely to survive much longer.

The tribes are arranged in descending units of tribe, clan, gubak, ube and family. The gubak, the basic unit, usually holds 20 to 30 families who drive a common herd between pastures. Ilbeks keep order and collect taxes, and the aksakals, the white-bearded elders, form the elite. The Shahsevan bred sheep, cattle, camels and horses, live in the felt dwelling called the alachig, and from the end of the 19th century began to turn to settled farming. Women weave kilims, jajims and horse blankets.
shahu-i: Shahu was the son of Sambhaji I and belonged to the Bhonsle dynasty. In 1689, at the age of seven, he was taken prisoner with his mother Yesubai after the Battle of Raigarh. Aurangzeb hoped to use the heir as a pawn against the Marathas and treated mother and son well. He called the boy, whose real name was Shivaji, Sadhu Shivaji, from which came the name Raja Shahu. In captivity Shahu was married to two daughters of Maratha sardars in Mughal service and was given the Bhavani sword of Shivaji and lands around Akkalkot, Supa, Baramati and Nevase.

Shahu left the Mughal camp at Doraha on 8 May 1707. His aunt Tarabai, who governed in the name of her son, denounced him as an impostor, and a civil war followed. At the Battle of Khed on 12 October 1707 the general Dhanaji Jadhav, already pledged to Shahu, did little more than skirmish, and Tarabai's forces were routed. Satara fell on 1 January 1708, when its commander Sheikh Mira imprisoned Tarabai's Pratinidhi and opened the gates. Shahu later won over the admiral Kanhoji Angre through Balaji Vishwanath, and the Treaty of Warana with Tarabai's son Sambhaji made Kolhapur subordinate to Satara.

Under the Peshwas Bajirao I and Balaji Bajirao the Marathas defeated the Nizam-ul-Mulk, Asaf Jah I of Hyderabad, at the Battle of Palkhed on 28 February 1728 and conquered Bundelkhand, Malwa, Gujarat, Gwalior and the Ganga-Yamuna Doab. His reign was the longest of any Maratha ruler. Contemporaries praised him for hearing petitions in person, abolishing irksome taxes and bringing barren land under cultivation.

In 1721 Shahu moved his throne from the citadel of Satara to the Rangmahal Palace in the city below, Shahunagar, which he supplied with piped water and a mint. He died there on 15 December 1749. His widow Sakvarbai and his concubines committed sati amid intrigues over the succession. His adopted son Rajaram II succeeded him, but power passed first to Tarabai and then to the Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, and the Chhatrapati became a figurehead. Another adopted son, Fatehsinh, became the first Raja of Akkalkot, founding the Lokhande Bhonsle dynasty there.
shahu-of-kolhapur: Shahu was born Yeshwantrao Ghatge on 26 June 1874, the son of Jaisingrao (Aabasaheb) Ghatge, chief of the Kagal (Sr.) estate and regent of Kolhapur State, and of Radhabai, who came from the royal Ghorpade family of Mudhol. He lost his mother at the age of three. After his adoption into the Kolhapur royal family on 17 March 1884 he studied at Rajkumar College in Rajkot and took lessons in administration from Sir Stuart Fraser of the Indian Civil Service, while a regency council appointed by the British government ran the state.

In 1891 he married Lakshmibai Khanvilkar, daughter of a Maratha nobleman from Baroda; they had two sons and two daughters. He ascended the throne on 2 April 1894, on coming of age, and was renamed Shahuji Maharaj. Over six feet five inches tall, he was a keen wrestler and patronised the sport throughout his rule.

A Brahmin priest of the royal family, Narayan Bhat, refused to perform Vedokta rites for Shahu, implying that he belonged to the Shudra varna. The Vedokta controversy that followed led Shahu to fight for the rights of the Maratha community. In 1916 he established the Deccan Rayat Association at Nipani to secure political rights for non-Brahmins.

Besides the reservation order of 26 July 1902, Shahu built hostels for many caste and religious communities, among them Muslims, Jains and Christians, opened Vedic schools to all castes and in 1917 made primary education compulsory and free. His laws sanctioned widow remarriage on 1 January 1917 and inter-caste and inter-religious marriage on 12 July 1919, and the Jogtini Act of 11 November 1920 banned the Devadasi system.

He opened the Shahu Chhatrapati Spinning and Weaving Mill in 1906, founded co-operative societies and the King Edward Agricultural Institute, and began the Radhanagari Dam on the Bhogawati River in 1907; completed in 1935, it enabled the irrigation of about 15,000 hectares. He built hundreds of taleems, or wrestling training centres, and Khasbag Stadium.

Between 1917 and 1921 Shahu met B. R. Ambedkar a number of times to discuss ways of ending caste segregation. He made Ambedkar chairman of a conference for the untouchables on 21-22 March 1920 and donated Rs. 2,500 when Ambedkar started his newspaper Mooknayak on 31 January 1921. Shahu died in Girgaon, Bombay, on 6 May 1922 and was succeeded by his eldest son, Rajaram III. In 2006 the Government of Maharashtra declared his birthday Social Justice Day, and in 2009 a statue of him was unveiled at Parliament House in New Delhi.
shaivism: The origins of Shaivism are unclear and debated. The earliest traceable root is the worship of the Vedic deity Rudra, who appears in the Rigveda, composed about 1500 to 1200 BCE. Chakravarti describes Shaivism as an amalgam of pre-Aryan traditions, Vedic Rudra and post-Vedic practices, including yoga, puja and bhakti. The earliest evidence of sectarian Rudra-Shiva worship appears with the Pashupata in the early centuries CE.

In the Gupta period, from about 320 to 500 CE, the Puranas contain extensive chapters on Shaivism, among them the Shiva, Skanda and Linga Puranas. After the Gupta Empire declined following the Hun invasions, new regional powers in central and northern India, such as the Maukharis and the Kalacuris, adopted Shaivism. In South India it was the predominant tradition, living alongside Buddhism and Jainism, before the Vaishnava Alvars launched the Bhakti movement in the 7th century.

Shaivism holds Shiva, whose name means the auspicious one, to be the supreme being. Its followers, called Shaivas, are estimated at about 385 million, mostly in India, Sri Lanka and Nepal. It divides broadly into Vedic and Puranic Shaivism, the householder religion of the majority, and non-Puranic or tantric Shaivism, which treats the Agama texts as superior revelations. Shiva is worshipped most often as the linga, and temples also feature the bull Nandi and the trident.

The Atimarga was the path of ascetics. The Mantramarga, open to householders too, sought special powers as well as liberation. Within it Shaiva Siddhanta is a devotional dualism, while the Trika and Kashmiri Shaivism are monistic. Lingayatism, founded by Basava in the 12th century, is a distinct tradition.

Shaivism reached Southeast Asia from South India. In Indonesia, temples and inscriptions of 400 to 700 CE suggest that Shiva was the highest god, and Shaivism and Buddhism coexisted in Java until about 1500, when both were replaced by Islam; the combination persists in Bali. Its influence was strong from the late 6th century in the Khmer and Cham kingdoms, and thousands of Shaiva temples were built there and in Indonesia. In Java they are called candi, in Bali pura and in Cambodia wat.

Shiva as Nataraja, lord of dance, appears in temples at Badami, Ellora, Khajuraho and Chidambaram, and is reflected in classical dances such as Bharatanatyam. Shaivism has also been a major source of yoga techniques, including those of Hatha Yoga.
shajar-al-durr: Shajar al-Durr, whose name means Tree of Pearls, was probably of Turkic or Armenian origin. As-Salih Ayyub bought her as a slave in the Levant before he became sultan, and she accompanied him to Al Karak during his detention there in 1239. When he became sultan in 1240 she went with him to Egypt and bore their son Khalil, and he later married her.

Ayyub died on 22 November 1249 at Al Mansurah while Louis IX of France's crusader army was attacking Egypt. Shajar al-Durr, the commander Fakhr ad-Din and the chief eunuch Jamal ad-Din Muhsin concealed his death, forging documents in his hand, until his son Turanshah arrived from Hasankeyf. She agreed to Baibars's plan to defend Al Mansurah, where the crusader force was trapped and annihilated.

After Turanshah's arrival in February 1250 the crusaders were defeated at Fariskur on 6 April and Louis IX was captured. Turanshah then sought to replace his father's officials and demanded his father's wealth from Shajar al-Durr, which enraged the Mamluks. Baibars and other Mamluks assassinated him on 2 May 1250; he was the last of the Ayyubid sultans. The Mamluks and emirs installed Shajar al-Durr, with Izz al-Din Aybak as atabeg, and she took titles including Queen of the Muslims, invoking her husband and her son. Louis IX gave up Damietta and left for Acre on 8 May 1250.

The Syrian Ayyubid emirs refused her homage, and the Abbasid Caliph al-Musta'sim in Baghdad would not recognise a woman as ruler, writing that if the Mamluks had no men he would send some. After about three months she abdicated and married Aybak, who became sultan.

By 1257 relations between Shajar al-Durr and Aybak had soured, and he decided to marry the daughter of Badr al-Din Lu'lu' of Mosul. Shajar al-Durr had him murdered by servants while he bathed. His Mamluks did not believe her account of a sudden death, and she was arrested. On 28 April 1257 she was beaten to death by the bondmaids of Aybak's son al-Mansur Ali and his mother.

She built a tomb for her husband at the Salihiyya madrasa in 1250, joining tomb and madrasa, and a tomb for herself, whose mihrab carries a mosaic of a tree with pearl-like fruit recalling her name. She is regarded as the first Mamluk ruler of Egypt, and she appears in the folk epic Sirat al-Zahir Baibars and in a 1935 film by Ahmed Galal.
shakhbut-bin-sultan-al-nahyan: Shakhbut was born on 1 June 1905, the eldest son of Sultan bin Zayed bin Khalifa Al Nahyan and Sheikha Salama bint Butti. He married twice. His first wife, his first cousin Sheikha Fakhera bint Hazza Al Nahyan, was the mother of all his children: two sons, Saeed and Sultan, and four daughters, Osha, Mozah, Qoot and Rawdha. His second marriage, to Mariam bint Rashid Al Otaiba, was childless.

Shakhbut came to power in 1928 after a coup against Sheikh Saqr bin Zayed Al Nahyan. As ruler he followed a strongly mercantilist policy and kept his reserves in gold. After oil was discovered in Abu Dhabi in 1958, the emirate's elites grew frustrated by his refusal to spend the petroleum royalties. On 24 April 1966 King Hussein of Jordan awarded him the Nahda Order, then Jordan's highest honour.

A few months later, at the request of those elites, the British deposed him in a bloodless coup carried out through the Trucial Oman Scouts on 6 August 1966, and Shakhbut's younger brother Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan took his place as ruler.

On Zayed's orders Shakhbut and his family went into exile in Iran, where they lived in Khuzestan province as guests of Sheikh Abdulkarim Al-Faisali of the Banu Tamim tribe. Both of his sons died young while living in exile with him. Shakhbut died on 11 February 1989. His descendants, through the sons of Saeed and Sultan, continue to live in the emirate of Abu Dhabi.
shaki-azerbaijan: Shaki lies in north-western Azerbaijan on the southern side of the Greater Caucasus, about 240 km from Baku, surrounded by peaks that in places reach 3,000 to 3,600 metres. The Kish and Gurjhana are its main rivers. The city was known as Nukha until 1968. Azerbaijani historians trace its name to the Sakas, an Iranian people who reached the South Caucasus in the 7th century BCE, and traces of large settlements date back more than 2,700 years.

Shaki was one of the larger cities of the Caucasian Albanian states in the 1st century. After an Arab invasion in 654 it was annexed to the third emirate of Arminiya, and around the turn of the 9th century Armenian Smbatean princes ruled it as an autonomous principality, Shaki or Hereti. The Kiurikian dynasty ruled it from 1038 to 1105, and in 1117 King David IV of Georgia captured it. Timur took it in 1392. The Safavid shah Ismail I conquered the area in the early 1500s, and in 1551 Shah Tahmasp appointed the first Qizilbash governor. The Ottomans briefly held it twice.

In 1743 Haji Chelebi, who claimed descent from the earlier hereditary rulers, proclaimed an independent Sheki Khanate. Nadir Shah sent an army against him, but after Nadir's death Haji Chelebi declared himself khan again. The khanate raised silkworms and traded, and it defeated the army of Heraclius II of Kakheti in 1751. By the treaty of Kyurekchay of 21 May 1805 it agreed to annexation by Russia, which formally took the area by the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813. The khanate was abolished in 1819 and the Shaki province established in its place.

In the mid-19th century the city became an international silk centre, and more than 200 European companies opened offices there. A rising against collectivisation broke out in a village of the district in 1930 and was put down.

Because the town was devastated many times, its oldest surviving monuments date only from the 16th to 19th centuries. Among them is the Palace of Shaki Khans, built in 1762 without a single nail as a summer residence and decorated with shebeke, wooden lattices of coloured glass held without glue or nails. Others are the Shaki fortress, the Khan's Mosque and two caravanserais. The historic centre with the Khan's Palace was added to UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2019. Shaki has its own dialect of Azerbaijani and is known for sweet dishes such as Shaki halva.
shaktism: The earliest archaeological evidence of what appears to be an Upper Paleolithic shrine for Shakti worship comes from the site of Baghor I in the Sidhi district of Madhya Pradesh, dated to between 9000 and 8000 BCE. The origins of Shakti worship may also be traced to the Indus Valley Civilisation. Among the earliest evidence of reverence for the female aspect of the deity in Hinduism is the Devi Suktam hymn, chapter 10.125 of the Rig Veda. By the mid first millennium CE, goddesses such as Parvati, Durga, Kali, Lakshmi and Saraswati were already prominent. In eastern India, after the decline of Buddhism, Hindu and Buddhist goddesses were combined to form the Mahavidya, a group of ten goddesses.

Shaktas regard Shakti as the supreme, eternal reality of all existence, the same as the concept of Brahman in wider Hinduism, and as the source, embodiment and energy of the cosmos. Shaktism does not reject the masculine but rejects dualisms such as male and female, soul and body, affirming nature as divine. The Devi Mahatmya is considered as important as the Bhagavad Gita, and other revered scriptures include the Devi-Bhagavata Purana, the Kalika Purana and the Shakta Upanishads. A Shakta worships a personally chosen goddess, the ishta-devi, selected by family tradition, region, guru lineage or personal resonance.

Its two largest schools are the Srikula, the family of Tripura Sundari, which is strongest in South India and has been a force there since no later than the seventh century, and the Kalikula, the family of Kali, which prevails in northern and eastern India. Srividya, the best known school of the Srikula, views the goddess as benign and beautiful, while the Kalikula focuses on fierce forms such as Kali and Durga.

The most important Shakta festival is Navaratri, the nine nights, followed by the tenth day, Dusshera or Vijayadashami, which celebrates Durga's victory over demons described in the Devi Mahatmya. In Bengal the last four days are called Durga Puja and mark her slaying of the buffalo demon Mahishasura. Animal sacrifice to goddesses such as Kali is practised in parts of eastern India, the Himalayan states and Nepal, sometimes with a vegetable or sweet substitute, and many devotees find it distasteful.

Shakta temples are found across South Asia, and the major pilgrimage sites are called Shakta pithas, seats of the Devi. There has been significant sharing of ideas between Tantric Buddhism and Shakta Tantra. The Buddhist Aurangabad Caves of the 6th to 7th century show mother goddesses next to the Buddha, and the Sikh Dasam Granth includes sections on Chandi.
shakushain: Shakushain's revolt grew out of a long change in trade. In 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi gave the Matsumae clan the area around present-day Matsumae as a march fief, charged with defending Japan against the Ainu of the north. At first the Ainu travelled to the Matsumae domain and could trade freely with anyone, but in the first half of the 17th century the Tokugawa shogunate granted the Matsumae exclusive rights to trade with the Ainu. The Matsumae passed these rights to their samurai in place of fiefs, and the samurai, posted at trading stations across Hokkaido, forced goods on unwilling Ainu and overfished salmon with large nets. In 1665 the Matsumae set the exchange rate against the Ainu.

The fighting began in 1669 as a struggle over resources between Shakushain's people and another Ainu group led by Hae in the Shibuchari River basin, in what is now Shinhidaka. The Matsumae tried to mediate, but the conflict flared again, and Shakushain killed Hae's son. Hae sent emissaries to the Matsumae to ask for arms; some died of smallpox on the way back, and word reached the Ainu that the Matsumae had poisoned them. Shakushain then called on all the Ainu of Hokkaido to fight together. The coalition demanded full political independence and a return to direct trade with Honshū, and attacked Japanese people, ships, mining camps and trading forts, aiming also at the towns of the Matsumae domain.

At the end of 1669 Shakushain's forces surrendered and he was assassinated by Matsumae warriors, though the war went on for about three years more. The historian Brett Walker calls it a watershed in the conquest of Ezo: Shakushain, he writes, was a charismatic leader able to bridge regional differences among Ainu communities, and the shogunate answered by replacing local Matsumae generals with men of its own choosing.

The peace bound the Ainu to swear allegiance to the Matsumae. The Ainu remained autonomous, but the Matsumae quickly set up 60 new trading posts and held down prices, so that some settlements were reportedly close to famine, and Ainu unable to support themselves had to work in fish factories in Honshu for about a seventh of the pay of Japanese workers.
shallum-of-israel: Shallum was the fifteenth king of the ancient Kingdom of Israel and is named in the Books of Kings as the son of Jabesh. Before he took the throne he was a captain in the army of King Zechariah, whom he later killed. His name is given in Hebrew as Šallūm, which means "retribution".

The passage that names his father may instead refer to a place, so that Shallum would be "the son" of a city called Jabesh. On this reading he came from Jabesh-Gilead, a city that appears several times in the biblical texts: in the Book of Judges its men are killed and its unmarried women given to the Tribe of Benjamin, and in the Books of Samuel Saul relieves it from a siege by Nahash of Ammon.

According to 2 Kings 15:10, Shallum "conspired against Zechariah, and smote him before the people; and slew him, and reigned in his stead". The Biblical sources present this as the fulfilment of a prophecy that the House of Jehu, represented by Zechariah, would hold the throne for only four generations. Greek versions of the text name the place of the killing as Ibleam or Keblaam, while the Hebrew text leaves it unclear. He ruled from Samaria and came to the throne in the 39th regnal year of Uzziah, king of Judah.

Shallum reigned only "a month of days in Samaria". Menahem, another captain from Zechariah's army, then rose up against him and put him to death, and Menahem became king in his place (2 Kings 15:14-17). The historian Josephus retold the episode in Antiquities of the Jews, where the king appears as Sellemos and reigns for thirty days. Unlike the Bible, Josephus makes Shallum a friend of Zechariah, which sharpens the pathos of the murder, and he has Menahem, whom he calls a general based at Tirzah, march on Samaria with his whole army. He leaves out the prophecy, the city of Samaria and the dating by Uzziah's reign.
shalmaneser-iii: Shalmaneser III, whose name means the god Shulmanu is pre-eminent, succeeded Ashurnasirpal II, and his accession year began in 859 BCE with a first campaign. His reign was a constant series of campaigns against the eastern tribes, the Babylonians, Mesopotamia, Syria, Kizzuwadna and Urartu. His armies reached Lake Van and the Taurus Mountains, the Neo-Hittites of Carchemish were forced to pay tribute, and Hamath and Aram-Damascus were subdued. His annals of the 850s BCE are where the Arabs and Chaldeans first appear in recorded history. He reported destroying the Urartian cities of Sugunia in 858 BCE and Araškun in 853 BCE.

In 853 BCE eleven states, led by Hadadezer of Aram-Damascus, Irhuleni of Hamath and Ahab of Israel, with Gindibu, king of the Arabs, fought him at the Battle of Qarqar. The result was not decisive, and he had to fight them several times in the following years. In 851 BCE a revolt in Babylon led him to march against Marduk-bēl-ušate, who rebelled against his own brother Marduk-zakir-shumi I, an ally of Shalmaneser, and was killed. In 841 BCE he campaigned against Hazael of Damascus, devastating its territory without taking the city, and Jehu of Israel and the Phoenician cities sent him tribute.

Shalmaneser built a palace at Kalhu, the biblical Calah and modern Nimrud, and left several editions of royal annals recording his campaigns. The last is carved on the Black Obelisk from Calah, a black limestone relief that is the most complete Assyrian obelisk found. Its second register carries the earliest surviving picture of an Israelite, Jehu, whose tribute is described in a cuneiform caption that calls him son of Omri, an error. The monument was erected in 825 BCE, in a time of civil war, and was discovered by Sir Austen Henry Layard in 1846. The Kurkh Monolith names Ahab in connection with Qarqar.

In 836 BCE Shalmaneser sent an expedition against the Tibareni, followed by one against Cappadocia, and in 832 BCE another against Urartu. In the following year age made him hand command of the army to the commander-in-chief Dayyan-Assur. A revolt began in his 32nd year, with Nineveh and other cities rising under his son Assur-danin-pal, and civil war lasted two years. In his final year, 824 BCE, he died and was succeeded by Shamshi-Adad V, who suppressed the revolt in his third year. Shalmaneser had expanded the frontiers of the empire and stabilised its hold on the Khabur and the Zagros frontier region contested with Urartu.
shalmaneser-v: Shalmaneser V was the son and heir of Tiglath-Pileser III. His name, Salmānu-ašarēd in Assyria, means Salmānu is foremost, and it was a regnal name borne by four earlier Assyrian kings. Some later sources, among them the Ptolemaic Canon and the Babylonian King List, call him Ululayu, which was possibly his birth name.

Letters sent to his father while he was crown prince, signed Ululayu, report that Assyria and its forts are well. They show him detaining emissaries and moving goods, and his duties appear to have been mostly diplomatic or concerned with the palace household. Two Assyriologists have suggested that he acted as regent at Nimrud while his father was on campaign, though they note this is speculative.

Shalmaneser appears to have become king of both Assyria and Babylonia without challenge, although he faced some resistance from the Chaldean tribes in the south. Few contemporary sources survive. Apart from inscriptions on lion-shaped weights, no commemorative inscription can be attributed to him with confidence, and he built little in the great cities of the Assyrian heartland, so he probably spent much of his short reign at war. He held the office of eponym in his fourth year rather than his second, a change that later kings seem to have respected.

He campaigned widely in the west, against Phoenician cities and against the kingdom of Tabal in Anatolia. The Greek historian Menander of Ephesus records a five-year siege of Tyre, probably in his reign. His best-known undertaking was the siege of Samaria, capital of the Kingdom of Israel, which ended the kingdom and made it the Assyrian province of Samerina. The Babylonian Chronicle and the Bible ascribe the conquest to Shalmaneser, but Sargon II claims it in his own inscriptions. One reconstruction places the start of the siege in 725 or 724 BCE and its end in 722 BCE, near the end of Shalmaneser's reign. Nearly thirty thousand people were deported, and Sargon took responsibility for the resettlement.

Shalmaneser was deposed in 722 BCE and replaced by Sargon II. The circumstances are unclear but were probably violent, and the Babylonian Chronicle says only that he met the fate. A single inscription of Sargon portrays him as a godless tyrant who deprived the city of Assur of its privileges, but this serves chiefly to justify Sargon's own rise.

Sargon's early years saw opposition from a significant faction of Assyrians, over six thousand of whom he resettled as guilty. It is unlikely that Sargon was a legitimate heir, and he may have been unrelated to Shalmaneser, in which case Shalmaneser was the last king of the Adaside dynasty, which had ruled Assyria for almost a thousand years.
shamakhi: Shamakhi lies in the central part of Shirvan, at about 749 metres above sea level, in the most seismic area of the Caucasus. Eleven major earthquakes have struck it, and each time it was rebuilt. The first mention of the place, as Kamachia, is by Claudius Ptolemaeus in the 1st or 2nd century CE, and it served as the capital of the Shirvanshah realm from the 8th to the 15th centuries.

Shamakhi was a key town on the Silk Road and kept links with India and China in the 12th century. The friar William of Rubruck passed through it, and in 1476 the Venetian diplomat Giosafat Barbaro described a good city of four to five thousand houses that produced silk and cotton. The Safavid ruler Ismail I took it in 1500–1501, and from 1538 it was the capital of a Safavid province of Shirvan. The Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi, in 1647, described about 7,000 houses, seventy mosques and forty caravanserais. Its population included Persians, Armenians and Georgians as well as Turkish speakers, and its crafts included carpet weaving, in which the buta motif is characteristic.

In 1721 Lezgins from Shirvan and Dagestan, helped by the Sunni inhabitants, sacked the city, massacring thousands of its Shia inhabitants and robbing its Christian inhabitants and foreign nationals, many of them Russian merchants. Russian forces cited the attack as one pretext for entering Shirvan in 1723. The Ottomans held the town until the rise of Nader Shah, who in 1742 destroyed it and built a new town of the same name about 26 km to the west, which was later abandoned. Russia annexed the Shirvan Khanate in 1805, and Iran ceded the town in 1813. After the earthquake of 1859 the capital of the province was moved to Baku, and the importance of Shamakhi declined sharply.

Shamakhi is the administrative centre of the Shamakhi District of Azerbaijan. It is known for its traditional dancers and for perhaps giving its name to the Soumak rugs. The Juma Mosque is the only building to have survived eight of the eleven earthquakes, although the earthquake of 1902 destroyed it.
shamanism: Shamanism is a spiritual practice in which a practitioner, the shaman, interacts with the spirit world through altered states of consciousness such as trance. The aim is usually to direct spirits or spiritual energies into the physical world for healing, divination or some other help to human beings. There is no single agreed definition among anthropologists. Manvir Singh argues that the most justifiable one has three features: entering non-ordinary states, engaging with unseen realities, and providing services such as healing and divination. Ronald Hutton noted four definitions in use by the early 21st century, one of which restricts the word to the Indigenous religions of Siberia and neighbouring parts of Asia.

The English word derives from the Russian šamán, which comes from a Tungusic word, perhaps from the Evenki or Manchu language. It is sometimes linked to a Tungus root meaning to know, a connection Juha Janhunen questions on linguistic grounds. Mircea Eliade suggested that the Sanskrit śramaṇa, a wandering monastic, which spread with Buddhism across Central Asia, could be the ultimate origin.

Shamanism rests on the premise that the visible world is pervaded by invisible forces or spirits that affect the lives of the living. Beliefs identified by Eliade include that spirits can be benevolent or malevolent, that the shaman can treat sickness caused by malevolent spirits, and that the shaman's spirit can leave the body to enter the supernatural world to search for answers. Illness is often attributed to the spiritual realm, and healing may consist of retrieving the lost soul of the sick person. Shamans may also release the souls of game animals, and among peoples such as the Tucano, shamanic belief supports restrictions on hunting.

Shamans enter the spirit world through an ecstatic trance, brought on by ritual performance or by entheogens. Shamans often say they were called through dreams or signs, though some say their powers are inherited, and training generally takes years. Many describe an initiatory crisis of illness or psychological distress. Among several peoples of Siberia the drum, usually made of animal skin stretched over a bent wooden hoop, helps the shaman reach an altered state or travel between the physical and spiritual worlds.

Some scholars suggest that shamanic practices originate as early as the Paleolithic. A burial dating to about 30,000 years ago in what is now the Czech Republic is interpreted by some researchers as that of a shaman. The anthropologist Alice Kehoe criticizes the term, arguing that drumming, trance and chanting also occur outside shamanism and cannot usefully be generalized into a global religion, and she doubts that shamanism is an unchanged survival from the Paleolithic. Traditional Indigenous shamanism is believed to be declining, while some communities are reclaiming their traditions.
shamash-shum-ukin: Šamaš-šuma-ukin was a son of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon and the elder brother of Esarhaddon's successor Ashurbanipal. He was probably the second eldest son, younger only than the crown prince Sin-nadin-apli. When Sin-nadin-apli died unexpectedly in 674 BCE, Esarhaddon drew up new succession plans to avoid a crisis after his own death. Ashurbanipal, the fourth eldest son, was to inherit Assyria, while Šamaš-šuma-ukin was designated heir to Babylonia, the two being called equal brothers. He was nevertheless to swear an oath of allegiance to Ashurbanipal. Why the elder son was bypassed for Assyria is not known.

Ashurbanipal became king of Assyria at once on Esarhaddon's death, and Šamaš-šuma-ukin was crowned king of Babylon in the spring of the next year. At his coronation the statue of Marduk, taken from the city by his grandfather Sennacherib twenty years before, was returned to Babylon. Although he was ethnically and culturally Assyrian, he assimilated well: his inscriptions use Babylonian imagery to an unprecedented extent, he took part in the Babylonian New Year's festival, rebuilt the walls of Sippar, restored shrines and increased the land of the Ishtar temple in Uruk.

He remained a closely monitored vassal. Contemporary records show him in control only of Babylon and its vicinity, and governors of cities such as Nippur, Uruk and Ur regarded Ashurbanipal as their king. When the Elamite king Teumman invaded Babylonia in 653 BCE he had to rely on Ashurbanipal for troops. Resentment grew, and in 652 BCE he revolted, seeking independence for Babylonia rather than the Assyrian throne. His allies included Chaldeans, Arameans and Elamites, and perhaps the Medes. For two years battles were fought across Babylonia, with several minor players repeatedly changing sides.

The Elamites were defeated near Der, and by 650 BCE Ashurbanipal's forces had besieged Sippar, Borsippa, Kutha and Babylon. Babylon fell in 648 BCE after a siege of two years, with famine in the city, and was plundered. Ashurbanipal's inscriptions describe a bloodbath. Šamaš-šuma-ukin's fate is unclear: historians traditionally hold that he burned himself in his palace, but contemporary texts say only that he met a cruel death and that the gods consigned him to a fire. Ashurbanipal then placed his official Kandalanu on the Babylonian throne as a vassal.

Assyrian scribes found the episode hard to record, since Šamaš-šuma-ukin was a legitimately installed king and a member of the royal family. Ashurbanipal's inscriptions often call him only the king, and later Assyrian kings do not mention him. Steles he had erected were mutilated, erasing his face, which points to a large-scale damnatio memoriae.
shambaa-people: The Shambaa call their highland home Shambaai, where the bananas thrive, and set it against the nyika, the dry plains below, where malaria is endemic and which highlanders feared to stay in even for a night. Some Shambaa hold that they have always lived in the mountains, while many old clans of southern Usambara say they came up from Zigualand during famines. Before the Kilindi there was no central authority: the descendants of one ancestor lived on one hill and sacrificed to their ancestors together, and villages were linked by marriage, shared irrigation works, rituals and the elders' meetings that settled disputes.

In the Kilindi tradition the kingdom was founded by Mbegha, a hunter driven from Ngulu by his kin, who killed the wild pigs ruining Shambaa crops, gave away meat and was made king. Historians note that this is the story as the Kilindi wished it told, since questioning it could mean death. His son Bughe set up the capital at Vuga. Under Kimweri ye Nyumbai, who reigned from about 1815 to 1862, the kingdom reached its height, though the Zigua had taken guns and the Pangani valley in the 1830s.

After Kimweri's death the kingdom split between his grandson Shekulwavu and his son Semboja, whose base at Mazinde lay near the caravan route. In the Kiva rebellion of 1869 the Bondei, subjects on the eastern plains who paid tribute but gained little, killed every Kilindi they could capture. Afterwards Bonde stayed independent, Shekulwavu's survivors held the east and Semboja's followers the west, including Vuga, and both sides sought foreign allies.

The Shambaa speak Shambala, or Kisambaa, a North East Coastal Bantu language mutually intelligible with Bondei and Zigua; long intermarriage has led some to call the three Boshazi. Bananas were long their main food. The missionary Johann Krapf described the crop in 1848 and 1850, and German missionaries estimated in the early 1890s that bananas covered up to 45 per cent of arable land. They also grew maize, taro, beans, millet, sorghum, sugar cane, yams and sweet potatoes. Their number was estimated at 664,000 in 2001.
shams-al-dawla: Shams al-Dawla, whose own name was Abu Taher and whose regnal name means Sun of the State, was a son of the Buyid ruler Fakhr al-Dawla. When his father died in 997, his elder brother Abu Taleb Rostam, known as Majd al-Dawla, took power in the bulk of their father's possessions in Jibal, while Abu Taher received the governorships of Hamadan and Kirmanshah. Since both sons were still minors, their mother, known as the Sayyida, assumed the regency.

Both brothers at first took the title of Shâhanshâh, implying that they were subordinate to no one. They abandoned it when they accepted the authority of their cousin Baha' al-Dawla, by 1009 or 1010 at the latest. In 1006 or 1007 Majd al-Dawla tried to throw off his mother's regency. The Sayyida gained the support of the Kurdish ruler Badr ibn Hasanwaih and of Shams al-Dawla, whose forces laid siege to Ray and fought several battles with Majd al-Dawla's troops.

When Ray was finally taken, Majd al-Dawla was imprisoned for a year, and Shams al-Dawla ruled the city during that time; when the Sayyida released his brother, he returned to Hamadan. Around 1013, after the death of Badr ibn Hasanwaih, Shams al-Dawla occupied part of Badr's territory. Later in his reign he tried to replace Majd al-Dawla as ruler of Ray, but the Sayyida foiled his plans.

In 1015 Shams al-Dawla called upon the prominent Persian scholar Avicenna to treat him. During Avicenna's stay at his court Shams al-Dawla made him his vizier, so that the physician who attended the ruler also served as his chief minister. Shams al-Dawla died in 1021, having ruled Hamadan since 997, and was succeeded by his son Sama' al-Dawla.
shamshi-adad-i: Shamshi-Adad I was an Amorite ruler of Ekallatum who became king of Assyria and conquered lands across much of Syria, Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia, creating what is called the Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia. He inherited the throne of Ekallatum from Ila-kabkabu, whom the later Assyrian King List names as his father. When Naram-Sin of Eshnunna attacked Ekallatum, Shamshi-Adad fled to Babylonia and stayed in exile until Naram-Sin died.

He then retook Ekallatum, overthrew King Erishum II of Assyria and took Assur, emerging as the first Amorite king of Assyria. Later Assyrian tradition regarded him as an Amorite, though earlier archaeologists wrongly took him for a native Assyrian. At Assur he held the title Governor of Assur and rebuilt the temple of the god Assur, whose bricks carry his name as builder.

He took over the long-abandoned town of Shekhna, now Tell Leilan, and renamed it Šubat-Enlil, "the residence of the god Enlil", making it his capital. A main target of his expansion was Mari, which controlled the caravan route between Anatolia and Mesopotamia. Its king Yahdun-Lim was assassinated by his own servants, possibly on Shamshi-Adad's orders, and the heir Zimri-Lim fled to Yamhad. Shamshi-Adad occupied Mari and placed his sons in charge: Ishme-Dagan I at Ekallatum and Yasmah-Adad at Mari. He proclaimed himself "King of the Universe", a title Sargon of Akkad had used.

His relations with Eshnunna alternated between alliance and war. Around 1781 BCE he joined King Dadusha in a campaign between the two Zab rivers, then turned on Dadusha and attacked cities including Shaduppum, Nerebtum and Andarig. His campaigns were carefully planned, and his army used encircling ramparts and battering rams.

His letters to his sons show a ruler who controlled state business closely. He scolded Yasmah-Adad: "Are you a child, not a man, have you no beard on your chin?" He also arranged for Yasmah-Adad to marry Beltum, daughter of Ishi-Addu of Qatna, and insisted that she be kept in a leading position in the palace.

The kingdom lacked cohesion, and after his death around 1776 BCE Eshnunna captured cities around Assur while old rivals moved against his sons. Zimri-Lim expelled Yasmah-Adad from Mari, and under Ishme-Dagan I the rest was lost to a coalition of Mari, Andarig and Eshnunna and then to the Amorite ruler Hammurabi of Babylon.
shamsuddin-ilyas-shah: Ilyas Shah was a Sunni Muslim whose origins lay in the Sistan region, in what is now eastern Iran and southern Afghanistan, though whether he was born there is disputed. According to Syed A M R Haque, his forebears came to the subcontinent as Muslim missionaries and were granted jagirs in Bengal by the Delhi Sultanate in 1227. He rose through the Delhi Sultanate's service, by one account first under Malik Firuz in Delhi and later under Izzuddin Yahya, an imperial provincial governor in Bengal. In the early 14th century the sultanate ruled Bengal as three provinces, based at Satgaon, Sonargaon and Lakhnauti.

After Yahya's death in 1338 Ilyas took the title Shams ad-Din and fought a long war, from 1339 to 1352, against Sultan Alauddin Ali Shah and Sultan Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah. Having united Bengal, he moved his capital to Pandua, once a seat of the Gaur kings and Pala emperors. He kept an army of 90,000 cavalry and many elephants. In 1346 he led the first Muslim army into Nepal, occupying Tirhut and raiding the Kathmandu Valley, where his troops sacked the temple of Swayambhunath and looted Kathmandu for three days. He also invaded Orissa, sacking Jajpur and Cuttack, and was the first Muslim king to capture Guwahati.

When Firuz Shah Tughluq invaded in November 1353 and occupied Pandua, Ilyas held out in the fortress of Ekdala for two months, then pursued the withdrawing army as far as Varanasi. Firuz Shah returned to Delhi in 1355, and Ilyas's realm reached the Koshi River. His coins call him the second Alexander. Persian became his court language, and later in his reign he exchanged gifts with Firuz Shah, sending elephants for Turkish and Arabian horses.

Ilyas Shah died in January 1358 and was buried in Hajipur, the former village of Ukkacala, which he had fortified and which was renamed in his honour. In 1587 Makhsus Shah, brother of Akbar's governor of Bihar, built a congregational mosque inside his fort there. A mazar on SDO Road attributed to him is revered by Muslims and Hindus, who hold a mela at his Urus each year. His dynasty ruled Bengal for 145 years.
shan-state: Shan State borders China (Yunnan) to the north, Laos to the east, Thailand to the south, and five administrative divisions of Myanmar to the west. It covers 155,800 square kilometres, almost a quarter of the country's area, and most of it is a hilly plateau, the Shan Plateau, cut by the gorge of the Thanlwin or Salween River. Inle Lake, where the Intha people live in floating villages, is the second largest natural expanse of water in the country. Taunggyi is the capital, and the Tai, or Shan, are the majority among the several ethnic groups of the state.

The Shan States were founded in the Shan Hills during the Pagan Kingdom, and their founding accelerated after 1287, when the Mongols overthrew Pagan and the Tai who came south with them stayed. The most powerful were Mong Yang and Mong Kawng in present-day Kachin State, followed by Hsenwi, Hsipaw and Mong Mit. They were multi-ethnic, including Chin, Kachin, Wa, Pa O and Kayah peoples. A Mohnyin-led confederation of Shan states conquered Ava in 1527.

In 1555 King Bayinnaung dislodged the Shan king from Ava and by 1557 had conquered all the Burmese Shan states, reducing them to governorships. The saophas, the rulers, kept their regalia and feudal rights, but their sons had to live in the Burmese king's palace as hostages, a policy continued until 1885. Several northern states were annexed by the Qing dynasty in the 1730s. The Konbaung dynasty's reassertion of control led to war with China between 1765 and 1769, and its success laid the foundation for the present boundary. Burma lost southern Lan Na in 1776 and northern Lan Na in 1786 to Siam.

The British captured Mandalay on 28 November 1885, but it took until 1890 to subdue all the Shan states, which then were ruled by their saophas as feudatory princely states. In October 1922 the Shan and Karenni states were merged as the Federated Shan States. At the Panglong Conference in February 1947 a unitary Shan State was agreed, including the former Wa states, with the right of secession after ten years. Rebellions and the Chinese Nationalist invasion of 1950 followed independence, and in the 1960s eastern Shan State became a major opium-growing area, part of the Golden Triangle.
shandong: Shandong lies on the eastern edge of the North China Plain and in the lower reaches of the Yellow River, and extends into the sea as the Shandong Peninsula. It borders the Bohai Sea to the north, Hebei to the northwest, Henan to the west, Jiangsu to the south and the Yellow Sea to the east. The name means east of the mountain, and refers to its position east of the Taihang Mountains; it came into use when the Jin dynasty established the military command offices of Shandong East Circuit and Shandong West Circuit in 1168. The province is a centre of Taoism, Chinese Buddhism and Confucianism, and Mount Tai has one of the longest histories of continuous religious worship in the world.

A succession of Neolithic cultures lived in Shandong, among them the Houli, Beixin, Dawenkou, Longshan and Yueshi cultures. The Qin dynasty conquered Qi and founded the first centralised Chinese state in 221 BCE, and the Han dynasty then created commanderies under the Qingzhou and Yanzhou inspectorates. The Ming dynasty created the modern province, and in 1376 moved its capital from Qingzhou to Jinan, which remained the capital for seven centuries.

After the Second Opium War the Qing court opened Cheefoo as a trade port, and Western powers established consulates, missionaries and factories there. In the 1880s Shandong became the base of the Beiyang Fleet, which the Imperial Japanese Navy defeated in 1894. After the killing of two German Catholic missionaries in the Juye Incident, the Qing government had to cede Qingdao to the German Empire, and in 1898 Weihaiwei went to Britain. During the warlord era the Fengtian clique installed Zhang Zongchang as military governor in April 1925; he ruled until 1928 and was succeeded by Han Fuju. The Jiaozhou–Jinan Railway, constructed by Germans from 1899 to 1904, connects Jinan with Qingdao and remains the main east–west line across the province.

Shandong is a coastal province of eastern China with Jinan as its capital, and the 2020 census counted 101.5 million people. Qufu, the birthplace of Confucius, later became the centre of Confucianism, and the Buddhist temples in the mountains south of Jinan were once among the foremost in China. Shandong cuisine is one of the eight great traditions of Chinese cooking. Its literature largely reflects Confucianism, and classics such as the Analects, Mencius and the Zuo Zhuan come from the province. Qingdao keeps German-era architecture.
shang-yang: Shang Yang, also called Wei Yang, was originally surnamed Gongsun. According to the Shiji he was the son of a concubine of the ruling ducal family of the minor state of Wey. As a young man he studied law and obtained a position under Prime Minister Shuzuo of the state of Wei, then left that lowly post, with the support of Duke Xiao of Qin, to become chief adviser in Qin. He served as Qin's chief minister for twenty years.

He launched two series of reforms. The first, in 356 BCE, put into force Li Kui's Book of Law, with the addition of a rule punishing those who knew of a crime and failed to inform the government. Land was assigned to soldiers according to their military success, nobles unwilling to fight lost their land rights, and the army was divided into twenty grades according to battlefield achievement. The cultivation of wasteland and immigration were encouraged, and agriculture was favoured over luxury commerce. The second set, in 350 BCE, brought a standardised system of land allocation and tax reforms.

Most of the measures were taken from policies tried elsewhere, such as those of Wu Qi of Chu, but his were more thorough and extreme and placed policy in the ruler's hands. He partly abolished primogeniture and doubled the tax on households with more than one adult son, to break large clans into nuclear families. He also moved the capital from Yueyang to Xianyang to reduce the influence of nobles.

The Qin nobility despised Shang Yang, and he was vulnerable after the death of Duke Xiao. The next ruler, King Huiwen, ordered the nine familial exterminations against him on grounds of fomenting rebellion. He was executed by being torn apart by chariots, and his family was killed. Sima Qian tells it differently: he fled to Wei, was expelled, raised a rebel army in his fief and died in battle. King Huiwen kept his reforms.

Han Fei credits him with the theories of fixing the standards and equality before the law, and the Book of Lord Shang is likely the work of both him and his followers. Sima Qian reports that after ten years of the ordinances the commoners of Qin were delighted, and that no one picked up lost articles on the road.
shang-zhixin: Shang Zhixin was born in 1636, the eldest son of Shang Kexi, who had abandoned the Ming dynasty for the Qing and held the title Prince of Pingnan, the prince who pacifies the south.
