In 1673 Shang Kexi, pleading old age, asked the Kangxi Emperor to let him retire to his adopted homeland of Liaodong, and passed his position to Shang Zhixin, who took charge of the defence of Guangdong province.

The court, pursuing a policy of centralisation, soon decided to abolish the Pingnan Feudatory on the pretext that Shang Zhixin was difficult to control. Shang Kexi was willing to move his family back to Haicheng, but the rising of the feudatories under Wu Sangui and Geng Jingzhong ended the plan. Shang Zhixin was ordered to return military command to his father, who stayed loyal, many of his men deserted to the rebels, and from 1673 to 1676 Guangzhou held out as a Qing fortress in rebel territory.

Early in 1676 troops loyal to Shang Zhixin put his father under house arrest, and he joined Wu Sangui. After Shang Kexi's death late that year, and the surrender of rebel generals such as Wang Fuchen, he went back over to the Qing. Ordered to lead troops against Wu Sangui, he made only token efforts, hoping to preserve his own forces.

In 1679 the emperor stripped him of much of his military power. In 1680, with a Qing victory near, he was arrested, taken to Beijing and ordered to kill himself; in return his family was spared from punishment, although four of his 36 brothers were executed at the time of his suicide. He was known for the cruelty of his rule, in which some of his personal enemies were torn apart by hunting dogs.
shangdu: Shangdu, meaning Upper Capital, lies in what is now Zhenglan Banner, Inner Mongolia, in the grasslands north of the Great Wall, about 350 km north of Beijing and 28 km north-west of present-day Duolun County. It was designed by the architect Liu Bingzhong, a trusted adviser to Kublai Khan and a former Buddhist monk, as a seasonal retreat that blended Mongolian steppe traditions with Chinese urban planning.

The city was first called Kaiping and was established between 1252 and 1256. In 1264 Kublai Khan renamed it Shangdu and made it the summer capital of the Yuan dynasty. It was laid out in three parts: an outer city, an inner city and a central imperial palace whose enclosure measured about 550 metres on each side, roughly 40 per cent of the later Forbidden City in Beijing. Kublai Khan held court there, received foreign envoys and conducted affairs of state. At its height the city had a population of over 100,000 and included gardens, hunting grounds, temples and administrative quarters.

Marco Polo visited around 1275 and described a marble palace whose rooms were gilded and painted with figures, set within a walled park with fountains and rivers. He also recounted a portable cane palace with lacquered dragons that could be taken apart and moved at the emperor's command. When the Yuan dynasty fell, the last Yuan emperor, Toghon Temür, is credited with a lament for his Yellow Steppe of Xanadu. The city was largely destroyed and abandoned, and though its original name, Kaiping, was briefly restored, the settlement never recovered.

In 1872 the British diplomat Steven Bushell visited the ruins and noted surviving temples, marble blocks and decorative tiles, but by the late 20th century local residents of Dolon Nor had scavenged many of these materials for building. The Chinese government has worked to preserve and study the site since 2002, and UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2012.

In the West the name entered literature through Samuel Purchas, who in 1614 described Xandu as a pleasure palace with a vast park, drawing on Marco Polo. Samuel Taylor Coleridge, inspired by Purchas, wrote the poem Kubla Khan, begun in 1797, whose opening line has Kubla Khan decree a stately pleasure-dome in Xanadu.
shanghai: Shanghai lies on the Yangtze Estuary of China's east coast, with the Yangtze River to the north, Hangzhou Bay to the south and the East China Sea to the east. The Huangpu River bisects the city. The land is an alluvial plain formed by the Yangtze's deposition and by land reclamation, and most of it is flat, with an average elevation of four metres. The soil is soft, so skyscrapers have to be built on deep concrete piles to avoid sinking.

The western part of the area was inhabited 6,000 years ago. In the Spring and Autumn period it belonged to the Kingdom of Wu, which was conquered by Yue and then by Chu. The name Shanghai, on the sea, is first found in the 11th-century Song dynasty, and in 1280 the place was renamed Shanghai.

Originally a fishing village and market town, Shanghai grew to prominence in the 19th century through trade and its port. It was one of five treaty ports forced open to European trade after the First Opium War, and the Shanghai International Settlement and the French Concession were set up there. In the 1930s it was a primary commercial and financial hub of Asia. In the Second World War it fell under Japanese rule after the Battle of Shanghai, and the Communists took it during the Chinese Civil War. The reform and opening up supported by Deng Xiaoping led to extensive redevelopment by the 1990s, especially in the Pudong New Area.

Shanghai is one of the four municipalities under the direct administration of the Central People's Government and is divided into 16 districts. Its historic sites include the City God Temple, Yu Garden and the row of early 20th-century buildings along the Bund.
shanghai-french-concession: The concession was established on 6 April 1849, when the French consul Charles de Montigny obtained a proclamation from Lin Gui, the circuit intendant of Shanghai. It began as a narrow collar of land of 66 hectares around the northern end of the walled Old City, south of the British settlement and about a third of its size. A riverside strip for the quai de France was added in 1861, an extension agreed in 1899 doubled it, and in 1914 the government of Yuan Shikai gave France police and tax powers over its extra-settlement roads, an area 15 times the original grant, in return for evicting revolutionaries.

France left the International Settlement's Municipal Council in 1862, and the concession was run by its own Municipal Administrative Council under the consul-general and policed by the Shanghai French Police, with many men from Annam. Its newer western part, its avenues planted with London planes from 1902, became by the 1920s the premier residential area of Shanghai. Russian émigrés, 41 in 1915 and 7,000 after the revolution, shaped its shops and music; Sun Yat-sen and Soong Ching-ling lived on Rue Molière, and Eileen Chang finished Love in a Fallen City there.

In 1937, during the Battle of Shanghai, Chinese bombs fell on the concession twice by mistake, killing several hundred people, and Vice Admiral Jules Le Bigot halted Japanese troops at its entrance by sitting on a folding chair in the street. Refugees from the Chinese districts raised its population to 825,342. Vichy France handed it to the Wang Jingwei government on 30 July 1943, and in February 1946 France gave up all its concessions in China.

The former concession lies in the north-eastern part of Xuhui District and the western part of Huangpu District, the former Luwan District. Large parts of it are designated historical-cultural conservation zones, among them the Hengfu area, and its plane-tree avenues, shikumen houses and Art Deco buildings such as the Normandie Apartments survive.
shango: In Yoruba tradition Shango is a royal ancestor as well as a god: as the third Alaafin of Oyo he is said to have brought the empire prosperity before his deification. According to Professor Mason's Mythological Account of Heroes and Kings, he was, unlike his peaceful brother Ajaka, a powerful, bellicose and violent ruler, whose seven years on the throne were filled with campaigns and battles. A related deity of Yorubaland, Ara, whose name means thunder, is often closely associated with him.

Two narratives describe him. In one he casts a thunderstone to earth against anyone who offends him, and worshippers in Yorubaland in Nigeria avoid cowpea for fear of his wrath. In the other he breathes fire and smoke through his nostrils and is angered by his quarrelsome wives. He was feared for tyranny and destructive power but revered for bravery and fairness. His necklaces are of red and white beads, usually in groups of four or six, his sacred numbers, and stones made by lightning are kept at sacred sites and used in rituals.

He is worshipped on the fifth day of the week, Ojo Jakuta, with the bata drum, red clothing and foods such as guguru, bitter cola, àmàlà and gbegiri soup. Shango is still called on during coronation ceremonies in Nigeria.

Devotion to him gave its name to Yoruba religions in Trinidad and in Recife, Brazil. In Haiti he is Ogou Chango of the Nago nation, and Palo knows him as Siete Rayos. In Candomblé, Xangô is believed to have many manifestations, among them Ayrá, Agodo and Afonja. He gained strong importance among the enslaved in Brazil for his strength, resistance and aggression and became patron of plantations and many terreiros, while Oko, the orixá of agriculture, found little favour. The main barracão of the terreiro Casa Branca is dedicated to him, and his ritual dish, amalá, is served on Wednesday at his altar. He is the protagonist of Duro Ladipo's play Ọba kò so of 1963.
shangqiu: Shangqiu lies in the easternmost part of Henan province, on the North China Plain, where the land is mostly flat and the soil fertile. Its name means Hills of Shang. The city and its surroundings were an important base of the Shang dynasty. Tradition places the early rulers Shennong, Zhuanxu and Ku in this area, together with Ku's son Xie, who helped Yu the Great to control the floods and received the land of Shang as a fief.

According to tradition, Xie's thirteenth-generation descendant Tang overthrew the Xia dynasty and founded the Shang, whose first capital, Nanbo, lay south of present-day Shangqiu. When the Zhou replaced the Shang around the 11th century BCE, the Shang royal descendants were given the area, which became the State of Song, with its capital Suiyang. Song was a major power in the Spring and Autumn period, declined in the Warring States period and fell to Qi and Wei in 286 BCE. Under the Han, Suiyang was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang, and a failed siege of it brought the collapse of the main rebel army in the Rebellion of the Seven States.

A ten-month siege of Suiyang in 757, during the An Lushan rebellion, turned the war in the Tang's favour. Zhao Kuangyin was military governor of a region centred on Songzhou before he founded the Song dynasty in 960 and took its name from it. The city was the Southern Capital of the Northern Song. After the Jurchens captured Kaifeng in 1127 the court withdrew to Shangqiu because of its link with Emperor Taizu, and Gaozong was crowned there on 12 June 1127. The capital moved to Yangzhou in 1128 and to Hangzhou in 1129. The present name dates from 1545, when Shangqiu County was created.

Shangqiu is a prefecture-level city of Henan. The Longhai railway, completed in 1916, made it a regional transport centre, and the Beijing-Kowloon line crosses it there. The Suiyang old city, built in 1511 under the Ming, is one of the best preserved traditional cities in China and was listed as a historical city by the central government in 1986. The philosophers Zhuangzi and Mozi are said to have come from the area.
shanhai-pass: The Shanhai Pass, whose name means Mountain-Sea Pass, commands the narrowest choke point of the Liaoxi Corridor, a coastal plain between the foothills of the Yan Mountains and the Bohai Sea. This is the only easily traversable land route between North China and the Northeast. It lies in what is now Shanhaiguan District of Qinhuangdao in Hebei, on the east bank of the Shi River, with walls running from the mountains to the shore of Liaodong Bay. An army wishing to avoid a costly siege had to circumvent it through narrow mountain passes deep in the Yan Mountains, which made long supply lines and large invasions difficult.

Passes stood here under the Northern Qi, Sui and Tang dynasties, and by 785 a garrison had been established at Yuguan, as the Tang called the site. The area was later controlled by the Liao dynasty, and garrisons were built under the Jin and Yuan. In 1381 the Ming general Xu Da was ordered to repair the old Yongping and Jieling passes, and from this the present pass took shape. It was reinforced heavily after the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing, and in the late sixteenth century the general Qi Jiguang began building a military city around it, with forts to the east, south and north.

In 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng entered Beijing, ending the Ming dynasty, and tried to win over Wu Sangui, the Ming general commanding the Ningyuan garrison. Instead of submitting to Li's Shun dynasty, Wu contacted the Manchu Qing and proposed a joint effort to drive the rebels out of the capital. The Qing regent Dorgon marched to the pass, and together Wu and the Manchus defeated Li's army near it. Li abandoned Beijing, and the Qing army entered unopposed.

The pass is square, with a perimeter of about four kilometres and walls 14 metres high and 7 metres thick, surrounded on three sides by a moat. Of its four gates only the Zhendong Gate in the east wall survives. It is one of the best preserved passes of the Great Wall, and the point where the wall meets the sea is known as the Old Dragon's Head. It was listed as part of the Great Wall as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
shantarakshita: Śāntarakṣita, whose name means protected by the One who is at peace, lived from 725 to 788 according to the dates given for him. Few historical records of him exist, and most of the available material is hagiographic. According to the 19th-century commentator Ju Mipham, he was the son of the king of Zahor, which some sources place around Bhagalpur and Banka in eastern Bihar. He was an Indian monk of the Mulasarvastivada lineage who lived under the Pala Empire. Tibetan sources say he studied under Jñānagarbha at Nalanda and became its abbot after mastering all branches of learning. Tibetan sources call him, Jñānagarbha and Kamalaśīla the three eastern Svātantrikas.

King Trisong Detsen invited him to Tibet to help establish Buddhism, and a first journey can be dated to 763. According to Tibetan sources such as the Blue Annals, that visit failed because of the activities of local spirits, and he spent six years in Nepal before returning. He came back with the tantric adept Padmasambhava, who performed the rites that appeased the spirits, and he then oversaw the building of Samye, modelled on the Indian monastery of Uddaṇḍapura.

He ordained the first seven Tibetan monastics there, with the help of twelve Indian monks, about 779, and stayed as abbot for the rest of his life. At Samye he set up a monastic curriculum on the Indian model and oversaw the translation of scriptures into Tibetan, with scholars such as Vimalamitra, Buddhaguhya, Śāntigarbha and Viśuddhasiṃha. He and his students first taught the ten good actions, the six paramitas and dependent origination. Tibetan sources say he died suddenly after being kicked by a horse.

Around eleven works may be his. His Tattvasaṅgraha is a compendium of more than 3,600 verses in 26 chapters that sets out and refutes the non-Buddhist views of his time, including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya and the Cārvākas. A Sanskrit copy, with the commentary of his pupil Kamalaśīla, was found in 1873 by Dr G. Bühler in a Jain temple at Jaisalmer. His Madhyamakālaṅkāra, the Ornament of the Middle Way, sets out his synthesis of Madhyamaka with Yogācāra and the epistemology of Dharmakirti. It argues for emptiness by showing that things have neither a single nor a manifold nature, and it accepts mind-only teaching on the conventional level.

His approach stayed the main Tibetan reading of Madhyamaka until the 11th and 12th centuries, when Candrakirti's work began to be translated. Tsongkhapa later criticised it, and Prasaṅgika Madhyamaka replaced it as the dominant view. In the 19th century Ju Mipham revived it as part of the Rimé movement, and the Madhyamakālaṅkāra is now studied by all Nyingma shedra students.
shanxi: Shanxi lies on a plateau made up of higher ground to the east, in the Taihang Mountains, and to the west, in the Lüliang Mountains, with a series of valleys in the centre through which the Fen River runs. The name means west of the mountains, a reference to its position west of the Taihang range. The Great Wall forms most of the northern border with Inner Mongolia, and the province also borders Hebei to the east, Henan to the south and Shaanxi to the west. The highest peak is Mount Wutai, at 3,058 metres, and the total area is 156,700 square kilometres.

The state of Jin, which existed in what is now Shanxi during the Spring and Autumn period (c. 770 – c. 481 BCE), gave the province its one-character abbreviation, Jin. Jin split into three states, Han, Zhao and Wei, in 403 BCE, a date sometimes taken as the start of the Warring States period, and all of them had fallen to the state of Qin by 221 BCE. The Han dynasty ruled the region as Bingzhou. During the Sixteen Kingdoms period several regimes controlled it in turn, followed by the Northern Wei (386–534), a Xianbei kingdom with one of its early capitals at present-day Datong.

Under the Ming and Qing dynasties Shanxi merchants, also called Jin merchants, dominated China's commerce and finance, a phenomenon that lasted for centuries from the Song to the Qing. Their networks reached Russia, Japan, Korea, Central Asia, Southeast Asia and South Asia. They controlled the overland tea trade with Russia and Mongolia, monopolised trade routes across the Great Wall and handled the Qing government's tax remittances between provinces.

After the Qing collapsed, Shanxi was governed for nearly four decades by Yan Xishan and kept a high degree of de facto autonomy within the Republic of China. When Japan invaded in 1937, Shanxi was one of the first areas attacked, and Yan invited Communist forces to re-enter the province. They arrived in time to help defeat a stronger Japanese force at the Pingxing Pass, in the Battle of Pingxingguan.

Shanxi is a province of North China whose capital and largest city is Taiyuan. The population is more than 99 per cent Han Chinese, and the dominant local language, Jin Chinese, is the only major Sinitic variety in northern China that is not classified within the Mandarin group. The province holds roughly one third of China's coal reserves. It has by far the largest number of historic buildings of any Chinese province, over 28,000 ancient structures, and three UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Pingyao Ancient City, the Yungang Grottoes and Mount Wutai.
shaoxing: Shaoxing is a prefecture-level city on the southern shore of Hangzhou Bay in north-eastern Zhejiang province, on the south bank of the Qiantang River estuary. It borders Ningbo to the east, Taizhou to the south-east, Jinhua to the south-west and Hangzhou to the west. The city was first named Shaoxing in 1131 during the Southern Song dynasty, after the reign period of Emperor Gaozong of Song.

The city lies north of the Kuaiji Mountains, an important centre of the people of Yue in the Spring and Autumn period. Chinese legend connected the mountains with events in the life of Yu the Great, the founder of the Xia. Around the early 5th century BCE, in the time of the Yue king Goujian, his people began to establish permanent centres on the plain north of the hills. After his release from captivity in Wu, Goujian commissioned his adviser Fan Li to build a major triangular fortification in the area of the present Yuecheng District.

After the Qin conquest in 222 BCE the First Emperor visited Mount Kuaiji in the last year of his reign, 210 BCE, and sacrificed to the spirit of Yu. The stele he erected is lost, but Sima Qian saw it and preserved its text in his Records of the Grand Historian. The area's capital was known as Kuaiji until the 12th century, when it was renamed Shaoxing.

Under the Ming and Qing dynasties Shaoxing was a prefecture of eight counties. From the later Ming through the Qing it was known, sometimes with disapproval, for its network of natives in the imperial bureaucracy, who cooperated out of loyalty to their place of origin. It also supplied unofficial legal specialists, the Shaoxing masters, whose knowledge of the Qing legal code let officials trained in the Confucian Classics judge local cases. In the early 20th century the prefecture was abolished and its name applied to a new county.

Shaoxing is a prefecture-level city administering three districts, two county-level cities and one county. It is known for Shaoxing rice wine, brewed with the water of Mirror Lake, and for Yue opera, sung in the local dialect. Its sites include the Tomb of Yu the Great, the Orchid Pavilion, commemorating the calligrapher Wang Xizhi, and the Shen Garden, associated with the poet Lu You. Several places connected with the writer Lu Xun, who was born in the city, survive.
shapsugs: The Shapsugs are one of the twelve major Circassian tribes and were historically among the largest groups of the Black Sea Adyghe. The Little Shapsug lived between the Dzhubga and Shakhe rivers, while the Greater Shapsug held high mountain country on the northern slopes of the Caucasus. They controlled the ports of Dzhubga and Tuapse and the gorges behind them. Before the Russo-Caucasian War, sources put their number between 150,000 and 300,000.

The tribe consisted of five aristocratic families and 81 free clans, and it is classed as one of the three democratic Adyghe tribes. The Shapsugs supported other Adyghe tribes in their struggle against the Crimean Khanate. In the Caucasian War they were among the most stubborn opponents of Imperial Russia and joined the alliance of Shamil, which lasted until 1859. In late 1860 representatives of three Adyghe tribes, the Shapsug, Ubykh and Natukhai, met in a council that named Sochi the last capital of the Circassian resistance.

Traditional Shapsug culture had much in common with that of the other Circassian tribes. The Shapsugs practised agriculture, cattle and horse breeding, horticulture, viticulture and beekeeping. In pre-Islamic and pre-Christian times they worshipped Circassian gods, among them Shible, god of thunder and lightning, Sozeresh, god of fertility, Tlepsh, god of blacksmithing, and Keshkogwasha, god of the Black Sea. In droughts they performed the Hantse Guashe ceremony, carrying a dressed doll through the village and drowning it in the river. Since the early 19th century they have been mainly Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. Their speech is a sub-dialect of the West Adyghe dialect of Adyghe, and before the exile there were two major varieties of it.

The Shapsugs were among the last to lay down their weapons in 1864, and some fought on into the 1880s. After the war the overwhelming majority were forcibly evicted to the Ottoman Empire and elsewhere in the Middle East, and only a small part of the tribe stayed on its native land. On 6 September 1924 the Bolsheviks created a Shapsug national district of about 3,400 people, which was renamed Lazarevsky district in 1945. A resolution of 12 June 1992 re-established it, after the tribe's first congress in 1990.

Today the largest Shapsug communities are in Turkey, with others in Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq. The first Circassians to settle in Amman were Shapsugs. In Russia the census of 2002 counted 3,231 Shapsugs.
shapur-i: Shapur was a son of Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian Empire, and his wife Murrod, whom Shapur names as his mother in his inscriptions. A semi-historical biography of Ardashir tells that the Parthian king's daughter Zijanak tried to poison her husband and was hidden with her son for seven years, but modern historians treat this as a story meant to link the Sasanians with the Parthian nobility. Shapur took part in his father's war against the Arsacids, including the Battle of Hormozdgan on 28 April 224, in which Artabanus IV was defeated and killed. Ardashir considered him the gentlest, wisest, bravest and ablest of his children and named him his successor.

In the east Shapur annexed most of the land of the Kushans and founded the city of Nishapur. In the west he seized Nisibis and Carrhae and advanced into Syria. Gordian III's forces defeated him at the Battle of Resaena, but he then won the Battle of Misiche and forced Philip the Arab to sign a peace in 244 and pay 500,000 gold denarii, which the Romans called a most shameful treaty. Later he annihilated a Roman force of 60,000 at the Battle of Barbalissos and ravaged Syria.

Emperor Valerian recovered Antioch by 257, but he pursued the Persians to Edessa, where he and the Roman army were captured. Shapur then took Caesarea and deported many thousands of Roman subjects, who built a dyke near Shushtar and the city of Bishapur. Captives of Antioch were settled in Gundeshapur. He did not seem interested in permanently occupying Roman provinces, preferring plunder, and in the 260s Odaenathus of Palmyra and Roman forces forced his withdrawal.

Shapur was the first Iranian monarch to style himself King of Kings of Iranians and non-Iranians, a title that became regular under his son Hormizd I. He called himself Mazda-worshipping, founded many fire temples, and treated Zoroastrian priests generously. He was tolerant of Mani, who joined his court and dedicated to him the Shabuhragan, but Shapur remained a Zoroastrian. According to Shapur's inscription at Hajiabad he was still active at court in his later years. He died of illness in Bishapur and was succeeded by Hormizd I; two other sons, Bahram I and Narseh, also became kings. His victory over Valerian is shown in reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam.
shapur-ii: Shapur II was the son of Hormizd II, who died in 309. His successor, Adur Narseh, was killed by nobles after a few months, and they blinded the second son and imprisoned the third, who later escaped to the Roman Empire. The throne was kept for Shapur, who took the title of King of Kings at birth. Sources differ on whether he was born after his father's death or was an infant, and a legend that he was crowned before birth is regarded as fiction by modern historians. The nobility and priesthood held power until 325, when he reached the age of sixteen.

At sixteen Shapur led an expedition against Arab tribes that had raided Pars, defeating the Iyad in Asoristan, crossing the Persian Gulf to al-Khatt and attacking the Banu Tamim in the Hajar Mountains. He deported several tribes and ordered a wall built near al-Hira. Historians consider the accounts of his cruelty exaggerated.

His main aim in the west was to undo the Peace of Nisibis of 298, which had given Rome provinces in Mesopotamia. In 337 he broke the peace, and he besieged Nisibis three times without taking it, while the Battle of Singara in 344 was indecisive. Nomad invasions in the east halted the war by 350. In 359 he took Amida after a siege of seventy-three days and deported its people to Khuzistan. After the Roman emperor Julian was killed in 363, his successor Jovian gave up the districts beyond the Tigris, Nisibis and Singara. Armenia remained contested: a joint Roman and Armenian army defeated Persian forces in 371, and a seven-year truce followed.

In the east he gained territory in what is now Afghanistan and Pakistan around 350, but from about 360 Bactria fell to the Kidarites. Under Shapur the collection of the Avesta was completed, heresy and apostasy were punished, and Christians were persecuted, a reaction to the Christianization of the Roman Empire under Constantine.

Shapur died in 379 and was succeeded by his brother Ardashir II, who agreed to rule until Shapur's son, Shapur III, came of age. At his death the empire was larger and stronger than when he took the throne. His death began a conflict of about 125 years between the great nobles, the wuzurgan, and the kings.
shar-kali-sharri: Shar-Kali-Sharri reigned about 2218 to 2193 BCE by the middle chronology, as ruler of Akkad, and succeeded his father Naram-Sin, who had deified himself in his lifetime. In the 1870s Assyriologists thought he was the same person as Sargon of Akkad, the first ruler, a mistake recognised in the 1910s.

His name was sometimes written with the sign marking a god, and he was later deified: two of his titles are "heroic god of Akkade" and "god of the land of Warium". It has been suggested that he was governor of Nippur before he took the crown, since texts show that he was crowned there, with his sister Tudanapšum, high priestess of Enlil at Nippur, taking part. His queen was Tuta-sar-libbis.

According to the Sumerian King List his reign lasted 25 years, matching the year names from his rule. He completed the establishment of direct Akkadian rule begun by his predecessor, with governors in cities such as Adab and Lagash who called themselves his servants. Early in his reign he made a royal progress to Sumer lasting at least six months, taking in Umma, Zabala, Isin, Girsu and Nippur, accompanied by at least five generals.

Work on the Ekur, the temple of Enlil at Nippur, begun by Naram-Sin, was completed under him and appears in seven of his year names, which name the general Puzur-Eshtar as its builder. He also built temples to Annunitum and Ilaba at Babylon and another to Ilaba at Zabala.

His year names suggest a fairly peaceful reign with the usual clashes with the nomadic MAR.TU, the Gutians and the Elamites, and economic texts point to reasonable prosperity. The Gutians were growing in influence, and at some point they made Adab their capital. A later Neo-Babylonian copy of one of his inscriptions says that he faced a widespread revolt and overcame it, though it may reflect the Great Revolt faced by Naram-Sin.

Tradition held that the Akkadian Empire began to unravel in his reign. According to the Sumerian King List and later literary compositions, after his death in about 2193 BCE the region fell into anarchy and no king could dominate for long. The king list asks: "Then who was king? Who was not the king?" and names four rulers, Igigi, Imi, Nanum and Ilulu, who together ruled only three years. Akkad then recovered a degree of order under Dudu, who reigned 21 years, and Shu-turul, who reigned 15. Puzer-Mama, a later governor of Lagash, declared himself ruler, possibly on Shar-Kali-Sharri's death, and began the second dynasty of Lagash.
sharaf-al-dawla: Before he took the title Sharaf al-Dawla he was known as Shirdil Abu'l-Fawaris. When his father 'Adud al-Dawla conquered Kerman in 968, Shirdil was made viceroy of the province. For some time after 977 he lived in Baghdad before being sent back to Kerman. As the eldest son he saw himself as his father's heir, and 'Adud al-Dawla's apparent preference for his second son Marzuban made him hostile to his brother. 'Adud al-Dawla had named no definite successor when he died in 983, and Marzuban, now called Samsam al-Dawla, took power in Baghdad as senior amir.

Shirdil pressed his own claim, invaded Fars from Kerman and took the title Sharaf al-Dawla. He was soon surrounded by rivals: Samsam al-Dawla in Baghdad, his brothers Taj al-Dawla and Diya' al-Dawla in Basra and Khuzestan, and Fakhr al-Dawla in Ray. He supported the Samanids when Fakhr al-Dawla tried to take Khorasan from them, yet the rulers of Basra and Khuzestan acknowledged Fakhr al-Dawla as senior amir, making him the most powerful of the Buyids.

Sharaf al-Dawla nevertheless gained ground. He recovered Buyid Oman, which had gone over to Samsam al-Dawla, and early in 986 took Basra and Khuzestan, driving his two brothers to Fakhr al-Dawla's lands. By May or June 986 Samsam al-Dawla recognised him as senior amir. Anarchy in Iraq then drew him there. In Baghdad he deposed Samsam al-Dawla and imprisoned him in Fars with his official Fuladh ibn Manadhar, and had the Daylamite officer Ziyar ibn Shahrakawayh executed. In July 987 the caliph proclaimed him senior amir.

His next aim was to subdue the Kurd Badr ibn Hasanwayh, an ally of Fakhr al-Dawla who had taken Diyarbakr during Samsam al-Dawla's rule, but the campaign failed, and he died not long afterwards. He had largely preserved his father's empire, although the Buyids of Ray under Fakhr al-Dawla had become effectively independent. After his death Samsam al-Dawla escaped from prison and seized Fars, Kerman and Khuzestan.
sharaf-khan-bidlisi: Sharaf Khan was born on 25 February 1543 in a village of central Iran, between Arak and Qom, while his father Shamsheddin, a Kurdish beg, was in exile. He belonged to the ruling house of the Rojakî tribal confederation, whose members ruled the Bitlis Emirate, which had been an independent emirate at intervals since at least the 9th century. He preferred the royal title of emir or mir to the tribal title of khan, and was most commonly known as Mir Sharaf.

His family came under the protection of the Safavid dynasty, and he was schooled at the court of Shah Tahmasp I. In 1596 he recalled that at the age of nine he entered the private harem and served for three years, from 1551 to 1554, as a page in the inner palace. His education covered the Quran, the principles of sharia, piety and purity, and later the martial arts, archery, polo, racing, swordsmanship and the precepts of chivalry.

In 1576 Tahmasp gave him the title of Mir of Mirs and made him leader of all the Kurdish tribes of Iran. Two years later he changed sides and supported the Ottomans in their war against Iran, offering them 400 soldiers. Sultan Murad III granted him the title of emir in 1578, and he became Mir of the Emirate of Bitlis. Between 1578 and 1588 he took part in nearly all the Ottoman wars against the Persians. In 1597 he handed the authority of his dynasty to his son Šams-al-Dīn.

The Sharafnama is divided into four parts. The first treats the five Kurdish dynasties that held royal status: the Marwanids of Amed, the Hasanwayhids of Dinavar and Sharizur, the Fadluyids of the Great Lur, the princes of Little Lur, and Saladin and the Ayyubids. The second lists dynasties that struck coins and had the khutba recited in their names, the third the families of hereditary governors, and the fourth the history of the mirs of Bitlis.

He wrote only in Persian, which he had mastered at the court in Qazvin, aiming at a wide readership across the Persian-speaking lands and at greater standing for his dynasty. He sent copies to the Kurdish leaders of Kilis, Husayn Jānbūlād, and of Ardalan, Halo Khan. Through later translations the work has shaped Kurdish literature and societies.
sharafnama: The title means The Book of Honor. The work deals with the Kurdish dynasties, among them the Ayyubid dynasty of Saladin, and with the ancient and medieval Kurdish principalities of the Middle East and the Caucasus, and it also mentions the pre-Islamic ancestors of the Kurds. It is regarded as the oldest source on Kurdish history. Its author, Sharaf al-Din Bitlisi (1543–1599), was a historian and poet as well as a prince.

Although it is a history of the Kurds, the book was written in Persian, a choice that the author's upbringing made almost inevitable. His father, Shams al-Din Khan, had sought refuge at the court of the Safavid Shah Tahmasp I, who reigned from 1524 to 1576, and Sharaf Khan was educated alongside the princes in the shah's palace at Qazvin, where he came to master Persian like a native speaker. Writing in Persian let him reach a wide readership across the Persian-speaking lands and added to his dynasty's standing in the wider world.

On finishing the book he sent copies to two other Kurdish rulers, Husayn Jānbūlād of Kilis and Halo Khan of Ardalan. The gesture may have been meant to show the authority of the ruler of Bidlis and to win wider recognition for it. It also suggests that Persian was read and written at the courts of other Kurdish princes.

The French scholar François Charmoy translated the book from Persian into French in 1873–1875 and published his translation in Saint Petersburg, where a Kurdish–French dictionary by Alexandre Jaba also appeared in 1879. The Sharafnama has since been translated into German, Arabic, English, Ottoman, Russian and Turkish. In 1972 the Kurdish scholar Abdurrahman Sharafkandi translated it from Persian into Kurdish, giving Kurdish readers the history of their princely houses in their own language.
sharif-ali: Bruneian tradition makes Sharif Ali an Arab of Taif descent and a descendant of Muhammad through his grandson Hasan ibn Ali, known as Al-Amir Sharif 'Ali bin Sharif Ajlan bin Sharif Rumaythah bin Sharif Abu Numayy and once Emir of Mecca. The only unambiguous token of his descent from his father, Sharif Abu Numaie, is the sword Pedang Si Bongkok, which he is said to have brought with him and which is still kept in the palace as a royal heirloom. He came to Brunei as a missionary and married Puteri Ratna Kesuma, daughter of Sultan Ahmad, who had no male heir, and the people urged him to take the throne.

Under him Islamic teaching was firmly set in Brunei's Malay Muslim Monarchy. Islamic laws such as the fast were introduced, while local customs in keeping with Islam were kept. Besides building the first mosque, he fixed the direction of the qibla and sometimes gave the Friday sermon himself. He added Islamic symbolism to the royal regalia, above all the flag Tunggul Alam Bernaga, whose three wings stand for iman, Islam and ihsan, and he gave the country the title Darussalam. Archaeological evidence shows that Chinese builders worked on the stone ramparts of Kota Batu, which he designed.

According to the Boxer Codex the Bruneians descended from a Sultan Yusuf, who sailed from a city near Mecca with a large following and fought the Visayans after landing in Borneo; some scholars, among them John S. Carroll, identify him with Sharif Ali.

His son, Pengiran Muda Besar Sulaiman, succeeded him, and Sultan Bolkiah and Sultan Muhammad Hasan later continued his work. A gravestone at Kota Batu next to the Brunei Museum was long held to be his, but closer study showed it to be the grave of a man named Asueri, neither a sultan nor a sharif, and his date of death is unknown. Sultan Sharif Ali Islamic University, founded on 1 January 2007, a mosque at Kampong Sengkurong and a secondary school at Kampong Salambigar bear his name.
sharif-kabungsuan: Maguindanao genealogy records state that Kabungsuwan's father was an Arab and a sharif, a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and that his mother was Malay. In Maguindanao tradition his name means the youngest, for he is said to have been the youngest of three children. His eldest brother, Ahmad, is said to have founded the Bruneian Sultanate, and his other brother, Alawi, to have set up the Sulu Sultanate. He came from Johore before settling in Mindanao.

A Sunni scholar, Kabungsuwan is generally regarded as the man who brought Islam to the Lanao and Maguindanao areas of Mindanao. Several tarsilas, written genealogies, tell of his arrival. Most say that he came with a group of seafarers, that their first dealings with the local people involved some force, and that there were already Muslims in Mindanao when they landed near the mouth of the Pulangi River.

He traded at T'buk, the old name of Malabang in Lanao, married a local princess and established the Sultanate of Maguindanao, of which he was the first sultan, usually centred in the valley of Cotabato. He formed alliances with influential royal families of Sulu, Borneo and Ternate, and these led in time to Islam becoming the dominant religion around Lake Lanao by the 19th century.

Kabungsuwan's memory is kept above all in the genealogies of the Maguindanao, which trace the sultanate and its faith to him. The former Philippine province of Shariff Kabunsuan was named after him, using the Maguindanaon form of his name, Muhammad Kabunsuan.
sharif-of-mecca: The word sharif is Arabic for noble or highborn and describes the descendants of Hashim ibn Abd Manaf; the title is sometimes written Sheriff or Sherif, the form T. E. Lawrence used in Seven Pillars of Wisdom. The office dates from the late Abbasid era. Its holder was the traditional steward of the holy cities, charged with protecting Mecca and its surroundings and with the safety of the pilgrims performing the Hajj.

Until 1200 the office was held by a member of the Hashim clan, and descendants of the wider Banu Hashim kept it into the 20th century, ruling on behalf of Muslim powers such as the Ayyubids and the Mamluks. In 1517 the sharif acknowledged the supremacy of the Ottoman caliph but kept a large measure of local autonomy. During the Ottoman era the sharifate extended its rule north to Medina, until then a sharifate of its own, and south to the frontiers of 'Asir, and it regularly raided Nejd.

Hussein bin Ali, sharif from 1908, rebelled against Ottoman rule in the Arab Revolt of 1916. After the Ottoman defeat in 1918 he formed the independent Kingdom of Hejaz and later declared himself caliph, while the British gave his sons Faisal and Abdullah the new states of Iraq and Transjordan. Facing growing attacks by Ibn Saud, Hussein abdicated in 1924 in favour of his eldest son, Ali bin Hussein, the last Grand Sharif. Ibn Saud took the Hejaz at the end of 1925 and expelled the Hashemites, and the House of Saud has overseen Mecca, Medina and the Hajj since then.
sharif-ul-hashim-of-sulu: Very little is known of the early life of Sharif ul-Hashim. His birth is given as 17 November 1405, in Johore, in present-day Malaysia, and his proper name as Sayyid Abu Bakr bin Abirin Al-Hashmi. He was a Sunni Sufi scholar of the Shafi'i school of law and the Ash'ari creed. The titles Sayyid and Shareef that he bore denote an accepted descendant of the Islamic prophet Muhammad through both the Imams Hassan and Hussain.

His genealogy traces his maternal line to Sayyed Zainul Abidin of Hadhramaut in Yemen, who belonged to the fourteenth generation from Hussain, the grandson of Muhammad. Sharif ul-Hashim was of the Ba 'Alawiyya of Yemen, as were other missionaries who are known locally as Lumpang Basih.

As sultan he took the regnal name Paduka Mahasari Maulana al Sultan Sharif ul-Hashim, rendered as The Master, His Majesty, Protector and Sultan, Sharif of Hashim. The last part refers to his descent from the Hashim clan, to which Muhammad belonged, and the name is usually shortened to Sharif ul-Hashim. He was also known in full as Sayyid wal-Shareef Abu Bakr ibn Abirin Al-Hashmi.

During his reign he promulgated the first Sulu code of laws, called the Diwan, which was based on the Quran. He introduced Islamic political institutions to Sulu and consolidated Islam as the religion of the state.

The sultanate remained in the hands of his descendants. His eldest son, Sharif Kamal ud-Din, succeeded him and reigned from 1480 to 1505. Another son, Sharif Ala ud-Din, was never proclaimed sultan of Sulu, although he is styled sultan in the lists of the family. A grandson, Sultan Sharif Mu-izz ul-Mutawadi-in, ruled Sulu from 1527 to 1548.
sharof-rashidov: Sharof Rashidov was born on 6 November 1917, the day before the Russian Revolution, into a poor Uzbek peasant family in the village of Sovungarlik, in what is now the Jizzakh region. After the Jizzakh Pedagogical College in 1935 he taught at a secondary school. He graduated in philology from Samarkand State University in 1941, and that year he was sent to the Eastern Front as a junior lieutenant. He fought in the Battle of Moscow, received two Orders of the Red Star and was demobilised in 1943 after being severely wounded. He also wrote, and his epic Chegarachi appeared in 1937.

Rashidov sat in the Supreme Soviet of the Uzbek SSR from 1947, chaired its Presidium from 1950 to 1959, and in March 1959 became First Secretary of the Communist Party of Uzbekistan, a post he held until his death. He led the Samarkand faction and purged Tashkent-aligned politicians. In 1969 rivals from the Tashkent, Fergana and Bukhara factions tried to depose him; he prevailed, and the plotters lost their power.

He enjoyed the support of Brezhnev, who sent resources for industrialisation and shielded him from investigation, and the republic had an unusually high degree of autonomy. Critics likened him to a khan for his control, and he kept a network of informers. Uzbekistan saw rapid growth, with the Muruntau gold mine opening in 1969 and Tashkent rebuilt after the earthquake of 1966.

He promoted relatives to office: at least fourteen held important government posts. Moscow demanded ever more cotton, and the republic's government reported inflated figures for irrigated and harvested land and output. Bribes, tribute and forgery created the appearance of fulfilled quotas, and wealth from central Soviet funds passed to the republic and to the Rashidov family. The push for cotton also contributed to the shrinking of the Aral Sea. Yuri Andropov, who knew of the scheme, began to break up the cotton mafia after Brezhnev's death.

Rashidov died on 31 October 1983 while visiting the Karakalpak ASSR. Most sources indicate a heart attack, with the strain of the corruption investigation often suggested as a factor, but some accounts allege suicide. Inomjon Usmonxoʻjayev succeeded him. He was first buried in Tashkent's Lenin Square, but after the cotton scandal drew attention his remains were disinterred in 1986 and reburied in his home district. After Uzbek independence Islam Karimov rehabilitated his image, a district was named after him, and a museum in Jizzakh is dedicated to him.
sharpeville-massacre: Sharpeville was built in 1943 to replace Topville, a nearby township where overcrowding and illness were widespread, and from 1958 about 10,000 Africans were forcibly removed to it. Unemployment and crime were high, and a new police station was used to check passes, deport illegal residents and raid illegal shebeens.

Pass laws, meant to control the movement and employment of Africans, were updated in the 1950s. Everyone over sixteen had to carry a passbook containing an identity card, labour bureau authorisation, the employer's name and personal details. Under Hendrik Verwoerd the National Party government used these laws to enforce greater segregation and in 1959–1960 extended them to women. The Pan-Africanist Congress, led by its founding president Robert Sobukwe, called on people to leave their passbooks at home and offer themselves for arrest.

About 5,000 people gathered at the Sharpeville police station on 21 March 1960. The mood was at first peaceful and festive, and fewer than 20 police were in the station. The crowd later grew to about 20,000, and 130 police with four Saracen armoured personnel carriers arrived. There is no evidence that anyone in the crowd was armed with anything other than stones. Jets flew low over the crowd to scatter it, and the protesters threw stones, striking three policemen.

At 13:30 the police began shooting without a warning to disperse and fired 1,344 rounds within two minutes. The police record listed 69 killed and 180 injured, and many people were shot in the back as they fled. Police reports in 1960 claimed that young, inexperienced officers panicked. In 1998 the Truth and Reconciliation Commission found a degree of deliberation in the decision to open fire. The photographer Ian Berry, who recorded the scene, had at first thought the police were firing blanks.

Strikes, marches and riots spread across the country in the following week. On 30 March 1960 the government declared a state of emergency and detained more than 18,000 people, among them Nelson Mandela. The United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 134 on 1 April, and South Africa became increasingly isolated; the event also played a part in its departure from the Commonwealth of Nations in 1961.

The banning of the Pan-Africanist Congress and the African National Congress followed, and the killings were one of the catalysts for a shift from nonviolent resistance to armed struggle. Poqo, the military wing of the PAC, and Umkhonto we Sizwe, that of the ANC, were founded soon afterwards. Since 1994 21 March has been Human Rights Day in South Africa, and a memorial opened in 2002 as part of the Sharpeville Human Rights Precinct.
sharur-district: Sharur is one of the seven districts of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic of Azerbaijan. It borders the districts of Kangarli and Sadarak, the Vayots Dzor and Ararat provinces of Armenia, and the West Azerbaijan Province of Iran. Its capital and largest city is Sharur. The area has full-flowing rivers and fertile soils that favoured early plant-growing, and its people have long been engaged in agriculture, horticulture, viticulture, cotton growing and beekeeping.

Research indicates that people settled in the area in the late glacial period. Excavations have revealed settlements and burial places of the Neolithic, the Bronze Age and the Antique period. The settlement of Oghlangaya, covering 40 hectares on the Garatepe mountain, dates to the second and first millennia BCE, and mid Bronze Age monuments have been found along the Araz River and the Arpachay. Research in 1980 to 1990 uncovered a Stone Age cave with many stone tools. The place appears as Sharuk in the epic of the Book of Dede Korkut.

When the Nakhichevan Khanate was disestablished and annexed to the Russian Empire in 1828, the Sharur area was included in the Nakhichevan Uyezd of the Armenian Oblast and later in the Erivan Governorate. In 1870 the Sharur and Daralayaz mahals were detached as a separate district, the Sharur-Daralayaz Uyezd, which had 76,551 inhabitants in the Russian census of 1897. After the brief independence of Armenia and Azerbaijan in 1918 to 1920, the Sharur area, mostly controlled by local Azerbaijanis, was assigned to the Nakhichevan ASSR within the Azerbaijan SSR.

On 8 August 1930 the Sharur Uyezd was reorganised as the Norashen raion. It was renamed Ilich, or Ilichyovsk, in honour of Vladimir Lenin from 1964 to 1991, and on 28 February 1991 the name Sharur was restored. The district's administrative centre is the city of Sharur.
shashanka: Little is known of Shashanka's early life. A seal-matrix found at the hill fort of Rohtasgarh in Rohtas district names him Mahasamanta, great feudatory, which suggests that he began as military governor of this Magadhan outpost, probably under the Later Gupta ruler Mahasenagupta (r. c. 562–601). Historians disagree about his origins. Padmanath Bhattacharya and R. D. Banerji linked him to the Guptas by descent, and D. K. Ganguly saw him as a native of Magadha who served the Maukhari kings, while Srivastava rejected a Magadhan origin, since the poet Banabhatta calls him King of Gauda and the Chinese monk Xuanzang ruler of Karnasuvarna. His name means moon, an epithet of Shiva.

By 605, after Mahasenagupta's death, Shashanka had established what became the Gauda Kingdom, issued gold coins and taken the title Maharajadhiraja. Between 595 and 600 the Gauda army fought the Varman kings of Kamarupa; the Doobi copper plates record the defeat of the princes Bhaskaravarman and Supratisthita, who were taken to Gauda as prisoners and soon released. The only account of the killing of Rajyavardhana is the Harshacharita of Banabhatta, a companion of Harsha, and neither man was present. In the war that followed Shashanka withdrew from Kannauj but kept his own lands, and by the end of his reign his domain stretched from Vanga to Bhuvanesha.

He continued Gupta traditions such as land grants to Brahmins, invited Sakadvipi and Vedic Brahmins into his kingdom, and issued gold and silver coins. Three of his copper plates are known: two from Midnapore, of his 8th and 10th regnal years, and an undated one from Egra near Kharagpur. He is credited with starting the Bengali era, Bangabda.

His son Manava succeeded him and ruled for eight months, after which Gauda was divided between Harsha and Bhaskaravarman, who took Karnasuvarna. A 12th-century text accuses Shashanka of destroying the Buddhist stupas of Bengal and cutting down the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya; R. C. Majumdar doubted the account, written some 500 years later, while Radhagovinda Basak saw no reason to reject it. Many historians regard him as the first king to attempt to unite Bengal. Folklore credits him with digging the Sarasanka dighi, a lake of over 140 acres in Midnapore, and Rakhaldas Bandyopadhyay made him the subject of a historical novel in 1914.
shashe-river: The Shashe, also spelled Shashi, is a major left-bank tributary of the Limpopo River. It rises north-west of Francistown in Botswana. It is a highly ephemeral river, which usually flows on only a few days of the year, yet it contributes 12.2% of the mean annual runoff of the Limpopo Basin. Its main tributaries are the Simukwe, Shashani, Thuli, Tati and Ramokgwebana rivers.

The lower Shashe is a channel filled with sand, with extensive alluvial aquifers in the channel and beneath the alluvial plains. These feed several irrigation schemes, among them Sibasa and Shashi. More than two million years ago the Upper Zambezi River flowed south through what is now the Makgadikgadi Pan, a vast seasonal wetland, into the Shashe and on to the Limpopo.

The Shashe Dam near Francistown was built to supply water to the industrial city of Selebi-Phikwe. In 1982 the groundwater of Francistown's wells was found to carry high levels of nitrate and to be too little for the town's needs, so its public supply was moved to the dam. The dam also serves surrounding villages, the Phoenix Mine and the Mupane Gold Mine.

Further downstream the Dikgatlhong Dam, near the village of Robelela, was completed in December 2011. When full it holds 400,000,000 cubic metres, far more than the Gaborone Dam with 141,000,000. A pipeline links it to the North-South Carrier at the break pressure tank at Moralane, which takes the water south to Gaborone.

A road bridge and a rail bridge cross the river south of Francistown, but the lower course along the border of Botswana and Zimbabwe has no bridge. At Tuli, where both banks lie in Zimbabwe, there are two legal crossing points. The river passes through the Shashi Irrigation Scheme and the Tuli Block, and its confluence with the Limpopo lies within the Greater Mapungubwe Transfrontier Conservation Area.
shatapatha-brahmana: The text belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda and is often described as the most complete and systematic of the Brahmanas, the commentaries on the Vedas. Arthur Berriedale Keith placed it linguistically in the later part of the Brahmana period, the 8th to 6th centuries BCE, and Asko Parpola dates it to around 700 BCE. Scholars have rejected claims of a much earlier date: Witzel noted that it refers clearly to iron and reflects developments later than the Atharvaveda and only slightly earlier than the time of the Buddha.

It survives in two recensions, the Madhyandina and the Kanva. The 14 books of the Madhyandina fall into two parts: the first nine comment closely, often line by line, on the first 18 books of the Yajurveda's samhita, and the remaining five cover supplementary and newer ritual material. The last book closes with the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. Julius Eggeling, its English translator in five volumes, suggested the name may come from the Madhyandina's exactly one hundred adhyayas, though the Kanva, with one hundred and four, has the same name.

Its rules for the layering, size and shape of bricks in fire altars are, in the view of Frits Staal, part of the ritual geometry that later produced the Sulba Sutras. A. A. Macdonell noted that, unlike the Samhitas, it expressly calls the Earth circular, comparing it to a wheel.

Scholars from Macdonell and Keith to D. A. Soifer hold that several avatars of Vishnu and their Puranic legends either begin or were greatly developed in this text: Matsya, the fish that guides Manu's ship to a mountain peak, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha and Vamana, the first five of the Dashavatara. It repeatedly identifies Vishnu with the sacrifice. Soifer sees in its story of Indra and the asura Namuchi the prototype of the Narasimha myth. The text also tells of a boar called Emûsha who raised up the earth when it was only the size of a span.
shatrunjaya: The Shatrunjaya hills, also spelled Shetrunjaya, stand on the banks of the Shetrunji River near the city of Palitana in the Bhavnagar district of Gujarat. The name is explained as place of victory against inner enemies, or that which conquers enemies. The Gulf of Khambhat lies to the south and the town of Bhavnagar to the north, about 56 kilometres from Palitana, which lies at the foot of the hills. A river flows between the two main hills, and a path along the ridge descends about 13 kilometres into the Aadpur Valley. The country is rugged and prone to drought.

In Jain tradition the hill was sanctified when Rishabha, the first Tirthankara of Jainism, delivered his sermons on its summit. It was originally known as Pundarikgiri, because Pundarik Swami, a chief Ganadhara and the grandson of Rishabha, is believed to have attained nirvana there. His shrine stands opposite the main temple of Adinath, which was built by Bharata, the son of Rishabha.

The hill is also called Siddhakshetra or Siddhanchal, since many Tirthankaras are said to have attained enlightenment there, and according to legend the hills form part of the Girnar ranges. They resemble other places where Jain temples have been built, among them sites in Bihar, Gwalior, Mount Abu and Girnar. Other spellings of the name include Śatruñjaya, Satrunjaya, Shetrunja and Shetrunjo.

Shatrunjaya is considered the most sacred pilgrimage site in Jainism, and its hills hold 865 temples. The Palitana temples cover both hills and the saddle between them, and pilgrims reach them by about 3,750 stone steps cut into the mountain, a climb of some 3.5 kilometres that usually takes around two hours. The hills are closed to pilgrims for four months during the monsoon.

On the full moon day of the month of Kartik in the Jain calendar, in October or November, thousands of Jains gather at the foot of the hills for the Shri Shatrunjay Teerth Yatra. Many regard it as a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage, in which devotees walk around the Shatrunjaya hills on foot, a distance of about 216 kilometres, offering prayers as they go.
shatt-al-arab: The Shatt al-Arab, Arabic for River of the Arabs, is about 200 km long. It forms where the Euphrates and Tigris meet at al-Qurnah in the Basra Governorate and flows into the Persian Gulf south of the city of al-Faw. It is about 232 m wide at Basra and 800 m at its mouth. The Karun joins it from the Iranian side at Khorramshahr and deposits large amounts of silt, so that continuous dredging is needed to keep the river navigable. In Iran it is known as the Arvand Rud, the Valiant River. In the mid-1970s its banks held 17 to 18 million date palms.

Control of the river was disputed in the age of the Ottomans and the Safavids. The Safavids gained most of present-day Iraq in the early 16th century, but lost it to the Ottomans after the Peace of Amasya in 1555. Abbas I recovered the river, and the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639 permanently ceded it to the Ottomans, although it never marked the southern frontier precisely. Nader Shah restored Iranian control for a time, until the Treaty of Kerden of 1746. Treaties of Erzurum in 1823 and 1847 and a protocol of 1913 again failed to settle the boundary.

In 1937 Iran and Iraq signed a treaty that placed the border at the low-water mark on the eastern bank, except at Abadan and Khorramshahr, so that Iraq controlled almost the whole waterway; ships had to fly the Iraqi flag and take an Iraqi pilot, and Iran paid tolls. Iran abrogated the treaty in April 1969. In March 1975 the Algiers Accord fixed the border on a line close to the thalweg, the deepest channel, in exchange for an end to Iranian support for the Iraqi Kurds.

Saddam Hussein abrogated that treaty in 1980 and invaded Iran, and the waterway was the scene of much of the fighting in the Iran-Iraq War, which lasted until 1988. When Iran captured al-Faw in 1986, Iraq's shipping through the river virtually stopped.

The southern part of the river forms the border between Iraq and Iran down to its mouth. It is Iraq's only outlet to the Persian Gulf, and Basra is a major port for loading oil tankers. Kuwait's Bubiyan Island is part of its delta. By 2002 more than 14 million of the date palms had been destroyed by war, salt and pests.
shatuo: The Shatuo descended mainly from the Chuyue, one of four Chuy tribes formed after the fall of the Yueban state at the end of the 480s. The Chuyue who stayed in the Western Turkic Kaganate lived east of the lake Barkul and were called Shatuo in Chinese, meaning sandy slope or desert. Other accounts traced them to the Tiele: the epitaph of Li Keyong names as his clan's progenitor Yidu, lord of the Xueyantuo. They had three sub-tribes, the Chuyue, Suoge and Anqing, the last of Sogdian origin. The early Shatuo seem to have practised some aspects of Manichaeism alongside reverence for spirits, divination and a Sky God.

Never numerous, the Shatuo were known as brave warriors, archers and siege fighters. They served in Emperor Taizong of Tang's campaigns against Goryeo in the 640s, and their chief Shatuo Jinshan began sending tribute to the Tang court in 702. During the An Lushan rebellion of the 750s they gave the Tang significant military aid. In 808, 30,000 Shatuo under Zhuye Jinzhong defected from the Tibetans to China, losing their leader in the flight, and in 809 the Tang resettled them in Hedong, in northern Shanxi. There they traded in horses, sheep and cattle, settled, intermarried with their neighbours and grew from about 30,000 people to 50,000-60,000 warriors by the end of the century.

Zhuye Chixin helped destroy the Uyghur Khaganate in 839 and 843 and was renamed Li Guochang in 869. His son Li Keyong, called the Dragon with a Single Eye, drove Huang Chao from Chang'an in 883, yet the Shatuo sacked the city in 885. Jinyang, a fortress city with a wall of 20 km, became their capital.

Li Keyong's son Li Cunxu destroyed the Later Liang in 923 and proclaimed the Later Tang. Shi Jingtang founded the Later Jin in 936, ceding the Sixteen Prefectures to the Khitan Liao, and Liu Zhiyuan founded the Later Han in 947. The Later Han's remnants set up the Northern Han in Shanxi, which survived under Liao protection until the Song took it in 979. Before the 12th century the Shatuo had disappeared as a distinct people, assimilated into the population around them; those left on the steppe were absorbed into other tribes and may have become the Ongud, the White Tatars.
shaushtatar: Shaushtatar, also written Šauštatar, was the son and successor of Baratarna. By the time he came to the throne his father had installed Hurrian client kings in a number of cities, which made it easier for him to turn Mitanni into a Mesopotamian power. His name draws on the Hurrian word šauša, meaning big or great; the divine name Šauša referred to the local form of the great goddess Ištar.

No longer under constant threat from the Egyptians, Shaushtatar turned against Assyria. He invaded it and sacked and looted its capital, Assur. He then led his army west across the Euphrates River, bringing the northern Syrian states under his sway as he advanced to the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. Mukish, Nuzi, Assur and Kizzuwatna became vassals of Mitanni, so that its rule reached from Assyria and Nuzi in the east to Mukish and Kizzuwatna in the west.

He came into conflict with the Egyptian pharaoh Thutmose III over territory in Syria, and he sought to push Mitanni's power further south, perhaps into Palestine. Much of southern Syria still lay within the Egyptian sphere of influence. Although Palestine then had a large Hurrian population, a war with Egypt would have been hard to win. Shaushtatar died while it was still being planned, and his son Artatama I negotiated an alliance with the pharaoh Amenhotep II.

Shaushtatar is known from documents of his own reign. Two tablets recording legal decisions, AIT 13 and AIT 14, were found at Alalakh; they name Niqmepa, king of Mukish, and so tie the reign to that of a neighbouring ruler. Another tablet in his name, granting land, was found at Tall Bazi.
shawnee: The Shawnee are a Native American people of the Northeastern Woodlands, and their language is an Algonquian language. Their precontact homeland was likely centred in southern Ohio. Some scholars propose that they descend from the Fort Ancient culture of the Ohio region, which flourished from about 1000 to 1650 CE, though others suggest that they entered the region later and occupied Fort Ancient sites. In the 17th century Europeans met them over a wide area. A Dutch map of 1614 shows a group called Sawwanew east of the Delaware River, while French accounts place them along the Ohio River.

In the early 18th century they were concentrated mainly in eastern Pennsylvania, then dispersed again across Pennsylvania, West Virginia, Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana and Illinois. Shawnee towns might have forty to one hundred bark-covered houses, similar to Iroquois longhouses, with a council house for public deliberations. They fought to keep their homelands in the French and Indian War, Pontiac's War, Lord Dunmore's War and the American Revolutionary War, in which most allied with the British. Cornstalk led a minority that favoured neutrality.

After the Revolution the Shawnee and the Miami formed a powerful alliance in the Ohio Valley. Defeat at the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794 led most Shawnee bands to sign the Treaty of Greenville the next year, ceding large parts of their homeland; other groups refused and moved to Missouri. Tecumseh did not sign it, and he later organised the intertribal alliance known as Tecumseh's confederacy. After his death and the end of the War of 1812 the Shawnee signed further treaties, and the 1830 Indian Removal Act sent them west of the Mississippi River, later to Indian Territory.

Before contact the Shawnee had a patrilineal social system, unlike many other peoples whose descent was traced through the mother. The tribe had five divisions, among them the Chillicothe, the Hathawekela, the Kispoko, the Mekoche and the Pekowi, and a 1935 study found six clans or name groups, each present in all five divisions. Today Shawnee people are enrolled in three federally recognised tribes, the Absentee-Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma, the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma and the Shawnee Tribe, all headquartered in Oklahoma. The Shawnee language is still spoken by fewer than 100 people, according to estimates of 2017.
shaybanids: The Shaybanids, more accurately the Abu'l-Khayrid Shibanids, were a dynasty of Uzbek origin descended in the male line from Shiban, the fifth son of Jochi and a grandson of Genghis Khan. As the lineages of Batu and Orda died out in the civil wars of the 14th century, the Shaybanids under Abu'l-Khayr Khan declared themselves the only legitimate successors to Jochi and claimed his whole ulus, including parts of Siberia and Kazakhstan. Their rivals, the Tukay-Timurid dynasty, who claimed descent from another son of Jochi, ended up in control of the Great Horde and its successor khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea.

Under Abu'l-Khayr Khan, who led the Shaybanids from 1428 to 1468, the dynasty began consolidating the Uzbek tribes, first around Tyumen and the Tura River and then down to the Syr Darya region. His grandson Muhammad Shaybani, who ruled from 1500 and gave the dynasty its name, conquered Samarkand, Herat, Balkh and Bukhara, which ended the Timurid dynasty and created the short-lived Shaybanid Empire. Shaybanid descendants ruled the Khanate of Bukhara from 1505 to 1598 and the Khanate of Khwarazm, or Khiva, from 1511 to 1695. The Shaybanids also ruled the Khanate of Sibir from 1563, whose last khan, Kuchum, was deposed by the Russians in 1598.

Muhammad Shaybani and his successors began a programme of translating Persian literature into Chagatai Turkish, although Persian remained the main language of administration. By the 17th century most Shaybanid Uzbeks had been assimilated into a Chagatai Karluk culture and had made peace with the Timurid dynasty in India by proclaiming themselves heirs and protectors of the Timurid heritage. The Kalan Mosque, built in 1121, was entirely rebuilt in the early 16th century, and in 1530 Ubaidullah Khan added the Mir Arab Madrasa opposite it. Abdullah II built the Modari Khan Madrasa in 1567 and the Abdullah II Madrasa between 1588 and 1590.
shaykh-haydar: Haydar was born in June or July 1459 in Amid, present-day Diyarbakır, to Shaykh Junayd and Khadija Begum, a sister of Uzun Hasan of the Ak Koyunlu. Less than a year later his father was killed at the Battle of Tabasaran. In 1469–70 Uzun Hasan, who had defeated Jahan Shah of the Kara Koyunlu at the Battle of Chapakchur, installed Haydar in Ardabil, and followers of the order from northern Syria and eastern Anatolia came there to join him.

Haydar kept the political aims of his father. Under him the Safavid order became a political movement with an increasingly extreme, heterodox Twelver Shi'i colouring, and his followers regarded him as a divine figure. He had them wear a scarlet headgear of twelve gores in memory of the Twelve Imams. He made alliances with leaders of the Talish, Shirvan and southern Dagestan and led three campaigns into the North Caucasus, which the historian Roger Savory describes as meant to drill his men against the infidels of Circassia and Dagestan.

To avoid the lands of the hostile Shirvanshahs, Haydar had boats built at Khalkhal and Astara and reached coastal Dagestan by the Caspian Sea. His first seaborne raid plundered the town of Qaytaq and the Hamiri plain, and a first campaign by land followed in 1478. In 1471–1472 he married Halima, also called Alamshah Begum, a daughter of Uzun Hasan by Despina Khatun of Trebizond; ten sons and four daughters survived him.

On his third campaign, in 1488, Haydar sacked Shamakhi. Outside the Bayqird Castle in Tabasaran he and his men were cornered and, on 9 July 1488, killed by the forces of the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yassar and the Ak Koyunlu Sultan Ya'qub, son of Uzun Hasan. The Ak Koyunlu had him beheaded and buried the head in Tabriz. He died not far from where his father had fallen.

His son Ali Mirza succeeded him as head of the order, followed by a younger son who became Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty. Ismail later moved his father's remains to the Safavid shrine at Ardabil, where Haydar's tomb became a place of pilgrimage.
shaykh-junayd: Junayd was the son of Shaykh Ibrahim and the grandson of Khvajeh Ali Safavi, hereditary leaders of the Safavid order, a Sufi order based at Ardabil in north-western Iran. He took over the leadership of the order on his father's death in 1447. Until then the Safaviyya had been organised around a saint and ascetic; under Junayd it became an active military movement with a policy of conquest, aimed at winning him a principality of his own.

Junayd was the first Safavid spiritual leader to espouse specifically Shia teachings, in particular those of the Twelver ghulat, and his followers regarded him as a divine incarnation. He drew so many disciples at Ardabil that in 1448 Jahan Shah, the Kara Koyunlu prince, drove him into exile. In Anatolia and Syria he carried on missionary work and gathered a following among the Turkmen.

He then went to the court of Uzun Hassan at Diyarbakır, where, at some point between 1456 and 1459, he married Uzun Hassan's sister, Khadija Khatun. Barred from returning to Ardabil, he lived in Shirvan, and there he was killed on 4 March 1460 in a local skirmish near the Samur River, in what is now Azerbaijan.

Junayd was buried where he fell, and his mausoleum stands in the village of Khazra in Azerbaijan. His death began a lasting hostility between the mainly Sunni Shirvanshah and the increasingly heterodox Shia Safaviyya. He was succeeded by his son Shaykh Haydar, who married his cousin Halima Alamshah Khatun, daughter of Uzun Hassan and Theodora Despina Khatun; they had three sons and three daughters. One of their sons was Shah Ismail I, who founded the Safavid dynasty and was the father of Shah Tahmasp I.
shays-rebellion: The hill towns of central and western Massachusetts lived largely by subsistence farming and credit, while the coastal merchants who dominated the state government traded with Europe and the West Indies. In 1784 London merchant houses withdrew loans and demanded hard currency, and New England merchants passed the demand on to their customers. Farmers who could not pay began to lose land and possessions through the courts. After James Bowdoin became governor in 1785 he stepped up the collection of back taxes, and the legislature added a property tax that even John Adams thought heavier than the people could bear.

When the legislature adjourned in August 1786 without considering the petitions sent to Boston, protesters calling themselves Regulators stopped the county court from sitting at Northampton on 29 August, then at Worcester, Great Barrington, Concord and Taunton. The state answered with a Riot Act and a suspension of habeas corpus, and on 30 November Job Shattuck was arrested at Groton. With the federal government unable to pay for troops, Benjamin Lincoln raised more than £6,000 from over 125 merchants for an army of 3,000 men from the eastern counties.

On 25 January 1787 the forces of Shays and Eli Parsons approached the Springfield Armory, unaware that Luke Day had postponed his attack and that his message had been intercepted. William Shepard's militia fired warning shots and then grapeshot from two cannons, killing four and wounding 20. Lincoln's night march through a snowstorm surprised the rebel camp at Petersham, and at the end of February about 120 rebels who had crossed from New York raided Stockbridge, leading to the bloodiest clash of the rising at Sheffield.

Four thousand people signed confessions in exchange for amnesty. Eighteen men were sentenced to death, but most were pardoned or had their sentences commuted; John Bly and Charles Rose were hanged on 6 December 1787. Shays was pardoned in 1788 and died poor in New York in 1825. Bowdoin lost the election of 1787 to John Hancock, and the legislature cut taxes and placed a moratorium on debts. Historians remain divided on how far the rising shaped the Constitution, though most agree it drew some Anti-Federalists towards a stronger government; Massachusetts ratified by 187 votes to 168 on 6 February 1788.
shebelle-river: The Shebelle River begins in the highlands of Ethiopia and flows south-east into Somalia towards Mogadishu, and its length is 1,820 km. Near Mogadishu it turns sharply south-west and follows the coast. Below Mogadishu the river becomes seasonal. Its flow varies with the rains: it has been described as reaching the Jubba River, and so the ocean, only in seasons of heavy rainfall, and in drier years it dwindles into wetlands and sandy plains. Its tributaries include the Erer, Galetti and Wabe rivers, and it was known historically as the Nile of Mogadishu.

The area around it is inhabited by the Arsi Oromo and by Somali people in the Somali Region of Ethiopia and in Somalia. In the lower basin, farming has largely replaced the traditional nomadic herding way of life.

In the Middle Ages the Shebelle was under the control of the Ajuran Empire, which rose to prominence in the thirteenth century and monopolised the water of the Shebelle and the Jubba. Its rulers built many limestone wells and cisterns by hydraulic engineering, and developed systems of agriculture and taxation that remained in use in parts of the Horn of Africa until the nineteenth century. The wells drew Somali and Oromo nomads with their livestock, and officials of the state mediated their disputes.

Irrigation ditches called kelliyo carried water from the Shebelle and Jubba to plantations growing sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton, supported by dikes and dams. The farms of Afgooye, Bardhere and other places grew more productive, and the crops were sold at the coastal ports of Mogadishu, Merca, Barawa and others to merchants who traded with Arabia, Persia, India, Venice, Egypt, Portugal and as far as Java and China.

The source of the river is cultivated by the Arsi Oromo. In 1989, with the help of Soviet engineers, the Melka Wakena Dam was built on its upper reaches in the Bale Mountains, producing 153 megawatts. Along the lower river, the cultivation of bananas contributes significantly to Somalia's export industry. The river has a history of destructive flash floods, among them the hidigsayley of 1965 and the kabahay of 1978.
sheberghan: Sheberghan lies at an altitude of 335 metres along the banks of the Sari Pul River, about 130 kilometres west of Mazar-i-Sharif on the Afghanistan Ring Road. It sits astride the main route between Balkh and Herat, controls the direct route north to the Amu Darya, about 90 kilometres away, and a branch route south to Sar-e Pol. For millennia it has been the focal point of power in the north-eastern corner of Bactria.

The name is a corruption of its classical Persian name, Shaporgân, meaning King Shapur's town. Two Sasanian kings bore the name Shapur and both built many cities; it is more likely that Shapur I, governor of the eastern provinces, built a roadway between a few important cities, among them Nishapur, Bishapur and Peshawar.

Sheberghan was a flourishing settlement along the Silk Road. A few kilometres north-east lies the fortified town of Yemshi-tepe, about 500 metres from the necropolis of Tillia Tepe. A joint Soviet-Afghan team excavated there from 1969 to 1979, and six royal tombs yielded a vast amount of gold and other treasure, together with coins of the early 1st century CE and none later. A team that began work in 1977, 5 kilometres north of the town, found mud-brick columns and a cross-shaped altar of a temple dating to at least 1000 BCE. The town has been proposed as the site of Xidun, one of the five divisions of the early Kushan Empire.

Marco Polo visited in the 13th century and wrote of its honey-sweet melons. The town later became the capital of an independent Uzbek khanate, which the Anglo-Russian border agreement of 1873 allotted to Afghanistan. In 1856 J. P. Ferrier described a citadel where the governor Rustem Khan lived, good gardens and excellent cultivation, and a town of 12,000 people, mostly Uzbeks. He added that its water came from the mountains of the Khanate of Sirpool and that disputes over it often threatened war.

Sheberghan is the capital of Jowzjan Province and has an estimated population of 213,411, mostly Turkmens and Uzbeks, with Tajiks, Pashtuns, Hazaras and Arabs as well. Turkmeni is the first language of many natives, though Dari and Pashto are the official languages of Afghanistan. Jowzjan University stands in the centre. Irrigated land around the city supplies fruit and vegetables to other cities, and natural gas has been worked nearby since 1967, when the Khowaja Gogerak field was opened with Soviet help and a pipeline linked Sheberghan with Keleft in the Soviet Union.
shechem: Shechem lay in a narrow valley between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, two of the largest mountains in Samaria. The valley was a principal highway for merchants and travellers moving between the northern and southern hills, which made the city a trade hub. Many springs made wells easy to dig, and the fertile soil supported agriculture and livestock.
