The site was identified as Tell Balata after a German party led by Hermann Thiersch came upon it in 1903.

The oldest settlement dates to the Chalcolithic period, around 3500 to 3000 BCE. The first substantial building belongs to the Middle Bronze Age IIA, around 1900 BCE, and the city is mentioned on the stele of Sebek-khu, a noble at the court of Senusret III. In the Middle Bronze IIC, around 1590 to 1550 BCE, it reached its largest size and power, with a Fortress Temple and cyclopean walls. In the Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE, Šakmu was the centre of a kingdom made by the Canaanite prince Labaya, who recruited Habiru mercenaries.

In the Iron Age II the city, in the northern Kingdom of Israel, had an estimated 1,200 inhabitants in the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. In the Hellenistic and Roman periods it was the main settlement of the Samaritans, whose religious centre stood on Mount Gerizim. Josephus says Sextus Vettulenus Cerialis destroyed it in the First Jewish-Roman War, and in 72 CE Vespasian built Flavia Neapolis two kilometres to the west, the origin of the name Nablus.

The Hebrew Bible mentions Shechem some sixty times. Genesis tells that Abraham built an altar at the oak of Moreh there, and that Jacob's sons Simeon and Levi killed the city's men after the abduction of their sister Dinah. Joshua assembled the Israelites there to choose whom to serve. Abimelech, son of Gideon, was made king there and later destroyed the city. After Solomon's death the northern tribes met at Shechem, and Jeroboam fortified it as the capital of the new kingdom. The kings later moved to Tirzah and then to Samaria, and Shechem lost importance.

Around 128 BCE the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed the Samaritan temple on Mount Gerizim and in 107 BCE the city, which never recovered. Jacob's Well and Joseph's tomb stand nearby, and some scholars identify Shechem with the Samaritan city of Sychar in the Gospel of John.
shefqet-verlaci: Shefqet Bey Vërlaci was born on 15 December 1877 in Elbasan, then in the Manastir Vilayet of the Ottoman Empire. By 1922 he was the largest landowner in Albania. He led the Progressive Party, the largest conservative party in the country, whose members included North Albanian clan chiefs and leading Muslim landowners and which firmly opposed any agrarian reform that would reduce their estates. He was first elected a deputy in the elections of 5 April 1921.

In late 1922 Ahmed Zogu became engaged to Vërlaci's daughter, which won him Vërlaci's support and the post of prime minister. On 3 March 1924, after a financial scandal and an attempt on his life, Zogu had to hand the premiership to Vërlaci, who held it until 27 May and then fled to Italy. Under the government of Fan Noli that followed, a special tribunal sentenced him to death in absentia and confiscated his property. After Zogu was crowned king in 1928 he married Countess Géraldine of the Apponyi family, and relations between the two men stayed bitter for years.

On 12 April 1939, after the Italian invasion, Vërlaci became prime minister of the government formed under Italian occupation, and until 16 April, when King Victor Emmanuel III accepted the Albanian crown, he was also acting head of state. He led the government until late 1941; sources differ on whether he left office on 10 November, 3 December or 4 December.

Victor Emmanuel III also named him a senator of the Kingdom of Italy, where the Senate recorded him as residing in Tirana and gave his profession as possidente, landowner. Vërlaci died on 21 July 1946 and is buried in the Protestant Cemetery in Rome. He was the father of Behie, Fazilet, Ismail and Mehtab.
sheikh-adi-ibn-musafir: His birthplace, the village of Bait Far, lay in a region that medieval Arabic geographers called Shuf al-Akrad, the Shuf of the Kurds; the historian Ibn al-Mustawfi preserves an account placing his birth there on the authority of the sheikh's own nephew. His ancestry has been disputed since the medieval period. Western scholarship widely identifies him as an Arab of Umayyad descent, which other scholars dispute. Leaving Baalbek while still very young, he met the leading mystics and theologians of Baghdad, lived unmarried and ascetically, worked the land and wove his own garments from cotton he grew.

Around the age of thirty he went to the Hakkari mountains. Al-Dhahabi records a vision telling him to go to Lalish, where God by his hand would revive many dead souls. Disciples such as Mahmarashan and Pir Dawud Kharbanda spread his teaching, and people came from around Mosul, Syria and Iran with offerings, which he gave to the poor. In Yazidi history he united scattered tribes and returned to them their ancient temple, which members of other faiths had occupied. A hagiography of 1509 says he preached through the villages south of the Hakkari mountains and spoke Kurdish where necessary.

Yazidi hymns tell of miracles, among them a gift of poison from Imad al-Din Zangi, ruler of the Zangid dynasty, turned into oil and honey. Medieval Muslim writers saw him differently: Yaqut al-Hamawi called him the sheikh and imam of the Kurds, and Rudolf Frank found the Islamic sources unanimous in describing a Sunni Sufi.

Yazidi sacred texts attributed to him survive orally among the Qawals and in mişûr manuscripts, the earliest from 1207–1208. In his Qasida, a poem in Arabic in the first person, he declares that in the secret of his knowledge there is no God but him. Four prose works in a Berlin codex copied in Damascus in 1509 had his name replaced with that of Ahmed ibn al-Rifai, by a Muslim who, Frank concluded, took offence at it. In Yazidi belief he heads a council of seven saints, each the earthly counterpart of one of the seven great angels, and his death is understood as an ascension to heaven.
sheikh-lotfollah-mosque: Construction began in 1011 AH (1602/1603 CE) and finished in 1028 AH (1618/1619 CE). The architect was Muhammad Reza, son of Husayn, a builder from Isfahan whose name appears on an inscription around the mihrab. The mosque was meant for the royal court alone, unlike the public Shah Mosque, so it has no minarets and is smaller. Shah Abbas had a tunnel built from the Ali Qapu Palace under the square to it, ending in a winding passage with guards, apparently to shield the women of the harem.

It was named in 1622 after Shaykh Lutfallah Maysi al-Amili, a prominent scholar and father-in-law of Shah Abbas, who came to Isfahan at the shah's orders and lived on the site but was never involved in the building. Reza Shah Pahlavi had the mosque restored in the 1920s, on the advice of Arthur Upham Pope.

The building is closer to a mausoleum in type than to a four-iwan mosque, which historians ascribe either to private worship by the shah's family or to its use as a women's sanctuary. It has a single domed chamber, 19 metres on a side, with no courtyard and no interior iwans. Because the square runs north to south and the qibla lies to the south-west, the architect joined the entrance to the chamber by an L-shaped vestibule, so the dome stands 6.5 metres off the axis of the portal iwan as seen from the square.

The visitor passes through two dim corridors before facing the mihrab in a room lit by nearly a score of windows. The dome, one of the few single-shell domes of Safavid architecture, is 13 metres across. Concentric rings of lozenge-shaped tilework shrink towards a central sunburst, often called a peacock because the light through the opening forms its tail.

The mosque is regarded as a masterpiece of Safavid architecture and is registered with Naqsh-e Jahan Square as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was added to the Iran National Heritage List on 6 January 1932. In The Road to Oxiana, Robert Byron wrote that he knew of no finer example of the Persian Islamic genius than the interior of the dome. The dome's design is said to derive from the Shah Vali Mosque in Taft, Yazd.
sheikh-mujibur-rahman: Mujib was born on 17 March 1920 in the village of Tungipara in the Faridpur district of Bengal, into a Bengali Muslim family of small landlords. His father was a law clerk in the courthouse of Gopalganj. He became a student activist, and in 1943 was elected a councillor of the Muslim League. At Islamia College in Calcutta he worked under his mentor Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy and campaigned for inclusion of the Sylhet district in Pakistan in the 1947 referendum. After partition he studied law at the University of Dhaka, from which he was expelled in 1949 for inciting employees against the university.

In 1948 Mujib founded the East Pakistan Students' League and was drawn into the Bengali language movement, which opposed making Urdu the sole national language. In 1949 he became a joint secretary of the Awami Muslim League, later the Awami League, and after Suhrawardy's death in 1963 its general secretary. He was elected to the East Bengal Legislative Assembly in 1954 and briefly served in the cabinet of A. K. Fazlul Huq. He spent many years in prison. The government of President Ayub Khan arrested him in 1967 in the Agartala Conspiracy Case, accusing him of plotting with Indian agents. Mass protests forced it to drop the charges on 22 February 1969, and he was then given the title Bangabandhu, Friend of Bengal.

In 1970 the Awami League won Pakistan's first general election, but the military government of President Yahya Khan refused to transfer power. On 7 March 1971 Mujib gave a speech that called vaguely for independence. The army arrested him late on 25 March and began a crackdown on Bengali civilians. In the early hours of 26 March the Proclamation of Bangladeshi Independence was issued in his name, and nationalists declared him head of the provisional government while he was held in West Pakistan.

Mujib returned to Bangladesh in January 1972. His government drew up a secular constitution, held the first general election and normalised relations with most countries. In 1974 he gave the first speech in Bengali to the United Nations General Assembly. The country suffered a severe famine in 1974, and the government formed a paramilitary force, the Jatiya Rakkhi Bahini, against a left-wing insurgency; it was later accused of human rights abuses. In 1975 he introduced a one-party system as the Second Revolution and became president. He was assassinated with most of his family at his Dhanmondi residence in a military coup on 15 August 1975. UNESCO has listed his speech of 7 March 1971 in its Memory of the World Register.
shen-buhai: According to Sima Qian, Shen Buhai was born in the central State of Zheng and served there as a minor official. After the State of Han conquered Zheng in 376 BCE he rose through the ranks of its officials. Sima Qian probably knew little of his life beyond what the Han Feizi records. His birth is often given as about 400 BCE, a compromise date proposed by the sinologist Alfred Forke, and his given name Buhai means does not harm.

The Shiji dates his appointment as chancellor to the eighth year of Marquis Zhao, traditionally 351 BCE, though Ch'ien Mu and Herrlee Creel thought it more probably came around 354 or 355 BCE. In office he reformed the state's administration and military defences and, to a lesser extent, issued new laws. The Han Feizi blames him for failing to consolidate the old laws, and the Huainanzi says that in his time the officials of Han were at cross-purposes. No early text links him with penal law, only with the control of officials.

His writings, the Shenzi in six chapters, are lost; Creel, with T. H. Tsien, gathered fragments totalling 1347 characters. Shen held that a bureaucracy needed men qualified for their posts, kept under constant watch, with performance matched against office titles. He appears to have opposed punishment, hoping strict administration would make it unnecessary, and his ruler acts inactive, revealing nothing while others reveal themselves. Sima Qian traced his thought to Huang-Lao Daoism, and Creel noted a striking resemblance to Laozi.

In 141 BCE Confucians had his name listed among the Legalist thinkers banned from government under Emperor Wu of Han, and study of his ideas declined, though his methods of checking skills and reports remained in use. Xun Kuang criticised him as one of the Twelve Masters. Creel named possible heirs from Emperor Qinshihuang to Emperor Wen of Sui, and some scholars see him as an influence on the civil service examination.
shen-dao: Very little is known of his life, and the records are brief; he is usually called Shenzi, Master Shen, after his writings. David R. Knechtges placed him as an itinerant philosopher from the state of Zhao who travelled to Linzi in 300 BCE to join the Jixia Academy and probably left after the state of Yan captured the city in 285 BCE. Sima Qian discussed him among the Jixia scholars and took him as rooted in Huang-Lao, while later Confucian archivists classed him as a Legalist. His surviving fragments are the most substantial of any Jixia scholar.

Much of his work concerned fa, a concept covering administrative standards, methods and laws, and he held that reward and punishment should follow fa rather than the ruler's own judgement, and should be proportionate rather than extreme. Xun Kuang called him obsessed by fa. His best-known saying, preserved in the Tang encyclopedia Qunshu Zhiyao, is that even a law that is not good is better than having no law. He also argued for the non-action of the ruler, who should rest while his ministers labour.

The Han Feizi made him its figure for shi, positional power, in its chapter Objection to Positional Power, though his idea of power was more naturalistic, likened to a dragon riding the wind. The Zhuangzi described him as impartial and unselfish, and appears to quote him: a clod of earth does not err with regard to the Tao. A. C. Graham called him a theoretician of centralised power.

The Book of Han listed the Shenzi in forty-two chapters, but that edition was lost between the Tang and Song dynasties, and the Qunshu Zhiyao remains the fullest source. Paul Thompson reconstructed the fragments in The Shen Tzu Fragments in 1979, and Eirik Lang Harris published a complete translation in 2016. In 2007 the Shanghai Museum published six Chu bamboo slips of sayings of Shenzi, though scholars are not sure they belong to the same tradition.
shen-kuo: Shen Kuo was born in Qiantang, modern Hangzhou, in 1031. His father, Shen Zhou, was a lower gentry figure serving in provincial posts, and his mother, from the Xu family of Suzhou, was well educated and gave Shen Kuo and his brother their first schooling, including the military doctrines of her elder brother Xu Dong. Lacking the prominent clan history of many northern elite families, Shen relied on his own ability. In 1063 he passed the imperial examinations, placing in the higher category of candidates. At Yangzhou he drew the notice of the fiscal intendant Zhang Chu, who recommended him for a post in the financial administration at court and whose daughter he later married.

Shen rose to be a finance minister, a state inspector, head official of the Bureau of Astronomy, Assistant Minister of Imperial Hospitality and an academic chancellor. Politically he belonged to the New Policies Group of the Reformist faction led by Chancellor Wang Anshi. With his colleague Wei Pu he planned a five-year project of daily observations to chart the paths of the Moon and planets, but political opponents blocked it. In 1075 he reported on his reforms of the calendar, which the court adopted only in part.

Chancellor Cai Que later held him responsible for a disaster and loss of life, removed him from office and placed him on probation in a fixed residence for six years. Cut off from government, Shen devoted himself to scholarship, and after he completed two geographical atlases for a state programme the court lifted the probation and pardoned him. His largest atlas had twenty-three maps of China and foreign regions at a uniform scale of 1:900,000. He spent his last years at his Dream Brook estate.

The Dream Pool Essays of 1088 contains some 507 essays across physics, mathematics, astronomy and medicine, and argues that technology does not conflict with Confucian precepts. In it Shen is the first to describe the magnetic needle compass, with experiments on suspended needles and the concept of true north through magnetic declination. He also described Bi Sheng's ceramic movable type, the drydock and the pound lock, and he offered a hypothesis of land formation from marine fossils and silt, and another of gradual climate change after finding petrified bamboo in a dry northern region. He improved the armillary sphere, the gnomon and the water clock.

As an archaeologist he held that ancient objects should be studied for how they were made and used, and he credited their manufacture to common artisans rather than to sages. Only six of his books survive, four of them significantly altered since he wrote them. Joseph Needham ranked his mind among the best scientific minds in Chinese history.
shen-yue: Shen Yue, whose courtesy name was Xiuwen, was born in Huzhou, Zhejiang, in 441 and died on 1 May 513. He was the grandson of the general Shen Linzi. He served emperors of the Liu Song dynasty, the Southern Qi dynasty and the Liang dynasty of the Southern Dynasties, and became a prominent scholar of the Liang.

Xiao Yan ascended the throne as Emperor Wu of Liang on 30 April 502. He first meant to treat the deposed Emperor He of Qi, Xiao Baorong, well by making him Prince of Baling and giving him Nanhai Commandery as a fief. Shen Yue advised him, quoting Cao Cao, 'Do not endure genuine disaster in the pursuit of ethereal reputation', and Emperor Wu then ordered Xiao Baorong killed. Shortly before his own death Shen fell gravely ill and dreamt that Xiao Baorong cut off his tongue with a sword. A shaman confirmed the dream, and Shen summoned priests and monks to inform and appease Xiao Baorong's spirit that persuading him to give up the throne had not been his idea.

Shen Yue was largely responsible for writing and compiling the Book of Song, a history of the Liu Song dynasty, of which his Treatise on Music, in volumes 19 to 22, is one of the most important sections. Pei Ziye distilled the history into a shorter Summary of Song, and Shen is recorded to have said of it, 'This is a standard which I cannot reach.' Shen was the leading scholar on the musical practices of his time and wrote essays on the qilin and on omens.

He is probably best known as the originator of the first deliberately applied rules of tonal euphony in Chinese prosody, the 'four tones and eight defects', which became the theoretical basis of the regulated verse of the Tang dynasty. He was also the first to apply the term Yuefu generically to Han ballad-style poetry, and he wrote the Six Poems on Remembering, which describe his beloved at six times of day.
shendi: Shendi, also written Shandi, lies on the south-eastern bank of the Nile, 150 km north-east of Khartoum and about 45 km south-west of the ancient city of Meroë, in the River Nile state. Its main suburb on the west bank is Matamma, from which a traditional trade route crosses the Bayuda Desert to Merowe and Napata. The name has been traced to an old Nubian word for lip, after the bend of the river, to a Meroitic word for ram, and to words in Daju and Beja.

The ground between the river and the flood plain has been inhabited almost continuously for about four thousand years; excavations at Shanan Castle found traces of a large Neolithic settlement. The traveller James Bruce stopped there in 1772 and described its weekly market as the largest in Nubia, with cattle, horses, gum arabic, honey and coffee from the south, sugar and cotton from Egypt, and spices and glassware arriving through the port of Suakin. He noted that a woman named Sitna ruled the town.

When the traveller Burckhardt came in 1814, the king, al-Mak Muhammad al-Nimr, owed allegiance to Sennar but was otherwise independent. In November 1822 the army of Muhammad Ali Pasha, governor of Ottoman Egypt, reached Shendi on its way to Sennar. Accounts say Ismail Kamel Pasha insulted Mek Nimr with heavy demands for livestock and slaves, and that Nimr invited him to a feast and had the place set on fire.

Muhammad Ali ordered his son-in-law Muhammad Bey al-Daftardar back from Kordofan, and in 1823 Shendi was destroyed and most of its people were killed. Mek Nimr withdrew south towards Sennar and the border of Abyssinia. For the rest of the 19th century Shendi was a minor village, its trade moving to Khartoum, the seat of Turkish-Egyptian rule.

Shendi is the historic centre of the Ja'alin, to whom most of its people belong. It is a farming town with the largest area of mango cultivation in Sudan, and it has one of the country's earliest textile factories. Shendi University, a public university, was founded in 1994.
sheng-shicai: Sheng Shicai was an ethnic Han Chinese born in Kaiyuan, Manchuria, to a well-to-do peasant family. He studied in Mukden and Shanghai and then in Tokyo, where he took political economy at Waseda University and met leftist publications such as The ABC of Communism. By his own admission he became a Marxist in 1919, the year he took part in the May Fourth Movement. He then chose a military career, trained in Kwantung and the Northeastern Military Academy, served under Guo Songling and was sent to the Imperial Japanese Army Academy. In 1927 he joined the Northern Expedition. He reached Xinjiang in the winter of 1929–30 at the invitation of its governor Jin Shuren, who made him Chief of Staff of the Frontier Army.

On 12 April 1933, amid the Kumul Rebellion and fighting with the Hui commander Ma Zhongying, White Russians and provincial officials overthrew Jin, and two days later the coup leaders appointed Sheng military governor, or duban. He had the coup leaders removed, and by June 1934, with help from the Soviet Union, which he had invited to intervene, he had defeated Ma Zhongying and Zhang Peiyuan, subordinating himself to the Soviets in return.

In 1934 his government published an administrative plan promising racial equality and religious freedom, and it gave non-Han peoples a place in the provincial government for the first time. The Soviets gained a monopoly over trade and exploited the province's rare materials and oil, and Sheng joined the Soviet Communist Party in August 1938.

In 1937, in parallel with Stalin's Great Purge, Sheng carried out his own, which swept the Uyghur and Hui political elite and later struck Han Chinese sent from Moscow; an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 people died. In July 1942, with the Soviet Union at war with Germany, he approached the Nationalist government and expelled Soviet personnel, and he purged the Chinese Communists whom he had brought in to fill posts. In 1944 he tried to turn back to the Soviets, but Stalin refused to intervene, and the Nationalist government removed him. On 29 August 1944 he was named Minister of Agriculture and Forestry.

He left Xinjiang on 11 September 1944 with 135 truckloads of wealth, held the ministry until July 1945 and later advised Hu Zongnan in Xi'an. After the Chinese Civil War he went with the Kuomintang to Taiwan, where he lived in retirement and died in Taipei in 1970. He was called the King of Xinjiang during his rule.
shengzong-of-liao: Shengzong's personal name was Wenshunu. He succeeded his father, Emperor Jingzong, in 982 while still a boy, and because he was too young to rule his mother, Empress Dowager Xiao, became regent. Emperor Taizong of the Northern Song dynasty tried to exploit the situation in 986 by sending three large armies against the Liao southern capital, present-day Beijing, in the contested Sixteen Prefectures. The young emperor and his mother led Liao cavalry against them and defeated the Song at the Battle of the Qigou Pass in June.

The empress dowager made Yelü Xiuge her senior general, and attacks on the Song went on into the following year. In 1004 the Liao invaded Song territory on a large scale and camped at Shanyuan, about 100 miles north of the Song capital, Kaifeng. Under the treaty signed in mid-January 1005 the Song paid 200,000 bolts of silk and 100,000 taels of silver each year in exchange for peace. With modifications the arrangement lasted until the end of the Liao, and the Jurchen Jin dynasty later continued it with the Song.

Examinations for officials on the Tang and Song model were institutionalised in 988. At first only three to five candidates passed; by 1014 between 30 and 130 passed the triennial examinations. Most holders of the jinshi degree were never appointed, since Khitan aristocrats, who were barred from the examinations and rose through patronage, were far more likely to receive office. A feudal reform freed most slaves, and the economy came to rest on raising horses and sheep, on agriculture and on fishing rather than on expansion and plunder.

Shengzong began the active patronage of Buddhism and rebuilt temples such as the Monastery of Solitary Joy. By one estimate, perhaps exaggerated, a tenth of the Liao population were monks or nuns within a century of his reign. Most shrines stood in the south among the settled Chinese population, and the Khitan seem to have kept their animistic beliefs and rituals. He died on 25 June 1031 as the longest-reigning monarch of the Liao, and his reign is widely praised as the dynasty's golden age of peace and prosperity.
shenyang: Shenyang lies in the central part of Liaoning province. Its western districts are on the alluvial plain of the Liao River system and its eastern part reaches into the forested hinterland of the Changbai Mountains. The name means the yang side of the Shen River, the old name of the Hun River, which runs on the southern side of the city; in Chinese naming custom a river's north bank is the sunny, or yang, side. Humans lived here as early as 8,000 years ago, and the remains of the Xinle culture, a late Neolithic society over 6,800 years old, are kept in a museum in Huanggu District.

In the 14th century the city came under the Ming dynasty, for which it was an important military stronghold. In 1625 the Jurchen leader Nurhaci captured Shenyang and moved his whole administration to it. The Manchu name was Simiyan hoton, and in 1634 the official name became Mukden, or Shengjing, meaning rising capital, from the Manchu word mukdembi, to rise. The imperial palace was built from 1626 on Nurhaci's orders, with more than 300 rooms and 20 gardens.

After the First Sino-Japanese War Japan obtained the Liaodong Peninsula by the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 but had to give it up under the Triple Intervention. A secret treaty of 1896 allowed Russia to build a railway through Manchuria, and after the Boxer Rebellion of 1900 Russian forces occupied most of Manchuria, making Mukden a Russian stronghold. The Battle of Mukden of 1905 was fought south of the city, and Japanese influence grew afterwards. In 1914 the city took back the name Shenyang, though Mukden stayed in use in English and in Japan for decades.

The Mukden incident of 1931 led to the Japanese invasion and occupation of the rest of Manchuria and the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Red Army occupied the city in August 1945, and British and American reports say Soviet troops looted and terrorised its people. The Communists captured it in 1948 after the Liaoshen campaign.

Shenyang is the capital of Liaoning province, with 9,070,093 residents at the 2020 census. It has been a centre of heavy industry since the 1930s, and many factories were built in Tiexi district in the first five-year plan, 1951 to 1956. After the 1980s heavy industry declined and hundreds of thousands of workers were laid off. It is the railway hub of north-eastern China.
shenzhen: Shenzhen lies on the east bank of the Pearl River estuary on the central coast of Guangdong. It borders Hong Kong to the south, Dongguan to the north, Huizhou to the northeast and Macau to the southwest. Although it sits about a degree south of the Tropic of Cancer, it has a warm, humid subtropical climate shaped by the monsoon and the Siberian anticyclone, with mild winters and a rainy season that lasts until late September or early October.

The city roughly follows the administrative boundaries of the historical Bao'an County. Its name means deep ditch in the local vernacular, from words used for irrigation ditches. The earliest recorded mention of the name dates from 1410, under the Ming dynasty, but no market town was established there until the Qing dynasty.

Humans have lived in the area for some 6,700 years, with the oldest evidence from the mid-Neolithic period. Historic counties were first established there about 1,700 years ago, and the towns of Nantou and Dapeng were built over 600 years ago. After the Second Opium War the United Kingdom seized Hong Kong Island and was leased the New Territories, which fixed the modern boundary between Hong Kong and the area of Shenzhen, then a village on the border.

In 1953 the Bao'an County government moved to Shenzhen, which was closer to the Kowloon–Canton Railway and had a larger economy than Nantou. From the 1950s to the end of the 1970s the county received a large influx of refugees trying to reach Hong Kong; between 100,000 and 560,000 are said to have lived there. The place became a city by 1979. In May 1980 the Central Committee designated it the first special economic zone in China, as part of the reform and opening up promoted by Deng Xiaoping, an experiment in market capitalism within a community guided by socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then had a population of 30,000.

Shenzhen is a prefecture-level city with nine districts and one new district. Its permanent population was recorded as 17,560,000 in 2020, many of them migrants from other parts of China, so that the population is younger than that of most Chinese cities. Before the zone was established the local communities spoke Cantonese or Hakka, and the main local cuisine is Cantonese.

The city is a centre of the technology and manufacturing industries, and is home to the Shenzhen Stock Exchange and companies such as Huawei, Tencent and DJI. Its port is one of the large container ports of the world. The Shenzhen Metro, a rapid transit system, serves the city, and the city is part of the Pearl River Delta Metropolitan Region together with Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, among others.
shephelah: The Shephelah, also written Shfela and known as the Judaean Foothills, is a transitional region of soft, rolling hills between the Judaean Mountains and the Coastal Plain. It is about 60 kilometres long from north to south. It is divided into a western Low Shephelah, rising to no more than about 200 metres above the Coastal Plain, and an eastern High Shephelah, between 250 and 450 metres above sea level.

A series of east-west valleys cuts it into districts: from north to south the valleys of Ayalon, Sorek, Elah, Guvrin, Lachish and Adorayim. The Ayalon was the primary access corridor to Jerusalem along the ascent of Horon, and passage between the east-west and north-south valleys has dictated the communication routes throughout history. The hills are of soft chalk covered with marl, unlike the hard chalk and dolomite of the Judaean Hills, and bell-shaped caves are a feature of the south, as at Beit Guvrin.

Surveys have found habitation in the Late Bronze period. In the early Iron Age the population of what is widely believed to have been a Canaanite enclave between Philistia and the Israelite and Judahite highlands declined, although a string of settlements survived on the eastern edge.

Growth resumed in the Iron Age IIA-B, beginning with the short-lived settlement at Khirbet Qeiyafa, and the incoming settlers, identified with the highland culture, expanded as Philistia declined. By the 8th century BCE it was the most densely populated region of the Kingdom of Judah, but the Assyrian invasion of 701 BCE destroyed most excavated sites and left it largely depopulated in the following century.

After Babylon destroyed Judah in 587 BCE the Edomites gradually took the region, which became the core of Idumea. It flourished in the Hellenistic period, was strongly affected by the First Jewish-Roman War of 66 to 70, and was largely depopulated of Jews after the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 136. It flourished again in the Byzantine period and saw one of the major battles of the Muslim conquest of the Levant in the 7th century. In the late Mamluk and early Ottoman periods permanent villages contracted, and ruins were reused as seasonal shelters.

The Shephelah is largely rural with many farms, and the cities of Ashdod, Ashkelon, Rehovot, Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Gat roughly surround it. The Hebrew Bible mentions it many times and assigns land in it to the tribes of Judah and Dan. Its archaeological sites include Lachish, Azekah, Gezer, Maresha and Tel Burna.
sher-shah-suri: Sher Shah was born Farid Khan in Sasaram in present-day Bihar, a Pashtun of the Sur clan. His birth year is disputed, with some accounts giving 1472 and others 1486. His grandfather Ibrahim Khan Sur migrated from the region of Roh in present-day Afghanistan and began as a horse trader, and his father Hasan Khan Sur held jagirs in Bihar. He received the title Sher Khan, from Persian for lion, after killing a tiger that leapt at the governor of Bihar.

He managed his father's jagirs for 21 years, reforming land revenue assessment and the commissions of tax collectors, until the resentment of his stepmother and step-brothers led him to resign in 1518. He went to Agra, observed the Mughal leadership of Babur and then entered the service of the governor of Bihar. When Sultan Mohammad of Bihar died in October 1528, the queen Dudu Bibi became regent and Sher Shah her deputy governor.

By 1530 Sher Shah was regent and de facto ruler of Bihar. He gained the fort of Chunar by marrying the widow of its governor, defeated the Lohani chiefs of Bihar and the Sultan of Bengal at Surajgarh in March 1534, and in 1538 took Rohtasgarh and Gauda while the Mughal emperor Humayun was engaged elsewhere. After defeating the Mughals he took Agra and Delhi. He then conquered Malwa in 1542, and in 1543 took Raisen, where the Rajputs who left the fort under a promise of safe conduct were massacred, an act considered the darkest mark on his reign.

He ordered the empire's administration and army. He divided Bengal into 47 administrative divisions, paid his soldiers fixed salaries, assigned roles through the Dagh system and promoted by merit. He abolished taxes at provincial borders, leaving only a levy on goods brought in and one on goods sold. He extended the Grand Trunk Road from Chittagong to Kabul and issued a silver coin of 178 grains called the rupee, the precursor of the modern rupee.

Sher Shah besieged Kalinjar fort for seven months, and the circumstances of his death are uncertain. In one account a bomb thrown at the fort fell back on a store of bombs, and he was found half-burned and lived two more days, ordering the assault until he heard the fort had fallen. He died on 22 May 1545. His son Jalal Khan, known as Islam Shah Suri, won the succession and ruled until 1553, after which the Sur Empire fell apart in civil war until the Mughals reconquered it. Historians debate his religious policy, and many hold that he showed tolerance toward Hindus.
sher-singh: Sher Singh was born on 4 December 1807, the elder of twins of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and Maharani Mehtab Kaur, and his father's second son; his twin was Tara Singh. In 1820 Ranjit Singh gave him a seat in the Darbar with civil and military honours. He was Governor of Kashmir from 1831 to 1834, during which a famine that broke out in 1831 cut the population from 800,000 to 200,000, and in 1834 he commanded the force that took Peshawar from the Afghans.

In 1831 he led the Sikh troops against the camp at Balakot of Barelvi, who had declared jihad against the Sikhs. The Sikhs closed in from all sides, and about 500 of his followers were killed, among them Shah Ismail Dehlvi; Sher Singh received Rs. 50,000 and a letter of appreciation.

In January 1841 Sher Singh, an experienced soldier with the backing of the Sikh Army, marched on Lahore and took the throne after a long siege of the Lahore Fort, ending the regency of Maharani Chand Kaur; thousands died in the siege, and he was proclaimed Maharaja by the wazir Dhian Singh Dogra. Continuing his father's friendly ties with the British, he let their army retreat from Afghanistan through the Punjab in 1842, though many of his officials wished to raid it. He was a patron of the painters Kehar Singh and August Schoefft, followed wrestling and began a communal cleaning of the Amrit Sarovar of the Golden Temple complex.

Lehna Singh Sandhawalia, Ajit Singh Sandhawalia and Dhian Singh plotted his death, and historians disagree on how he died. In one account, at the Shah Bilawal Baradari in Lahore, Ajit Singh asked him to inspect a new shotgun, shot him and beheaded him with his sword. The Sandhawalias also killed Dhian Singh and Sher Singh's son Partap Singh, and father and son were cremated together at the Shah Bilawal Baradari, where both their samadhis stand.
sherborne: Sherborne lies on the River Yeo, on the edge of the Blackmore Vale, six miles east of Yeovil, in north-west Dorset. Its name was scir burne, meaning clear stream, after a brook running through the centre, and the Domesday Book gives it so. The A30 road from London to Penzance passes through. Much of the old town, including much of the abbey and many medieval and Georgian buildings, is built from a honey-brown local material called Sherborne Stone. The town became a borough in 1227.

In 705 the diocese of Wessex was split between Sherborne and Winchester, and King Ine founded an abbey for Saint Aldhelm, first Bishop of Sherborne, whose see covered Dorset, Somerset and Devon. The large diocese lasted until about 909, when it was divided into three sees, Sherborne keeping Dorset. In 1075 the bishop's seat moved to Old Sarum and the church became a Benedictine monastery. The abbey was damaged by fire in 1437 after tension between the town and the monastery came to a head, but much of the Norman structure stands. In 1539, after the Dissolution of the Monasteries, Sir John Horsey bought the buildings and the abbey church became the parish church.

In the 12th century Roger de Caen, Bishop of Salisbury and Chancellor of England, built a fortified palace. Sir Thomas Fairfax besieged it in 1645 in the English Civil War, and it was left in ruins. In 1594 Sir Walter Raleigh built an Elizabethan mansion in the grounds, known as Sherborne Castle.

Sherborne had 10,361 residents at the census of 2021. A school is said to have existed there since the time of King Alfred, who was educated there; it was refounded in 1550 as King Edward's Grammar School, using some of the abbey buildings, and is now Sherborne School. Its alumni include Cecil Day-Lewis, Alan Turing and John le Carré. The town holds 378 listed buildings, among them St Johns' House, an almshouse founded in 1437, and the Abbey Gatehouse, which has housed Sherborne Museum since 1966. The Pack Monday Fair, held for centuries on the Monday after 10 October, was originally an agricultural fair.
sherbro-island: Sherbro Island lies in the Atlantic Ocean within Bonthe District, in the Southern Province of Sierra Leone, separated from the mainland by the Sherbro River to the north and the Sherbro Strait to the east. It is 32 miles (51 km) long and up to 15 miles (24 km) wide, covering about 230 square miles (600 km2), with Cape St. Ann at its western end and the port of Bonthe, its commercial centre, at the east. It is believed to be a breeding ground for green and leatherback sea turtles, and African manatees live in the delta of the Sherbro river system to the north.

The island was long home to the Sherbro people, who fished and traded by boat with villages along the coast. During the Mane invasion of the 16th century it was the centre of one of their main kingdoms, and its king in the first half of the 17th century, Sherabola or Selboele, gave the island its name. Portuguese, Spanish and Dutch traders came in the 17th century, followed by England's Royal African Company, which by the early 18th century was trading in slaves and kept a fort on York Island in the Sherbro Estuary for shipping enslaved Africans to the Americas. Its agent Thomas Corker of Falmouth married the daughter of a Sherbro chief, and their two sons founded a family of traders and chiefs.

After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 the old fort served as a base against illegal slavers. In 1815 Paul Cuffe, an African-American ship maker of Boston, settled 88 American freedmen on the island. The American Colonization Society later sent the ship Elizabeth from New York with 86 free African Americans, among them the missionary Daniel Coker, and three agents; disease killed more than a quarter of the settlers, and in April 1822 the survivors moved to Providence Island at Cape Mesurado. The British colony at Freetown acquired the island from the Sherbro in 1861, and it was governed from there until Sierra Leone became independent in 1961.

The Sherbro remain by far the largest group on the island, whose population the government recorded as 28,457 in May 2013. Swamp-rice cultivation and fishing are its main livelihoods, and it has more than 65 miles (105 km) of beaches.
sherburn-in-elmet: Sherburn stands on a low hill of Permian limestone that juts into the valley of the River Ouse, west of Selby and south of Tadcaster. Its name comes from the Old English scir, bright or pure, and burn, a stream or spring, perhaps for the clear water of the hill beside the muddy streams of the plain below; the earliest record of it, Scyreburnan, dates from 963. The ridge is still a source of clear water, for the brewers of Tadcaster among others.

A Roman road from Castleford to Tadcaster and York ran along the ridge, on the line of today's Low Street and Finkle Hill, though little sign of Roman settlement has been found. Elmet, the little-understood post-Roman Brittonic kingdom around what is now Leeds, is also recalled in the names of Barwick-in-Elmet and Scholes-in-Elmet.

Beside All Saints' Church an earthwork marks Hall Garth, a high-status dwelling that King Athelstan gave, with the manor of Cawood, to the Archbishops of York after his victory over the Scots and Norse at Brunanburh in 937. It is sometimes wrongly called Athelstan's Palace and cannot be dated with certainty to the time before Elmet was absorbed into Northumbria in 616/7. The church, a Grade I listed building on the site of an Anglo-Saxon one, has a 12th-century nave and north aisle; Anthony Salvin restored its east end in 1857.

Local legend holds that Edward IV watched the Battle of Towton in 1461 from the church tower, but the main fighting, three to four miles away, could not have been seen clearly from a tower then lower than it is today. In the English Civil War the Royalists garrisoned the town for Charles I. On 15 October 1645 a Cavalier force under Lord Digby and Sir Marmaduke Langdale defeated the Parliamentarian garrison, until Colonel Copley's counterattack routed it: the last significant Royalist force in the North during the First English Civil War.

Sherburn in Elmet is a civil parish of North Yorkshire. It belonged to Selby District from 1974 to 2023 and is now administered by the unitary North Yorkshire Council. The 2021 census counted 8,572 people, and its railway station has services to York, Hull and Sheffield.
shetland: Shetland lies between Orkney, the Faroe Islands and Norway, about 80 kilometres northeast of Orkney, 170 kilometres from mainland Scotland and 220 kilometres west of Norway. The largest island, known as the Mainland, is the fifth-largest in the British Isles, and 16 of the islands are inhabited. The climate is oceanic and the coastline rugged, on islands that are virtually treeless. Almost all place names are of Norse origin. The name may derive from the Old Norse hjalt, hilt, and land.

Humans have lived in Shetland since the Mesolithic period. Because people built in stone on treeless islands from at least the early Neolithic, the islands hold over 5,000 archaeological sites. Norse settlers colonised Shetland in the late 8th and 9th centuries; the fate of the preceding population is unresolved, though there is no established archaeological evidence that settlement involved violent extermination.

From the mid-13th century Scottish monarchs sought to control the islands around their seas. This led King Haakon IV of Norway to invade Scotland; after the stalemate at the Battle of Largs he retreated to Orkney and died in December 1263. Under the 1266 Treaty of Perth the Hebrides and Mann passed to Scotland, but the Scots recognised continuing Norwegian sovereignty over Orkney and Shetland.

After 1380 Norway formed a union with Denmark and royal interest in the islands declined. Orkney in 1468 and Shetland in 1469 were pledged by Christian I as security for the unpaid dowry of his daughter Margaret on her marriage to James III of Scotland, with a right of redemption, and the islands were absorbed into Scotland in 1472. Later Danish rulers made repeated attempts to recover them. Shetland kept its own legal system until 1612.

Shetland is the northernmost region of the United Kingdom. Its administrative centre and only burgh is Lerwick, capital since 1708, when it replaced Scalloway. The Norse heritage is reflected in the Up Helly Aa fire festivals and a strong fiddle tradition, and writers have often used the Shetland dialect of Scots. Oil and gas were first landed at Sullom Voe in 1978.
shi-chaoyi: The year of Shi Chaoyi's birth is not known. He was the oldest son of Shi Siming, a childhood friend of An Lushan who had served under him, and he was not the son of Shi Siming's wife, Lady Xin. In 757 Shi Siming turned against An Lushan's son and successor An Qingxu and submitted to Emperor Suzong of Tang with the Fanyang region, and he made Shi Chaoyi prefect of Ji Prefecture. When Shi Siming turned against the Tang again and killed An Qingxu in 759, he left Shi Chaoyi to defend Yecheng.

After claiming the title of emperor of Yan in 759, Shi Siming created Shi Chaoyi the Prince of Huai but not crown prince, favouring Lady Xin's son Shi Chaoqing instead. Shi Siming was described as cruel and prone to kill, while Shi Chaoyi was considered kind and was favoured by the soldiers. In spring 761 Shi Chaoyi served as forward commander in an attack on Shan Prefecture but was repeatedly repelled by the Tang general Wei Boyu, and his father threatened to kill him once the prefecture fell.

That night his followers Luo Yue and Cai Wenjing warned him that they would defect to the Tang unless he acted. With the agreement of Shi Siming's guard commander, Luo led 300 soldiers who seized Shi Siming and later strangled him on the road back to Luoyang. Shi Chaoyi claimed the Yan throne and sent messengers to Fanyang to have Empress Xin and Shi Chaoqing killed.

He was considered kind and humble and willing to listen to his advisers, but the Luoyang region he held directly had already been ravaged by war. Many Yan generals had been followers of An Lushan, considered themselves the equals of Shi Siming and were only nominally submissive to his younger son. Shi Chaoyi suffered a number of losses to Tang generals, and his attacks on Lu Prefecture and Songzhou failed.

Luoyang fell in winter 762, when the Tang forces were aided by Dengli Khan of the Uyghur Khaganate. Shi Chaoyi fled, but his generals, among them Zhang Xiancheng, Xue Song, Tian Chengsi and Li Huaixian, turned against him one after another when he asked them for aid. He hoped to escape to the Xi or the Khitan, but in spring 763 he was intercepted by troops Li Huaixian had sent to capture him, and he hanged himself to avoid capture. Li Huaixian had his head delivered to Chang'an, where it arrived on 17 February.
shi-chonggui: Shi Chonggui was born in Taiyuan in 914, the son of the cavalry officer Shi Jingru and Lady An. His father died early, and his uncle Shi Jingtang adopted him and gave him responsibilities in the circuits he governed. When Shi Jingtang rebelled against the Later Tang emperor Li Congke in 936, Shi Chonggui helped guard him during the siege of Taiyuan. Emperor Taizong of the Khitan then chose him to hold Taiyuan while the allied armies marched on Luoyang, and he later became mayor of Kaifeng and Prince of Zheng.

When Shi Jingtang died in 942, the chancellor Feng Dao and the guard general Jing Yanguang passed over his young son Shi Chongrui and put Shi Chonggui on the throne, judging that the unsettled realm needed an older ruler. Under Jing's influence the new emperor announced his succession to Emperor Taizong in a letter calling himself grandson but not subject, and Jing had the Liao trade envoy Qiao Rong arrested and Khitan merchants executed.

Liao invaded early in 944. Shi Chonggui led troops himself to relieve generals besieged at Qicheng, dismissed Jing, and put down the rebellion of Yang Guangyuan. A second invasion late in 944 ended with a Later Jin victory near Yangcheng, after which he refused Liao's terms for peace and, according to the histories, grew arrogant and extravagant. In 946 he sent his uncle by marriage Du Wei north to recover the Sixteen Prefectures, but Du was surrounded at Zhongdu Bridge and surrendered the army on Taizong's promise to make him emperor. With Kaifeng left undefended, Shi Chonggui surrendered, ending Later Jin.

Taizong named him the Marquess of Fuyi, the marquess who turned against righteousness, and sent him and his family into exile deep in Liao territory, a journey on which they often went without food. Under Emperor Shizong they were settled at Liaoyang and later at Jian Prefecture, where his followers farmed the land. His tombstone, received by the Chaoyang City Museum in 2000, records that he died in 974, honoured by the Liao court as Prince of Jin, with official mourning held for him.
shi-hu: Shi Hu, courtesy name Jilong, was the son of Koumi, whose father was a cousin of Shi Le's father Zhouhezhu. Koumi died early, and the boy was raised by Zhouhezhu and Shi Le's mother Lady Wang, so he was sometimes called Shi Le's brother. Separated from Shi Le in a famine among the Jie in the early 300s, he was later found by Liu Kun, the Jin governor of Bing Province, and sent to him. In Shi Le's army he became feared for his bravery, archery and horsemanship, and for his cruelty.

Shi Le relied on him against his chief enemies and made him Marquess of Fanyang. In 313 he drove Liu Yan out of Yecheng, which he came to treat as his own. In 321 he captured Duan Pidi, ending the last major pocket of Jin resistance in northern China, and after taking Guanggu from Cao Ni in 323 he slaughtered most of its people, leaving 700 alive for the governor Liu Zheng to rule. In 329 he took Shanggui and killed the Former Zhao princes Liu Xi and Liu Yin, ending Former Zhao.

When Shi Le fell ill in 333, Shi Hu cut him off from the court. After Shi Le's death he seized the crown prince Shi Hong, executed the advisers Cheng Xia and Xu Guang, and had himself made King of Wei. He crushed revolts at Luoyang and Chang'an, and in late 334 deposed Shi Hong and had him put to death, taking the title Regent Heavenly King.

In 335 he moved the capital from Xiangguo to Yecheng. A professed Buddhist who revered the monk Fotu Cheng, he issued an edict proclaiming religious freedom. From 336 he built luxurious palaces, among them the Taiwu Palace, and the taxes, labour and conscription they demanded weighed heavily on the people. In 338 he joined Murong Huang of Former Yan to destroy the Duan tribe, then besieged the Former Yan capital Jicheng for nearly 20 days and withdrew with heavy losses.

He had two crown princes executed: Shi Sui in 337, with his wife and 26 children, and Shi Xuan in 348, burned alive after he murdered his brother Shi Tao. In spring 349 Shi Hu took the title of emperor and named his young son Shi Shi heir. He died in 349, and within two years his sons' wars and his adopted grandson Shi Min, who took back his father's family name Ran, had destroyed the state and massacred most of the Jie.
shi-jingtang: Shi Jingtang was born on 30 March 892 to Nieliji, known by the Chinese name Shi Shaoyong, a general under the warlord Li Keyong and his son Li Cunxu. The Old History of the Five Dynasties traced the family to the Han prime minister Shi Fen, apparently to give him Han Chinese ancestry; the New History of the Five Dynasties doubted this, and he most likely came from the Shi clan of the Shatuo sub-tribe Anqing, of ultimately Sogdian origin.

Li Siyuan, then prefect of Dai Prefecture, was impressed by him and gave him his daughter in marriage, and Shi became one of Li Siyuan's two leading officers beside Li Siyuan's adoptive son Li Congke, with whom he had a quiet rivalry. When mutineers at Yedu forced Li Siyuan to join them in 926, Shi persuaded him that he could never clear himself with the emperor Li Cunxu and urged him to march south. After Li Cunxu was killed, Shi helped block Li Jiji's army so that Li Siyuan could take the throne.

Li Siyuan made him military governor of Baoyi, then deputy commander of the imperial guards, governor of Xuanwu after Zhu Shouyin's revolt in 927, and in 928 defender of Yedu with an honorary chancellor's title. Under Li Conghou the chiefs of staff Zhu Hongzhao and Feng Yun, wary of him, ordered in 934 that he be moved from Hedong to Chengde; Li Congke rebelled instead and seized the throne. Shi, frail from illness, was allowed back to Hedong, but by 936 he was widely expected to rebel.

For the help of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty he was called the adopted son of Emperor Taizong of Liao, though ten years older. In spring 937 he moved the capital from Luoyang to Daliang to be nearer Fan Yanguang, whom he expected to rebel. Fan rose that summer and drew the general Zhang Congbin into revolt at Luoyang, where Zhang killed two of Shi's sons, Shi Chongxin and Shi Chongyi. Du Chongwei defeated Zhang, and Fan surrendered in the autumn of 938.

In 940 Li Jinquan of Anyuan rebelled and turned to Southern Tang, but Ma Quanjie defeated its force and peace followed.An Chongrong of Chengde, who saw Shi's submission to Liao as weakness, called on him in 941 to break with Liao, and Shi went to Yedu to prepare against him, leaving his adopted son Shi Chonggui in charge at Daliang. He died on 28 July 942, and Shi Chonggui succeeded him.
shi-lang: Shi Lang, also known as Secoe or Sego, was born in Fujian to a distinguished lineage. He studied military strategy as a youth and became especially skilled in naval warfare. The Kangxi Emperor later described him as a fierce warrior highly adept in command, though he was also blunt and lacking in courtesy. After minor operations with his father, he joined Zheng Zhilong's fleet as captain of the left vanguard and served in it through most of the early 1640s. After a personal dispute, Koxinga killed Shi's father, brother and son, and Shi went over to the Qing.

The Qing valued his naval experience and his contacts in the main trading ports of East Asia. In 1656 he accompanied Prince Jidu, a son of Jirgalang, on an expedition in Fujian and became Assistant Brigadier-General. In the campaign of 1663 against the Zheng family he commanded Dutch ships and men. A plan he submitted in 1668 to drive the Ming remnants from Taiwan and the Pescadores was not taken up, and he received a post in the Imperial Bodyguard, attached to the Chinese Bordered Yellow Banner.

In 1681, after the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, the Kangxi Emperor chose him on the advice of Li Guangdi to lead an attack on Taiwan. Shi insisted on a command independent of Yao Qisheng, the Governor-General of Fujian. On 8 July 1683 he sailed from Tongshan with 300 warships and 20,000 soldiers, and on 16 and 17 July he defeated the Zheng commander Liu Guoxuan near the Pescadores. On 3 October he reached Taiwan and received the formal surrender of Liu Guoxuan and Zheng Keshuang.

Named General Who Maintains Peace on the Seas and a hereditary marquis, Shi stayed at his post in Fujian. He seized almost half the developed land of southern Taiwan for his own profit, extorted money from local communities and pursued policies meant to isolate the island: the coastal provinces were forbidden to deal with it, and settlers could not bring their families. Though later charged with arrogance, he was received by the emperor in Beijing in 1688. He died in office in 1696.

He received the posthumous name Xiangzhuang, and in 1732 his name was entered in the Temple of Eminent Statesmen. In China he is generally denounced as a traitor to the Ming loyalist cause, and in Taiwan he is remembered as a conqueror and a cruel governor.
shi-le: Shi Le, courtesy name Shilong, was born in 274 to a family of minor Jie chiefs in Bing Province, modern Shanxi, and grew up in Wuxiang. The Jie seem not to have used family names, and his original name was probably Bèi. During a great famine in Bing Province in 302 or 303 he was captured by Jin officials and sold as a slave, but his owner, Shi Huan, freed him. He led bandits and joined a rebellion in support of Sima Ying, Prince of Chengdu, under his friend Ji Sang, who gave him the name Shi Le. After its defeat in 307 he joined Liu Yuan, founder of Han-Zhao.

Shi led a roving army that pillaged across central China, and unlike many rebel leaders he took learned men as advisers. In 311 his cavalry destroyed the largest Jin force left in central China at Ku, as it escorted the funeral train of the regent Sima Yue, and he executed the captured princes and officials. On the advice of Zhang Bin he made Xiangguo his headquarters in 312, and in 314 he feigned submission to the Jin governor Wang Jun before seizing his base at Ji and executing him.

His army, under his nephew Shi Hu, became known for cruelty to civilians. In 319 the Han-Zhao emperor Liu Yao, suspecting rebellion, killed Shi's envoy, and Shi declared himself Prince of Zhao. In 328 he captured Liu Yao outside Luoyang and executed him when Liu refused to order his heir to surrender; Shi Hu then took Shanggui and killed the last princes of Former Zhao.

In 330 Shi Le took the title Heavenly King and later that year emperor, and he made his son Shi Hong, Prince of Qin, Grand Chanyu over the five nomadic tribes. Shi Hu resented being passed over. Shi Le ignored his advisers Cheng Xia and Xu Guang, who urged him to curb Shi Hu, and when he died in 333 Shi Hu seized power and killed them. Shi Le was buried in secret, an empty coffin placed in the imperial tomb; his descendants all died at Shi Hu's hands. He is the only Chinese emperor to have risen from slavery, and he gave the Kuchan Buddhist monk Fotudeng great influence at his court.
shi-siming: Shi Siming was born Shi Sugan, one day before An Lushan, and the two grew up together. He was poor and of low station, but known for his bravery, and Lady Xin, a daughter of the local gentry, married him against her family's wishes. Like An he understood six non-Han languages, and both served as interpreters in military interrogation under the generals Wu Zhiyi and Zhang Shougui. Emperor Xuanzong, impressed with him at Chang'an, gave him the name Siming, thinking of brightness.

Shi rose to command at Pinglu and in 751 rallied An's broken troops after a defeat by the Xi. When An rose against Xuanzong in 755, Shi fought for him north of the Yellow River, capturing the rebel governor Yan Gaoqing at Changshan in 756, though he fared badly against the Tang generals Li Guangbi and Guo Ziyi until they withdrew after the fall of Chang'an. After An Lushan was killed by his son An Qingxu in 757, Shi besieged Taiyuan in vain, then held Fanyang, hoarded its supplies and ignored his new master's orders.

Late in 757 he submitted to Emperor Suzong, who made him military governor of Fanyang and Prince of Guiyi. Tang generals doubted him, and in 759, when the court had Wu Cheng'en try to arrange his killing, Shi put Wu to death and turned south. On 7 April 759 his army met the Tang forces besieging An Qingxu at Yecheng; a sudden storm threw both sides into panic and the siege was lifted. Shi then met An Qingxu, rebuked him for killing his father, and had him executed with his four brothers.

As emperor of Yan, Shi took Bian Prefecture and Luoyang, but Tang forces held him at Heyang and Shan Prefecture. He was described as cruel, and he favoured his son Shi Chaoqing over his eldest son Shi Chaoyi. In spring 761, angered by Shi Chaoyi's failures before Shan Prefecture, he threatened to kill him. That night Shi Chaoyi's subordinate Luo Yue, with his son's agreement, seized Shi with 300 soldiers and strangled him on the road to Luoyang. Shi Chaoyi took the throne and committed suicide in 763 after his defeat by Tang forces.
shiba-clan: The Shiba descended from Ashikaga Yasuuji and from the Seiwa-Genji. The clan name dates from the end of the 13th century and from Shiba Ieuji, a son of Yasuuji. The family was based in Mutsu Province, in the north of Honshū, and also inherited the governorship of Owari Province, in present-day Aichi Prefecture. In the Kamakura period it was treated as a cadet branch of the Ashikaga clan and used the Ashikaga name; Shiba became its family name only in the Muromachi period.

Shiba Takatsune (1305–1367) raised the clan's standing when he sided with Ashikaga Takauji (1305–1358) in the fighting against Emperor Go-Daigo in 1335. Once the Ashikaga shogunate was established, Takauji made him shugo governor of Echizen and Wakasa provinces. His son Shiba Yoshimasa (1350–1410) held the office of kanrei, deputy of the shogun, from 1379 to 1397, and the office was held after him by his son Shiba Yoshishige (1371–1418) and his grandson Shiba Yoshiatsu (1397–1434).

By the mid-15th century the Shiba were divided by factional dispute. The feud within the clan and with other clans was one cause of the Ōnin War (1467–1477), and the Shiba were unable to make the transition to Sengoku daimyō. They lost Echizen to the Asakura in the 1470s, when Asakura Toshikage took their power by usurpation.

By 1550 the clan was represented by Shiba Yoshimune of Owari Province, whose seat was Kiyosu Castle. He was a figurehead behind whom the Yamato no kami branch of the Oda clan ruled. When Oda Nobutomo killed Yoshimune in 1554, the clan effectively came to an end, although his son Shiba Yoshikane lived until 1572.
shibam: Shibam stands in Wadi Hadhramaut in the desert of Ramlat al-Sab'atayn, in the central-western part of the Hadhramaut Governorate. Its main road links Sanaa and other cities of western Yemen with the far eastern territories, and another road from the village of Alajlanya links it to Mukalla, the governorate's capital on the Indian Ocean. The nearest towns are Seiyun, which has an airport, and Tarim, both to the east. The climate is hot desert, with June the hottest month. The town is officially called the Old Walled City of Shibam, from the fortified wall that surrounds it.

The first known inscription about the city dates from the 3rd century CE. According to the geographer al-Hamdani, its origins go back to the pre-Islamic period, and it became the capital of the Kingdom of Hadhramaut in 300 CE, after the destruction of the earlier capital, Shabwa, in the far west of the valley. Its position along ancient trade routes contributed to its prosperity. Whether the present town stands on the site of the ancient city is unclear.

One theory explains its rise of more than six metres above the surrounding plain by the accumulation of ruins, but no excavations support this, and it might be a natural outcrop of the mountain spur behind it. Two archaeological sites lie nearby: Jujah, a quarry for large squared building stones, and Gabusa, where an Assyrian-style bronze lion's head was found.

Shibam has been inhabited continuously for an estimated 1,700 years, although the present town dates to 1533, and many houses have been rebuilt numerous times in recent centuries. In the 20th century it was one of the three major cities of the Qu'aiti Sultanate, with Mukalla and Ash-Shihr. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1982.

The houses of Shibam are all built of mud brick, and about 500 of them are tower blocks of five to eleven storeys, with one or two rooms on each floor. The design was meant to protect residents from Bedouin attacks. Some towers stand over 30 metres high, which makes the town one of the oldest and best examples of urban planning on the principle of vertical construction, and it is often called the oldest skyscraper city in the world.

The walls must be maintained routinely with fresh layers of mud against rain and erosion. A tropical storm in 2008 flooded the town and brought down some buildings, and in 2015 UNESCO listed it, with Old Sanaa, as cultural heritage at risk.
shibam-kawkaban: Shibam Kawkaban lies in Shibam Kawkaban District of Al Mahwit Governorate, 38 km west-northwest of Sanaa. Shibam is a market town at the edge of a large agricultural plain; above it, at the summit of the cliffs to the south-west, stands the fortress town of Kawkaban, whose name means two planets in Arabic. Its citadel, about 2,931 m above sea level, is walled on the north and naturally fortified on the other sides. Fertile farmland, the strength of the fortress and the nearness of Sanaa made the place strategically important throughout Yemen's history.

Inscriptions of the 3rd century name Shibam as the centre of the Dhu Hagaran Shibam tribe. The 10th-century writer Abu Muhammad al-Hasan al-Hamdani recorded that the town was originally called Yuḥbis and took the name Shibam from a man of the Banu Hamdan tribe who settled there. He described it as the centre of the mikhlaf of 'Aqyan, with 30 mosques in his day and inhabitants of the Banu Fahd branch of Himyar. The Yuʿfirid dynasty, which came from Shibam Kawkaban, made it their capital.

From the 1500s the town was a stronghold of the Alid Sharaf al-Din dynasty, which produced two Zaydi Imams of Yemen. It was also home to a Jewish community until the mid-20th century; the Jewish poet Zechariah Dhahiri lived there. In May 1902 the German explorer Hermann Burchardt found Kawkaban almost deserted: a town that 40 years earlier had counted 30,000 inhabitants now held hardly a few hundred, with some Jewish families still in its quarter.

The census of 1975 counted about 2,000 inhabitants. The town keeps several old mosques, among them al Madrasa, al Mansoor, al Sharefa and Harabat, an old market at its centre and rainwater reservoirs called Meseda, Alasdad and Sedalhamam. Kawkaban is known for its lavish tower-houses. In February 2016, during the Yemeni Civil War, aircraft of the Saudi-led coalition struck the citadel, killing seven residents and destroying the historic gateway and houses 700 years old.
shiban: Shiban, also written Siban or Shayban, was the fifth son of Jochi and a younger brother of Batu Khan, the founder of the Golden Horde. Because he had not come of age when his father died in 1227, he received no lands at that time. In the Mongol invasion of Europe he made a decisive attack on the army of Béla IV at the Battle of Mohi in 1241.

According to Abulghazi, Batu rewarded him after the campaign with winter quarters east of the Ural Mountains on the lower Syr Darya, Chu and Sary su rivers, and summer quarters along the Ural River on the eastern side of the mountains. His brother Orda Khan gave him 15,000 families and four clans, the Kuchis, Naimans, Karluks and Buiruks. Shiban's lands thus lay between those of Batu and Orda, between the Ural mountains and the Caspian Sea. How long he lived is not known.

Shiban left twelve sons. One, Balagha, helped Hulagu Khan take Baghdad in 1258 and died in unknown circumstances. His descendants, the Shaybanids, rose to importance about two centuries after him. After the line of Batu died out in 1359, several of them took the throne of the Golden Horde and of its successor states, among them the Khanate of Sibir and the Uzbek Khanate. Two branches settled in Central Asia and founded the khanates of Transoxiana, later Bukhara, and Khwarazm, later Khiva.
shibata-katsuie: Katsuie, also known as Gonroku, was born in the village of Kamiyashiro, now part of Meitō-ku in Nagoya, into a branch of the Shiba clan, which descended from the Ashikaga and had once been overlords of the Oda. He served Oda Nobuhide and then Oda Nobuyuki, fighting at the Battle of Kanōguchi against the Saito clan in 1547 and at the second Battle of Azukizaka against the Imagawa clan in 1548. In 1556, when control of the Oda clan was contested, he backed Nobuyuki against his elder brother Oda Nobunaga and was defeated at the Battle of Inō. Nobunaga had his brother executed but spared Katsuie, impressed by his loyalty and courage.

In Nobunaga's service Katsuie was made a bugyō in 1565. In 1570, during the Battle of Anegawa, he held Chōkō-ji castle against 4,000 soldiers of the Rokkaku clan and drove them off with an all-out attack, which with other victories earned him the name Oni Shibata, Demon Shibata. He was severely wounded at the first Siege of Nagashima in 1571, fought the forces of Shogun Ashikaga Yoshiaki in Omi and Settsu provinces from 1573, and led the right wing at the third Siege of Nagashima in 1574.

At the Battle of Nagashino in 1575 he and Hashiba Hideyoshi guarded the left flank. In 1576 he took command of Kitanosho Castle and was ordered to conquer the Hokuriku region; in 1577 he led the army sent against Uesugi Kenshin at the Battle of Tedorigawa, and from 1581 he campaigned in Etchū Province with Maeda Toshiie and Sassa Narimasa.

Katsuie was besieging Uozu when Nobunaga died in the Honnō-ji incident in 1582. At the meeting at Kiyosu Castle on the succession he first supported Nobunaga's grandson Samboshi and then Oda Nobutaka, Nobunaga's third son, and allied with Nobutaka and Takigawa Kazumasu against Toyotomi Hideyoshi. In 1583 his nephew Sakuma Morimasa ignored his orders to withdraw at Shizugatake and was captured and beheaded. Katsuie fell back to Kitanosho, which was taken in three days. His wife Oichi let their daughters escape but stayed to die with him, and after setting the castle on fire he committed seppuku. His death poem asks the bird of the mountain to carry his name beyond the clouds.
shibi-khagan: Shibi Qaghan succeeded Yami Qaghan as khagan, and from 613 to 615 he gave active support to agrarian rebels inside China. The Sui official Pei Ju, judging him too strong to control, proposed marrying a princess to his brother Ashina Chiji, who declined in fear. Pei then lured Shibi's strategist Shishuhu to Mayi and killed him on a false charge of plotting against his master. Knowing the charge was false, Shibi resolved to break with the Sui.

In the autumn of 615 he fell on Yanmen Commandery while Emperor Yang was visiting it, overrunning most of its settlements. Warned by Shibi's wife, Princess Yicheng, a member of the Sui imperial family, the emperor and Empress Xiao escaped to the commandery seat, which the Turks besieged from 11 September. On the advice of the empress's brother Xiao Yu, messengers were sent to Yicheng, who was directing affairs at the Turkic capital; she falsely told Shibi that the north was under attack, and he lifted the siege.

As Sui rule broke down he backed warlords who claimed the title of emperor. He made Liang Shidu Tardu Bilge khagan and gave him a flag with a wolf's head, the emblem of the Turks, and Liang guided his forces into the Ordos Desert. Liu Wuzhou, who sent him the ladies of Fenyang Palace as tribute and received horses in return, was named Dingyang Khagan.

When Li Yuan, the future founder of the Tang dynasty, rose in 617, his envoy Liu Wenjing promised that the land would go to Li and the money, silk, gold and treasures to the khagan. Shibi, though not wholehearted, sent men under his general Kangqiaoli Tegin and horses, which Li Yuan wanted more than soldiers, and Ashina Chiji went with the Tang army to Chang'an.

In 618 he sent an ambassador, Kutlug Tegin, to the new Tang court. In February 619 he prepared a major incursion into Chinese territory, joined by Liu Wuzhou and Liang Shidu, but he died while campaigning near Taiyuan. His sons included Ashina Shibobi and Ashina Jiesheshuai.
shibtu: Shibtu, whose Amorite name means the Old One, perhaps the Eldest, was born into the royal house of Yamhad at Aleppo, one of the most powerful kingdoms of the Near East in the early 18th century BCE. Her mother was Queen Gashera, and her brother Hammurabi later succeeded their father. Zimri-Lim had recovered Mari with Yarim-Lim's support, and their alliance was sealed by her marriage, which took place by proxy in about 1773 BCE, the second year of his reign: his envoys placed the veil on the bride at Aleppo after long talks over her dowry and the counter-dowry.

Zimri-Lim already had a main wife, Dam-hurasim, apparently a daughter of the king of Qatna, and Shibtu arrived in a secondary position. After the death of the queen mother Addu-duri she rose to the first rank. She stayed in the palace when the king was away, managing its staff, stores and estates, and her letters often open by saying that the palace is well. Yet she remained subordinate: she reported to him in detail and refused to hand over gold to the steward Mukannishum without a written order from the king.

She took a large part in religious affairs. She made offerings, among them gifts to the goddess Ishtar of Tuba in her homeland, reported prophecies uttered in the sanctuaries, and at the king's request had omens taken from the entrails of lambs. One such reading wrongly predicted that Hammurabi of Babylon would never prevail over Mari. Zimri-Lim's letters to her also deal with the choice of captive women for his household and with an infection spreading among the palace women, which he told her to contain by keeping the sick woman's cup, seat and bed apart.

Shibtu bore twins, a boy and a girl, probably the Hadni-Addu and Shubultum listed with her in the Small Eastern Palace. When Hammurabi's troops took Mari in 1761 BCE and the palace was looted and destroyed, she and the king disappear from the record. The scholar J.-M. Durand has suggested from a tablet listing her dowry that Zimri-Lim may have died before the fall, and that Shibtu either fled to Aleppo with her dowry or was remarried to Dadi-hadun, a vassal king.
shiga-prefecture: Shiga Prefecture borders Fukui Prefecture to the north, Gifu to the northeast, Mie to the southeast and Kyoto to the west. Lake Biwa, Japan's largest lake, lies at its centre and occupies one-sixth of its area. The Seta River is the only natural river that flows out of the lake, running through Kyoto to Osaka Bay. The lake divides the prefecture into four areas: Kohoku to the north, Kosei to the west, Kotō to the east and Konan to the south. Mountain ranges enclose it, among them the Hira Mountains, Mount Hiei, the Ibuki Mountains and the Suzuka Mountains. Southern Shiga is usually warm, while the north is cold with high snowfall.

Shiga was known as Ōmi Province, or Gōshū, before the prefectural system was established. Ōmi neighboured Nara and Kyoto, at the junction of western and eastern Japan. Between 667 and 672 Emperor Tenji founded a palace at Ōtsu, and in 742 Emperor Shōmu founded one at Shigaraki. In the early Heian period Saichō, born in the north of Ōtsu, founded Enryaku-ji, the centre of Tendai. Oda Nobunaga subjugated Ōmi and built Azuchi Castle on the eastern shore of Lake Biwa in 1579.

In 1600 Ishida Mitsunari, based at Sawayama Castle, made war against Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara. Afterwards Ieyasu made Ii Naomasa lord of Sawayama, and Naomasa established the Hikone Domain. Ii Naosuke, of that house, became the Tokugawa shogunate's Tairō and concluded commercial treaties with the Western powers. With the abolition of the han system eight prefectures were formed in Ōmi, and they were unified into Shiga Prefecture in September 1872. It is named after Shiga District, to which Ōtsu belonged until 1898.

Ōtsu is the capital and largest city; other major cities include Kusatsu, Nagahama and Higashiōmi. Hikone Castle is one of four national treasure castles in Japan, and Enryaku-ji is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The southern half adjoins Kyoto and forms part of Greater Kyoto. The Hikiyama festival of floats, held in ten areas including Nagahama each April, was designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1979.
shihab-dynasty: According to the 19th-century historian Mikhail Mishaqa, the Banu Shihab descended from the Banu Makhzum clan of the Quraysh, and their ancestor Harith fell at the Bab Sharqi gate during the Muslim siege of Damascus in 634. The tribe later settled in the Hauran and in 1172 moved from Shahba to Wadi al-Taym, at the foot of Mount Hermon. The family histories say Nur al-Din made their leader Munqidh ibn Amr governor of Wadi al-Taym in 1174 and that his descendants governed it through Mamluk rule. Under the Ottomans, Ahmad Shihab held its tax farm at intervals from 1592 to 1630 and fought beside his cousin Fakhr al-Din II, and marriages bound the Shihabs to the Ma'n dynasty.

When Ahmad Ma'n died without a male heir in 1697, the Qaysi Druze sheikhs chose Bashir Shihab I, his sister's son. The Ottomans appointed instead Haydar Shihab, Ahmad Ma'n's grandson, with Bashir as regent during his minority. The emir held a large tax farm covering the Chouf, Gharb, Matn and Keserwan, renewed each year by the Ottoman authorities, and made Deir al-Qamar his seat. Ousted in 1709, Haydar returned in 1711 and routed the Yamani faction at the Battle of Ain Dara; the Yamani Druze left for the Hauran, Maronite newcomers took their place, and the Shihabs became the paramount power in Mount Lebanon.

Later emirs fought each other and the governors of Sidon. Yusuf, raised a Maronite but presenting himself as a Sunni, began Shihab patronage of the Maronite bishops and monks, while Ahmad Pasha al-Jazzar played rival emirs against one another. Bashir Shihab II stayed neutral when Napoleon besieged Acre in 1799, then allied with Muhammad Ali of Egypt and helped Ibrahim Pasha take Acre on 27 May 1832 and Damascus on 14 June 1832. After the London Treaty of 15 July 1840 Ottoman and British troops landed, and on 14 October 1840 Bashir surrendered and went into exile. On 13 January 1842 the sultan deposed Bashir Shihab III, ending Shihab rule.

The Shihabs remain one of the most prominent families in Lebanon and bear the title emir; some are Sunni and others Maronite Catholics, though they share common roots. Fuad Chehab, the third president of Lebanon after independence, and the former prime minister Khaled Chehab belonged to the family, and descendants of Bashir II in Turkey are known as the Paksoy family. The 11th-century citadel of Hasbaya is still the family's private property.
shikoku: Shikoku is 225 kilometres long and between 50 and 150 kilometres wide, and lies south of Honshu and north-east of Kyushu. With its surrounding islands it covers about 18,800 square kilometres. Mountains running east and west divide it into a narrow northern zone facing the Seto Inland Sea and a larger, sparsely populated southern part facing the Pacific Ocean.
