Mount Ishizuchi in Ehime, at 1,982 metres, is the highest mountain. The major river is the Yoshino, which runs 196 kilometres from near Mount Ishizuchi to the sea at the city of Tokushima. Unlike Japan's other main islands, Shikoku has no active volcanoes, although a major volcanic caldera near Mount Ishizuchi was active around 14 million years ago.

The island's ancient names include Iyo-no-futana-shima, Iyo-shima and Futana-shima. Its present name, meaning four provinces, refers to the four former provinces that make it up: Awa, Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo. Shikoku has historically been quite isolated and therefore kept the original characteristics of Japan for longer, especially in vegetation and some architectural techniques. Until the Great Seto Bridge network opened in 1988, the central part of the island was isolated from the rest of Japan.

Shikoku is known for a pilgrimage of 88 temples, established by the Heian-period Buddhist priest Kūkai, a native of present-day Zentsūji in Kagawa Prefecture. According to legend Kūkai still appears to pilgrims. Pilgrims wear white jackets bearing the characters dōgyō ninin, meaning two travelling together. Because of wheat production, Sanuki udon became an important part of the diet in Kagawa Prefecture, formerly Sanuki Province, in the Edo period.

Shikoku is the smallest of Japan's four main islands and has the smallest population, about 3.4 million. It consists of four prefectures: Ehime, Kagawa, Kōchi and Tokushima. Matsuyama, the capital of Ehime Prefecture, is the largest city, and most inhabitants live in the north. Three expressways, which together form the Honshū–Shikoku Bridge Project, connect the island to Honshu. Annual festivals include the Awa Odori in Tokushima, held in August at the time of the Obon festival, and the Yosakoi festival in Kōchi.
shillong: Shillong lies in the middle of the Shillong Plateau, the only major uplifted structure in the northern Indian shield, and is surrounded by hills. Three of these are revered in Khasi tradition: Lum Sohpetbneng, Lum Diengiei and Lum Shyllong. The name comes from Lei Shyllong, a powerful deity believed to live on Shillong Peak, which overlooks the city. The city is about 100 kilometres from Guwahati by road, through hills and past Umiam Lake. Its climate is subtropical highland, with cool, very rainy summers and cool, dry winters. Its biggest market is Ïewduh.

During the First Anglo-Burmese War the British wanted a road connecting Sylhet and Assam across the Khasi and Jaintia Hills. David Scott, an East India Company civil servant and agent of the governor-general for the North East Frontier, overcame opposition from the Khasi chiefs, the Syiems, and in 1829 negotiated with the Syiem of Sohra for a sanatorium for the British. In early 1829 a Khasi confederation rose against British occupation, but by January 1833 its leader, Tirot Sing, had surrendered to Scott and was detained in Dacca. The British disliked the climate and facilities of Sohra, also known as Cherrapunjee, and moved to Shillong, which took its name because the new town lay below Shillong Peak.

The British designated Shillong the civil station of the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in 1864. In 1874 a separate Chief Commissionership of Assam was formed with its seat at Shillong, chosen for its convenient position between the Brahmaputra and Surma valleys and for its much cooler climate. It included Sylhet, the Naga Hills, the Lushai Hills and the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo Hills. A proclamation of 1878 made Shillong and its suburbs a station under the Bengal Municipal Act of 1876, with the villages of Mawkhar and Laban included by agreement with Haiñ Manik Syiem of Mylliem, dated 15 November 1878. An earthquake of 12 June 1897, of moment magnitude 8.1, killed 27 people in Shillong and destroyed much of the town.

Shillong was capital of undivided Assam under British rule and for 25 years in independent India. When the state of Meghalaya was created on 21 January 1972 it became the capital of Meghalaya, and Assam moved its capital to Dispur in Guwahati. It is the headquarters of the East Khasi Hills district. The rolling hills reminded the British of Scotland, so they called it the Scotland of the East.
shilluk-people: The Shilluk, who call themselves Chollo, are a major Luo Nilotic people living on the western bank of the White Nile in the Upper Nile state of South Sudan. They speak Dhøg Cøllø, which belongs to the Luo branch of the Western Nilotic subfamily, and they are the third-largest ethnic group of South Sudan after the Dinka and the Nuer. According to one account they formed their kingdom in 1454. Its king, the reth, came from the divine lineage of the culture hero Nyikang, who is believed to affect the nation's health.

The kingdom was historically a patriarchal monarchy, and society was somewhat hierarchical, with castes of royals, nobles, commoners and enslaved people. Today the Shilluk are governed by an elected headman chosen by a council of hamlet heads. Before the Second Sudanese Civil War the Shilluk also lived on the northern bank of the Sobat River, near where it joins the Nile.

Christian missions divided them: the Episcopal Church of Sudan dates its beginning to the late 19th century, when the Church Mission Society sent missionaries, the Catholic Church ran stations at Lul, Detwoc, Tonga and Yoynyang on the western bank, and the American Inland Mission ran one at Doleib Hill. The Shilluk were a minority in the Sudan People's Liberation Movement for most of the Second Sudanese Civil War.

In the summer of 2010 the Sudan People's Liberation Army, trying to disarm the people and stop a local Shilluk rebellion, burned several villages in the Shilluk Kingdom and killed an untold number of civilians. More than 10,000 people were displaced during the rainy season and fled into the forest, often without bedding, shelter or food, and many children died from hunger and cold. Violence began again in April 2011 with a crackdown on rebel-controlled regions, and broke out again in late 2022.

Most Shilluk are settled farmers, and both sexes do agricultural work. As among most Nilotic peoples, cattle-raising is a large part of the economy, though agriculture and fishing matter more than usual. Marriage involves bride-wealth, which traditionally included about ten head of cattle, several sheep and symbolic spears, although the amount depended on the groom's means. The ceremonies include a cattle exchange, a wedding feast at the bride's home and a symbolic mock battle between the families. Most Shilluk have converted to Christianity, some follow the traditional religion or a mixture of the two, and a few have converted to Islam.
shimabara-rebellion: Shimabara had been the domain of the Christian Arima clan, which was moved out in 1614 and replaced by the anti-Christian Matsukura. The new lord, Matsukura Shigemasa, hoped to rise in the shogunate by sponsoring costly projects, among them work on Edo Castle and a planned invasion of Luzon, and built a new castle at Shimabara. He placed a heavily disproportionate tax burden on his people and persecuted Christianity strictly, policies his heir Matsukura Katsuie continued. The Amakusa Islands suffered similar treatment under the Terasawa family, and the region held many unemployed samurai, former retainers of the Arima, Konishi and other houses.

Discontented rōnin and impoverished peasants plotted in secret, and the uprising broke out on 17 December 1637 with the assassination of the magistrate Hayashi Hyōzaemon. A charismatic 16-year-old, Amakusa Shirō, emerged as leader. The rebels besieged Tomioka and Hondo castles and Shimabara Castle but were forced back by armies from neighbouring Kyushu domains. They gathered at the ruins of Hara Castle, former seat of the Arima, and used weapons and provisions plundered from the Matsukura storehouses.

The shogunate's allied army, under Itakura Shigemasa, besieged Hara Castle. The swordsman Miyamoto Musashi was present as an adviser to Hosokawa Tadatoshi. The Dutch supplied gunpowder and cannon, and the ship de Ryp bombarded the castle before withdrawing. Itakura was killed in a failed advance and replaced by Matsudaira Nobutsuna. On 3 February 1638 a surprise attack killed 2,000 warriors of the Hizen Domain, but the castle's food and ammunition then ran out. Troops of the Kuroda clan stormed the outer defences on 12 April 1638, and the rebels were routed on 15 April.

The shogunate executed an estimated 37,000 rebels and sympathizers. Amakusa Shirō's head was displayed in Nagasaki, and Hara Castle was burned and buried with the dead. Katsuie was beheaded in Edo, the only daimyō decapitated in the Edo period, and Terasawa Katataka's lands were confiscated. Portuguese traders, suspected of helping the rebels, were expelled, and national seclusion was stricter by 1639. Christianity survived only underground.

Migrants from other parts of Japan resettled the peninsula, whose towns had lost most of their men, and every inhabitant was registered with a local temple. The rebellion is often portrayed as Christian, but the academic consensus is that it was driven chiefly by peasant anger at misgovernment, with Christians joining later. Apart from local peasant risings, it was the last large-scale armed clash in Japan until the Boshin War.
shimane-prefecture: Shimane Prefecture lies on the Sea of Japan side of the Chūgoku region of Honshu, with the Chūgoku Mountains to the south. It borders Yamaguchi, Hiroshima and Tottori prefectures. The mountains make the interior harder to live in, and over two thirds of the population lives along the coast. Rice is grown mostly on the Izumo plain. The Shimane peninsula encloses two brackish lakes, Lake Shinji and Nakaumi, and the Oki Islands off the coast also belong to the prefecture. The largest cities are Matsue, the capital, Izumo, Hamada and Masuda.

The history of Shimane begins with mythology. The Shinto god Ōkuninushi was believed to live in Izumo, an old province, and Izumo Shrine honours him. The area was divided into the provinces of Iwami, Izumo and Oki until the abolition of the han in 1871. In the Nara period Kakinomoto no Hitomaro wrote a poem on Shimane's nature when he was sent as governor. In the Kamakura period the shogunate exiled the emperors Go-Toba and Go-Daigo to Oki, and Go-Daigo escaped and rallied supporters against the shogunate.

In the Muromachi period the Kyōgoku clan controlled Izumo and Oki. After the Ōnin War the Amago clan expanded its power from Gassantoda Castle and the Masuda clan dominated Iwami. Many battles were fought between them for the silver of the Iwami Ginzan mine, which lay between their territories. Mōri Motonari conquered Izumo, Iwami and Oki in 1566. After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, which the Mōri lost, Horio Yoshiharu entered Izumo and Oki and built Matsue Castle. In 1638 Matsudaira Naomasa, a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu, became ruler because the Horio had no heir, and his family ruled until the han were abolished. The Iwami mine, under direct shogunate control, was one of the nation's largest silver mines by the early 17th century.

After the abolition of the han in 1871 the old Shimane and Hamada provinces formed the area of the present prefecture. Oki became part of Tottori that year, Hamada Prefecture was merged into Shimane in 1876, and the present border was formed in 1881.

Shimane is the second-least populous prefecture of Japan. Izumo-taisha, one of the oldest Shinto shrines in Japan, stands at Izumo, and Matsue Castle dates from the Tokugawa era. The Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine, with its cultural background, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Izumo-taisha main shrine and the Kamosu Shrine main shrine are National Treasures.
shimashki-dynasty: A list of twelve kings of Shimashki survives in the Elamite king-list of Susa, which also lists the kings of the Awan dynasty. How accurate it is, and whether its order is chronological, is uncertain, though some of its kings appear in the records of neighbouring peoples. Shimashki probably lay near today's Masjed Soleyman. It is first mentioned in an inscription of Puzur-Inshushinak, king of Awan, around 2100 BCE, which shows a king of Shimashki seizing his feet in submission. The historian Daryaee suggests that Shimashki was better thought of as an alliance of peoples than a unitary state.

Its early kings appear in the records of the Third Dynasty of Ur. Girnamme, a contemporary of Shu-Sin of Ur, took part in the marriage of Shu-Sin's daughter, and with Tazitta and Ebarti I he is named in Mesopotamian texts of 2044 to 2032 BCE that record food rations for messengers. The confederacy then led an alliance that defeated Ibbi-Sin, the last ruler of Ur, looted the capital and held it by military occupation for 21 years. The campaign was a joint effort of Kindattu and his ally Ishbi-Erra, whose hymn claims that he later expelled Kindattu from Mesopotamia.

Kindattu's son Idaddu I called himself king of Shimashki and Elam. Tan-Ruhurater married Mê-Kubi, daughter of Bilalama, governor of Eshnunna, and his son Idaddu II oversaw building works as governor of Susa and was, according to Gwendolyn Leick, the last Shimashkian king. The rulers of Shimashki were drawn into a long conflict with the kings of Isin and Larsa.

Under the Shimashki and the Sukkalmah dynasty that followed them, Elam became one of the most powerful kingdoms of West Asia, reaching Mesopotamia and Syria through trade, war and diplomacy. Its expansion was halted only by the Babylonian king Hammurabi in the 18th century BCE, after which the Elamite forces along the Tigris withdrew to Susa.
shimazu-clan: The Shimazu were the daimyō of the Satsuma domain, which spread over Satsuma, Ōsumi and Hyūga provinces. They were tozama, or outsider, daimyō, as opposed to the fudai families that were hereditary vassals or allies of the Tokugawa. The founder, Shimazu Tadahisa (died 1227), is said to have been a son of the shōgun Minamoto no Yoritomo. He received the domain of Shioda in Shinano Province in 1186 and was then named shugo of Satsuma. He went to Satsuma in 1196 and subdued Hyūga and Ōsumi.

The clan claims descent from the Seiwa Genji on its father's side and from the Koremune clan through Tadahisa's wife. Older sources record Tadahisa himself under the name Koremune, and Japanese historians have questioned his Genji lineage; the general view is that he was of Koremune descent.

At their peak the Shimazu were the wealthiest and most powerful tozama family, with an income above 700,000 koku. Shimazu Yoshihisa, the 16th head, retired in 1587 after Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Kyushu Campaign. His successor Yoshihiro led the clan at the Battle of Sekigahara. In 1609 the Shimazu invaded the Ryūkyū Kingdom, which the shōgun allowed in order to appease them after their loss at Sekigahara. The trade it brought, and the prestige of being the only daimyō family to control an entire foreign country, secured their standing.

Shimazu women married into the shogunal house: a daughter of Shigehide became the wife of the 11th shōgun, Tokugawa Ienari, in 1789, and in 1856 Nariakira's adopted daughter Tenshō-in became the wife of the 13th shōgun, Tokugawa Iesada. Hisamitsu, regent for Tadayoshi, was daimyō of Satsuma at the time of the Boshin War and the Meiji Restoration, in which Satsuma played a major role.

The Shimazu are known as the first in Japan to use matchlock arquebuses on the battlefield and began producing them at home. In their campaign to conquer Kyushu in the 1580s they lured opponents into an ambush by arquebus troops on both sides, then sent central forces to rout them, and so beat larger clans such as the Itō, Ryūzōji and Ōtomo. The clan was known for the loyalty of its retainers. Its seven most significant vassal families, the shichi-tō, were the Niiro, Hokugō, Ijuin, Machida, Kawakami, Ata and Kajiki. In 1884 both Hisamitsu and Tadayoshi were created princes.
shimazu-nariakira: Nariakira was born on 28 April 1809 at the Satsuma estate in Edo, the son of Shimazu Narioki, and was named heir at the age of three. Like his grandfather Shigehide, he was drawn to Western learning: he studied Shigehide's clocks, telescopes and microscopes, learned Roman letters, which he later used as a private code, and met the German physician Philipp Franz von Siebold. His father and the chief adviser Zusho Hirosato distrusted his costly plans, and his father's consort Yura pressed the claims of her son, his half-brother Shimazu Hisamitsu.

In 1846 the shogunal official Abe Masahiro sent him to Satsuma to deal with French and British demands for treaties with the Ryūkyū Kingdom, and the two agreed to allow such relations there rather than risk conflict. His father then sidelined him, and his followers, who blamed Yura for the deaths of his eldest children, were made to commit seppuku. With help from Date Munenari of Uwajima, Abe intervened: Zusho committed seppuku on 18 December 1848 after taking the blame for illegal trade, and Narioki was pressed to retire.

As daimyō, Nariakira had the Iroha-maru, one of the first Western-style ships built in Japan, made by the physician Minayoshi Hotoku, and set up a shipyard at Sakurajima. He brought Western-style cavalry into the domain's army, founded the Rangaku Koshujo for Dutch and Western studies, and in 1848 obtained the first daguerreotype camera imported into Japan. He promoted Saigō Takamori to be his attendant in 1854 and pardoned Ōkubo Toshimichi, who had been exiled for supporting him.

In July 1858, while supervising manoeuvres at Tempozan for sending 3,000 Satsuma soldiers to Edo, he was overcome by the heat and died at Tsurumaru Castle. Saigō and Ōkubo took up his views, among them centring government on the emperor and Westernizing the military, which later underlay the Meiji government. He was deified as the kami Terukuni Daimyōjin. His portrait, made on 17 September 1857, is the oldest surviving daguerreotype by a Japanese photographer and in 1999 became the first photograph designated an Important Cultural Property.
shimazu-takahisa: Takahisa was a son of Shimazu Tadayoshi and is said to have been born in Izaku Castle in 1514. In 1526 he was adopted as the successor of Shimazu Katsuhisa and became head of the clan, the fifteenth to hold that position. As daimyō he launched a series of campaigns to reclaim three provinces, Satsuma, Osumi and Hyūga, in the warring years of Japan's Sengoku period.

Takahisa actively promoted relations with foreign peoples and countries. After a number of Portuguese were shipwrecked on Tanegashima in 1543, he became the first daimyō to bring Western firearms into Japan, and in 1549 he used firearms of Portuguese origin to take Kajiki castle. In the same year he welcomed the Jesuit Francis Xavier, meeting him at Ijyuin Castle, and granted him protection to preach in his domain. Under pressure from local Buddhist monks he later withdrew his support for Christianity. He also maintained a diplomatic relationship with the Ryūkyū Kingdom.

His authority over his own vassals was not secure. In 1554 he had to take action against rebellious kokujin vassals, the Ito and Kimotsuki clans, at the Siege of Iwatsurugi Castle. His notable retainers included Ijuin Tadaaki, Niiro Tadamoto and Tanegashima Tokitaka.

Takahisa nurtured the leaders of the next generation: his sons Shimazu Yoshihisa, Yoshihiro, Toshihisa and Iehisa, under whom the Shimazu clan for a time extended its power across the island of Kyūshū. He is also said to have had a daughter whose name is unknown. In 1570 he handed the headship of the clan to Yoshihisa, and he died in 1571.
shimazu-yoshihiro: Yoshihiro was the second son of Shimazu Takahisa and is said to have been born in Izaku Castle. As lord of Iino Castle he defeated the Itō clan with Niiro Tadamoto at the Battle of Kizaki in 1572, and with his brothers beat the Otomo clan at the Battle of Mimigawa in 1578. In 1587, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi's armies came to subdue Kyūshū, he pressed for war even after his brother Yoshihisa had surrendered, and gave in only after repeated requests. He was long believed to have become the 17th head of the clan, but it is now thought that Yoshihisa kept that position.

Under Hideyoshi he fought in Korea in both 1592 and 1597. In 1597, with Tōdō Takatora, Katō Yoshiaki and Konishi Yukinaga, he defeated the navy of Wŏn Kyun, and at Sacheon in 1598 his 7,000 soldiers beat a Ming army of 37,000. At the Battle of Noryang, the last of the war, he sought to cross the strait and join Konishi; afterwards he rescued the Japanese commanders and returned home.

Recent research holds that he sided with Ishida Mitsunari from the start, not after a slight at Fushimi as novels of the Edo Period claimed. At Sekigahara his 1,500 men held their ground without fighting. Stranded among at least 30,000 of Tokugawa Ieyasu's troops, he was dissuaded by his nephew Shimazu Toyohisa from a last charge and instead cut through the enemy in a fighting retreat known as sutegamari, in which Toyohisa and most of his men died and Ii Naomasa was wounded. He then returned to Satsuma by ship.

In 1602 Ieyasu allowed the clan to keep its domain and let Yoshihiro's son Shimazu Tadatsune succeed him. Yoshihiro retired to Sakurajima and taught the younger generation. A devoted Buddhist, he had raised a monument to enemy dead of the Korean war. When he died in 1619, several retainers who had fought beside him took their own lives, and in 1918 Emperor Taishō gave him the posthumous senior third rank.
shimazu-yoshihisa: Yoshihisa was the eldest son of Shimazu Takahisa; his mother was a daughter of Iriki'in Shigesato, and Shimazu Yoshihiro, Shimazu Toshihisa and Shimazu Iehisa were his brothers. His childhood name was Torajumaru, though he went by Matasaburō. At his coming of age he took the name Tadayoshi, changed it to Yoshitatsu after receiving a character from the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiteru, and later took the name Yoshihisa. He married his own aunt and, after her death, a daughter of Tanegashima Tokitaka. In 1566 he became the sixteenth chief of the clan.

Working with his three brothers, he set out to unify Kyūshū. He defeated the Itō clan at the battle of Kizaki in 1572 and at the Siege of Takabaru in 1576, took Minamata castle in Higo Province in 1581, and after Okitanawate also defeated the Aso clan. When the Ōtomo and Ryūzōji appealed to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Yoshihisa derided his request to make peace. In 1586 his army attacked Tachibana castle, defended by Tachibana Muneshige and his wife Tachibana Ginchiyo, and the Ōtomo leaders went to Osaka to win Hideyoshi's help.

Hideyoshi mobilised 200,000 soldiers and 20,000 pack animals. His vanguard under Toyotomi Hidenaga, joined by Mōri forces under Kobayakawa Takakage, drove the Shimazu back in Hyūga and Bungo; they fought well but had few firearms and lacked discipline and training. In June 1587 they were routed in Satsuma itself, Hideyoshi besieged Kagoshima castle, and Yoshihisa sued for peace and shaved his head as a sign that he would become a monk, taking the name Ryūhaku.

His conquests went to Hideyoshi's generals Kato, Konishi and Kuroda. Yoshihiro commanded the clan's troops, though Yoshihisa is believed to have kept managing the domain's daily affairs, and having no son he adopted Yoshihiro's son Shimazu Tadatsune as heir. Hosokawa Fujitaka taught him classical literature, and he at first favoured Christian missionaries such as Luís de Almeida. Asked by Tokugawa Ieyasu how he had unified Kyushu, he credited his brothers and retainers. He died of illness at Kokubu Castle in 1611 and was buried at the former site of Fukushoji in Kagoshima, where his tombstone remains.
shimla: Shimla stands in the south-western ranges of the Himalayas at an average altitude of 2,206 metres, along a ridge with seven spurs. It stretches nearly 9.2 kilometres from east to west and lies within the historical cultural Mahasu region. The nearest river, the Sutlej, is about 21 kilometres away. According to one theory the name comes from Shyamalaya, a blue slate house on Jakhu Hill built by a fakir. According to another it comes from Shamli or Shyamala, the Hindu goddess Kali, whose temple is said to have stood on the Jakhu hillside.

In the 18th century most of the area was dense forest, with the Jakhu Temple, a few houses and nearby villages. Bhimsen Thapa of Nepal captured it in 1806, and the British East India Company took control under the Sugauli Treaty after the Anglo-Nepalese War, with David Ochterlony storming the fort of Malaun in May 1815. The surveying Gerard brothers described Shimla on 30 August 1817 as a middling-sized village.

In 1819 Lieutenant Ross built a wood cottage, and in 1822 Charles Pratt Kennedy built the first permanent house, Kennedy Cottage. In 1830 the British acquired the surrounding land from the chiefs of Keonthal and Patiala. The settlement grew from 30 houses in 1830 to 1,141 in 1881.

Officers came for the climate, which they found like Britain's. By the late 1830s the town had theatre and art exhibitions, and businessmen, mainly from the Sood and Parsi communities, arrived to supply the growing European population. Christ Church's foundation was laid on 9 September 1844. In 1863 the Viceroy John Lawrence decided to move the summer capital there, though it meant shifting the administration twice a year from Calcutta, over 1,600 kilometres away.

The Viceregal Lodge was later built on Observatory Hill. A fire cleared the Upper Bazaar, where the native Indian population lived, and its people were moved to the Middle and Lower Bazaars so that the east end could become the centre of the European town.

Shimla is the capital of Himachal Pradesh and its largest city. After partition it briefly served as capital of East Punjab until Chandigarh was built. Buildings of the colonial era in Tudorbethan and neo-Gothic styles survive, including the Viceregal Lodge and Christ Church, along with temples such as Jakhu Temple. The Kalka-Shimla Railway, built by the British, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The city hosted the Simla Deputation of 1906 and the Shimla Agreement of 1972.
shimonoseki: Shimonoseki is the westernmost point of Honshu and of Yamaguchi Prefecture. It borders the Sea of Japan to the west and the Seto Inland Sea to the south, across the Kanmon Straits. The city is long from north to south and fan-shaped, opening towards the Seto Inland Sea, and the Asa and Ariho rivers run through it. It was formerly called Bakan. Its climate is humid subtropical, with hot summers and cool winters, and it is nicknamed the home of fugu, for the pufferfish caught and cooked locally.

Shimonoseki was part of ancient Nagato Province and has prospered since ancient times as the gateway to Honshu from the Asian continent, including Kyushu, China and the Korean Peninsula. According to the Nihon Shoki, Emperor Chuai built a palace on the site of the present city hall in the Kofun period. The name appears in Heian period documents from 869 as the site of a checkpoint controlling maritime access to the Seto Inland Sea, although by the Kamakura period the name Akamanoseki was more common.

During the Genpei War the Heike and Genji fought the Battle of Dan-no-ura near the present Kanmon Bridge. In the Muromachi period the Ōuchi clan, shugo of both Nagato and Buzen in Kyushu, controlled trade and diplomatic missions from Ming China and Joseon Korea.

In the Edo period the area belonged to Chōfu Domain, ruled by the Mōri clan. In February 1691 the German explorer Engelbert Kaempfer visited the town during his two-year stay in Japan and described it as a major port for supplying ships, with around 400 to 500 houses. The Bombardment of Shimonoseki took place in 1864, and in 1895 the Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed, by which a defeated China handed over Taiwan, Penghu and Port Arthur to Japan. Akamagaseki city was established on 1 April 1889 under the modern municipal system and renamed Shimonoseki on 1 June 1902.

Shimonoseki is the largest city in Yamaguchi Prefecture. It has long had a thriving industry in shipping, trade and finance, and it remains the economic centre of the prefecture. It is the largest harvester of pufferfish in Japan. In 2005 it absorbed the towns of Hōhoku, Kikugawa, Toyota and Toyoura, and in the same year it was designated a core city with increased local autonomy. Universities in the city include Shimonoseki City University and the National Fisheries University.
shimosa-province: Shimōsa Province lay in the area of modern Chiba and Ibaraki prefectures and the bordering parts of Saitama Prefecture and Tokyo, in the parts that lay east of the lower reaches of the old Tone River before it was diverted eastward. It lies to the north of the Bōsō Peninsula, whose name takes its second kanji from Kazusa and Shimōsa Provinces. Its short names were Sōshū and Hokusō. It was classed as one of the provinces of the Tōkaidō and bordered Kazusa to the south, Musashi and Kōzuke to the west, and Hitachi and Shimotsuke to the north. Under the Engishiki classification it ranked as a 'great country' and a far country.

Shimōsa was originally part of a larger territory called Fusa Province, which was divided into upper and lower parts, Kazusa and Shimōsa, in the reign of Emperor Kōtoku (645–654). The Imperial Court in the Nara period knew it for its fertile lands, and records mention that it supplied hemp to the court. It was divided into 11, later 12, counties. The location of its capital is not precisely known but is believed to lie in the modern city of Ichikawa, near the ruins of the Kokubun-ji. Its Ichinomiya is the Katori Jingū in the modern city of Katori.

In the Heian period the province was divided into many shōen held by local samurai clans, chiefly the Chiba clan, which sided with Minamoto no Yoritomo in the Genpei War. Much of it stayed under Chiba control in the Kamakura period. By the early Muromachi period it was a highly contested region fragmented among samurai clans, and in the Sengoku period the Later Hōjō clan held sway after the Battle of Kōnodai in 1538 against the Ashikaga and Satomi clans.

After Tokugawa Ieyasu was installed in Edo, following the Battle of Odawara, he created eleven han within Shimōsa to reward his followers and kept the rest as tenryō territory held directly by the shōgun and administered by various hatamoto. The whole province had an assessed revenue of 681,062 koku. After the Meiji Restoration the domains and tenryō became short-lived prefectures in July 1871, with the abolition of the han system. Most of the province became part of the new Chiba Prefecture on 15 June 1873, four districts (Yūki, Toyoda, Sashima and Okada) went to the new Ibaraki Prefecture, and the part west of the Edogawa River went to Saitama Prefecture.
shin-saimdang: Shin Saimdang was the third of five daughters of Shin Myeong-hwa, a government official of the Pyongsan Shin clan who was a friend of the scholar Cho Kwangjo but not politically active, and Lady Yi of the Yongin Yi clan. Her father lived largely apart from the family for 16 years in Hanseong while he prepared for the civil examinations, and he never went beyond the jinsa test.

Because her mother kept living with her own parents after marriage, she had more freedom in educating her daughters. Having no brothers, Saimdang received an education that would normally have been given to a son, learning the Thousand Character Classic from her father and studying Neo-Confucianism, history and literature, which surprised her father's visitors.

Her father chose Yi Won-su as her husband, although many thought it poor judgement, since his family was poor and he had no post. Shin Myeong-hwa put first a husband who would let her continue her art, and Yi Won-su did not object. She married him on 20 August 1522, at 17, and with his consent kept spending time at her parents' home in Gangneung. The couple had eight children, five boys and three girls, and at 33 she went back to Gangneung to give birth to her third son, Yi I.

Her paintings are known for delicate beauty, with insects, flowers, butterflies, orchids, grapes, fish and landscapes among her favourite themes. About 40 works in ink and stone colours remain, although many others may exist. Little of her calligraphy survives, but the scholar Eo Suk-kwon compared her grapes and landscapes to those of the artist Ahn Gyeon. In 1868 the governor of Gangneung remarked on her calligraphy as filled with nobility, elegance, serenity and purity.

Saimdang disapproved when her husband took up with a kisaeng named Kwon, and the couple's relationship cooled; she asked him not to remarry after her death. She died suddenly in 1551, aged 46, after moving to the Pyongan region. Her son Yi I had prayed daily for her recovery at the shrine of his maternal grandfather.

After her death Yi Won-su did not marry Kwon but brought her to live with the children, causing conflict with Yi I, who ran away from home. Her respectful nickname was Eojin, Wise Mother, and she is often held up as a model of Confucian ideals. Along with Queen Munjeong, Jeong Nan-jeong and Hwang Jin-yi she is considered one of the most significant women of the period.
shin-sawbu: Shin Sawbu was born on 11 February 1394, the only daughter of the Mon King Razadarit by his junior queen Thuddhamaya, and was named Vihāradevī, meaning queen of the monastery in Sanskrit and Pali. At 20 she married Binnya Bwe, a nephew of Razadarit, and had a son, Binnya Waru, and two daughters. Her husband died when she was 25.

After Razadarit's death in 1421 his sons quarrelled, and King Thihathu of Ava came south with an army in November 1423. To make peace, her brother Binnya Ran presented her to Thihathu in December 1423. Thihathu died in 1425, and she stayed at Ava, where she became patron of two Mon monks, Dhammanyana and Pitakahara. In 1429 they helped her escape and return to Pegu.

She came to the throne early in 1454, when the male line of Pegu had been exhausted; two of her brothers and her son had already reigned there. Her successor was the monk Pitakahara, who left the sangha, took the titles Punnaraja and Dhammazedi and married her younger daughter Mipakathin. A Mon tradition tells that she hid a layman's dress and small models of the five regalia in one monk's alms bowl and let the lot decide. Some historians, among them Guillon, hold that she and Dhammazedi ruled jointly, he at Pegu and she at Dagon, the traditional appanage of Mon queens.

At Dagon she enlarged and paved the platform of the Shwedagon Pagoda, set stone posts and lamps around it, strengthened its sevenfold wall and extended its glebe lands to Danok. She had her own weight in gold, 25 viss, beaten into leaf to cover the pagoda. Three stone inscriptions survive from her reign, among them one recording a land dedication of 25 September 1455.

She died at Dagon in 1471 and is said to have worn a crown to the end. The stupa said to hold her remains stands at a monastery in Sanchaung Township of Yangon, near the Shwedagon. Her Mon name Binnya Thau means Old Queen, and a chronicle tells that she took it after an old man mocked her in the street. At the end of the nineteenth century some Mons are said to have regarded Queen Victoria as her reincarnation. Shin Saw Pu Road in Yangon is named after her.
shina-language: Shina, also known by its exonym Gilgiti, is an Indo-Aryan language of the Dardic branch of the Indo-European family. It is spoken primarily by the Shina people of northern Pakistan, in Gilgit-Baltistan and Kohistan. A small community of speakers lives in the Gurez valley of Jammu and Kashmir and the Dras valley of Ladakh in India. Related outliers include Brokskat in Ladakh, Kundal Shahi in Azad Kashmir, Palula and Sawi in Chitral and Kunar, Ushojo in the Swat Valley and Kalkoti in Dir.

Ethnologue estimated 1,146,000 speakers in Pakistan in 2018, most of them in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Gilgit-Baltistan. In Ladakh, the speakers in the far north of Kargil district numbered about 32,200 in the 2011 census, and in the Kashmir Valley Shina people form the majority in Gurez. Under the influence of Urdu and English, and the religious weight of Arabic and Persian, the language keeps adding loan words.

Shina words are often distinguished by three contrasting tones: level, rising and falling. The tone is heard only on long vowels. Where the stress falls on the first mora of a long vowel the tone is falling, and where it falls on the second mora the tone is rising. The word written the means the imperative Do! with a level tone, while Thée means Will you do? and Theé means after having done. There are five vowels, each short or long, and all but one can also be nasalised. In the dialects of Dras in India the original initial and final consonant clusters have been preserved, while those spoken in Pakistan have lost them.

Shina is one of the few Dardic languages with a written tradition, yet it was unwritten until a few decades ago and remains mostly spoken. Since the first attempts to represent its phonology accurately in the 1960s, several orthographies have been proposed. Debates have centred on how to write retroflex sounds absent from Urdu and whether to mark vowel length and tone. Only in the late 2010s was the orthography standardised, and primers and dictionaries endorsed by the government of Gilgit-Baltistan have been published. The alphabet is a Perso-Arabic one, developed by writers including Professor Muhammad Amin Ziya, Shakeel Ahmad Shakeel and Razwal Kohistani. Diacritics mark the rising and falling tones.
shinano-province: Shinano Province, also called Shinshu, was an old province of Japan that is now Nagano Prefecture. It bordered Echigo, Etchu, Hida, Kai, Kozuke, Mino, Mikawa, Musashi, Suruga and Totomi Provinces, and its ancient capital stood near modern Matsumoto, which became an important city of the province. The province consisted of sixteen districts, among them Azumi, Chiisagata, Chikuma, Hanishina, Minochi, Saku, Sarashina and Takai, together with the four districts of the former Suwa Province: Ina, Kamiina, Shimoina and Suwa. The Suwa Taisha was designated the chief Shinto shrine, the ichinomiya, of the province. The aircraft carrier Shinano of the Second World War was named after it.

In 713 the road across Mino and Shinano was widened to take the growing numbers of travellers through the Kiso District. In the Sengoku period the province was often split among fiefs, and castle towns such as Komoro, Ina and Ueda developed. Shinano was one of the main centres of Takeda Shingen's power in his wars with Uesugi Kenshin and others.

After Oda Nobunaga's assassination in the Honno-ji Incident, Shinano was contested between Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Go-Hojo clan of Odawara Castle. The Tokugawa, Uesugi and Hojo each hoped to seize Shinano, the Ueno region and Kai Province, which were then ruled by the remnants of the many small clans that had served the Takeda. The three-way conflict became known as the Tensho-Jingo War.

It turned in favour of the Tokugawa, helped by the defection of Sanada Masayuki to their side, and the Hojo negotiated a truce, sending Hojo Ujinobu while the Tokugawa sent Ii Naomasa to the preliminary meetings. In October representatives of the Oda clan, Oda Nobukatsu and Oda Nobutaka, and Toyotomi mediated until the truce was concluded.

In 1871 the han system was abolished and prefectures established. The former domains, among them Komoro, Ueda, Matsushiro, Suzaka, Iiyama, Suwa/Takashima, Iida and Matsumoto, were merged into Nagano, first called Nakano Prefecture in 1870, and Chikuma prefectures. When the prefectures were merged again in 1875/76, Chikuma was split, its western part covering Hida Province going to Gifu and its eastern part in Shinano to Nagano. Since then Nagano has been essentially contiguous with Shinano.
shingon-buddhism: The word shingon is the Japanese reading of the Chinese zhenyan, which translates the Sanskrit mantra. The Zhenyan lineage was founded in China in about the 7th and 8th centuries by Indian masters such as Śubhakarasiṃha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra. Kūkai, born into the aristocratic Saeki clan in Shikoku, converted to Buddhism in his twenties and practised as an ascetic in the mountains. In 804 he went to Chang-an, where he studied under Huiguo, a student of Amoghavajra, and brought back many texts, mandalas and ritual items. In 809 he was allowed to reside at Takaosanji, now Jingo-ji, and under Emperor Saga's patronage he began to give esoteric initiations. He established his tradition on Mount Kōya, which remains its central pilgrimage centre.

Shingon teaches that buddhahood can be attained in this very body, through practices that use the three mysteries of mudra, mantra and mandala: gestures of the body, sacred formulas of speech and meditation of the mind. At its centre stands Mahāvairocana, or Dainichi, the universal Buddha who is the basis of all phenomena. Another influential doctrine is that all beings are originally enlightened. Practice depends on initiation by ordained masters. A central meditation is Ajikan, contemplation of the letter A in a white moon disk upon a lotus, and the goma fire ritual has roots in the Vedic homa.

After Kūkai, Tō-ji rose under Kangen to be the head temple, and Mount Kōya declined before recovering in the 11th century with the support of Fujiwara nobles such as Fujiwara no Michinaga. In 1615 Tokugawa Ieyasu issued regulations that brought the school into the administrative temple system. After the Meiji Restoration the state separated Shinto from Buddhism, and many Shingon temples closed after confiscations of land. In 1941 the schools were forcibly merged, and after the war they separated again. About eighteen major schools now exist. Shingon influenced Tendai, Shugendo, Shinto and the ritual repertoire of Soto Zen, and shaped medieval Japanese aesthetics and art.
shining-path: The Shining Path, officially the Communist Party of Peru, was founded in 1969 by Abimael Guzmán, a former university philosophy professor whom his followers called Presidente Gonzalo, together with 11 others. Guzmán was heavily influenced by a trip to China and admired Mao Zedong. Its common name comes from a maxim of Mariátegui: Marxism–Leninism will open the shining path to revolution.

From 1970 to 1977 it built a student organization and regional committees in Lima and the central sierra. It first gained a foothold at San Cristóbal of Huamanga University in Ayacucho, where Guzmán taught, and between 1973 and 1975 controlled the student councils at the universities of Huancayo and La Cantuta.

By 1980 it had about 500 members. When Peru's military government allowed elections for the first time in twelve years, the Shining Path declined to take part and began a guerrilla war in the highlands of the Ayacucho Region. On 17 May 1980, on the eve of the presidential elections, it burned ballot boxes in the town of Chuschi, its first act of war. Through the 1980s it grew in territory and militants, particularly in the Andean highlands, gaining some peasant sympathy by filling a political gap left by the central government and offering what it called popular justice: public trials with swift sentences, including public executions.

The government's response was initially tepid. On 29 December 1981 it declared an emergency zone in Ayacucho, Huancavelica and Apurímac and let the military detain any suspect. The military abused this power, arresting many innocent people and subjecting some to torture and rape.

On 12 September 1992 the Special Intelligence Group captured Guzmán and several leaders in an apartment above a dance studio in Lima. The leadership vacuum was large, and the organization suffered defeats from rural self-defence organizations of campesinos, supposedly its social base. When Guzmán called for peace talks, it split between those for and those against them.

The party was designed on a concentric model, with Communist Party organs at the centre, the paramilitary wing around them and the political wing on the outside, so that the party controlled both. Its ideology moved from Marxism–Leninism–Mao Zedong thought to Marxism–Leninism–Maoism–Gonzalo thought, and some authors see a cult of personality around Guzmán.

It has been widely condemned for brutality against peasants, as in the Lucanamarca massacre, and against trade unionists, rival Marxist groups and elected officials. The Asháninka minority suffered disproportionately, with about 6,000 killed, over 10% of their 1993 population.
shinkolobwe: The mine, also called Kasolo, Chinkolobew or Shainkolobwe, lies 20 km west of Likasi (formerly Jadotville), 20 km south of Kambove and about 145 km north-west of Lubumbashi, and takes its name from the long-gone nearby village of Shinkolobwe. The English geologist Robert Rich Sharp (1881-1960) found the deposits. Uranium minerals, with cobalt, silver, nickel, bismuth and arsenic, occur in veinlets along fractures in the dolomitic shales of the Precambrian Mine Series, where uraninite mineralisation occurred 630 million years ago. Many new minerals were first identified there, among them becquerelite, curite, soddyite and sharpite.

The first mine opened in the Belgian Congo in 1921, and only the richest ore was sent to Olen in Belgium for the extraction of radium and uranium, the rest being held in reserve. Open-cut mining was suspended in 1936. Britain and France showed interest in the Belgian stock of ore in 1939, but after the Nazis occupied Belgium in 1940 they took 1,200 tons of it, most of which the Alsos Mission recovered in 1945.

Edgar Sengier, director of Union Minière du Haut Katanga, had stockpiled 1,200 tonnes of ore in a warehouse on Staten Island, New York. Colonel Ken Nichols bought it, with another 3,000 tonnes stored above ground at the mine, for the Manhattan Project, and after the agreement of September 1942 an average of 400 tons of uranium oxide a month was shipped to the United States. The mine was reopened, its location removed from maps and journalists kept away.

After the war the United States received 1,440 tons of uranium concentrates from the Belgian Congo in 1947, 2,792 in 1951 and 1,600 in 1953, and a garrison guarded the site, supported by a NATO base at Kamina. With new uranium mines opening in the United States and the Congo becoming independent, the Americans left in 1960 and Union Minière sealed the mine with concrete.

The mine was officially closed by presidential decree on 28 January 2004. In July 2004 part of the old mine collapsed, killing eight people and injuring thirteen. Industrial production has ceased and cement lids seal the shafts, but a United Nations report of June 2006 found that artisanal mining was still going on there.
shinran: Shinran was born on 21 May 1173 at Hino, now part of Fushimi in Kyoto, to Lord Hino Arinori, of a lesser branch of the Fujiwara clan that had lost its rank after a scandal. The family was known for scholars and civil servants. His father died early and he was educated by his uncle Hino Munenari. His birth name was Matsuwakamaro, and he later used the names Han'en, Shakkū, Zenshin and finally Shinran. He trained as a Tendai monk on Mount Hiei.

Dissatisfied with his spiritual life, he went on retreat at the Rokkaku-dō temple in 1201. There he had a vision of Avalokiteśvara as Prince Shōtoku, which directed him to the Pure Land teacher Hōnen. He became Hōnen's disciple and gave up the Tendai practices for the recitation of the nembutsu.

In 1207 the retired emperor Go-Toba banned Hōnen's nembutsu community after two followers were accused of arranging liaisons with court ladies and were executed. Hōnen and seven disciples, Shinran among them, were defrocked and exiled to different provinces. Shinran went to Echigo, and he and Hōnen never met again. He saw the exile as a chance to spread the teaching. He and his wife Eshinni had at least six children there.

In the 1230s he left the Kantō region for Kyoto, where he lived frugally on gifts from his followers, studying, writing and copying documents. He called himself Gutoku, the Bald Fool, neither monk nor layman. He died at the Zempōin temple in 1263, aged 89, having rejected the usual rites for the dying and held that faith alone ensured birth in the Pure Land. He named no successor and did not mean to found a new lineage.

His major work, the Kyōgyōshinshō, is a systematic exposition and defence of Pure Land doctrine. Shinran taught that liberation comes from the entrusting mind, shinjin, awakened by Amida's compassionate other-power and not by any merit of one's own. The nembutsu is a grateful response to Amida's grace rather than a practice that earns merit. He singled out the Sutra of Immeasurable Life as the main Pure Land sutra.

He never presented himself as the founder of a sect, but his teaching came to be seen as a school, the True Pure Land school, Jōdo Shinshū. He has often been compared to Martin Luther and John Calvin, a comparison first made in the 16th century by the Jesuit Alessandro Valignano, though the scholar Ducor calls it superficial.
shinsengumi: Japan's forced opening to the West in 1854 increased internal instability, and loyalists, particularly in the Chōshū Domain, began to rebel in Kyoto in the name of sonnō jōi, 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'. In response the Tokugawa shogunate formed the Rōshigumi on 19 October 1862, a squad of 234 rōnin drawn from the sword schools of Edo, to protect the 14th shōgun, Tokugawa Iemochi, on a journey to Kyoto to meet Emperor Kōmei. The squad's leader, Kiyokawa Hachirō, who was loyal to the emperor, planned to gather other rōnin to police the city, and when this scheme came out the squad was ordered back to Edo.

Nineteen members, mainly from the Mito clan, stayed in Kyoto and formed the Mibu Rōshigumi. On 18 August 1863 Matsudaira Katamori, who had judged that the mission should become patrolling Kyoto's streets in the name of the Tokugawa bakufu, renamed it the Shinsengumi, meaning Newly Selected Corps.

Early on there was internal strife. Matsudaira Katamori ordered the killing of the erratic Serizawa Kamo, and in October 1863 Hijikata Toshizō led a group that assassinated him. On 8 July 1864, in the Ikedaya incident, thirty Shinsengumi suppressed a cell of twenty Chōshū revolutionaries, possibly preventing the burning of Kyoto; the incident led to soldiers enlisting in the squad.

In January 1868 they fought for the shogunate at the Battle of Toba–Fushimi. Reformed as the Kōyō Chinbutai, they lost the Battle of Kōshū-Katsunuma on 29 March 1868. Kondō was captured by Imperial forces and beheaded on 17 May 1868. Hijikata went on to fight at Aizu and, in December 1868, joined the Republic of Ezo in the north. He was killed by a gunshot at the Battle of Hakodate on 20 June 1869, and the last commander, Sōma Kazue, surrendered with the survivors three days later.

At its peak the Shinsengumi had about 300 members. It was the first samurai group of the Tokugawa era to admit people from non-samurai classes such as farmers and merchants, though it is a misconception that most members were of those classes: of 106 members whose origins are recorded, 87 were samurai. Its code, created by Hijikata Toshizō, had five articles, forbidding deviation from the samurai code, leaving the group, raising money privately, taking part in others' litigation and engaging in private fights. The penalty for breaking any rule was seppuku. Its first uniform was a light-blue haori with white mountain stripes. After about a year the corps appears to have adopted an all-black uniform instead.
shinto: Shinto has no single founder, no canonical text and no central authority, so beliefs and practices vary widely. One proposed broad definition is that Shinto is a belief in kami, the supernatural beings that practitioners hold to inhabit all things, including forces of nature and prominent places. They are not regarded as omnipotent, omniscient or necessarily immortal, and the dead may become kami. Kami are worshipped at household shrines called kamidana and at public shrines called jinja, where priests known as kannushi offer food and drink. Shinto stresses ritual over doctrine, and above all purity: humans are seen as fundamentally pure, and pollution, or kegare, is a temporary condition removed by rites of purification.

Kami veneration has been traced back to the Yayoi period, from 300 BCE to 250 CE, when bronze bells, weapons and mirrors seem to have played a role in ritual. Historians debate when it is suitable to speak of Shinto as a distinct religion. Buddhism reached Japan at the end of the Kofun period and spread quickly, and the two merged so closely, in a process called shinbutsu-shūgō, that kami came to be seen as part of Buddhist cosmology.

The earliest written tradition of kami worship is in the 8th-century Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, which were commissioned by ruling elites to legitimise and consolidate their rule. They describe a universe in three parts: the Plane of High Heaven, where the kami live, the world of humans, and the Nether World. Although never of great importance to Japanese religious life, their accounts were proclaimed factual by the government in the early 20th century.

Japan has around 100,000 public shrines, about 80,000 of them affiliated with the Association of Shinto Shrines, which shrines formed in 1946. Festivals, called matsuri, mark the seasons of the agricultural year and give thanks to the kami, while rites of passage include a child's first visit to a shrine and weddings. Shinto was formally separated from the state during the U.S. occupation after World War II. A new constitution separated religion from the state, and the emperor declared that he was not a kami.

Numerically Shinto is the largest religion in Japan, with Buddhism second, but most people take part in both. Many Japanese say they have no religion, partly because they dislike the connotations of the Japanese word shūkyō, which suggests sect doctrine. Aspects of Shinto have been taken into new religious movements such as Tenrikyo and Oomoto.
shiraz: Shiraz is the capital of Fars province, historically known by the exonym Persia proper. It lies in a green plain at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, 1,500 metres above sea level, and has been a regional trade centre for over a thousand years. The earliest reference to the city, as Tiraziš, is on Elamite clay tablets dated to 2000 BCE, and tablets from the Persepolis treasury archives mention major workshops there. The name became Old Persian Širājiš and then the modern Persian Shirāz.

The Arab Muslim army conquered Fars in expeditions between 640 and 653 and captured the area around Shiraz in 641. Because the Sasanian capital Istakhr was deeply associated with the Sasanian Empire and the Zoroastrian religion, the Arabs sought to establish a rival cultural and administrative centre in nearby Shiraz. It was founded or restored in 693 by Muhammad ibn Yusuf al-Thaqafi, brother of the Umayyad viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, or by the latter's kinsman Muhammad ibn Qasim. In the 13th century it became a leading centre of the arts and letters, through its ruler's encouragement and the presence of Persian scholars and artists.

Ismail I, founder of the Safavid dynasty, captured Shiraz in 1504. After the fall of the Safavids the city declined, and a revolt of its governor against Nader Shah ended with a siege of many months and a sack. By Nader Shah's murder in 1747 most of its historical buildings were damaged or ruined, and its population had fallen to 50,000, a quarter of that in the 16th century. Karim Khan, de facto ruler of Iran from 1760 until 1779, made Shiraz his capital.

Shiraz is the fifth-most-populous city of Iran, with 1,995,500 inhabitants at the 2021 census. It is known as the city of poets, gardens, wine, nightingales and flowers. Hafez and Saadi were born there, and their tombs lie on the north side of the present city. The Eram garden is among its old gardens, and the Arg of Karim Khan, the citadel, stands beside the Vakil Bazaar and Vakil Bath. Shiraz has historically had major Jewish and Christian communities.
shire-highlands: The highlands cover roughly 7250 square kilometres and rise from 600 to 1100 metres, with hills and mountains above that; the highest is Zomba Mountain at 2087 metres. They are bounded west and south by the valley of the Shire River, an extension of the African Rift Valley, while the Phalombe Plain separates them from the Mulanje Massif to the east. Their streams drain to the Shire or into the closed basin of Lake Chilwa. The cooler, wetter climate supports the forests, woodlands and grasslands of the South Malawi montane forest-grassland mosaic.

The highlands have been inhabited for thousands of years. In the middle of the 19th century Yao people migrated from the northern Mozambican coast and founded chiefdoms there, among them Malemia, Mlumbe, Kawinga and Mpama; their chiefs traded in ivory and slaves through the port of Quelimane. In 1861, encouraged by David Livingstone, Bishop Charles Mackenzie of the Universities' Mission to Central Africa set up a station at Magomero near Zomba, withdrawn after his death in 1863.

In 1891 Harry Johnston became Commissioner of the British Central Africa Protectorate and made Zomba his headquarters. Between 1891 and 1895 he subordinated the Yao chiefs to British rule, often by force, abolished the slave trade and by 1894 had granted British settlers, missionaries and companies freehold rights to 3776 square kilometres, over half the highlands. A railway was built across them between 1903 and 1907, from Blantyre to the river port of Chiromo. Coffee declined by 1900 through drought and Brazilian competition, and tea plantations were established around Thyolo in the 1930s.

The highlands are a major agricultural area and the most densely populated part of Malawi. Yao people predominate in the north and Chewa people in the centre and south, and Lomwe people also live there. Blantyre is the largest city; Zomba, the second, was the capital of Nyasaland and of independent Malawi until 1975. Tea remains important, beside tobacco, groundnuts and maize.
shirkuh: Asad al-Dīn Shīrkūh was a Kurdish commander who served the Zengid dynasty and then the Fatimid Caliphate. He was the uncle of Saladin, and his efforts in Egypt were a key factor in establishing the Ayyubid dynasty there. His name may mean the mountain lion, and his honorific Asad ad-Din means the lion of faith. Latin writers called him Siraconus.

He came from a Kurdish village in Armenia near the city of Dvin, the son of the Kurdish chief Shadhi ibn Marwan and brother of Najm ad-Din Ayyub, ancestor of the Ayyubid dynasty. When the last Shaddadid was deposed in Dvin in 1130 the family moved to Baghdad and then to Tikrit, where Shadhi was made governor. In 1138 Shirkuh killed a man he was quarrelling with in Tikrit, and the brothers were exiled; Saladin was supposedly born the night they left. They entered Zengid service, and Shirkuh received Homs, ar-Rahba and other appanages. In 1154 the brothers negotiated the surrender of Damascus to Nur ad-Din.

In 1163 Shawar asked Nur ad-Din to intervene in Egypt in his dispute with Dirgham over the Fatimid vizierate. Nur ad-Din sent Shirkuh, with a grant of 200,000 dinars and 2,000 soldiers chosen from his regiments, in the first of three ventures into Egypt; Saladin went as his advisor. Shawar was restored and Dirgham killed, but Shawar quarrelled with Shirkuh and allied with Amalric I of Jerusalem, who besieged Shirkuh at Bilbeis in 1164. Nur ad-Din meanwhile attacked the Crusader states and almost captured the Principality of Antioch.

The Fatimid caliph al-Adid invited Shirkuh back in 1167 to help defeat the Crusaders attacking Cairo. Shawar again allied with Amalric, who besieged Shirkuh in Alexandria until he agreed to leave. A Crusader garrison stayed in Egypt, and Amalric allied with the Byzantine Empire. Shawar switched sides to Shirkuh, and after a pitched battle the Crusaders retreated. In January 1169 Shirkuh entered Cairo, was welcomed by al-Adid, and had Shawar executed.

Shirkuh accepted the office of vizier but died two months later, in March 1169, of a severe quinsy, according to Baha ad-Din ibn Shaddad, who says he was given to rich meats and suffered many bouts of indigestion. His nephew Saladin succeeded him as vizier and from 1174 also succeeded Nur ad-Din, uniting Egypt and Syria. Some historians hold that Shirkuh's death helped Saladin consolidate his position as undisputed head of the Ayyubid family. In 1179 Saladin gave Homs to Shirkuh's son Muhammad, whose descendants ruled it until 1263.
shirvanshah: The title Shirvanshah most likely dates from before the rise of Islam. The geographer Ibn Khordadbeh (died 913) records that the first Sasanian ruler, Ardashir I, granted it to a local ruler of Shirvan. Al-Baladhuri mentions a Shirvanshah and a neighbouring Layzanshah who submitted to the Arab commander Salman ibn Rab'ia al-Bahili (died 650) during the first Arab incursion into the eastern Caucasus. The name also appears as Shirwan Shah, Sharvanshah and Sharwanshah. Much of what is known of the early holders comes from the Jamiʿ al-Duwal of the 17th-century Ottoman historian Munejjim-bashi, who drew on the lost Arabic History of Darband.

The first Yazidid to take the title was Haytham ibn Khalid in 861, a grandson of Yazid ibn Mazyad al-Shaybani, whom Harun al-Rashid had twice appointed governor of Arminiya. In using it the Yazidids showed their adherence to ancient Iranian ideals. By 982 the Shirvanshahs had also assumed the titles Layzanshah and Khursanshah for the principalities they absorbed north of the Kur River, and Manuchihr III additionally styled himself Khāqān-e Kabir, or Great Khan, which gave his eulogist Khaqani his pen name. The Bagrationi kings of Georgia, who held parts of the region in the 12th century, occasionally used the title of Shirvanshah themselves.

From the reign of Manuchihr I (1027–1034) the rulers' names became almost entirely Persian, such as Manuchihr, Qubad and Faridun, and they claimed descent from Sasanian figures such as Bahram Gur and Khosrow I Anushirvan. In 1382 the throne passed to Ibrahim I, a distant relative, which began the Darbandid line. Akhsitan I moved the royal residence from Shamakhi to Baku after Shamakhi fell to the Eldiguzid ruler Qizil Arslan.

The Shirvanshahs patronised Persian literature, and in the 12th century their realm drew poets including Khaqani, Nizami Ganjavi and Falaki Shirvani. Khaqani addressed Akhsitan I as the most just descendant of Bahram and presented Shirvan as heir to the Sasanian Empire. Nizami called Akhsitan I the 'king of Iran' in Layla and Majnun.

In 1500 Ismail I of the Safavids defeated and killed the Shirvanshah Farrukh Yasar, but he let the dynasty continue as vassals. Shah Tahmasp I dismissed Shahrukh in 1538 for repeated disloyalty and made Shirvan a Safavid province. The Palace of the Shirvanshahs, among the buildings raised at Baku and Shamakhi in the 15th century, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
shishunaga-dynasty: The Shaishunaga dynasty was possibly the second ruling dynasty of Magadha. According to the Buddhist text Mahavamsa it followed Nagadashaka of the Haryanka dynasty. The Brahminic Puranas give a different list of kings with a different chronology, and Jain texts do not mention the dynasty at all. They say instead that Udayin of the Haryanka dynasty was killed by an assassin from a rival kingdom and, being childless, was succeeded by Nanda, whom his ministers chose. Shishunaga, the founder, had been an amatya, or minister, of the last Haryanka ruler, Nāgadāsaka, and came to the throne after a popular rebellion in c. 413 BCE.

Shishunaga founded his dynasty in 413 BCE with a capital at Rajgir and later Pataliputra, in what is now Bihar. Buddhist sources say he had a secondary capital at Vaishali, formerly the capital of Vajji, until Magadha conquered it. He ended the Pradyota dynasty of Avanti, which ended the centuries-old rivalry between the two kingdoms, and annexed Avanti into Magadha.

According to the Puranas, Shishunaga was succeeded by his son Kakavarna, and according to the Sinhala chronicles by Kalashoka; some historians hold that the two are the same. The Second Buddhist council at Vaishali and the final transfer of the capital to Pataliputra are the two main events of his reign. According to the Harshacharita he was killed by a dagger thrust into his throat. Buddhist tradition says ten sons of Kalashoka ruled simultaneously, while the Bhagavata Purana lists seven kings after Kākavarṇa.

Other Puranas count Nandivardhana as the ninth Shaishunaga king and his son Mahanandin as the tenth and last. Mahanandin was killed by Mahapadma, his illegitimate son, and the Puranas say the Nanda Empire, founded by Mahapadma Nanda, followed the Shaishunagas in c. 345 BCE. The Buddhist tradition says Kalashoka's sons were ousted by Ugrasena Nanda. The historian K. T. S. Sarao, who favours the Buddhist short chronology, dates Udayin's reign to c. 373–357 BCE and suggests that the lists of successors may describe rulers in different places at the same time while Magadha was divided. Keay, another supporter of the short chronology, likewise says the succession in this period is very uncertain.
shishuo-xinyu: The book holds around 1,130 anecdotes and character sketches of some 600 literati, musicians and painters of the Han and Wei–Jin periods, the 2nd to the 4th centuries. They are grouped under headings that each name a quality or failing, from Virtuous Conduct, Speech and Conversation and Affairs of State to Taunting and Teasing, Extravagance and Ostentation and Hostility and Alienation. Chapter 19, Worthy Beauties, has 32 stories about outstanding women. The work is thus both a biographical source and a record of the colloquial language of its time.

The original text was divided into eight juan, or scrolls, though current editions generally run to ten volumes. Its compiler, Liu Yiqing, lived from 403 to 26 February 444 and was a member of the ruling house of the Liu Song dynasty.

Most of its anecdotes and people are attested in other sources, yet traditional Chinese bibliographers did not class the book as history. They placed it among the xiao shuo, or minor tales, a term later used for fiction; some attribute this to its colloquial language and to its departure from the conventions of the Twenty-Four Histories. Its mixture of literary and vernacular styles set the scene for the later tradition of informal Chinese literature, and in the 20th century the novelist Lu Xun spoke highly of its aesthetic merits.

The oldest surviving copies are hand-written fragments from the Tang dynasty. Woodblock editions followed under the Southern Song: one by Dong Fen in 1138, whose original is kept in Japan, one by Lu You in 1188 and one from Hunan in 1189. The whole text, with the annotations and commentary of the Liang dynasty scholar Liu Xiaobiao, was translated into English by the sinologist Richard B. Mather and published in 2002 as Shih-shuo Hsin-yü: A New Account of Tales of the World.
shishupala: Shishupala, whose name means protector of children, was the son of King Damaghosha of Chedi and Srutashrava, a sister of Kunti, and is also called Chaidya, King of Chedi. The Mahabharata says he was born with three eyes and four arms. His parents meant to cast him out, but a voice from heaven warned that his time had not come, that the extra limbs would vanish when a certain person took him on his lap, and that he would die at that person's hands. When his cousin Krishna placed the child on his lap the eye and arms disappeared, and Shishupala's mother persuaded Krishna to pardon her son for a hundred offences.

Rukmi, the prince of Vidarbha, was a close friend and wanted his sister Rukmini to marry Shishupala, but before the ceremony she eloped with Krishna, which deepened Shishupala's enmity. When Yudhishthira undertook the Rajasuya Yajna, he sent Bhima to obtain the fealty of Shishupala, by then king after his father's death. Shishupala accepted Yudhishthira's supremacy without protest and was invited to the final ceremony at Indraprastha.

There the Pandavas chose Krishna as the guest of honour. Shishupala called him a mere cowherd unworthy of honour as a king, and mocked Bhishma's lifelong vow of celibacy as cowardice; Krishna calmed the angry Bhishma and pardoned this hundredth offence. At the next insult he released the Sudarshana Chakra and killed Shishupala on the spot, and Shishupala's soul attained salvation by merging into Krishna's body. He is held to be the third and last birth of Jaya, the gatekeeper of Vishnu. His sons were killed in the Kurukshetra War.

Māgha's Shishupala Vadha, composed in the 7th or 8th century, tells the story in 20 cantos of about 1800 highly ornate stanzas. It is counted among the six Sanskrit mahakavyas, the great epics, and is admired more for its descriptions and lyrical quality than for its plot.
shitthaung-temple: King Min Bin built the temple to commemorate his conquest of Bengal, and it is also known as the Temple of Victory. It stands on the western face of Pokhaung Hill, north of the Royal Palace of Mrauk U and next to the Andaw-thein Temple; the Htukkanthein Temple, an ordination hall, lies close by. A flight of stairs and a tazaung on its east side are a later addition, about 75 years old.

Its plan is typical of Burmese Buddhist temples: a central bell-shaped stupa with four smaller stupas at the corners and many still smaller ones around them. At its heart is a central hall lined with hundreds of Buddha statues, some in their original places and others brought from nearby excavations.

Its most notable feature is the three layers of maze-like corridors that encircle the main hall. Their walls carry reliefs of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, kings of the spiritual abodes, devas and guardian spirits, the 550 Jatakas, scenes of Arakanese culture, and animals both real and mythical.

The temple is the main attraction of Mrauk U, but like many of the town's monuments it has suffered from the monsoon rains of its tropical setting. In 2003 the central stupa was found to be leaking, and water was dissolving some of the carved figures in two of its chambers. The local archaeological department poured concrete over the stupas, which saved the statues inside but spoiled the outer appearance of what had been the focal pagoda for most northern Arakanese. Many Arakanese criticised the defacing of the temple, though since it protected the carvings within, it was less widely condemned than had been expected.
shiva: The name Shiva means auspicious, propitious or gracious. In the Rig Veda (c. 1700 to 1100 BCE) the word is an adjective applied to several deities, among them Rudra, a fearsome god of the roaring storm. Shiva is associated with Rudra, and the Hindu scriptures treat the two as the same figure. The Shiva of later Hinduism is, however, regarded as an amalgamation of various older Vedic and non-Vedic deities into a single god, a process linked to the Hindu synthesis of post-Vedic times. How this composite figure formed is not well documented and has attracted much speculation.

Some authors have read Mesolithic rock paintings at Bhimbetka as depictions of Shiva, but Howard Morphy holds that in context they more probably show hunting parties with animals. The Yajurveda gives both terrifying (rudra) and benign (shiva) attributes, and later texts such as the Atharvashiras Upanishad declare that all gods are Rudra.

For Shaivas, the followers of Shaivism, Shiva is the Supreme Lord who creates, protects and transforms the universe. In the Shakta tradition the Goddess is the equal and complementary partner of Shiva. Within the Trimurti he is the destroyer or transformer beside Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver, though ancient and medieval texts also contain many triads that do not include him.

Shiva is a god of ambiguity: fierce and benevolent, an ascetic yogi on Kailasa and a householder with his wife Parvati and their children Ganesha and Kartikeya. His attributes include the third eye, with which he burned Kama, desire, to ashes, the crescent moon in his hair, the river Ganga flowing from his matted locks and the trident. He is shown as Nataraja, Lord of Dance, and is usually worshipped in the aniconic form of the linga, which the Linga Purana presents as the manifested sign of the signless.

Shiva is revered across India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Indonesia, especially Java and Bali, where he is known as Batara Guru, a spiritual teacher blended with local spirits and heroes. His worship spread in Central Asia under the Kushan and Hephthalite empires, and wall paintings from Penjikent in Sogdia show him with a halo, a sacred thread and a tiger skin.

The Siva Sutta shows him conversing with the Buddha, and he appears as Mahakala in Vajrayana, as Maheshvara in Mahayana and as Ishana in Theravada Buddhism, in most forms ranked below Mahabrahma or Sakra. The Japuji Sahib of the Guru Granth Sahib names Shiva beside Vishnu and Brahma.
shivaji: Shivaji was born in the hill fort of Shivneri near Junnar, now in Pune district, and was named after a local deity, the goddess Shivai Devi. Scholars disagree on his date of birth. He belonged to the Bhonsle family. His father Shahaji served as a chieftain in the Maratha uplands under the Sultanate of Bijapur, hoping for rewards of jagir land, and Shahaji's campaigns against the Mughals were generally unsuccessful.

In 1647 the 16-year-old Shivaji captured Torna Fort, by stratagem or bribery, while the Bijapur court was in confusion, and used the treasure found there to build Rajgad, which served as his seat for over a decade. In 1657 Bijapur sent the veteran general Afzal Khan to arrest him. After Shivaji defeated forces sent against him, Siddi Jauhar besieged him at Panhala in 1660. Shivaji escaped by night, and at the pass of Ghod Khind the sardar Baji Prabhu Deshpande and 300 soldiers volunteered to fight to the death to hold back the pursuers.

Until 1657 Shivaji kept peaceful relations with the Mughal Empire, then raided its Deccan territory. After his defeat by Jai Singh I at Purandar he entered Mughal vassalage. In 1666 Aurangzeb summoned him to Agra, where he took offence at being made to stand among low-ranking nobles and was placed under house arrest, and he later escaped. Peace followed until 1670, when Shivaji recovered much of the territory he had surrendered.
In 1674 he was formally crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad Fort despite opposition from local Brahmins, a title that gave him a legal basis to rule and set him above other Maratha leaders.

Shivaji set up the Ashta Pradhan Mandal, a council of eight ministers who advised him on political and administrative matters. At his court Marathi replaced Persian, his royal seal was engraved in Sanskrit, and in 1677 his official Raghunath Pandit produced the Rājavyavahārakośa, a thesaurus of state usage. He employed people of all castes and religions, including Muslims and Europeans, and many commentators regard his religious policies as tolerant.

His army was small but effective, built on Maratha and Kunbi peasants. He avoided pitched battles against the heavy Mughal cavalry and used guerrilla tactics, known in Marathi as Ganimi Kawa, cutting supply lines and luring enemies into hills and jungle. Hill forts were central to his strategy: the historian Jadunath Sarkar counted some 240–280 at his death, each held by three officers of equal status so that no single traitor could hand it over.
shkoder: Shkodër extends over the Mbishkodra Plain between Lake Shkodër and the foothills of the Albanian Alps, on a hill where the lake drains into the Buna. It is bounded by the Kir to the east, the Drin to the south and the Buna to the west. Lake Shkodër, the largest lake in southern Europe, forms the frontier between Albania and Montenegro. The city has been continuously inhabited since the Early Bronze Age and has roughly 2,200 years of recorded history. Its ancient name Skodra, in Latin Scodra, is certainly pre-Roman, and the forms Scutari and Skadar later spread in Italian, English and Serbo-Croatian.

An urban settlement called Skodra was founded in the 4th century BCE by the Illyrian tribe of the Labeatae. It became the capital of the Illyrian kingdom under the Ardiaei and Labeatae. The Romans annexed and sacked it after the third Illyrian War in 168 BCE, when King Gentius was defeated. In the 3rd century CE it became the capital of Praevalitana under Diocletian's reform, and in the 4th century the Archdiocese of Scodra was founded.

In the Middle Ages the city passed among Byzantines, Serbian rulers of Zeta and the Balšić family, who surrendered it to the Republic of Venice in 1396 as a protection against the Ottomans. Mehmed II laid siege to it in 1478 and 1479; an agreement between Venice and the Ottomans ended the siege, letting the citizens leave unharmed. It then became the seat of the Ottoman Sanjak of Scutari. From 1757 to 1831 it was the centre of the pashalik of the Bushati family, and in the later 19th century the centre of a vilayet and a trading hub with over 3,500 shops.

The city was important in the Albanian national movement. After the Balkan Wars Montenegro left it to the new Albania in May 1913. Under the communist regime the Shkodër Bazaar and the port on the Buna were demolished.

Shkodër is regarded as the traditional capital of northern Albania and the centre of Roman Catholicism in Albania, with the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Shkodër-Pult. Its mosques and churches reflect its religious diversity. Rozafa Castle, linked to a legend of a woman who sacrificed herself so it could be built, and the Marubi National Museum of Photography are among its landmarks.
shkumbin: The Shkumbin is 181.4 km long and drains a basin of 2,444 square kilometres. It rises in the eastern Valamara Mountains of south-eastern Albania, between Maja e Valamarës and Gur i Topit, and runs north through Proptisht and Qukës in many deep gorges and canyons. It then flows inside a syncline between the Mokra and Shebenik mountains to the east and the Polis mountains to the west. Near Librazhd it turns about 50 km west of its source and joins the Rapun stream, crosses the Myzeqe Plain and forms a small delta in the Karavasta Lagoon, close to the Adriatic Sea.

The name comes from the Latin Scampinus, also recorded as Scampis, which replaced the Illyrian name of the river, Genusus. A Slavic origin has been rejected. The Latin name entered Proto-Albanian as a loanword, which fits the existence of a large Roman town near present-day Elbasan that gave the river its new name.

In antiquity several Illyrian peoples lived in the valley. The Parthini held the middle valley. To their west lived the Taulantii, on the coast and in the lower valley, and to their east the Dassaretii, around Lake Ohrid and in the upper valley.

The Via Egnatia followed the river and made it a strategically important corridor between east and west. The road began in two branches, a northern one from Epidamnos and a southern one from Apollonia, which converged at Ad Quintum near modern Elbasan and continued east through the Shkumbin valley. In Roman imperial times the boundary between the provinces of Illyricum and Epirus Nova ran roughly along the valley, which also formed approximately the border between the Latin and Greek-speaking areas.

The river is roughly the geographical dividing line between the Tosk and Gheg dialects of Albanian, with Gheg spoken north of it and Tosk south.
