In both, a plaque recording his boast about the stele of Naram-Sin serves as the example of a conqueror once mighty and now almost unknown, and the story turns on that lesson.
shuubiyya: The name comes from verse 49:13 of the Quran, which says God made mankind into peoples (šuʿūb) and tribes that they may know one another, and that the most noble in God's sight is the most righteous; Islamic scholars read the verse as a declaration of the equality of all human beings. The movement arose among non-Arab Muslims, mainly of Persian descent, as a response to the privileged standing of Arabs in the early Islamic empire. It spoke at first through Arabic literature and administration, where Persian scholars and secretaries (kuttab) asserted equality (taswiya) or superiority (tafdīl). Egyptians, Berbers and Arameans also took part.

Under the Samanid Empire the sentiment grew into a revival of Persian literature and new forms of poetry. Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, completed in the early 11th century and sparing in Arabic words, is often associated with it. Not every scholar of Iranian descent shared the view: Al-Biruni wrote that he would rather be reviled in Arabic than praised in Persian, and Ibn al-Muqaffa', as Al-Jahiz recorded, denied that the Persians surpassed other nations in intellect, calling them a people who had been taught and learned.

Opposition was fierce. Abu Hayyan al-Tawhidi recorded rebuttals in his Al-Imta' wa al-Mu'anasa, among them the answer to the Samanid vizier Al-Jayhani that the sciences he claimed for the Persians were of Greek origin, and attacks on the Zoroastrian practice of marriage between close kin. The Buyid vizier Sahib ibn 'Abbad had Badi' al-Zaman al-Hamadani answer a Shu'ubi poet at his court, then banished the poet. In the 12th century Al-Zamakhshari refused ever to join the Shu'ubiyya. Two centuries after the movement ended in the east, another form arose in al-Andalus, driven mainly by Berbers; the epistle of the poet Ibn Gharsiya is a noted example.

Among the first Western scholars to study the movement closely, in the late 19th century, was the Hungarian Ignaz Goldziher, in the first volume of his Muslim Studies. In 1966 Sami Hanna and G. H. Gardner published an essay, Al-Shu'ubiyah Updated, and in 1972 Leonard C. Biegel coined the term Neo-Shu'ubiyah for modern non-Arab nationalisms in the Middle East, such as Assyrian and Kurdish nationalism, Berberism, Coptic nationalism, Pharaonism and Phoenicianism.
shwebo: Shwebo lies 110 km north-west of Mandalay between the Irrawaddy and the Mu rivers. In Pali it is called Ratanāsiṅga, Jewel-Horn, or Ratanāsikhā, Apex of Jewels. Five names were conferred on the city: Moksobo, its name as a village; Ratanāsiṅga; Konbaung; Yangyi-Aung, Conquering a Great Foe; and Shwebo, Goldham.

Until 1752 Moksobo was a village of about 300 houses. On 29 February 1752 its chief, Aung Zeya, founded the Konbaung dynasty to resist the coming invasion of Hanthawaddy forces from Lower Burma. Taking the royal title Alaungpaya, he won the allegiance of 46 surrounding villages, built a stockade and dug a moat round the village, and renamed it Shwebo. For the next eight years he led the reunification of Burma from there.

After Alaungpaya's death in 1760 his successor, Naungdawgyi, moved the capital to Sagaing, closer to the Irrawaddy. Shwebo nonetheless remained important throughout the Konbaung era, which lasted until 1885. The region supplied a disproportionate share of the soldiers in Konbaung armies and was usually held as an appanage by the most senior prince, often the crown prince. In 1853 the Prince of Mindon went to Shwebo to raise the standard of rebellion in his successful bid to overthrow his half-brother Pagan.

Shwebo is a city of the Sagaing Region, with 88,914 people counted in 2021. It stands in the Dry Valley, in the rain shadow of the Arakan Mountains, on the boundary between a tropical savanna and a hot semi-arid climate. It is the seat of Shwebo University and the site of Shwebo Palace, and it lies on the Mandalay-Myitkyina railway line.
shwezigon-pagoda: The chronicles of the kings of Burma attribute the start of construction to King Anawrahta, founder of the Pagan Empire, in 1059-1060. According to legend, Anawrahta chose the site by sending out a white elephant carrying a relic of the Buddha, a frontal bone or a replica of the tooth relic, declaring that the pagoda would rise wherever it stopped. It stopped on a dune, hence the name Shwezigon, golden pagoda on a dune. Anawrahta built the lower terraces, and the rest of the structure is credited to his son Kyansittha, who dedicated a stone pillar with Mon language inscriptions in the compound.

The stupa rises on five square terraces around a solid core, steep as a pyramid and topped with umbrellas, so that the whole appears as a cone. Stairways from the four cardinal directions lead up to an octagonal platform carrying the gilded stupa, and 550 glazed terracotta tiles showing the Jataka tales are set into three of the terraces; there were once 584. Great chinthes guard the entrances, of which only the southern and western are in use.

Four bronze standing Buddhas, 12 to 13 feet high, face the four sides: Kakusandha to the north, Koṇāgamana to the east, Kassapa to the south and Gautama to the west. Below the Kassapa statue a pair of footprints with a chakra at their centre is carved on a sandstone slab. At the outer limits a shrine holds the 37 nats with a carved wooden figure of Thagyamin, king of the nats, believed to be 900 years old.

Worshippers believe the pagoda enshrines the Buddha's collar-bone and frontal bone from Prome and his tooth from Ceylon, although the relics have not been found and are believed stolen. Inside the solid body runs a maze of narrow passages where devotees fix dedicatory slabs on payment of a donation, praying for blessings. Earthquakes have damaged the pagoda many times; King Bayinnaung renovated it in the late 16th century, and after the 1975 earthquake it was strengthened with more than 30,000 copper plates given by devotees and gilded again in 1983-1984.
si-inthrathit: Si Inthrathit was born to the royal family of Sukhothai, though his exact lineage is unclear. Legend makes him a descendant of King Patumsuriyawong, whom some historians identify with the Khmer king Suryavarman II. Before he became king he was chief of Bang Yang, a territory in what is now north-central Thailand that then lay in the westernmost part of the Khmer Empire. He was first known as Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao, interpreted as the lord who rules the sky. Inscriptions are often missing their top or bottom portions, where dates would stand, and this uncertainty over the name led to his being called simply Hao in his early life.

Bang Klang Hao and Khun Pha Mueang of Mueang Rat decided to rebel and declare independence from Angkor. Khmer control and its heavy taxes were the main motives, and the Khmer preoccupation with great architectural works weakened their defences and indirectly helped the rising. Bang Klang Hao captured Si Satchanalai and gave it to Pha Mueang, who in return gave him Sukhothai.

He was then declared king at Sukhothai and took a regnal name of Sanskrit origin, Si Inthrathit, translated from Adityan Indra. His skill and bravery impressed the people, who gave him the title Phra Ruang, meaning glorious prince. The title passed to all later rulers of Sukhothai, which gave rise to the first Thai royal dynasty, the Phra Ruang.

Si Inthrathit and his queen, Sueang, had three sons. The eldest died young, and the second was named Ban Mueang. The third defeated a Khmer prince in combat on elephants and was named Ram Khamhaeng, meaning Rama the Bold, in tribute to the feat. Si Inthrathit died around 1270 and was succeeded by Ban Mueang. His dynasty is regarded as the first historical Siamese dynasty, both because it arose in the region foreigners later called Siam and because it was the royal house that freed the Thai principalities from the Khmer Empire.
siad-barre: Mohamed Siad Barre was born to pastoral parents at a time when no birth records were kept, and guesses at his birth year range from 1909 to 1921. His father was Marehan and his mother Ogaden, both of the Darod clan family. By concealing his unofficial birthplace, as many others did, he became eligible for the Italian colonial police force and military in Somalia. He rose to command the Somali National Army.

After the assassination of President Abdirashid Shermarke, Barre came to power in the coup of 21 October 1969. The Supreme Revolutionary Council renamed the country the Somali Democratic Republic and made it a one-party Marxist–Leninist state, and a personality cult styled him the Victorious Leader. Early policies included the nationalisation of banks, industry and land, public works, and a literacy campaign. In 1972 Somali became the language of instruction, replacing Italian in the south and English in the north, and in 1973 highways linked the two regions. Somalia joined the Arab League in 1974, the year Barre chaired the Organization of African Unity. A law of 1970 allowed the security service to detain critics indefinitely without trial.

In 1977 Barre launched the Ogaden War against Ethiopia, and between September 1977 and March 1978 his forces captured virtually the whole Somali region. The Soviet Union then turned against him; he expelled its advisers and moved towards the United States, which gave about US$100 million a year in aid until 1989. His popularity declined after the defeat. After a coup attempt in 1978 most of those accused were summarily executed, and survivors who escaped abroad formed the first of the groups that opposed his regime by force. In May 1986 he was badly injured in a car accident.

Barre fled Mogadishu on 26 January 1991 as the Somali Rebellion ended his government, and the Somali Civil War followed. He twice tried to retake the capital from his family's stronghold at Burdhubo, but was overwhelmed by the army of Mohamed Farrah Aidid in May 1991 and went into exile, first in Nairobi and then in Nigeria. He died of a heart attack in Lagos on 2 January 1995, and his body was returned to Garbaharey for burial.
siamun: Siamun, whose throne name was Netjerkheperre-Setepenamun, was the sixth pharaoh of the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt. He was the son of Psusennes I and may have been a child when his father died, which could have led Osorkon the Elder to act as king-regent. A queen Karimala, known from an inscription in the temple of Semna, may have been his wife and the daughter of Osorkon the Elder; Chris Bennett argued in 1999 for this marriage. Siamun was not succeeded by a son but by a cousin, Psusennes II, which suggests a crisis over the succession.

The highest attested year of Siamun is year 17, recorded in the Karnak Priestly Annals at the induction of Hori, son of Nespaneferhor, into the priesthood. Rolf Krauss calculated from a lunar feast that this year equals 970 BCE, which would put his accession in 986 BCE. The inscription is the first in which the word pharaoh is used as a title attached to a king's royal name; before then it had referred only to the office of the king.

According to Nicolas Grimal, Siamun doubled the size of the Temple of Amun at Tanis, worked at the Temple of Horus at Mesen, and built at Heliopolis and Piramesse. At Memphis he dedicated a new temple to Amun and favoured the priests of Ptah.

A fragmentary relief from the Temple of Amun at Tanis shows a pharaoh named Siamun smiting enemies and holding a double-bladed axe. Kenneth Kitchen argued that its shape is Aegean rather than Canaanite, so that Siamun's foes were Philistines and the scene commemorated a recent victory at Gezer. Paul S. Ash replied that the relief shows a fictitious battle, that Philistines are never shown with axes and that nothing in it points to Philistia or the Levant.

Excavations at Gezer show Egyptian destruction of the city in the 10th century BCE, in Siamun's time. Some scholars, among them Kitchen and William G. Dever, identify him with the pharaoh of the Bible who gave his daughter in marriage to King Solomon and took Gezer for him. Paul S. Ash and Mark W. Chavalas challenge this, and Edward Lipinski argues that Siamun died before Solomon's accession and that Shoshenq I was more likely the conqueror of Gezer.

Siamun's original tomb has never been found. Ushabtis bearing his name were found on two decayed mummies in the antechamber of the tomb of Psusennes I, and it has been proposed that he was reburied there after the Nile flooded his own tomb.
siberia: Siberia is a geographic and historic concept, not a political entity, so it has no single precise border. It stretches from the Ural Mountains to the Pacific Ocean and from the lands inside the Arctic Circle to the northern borders of Kazakhstan, Mongolia and China, and it covers over 13.1 million square kilometres, about three-quarters of Russia's area. Great rivers such as the Ob, the Yenisey and the Lena cross it. The climate runs from Arctic to temperate, with long, extremely cold winters; the January average is −25 °C.

Many nomadic groups lived in parts of Siberia over the millennia, among them the Xiongnu, the Huns, the Scythians and the Nenets. Later states reaching into the region included the Turkic khaganates, the Kyrgyz Khaganate, the Mongol Empire and the Khanate of Sibir. The Russian conquest began with the fall of the Khanate of Sibir in 1582. By the mid-17th century Russia controlled areas reaching the Pacific, and some 230,000 Russians had settled in Siberia by 1709.

Siberia became a destination for internal exiles, with more than 800,000 people exiled in the 19th century. The Trans-Siberian Railway, built in 1891–1916, tied the region to industrialising Russia, and around seven million Russians moved to Siberia between 1801 and 1914. In the Soviet period the Gulag administered penal labour camps, many of them in Siberia; according to semi-official Soviet estimates, more than 14 million people passed through the camps and prisons between 1929 and 1953.

Siberia holds roughly a quarter of Russia's population. Its largest cities are Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk and Omsk. More than 85 per cent of its people are of European descent, chiefly Russian, and the predominant religious group is the Russian Orthodox Church. Indigenous peoples include the Yakuts, Tuvans, Altai, Khakas and Buryats, and Siberia is traditionally regarded as the archetypal home of shamanism. The Trans-Siberian Railway still runs from Moscow to Vladivostok.
sibghatullah-mojaddedi: Sibghatullah Mojaddedi was born in Kabul, into the Mojaddedis, a well-known Pashtun family of religious scholars who trace their ancestry to the 16th-century scholar and Naqshbandi Sufi Mujaddid Ahmad Sirhindi. He studied Islamic law at al-Azhar University in Cairo and returned to Afghanistan in 1952 to teach in high schools and at Kabul University, where he became known as an advocate of Afghan political independence. In 1959 he was accused of conspiring against the Soviet prime minister Nikita Khrushchev and was imprisoned without trial until 1964. After his release he was forced into exile for outspoken comments on Soviet influence, living in several countries including Denmark and Pakistan.

After the Saur Revolution of 1978 the communist Khalq government killed Mojaddedi's brother and several relatives. From exile in Peshawar he founded the Jebh-e-Nejat-e Melli, the Afghan National Liberation Front, and on 13 March 1979 was the first person to call for nationwide jihad against the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan. His militia was most prominent in Kunar Province. He envisioned an Islamic republic, possibly with a restored monarchy. In 1988 he was elected head of the Afghan Interim Government in Peshawar.

In April 1992 he was elected chair of the Islamic Jihad Council set up to form a post-Soviet government, and on 28 April he entered Kabul amid a large crowd. He offered a general amnesty to all Afghans except the deposed president Mohammad Najibullah. All mujahideen factions supported his election except Hezb-e Islami Gulbuddin, whose forces fired rockets at the capital. In May 1992 Burhanuddin Rabbani set up a new leadership council that undermined his authority, and Mojaddedi resigned and handed over power. Sources differ on whether his time in office lasted two or three months.

After the fall of the Taliban in 2001 Mojaddedi returned from Pakistan and chaired the loya jirga of 2003 that approved Afghanistan's new constitution. Amnesty International said that he and the jirga's leadership curtailed freedom of speech there. In 2005 he became chairman of the Meshrano Jirga, the upper house of the National Assembly. On 12 March 2006 two suicide bombers attacked his car in Kabul, killing four pedestrians and slightly injuring him. He died on 11 February 2019. He is considered to have been a moderate leader.
sibiu: Sibiu lies in the historical region of Transylvania, some 275 kilometres north-west of Bucharest, near the geographical centre of Romania. It straddles the Cibin River, a tributary of the Olt, in the Cibin Depression, about 20 kilometres from the Făgăraș Mountains. Its position makes it one of the important transport hubs of the country. In German the city is Hermannstadt, in Hungarian Nagyszeben, in Latin Cibinium and in the dialect of the Transylvanian Saxons Härmeschtat. It is nicknamed the Town with Eyes, for the eyebrow dormers on many old buildings.

The town was founded by Saxon settlers from territories of the Holy Roman Empire and the Kingdom of France, brought by King Géza II of Hungary in the mid to late 12th century as part of the Ostsiedlung. In 1191 Pope Celestine III confirmed the free prepositure of the Saxons in Transylvania, with its headquarters at Cibinium. The German name Hermannstadt dates from 1366. By the 14th century Sibiu was an important trade centre, and in 1376 its craftsmen were divided into 19 guilds. It was the most important of the seven cities that gave Transylvania its German name, Siebenbürgen.

Sibiu was home to the Transylvanian Saxon University, the community of ministers, councilmen and officials that built a legal and political order for the Saxons from the 1400s. After the Ottomans withdrew in the late 17th century it became capital of the Principality of Transylvania. In the 18th and 19th centuries it also became a major centre of Transylvanian Romanians, housing the first Romanian-owned bank and the cultural association ASTRA. Between 1848 and 1867 it was the meeting place of the Transylvanian Diet. From the 1950s to 1990 most of its ethnic Germans emigrated.

Sibiu is the seat of Sibiu County. Its museums are organised around the Brukenthal National Museum and the ASTRA National Museum Complex, which includes a 96-hectare open-air museum. The Radu Stanca National Theatre, with origins in 1787, has Romanian and German sections. Several fortified villages near the city were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993, and Sibiu was a European Capital of Culture in 2007, together with Luxembourg City.
sibu: Sibu lies on the island of Borneo at the confluence of the Rajang and Igan rivers, about 60 kilometres from the South China Sea and 191.5 kilometres (119 mi) north-east of Kuching. The town stands on deep peat soil, on which buildings and roads slowly sink after completion, and its position in lowland peat swamps has exposed it to frequent floods, about one to three a year. It has a tropical rainforest climate, with annual rainfall of about 3,200 millimetres. Before 1873 it was known as Maling, after a bend in the Rajang called Tanjung Maling; the name Sibu comes from the pulasan fruit, known in the Iban language as Buah Sibau.

In the 17th and 18th centuries the Rajang basin saw tribal conflicts involving the Iban and the indigenous peoples living there, and Iban groups at times allied with Malay communities to attack the Kayan or raid passing Chinese and Indonesian vessels. James Brooke acquired the territory of Sarawak from the Bruneian Empire in 1841, and the Sibu region was incorporated in 1853. The earliest inhabitants were the Melanau, followed by Iban and Malay communities in the 1850s. In 1862 Rajah Brooke had Sibu Fort built as the administrative centre, and on 1 June 1873 the third division of Sarawak, later the Sibu Division, was established.

Wong Nai Siong, a Christian scholar from Minqing County, Fujian, learned of Sarawak through his son-in-law Dr Lim Boon Keng and sought a place of settlement overseas after the Qing response to the Boxer Rebellion, which targeted Chinese Christians. Japanese aircraft raided Sibu on 25 December 1941, and Andrew MacPherson, Resident of the Third Division, was killed by Japanese forces with his officers while trying to reach Dutch Borneo. After 1945 Charles Vyner Brooke, the last Rajah, ceded Sarawak to become a British crown colony, and the local anti-cession movement included Rosli Dhobi, a nationalist from Sibu. In the early 1950s communists established a presence in Sibu, Sarikei and Bintangor.

Sibu is a city of 129.5 square kilometres and the capital of Sibu District within Sibu Division in Sarawak, Malaysia. Its local council traces its origins to 31 January 1925, under the Brooke administration, and became the Sibu Municipal Council on 1 November 1981. The highest point is Bukit Aup Jubilee Park, at 59 metres above sea level.
sibylla-queen-of-jerusalem: Sibylla was the elder child of Amalric, then count of Jaffa and Ascalon, and his first wife Agnes of Courtenay. When Baldwin III died in 1163 the High Court forced Amalric to annul the marriage as a condition of accepting him as king, though Pope Alexander III declared the children legitimate.

Amalric died on 11 July 1174. His son Baldwin IV, aged 13, was chosen king despite fears of leprosy, and Sibylla became his heir presumptive. The High Court and the regent, Count Raymond III of Tripoli, arranged her marriage to William Longsword of Montferrat in 1176. William died in June 1177 while she was pregnant, leaving her countess of Jaffa and Ascalon, and in the winter of 1177–78 she gave birth to a son, Baldwin.

In 1180 Baldwin IV arranged her marriage to Guy of Lusignan, a Poitevin knight. William of Tyre reports that Raymond of Tripoli and Bohemond III of Antioch were marching on Jerusalem to stage a coup, and the historian Bernard Hamilton concludes that the quick marriage foiled their plan. It divided the nobility into factions for and against Guy. In 1183 the king, by then blind and unable to walk unaided, had Sibylla's five-year-old son crowned co-king as Baldwin V and tried to have her marriage annulled, but she and Guy refused to leave Ascalon.

Baldwin V died in August 1186. Sibylla secured Jerusalem and gained the support of Raynald of Châtillon, Gerard of Ridefort and the patriarch Heraclius. Her backers required her to leave Guy in return for recognition, and she agreed on condition that she could choose her next husband. At her coronation, probably in mid-September, the patriarch gave her a second crown and asked her to name a consort, and she crowned Guy herself. Saladin invaded in April 1187. Guy was captured at the Horns of Hattin on 4 July, and Sibylla commanded the defence of Jerusalem until it surrendered. She won Guy's release in July 1188.

Conrad of Montferrat refused to admit the couple to Tyre. Sibylla accompanied Guy to the siege of Acre in the Third Crusade, and an epidemic struck the camp in 1190. She died in late summer or autumn, with her daughters Alice and Maria. Her half-sister Isabella I succeeded her.

Hamilton rejects the chronicler Ernoul's portrait of her as fickle and foolish, saying that it bears little relation to the known facts. Roger of Wendover called her a most praiseworthy woman, and the historian Helen J. Nicholson attributes the distortion of her image to contemporary gender ideals.
sicca-veneria: Sicca Veneria stood 175 kilometres west of Tunis and some 40 kilometres east of the present border between Tunisia and Algeria. Its site is the cliff face of Jebel Dyr, a table-topped mountain, at about 780 metres, the highest elevation of any city in Tunisia. From antiquity the town was the principal city of the High-Tell Mountains and of the north-west of the country, and until recent times it was the political centre, the most important religious centre and the dominant stronghold of that region. The great mesa known as the Jugurtha Tableland can be seen from it.

The character of the worship of Venus at the Roman colony suggests that it began as a Phoenician settlement. It was later a Numidian stronghold, and under the Caesars it became a fashionable residential city and one of the chief centres of Christianity in North Africa. The Christian apologist Arnobius the Elder, who died in 330, lived and taught here, and the early Christian writer Lactantius, who lived from about 250 to 325, is also associated with the town.

In the early 5th century a priest of Sicca named Apiarius provoked a dispute between the churches of Carthage and Rome over the jurisdiction of the bishops of Africa, when he appealed to Rome against his excommunication by Carthage. In 499 Fulgentius of Ruspe was ordered to be scourged here by an Arian priest.

Around 439 the Vandals conquered the African Romans near the coast, and the town eventually became part of the Berber Kingdom of Dorsale. It was raided in 688 during the Umayyad conquest of North Africa. The name El Kef has been used since the 16th century. A kasbah to house a permanent garrison was built in the 17th century and fortified ramparts were added in 1740, yet Algerian forces still took and pillaged the city in 1756, and French troops occupied it from 1881.

The modern city of El Kef is the capital of the Kef Governorate and had a population of 45,191 at the 2004 census. Roman remains include fragments of a large temple dedicated to Hercules, baths, ancient cisterns and the ruins of a Christian basilica whose apse is intact. A well preserved three-aisled basilica of the beginning of the 5th century, named Dar El Kous and dedicated to Saint Peter, has also been found. The city is a centre of Sufi devotion, with the Sidi Bou Makhlouf Mausoleum, and it was the provisional capital of Tunisia during the Second World War.
sicels: The Sicels, who in Latin were the Siculi, were an Indo-European people of eastern Sicily in the Iron Age, speaking the Siculian language. The earliest literary mention is in the Odyssey. Thucydides and other classical writers knew traditions that the Sicels had once lived in central Italy and were dislodged by Umbrian and Sabine tribes before crossing into Sicily. The common assumption is that they arrived early in the first millennium BCE and introduced iron and the domesticated horse, though archaeology points to an arrival between the thirteenth and eleventh centuries BCE. The name Shekelesh, given to one of the Sea Peoples in an inscription of about 1207 BCE, may be related.

Their social organisation appears to have been tribal, based on agriculture. Their best-known necropolis is Pantalica near Syracuse, and the second largest is Cassibile near Noto; elite tombs were oven-shaped, in the form of beehives. The chief Sicel towns were Agyrium, Centuripa, Henna and three places named Hybla. Their cult of the Palici, twin sons of the volcanic god Adranus, is known in a version influenced by Greek myth. In the temple of Adranus the Sicels kept an eternal fire.

Little is known of the language, which survives in glosses of ancient writers and a few inscriptions, such as the ninety-nine letters on a jug found at Centuripe in 1824. The verb pibe, drink, is cognate with Latin bibe, the best evidence that Sicel was Indo-European.

Greek colonists came both from Chalcidian cities, which kept good relations with the Sicels, and from Dorian ones, which did not. The Sicels were forced out of most advantageous port sites and withdrew into the interior. At Morgantina, Sicels and Greeks lived side by side, so that historians argue whether it was a Greek polis or a Sicel city. In the middle of the fifth century BCE Ducetius created an organised Sicel state in opposition to Syracuse, including several cities in the centre and south of the island. His army was defeated at the Battle of Nomae in 450 BCE, and he died ten years later; without him the movement collapsed and the increasingly Greek culture lost its distinct character.
sichelgaita: Sichelgaita, also called Sigelgaita or Gaita, was a daughter of Prince Guaimar IV of Salerno and his wife Gemma. Her father had expanded the principality over large parts of Southern Italy until he and his brother were murdered by her four maternal uncles in 1052. His Norman allies avenged him and made her brother Gisulf II prince. Robert Guiscard, who had inherited Apulia and Calabria from his brother Humphrey in 1057, needed a marriage alliance and divorced his first wife, Alberada, on grounds of consanguinity to marry her.

In the first years of the marriage her chief task was to bear heirs, and from 1065 she appears in charters beside Robert. Her Lombard ancestry gave his rule legitimacy among vassals who might otherwise have rebelled against a foreigner. When Robert was close to death in 1073 she made the vassals swear allegiance to her son Roger as heir over her stepson Bohemond. She tried to mediate between Robert and Gisulf, but Robert besieged Salerno in 1076; the city surrendered that December and the citadel held out until May 1077. Salerno became the couple's capital, and charters there twice title her duke.

In 1080 she conducted the siege of Trani, which ended with the surrender of the rebel Peter II of Trani, while Robert moved against Taranto. She is said to have argued against attacking the Byzantine Empire, since Christians should not fight Christians, yet she joined the campaign. The Byzantine historian Anna Comnena's picture of her rallying the troops with a spear is read by the historian Skinner as an attempt to belittle the Normans, while William of Apulia wrote that she fled wounded by an arrow. Whether she fought is not known; the historian David Balfour finds no evidence that she was ever a combatant.

Robert died on Kefalonia on 17 July 1085 with Sichelgaita at his side. She secured his titles for Roger Borsa and remained active in government, signing charters with her son, among them one placing the Jews of Bari under the city's archbishop. Orderic Vitalis claimed she tried to poison Bohemond, a story John Julius Norwich considers unfounded. In 1086 she gave the town of Cetraro to Monte Cassino in Robert's honour. She died on 16 April 1090 and was buried at Monte Cassino at her own request.
sicilian-expedition: Athens had ties in Sicily from at least the mid-5th century BCE. To small Sicilian cities it was a counter to Syracuse, a Dorian city close to Corinth, Athens's commercial rival. Athens and Sparta had been formally at peace since the Peace of Nicias in 421 BCE, but control of Athenian policy was divided between a peace party led by Nicias and a war party led by Alcibiades. In 416 BCE the city of Segesta went to war against Selinus and sent to Athens for help, offering 60 talents of uncoined silver and deceiving the Athenian ambassadors about its wealth. The assembly approved sixty triremes under Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus. Before sailing, many hermai were mutilated and Alcibiades was accused; he was recalled for trial.

The fleet gathered at Corcyra with 134 triremes and 5,100 hoplites. Segesta proved not to have the money, and the generals disagreed: Nicias proposed a show of force and return, Alcibiades revolts, and Lamachus an immediate attack. The Athenians won the first battle south of Syracuse and withdrew to Catana for the winter. The Spartan general Gylippus landed at Himera and defeated them on the Epipolae, and the Syracusans completed a counter-wall.

Demosthenes and Eurymedon arrived with 73 ships and 5,000 hoplites, but Demosthenes's night attack on the counter-wall failed. A lunar eclipse on 28 August led the superstitious Nicias to delay departure by 27 days. The Syracusans blockaded the harbour from 3 September, and the Athenians were defeated in a last naval battle on 9 September. On 13 September about 40,000 survivors left camp. Demosthenes surrendered with 6,000 men, and the rest were nearly all massacred at the river Assinarus, where Nicias surrendered to Gylippus.

Athens lost two hundred ships and thousands of soldiers. The defeat encouraged its enemies in mainland Greece and Persia, and allies in the Aegean revolted. Some historians regard it as the turning point of the war, though Athens fought on for another decade. Historians disagree on the cause: J. B. Bury blamed chiefly the incompetence of Nicias, made worse by the recall of Alcibiades, while others see the plan as sound, and the proposal of Lamachus for an immediate attack is often held to have been the best option.
sicilian-vespers: The rising had its origin in the struggle between the papacy and the Hohenstaufen Holy Roman Emperors for control of Italy. In 1245 Pope Innocent IV excommunicated Frederick II and declared him deposed. After Frederick's death in 1250 and that of his son Conrad IV in 1254, Frederick's illegitimate son Manfred seized the Kingdom of Sicily and reigned from 1258 to 1266. The popes would not recognise him. Pope Urban IV chose Charles of Anjou, who defeated and killed Manfred at the Battle of Benevento in 1266. Conradin, who invaded in 1268, was defeated at the Battle of Tagliacozzo and executed, leaving Charles undisputed master of the kingdom.

Charles regarded Sicily as a springboard for Mediterranean ambitions, including the capture of Constantinople. Sicilian nobles had no share in government, and the heavy taxes he imposed were spent on wars outside the island. Byzantine agents and Peter III of Aragon, Manfred's son-in-law, who saw his wife Constance as the rightful heir, fomented the unrest.

The revolt began at the Vespers prayer on Easter Monday, 30 March 1282, at the Church of the Holy Spirit just outside Palermo. The accounts differ on the spark. In Steven Runciman's version, a French sergeant named Drouet pestered a married woman, her husband killed him, and the crowd killed the other Frenchmen as the church bells rang. By the next morning some two thousand French men and women lay dead. According to Runciman, foreign friars were made to pronounce the word ciciri, which French speakers could not say correctly. Local tradition made John of Procida the mastermind, but modern sources consider that an exaggeration or an error.

The rebels controlled most of the island within a fortnight and all of it within six weeks except Messina, which rose on 28 April and burned Charles's fleet in its harbour. About 13,000 French men and women were slain or expelled. The towns asked Pope Martin IV to recognise them as free communes under his suzerainty, but the French pope directed them to accept Charles. They then turned to Peter III of Aragon, who landed at Trapani on 30 August 1282 and was crowned in Palermo on 4 September, becoming Peter I of Sicily.

Peter's involvement changed the revolt from a local rising into a European war, the War of the Sicilian Vespers. With the pope's blessing Charles's fleet from Naples blockaded Messina and tried several landings on the island, but all were repulsed. Pope Martin IV excommunicated Peter III, Michael VIII Palaiologos and John of Procida in 1282. Bartholomaeus of Neocastro later wrote the Historia Sicula, an important if sometimes contradictory source.
sicily: Sicily is roughly triangular, which gave it the ancient name Trinacria, from the Greek for having three headlands. The Strait of Messina, about 3 km wide in the north and about 16 km wide in the south, separates it from Calabria. The island covers 25,711 km2, and the Autonomous Region of Sicily, which includes the smaller islands of Lipari, Egadi, Ustica and Pantelleria, covers 27,708 km2. Inland the terrain is mostly hilly and intensively cultivated, and the mountain ranges of Madonie, Nebrodi and Peloritani along the north coast extend the mainland Apennines. Mount Etna dominates the east coast, and the fertile soil is the result of past volcanic eruptions.

Humans first colonized Sicily towards the end of the Late Pleistocene, around 16,000 years ago, and dolmens date to the second half of the third millennium BCE. The original classical-era inhabitants were three peoples: the Sicani, the Elymians and the Sicels. Thucydides writes that the Sicani, the earliest, arrived from the Iberian Peninsula. The Elymians are thought to have come from the Aegean. The Sicels, whose name the island bears, are thought to have originated in Liguria and arrived from mainland Italy in 1200 BCE, forcing the Sicani to the middle of the island. By around 750 BCE there were three Phoenician and about twelve Greek colonies along the coasts, and Sicily became a centre of Magna Graecia.

The Sicilian Wars of 580-265 BCE were fought between Carthaginians and Greeks, and the Punic Wars of 264-146 BCE between Rome and Carthage. The name Sicilia was given to the Roman province in 241 BCE. Later rulers included the Vandals, the Ostrogoths, the Byzantine Empire and the Emirate of Sicily. The Norman conquest created the County of Sicily in 1071 and the Kingdom of Sicily in 1130. After the Sicilian Vespers in 1282 the island was ruled by the Crown of Aragon and then Spain. In 1816 the kingdom joined with Naples to form the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and after Garibaldi's Expedition of the Thousand and a plebiscite the island joined Italy in 1860.

Sicily is one of Italy's twenty regions and one of its five autonomous ones, with special status granted on 15 May 1946. Its capital is Palermo. It has seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Valle dei Templi at Agrigento, the Roman mosaics of the Villa Romana del Casale, the Aeolian Islands and the Late Baroque towns of the Val di Noto. Millions of people of Sicilian origin live abroad, the result of emigration that began after Italian unification, first to the United States between the 1880s and the 1920s.
siculo-arabic: Siculo-Arabic, or Sicilian Arabic, is a group of Arabic varieties spoken in the Emirate of Sicily from the 9th century and persisting under the Normans until the 13th century. It descends from the Arabic brought to the island by the Muslim conquest of Byzantine Sicily, which was piecemeal and slow. Sicily was a frontier zone even after the fall of Taormina in 962 completed the invasion.

African Romance and Byzantine Greek continued in use long after the conquest. The speakers of Siculo-Arabic were largely Sicilian Muslims, although the foundation charter of the church of Santa Maria dell'Ammiraglio, written in both Greek and Arabic, suggests that it was also the mother tongue of many Orthodox Christians of Palermo. It is attested only in writings from the 9th to the 13th centuries.

When the Normans came to Sicily the island had two main non-Latin language groups: Arabic speakers, mostly in Palermo, Agrigento, Butera, Enna and Noto, and Greek speakers, mostly in Messina, Taormina, Cefalu, Catania and Syracuse. In 1086 the Normans secured the conversion of ibn Hamud, the last important Kalbid ruler of Enna, and this, together with their adoption of many Arab ways of government, led to the emergence of a Christian Siculo-Arabic.

The Norman chancery worked in Arabic, Greek and Latin, and its documents are among the main sources for Arabic in Sicily. In 1154 the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi completed at the court of Roger II of Sicily the world map and description known as the Tabula Rogeriana.

The Hohenstaufens dropped Arabic as a language of government in 1198 and expelled the remaining Muslims to Lucera and North Africa in the 13th century, so that the only remaining speakers were Christians. After the Kingdom of Aragon took Sicily in 1282 and made Latin the only official language, Greek and Arabic official records ceased by the 14th century.

Maltese is the sole surviving descendant of Siculo-Arabic. It evolved over some 800 years through a gradual Latinisation that followed the re-Christianisation of Malta, complete by 1250, and it received a strong Romance superstrate. Hardly any records survive from the 14th century, and the earliest record of Maltese is Il-Kantilena by Pietru Caxaro, from the late 15th century, written in the Latin script. Present-day Sicilian, an Italo-Dalmatian language, kept relatively little from Siculo-Arabic, about 300 words, mostly relating to agriculture.
siddis: The Siddi, also called Sheedi, Sidi or Siddhi, are an ethnic group living in Pakistan and India. They are primarily descended from Bantu peoples of the Zanj coast in Southeast Africa, most of whom came to the Indian subcontinent through the Indian Ocean slave trade. Others arrived as merchants, sailors, indentured servants and mercenaries. Most were or became Muslims.

The origin of the name is disputed: one theory derives it from the Arabic sahibi, another from Sayyid, the title of the captains of the Arab vessels that first brought settlers. The first Siddis are thought to have arrived in 628 CE at the port of Bharuch, and others, called Zanjis, came as soldiers with Muhammad bin Qasim's Arab army in 712 CE.

Some Siddis escaped slavery and founded communities in forested areas, and others were brought as slaves by the Deccan Sultanates, adopted Deccani Muslim culture and identified with the Deccani faction against Iranian Shia immigrants. Several former slaves rose to high rank in the military and administration, most prominently Malik Ambar.

African presence in Sindh is documented from 711, but large-scale importation took place from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, during the Omani-Arab slave trade: captives mostly from modern Kenya and Tanzania were sold at Zanzibar and shipped to Muscat and then Karachi. Hoshu Sheedi died fighting the British at the Battle of Hyderabad in 1843 and is remembered as a hero. After the British defeated the Talpurs they banned slavery in Sindh. In Balochistan the ruler of Kalat formally abolished slavery in 1914, though domestic slavery persisted until the late 1950s.

In India the Siddi are recognised as a scheduled tribe in Goa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Daman and Diu. A plurality of those in Karnataka are Hindus (41.8 percent), followed by Muslims and Christians, while about 98.7 percent of those in Gujarat are Muslims. In Pakistan they live mainly along the Makran coast and in southern Sindh, and in Karachi chiefly in Lyari, where many have traditionally worked as fishermen and sailors and in the port. They speak local languages, among them Balochi and Sindhi, and many have assimilated into the wider Baloch identity.

They have kept ancestral practices especially in music and dance. The Goma, also called Dhamal in Gujarat, derives from the Bantu ngoma, meaning a drum, and at its climax some dancers are believed to carry the presence of past Siddi saints. In Pakistan the annual Sheedi Mela festival, with a visit to the sacred alligators at Mangopir, is the main event of the community's calendar.
sidereus-nuncius: The first telescopes appeared in the Netherlands in 1608, when the Middelburg spectacle-maker Hans Lippershey tried to obtain a patent on one. By 1609 Galileo had learned of the invention and built his own improved version. He was not the first person to aim the new instrument at the night sky, but his was the first published study of celestial bodies made with one. The improved telescope he used for the observations in the book magnified 20 times. The Latin nuncius usually meant messenger but could also mean message.

The book contains more than seventy drawings and diagrams of the Moon, of constellations and of the Medicean Stars of Jupiter. Galileo saw that the line dividing lunar day from night was smooth across the darker regions and irregular across the brighter ones, and concluded that the dark regions are low and flat and the bright ones mountainous. He judged, quite accurately, that the lunar mountains were at least four miles high. He saw at least ten times more stars than the naked eye shows, thirty-five in the Pleiades where observers had seen six, and deduced that the Milky Way is a congeries of innumerable stars.

In the last part Galileo reported four objects in a line near Jupiter. Their changing positions from night to night, always in the same line, persuaded him that they were orbiting the planet, and he drew their positions nightly from late January to early March 1610. He named them the Medicean Stars after the four Medici brothers and dedicated the book to Cosimo II de' Medici, hoping for patronage in Florence.

Reactions ranged from praise to hostility and disbelief. Some said the telescope had a lens defect and produced illusory points of light, and Martin Horký published a pamphlet alleging poor lenses and personal ambition. Johannes Kepler was the first astronomer to support Galileo publicly, in an open letter of April 1610. Simon Marius, who claimed in Mundus Jovialis (1614) to have seen the moons first, named them Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, the names now in use. Galileo's imperfect Moon contradicted the Aristotelian and Ptolemaic view of perfect heavens.
sidetic-language: Coins from Side bearing legends in an unknown script were first found in the 19th century. In 1914 an altar with a Greek and a Sidetic inscription came to light at Side, but the Sidetic text could not be read until a second Greek–Sidetic bilingual was found in 1949, which allowed Hellmut Theodor Bossert to identify 14 letters. In 1964 a large stone block near the east gate of Side yielded two longer texts, and in 1972 a text was found outside the city for the first time, at neighbouring Lyrbe-Seleukia. The longest inscription, a list of names of six complete lines also read as the Athenodoros memorial, was found in 1995.

The Greek historian Arrian, in his Anabasis Alexandri of the mid-2nd century CE, mentions a peculiar indigenous language at Side. Two words survive in Greek writers: zeigarê, cicada, recorded by the lexicographer Hesychius, and laerkinon, valerian, cited by Galen. Some puzzling signs in the third book of Hippocrates' Epidemics may be notes by the physician Mnemon of Side in Sidetic script.

Sidetic was written from right to left in an alphabet of 31 letters in the inscriptions and four more found only on coins, a few of them clearly taken from Greek. The values of two thirds of the letters are now firmly established. The frequent vertical strokes are read by most scholars as a sibilant, which would fit an Anatolian genitive ending, and by others as word dividers.

By the time of the inscriptions the language was strongly influenced by Greek, with loanwords such as istratag, from strategos, commander, and anathema-, votive offering. Few words go back to Luwian roots: maśara, for the gods, and perhaps malwadas, votive offering. No verb has been securely identified, though ozad, he offered, is a promising candidate with the common Anatolian past ending -d. As in neighbouring Pamphylian, names often lose their first vowel or an inner one, as in Poloniw for Apollonios and Artmon for Artemon. The Sidetic alphabet was added to the Unicode Standard in September 2025, in version 17.0.
sidi-bel-abbes: Sidi Bel Abbès is named after Sidi bel Abbass, a Muslim marabout who is buried there. It lies 75 km from the Mediterranean, astride the Sig River, in a semi-arid climate, with Oran 70 km to the north and Tlemcen 90 km to the west. It is the commercial centre of an area of vineyards, market gardens, orchards and grain fields, and its economy rests on cereals, wheat and barley and the grape industry.

The present city developed around a French camp built in 1843 on the Wadi Sig. In 1849 a planned agricultural town was established around the existing military post, and the town was surrounded by a wall with four gates. It was closely associated with the French Foreign Legion until 1962, as the site of its basic training camp and the headquarters of its 1st Foreign Regiment. The main buildings stood in the French military district of the Quartier Vienot. In the late 1890s the town, described as having a Spanish appearance, had a civilian population of about 30,000.
In the 1930s much of the old city walls were demolished, and wide boulevards and squares replaced the traditional quarters, so that the town lost much of its former character.

Sidi Bel Abbès is the capital of the province of the same name and has the Djillali Liabès University. French-style landmarks remain, among them Place Carnot, renamed Place 1er Novembre after independence, Perrin Castle, and the town hall, which was formerly a cathedral. Raï music is the best-known music of the city. Natives of Sidi Bel Abbès include the French politician René Viviani, the mathematician Gaston Julia, known for the Julia set, and the boxer Marcel Cerdan.
sidi-saiyyed-mosque: A marble tablet on the wall of the mosque names its builder as Shaikh Sa'id Al-Habshi Sultani. Sidi Sa'id had been a slave of Rumi Khan, a Turkish general who came to Gujarat from Yemen with his Habshi slaves. He later served Sultan Mahmud III and, after the sultan's death, the Abyssinian general Jhujhar Khan, who granted him a jagir when he retired from military service. He became a prominent nobleman: he collected a library, owned over a hundred slaves, made the Hajj and set up a langar, a public kitchen. He rebuilt a smaller brick mosque that stood on the site, and when he died in 1576 he was buried near it.

The Sunni mosque, known locally as Sidi Saiyyed ni Jali, is entirely arcuated. It is known for its ten carved stone latticework windows, or jalis, in the side and rear arches. The rear wall is filled with square pierced stone panels in geometric designs, while the two bays flanking the central aisle hold reticulated slabs carved with intertwined trees, foliage and a palm motif. This window, the Sidi Saiyyed Jali, is the unofficial symbol of Ahmedabad and inspired the logo of the Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad. The central window arch is walled with stone, possibly because the mosque was not finished to plan before the Mughals invaded Gujarat.

During British colonial rule the building served as an office, or kachery, for the Mamlatdar of Dascrohi taluka. Doors were fitted, the mihrabs were turned into presses and the interior was whitewashed. On an official visit to Ahmedabad, Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India, ordered the office to leave the premises as part of his wider policy of preserving historic monuments. The mosque is now designated a Monument of National Importance.
sidney-holland: Holland was born on 18 October 1893 at Greendale in Canterbury, the youngest of eight children of Henry Holland, a farmer and merchant who was Mayor of Christchurch and later a Reform Party MP. In the First World War he served with the New Zealand Field Artillery and saw action at the Battle of Messines before being invalided home with a severe illness that cost him a lung. With a brother he founded the Midland Engineering Company in Christchurch, which made horticultural spray pumps and shared its profits with its employees.

From 1925 to 1935 he was his father's unofficial secretary and campaign manager, and in 1935 he took his father's seat of Christchurch North despite Labour's landslide. In 1940 he replaced Adam Hamilton as leader of the new National Party, and in 1941 he drew rival conservative groups into it. He was deputy chairman of the War Cabinet of 1942, which broke up that September over a miners' strike in the Waikato. In opposition he attacked Labour's socialism and the power of the unions, while bringing National to accept the main elements of the welfare state, and he won the election of 30 November 1949.

His government, in which he was also Minister of Finance, ended butter and petrol rationing and other state controls and reinstated the death penalty; eight executions followed. In the waterfront dispute of 1951 it imposed emergency regulations that sharply curtailed civil liberties, used the armed forces to unload ships and deregistered the Waterside Workers' Union, which gave in after 151 days. Holland then called a snap election and won a larger majority. The historian Redmer Yska holds that he exploited anti-Communist feeling during the dispute.

In September 1951 New Zealand signed the ANZUS agreement, and troops went to the Korean War and, from 1955, to the Malayan Emergency. National won a third term in 1954 although Labour polled more votes. During the Suez Crisis in 1956 Holland suffered a mild heart attack or stroke at his desk, and on 12 August 1957 he announced his retirement; Keith Holyoake succeeded him on 20 September. He was knighted and died in Wellington Hospital in 1961.
sidoarjo: Sidoarjo Regency covers about 719.34 km2, the smallest regency of East Java, and borders Surabaya, Gresik, Pasuruan, Mojokerto and the Madura Strait. Its northern districts, such as Waru and Taman, adjoin Surabaya and are the most densely settled. Coastal districts such as Sedati and Porong lie between 0 and 3 metres above sea level and are given over to shrimp and milkfish ponds, which earned the regency the nicknames Delta City and Shrimp City. The climate is tropical savanna, with heavy rain from December to April.

The area belonged to the Kahuripan kingdom founded by Airlangga around 1019, with its capital at the mouth of the Brantas River, before the kingdom was divided into Janggala and Kediri in 1045. Janggala's capital lay at Hujung Galuh, partly within present-day Sidoarjo and Surabaya, which grew into a major port of the Majapahit Empire in the 14th century. The red-brick Pari Temple, built around 1371 in the reign of Hayam Wuruk, and Dermo Temple, believed to date from the mid-14th century, survive from that age. In the colonial period the district was known for sugarcane and had 10 sugar mills, the oldest, Watu Tulis, built in 1838.

From May 2006 hot mud flowed from a natural gas well drilled by Lapindo Brantas in Porong District, displacing more than 10,000 people. The flow began on 28 May, when the drill penetrated a layer of liquid sediment, and attempts to pump concrete into the well failed. Some scientists suggested that the Yogyakarta earthquake of the day before had opened paths for the mud; others blamed the drilling. The daily flow grew from some 50,000 cubic metres in August to some 125,000 in September, and on 26 September barriers failed and more villages were flooded.

The regency has its capital in Sidoarjo District and is divided into 18 districts. With an estimated population of about two million in 2025, it is part of the Gerbangkertosusila metropolitan area around Surabaya. Juanda International Airport lies in Sedati, and manufacturing accounts for nearly 40% of the economy.
sidon: Sidon stands on a mainland promontory with two harbours. Its Phoenician name, Ṣīdūn, probably meant fishery or fishing town. As a Roman colony it was renamed Colonia Aurelia Pia Sidon, and the Crusaders called it Sagittus in Latin and Saete or Sayette in Old French. Excavations show that the site has been inhabited since early prehistory: a stone tool assemblage of the Acheulean was found at Sidon II, and a Neolithic one at Sidon III. A settlement of the late Early Bronze Age I lies near the ruined Crusader castle.

Sidon may have been the oldest of the Phoenician cities, and a great Mediterranean trading network grew from it and other ports. Homer praised the skill of its craftsmen in glass and purple dye and of its women in embroidery. Tradition says a colonising party from Sidon founded Tyre, and the two cities later each claimed to be the mother city of Phoenicia. Around 1350 BCE it was part of the Egyptian Empire and ruled by Zimredda.

It was conquered in turn by the Assyrians, Babylonians, Egyptians, Persians, Greeks and Romans. Persian rule began in the 6th century BCE, and in exchange for its help in the conquest of Egypt, Cambyses II gave Sidon the territories of Dor, Joppa and the Plain of Sharon. Alexander the Great occupied it in 333 BCE.

Under Rome the city kept minting its own silver coins, and Herod built a theatre there. On 4 December 1110 King Baldwin I of Jerusalem and King Sigurd I of Norway captured it, and it became the centre of the Lordship of Sidon, a vassal state of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin took it in 1187, and German Crusaders restored Christian rule in 1197. The Ayyubids destroyed it in 1249 and the Mongols under Kitbuqa again in 1260.

After Ottoman Turkish rule began in the early 16th century it became the capital of the Sidon Eyalet and regained much of its earlier commercial importance. In the 18th century the Hammud family of notables dominated the city and monopolised cotton exports. After the First World War it was part of the French Mandate of Lebanon.

Sidon is the capital of the South Governorate of Lebanon, and Beirut and Tyre are each about 40 kilometres away. The Sidon Sea Castle, built by the Crusaders in the early 13th century, stands near the port. The Khan al-Franj is a 16th-century caravanserai named for the French merchants it housed, though it was once wrongly credited to Emir Fakhreddine II. The Sidon Soap Museum traces the history of soap making in the region. Palestinian refugees who arrived after 1948 were settled in the camps of Ein el-Hilweh and Mieh Mieh.
sidon-sea-castle: Sidon, an ancient Phoenician city on the Mediterranean coast of Lebanon, is said to have been inhabited since 4000 BCE. The small island on which the castle stands was earlier the site of a temple to Melqart, the Phoenician counterpart of Heracles. It may also have held the palace of the Phoenician king and other monuments, destroyed by the Assyrian king Esarhaddon and later by earthquakes. The records of Sennacherib's attacks on Sidon mention Great Sidon, Little Sidon, fortresses, pastures, cisterns and fortifications. The island also served as a refuge from attacks on the city.

The crusaders built the fortress in 1228 and joined the island to the mainland by a narrow roadway 80 m long. The castle was damaged in several wars and repaired several times. The Mamluks partly destroyed it when they took the city and later rebuilt it. After falling into disuse it was restored in the 17th century by Emir Fakhreddine II, and suffered great damage again afterwards.

The castle today consists mainly of two towers joined by a wall. Roman columns were laid in the outer walls as horizontal reinforcement, a feature often seen in fortifications built on or near Roman sites. The rectangular west tower, to the left of the entrance, is the better preserved. It holds a large vaulted room scattered with carved capitals and rusting cannonballs, and a winding staircase leads to the roof, where there is a small domed mosque of the Ottoman era and a view over the old city and the fishing harbour.

The east tower is less well preserved and was built in two phases: its lower part dates from the crusader period and its upper level from the Mamluks. Remains of the old Phoenician city lie under the sea around the castle, among them walls, columns, stairways, buildings, statues and cisterns. The castle is one of the most prominent historical sites of Sidon.
sidonio-pais: Sidónio Bernardino Cardoso da Silva Pais was born in Caminha on 1 May 1872, the eldest child of a notary of Jewish descent. He entered the Army School in 1888 and studied artillery, rising from sub-lieutenant in 1892 to major in 1916, and took a doctorate in mathematics at the University of Coimbra in 1898, where he became a professor.

A republican, he served as vice-chancellor of the university from 23 October 1910. After the First Portuguese Republic was established in 1910 he sat in the Constituent Assembly that drafted the Constitution of 1911 and was minister of public works and then finance minister. From 17 August 1912 he was Portugal's minister plenipotentiary in Berlin, until Germany declared war on Portugal on 9 March 1916.

Back in Portugal he became the main opposition leader to Afonso Costa's Democratic Party government, which was criticised for the effects of the war effort and the poor results of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps. From 5 to 8 December 1917 he led an insurrection of about 250 troops, which succeeded after three days of heavy fighting.

Costa handed power to Pais's military junta, which removed President Bernardino Machado and forced him into exile. Pais became prime minister on 11 December and took the presidency's functions on 27 December, in violation of the 1911 Constitution. He then issued decrees without consulting Congress and suspended parts of the Constitution, and his supporters called the result the New Republic.

On 23 February 1918 he amended the Law of Separation of Church and State, which angered traditional Republicans and Freemasons but won Catholics. On 11 March 1918 he decreed election of the president by universal suffrage and was elected on 28 April with 470,831 votes. In April the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps was destroyed at the Battle of the Lys, and conflict at home grew until he declared a state of emergency on 13 October 1918.

Pais escaped an assassination attempt on 5 December 1918. On the evening of 14 December, at Rossio station in Lisbon, as he left to take a train to Porto, the left-wing activist José Júlio da Costa shot him in the arm and the stomach, and he died on the way to hospital shortly before midnight.

Four bystanders were also killed by the guards. Tens of thousands attended his funeral. The writer Fernando Pessoa called him the President-King, and he remains one of the most divisive figures in modern Portuguese history. He is the only Portuguese president to have been assassinated, and the New Republic has been seen as a precursor of Salazar's Estado Novo.
sidonius-apollinaris: Gaius Sollius Modestus Apollinaris Sidonius was born at Lugdunum, the modern Lyon, into the Gallo-Roman aristocracy. His father was Prefect of Gaul under Valentinian III, and his grandfather Apollinaris held the same office from 408 to 409. Around 452 he married Papianilla, the daughter of Emperor Avitus.

His father-in-law became emperor in 455, and Sidonius wrote a panegyric for him. When Majorian deprived Avitus of the empire in 457 and seized Lyons, Sidonius fell into his hands, but his reputation for learning earned him respectful treatment. He composed a panegyric for Majorian, which won him a statue at Rome and the title of comes. In 468 the emperor Anthemius appointed him Urban Prefect of Rome, probably in part to win the support of the aristocrats of Gaul, and later made him a Patrician and Senator.

Sidonius was elected bishop of Clermont in succession to Eparchius, a relative of his wife. He says little about it and seems not to have wanted the post. He declared that he would give up pagan poetry as incompatible with religious life, but he went on writing verse privately. From 473 to 475 he and his brother-in-law Ecdicus led the defence of Clermont, which the Visigoths under King Euric attacked every year.

When the city was finally conquered he was imprisoned and exiled to Liviana, but Euric allowed him to return as bishop in 476 or 477 after the intervention of his adviser Leo. Sidonius accepted a degree of collaboration with the Visigothic court as necessary to keep the Roman aristocracy of Gaul together, yet he remained hostile to the Goths. He wrote to a senator, You shun barbarians because they have a bad reputation; I avoid them, even when they have a good one.

Twenty-four Carmina survive, occasional verse including panegyrics on emperors that draw on Statius, Ausonius and Claudian. Nine books of Letters preserve 147 documents addressed to 117 people, published in part in the early 470s and gathered in their final form around 477. Eric Goldberg calls him the single most important surviving author from 5th-century Gaul.

His Latin is deliberately elaborate and dense with classical and biblical allusion, which Sigrid Mratschek sees as a bulwark against the barbarians and a refuge from the dissolution of the old order. His letters cannot be read as plain description, since he modelled them on earlier letter writers, above all Pliny the Younger.
siege-engine: Siege engines ranged from the size of a small house to that of a large building. Some were built in place to attack from a distance, while others stood on wheels so that they could be advanced to the walls. From antiquity until the development of gunpowder they were made largely of wood, bound with rope or leather and possibly strengthened with a few pieces of metal at points of stress. Those that threw projectiles built up force by tension, by torsion or, in the trebuchet, by human power or a counterweight.

The earliest siege engines appear to be simple movable roofed towers, used with scaling ladders, depicted during the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The Assyrians used battering rams, and in Kush siege towers and rams were built from the 8th century BCE. The Carthaginians used towers and rams against the Greek colonies of Sicily, which influenced Dionysius I of Syracuse, who developed a catapult in 399 BCE. Philip II of Macedonia and Alexander the Great were the first rulers to use siege engines to a large extent. The Helepolis of Demetrius Poliorcetes, of 304 BCE, was nine stories high, plated with iron, 40 metres tall and weighed 180 tonnes.

The Romans preferred to build earthen ramps or simply to scale the walls, their soldiers working under shelters called vineae. Roman legions first used siege towers around 200 BCE, and the onager was the main Roman invention in the field. In China the earliest documented siege artillery, a levered traction catapult and a large siege crossbow, is described in the Mozi, a Mohist text of about the 4th to 3rd century BCE.

Medieval armies used catapults such as the mangonel, the ballista, the traction trebuchet, first designed in China in the 3rd century BCE, and the counterweight trebuchet, first described by Mardi bin Ali al-Tarsusi in the 12th century though of unknown origin. Besiegers could also starve a castle out, set fires against its walls, dig mines under the foundations or throw diseased animals and human corpses over the walls to spread disease.

With gunpowder came the cannon, the petard and the mortar, which proved so effective that fortifications had to be built low and thick, as in the designs of Vauban. Specialised siege artillery culminated in the two world wars, with guns such as Big Bertha and the German Schwerer Gustav, a railway gun of 80 cm calibre. Such guns took so long to move and deploy that they were vulnerable to air attack and unsuited to rapid warfare.
siege-of-acre-1189-1191: After Saladin defeated the army of Jerusalem at Hattin, he released Guy of Jerusalem, who was blamed for the disaster. Conrad of Montferrat, who held Tyre, refused Guy entry, claiming to administer the city until kings from Europe settled the succession. Guy therefore turned to Acre, a port on a peninsula in the Gulf of Haifa, 50 km to the south, which Saladin had decided to fortify rather than destroy. In August 1189 Guy marched along the coast, while Pisan and Sicilian contingents that had arrived earlier went by sea.

Guy's army of 7,000 to 9,000 infantry and 400 to 700 knights failed in a first assault and camped outside the walls, waiting for reinforcements from Europe. Saladin attacked the camp on 15 September 1189 without success, and on 4 October a pitched battle east of the city ended with the Crusaders repelling the relieving army, though the Templar Grand Master Gerard de Ridefort was killed. Saladin then surrounded both the city and the Crusader camp, so that the siege was double. Disease spread in the camp and the water was fouled. Queen Sibylla died in 1190, and with her Guy lost his claim to the throne.

Philip II of France arrived on 20 April 1191 and Richard I of England on 8 June, after conquering Cyprus on the way. Richard's engines, including the mangonels called God's Own Catapult and Bad Neighbour, opened breaches, and on 12 July the garrison offered terms that were accepted. The Muslim garrison was taken captive and Conrad raised the banners of Jerusalem, France, England and Austria over the city.

The surrender terms involved ransom payments and an exchange of prisoners. On 11 August Saladin delivered the first of three payments, which Richard rejected because some Christian nobles were omitted. On 20 August Richard, who thought Saladin had delayed too long, had 2,700 prisoners from the garrison beheaded, and Saladin killed the Christian prisoners he held. Leopold V of Austria left after a quarrel with Richard, and Philip returned to France on 31 July. The Crusaders marched south and Saladin was defeated at Arsuf on 7 September. Acre became the capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, whose territory shrank to a strip along the Mediterranean coast.
siege-of-amida-359: Shapur II sought to regain territory lost to the Roman Empire. After a decade of war against the Xionites he made peace with them, and their king Grumbates joined him against the Romans. In 359 he invaded while Emperor Constantius II was occupied in the west. Constantius had come to doubt the loyalty of the general Ursicinus and gave the eastern command to Sabinianus, but Ursicinus, on whose staff Ammianus Marcellinus served, moved his headquarters to Amida, where several legions gathered beside the garrison of Legio V Parthica.

Shapur meant to bypass fortress cities such as Nisibis and march into Syria, but he turned on Amida, where his vanguard nearly captured Ursicinus. When the son of Grumbates was killed by an arrow from the walls while inspecting the defences, the Sassanids attacked the city; Ammianus likens the death to that of Patroclus at Troy.

Early in the siege 70 Persian archers, helped by a Roman renegade, entered a tower on the south side and shot into the city until their arrows ran out and they were killed. Assaults on the walls were driven back and many siege towers burned. Albanian, Saka and Chionite cavalry ringed the city, war elephants were used on the west, and a plague in the city ended after ten days with a light rain. Two Gallic legions made a night sortie that inflicted heavy losses on the Persian camp.

The Persians then raised earth mounds against the walls, and the Romans built higher mounds inside. When one of these collapsed, the attackers reached the ramparts and broke in. A massacre followed, and Count Aelianus, who had directed the defence, was crucified with his surviving officers.

The city was sacked and its people deported to Khuzestan. With autumn come, Shapur could advance no further; he had lost as many as 30,000 men and his eastern allies deserted him. In 360 he took Bezabde and Singara, and after Emperor Julian was killed in Persia in 363 his successor Jovian made a peace that ceded Nisibis and the districts on the Tigris. The historian Khodadad Rezakhani has suggested that the king whom Ammianus describes before the walls, wearing a ram's head, may have been the Kidarite ruler Peroz.
siege-of-baghdad-1258: Baghdad was founded in 762 by al-Mansur, the second Abbasid caliph, and became the centre of the Islamic Golden Age. From the tenth century the Abbasids lost power, and the Buyids occupied Baghdad in 945 and the Seljuks in 1055. From 1230 Mongol generals raided Mesopotamia almost every year, though Baghdad remained unconquered.

After Möngke Khan became khan in 1251, he sent his brother Hulegu west to destroy the Nizari Ismaili Assassins and secure the submission of the caliphs, with one fifth of the empire's manpower. The Assassins' Grand Master surrendered on 19 November 1256. Hulegu had expected Caliph al-Musta'sim to provide troops, and the caliph's ministers persuaded him to refuse. A correspondence followed in September 1257, in which the caliph's reply called Hulegu young and ignorant, and his envoys were mocked by mobs in Baghdad.

Hulegu's armies invaded Mesopotamia from several sides. On 16 January 1258 the Mongol vanguard under Baiju broke the dykes of the Dujayl Canal and flooded the camp of the caliph's army, which was then routed. Hulegu reached the eastern suburbs on 22 January and encircled the city with a palisade and a moat. The assault began on 29 or 30 January, with catapults, naphtha and arrows carrying guarantees of safety for those who had not fought. The Mongols held the eastern wall by 4 February.

Hulegu insisted on unconditional surrender. On 7 February a large number of unarmed soldiers and inhabitants left the city and were divided into groups and executed. The caliph surrendered on 10 February with his family and 3,000 dignitaries. The sack began on 13 February and lasted a week. Hulegu spared Christians, scholars, sayyids and merchants who traded with the Mongols. On 20 February al-Musta'sim and his family were put to death; the caliph was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses, as the Mongols avoided shedding royal blood.

The number of dead is unknown. Later Muslim writers gave 800,000 to two million, and Hulegu himself claimed two million, a figure described as obviously inflated. An epidemic among the survivors raised the toll, and scholars have debated whether it was plague. Hulegu left on 8 March, ordering Baghdad rebuilt.

The fall ended the 500-year-old Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad. A member of the dynasty reached Cairo and was installed by the Mamluks as al-Mustansir II, but he and his descendants were puppets of the Mamluk state. Power moved towards cities such as Tabriz, capital of the Ilkhanate that Hulegu founded. Under the Ilkhanate Baghdad prospered, unlike the exaggerations of later Muslim historians, though it declined relative to Tabriz. The fall has traditionally been seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age, though its real consequences are uncertain.
siege-of-belgrade-1521: The siege was the third major Ottoman attack on the Hungarian stronghold, in the Ottoman–Hungarian wars, at the time of the Ottoman Empire's widest reach to the west. Selim I died in 1520 and his son Suleiman became sultan. The Kingdom of Hungary was almost in ruins. The nobility was divided into parties, the lower nobility clashed with the higher nobility and the court, and John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania and one of the richest magnates of his time, openly opposed the weak regime of King Louis II. The king often lacked money even for his own needs, so the southern border defences could not be strengthened.

Suleiman launched his army in mid-May 1521. At first nobody, the sultan included, knew the target. Hain Ahmed Pasha proposed taking Šabac first, then crossing the Sava and striking Buda. His rival Piri Mehmed Pasha argued that unless Belgrade was captured first, the Hungarians could cut the army off on its return.

The sultan preferred Ahmed's plan but allowed Piri to besiege Belgrade with a small part of the army. The sultan took Šabac, and Piri took the fortress of Zemun. Suleiman then ordered Piri to lift the siege and join the main army as it built a bridge over the Sava, but Piri refused. The attempt to cross failed, because the Sava flooded and the bridge could not be used. The sultan told Piri that they would soon join him, and together they took the city on 24 August. At Šabac the Turks had slaughtered all the defenders. At Belgrade about 70 of 700 defenders survived, and Suleiman spared their lives. Most of the Serbian inhabitants were deported to Istanbul.

The fall of Belgrade showed that the Hungarian authorities could not resist Ottoman expansion, as the Battle of Mohács in 1526 would confirm. After the collapse of Hungary the leadership of the Christian struggle against the Ottoman advance passed to the Habsburg monarchy, which came to include Hungary. Belgrade came under a Christian ruler again only in 1688, when Maximilian of Bavaria conquered it for Austria.
siege-of-bursa: The siege of the city, then called Prusa, began in 1317 and ended with its capture on 6 April 1326. The Ottomans had never taken a city before, and their lack of experience and of proper siege equipment meant that it fell only after six or nine years. The historian Laonikos Chalkokondyles wrote that they profited from the Byzantine civil war of 1321–1328, in which the younger Andronikos fought his aged grandfather for the throne and brought in the Serbs, so that they could do nothing to stop the Turks; in his words, Prusa was besieged, starved out and taken, and other cities of Asia Minor fell as well.

Accounts differ on the fate of Osman I. Some sources say he died of natural causes just before the city fell, others that he lived long enough to hear of the victory on his deathbed and was then buried in Bursa.

Orhan made Bursa the first official Ottoman capital, and it remained so until 1366, when Edirne took its place. He encouraged the city's growth with imarets, hammams, mosques, inns and caravanserais, built a mosque and a medrese in what is now the Hisar district, and was buried there in a türbe beside his father. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, who visited in 1331, was impressed by the sultan and described a pleasant city with fine bazaars and wide streets, surrounded by gardens and running springs.

Bursa holds a special place in Ottoman history as the founding city and as the birthplace of Ottoman architecture, seen in the Hüdavendigar Mosque (1385), the Bayezid I Mosque (1395), the Bursa Grand Mosque (1399) and the Yeşil Mosque (1421). The historian Paul K. Davis wrote that its capture established Osman and his successors as the major power in Asia Minor and began the Ottoman Empire.
siege-of-dorostolon: In the course of the Rus'-Bulgarian war, Svyatoslav I of Kiev overran the eastern part of the First Bulgarian Empire and made Pereyaslavets on the Danube his capital. After John I seized the throne, the Byzantines launched a counter-offensive. They defeated the combined Rus' and Bulgarian forces at the Battle of Arcadiopolis and recaptured Pereyaslavets, and Svyatoslav was forced to fall back to the northern fortress of Dorostolon, also called Drustur or Dorostorum.

The emperor's army was reinforced by a fleet of 300 ships equipped with Greek fire. Several engagements before the walls showed the Byzantines that the Rus' lacked skill in cavalry warfare. Among the dead were John Kourkouas, a relative of the emperor, whose severed head the Rus' displayed from one of the towers, and Svyatoslav's second-in-command Ikmor, killed by Anemas, a son of the last emir of Crete, in revenge for Ikmor's killing of his father during the Byzantine siege of Crete.

Famine brought the Rus' and their Bulgarian allies to extremities. To appease their gods they drowned children in the Danube, but their position did not improve. One night a force of some 2,000 warriors, women among them, made a surprise sally to search for supplies, defeated a Byzantine force on the way and returned to the city. After the final defeat the Byzantines were astonished to find the bodies of armed women among the fallen.

Unable to break the siege, the Rus' agreed to a peace treaty under which they renounced their interests in the Bulgarian lands and in the city of Chersonesos in Crimea. Svyatoslav remarked bitterly that all his allies, the Magyars and the Pechenegs, had betrayed him at the decisive moment.
