He was allowed to withdraw his army to Berezan Island, and the Byzantines entered Dorostolon and renamed it Theodoropolis, after the reigning empress Theodora.
siege-of-isfahan: The Safavid Empire had been in decline since the late 17th century, through the shahs' lack of interest in ruling, royal intrigues, civil unrest and recurrent wars with the Ottomans. The Safavids, strongly in favour of Shia Islam, heavily oppressed the Sunni Pashtuns in what is now Afghanistan. Their leader Mir Wais Hotak, sent to Isfahan as a prisoner by Gurgin Khan, the governor of Georgia, won the shah's favour, returned to Kandahar, killed Gurgin Khan and led the Pashtuns in revolt.
Safavid punitive campaigns against the rebels were defeated. After Mir Wais Hotak died in 1715, his son Mahmud Hotak took up the struggle and led the Pashtun army towards the capital.

On 8 March 1722 the Afghans won a decisive victory over the Safavid army at the Battle of Gulnabad, close to Isfahan. The numbers are uncertain, but Mahmud is estimated to have had about 18,000 troops against a Persian army of around 40,000. The beaten Safavid forces fell back in disarray to the city.

Lacking artillery to breach the walls, the Afghans blockaded Isfahan to starve Shah Sultan Husayn and the defenders into surrender. Ill-organised attempts at relief failed, and the shah's Georgian vassal, Vakhtang VI, refused to come to his aid. The shah's son Tahmasp escaped with some 600 soldiers to raise a relief army. Famine took hold, and on 23 October the shah capitulated and abdicated in favour of Mahmud, who entered the city on 25 October 1722.

Afghan rule lasted until 1729, first under Mahmud and then under his cousin Ashraf, and most of the Safavid princes, as well as Shah Sultan Husayn, were executed. Russia and the Ottoman Empire took advantage of the crisis to seize Persian lands in Gilan and Azarbayjan and in the Kurdish and Luristan territories, dividing them by the Treaty of Constantinople in 1724.

In 1729 Shah Tahmasp II and his general Tahmasp Qoli Khan, later known as Nader Shah, defeated the Afghans in Khorasan, and Ashraf was killed. Afghan rule ended in 1730 and Tahmasp II was restored, but in 1736 Nader deposed Abbas III, the son of Tahmasp II, and was proclaimed shah himself.
siege-of-jerusalem-1099: In 1095 Pope Urban II called for a crusade at the Council of Clermont, aiming to aid Byzantium against the Seljuks and to liberate Jerusalem. The main forces left Constantinople in April 1097 and besieged Antioch from October 1097, and after it fell in June 1098 the advance stood still for months amid power struggles between Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond IV of Toulouse, epidemics and shortages. Raymond resumed the march south in January 1099, following the coast and making agreements with local Muslim rulers or paying tribute rather than besieging fortified cities. The army reached Jerusalem on 7 June 1099.

Jerusalem had been under Fatimid rule since the 10th century. The governor, Iftikhar ad-Dawla, denied the crusaders water, food and wood near the city, expelled Syrian Christians who might sympathise with them and let Jews stay. Of the crusaders, between 12,000 and 14,000 reached the city, against a garrison of roughly a thousand Arab and Sudanese troops and some 400 Egyptian elite cavalry.

An attack on 13 June, prompted by a hermit's prophecy, failed for lack of siege engines. Under Guglielmo Embriaco and Gaston of Béarn the crusaders built two wheeled siege towers, an iron-headed battering ram and many ladders in almost three weeks.

The assault began in the night of 13 to 14 July, with the main attacks from Mount Zion and on the eastern part of the northern wall. On 14 July the ram pierced the wall but stuck, and the attack stopped with heavy losses, perhaps a fifth or a quarter of the Western armies. It resumed at midday on Friday 15 July, and when the tower was pushed against the wall the crusaders entered the city. Governor Iftikhar escaped, with others, to Ascalon after negotiating.

Thousands of Muslims and Jews were massacred, and the Muslim holy sites on the Temple Mount became Christian shrines. Jews who had defended the city were burned in their synagogue. There are no reliable figures: contemporary Arab claims of 70,000 or more dead are unrealistic against a population of about 30,000, and modern estimates range from 3,000 to 10,000. Atrocities after storming a city were normal in medieval warfare on both sides.

On 22 July Godfrey of Bouillon became Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri, refusing the title of king, and defeated a Fatimid army at Ascalon on 12 August. After his death on 18 July 1100, his brother Baldwin was crowned on Christmas Day in the Church of the Nativity as the first King of Jerusalem.
siege-of-jerusalem-1187: The Kingdom of Jerusalem, weakened by internal disputes, was defeated at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187. Most of its nobility were taken prisoner, King Guy among them. By mid-September Saladin had taken Acre, Nablus, Jaffa, Toron, Sidon, Beirut and Ascalon, while Tyre held out thanks to the arrival of Conrad of Montferrat. Balian of Ibelin asked Saladin for safe passage to Jerusalem to fetch his wife, Maria Komnene, and their family. He was allowed to go on condition that he not bear arms or stay more than a day, but the patriarch Heraclius and the inhabitants begged him to organise the defence, and Heraclius absolved him of his oath.

The city was crowded with refugees and had fewer than fourteen knights, so Balian created sixty more from squires and burgesses. Saladin arrived on 20 September. For six days his archers and siege towers failed to take the walls. On 26 September he moved his camp to the Mount of Olives, where there was no major gate from which the Crusaders could sally, and a mined section of the wall collapsed on 29 September. Neither side could gain the breach. The clergy organised a barefoot procession round the walls, and the civilians were in despair.

At the end of September Balian rode out to offer surrender. Saladin insisted on an unconditional surrender and said he had sworn to take the city by force, until Balian threatened that the defenders would destroy the Muslim holy places and kill their own families and the 5,000 Muslim slaves. Saladin then agreed to a ransom of ten dinars for men, five for women and two for children, and accepted 30,000 dinars for 7,000 of the poor.

Balian surrendered the city on 2 October 1187. The takeover was relatively peaceful, in contrast to the Crusader capture of 1099. About 15,000 who could not pay were sold into slavery, though Saladin and his brother al-Adil freed many. The Christian cross on the Dome of the Rock was pulled down. Saladin spared the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, allowed local Christians to stay and Jews to resettle, and charged Frankish pilgrims a fee. Control of Christian affairs passed to the patriarch of Constantinople.

The Kingdom of Jerusalem continued, with its capital moved first to Tyre and later to Acre. On 29 October Pope Gregory VIII issued the bull Audita tremendi, and in 1189 the Third Crusade began under Richard I of England, Philip II of France and Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor.
siege-of-jerusalem-587-bce: After the Assyrians destroyed the northern Kingdom of Israel, Judah survived as a vassal and kept its monarchy. As Assyria declined in the late 7th century BCE, Judah lay between Egypt and the rising Neo-Babylonian Empire. Nebuchadnezzar II defeated Egypt at the Battle of Carchemish in 605 BCE, and between 604 and 603 BCE he conquered the whole Levant, making Judah a Babylonian vassal. In 601 BCE Jehoiakim of Judah revolted despite the warnings of the prophet Jeremiah. In 597 BCE the Babylonians besieged Jerusalem, which surrendered. Nebuchadnezzar pillaged the city and deported Jehoiakim's son Jeconiah and other prominent citizens, and installed Jeconiah's uncle Zedekiah as king.

Encouraged by Egypt, Zedekiah ceased to pay tribute and allied himself with Pharaoh Hophra, and Nebuchadnezzar returned to take Jerusalem. The siege began in January 589 BCE. Many Judeans fled to Moab, Ammon, Edom and other kingdoms. The only known records of this siege are in the Hebrew Bible, which describes severe deprivation in the city. Nebuchadnezzar broke through the walls in the eleventh year of Zedekiah's reign. According to the Bible, Zedekiah and his followers tried to escape but were caught on the plains of Jericho and taken to Riblah, where his sons were executed before his eyes and he was blinded and taken to Babylon.

The Bible says the general Nebuzaradan was sent to complete the destruction of the city and of Solomon's Temple and took most of the Judeans into captivity. Archaeology confirms that the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem systematically with fire and pulled down its wall, and towns near the city and on the kingdom's western frontier were destroyed as well.

Judah was abolished and became a Babylonian province centred on Mizpah, where a Judean named Gedaliah was made governor. He was assassinated about two months later, and many of those who remained fled to Egypt. Population fell from roughly 110,000 to between 15,000 and 40,000 through deportation, death and flight. In Babylonia the exiles were settled as ordinary residents, kept their identity and were known as the people of Judah.

After Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BCE, exiles were allowed to return, and the Second Temple was completed in 516 BCE under Zerubbabel. The destruction was a defining moment for Judaism: it fostered the view that national disaster stemmed from collective sin, while the prophets held that the covenant endured.
siege-of-jerusalem-597-bce: To spare Jerusalem, King Jehoiakim of Judah had changed his allegiance from Egypt to Babylon in his third year, paying tribute from the treasury while Nebuchadnezzar II took temple artefacts and members of the royal family and nobility as hostages. In 601 BCE Nebuchadnezzar tried to invade Egypt and was repulsed with heavy losses. The failure set off rebellions among the states of the Levant that owed allegiance to Babylon, Judah among them: Jehoiakim stopped paying tribute and took a pro-Egyptian position, despite the strong protests of the prophet Jeremiah.

According to the Nebuchadnezzar Chronicle, the king of Babylon assembled his army in the month of Chislev of his seventh year, 598 BCE, invaded the land of Hatti and laid siege to the city of Judah. On the second day of Adar, 16 March 597 BCE, he took the city and its king prisoner, installed a king of his own choice and received rich tribute.

Jehoiakim is thought to have died during the siege, possibly on 10 December 598 BCE, and was succeeded by his young son Jeconiah, who was either 8 or 18. The dating to 597 BCE rests on the chronicles that Donald Wiseman published in 1956; before then William F. Albright and others more often dated the capture to 598 BCE.

Nebuchadnezzar pillaged the city and its Temple and deported the king, his court and prominent citizens and craftsmen to Babylon before Nisan of 597 BCE. The Book of Kings counts 10,000 exiles together with 7,000 craftsmen and 1,000 smiths, 18,000 in all, while the Book of Jeremiah gives 3,023; if that figure counts only men, perhaps 15,000 to 30,000 Judeans were exiled. The deportation is considered the start of the Babylonian captivity and of the Jewish diaspora, and the Book of Ezekiel counts its dates from it.

Jeconiah's uncle, Zedekiah, was installed as vassal king, while Jeconiah was kept in Babylon. A decade later Zedekiah rebelled in turn, and the second siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE ended with the destruction of the city and Solomon's Temple and the end of the Kingdom of Judah.
siege-of-odawara-1590: The siege of 1590 was the third siege of Odawara and the main action of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's campaign to remove the Hōjō clan as a threat to his power. After the death of Oda Nobunaga in 1582, Hideyoshi had reunified the country by 1588. He asked Hōjō Ujimasa and his son Ujinao to attend the imperial visit to Jurakudai in Kyoto, but Ujimasa refused and proposed instead a date in the spring or summer of 1590, which Hideyoshi rejected. In May 1590 Hideyoshi launched the campaign. Ujimasa hoped that Date Masamune would come to his aid and that Tokugawa Ieyasu might change sides in a stalemate.

In the months before, the Hōjō had hastily strengthened the castle, and despite the overwhelming force against them the siege saw little fighting. The besiegers' camps were entertained by concubines, musicians, acrobats and jugglers, while the defenders slept on the ramparts with their arquebuses. Hideyoshi relied mostly on starvation; in one skirmish miners from Kai Province dug under the walls and let in men under Ii Naomasa.

Meanwhile an army led by Maeda Toshiie and Uesugi Kagekatsu took the Hōjō strongholds one by one, among them Matsuida, Minowa, Maebashi, Matsuyama, Hachigata and Hachiōji castles, and Hideyoshi's naval forces defeated the Izu suigun. Sakura Castle of the Chiba clan, allies of the Hōjō, fell to Honda Tadakatsu and Sakai Ietsugu, and the defenders of Oshi Castle, besieged by Ishida Mitsunari, gave up on hearing of the defeat at Odawara.

Ujimasa's brother Ujiteru was forced to commit suicide with him. The Chiba lost all their holdings, though many of their senior members entered the service of Ii Naomasa. The tea master Yamanoue Sōji, who served the Odawara lords, was sentenced to death by torture. The Hōjō lands that went to Ieyasu turned out to be a stepping-stone towards his later conquests and the office of shogun.
siege-of-osaka: When Toyotomi Hideyoshi died in 1598, Japan came to be governed by the Council of Five Elders, among whom Tokugawa Ieyasu held the most authority. After defeating Ishida Mitsunari at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Ieyasu essentially took control of Japan and abolished the council. The Tokugawa shogunate was established in 1603 with its capital at Edo. Hideyoshi's son Toyotomi Hideyori and his mother Yodo-dono were allowed to stay in Osaka Castle, Hideyoshi's residence. Ieyasu wanted a stable regime under his own clan, and the Toyotomi clan, led by Hideyori under the influence of Yodo-dono, was the only remaining obstacle.

In November 1614 Ieyasu led 164,000 men to Osaka, and the siege began on 19 November. The Sanada-maru, an earthwork barbican defended by Sanada Yukimura with 7,000 men, repelled the shogunate's armies repeatedly. Ieyasu then turned to artillery and tunnelling miners, and from 8 January 1615 he had the castle bombarded. The stone bases of Japanese castles withstood the guns of the time, but fire aimed at Yodo-dono's quarters killed two of her maids and terrified her.

Peace talks followed, and on 21 January Ieyasu issued a document, sealed with blood from his finger, promising that the rōnin would not be found guilty and that Hideyori's income would stay the same. The outer moat was filled in.

By April 1615 news came that the Toyotomi were again recruiting rōnin and trying to stop the filling of the moat, and Ieyasu ordered Hideyori to leave Osaka. Fighting resumed in the summer campaign, with battles at Kashii on 26 May and Dōmyōji on 2 June. The decisive Battle of Tennōji came with Tokugawa forces of around 155,000 led by the shōgun Tokugawa Hidetada. Mistakes on both sides almost changed the result, but Sanada Yukimura was killed by Nishio Munetsugu, which destroyed the Toyotomi army's morale. Hideyori's own force sallied out too late and was driven back, and the castle was soon ablaze and under artillery fire.

The siege ended the last major armed opposition to the Tokugawa shogunate. In July 1615 the era name was changed from Keichō to Genna, apparently to mark the end of civil war since the Ōnin War, and the end of the conflict is sometimes called the Genna Armistice. Furuta Oribe, a daimyo who had been in league with the Toyotomi and plotted to set Kyoto on fire, was ordered to commit seppuku on 11 June.
siege-of-paris-885-886: The Vikings first reached Paris in 845 and sacked it, and they attacked it three more times in the 860s, leaving once they had enough loot or bribes. The Edict of Pistres of 864 ordered bridges built across the Seine, two of them at Paris, one on each side of the Île de la Cité. The lands around Paris were held by the count of Paris, first Robert the Strong, who fortified the capital and fought the Norsemen until his death at the Battle of Brissarthe, and then his son Odo. Charles the Fat, already king of Germany and Italy, became king of West Francia in 884, which raised hopes of reuniting Charlemagne's empire.

Vikings under Sigfred and Sinric sailed up the Seine in 885. The poet Abbo Cernuus, an eyewitness, wrote of 700 ships and perhaps 30,000 or 40,000 men, but historians regard his numbers as a gross exaggeration, and some put the ships at about 300. They arrived on 24 or 25 November and, when their demand for tribute was refused, began the siege. Odo had no more than 200 men-at-arms, and he led the defence with Gozlin, Bishop of Paris, who fought with a bow and an axe. The Norse attacked the northeast tower with catapults, mining, rams and fire, but were repulsed, partly with hot wax and pitch.

They then camped on the right bank and kept the siege up for months. In February 886 rains swelled the river, and the wooden bridge gave way, isolating the northeast tower. Its twelve defenders refused to surrender and were killed. Odo twice slipped out to ask Charles for help. Gozlin died in May. After a last attack in the summer, Charles arrived in October and camped at Montmartre.

Charles did not attack. To the frustration of the Parisians he let the Norse sail up the Seine to raid Burgundy, which was in revolt, and when they left France the next spring he paid them 700 livres of silver, about 257 kg. When Charles died in 888, Odo was elected the first non-Carolingian king of the Franks. The siege showed the strategic value of Paris, and the attacks destroyed much of the Left Bank, which turned to farming, while later growth favoured the Right Bank.
siege-of-pelium: News of the Illyrian revolt under Cleitus and Glaukias of the Taulantii reached Alexander while he was campaigning on the Danube against northern tribes his father, Philip II of Macedon, had reduced to partial subjection. Pelium held one of the most important passes between Illyria and Macedonia. Without it Alexander would face a long march around the mountains to the south, giving the newly rebellious Greek cities, Athens and Thebes among them, time to prepare. His ally Langarus of the Agrianians covered his flank by raiding the country of the Autariatae, and Alexander arrived to find Cleitus holding Pelium and awaiting Glaukias. Cleitus is reported to have sacrificed three boys, three girls and three black rams before meeting the Macedonians.

Alexander came with 23,000 soldiers. He drove Cleitus's troops from the surrounding heights back inside the walls, failed to take the town by assault and began siege lines, but Glaukias arrived the next day and forced him back onto the plain, outnumbered and short of supplies. A foraging party under Philotas had to be rescued. To secure the narrow defile behind him, Alexander drew up his phalanx one hundred and twenty men deep and put it through silent drill in full view of the Illyrians, then charged with his cavalry as the phalanx raised its war cry; the tribesmen fled, and no armoured Macedonian soldier was killed.

Crossing the river to a safer camp, he held off an attack on his rear with a cavalry charge and archers shooting from mid-stream. Three days later scouts reported that the Illyrians, thinking him in retreat, had grown careless. At night he led his archers, shield-bearing guards, the Agrianians and the brigade of Coenus against them, catching many asleep; a great slaughter followed and many were captured.

Alexander built a new outpost at Pelium, as the Illyrians had burned the settlement, and accepted their submission. The campaign served as his testing ground as a general: he learned the mountain-fighting tactics of the Illyrians and used them later in the eastern satrapies of Persia. Illyrian forces crossed to Asia with his army in 334 BCE, and 3,000 more joined him in 327 BCE.
siege-of-turin: The War of the Spanish Succession began after the death of Charles II of Spain in November 1700, when his heir Philip of Anjou, grandson of Louis XIV, became king. Fighting in northern Italy centred on the Spanish-held Duchies of Milan and Mantua. Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy, first allied with France, then in October 1703 joined the Grand Alliance. The following year French armies under Louis de la Feuillade took Savoyard lands north of the Alps, and by the end of 1705 Turin was the only significant city still in Savoyard hands.
On 19 April 1706 the Duke of Vendôme won at Calcinato; Prince Eugene of Savoy then resumed command of the Imperial troops, and Vendôme was recalled to France in July after the defeat at Ramillies.

An army of 48,000 under de la Feuillade reached Turin on 12 May and had encircled it by 19 June. Siege operations began on 2 June. La Feuillade chose to fire on the citadel from gun positions 300 metres outside the city. Victor Amadeus left on 17 June with 7,000 cavalry, leaving the Austrian general Philipp von Daun in command. Prince Eugene began his advance on 15 August and joined Victor Amadeus at Carmagnola on 29 August. French assaults between 27 August and 3 September were repulsed with heavy loss. Pietro Micca was killed on 31 August after exploding a mine to stop the French entering the tunnels beneath the citadel.

Having concentrated at Collegno, near a weak spot in the French lines, Prince Eugene attacked on 7 September in eight columns. Charles of Württemberg broke through on the left, and repeated attacks by Leopold of Anhalt-Dessau, with a sortie led by von Daun, forced the French back. The French abandoned their siege artillery and retreated towards Pinerolo, and Victor Amadeus re-entered his capital that day.

The French withdrew from northern Italy, and Victor Amadeus recovered most of Piedmont, though Nice and the County of Savoy were returned only in 1713. The Convention of Milan of March 1707 ended the war in Italy and handed Milan and Mantua to Austria. After Italian unification Pietro Micca became an example of patriotism and loyalty to the new Italian state. In 2004 construction of an underground car park in the Piazza Vittorio Veneto uncovered 22 skeletons of the early 18th century, which a study of 2019 found to be almost certainly casualties of the siege.
siege-of-vicksburg: The siege followed manoeuvres in which Major General Ulysses S. Grant and his Army of the Tennessee crossed the Mississippi River at Bruinsburg, won battles at Port Gibson and Raymond and captured Jackson, the state capital, on 14 May 1863. Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton's Confederate Army of Mississippi failed to stop the advance at Champion Hill and Big Black River Bridge and withdrew into the fortress city of Vicksburg, the last major Confederate stronghold on the river.

Pemberton could put only 18,000 troops into his lines against more than 35,000 for Grant, but the line, about six and a half miles long, ran over steep hills studded with forts, redoubts and gun pits. General Joseph E. Johnston, whom many in the city expected to relieve it, never did.

Grant's assault on the Stockade Redan on 19 May was repulsed, at a cost of 157 killed, 777 wounded and eight missing against Confederate losses of eight killed and 62 wounded. A larger assault on 22 May was also repulsed. On 25 May Grant ordered the reduction of the city by regular approaches, to avoid further loss of life, and Union trenches closed round the Confederates, trapped between them and the gunboats on the river. On 25 June a mine packed with 2,200 pounds of gunpowder blew a crater under the 3rd Louisiana Redan, but the infantry that followed was pinned down and fell back.

On 3 July Pemberton asked about negotiations. Grant first demanded unconditional surrender, then offered to parole the prisoners, as he did not want to feed 30,000 Confederates in prison camps. Pemberton surrendered on 4 July.

With the surrender of Port Hudson to Major General Nathaniel P. Banks on 9 July, the Union gained command of the Mississippi River and held it for the rest of the war. The surrender cut the Trans-Mississippi Department off from the rest of the Confederacy, effectively splitting it in two. It is sometimes considered, together with Robert E. Lee's defeat at Gettysburg the day before, the turning point of the war, and Lincoln called Vicksburg the key to the war. The works around the city are kept by the National Park Service as Vicksburg National Military Park.
siege-of-vienna-1529: In August 1526 Suleiman decisively defeated King Louis II of Hungary at the Battle of Mohács, and the childless Louis died. Archduke Ferdinand I of Austria claimed the throne but won recognition only in western Hungary. A noble from Transylvania, John Zápolya, challenged him and was recognised as king by Suleiman in return for accepting vassal status. Hungary became divided into three zones: Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary and the Principality of Transylvania. Ferdinand captured Buda in 1527 but lost it in 1529 to an Ottoman counter-attack.

Historians offer conflicting interpretations of the Ottomans' long-term aims. Some argue that Suleiman wished to assert control over all of Hungary, including Royal Hungary, and others that he intended to use Hungary as a base for further invasion of Europe.

In the spring of 1529 Suleiman mustered a large army in Ottoman Bulgaria and launched his campaign on 10 May. Contemporary chroniclers gave figures from 120,000 to over 300,000, but modern estimates put his combat force at the walls of Vienna at between 75,000 and 100,000. Heavy spring rains bogged down his heavy cannon, which had to be abandoned, camels were lost in large numbers and sickness spread among the janissaries. Buda fell to the Ottomans on 8 September.

The defenders, no more than 21,000, were commanded by Niklas Graf Salm, a seventy-year-old German mercenary, with German Landsknecht pikemen, Spanish harquebusiers sent by Charles V and 2,000 Serbian hussars under Pavle Bakić. Salm strengthened the old walls and levelled buildings to clear room for defences. The siege lasted from 27 September to 15 October. The defenders raided Ottoman sappers and blew up mines, and on 6 October a force of 8,000 men attacked the Ottoman mining works, destroying many tunnels at heavy cost. A final assault on 14 October was beaten back. On 15 October Suleiman called off the siege, and the army returned through snow and mud, reaching Constantinople on 16 December.

During the campaign Ottoman troops pillaged the countryside around Vienna, killed many civilians and took survivors as slaves, an estimated 20,000 people, few of whom returned. Salm, wounded in the last assault, died on 4 May 1530.

The campaign had mixed results. Buda returned to the control of the Ottoman vassal Zápolya, and the devastation of Habsburg lands weakened Ferdinand, but Suleiman could not force him into open battle. The failure at Vienna began about 150 years of military tension between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans, which culminated in a second siege of Vienna in 1683. A further campaign in 1532 was stalled at Güns by Nikola Jurišić and turned back. The two campaigns marked the limit of Ottoman logistical capability to field large armies deep in central Europe at the time.
siege-of-xiangyang: Xiangyang guarded the Han River, a major tributary of the Yangtze, and the Southern Song treated its defence as seriously as that of the capital. Surrounded by mountains on three sides and the river on the fourth, the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng were stocked with supplies for long sieges and protected by double walls. A Mongol assault in 1257 failed when cavalry were trapped between the walls and killed.

After winning the succession war against his brother Ariq Böke, Kublai Khan resolved to complete the conquest of China. In 1267 he ordered Aju and the Song defector Liu Zheng to attack Xiangyang and Fancheng.

The Mongols blockaded the cities with a ring of forts, built a fleet of 5,000 ships to close the Han River and trained 70,000 marines. Their first trebuchets did little against a moat widened to 150 metres and walls hung with thick netting. Song relief forces were repeatedly beaten, losing 1,000 men in October 1270 and 2,000 in August 1271. In 1272 a force of 3,000 men under two commanders both named Zhang broke through with a hundred paddle wheel boats, but no further help followed.

The siege was decided by the counterweight trebuchet. The engineers Ismail and Al al-Din, sent by Abaqa, Ilkhan of Persia, built about 20 machines that could throw projectiles of over 300 kilograms some 500 metres. Fancheng fell within days early in 1273, and Lü Wenhuan surrendered Xiangyang on 14 March 1273, becoming its governor under Yuan rule.

With Xiangyang taken, the Yuan controlled the Han and Yangtze rivers, and Song fortresses defected as Lü Wenhuan ordered members of his family commanding Song forces to change sides. A Song attempt to negotiate a truce in 1275 failed, the Song emperor abdicated on 4 February 1276, and the dynasty collapsed after the Battle of Yamen. Both sides had used gunpowder weapons such as thunder crash bombs and fire lances during the siege. Political infighting at the Song court, where the Lü family was allowed to ignore the commander Li Tingzhi, also weakened the defence.
siege-of-yorktown: The French and American armies united north of New York City in the summer of 1781. Dispatches from France raised the possibility of help from the fleet of the Comte de Grasse, and Washington and Rochambeau disagreed on whether to ask him to support a siege of New York or operations against the British army in Virginia. On Rochambeau's advice, de Grasse said he would sail to the Chesapeake Bay, where Cornwallis was building a defensible deep-water port at Yorktown on Henry Clinton's orders. The Marquis de Lafayette shadowed him with a Continental force.

On 19 August the allies began their march south, 4,000 French and 3,000 American soldiers leaving Newport, Rhode Island. Washington sent false dispatches that reached Clinton, suggesting an attack on New York. At the Battle of the Chesapeake on 5 September de Grasse defeated a fleet under Sir Thomas Graves, cutting Cornwallis off by sea and landing the heavy siege guns.

Washington and Rochambeau reached Yorktown on 28 September 1781 with some 7,800 French soldiers, 3,100 militia and 8,000 Continentals. After dark on 6 October troops dug the first parallel, a trench about 2,000 yards long, and Washington struck the first blows with his pickaxe. Over the next days the allies set up their guns and the British fire weakened.

On the night of 14 October Washington sent two columns against Redoubts Nos. 9 and 10, ordering that no musket be loaded until the works were reached. A French column under the Count of Deux-Ponts took the first and an American one under Lieutenant Colonel Alexander Hamilton the second, which let the allies finish their second parallel. On 17 October Cornwallis asked for terms, and the articles of capitulation were signed on 19 October. Malaria, endemic in the Virginia marshes, had weakened the British; Cornwallis estimated that half his army was unfit to fight.

More than 7,000 British soldiers were captured. Cornwallis did not attend the surrender ceremony, and Charles O'Hara represented him. Washington refused to let the British soldiers be paroled and sent home, and required that they receive the same honours as the garrison of Charleston had been given. Negotiations between the United States and Great Britain followed, ending in the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

Germans served in all three armies, about a third of the forces, and the siege is called the German battle in some German writing. The battlefield is preserved in Colonial National Historical Park, and Yorktown Day is held every 19 October.
siege-tower: A siege tower, called a belfry in the Middle Ages, is a specialised siege engine built to protect assailants and ladders as they approach the walls of a fortification. It was often rectangular, with four wheels, and as high as the wall or higher, so that archers or crossbowmen on top could shoot into the fortification. The towers were mostly wooden and so flammable, and builders covered them with iron or fresh animal skins. Because of their size they were mostly built on the site of the siege, which took considerable time, and they were used mainly when ladders, mining or battering rams could not overcome the defences.

When a tower reached the wall, it dropped a gangplank across, and troops rushed onto the walls. Some towers also carried battering rams or housed spearmen, pikemen, swordsmen, archers and crossbowmen. Being large, a tower was often the first target of stone catapults, but it had projectiles of its own. A tower could be defeated by flooding the ground before the wall so that it bogged down in mud, and it needed level ground, so many hill-top forts were safe from it.
Small towers were sometimes placed on earth mounds, and the Roman siege ramp at Masada in 72 to 73 CE survives. Towers were also mounted on ships to attack coastal walls.

Evidence for siege towers in Egypt, China and Anatolia dates to the Bronze Age. A mobile tower appears in the tomb of General Intef at Thebes, and a stone relief of about 2000 BCE from Harpoot in Turkey is the earliest known depiction from Anatolia. The Neo-Assyrian king Ashurnasirpal II used them in the 9th century BCE. Piye, founder of the Kushite 25th dynasty, had one built at Ashmunein. The Helepolis of Demetrius I of Macedon at Rhodes in 305 BCE stood up to 40 metres high, had nine storeys and was manned by 200 soldiers.

Use reached its height in the Middle Ages. Avar attackers at Constantinople in 626 prepared twelve towers covered with hides, and at Kenilworth in 1266 a single tower carried 200 archers and 11 catapults. Defenders sprayed Ottoman towers with Greek fire in 1453. Large cannon made towers obsolete, though wooden battery towers, such as one built by Ivan Vyrodkov at Kazan in 1552, took on a similar role.
siege-warfare: A siege, from the Latin sedere, to sit, is a military blockade of a city or fortress, meant to conquer it by attrition or by a well-prepared assault. A siege arises when an attacker meets a place that cannot be taken by a quick assault and refuses to surrender. The attacker surrounds it to block supplies, reinforcements and escape, a step known as investment, and tries to reduce the fortifications with siege engines, artillery, mining or sapping, or through deception and treachery. Sieges were often decided by starvation, thirst or disease, which could strike either side.

City walls were essential to the first cities. The walls of Uruk in the ancient Near East were 9.5 km long and up to 12 m high, and some Indus Valley settlements were also fortified. The earliest known depictions of siege warfare, from the Protodynastic Period of Egypt about 3000 BCE, show the symbolic destruction of walls. Egyptian tomb reliefs of the 24th century BCE show the first siege equipment, wheeled ladders against Canaanite walls. Assyrian palace reliefs of the 9th to 7th centuries BCE show huge tower-shaped battering rams topped by archers.

Few siege works have been found archaeologically. The earliest known circumvallation, a trench 2.5 km long around Tell es-Safi/Gath, is thought to have been built by Hazael of Aram Damascus in the late 9th century BCE, and Sennacherib of Assyria built a siege system around Lachish in 701 BCE. During the Peloponnesian War a hundred sieges were attempted and fifty-eight ended in surrender.

Cannons were first used in Song dynasty China in the early 13th century but became significant only about 150 years later; by the 16th century they were essential to any army. In Spain the army of Ferdinand and Isabella took Moorish strongholds in Granada in 1482 to 1492 that had held out for centuries. The answer was the star-shaped fortress with low, thick walls and triangular bastions, the trace italienne. At the end of the 17th century Marshal Vauban and Menno van Coehoorn brought fortification to its height and turned the besieger's work into a methodical process.

Sieges dominated war in Western Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries, and a single siege could occupy a campaign, as at Ostend in 1601 to 1604. In the 20th century mobile warfare reduced the importance of the single fortress, though trench warfare of the First World War used siege techniques, and the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 was met with an airlift.
siegen: Siegen lies in the basin of the upper reaches of the river Sieg, from which side valleys branch off in many directions. To the north lies the Sauerland, to the north-west the Rothaargebirge and to the south-west the Westerwald. The city covers roughly 115 square kilometres at a median elevation of 290 metres, and about 60 per cent of it is wooded. It is the seat of the district of Siegen-Wittgenstein. Municipal reforms and amalgamations in 1975 lifted its population above 100,000.

The name Siegen comes from the possibly Celtic name of the river Sieg. The place, called Sigena, is first mentioned in a document of 1079. The history of the city is shaped by mining, which began locally as far back as La Tène times, and many old mines lie within its limits. Siegen belonged at first to the Archbishopric of Mainz. The Nassau overlords introduced the Reformation in 1530, and a Franciscan monastery was dissolved in 1533.

The town was first Lutheran, but in 1550 the Principality of Nassau converted to the Reformed Church. Catholic worship regained ground in 1623, when one fifth of the townsfolk and people in the surrounding area became Catholic again, and a Jesuit monastery was founded in 1626. After the town passed to Prussia in 1815 the Lutheran and Reformed churches were united, though the parishes kept a Reformed emphasis.

Siegen had 20,000 inhabitants in 1897 and 40,000 by 1939. In World War II it lost roughly 30 per cent of its people, about 12,000, and was about 80 per cent destroyed. Its population fell to 28,000 by 1945 and regained its prewar level only in 1952.

The Oberes Schloss on the Siegberg, first mentioned in 1259, was the family seat of the House of Nassau and has housed the Siegerland Museum since 1905. Its collection centres on works by Peter Paul Rubens, arguably the best-known native of Siegen, and includes portraits of members of the Houses of Nassau and Orange. The Unteres Schloss took its present form late in the 17th century and was the home of the Protestant line of Nassau-Siegen, whose crypt lies inside. The Nikolaikirche has an unusual eight-sided shape and a golden coronet on its tower, so Siegen is sometimes called the Krönchenstadt. The Martinikirche dates from the 11th century.
siegfried-of-westerburg: Siegfried was the second son of Siegfried IV, Count of Runkel in Westerburg, who died in 1266; his elder brother Henry I of Westerburg was later killed at the Battle of Worringen. He was consecrated archbishop in Lyon in March 1275, because Cologne had been under excommunication since 1268. In July 1275 he lifted the city's excommunication and signed a treaty of friendship with it, and in October 1279 he made the Peace of Pingsheim with the Counts of Jülich. On 27 April 1285 he gave Brühl town and market rights.

Around 1283 he took the side of Count Reinoud I of Guelders in the War of the Limburg Succession. At the Battle of Worringen on 5 June 1288 he faced Duke John I of Brabant, with citizens of Cologne and men of Berg fighting against him. Captured by John, he was handed to Count Adolf VIII of Berg and held at Schloss Burg. On 18 June 1288 he had to recognise the sovereignty of the city of Cologne.

Under peace treaties of 19 May 1289 he paid 12,000 marks to the Count of Berg, ceded Lünen, Werl, Menden and other places and the Vogtship over the Diocese of Essen to Eberhard II, Count of the Mark, pledged Deutz and tore down castles such as Worringen and Zons. He was released on 6 July 1289, having fallen ill in captivity. In January 1290 Pope Nicholas IV released him from his promises to Cologne.

Siegfried then made Bonn his residence and mint, calling it Verona in defiance of Cologne. He backed his brother-in-law Count Adolf of Nassau for the German crown; in the Treaty of Andernach of 27 April 1292 Adolf agreed to transfer imperial cities such as Dortmund and Duisburg to the archbishopric, and Siegfried crowned him at Aachen on 24 June 1292. The coalition of Worringen blocked this attempt at recovery, and Adolf's kingship collapsed as well. Siegfried died in Bonn on 7 April 1297 and was buried in Bonn Minster.
siem-reap: Siem Reap is the capital and largest city of Siem Reap province in north-western Cambodia, and the second-largest city of the country. It lies close to the ancient temples of Angkor, built during the Khmer Empire, and about 30 minutes north of the Tonlé Sap, the great lake and river system that is central to Cambodia. It has a tropical wet and dry climate, with a wet season from May to October.

In the Angkor period the site was probably occupied by a town called Dvijendrapura, whose position may be marked by the old temple of Prah Einkosei. A stele there, inscribed in Sanskrit and Old Khmer and dated to 968 and 970 CE, records endowments made by the princess Indralakṣmī and her husband Divākara-bhaṭṭa.

The name Siem Reap is commonly translated as defeat of Siam. According to oral tradition King Ang Chan I (1516–1566) gave it after repulsing a Siamese army sent by King Maha Chakkraphat in 1549. Scholars such as Michael Vickery regard this as a modern folk etymology and hold that the origin of the name is unknown. Sources date the decline of Angkor to more than a century earlier, when a military expedition from Ayutthaya captured and sacked Angkor Wat in 1431, beginning a long period of vassal rule over Cambodia. Siem Reap, with Battambang and Sisophon, was under Siamese administration from 1795 until 1907, and the provinces were known collectively as Inner Cambodia.

Siem Reap was little more than a village when French explorers such as Henri Mouhot reached Angkor in the 19th century, although European visitors had seen the ruins earlier, among them António da Madalena in 1586. In 1901 the École française d'Extrême-Orient began its long work of clearing and restoring the site, and the first Western tourists arrived that year. Following a Franco-Siamese treaty in 1907 the area passed to Cambodia under French protection and Siem Reap began to grow. The Grand Hotel d'Angkor opened in 1929. In 1975 the Khmer Rouge drove the population of Siem Reap into the countryside, as in every Cambodian town.

Siem Reap has French-colonial and Chinese-style architecture in the Old French Quarter and around the Old Market. It is the gateway to Angkor, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that includes Angkor Wat, with its five towers symbolising Mount Meru and its bas-reliefs of Hindu narratives, and Angkor Thom, the royal city built by Jayavarman VII at the end of the 12th century and known for the Bayon. Tourism is the centre of the local economy. The Angkor National Museum opened on 12 November 2007.
siemens: Siemens & Halske was founded by Werner von Siemens and Johann Georg Halske on 1 October 1847. Its first product was a telegraph that used a needle to point to the letters of a message instead of Morse code, and its first workshop opened on 12 October. In 1848 the company built the first long-distance telegraph line in Europe, 500 km from Berlin to Frankfurt am Main. Werner's brother Carl Wilhelm Siemens began to represent it in London in 1850. In 1867 it completed the Indo-European telegraph line of over 11,000 km from London to Calcutta.

The firm was incorporated in 1897 and in 1903 merged part of its activities with Schuckert & Co. of Nuremberg to form Siemens-Schuckert. In 1919 it helped found the Osram lightbulb company, and in the 1920s and 1930s it began to make radios, television sets and electron microscopes. It built the Ardnacrusha hydroelectric station on the River Shannon in the Irish Free State in the 1920s. In 1932 a third parent company, Siemens-Reiniger-Werke, was formed.

From 1933 to 1945 Siemens-Schuckert exploited the forced labour of deported people. It owned a plant at Auschwitz, and a Siemens factory stood in front of the Ravensbrück concentration camp, where women were forced to work. By the end of 1944 the company ran almost 400 relocated plants because Allied air raids had destroyed factories in Berlin and other cities.

In 1962 Siemens & Halske agreed to make up to 7 million Deutsche Marks available to Jewish former forced labourers. From new bases in Bavaria the firm made computers, semiconductors and pacemakers in the 1950s, and in 1966 the three parent companies merged to form Siemens AG. Beginning in 2005 a multinational bribery scandal led to a settlement in December 2008, in which the company paid about $1.6 billion to the US and Germany.

Siemens is incorporated in Germany with its headquarters in Munich. Its principal divisions are Digital Industries, Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, with a financial services arm, and it has repeatedly sold off parts of its business, among them Infineon Technologies in 1999, Osram in 2013, Siemens Healthineers in 2017 and Siemens Energy in 2020.
siemowit-ii-of-masovia: Siemowit was the eldest son of Bolesław II of Płock and his first wife Gaudemantė, or Sophia, a daughter of Grand Duke Traidenis of Lithuania, and was probably named after his paternal grandfather Siemowit I. In 1310, before his father's death, he received the districts of Warsaw and Liw. In the division of 1313 he took Rawa Mazowiecka as his capital, with Sochaczew, Zakroczym, Gostynin, Ciechanów and Wizna, while his younger brothers Trojden I and Wenceslaus received Czersk and Płock. The settlement satisfied none of them, and in 1316 the three fought a brief war whose details are unknown.

Between his powerful neighbours, King Władysław I the Elbow-high of Poland, the Teutonic Order, Lithuania and Bohemia, Siemowit often changed sides. With Władysław he helped place his nephew Bolesław Jerzy II on the throne of Halych in 1323, and in 1325 the Masovian dukes joined Władysław's coalition against Brandenburg. When Wenceslaus allied with the Teutonic Order and Władysław plundered Płock, Siemowit and Trojden made their own alliance with the Order at Brodnica on 2 January 1326, which guaranteed their independence; Lithuanians then invaded his lands.

In 1329 the brothers unexpectedly fought for Władysław against the Teutonic Knights in Kujawy, and a year later Siemowit obtained neutrality. In 1333 he refused the Order's offer of Brześć Kujawski and took Władysław's side for good. The Treaty of Kalisz of 8 July 1343, which made peace between Poland and the Order, eased the position of his duchy, and as a possible successor of Casimir III the Great he waived his rights to Chełmno and Eastern Pomerania.

Siemowit died in February 1345 and was buried either in Płock Cathedral, as Jan Długosz reports, or in the Dominican monastery of Warka. He never married and had no children, so his duchy was divided among his three surviving nephews, Bolesław III, Siemowit III and Casimir I.
siemowit-iii-of-masovia: Siemowit was the second son of Trojden I of Masovia and his wife Maria, a daughter of Yuri I of Galicia. In 1341, after the deaths of their father and elder brother, he and his younger brother Casimir I of Warsaw inherited the Duchy of Czersk, and in 1345, on the death of their uncle Siemowit II of Rawa, the Duchy of Rawa. When the brothers divided their lands in 1349, Siemowit kept Czersk, Liw and Rawa and gave the small region of Warsaw to Casimir.

At first Siemowit sought good relations with his powerful neighbours, the Teutonic Order, Poland and Bohemia; historians disagree whether he did homage to the Emperor Charles IV in 1346 or in 1351. On 18 September 1351 the two brothers recognised King Casimir III the Great of Poland as their suzerain, receiving Gostynin and Sochaczew and the Duchy of Płock. When his brother died in 1355, the king left the Duchy of Warsaw to Siemowit, who promised never to ally with Poland's enemies.

Relations with Casimir III grew close. Siemowit attended the marriage of Elizabeth of Pomerania to Charles IV in Kraków in 1363 and the conference of crowned kings and princes held there in September 1364. On the king's death in 1370, under agreements made between them, Płock, Wizna, Wyszogród and Zakroczym returned to Masovia. Siemowit promulgated a customary law in 1377 and reformed the administration, justice and the monetary system. In 1373 or 1374 he gave Warsaw and Rawa to his sons Siemowit IV and Janusz I.

In 1335 Siemowit married Euphemia, daughter of Nicholas II of Opava, and after her death Anna, daughter of Nicolas of Ziębice. When Anna became pregnant with their son Henry, Siemowit accused her of adultery, had her strangled and had the child cast away; Henry was later found to be his son and was made a bishop. Siemowit died on 16 June 1381 and was buried at Płock Cathedral.
siemowit-iv-of-masovia: Siemowit IV was the second son of Siemowit III, Duke of Masovia, and his first wife Euphemia, daughter of Nicholas II of Opava. In his father's lifetime he received his own district of Rawa Mazowiecka, around 1373 or 1374. When his father died on 16 June 1381, Masovia was divided between him and his elder brother Janusz I, and Siemowit obtained Rawa, Płock, Sochaczew, Gostynin, Płońsk and Wizna.

After the death of King Louis of Poland and Hungary on 10 September 1382, Siemowit claimed the crown with the support of the nobility of Greater Poland and Kujawy. In January 1383 he marched into Greater Poland, beginning the Greater Poland Civil War. When the dowager queen Elizabeth of Bosnia chose her youngest daughter Jadwiga to reign in Poland, his supporters hoped he would marry her. Archbishop Bodzanta of Gniezno proposed his candidacy at Sieradz, but the voivode of Kraków, John of Tęczyn, persuaded the nobles to wait for Jadwiga.

Siemowit then tried, probably with Bodzanta's knowledge, to abduct Jadwiga, but the Lesser Poland nobility closed the gates of Wawel. Proclaimed king by part of the nobility at Sieradz, he failed to take Kalisz, and his supporters signed an armistice on 29 September 1383. By a treaty of 12 December 1385 he gave back the lands he had taken for 10,000 silver marks, renounced his claim and did homage to Jadwiga and Jogaila. He married Jogaila's sister Alexandra and went with the royal party to Vilnius for the Christianization of Lithuania.

As a vassal Siemowit still pursued a policy of his own, minted his own coins and kept close ties with Sigismund of Hungary. To raise money he mortgaged Wizna, Płońsk and Zawkrze to the Teutonic Order. In the war of 1409–1410 he sent troops to the Battle of Grunwald, though it was his son Siemowit V who fought with two banners. Going blind after 1420, he left the government to his sons and died at Gostynin on 21 January 1426. He was buried in the ducal crypt of Płock Cathedral. He and Alexandra had thirteen children; their daughter Cymburgis married Ernest I, Duke of Austria, and among their grandchildren was Frederick III, Holy Roman Emperor.
sierra-leone: Sierra Leone lies on the south-west coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea to the north and east, Liberia to the south-east and the Atlantic Ocean to the west. It has about 400 km of coastline. The east is a plateau with high mountains, where Mount Bintumani reaches 1,948 m, and lowland plains of forest, bush and farmland cover about 43% of the land. Freetown stands on a mountainous coastal peninsula. The name comes from the Lion Mountains near Freetown, which the Portuguese explorer Pedro de Sintra named Serra Leoa, meaning lioness mountains, in 1462.

The area has been inhabited for at least 2,500 years. Iron technology was adopted by the 9th century and agriculture established on the coast by about 1000 CE. Dense rainforest and swamps, and the tsetse fly, whose disease killed the horses and zebu cattle of the Mandé people, protected the region against invasion by the Mandinka Empire and limited the influence of the Mali Empire. Susu traders brought Islam in the 18th century.

European contact began in the 15th century. Traders from the Dutch Republic, England and France set up stations that came to deal mainly in slaves, brought to the coast by traders from the interior. In 1808 the coastal Sierra Leone Colony was founded as part of the British Empire, to resettle Africans returning after the abolition of the slave trade, and in 1896 an inland Protectorate was created. Independence came in 1961 under Prime Minister Sir Milton Margai. A constitution of 1971 made the country a presidential republic under Siaka Stevens. In 1991 a civil war began between the government and the Revolutionary United Front. It lasted 11 years and ended in 2002 after intervention by ECOMOG forces and then the United Kingdom.

Freetown is the capital and largest city. The country is a presidential republic, and English is the official language, while Krio, derived from English and several African languages, is spoken across the country. About 18 ethnic groups live there, the Temne and Mende being the largest, and the Creole people descend from freed African-American and Afro-Caribbean slaves and liberated Africans. Bunce Island, near Freetown, holds the ruins of a slave fortress of the Atlantic slave trade.
sierra-leone-company: The company grew out of an earlier venture. In 1787 the Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor sent 411 people, among them 300 of London's Black Poor, many of them Black Loyalists, and 60 English working-class women, to found a free settlement; they built Granville Town, which disease and abandonment wasted and the neighbouring Temne people burned in 1789. The St. George's Bay Company, founded in 1790, re-established Granville Town in 1791 for the 60 remaining Old Settlers.

Both ventures were promoted by Granville Sharp, whose prospectus of 1790, Free English Territory in AFRICA, said the subscribers sought no present profit but a charitable measure. Early subscribers from the Clapham Sect included Henry Thornton, William Wilberforce, Thomas Clarkson, Thomas Gisbourne and Samuel Whitbread. The attorney general, Archibald Macdonald, blocked a royal charter, and slave-trade merchants in London, Liverpool, Bristol and Lancaster petitioned against incorporation by act of parliament. Thornton nevertheless guided the bill through, and on 30 May 1791 it passed by 87 votes to 9.

In 1792 John Clarkson led over 1100 Black settlers from Halifax, Nova Scotia, most of them former slaves of the American colonies freed by the British during the American Revolution. These Nova Scotian Settlers founded Freetown in March 1792, and their determination made it take shape and survive. The company issued a decimal currency of dollars and cents, struck by Matthew Boulton at the Soho Mint and dated 1791 and 1796.

When war broke out between Britain and France, the company lost supplies and ships to privateers and the French navy, and in September 1794 the French burned Freetown in a raid. The colonists rebuilt, helped by American merchants who sold the company vital supplies. The acting governor, Zachary Macaulay, and his council agreed to accept American Black settlers with a gift of land if they brought letters of good character from their clergy, became British subjects, paid their own passage and cleared a third of their land within two years. The company's ships traded along the coast, sending the Domingo to the River Gabon for wax, ivory and redwood in 1794.
sierra-leone-creole-people: The first settlers, the Black Poor, were 411 African Americans and Afro-Caribbeans who arrived from England in May 1787, many of them Black Loyalists who had joined the British in the American Revolutionary War on promises of freedom. They called their colony the Province of Freedom and their settlement Granville Town, after the abolitionist Granville Sharp, on land negotiated from the Temne chief King Tom. Most died of disease or in fighting with the indigenous peoples, and about 64 survived to found a second Granville Town.

Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia followed, among them Gullah people from South Carolina and the Sea Islands. They laid out their town on the grid of a North American colonial town, and most of them lived on five streets. About 551 Jamaican Maroons from Cudjoe's Town arrived in 1800 and fought the Temne when they attacked Freetown in 1801.

The last and largest group were the Liberated Africans, or Recaptives, freed from slave ships by the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron after 1808: Akan, Bakongo, Ewe, Wolof, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and many others. They took on the customs of the Nova Scotians and Europeans while keeping some of their own traditions, and over several generations the mingling of these peoples formed the Creole ethnicity. Creoles became educated in British institutions and held leading positions in colonial Sierra Leone and British West Africa. Between 1840 and 1900 at least six in ten black African Anglican clergy in West Africa were Creoles, many trained at Fourah Bay College.

In the nineteenth century Creoles settled across West Africa, in Lagos, Abeokuta, Accra, Banjul, Limbe and Fernando Pó among other places; the Saro of Nigeria and the Aku of the Gambia descend in part from them.

Creoles are more than 98 percent Christian and live mostly in Freetown and the Western Area, where they make up 1.2 percent of the population of Sierra Leone. Their culture joins West African, North American and British ways. A wedding opens with the gej or put stop, in which the bride's hand is asked for; a newborn is welcomed with the pull-na-doh naming ceremony on the seventh day; and awujoh feasts remember the dead. Twins take Yoruba names, Taiwo and Kehinde, and gumbe music, with its drum, maracash and saw, comes from the Jamaican Maroons.
sierra-madre-occidental: The range runs parallel to the Pacific coast, from just south of the Arizona-Sonora border through eastern Sonora, western Chihuahua, Sinaloa, Durango, Zacatecas, Nayarit and Jalisco to Guanajuato, where it joins the Sierra Madre del Sur and the Transverse Volcanic Axis of central Mexico.

It is a high plateau of volcanic rock, with an average elevation of 2,250 metres in the Sierra Tarahumara, cut by deep river valleys. Its rains feed rivers such as the Yaqui, the Fuerte and the Conchos, which supply irrigation to the arid country around. Pine-oak forests cover the slopes between about 1,500 and 3,000 metres. Gold and silver occur in veins in the older volcanic rocks.

The mountains are home to several nations speaking Uto-Aztecan languages, among them the Tarahumara in the centre, the Huichol in the south and the Tepehuanes on the eastern slopes. The farming Chalchihuites culture began around the first century CE, grew rapidly from about 300 CE until about 500 CE and declined in the ninth century. In the northern foothills the Mogollon culture appeared around 900 CE and was abandoned around 1000 to 1100.

Francisco de Ibarra came to Durango in 1554 and crossed the Sierra Madre in 1564. The first silver mine was founded at Santa Barbara in 1567, and missionaries followed the miners, with a strong presence by 1595. A missionary first met the Tarahumara in 1607. Opposition to the missions led to the Tepehuán Revolt, which began in 1616 at Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes in Durango and lasted two years. The discovery of silver at Parral in 1631 pushed the northern limit of settlement into Tarahumara lands.

Railways arrived in the 1880s and 1890s, most of them American, and allowed old mines to reopen at a profit. Foreign influence led to unrest, including the Tomochic rebellion of 1892, and loggers who arrived in the late 1800s drove the Tarahumara further into the canyons. Geronimo and other Apache moved into the mountains after leaving San Carlos in 1881 and raided from them until he surrendered in 1886.

The range is about 1,250 kilometres long. Copper Canyon, larger and in places deeper than the Grand Canyon, lies in the Sierra Tarahumara, and Basaseachic Falls National Park holds the highest waterfalls in Mexico. Few paved roads cross the mountains, and Creel, a town of about 5,000 inhabitants, is a stop on the railway.
sierra-morena: The Sierra Morena is one of the main mountain systems of Spain. It stretches for 450 kilometres from east to west across the south of the Iberian Peninsula, forming the southern edge of the Meseta Central and the watershed between the Guadiana to the north and west and the Guadalquivir to the south. It is the result of uplift produced by the northward pressure of the African Plate, and its hard Paleozoic rocks include granite and quartzite, with softer slate and gneiss.

Its peaks are not high; its highest point is the lowest among the mountain systems of the Iberian Peninsula, and the summits average between 600 and 1,300 metres. Seen from the south it looks like a true range, with steep slopes and gorges, but from the plateau in the north it barely rises above the surrounding land. The name probably means dark range and is likely derived from the dark colour of some of its rocks and vegetation.

The ranges hold valuable deposits of copper, gold, silver, iron, lead, mercury and other metals, some exploited since prehistoric times. Formerly a border area and a vast wilderness with little population, the Sierra Morena had mountain passes that were important for communication between Andalusia and central Spain. The Despeñaperros, a canyon with sheer walls over 500 metres high, is the natural way across the range into Andalusia, and the ancient Iberians used the passes to travel between the plateau and the Guadalquivir basin.

The mountains were long notorious as a haunt of bandits and highwaymen. In 1767, in the reign of Charles III of Spain, the Nuevas Poblaciones de Sierra Morena y Andalucía were begun to settle the zone, and the area around La Carolina received farmers that included German, Swiss and Flemish families, one aim being safe stopping places for carriages. The range saw many battles in the Spanish Civil War, among them Cerro Muriano in August 1936, the scene of Robert Capa's photograph of a falling militiaman.

Parts of the range are protected, including several natural parks and the Dehesas de Sierra Morena biosphere reserve. It is one of the last habitats of the endangered Iberian lynx. The range appears in Don Quixote, where Don Quixote and Sancho Panza retreat into it, in Voltaire's Candide and in Jan Potocki's The Manuscript Found in Saragossa.
sierra-nevada-de-santa-marta: The range is separate from the Andes that run through the north of the country. It covers about 17,000 square kilometres in the departments of Magdalena, Cesar and La Guajira and is the source of 36 rivers. It is completely surrounded by land below 200 metres, so the Andean backbone cannot be reached from it without descending below that level. Its highest point is either Pico Cristóbal Colón or Pico Simón Bolívar, and it is not yet determined which. Both are about 5,700 metres by satellite data and local maps, lower than the 5,775 metres often quoted. Several of its peaks are intervisible with Cerro Paramillo in Antioquia, a line of sight of just over 500 kilometres.

The rock is mainly Cretaceous schists and gneisses with quartz-dioritic intrusions of Tertiary age. Rainfall averages about 4,000 millimetres a year at 500 to 1,500 metres, and temperatures range from 0 to 27 °C. Vegetation changes with height: dry forest and scrub near the coast, montane and cloud forest above 500 to 1,000 metres, the Santa Marta Páramo between 3,300 and 5,000 metres, and a permanent snow cap above. The area has more than 3,000 species of vascular plants and about 20 endemic bird species, including the Santa Marta warbler and the Santa Marta parakeet.

The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta National Natural Park, established in 1964, is Colombia's second-oldest national park. It was designated a Biosphere reserve by UNESCO in 1979. All the watercourses that rise there drain to the Caribbean, either directly or through the Magdalena River system, and roughly 1.2 million people depend on their fresh water.

About 30,000 indigenous people of the Koguis, Arhuacos, Kankuamos and Wiwa peoples live in the area, in indigenous reserves in the mid-highlands. The park also holds the remnants of the Tairona culture. Access to the highest summits has been difficult for about ten years, because of local opposition on the southern side and armed turmoil; a documented ascent of Pico Cristóbal Colón was made in December 2015.
sierra-nevada-spain: The name Sierra Nevada means snow-covered mountain range. The range was formed during the Alpine Orogeny, the mountain-building event that also raised the European Alps and the Atlas Mountains of northern Africa, and its present form dates from the Paleogene and Neogene Periods, from 66 to 1.8 million years ago, when the African and Eurasian continental plates collided. At its foothills lies the city of Granada, with Almería and Motril a little further south.

A ridge running west-south-west to east-north-east is central to the range, and for a substantial distance the watershed stays above 3,000 metres. The southern side has several long, narrow river valleys leading south-west, while the steeper northern side is dominated by the Rio Genil, which starts near Mulhacén. The rock is chiefly soft micaceous schist. The climate is Mediterranean at lower levels and subarctic above 2,500 metres, so summer and winter daytime temperatures are some 12 degrees lower than in Granada, in an area otherwise known for high temperatures and abundant sunshine.

Parts of the range are included in the Sierra Nevada National Park, and the range has also been declared a biosphere reserve. It is one of the foremost plant biodiversity hotspots in the Western Mediterranean: 2,100 species of vascular plants have been recorded, of which 80 are endemic, including about 40 per cent of the high-elevation species. Evergreen oaks and maquis shrubland grow on dry, south-facing slopes, deciduous and conifer forests at higher elevations, and subalpine shrublands and grasslands at the highest. Wet grasslands on peat soils and around springs fed by snowmelt include many endemic species.

The high peaks make skiing possible at one of the most southerly ski resorts in Europe. The Sierra Nevada Observatory, the Calar Alto Observatory and the IRAM 30m telescope stand on the northern slopes at an elevation of 2,800 metres.
sierre: Sierre was first mentioned around 800 as Sidrium. The hill of Gerunden and the surrounding area were settled very early, and finds include neolithic objects, Bronze Age weapons and jewellery and Roman inscriptions. In the Roman period there seems to have been no major population centre but several scattered upper-class dwellings, and the duumvir of the Civitas Vallensium, Caius Cominus Chiu, lived there. In 515 King Sigismund of Burgundy gave the estate to the Abbey of Saint-Maurice as a fief, and by the 11th century it belonged to the Bishop of Sion.

The aristocratic families and residents lived on three hills, each with a castle serving as the residence of the bishop's representatives and as a refuge. The castles were razed in the middle of the 14th century when the noble families stood with the bishop in his war with the Zenden of the Upper Valais and the Counts of Savoy, and most residents settled farther north in Plan-Sierre.

The Contrée of Sierre began as a group that managed the common land, took on a larger political role in the 14th and 15th centuries and became the core of the Zenden of Sierre. As the capital of a Zenden, Sierre fought the French in the invasion of 1798 and 1799, and in 1799 French and Vaudois troops occupied it.

Sierre lies in the middle Rhône valley, on the right bank of the river, and is the capital of the district of Sierre. It is the last official French-speaking town in the canton before the language border, which is marked by the Raspille mountain stream and the forest of Finges. About 8 percent of its people speak German. It is nicknamed the City of the Sun for its average of 300 days of sunshine a year, and its coat of arms is a golden sun on red.

After 1848 the villages of the Noble Contrée became municipalities and the Zenden became the District of Sierre. At the beginning of the 20th century aluminium smelting, enabled by hydroelectricity, made the town economically important. Sierre is a starting point for the Val d'Anniviers and is linked to Crans-Montana by a funicular railway.
siete-partidas: The code was first called the Libro de las Leyes, the Book of Laws, and took its present name, from the number of its sections, only in the 14th century. One of its oldest versions says a commission of the leading Castilian jurists wrote it under Alfonso X's personal direction between 26 June 1256 and 28 August 1265; other spans have been proposed, but most historians hold that it was not completed until 1265. Its aim is debated: Alfonso was pursuing the crown of the Holy Roman Empire, and Aquilino Iglesias argued that the code was meant for the whole Empire, while García-Gallo and others pointed to its Spanish language and its references to Castile's own territorial organisation.

Resistance, above all among the nobility, led the Cortes to pass the Ordinances of Zamora in 1274, which restricted the code to cases under the king's own jurisdiction and left other matters to local fueros. Whether Alfonso X enacted it is unknown.

A prologue sets out the work's purpose, and each of the seven partidas begins with a letter of the king's name, forming the acrostic Alfonso. The parts contain 182 articles made up of 2802 laws, covering constitutional, civil, commercial and criminal law and procedure. Its provisions come with references to authors and texts, examples and a reasoned account of their religious, philosophical and historical background, and it has been called a humanist encyclopedia. Because each partida was written by a different person, some provisions contradict others.

The main editions were those of Alonso Díaz de Montalvo (Seville, 1491), of Gregorio López (Salamanca, 1555), authorised by royal decree on 7 September 1555 and most used in Spanish America, and of the Real Academia de la Historia (1807). The code was studied in universities and translated into Catalan, Portuguese, Galician and English. It reached Spanish America with Castilian law and Brazil with Portuguese law, stayed in force in Latin America until the codifications of 1822–1916, and gave the legal basis for the juntas formed after the imprisonment of Fernando VII in the Peninsular War. Samuel Parsons Scott's English translation appeared in 1931.
sigebert-i: Sigebert I was the third surviving son of four of the Frankish king Clotaire I and Ingund. When Clotaire died in 561 the kingdom was divided among his four sons according to Frankish custom. Sigebert received the north-eastern portion, Austrasia, with its capital at Rheims. Charibert took the kingdom centred on Paris, Guntram received Burgundy with its capital at Orléans, and the youngest, Chilperic, received Soissons, which became Neustria when he also obtained part of Charibert's share.

Sigebert added further territory when Charibert died in 567 or 568. Incursions by the Avars, a nomadic people related to the Huns, led him to move his capital from Rheims to Metz. He repelled their attacks twice, in 562 and about 568, and eventually made peace with them. About 567 he married Brunhilda, daughter of the Visigothic king Athanagild, who was baptised as a Catholic, having been an Arian. According to Gregory of Tours, he sought a wife abroad because his brothers were marrying slave women.

Chilperic then asked Athanagild for his other daughter, Galswintha, abandoned his other wives and married her, but soon had her murdered in order to marry his mistress Fredegund. Probably spurred by Brunhilda's anger at her sister's murder, Sigebert sought revenge. The brothers had already been at war, but their hostility grew into a long and bitter conflict that was continued by their descendants. In 573 Sigebert took Poitiers and Touraine and conquered most of his kingdom, and Chilperic hid in Tournai.

At his moment of triumph, when Chilperic's subjects had just declared him king at Vitry-en-Artois, Sigebert was struck down by two assassins working for Fredegund. His son Childebert succeeded him under the regency of Brunhilda. She and Childebert quickly put themselves under the protection of Guntram, who eventually adopted Childebert as his own son and heir. Sigebert and Brunhilda had two daughters, Ingund and Chlodosind. Gregory of Tours is the source for his marriage.
sigebert-iii: Sigebert was born around 630, the eldest son of Dagobert I, King of the Franks, and his concubine Ragnetrude. Dagobert recalled Saint Amand, whom he had banished for criticising his vices, and asked him to baptise the newborn. The ceremony took place at Orléans, with Charibert II, king of Aquitaine, as godfather. Dagobert entrusted the child's education to Pepin of Landen, who had been mayor of the palace in Austrasia under Chlotar II until 629, and Pepin took him to his domains in Aquitaine for three years.

In 633 a revolt of the nobles forced Dagobert to make the three-year-old Sigebert king of Austrasia, as Chlotar II had once made Dagobert. Dagobert refused to give power to Pepin. He placed Sigebert under the tutelage of Adalgisel as mayor of the palace and of Saint Cunibert, Bishop of Cologne, as regent, and kept Pepin in Neustria as a hostage. When Dagobert died in 639 the two Frankish kingdoms became independent again under Sigebert and his half-brother Clovis II, then about eleven and five years old.

Under Sigebert the mayor of the palace began to play the most important role in Austrasian politics, and he has been called the first roi fainéant, or do-nothing king, of the Merovingian dynasty. Pepin replaced Adalgisel in 639 and died the following year, and his son Grimoald succeeded him. When the Duchy of Thuringia rebelled, in the only war of the reign, Grimoald let the young king head the army, which was defeated by Duke Radulph. The Chronicle of Fredegar records that the rout left Sigebert weeping in his saddle. Sigebert lived as a pious adult and used his wealth to found monasteries, hospitals and churches, among them Stavelot-Malmedy and the Abbey of Saint Martin near Metz.

Sigebert died of natural causes on 1 February 656, aged about 25, and was buried at Saint Martin. His body was found incorrupt in 1063 and moved beside the altar; after the abbey was demolished in 1552 the relics went to Nancy Cathedral. He is venerated as a saint, with his feast on 1 February, and is patron saint of Nancy.

Grimoald had persuaded the childless king to adopt his son Childebert the Adopted, but Sigebert then had a son, Dagobert II. After Sigebert's death Grimoald had the seven-year-old Dagobert tonsured and sent to a monastery in Ireland and proclaimed Childebert king. Childebert was deposed after seven months and both he and Grimoald were killed. Dagobert II was recalled from Ireland in 676 and took his father's throne after about twenty years in exile.
sighnaq: Sighnaq lay in what is now Kyzylorda Region of Kazakhstan, in the district called Farab, between the settlements of Isfijab and Jand; its name means shelter. Medieval writers placed it differently: Sherif al-Din made it a border city of Turkestan 40 kilometres from Otrar, the geographer al-Muqaddasi put it 24 farsakhs up the Syr Darya from Otrar, and Mahmud Kashghari called it a town of the Oghuz. On this evidence the ruins at Sunak Kurgan, a few kilometres northeast of Tyumen Arik on the Orenburg-Tashkent railway, have been identified as the city.

In the 10th century the Oghuz Turks are believed to have had a semi-sedentary town near the frontier, where they traded with the Muslim states to the south; the Hudud al-'Alam records bows made there for export. In the 12th century it was the capital of a still pagan Kipchak khanate and suffered raids from Khwarezm, one in 1152 and another in 1195 under Kayir Toku Khan. Early in the thirteenth century Ala al-Din Muhammad annexed it, and in 1220 Genghis Khan took it after a siege and massacred the population.

Timur annexed the city in the late 14th century. In 1427 Baraq Khan, khan of the Golden Horde, claimed it from Tamerlane's son Shah Rukh, defeated the Timurids and occupied it, but they recovered it after his death around 1428. Abu'l-Khayr, founder of the Uzbek Khanate, conquered it in 1446, and in 1457 the Kalmyks defeated the Uzbeks at the Battle of Kök Kašane, 7 kilometres to the south, forcing Abu'l-Khayr to accept the terms of Uz Timur. Muhammad Shaybani, who refounded the Uzbek Khanate, was born in the region. In the sixteenth century the city belonged to the Kazakhs, then lost importance and disappeared.
sigibert-the-lame: Sigibert, also written Sigobert or Sigebert, was a king of the Ripuarian Franks in the area of Zülpich, the Latin Tolbiac, and Cologne. His father was named Childebert. He was presumably wounded in the knee at the Battle of Tolbiac against the Alamanni, fighting on the side of Clovis I, and he supported Clovis again against the Visigoths at the Battle of Vouillé in the spring of 507.

According to Gregory of Tours, Sigibert was killed although he had twice lent help to Clovis. His son Chlodoric sent assassins against him while he was staying away from his kingdom in a forest near Fulda, then told Clovis of the murder and offered him the finest treasures of his newly inherited kingdom as a sign of their new alliance. Clovis's messengers, sent to assess the treasure, asked Chlodoric to plunge his hand as deep as he could into his gold coins, and with his arm submerged they killed him.

Clovis then stood before Chlodoric's people, professed horror at the murder of Sigibert, and told them that the son had sent assassins to kill his father and had since met his own end. He offered them his protection, and so became their king. In Gregory's telling the episode is one of a series: Chlodoric died in the same campaign that killed the Frankish king Chararic, and Clovis had earlier killed Ragnachar and his brothers. After these murders, Gregory says, Clovis lamented that he had no family left, not from grief but so that any surviving relatives would make themselves known and could be marked for death.
sigismondo-pandolfo-malatesta: Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta was born in Brescia on 19 June 1417, the elder of the two illegitimate sons of Pandolfo III Malatesta. Following family tradition, he first served as a man-at-arms at the age of 13 against his relative Carlo II Malatesta of Pesaro, who sought to annex Rimini, Cesena and Fano. After his victory he and his brothers obtained the title of papal vicar for those cities. When his elder brother abdicated, he became lord of Rimini at the age of 15 and of Fano from 1432.

Sigismondo commanded a papal corps in 1432 but was excommunicated after occupying the papal city of Cervia, and was soon pardoned and made commander of the papal army.
