He fought in Romagna and the Marche alongside Francesco Sforza, whom he later betrayed, and served in turn under Venice, Florence, Siena and Naples. In 1445 he forced the Neapolitans to raise the siege of Piombino. Two of his wives died in mysterious circumstances, and rumours of poisoning and drowning spread, though the second charge, made by Sforza, was never confirmed. In 1456 he married his long-time mistress Isotta degli Atti.

The Peace of Lodi in 1454, from which he was excluded, turned the major Italian powers against him. On 25 December 1460 Pope Pius II tried him in his absence, excommunicated him as a heretic and accused him of a series of sins. His image was burnt in Rome and a league of the pope, the king of Naples, the Duke of Milan and Federico da Montefeltro fought him. After defeats near Senigallia in 1462, the war ended in 1463 with the loss of all his territories except Rimini and about 8 kilometres around it. He then served Venice as a field commander in the Peloponnesus from 1464 to 1466.

Sigismondo died at Castel Sismondo in 1468 and was succeeded by his legitimated son Sallustio. His contemporaries recognised his skill as a general, and he built the Rocche of Rimini and Fano. The Tempio Malatestiano in Rimini, designed by Leon Battista Alberti and decorated by artists including Piero della Francesca and Agostino di Duccio, was essentially a lay monument to Isotta and the first church to use the Roman triumphal arch as part of its structure. His reputation rested largely on Pius II's view of him, and chroniclers called him a tyrant. Ezra Pound's Malatesta Cantos admire him, and Adrian Stokes wrote The Stones of Rimini on the art of his court.
sigismund-archduke-of-austria: Sigismund was born on 26 October 1427 at the Tyrolean court in Innsbruck, the son of Duke Frederick IV of Austria of the Further Austrian line and his second wife Anna of Brunswick. He was a minor when his father died in 1439, and his first cousin Frederick V acted as regent until 1446. Frederick, elected King of the Romans in 1440, used the regency to extend his influence in the Further Austrian lands, and the income from the mines of Tyrol remained important to him. Sigismund married Princess Eleanor of Scotland, daughter of King James I, on 8 September 1449.

Sigismund took over Further Austria, which included the Sundgau, the Breisgau and smaller estates, in 1446. For much of his reign he disputed with Nicholas of Cusa, Prince-bishop of Brixen, over the Eisack, Puster and Inn valleys. In 1460, when he marched on the bishop's residence at Bruneck Castle, Pope Pius II excommunicated him. Nicholas died in 1464 before Sigismund submitted to obtain a papal pardon.

In 1469 he sold his Swabian lands on the Rhine, among them the Alsace landgraviate, Pfirt and the Breisgau, to Charles the Bold of Burgundy. Sources are unclear whether he did so to pay debts from a luxurious way of life or only lent them for better protection against the Swiss. In 1477 the Emperor Frederick raised him to archduke. In 1484 he married the 16-year-old Catherine of Saxony; neither marriage produced children.

Under a coinage reform of the late 1470s and early 1480s the silver mines of Tyrol were revived, and the large silver guldengroschen was struck there. It was later developed into the thaler, ancestor of many European coins and of the US dollar. In March 1487 he entered a pointless war with Venice after imprisoning 130 Venetian merchants at Bozen, and it ended with no decisive victory. By 1490 Tyrolean nobles compelled him to hand rule to Frederick's son Maximilian, though it is unclear whether he did so willingly. He died on 4 March 1496, and the Tyrolean branch of the Habsburgs died out, leaving Maximilian sole heir.
sigismund-holy-roman-emperor: Sigismund was the son of Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor, and his fourth and final wife, Elizabeth of Pomerania. His place and exact date of birth are disputed: his mother's letter points to 14 February 1368, and in 1892 Theodor Lindner gave 15 February and Nuremberg. In the Bohemian Crown lands he was nicknamed the ginger fox because of his hair. He was betrothed in 1374 to Mary, eldest daughter of King Louis I of Hungary, to augment the lands of the House of Luxembourg. After his father's death in 1378 he became Margrave of Brandenburg and was sent to the Hungarian court, where he learned the language, and in 1381 he was sent to Kraków to learn Polish.

Mary became queen of Hungary in 1382, and Sigismund married her in 1385. In 1396 he led the Crusade of Nicopolis, and was decisively defeated by the Ottoman Empire. Afterwards he founded the Order of the Dragon to fight the Turks. After King Rupert's death in 1410 three electors chose him as king of Germany, but a rival election made Jobst of Moravia king too; Jobst died on 18 January 1411, and Sigismund was elected again on 21 July 1411 and crowned at Aachen on 8 November 1414.

He took a leading part in the Council of Constance, which ended the Western Schism. It also had Jan Hus burned at the stake in July 1415, and historians debate Sigismund's complicity: he had granted Hus a safe conduct and protested against his imprisonment, and Hus was condemned by a Church court in his absence. When Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia died in 1419, Sigismund became titular king, but the Czech Estates, who distrusted him as the betrayer of Hus, did not acknowledge him for seventeen years. Three campaigns against the Hussites ended in disaster. He received the Iron Crown at Milan on 25 November 1431 and was crowned emperor in Rome on 31 May 1433.

Sigismund died on 9 December 1437 at Znojmo in Moravia and was buried at Nagyvárad, next to the tomb of King Saint Ladislaus I of Hungary. He was the last male member of the House of Luxembourg, and his only surviving legitimate child was Elisabeth of Luxembourg, so the succession passed on. Historian Thomas Brady Jr. remarks that he possessed a breadth of vision and a sense of grandeur unseen in a German monarch since the thirteenth century. His difficulties with the Hussites are now generally seen as the result of a lack of financial resources and other constraints, not of personal failings.
sigismund-i-the-old: Sigismund was born on 1 January 1467 at Kozienice, the fifth son of Casimir IV Jagiellon, and was not expected to rule. When Casimir died in 1492 he was the only son without titles or land. His efforts to get land from his brother Alexander and an Austrian throne failed, as did an invasion of Moldavia in 1497. His eldest brother Vladislaus II, king of Bohemia and Hungary, then granted him the duchies of Głogów in 1499 and Opava in 1501, and in 1504 he became governor of Silesia and Lower Lusatia.

After Alexander I died in 1506, the Lithuanian Ducal Council elected Sigismund grand duke on 20 September, and the Polish Senate at Piotrków elected him king on 8 December. He was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 24 January 1507. He summoned annual sessions of the Sejm and issued statutes between 1530 and 1538 that fixed the free election of the monarch. His reforms included a permanent conscription army in 1527 and the recovery of royal properties that had been pawned to nobles, which provoked the Chicken War of 1537, a revolt of the lesser nobility at Lwów. Sigismund rejected most of the demands and accepted only the principle that one person could not hold two offices.

War against Muscovy brought the loss of Smolensk in 1514 but a Polish and Lithuanian victory at Orsha on 8 September 1514, and the commander Jan Amor Tarnowski stopped a Muscovite invasion at Starodub in 1535. The Treaty of Kraków of 1525 ended two centuries of wars with the Teutonic Knights: the Order was secularised and his nephew Albert, who had become a Lutheran, became Duke of Prussia and paid homage to Poland. After the death of Janusz III of Masovia in 1526 Sigismund united that duchy and Warsaw with the kingdom.

Sigismund married first Barbara Zápolya and then Bona Sforza, daughter of the Duke of Milan, who supported his purchase of land and improvements of the royal estates. Under her influence Italian styles dominated at the height of the Polish Renaissance. His only surviving legitimate son, Sigismund Augustus, was made co-king in 1529 and took the throne when his father died on 1 April 1548.
sigismund-ii-augustus: Sigismund Augustus was born in Kraków on 1 August 1520, the elder of two sons of Sigismund I the Old and Bona Sforza of Milan, and the only one to survive infancy. He was educated by the leading scholars in the country. His mother wished to name him Augustus, either for the month of his birth or after the first Roman Emperor.

Because the Polish crown was elective, his parents secured his succession by having him chosen king in his father's lifetime. He was inaugurated as Grand Duke of Lithuania on 18 October 1529, named King of Poland alongside his father on 18 December and crowned at the age of nine on 20 February 1530 by Primate Jan Łaski. The nobles criticised this election, which became one of the reasons for the Lwów Rokosz in 1537. He began his reign as active Grand Duke in 1544 and at first opposed the Polish–Lithuanian union, hoping to leave his throne to heirs, since the Lithuanian throne was hereditary and the Polish was not.

He married Elizabeth of Austria on 5 May 1543, when she was 16 and he 22. Queen Bona plotted against her, and the couple settled in Vilnius. Elizabeth died in 1545 at 18. In July or August 1547 he secretly married Barbara Radziwiłł, who was despised by Bona. The deputies of his first Sejm, on 31 October 1548, threatened to renounce their allegiance unless he repudiated her, and he even considered abdicating. After his father's death on 1 April 1548 he declared her Queen on 17 April, and she died five months after her coronation. His third wife was Catherine of Austria. Neither marriage produced living children.

His reign saw the bloodless introduction of the Protestant Reformation into Poland and Lithuania, and the collapse of the Knights of the Sword in the north, which led to the Commonwealth's acquisition of Livonia as a Lutheran duchy. He kept a policy of tolerance towards minorities and peaceful relations with neighbours, except for the Northern Seven Years' War, fought to secure Baltic trade. He established the first regular Polish navy and the first regular postal service in Poland, and in 1569 oversaw the signing of the Union of Lublin, which formed the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Culture flourished under his patronage, and he collected tapestries from the Low Countries.

Sigismund Augustus died on 7 July 1572, the last male monarch of the Jagiellonian dynasty. The dynasty ended with the death of his sister Anna in 1596. His rule is widely considered the apex of the Polish Golden Age.
sigismund-iii-vasa: Sigismund was born on 20 June 1566 at Gripsholm Castle, the second child and only son of Catherine Jagiellon and Grand Duke John III of Sweden. The couple had been held prisoner there since 1563, after John staged a failed rebellion against his brother Eric XIV of Sweden. Catherine was a daughter of King Sigismund I the Old of Poland, and Sigismund was raised as a Catholic, although his younger sister Anna Vasa of Sweden was a Lutheran.

In 1587 he stood for election to the Polish throne after the death of Stephen Báthory. Queen Dowager Anna and several magnates backed him as a descendant of the Jagiellons, while nobles associated with the Zborowski family opposed him. He was elected on 19 August 1587.

Chancellor Jan Zamoyski was hostile to the king almost from his arrival, criticising his liking for Habsburg culture and his cold character. The king's friends came largely from the higher clergy and the Jesuits, and religious freedoms guaranteed by the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 came under pressure. When mob violence against non-Catholics broke out in Vilnius and Kraków in 1591, dissidents gathered in conventions and Sigismund had to yield to their demands. In 1606 his efforts to strengthen royal authority provoked the Zebrzydowski rebellion, an armed rising of nobles and magnates.

After succeeding his father in 1592 he also ruled Sweden, where the Uppsala Resolution of 1594 had promised to uphold the Lutheran faith. He placed his own commanders in the castles and appointed Catholics to high office, which angered many Swedes. A civil war began in 1597 under his uncle Duke Charles, who took most of the castles. Sigismund accepted a peace at Linköping, then fled to Poland with his sister, and Charles deposed him in 1599.

In the east he used the Russian Time of Troubles to invade from 1609, and the campaign ended with the seizure of Smolensk and the occupation of Moscow. A Polish–Ottoman war followed in 1620–1621 over Moldavia. In 1626 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden invaded and later annexed parts of Polish Livonia.

Towards the end of his reign Sigismund withdrew from politics and devoted himself to family matters and the performing arts. In his last days he was bedridden with gout and joint pain. His rule of nearly 45 years is seen as controversial: it brought considerable developments in architecture, the arts and culture, but also conspiracies, religious conflict and the long war with Sweden. His policies began the Counter-Reformation in Poland–Lithuania and weakened Protestantism there. Szymon Starowolski ranked him above his predecessors, while opponents thought he had lived too long. His son Władysław IV Vasa succeeded him and later commissioned the column in Warsaw that bears his name.
sigismund-of-burgundy: Sigismund was the son of King Gundobad and Caretene, and a student of Avitus of Vienne, the Chalcedonian bishop who converted him from the Arian faith of his Burgundian forebears. In 515 he was inspired to found a monastery dedicated to Saint Maurice at Agaune in Valais, and in 516 he succeeded his father as king. In 494 he had married Ostrogotha, an illegitimate daughter of Theodoric the Great, as part of Theodoric's negotiation for an alliance with the Burgundians, and they had a son, Sigeric, and a daughter, Suavegotha.

He quarrelled with Bishop Apollinaris of Valence over marriage rules. His treasurer Stephen lived in incest, and the province's four bishops ordered him to separate from his companion; Sigismund backed his official and exiled the bishops to Sardinia. After a time he let three of them return, but kept Apollinaris a close prisoner for a year. According to Gregory of Tours, in 517 Sigismund, urged on by his second wife, ordered his son Sigeric seized while drunk and drowned in a well, after Sigeric had rebuked her for wearing his late mother's ceremonial clothes. Overcome with remorse, the king withdrew to the monastery he had founded.

In 523 four Frankish kings, Chlodomer, Childebert I, Clotaire I and Theuderic I, sons of Clovis I, invaded Burgundy, a war that Clotilde is said to have provoked to avenge her father Chilperic II, whom Gundobad had killed in 493. Sigismund and his brother Godomar lost the battle. Godomar fled, and Sigismund put on a monk's habit and hid in a cell near his abbey. Chlodomer, king of Orléans, captured him and in 524 he was beheaded and his body thrown into a well; his wife and remaining children were also put to death.

Godomar succeeded him, rallied the Burgundians and, with help from Theodoric the Great, regained the kingdom, massacring the Frankish garrisons. Chlodomer was killed at the Battle of Vézeronce on 25 June 524, reportedly by Godomar. In 535 Sigismund's remains were recovered from the well and buried at Agaunum. He was venerated as a saint and as a patron of those suffering from fever, and the cult spread to Switzerland, France and Italy. In 1366 Charles IV moved his relics from Agaunum to Prague, making him a patron of the Kingdom of Bohemia.
sigmaringen: Sigmaringen lies in the Danube valley, surrounded by wooded hills, south of the Swabian Alps and about 40 km north of Lake Constance. It is the capital of the Sigmaringen district. The town is known for its castle, Schloss Sigmaringen, which was the seat of the principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen until 1850 and is still owned by the Hohenzollern family.

The first castle was built in the 11th century on the rock that protects the valley. The first written reference dates from 1077, when King Rudolf of Rheinfelden tried in vain to conquer it. The town was officially founded in 1250, and in 1325 it was sold to Ulrich III, Count of Württemberg. The castle was rebuilt into a chateau in 1460 and 1500. In 1535 Sigmaringen came into the hands of the Hohenzollern through the county of Werdenberg, and it belonged to the principality of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen from 1576. The Swedes occupied the castle in 1632 during the Thirty Years' War.

From 1806 to 1849 Sigmaringen was the capital of the sovereign principality and the residence of the princes of Hohenzollern. After the Sigmaringen Revolution of 1848 the princes of Hechingen and Sigmaringen abdicated, and both principalities fell to Prussia in 1850. Until 1945 the town was the seat of the Prussian government of the Province of Hohenzollern, and Karl Anton von Hohenzollern was Prime Minister of Prussia from 1858 to 1862. Carol I of Romania, born there in 1839, was king of Romania from 1866 to 1914, and Ferdinand I, born there in 1865, reigned from 1914 to 1927.

On 7 September 1944, after the Allied invasion of France, Philippe Pétain and members of the Vichy cabinet were relocated to Germany, against Pétain's fierce resistance. A government in exile headed by Fernand de Brinon was set up at Sigmaringen, with embassies of Germany, Italy and Japan. The writers Louis-Ferdinand Céline and Lucien Rebatet fled there with it, and Céline's novel D'un château l'autre describes its fall. Free French forces took the town on 22 April 1945.

Three railways meet in Sigmaringen: the Ulm to Sigmaringen line, the Tübingen to Sigmaringen line, and the line from Engstingen operated by the Hohenzollerische Landesbahn. Among the people born there are the Capuchin martyr Fidelis of Sigmaringen, born in 1577, and the physician Theodor Bilharz, who made discoveries in parasitology.
sigmund-freud: Sigmund Freud was born Sigismund Schlomo Freud on 6 May 1856 in the Moravian town of Freiberg, in the Austrian Empire, now Příbor in the Czech Republic. He was the first of eight children of Ashkenazi Jewish parents who both came from Galicia. His father, Jakob Freud, was a wool merchant, and his mother, Amalia Nathansohn, was Jakob's third wife. The family was struggling financially and living in a rented room when he was born. He was born with a caul, which his mother saw as a good omen.

Freud took almost nine years to finish his medical studies, because of his interest in neurophysiological research, including the sexual anatomy of eels, and in philosophy under Franz Brentano. He entered private practice in neurology for financial reasons and received his doctorate in medicine in 1881, aged 25. In the 1880s he worked chiefly on the anatomy of the brain. In 1891 his monograph Zur Auffassung der Aphasien entered the debates about aphasia, coined the term agnosia and counselled against too locationist a view of neurological deficits.

He was also an early researcher of cerebral palsy, then called cerebral paralysis, and showed that the disease existed long before other researchers studied it. He suggested that William John Little, who first identified it, was wrong that lack of oxygen at birth was a cause, and proposed instead that birth complications were a symptom. Freud died on 23 September 1939.

Freud founded psychoanalysis, a clinical method that treats conflicts in the psyche through dialogue between patient and analyst. He introduced free association, the interpretation of dreams and the analysis of transference. He widened the idea of sexuality to include infantile stages, which led to the Oedipus complex, and developed a theory of the unconscious and a model of the mind with id, ego and superego. His later work offered an interpretation and critique of religion and culture.

His books include The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality (1905), Totem and Taboo (1913), The Ego and the Id (1923), The Future of an Illusion (1927), Civilization and Its Discontents (1930) and Moses and Monotheism (1939). His talking cure gave the basic format for later psychotherapy. The neo-Freudians, among them Alfred Adler and Karen Horney, rejected his theory of instinctual drive, and Jacques Lacan approached psychoanalysis through linguistics and literature. His legacy remains controversial.
sigtuna: Sigtuna lies in Stockholm County on Skarven, a bay of Lake Mälaren. The present harbour town developed about 4 kilometres east of Old Sigtuna, which, according to Old Norse religion, was once the home of the widely revered god Odin. The name is closely linked with the higher land to the north, Signhildsberg, and its second element means a settlement. The first element may come from dialect words for seeping water or swamp, since the estate was surrounded by marshy terrain, or the name may be an old prestigious name meaning strong fortress, from a word for victory.

Sigtuna was founded on what was then the shore of Lake Mälaren just over a thousand years ago and took its name from an ancient royal estate several kilometres to the west. Some sources name King Eric the Victorious as founder and others King Olof Skötkonung. It operated as a royal and commercial centre for some 250 years and was one of the most important cities of Sweden. At the end of the 10th century and the beginning of the 11th, Sweden's first coins were minted there.

The Dominican monastery played an important role in the Swedish Middle Ages and produced many important church officials, among them many Swedish archbishops. Its church, St Mary's, built in the 13th century, remains largely intact. In 1187 raiders from across the Baltic Sea attacked and pillaged Sigtuna, possibly from Curonia, from the island of Saaremaa, or Karelians and Novgorodians, though excavations have not verified the tradition of destruction. The town began slowly to lose its importance in the 13th century because post-glacial rebound caused navigability problems. Its first known seal dates from 1311, and in the late 19th century it had only about 600 people, the smallest town in Sweden.

Sigtuna is a locality in Sigtuna Municipality, still often called a stad for historical reasons. It has a medieval-style town centre with the old main street, Stora gatan, the small old town hall, Viking runestones and several church ruins, among them St Per's Church from the 1100s, St Olof's Church from around the middle of the 11th century and St Lars's Church from the middle of the 13th. Its population growth in the second half of the 20th century is related to Stockholm Arlanda Airport, 10 kilometres away.
sigurd-eysteinsson: Sigurd was a son of Eystein Glumra. His life is known mainly from two Norse sagas, the Heimskringla and the Orkneyinga saga. They tell that after the Battle of Hafrsfjord unified the Norwegian kingdom, in or after 872, the Orkney and Shetland islands became a refuge for exiled Vikings who raided their former homeland, and that King Harald Fairhair subdued them with the help of Rognvald Eysteinsson of Møre. Rognvald's son Ivar was killed in the conquest, and Harald gave Rognvald the islands with the title of jarl in compensation.

With Harald's consent Rognvald passed the title and lands to his brother Sigurd, who was one of Harald's forecastlemen. The Historia Norwegiæ, written from a different source, confirms that Rognvald's family conquered the islands but gives no details. In league with Thorstein the Red, Sigurd extended his rule to the Scottish mainland and conquered Caithness and Sutherland at least as far south as Ekkjalsbakka, which some sources place in Moray but which more likely lay along the river Oykel. These conquests earned him the name the Mighty, in Old Norse ríki.

Near the end of his rule, the Orkneyinga saga says, Sigurd challenged a native ruler, Máel Brigte the Buck-Toothed, to a battle of 40 men a side and treacherously brought 80. After beheading Máel Brigte he strapped the head to his saddle, and the buck-tooth scratched his leg as he rode; the wound became infected and killed him. He was buried in a mound called Sigurd's Howe, most probably at Sidera or Cyderhall near Dornoch, though Burghead in Moray has also been named.

A time of instability followed. His son Guttorm died within months, and Rognvald's son Hallad, made earl next, could not contain the Viking raiders and returned to Norway in disgrace. The earldom then passed to Rognvald's youngest son, Einarr.
sigurd-syr: Icelandic poems and sagas, culminating in Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, present Sigurd Halvdansson Syr as a great-grandson of King Harald Fairhair through Harald's son Sigurd Rise, a little-known son of Harald by a Sami girl named Snæfríðr Svásadottir. Doubt has been cast on this descent: there is no contemporary record of the Halfdan said to be his father, and many modern historians regard the Fairhair genealogy as largely invented.

Heimskringla describes Sigurd as prudent, taciturn and modest though very wealthy, a careful manager of his property who took part in running it himself, wise and peaceful. He may have owned several large farms. His nickname Syr can be translated as sow or swine, and its origin is unknown. The historian P. A. Munch suggested that it referred to his devotion to farming, meaning one who roots in the soil; as Sigurd was a respected man of high birth, the name was most probably meant as an honour.

He was baptised in 998. According to Heimskringla, when King Olaf Tryggvason came to Ringerike to spread Christianity, Sigurd and his wife allowed themselves to be baptised. Sigurd had no great political ambition of his own and disliked the pomp of noble life, though he played the part expected of him. He fully backed the ambitions of his stepson Olaf, and in 1014, when Olaf wished to raise an army in Norway, Sigurd successfully asked the other petty kings of Norway to support him.

Sigurd died around 1018. The sagas remember him and Åsta Gudbrandsdatter as good and noble rulers, and they name their children as Guttorm, Gunnhild, who married Ketil Kalv of Ringnes in Stange, Halfdan, Ingerid, mother of Tore, the foster-father of King Magnus Barefoot, and Harald Hardrada, King of Norway from 1046 to 1066. Sigurd's place in Norwegian history rests largely on his links with his stepson Olaf II and his son Harald III.
sigurd-the-crusader: Sigurd was one of three sons of King Magnus III of Norway, all of them illegitimate and born to different mothers, the others being Øystein and Olaf. Before he was proclaimed king he was styled King of the Isles and Earl of Orkney. In 1098 he accompanied his father on an expedition to Orkney, the Hebrides and the Irish Sea, and was made Earl of Orkney, with the title King of the Isles after the overthrow of its king. A marriage was arranged between Sigurd and a daughter of the Irish ruler Muirchertach Ua Briain. When Magnus was ambushed and killed in Ulaid in 1103, the 14-year-old Sigurd returned to Norway, leaving his child bride behind.

The three brothers were proclaimed kings in 1103 and ruled jointly to avoid feuds. Olaf died in 1115 and Øystein in 1123, after which Sigurd ruled alone. Historians have regarded the period as a golden age of the medieval Kingdom of Norway. In 1107 he led the Norwegian Crusade to support the Kingdom of Jerusalem, with about 5,000 men in some 60 ships, according to the sagas. He fought at Lisbon and on Mediterranean islands, visited King Roger II of Sicily at Palermo, and was welcomed in the Holy Land by King Baldwin I of Jerusalem.

Sigurd joined Baldwin and the Doge of Venice, Ordelafo Faliero, at the siege of Sidon, which fell on 5 December 1110. He was given a splinter of the True Cross, which he kept. He sailed on to Cyprus and Constantinople, where he gave his ships and many treasures to Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, and many of his men stayed to serve in the Varangian Guard. He returned overland, through Hungary and Bavaria, and was back in Norway in 1111.

In his reign the tithe was introduced, which strengthened the church, and he founded the diocese of Stavanger. In 1123 he took part in a crusade to Småland in Sweden, whose inhabitants were reported to have returned to Old Norse gods.

According to the kings' sagas Morkinskinna and Heimskringla, Sigurd showed signs of mental illness in his last years. He died in 1130 and was buried in Hallvard's church in Oslo. He left no legitimate son. His illegitimate son Magnus became king and shared the throne uneasily with Harald Gille, and a struggle among claimants after Sigurd's death grew into a lengthy and devastating civil war. Scholars still debate the historical reliability of the sagas.
sihl: The Sihl rises on the north-eastern side of the Druesberg mountain in the municipality of Unteriberg and flows north past the village of Studen into the Sihlsee, an artificial reservoir about 8.5 kilometres long near Einsiedeln. The Sihlsee is Switzerland's largest artificial lake and is held back by a dam 33 metres high. Below it the river runs through a narrow glacial valley, takes in its tributary the Alp, passes the Sihlsprung rapids along the border between the cantons of Zug and Zürich, and enters the canton of Zürich for good at Sihlbrugg.

The name is first recorded in 1018 as Sylaha. It may be of Old European or Celtic origin, from a word for a quiet watercourse, with the Old High German element aha, flowing water, added. Industry was drawn to the lower valley around Langnau am Albis and Adliswil by the water power the river offered. Once the Sihlsee was built, water was diverted from it through a tunnel to the Etzelwerk hydroelectric station at Altendorf and into Lake Zürich, leaving less water downstream, poorer water quality and a river that in places dries out in winter. Before the reservoir the Minster was a direct tributary of the Sihl.

North of Sihlbrugg the river flows through a lightly populated, wooded valley beside the Sihlwald, a rare large original forest on the slopes of the Albis. In Zürich it passes several city quarters, runs for 1.2 kilometres under a viaduct of the A3 motorway, and flows through five culverts beneath the upper platforms of Zürich Hauptbahnhof before joining the Limmat at the Platzspitz park. Because a failure of the Sihlsee dam could send a flood wave 8 metres high into the city within two hours, Zürich has published evacuation plans, and work began in 2022 on a relief tunnel to Lake Zürich.
sihor: Sihor lies on the river Gautami, surrounded by hills, about 20 km from Bhavnagar, at an average elevation of 60 metres. According to Hasmukh Dhirajlal Sankalia its name comes from Siṁhapura, attested in inscriptions of the Maitraka and Chaulukya eras, after either the lion, native to Gujarat, or a man named Siṁha; over time the root became sīha and the suffix -pura was shortened to -or. Other forms of the name recorded are Saraswatpur, Sinhalpur, Sinhpur, Sinhor and Shihor.

Sihor was a capital of the Gohil Rajputs, and its many temples have earned it the local name Chhote Kashi, a small Varanasi. Its monuments include the 12th-century Brahma Kund, a stepped tank surrounded by images of Hindu deities and attributed to Raja Jayasimha Siddharaja, the 17th-century Vijay Vilas Palace of the maharajas with its paintings and wood carvings, the old fort and town walls, and the nine Shiva temples of the Navnath pilgrimage, built or renewed between about 1000 and 1600 and visited above all in the month of Shraavan.

Local tradition links the town with two figures. One makes it the home of Prince Vijaya, remembered as the first king of Sri Lanka, who is said to have sailed from nearby Ghogha; other traditions place his origin in Bengal. Another holds that Nana Sahib, a leader of the rising of 1857, lived out his life in Sihor and died there in 1909; a house in the old town, a tomb and a park are associated with him.

Sihor is a town and municipality in Bhavnagar district with a population of about 26,000 at the 2011 census. It became a railway junction when the Bhavnagar State Railway reached it in 1880, and it is known for its copper and brass ware, pottery, snuff making and rolling mills.
sijilmasa: Sijilmasa was a medieval Moroccan city and trade entrepôt at the northern edge of the Sahara. The ruins extend for five miles along the River Ziz in the Tafilalt oasis near the town of Rissani. Much of its economic success has been attributed to the oasis's large canal. Until the 14th century, as the northern terminus of the western trans-Sahara trade route, it was one of the most important trade centres of the Maghreb.

According to al-Bakri, Sufrite Kharijites first settled the town after the Berber revolts against the Umayyads. When they numbered about four thousand they elected a leader, 'Isa bin Mazid al-Aswad, who after 14 years was accused of corruption and executed. Abu al-Qasim Samgu bin Wasul al-Miknasi then led the town, and he and his descendants are known as the Midrar dynasty. Its wealth let the city assert its independence from the Abbasid Caliphate as early as 771. Ibn Hawqal, who visited between 947 and 951, reports a bill of 42,000 dinars issued to a trader at Awdaghust by a merchant of Sijilmasa, a sum he had never heard of elsewhere.

In 905 'Abd Allah al-Mahdi Billah, later regarded as the founder of the Fatimid dynasty, arrived in the Maghreb with his son al-Qa'im, fleeing the Abbasids, and hid in Sijilmasa for four years under the Midrar ruler Prince Yasa'. Yasa' imprisoned them. An Isma'ili army under Abu 'Abdallah reached the Tafilalt in the latter half of 909 and besieged the city. Yasa' was killed that year or the next, and the Midrar dynasty fragmented until the Maghrawa Berbers took the city. The Almoravids, led by Abdallah ibn Yasin, made it their first conquest, and it was the site of their first mint and their only mint from 1058 to 1100. The Almohads took it in 1146.

Ibn Battuta stayed there in 1352-1353 and praised its dates. By the early 16th century Leo Africanus found it destroyed, though its walls still stood. He reports that the last prince was assassinated by its citizens, whereas Ibn Khaldun attributes its fall to a lack of resources. Sultan Moulay Ismail had it rebuilt in the 18th century, and in 1818 the nomadic Ait Atta tribes conquered and destroyed it.

The ruins lie one kilometre north of Rissani and are recognised by the World Monuments Fund as an endangered site. The Moroccan-American Project of Sijilmassa, launched in 1988, led to six excavations. The Moroccan Ministry of Culture preserves the ruins.
sikandar-begum: Sikandar was born at Gauhar Mahal in Bhopal State on 10 September 1817, the daughter of Nasir Muhammad Khan and Qudsia Begum, both former rulers of the state. On 18 April 1835 she married Nawab Jahangir Mohammad Khan; their only child was Shah Jahan Begum. When the nine-year-old Shah Jahan came to the throne, Joseph Davey Cunningham, political agent of the Governor-General of India, announced Sikandar's appointment as regent, and the governor-general gave her the state's executive powers.

During the rising of 1857 she banned anti-British pamphlets, strengthened her intelligence network and bribed rebellious soldiers to change sides. In August sepoys attacked British garrisons at Sehore and Berasia, and in December, encouraged by her mother, they surrounded her palace; she sent her son-in-law Umrao Daulah to negotiate and ended the siege by raising their pay. The British recognised her as Nawab of Bhopal on 30 September 1860, made her a Knight Grand Commander in 1861 and raised her salute to 19 guns.

In 1863 she performed the Hajj with about 1,000 companions, mostly women, and wrote an Urdu memoir of the journey, translated into English in 1870, in which she called Mecca and Jeddah unclean and complained of Turkish customs officials. At home she divided the state into three districts and 21 sub-districts, repaid its debt and founded a customs office, a secretariat, a mint, a postal service and a modern judiciary with a court of appeal.

Sikandar founded the Victoria School for girls and Urdu and Hindi middle schools in every district, set up a Majlis-e-Shoora of nobles and intellectuals to recommend laws, and in 1862 made Urdu the court language in place of Persian. She built the Moti Masjid of red sandstone and the Moti Mahal and Shaukat Mahal palaces. A devout Muslim who wore no face veil and kept no purdah, she hunted tigers, played polo and commanded the army. She died of kidney failure on 30 October 1868 and was succeeded by her daughter.
sikandar-lodi: Sikandar Lodi was born Nizamudin Loadu on 17 July 1458, the second son of Bahlul Lodi, who had founded the Lodi dynasty. He became Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate after his father's death in July 1489 and ruled until his own death on 21 November 1517. He was the second and most successful Lodi ruler, a capable administrator who encouraged trade across his territory. He extended Lodi rule into Gwalior and Bihar, made a treaty with Alauddin Hussain Shah and the Sultanate of Bengal, and in 1503 commissioned the city of Agra.

His main wars were against the Tomar rajas of Gwalior. In 1500 Raja Man Singh Tomar sheltered rebels from Delhi, and in 1501 Sikandar captured Dholpur, a dependency of Gwalior. In 1504 he resumed the war and took the Mandrayal fort, and from September 1505 to May 1506 he ravaged the countryside around Gwalior but could not take the fort against Man Singh's hit-and-run tactics. He then took smaller forts, including Narwar after a year-long siege. An illness prevented his planned attack on Gwalior in 1516, and he died the next year.

Sikandar patronised learning, and under his influence poetry and music revived in Delhi, where the Hindu poet Dungar taught at a Muslim college. He wrote Persian poetry under the pen name Gul Rukhi, 'rose-faced', and prepared a diwan of 9000 verses.

Because his mother was Hindu, he adopted a strict Sunni orthodoxy as a political expedient to prove his Islamic credentials. He destroyed Hindu temples, and under pressure from the ulama allowed the execution of a Brahmin who declared Hinduism as true as Islam. He also established sharia courts in several towns, open to the non-Muslim population as well, even for property disputes.
sikandar-shah-bengal: Sikandar Shah, styled Abul Mujāhid, was the second sultan of the Ilyas Shahi dynasty and came to the throne on the death of his father, Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah. He continued his father's imperial ambitions, consolidating and expanding the Bengal Sultanate. When Firuz Shah Tughluq, the Sultan of Delhi, invaded Bengal in 1359, the Tughlaqs declared Zafar Khan Fars, a Persian noble and son-in-law of Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah, the legitimate ruler. The Delhi army numbered 80,000 cavalry, a large infantry and 470 elephants.

As his father had done, Sikandar Shah took refuge in the fortress of Ekdala, which the Bengal army held against the besiegers until the monsoon began. He also completed his father's Assam campaign: a coin bearing the mint name Chawlistan urf Kamrup points to his occupation of Guwahati, the capital of Kamrup. Local chiefs later joined the Kamata and Kachari ruler Mahamanikya against the army of occupation, and in 1362 Sikandar Shah advanced along the Brahmaputra to the Kopili River, where the allies fought him at Gachtal.

His reign of three decades was marked by stability and prosperity. Besides the Adina Mosque, which long remained the largest mosque in the Indian subcontinent, he built the tomb and mosque of Akhi Siraj, the Kotwali Gateway at the southern entrance of Lakhnauti, a vault at Ganagarampur in Dinajpur and a mosque at Mulla Simla in Hughli. He was known as sober and gentle, liked the company of learned people, respected the clergy and Sufis, and continued the tolerant practices of his father.

In 1390 one of Sikandar Shah's eighteen sons rebelled and occupied Sonargaon and Satgaon, and a war of succession followed. At the Battle of Goalpara, near the capital Pandua, Sikandar Shah was killed by the forces his son led, although the son had ordered that his father should not be harmed in any way. The son then took the throne of Bengal as Sultan Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah.
sikasso: Sikasso was a small village until Tieba Traoré, whose mother came from there, became faama, or ruler, of the Kénédougou Kingdom and moved the capital to it. He established his palace on the sacred Mamelon hill and built a massive tata, a defensive wall, against attacks by the Malinke conqueror Samori Ture and by the French colonial army. This made Sikasso the largest fortified city ever built in West Africa.

The city withstood a siege by Samori Ture that lasted fifteen months, from 1887 to 1888, before the French, who were allies of Kénédougou against him, relieved it. The French nevertheless contrived a diplomatic crisis to attack in 1898. They began a major artillery barrage against the tata on 15 April 1898, and the city fell on 1 May amid furious house-to-house fighting. It then had around 30,000 inhabitants.

Babemba Traoré, Tieba's brother and successor as faama, ordered his bodyguards to kill him rather than let him fall into French hands. He is remembered for upholding a Bambara saying, usually rendered as death is preferable to shame. About 4,000 captives were taken in the sack and shared out as slaves among the French and their African auxiliaries. They were marched west to the Niger, and many, too weak or starved to continue, died or were killed on the way.

Sikasso lies 375 kilometres south-east of Bamako, 100 kilometres north of Côte d'Ivoire and 45 kilometres west of Burkina Faso, and acts as a crossroads between the coastal countries and landlocked Mali and Burkina Faso. It is the capital of the Sikasso Cercle and the Sikasso Region and the second largest city of Mali, with 225,753 residents in the 2009 census. Its ethnic groups include the Senufo, the Bobo and the Minianka.

The surrounding country has abundant agriculture, and the city produces enough fruit and vegetables to feed itself. Its attractions include the large market, the Mamelon hill, the remains of Tieba Traoré's tata and the nearby Missirikoro Grotto. A festival of the balafon, a traditional Malian instrument, is held each June.
sikh-empire: By the mid-18th century a confederation of twelve Sikh states, the misls, was established in central and eastern Punjab, and their Dal Khalsa armies fought the Mughals and the invading Afghans under Ahmad Shah Abdali. Ranjit Singh was born in 1780 into the ruling family of the Sukerchakia misl and succeeded his father at the age of thirteen. After Zaman Shah Durrani invaded the Punjab and withdrew in 1797–98, Ranjit Singh captured Lahore, and in 1799 he moved his capital there from Gujranwala. He was formally crowned on 12 April 1801 by Sahib Singh Bedi, a descendant of Guru Nanak.

Ranjit Singh annexed the other misls, beginning with Amritsar in 1802, and by 1813 all were under his rule. Afghan influence east of the Indus ended with the fall of Multan in 1818, and Kashmir and Peshawar were later lost by the Durrani Afghans to the Sikhs. By 1840 Ladakh and Baltistan had come under Sikh suzerainty through Gulab Singh. At its height the empire reached from Gilgit in the north to the Sindh deserts in the south and from the Khyber Pass to the Sutlej. Ranjit Singh modernised his army with new training, weapons and artillery. The British policy of confining him to the north of the Sutlej led to the river becoming the boundary between the two states.

After Ranjit Singh's death in 1839 the empire was weakened by internal divisions, which the British East India Company is said to have stoked, and by political mismanagement. It was dissolved in 1849 after its defeat in the Second Anglo-Sikh War, and it was the last major region of the subcontinent to be conquered by the British.

The court at Lahore was known as the Lahore Darbar or Khalsa Darbar, and the state itself in its own chronicles as the Sarkar Khalsaji. In theory it rested on the ideals of the Khalsa, but in practice it was secular, with Sikhs, Hindus, Muslims and Christians serving at court. The Fakir brothers, Muslims who served as advisers, included Fakir Azizuddin, foreign minister and translator, who advised Ranjit Singh against war with the British in 1808. Land revenue provided about 70 percent of income, and the court observed Vaisakhi, Dussehra, Basant, Holi and Diwali. Estimates of the population vary widely, and most of its people were Muslims.
sikh-gurus: The Sikh gurus established the religion over about two and a half centuries, beginning in 1469, the year of the birth of Guru Nanak. Nine other human gurus succeeded him. The word guru is Sanskrit for a teacher, guide or master, and Bhai Vir Singh explained it as joining gu, meaning darkness, and ru, meaning light, so that the guru is the one who enlightens. The word Sikh derives from the Sanskrit shishya, a disciple or student, and Sikhs have a student and teacher relationship with their gurus.

According to Sikh belief all the gurus held the same light or soul, and each body was a vessel for it. When one guru died the successor inherited this light, which is why the gurus are also called mahalla, or house. They were formally called patiśāh, being seen as masters of both spiritual and temporal affairs.

Guru Nanak was succeeded by Guru Angad. By 1600 many claimants contested the guruship, which led to internal strife and divisions. Under Guru Gobind Singh reforms were introduced, among them the formal introduction of the Khalsa Panth and a steady ending of a personal, human guruship.

The last guru declared that after him the guruship would pass both to the Khalsa Panth and to the Granth Sahib. The Khalsa was to act in accordance with the scripture, and the authority once conferred on a personal leader passed to the community as a whole. In 1708 the tenth guru passed the guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs now regard as the living guru. The guruship of the Guru Panth, the Khalsa, declined after the rise of Ranjit Singh.

Each guru had a base of operations. Guru Nanak founded Kartarpur (Narowal) in the 1520s and stayed there until his death in 1539. Guru Angad lived at Khadur from 1539 to 1551, and Guru Amar Das founded Goindwal and lived there from 1551 to 1574. Guru Ram Das established Ramdaspur, now Amritsar, and stayed from 1574 to 1581.

Guru Arjan also lived at Amritsar and founded Kartarpur (Jalandhar), Hargobindpur and Tarn Taran. Guru Hargobind founded Kiratpur in 1634, and Guru Tegh Bahadur founded Anandpur in 1664, while also travelling as far as Dhaka and Patna. Guru Gobind Singh lived at Anandpur from 1675 to 1704, founded Paonta in 1685 and Damdama in 1705, and went south to Nanded, where he died in 1708.
sikhism: Sikhism, also called Sikhi, developed from the teachings of Guru Nanak (1469–1539), the first guru, and the nine gurus who followed him. Nanak was born in the village now called Nankana Sahib, in present-day Pakistan, to Punjabi Khatri Hindu parents. The hagiography Puratan Janamsakhi, composed more than two centuries after his death, says that after a disappearance of three days he declared, "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim". In 1526 he started a small commune at Kartarpur, and his disciples came to be known as Sikhs, a word meaning students or disciples.

In 1539 Nanak chose his disciple Lahiṇā, who became Guru Angad, as successor rather than either of his sons. The Mughal emperors tortured and executed two gurus, Guru Arjan (1563–1606) and Guru Tegh Bahadur (1621–1675), who refused to convert to Islam. In 1699 Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, an order meant to protect freedom of conscience, whose members express the qualities of the sant-sipāhī, the saint-soldier.

Sikhs hold that only one God exists, present in everything, a oneness expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar. The word for God is Waheguru. Central practices are remembrance of the divine name (simran), selfless service (sevā), honest work and sharing with those in need. Nanak is quoted as saying, "Truth is the highest virtue, but higher still is truthful living." Sikhism rejects the claim that any religious tradition has a monopoly on truth, and Sikhs do not actively proselytise, though voluntary converts are generally accepted.

The Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave to Sikhs fully initiated in the ceremony of ammrit sañcār, in which sweetened water is stirred with a double-edged sword. Baptised Sikhs wear the five Ks, which include the kesh, uncut hair, so that most religious Sikh men wear a turban. Gurdwaras are open to all.

The central scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh decreed in 1708 that it would be the final and perpetual guru, closing the line of human gurus, and Sikhs regard it as the eleventh and eternally living guru. Its earlier form, the Ādi Granth, was compiled primarily by Bhai Gurdas under Guru Arjan in 1603 and 1604. It contains the hymns of the gurus and of thirteen Hindu and two Muslim bhagats of the Bhakti tradition, among them Kabir and the Sufi saint Farid. It is written as poetry for recitation in thirty-one ragas. The Dasam Granth, containing texts attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, does not have the same authority.
sikhs: The word Sikh comes from the Sanskrit word for seeker, disciple or student. Guru Nanak, who lived from 1469 to 1539, was born into a Hindu Khatri family in the village of Talwandi, near Lahore, now Nankana Sahib. According to the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a Sikh is a person who faithfully believes in one immortal being, the Gurus from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, the Guru Granth Sahib and the teachings of the Gurus, and in the initiation called Amrit Sanchar, and who owes allegiance to no other religion. Early followers were mostly Khatris, and many Jats joined later.

Sikh political history may be said to begin in 1606, with the death of the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan. On 30 March 1699 Guru Gobind Singh initiated five people from varied social backgrounds, known as the Panj Piare, to form the Khalsa, the collective body of initiated Sikhs. In the 18th and 19th centuries the Punjab was ruled by Sikhs for significant periods, and Mughal and Afghan persecution in the 17th and 18th centuries left little room for art, which changed under Ranjit Singh and the Sikh rule at Lahore.

After the British annexed the Sikh kingdom, large numbers of Sikhs were recruited into the British Army, and the Sikhs stayed loyal during the 1857 mutiny. The Singh Sabha movements of 1873 and 1879 worked to define Sikh identity, and the Akali movement of the 1920s led to the Sikh Gurdwara Bill of 1925, which placed historic shrines under the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee. In 1947 the partition of the Punjab was marked by conflict, and Sikhs and Hindus moved east as Muslims moved west. Sikh migration abroad began in earnest in the second half of the 19th century.

Initiated Sikhs, known as Khalsa, wear five articles of faith: uncut hair, usually covered by a turban, a steel bracelet, a short sword, a cotton undergarment and a small wooden comb. Male Sikhs generally take the last name Singh, meaning lion, and female Sikhs Kaur, meaning princess, names given by the Gurus partly as a rejection of caste. Sikh devotional music, Gurmat Sangeet, sets the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib to ragas. About 25 to 30 million Sikhs live in the world, most of them in India.
siku-quanshu: The Qianlong Emperor of the Qing dynasty ordered the compilation. Local and provincial officers were put in charge of locating important books, and owners of rare books were encouraged to send them to the capital. At first few did, for fear of the Literary Inquisition, but the emperor then decreed that books would be returned to their owners after the compilation and that owners would not be punished if their books contained anti-Qing sentiment. Less than three months later four to five thousand books were handed in.

By March 1773 an editorial board of hundreds of editors, collators and copyists had been formed in Beijing, with more than 361 scholars and Ji Yun and Lu Xixiong as chief editors. About 3,826 scribes copied every word by hand, and each received a government position after transcribing a set number of sections instead of payment in cash. The work was completed in 1782.

The work is structured in four categories that follow the divisions of the imperial library: Classics, Histories, Letters, containing literature such as poetry and personal letters, and Masters, whose texts concern philosophy, arts and sciences. Each copy was bound into 36,381 volumes of about 2.3 million pages, divided into 44 subcategories. It includes most major Chinese texts, from pre-Classical Zhou works such as the I Ching to writings of the Qing, among them the Analects of Confucius, the Records of the Grand Historian and The Art of War. The Qianlong Emperor reviewed many of the works, and his opinions coloured the compilers' criteria, especially for works expressing anti-Qing sentiment.

The emperor commissioned seven copies, four kept in the north and three in the south, at Hangzhou, Zhenjiang and Yangzhou. The Old Summer Palace copy was destroyed in the Second Opium War in 1860, the Zhenjiang and Yangzhou copies were destroyed completely, and the Hangzhou copy was about 70 to 80 percent destroyed during the Taiping Rebellion. Four copies survive, in Beijing, Taipei, Lanzhou and Hangzhou.

It is said that the emperor did not keep his promise to return the books. A catalogue of over 2,855 rejected and banned books, the Siku Jinshu, was drawn up, and four to five hundred more were edited or censored, most of them late Ming works with anti-Qing sentiment. It has also been pointed out that most works banned under Qing censorship survive, while most of the works lost were not among those prohibited.
silent-night: The carol was composed in 1818 by Franz Xaver Gruber, schoolmaster and organist in the nearby village of Arnsdorf, to words by Father Joseph Mohr. On Christmas Eve 1818 Mohr brought the poem to Gruber and asked him to write a melody and guitar accompaniment for that night's mass, after river flooding had possibly damaged the church organ. The church was later destroyed by repeated flooding and replaced by the Silent-Night-Chapel. "Stille Nacht" was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 at the Nikolauskirche, the parish church of Oberndorf. Several films repeat the story of a broken organ, which appeared in a fictional account published in the U.S. in the 1930s.

A manuscript in Mohr's handwriting, found in 1995 and dated by researchers to about 1820, shows that he wrote the words in 1816 at the pilgrim church of Mariapfarr and that Gruber composed the music in 1818. It is the earliest manuscript known. Before its discovery the carol was often attributed to better-known composers such as Haydn, Mozart and Schubert.

Mohr's poem had six verses. The melody Gruber wrote was a moderato tune in 6/8 time with a siciliana rhythm. The melody changed slightly in the early decades of its spread, and the slow, meditative lullaby or pastorale sung today differs from Gruber's original, especially in its final strain. In 1859 the Episcopal priest John Freeman Young, then at Trinity Church in New York City, published the English translation sung most often today, made from three of the original six verses. The carol has been translated into about 300 languages. Its words and melody are in the public domain.

Karl Mauracher, an organ builder who serviced the Oberndorf organ, took the song home to the Zillertal, where two families of travelling folk singers, the Strassers and the Rainers, added it to their shows. The Rainers were singing it by about Christmas 1819 and performed it before Franz I of Austria and Alexander I of Russia. They gave its first performance in the U.S., in New York City in 1839. By the 1840s it was known in Lower Saxony and was reported to be a favourite of Frederick William IV of Prussia. The first edition appeared in 1833 in a collection of Four Genuine Tyrolean Songs.

The carol was first recorded in 1905, and more than 137,000 recordings are known. Composers who have arranged it include Carl Reinecke, John Rutter and David Willcocks, and UNESCO declared it an intangible cultural heritage in 2011.
silingi: The Silingi, in Latin Silingae, were a Germanic tribe within the larger Vandal group. Ptolemy first mentions them in the 2nd century, placing them south of the Suevic Semnones and, like the Semnones, on both sides of the Elbe. East of them, across a river probably the Oder, lived the Omani, a Lugian people, with the Calucones to the south. Some modern scholars guess that the Naharvali, whom Tacitus names as keepers of the Lugian sanctuary, were the same people, but the guess rests only on the area in which Tacitus places them. According to some historians, in the reign of Marcus Aurelius the Silingi were among the Vandals said to live in the Vandal mountains, possibly the Sudetes.

The Huns pushed the Vandals westward about 400. They crossed the Rhine into Gaul in 406 and the Pyrenees into Iberia in 409. The other main Vandal group, the Hasdingi, settled in Gallaecia, and the Silingi in Baetica. After attacks by the Visigoths, the remnants of the Silingi and the Alans submitted in 419 to the Hasdingian leader Gunderic, who had fled from Gallaecia to Baetica after a defeat by a Roman-Suebi coalition. After Genseric succeeded Gunderic in 428, the Vandals moved to North Africa and founded a kingdom centred on Carthage, which fell in the Vandalic War of 533–4 when Justinian I reconquered Africa for the Eastern Roman Empire.

Any Silingi who stayed in Silesia after the migrations of the 5th century were probably replaced slowly in the sixth by people of the Prague-Korchak cultures, supposed to be new Slavic tribes from the east.

Some historians connect the names Silesia and Silingi. Another view derives the name of the region from the old Polish word Ślągwa, meaning damp. The name of Silesia is often assumed to come from the river Ślęza or Mount Ślęża, a hill south-south-east of Wrocław that was a religious centre of the Silingi, though its sacred role goes back to the sun-worshipping people of the Lusatian culture as early as 1300 BCE. A student corps, Corps Silingia Breslau, founded in 1877, still bears the name.
silistra: Silistra lies on the southern bank of the lower Danube in the Bulgarian part of the historical region of Dobruja, at the point where the border with Romania stops following the river. It is the administrative centre of Silistra Province. The name is possibly derived from the root of Istrum, the old Thracian name of the lower Danube. Landmarks include a richly decorated Late Roman tomb, remains of the medieval fortress and an Ottoman fort.

After the Roman province of Moesia was founded in 12 CE, the Romans built a fort in 29 on the site of an earlier Thracian settlement and kept its name, Durostorum. After Trajan's Dacian Wars it was enlarged into a legionary fortress for the Legio XI Claudia, which stayed there from before 114 until about 400, and it grew into a city at the time of Marcus Aurelius.

Durostorum became a bishopric and a centre of Christianity in the region. The earliest saints of Bulgaria are Roman soldiers executed there in the Diocletian Persecution, among them Saint Dasius, and the Roman general Flavius Aëtius was born in the town in 396.

Around the end of the 7th century the town was incorporated into the First Bulgarian Empire, as Drastar, and its bishop was proclaimed the first patriarch of Bulgaria. In 895 Simeon I the Great held the fortress against besieging Hungarians. Sviatoslav I of Kiev captured it in 969, and the Byzantines took it two years later in the Battle of Dorostolon.

Tsar Samuel restored Bulgarian rule in 976, and the Byzantines regained the town in 1001. It joined the Second Bulgarian Empire after the rebellion of Asen and Peter in 1186 and withstood a three-month Mongol siege in 1279. It remained Bulgarian until the Ottoman conquest of the Balkans around 1400.

Under Ottoman rule Silistre was the centre of a sanjak and later of a large province. It was besieged between 14 April and 23 June 1854 during the Crimean War, an event that inspired Namık Kemal's play Vatan Yahut Silistre. Silistra joined Bulgaria in 1878. It passed to Romania in 1913, was held by Bulgaria from 1916, returned to Romania by the Treaty of Neuilly in 1919 and became Bulgarian again in 1940, a transfer confirmed in 1947.

Silistra is a cultural, industrial, transport and educational centre of north-eastern Bulgaria. The grave of the rabbi Eliezer Papo, who served the Jewish community from 1819 to 1826, is a place of pilgrimage. The Roman general Flavius Aëtius, who defeated Attila the Hun, is the town's best-known native.
silius-italicus: Silius was the son of a Greek father and a Roman mother. The main source for his life is a letter of Pliny the Younger written on the occasion of his death, with some inscriptions and epigrams by Martial. His birthplace is not securely identified: Italica in Hispania was once favoured because of his cognomen, but Latin usage would then have required the form Italicensis, and J. D. Campbell has suggested Patavium, modern Padua.

In early life Silius was a leading orator in the courts, and later a cautious politician, generally believed to have become an informer under Nero. He was consul in 68, the year of Nero's death, and a close ally of the emperor Vitellius, whom Pliny says he served wisely and amicably. He was proconsul of Asia in 77 and 78, as an inscription from Aphrodisias shows. He then left public life for his villas in Campania, where he collected books and sculpture, held learned conversations and gave recitations.

Silius bought Cicero's estate at Tusculum and the tomb of Virgil at Naples, which he restored, and marked Virgil's birthday more lavishly than his own. The Punica, composed between 83 and 101, takes Virgil as its main model and presents the war with Hannibal as a continuation of Juno's grudge against Rome. Scipio Africanus is its hero, and Stoic ideas of virtue and trial run through it.

Stricken by an incurable tumour after the age of 75, Silius starved himself to death around 101, keeping a cheerful countenance to the end. Pliny remarked that he was the last person to die who had been consul under Nero, and judged that he wrote poetry with more eagerness than genius. The poem seems to have been mostly unknown in the Middle Ages; its manuscript was discovered by Poggio Bracciolini in 1417 at the Abbey of Saint Gall during the Council of Constance.
silk: Silk is a natural protein fibre, composed mainly of fibroin with a smaller coating of sericin, most commonly made from the cocoons of insect larvae. The best-known silk comes from the mulberry silkworm, Bombyx mori, reared in captivity in a process called sericulture. The production of silk originated in central China in the Neolithic period. The earliest evidence is the silk protein fibroin found in soil from two tombs at Jiahu in Henan, about 8,500 years old, and the earliest surviving silk fabric, from about 3630 BCE, wrapped the body of a child at a Yangshao culture site in Henan.

Silk production remained confined to China until the Silk Road opened, at some point in the latter part of the 1st millennium BCE, and China kept a virtual monopoly on it for another thousand years. Wild silks were spun in China, South Asia and Europe from ancient times, but always on a far smaller scale.

The Roman Empire knew of silk and traded in it, and Chinese silk was the most highly priced luxury good it imported. Under the emperor Tiberius, sumptuary laws forbade men to wear silk, but they proved ineffectual. The secret of silk-making reached Europe only around 550, by way of the Byzantine Empire; contemporary accounts say monks working for the emperor Justinian I smuggled silkworm eggs from China to Constantinople inside hollow canes. The best looms and weavers worked inside the Great Palace there, and the cloth was used for imperial robes and as diplomatic gifts.

Italy was the leading producer in the medieval period, beginning at Catanzaro in the 11th century. Bengal was the leading exporter of silk between the 16th and 19th centuries, and silkworms were brought to Oaxaca from Spain in the 1530s.

Silk is not spun like other natural fibres. The cocoons are soaked in boiling water to remove the sericin and free the end of the filament, which is then reeled off in one continuous length. A caterpillar spins about one mile (1.6 km) of filament in two or three days, and since one thread is too fine for commercial use, three to ten strands are twisted together. The flat surfaces of the fibrils reflect light at many angles, which gives silk its natural sheen. It was used for clothing and furnishings, and also in parachutes and bicycle tyres.
silla-tang-war: After the Goguryeo–Tang War ended in 668, the lands of Baekje and Goguryeo were occupied by the Silla–Tang alliance, and many of their people were forcibly resettled by the Tang. Emperor Gaozong of Tang created the Protectorate General to Pacify the East, based in Pyongyang, and divided Goguryeo's territory into 9 commanderies, 42 prefectures and 100 counties. Silla resented this: Emperor Taizong of Tang had promised it Baekje and the lands south of Pyongyang in return for its help, but Gaozong reneged on the promise.

King Munmu of Silla assembled an army that included the remnants of the Baekje and Goguryeo forces, aiming to drive the Tang from the peninsula. Revolts in the former Goguryeo lands, the first in 669, aided his cause.

In 671 Silla drove the Tang out of most of the former Baekje territory. In February 675 the Tang defeated Silla at Chiljung Fortress in Gyeonggi; Munmu sent a tributary mission with apologies, and Gaozong, who accepted them, withdrew troops to meet the Tibetan threat in the west. Silla then renewed its advance. Xue Rengui, who crossed the Yellow Sea to supply the army of Li Jinxing, was defeated at Cheonseong with the loss of 1,400 men, 1,000 horses and 40 warships.

According to the Samguk Sagi, Li Jinxing led 200,000 soldiers at Maeso Fortress in September 675 and was defeated, and 30,080 war horses were captured. Chinese and Korean sources each tend to omit or play down the battles their side lost, and the Zizhi Tongjian does not mention Maeso. In November 676 a Silla victory at Gibeolpo, a naval battle of which little more is known, ended the war.

The Tang moved the seat of the protectorate to Liaoyang, which ended their designs on Silla. The frontier between Tang and Unified Silla ran from the mouth of the Taedong River to the East Korea Bay; the lands to the north stayed under Tang rule and later mostly passed to Balhae. Relations were restored in the early 8th century under King Seongdeok of Silla and Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, and in 736 the Tang formally recognised Silla's rule south of the Taedong River.
sillustani: The cemetery stands on the shore of Lake Umayo near Puno. Its tombs are the remains of the Qulla people, most likely Puquina speakers, whom the Inca Empire conquered in the 15th century. Chullpas of this kind are found throughout the south Central Andes and across the Altiplano, and above-ground burial in the region goes back at least to the mature Tiwanaku period, about 500 to 950, but Sillustani is considered the best preserved example.

Veneration of the dead and kinship were central to Aymara culture, and the towers were built for the Aymara elite of the immediate pre-Inca and Inca periods. Each held a whole group, most likely an extended family, and they were probably limited to the nobility. The bodies were not deliberately mummified but survived for centuries in the dry air of the closed tombs, most of the bundles in a fetal position. The only openings face east, where the Sun was believed to be reborn by Mother Earth each day, and some stones are carved with animal shapes. Many chullpas show pre-Inca work later faced with Inca stone blocks.

The word chullpa, used in the 19th century, comes from the dictionary of Ludovico Bertonio of 1612, though Bertonio applied it to the basket burials of semi-nomadic herders and called the stone towers uta amaya, houses of the soul.

Grave robbers have dynamited many of the tombs, and others were never finished. A large ramp beside one chullpa shows how stones were raised onto the walls, much as Father Cobo saw Inca builders do at the Cusco Cathedral. In 2005 a restoration directed by the archaeologist Eduardo Arizaca Medina used wooden ramps and pry bars to set the stones.
siloam-tunnel: Jerusalem stands on a mountain and is naturally defensible, but its main source of fresh water, the Gihon Spring, lies on the side of the cliff above the Kidron Valley, so a defensible wall would leave the spring outside. The Canaanites removed this weakness by building a strongly fortified tower around the spring and linking it to the city walls by a wall carrying a protected corridor. A Canaanite tunnel had collected the spring water since about 1800 BCE and led it south through the bedrock to fields in the Kidron Valley.

The best-known explanation of the Siloam tunnel is that Hezekiah of Judah, fearing a siege by the Assyrians under Sennacherib, diverted the spring's water into the city. The Bible says he blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channelled the water down to the west side of the city (2 Chronicles 32:30).

The curving tunnel runs from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam and is 533 metres long. The engineers moved the water by using a height difference of about 30 centimetres between the two ends, a gradient of 0.06 per cent. According to the Siloam inscription, the tunnel was carved out of the living rock by two teams, one starting at each end and meeting in the middle. The inscription is partly unreadable, and several directional errors are visible in the tunnel itself.

Aharon Horovitz interprets the tunnel as a means of keeping the whole outflow of the spring inside the walls, to keep water from a besieging army. Both the spring and the pool would have been used by the inhabitants as water sources, whereas the earlier channel had released unused water into the Kidron Valley, where besiegers could have taken it.

Franciscus Quaresmius first described the tunnel in modern times, in 1625. Edward Robinson explored it in 1838 and Charles Warren in 1865. Neither Quaresmius nor Robinson linked it to Hezekiah, but in 1871 Warren suggested the Pool of Siloam may have been dug by him, and later wrote that the inscription agreed well with the biblical account.

Radiocarbon dating of organic matter in the plaster and uranium-thorium dating of speleothems supported a date in Hezekiah's reign. Excavations by Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron cast doubt on it in 2011, and they suggested a date several decades earlier, in the last part of the 9th century or early 8th century BCE. De Groot and Fadida support this on the basis of pottery. They note that the biblical passage on Hezekiah's waterworks names no place in the city and may refer to waterworks in the Mamilla area.
silver: Silver was known in prehistoric times. Copper, silver and gold occur in elemental form in nature and were probably the first primitive forms of money, replacing simple barter. Unlike copper, silver did not lead to the growth of metallurgy, because of its low structural strength; it was used mostly for ornament or as money. Native silver was much scarcer than native gold, and in Egypt silver was more expensive than gold until about the fifteenth century BCE.

The discovery of cupellation, which extracts silver from its ores, changed this. Slag heaps in Asia Minor and on the Aegean islands show silver being separated from lead as early as the 4th millennium BCE, and Sardinia was one of the earliest extraction centres in Europe, in the early Chalcolithic. The techniques spread widely only later.

Silver is a soft, ductile and malleable metal, slightly less malleable than gold, with a brilliant white lustre that takes a high polish; the name of the metal has become the name of a colour. It is one of the seven metals of antiquity and sits in group 11 of the periodic table with copper and gold. Because pure silver is so soft, silver used for jewellery, coinage and household objects is usually alloyed with copper.

The English word comes from Old English seolfor and siolfor, with cognates in Old High German silabar, Gothic silubr and Old Norse silfr. The chemical symbol Ag comes from the Latin argentum, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'white' or 'shining'.

The earliest known coins were minted in the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor around 600 BCE, of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver. Silver standards, in which the unit of account is a fixed weight of silver, were then widespread until the 20th century. Notable silver coins include the Greek drachma, the Roman denarius, the Islamic dirham, the karshapana of ancient India, the rupee of the Mughal Empire and the Spanish dollar.

Apart from coinage, the major use throughout most of history was in jewellery and general-use items such as table silver. In Hesiod's Works and Days the successive ages of humanity are named after metals, among them silver, and Ovid, in the Metamorphoses, describes a silver age that excels bronze but is excelled by gold.
silvio-pellico: Silvio Pellico was born at Saluzzo in Piedmont on 24 June 1789 and spent his early life at Pinerolo and Turin, taught by a priest named Manavella. At ten he wrote a tragedy inspired by a translation of the Ossianic poems. After his twin sister Rosina married in Lyon he lived there for four years, studying French literature. He returned to Italy in 1809 and settled in Milan, where he joined the circle around Ugo Foscolo and Vincenzo Monti, and in 1810 became professor of French at the Collegio degli Orfani Militari.

His tragedy Francesca da Rimini, staged in Milan in 1815 and published three years later, was among the first and most successful inspired by Dante's episode in the fifth canto of the Inferno. Stendhal reviewed it enthusiastically and Lord Byron translated it into English. As a tutor he served the sons of Count Briche and of Count Porro Lambertenghi, and tried to weaken Austrian rule by indirect educational means. He was secretary and chief editor of the literary journal Il Conciliatore, which the Austrian censors allowed to run for only a year.

In October 1820 he was arrested on a charge of Carbonarism and held in the Santa Margherita prison, then moved to the Piombi at Venice in February 1821. A sentence of death passed in February 1822 was commuted to fifteen years in harsh conditions, and in April he was placed in the Spielberg at Brünn, today's Brno. There he composed the tragedy Leoniero da Dertona, which he had to keep in memory. He was released in 1830.

His account of his imprisonment, My Prisons, appeared in 1832 and gave him European fame. It was translated into virtually every European language in his lifetime and contributed to the movement for Italian unification against Austrian occupation. It won him the friendship of the Marchesa Juliette Colbert de Barolo, a reformer of the Turin prisons, who gave him a yearly pension in 1834. After his parents' deaths in 1838 he lived in her house, assisted her charities and wrote chiefly on religious themes, best known of them the essay Dei doveri degli uomini. He died in Turin on 31 January 1854 and was buried in the Camposanto.
silvius-i-nimrod-duke-of-wurttemberg-oel: Silvius Nimrod was born on 2 May 1622 at Weiltingen, a son of Duke Julius Frederick of Württemberg-Weiltingen and Anna Sabina of Schleswig-Holstein-Sonderburg. As a young man he served in the Thirty Years' War: in 1638 he was with the army of Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar during the siege of Breisach. On 1 May 1647 he married Elisabeth Marie, Duchess of Oels (1625–1686), at Oels. Her father, Duke Charles Frederick I, died a few weeks after the wedding.

Charles Frederick had been the last reigning duke of Oels, so the duchy fell to the Crown of Bohemia as a vacant fief, and Emperor Ferdinand III inherited it in his capacity as King of Bohemia. Only after lengthy negotiations was Silvius Nimrod invested with the duchy, in Vienna on 15 December 1648, in exchange for 20000 guilders and the Moravian lordship of Jevišovice. He then set about rebuilding a duchy that had suffered in the war, giving particular attention to education and the Church.

In 1652 he founded the Order of the Skull, which lasted until the 19th century. The poet Angelus Silesius served as his court physician from 1647 to 1652, and Matthäus Apelt had been his ducal councillor and director of court music until 1639.

Silvius Nimrod died of a stroke in April 1664 while visiting Brzezinka in Silesia. Under his will, Duke Christian of Liegnitz-Brieg became guardian of his children, who were still minors. To prevent an imperial guardianship, which would probably have meant a Catholic upbringing, Christian sent the young princes to study at the Collegium illustre in Tübingen. The couple had five sons and two daughters, several of whom died young; Silvius II Frederick (1651–1697) and Christian Ulrich I (1652–1704) were among the sons who outlived their father.
sima-qian: Sima Qian was born at Xiayang in Zuopingyi, near present-day Hancheng in Shaanxi. His father, Sima Tan, was appointed grand historian at the imperial court, a relatively low-ranking post whose main duty was to draw up the yearly calendar, identifying ritually auspicious and inauspicious days, and which also involved recording events at court and across the country.

In 126 BCE, at about the age of twenty, he made an extensive tour of Han China. Starting from Chang'an, he went south across the Yangtze to the Changsha Kingdom, where he visited the Miluo River, traditionally the place where the poet Qu Yuan drowned himself. He visited the grave of the general Han Xin at Huaiyin and Qufu, the hometown of Confucius, where he studied ritual.

After his travels Sima became a Palace Attendant to Emperor Wu of Han. His father had conceived a complete history of China but left only preparatory sketches, and summoned his son to continue it. Sima Qian succeeded him as grand historian and in 105 BCE was among the scholars chosen to reform the calendar. The resulting Taichu calendar, promulgated in 104 BCE, is the first Chinese calendar whose full method of calculation has been preserved.

In 99 BCE he became embroiled in the Li Ling affair. The general Li Ling had been defeated and captured in a campaign against the Xiongnu, and every official condemned him. Sima alone defended him, though Li had never been his friend. Emperor Wu took this as an attack on his brother-in-law Li Guangli and sentenced Sima to death. Execution could be commuted by money or by castration; lacking the money, Sima chose castration and spent three years in prison. On his release he lived on as a palace eunuch to finish his history, rather than die as a disgraced gentleman-scholar was expected to.

The Shiji, or Records of the Grand Historian, runs to over 500,000 characters in 130 chapters and covers more than two thousand years, from the Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu.
