It combined basic annals of sovereigns, tables, treatises on music, ritual and economics, house chronicles and ordered biographies. Earlier histories had recounted particular events or regions. Sima treated the known world and was the first Chinese historian to treat the Xiongnu as human beings implicitly the equals of the Han. His Letter to Ren An is admired as prose. His grandson Yang Yun released the work during the reign of Emperor Xuan.
sima-yi: Sima Yi, courtesy name Zhongda, came from Xiaojing in Wen County, Henei Commandery, and traced his ancestry to Sima Ang, King of Yin, who briefly ruled one of the Eighteen Kingdoms in the transition from the Qin to the Western Han. He showed intelligence and ambition young and knew the Confucian classics well. Before he was about 19, the commandery administrator Yang Jun, known for spotting talent, called him an extraordinary talent, and Cui Yan, a friend of his elder brother Sima Lang, said Sima Lang could not compare with him. He formally began his political career in 208 under the Imperial Chancellor Cao Cao.

In 215 Sima Yi accompanied Cao Cao against Zhang Lu at Yangping and urged him to attack Liu Bei in Yi Province, but Cao Cao declined. He also warned that Hu Xiu and Fu Fang were unfit to guard the border at Jing Province, and in 219, at the Battle of Fancheng, both defected to Guan Yu. When Cao Cao died in March 220 he supervised the funeral arrangements.

Under Cao Rui he defeated Zhuge Jin's attack on Xiangyang, and in July 227 he was sent to garrison Wan and given the military affairs of Jing and Yu provinces. In March 230 he was promoted to General-in-Chief. He is best known for defending Wei against a series of invasions by Shu between 231 and 234, and in 238 he led an army against Gongsun Yuan in Liaodong. Sun Quan wrote that Sima Yi used strategy like a god.

In 239 he became a regent for the young Cao Fang alongside Cao Shuang. Their relations soured over Cao Shuang's corruption, extravagance and attempts to curtail Sima Yi's influence, and in February 249, after careful preparation, Sima Yi ousted Cao Shuang in a coup and had him and his associates executed.

Afterwards Sima Yi was the main authority in Wei. In June 251 he faced Wang Ling's rebellion, which he dealt with swiftly. He died on 7 September 251 at the age of 71 or 72 and was succeeded by his eldest son Sima Shi. For the rest of Wei's history power passed increasingly to the Sima clan, and his grandson Sima Yan founded the Jin dynasty in February 266, honouring him as Emperor Xuan of Jin with the temple name Gaozu.

He was the last common ancestor of all Jin emperors: the Western Jin descended from his son Sima Zhao, the Eastern Jin from his son Sima Zhou. In 249 Wang Guang said that Sima Yi gave his assignments to the worthy and capable and had left nothing that Cao Shuang did wrong uncorrected.
simalungun-people: The Simalungun live in the Eastern Batak lands, bordering the Toba Batak to the south and west and the Karo Batak to the north. Their language is closely related to Toba Batak, while their culture is closest to that of the Karo. Long before Dutch rule, the peoples later called collectively the Eastern Batak, such as Sin Raya, Sin Silou and Sin Bandar, claimed the area as their homeland. The name Simalungun comes from Simeloengoen, the name the Dutch gave to their colonial area of the Eastern Batak kingdoms, and the people themselves still use it.

The kingdoms were ruled by raja, regarded as living gods. The head of a village was installed by the king and loyal to him, and lived in the Rumah Bolon, the largest and most ornate house; the chief village of each kingdom was called a pematang. Villagers bathed at a communal tapian fed by bamboo pipes, pounded rice at a shared block, the losung, with a hole for each family, and held Robu Tabu days, when outsiders were kept away, to drive out spirits.

Simalungun people belong to one of four clans, Saragih, Damanik, Purba and Sinaga, whose names they bear as surnames. Each clan has subclans, though people may identify by the clan name to stress common kinship. Many still speak the Simalungun language alongside Toba Batak and Indonesian.

In 1870 the Dutch established the Residency of East Sumatra, centred on Medan in the Sultanate of Deli, and one by one the Eastern Batak kingdoms gave way to Dutch expansion. The Netherlands East Indies government signed surrender agreements with the seven kingdoms of Siantar, Tanoh Jawa, Panei, Dolok Silou, Raya, Purba and Silimahuta, forming the unit Simeloengoen en Karolanden, and in 1908 the colonial seat was set at Pematang Siantar. Dutch rule encouraged the migration of plantation labourers into the region.

In 1946 a social revolution in East Sumatra, which the Simalungun regard as a tragedy, deposed the monarchies, and many members of the royal families were kidnapped and killed. The families are still acknowledged among the Simalungun, but their titles are now ceremonial. The German missionary August Theis reached the region on 2 September 1903, a day the Simalungun church commemorates. Wismar Djaulung Saragih Sumbayak, whom he baptised in 1910, wrote the first Simalungun dictionary and campaigned for schooling in Simalungun, work that led to the Simalungun Protestant Christian Church.
simcoe-county: Simcoe County stretches from the shores of Lake Simcoe in the east to Georgian Bay in the west, north of the Greater Toronto Area, and covers 4,818.93 square kilometres. The Niagara Escarpment crosses parts of its west, and the Minesing Wetlands in its centre are listed under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance. It is informally divided along County Road 90 into South Simcoe, closely tied to Toronto, and North Simcoe, more connected with the Muskoka area to the north.

The former Wendake country near Nottawasaga Bay saw the earliest French exploration and settlement in Ontario. Carhagouha and Sainte-Marie among the Hurons mark the first known contacts between the Huron and French missionaries, and the Huron capital, Ossossané, was at one time the largest aboriginal settlement in North America outside Mexico.

The county was established within the Home District in 1798 by the Legislative Assembly of Upper Canada and at first existed only for military enlistment. It became a constituency in 1823 but sent its own member, John Cawthra, only in 1828, since the vote depended on title to property and its first registrar of deeds was appointed in 1826. Separated from the Home District in 1837, it was proclaimed a distinct District of Simcoe on 11 January 1843, once its jail and courthouse stood, with James R. Gowan as first judge.

On 1 January 1850 the district gave way to a county organised for municipal purposes. It gave five western townships to Grey County in 1852 and Mono and Mulmur to the new Dufferin County in 1881, and its unorganised northern territory went to the districts of Muskoka and Parry Sound, finally in 1888. Mara and Rama townships joined it in 1974.

Since 1994 the county has been made up of 16 towns and townships, with its seat at Midhurst; Barrie and Orillia lie within it but are separate single-tier cities. Its 2021 census population was 533,169. Its institutions include Canadian Forces Base Borden, Georgian College and the Ontario Provincial Police headquarters.
simele-massacre: Most of the Assyrians affected belonged to the Church of the East and came from the Hakkari and Barwari mountains; survivors of the Assyrian genocide of 1915 were resettled after 1925 in villages of northern Iraq, often on land Kurdish landlords could reclaim. Many had served in the Assyrian Levies under British command, whom Iraqi nationalists saw as a British proxy. When Britain granted the Kingdom of Iraq independence in 1932, Patriarch Shimun XXI Eshai sought an autonomous homeland and took his case to the League of Nations. In June 1933 he was detained in Baghdad after refusing to give up his temporal authority.

On 21 July 1933 more than 600 Assyrians led by Malik Yaqo crossed into Syria seeking asylum from the French, who refused it and sent them back on 4 August. At Dirabun on the Tigris they clashed with an Iraqi brigade, which lost 33 soldiers; historians disagree on who began the fighting. Exaggerated stories of Assyrian atrocities and rumours of plots against Iraqi cities spread, and the army under Bakr Sidqi moved north. From 8 August troops shot Assyrian men found between Zakho and Duhok, while Kurdish, Arab and Yazidi tribes were encouraged to loot more than 60 villages.

Refugees gathered at the police post in Simele, where officials told them they were safe. On 11 August they were sent back to their homes; troops in armoured cars arrived, the flag over the post was pulled down, and the soldiers fired on the disarmed men, then killed them methodically in the houses where they sheltered. The British inspector R. R. Stafford called it as foul a crime as any in the annals of the Middle East. The main campaign lasted until 16 August.

Crowds in Mosul cheered the returning troops, Crown Prince Ghazi gave colours to those who had taken part, and Bakr Sidqi was promoted; he later led Iraq's first military coup. Shimun was flown into exile in Cyprus on 18 August. Over 20,000 Assyrians became refugees, many settling along the Khabur River in Syria. Britain, though protesting, rejected an international inquiry. The massacre shaped modern Assyrian identity, influenced Raphael Lemkin's coining of the word genocide, and is remembered on 7 August as Assyrian Martyrs Day.
simeon-i-of-bulgaria: Simeon was born in 864 or 865, the third son of Prince Boris I, who made Bulgaria Christian. Boris intended him for the church and sent him to Constantinople at thirteen or fourteen, where he spent about a decade and became so fluent in Greek that Byzantine chronicles called him the half-Greek. About 888 he returned to the royal monastery at Preslav and translated religious works from Greek into Medieval Bulgarian. When his elder brother Vladimir tried to reintroduce paganism, Boris had him imprisoned and blinded and appointed Simeon. An assembly at Preslav made Bulgarian the only language of state and church and moved the capital from Pliska to Preslav.

The long peace with Byzantium ended when Emperor Leo VI moved the market for Bulgarian goods from Constantinople to Thessaloniki, where merchants were heavily taxed. The Byzantines induced the Magyars to attack Bulgaria in 895, but in 896 Simeon, with Pecheneg allies, defeated them at the Battle of Southern Buh, and he then destroyed a Byzantine army at Bulgarophygon. Peace brought an annual tribute from Byzantium. After Leo's death in 912, Simeon reached Constantinople in 913 and was recognised as Emperor of the Bulgarians by Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos, though Zoe, mother of the young Constantine VII, disowned the recognition in 914.

On 20 August 917, at the river Achelous, the Bulgarians routed a Byzantine army, in one of the largest battles in medieval history. Simeon annexed Serbia in 924 after a revolt there. He met Romanos Lekapenos on the Golden Horn on 9 September 924, and about 925 raised the Bulgarian Church to a patriarchate; Pope John X recognised his imperial title. In 926 his troops were defeated by King Tomislav of Croatia at the Battle of the Bosnian Highlands. Simeon died of heart failure in Preslav on 27 May 927 and was succeeded by his son Peter I.

Simeon's reign saw the first and most productive period of medieval Bulgarian literature. The Preslav Literary School and the Ohrid Literary School, where the Cyrillic alphabet was developed, produced translations of the Bible and of works by John Chrysostom and Basil of Caesarea, and original works such as John Exarch's Six Days and Černorizec Hrabǎr's An Account of Letters. Disciples of Cyril and Methodius, among them Naum and Constantine of Preslav, took part. Preslav had more than twenty cross-domed churches and a Golden Church, and it was Simeon's imperial capital.
simeon-uros: Simeon Uroš, nicknamed Siniša, was born around 1326, the son of King Stephen Uroš III of Serbia and his second wife Maria Palaiologina, daughter of the Byzantine prince and rebel John Palaiologos. His half-brother Stephen Dušan had been crowned young king, the designated heir, in 1322. After Dušan was proclaimed Emperor of Serbs and Greeks in 1345 and crowned in 1346, he gave Byzantine titles to his magnates, and Simeon and Jovan Asen received the title of despot.

When Serbia had conquered Epirus, Acarnania and Thessaly, Simeon was made their governor. He strengthened his standing among the local nobles by marrying Thomais Orsini, daughter of John II Orsini, a former ruler of Epirus.

Soon after Dušan's death in 1355, Simeon's brother-in-law Nikephoros II Orsini, the deposed ruler of Epirus, won over the nobles of Thessaly and Epirus, and in 1356 drove Simeon to Kastoria. There Simeon proclaimed himself Emperor of Serbs and Greeks against his nephew Stephen Uroš V. Some magnates backed him, but the nobility of Serbia and Macedonia rejected him, and after a failed invasion of Zeta in 1358 he gave up his hopes in Serbia.

In 1359 Nikephoros was killed fighting Albanian clans, and Simeon was acknowledged in Thessaly and then in the towns of Epirus. He also used his mother's family name, Palaiologos. When Radoslav Hlapen of Vodena tried to take Thessaly for his stepson Thomas Preljubović, Simeon recognised his conquests, handed him Kastoria and married his daughter Maria to Thomas. In 1366 he gave Ioannina to Thomas, who held it as a vassal despot.

From Trikala Simeon ruled his last decade in relative peace, over a court of Byzantine, Serbian and Albanian nobles in which his wife's Byzantine relatives were favoured. He founded and richly endowed the monasteries of Meteora. He died in 1370 and was succeeded by his son John Uroš; another son, Stephen Uroš, became prince of Pharsalos.
simferopol: Simferopol lies in the south-central Crimean Peninsula on the Salhir River, near the artificial Simferopol Reservoir, which supplies the city's drinking water and has the biggest earth dam in Europe. It has a humid subtropical climate. The city is a political, economic and transport hub of the peninsula and has a major railway station.

Its name comes from the Greek Sympheropoli, meaning city of common good or usefulness. In Crimean Tatar the city is Aqmescit, the white mosque. The colour does not describe a building: Turkic peoples give a colour to each cardinal point, and white is the west, so the name means the Western Mosque.

The Crimean Scythians lived in the area from the 3rd century BCE to the 4th century CE, and the remnants of their capital, Scythian Neapolis, lie within the city. The Crimean Tatars later founded Aqmescit, which was for a time the residence of the Qalğa-Sultan, the second most important office in the Crimean Khanate after the Khan.

After Catherine II annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1784, the new city of Simferopol was founded on the site of Aqmescit, in line with her Greek Plan of Greek place names for the new southern lands. It became the administrative centre of the Taurida Governorate in 1802. After the Crimean War of 1854-1856 more than 30,000 Russian soldiers were buried near the city. In 1870 about 57 per cent of the population were Eastern Orthodox, with Jewish, Karaite, Catholic and other communities beside them.

The Red Army took the city on 13 November 1920, and it became capital of the Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic in 1921. German forces occupied it from 1 November 1941 to 13 April 1944 and killed over 22,000 local people, mostly Jews, Russians, Krymchaks and Romani, including an estimated 14,300 from 9 December 1941. On 18 May 1944 the city's Crimean Tatars were deported with their whole nation to Central Asia. Crimea was transferred to the Ukrainian SSR on 26 April 1954. After 1991 Simferopol was capital of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. Russia annexed Crimea in 2014; the city is internationally recognised as part of Ukraine.
simla-convention: Tibet had been a self-governing protectorate under Qing China, but as the Qing weakened, Britain feared Russian influence there, carried through the contacts between the Buryat Agvan Dorzhiev and the 13th Dalai Lama. British forces under Francis Younghusband entered Tibet in 1904 and concluded the Lhasa Convention. In 1906 the Chinese envoy Tang Shaoyi insisted on Chinese sovereignty, and in the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 Britain and Russia acknowledged Chinese suzerainty. A Qing expedition of 1910 came close to reconquering Tibet before the dynasty fell in the 1911 Revolution.

The conference opened at the Viceregal Lodge in Simla on 13 October 1913 and held eight formal sessions in Simla and Delhi. Sir Henry McMahon, Foreign Secretary of British India, represented Britain, assisted by Charles Alfred Bell and Archibald Rose; Ivan Chen represented the Republic of China; and Paljor Dorje Shatra, known as Lonchen Shatra, represented Tibet. Shatra opened by declaring Tibet an independent state and claiming frontiers reaching the Kuenlun Range, while Chen claimed Chinese occupation as far west as Giamda. Shatra backed his case with taxation and administrative records for the regions up to Tachienlu.

On 17 February 1914 McMahon proposed the division into Inner and Outer Tibet, with a map of both lines. China repudiated Chen's initialling of 27 April as unauthorised and asked to move the talks to London or Beijing, which Britain refused. At the final session on 3 July, convened at 11:15 pm to give Chen time for instructions that never came, Chen declined, and Britain and Tibet adopted the convention with a bilateral declaration denying China any privileges under it until China accepted it. The border with British India, later the McMahon Line, had been negotiated by the British and Tibetans alone.

In 1915 the Government of India regarded the bipartite treaty as for the present invalid, and in 1921, with the Anglo-Russian Convention held to have lapsed, Britain felt free to deal with Tibet directly. Britain sold the Tibetans 5,000 guns and half a million rounds, and in fighting from 1917 they recaptured Chamdo before a truce arranged by the British set the border on the Upper Yangtse. The Tibetologist Melvyn Goldstein judged that Simla did nothing to resolve the Tibet question. On 29 October 2008 Britain dropped its old position of Chinese suzerainty and recognised Chinese sovereignty over Tibet.
simmern: Simmern lies in the Hunsrück, in a basin called the Simmerner Mulde, with the old town centre in the valley of the Simmerbach and newer districts on the surrounding heights. The Külzbach joins the Simmerbach on the western outskirts, and the 50th parallel of north latitude runs through the municipal area. The Moselle, the Rhine and the Nahe are each about 25 kilometres away, and Mainz is 55 kilometres to the east. In the Middle Ages the town lay on the army road from Bingen to Trier.

Simmern was first mentioned in 1072, though the site had been settled in Roman times. It belonged first to the counts of the Nahegau and then to the Raugraves, who were given it as a fief by the Electorate of Trier between 1323 and 1330. Emperor Louis the Bavarian granted town rights in 1330, with the right to fortify, and the town built a double wall with towers and gates. Its weekly and yearly markets drew dealers from across the Hunsrück. Before the end of the 14th century it passed to the Wittelsbach counts palatine.

After the death of King Ruprecht III the Wittelsbachs divided into several lines, among them the Palatinate-Simmern line, which kept its residence in the town. Duke Johann II ruled from 1509 to 1557, had the town's first printing shop built, promoted the arts, especially sculpture, and introduced the Reformation. His successor Friedrich III, called the Pious, turned to Calvinism in 1563. In 1559 the Palatinate-Simmern line succeeded the extinct main line as electors at Heidelberg.

Friedrich V, the Winter King, brought the Thirty Years' War to the Palatinate, but Simmern, fortified by Karl I Ludwig, came through relatively unscathed. When the Palatine line died out in 1685, France claimed the inheritance, and the Nine Years' War began in 1688. On 17 September 1689 French troops left almost all of Simmern in rubble and razed the ducal residence. Only Saint Stephen's Church, the Powder Tower and a few houses survived. The French annexed the town after the Revolution, and in 1815 it was assigned to Prussia at the Congress of Vienna.

Simmern has been part of Rhineland-Palatinate since 1946. It is the district seat of the Rhein-Hunsrück-Kreis and has carried the name element Hunsrück since 1 June 1980. Its Powder Tower is also known as the Schinderhannes Tower, after the robber Johannes Bückler, who was held there for half a year in 1799 and escaped.
simon-august-count-of-lippe-detmold: Simon August was born in Detmold on 12 June 1727, the son of Simon Henry Adolph and Johanna Wilhelmine of Nassau-Idstein. He came to power in 1734 while still a child, and until 1747 he ruled under the guardianship of his mother.

Influenced by the Enlightenment, Simon August issued fiscal and social legislation. In 1749, together with Adolf von Hillensberg, he introduced a budget in Lippe, so that money would not be spent when no revenue was available to cover it. Two present-day institutions, the Sparkasse Detmold and a fire insurance company, are direct continuations of companies he founded.

He also took an interest in the resources of his small territory. He acquired a salt mine at Bad Salzuflen and built a spa at Bad Meinberg. In 1775 he set up a relief fund for the poor, and a census held in 1776 counted 49,416 inhabitants in his lands.

Simon August married four times. His first wife, Polyxena Louise, a daughter of Charles August, Prince of Nassau-Weilburg, whom he married at Kirchheimbolanden in 1750, bore a daughter who died in infancy. In 1765 he married Maria Leopoldine of Anhalt-Dessau, mother of his heir Leopold, born in Detmold in 1767. After her death in 1769 he married her sister Casimire, who bore a second son, Casimir August, in 1777. His fourth marriage, to Christine of Solms-Braunfels at Braunfels Castle in 1780, was childless. He died at Detmold on 1 May 1782, and his son Leopold I took up the government.
simon-bar-giora: His name means Simon, son of Giora, and Giora is the Aramaic for convert or sojourner; most scholars today agree that his father was a Gentile convert to Judaism. Josephus calls him a Gerasene by origin. Which Gerasa he meant is debated: Gerasa in the Decapolis is one possibility, but given Simon's later activity in Acrabatene and around Bethoron, a place in Judaea is generally thought more likely.

In 66 he led attacks on the Roman army of Cestius Gallus as it approached Beth Horon, throwing its rear into disorder and carrying off pack animals with its weapons. The Jerusalem authorities, hoping to moderate the revolt, refused him a command, and he turned to raiding wealthy houses in Acrabbene before taking refuge with the rebels at Masada. After Ananus ben Ananus was killed, he left the fortress, proclaimed liberty for slaves and gathered a large following, sacking villages in Idumea and plundering Hebron. When Zealots in Jerusalem captured his wife, he mutilated captives taken outside the city until she was released.

In spring 69 the Roman advance drove him into Jerusalem, where the remaining authorities invited him in to drive out John of Giscala. With fifteen thousand soldiers he held the upper city and part of the lower, living in the tower of Phasael. The factions destroyed each other's grain stores in a sabbatical year, when grain was already short. He ordered the execution of the High Priest Matthias ben Boethus and three of his sons as suspected friends of Rome, and Josephus wrote that he was a greater terror to the people than the Romans themselves.

When Titus took Jerusalem in 70, five months after the siege began, Simon hid in passages beneath the Temple Mount and tried to dig his way out until his food ran out. Dressed in the garments of a Judean king, he rose from the ground where the Temple had stood and was taken prisoner. He was held in the Mamertine Prison, paraded in chains through Rome in the triumph, tortured and executed in the Forum near the Temple of Jupiter. Cassius Dio calls him the leader of the Judeans.
simon-bar-kokhba: Documents found in the twentieth century in the Cave of Letters give his name as Shimon bar Kosevah, with variants. The name may point to his father or his place of origin; Khirbet Kuwayzibah is a likely candidate, and Emil Schürer thought it may refer to the village of Chozeba. The name Bar Kokhba, son of the star, comes from Rabbi Akiva, who regarded him as the Jewish messiah and, according to the Jerusalem Talmud, applied to him the Star Prophecy of Numbers 24:17, "There shall come a star out of Jacob". It appears in ecclesiastical sources, not in the Talmud, until the 16th century.

The Romans had devastated Judaea in the First Jewish–Roman War (66–73 CE), and a series of laws passed by Roman emperors gave the incentive for a second rebellion, which began in 132 CE under the governor Tineius Rufus. Bar Kokhba established a Jewish state that lasted about three years, with himself as nasi, or prince. For many Jews the turn of events heralded the Messianic Age. The Romans fared very poorly at first against a unified Jewish force, but then adopted a scorched earth policy that slowly wore down the population. According to the archaeologist Yigael Yadin, Bar Kokhba tried to revive Hebrew as the official language of the state.

Letters found in the Cave of Letters above the Dead Sea, some possibly by him, are now in the Israel Museum. Rabbinic literature portrays him as irascible, telling that he made recruits prove their valour by cutting off a finger and killed his uncle, Rabbi Elazar Hamudaʻi, on suspicion of collaboration.

In the last phase of the war Bar Kokhba took refuge in the fortress of Betar, which the Romans took after a siege; he was killed in 135. Cassius Dio, writing several decades later, says 580,000 Jews were killed in the war and some 50 fortified towns and 985 villages razed. The victory was so costly that Hadrian left out the customary greeting in his report to the Senate.

Hadrian barred Jews from Aelia Capitolina, the city he built on the ruins of Jerusalem, and merged Judaea, Galilee and Samaria into the province of Syria Palaestina, commonly seen as an attempt to sever the link with Judaea. Rebels who survived were killed or enslaved within the next year.
simon-bolivar: Simón Bolívar was born on 24 July 1783 in Caracas, the youngest of four children of Juan Vicente Bolívar y Ponte and María de la Concepción Palacios y Blanco, in a wealthy creole family. His father died of tuberculosis in 1786 and his mother in 1792, and he was raised partly by an enslaved woman named Hipólita, whom he viewed as both a motherly and a fatherly figure. In 1799 he was sent to Madrid, where he married María Teresa Rodríguez del Toro y Alaysa in 1802; she died of yellow fever in 1803. On a second journey to Europe he reached Rome, where he swore to end Spanish rule in the Americas.

After Napoleon's invasion of the Iberian peninsula, Venezuelan creoles sought their own government, and Bolívar helped secure Francisco de Miranda's election to the congress that declared Venezuela independent on 5 July 1811, creating the first Republic of Venezuela. The republic fell in 1812, and Bolívar went into exile in Curaçao and Cartagena. After Spanish forces subdued New Granada, he wrote the Jamaica Letter in 1815 in Kingston, laying out his ideology and vision of the future of the Americas.

In Haiti Alexandre Pétion, after Bolívar pledged to free every slave in the areas he occupied, gave him money and military supplies. In February 1819 the congress at Angostura elected him president. In May he marched over the Andes with more than 2,000 soldiers, and on 7 August 1819 the Royalists were routed at the Battle of Boyacá. Allies and Bolívar defeated the Spanish in Venezuela and Panama in 1821, Ecuador in 1822, Peru in 1824 and Bolivia in 1825, and Venezuela, New Granada, Ecuador and Panama were merged into Gran Colombia.

In his final years Bolívar became disillusioned with the republics and was successively removed from his offices. He left Bogotá on 8 May 1830 intending to go into exile in England, but with his health failing and no ship available he was taken to the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino near Santa Marta, where he died of tuberculosis on 17 December 1830, aged 47. In 1842 his remains were returned to Caracas, and in 1876 they were moved to the National Pantheon of Venezuela. He is regarded as a hero and national and cultural icon throughout Latin America, and Bolivia and Venezuela, as the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, are named after him.
simon-de-anda-y-salazar: Simón de Anda y Salazar was born on 28 October 1709 in the Basque Country of northern Spain, near the town of Subijana. He served in the Philippines as an oidor, a judge, of the Royal Audience of Manila. During the British attack on the city, the Governor-General and the Audiencia appointed him Lieutenant Governor, and on the night of 5 October 1762, during the Battle of Manila, he left the city with much of the treasury and its documents.

When the acting governor, Archbishop Manuel Rojo, was captured by the British and surrendered the Philippines, Anda rejected the act as illegal. He assumed full authority on behalf of the Real Audiencia, set up a provisional government and raised an army, and kept up the campaign against the British. He returned unopened every letter that did not address him as Governor-General of the Philippines, which the British refused to do until Rojo's death on 30 January 1764, so early negotiations failed.

In March 1764 Brigadier Francisco de la Torre brought orders from both kings to hand Manila back to Spain under the Treaty of Paris of 1763, and on 1 April 1764 the British garrison marched out. Anda then travelled to Spain, where the Cortes received him well and the king made him a Councilor of Castile, although he had written to the king complaining of disorders in the Philippines, many of them laid at the door of the friars.

Anda returned to the Philippines on 12 April 1768 and by royal decree became Governor-General in July 1770. He proceeded against his predecessor and other officials, reformed the Spanish and Philippine army and undertook public works. He opposed the king's order of 9 November 1774 to secularise the curacies held by the regular clergy, which was repealed after his death. He died on 30 October 1776 in the Hospital de San Felipe in Cavite, aged 67. Monuments to him stand in Manila and Bacolor, and the municipalities of Anda in Bohol and Pangasinan bear his name.
simon-de-la-loubere: Simon de la Loubère was born on 21 April 1642. The embassy he led to Siam in 1687 is known as the La Loubère-Céberet mission. On reaching Bangkok it was received by Ok-khun Chamnan, who in turn led the Siamese embassy that sailed with La Loubère on board the Gaillard on 3 January 1688. On his return he wrote, as Louis XIV had requested, an account of all that had appeared most singular to him in the country, observed as exactly as he could.

Following the publication of Du Royaume de Siam, La Loubère was elected to the Académie française, where he held Seat 16 from 1693 until his death on 26 March 1729. He was a friend of the German scientist Gottfried Leibniz, to whom he wrote in a letter of 22 January 1681 that he had no greater joy than to discuss philosophy and mathematics with him.

The obscure manuscript on Siamese astronomy that he brought back, now called the Siamese Manuscript, interested Jean Dominique Cassini enough that the astronomer spent a couple of years deciphering its contents, finding along the way that the document had originated in India. The Siamese method of making magic squares, also called the La Loubère method, is a simple way of building squares of odd order. It had apparently been brought from Surat, India, by another Frenchman named Vincent, who sailed on the return ship with La Loubère.

His book of 1691 also gives one of the earliest accounts of a parachute: a man who entertained the king of Siam by jumping from a high place with two large umbrellas, landing in trees, on rooftops and sometimes in rivers. His other writings include the Traité de l'origine des jeux floraux de Toulouse of 1715 and De la Résolution des équations, ou de l'Extraction de leurs racines, which appeared in 1732, after his death.
simon-de-montfort-5th-earl-of-leicester: Simon de Montfort was the son of Simon de Montfort, lord of Montfort l'Amaury near Paris, and Amicia de Beaumont, daughter of Robert de Beaumont, 3rd Earl of Leicester. He succeeded his father as lord of Montfort in 1188 and in 1190 married Alix de Montmorency, who shared his religious zeal and went with him on campaigns.

In 1199 he took the cross and joined the Fourth Crusade. He opposed the attack on Zara, which was sacked in 1202, did not take part in it, and left the crusade with his followers when it was diverted to Constantinople, travelling instead to the court of King Emeric of Hungary and on to Acre. He became Earl of Leicester in 1204, but King John of England took the lands and their revenues in 1207.

In 1209 Simon joined the first campaign of the Albigensian Crusade, and after the Siege of Carcassonne he was elected its leader and viscount of the confiscated lands of the Trencavel family. He was rewarded with territory taken from Raymond VI of Toulouse. In 1210 he burned 140 Cathars at Minerve who refused to recant, sparing those who did. Before the sack of Lastours he had prisoners from Bram blinded and mutilated, leaving one with a single eye to lead the rest.

He was described as deeply committed to the Dominican order, and Dominic Guzman spent winters at Fanjeau, his headquarters. The Cistercian Peter de Vaux de Cernay wrote an account of the crusade that historians generally consider propaganda.

In 1213 he defeated Peter II of Aragon at the Battle of Muret, which completed the defeat of the Albigensians; he then carried on the campaign as a war of conquest and in 1215 was made Count of Toulouse and Duke of Narbonne. He besieged Beaucaire from 6 June to 24 August 1216. Raymond VII of Toulouse returned to the city in October 1217, and Simon besieged it.

After nine months of siege he was killed on 25 June 1218 during a sally, when a stone from a mangonel smashed his head; according to one source it was worked by the women of Toulouse. He was buried in the Cathedral of Saint-Nazaire at Carcassonne, and his body was later moved to Montfort l'Amaury. His French estates passed to his eldest son Amaury, and his second son Simon later gained the earldom of Leicester and led the barons' rebellion against Henry III of England.
simon-de-montfort-6th-earl-of-leicester: Simon de Montfort was a younger son of Simon de Montfort, 5th Earl of Leicester, leader of the crusade against the Cathars, and Alix de Montmorency. His father was killed at the Siege of Toulouse in 1218. Simon's elder brother Amaury gave up the family's claim to the English earldom of Leicester in return for all the possessions in France, and Simon arrived in England in 1229 with no knowledge of English. Henry III received him well, and he was formally recognised as Earl of Leicester in February 1239. In January 1238 he secretly married the king's sister Eleanor, who had earlier vowed perpetual chastity; Archbishop Edmund Rich condemned the match.

The friendship with Henry broke down over a debt for which Simon had named the king as security without his approval, and Simon and Eleanor fled to France in 1239. He went on the Barons' Crusade and later served as the king's lieutenant in Gascony, but quarrelled with Henry again and retired to France in 1252. At the Oxford Parliament of 1258 he stood at the head of the opposition and sat on the Council of Fifteen set up to control the administration. After Henry revoked the Provisions of Oxford in 1261 Montfort left England, returning in 1263 at the barons' invitation to lead a rebellion.

The Mise of Amiens, Louis IX's arbitration of January 1264, annulled the Provisions. In the civil war that followed Montfort won the Battle of Lewes on 14 May 1264 and captured the king, Prince Edward and Richard of Cornwall. His Great Parliament of 1265 summoned two representatives from each county and from a selected list of boroughs. His cause was marked by violence against Jews: he had expelled the Jews of Leicester, and his followers seized debt records and killed Jews in London, Worcester, Winchester and Derby and elsewhere.

Prince Edward escaped in May 1265, and Gilbert de Clare, Earl of Gloucester, deserted Montfort. At Evesham on 4 August 1265 Montfort led an uphill charge against a superior army, described by one chronicler as the murder of Evesham, and was killed along with his son Henry. His body was mutilated. A popular cult grew at his grave, and a miracle book records some 200 alleged miracles. He is remembered as a father of representative government, and also as responsible for persecution of Jews. De Montfort University in Leicester is named after him.
simon-i-of-kartli: Simon, also called Svimon and known as Simon I the Great, was the eldest son of King Luarsab I of the Bagrationi dynasty and of Tamar, daughter of Bagrat III of Imereti. In 1556 he commanded his father's army against Persian invaders at the Battle of Garisi, having been proclaimed co-ruler and heir just before it. Luarsab was mortally wounded, but Simon won the battle and soon succeeded him.

With Tbilisi in Persian hands, Simon ruled from Gori. In 1559 he allied with Levan of Kakheti and married his daughter Nestan-Darejan. His attempts to recover Tbilisi from 1560 ended in defeat at Tsikhedidi in April 1561. His brother David submitted to Shah Tahmasp I, converted to Islam and returned with a Persian army; Simon won at Dighomi in 1567 and Samadlo in 1569 but was taken prisoner at Partskhisi in 1569. Refusing to convert, he was held for nine years in the fortress of Alamut.

In 1578, at the start of the Ottoman–Safavid War, Shah Mohammad Khodabanda released him to rule Kartli, on condition that he accept Islam, and gave him cannon and 5,000 Qizilbash. Back in Georgia Simon returned to Christianity and led the resistance against the Ottomans, recovering most of Kartli by 1579 and defeating the main Ottoman army at Mukhrani in 1582. He also sought help from Pope Clement VIII, Emperor Rudolph II and Philip II of Spain, without result. After Ferhad Pasha conquered Kartli by 1588 he made peace and paid tribute, and the treaty of Constantinople of 21 March 1590 recognised all Georgia as Ottoman. He fought on from 1595 and retook Gori in 1599.

Sultan Mehmed III then sent Jafar Pasha, beylerbey of Tabriz, against him. Simon was heavily defeated at Nakhiduri and captured as he tried to escape, and the sultan ordered three days of celebration across his realm. Taken to Constantinople, where the Georgian noblewoman Gulchara cared for him, he died in the Fortress of the Seven Towers (Yedikule) in 1611 without converting to Sunni Islam. The Georgians redeemed his body and buried it beside his father in Svetitskhoveli Cathedral at Mtskheta. His son George X ruled Kartli from 1599 to 1606.
simon-kimbangu: Kimbangu was born at Nkamba, near Thysville. According to the Kimbanguist narrative, the traditional religious leader Papa Kuyela and Mama Luezi found the infant in the bush during a storm and adopted him, and his followers hold that his coming had been foretold in the 1600s by Kimpa Vita, who was burnt alive for her message of the Holy Spirit and the liberation of Africa. He became a Baptist and worked for several years as a catechist. Kimbanguist accounts add that he refused a call from Christ at first and sought work in Leopoldville before returning to Nkamba in 1921.

His ministry of preaching and healing lasted from April to September 1921, and his disciples hold that he cured the sick, raised the dead and prophesied the liberation of black people. Bertram Melbourne holds that the Protestant and Catholic establishments appealed to the colonial authorities, while David van Reybrouck describes the Belgian administrator Léon Morel calling the missionaries to a meeting at Thysville, where the Catholics urged firm intervention and the Protestants a softer approach. Kimbangu and his followers were arrested on 6 June 1921, but he escaped into the bush with some disciples and his son Charles.

He went on preaching in hiding and gave himself up in September. A military court tried him without a lawyer and found him guilty of undermining public security and disturbing the peace. Asked by the Italian judge de Rossi to state his claims, he answered that he was not a prophet but the special envoy of Jesus, the Muanda Velela, the Holy Spirit in Kikongo. On 3 October 1921 he was sentenced to death.

Kimbangu died in prison at Elisabethville on 12 October 1951. In 1960 his body was exhumed and reburied at Nkamba with full military honours, and the Congolese government later made 6 April, the day his healing and prophetic work began, a holiday dedicated to the fight of Simon Kimbangu and the African consciousness.

After his trial the administration tried to suppress the movement: followers were banished across the country and their faith was outlawed, and in 1940 the leading exiles were put in guarded work camps under forced labour, where many died. The church spread underground and was recognised by the Belgian government in 1959. His son Joseph Diangienda, whom Kimbanguists regard as his second incarnation, organised it until his death in Switzerland on 8 July 1992, followed by his elder brother Salomon Dialungana Kiangani and then by Salomon's son Simon Kimbangu Kiangani at Nkamba.
simon-patino: Patiño's biographers disagree about his early life. Many wrote that he was a cholo of mixed Quechua and Spanish descent, born to a poor mother, while his authorised biography held that he was of European ancestry alone and the son of a provincial leader. He was in fact the illegitimate son of Julio Abasto and María Patiño of Cochabamba. Before entering mining he either managed a store in Oruro or spent years in private schools.

Patiño worked for the silver company Compañía Huanchaca de Bolivia and then for Fricke y Compañía, collecting debts for its store. In 1894 he accepted the deed to a rocky mountainside in settlement of a debt of $250 owed by a prospector, and was dismissed for taking worthless property; legend has it that he had to repay the store himself. The first years of work yielded little, but the rich tin vein found in 1900 changed his fortunes.

Over the following decade he gained control of nearby mines and of other important Bolivian mines, among them Catavi, Siglo XX, Uncia and Huanuni. He bought out Chilean interests in his company, acquired tin smelters in England and Germany and in 1924 merged his Bolivian mining and railway assets into Patiño Mines & Enterprise Consolidated Inc., registered in Delaware. By the 1940s he controlled the international tin market, and during the Second World War he was believed to be one of the five wealthiest men in the world.

Patiño had divided his time between Europe and Bolivia since about 1912, and after a heart attack in 1924 he settled abroad, in Paris, New York and finally Buenos Aires. While in Paris he served as Bolivia's minister to France and represented it at the Évian Conference in 1938. He married Albina Rodriguez, with whom he had five children. He was buried in a white mausoleum in the province of Cochabamba. The Bolivian Revolution of 1952 confiscated the Patiño mines.
simon-stevin: Very little is known with certainty about Stevin's life. He is assumed to have been born in Bruges, since he enrolled at Leiden University as Simon Stevinus Brugensis, into a family likely to have been Calvinist. He left Bruges in 1571, perhaps to escape the persecution of Protestants by the Spanish rulers, and began a career as a merchant's clerk in Antwerp. He served as city clerk of Bruges from 1577 to 1581, then moved to Leiden, where he attended the Latin school and enrolled at the university on 16 February 1583. There he befriended Prince Maurice of Nassau, the second son of William the Silent.

After William's assassination, Stevin became the principal adviser and tutor of Maurice. He directed the waterstaet, the authority for public works and water management, from 1592 and later served as quartermaster-general of the army of the States-General. Maurice asked him to found an engineering school within the University of Leiden. His work on sluices and spillways to control flooding included improvements to windmills that raised their efficiency in pumping water from the polders threefold, for which he received a patent in 1586. Around 1600 he used a land yacht, a carriage with sails, on the beach between Scheveningen and Petten, with Maurice and twenty-six others, and it outran horses.

Stevin wrote De Thiende, a 35-page booklet first published in Dutch in 1585, which taught calculation without fractions by using decimal fractions. It was addressed to stargazers, surveyors and tradespeople. Decimal fractions had been introduced earlier by medieval Islamic scholars, and his notation was unwieldy. He derived the balance of forces on inclined planes, discovered the hydrostatic paradox, distinguished stable from unstable equilibria and in 1586 demonstrated that bodies of different weight fall with the same acceleration. He was the first to explain the tides by the attraction of the moon.

He believed Dutch ideal for scientific writing and wrote all his works in it, so that people who lacked Latin could use them. He coined Dutch terms such as wiskunde for mathematics, natuurkunde for physics and scheikunde for chemistry. He died in 1620 in Leiden or The Hague, leaving a widow and two children.
simon-thassi: Simon Thassi was the second son of Mattathias and one of the Maccabean brothers who led the revolt against the Seleucid Empire with Judas Maccabaeus and Jonathan Apphus. His epithet Thassi suggests "the Wise", and it can also mean "the Director", "the Guide", "the Man of Counsel" and "the Zealous". He is also called Simon the Hasmonean, Simon Maccabee or Simon Maccabeus.

The Seleucid king Antiochus VI appointed him strategos, or military commander, of the coast from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt. In that post he took Beth-zur and Joppa, garrisoned them with Jewish troops and built the fortress of Adida.

When the Seleucid general Diodotus Tryphon captured Jonathan, the people assembled at Jerusalem chose Simon as their leader. He completed the fortification of the city and secured Joppa, and at Hadid he blocked Tryphon's advance. Tryphon demanded a ransom and Jonathan's sons as hostages. Josephus and 1 Maccabees both say Simon agreed, although he knew he would be deceived, so that the people could see he had done all he could. Jonathan was killed anyway and the hostages were not returned.

Simon then sided with the Seleucid king Demetrius II and asked for freedom from taxation, which was granted. This implied recognition of Judea's political independence. A large assembly of priests, people and elders decreed that he should be leader and high priest "forever, until there should arise a faithful prophet". He became High Priest and Ethnarch, the first prince of the Hasmonean dynasty. The Roman Senate recognised the new dynasty about 139 BCE, when his delegation was in Rome.

Simon and two of his sons, Mattathias and Judah, were killed at a banquet at Dok by his son-in-law Ptolemy, the Seleucid governor at Jericho. His third son John Hyrcanus succeeded him as high priest and ruler, but at first could not capture Ptolemy, who held John's mother hostage.

The name Simon, and its Hebrew form Simeon, became the most popular male name for some three centuries in the Hasmonean Kingdom and Roman Judaea, both to honour the leader who had won independence and because it did not sound strange to Greek ears.
simon-van-der-stel: Simon van der Stel was born at sea on 14 October 1639, while his father, Adriaan van der Stel, an official of the Dutch East India Company (VOC), was on his way to take up his post as the first Dutch governor of Mauritius. His mother, Maria Lievens, was the daughter of a freed slave, which made Simon the first person not born in Europe and of mixed heritage to be appointed Commander and Governor of the Cape Colony. He spent his youth on Mauritius.

In 1645 Adriaan left for Dutch Ceylon, where he was murdered in 1646 by the troops of Rajasinha II of Kandy. Simon, his mother and his sisters returned to Batavia. Little is known of him until he returned to the Dutch Republic in 1659. There he associated with the cloth dealer Willem Six, and in 1663 married his daughter, Johanna Jacoba Six; they had six children.

Van der Stel was appointed Commander at the Cape in 1679 through the influence of his relative Joan Huydecoper van Maarsseveen. His wife stayed behind and he never saw her again, though he sent her money and she sent furnishings and paintings for his house at Groot Constantia. In 1685 he received Constantia as a reward for good and faithful services to the VOC, and in 1685-86 he led an expedition to the Copper Mountains at Springbok in Namaqualand, making botanical, zoological and geographic observations.

In 1691 the VOC replaced the office of Commander with that of Governor, and Van der Stel was promoted. He could be very harsh: in June 1689 he imprisoned in appalling conditions the crews and priests of the French ships Le Coche and La Normande, whose diamonds and jewellery he seems to have appropriated. His sons all spent time with him at the Cape; Willem Adriaan succeeded him as Governor, and Adrian became governor of Amboyna.

Van der Stel retired in 1699 and devoted himself to his wine estates at Constantia, where he died on 24 June 1712; the estate was sold in parts at a four-day auction in 1716. He is considered one of the founders of South African viticulture. Stellenbosch, Simon's Town and the Simonsberg mountain bear his name, as did the South African Navy ship SAS Simon van der Stel in 1952. Jean-Jacques Rousseau named him in his Discourse on Inequality, and his travel journals are kept in the Fagel Collection of Trinity College Dublin.
simon-vratsian: Vratsian was born Simavon Grouzian on 5 April 1882 in the village of Metz Sala near Nor Nakhichevan in the Russian Empire. A schoolteacher, believing the name came from the Russian word for Georgian, turned it into Vratsian. After Armenian and Russian schools he joined the Armenian Revolutionary Federation in 1898, by his own account by mistake while looking for a meeting of the rival Hunchak Party. He studied at the Gevorgian Seminary in Echmiadzin from 1900 to 1906 and at the party's congress in Vienna in 1907 supported the adoption of socialism in its programme.

In 1908 he went to Saint Petersburg to study law and education, but had to leave Russia as the Tsarist authorities pressed the party. He taught in Erzurum, edited the Hairenik newspaper in Boston from 1911 and in 1914 was elected to the party's Bureau. Jailed as a Russian spy in August 1914, he escaped to Transcaucasia and worked with the Armenian volunteer units of the Russian army. In 1919 he became a minister in the cabinet of Alexander Khatisian and kept his posts under Hamo Ohanjanyan.

Vratsian became prime minister on 23 November 1920 and on 2 December surrendered Armenia to the Bolsheviks. In February 1921 he came out of hiding as chairman of the Committee for the Salvation of the Fatherland, which led the February Uprising that briefly overthrew Soviet rule. When the rebels fell back to Zangezur in April he became premier of the Republic of Mountainous Armenia, and in July he escaped to Persia.

In exile Vratsian edited the party newspaper Droshak in Paris from 1924 to 1933, and in 1945 he presented a petition to the UN General Assembly at San Francisco asking for the Armenian lands held by Turkey. From 1952 he lived in Beirut, where he was principal of the Collège Arménien; the historians Richard G. Hovannisian and Gerard Libaridian were among his students. He wrote a six-volume memoir, On the Path of Life, and a history of the First Republic. He died in Beirut on 21 May 1969.
simone-boccanegra: Simone Boccanegra belonged to a wealthy Genoese family of merchants. One of its members, Guglielmo Boccanegra, had become the virtual ruler of the Republic of Genoa in 1257 after an insurrection against the government of the old aristocracy, and in 1260 commissioned the Palazzo San Giorgio. Simone's mother was a Pisan aristocrat. His brother Egidio served as grand admiral of Alfonso XI of Castile and defeated a Moroccan fleet off Algeciras in 1344, and another brother, Niccolò, was Capitano del popolo in Pisa.

Boccanegra was elected doge for life on 23 December 1339. His first acts excluded the old mercantile patriciate from public life, and new mercantile houses rose in its place: the Adorno, Guarco, Fregoso and Montaldo. Genoese control was extended along both the French and Italian Rivieras, except for the Grimaldi holdings at Monaco and Ventimiglia. Conspiracies began at once, and the first conspirator was beheaded on 20 December 1339. He kept a bodyguard of 103 mounted soldiers drawn from Pisa. He was later forced to resign at a public meeting he had himself called, and lived in exile, mostly in Tuscany, while Genoa submitted to Giovanni Visconti of Milan in 1353.

When a revolt against the Visconti broke out on 14 November 1356, Boccanegra appeared at the church of San Siro and rallied the commoners, and was restored as doge. In 1358 Genoa obtained the surrender of the envoys of the revolt in Corsica.

By 1362 his popularity was waning, and conspiracies were uncovered that autumn. In January 1363 King Peter I of Cyprus visited Genoa and knighted the doge's two-year-old son. Boccanegra died suddenly on 14 March 1363, after a banquet for the king. The chronicler Giorgio Stella says a revolt overthrew his regime as he lay ill and Gabriele Adorno was elected doge; his modern biographer Petti Balbi holds that he died a natural death. His tomb sculpture, from the lost church of San Francesco in Castelletto, is now in the Museum of Sant'Agostino. Antonio García Gutiérrez's play of 1843 and Giuseppe Verdi's opera of 1857 told his story.
simone-de-beauvoir: Beauvoir was born on 9 January 1908 in Montparnasse, in Paris. Her father, Georges Bertrand de Beauvoir, was initially a lawyer but aspired to be an actor, and her mother, Françoise, was a devout Catholic and a banker's daughter. The promised dowry was lost when Françoise's father was jailed. Her parents were often absent, and she was raised chiefly by a nanny, Louise. She had a younger sister, Hélène, born on 6 June 1910. Intellectually precocious and encouraged by her father, she wrote that the contrast between her father's individualism and pagan standards and her mother's rigid conventional morality made her life an endless disputation, the main reason she became an intellectual.

After her studies Beauvoir saw teaching as a way to earn her own living. She did her practice teaching at the same secondary school as Maurice Merleau-Ponty and Claude Lévi-Strauss, and from 1929 to 1943 she taught at lycées in Marseille, Rouen and Paris until she could live on her writing. She then became a public intellectual. Her first novel, She Came to Stay, appeared in 1943, followed by The Blood of Others (1945), which tells a love story between two young students in the French Resistance during the Second World War.

With Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty she co-founded Les Temps Modernes, a monthly political journal that carried communists, Catholics, Gaullists and socialists, whose first issue appeared on 1 October 1945. Sartre and Merleau-Ponty later quarrelled, and Beauvoir sided with Sartre. She remained an editor until her death and in later years held the editorial meetings in her flat.

Her first philosophical essay, Pyrrhus et Cinéas (1944), was followed by The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), in which she argues that the freedom of the self requires the freedom of others. The Second Sex (1949) turned the existentialist principle that existence precedes essence into a feminist one: One is not born, but rather becomes, woman. It articulated the distinction between biological sex and the social construction of gender, and showed how sexual difference is used to trap women in the role of the Other. The Mandarins (1954), a roman à clef about Sartre's and Beauvoir's circle after the war, won the Prix Goncourt.

Beauvoir at first denied being a feminist but later admitted it. The Second Sex opened the way for second-wave feminism, and Kate Millett, Shulamith Firestone, Juliet Mitchell, Ann Oakley and Germaine Greer read it in translation and acknowledged their debt to her. Betty Friedan said that reading it in the early 1950s led to her own analysis of women's existence.
simone-martini: Simone Martini was born in Siena around 1284. It is thought that he was a pupil of Duccio di Buoninsegna, the leading Sienese painter of his time, although the Renaissance biographer Giorgio Vasari instead made him a pupil of Giotto di Bondone, with whom he went to Rome. His brother-in-law was the artist Lippo Memmi. Very little documentation of his life survives, and many attributions to him are debated by art historians.

Among his first documented works is the Maestà of 1315 in the Palazzo Pubblico in Siena. Lippo Memmi painted a similar Maestà for the Palazzo Comunale in San Gimignano soon afterwards, an example of the lasting influence of his models. During a stay in Naples at the request of the king he painted Saint Louis of Toulouse Crowning His Brother Robert of Anjou in 1317, now in the Museo di Capodimonte, and he painted a polyptych of Saint Catherine of Alexandria in Pisa in 1319.

He also painted the Annunciation with St. Margaret and St. Ansanus of 1333, now in the Uffizi in Florence, and frescoes in the San Martino Chapel in the lower church of the Basilica of San Francesco in Assisi. A Christ Discovered in the Temple of 1342 is in the Walker Art Gallery in Liverpool.

His Sienese style contrasts with the sobriety and monumentality of Florentine art and is noted for soft, stylised, decorative features, sinuous line and courtly elegance. His art owes much to French manuscript illumination and ivory carving, examples of which reached Siena along the Via Francigena, a main pilgrimage and trade route. He greatly influenced the International Gothic style.

He likely moved to Avignon in 1334 or 1335 and died there in July 1344 in the service of the papal court. He was commissioned to paint frescoes for the porch of Avignon Cathedral, of which only faint sinopia outlines remain. According to Vasari, he painted a portrait of Laura de Noves for his friend Petrarch, who refers to it in two sonnets of the Canzoniere.
simonides-of-ceos: Few clear facts about Simonides' life have survived, and ancient sources are uncertain even about his date of birth. Modern scholars generally accept 556 to 468 BCE, though this would make him about fifty years older than his nephew Bacchylides. He was the son of Leoprepes and was born in Ioulis on Ceos, an island with a rich musical culture, where choirs were trained at a school in Carthaea, and a tradition of athletic competition that made it fertile ground for the victory ode, a genre of choral lyric he pioneered. About the age of thirty he was drawn to Athens by the court of the tyrant Hipparchus, where his rivalry with the chorus-trainer Lasus of Hermione later became a joke.

After the assassination of Hipparchus in 514 BCE Simonides withdrew to Thessaly, under the patronage of the Scopadae and Aleuadae. A tradition related by Cicero and Quintilian says that Scopas refused to pay him in full for an ode that spoke too much of Castor and Pollux, and that the poet was called out of the banquet hall just before it collapsed, which was said to have led him to devise a system of mnemonics based on places. Quintilian dismisses the story as fiction.

He returned to Athens during the Persian Wars and became a prominent international figure as the author of commemorative verses. After the defeat of the second Persian invasion he composed epitaphs for Athenians, Spartans and Corinthians, a song for Leonidas and his men, and poems on the battles of Artemisium, Salamis and Plataea. His last years were spent in Sicily as a friend of Hieron of Syracuse, and he is said to have made peace between Hieron and Theron of Acragas. Callimachus records that he was buried outside Acragas.

Simonides wrote choral lyrics, elegiac verses, dirges, paeans and dithyrambs, and an epigram credits him with 57 victories in dithyrambic competitions. He is generally credited with popularising the victory ode, an extension of the hymn, and with establishing the choral dirge as a recognised form. Only a small part of his poetry survives, in papyrus fragments and quotations, and modern scholars consider just one of the epigrams attributed to him unquestionably authentic, an inscription for the seer Megistius, which places even the Thermopylae epitaph in doubt.

His style is clear and simple, with restraint and balance, and Quintilian praised his power to excite pity. Aristophanes made him a type of the miser, and a tradition holds that he was the first poet to charge fees. Plato quotes his poem on the difficulty of being truly good, which holds that only a god can be perfect and that a man is good enough if he does nothing shameful willingly.
simplon-pass: The Simplon Pass is a high mountain pass between the Pennine Alps and the Lepontine Alps in Switzerland. It connects Brig in the canton of Valais with Domodossola in Piedmont, Italy. The pass itself and the villages on each side of it, such as Gondo, lie in Switzerland. Its lowest point, which is also the lowest point of the watershed between the basins of the Rhône and the Po in Switzerland, lies in marshland about 500 metres west of the settlement of Simplon Pass. Peaks that can be climbed from the pass include the Wasenhorn, the Hubschhorn, the Breithorn and Monte Leone.

A passage through the mountains had been used locally for several centuries, but the pass acquired international significance during the Napoleonic occupation. Between 1801 and 1805 the engineer Nicolas Céard built the Simplon Road at the direction of the emperor, so that artillery could be moved between the Rhône valley and Italy. From then on the pass could be used by road vehicles: first post carriages, replaced early in the twentieth century by post buses. The former département of Simplon, the Swiss canton of Valais, was named after the pass.

The cantonal authorities made a plan in 1950 to keep the road open all year instead of closing it between October and late April, as was usual at this altitude. It called for avalanche shelters and wider tunnels for full-size coaches. In October 1970 journalists were told that the work had been finished on 37 of the 42.5 kilometres between Brig and the Italian frontier at Gondo. The Simplon Tunnel, 20 kilometres long, opened in 1906, and the Orient Express used the Simplon route intermittently during the twentieth century on its way between Istanbul and Paris.

The road remains one of the few major Alpine passes kept open throughout the year. The Hospice du Simplon at the top is owned by the Congregation of Canons Regular at Grand-Saint-Bernard. A granite eagle about nine metres high, designed by the architect Erwin Friedrich Baumann and inaugurated in September 1944, commemorates the 11th Alpine Brigade of the Swiss Army; a memorial of 2005 marks the 200th anniversary of the Napoleon Road.
simtokha-dzong: Its formal name, Sangak Zabdhon Phodrang, means Palace of the Profound Meaning of Secret Mantras. Tradition holds that the dzong guarded against a demoness who had vanished into a rock near the site, and the name Simtokha is explained from simmo, demoness, and do, stone. With it Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, who unified Bhutan, brought the dzong as castle-monastery into use in the country for the first time, and it served as both a monastic and an administrative centre.

Early on, five disaffected lamas joined an invading Tibetan army opposed to the Buddhist practice of the dzong under the Zhabdrung; they were defeated, and their leader Palden Lama died in the battle. A second Tibetan attack in 1630 held the dzong for a while, until part of it caught fire and the collapsing roof killed the invaders. Mingyur Tenpa, the third Druk Desi or regent, completed the first renovation and extension in 1670, and the most recent refurbishment was carried out by architects from Japan.

The small dzong stands on a ridge about 5 kilometres south of Thimphu, commanding the valley and the roads to the Dochula Pass and eastern Bhutan, at the meeting point of three western regions: Sha, Wang and Pa. It rises over three floors, entered by a single gate on the south. Prayer wheels and some 300 slate carvings of saints and philosophers line the outside. The main chapel holds a large image of the Sakyamuni Buddha flanked by eight bodhisattvas, with dark murals said to be among the oldest in Bhutan, and the ceiling of the assembly hall bears a cosmic mandala in which the circles stand for the twelve months.

In 1961 the third Druk Gyalpo, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, established a Buddhist school of linguistics in the dzong at the suggestion of Queen Mayum Choying Wangmo Dorje. On 17 August 2019 the Bhutanese Prime Minister Lotay Tshering and the Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi met there for an exchange of documents, the first time the monument served as a venue for international diplomacy.
simurgh: The Persian word sīmurğ derives from Middle Persian sēnmurw, which comes from Avestan mərəγō Saēnō, the bird Saēna, originally a raptor, likely an eagle, falcon or sparrowhawk. In Persian the phrase sī murğ also means thirty birds, a play on words used by Attar of Nishapur.

The figure appears in all periods of Iranian art and literature, and in the iconography of Georgia, medieval Armenia and the Eastern Roman Empire. The Sasanians used it heavily, as a tribal emblem and in their art and propaganda. Through Persian influence it reached the Arabic-speaking world, where it was conflated with other mythical birds such as the ghoghnus and developed into the rukh, the origin of the English word roc. Representations were adopted in early Umayyad art and coinage.

In Iranian art the simurgh is a winged creature in the shape of a bird, gigantic enough to carry off an elephant or a whale. It appears as a peacock with the head of a dog and the claws of a lion, and sometimes with a human face. It is inherently benevolent, and being part mammal it suckles its young.

The simurgh was thought to purify land and water and so bestow fertility, and it mediated between earth and sky. It roosted in Gaokerena, the Hōm tree of life in the middle of the sea Vourukasha, whose all-healing seeds it scattered when it took flight. It is also linked with farr, divine glory, the mandate underlying a king's authority; it appears resting on the head or shoulder of would-be kings and clerics as a sign that Ormuzd accepts them.

In Ferdowsi's Shahnameh the simurgh raises Zal, son of Saam, who was born albino and abandoned on the mountain Alborz. She gives him three golden feathers to burn if he needs her help. When his wife Rudaba is near death in labour, Zal burns a feather and the simurgh instructs him in performing a caesarean section, so that Rostam is born. The simurgh later heals Rostam and his horse Rakhsh after Esfandiyar's arrows and tells Rostam how to make the double-headed arrow that blinds Esfandiyar. In the fifth trial of Esfandiyar, a different simurgh is killed.

In Persian Sufi poetry it is a metaphor for God. In Attar's 12th-century Conference of the Birds, a group of pilgrim birds led by the hoopoe seeks the simurgh and at last finds only a lake in which they see their own reflection, a pun on thirty birds.
sin-iddinam: Sîn-iddinam's presumed reign of seven years rests on the Larsa King List (the Larsa Date List) and on the seven year names known for him. His name was written with the divine sign, as dsuen-i-din-na-am, for the whole of his reign, while his father Nur-Adad had been deified only late in his own. Until Nur-Adad's time the kings of Larsa had called themselves King of Ur, and Sîn-iddinam took the title Provider of Ur instead.

Two of his letters describe the crisis in Larsa that came before his father's accession: house was turned against house, battle was waged in the public square, murder was done with weapons, ruin set in in all the streets and brother consumed brother, while deserting troops perished by hunger or weapons. It has been suggested that the disruption was caused by Šimaškian incursions.

His year names also record that Ibrat, the main city, was seized together with Malgium and other places. His defeat of an army of Babylon fell roughly in the 43rd year of Sumu-la-El of Babylon, about 1847 BCE. He concluded a treaty with Ibal-pi-El I of Eshnunna and Sîn-kāšid of Uruk against Sabium of Babylon and his ally Ikūn-pī-Sîn of Nerebtum.

His building work on the E-Babbar, the temple of the god Utu at Larsa, is recorded on a number of plaques and clay cones, and a large number of his clay barrels commemorating the wall of Mashkan-shapir were found at that site. A cache of tablets found at Tell Waresh 2, near Nippur, includes some that carry his year names. He is also known for a prayer to Utu, whom he calls Father of the black-headed ones. His cult statue, still anointed under Rim-Sin (c. 1823–1763 BCE), stood in the temple of Nanna at Ur.
sinaloa: Sinaloa is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the Federal Entities of Mexico. It covers 58,328 square kilometres and is divided into 20 municipalities. It borders Sonora, Chihuahua, Durango and Nayarit, and faces Baja California Sur across the Gulf of California. The Sierra Madre Occidental dominates the east, and many rivers flow from it to the gulf through fertile valleys and a narrow coastal plain. The most popular explanation of the name, attributed to Eustaquio Buelna, combines the Cahita words sina, the pitahaya plant, and lobola, rounded.

Sinaloa belongs to the northern limit of Mesoamerica, and the Fuerte River marks the start of Aridoamerica to the north. Before European contact it was inhabited by groups such as the Cahitas, the Tahues, the Acaxees and the Xiximes. In 1531 Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán, with a force of over 10,000 men, established a Spanish and allied Indian outpost at San Miguel de Culiacán. Over the next decade the Cahíta suffered severe depopulation from conquest and from smallpox and other diseases brought by Europeans.

Starting in 1599 Jesuit missionaries spread out from a base at what is now Sinaloa de Leyva, and by 1610 Spanish influence reached the northern edge of the territory. Their movement into the east prompted the Acaxee Rebellion of 1601; the Spanish executed 48 Acaxee leaders. After independence Sinaloa was joined with Sonora as the Estado de Occidente, and in 1830 it separated to become the 20th state of the First Mexican Republic, with Culiacán as its capital. Los Mochis was founded in 1893 by American settlers led by Albert K. Owen as the Topolobampo colony, inspired by utopian socialism.

The capital and largest city is Culiacán; other large cities include Mazatlán, a tourist resort, and Los Mochis. Irrigation projects built after the revolution turned arid land into farmland and earned Sinaloa the name granary of Mexico. Banda music, popularized there in the late 19th century, is its best-known cultural tradition, and ulama, a form of the ancient Mesoamerican ballgame, is still played in a few rural communities near Mazatlán.
sinan-pasha-ottoman-admiral: Known in full as Sinanuddin Yusuf Pasha, he was of Croatian descent, and his brother, the grand vizier Rüstem Pasha, was married to Mihrimah Sultan, a daughter of Suleiman the Magnificent and Hurrem Sultan. He held the rank of Kapudan Pasha under Suleiman and was succeeded in it by Piali Pasha. With Turgut Reis (Dragut) he led several naval expeditions in the Mediterranean Sea, particularly along the coasts of Italy and North Africa.

Sinan was less expert in naval affairs than Turgut, who was the more popular commander among the admirals and captains, and the two often clashed. After the conquest of Tripoli in 1551 the whole fleet left Sinan on the shore and followed Turgut into the Tyrrhenian Sea, declaring that it would accept only Turgut as its commander. Turgut called this mutiny and treason and ordered the ships back to take Sinan with them. Suleiman, who favoured Turgut's talent, told Sinan to do whatever Turgut said, and most Ottoman seamen of the time believed Turgut deserved Sinan's rank.

Sinan was nonetheless seen as a good and clever naval strategist and was one of the sultan's favourite military strategists and a friend. Accounts of his character conflict. The Ottoman historian Peçevî called him proud and megalomaniac, a man who would not listen to the opinions and complaints of others and had a cold gaze, while Spanish historians of the period described him as tall and strong, with a handsome face, a gallant heart and a very kind manner.

Sinan Pasha died in his palace, which stood on the site of the present Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul. He had ordered the building of a large mosque bearing his name in the Beşiktaş district and wished to be buried there, but it could not be finished in time, and he was buried instead in the garden of the Mihrimah Sultan Mosque in Üsküdar, designed by the architect Mimar Sinan. Although he had two daughters and a son, he left his whole fortune to Mihrimah Sultan, his brother's wife.
sinchi-roca: Sinchi Roca, written Sinchi Rocca or Cinchi Roca in Hispanicized spellings and Sinchi Ruq'a in Quechua, where the name is glossed as "valorous generous Inca", belonged to the Hurin dynasty, the first dynasty of the Kingdom of Cusco. Tradition makes him the son of two of the original Inca siblings, Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo, who may have conceived him at Huaynacancha. His wife was Mama Cura of the Sanu lineage, a daughter of Sitic-huaman, and their children included Lloque Yupanqui and a son named Sapaca. His dates are given as about 1230 to about 1260.

In one of the Inca foundation myths Sinchi Roca led his family into the valley of Cuzco. He is thought to have divided his land into territories and to have begun the first census of the Inca population. He is also said to have ordered all Inca to pierce their ears as a sign of nobility. The chronicler Pedro Cieza de León states that he built terraces and brought in large quantities of soil to improve the fertility of the valley.

Sixteenth-century Spanish writers, Cabello de Balboa among them, affirm that Sinchi Roca was the first Inca to wear the mascapaicha, later the sign of Inca sovereignty. It was a fringe of red wool, each strand passed through a small gold tube, set above the forehead beneath two or three black and white feathers of the sacred Andean mountain caracara and held by a braided headband called the llautu. The word sinchi later came to mean a warlord, while Capac, one of his father's names, became the title of a sovereign.
sindh: Sindh lies in the south-east of Pakistan and is bounded by the Arabian Sea to the south, Balochistan to the west and Punjab to the north; to the east it shares a border with the Indian states of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Its landscape is mostly alluvial plain on either side of the Indus River, with the Thar Desert in the east and the Kirthar Mountains in the west. The name Sind is a Persian derivative of the Sanskrit sindhu, meaning river, and the Greeks under Alexander the Great called the Indus Indos. The spelling Sindh replaced the older Sind in 1988.

Settled life began around Sindh and Punjab some 9,000 years ago and developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation. Mohenjo-daro, built around 2500 BCE, was one of the largest settlements of that civilisation, with standardised bricks, street grids and covered sewerage. It was abandoned in the 19th century BCE as the civilisation declined, and was not rediscovered until the 1920s. Around 1000 BCE the Indo-Aryan kingdom of Sindhu-Sauvira emerged and lasted until the Achaemenids captured the region in 518 BCE, after whom came the Macedonians, Mauryans, Indo-Greeks, Indo-Scythians, Guptas and Sasanians.

The first Muslim naval raids came in 636 under the caliph Umar. Arab forces conquered Sindh in 712 under the Umayyad Caliphate and made it a province, which laid the foundations of the Muslim period in South Asia. The Habbari Emirate emerged in the 9th century, and between the 11th and 16th centuries the Soomra, Samma and Arghun dynasties ruled, mostly as vassals of the Delhi Sultanate. Akbar, himself born at Umerkot in Sindh, sent an army in 1591 to 1593 to take lower Sindh from the Tarkhan dynasty. Mughal rule ran from the provincial capital Thatta, while the Kalhora dynasty held upper Sindh from Khudabad. The Talpur dynasty ruled from 1783, and the East India Company later captured the province.

Sindh became a separate province in 1936. After the Lahore Resolution of 1940 it was the first province to endorse the Pakistan Movement, and it joined the Dominion of Pakistan in 1947. It was merged into West Pakistan in 1955 and restored as a province in 1970.

Karachi, on the southern coast, is the provincial capital and the largest city. Sindhi, spoken by about 60 per cent of the population at the 2023 census, is the most widely spoken language, and about 90 per cent of residents are Muslim. Sufism is an important marker of Sindhi identity for Muslims and Hindus alike, and the poet Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai lived here. Two World Heritage Sites lie in the province, Mohenjo-daro and the Makli Necropolis near Thatta.
sindhudurg-district: Sindhudurg is the southernmost district of Maharashtra, about 5,207 square kilometres in area. It is bordered on the north by Ratnagiri district, on the south by Goa, on the south-east by Belagavi district of Karnataka, and on the west by the Arabian Sea. To the east, across the crest of the Western Ghats, lies Kolhapur district. It is part of the Konkan, a narrow coastal plain between the Ghats and the sea, with a warm, humid climate and rains from June to October. The district has deposits of iron, bauxite and manganese, and most people speak Malvani, a distinct dialect of Konkani and Marathi, and are fluent in Marathi too.

The name Konkan is of Indian origin and great antiquity, though its derivation has never been definitively explained. Tradition places the Pandavas in the region during the 13th year of their exile. In the middle of the sixth century kings of the Maurya and Nala dynasties appear to have ruled in the Konkan, and Ratnagiri district was under the Silahars. In the 16th century Portuguese power rose on the west coast. A local sultan lost his hold on the district in 1675 with the rise of Shivaji, and the district became part of the Maratha Empire, which ruled it until 1817, when the whole Konkan passed to the British.

Shivaji built the sea fort of Sindhudurg near Malvan, whose name means Sea Fort.
