The city is the seat of the Ss. Cyril and Methodius University, the Macedonian Academy of Sciences and Arts and the National Theatre.
skradin: Skradin lies near the Krka river and at the entrance to the Krka National Park, 17 kilometres from Šibenik and 100 kilometres from Split, in Šibenik-Knin County. The park's main attraction is the series of waterfalls called Slapovi Krke, the biggest of which, Skradinski buk, is named after the town. The municipality had a population of 3,349 at the 2021 census, and the town itself 508.

In antiquity the town was known as Scardon and Scardona, a name found in Strabo, Procopius, Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy. Its ending is thought to be an Illyrian suffix, and the prevailing theory links the root of the name to a term meaning steep. After the Roman conquest Skradin became an administrative and military centre of the region and was mentioned as a municipium in 530. It was destroyed in the Migration Period in the 7th century and restored under Croatian rulers in the early Middle Ages. In the 10th century it was one of the fortified towns of Croatia, the centre of the Skradin županija.

Skradin flourished in the late 13th and early 14th centuries as the capital of the Šubić bans Paul I and Mladen II. They built the Turina fortress on the hill above the harbour, raised the settlement below it to a free city with its own statute and administration, and founded richly endowed monasteries that housed Dominicans, Franciscans and other orders.

The Ottomans conquered the town in 1522 and held it, with some interruptions, until 1684. The Ottoman-Venetian wars devastated it and it was relocated. In October 1683 uskoks from Venetian Dalmatia, mainly Morlachs from Ravni Kotari, took Skradin and other border towns whose Muslim population had fled, and the Venetians finally took it in 1684. It became the centre of a municipality in 1705, and was later occupied by Napoleon as part of the French Empire and then by Austria-Hungary. The centre of the region shifted to Šibenik, and the Diocese of Skradin was abandoned in 1828.
skule-bardsson: Skule was born around 1189 to Bård Guttormsson. Under an arrangement by which he and King Haakon Haakonsson shared power, he held much of the real authority in the kingdom. His centre of power was Nidaros, and he had nobles bound to him as liegemen, such as Endrid Bookling and Alf of Leifa-steads, men whose standing probably lay somewhere between a European count and a high ministerialis. To ease the rivalry, Skule's elder daughter Margaret Skulesdatter was married to King Haakon in 1225, making the duke the king's father-in-law.

Believing that he had too little power, Skule joined the opposition to Haakon from time to time. In 1237, in a further attempt at compromise, he was given the first Norwegian title of duke (hertug), but he later took up his rebellion again, and the Icelander writer Snorre Sturlason was among his allies. Skule also clashed with Arnbjorn Jonsson over the Borg stewardship, which Arnbjorn gave up when Abbot Bjorn showed him that the king had granted it to Skule.

In 1239 his supporters proclaimed him king of Norway at the Øyrating, the traditional thing of Trøndelag. He tried without success to win over his other son-in-law, Jarl Knut Haakonsson. His party was called the Vårbelgs, after the poor-quality spring pelts worn by poor people. Skule raised an army against Haakon, won a battle at Låka in Nannestad, but was beaten at Oslo.

In May 1240 Haakon and his supporters defeated Skule. He took refuge in Elgeseter Priory at Nidaros, but Haakon's men burned down the monastery and killed him. His rising was the last phase of the civil wars that had divided Norway since about 1130, conflicts fed by unclear succession laws, social conditions and the struggle between church and king, and fought in the end between the Bagler and Birkebeiner parties. Henrik Ibsen's play Kongs-Emnerne (1863) dramatises the dispute between Duke Skule and King Haakon.
skype: Skype was founded in 2003 by Niklas Zennström from Sweden and Janus Friis from Denmark, and its software was created by Estonian developers. Friis and one of the Estonians, Toivo Annus, are credited with the idea of cutting the cost of voice calls by using a peer-to-peer protocol like that of Kazaa. An early alpha version was tested in the spring of 2003, and the first public beta was released on 29 August 2003. The name came from the words sky and peer-to-peer, which became Skyper. Some domain names for Skyper were already taken, so the final r was dropped.

Skype was a proprietary telecommunications application best known for videotelephony, videoconferencing and voice calls. It also offered instant messaging, file transfer and paid calls to landline and mobile telephones over traditional networks. Registered users had a unique Skype ID and could hold voice chats between pairs of users and conference calls using a proprietary audio codec. It originally ran as a hybrid of peer-to-peer and client-server systems. An early web page described it as highly secure with end-to-end encryption, but its protocol was never made public, so the claim could not be independently verified.

In September 2005 eBay agreed to acquire Skype Technologies, based in Luxembourg. In 2009 eBay sold 65 per cent of it to Silver Lake, Andreessen Horowitz and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board. Microsoft acquired it on 10 May 2011 for 8.5 billion US dollars and used it to replace its own Windows Live Messenger, which it discontinued in April 2013. In 2011 most of the development team and 44 per cent of the division's employees were in Tallinn and Tartu, in Estonia.

At the end of 2010 there were over 660 million registered users worldwide. In February 2012 there were 34 million users online at one time, and by January 2013 more than 50 million. In 2011 its free version was reported to be used increasingly by teachers and schools for global education projects and language learning. Microsoft retired Skype in favour of Microsoft Teams on 5 May 2025.
slane: The Irish name Baile Shláine means the town of Sláine mac Dela. The village stands on a steep hillside on the left bank of the Boyne, where the N2 road from Dublin to Monaghan meets the N51 from Drogheda to Navan. The Hill of Slane rises 158 metres above its surroundings to the north; in the Metrical Dindshenchas the Fir Bolg king Sláine mac Dela was said to be buried there. The Neolithic tombs of Brú na Bóinne, Newgrange among them, lie 5 kilometres downstream, and the site of the Battle of the Boyne 10 kilometres to the east.

The story of the Paschal fire comes from the highly mythologised seventh-century Life of Patrick by Muirchu moccu Machtheni, which sets it in 433 in defiance of the High King Laoire. Historians and archaeologists agree that Muirchu moved to Slane a fire lit elsewhere; it is somewhat more certain that Patrick appointed Saint Erc bishop of Slane. The Annals of the Four Masters record that in 948 the round tower was burned by the Vikings with relics and people inside, among them Caeineachair, the lector of Slane. The friary on the hill was restored in 1512 and abandoned in 1723.

Richard Fleming built a motte and bailey near the hilltop in the 1170s, and the Flemings were lords of Slane until the Williamite confiscations of the seventeenth century, when the Conyngham family replaced them. The Conynghams rebuilt the castle and laid out the village as a model settlement of the eighteenth century, with four nearly identical Georgian houses at the crossroads known as The Square. United Irishmen were hanged on Gallows Hill in the village after the failed rising of 1798.

The 2022 census counted 1,445 inhabitants. Slane Mill, a five-storey stone building finished in 1766 by the engineer David Jebb after the Boyne Navigation reached Slane, was then the largest flour mill in Ireland, and its 14th-century bridge still carries the N2 across the river. The grounds of Slane Castle, about 1 kilometre upstream, have been the site of large rock concerts since 1981.
slavery: Slavery predates written records and has existed in many cultures. It is rare among hunter-gatherers, because it requires economic surpluses and a substantial population density, and became widespread only with the invention of agriculture in the Neolithic Revolution about 11,000 years ago. It was practised in almost every ancient civilisation, through debt bondage, punishment for crime, the enslavement of prisoners of war, child abandonment and the enslavement of slaves' offspring.

The English word slave came through Old French esclave from Byzantine Greek sklábos. According to a widespread view, known since the 18th century, this derives from the self-name of a Slavic tribe, because its people were often captured and enslaved; the view has been disputed since the 19th century.

Slavery is the ownership of a person as property, especially with regard to their labour, and typically involves compulsory work, with place of work and residence dictated by the holder. Many cases of enslavement followed a breach of the law, indebtedness, military defeat or the pursuit of cheaper labour; others were instituted along lines of race or sex. In chattel slavery the slave is legally the personal property of the owner and can be bought and sold like livestock. Depending on era and country, slaves sometimes had limited legal rights: a 1686 statute in the Province of New York punished those who deliberately killed slaves.

Chattel slavery was widely accepted, and in ancient Greece and the Roman Empire was considered a keystone of society. Other examples are medieval Egypt, Sub-Saharan Africa, Brazil, the antebellum United States, Cuba and Haiti. In the Senegambia region between 1300 and 1900 close to one-third of the population was enslaved, and in early Islamic states of the western Sahel, including Ghana, Mali, Segou and Songhai, about a third.

Economists have argued that slavery becomes desirable where land is abundant and labour scarce, and that slavery and then serfdom declined in Europe as the population grew, then returned in the Americas and Russia where large areas had few inhabitants. It was common where tasks were simple and easy to supervise, as on large plantations of sugarcane and cotton.
slavery-abolition-act-1833: Slavery had been judged to have no legal basis in England in 1772, in Lord Mansfield's judgment in the Somerset case. By 1783 a movement to end the slave trade had begun among the British public, and the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade was founded in 1787. The Slave Trade Act 1807 outlawed the slave trade within the Empire but not slavery, and the Slave Trade Felony Act 1811 made it a felony. The Anti-Slavery Society was founded in London in 1823. In the 1820s abolitionists and the Colonial Office followed a policy of gradualism, beginning with amelioration measures put in place by the Order in Council of 1824 which the colonies only partly carried out.

Two events changed the balance. The Baptist War, a slave revolt in Jamaica organised by the Baptist minister Samuel Sharpe, broke out in the Christmas holiday of 1831 and was suppressed about ten days later, and two parliamentary inquiries followed. The Reform Act 1832 swept away the rotten borough seats that the West India lobby had bought to resist abolition. In March 1833 Edward Stanley, the Colonial Secretary, introduced a bill with two innovations, apprenticeship and compensation for owners; the apprenticeship was cut from twelve years to six, and compensation rose from 15 to 20 million pounds. Members of the Commons, anxious about property rights, approved the full amount.

The act passed the Commons on 7 August 1833 and the Lords on 20 August, received royal assent on 28 August and came into force on 1 August 1834. Children under six were freed at once. Others became apprentices: field workers, the praedial class, until 1 August 1840, and the non-praedial class, including house servants, until 1 August 1838. Apprentices owed up to 45 hours of unpaid work a week in return for food, clothing, medical care and housing, and could buy their discharge.

The act excluded the territories of the East India Company, Ceylon and Saint Helena, which the Indian Slavery Act 1843 brought in. The act gave 20 million pounds to owners, not to the enslaved, financed by a loan of 15 million pounds from Nathan Mayer Rothschild and Moses Montefiore. About 42,000 people in the colonies and 3,500 in Britain received compensation. Antigua and Bermuda gave immediate freedom instead of apprenticeship.

Abolitionists opposed apprenticeship from the start. After a campaign in 1837 and 1838, and an amendment of April 1838 that banned flogging of apprentices, the colonial legislatures ended apprenticeship on 1 August 1838. Barbados acted first, on 16 May, and Jamaica was the last, in the middle of June. Around 800,000 freed slaves were attested in the claims process. The act was repealed by the Statute Law (Repeals) Act 1998, and other laws still forbid slavery.
slavko-kvaternik: Slavko Kvaternik was born on 25 August 1878 in Moravice, then called Komorske Moravice, in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia of Austria-Hungary. His father Ljudevit was a postman, and his mother Marija, née Frank, was Catholic and of German descent from Bavaria. He was educated at a military academy and served in the Austro-Hungarian Army in the First World War, receiving the German Iron Cross 1st Class in 1918. He married Olga Frank, daughter of the Croatian nationalist politician Josip Frank, who was of Jewish descent and had converted to Catholicism. Their son Dido became a member of the Ustasha.

In 1918 Kvaternik joined the newly formed National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and became its Chief of General Staff. At the end of that year he commanded Croatian troops in the successful occupation of Međimurje. He later transferred to the Royal Yugoslav Army, where he stayed until 1921. In 1929 he was one of the founders of the Ustasha, the Croatian Revolutionary Movement, in Italy.

After Germany invaded Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941, the Ustaše formed their government under Ante Pavelić. Four days later Kvaternik proclaimed the Independent State of Croatia and formed its first Ustasha government. At his request, Vladko Maček, leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, who had refused to head the new state for the Germans, told the people to cooperate with the new regime. Kvaternik was commander-in-chief of the armed forces, with the title of vojskovođa, or marshal, and was the second most powerful man in the state as a member of the Doglavnik's Council.

In May 1942 he ordered the deportation of Serbs from 12 villages in Petrinja County and six in Glina County to the Jasenovac and Stara Gradiška concentration camps. About 1,200 to 1,250 people were deported from Petrinja County, and at least 471 of those deported from Glina County died in the camps.

Olga Frank had committed suicide at the end of August 1941, probably because of her Jewish origins and the roles of her husband and especially her son in the Independent State of Croatia. After the war Kvaternik was captured by the United States Army and extradited to Yugoslavia, where he was tried and sentenced to death for crimes committed under the regime. He was hanged in Zagreb on 7 June 1947. He had received the Military Order of the Iron Trefoil, first class, which gave him the title of vitez, or knight.
slavonia: Slavonia lies in the Pannonian Basin, largely bordered by the Danube, Drava and Sava rivers. Its west consists of the Sava and Drava valleys and the mountains around the Požega Valley, and its east of plains, under a moderate continental climate. The name comes from the Slavs who settled there and called themselves Slověne; the land between the Sava and the Drava was Slověnьje in Proto-Slavic. Finds of the Starčevo culture near Slavonski Brod are dated to 6100–5200 BCE, and finds of the Vučedol culture near Vukovar to 3000–2500 BCE.

The Romans completed their conquest in 11 BCE and created the province of Illyricum, which was soon renamed Pannonia. After the Western Roman Empire fell, the Ostrogoths and then the Lombards held the area until the Lombards withdrew in 568, and Avars and Slavs controlled it by 582. A Slavic principality whose rulers were vassals of the Francs followed the fall of the Avar Khaganate, before Hungarian tribes overwhelmed it. Croatian influence spread north under King Tomislav, and in 1102 Croatia and Hungary entered a personal union under Coloman. From the 13th century a separate ban governed a Kingdom of Slavonia, and Croatia and Slavonia shared one ban from 1476.

The Ottomans took Đakovo in 1536 and Požega in 1537, and completed their conquest of Slavonia in 1552 with the capture of Virovitica. Požega became the chief Ottoman centre. The frontier steadied after the Battle of Sisak in 1593. During the Great Turkish War the Ottomans left the region between 1684 and 1691, and the Treaty of Karlowitz transferred it to the Habsburgs, with Osijek as the administrative centre of the restored kingdom. The Croatian-Hungarian Settlement of 1868 united Croatia and Slavonia, and in 1918 the region joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs and then Yugoslavia. Fighting in 1991–1995 included the Battle of Vukovar in 1991.

Slavonia roughly corresponds to five Croatian counties: Brod-Posavina, Osijek-Baranja, Požega-Slavonia, Virovitica-Podravina and Vukovar-Syrmia. Its largest city is Osijek, followed by Slavonski Brod and Vinkovci. Tamburica music is characteristic of the region, and the traditional song form bećarac is recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage. Erdut, Ilok and Kutjevo are centres of winemaking.
slavonic-bulgarian-history: Paisius travelled widely in the Ottoman Empire and beyond to collect sources. In 1758 he went to the monastery of Sremski Karlovci, and he drew on the Russian translation of Caesar Baronius's Annales Ecclesiastici, Mavro Orbini's Kingdom of the Slavs, monastic registers and chronicles, marginal notes in psalters, charters of donation issued by Bulgarian rulers, and lives of Bulgarian saints kept in monastic libraries. He began intensive work on the manuscript at Hilandar in 1761, but disagreements with the other monks led him to move to the Zograf Monastery, where he finished it. It is his only literary work, and he distributed the manuscript himself.

The book has an introduction, a preface adapted from Baronius on the value of history, seven chapters and an autobiographical epilogue. It traces the medieval Bulgarian state through its battles and its struggle against the Byzantine Empire to its fall under Ottoman rule, and devotes a whole chapter to Cyril and Methodius and the Glagolitic script. Paisius regarded the Bulgarians as descendants of Meshech. He used "Greek" for the Byzantines and gave the word an ethnic meaning, depicting Greeks as cunning and haughty and blaming them for the Ottoman conquest, and he was the first author to call Ottoman rule a yoke and slavery.

Sophronius of Vratsa made the first copy in 1765 at Paisius's request, and 60 copies are known. It was printed in Hristaki Pavlovich's Tsarstvenik, used in Bulgarian schools, but became popular only after the mid-19th century. In the 1980s the Bulgarian Committee for State Security stole the original from Zograf, leaving a copy in its place; the theft caused a scandal when revealed in the 1990s, and the manuscript was returned on 12 January 1998. Historians judge it more polemic than history: Richard Frucht calls it filled with self-serving errors, and Raymond Detrez finds little scientific value in it.
slavs: The oldest mention of the Slavic name is from the 6th century, when Procopius wrote Sklaboi and related forms in Byzantine Greek and his contemporary Jordanes wrote Sclaveni in Latin. It is usually derived from slovo, word, so that it meant people who speak the same language, in contrast to the Slavic word for Germans, němьcь, meaning mute people.

Roman sources of the 1st and 2nd centuries refer to early Slavic peoples as Veneti, living east of the Suebi and west of the Sarmatians between the upper Vistula and the Dnieper. The Slavs, called Antes and Sclaveni, first appear in Byzantine records in the early 6th century, emerging from the area of the Carpathian Mountains, the lower Danube and the Black Sea to invade the Danubian provinces of the Eastern Empire under Justinian I.

The westward movement of Germanic tribes in the 5th and 6th centuries, together with that of the Huns and later the Avars and Bulgars, began the great migration of the Slavs, who settled lands the Germanic tribes had left. They moved west towards the Oder and the Elbe-Saale line, south into Bohemia, Moravia, the Pannonian plain and the Balkans, and north along the upper Dnieper. By the end of the 6th century they had settled the Eastern Alps.

In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo supported the Slavs against their Avar rulers and became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first known Slav state in Central Europe. The First Bulgarian Empire was founded in 681 as an alliance of the ruling Bulgars and the numerous Slavs, and Old Church Slavonic became its official language in 864. The Principality of Serbia dates from the 8th century, and the Duchy of Bohemia and Kievan Rus' from the 9th.

From the mid-19th century a pan-Slavic movement stressed the common heritage of the Slavic peoples, especially in the Balkans, where South Slavs had long been ruled by other empires. In 1918 the Slavs established Czechoslovakia, the Second Polish Republic and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes.

Procopius, in 545, described the Sclaveni and Antae as having once shared the name Sporoi. He wrote that they lived under a democracy, believed in one god, the maker of lightning, to whom they sacrificed, and lived in scattered housing, often changing settlement. In war they were mainly foot soldiers with shields, spears and bows and little armour.
slobodan-milosevic: Milošević was born in Požarevac, four months after the Axis invasion of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and was raised during the occupation. His ancestral roots were in Montenegro. His father, a Serbian Orthodox theologian, died by suicide in 1962, and his mother, a teacher and active member of the Communist Party, in 1972. He studied law at the University of Belgrade, where he befriended Ivan Stambolić, whose uncle Petar Stambolić had been president of the Serbian Executive Council. The connection proved crucial for his career, as the two climbed through the party hierarchy.

Milošević was elected president of the Belgrade city committee of the League of Communists in 1984. In 1987 he emerged as a force in Serbian politics by declaring support for Serbs in Kosovo, who said the provincial government, dominated by ethnic Albanians, was oppressing them; he called for reducing Kosovo's autonomy. From 1988 the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution, a series of rallies in Vojvodina and Montenegro, led to the resignation of their governments and the election of officials allied with him. His supporters call it a genuine grass-roots movement.

He became president of Serbia in 1989 and led the Socialist Party of Serbia from its foundation in 1990. Under United Nations sanctions during the Yugoslav Wars, Serbia's economy collapsed. In 1997 he became president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Counteraction against the Kosovo Liberation Army escalated into armed conflict in 1998 and NATO air strikes in 1999. After a disputed presidential election in 2000 he resigned amid demonstrations.

The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia indicted him in May 1999 for crimes in Kosovo, and later for Croatia and Bosnia, including genocide. Arrested in 2001 by Yugoslav authorities on suspicion of corruption, he was extradited to the tribunal, which he denounced as illegal; he refused counsel and conducted his own defence. He was found dead in his cell in The Hague on 11 March 2006, of a heart attack, before the trial concluded. Later verdicts found him part of a joint criminal enterprise that used violence to remove Croats, Bosniaks and Albanians from parts of Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo. He remains a controversial figure in Serbia and the Balkans.
slovakia: Slovakia covers about 49,000 km2 and is mostly mountainous, with the Carpathian Mountains across most of the northern half. The Tatra Mountains hold 29 peaks above 2,500 metres, and Gerlachovský štít, at 2,655 metres, is the highest point in the country. The largest lowland is the Danubian Lowland in the southwest, followed by the Eastern Slovak Lowland in the southeast. Forests cover 41% of the land, nine national parks cover 6.5%, and hundreds of caves lie under the mountains, five of them on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The name means the Land of the Slavs, and the present Slovak form Slovensko is first attested in 1675.

The oldest human artefacts, stone tools dated to 270,000 BCE, come from near Nové Mesto nad Váhom, and a Neanderthal cranium of about 200,000 BCE was found near Gánovce. Slavs arrived in the 5th and 6th centuries, and parts of the territory came under the Avar Khaganate before the Principality of Nitra was annexed by the Principality of Moravia, later Great Moravia. The land passed into the Principality of Hungary, which became the Kingdom of Hungary in 1000. The Mongol invasion of 1241 and 1242 destroyed much of it, and the south was part of Ottoman provinces in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Slovak Uprising of 1848 did not achieve its aim but helped to cement a Slovak national identity. Czechoslovakia was proclaimed in 1918, with its borders set by the Treaty of Saint Germain in 1919 and the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The first Slovak Republic, established in 1939 as a one-party clerical fascist client state under Nazi Germany, joined the Axis in 1940. Czechoslovakia became a communist state after the Soviet-backed coup of 1948, the Prague Spring was suppressed by the Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968, and the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule.

Slovakia became independent on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia, and its constitution, ratified on 1 September 1992, took effect that day. It is a parliamentary democratic republic with a directly elected president of limited powers and a 150-seat National Council. It joined the European Union and NATO in 2004, the Schengen Area in 2007 and the eurozone in 2009.

The 2021 census recorded 83.8% Slovaks and 7.8% Hungarians, the largest minority, and 55.8% of the population identified as Catholic. About 90,000 Jews lived in Slovakia before the Second World War, and most were murdered in the Holocaust; about 2,300 remain.
slovenes: In the 6th century CE Slavic people settled the region between the Alps and the Adriatic Sea in two waves: the first came from the Moravian lands around 550, and the second, from the southeast, followed the migration of the Lombards to Italy in 568. From 623 to 658 Slavic peoples between the upper Elbe River and the Karawanks mountain range united under King Samo in what is known as Samo's Tribal Union. It collapsed after his death, but a smaller principality, Carantania, remained, centred on present-day Carinthia. Facing the danger of Avar tribes, the Carantanians accepted a union with Bavaria in 745 and later recognised Frankish rule and accepted Christianity.

The last Slavic state formation in the region, the principality of Prince Kocel, lost its independence in 874. Slovene ethnic territory then shrank under pressure from Germans in the west and the arrival of Hungarians in the Pannonian plain, and it stabilised in its present form in the 15th century. The first mentions of a common Slovene identity date from the 16th century, when the Protestant preacher Primož Trubar and his followers printed the first books in Slovene and Jurij Dalmatin translated the whole Bible.

Under Maria Theresa and Emperor Joseph II, reforms included compulsory primary education in Slovene in 1774, and a national revival began. In 1848 the first Slovene political programme, United Slovenia, demanded an autonomous kingdom of all Slovene-speaking lands within the Austrian Empire. It failed, but it remained a platform for later activity, including mass rallies called tabori. The first Slovene political parties appeared in the 1890s, all loyal to Austria.

After the First World War most Slovenes joined the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, then the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. In the territory given to Italy, about 327,000 of 1.3 million Slovenes were subjected to forced Fascist Italianization. In the Second World War Slovenia was divided among Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy and Hungary. After the war it formed part of socialist Yugoslavia, and in 1991 it became independent after a brief ten-day war.

Most ethnic Slovenes are Roman Catholic, with historical Protestant minorities, especially Lutherans in Prekmurje. The Freising manuscripts are the first written words in Slovene. Anton Tomaž Linhart was the first to define Slovenes as a separate branch of the Slavic people, in his work of 1791. Between 1880 and the First World War the largest numbers of Slovenes emigrated to America, and the largest group in the United States settled in Cleveland, Ohio.
slovenia: Slovenia covers 20,271 km2 and is mostly mountainous and forested. Four major European geographic regions meet there: the Alps, the Dinarides, the Pannonian Plain and the Mediterranean Sea. The highest peak, Triglav, at 2,864 metres, appears on the national coat of arms and flag. The Adriatic coastline stretches approximately 47 kilometres, the southwest has a limestone Karst Plateau of underground rivers, gorges and caves, and the landscape of the northeast is essentially flat. The name means land of the Slavs.

Evidence of habitation dates to around 250,000 years ago. A pierced cave bear bone from Divje Babe cave near Cerkno, dated to 43100 ± 700 years before present, is considered a kind of flute and possibly the oldest musical instrument discovered. Pile dwellings over 4,500 years old in the Ljubljana Marsh are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Ljubljana Marshes Wooden Wheel is the world's oldest wooden wheel. In Roman times the area was divided between Venetia et Histria and the provinces of Pannonia and Noricum, with posts at Emona (Ljubljana), Poetovio (Ptuj) and Celeia (Celje). In 394 the Battle of the Frigidus took place in the Vipava Valley, where Theodosius I defeated the usurper Eugenius.

Slavic tribes migrated to the Alpine area in the early Middle Ages. From 623 or 624 King Samo united the Alpine and Western Slavs against the Avars, and after his death around 658 the ancestors of the Slovenes formed Carantania and Carniola. Charlemagne decisively defeated the Avars in 803. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes was formed in December 1918 and became known as Yugoslavia in 1929. Nazi Germany, Fascist Italy, Hungary and the Independent State of Croatia partitioned Slovenia in 1941.

Slovenia was established in 1945 as one of six republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and modern Slovenia emerged in June 1991, when it declared independence and became a sovereign state after the brief Ten-Day War. It is a parliamentary republic whose head of state is a president elected for five years, and legislative power rests mainly with the 90-member National Assembly. In 2007 it was the first new member state of the European Union to adopt the euro. The population is about 2.1 million, and Slovenes make up 83.1% of the inhabitants. Four sites are on UNESCO's World Heritage list, among them the Škocjan Caves and the Idrija Mercury mining site.
slupsk: Słupsk lies on the Słupia River in northern Poland, in the historical region of Pomerania, or more exactly in the part now called Central Pomerania. The town grew from a few medieval settlements on the banks of the river, at a ford on a trade route linking the territories of the present Pomeranian and West Pomeranian voivodeships. This led to the building of a grod, a West Slavic fortified settlement, on an islet in the river. It stood on an artificial hill, was protected by a palisade and had a natural moat formed by branches of the Słupia, and swamps around it gave good defence.

Records confirm that the area was part of the Polish realm under Mieszko I and in the 11th century. Słupsk received city rights in 1265. By the 14th century it was a centre of local administration and trade and an associate of the Hanseatic League. Between 1368 and 1478 it was the residence of the Dukes of Słupsk, who until 1474 were vassals of the Kingdom of Poland. Under a peace treaty Słupsk became part of Brandenburg-Prussia, and in 1815 it joined the new Prussian Province of Pomerania.

As Stolp, the town was not directly affected by fighting in the First World War. It stood close to the border of the Polish Corridor, and Polish claims to it were refused during the Treaty of Versailles negotiations. In the interwar years it was the regional centre of the eastern part of Eastern Pomerania and was known as Little Paris. During the Second World War the Nazis created a labour camp in 1941 and, in 1944, a subcamp of the Stutthof concentration camp at the railway repair works, where over 600 Jewish prisoners were held, and a forced labour camp for women and children, in which over 200 children died.

After the war the city became part of Poland. Most of the German population fled or was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement, and Poles, many of them expelled from the former eastern territories annexed by the Soviet Union, settled the city.

Słupsk is a city with powiat rights in the Pomeranian Voivodeship and the seat of Słupsk County. From 1975 to 1998 it was the capital of its own voivodeship. Its monuments include the Renaissance Ducal Castle, which houses the Museum of Middle Pomerania, and the Castle Mill, the oldest preserved industrial structure in Poland. The city is also the seat of the Pomeranian University in Słupsk.
slutsk: Slutsk was first mentioned in writing in 1116. It was at first part of the Principality of Turov and Pinsk but became the capital of a separate principality in 1160, and from the 1320s or 1330s it belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Casimir IV Jagiellon vested it with Magdeburg town rights in 1441. It was a private town of the Olelkovich and Radziwiłł families, who made it a centre of the Polish Reformed Church with a gymnasium and a strong fortress. Scottish immigrants settled there in the middle of the 17th century.
Later the town became known for kontusz belts, among the most expensive garments of the szlachta, so that such belts worn over the żupan were often called belts of Slutsk whatever their real origin.

In 1778 it became a county seat within the Nowogródek Voivodeship, and after the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 it was part of the Russian Empire. Germany occupied it in 1918, and Poland held it in 1919 and 1920. In 1920 it was the centre of a major anti-Bolshevik uprising known as the Slutsk defence action.

The first Jews are recorded in 1583, and the community was formally recognised in 1601. By 1691 Slutsk was one of the five leading communities of the Lithuanian Jewish Council. In 1750 there were 1,593 Jews, a third of the population, and three quarters of the town's merchants were Jewish. By 1897 there were 10,264 Jewish inhabitants, 77 percent of the population. The town was important for Torah study, and the Slutsk-Kletsk Yeshiva was founded there in 1883 by Rabbi Yaakov Dovid Wilovsky.

German forces occupied Slutsk on 26 June 1941. On 27 and 28 October 1941 Jews were taken to pits in the Gorovakha ravine and shot in what is known as the Slutsk affair, with 3,400 victims by German sources and 8,000 by Soviet ones. Thousands more were killed in 1942, and the town ghetto was liquidated on 8 February 1943. The Red Army recaptured the town on 30 June 1944.

Slutsk lies on the Sluch River 105 kilometres south of Minsk and is the administrative centre of Slutsk District in the Minsk Region of Belarus. Its symbol is the woven belt, to which the Museum of the History of Slutsk Belts is dedicated.
smallpox-vaccine: Smallpox in its severe form, variola major, killed up to 35 per cent of those infected in some outbreaks. Before the vaccine, immunity was induced by inoculation, or variolation, which probably occurred in Africa and China well before it reached Europe. The first clear reference is by the Chinese author Wan Quan in a work of 1549, and in China powdered smallpox scabs were blown up the noses of the healthy; the method carried a mortality of 0.5 to 2.0 per cent, against 20 to 30 per cent for the disease itself. Two reports on the Chinese practice reached the Royal Society in London in 1700.

Edward Jenner was born in Berkeley, England, and as a child was variolated and nearly died. As an apprentice he noticed that people who caught cowpox from cattle did not catch smallpox, though the idea was not taken up at the time. In 1768 Dr John Fewster had reported that variolation caused no reaction in people who had had cowpox. Jenner trained in London from 1770 to 1772 as the private pupil of John Hunter, and in 1796 demonstrated that cowpox infection conferred immunity to smallpox.

The word vaccine comes from Jenner's term variolae vaccinae, smallpox of the cow, from the Latin vacca. Jenner's friend Richard Dunning first printed vaccination in 1800, and in 1881 Louis Pasteur proposed widening both terms to cover other protective inoculations, to honour Jenner. The vaccine virus is called vaccinia, and in 1939 Allan Watt Downie showed that it was serologically distinct from cowpox. Genome sequencing later found it most closely related to horsepox, identified in the 2010s as its likely ancestor.

From 1796 to the 1880s the vaccine passed from arm to arm. It was maintained in cattle from the 1840s, and calf lymph became the leading vaccine in the 1880s. Without adequate safety methods, contaminated vaccine at times transmitted erysipelas, tetanus, septicaemia and tuberculosis, and arm-to-arm transfer risked syphilis. Second-generation vaccines, grown in membranes or cell cultures, gave greater purity, and third-generation ones used attenuated vaccinia strains.

An international search for outbreaks, backed by vaccination, began in 1967 under a World Health Organization unit headed by Donald Henderson. The last case in the Americas was in Brazil in 1971, in south-east Asia in Indonesia in 1972, on the Indian subcontinent in Bangladesh in 1975, and the last endemic case anywhere occurred in Somalia in October 1977. A commission chaired by Frank Fenner concluded in December 1979 that smallpox had been eradicated, and the WHO endorsed this in May 1980. After the attacks of 2001 many governments rebuilt vaccine stockpiles, and smallpox vaccines were later used against the mpox outbreak, for which the WHO declared an emergency on 23 July 2022.
smbat-i-of-armenia: Smbat I, born about 850, was the son of Ashot I, the first king of the Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia. When Ashot I died in 890 Smbat was campaigning in Gugark and could not attend the funeral. He took the throne after the mourning rites, but his uncle Abas Sparapet, the Commander-in-Chief, also wanted the crown and withdrew to the district of Vanand to await a chance to rebel. The Georgian prince Adarnase Bagratuni dressed Smbat in royal garments as a sign of recognition, and Abas, seeing this as betrayal, had Adarnase arrested. After the Catholicos of Armenia intervened, Smbat resumed hostilities, and Abas withdrew into Kars and sought peace. Smbat secured the throne in 892.

In 892 the Arab Caliphate recognised Smbat's authority, and he captured Dvin, the last Arab stronghold in Armenia. In 893 he concluded a largely commercial treaty with the Byzantine Empire under Leo VI, which also served as an alliance. Afshin, the ruler of the Sajid emirate of Azerbaijan, invaded in protest but withdrew after Smbat's diplomacy. An earthquake in 894 left Dvin half ruined and killed about 70,000 people. Afshin invaded again and was defeated near Doghs in Aragatsotn. Smbat then campaigned in Gugark, crowned Adarnase Bagratuni King of Georgia in 899 and, in 903, conquered the Kingdom of Abkhazia and annexed districts including Klarjeti and Ardahan.

In 901 Yusuf succeeded Afshin and took Dvin, which Smbat recaptured. Yusuf encouraged the rebellion of Gagik Artsruni and sent him a crown, recognising him as king. In 909 he invaded again, and in 910 Smbat was defeated at Dzknavachar after the Sevordi princes betrayed him, while Arab emirs who had paid him tribute revolted. Smbat took refuge in the Kapuyt Fortress, which Yusuf besieged.

Smbat surrendered in 914 in the hope of ending the Arab onslaught after Yusuf guaranteed his safety, but Yusuf broke his oath. He took him to Yernjak and tortured him, and tried to make him order the defenders of the Armenian fortresses to yield, which Smbat refused. Yusuf had him beheaded and his body crucified at the gates of Dvin. The contemporary Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi writes that the place where the cross stood became a site of pilgrimage for Christians and non-Christians. Later Armenian authors said the body was taken down and brought to the monastery at Artsvanist. He is remembered as Smbat the Martyr.
smendes: Smendes may have been a son of Hrere, Chief of the Harem of Amun-Re and probably the wife of a high priest of Amun. If so, he was the brother of Nodjmet and the brother-in-law of the High Priests Herihor and Piankh. He married Tentamun, likely a daughter of Ramesses IX, and he is described as son-in-law of Ramesses XI. His birth name was Nesbanebdjed, meaning He of the Ram, Lord of Mendes; Smendes is the Greek form used by later writers such as Josephus and Sextus Africanus.

Smendes succeeded Ramesses XI, the last ruler of the Twentieth Dynasty, and founded the Twenty-First. He may have resided at Tanis or at Memphis, and blocks and statues at Tanis bear his names, some of them reused from earlier Ramesside kings. Tanis became the capital under Psusennes I, but the move from Pi-Ramesses may have begun with Smendes.

He ruled a divided Egypt. His nominal authority in Upper Egypt is attested by a quarry stela at Ed-Dibabiya, which tells how he, residing in Memphis, ordered repairs to the temple of Luxor after a flood threat, and by a graffito at the Temple of Monthu at Karnak. Middle and Upper Egypt were effectively under the High Priests of Amun, such as Pinedjem I, Masaharta and Menkheperre.

Manetho's Epitome assigns him twenty-six years. A date in Year 25 on the Banishment Stela, recording how Menkheperre put down a revolt at Thebes and exiled its leaders to the oases of the Western Desert, can refer only to Smendes. His throne name, Hedjkheperre Setepenre, was later adopted by five kings, among them Shoshenq I.

He appears in the Report of Wenamun, a story in which a priest of Amun sent by Herihor to Byblos for timber first calls on Smendes at Tanis and receives a ship from him. Egyptologists question its historical accuracy, and since Karl Jansen-Winkeln proposed reversing the order of Herihor and Piankh, Arno Egberts has argued that the tale is set in Smendes's fifth year. He was succeeded by Amenemnisu, who may have been his son. His tomb has not been found; a canopic jar of his is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
smithsonian: The Smithsonian Institution was founded on 10 August 1846 by act of the United States Congress, which created it for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. It is named after its founding donor, the British scientist James Smithson. It operates as a trust instrumentality and is not formally part of any of the three branches of the federal government, and the legislation called for a Board of Regents to govern it, which includes the chief justice and the vice president as ex officio members.

Earlier, in 1816, a group of Washington citizens had founded the Columbian Institute for the Promotion of Arts and Sciences, chartered by Congress in 1818, whose members included John Quincy Adams, Andrew Jackson and Henry Clay. Its charter expired in 1838.

The first secretary, Joseph Henry, wanted the institution to be a centre of scientific research, but it also became the depository for various Washington and United States government collections. The thousands of specimens and artefacts gathered by the United States Exploring Expedition, which circumnavigated the globe between 1838 and 1842, joined the collections, as did the finds of military and civilian surveys of the American West, including many Native American artefacts. In 1846 the regents planned weather observation, and in 1847 money was appropriated for meteorological research. From 1857 to 1866 it was a magnet for young scientists who formed the Megatherium Club.

Building the Smithsonian Institution Building, known as the Castle and designed by James Renwick Jr., began in 1849, and it opened in 1855. The Arts and Industries Building followed in 1881, built after the Philadelphia Centennial Exposition of 1876 earned enough income. The National Zoological Park, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, opened in 1889, and the National Museum of Natural History in June 1911. The institution was originally organised as the United States National Museum, a name that ceased to exist administratively in 1967.

Today the Smithsonian is a group of museums, libraries, research centres and a zoo, mostly in Washington, D.C., with others in Maryland, New York and Virginia, and it has affiliated museums across the United States and in Panama and Puerto Rico. Its collections are among the largest of any museum complex, and the National Museum of Natural History holds most of the items, mainly scientific specimens. Only a small fraction is on public display at any time, and the rest is kept for research. Almost all visitors are admitted without charge.

In 2020 it released about 2.8 million images and 173 years of staff-created data into the public domain under a Creative Commons Zero dedication. It publishes Smithsonian magazine, begun at the suggestion of Secretary S. Dillon Ripley, and awards such as the James Smithson Medal, established in 1965.
smolensk: Smolensk stands on the Dnieper River, 360 kilometres west-southwest of Moscow, and is the administrative centre of Smolensk Oblast. In the early medieval period it lay on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks. Rus' travellers sailed up the Western Dvina and portaged their boats to the upper Dnieper, and at Smolensk they are supposed to have mended leaks with tar, which one explanation gives for the name. Others derive it from the Smolnya River or from a Slavic tribe, the Smolyans. The Byzantine emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus described the city around 950 as a key station on the route.

The Ustyug Chronicle of the 16th century first mentions Smolensk under 863, and the Primary Chronicle names it as the centre of the Krivichi. After Oleg the Wise took Kiev in 882, it became part of Kievan Rus'. The Principality of Smolensk was founded in 1054 and by the end of the 12th century was one of the strongest in Eastern Europe, its princes often holding the Kievan throne. The Svirskaya church of 1197 was admired as the most beautiful building east of Kiev. The city had its own veche from the start.

Spared by Mongol armies in 1240, Smolensk paid tribute to the Golden Horde and became a pawn between Lithuania and Moscow. Vytautas the Great of Lithuania took it in 1395, 1404 and 1408, and Vasily III of Russia took it in 1514. Boris Godunov fortified it, building the stone kremlin of 1597-1602, the largest in Russia. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth captured it in 1611 after a siege of twenty months and kept it through the Smolensk War that began in 1632. Russia retook it on 23 September 1654, and the Truce of Andrusovo in 1667 ended Polish claims.

Smolensk was the seat of a governorate from 1708. In August 1812 Napoleon entered the city after a battle in which total losses were estimated at 30,000, and the Eagles monument of 1912 marks the centenary. German forces occupied it in 1941-1943. Some 18 kilometres away, at Katyn in 1940, the NKVD murdered some 22,000 Polish prisoners of war. The population was 316,570 in the 2021 census.
sneferu: Sneferu, whose name means He has perfected me, was the first pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty. Estimates of the length of his reign vary: the Turin Canon gives 24 years, now considered an underestimate, while Rolf Krauss suggests 30 years and Rainer Stadelmann 48. The Papyrus Prisse, a Middle Kingdom source, names Huni as his predecessor and calls Sneferu a beneficent king. His main wife, Hetepheres I, was the mother of Khufu, who built the Great Pyramid at Giza. Among his children were the viziers Nefermaat I and Kanefer, Ankhhaf, and Rahotep, high priest of Re at Heliopolis.

Sneferu's building needed labour and materials. The Palermo Stone records his smiting of Nubia, with 7,000 captives and 200,000 sheep and goats brought back, the building of boats of cedar, and the arrival of 40 ships laden with wood. His campaigns in Libya are credited with 11,000 prisoners and 13,100 head of cattle, and there was activity at the turquoise mines of Sinai. Such raids must have been devastating for the peoples attacked, and it has been suggested that the campaigns into Nubia contributed to the spread of the A-Group culture there.

Three pyramids are attributed to Sneferu, and under him pyramid design changed from stepped to true. At Meidum the structure was first conceived with seven steps and later given a limestone facing to make a smooth, angled pyramid, though some scholars once credited it to Huni. At Dahshur, the Bent Pyramid changes its angle of inclination from 55 degrees to about 43 degrees in its upper levels, probably because of unstable construction layers. Its top layers were laid horizontally, ending the step-pyramid concept. The Red Pyramid, his last, has a simpler interior, and fragments of human remains found in its passage in 1950 may or may not be his. Cedar for his building was most likely brought from Lebanon.
snorri-sturluson: Snorri Sturluson was born in 1179 at Hvammur í Dölum into the wealthy Sturlungar clan, the son of Sturla Þórðarson and Guðný Böðvarsdóttir. At the age of three or four he was sent to be fostered at Oddi by Jón Loftsson, a relative of the Norwegian royal family, after a lawsuit involving his father was settled. At Oddi he received an excellent education and made connections that helped his later career. In 1199 he married Herdís, daughter of Bersi Vermundarson, and inherited an estate at Borg and a chieftainship. In 1206 he settled at Reykholt.

Snorri became known as a poet and worked as a lawyer. In 1215 he became lawspeaker of the Althing. In 1218 he sailed to Norway at the royal invitation and became acquainted with the young King Haakon IV and his co-regent Jarl Skúli, who gave him gifts and made him a skutilsvein. He returned in 1220 and was lawspeaker again from 1222 to 1232, supporting union with Norway, which made him enemies among the chiefs. From 1224 to 1230 he was the most powerful chieftain in Iceland.

Feuding followed, above all with his brother Sighvatur and nephew Sturla Sighvatsson, who drove him into the countryside with a force of 1000 men. In 1237 he went to Norway again. After Sighvatur and four of his sons were killed at the Battle of Örlygsstaðir in August 1238, Snorri disobeyed the king's order to stay and returned to Iceland in 1239, his words út vil ek, "I will go home", becoming proverbial.

Haakon sent agents to Gissur Þorvaldsson with a secret letter ordering Snorri to be killed or captured. Gissur led seventy men in a raid on Snorri's house at Reykholt in the autumn of 1241, and Snorri was killed in the cellar. His reported last words were Eigi skal hǫggva, "Do not strike!". The killing was unpopular in Iceland and Norway, and in 1262 the Althing ratified union with Norway.

Snorri's writings, the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, shed light on peoples of northern Europe in periods for which information is scarce, including relations between England and Scandinavia in the 10th and 11th centuries, and give an early account of the discovery of Vinland. The historian Halvdan Koht judged his work unsurpassed among the historical literature of the Middle Ages, while Gwyn Jones called him never servile to fact. In the mid-19th century Heimskringla helped to form Norwegian national identity.
snowdonia: Snowdonia, or Eryri, is a mountainous region and national park in North Wales. It contains all 15 mountains in Wales over 3,000 feet, including Snowdon, called Yr Wyddfa in Welsh, which is the highest in Wales and in Britain south of the Scottish Highlands. These peaks belong to the Snowdon, Glyderau and Carneddau ranges in the north, with the Moelwynion and Moel Hebog ranges to the south. Further south lie the Rhinogydd, Cadair Idris and the Aran ranges. Llyn Tegid, or Bala Lake, is the largest natural water body in Wales.

Glaciation through a succession of ice ages carved the rocky landscape from folded and faulted sedimentary and igneous rocks, and the last ice age ended just over 11,500 years ago. Visiting Cwm Idwal in 1841, Charles Darwin realised that the landscape was the product of glaciation. Low-grade metamorphism of Cambrian and Ordovician mudstones produced the slates whose extraction once formed the mainstay of the local economy.

The earliest evidence for human settlement dates from around 4000–3000 BCE, with extensive traces of prehistoric field systems, enclosures and hut circles. There are Neolithic and Bronze Age burial chambers such as Bryn Cader Faner and Iron Age hillforts such as Bryn y Castell near Ffestiniog. The Romans finally conquered the region by 77–78 CE, and remains of their marching and practice camps survive, with a fort and amphitheatre at Tomen y Mur. Roads connected the area with Segontium, now Caernarfon, and with Deva Victrix, now Chester.

The economy was traditionally centred on farming, and from the early 19th century increasingly on mining and quarrying. The region was once the most important producer of slate in the world. Sheep farming remains central to the farming economy, and large areas were planted with conifers in the 20th century.

Snowdon means snow hill, from the Old English snāw and dūn, and is first recorded as Snawdune in 1095. Snowdonia is derived from it and is first recorded in 1284, but was probably not in common use until it was re-popularised in the 19th century. Eryri is first recorded in 1191 and probably derives from eryr, meaning ridge; a popular reading, place of the eagle, rests on the fact that eryr also means eagle.

Before 1951 Snowdonia generally meant a smaller upland area centred on the Snowdon massif. The national park, established in October 1951, covers 823 square miles and most of central and southern Gwynedd and the western part of Conwy County Borough. It was the first of the three national parks of Wales and the third in the United Kingdom, after the Peak District and the Lake District. Northern Snowdonia is the only place in Britain where the Snowdon lily grows.
so-yoshitoshi: Yoshitoshi, whose name is sometimes read Yoshitomo, was the fifth son of Sō Masamori. He became head of the family in 1580, after his adoptive father Sō Yoshishige was defeated in a prelude to Toyotomi Hideyoshi's Kyūshū Campaign. Under the influence of Konishi Yukinaga, whose daughter he married, he was baptized with the name Dario; his wife took the name Maria. In 1587 Hideyoshi confirmed the Sō clan in possession of Tsushima, then the single checkpoint for all Japanese ships bound for Korea, and Yoshitoshi entered his service.

Hideyoshi's ultimate aim was the conquest of Ming China, and in 1589 Yoshitoshi was charged with delivering to Joseon Korea the demand that it join the campaign or face war. With a stake in peace through his house's trading privileges, he delayed for nearly two years, and when pressed he turned the mission into an effort to improve relations, securing a Korean embassy to Japan in 1590. King Seonjo refused Japanese troops passage to China, and Hideyoshi decided on invasion.

Because of Tsushima's position and his knowledge of Korea, Yoshitoshi led the first major land assault of the war, the Siege of Busan on 13 April 1592, supported by Konishi Yukinaga, and he kept his command through several later engagements. The campaigns had failed by 1598, and he returned to Tsushima. The Sō took no part in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, and as a tozama clan were allowed to keep their domain.

After Sekigahara he helped Tokugawa Ieyasu reopen relations with Joseon, arranging an audience for the envoy Yujeong at Fushimi Castle. In 1603 he was granted Fuchū Domain, assessed at 100,000 koku. When Joseon demanded in 1606 a formal letter from the shogun asking for peace and the surrender of the soldiers who had defiled the royal tombs near Hanseong, he sent a forged letter and a group of criminals instead, and a Korean emissary came in 1608. He died on 31 January 1615. His descendants held the domain until the abolition of the han system and served as the shogunate's intermediaries with Joseon throughout the Edo period.
soap: Toilet soaps are made by saponification, in which an alkaline solution, often lye, breaks down the triglycerides of vegetable or animal oils and fats into salts of fatty acids and frees glycerol. Sodium soaps, made with soda lye, are firm, while potassium soaps, made with potash lye, are softer or often liquid. Soap made from pure olive oil is sometimes called Castile soap or Marseille soap. Soap cleans by gathering oil and dirt into tiny spheres called micelles, which the water then carries away.

Proto-soaps, which mixed fat and alkali for cleansing, are mentioned in Sumerian, Babylonian and Egyptian texts. The Ebers papyrus of about 1550 BCE shows that the Egyptians made a soap-like product as a medicine from animal fats or vegetable oils and trona. True soaps differed from these: they foamed, were made deliberately and could be hard or soft, because their makers understood sources of lye. It is uncertain who invented true soap, which may have arisen independently in various societies.

The Romans cleaned the body by rubbing oil into the skin and scraping it off with a strigil, and they did not use soap until at least the first century CE. Pliny the Elder describes soap as an invention of the Gauls, made from tallow and ashes. In the second century CE the physician Galen described soap-making with lye and rated Germanic soaps the best and those of Gaul second.

During the Islamic Golden Age hard, pleasantly scented toilet soap was produced in West Asia and North Africa, and soap-making became an established industry. Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi gave recipes, and in Syria soap was made from olive oil, alkali and lime and exported to the rest of the Muslim world and to Europe.

In Europe the soapmakers of Naples formed a guild in the late sixth century, and by the 15th century soap was made on an industrial scale in Antwerp, Castile, Marseille, Naples and Venice. In England a soap tax kept soap a luxury until it was repealed in 1853. Industrially made bar soaps became available in the late 18th century, and William Hesketh Lever and his brother bought a soap works in Warrington in 1886, which became Lever Brothers and later Unilever.
soba: Soba is an archaeological site and former town in what is now central Sudan. It was the capital of Alodia from the sixth century. E. A. Wallis Budge identified it with a group of ruins on the Blue Nile 19 kilometres from Khartoum, where the remains of a Meroitic temple that had been converted into a Christian church stand. At its height the city covered about 275 hectares.

In the 10th century Ibn Selim el-Aswani described Soba as large and wealthy, with fine buildings. The city was built mainly of red brick, and after it was abandoned its ruins were plundered for building material when Khartoum was founded in 1821. From the 1900s modern buildings began to cover the remains, and modern development now covers about half of the site. Since the 1990s the growth of suburbs in Greater Khartoum has continued to threaten what is left.

Excavations carried out before 2019 covered only about 1% of the city's area. They were made by expeditions of the Sudanese National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums and the British Institute in Eastern Africa, among others, mostly as salvage excavations during the building of a tarmac road and the construction that followed along it.

In 2019 the interdisciplinary project Soba, the heart of Alwa began, run by the Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology of the University of Warsaw and the Institute of Archaeology and Ethnology of the Polish Academy of Sciences and directed by Mariusz Drzewiecki. It set out to study the topography of Soba and the extent, layout and character of each quarter of the city. A magnetic geophysical survey revealed unknown parts of the medieval town: in one quarter large architectural complexes stood apart from each other, while another shows a clear grid of streets. Test trenches were dug at key points and where the survey's results were unclear.
sobek: Sobek, also known by the Greek name Suchus, was present in the Egyptian pantheon from the Old Kingdom to the Roman period. He is first known from the Pyramid Texts, in spell PT 317, which praises the pharaoh as the living incarnation of the crocodile god and calls him Neith's son. Scholars debate the origin of his name, Sbk. Many derive it from a causative of the verb meaning to impregnate, while others see a participle of a verb meaning to unite, so that it could mean he who unites the dismembered limbs of Osiris.

He gained prominence in the Middle Kingdom, above all under the Twelfth Dynasty pharaoh Amenemhat III, who took a particular interest in the Faiyum, the region most closely tied to Sobek, and with his contemporaries built projects to promote the god there. In this period Sobek was often fused with Horus, which brought him closer to the kings and into the divine triad of Horus, Osiris and Isis.

Sobek is associated with the Nile crocodile and is usually shown as a crocodile or a crocodile-headed man. He stood for pharaonic power, fertility and military prowess, and was also a protective god, invoked against the dangers of the Nile. His character is aggressive. Epithets include he who loves robbery and pointed of teeth, yet he also appears as a healer: through his link with Isis he helped heal the murdered Osiris.

Through Horus he gained a role as a solar deity, strengthened in later periods by Sobek-Ra, a fusion with the sun god Ra, which became prominent only in the last dynasties. In Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt a local text, the Book of the Faiyum, centred on Sobek, describing the daily journey of Sobek-Ra with the sun and his rising from the primal waters of Lake Moeris in creation.

The whole Faiyum, the Land of the Lake, was a cult centre, and many towns had their own forms of the god, such as Soknebtunis at Tebtunis and Sokonnokonni at Bacchias. At Karanis Pnepheros and Petsuchos were worshipped, with mummified crocodiles serving as images of Petsuchos. The chief form, Sobek Shedety, was the patron of Shedet, known as Crocodilopolis, whose temple Ptolemy II is thought to have begun to enlarge. Its priests held titles such as prophet of the crocodile-gods.

Outside the Faiyum the biggest centre was Kom Ombo, about 30 miles north of Aswan, built in the Graeco-Roman period, where the temple was called the Per-Sobek, house of Sobek. In later periods he became a subject of personal piety and a recipient of votive offerings. Crocodiles were raised as living incarnations of the god and mummified in a ritual when they died, and mummified crocodile eggs were also offered.
sobekhotep-iv: Khaneferre Sobekhotep IV was one of the more powerful kings of the Thirteenth Dynasty of Egypt. On a stela found in the Amun temple at Karnak he states that he was born in Thebes. His father was the god's father Haankhef and his mother the king's mother Kemi. He was the youngest brother of Neferhotep I and Sihathor. When turmoil and the lack of heirs led Neferhotep I to appoint Sihathor as junior coregent, Sihathor died within a year, and Sobekhotep became coregent in his place. He may have had several wives, but only one is certain, the king's wife Tjan, whose children included Amenhotep and Nebetiunet.

Sobekhotep reigned at least eight years, and perhaps about ten. His control of Memphis, Middle Egypt and Thebes is well attested, but he is thought not to have ruled a united Egypt, since Kim Ryholt holds that the 14th Dynasty already controlled the eastern Delta. N. Moeller and G. Marouard argue instead that it was held by the Hyksos king Khyan, on the evidence of sealings of Khyan and of Sobekhotep IV found together at Tell Edfu. Robert Porter and Alexander Ilin-Tomich dispute this, and Ryholt and Nicolas Grimal put the two kings about a hundred years apart.

He is known from many monuments, including stelae, statues and seals. A stela from Karnak reports gifts to the temple of Amun-Ra, and inscribed blocks at Abydos attest building at the local temple. The vizier Neferkare Iymeru reports that he built a canal and a house of millions of years for the king. Four stelae record an expedition in year 6 to the amethyst mines of Wadi el-Hudi, and further stelae are dated to year 8 at Edfu and year 9 at Wadi Hammamat. A stela (BM EA 1060) is thought to describe military activity in Wawat. The court continued the administration of Neferhotep I, with Iymeru as vizier.

His tomb has not been located with certainty. He was perhaps buried at Abydos, where Josef W. Wegner found a huge tomb naming a pharaoh Sobekhotep beside the funerary complex of Senusret III. It was first attributed to Sobekhotep I, but the style of the burial suggests a date under Sobekhotep IV.
sobekneferu: Sobekneferu, whose name means Beauty of Sobek, is usually presumed to have been a daughter of Amenemhat III, though the link between him and his two successors, Amenemhat IV and Sobekneferu, is uncertain. Her mother is unknown, and either of Amenemhat III's two known wives, Aat and Khenemetneferhedjet III, is a candidate. The ancient historian Manetho states that Amenemhat IV and she were brother and sister, and there is speculation about a marriage between them, but no contemporary evidence for it.

The reasons for her accession are obscure. Amenemhat IV may have left no male heir, or there may have been a dispute over legitimacy. She never associated herself with Amenemhat IV and asserted her legitimacy instead through Amenemhat III. She adopted the full royal titulary, modifying the traditional titles to mark her womanhood, as with daughter of Re and female Horus, and was the first ruler to carry the name of the crocodile god Sobek in both her birth name and her throne name, Sobekkare.

The Turin Canon credits her with a reign of three years, ten months and 24 days. Contemporary evidence is scant: a few partial statues, seals and inscriptions, mostly from the Faiyum, where she is credited with completing the Labyrinth, the mortuary temple of Amenemhat III's pyramid at Hawara. A graffito at the fortress of Kumma in Nubia records the height of the Nile inundation in her third regnal year, which shows that she kept authority across Egypt.

Her funerary monument has not been identified. A papyrus from Harageh mentions a site called Sekhem Sobekneferu that may refer to it, and a storeroom administrator named on a stela is evidence of an active funerary cult.

Her death brought the Twelfth Dynasty and the Middle Kingdom to a close and began the Second Intermediate Period. The transition seems to have been smooth, as there is no evidence of a violent collapse. The early Thirteenth Dynasty was marked by a rapid succession of short-lived rulers, the first of whom is debated, with Wegaf and Sobekhotep I the main candidates. Sobekhotep I appears to have modelled his throne name on her Nebty name, which suggests that he sought legitimacy from her and held her in esteem.

Later king lists record her. She appears on the Karnak list of the Thutmosid period and on the Saqqara Tablet and the Turin Canon of the Ramesside period, and in the work of Manetho. The Abydos King List omits her, along with all other female kings and the rulers of the intermediate periods and the Amarna period, which shows whom Seti I and Ramesses II regarded as legitimate rulers.
sobhuza-i: Sobhuza, also known as Ngwane IV, was the son of King Ndvungunye, also called Zikodze, who died after being struck by lightning, and of Somnjalose Simelane. His name Somhlolo means man of mysteries. Somnjalose was the younger sister and inhlanti, or support bride, of Ndvungunye's senior wife Lojiba Simelane, who had no sons. Under the Ngwane royal rules of kinship Sobhuza counted as Lojiba's son, so when he became king it was Lojiba, not his own mother, who became Indlovukati, the Queen Mother.

The kingdom he inherited, KaNgwane, was centred along the Pongola River south of modern Eswatini. The Dlamini kings, who had earlier ruled in and around the Lubombo Mountains, had built it under his grandfather Ngwane III around 1750 by taking in more than a dozen smaller chiefdoms. In the 1810s and 1820s it was threatened by the stronger Ndwandwe and Zulu kingdoms, and Sobhuza moved his royal centre from Zombodze in the Shiselweni region north to a new Zombodze in central Eswatini, leaving the old centres as southern outposts.

From there he conquered many local chiefdoms, and KaNgwane became a kingdom comparable to those of the Zulu, the Pedi and the Maroti. To make peace with the Ndwandwe, with whom his people were constantly in conflict, he married Tsandzile Ndwandwe, a daughter of Zwide. She bore him Mswati II and Mzamose Dlamini. The clans conquered before and during his rule are known as the Emakhandzambili.

Sobhuza was buried at the royal burial site of Mbilaneni. After a short regency by Lojiba, his son Mswati II succeeded him, with Tsandzile as Queen Mother. He left a country said to reach Barberton in the north, Carolina in the west, the Pongola River in the south and the Lubombo Mountains in the east, larger than present-day Eswatini. He is greatly revered in Eswatini, where Swazis mark Somhlolo Day on 6 September as their Independence Day and the national stadium bears his name.
sobhuza-ii: Sobhuza was born on 22 July 1899 at the Zombodze Royal Residence, the son of King Bhunu (Ngwane V) and Inkhosikati Lomawa Ndwandwe. His father died suddenly while dancing the incwala when the boy was four months old, and Sobhuza was chosen king soon afterwards. His grandmother Labotsibeni Mdluli served as regent, with his great-uncle Prince Malunge helping to lead the nation. He studied at Lovedale in the Eastern Cape and in England before taking power on 22 December 1921, at the age of twenty-two.

Early in his reign Sobhuza tried to recover land occupied by white settlers in 1907. He led a delegation to London to petition King George V and in 1929 took the question to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, but lost under the Foreign Jurisdictions Act 1890, which placed the acts of British administrations in protectorates beyond the reach of British courts. In the colonial period his role was largely ceremonial, though he kept great influence as traditional head of the nation.

In the early 1960s he helped to bring about independence. He opposed the constitution proposed by the British, which would have made him a constitutional monarch, and through his advisory council formed the Imbokodvo National Movement, which won all the seats in the 1967 elections. Independence came on 6 September 1968. On 12 April 1973 he repealed the constitution and dissolved parliament, ruling as an absolute monarch. A constitution of 1978 provided for an electoral college of eighty members chosen by forty local councils known as tinkhundla.

Sobhuza marked his Diamond Jubilee in 1981. He died on 21 August 1982 at Embo State House, aged 83. His reign of 82 years and 254 days is the longest precisely dated of any monarch on record. He kept many consorts, according to the Swaziland National Trust Commission 70 wives, who bore him 210 children, and was known as the Bull of the Swazi. A regent ruled after his death, and his young son Prince Makhosetive was crowned Mswati III in 1986. Much of the land and mineral wealth once owned by non-Swazi interests had come under Swazi control during his reign.
sobibor-extermination-camp: Sobibor was one of four extermination camps of Operation Reinhard, the deadliest phase of the Holocaust. At the Wannsee Conference on 20 January 1942 Reinhard Heydrich announced a plan to murder the Jews systematically through a network of such camps. In March 1942 SS-Hauptsturmführer Richard Thomalla, who had earlier overseen the building of Bełżec, took over construction at Sobibor, in the forest near the village of Żłobek Duży in the General Government. He allotted a larger area than at Bełżec, so that all the camp's facilities lay within its perimeter.

Double barbed-wire fences thatched with pine branches blocked the view inside. The site had a front compound for the personnel and four numbered compounds. Eighteen to twenty-two German and Austrian SS officers served at a time, nearly all of them veterans of Aktion T4, backed by a larger group of watchmen, generally of Soviet origin.

Sobibor became fully operational on 16 or 18 May 1942. Arriving Jews were told they were in a transit camp, made to hand over valuables and undress, and sent along a 100-metre path called the Road to Heaven to gas chambers, where they were murdered with carbon monoxide from the exhaust of a tank engine. Most were killed within hours. Between 170,000 and 250,000 people were murdered there. No complete record survives; the figure of 250,000 was proposed in 1947 by the Polish judge Zbigniew Łukaszewicz, while Jules Schelvis arrived at 170,165.

The only prisoners who lived there were about 600 forced labourers who worked in the camp, and few survived more than a few months. They were flogged for trifles, and in the summer of 1943 a penal brigade was formed whose members had to work while running.

In the summer of 1943 rumours spread that the camp would close, and the prisoners understood this meant their own deaths. On 14 October 1943 members of the underground killed eleven SS men, but the plan to march out of the gate was disrupted, and the prisoners escaped over the fences and through a minefield under machine-gun fire. About 300 got out, of whom roughly 60 survived the war. The Germans then demolished most of the camp to hide their crimes from the advancing Red Army.

After the war several trials took place. Erich Bauer was sentenced to death on 8 May 1950, commuted to life imprisonment. The site was long neglected, and the camp became better known through the miniseries Holocaust in 1978 and the film Escape from Sobibor in 1987. A museum now stands there, and archaeologists continue to investigate the site.
sobornoe-ulozhenie: The code replaced the Sudebnik of 1550 of Ivan IV. After the Time of Troubles the new Romanov government legislated actively: where 100 edicts had been issued between 1550 and 1610, 348 followed between 1611 and 1648. Each new edict was attached to the edict book of the prikaz that had asked for it and was often known only to its officials, so that many were obsolete and some contradicted one another. The Salt Riot of 1648 in Moscow gave the immediate impulse: the rioters demanded a Zemsky Sobor and a new code, and the tsar summoned the assembly as a concession.

A committee headed by Prince Nikita Odoyevsky, with Prince Semyon Prozorovsky, Fyodor Volkonsky and the scribes Gavrila Leontyev and Fyodor Griboyedov, drafted the code. The Zemsky Sobor sat in two houses, one of the tsar, the Boyar Duma and the Consecrated Sobor, the other of elected men of different ranks, and deputies of the nobility and the posad people shaped many of its norms. Drafting ended on 29 January 1649.

The code drew on the books of the prikazes, the Sudebnik of 1497 and that of Ivan IV, the Statutes of Lithuania of 1588 as a model of legal technique, and petitions. It was the first attempt by Russian legislators to arrange legal norms by areas of law, and it gave much attention to procedure.

Besides its provisions on serfs, the code required internal passports for travel between towns and granted the nobility, who agreed to serve in the army, the exclusive right to own serfs. It forbade boyars to accept taxpayers as bondsmen, barred the clergy from acquiring landed estates and reduced the competence of the church courts.

The original is a scroll of 959 narrow columns bearing 315 signatures of Sobor members; under Catherine II a silver ark was made to hold it, and it is kept in the Kremlin Armoury. The code was printed twice in 1649, in 1200 copies each time, and signed copies went to all the prikazes in Moscow as a guide for policy and law. It remained in force until 1832, when its articles were revised under the direction of Mikhail Speransky.
soca: The Soča, known in Italian as Isonzo, is a river 138 kilometres long that flows through western Slovenia for 96 kilometres and north-eastern Italy for 43 kilometres. Its source lies in the Trenta Valley in the Julian Alps at an elevation of 876 metres. It runs past Bovec, Kobarid, Tolmin, Kanal ob Soči, Nova Gorica, where the Solkan Bridge crosses it, and Gorizia, and enters the Adriatic Sea close to Monfalcone.

Antiquity recorded the river as Aesontius, Sontius and Isontius. The Slovene name derives from a form borrowed from Latin and Romance Sontius, which is probably based on an older substrate name meaning a swift, rushing river. Other names are Lusinç in Friulian and Sontig in German.

The present course is the result of several dramatic changes over the past 2,000 years. According to the Roman historian Strabo, the river called Aesontius, which in Roman times flowed past Aquileia to the Adriatic, was essentially the Natisone and Torre river system. In 585 a landslide cut off the upper part of the Natisone riverbed, and the Bontius River captured the stream. In the following centuries the estuary of this new river, the Soča, moved eastward until it captured the short coastal Sdobba River, through which the Isonzo now reaches the sea.

Before the First World War the river ran parallel to the border between the Kingdom of Italy and the Austro-Hungarian Empire. Between May 1915 and November 1917 the valley was the stage of the twelve battles of the Isonzo on the Italian front, in which over half a million Austro-Hungarian and Italian soldiers were killed. The twelfth battle, fought from 24 October to 7 November 1917, is also known as the Battle of Caporetto.

The river is marketed as the Emerald Beauty for its emerald-green water, which is said to keep its colour along its whole length. The Soča Valley attracts visitors to the Big Soča Gorge, the Little Soča Gorge, Kozjak Falls and the Tolmin Gorges. The upper course is home to the marble trout, native to the rivers of the northern Adriatic basin and now endangered. The Italian poet Giuseppe Ungaretti described the river in I fiumi (1916), and the Slovene poet Simon Gregorčič wrote Soči, one of the masterpieces of Slovene poetry.
