sochi: Sochi lies on the Sochi River along the Black Sea, in the North Caucasus of southern Russia. Greater Sochi is elongated along the coast for 145 kilometres and is about 1,603 kilometres from Moscow. It has a humid subtropical climate, with daytime temperatures of 25 to 29 °C in July and August and about 10 °C in January and February. The Caucasus Nature Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies just to the north, and the city has the region's most northerly tea plantations.

The name is the Russified form of a Circassian name that comes from the Ubykh Ş̂uaça, a compound of the words for sea and side, and roughly means seaside or coast. Georgian sources offer another derivation, from the Georgian word for the fir tree.

In antiquity the Zygii, a Proto-Adyghe people, lived in the area under the Kingdom of Pontus and then the influence of the Roman Empire. From the 6th to the 11th century it belonged successively to the Georgian kingdoms of Lazica and Abkhazia, which built about a dozen churches within the present city boundaries; the northern wall of an 11th-century Byzantine basilica still stands in the Loo microdistrict. The Christian settlements along the coast were later destroyed by invading Alans, Khazars, Mongols and other nomadic powers whose control was slight.

Russia occupied the coastline in 1829 as a result of the Russo-Circassian War and the Russo-Turkish War of 1828 to 1829, but the Circassians did not accept Russian control and kept resisting the new outposts. Supplying weapons to them from abroad caused a diplomatic conflict between the Russian and British empires in 1836 over the mission of the Vixen. Lazarevskoye was founded as a Russian military outpost in 1839 and named after Admiral Mikhail Lazarev. The Michael Archangel Cathedral, built in 1873 to 1891, commemorates the end of the Caucasian War.

In the Russian Civil War the coast saw armed clashes among the Red Army, White forces and the Democratic Republic of Georgia. A railway from Tuapse to Georgia, running within a kilometre or two of the shore, opened in 1923. After the Crimean resorts passed from the Russian SFSR to the Ukrainian SSR in 1954, Sochi became the unofficial summer capital of the country. In 1961 Soviet officials formed Greater Sochi, stretching 140 kilometres from the southern part of Tuapse to Adler.

Sochi is the largest resort city in Russia, with sanatoriums, hotels and beaches along its coast, and it is divided into four city districts. It hosted the Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games in 2014, with the alpine and Nordic events at the ski resort of Rosa Khutor in Krasnaya Polyana.
socialism: The history of socialism has its origins in the Age of Enlightenment and the French Revolution of 1789, although it has precedents in earlier movements and ideas. Pierre Leroux claimed to have first used the word socialism, in the Parisian journal Le Globe in 1832. He was a follower of Henri de Saint-Simon, one of the founders of what would later be labelled utopian socialism. The utopian socialists condemned liberal individualism for failing to address the poverty, oppression and wealth inequality of the Industrial Revolution. Saint-Simon proposed economic planning and scientific administration, while Robert Owen proposed cooperatives.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1847 and 1848, just before the Revolutions of 1848, and called their position scientific socialism. In the last third of the 19th century parties dedicated to democratic socialism arose in Europe, drawing mainly on Marxism. For one week in December 1899 the Australian Labor Party formed the first socialist government in the world, when it was elected in the Colony of Queensland under Premier Anderson Dawson.

Socialism encompasses diverse economic and social systems characterised by social ownership of the means of production, which can be public, community, collective, cooperative or employee ownership. Systems are divided into non-market forms and market socialism, which retains monetary prices and factor markets. In his Dictionary of Socialism (1924), Angelo S. Rappoport analysed forty definitions and found common elements: criticism of the social effects of private ownership of capital, a view that the solution is some form of collective control, and agreement that the result should be a society based on social justice. Major movements include anarchism, communism, the labour movement, Marxism, social democracy and syndicalism.

By the early 1920s communism and social democracy had become the two dominant tendencies within the international socialist movement. In the first half of the 20th century the Soviet Union and the communist parties of the Third International came to represent socialism as a centrally planned economy directed by a state that owns all the means of production, although other trends condemned what they saw as its lack of democracy. The People's Republic of China, founded in 1949, introduced socialism through a state-led economy, land redistribution and the Anti-Rightist Movement, followed by the Great Leap Forward.

Elsewhere reformist social democrats and democratic socialists came to power through the ballot box. In the UK, Herbert Morrison said that socialism is what the Labour government does, while Aneurin Bevan argued that it requires the main streams of economic activity to be brought under public direction. Such governments established mixed economies with partial nationalisation and social welfare, as in the Nordic model.
socialist-party-of-albania: The Party of Labour of Albania, founded by Enver Hoxha, had ruled the country for over four decades. Hoxha's successor, Ramiz Alia, was forced to introduce limited reforms in the late 1980s, and on 11 December 1990 he announced that the party had given up its monopoly of power. It won the Constitutional Assembly election of 1991, the first free elections held in Albania in almost 80 years, by which time it was no longer a Marxist-Leninist party. At an extraordinary congress held from 10 to 13 June 1991 it reorganised itself as the Socialist Party in order to survive in the new system.

Fatos Nano, a man from the intelligentsia, was elected the first chairman. He helped to reform the old communist party and brought it into the Socialist International. In 2004 a faction led by Ilir Meta broke away and formed the Socialist Movement for Integration. On 10 October 2005, after losing the parliamentary election of that year, Nano resigned and was succeeded by Edi Rama.

Under Rama the party formed the Alliance for a European Albania, which united several parties and won the parliamentary election of 2013, returning the Socialists to government after eight years. Running alone, the party won the elections of 2017 and 2021 with 74 seats in each, enough to govern by itself, though it has had the outside support of the Social Democratic Party in parliament.

The party is described as social-democratic. Its platform of 2013 pledged to replace the flat tax with a progressive tax and supported universal health care. It is pro-European, supports Albania's accession to the European Union and its membership of NATO, and regards Kosovo as the country's main strategic partner and ally. It is an associate of the Party of European Socialists. Its emblem is based on the fist and rose designed by José María Cruz Novillo for the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party in 1977, used without that party's official consent.
socialist-party-of-chile: Socialist thought in Chile goes back to the mid-19th century, when Francisco Bilbao and Santiago Arcos opened a debate on civil rights and social equality. Its ideas took hold in the labour movement early in the 20th century. The Great Depression plunged the working and middle classes into crisis and drew them to socialist ideas, which found expression in the short-lived Socialist Republic of Chile in 1932.

The party was founded on 19 April 1933 at a conference in Santiago, where delegates of four groups, among them the New Public Action headed by Eugenio Matte and the Revolutionary Socialist Action of Oscar Schnake, wrote its founding document. Schnake was elected its first Secretary General. Colonel Marmaduque Grove and Salvador Allende were among its founders.

The party declined in the 1940s. In 1948 the Law for the Defense of Democracy banned the communists, and the socialists divided over it: an anticommunist group around Bernardo Ibanez was expelled, and the electoral registrar gave it the name Socialist Party of Chile, forcing the group of Raul Ampuero to call itself the Socialist Popular Party.

In 1969 the party's Central Committee proclaimed Allende its presidential candidate, by 13 votes in favour and 14 abstentions, and in October of that year the Popular Unity coalition formed, which won the presidential election of September 1970. Allende was proclaimed President on 24 October 1970, with the declared commitment to build socialism while respecting democratic and institutional mechanisms.

On 11 September 1973 General Augusto Pinochet led the military coup against Allende, who refused to give up power and committed suicide in his office in the Palace of La Moneda during an air bombardment. The junta banned the leftist parties. Within weeks four members of the Socialist Central Committee and seven regional secretaries had been murdered, twelve other members of the committee were imprisoned, and Altamirano escaped to Havana. The bodies of Carlos Lorca and others were never found. The party split, and in the 1980s socialist factions returned as opponents of the dictatorship.

In 1989 the renewal wing of the party, led by Jorge Arrate, decided to join the Socialist International and to back the Christian Democrat Patricio Aylwin, who won the presidential election of that year. The party reunited on 27 December 1989. Its members won the presidency with Ricardo Lagos in 2000 and with Michelle Bachelet in 2006 and 2014.
socialist-realism: Socialist realism grew out of earlier Russian realism, such as the work of the Peredvizhniki and Ilya Yefimovich Repin, which lacked the later political connotation. After the Bolsheviks took power on 25 October 1917 there was a marked shift in artistic styles, following a short period of artistic exploration. The term is attributed to the writer Maxim Gorky, who introduced the concept in 1933 in a literary rather than a visual context. The First Congress of Soviet Writers in 1934 proclaimed it the only acceptable method for Soviet cultural production in all media. Its formal objective was to depict reality in its revolutionary development, though no definitive guidelines on style or subject matter were given.

Works were usually characterised by unambiguous narratives or iconography relating to Marxist-Leninist ideology, such as the emancipation of the proletariat. In the visual arts the style often relied on the conventions of academic art and classical sculpture. Key concepts that were to assure loyalty to the party included partiinost (party-mindedness), ideinost (ideological content), klassovost (class content) and pravdivost (truthfulness). Content counted for more than form, which allowed works to be condemned as formalism. Optimism was required: the present and the future were idealised, and tragedy and negativity were not permitted unless shown in a different time or place. The Soviet mass song, including Isaakovsky's Katiusha and Aleksandrov's Sacred War, was a leading genre in music of the 1930s and the war.

Leon Trotsky, Stalin's adversary, criticised the approach, regarding it as an arbitrary construct of the Stalinist bureaucracy and holding that literary schools had been strangled one after the other. After the Russian Revolution socialist realism became an international literary movement, and it was taken up in East Germany, China and Indonesia, where the group Lekra pushed artists to follow it. In art, from the mid-1960s more relaxed and decorative styles became acceptable in the Warsaw Pact bloc. In the non-communist world it had little mainstream impact and was widely seen as a means of imposing state control on artists.
socialist-republic-of-the-union-of-burma: The state grew out of military rule. In 1958, with the ruling AFPFL split in two, Prime Minister U Nu invited General Ne Win, the Army Chief of Staff, to serve as interim prime minister, and this caretaker government held power until the February 1960 election returned U Nu. On 2 March 1962 Ne Win and the Tatmadaw, the armed forces, overthrew U Nu's government. The coup leaders set up the Revolutionary Council of the Union of Burma, which in April declared the Burmese Way to Socialism the state ideology and on 4 July founded the Burma Socialist Programme Party (BSPP).

The constitution of 1974 replaced the Revolutionary Council with the Pyithu Hluttaw, whose members all belonged to the BSPP. Ne Win was both head of state and head of government, and although the party tried to become a mass party, military officers dominated its leadership throughout.

Under the Enterprise Nationalization Law, the major industries, among them import-export trade, rice, banking, mining, teak and rubber, were nationalised on 1 June 1963; around 15,000 private firms were taken over in all, and the government's Burma Oil Company replaced American and British oil firms. The law fell hardest on Burmese Indians, the Burmese Chinese, the Anglo-Burmese and the British, and by September 1964 approximately 100,000 Indian nationals had left the country. The Ford Foundation, the Asia Foundation and the World Bank were shut out, visas for foreigners were limited to 24 hours, and privately owned newspapers were banned in December 1965.

The black market came to make up about 80% of the economy. Foreign exchange reserves fell from $214 million in 1964 to $50 million in 1971. After the first BSPP congress in 1971 the government asked to rejoin the World Bank, joined the Asian Development Bank and launched a Twenty-year plan, reforms that brought living standards back to pre-war levels.

By 1988 foreign debt had reached $4.9 billion, about three-fourths of national GDP. Ne Win's attempt to base the kyat on denominations divisible by 9, a number he considered auspicious, wiped out the savings of millions of people and led to the 8888 Uprising. On 18 September 1988 the Tatmadaw staged a coup against the BSPP, violently ended the protests and set up the State Law and Order Restoration Council. Scholars have largely described the Burmese Way to Socialism as an abject failure, although real per capita GDP still grew by about 1.3% a year between 1962 and 1987.
socialist-revolutionary-party: The party's ideas rested on the Narodnik populist movement of the 1860s and 1870s, revived by the neo-populists, especially Viktor Chernov, who entered a dialogue with Marxism to attract the growing urban workforce to a programme that was traditionally peasant-oriented. The party was established in 1902 out of the Northern Union of Socialist Revolutionaries, founded in 1896, and local groups such as the Workers' Party of Political Liberation of Russia, created by Catherine Breshkovsky and Grigory Gershuni in 1899.

The Socialist Revolutionaries, or SRs, were agrarian socialists and supporters of a democratic socialist republic. They won a mass following among the peasantry by endorsing the overthrow of the Tsar and the socialization of land, its division among peasant tenants, as against the Bolshevik programme of nationalization.

Until about 1909 the party relied heavily on assassinations of officials, carried out by its Combat Organisation, which killed two Ministers of the Interior, Dmitry Sipyagin and Vyacheslav von Plehve, and Grand Duke Sergei Aleksandrovich. Its leader after 1903, Yevno Azef, was an agent of the Okhrana secret police. When he was exposed in 1908 the Central Committee resigned, and the party then renounced individual terror.

After the February Revolution of 1917 the SRs returned to active politics. Alexander Kerensky, a nominal member, became head of the Provisional Government in July, and Chernov served as Minister of Agriculture but found his land reforms blocked. A split over the war and land redistribution produced the Left SRs in the autumn, and it became final on 25 October when the Left SRs stayed at the Congress of Soviets while the mainstream party walked out. In the Constituent Assembly election two weeks after the Bolsheviks took power, the SRs won 37.6% of the vote against the Bolsheviks' 24%; the Bolsheviks dissolved the Assembly by force in January 1918.

The Left SRs governed with the Bolsheviks from late November 1917 and resigned their positions after the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Two Left SR Chekists assassinated the German ambassador Count Wilhelm Mirbach on 6 July 1918, and the Left SRs' attempted rising failed, leading to arrests and executions. Fanny Kaplan, a former SR, tried to kill Lenin on 30 August. A trial of SRs in Moscow in 1922 drew protests from Eugene V. Debs, H. G. Wells, Karl Kautsky and Albert Einstein. A small remnant operated in exile, with a delegation in Prague, and belonged to the Labour and Socialist International from 1923 to 1940.
society-of-mary-marists: After his ordination Jean-Claude Colin served as assistant to his elder brother Pierre, the parish priest at Cerdon, where he began drafting a rule for a group of priests and, with Jeanne-Marie Chavoin, founded the Sisters of the Holy Name of Mary. The church authorities of Lyon received the plan coolly, fearing to lose priests. In 1823 Bishop Devie of Belley let Colin and a few companions form a travelling mission band for the rural districts and then gave them his minor seminary, though he too wanted no more than a diocesan institute.

Rome proposed the mission to Western Oceania to the Marists, and on their acceptance Pope Gregory XVI's brief of 29 April 1836 approved the Marist Fathers as a religious institute with simple vows under a Superior General. Colin was elected to that office on 24 September 1836, and the first professions were made the same day, among them those of Peter Chanel and Marcellin Champagnat.

Under Bishop Jean Baptiste Pompallier, vicar apostolic living in New Zealand, Marists went to Wallis and Futuna in 1837, Tonga in 1842, New Caledonia in 1843, where Brother Blaise Marmoiton was killed, Fiji in 1844 and Samoa in 1845, against much Protestant opposition. The vicariate was divided among Marist bishops; Melanesia and Micronesia were given up after Bishop Epalle was killed at Isabella Island, and only the Solomon Islands returned to the Marists in 1898. Besides their religious work they did much to make known the languages, fauna and flora of the South Sea Islands.

Foundations followed in Great Britain from 1850 at Cardinal Wiseman's request, and in the United States from 1863, when Archbishop Odin called the Marists to Louisiana; from there they spread to eleven states and to Mexico.

The Society has five independent branches: the Marist Fathers; the Marist Brothers, founded by Champagnat in 1817; the Marist Sisters, founded by Chavoin in 1824; the Missionary Sisters of the Society of Mary, approved in 1931; and the Third Order of Mary, whose rule Pierre-Julien Eymard wrote and whose best-known member was Jean-Marie Vianney. Marists aim to be hidden and unknown, saying no to greed, pride and power, and Colin asked them to think, judge, feel and act as Mary in all things. The Society has its Generalate in Rome and around 500 members.
society-of-united-irishmen: The Society of United Irishmen was a sworn association formed in the wake of the French Revolution to secure representative government in Ireland. It was founded at a gathering in a Belfast tavern in October 1791. Apart from Thomas Russell, a former army officer from Cork, and Theobald Wolfe Tone, a Dublin political writer, the participants were Presbyterians, Dissenters from the established Church of Ireland who shared in part the disabilities of the Catholic majority. They resolved to reform the government on 'principles of civil, political and religious liberty'. Tone had written An Argument on behalf of the Catholics of Ireland, and Russell invited him to the meeting for that reason. The society recruited through freemasonry-style ritual among tradesmen, artisans and tenant farmers.

From February 1793 Britain was at war with the French Republic, and tension rose in Belfast. Legislation banned extra-parliamentary conventions and suppressed the Irish Volunteers, and in May 1794 the Society was proscribed. Its aims were then restated in uncompromising terms: Catholic emancipation and parliamentary reform became universal manhood suffrage and a republic. In March 1796 Tone wrote that independence must be had at all hazards. In September 1796 arrests removed leaders including Russell, Charles Teeling, Henry Joy McCracken and Robert Simms, and on 15 December Tone arrived off Bantry Bay with a French fleet of about 14,450 men under Louis Lazare Hoche, but a gale prevented a landing.

Martial-law seizures from May 1798 forced the conspiracy into the open and produced a series of local risings. On 22 August 1798 some 1,100 French troops landed at Killala in County Mayo. They won the Races of Castlebar, but General Humbert surrendered on 8 September. The last action of the rebellion was a slaughter of some 2,000 poorly armed insurgents outside Killala on 23 September. A renewed conspiracy led by Robert Emmet failed in 1803, when an attempted rising in Dublin misfired.

After the rebellion the British government pressed a union upon the Irish Parliament, and the Acts of Union of 1801 abolished it. Some United Irishmen, among them Archibald Hamilton Rowan, hailed the downfall of that assembly. Exiles formed a United Irish society in the United States, and in Newfoundland a mutiny of 1800 in which eight men were hanged was reported as United Irish. Since the centenary of 1798, Ireland's unionist, nationalist and republican traditions have all claimed and disputed the legacy of the United Irishmen.
socotra: Socotra is the largest of six islands in its archipelago and makes up about 95 per cent of its land. It lies 380 kilometres south of the Arabian Peninsula and 232 kilometres east of the Horn of Africa. It is culturally and administratively part of Yemen but geographically belongs to Africa, since it is a continental fragment linked to the Somali plate. The archipelago was once part of Gondwana and detached in the Miocene.

The island has coastal plains with dunes, limestone plateaus where goats and sheep were herded for centuries, and the granite Hajhir Mountains, which rise to 1,503 metres. About 37 per cent of its plant species and 90 per cent of its reptile species are found nowhere else. The inhabitants speak Arabic and Soqotri, a Semitic language related to Mehri.

Oldowan stone tools were found near Hadibo in 2008. In antiquity the island played a part in international trade and appears in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, a Greek navigation aid of the first century CE, as the island of Dioscurides. Sailors who visited between the first century BCE and the sixth century CE left nearly 250 inscriptions and drawings in Hoq Cave, in South Arabian, Ethiopic, Brāhmī, Greek, Palmyrene and Bactrian. They are a main source for Indian Ocean trade at that time. Christians lived there in the 6th century.

In 880 an Aksumite force conquered the island, and it was later dislodged by an armada from Oman. The geographer Ibn al-Mujawir, who arrived from India in 1222, described indigenous mountain dwellers and foreign coastal dwellers, among them large settlements of Indian traders. In 1507 a Portuguese fleet under Tristão da Cunha and Afonso de Albuquerque captured the port of Suq after a hard fight with the Mahra Sultanate, hoping for a base on the route to India. Famine and sickness struck the garrison, and the Portuguese left in 1511. The Mahra sultans regained control and the inhabitants were converted to Islam.

The East India Company kept a garrison on Socotra in 1834 and 1835, but the sultan refused to sell the island. In 1886 the British government made a protectorate treaty with him. The Mahra Sultanate was abolished in October 1967, and on 30 November 1967 Socotra became part of South Yemen.

Socotra is a Yemeni island, and its principal town, Hadibu, lies on the north coast. The Dragon's Blood Tree, Dracaena cinnabari, which has an umbrella-like crown and a red sap, is the best-known of its endemic plants. UNESCO recognised the archipelago as a World Heritage Site in 2008.
socrates: Socrates left no writings, and what is known of him comes from others: his pupils Plato and Xenophon, the comic dramatist Aristophanes, and Aristotle, who was born after his death. These accounts often contradict one another, a difficulty scholars call the Socratic problem. Xenophon wrote about him in the Memorabilia, the Oeconomicus, the Symposium and the Apology. How far Plato's dialogues portray the historical Socrates is debated, and some scholars distinguish an earlier, more faithful portrait from a later one carrying Plato's own views.

Socrates was born in 470 or 469 BCE in the Athenian deme of Alopece, to Sophroniscus, a stoneworker, and Phaenarete, a midwife. He had the usual education of a well-off Athenian and served in three campaigns of the Peloponnesian War, according to Plato. He married Xanthippe, with whom he had three sons, and also a daughter of the statesman Aristides. He was indifferent to comfort, owned one ragged coat and walked barefoot, and he criticised both the democrats and the oligarchs of Athens.

The method named for him, the elenchus, is shown mainly in Plato's early dialogues. Socrates asks an apparent expert for a definition, and further questions lead the expert to contradict it. A new definition is then tested in the same way. The discussion usually ends in an impasse, with the interlocutor unable to define what he thought he understood. Socrates frequently proclaimed his ignorance, saying he was sure only that he did not know.

Scholars dispute what the method achieves. In 1982 Gregory Vlastos argued that it could show only that an interlocutor's beliefs were inconsistent. Because Socrates taught no fixed doctrine, later schools drew different conclusions.

In 399 BCE Socrates was accused of impiety and of corrupting the youth. The accusation was brought by a poet, Meletus, with Anytus and Lycon. The trial came after the defeat of Athens by Sparta at the Battle of Aegospotami in 404 BCE and the rule of the Thirty Tyrants, and it probably lasted most of a day. A jury of hundreds of citizens found him guilty. He proposed free meals from the state, or alternatively a fine of one mina of silver, and the jurors ordered his death. Plato relates that he was put to death with hemlock after refusing offers to help him escape.

Almost every philosophical current after Socrates traced its roots to him, among them Plato's Academy, Aristotle's Lyceum, the Cynics and the Stoics, except the Epicureans and the Pyrrhonists. He was considered to have shifted philosophy from the natural world to human affairs.
sodom-and-gomorrah: In Genesis, Sodom and Gomorrah are two of the cities of the plain. Lot, the nephew of the patriarch Abraham, settled in the Jordan Valley and moved his tent as far as Sodom. Genesis 14:2 names Bera as king of Sodom and Birsha as king of Gomorrah. The two cities rebelled against Chedorlaomer of Elam, to whom they were subject, and he defeated them at the Battle of Siddim and took many captives, including Lot. Abraham gathered his men, rescued Lot and freed the cities.

The Genesis account then tells that God resolved to destroy Sodom because of its reputation for wickedness. Abraham asked whether the righteous would be swept away with the wicked, and obtained God's agreement to spare the city if ten righteous people could be found. Two angels came to Lot's house in the evening. The men of the town surrounded it and demanded that Lot surrender the visitors so that they might know them, and the angels struck the crowd blind. Lot and his daughters were spared, while Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt for looking back.

Genesis names no single sin as the cause. Other texts attribute various sins, sexual and nonsexual, and Ezekiel, Isaiah and Jeremiah describe the crimes of Sodom as concerning the poor treatment of the less fortunate, as well as adultery and lies. Since 1955 scholars have increasingly read the central sin as inhospitality to guests, while debate turns on the Hebrew verb yada, to know, in Genesis 19:5. The reading that the sin was homosexuality is traced to Philo of Alexandria, and became accepted Church teaching in the 12th century. The Quran refers to the people of Lut and their destruction, associated primarily with idolatrous practices.

The cities may have been based on real places along the Dead Sea, and Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira have been suggested as candidates, though the archaeological evidence is inconclusive. Strabo placed Sodom at a hill of limestone and salt at the south-western tip of the Dead Sea, near Mount Sodom, and some scholars believe the cities lie flooded beneath the southern basin of the sea. One proposal is an earthquake between 2100 and 1900 BCE along the Jordan Rift Valley, but no contemporary account of seismic activity supports it, and volcanic and meteor explanations have been dismissed as unlikely. The names became a byword for destruction and desolation in the prophets and the New Testament.
sofala: Sofala, now called Nova Sofala, lies on the Sofala Bank in Sofala Province. It stood at the edge of a wide estuary of the Buzi River, which linked it to the inland market town of Manica and on to the gold fields of Great Zimbabwe. The approach was hard: a long shifting sand bank and dangerous shoals let boats in safely only at high tide, and the shore was mangrove swamp full of malarial mosquitoes. The town was made up of two parts, one on a sand flat by the water and one on higher ground.

Sofala emerged as a small trading post in the 10th century. Its first recorded users were merchants from Mogadishu, who are said to have kept it secret from their rivals in Kilwa. In the 1180s Sultan Suleiman Hassan of Kilwa took control of it and brought it into the Swahili cultural sphere; river dhows on the Buzi and Save carried gold down to the coast. Formally the town still belonged to the Kingdom of Mwenemutapa, to which the Swahili paid tribute, and it kept wide autonomy, with its own elite and settlements as far south as Cape Correntes.

Pêro da Covilhã, travelling in disguise, visited in 1489, and in 1502 the first Portuguese ships entered the harbour. Sheikh Isuf, who refused to recognise the usurper Emir Ibrahim of Kilwa, made a treaty of trade and alliance with Portugal, and in 1505 Pêro de Anaia built Fort São Caetano, the second Portuguese fort in East Africa. Fevers soon wasted the garrison, and after Vasco Gomes de Abreu took the island of Mozambique in late 1507 most of its operations moved there, though the governors kept the title Captain of Sofala.

By then the old gold fields were largely worked out and the trade had moved north, towards Quelimane and Angoche. The sea has since reclaimed much of old Sofala, and few ruins remain. Its harbour has silted up, and Beira, founded in 1890 some 32 kilometres to the north, took its place.
sofia: Sofia lies in western Bulgaria in the Sofia Valley, at the northern foot of the Vitosha mountain, on an average altitude of 550 metres. It is surrounded by mountains: Vitosha to the south, Lyulin to the west and the Balkan Mountains to the north. It is built west of the Iskar. Its development as a settlement owes much to its central position in the Balkans: three mountain passes lead to the city and have been key roads since antiquity, and Vitosha is the watershed between the Black and Aegean seas. Hot water springs still flow abundantly in the centre.

The area has a history of nearly 7,000 years. A Neolithic village at Slatina is documented. The earliest tribes were the Thracian Tilataei, and in the 500s BCE the area joined the Odrysian kingdom. In 339 BCE Philip II of Macedon destroyed and ravaged the town for the first time. The Celtic tribe Serdi gave the city its name, Serdica; the earliest mention is an Athenian inscription of the 1st century BCE, and according to Dio Cassius the Roman general Crassus subdued the Serdi. The emperor Marcus Ulpius Traianus gave it the name Ulpia Serdica.

During the decline of the Roman Empire the city was raided by Huns, Visigoths, Avars and Slavs. In 809 Khan Krum incorporated it into the First Bulgarian Empire, and it became known as Sredets. In 1018 the Byzantines ended Bulgarian rule until 1194, when the Second Bulgarian Empire took it back. Sredets was a major administrative, economic, cultural and literary hub until the Ottoman conquest in 1382. From 1530 to 1836 Sofia was the regional capital of Rumelia Eyalet, the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province.

Its population fell from 70,000 in the late 18th century to 19,000 in 1870 and 11,649 in 1878. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878, and Sofia was selected as the capital of the Third Bulgarian State the next year, beginning a period of intense demographic and economic growth. After the Liberation War, knyaz Alexander Battenberg invited architects from Austria-Hungary to shape the new capital.

Sofia is the capital and largest city of Bulgaria. Ancient Roman, Byzantine and medieval Bulgarian buildings survive in the centre, among them the 4th-century Rotunda of St. George, the walls of the Serdica fortress and part of the Amphitheatre of Serdica. The Boyana Church was included on the World Heritage List in 1979.
soga-clan: The Soga were an uji, an aristocratic kin group, of the Asuka period, and they held the hereditary rank of Great Omi. Tradition makes their founder Soga no Ishikawa, a son of Takenouchi no Sukune and great-grandson of Emperor Kōgen. Because of the clan's close ties to Korea, some scholars have suggested an immigrant origin: the linguist Alexander Vovin derived the name from Korean words meaning prince of the metal clan, and members bore names such as Soga no Karako, Korean person of Soga. The present consensus does not accept an immigrant origin, holding only that the clan was deeply engaged in foreign affairs.

Soga no Iname served as Great Minister from 536 until his death in 570. He married two daughters to Emperor Kinmei, one of whom bore Emperor Yōmei, and the next five emperors all had a wife or mother descended from him. The Soga favoured Buddhism, brought by monks from Baekje, and Chinese models of government. The rival Mononobe and Nakatomi clans opposed the new faith, and when an epidemic followed the arrival of a Buddhist statue it was blamed on the anger of the kami and the Soga temple at the palace was burned. After some fifty years of conflict Buddhism took hold under Soga protection.

By 644 Soga no Emishi and his son Soga no Iruka were building lavish palaces and tombs and styling themselves sovereigns. Nakatomi no Kamatari conspired with Prince Naka no Ōe and Soga no Kurayamada no Ishikawa no Maro, and the prince attacked Iruka at a court ceremony before Empress Kōgyoku; his guards finished him off. Emishi killed himself by burning his residence, destroying many court documents. The Empress abdicated in favour of her brother, Emperor Kōtoku, and the Taika Reform followed two years later. The coup is known as the Isshi incident.

The Soga were the first of many families to dominate the imperial house by shaping the succession and government policy. The Fusō Ryakuki records that at the raising of the pillars of Asuka Temple in 593 a hundred men under Soga no Umako wore Baekje dress. In 2005 the remains of a building in Nara that may have been Iruka's residence were found, consistent with the account of the Nihon Shoki.
sogdians: Sogdia, or Sogdiana, lay between the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, including the fertile valley of the Zeravshan, in what is now Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its Bronze Age urban culture appears at Sarazm in Tajikistan, as early as the 4th millennium BCE. The Sogdian city-states, centred on Samarkand, were never politically united. Sogdian is an Eastern Iranian language, no longer spoken, although Yaghnobi, a descendant of one of its dialects, is still spoken by the Yaghnobis of Tajikistan. Sogdiana was a province of the Achaemenid Empire, named on the Behistun Inscription of Darius I, and Cyrus the Great conquered it in 546 to 539 BCE.

Alexander the Great's forces captured the Sogdian Rock in 327 BCE, and Roxana, daughter of the Sogdian nobleman Oxyartes, married Alexander. Sogdia later passed to the Seleucid Empire, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, the Sakas and the Yuezhi, and the Sasanian Empire conquered it in 260 CE.

The Hephthalites took it around 479, and the First Turkic Khaganate and the Sasanians defeated them perhaps in 557, after which the Turks kept the land north of the Oxus. Qutayba ibn Muslim began the Muslim conquest of Sogdia in the early 8th century, and Sogdians, aided by the Turgesh, expelled the Umayyad garrison from Samarkand.

Conversion to Islam was virtually complete by the end of the Samanid Empire in 999, and Sogdian was largely supplanted by New Persian. Genghis Khan later destroyed Bukhara and Samarkand, but in 1370 Samarkand revived as the capital of the Timurid Empire.

The Sogdians turned their energies to trade so thoroughly that the Saka of Khotan called all merchants suli, Sogdian. They learned trade from the Kushans and became the main Silk Road middlemen after the Kushan collapse, establishing a trading network across the 1,500 miles from Sogdiana to China. In 568 a Sogdian diplomat, Maniah, persuaded Istämi, ruler of the First Turkic Khaganate, to send an embassy to Constantinople, where Justin II agreed to an alliance against Sasanian Persia and a direct silk trade.

Other Sogdians settled in China for generations and rose to prominence in the military and government of the Tang dynasty. They first practised Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism, Buddhism and, to a lesser extent, the Church of the East. The 6th century is thought to be the peak of Sogdian culture, and the Afrasiab paintings of Samarkand and the murals of Panjakent are rare surviving examples of its art.
sognefjord: The Sognefjord, nicknamed the King of the Fjords, stretches 205 kilometres inland from the ocean to the small village of Skjolden in Luster Municipality. It gives its name to the surrounding district of Sogn; the name is related to the Norwegian word súg-, to suck, presumably from the surge of the tidal currents at the fjord's mouth. The fjord is up to six kilometres wide, and its main branch averages less than five. It reaches 1,308 metres below sea level, with the deepest parts near Høyanger, and is more than 1,000 metres deep for about 100 kilometres.

Cliffs rise almost sheer from the water to 1,000 metres and more. The inner end lies south-east of a mountain range covered by the Jostedalsbreen, continental Europe's largest glacier, so its climate is less wet than the outer coast. The whole system, with its branches, holds about 500 cubic kilometres of water. The main branches include the Aurlandsfjord, the Fjærlandsfjord and the Nærøyfjord, 18 km long, a World Heritage Site that is only 300 metres across at its narrowest. The innermost arm, the Lustrafjord, is 42 km long.

The valley predates the Quaternary glaciations. The fjords of western Norway formed in connection with the eastward tilting of much of Norway during the Cenozoic uplift of the Scandinavian Mountains, which let rivers cut deeply into the older landscape. An estimated 7,610 cubic kilometres of rock has eroded from the drainage basin since then. During the last glaciation the ice reached a maximum thickness of nearly 3,000 metres, and the confluence of tributary fjords excavated the deepest basin.

In earlier times, transport between Bergen and the Scandinavian inland went by boat between Bergen and Skjolden and from there over the highlands on a simple road, or by boat to Lærdal and through the mountain pass to Valdres. Around the inner end of the fjord three of Norway's stave churches have survived: Kaupanger and Urnes along the shoreline, and Borgund, 30 km into the Lærdal valley.

The fjord runs through ten municipalities, among them Solund, Sogndal, Aurland, Årdal and Luster, and boats and ferries connect the settlements along it and its side arms. Gudvangen lies by the Nærøyfjord, and from Flåm the Flåm Railway climbs 864 metres to Myrdal Station over 20 kilometres. The Nærøyfjord and the Geirangerfjord are listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Summer tourists are an important part of the local economy.
sohar: Sohar, historically known as Mazun, lies on the Gulf of Oman and is the capital and largest city of the Al Batinah North Governorate. It is an ancient capital of Oman and has been credited as the mythical birthplace of Sinbad the Sailor. Because it was the largest town in the region, it has been argued that Sohar is the ancient town called Omanah mentioned by Pliny the Elder in his Natural History, a settlement believed to have given Oman its name.

According to al-Tabari, in 893 or 894 CE, under the Abbasids, local factions disputed who should rule Oman. One faction that approached the Abbasids was the Bani Sama, who were based in Buraimi before moving to Sohar. They called themselves the Wajihid Dynasty and assumed leadership of the region.

By the 10th century Sohar was one of the richest ports of the Persian Gulf. Ibn Hawqal and al-Maqdisi praised it as flourishing, populous, beautiful, pleasant and delightful, and compared it favourably with the ports of China. Aloes, wood, bamboo, sandalwood and spices came from India and frankincense from Dhofar. The Buwayhids sacked the city in 971 and its trade declined. Merchants of Kish across the gulf briefly took control around 1100. Sohar then became the first seat of the Sultanate of Sohar under the Bani Nabhan dynasty, who had been appointed governors by their Buyid suzerains. Its fort was built in the late 13th century by the Princes of Hormuz while the city remained under Nabhani control.

After a period of ruin, Sohar was re-established in the 15th century as a minor port under the Hormuzi-Qalhati sphere of influence, and it was still an international port until at least the 16th century. In the early 16th century the Portuguese Empire conquered it and used it to control the entrances to the Persian Gulf, as part of a web of fortresses from Bahrain to Hormuz. It appears in António Bocarro's 17th-century Book of Fortresses.

The population was 140,006 at the 2010 census. The development of the Port of Sohar, established in 2002 and operated by the Sohar Industrial Port Company, made the town a major industrial hub of Oman, with steel and aluminium industries in the industrial area.
soil-erosion: Soil erosion is the wearing away of the upper layer of soil, a form of soil degradation. It is a natural process driven by erosive agents: water, ice, snow, air, plants and animals, humans included. It may go on slowly and almost unnoticed or at a rate that causes a serious loss of topsoil. Rainfall and the runoff it produces cause four main types: splash erosion, sheet erosion, rill erosion and gully erosion, from the least severe stage to the most. Stream erosion deepens and widens valleys, and most of it happens in floods. Mass movement, driven by gravity, includes landslides and the slow scree slope.

Heavy rainfall on soil not protected by vegetation is the main climatic factor. Clay-rich soils resist erosion better than sandy or silty ones, as do soils high in organic matter. Plant roots bind the soil, and removing vegetation raises the rate of erosion. Long, steep slopes erode faster than short, gentle ones.

Human activity increases erosion. Unsustainable farming raises rates by one to two orders of magnitude over the natural rate. Tillage breaks the soil into fine particles, and monocropping, farming on steep slopes and heavy grazing add to the loss. In an undisturbed forest a layer of leaf litter and humus absorbs the impact of rain, and clearing the trees removes it. On-site effects include falling farm yields and, in some cases, desertification. Off-site effects include silted waterways and airborne dust.

The most effective known way to prevent erosion is to increase vegetation cover. Terracing has been practised for thousands of years by people all over the world. Windbreaks, rows of trees and shrubs along field edges, shelter fields against wind. Mixed cropping, crop rotation and crop residues left under conservation tillage have also been shown to cut rates of erosion. The model most widely used for predicting soil loss by water, the Universal Soil Loss Equation, was developed in the 1960s and 1970s.
soissons: Soissons is a commune in the department of Aisne in northern France, on the river Aisne about 100 kilometres north-east of Paris. It is one of the most ancient towns of France and is probably the ancient capital of the Suessiones. It has been the see of a Roman Catholic diocese since about 300, and a number of church synods, called the Council of Soissons, met there.

The town enters written history under its Celtic name Noviodunum, meaning new hillfort, as the capital of the Suessiones. Julius Caesar mentions it in 57 BCE: after leaving the Aisne he reached Noviodunum in one long day's march, found it surrounded by a high wall and a broad ditch, and received its surrender. From 457 to 486, under Aegidius and his son Syagrius, it was the capital of the Kingdom of Soissons, until it fell to the Frankish king Clovis I after the Battle of Soissons in 486.

As part of Neustria, the region and the Abbey of Saint-Médard, founded in the sixth century, played a political part under the Merovingian dynasty. After the death of Clovis I in 511 Soissons became the capital of one of the four kingdoms into which his lands were divided, until Chlothar II amalgamated the Frankish lands in 613. The Council of Soissons of 744 met at the instigation of Pepin the Short and Saint Boniface and condemned the bishop Adalbert and the missionary Clement of Ireland.

During the Hundred Years' War French forces committed a massacre of English archers in the town's garrison, in which many townsfolk were also killed. Henry V of England, noting that the town was dedicated to Saints Crispin and Crispinian, claimed to avenge their honour at Agincourt on Saint Crispin's Day 1415. Joan of Arc's forces liberated Soissons on 23 July 1429. The Congress of Soissons, held from June 1728 to July 1729, sought to settle disputes between Great Britain and Spain and led to the Treaty of Seville. The Prussians besieged the town for over a month in the Franco-Prussian War, and it surrendered in October 1870. It was heavily bombarded in World War I.

Soissons is a commercial and manufacturing centre. Its Gothic cathedral of Saint-Gervais-et-Saint-Protais was begun about 1177, and its choir was completed in 1211, earlier than Chartres Cathedral. The other principal sites are the ruins of the Abbey of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes and the crypt of the former Abbey of Saint-Médard. The Passerelle des Anglais, a footbridge over the Aisne, was rebuilt in 1914 by British soldiers and again in 1950.
sojourner-truth: Sojourner Truth was born Isabella Bomefree, later also given as Baumfree, and estimated that she was born between 1797 and 1800. She was one of ten or twelve children of James and Elizabeth Bomefree, who were held as slaves by the Hardenbergh family at Swartekill in the town of Esopus, New York. Her first language was Dutch, and she spoke with a Dutch accent for the rest of her life. When she was an infant, her brother and sister were sold to a different estate.

New York began to legislate the abolition of slavery in 1799, but emancipation was not complete until 4 July 1827. Her owner, Dumont, had promised to free her a year earlier if she did well, then changed his mind. Late in 1826 she walked away with her infant daughter Sophia, leaving her other children, who were not freed until they had served as bound servants. Isaac and Maria Van Wagenen of New Paltz took her in. In 1828 she went to court to recover her son and became the first Black woman to win such a case against a white man.

On 1 June 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth, after hearing the Spirit of God calling her to preach the truth, and set out to travel and preach against slavery. In 1844 she joined the Northampton Association of Education and Industry in Florence, Massachusetts, a community founded by abolitionists, where she met William Lloyd Garrison and Frederick Douglass and gave her first anti-slavery speech.

In May 1851 she spoke at the Ohio Women's Rights Convention in Akron. The first report, by Marius Robinson in the Anti-Slavery Bugle, does not contain the question Ain't I a Woman. A version published twelve years later by Frances Dana Barker Gage, in a speech pattern associated with enslaved people in the South, became the most widely circulated, though Truth, raised in New York, is unlikely to have spoken so. During the Civil War she helped recruit Black men into the Union army, and afterwards she tried unsuccessfully to secure land grants for formerly enslaved people.

Truth died at her home in Battle Creek, Michigan, on 26 November 1883, and about a thousand people attended her funeral. A memorial bust was unveiled in 2009 in Emancipation Hall in the Capitol Visitor Center, making her the first African American woman with a statue in the Capitol.
sokollu-mehmed-pasha: Sokollu's birth name was probably Bajica, and he was of Bosnian Serb origin, said to have been born into a modest shepherd family near Sokolovići, in the vicinity of modern Rudo. His father was named Dimitrije. His name Sokollu is a demonym from his place of birth. His family relations are disputed: Makarije Sokolović is traditionally called his brother, but some historians think he was a nephew or distant relative. Renamed Mehmed, he was educated first in Edirne and then in Constantinople, as an apprentice janissary and at the palace school in Topkapı Palace. He spoke Turkish, Serbian, Persian, Arabic, Venetian and Latin.

Mehmed became Imperial Chamberlain in 1541 and then head of the Sultan's squires, growing close to Suleiman. He is said to have excelled at the Battle of Mohács and the first Siege of Vienna. When Hayreddin Barbarossa died in 1546 he became his successor as Kapudan Pasha, took part in the expedition against Tripoli and greatly strengthened the fleet's arsenal. In 1551 he became Governor-General of Rumelia, based at Sofia. In 1555 he was made Third Vizier, and in 1559 he defeated the forces of Prince Bayezid at Konya in a rebellion against the heir Selim; Bayezid fled to Persia, and the Shah later handed him and his four sons over to be executed.

In 1562 Mehmed married Ismihan Sultan, a granddaughter of Suleiman, and in 1561 he had become Second Vizier. Suleiman made him Grand Vizier in June 1565, after the death of Semiz Ali Pasha. In 1566 war with Emperor Maximilian II began, and Mehmed prepared the army for the Sultan's advance, and his forces were sent to besiege Szigetvár. He served as Grand Vizier under Suleiman, Selim II and Murad III. Although he became a Muslim he remembered his Orthodox roots, and in 1557 he helped restore the Serbian Patriarchate of Peć, with Makarije Sokolović as its patriarch. He placed members of his family in important positions.

Sokollu Mehmed Pasha was assassinated on 11 October 1579. Some claim that the killer was a janissary in the pay of Safiye Sultan, wife of Murad III. Afterwards Murad III changed grand viziers ten times in sixteen years, which is taken as a sign of the instability that followed. He endowed buildings in Edirne, Halep, Medina, Belgrade and Bosnia, where his bridges are especially remembered, notably the eleven-arched bridge at Višegrad. In Istanbul the architect Mimar Sinan built his mosque complex in Kadırga and his tomb at Eyüp, where he is buried.
sokoto-caliphate: In the 17th and 18th centuries the major power of the region had been the Bornu Empire, but by 1759 its rulers had lost control of the oasis town of Bilma and of the trans-Saharan trade, and its vassal cities became autonomous. After the fall of the Songhai Empire in 1591, several Hausa sultanates grew to fill the void, among them Gobir, Kebbi and Zamfara. They fought one another regularly, especially in slave raids, and imposed high taxes to pay for the warfare.

Usman dan Fodio, an Islamic scholar and urbanised Fulani, had preached in Gobir with the support of its Hausa leaders. When his former student Yunfa became sultan of Gobir he restricted dan Fodio's activities and in 1802 attempted to assassinate him. Dan Fodio went into exile at Gudu in February 1804, where his followers pledged allegiance to him as Commander of the Faithful. By 1808 the new state controlled Hausaland and several surrounding states.

From 1808 to the mid-1830s the state expanded, annexing the plains to the west and key parts of Yorubaland, until it included more than thirty emirates and stretched from present-day Burkina Faso to Cameroon. The sultan ruled from Sokoto, and for a brief period under Muhammad Bello from Wurno. Each emir was appointed by the sultan but kept wide autonomy. Bello, the second sultan, consolidated the state through ribats, walled settlements with schools and markets, where pastoral Fulani were settled and plantations grew.

Slaves worked the plantations, and by 1900 Sokoto held at least 1 million and perhaps as many as 2.5 million of them. The jihad also inspired risings elsewhere, such as the Massina Empire in present-day Mali. British forces under Frederick Lugard moved into the caliphate in 1901 and exploited rivalries between the emirs. In 1903 the British, French and Germans conquered the area, and the twelfth and last caliph, Attahiru, was killed by British forces.

The caliphate was a loose confederation of emirates that recognised the suzerainty of the Sultan of Sokoto. Emirs travelled yearly to pledge allegiance and deliver taxes in crops, cowry shells and slaves, and a council of the emirs chose each new sultan. Hausa became the language of administration and the main medium of poetry. Usman, his brother Abdullahi and his son Bello wrote more than three hundred books between them, and Nana Asma'u started the Yan Taru movement in 1838, which encouraged the education of women.
sol-plaatje: Solomon Tshekisho Plaatje was born on 9 October 1876 at Doornfontein near Boshof in the Orange Free State, the sixth of eight sons of Johannes and Martha, Tswana Christians who worked for missionaries. The surname came from a nickname a Boer farmer gave his grandfather, Selogilwe Mogodi. When he was four the family moved to Pniel near Kimberley, where Wilhelmine Westphal, wife of the German missionary Ernst Westphal, gave him extra lessons, music among them. He became a pupil-teacher in February 1892.

In 1894 he moved to Kimberley as a telegraph messenger and passed the colony's clerical examination with the top marks in Dutch and typing. Under the Cape's qualified franchise he could vote at 21, a right later lost under the Union of South Africa. During the Siege of Mafeking he was a court interpreter and kept a diary, published long after his death.

Plaatje spent much of his life working for the enfranchisement of African people. He travelled to England with the congress's deputation against the Natives Land Act, 1913, and later to Canada and the United States, where he met Marcus Garvey and W. E. B. Du Bois. Fluent in at least seven languages, he edited and part-owned Kuranta ya Becoana in Mahikeng and, in Kimberley, Tsala ya Becoana and Tsala ya Batho.

He wrote Mhudi in 1919, but it appeared only in 1930, after R. R. R. Dhlomo's An African Tragedy of 1928. On one of his three visits to Britain, short of money, he acted in George Lattimore's revue Cradle of the World. His recording of Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika with Sylvia Colenso at the piano is believed to be the earliest surviving recording of the future national anthem.

Plaatje married Elizabeth Lilith M'belle, with whom he had six children. He died of pneumonia at Pimville, Johannesburg, on 19 June 1932 and was buried in Kimberley before more than a thousand mourners. His biographer Brian Willan writes that his political career was long forgotten and his manuscripts lost. Interest revived in the 1970s, and Mhudi was reissued in 1978. His Kimberley home at 32 Angel Street became a museum, his grave a national monument in 1998, and Sol Plaatje University opened in 2014.
solapur: Solapur lies on the Deccan Plateau in the south-western part of Maharashtra, close to the border with Karnataka, at an average elevation of 458 metres. It is about 410 km from Mumbai, 245 km from Pune and 305 km from Hyderabad, and it stands on a major highway and at a junction of railway lines between Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore and Hyderabad. The climate is dry, with three seasons, summer, monsoon and winter. The name is believed to come from the Marathi words sola, sixteen, and pura, village: the present city was considered to spread over sixteen villages, among them Ahmedpur, Fatehpur and Sonallagi.

The area was ruled by various dynasties, among them the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Yadavas and Bahamanis. Inscriptions from the time of the Kalachuris of Kalyani show the town was called Sonnalage, an old Kannada name later pronounced Sonnalagi, and it was the main commercial hub of the Yadavas of Devagiri. A Sanskrit inscription found at Kamati in Mohol gives the name Sonalipur, and inscriptions in the fort give Sonalpur and Sandalpur.

The Solapur district was formed in stages in the 19th century: in 1838 it became a sub-district of Ahmednagar, and in 1871 it was reformed with subdivisions from Satara. After the reorganisation of 1956 Solapur belonged to Bombay State, and in 1960 it became a district of Maharashtra.

Weavers of the Padmashali community moved to Solapur and other places in search of work when imported English cloth undercut hand weaving. Many worked in cotton mills. The Manacha Shri Ajoba Ganpati temple began celebrating the Ganesh festival in 1885, and Lokmanya Tilak, who visited Solapur, started the Ganesh festival in Pune in 1893. During the independence movement the Solapur Municipal Council hoisted the Indian national flag on its building on 6 April 1930, in the spirit of Gandhi's Dandi March.

Residents enjoyed full freedom from 9 to 11 May 1930. Four men, Mallappa Dhanshetti, Abdul Rasool Qurban Hussein, Jagannath Bhagwan Shinde and Shrikisan Laxminarayan Sarada, were hanged by the British on 12 January 1931 at Pune, and the city became known as the City of Hutatmas, the City of Martyrs.

Solapur is a city of Marathi, Kannada and Telugu cultural influences. It has long been a centre of cotton mills, power looms and handlooms, and Solapuri chadars were the first product in Maharashtra to receive a Geographical Indication tag. It also leads Maharashtra in the production of beedi cigarettes. The chief deity of the city is Shri Shivyogi Siddheshwar, and the Gadda Yatra fair, with the Nandi-dhawaj procession at Makar Sankranti, is associated with his marriage. The Shri Siddheshwar Swami Temple and the Bhuikot Fort are its main sights.
solar-cell: Edmond Becquerel demonstrated the photovoltaic effect experimentally and in 1839, at the age of 19, built the first photovoltaic cell in his father's laboratory. In a 20 February 1873 issue of Nature, Willoughby Smith described the effect of light on selenium during the passage of an electric current. In 1876 William Grylls Adams and Richard Evans Day constructed the first solid-state photovoltaic cell, and in 1883 Charles Fritts built another by coating selenium with a thin layer of gold to form the junctions; his device was only about 1 per cent efficient.

A solar cell is an electronic device whose electrical characteristics change when it is exposed to light. Its operation needs three things: the absorption of light, the separation of charge carriers of opposite types and their separate extraction to an external circuit. Most cells are made of semiconducting material, usually silicon, fabricated into a p-n junction, formed by doping one side p-type and the other n-type with small amounts of boron or phosphorus. A single silicon cell produces an open-circuit voltage of about 0.5 to 0.6 volts, so cells are joined into modules, and strings of modules into arrays, which give direct current that an inverter often converts to alternating current.

Almost all commercial cells are of crystalline silicon, cut into wafers 160 to 240 micrometres thick. Thin-film cells, of which cadmium telluride is the main kind, use less material, while multi-junction cells stack layers that absorb different parts of the spectrum and were first developed for satellites.

The first prominent application was in space. Solar cells were proposed and flown on the Vanguard satellite in 1958 as an alternative to its battery, which allowed the mission to last longer without changes to the spacecraft. In 1959 the United States launched Explorer 6, with large wing-shaped arrays of 9600 Hoffman solar cells, and such arrays became a common feature of satellites.

Costs stayed high through the 1960s because space users would pay for the best cells, and in 1971 a cell cost some $100,000 per watt. Terrestrial research grew with a programme of the US National Science Foundation that ran from 1969 to 1977 and with the Cherry Hill Conference of 1973. Adjusted for inflation, a solar module cost $96 per watt in the mid-1970s and 30 cents per watt in 2018. Solar cells are also used to power calculators and watches.
soleb: Soleb lies on the western bank of the Nile north of the Third Cataract, in ancient Nubia and present-day Sudan. Besides the temple, the site holds a vast necropolis of small tomb chapels decorated with pyramids. The earliest royal tombs there date to the 18th Dynasty, while others belong to the Ramesside and Meroitic periods. At Sedeinga, Amenhotep III built a companion temple to Queen Tiye as a manifestation of the Eye of Ra.

The sandstone temple is the southernmost known to have been built by Amenhotep III. It was consecrated to Amun Re and to the pharaoh himself, shown deified with ram's horns, and its architect may have been Amenhotep, son of Hapu. Several rulers of the Amarna Period attended to it. Akhenaten is at first shown there worshipping his father and Amun, but he later rededicated the temple to the Aten. Under Tutankhamun, who reversed his father's religious reforms, it was rededicated to Amun Re.

The Prudhoe Lions, inscribed with the name of Amenhotep III, stood as guardian figures at the temple; they depict lionesses, symbols of the goddess Sekhmet. Tutankhamun finished the second lion and added his name, and Ay later added his own.

Major Felix visited the site in 1829 and recognised that the prisoners named on its columns commemorated victories of Amenhotep III, and Karl Richard Lepsius described it in 1844. Part of the hypostyle hall lay ruined and buried in sand; the expedition led by Michela Schiff Giorgini in 1957–1963 reconstructed further parts of the temple, including more of the prisoner inscriptions, from identified pieces. Each figure is a bound prisoner whose shield names his town or land, and three lists survive.

One name, tꜣ šꜣsw yhwꜣ, is translated as land of the Shasu, those of Yhwꜣ. Some scholars, noting its likeness to the name of the Israelite god Yahweh, connect these Shasu with the Israelites, while Shalomi Hen considers the evidence too scanty for such an identification. Jude Flurry argues that the lists may exaggerate Egyptian victories, though they show who Egypt's enemies were.
solidarity-forever: Ralph Chaplin completed the song on 15 January 1915 in Chicago, on the day of a hunger demonstration. He was a dedicated member of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), a writer for Solidarity, its official paper in the eastern United States, and a cartoonist for the organisation. The words are sung to the tune of John Brown's Body and The Battle Hymn of the Republic.

The song puts into verse the outlook of the IWW's Preamble, printed inside the cover of every Little Red Songbook, which opens: "The working class and the employing class have nothing in common." Its third stanza, beginning "It is we who plowed the prairies", claims for workers the creation of value, and the fourth and fifth justify their claim to the world. The second assumes two opposed classes, the first and fifth set out the strategy of union solidarity, and the last foresees a new world brought to birth "from the ashes of the old".

Many performers drop the second and fourth stanzas, the most radical, and Pete Seeger's version also rewrites the last. Since the 1970s women have added verses on their concerns as union members, and the centennial edition of the Little Red Songbook includes two new verses credited to Steve Suffet.

Although written for the IWW, the song was adopted by other unions, among them the AFL–CIO, and it is sung at union meetings, protests and rallies in the United States, Australia, New Zealand and Canada and at conferences of the Australian Labor Party and the Canadian New Democratic Party. It has been translated into French, German, Polish, Spanish, Swahili and Yiddish, and it may have inspired The Battle Hymn of Cooperation of the consumer cooperative movement.

Chaplin disliked its popularity. Late in his life, by then an opponent of Communists in the labour movement, he wrote an article, Why I wrote Solidarity Forever, attacking the industrial unions of the period after the Wagner Act and declaring that "when the labor movement ceases to be a Cause and becomes a business, the end product can hardly be called progress." The IWW's songbook also prints a satire, Aristocracy Forever.
solidarity-polish-trade-union: In the 1970s Poland's government raised food prices while wages stagnated, and protests in 1976 were followed by a crackdown on dissent. Groups such as KOR and ROPCiO began to form underground networks to monitor and oppose the government, with labour unions an important part of them. In 1979 the Polish economy shrank for the first time since World War II, and foreign debt reached around 18 billion dollars by 1980. The writings of the philosopher Leszek Kołakowski, banned in Poland, circulated in underground copies, and Pope John Paul II's 1979 visit to Poland was, in Lech Wałęsa's words, a significant factor in the creation of the union.

Anna Walentynowicz was dismissed from the Gdańsk Shipyard on 7 August 1980, five months before she was due to retire, for taking part in the illegal trade union. Workers struck in her defence on 14 August, and she and Alina Pienkowska turned a strike over bread and butter into a solidarity strike with other establishments. The government signed the agreement allowing the union to exist on 31 August 1980. On 17 September more than twenty founding committees merged into one national organisation, and it was registered on 10 November 1980.

Solidarity brought together people linked to the Catholic Church and members of the anti-Soviet left, and it advocated non-violence. In September 1981 its first national congress elected Wałęsa president and adopted a programme called the Self-governing Republic. The government imposed martial law on 13 December 1981 under General Wojciech Jaruzelski, arresting the regional delegates. The union survived underground with financial support from the Vatican and the United States.

The Round Table talks of 6 February to 5 April 1989 led to semi-free elections on 4 June 1989, in which the opposition won 99 of the 100 Senate seats and all 161 contestable seats in the Sejm. A Solidarity-led coalition government was formed by the end of August, with Tadeusz Mazowiecki as prime minister, and in December 1990 Wałęsa was elected President of Poland.

The union's survival was unprecedented in the Eastern bloc, where Soviet-led invasions had quelled the Hungarian Uprising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968. Its electoral victory in 1989 set off a mostly bloodless chain of events across Central and Eastern Europe known as the Revolutions of 1989. Wałęsa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983. Organised as one big union by region rather than by craft, the union reached about 10 million members in September 1981, a third of the working-age population. After 1989 it became a more traditional trade union, and a political arm, Solidarity Electoral Action, won the parliamentary election of 1997.
solidus: The solidus, from the Latin for solid, was a highly pure gold coin of the Later Roman and Byzantine empires. It replaced the aureus in the early 4th century, and Constantine the Great struck it for mass circulation from about 312. His coins were struck at 72 to a Roman pound of gold, about 326.6 g, so each weighed about 4.5 grams. The weight stayed relatively constant for seven centuries, and the solidus was also a unit of weight, one seventy-second of a Roman pound. In Western Europe it was the main gold coin of commerce from late Roman times to the Early Middle Ages. In the Greek-speaking world it was called the nomisma.

In theory it was pure gold, but the limits of refining meant coins were often about 23 carats, or 95.8% gold. It bore no face value throughout its manufacture. Fractions were produced, the semissis, a half, and the tremissis, a third, and these were especially popular in the West, where few purchases required a coin as large as the solidus.

From the 4th to the 11th centuries solidi were mostly minted at Constantinople. After 476 the Germanic successor kingdoms, such as the Ostrogothic Kingdom and the Franks, struck imitations bearing the portrait and title of the emperor in Constantinople. Justinian I's reconquests reopened mints such as Carthage, which struck great numbers until the Arab conquest in 698.

Although imperial law forbade merchants to export solidi, it was loosely enforced, and many have been found in Russia, Central Europe, Georgia and Syria. The word soldier is ultimately derived from solidus, referring to those paid in solidi.

Michael IV began debasing the coin in 1034. Its fineness fell to about 21 carats under Constantine IX Monomachos, 16 under Romanos IV Diogenes and, after the defeat at Manzikert, to 14 under Michael VII Doukas and between 0 and 8 carats in the first eleven years of Alexios I Komnenos. In 1092 Alexios abolished the solidus and introduced the hyperpyron, at about 20.5 carats, which stayed stable until the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

In medieval Europe, where the only coin in circulation was the silver penny, the solidus survived as a unit of account worth 12 deniers. Its name gave the French sou, the Italian soldo, the Spanish sueldo and the English shilling, whose abbreviation s. comes from solidus, and the word soldier is ultimately derived from it, referring to those paid in solidi.
solingen: Solingen lies 25 kilometres east of Düsseldorf along the northern edge of the Bergisches Land, south of the Ruhr, and after Wuppertal is the second-largest city of the Bergisches Land. The city covers 89.45 square kilometres, about half of it used for agriculture, horticulture or forestry. The Wupper, a right tributary of the Rhine, flows through it for 26 kilometres. Solingen is called the Klingenstadt, the City of Blades, and its local dialect, a variety of Limburgish, calls the city Solich.

A chronicler first mentioned the area in 1067 as Solonchon, and the modern form of the name seems to have been in use from the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Smelters of blacksmiths more than 2,000 years old have been found around the town. Swords from Solingen have turned up in the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of the British Isles and were traded across Europe. It was a tiny village for centuries and became a fortified town in the 15th century. In the late 17th century a group of Solingen swordsmiths broke their guild oaths and took their sword-making secrets to Shotley Bridge in County Durham, England.

Plague killed about 1,800 people in 1614 to 1619. In the Thirty Years' War Solingen was heavily fought over, repeatedly attacked and plundered, and Burg Castle was destroyed. Ohligs, whose chief products early in the 20th century were cutlery and hardware, became part of Solingen in 1929. A British air raid in 1944 destroyed the Old Town completely, killing 1,800 people and injuring over 1,500, so few pre-war sites remain in the centre. From 1945 to 1949 Solingen lay in the British occupation zone, and reconstruction of the old town began in 1949. The independent town of Burg an der Wupper was incorporated in 1975.

Solingen's firms still make swords, knives, scissors and razors. The German Blade Museum shows swords and cutlery of all periods, and the Rhineland Industrial Museum is in the Hendrichs Drop Forge. Burg Castle was the castle of the counts of Berg. The Müngsten Bridge, built in 1897 and originally named the Kaiser-Wilhelm-Brücke, carries a railway 107 metres above the ground between Solingen and Remscheid and is the tallest railway bridge in Germany.
solomon: Solomon was born in Jerusalem, the second child of David and his wife Bathsheba, the widow of Uriah the Hittite. The first child of the union, a son conceived while Uriah was alive, died seven days after birth, which the Hebrew Bible suggests was a judgment from God. Solomon had three named full brothers and six known older half-brothers. His two names, Solomon and Jedidiah, are traditionally taken to mean peaceful and friend of God. The conventional dates of his reign, about 970 to 931 BCE, derive from biblical chronology.

According to the Hebrew Bible, God appeared to Solomon in a dream and asked what he wanted. Solomon asked for wisdom in order to rule his people, and God, pleased that he had not asked for long life or the death of his enemies, promised it. The account describes a reign of forty years in which Israel reached a height of splendour and wealth. He allied himself with Hiram I, king of Tyre, who sent materials and an architect for the Temple that David had gathered materials to build. The account also gives him 700 wives and 300 concubines, many of them foreign princesses, and disapproves of his building temples to their gods. It tells of a visit by the Queen of Sheba.

Solomon died of natural causes at around 55 years of age. His son Rehoboam succeeded him, but ten of the tribes refused him and followed Jeroboam, splitting the monarchy into the northern Kingdom of Israel and the smaller southern Kingdom of Judah. The historicity of Solomon is much debated. Current scholarship generally allows that a historical Solomon is possible, but regards the biblical picture of his opulence as almost surely an anachronistic exaggeration. Tradition ascribes to him the books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Song of Songs. He is revered in Islam as the prophet Sulaiman ibn Dawud, and the Solomon Islands were named for him by Álvaro de Mendaña in 1568.
solomon-i-of-imereti: Solomon, later called the Great, was a son of Alexander V of Imereti by his second wife, Princess Tamar Abashidze, and succeeded his father on his death in 1752. He at once took stern measures against the rebellious nobles and against the slave trade from which they profited together with the Ottoman authorities. The aristocratic opposition staged a coup that same year, but Solomon soon regained the crown and began reforms meant to steady a kingdom torn by chronic civil war.

The Ottomans regarded Imereti as their sphere of influence and sent an army, but Solomon rallied his nobles and defeated it at the Battle of Khresili in 1757. In the same year he allied with his kinsman Heraclius II, who ruled eastern Georgia. He beat back two further Ottoman invasions, of 20,000 and 13,000 men, and one of two raids by North Caucasian tribes that the Ottomans instigated. The Ottomans briefly took Kutaisi in 1765 and put his cousin Teimuraz on the throne, but Solomon returned and again freed Imereti of the Turks.

In May 1769, after a new Russo-Turkish war had broken out, Solomon met Heraclius in Tbilisi, and the two kings asked Russia for five regiments, joining the war in return for a guarantee of Georgian interests at the peace. Russia sent only a small force under General Gottlieb Heinrich Totleben, whose rudeness alienated the Georgians, and he was soon recalled. Solomon took part in the siege of Şorapani in 1769 and the siege of Poti in 1770–1771.

After the war he forced his autonomist vassals, the princes of Mingrelia and Guria, into submission. The Ottomans signed a treaty under which Imereti was no longer their vassal, with a symbolic tribute of 60 women a year that Solomon never paid. In 1779 he crushed an insurrection in Abkhazia sponsored by the Ottomans.

In his last years Solomon made a series of raids into the historic Georgian lands of the south-west held by the Turks. His son Prince Alexander led a brief revolt against him in 1778 before they were reconciled, and died before his father in 1780. Solomon died in 1784 and was buried at the Gelati Monastery. The Georgian Orthodox Church canonised him on 22 December 2016.
solomon-ii-of-imereti: Solomon was born David, a member of the Bagrationi dynasty, the son of Prince Archil of Imereti, brother of King Solomon I of Imereti, and of Helen, a daughter of King Heraclius II of Georgia. Solomon I died in 1784 without a male heir and named his nephew David as his successor. Another uncle, David II, kept both him and a rival prince, George, from the crown and seized the throne himself, which led to a civil war.

Heraclius II sent an army on behalf of his grandson and defeated David II at the Battle of Matkhoji on 11 June 1789, after which David was crowned as Solomon II. David II kept up his attempts to regain the throne until his final defeat in 1792. Ruling under his grandfather's protection, Solomon continued Solomon I's policy of curbing the powers of the feudal aristocracy. In 1795 he and Heraclius fought the Persians with a small Imeretian force at the Battle of Krtsanisi and were completely defeated.

After the death of Heraclius in 1798 and the Russian annexation of Kartli-Kakheti in 1800, his position grew precarious. His vassals, the princes of Mingrelia and Guria, placed themselves under Russian protection and claimed parts of the royal domains. Solomon sought Ottoman and Persian support, but the Russian commander in Georgia, Prince Pavel Tsitsianov, marched into Imereti and forced him to accept vassalage in the convention of Elaznauri of 25 April 1804.

Relations with Russia stayed strained. On 20 February 1810 the Russian administration removed him from the throne. Solomon rallied the people and appealed to Turkey, Persia and Napoleonic France. Insurgents once defeated one of the two Russian units sent from Tbilisi, but Lieutenant-General Rozen, helped by Georgian nobles who changed sides, defeated Solomon in the Khanistsqali valley.

Solomon died at Trebizond and was buried in the Saint Gregory of Nyssa Church; in 1990 his body was moved to Gelati Monastery in Georgia. His marriage to Princess Mariam Dadiani, daughter of Katsia Dadiani, Prince of Mingrelia, was childless.
