sonoma-california: When the first Spaniards arrived, the area lay near the north-eastern corner of the territory of the Coast Miwok, with the Southern Pomo to the north-west, the Wappo to the north-east and the Suisun and Patwin peoples to the east. Mission San Francisco Solano, founded in 1823 by the priest José Altimira, Giovanni Toscano and Giovanni Álvarez under Governor Luis Antonio Argüello, was the only mission built by the Mexican authorities rather than the Spanish. It formed part of a plan to fortify the area north of San Francisco Bay against Russian expansion southward from Russian America.

After the Mexican secularization act of 1833, Governor José Figueroa made Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo administrator of the mission and military commander of the Northern Frontier. In 1835, with the help of William A. Richardson, Vallejo laid out the streets, lots, central plaza and main avenue of the Pueblo de Sonoma on a grid prescribed by the Spanish Laws of the Indies. The Sonoma Barracks housed his troops. The pueblo remained under military control until a town council was established in 1844.

Before dawn on 14 June 1846 thirty-three Americans already in rebellion against the Mexican provincial government arrived in Sonoma, some of them from the camp of the army captain John C. Frémont. They met no resistance. They took Vallejo and three associates prisoner, though Vallejo had invited their leaders into his home to negotiate, and William Ide urged the rebels to stay and found a new republic. The remaining twenty-four made the Sonoma Barracks their headquarters and within days created their Bear Flag. The Californios called them Los Osos, the Bears. The Bear Flag Revolt ended and the California Republic ceased on 9 July 1846, when Lieutenant Joseph Warren Revere of the United States Navy raised the American flag before the barracks.

After California became a state in 1850, Sonoma was the first seat of Sonoma County, but an election of 1854 moved the seat to Santa Rosa. Disputes over land titles from Vallejo's grants took some thirty years of lawsuits to settle. The City Hall in the middle of the Plaza was dedicated in 1908.

Sonoma is a city in Sonoma County in the North Bay region of the San Francisco Bay Area, one of the principal cities of California's wine country and the centre of the Sonoma Valley wine region. It had 10,739 residents in the 2020 census. The Plaza, laid out by Vallejo, remains the centre of town.
sonora: Sonora is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the Federal Entities of Mexico, and it is divided into 72 municipalities. With a territory of 184,934 square kilometres it is the second largest state of the country. It borders Chihuahua, Baja California and Sinaloa, and to the north it adjoins Arizona and New Mexico along a border 588 kilometres long. The east is dominated by the Sierra Madre Occidental, the centre is plains and rolling hills, and the southwest has a long coast on the Gulf of California. Most of the state is arid or semiarid.

Sonora is home to eight indigenous peoples, among them the Mayo, the O'odham, the Yaqui and the Seri. Evidence of human presence goes back over 10,000 years. The cultures of the region are considered a zone separate from Mesoamerica: they farmed in a dry climate and had no true cities, only small settlements clustered around water sources.

Little reliable information remains about the 16th century after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire. Francisco Vázquez de Coronado passed through in 1540 and called part of the area Valle de la Sonora, the first record of the name. Unlike in central Mexico, no central power existed for the Spaniards to take over, and the Yaqui resisted intrusion until the 17th century. Lasting Spanish settlement became possible only with the mission system.

Sonora became part of an independent Mexico in 1821. The former province of Sonora, Ostimuri, y Sinaloa was divided in 1823 into the states of Sonora and Sinaloa, reunited in 1824 and separated again in 1831, when Sonora wrote its first state constitution. With the Gadsden Purchase it lost more than a quarter of its territory. The Cananea miners' strike of 1906, a prelude to the Mexican Revolution, ended when federal troops put it down brutally.

The capital and largest city is Hermosillo; other large cities include Ciudad Obregón, Nogales and San Luis Río Colorado. Agriculture is the most important economic activity, with irrigation in valleys such as the Yaqui and the Mayo, and Sonora is one of Mexico's two largest wheat-producing states. Livestock and mining have mattered since the colonial period. The El Pinacate biosphere reserve protects a field of dormant volcanic craters.
sonsonate: Sonsonate was founded in 1552 as the Villa del Espíritu Santo on vacant lots near the town of the Izalcos. This first foundation was very short-lived: in 1553 the settlement was moved to its present site, in a cocoa-producing area, and named the Villa de la Santísima Trinidad de Sonsonate. In time it came to be known simply as Sonsonate. It was the third Spanish town founded in the territory of present-day El Salvador.

The name comes from the Río Grande, or Sonsonate, which crosses the plain from north to south and flows into the Pacific Ocean. Early reports said the city took its name from the Sensunat river, which they interpreted as "four hundred waters". Fray Francisco Vásquez read it as "four hundred eyes of water", and Santiago I. Barberena derived it from the Nahuat words sentzunti, four hundred, and at, water, giving the place name Sentzunhat.

Throughout the period of Spanish domination, Sonsonate was the capital of the Mayor's Office of Sonsonate, a territory separate from the one administered from San Salvador, which is now the national capital. Historically the area produced cotton, and as late as 1850 most of the cotton grown was kept for local use.

Sonsonate is a city and municipal seat in western El Salvador, with an estimated population of 71,980 in 2020, and it is the second most important city of the west of the country. One of its main cultural attractions is the Holy Week celebration, which the Legislative Assembly of El Salvador recognised by decree in 2013 as part of the country's religious heritage. Tobacco farming, cattle ranching and tourism, based on its volcanoes and coral reef, are important local industries.
sook-ching: The Japanese 25th Army saw the Chinese of Singapore and Malaya as the likely centre of resistance to Japanese expansion, partly because of the money they had raised for China after the invasion of Manchuria and during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Its military government section drew up an "Implementation Guideline for Manipulating Overseas Chinese" on or around 28 December 1941, before the landing, and the chief of staff Sōsaku Suzuki told the Kenpeitai commander Oishi Masayuki to prepare a purge. The historian Hirofumi Hayashi concludes that the massacre was premeditated; the staff officer Tsuji Masanobu is named as its chief planner.

The killings ran from 18 February to 4 March 1942. Oishi, with 200 regular Kenpeitai officers and about 1,000 auxiliaries, ordered Chinese males aged 18 to 50 to report to screening centres. On paper the targets were communists, volunteers who had fought for the British, financiers of Chinese resistance and gangsters, but in practice the selection was arbitrary: hooded informants or officers picked out men at will, and at one centre all who passed through a particular entrance were taken away to be shot. Those released were stamped "examined"; the others were driven by truck to sites such as Changi Beach, Punggol Point and Sentosa.

At Tsuji's urging the operation was extended to Malaya, where the Japanese, lacking time and men to screen a scattered population, carried out indiscriminate massacres, chiefly in the southern states: about 2,000 died at Kota Tinggi on 28 February 1942, and 1,474 at Joo Loong Loong on 18 March. Japan later admitted about 6,000 deaths in Singapore, while Lee Kuan Yew, who himself nearly became a victim, put the toll far higher.

In 1947 a British war crimes court tried seven officers; Saburo Kawamura and Masayuki Oishi were hanged on 26 June 1947, while Tsuji escaped, later became a politician in Japan and disappeared in Laos in 1961. After mass graves were found at Siglap in 1962, Singapore's Chinese community boycotted Japanese imports for a week in September 1963. On 25 October 1966 Japan agreed to pay S$50 million, half as a grant and half as a loan, as a gesture of atonement, without an apology or acceptance of legal responsibility. The Civilian War Memorial on Beach Road, unveiled on 15 February 1967, holds the remains found from 1962 to 1966.
sophia-albertina-of-sweden: Sophia Albertina was born on 8 October 1753, the daughter of King Adolf Frederick and Louisa Ulrika of Prussia, and was named after her grandmothers, Queen Sophia Dorothea of Prussia and Margravine Albertina Frederica of Baden-Durlach. She lived under her mother's strict control until the queen dowager's death in 1782 and sided with her in the quarrels with Gustav III, burning some of her mother's papers before the king could see them. Marriages to Crown Prince Frederick William of Prussia, to her cousin Prince Peter of Holstein-Gottorp and to King Stanisław August Poniatowski were proposed, and none took place.

In 1767 her uncle Frederick the Great had her made coadjutrix of Quedlinburg Abbey, a convent of Lutheran women, and in 1787 she succeeded her aunt Anna Amalia of Prussia, taking her oath on 15 October. As reigning head of a state of the Holy Roman Empire she founded schools for poor children, opened the city's first theatre and raised the pay of the clergy, governing with her chancellor Sebastian von Moltzer. In the German Mediatization the state was incorporated into Prussia; she kept the title and income for life and left in September 1803.

At the Riksdag of 1789 she watched the sessions through a secret window and, with her sister-in-law Hedvig Elisabeth Charlotte, was associated with the social boycott of the king by noblewomen opposed to the Union and Security Act. She intervened for Magdalena Rudenschöld during the Armfelt conspiracy and had her death sentence revoked. In 1795 she came to believe that her chambermaid Lolotte Forssberg was her sister, which caused a scandal in Sweden and Prussia; in 1799 she declared Forssberg her illegitimate half-sister.

In 1807 she lost her Quedlinburg income when the Kingdom of Westphalia annexed it, and Napoleon did not answer her appeal. In the Revolution of 1809 she greeted Georg Adlersparre from her balcony. Charles XIV John used her presence, as the last of the old dynasty, to lend his own legitimacy; she placed the bridal crown on Josephine of Leuchtenberg in 1823. She died on 17 March 1829. Sofia Albertina Church in Landskrona, opened in 1788, bears her name.
sophia-dorothea-of-celle: Sophia Dorothea was born in Celle on 15 September 1666, the only surviving daughter of George William, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and his morganatic wife Éléonore Desmier d'Olbreuse, a French Huguenot noblewoman. By imperial order of 22 July 1674 she and her mother received the title of Countess of Harburg and Wilhelmsburg. A betrothal to the Hereditary Prince of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel ended in 1676 when he was mortally wounded at the siege of Philippsburg. George William's brother Ernest Augustus and his wife Sophia of the Palatinate then had misgivings about a match with their son George Louis because of the circumstances of her birth. To remove them her father declared Éléonore his lawful wife, and the family recognised Sophia Dorothea as a princess in 1680.

The wedding took place on 21 November 1682, in the face of opposition from Sophia Dorothea and her mother. The marriage failed. George Louis and his mother thought her birth and manners inferior, and the Electress Sophia wrote that the 100,000 thalers a year that came with her were what tempted her son. The couple had two children, the future George II, born in 1683, and a daughter Sophia Dorothea, born in 1687, who became queen in Prussia. George Louis took a mistress, Melusine von der Schulenburg.

Around 1690 she met again Count Philip Christoph von Königsmarck, whom she had known as a page at Celle. By 1694 the court believed they were lovers, which she denied for the rest of her life. They planned to flee together. On the night of 11 July 1694, after meeting her in the Leineschloss, Königsmarck disappeared without trace; it appears he was killed on the orders, direct or tacit, of George Louis or his father. The marriage was dissolved on 28 December 1694, with Sophia Dorothea named as the guilty party. She was forbidden to remarry or to see her children.

She was confined at Ahlden House, guarded day and night by forty men at arms, and known as the Duchess of Ahlden. Her father died in 1705 without seeing her. After a fire at Ahlden in 1715 she gave considerable sums towards rebuilding the town. She suffered a stroke in early 1726 and died on 13 November 1726, aged sixty. She was buried secretly in May 1727 beside her parents in the Stadtkirche in Celle.
Her love letters with Königsmarck, which survive in large part at Lund University, were published in the middle of the 19th century, and their authenticity is now established beyond doubt.
sophia-of-hanover: Sophia was born on 14 October 1630 at the Wassenaer Hof in The Hague, the twelfth child and fifth daughter of Frederick V of the Palatinate and Elizabeth Stuart, known as the Winter King and Queen because they had to flee Bohemia after ruling for a year. Her father died when she was two, and she was raised in Leiden away from her mother. Her lack of a dowry and the family's uncertain position hurt the sisters' marriage prospects. In 1649 her cousin Charles II of England, then in exile at The Hague, courted her, but she rebuffed him. After the Peace of Westphalia restored the Rhine Palatine to her brother Charles, she settled with him in Heidelberg in 1650.

A marriage contract was first drawn up with George William, Duke of Brunswick, but he withdrew and proposed that she marry his brother Ernest Augustus, promising never to marry himself, so that his lands would pass to the couple. The new contract was signed on 5 June 1658, and they married at Heidelberg on 30 September. Sophia bore ten children, of whom seven survived. In 1692 Ernest Augustus had the House of Hanover raised to electoral rank, and she became Electress of Hanover, the title by which she is best remembered.

The Act of Settlement of 1701 named her and the Protestant heirs of her body as next in the succession after William III and Princess Anne, to keep out the Catholic James Francis Edward Stuart. Some politicians wanted her to come to England, but Anne was opposed to a rival court, and the plan was dropped.

Sophia was a patron of the arts and, with Ernest Augustus, improved Herrenhausen Palace and guided the creation of its gardens. She was a friend of Gottfried Leibniz from 1676 until her death, and their correspondence shows her wide reading, which included Descartes and Spinoza. On 8 June 1714, aged 83, she collapsed and died in the Herrenhausen Gardens in the arms of her granddaughter-in-law Caroline of Ansbach. Queen Anne died on 1 August 1714, and Sophia's eldest son, George Louis, became George I of Great Britain. Sophia was buried in the chapel of Leine Palace in Hanover, and in 1957 her remains were moved to the mausoleum of Ernest Augustus I in the Berggarten.
sophia-palaiologina: Sophia, born Zoe Palaiologina, was the daughter of Thomas Palaiologos, Despot of the Morea and younger brother of Constantine XI, and of Catherine, heiress of Centurione II Zaccaria, the last independent Prince of Achaea. After the Ottoman army breached the Hexamilion wall in 1460, the family fled to Corfu and then Rome. Her mother died on Corfu in 1462, and when her dying father recalled the children to Rome in 1465 they were adopted by the Papacy and lived at the court of Pope Sixtus IV. Cardinal Basilios Bessarion, a Greek humanist and scholar, had charge of the children. They received 3,600 crowns for clothes, horses and servants.

After Maria of Tver, the first wife of Ivan III, died in 1467, Pope Paul II proposed Sophia as his bride in 1469, probably hoping to extend Catholic influence in Russia and unite the Orthodox and Catholic churches. Ivan Fryazin, acting as proxy for the grand prince, married her at St. Peter's Basilica on 1 June 1472. She reached Moscow on 12 November 1472, when the wedding was held at the Dormition Cathedral. The papal plan failed at once: she returned to the faith of her fathers after the wedding, and the papal legate was not allowed to enter Moscow carrying the Latin cross.

She did not keep to the isolation of elite Russian women and received foreign envoys, among them the Venetian Ambrogio Contarini in 1476. She is believed to have introduced grand Byzantine ceremony to the Kremlin and to have urged Ivan to end his tributary relationship with the Mongols. She bore eleven children between 1474 and 1490, among them the future Vasili III.

The court divided between supporters of the heir Ivan the Young, Ivan III's son by his first wife, and Sophia's party. When Ivan the Young died in 1490, rumour said that she had poisoned him, but modern historians say the claim cannot be verified for lack of sources.

In 1498 Ivan the Young's son Dmitry was crowned co-ruler, while Sophia and Vasili were left out, though they returned to favour in 1499. In April 1502 the struggle ended: Ivan III placed Dmitry and his mother Elena under guard, and Vasili was crowned grand prince. Sophia died on 7 April 1503. She was buried in the Ascension Convent in the Kremlin, and when the convent was demolished in 1929 her remains were moved to the Cathedral of the Archangel.
sophie-of-brabant: Sophie was born at Wartburg Castle near Eisenach on 20 March 1224, the eldest daughter and second child of her parents; the Cronica Reinhardsbrunnensis recorded her birth. Her mother was a daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary and Gertrude of Merania. When Sophie was three her father set out on the Sixth Crusade and died of a fever on the way. Her brother Hermann succeeded him under the regency of their uncle Henry Raspe.

On the orders of their mother's confessor, Konrad of Marburg, the children were sent to Bollenstein Castle under the care of their great-uncle Egbert, Bishop of Bamberg. After Elisabeth died in 1231 Henry Raspe took control of Thuringia, and Hermann died in 1241 without ever having reigned.

In 1241, at the age of 17, Sophie married Henry II, Duke of Brabant and Lothier, as his second wife, a marriage recorded in the Annales Parchenses. She was the only one of his wives to be styled duchess, since his first wife, Marie of Hohenstaufen, had died before he succeeded to the duchy. They had two children, Elisabeth, who married Albert I, Duke of Brunswick-Luneburg, and Henry, born on 24 June 1244, and she also raised six stepchildren.

When Henry Raspe died without issue in 1247, Sophie claimed the Ludowinger lands of Thuringia and Hesse against her cousin Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, and the Archbishopric of Mainz, which held them to be its fiefs. Backed by the Hessian nobility, she fought a war that lasted 17 years and won a partial victory in 1264: her cousin received Thuringia, while Hesse went to her son by right of his mother.

She was described as an energetic and courageous woman, proud of her saintly ancestry, and she opened her letters and charters with the words We, Sophie, duchess of Brabant, daughter of St. Elisabeth. After her husband's death she lived in a castle beside the Dijle at Sint-Agatha-Rode. She died in Marburg on 29 May 1275 and was buried in Villers Abbey. As founder of the Brabant dynasty of Hesse she stood at the start of an independent landgraviate that grew into a powerful principality; a statue of her and her son stands in front of Marburg's town hall.
sophocles: Sophocles was the son of Sophillus, a wealthy member of the rural deme of Hippeius Colonus in Attica, which later became the setting of his play Oedipus at Colonus. He was probably born there a few years before the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE, and 496 or 497 BCE is the most likely year. His father manufactured armour, and he was highly educated.

In 480 BCE he was chosen to lead the paean, a choral chant to a god, for the Greek victory over the Persians at the Battle of Salamis. He lived through both the Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War, and died at the age of 90 or 91 in the winter of 406/5 BCE.

His first artistic triumph came in 468 BCE, when he took first prize at the Dionysia and beat Aeschylus, the reigning master of Athenian drama. According to Plutarch, the archon departed from the custom of choosing judges by lot and asked Cimon and the other generals present to decide. His first production was probably in 470 BCE. For almost 50 years he was the most successful playwright in the dramatic competitions at the festivals of the Lenaea and the Dionysia. He competed 30 times and won 24, and was never placed lower than second. Aeschylus won 13 competitions and Euripides four.

He also served Athens in public office. In 443/2 BCE he was one of the Hellenotamiai, the treasurers of Athena, and in 441 BCE, according to the Vita Sophoclis, he was elected one of the ten generals as a junior colleague of Pericles and served in the campaign against Samos. In 411 BCE he was chosen as one of the commissioners, the probouloi, who responded to the destruction of the Athenian expedition in Sicily. Foreign rulers invited him to their courts, but he never accepted.

Sophocles wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete: Ajax, Antigone, Women of Trachis, Oedipus Rex, Electra, Philoctetes and Oedipus at Colonus. Only Philoctetes, of 409 BCE, and Oedipus at Colonus, staged in 401 BCE after his death by his grandson, can be dated securely. The three Theban plays, Oedipus Rex, Oedipus at Colonus and Antigone, were written for separate competitions many years apart, and they are not a trilogy, which explains some inconsistencies among them.

He is known for innovations in dramatic structure and a deeper development of character than earlier playwrights. Aristotle credits him with adding a third actor, which reduced the role of the chorus, though Themistius attributes this to Aeschylus. Aristotle also used Oedipus Rex in his Poetics as an example of the highest achievement in tragedy. Fragments of the satyr play Ichneutae were discovered in Egypt in 1907, and fragments of the Epigoni in 2005.
sophonisba: Sophonisba was a Carthaginian noblewoman of the Second Punic War, the daughter of Hasdrubal Gisco, and she is dated to about 206 to 203 BCE. Her Punic name is given as Ṣaponi-Baʿal, 'May Baʿal watch over me'. The form Sophonisba is not known until the 15th century, in a few late manuscripts of Livy. Her story is told by Livy, Diodorus, Appian and Cassius Dio, but Polybius, who had met Masinissa, never names her.

In 206 BCE Sophonisba was betrothed to Masinissa, a leader of the eastern Numidian Massylii, to seal an alliance between Carthage and the Massylii. The Carthaginian Senate forbade the wedding and ordered her to marry Syphax, chieftain of the western Masaesyli, who until then had been allied to Rome. Cassius Dio suggests that Syphax was thought the better ally. Appian says he was in love with her and pressed for the marriage with revolts and threats of attack alongside Roman forces. She married Syphax in 206 BCE, and Masinissa secretly allied himself with Scipio Africanus.

Classical writers praise her virtues and skill, and Cassius Dio says she was highly educated in music and literature. Modern historians have therefore seen her as a political agent for Carthage rather than a pawn. She is said to have made Syphax join Hasdrubal against Scipio and Masinissa at the battles of Utica and the Great Plains, where the Punic forces were defeated.

Syphax was defeated and captured at the Battle of Cirta in 203 BCE. Masinissa freed Sophonisba and married her, accepting that she had been forced to marry Syphax. Scipio refused the arrangement, fearing that she would turn Masinissa against Rome as she had Syphax, and demanded her surrender so that she could appear in a triumph at Rome. Masinissa asked her to die as a Carthaginian princess, and she drank a cup of poison he offered her, reproaching him for making the marriage so short and bitter.

Her story furnished tragedies and later operas from the 16th to the 19th centuries, more than any other with Cleopatra's. Petrarch told it in his epic Africa, and Gian Giorgio Trissino in 1515, John Marston in 1606 and Pierre Corneille in 1663 wrote plays on it.
sopocani-monastery: The monastery stands near the source of the Raška River in the region of Ras, the centre of the medieval Serbian state, 15 kilometres west of Novi Pazar. It was an endowment of King Stefan Uroš I, a son of Stefan the First-Crowned and a grandson of Stefan Nemanja, and was meant as his burial place. The church is dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The painting of its main parts can be dated indirectly to between 1263 and 1270. Stefan Uroš I was buried there, as were Anna Dandolo and Joanikije I. The church was extended and renovated in the mid-14th century by his great-grandson Dušan, when it took on the character of a cathedral.

Of a larger complex that once held dining rooms and residential buildings inside a high stone wall with two gates, only the Church of the Holy Trinity remains. The decoration follows a plan formed over the 13th century. The chancel has liturgical scenes, the nave shows Christ's work of salvation through the cycle of the Great Feasts, and the narthex has Old Testament, dogmatic and eschatological themes. Portraits of the Nemanjić family and scenes from the lives of Simeon Nemanja and Saint Sava appear as well, and Archbishop Sava II, head of the Serbian Orthodox Church from 1263, is shown in the procession of archbishops near the altar.

The style draws on late Byzantine art and shows a transition from the Komnenian to the Palaiologan period. The fresco of the Dormition of the Virgin on the western wall of the nave, with stately compositions and monumental figures, is the best known. Some experts on Serbian medieval art consider the frescoes the most beautiful of their time. The origins of the painters are unknown. Stefan Uroš I ordered gold-sheet tesserae for the outlines of some of the more prominent frescoes.

The monks had to leave the monastery temporarily several times in the 16th century because of the Ottoman threat. In 1689 the Ottoman Turks set fire to it and carried off the lead from the church roof. The brotherhood fled with relics to Kosovo and did not return, and the site stayed deserted for over two hundred years. The vaults caved in and the dome fell. Large restoration campaigns took place in 1925-1929 and 1949-1958, and the church has been settled again by monks.

Copying of Sopoćani's work in 1370-1375 created a Sopoćani style that spread to other churches, and in the early 20th century its art inspired modern Serbian artists. It was declared a Monument of Culture of Exceptional Importance in 1979 and was added that year to the World Heritage list together with Stari Ras.
sopron: An Iron Age hilltop settlement with a burial ground lay near Sopron-Várhely. Under Roman rule the city of Scarbantia stood here, and the site of its forum is now the main square. By the time Hungarians arrived the city was in ruins. From the 9th to the 11th centuries they strengthened the old Roman walls and built a castle, and the city takes its Hungarian name from a castle steward named Suprun. The city was mentioned as important in 1153. In 1273 King Otakar II of Bohemia occupied the castle, but the city opened its gates to King Ladislaus IV of Hungary, who raised it to the rank of free royal town.

The Ottomans ravaged the city in 1529 without occupying it, and many Hungarians fled there from occupied areas. A fire destroyed the city in 1676, and Baroque buildings replaced the medieval ones over the following decades. After the compromise of 1867 until 1918 it was part of the Habsburg-ruled Kingdom of Hungary, with the dual name Sopron and Ödenburg. In 1910 its 33,931 inhabitants were 51 per cent German and 44.3 per cent Hungarian.

After the breakup of the Austro-Hungarian Empire the German-inhabited parts of four western Hungarian counties were first awarded to Austria by the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919. After local unrest and Italian mediation in the Venice Protocol, a controversial plebiscite on 14 December 1921 decided the status of Sopron and eight surrounding villages, and 65 per cent voted for Hungary. Since then the city has been called Civitas Fidelissima, the Most Loyal City, and the anniversary is a city holiday. The western parts of the counties formed the Austrian state of Burgenland.

Sopron was bombed several times in World War II, and the Red Army captured it on 1 April 1945. On 19 August 1989 it was the site of the Pan-European Picnic on the border with Austria, which over 600 East Germans used to escape to the West and which helped pave the way for the mass flight that preceded the fall of the Berlin Wall.

Walls and foundations from Roman times remain in the old town, together with Medieval, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, among them the Esterházy Palace and the Firewatch Tower. Sopron is also a wine-producing region, known for Kékfrankos red and Traminer white wines, and its street signs are in Hungarian and German.
soqotri-language: Soqotri is a South Semitic language spoken by the Soqotrans on the islands of the Socotra Archipelago in Yemen, namely Socotra, Abd al Kuri, Darsah and Samha, and by Soqotri immigrants in the Gulf Arab states, mainly in Ajman. It is one of six Modern South Arabian languages. It is often mistaken for a variety of Arabic, but scholars consider that there are no longer grounds for associating the Modern South Arabian languages so directly with Arabic and regard them as Semitic languages in their own right.

The 1990 census counted 57,000 speakers in Yemen, and 71,400 in all countries. It has no official status. It has three main dialects, Eastern, Central and Western, and its dialects are very rich for the size of the islands.

Soqotri was isolated from the Arabian mainland throughout its history, and it developed phonetic features absent even from related mainland languages. It lost the interdental consonants, which merged with t, d and an emphatic t, so that Soqotri has dor for "blood" where Mehri has ðōrə. Its emphatics were once ejectives and have largely become pharyngealised, except for one.

Poetry and song were a normal part of everyday life, a way of communicating with other people, animals, the spirits of the dead, jinn, sorcerers and the divine. The couplet is the basic unit of Soqotri poetry and song. Older speakers in remote places still use the dual in verbs, nouns and pronouns, while younger speakers and those in contact with Arabic often use plurals instead.

Lieutenant Wellstedt, part of a surveying mission in 1835, collected the first list, of 236 Soqotri words, 41 of which he noted as Arabic loans. Soqotri was traditionally unwritten. A Russian team led by Vitaly Naumkin developed an Arabic-based alphabet for it in 2014 after five years of work, published in his Corpus of Soqotri Oral Literature, and it has helped narrators of oral lore work with researchers. Soqotri is regarded as severely endangered, because Arabic is the language of national identity and many young people see Soqotri as irrelevant to improving the island's socio-economic status.
sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz: Juana Inés de Asbaje y Ramírez de Santillana was born at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City, the illegitimate daughter of Don Pedro Manuel de Asuaje y Vargas-Machuca, a Spanish navy captain from the Canary Islands involved in transatlantic shipping and trade, and Doña Isabel Ramírez de Santillana y Rendón, a criolla whose father leased the Hacienda de Panoayan.

In 1667 she entered the Monastery of St. Joseph, a community of Discalced Carmelite nuns, but stayed only a few months. In 1669 she entered the Hieronymite convent, whose rules were more relaxed, and took the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. She chose the convent so that she could study as she wished, wanting in her words no fixed occupation that might curtail her freedom to study. Octavio Paz and Diane Marting hold that she also refused marriage, and that the convent gave her authority and freedom without it.

First Dream is a long philosophical and descriptive silva, a poetic form combining verses of seven and eleven syllables. It describes the shadow of night, the sleep of a person and the soul's vision of itself at the summit of its own intellect. Her poem Hombres Necios, written in the 1680s, explores the double standards of men and is among the first proto-feminist literary works in the Americas. Her comedies, among them Pawns of a House, first performed on 4 October 1683, are read by some scholars as questioning the relations of men and women through humour.

She was also interested in science, mathematics and music, and wrote a treatise, El Caracol, now lost, that sought to simplify musical notation and to solve problems of Pythagorean tuning. One surviving musical work attributed to her is the four-part villancico Madre, la de los primores. Her contemporaries nicknamed her The Tenth Muse and The Phoenix of America.

Sor Juana died on 17 April 1695. She wrote most of her work in the convent of San Jerónimo; its buildings in the historic centre of Mexico City now house the University of the Cloister of Sor Juana, founded by the Mexican government in 1979. Her works were rediscovered after her death, and Octavio Paz did much to restore her importance in his 1982 book on her life and times. Scholars have presented her as a candidate for Catholic sainthood, a symbol of Mexican nationalism and, in recent decades, a feminist before the time of feminism.
sora-lazio: Sora lies in the province of Frosinone, built on a plain on the banks of the Liri. It is 115 km from the centre of Rome and 138 km from the centre of Naples, and its municipality borders Abruzzo. Above the town, on a precipitous rock 540 metres high that guards the valley of the Liri and the entrance to the Abruzzi, stand remains of polygonal walls, where possibly the citadel of the original Volscian town lay, together with remains of medieval fortifications.

The Romans captured Sora in 345, 314 and 305 BCE before they confirmed its annexation by a colony 4,000 strong in 303 BCE. In 209 BCE it was one of the colonies that refused further contributions to the war against Hannibal. By the lex Julia it became a municipium, and under Augustus it was colonised by soldiers of the legio IV Sorana, which had mainly been enrolled there.

In the early Middle Ages Sora lay in the Ducatus Romanus under the authority of the pope, and the Lombards of Gisulf I of Benevento captured it in 705. The castle of Sorella on the rocky height above the town was a stronghold of some note. In 1229, during the War of the Keys, Sora submitted to the Papacy and was then sacked by Emperor Frederick II, who had its inhabitants hanged.

In 1443 King Alfonso of Naples made Sora the seat of an independent duchy. Pope Pius II seized it, but Pope Sixtus IV restored it to the Cantelmi, and it ultimately passed to the duke Giovanni della Rovere. Francesco Maria I della Rovere defended the city against Cesare Borgia. Pope Gregory XIII bought it for 11,000 ducats and placed it under his son Giacomo Boncompagni, the first duke of Sora of that family.

Sora is a town and comune of Lazio and the seat of some important manufacturing, especially paper mills. The original cathedral, consecrated by Pope Adrian IV in 1155, was destroyed by the earthquake of 1634. Among the town's churches are the Sanctuary of the Madonna della Figura and San Silvestro Papa. Caesar Baronius, the cardinal and ecclesiastical historian, was born there, as was the film director Vittorio De Sica.
soraya-esfandiary-bakhtiary: Soraya was born on 22 June 1932 at the English Missionary Hospital in Isfahan, the elder of two children and the only daughter of Khalil Esfandiary-Bakhtiary, a Bakhtiari nobleman who became Iranian ambassador to West Germany in the 1950s, and his Russian-born German wife Eva Karl. Her family had long served in the Iranian government and diplomatic corps, and a great-uncle, Sardar Assad, was a leader in the Persian Constitutional Revolution. She was raised in Berlin and Isfahan and educated in London and Switzerland.

In 1948 a relative introduced her to the recently divorced Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi by means of a photograph taken in London, and they were soon engaged. She married the Shah at the Marble Palace in Tehran on 12 February 1951, in a wedding with 2,000 guests and a gown designed by Christian Dior. Her upbringing had been German and Catholic, and some Muslim clerics objected to a half-European girl who had not been raised a Muslim.

As queen she headed the family charity in Iran. In August 1953 she followed the Shah to Rome when he fled during the confrontation with Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh, and he returned after the coup that overthrew Mosaddegh. In 1954 the Shah, concerned that she had not given him an heir, took her to the United States to consult doctors, and in Boston she was told she was infertile. A photograph of her water-skiing in a bikini at Miami caused controversy and was banned in Iran.

The marriage disintegrated by early 1958. The Shah's mother pressed him to divorce her, and Soraya refused to accept that he take a second wife. The divorce was announced in March 1958 and the marriage ended officially on 6 April. She received a penthouse in Paris and a monthly allowance. Afterwards she briefly acted in films, using her first name only, and starred in I tre volti in 1965 and became the companion of its director, Franco Indovina, who died in a plane crash in 1972.

Soraya wrote two memoirs, one published in 1964 and Le Palais des solitudes in 1991, in which she described her depression. She died on 25 October 2001 in her apartment in Paris, aged 69, and was buried in Munich beside her parents and brother. Her belongings were sold at auction in Paris in 2002 for more than 8.3 million dollars, and a dispute over her estate continued until 2016. Her divorce inspired the song Je veux pleurer comme Soraya, released in 1995.
sorbs: The name Sorbs, in Upper Sorbian Serbja and in Lower Sorbian Serby, derives from medieval groups called Surbi or Sorabi, and the Sorbs are also known as Lusatian Serbs. By the 6th century Slavs occupied the area west of the Oder formerly inhabited by Germanic peoples. The Sorbs are first mentioned in the 6th or 7th century. According to the 7th-century Chronicle of Fredegar, the Surbi lived in the Saale-Elbe valley and were vassals of the Merovingian dynasty. In the Early Middle Ages they formed their own principality, which for a short time became part of Samo's Empire and of Great Moravia, and was ultimately conquered by East Francia and the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1002 Bolesław I of Poland took over Lusatia, and the Peace of Bautzen confirmed it as part of Poland, but it returned to German rule in 1031. In the 1070s southern Lusatia passed to the Czechs within the Duchy of Bohemia. From 1376 to 1469 and from 1490 to 1635 Lusatia belonged to the Lands of the Bohemian Crown, and under Bohemian rule the Sorbs were allowed to return to cities, offices and crafts and to use their language in public. From the beginning of the 16th century the rest of the Sorbian-inhabited area underwent Germanization.

The Congress of Vienna in 1815 divided Lusatia between Prussia and Saxony. Bans on the use of Sorbian languages followed until 1835, and many Sorbs emigrated, mainly to Serbin in Texas and to Australia. In 1848, 5,000 Sorbs signed a petition to the Saxon government demanding equality for Sorbian in churches, courts, schools and government departments. After 1871 policies in united Germany sought to Germanize them, and under the Nazi regime the Sorbs were denied as a distinct Slavic people and called Sorbian-speaking Germans. In East Germany the Sorbs were recognised as an ethnic minority, and more than 100 Sorbian schools and several academic institutions were founded, and the Domowina was re-established.

The oldest known relic of Sorbian literature, from about 1530, is the Bautzen townsmen's oath, and the first Sorbian book, Albin Moller's songbook, was printed in 1574. Traditions that are preserved include Easter horseback riding, the Bird Wedding and the painting of Easter eggs. The Sorbs' flag of blue, red and white stripes was first used in 1842. Upper Lusatia, with its Catholic majority, is where Upper Sorbian customs are most alive, and in some places children grow up speaking Sorbian. Lower Lusatia, around Cottbus, is predominantly Protestant, and some primary schools teach bilingually. In 1900 about 87 per cent of the Sorbs were Lutheran, but today most speakers of Upper Sorbian are Catholic.
sordello: Sordello was born in the municipality of Goito in the province of Mantua. About 1220 he was involved in a tavern brawl in Florence. In 1226, while at the court of Richard of Bonifazio in Verona, he carried off his master's wife, Cunizza, at the instigation of her brother Ezzelino III da Romano. The scandal led to his flight to Provence in 1229, where he seems to have stayed for some time.

In Provence Sordello entered the service of Charles of Anjou and probably went with him on his expedition to Naples in 1265; in 1266 he was a prisoner in Naples. The last document that mentions him dates from 1269, and he is thought to have died in Provence. As far as the facts of his life go, he was the best known of the Italian troubadours. His works include a didactic poem, L'ensenhamen d'onor, love songs and satirical pieces. In his sirventes-planh of 1237 on the death of his patron Blacatz he invites the princes of Christendom to feed on the dead hero's heart, the closest parallel in his own work to the invective against negligent princes that Dante gives him.

Dante Alighieri praised Sordello around 1305 in De vulgari eloquentia and made him a character in cantos 6, 7 and 8 of the Purgatorio. Dante places him in Ante-Purgatory among those who repented late or died by violence, which suggests that Dante thought he was murdered, though this may be Dante's own conjecture. When Virgil names Mantua, the city of both poets, Sordello embraces him, and Dante uses this patriotism to begin a denunciation of Italy's corruption and lack of leadership.

Sordello then leads the travellers to the Valley of Rulers and points out kings and princes there, among them Rudolph I of Germany, Ottokar II of Bohemia, Philip III of France and Peter III of Aragon. Robert Browning made him the hero of his poem Sordello (1840). Oscar Wilde, Ezra Pound, Samuel Beckett, Roberto Bolaño and Robert Shea also wrote of him.
soren-kierkegaard: Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born on 5 May 1813 in Copenhagen, the youngest of seven children of an affluent family. His father, Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard, was a devoutly Christian wool merchant from Jutland who was devoted to the rationalist philosophy of Christian Wolff. The figure of Socrates, whom Kierkegaard met in Plato's dialogues, later shaped his interest in irony and indirect communication.

He met Regine Olsen on 8 May 1837 and proposed to her on 8 September 1840, after passing his theological examinations. He broke off the engagement on 11 August 1841, and after she pleaded with him he ended it verbally on 11 October 1841. His journals blame his melancholy, but his precise motive remains unclear, and the broken engagement is generally considered to have had a major influence on his work.

Kierkegaard published some works under pseudonyms, each presenting a distinct viewpoint, as a way of indirect communication. Either/Or, considered his magnum opus, and Fear and Trembling, his central writing on religion, both appeared in 1843. Critics have accused him of playing with viewpoints without committing to one, though he said all his work came from a service to Christianity.

His key ideas include subjective and objective truth, the knight of faith, anxiety, faith as a passion and the three stages on life's way. He wrote, "Christianity teaches that the way is to become subjective, to become a subject." He attacked Hegelianism by parody, though he admired Hegel personally. A dispute that began with an article by Peder Ludvig Møller in December 1845 led him to ask the satirical paper The Corsair to satirise him. His journals run to over 7,000 pages.

In his last years Kierkegaard attacked the Church of Denmark in newspaper articles and in a series of self-published pamphlets, The Moment. The attack began after Hans Lassen Martensen called the dead Bishop Jacob Peter Mynster a truth-witness, which Kierkegaard strongly objected to. He later said his earlier writing had been preparation for it. He collapsed in the street, spent over a month in Frederiks Hospital, refused communion, and died on 11 November 1855. His nephew Henrik Lund protested at the funeral against burial by the official church.

His work was written in Danish and was at first read mainly in Scandinavia, but was translated into French, German and other languages around the turn of the 20th century. Georg Brandes published the first book on his life and philosophy in 1879. His fame grew greatly in the 1930s, when the existentialist movement named him a precursor, and philosophers both theistic and atheistic drew from him the notions of angst, despair and the importance of the individual.
sorghaghtani-beki: Sorghaghtani was the daughter of Jakha Gambhu, the younger brother of the Keraite leader Toghrul. Around 1203 Temüjin proposed a marriage between his eldest son Jochi and a daughter or granddaughter of Toghrul. Toghrul refused and later tried to kill Temüjin by inviting him to discuss the proposal. Temüjin escaped, the Keraites were routed in the war that followed, and Toghrul was killed, possibly by the Naimans.

Unlike his brother, Jakha usually supported Temüjin. He gave two daughters to him and one to Jochi. Genghis Khan married the elder, Ibaqa Beki, and gave the young Sorghaghtani, still a teenager, to his son Tolui. Jakha was killed by the general Jürchedei when the Keraites revolted after 1204.

Mongol women held great authority at home, since the men were often away. Sorghaghtani was illiterate but valued literacy, and each of her sons learned a different language for a different region. She was a Christian of the Church of the East and respected other faiths: she financed a madrasa in Bukhara and gave alms to both Christians and Muslims.

Tolui died in 1232, aged 41. Ögedei Khan confirmed her authority over his estates, which included parts of northern China, and reportedly consulted her on many matters. He proposed marriage to her, and then marriage to his son Güyük, but she refused, saying her four sons needed her attention. In 1236 she asked for part of Hebei as her appanage, and Ögedei, after hesitating, agreed.

After Ögedei died in 1241, his wife Töregene Khatun ruled as regent until Güyük was elected Khagan in 1246. Güyük moved against Sorghaghtani and other powerful women. She had meanwhile allied herself secretly with Batu Khan, and when Güyük died in 1248 on a march westward some speculated that she had taken direct action. She and Batu then promoted her eldest son Möngke, who was formally named Great Khan at a kurultai in the Mongol homeland. The families of Ögedei and Güyük tried and failed to overthrow him.

Sorghaghtani died in February or March 1252, a few months after Möngke's accession, and was buried in a Christian church in Gansu. Her sons Möngke, Kublai, Hülegü and Ariq Böke each held power: Kublai as Great Khan and ruler of the Yuan dynasty, Hülegü as khan of the Ilkhanate, and Ariq Böke briefly as a rival Great Khan before Kublai captured him in 1264.

In 1310 she was honoured as Empress in a ceremony that included a mass, and in 1335 she was enshrined in a church in Ganzhou, where sacrifices were ordered. The Persian historian Rashid al-Din Hamadani called her extremely intelligent and able, and the Syriac scholar Bar Hebraeus also praised her. European accounts sometimes presented Mongol princesses such as her as daughters of Prester John.
sorghum: Sorghum bicolor was domesticated from a wild ancestor more than 5,000 years ago in eastern Sudan, in the area of the Rivers Atbara and Gash. It has been found at an archaeological site near Kassala dating from 3500 to 3000 BCE, and is associated with the Neolithic Butana Group culture. Sorghum bread from graves in Predynastic Egypt, some 5,100 years ago, is displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Turin.

About 4,000 years ago the crop spread to the Indian subcontinent, and about 3,000 years ago it reached West Africa. Wetter conditions in parts of the Horn of Africa between about 2,500 and 1,000 years ago supported its expansion and contributed to complex agricultural societies such as Aksum.

Sorghum is a large stout grass, typically annual, that grows in clumps and may reach over 4 metres high. Its bushy flowerheads carry up to 3,000 seeds each. It is also called great millet, Indian millet, Guinea corn, jowar and milo. Most varieties tolerate drought and heat, and the plant can grow in soils from heavy clay to sandy ground and recover after some drought. It suppresses weeds by producing a chemical called sorgoleone, and is usually grown by small farmers without fertilizer. Its name comes from the Italian sorgo, most likely from medieval Latin surgum and perhaps from Latin syricum, grass of Syria.

The first domesticated form had tight husks that had to be removed by force. Four further races evolved through cultivation with larger, free-threshing grains: caudatum in the Sahel, durra most likely in India, guinea in West Africa and magentiferum, from which came the varieties of Southern Africa.

Sorghum remained the staple food of the medieval kingdom of Alodia and of most Sub-Saharan cultures before European colonialism. In the Middle Ages the Arab Agricultural Revolution spread it, with other crops, across the Arab world as far as Al-Andalus. The grain is eaten as porridge, couscous or flatbread, such as the Indian jōḷada roṭṭi, and has no gluten. It is brewed into drinks: malwa beer in South Africa, and in China and Taiwan kaoliang liquor, a type of baijiu.

In the 19th century sweet sorghum, called the Chinese sugar-cane, was promoted as a source of sugar for the northern United States and the West Indies. Red leaf-sheaths have dyed leather in Nigeria and wool in Algeria, and in India the panicle stalks are used as broom bristles.
soria: Soria sits on the banks of the upper Douro, at about 1,065 metres above sea level, which makes it the second highest provincial capital in Spain. Its oceanic climate has very cold winters by Spanish standards and scant rainfall. The name may come from dauria, a form of the name of the river Durius, the Douro. Older explanations, that it descended from a castle named Oria after a Greek knight called Doricus, or that the first inhabitants were Dorians or Suebi, have been abandoned for lack of evidence.

The first recorded inhabitants of the area were the Celtiberians, around the 4th century BCE. After the Arab conquest the town grew in importance because it lay near the border of the Christian lands. In 869 it was the centre of a rebellion by Suleyman ibn-Abus against the emir of Córdoba. Soria itself enters history with its repopulation between 1109 and 1114 by the Aragonese king Alfonso I the Battler, who held the territory until 1134. It received a short fuero in 1120, confirmed by Alfonso VII of León in 1143.

Because Soria lay where several kingdoms met, it was at the centre of medieval conflicts. Alfonso VIII of Castile, who was born there, rewarded its support with privileges that it kept into modern times, and Alfonso X held his court there when he received the offer of the throne of the Holy Roman Empire. It prospered in the late Middle Ages through its border location and its control of the cattle industry, but lost importance after the union of Aragon and Castile in 1479 and the decree of exile of the Jews in 1492. French troops captured it and set it on fire in 1808.

Soria is a city and municipality in Castile and León and the capital of its province. Its heritage includes extensive medieval walls, Renaissance palaces and distinctive Romanesque churches such as San Juan de Rabanera. A few kilometres to the north lie the ruins of Numantia, a Celtiberian town whose inhabitants destroyed it rather than let it fall to Scipio, and the Numantine Museum holds finds from it. Antonio Machado spent five years teaching French in a secondary school in Soria, an experience that shaped his poetry.
sorrento: Sorrento is a city and comune on the Sorrentine Peninsula, overlooking the Bay of Naples, with views of Vesuvius and the island of Capri. The Amalfi Drive, a narrow road along high cliffs above the Tyrrhenian Sea, connects it with Amalfi. In antiquity its position was protected by deep gorges, and only about 300 metres on the south-west needed walls. The line of those walls is followed by the modern town.

From the 8th century BCE the area had a community of indigenous villages that was a crossing point for Etruscan traffic, and it later fell to the Osci, whose ruins at Surrentum date from about 600 BCE. Before coming under the Roman Republic Surrentum was subject to Nuceria. Its temples included those of Athena and of the Sirens. It was known in antiquity for wine, fish and red Campanian vases. An inscription shows that Titus restored the town's clock and its decoration in the year after the earthquake of 79 CE.

Sorrento became an archbishopric around 420. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire it was ruled by the Ostrogoths and then returned to the Eastern Empire. In the 9th century it became an autonomous duchy, ruled by figures elected by the people who received honorary titles from the Byzantine emperor. It fought Amalfi, the Saracens and the Lombard duchies, and with Neapolitan help resisted a siege by Benevento in 839. Guaimar IV of Salerno acquired the city in 1035, and what remained of its independence ended in 1137, when Roger II of Sicily conquered it and annexed it to the Kingdom of Sicily.

On 13 June 1558 the Ottoman navy under Dragut and Piali sacked the town and reportedly took 2,000 captives, which led to a new line of walls. In 1648 there was a revolt against Spanish domination, led by Giovanni Grillo, and in 1861 Sorrento was annexed to the new Kingdom of Italy.

Sorrento was the birthplace of the poet Torquato Tasso, author of the Gerusalemme Liberata. Visitors have included Lord Byron, Keats, Goethe, Ibsen and Nietzsche, who wrote Human, All Too Human there in 1876. The song Torna a Surriento, with words by Giambattista De Curtis and music by his brother Ernesto, is named for it. Its cathedral dates from the 14th century and has 11th-century doors from Constantinople. It is a tourist resort, known for ceramics, lacework and marquetry, and it produces limoncello.
soshangane: Soshangane, born Soshangana Nxumalo, was born around 1780 in present-day KwaNongoma, the son of Zikode kaGasa, a chief of the junior branch of the Nxumalo clan of the Ndwandwe people. His family lived in the Mkhuze region near eTshanini Mountain, while the senior branch under Zwide lived at Magudu near the Pongola valley. Under Zwide the Ndwandwe confederacy grew by absorbing smaller communities and by turning age groups formed at state-wide initiation rites into military regiments. Soshangane was one of Zwide's generals, beside Mzilikazi Khumalo, Nxaba Msene and Zwangendaba.

Fleeing the Zulu king with his brothers and his people, he moved along the eastern foothills of the Lubombo to the upper Ntembe River, where Captain W. Owen met them in 1822, a meeting described as the first recorded encounter between the English and the Nguni. For about five years he grew strong by raiding in the Tembe area, defeating the Ronga clans around Delagoa Bay, taking their cattle and young women and drafting their young men into his army. Ndwandwe refugees joined him after Shaka defeated Sikhunyani in 1826, and in 1828 he defeated Shaka's army.

Around 1825 he entered the country between the Matsolo and Nkomati rivers, where a brief alliance with Zwangendaba broke down over his ambition to found his own kingdom. In 1835 he drove out Nxaba Msene, who had ruled Sofala for about ten years, and he then conquered the Ndau and the Manyika.

Soshangane gave chiefdoms to his sons and close relatives, who heard subjects' problems before they reached the king, so that his elder sons gained political experience and followers. Regiments called mangas or impis, commanded by indunas and modelled on Shaka's, dominated the local peasantry; some twenty-four age sets of regiments were formed while the state lasted. Intermarriage with the Rhonga, Tonga and Chopi diluted the Nguni's distinctiveness, and the rulers required subjects to adopt customs such as pierced earlobes. He ruled until his death in 1858.
sosso-empire: The kingdom was inhabited by the Soninke ancestors of the present-day Sosso people and lay south of Wagadou and north of Beledougou. Its name may come from the word for horse, as it held a monopoly of the horse trade with its southern neighbours; Kaniaga is the Malinke name of the region. The Sosso began as a clan of slaves of the Kaya Magha, the ruler of the Ghana Empire, who gradually gained power in the royal bureaucracy and army and served as governors of provinces. Soumaoro Kante was said to have been head of all the royal slaves and governor of a province in northern Beledougou.

Oral histories collected in Sokolo and Goumbou say that a succession war between half-brothers of the ruling Diarrisso family so weakened Wagadu that it fell easily to Soumaoro, an event Heinrich Barth dated to about 1203. Soumaoro conquered Diarra and Gajaaga and subdued the Mandinka chieftaincies to the south, where the goldfields of Bure lay. Besides the capital, oral tradition remembers four cities, among them Kukuba, his fortress, on the cliff above Bamako now called Koulouba. Mande tradition remembers him as cruel: many Soninke left to escape his rule, and religious persecution drove Muslim traders from Koumbi Saleh to Djenne and Oualata.

At the Battle of Kirina, around 1235, Sundiata Keita led a coalition of smaller states that defeated the Sosso and killed Soumaoro, then destroyed the capital. The whole Kaniaga region passed to the Mali Empire, and the Sosso moved west into Senegambia or south into the Futa Jallon, where they became ancestors of the Susu and Yalunka peoples, though these peoples may have been there earlier.

The kingdom's history rests largely on oral tradition, which can compress several rulers into one: there may have been several Kante kings, but only Soumaoro is remembered. The colonial historian Maurice Delafosse's account of a mercenary general named Kemoko or Diarra Kante as Soumaoro's father was assembled from mixed traditions and invented detail. Stephen Bühnen has placed Sosso in the Futa Jallon, a view most Africanists reject. A town named Sosso still exists in Mali, near Boron in the Koulikoro Region.
sosurim-of-goguryeo: Born Go Gu-Bu, Sosurim was the first son of King Gogugwon and a grandson of King Micheon. He was made crown prince in 355 and helped his father govern and rebuild royal authority, which had been badly weakened after the Later Yan dug up the grave of King Micheon. He became the 17th ruler of Goguryeo, the northernmost of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, when his father was killed in the assault of the Baekje king Geunchogo on Pyongyang Castle.

Sosurim is considered to have strengthened central authority by setting up state religious institutions that stood above tribal factions. According to tradition, the king of Former Qin sent the monk Sundo with images and scriptures of the Buddha, and the monk Ado, a native of Goguryeo, came two years later. With royal support the first temple of the Korean kingdoms, Heungguk monastery, was said to have been built near the capital. Tombs of the mid-4th century already show Buddhist influence, but it is generally accepted that Sosurim fixed Buddhism in the state's ideology and administration.

The year 372 also mattered for Confucianism and Daoism: the Taehak was meant to educate the children of the nobility, and the code of laws of 373 laid down penal law and codified regional customs. In 374, 375 and 376 Sosurim attacked Baekje to the south, and in 378 Goguryeo was attacked by the Khitan from the north.

Sosurim died in 384 and was buried at Sosurim, probably a forest near the second capital, Gungnae. He had no children by his wife, whose name is not known. Much of his reign was spent holding the kingdom together and strengthening the crown, and he never avenged his father's death. His reforms laid the foundations for the conquests of his nephew, King Gwanggaeto the Great. He has been portrayed in the Korean television series The Legend (2007) and The King of Legend (2010–2011).
sotho-people: The Basotho are a Sotho-Tswana people, a mixture of Bantu-speaking clans that mixed with the San who already lived in southern Africa. Their ancestors are believed to have come from north-east Africa and to have migrated south in the fifth century CE. Separation from the Batswana is assumed to have taken place by the 14th century, and by the 16th century iron-working was well established in Basotho communities.

By at least the 17th century a series of Basotho kingdoms covered the southern part of the African plateau, in what is now the Free State, parts of Gauteng and the North West. Society was highly decentralised: each kraal, or extended clan, was ruled by its own chief, and chiefdoms were united only in loose confederations.

In the 1820s refugees from the Zulu expansion under Shaka came into contact with the Basotho of the highveld. In 1823 one group, the Kololo, migrated north and in 1845 conquered Barotseland. Moshoeshoe I meanwhile unified a loose confederacy of Basotho clans and Nguni peoples, and shaped refugee groups escaping the Difaqane into a cohesive nation.

He established his capital at Butha-Buthe in 1822 and later moved it to Thaba Bosiu. To meet the advance of the Boer voortrekkers he encouraged French missionaries of the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society, who advised him on foreign affairs, helped him to buy weapons and, between 1837 and 1855, set down Sesotho orthography and printed its first books.

After losing the western lowlands to the Boers in the Free State–Basotho Wars, Moshoeshoe appealed to Queen Victoria in 1868 to make Basutoland a British protectorate, with a British administration at Maseru. Borders were drawn in 1869, leaving large numbers of Sesotho speakers in the Orange Free State. Moshoeshoe died in 1870 and was buried on the summit of Thaba Bosiu. Basutoland became independent in 1966 as the Kingdom of Lesotho.

Sesotho is the first language of about 1.5 million people in Lesotho and of almost 4 million in South Africa according to the 2011 census, where it is one of eleven official languages. Missionary printing opened the way to a written literature, including Thomas Mofolo's epic Chaka. Because of the central part missionaries played in securing Moshoeshoe's kingdom, most Basotho became Christian, often blending Christianity with older beliefs in Modimo, a supreme being approached through the ancestors. Lesotho men have long migrated to South African cities to work in the mines. Traditional dress includes the mokorotlo, a conical hat, and the Basotho blanket, worn over the shoulders or waist.
soto-cano-air-base: The base lies in the Comayagua Valley, about 8 kilometres south of Comayagua and 97 kilometres from the capital, Tegucigalpa, at an elevation of 628 metres. It measures about 3.2 by 9.7 kilometres and is ringed to the east and west by mountain peaks of about 2,438 metres. Its full name is José Enrique Soto Cano Air Base, and it is a Honduran military installation, the home of the Honduran Air Force and its academy.

The airbase became operational in 1940, when the Honduran Air Force Academy moved there from Toncontin in Tegucigalpa to what was then called Palmerola. In the 1980s the United States government used Palmerola as a base of operations in support of its foreign policy aims, and the U.S. military's Joint Task Force Bravo is headquartered there. Because the Constitution of Honduras does not permit a permanent foreign presence, the task force stays on a semi-permanent basis under a handshake agreement, an annex to the 1954 military assistance agreement between the two countries, which can be ended at little notice.

In 1990 President Rafael Leonardo Callejas authorised commercial cargo flights from the base. In 2008 President Manuel Zelaya announced that commercial flights would move there after the crash of TACA Flight 390 at Toncontín International Airport, and the military was put in charge of building a civilian terminal; the work was cancelled after Zelaya was removed from office in the coup of 28 June 2009. Talks on a new airport at Palmerola resumed in April 2011, though in September 2011 President Lobo said officials were still evaluating the project.

The U.S. contingent, made up of military personnel and U.S. and Honduran civilians, is organised in five support commands, among them an air base squadron and an aviation battalion flying Black Hawk and Chinook helicopters. Its missions are mainly humanitarian aid and disaster relief across Central America. U.S. forces are guests on the base, which is not a U.S. installation but the home of the Honduran Air Force Academy.
souda-bay: The bay is about 15 km long and only two to four km wide. It lies between the Akrotiri peninsula and Cape Drapano and runs from west to east, with hills on both sides and a low, narrow isthmus in the west near Chania. Near its mouth, between Akrotiri and the town of Kalives, lies a group of small islands with Venetian fortifications; the largest, Souda Island, gives the bay its name. In antiquity the bay's port served Aptera, founded in the 7th century BCE and destroyed by the Saracens in the 820s.

The Venetians occupied the area in 1207. After an Ottoman force landed at Souda in 1571 and devastated the district of Chania, they fortified Souda Island between 1570 and 1573, and they held the islands of the bay until 1715, more than thirty years after Crete fell to the Ottomans. In 1822 an Egyptian army of about 10,000 under Hassan Pasha landed at Souda against the Cretan Revolution of 1821. After the revolt of 1866–69 the Ottomans built fortresses at Aptera and Kalami, barracks, a military hospital and a naval base, opened in 1872 in the presence of Sultan Abdul Aziz, and founded the town of Souda as the new port of Chania.

Prince George of Greece, first High Commissioner of the Cretan State, landed at Souda Bay on 9 December 1898. In 1913 the union of Crete with Greece was marked on Souda Island, where the Greek flag was raised on 1 May. In April 1941 some 25,000 British and Commonwealth troops withdrawn from mainland Greece, mainly from New Zealand and Australia, landed at the bay; after the German attack in May they retreated to Sfakia, and the Germans held the area until 1945.

The bay holds the Hellenic Navy's Crete Naval Station, the Hellenic Air Force's Souda Air Base on the Akrotiri peninsula and the NATO Missile Firing Installation. The Souda Bay Allied War Cemetery, designed by Louis de Soissons, is the principal Allied war cemetery on the island. The Ottoman fortress at Kalami is still used as a prison.
soufriere-hills: The Soufrière Hills is a complex stratovolcano of andesitic rock, with many lava domes forming its summit. Montserrat is an overseas territory of the United Kingdom. Chances Peak was the island's highest summit until the mid-1990s, but rising and falling lava domes have since eclipsed it. The Centre Hills in the middle of the island and the Silver Hills in the north are older volcanic massifs related to the subduction zone. Many Caribbean volcanoes bear the name Soufrière, French for sulphur outlet, among them La Soufrière on Saint Vincent and La Grande Soufrière on Guadeloupe. An explosive eruption formed the crater at the summit around 2460 BCE, and about 1550 CE lava erupted at Castle Peak.

There had been seismic activity in 1897-1898, 1933-1937 and 1966-1967, but the eruption that began on 18 July 1995 was the first since the turn of the 20th century. The first phreatic explosion came on 21 August 1995, and after 18 weeks of such activity an andesitic lava dome began to form. Pyroclastic flows were first observed on 27 March 1996, and on 3 April 1996 southern Montserrat, including the capital Plymouth, was permanently evacuated after earlier evacuations. A major flow on 17 September 1996 damaged the village of Long Ground. A large eruption on 25 June 1997 killed nineteen people and destroyed the airport, and by August 1997 pyroclastic flows had buried much of the south of the island, including most of Plymouth.

About 7,000 people, two thirds of the population, left Montserrat, 4,000 of them for the United Kingdom, and the destroyer HMS Liverpool took a major part in the evacuation. The British and Montserrat governments led the aid effort, including a package of 41 million pounds. Riots followed an offer of 10 million pounds, as people protested that the British Government was not doing enough, and Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne resigned after allegations that he was too pro-British. The tourist industry collapsed, though it began to recover within fifteen years.

The volcano kept erupting until 2010, and its last eruption was in 2013. An eruption began without warning at 11:27 pm on 28 July 2008, with an ash column about 12,000 metres high and flows reaching Plymouth. On 11 February 2010 a partial collapse of the lava dome sent ash clouds over Guadeloupe and Antigua. The volcano is monitored by the Montserrat Volcano Observatory, operated by the British Geological Survey.
souliotes: Most scholars agree that the first inhabitants of Souli settled there in the middle of the 16th century as groups of shepherds from southern Albania and the plains of Thesprotia; Vasso Psimouli traces them to Albanian pastoralists who arrived in large kinship groups in the mid-14th century. The community was named after the hilltop village of Souli, and its core was four villages, Souli, Avariko, Kiafa and Samoniva, later ringed by seven more. Psimouli estimates their population at about 4,500, while Souliot leaders claimed about 20,000 in 1800. The theory that they descended from the ancient Selloi found little acceptance among historians.

The Souliotes were organised in patrilineal clans, each called a fara, descended from a common ancestor and led by a single clan leader, with shared rights to springs and pastures. Blood vengeance governed relations between clans, and their houses were fortified towers. They spoke Albanian at home and learnt Greek from their neighbours. They paid a small tax to a sipahi, which gave them standing in the Ottoman timar system, and they lived also from brigandage and from protection offered to subject villages. As Orthodox Christians they belonged to the Rum millet, and their faith set them apart from the neighbouring Muslim Chams.

The first recorded revolt in Souli came in 1685, during the Ottoman-Venetian War, together with the people of Himara. From 1789 Ali Pasha of Ioannina campaigned against them repeatedly; after years of siege, artillery and famine their clans split, and they gave up their homeland. Many went to the Ionian Islands, while Kitsos Botsaris led 1,200 Souliotes to Agrafa, where most were killed in a siege at the monastery of the Assumption of Mary in 1804.

In 1820, when the Sultan declared Ali Pasha an outlaw, the Souliotes first joined the Sultan's army and then went over to Ali in return for their resettlement, retaking Souli on 12 December 1820. In the Greek War of Independence Markos Botsaris commanded the defence of Messolonghi in its first siege in 1822. Souli lay outside the new Greek state, so the Souliotes settled in Greece as refugees, where they came to identify wholly with the Greek nation and some reached high office, including that of prime minister.
sound-toll: The Danish Crown had collected tolls in the Great Belt for at least a century before the dues on the Øresund began. Every foreign ship passing the strait, whether bound for Denmark or not, had to stop at Helsingør and pay, and cannons at both Helsingør and Helsingborg could fire on and sink a ship that refused. Tolls were also taken in the Great Belt and the Little Belt so that ships could not simply go another way, and at times foreign vessels were forbidden any route but the Øresund, on pain of confiscation or sinking.
In 1567 the toll became a tax of 1–2% on the value of the cargo, which tripled the revenue. To stop captains understating their cargo, the Crown kept the right to buy it at the declared value.

The dues angered the trading nations of the Baltic, Sweden above all. Sweden had been exempt while it shared the Kalmar Union with Denmark, but after the Kalmar War and the Treaty of Knäred in 1613 Denmark-Norway charged dues on cargoes from Sweden's Baltic lands. The dispute was an official cause of the Torstenson War in 1643. At the Treaty of Brömsebro in 1645 Denmark-Norway ceded Jämtland, Härjedalen, Gotland and Saaremaa, and Swedish ships were freed from the dues. After the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658 the eastern shore of the Sound became Swedish, and the exemption was withdrawn at the Treaty of Frederiksborg in 1720, after Sweden's defeat in the Great Northern War.

In the 16th and 17th centuries the dues made up as much as two thirds of Denmark's state income, and for several centuries they remained the Crown's most important source of income, which left the kings fairly independent of the Privy Council and the aristocracy. The Copenhagen Convention came into force on 14 March 1857. It abolished the dues and made all the Danish straits international waterways, open to all commercial shipping.
souphanouvong: Souphanouvong was born on 13 July 1909 at the Palace Sisouvanna, Xieng Dong, Luang Prabang, a son of Prince Bounkhong, the last viceroy of Luang Prabang. Unlike his half-brothers Souvanna Phouma and Phetsarath Ratanavongsa, whose mothers were of royal birth, his mother was a commoner, Mom Kham Ouane. He attended the Lycée Albert Sarraut in Hanoi and studied civil engineering at the École nationale des ponts et chaussées in Paris. After graduating in 1937 he returned to French Indochina and worked at the public works bureau in Nha Trang, building bridges and roads in central Vietnam and Laos, until 1945.

After the Japanese surrender he sought the support of the Việt Minh for Lao independence from French rule and met their leader, Hồ Chí Minh, who greatly impressed him. He became a leader of the Lao Issara movement, serving as its provincial chairman in Thakhek, then as foreign minister of its government and commander-in-chief of its army. Wounded in defeat by the French at Thakhek on 21 March 1946, he fled to Bangkok, where he remained in exile, resigning as foreign minister in March 1949 after disputes over continued cooperation with the Việt Minh.

In August 1950 he convened the first congress of the Lao Freedom Front, the Pathet Lao, supported by North Vietnam, and was elected its president, becoming known as the Red Prince. The movement was led by Kaysone Phomvihane, however, and Souphanouvong was more of a figurehead. In 1958 he served in Souvanna Phouma's unity government and was elected to the National Assembly with the most votes of any candidate. He was arrested in July 1959, escaped in May 1960, and helped negotiate the Geneva agreement on the neutrality of Laos in 1962. He publicly professed Marxism-Leninism only in 1967.

After the communist seizure of power in 1975 Souphanouvong became the first president of the Lao People's Democratic Republic, and he was president of the Supreme People's Assembly from 1975 to 1988. In 1991 he became an adviser to the Central Committee of the party. He was married to Nguyen Thi Ky Nam, a Vietnamese woman, and they had ten children. He spoke eight languages, including Greek and Latin. He died in Vientiane on 9 January 1995 of heart disease, and the government decreed five days of mourning. He was buried in a stupa next to the Pha That Luang, and in 2012 his remains were moved to the new national cemetery in Vientiane.
sourigna-vongsa: His father was Tone Kham. In 1637 the nobles of Lan Xang elected Sourigna Vongsa king over his two older brothers, and he secured the throne at once by removing possible rivals: one brother was sent to Vietnam, the other into a solitary priesthood, and his cousins were sent west towards Siam. He was a strict and austere monarch who ran the country by firm laws, and his reign of 57 years is regarded as the golden age of Laos in territory, prestige and power.

Within five years his reputation had reached the representatives of the Dutch East India Company at Phnom Penh. The Dutchman Van Wuystoff and the Jesuit Giovanni Maria Leria both reached Vientiane in 1641, and Leria stayed six years. Much of what is known of seventeenth-century Laos comes from their accounts, Leria's published by John Philip de Marini. Both were struck by the country's prosperity, its free market and its trade, which supplied Europe with gum benzoin, lac and musk, and by its many monasteries and monks; de Marini wrote that monks went from Siam to Laos as to a university.

The king claimed to recognise no equal, but he concluded friendly treaties with his neighbours. With King Narai of Ayutthaya he built the Phra That Si Song Rak, the Stupa of the Affectionate Two, at Dan Sai, now in Loei province of Thailand, to mark their friendship and the boundary between their kingdoms. Unlike Narai, who received ambassadors with great pomp, Sourigna Vongsa wore no crown and preferred to sit on reed mats, and visitors noted that he spent his wealth in the service of religion. De Marini nonetheless described a palace so extensive that one would take it for a city.

Sourigna Vongsa had two sons, and he lost both. The elder was executed for adultery. In February 1686 the younger fled to Ayutthaya with his mother, his stepmother and 600 followers after the king ordered their execution, having found that the son was living with his half-sister with their knowledge. When Sourigna Vongsa died in 1694 he left no heir, and in the chaos that followed Lan Xang split into the three kingdoms of Vientiane, Luang Phrabang and Champasak.
The wealth of his golden age went chiefly to religion rather than to equipping the army with European weapons, and this was one of the main reasons for the kingdom's decline after his rule.
sourou-migan-apithy: Sourou-Migan Apithy was born on 8 April 1913 in Porto-Novo. He descended from an Ogu royal family but was not born into privilege, and his middle name, Migan, signified family ties with the chief ministers of the old Dahomeyan kingdoms.
