Spartan women of the citizen class had more status than women elsewhere in Greece. Thucydides remarked that the city had no splendid temples and resembled a group of villages.

Admiration of Sparta, called Laconophilia, was widespread even in rival Athens, and many philosophers described it as an ideal state. The French classicist François Ollier warned in 1933 that all surviving accounts were written by non-Spartans, who often idealised it, a distortion now called the Spartan Mirage.
spartacist-uprising: On 10 November 1918, after the collapse of the German Empire, a Council of the People's Deputies under Friedrich Ebert of the Majority Social Democratic Party (MSPD) and Hugo Haase of the more left-wing Independent Social Democratic Party (USPD) formed a provisional government. In the secret Ebert-Groener Pact the army command promised its loyalty, and Ebert promised prompt action against leftist uprisings. The MSPD sought elections to a constituent assembly, while the USPD and part of the working class wanted a council republic. Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht founded the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) on 1 January 1919. The dismissal of Berlin's police chief Emil Eichhorn on 4 January was the immediate trigger.

A protest on 5 January drew 100,000 people, and armed demonstrators occupied the printing plants of the newspaper Vorwärts and the Berliner Tageblatt. That evening about 70 leaders voted to form a revolutionary committee to overthrow the government. Up to 500,000 people answered its call for a general strike on 7 January, but the committee could not agree on how to proceed and the crowds went home. Negotiations with Ebert failed over the occupied buildings and Eichhorn's reinstatement.

Ebert gave Gustav Noske command of the troops around Berlin, and Freikorps units formed from former frontline soldiers were mustered. On 11 January the Vorwärts building was taken with flame throwers, machine guns, mortars and artillery. Many insurgents surrendered, and seven men who came to negotiate were taken to the Dragoon Barracks and shot. An investigative committee of the Prussian parliament put the death toll at 156.

On the evening of 15 January Luxemburg and Liebknecht were arrested in Wilmersdorf and taken to the Eden Hotel, where Captain Waldemar Pabst had them interrogated and beaten. Luxemburg was shot in the temple and thrown into the Landwehr Canal; Liebknecht was shot in the Tiergarten as a supposed fugitive. At the trial in May 1919 Otto Runge received two years in prison and Kurt Vogel 28 months, and Pabst was not charged. Elections to the National Assembly were held on 19 January, and it finalised the Weimar Constitution. The MSPD received 37.9 per cent, and its part in the suppression weighed on it throughout the Weimar Republic.
spartacus: No contemporary sources for Spartacus exist. The accounts of Plutarch and Appian were written more than a century after his death, by people who were not involved, and they contradict one another. Plutarch calls him a Thracian of nomadic stock, possibly of the Maedi tribe, who lived in what is now south-western Bulgaria. Appian says he had once served as a soldier with the Romans, but had since been a prisoner and was sold as a gladiator.

Plutarch adds that his wife, a prophetess of the Maedi, was enslaved with him. One modern author estimates that he was about 30 when the revolt began. He was trained as a murmillo at the gladiatorial school of Lentulus Batiatus near Capua.

In 73 BCE about 70 slaves plotted to escape the school. They seized kitchen utensils, fought their way out, took wagons of gladiatorial weapons and defeated the soldiers sent after them. They retired to Mount Vesuvius and chose Spartacus and two Gallic slaves, Crixus and Oenomaus, as leaders. The Roman legions were busy with a revolt in Hispania and the Third Mithridatic War, and Rome first sent a militia under the praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber. Spartacus's men climbed down the mountain on ropes of vines and attacked the camp from behind. Slaves, herdsmen and shepherds then flocked to the rebels, swelling their numbers to some 70,000.

In 72 BCE the Senate sent two consular legions, which beat a group of 30,000 rebels under Crixus and were then defeated by Spartacus. The Senate then gave command of eight legions to Marcus Licinius Crassus. According to Plutarch, Spartacus bargained with Cilician pirates to carry some 2,000 men to Sicily, but they betrayed him. Crassus fortified the isthmus at Rhegium, and the rebels broke through and marched towards Brundusium.

In the final battle in 71 BCE, which one account places in the High Sele Valley in Lucania, the rebels were routed and most were killed. Plutarch, Appian and Florus claim that Spartacus died in it, though Appian adds that his body was never found. Six thousand captured survivors were crucified along the Appian Way from Rome to Capua. The ancient historians disagree about his aims: Plutarch says he wanted to escape over the Alps and send his men home, while Appian and Florus say he intended to march on Rome. None of his actions suggests that he aimed to abolish slavery.
In later centuries he became a symbol of resistance. Voltaire called the Third Servile War the only just war in history, and Karl Marx admired him. The German Spartacus League took his name.
spartiates: Classical accounts credited the Spartan constitution to the lawgiver Lycurgus, but the sources' dates for him are so inconsistent that it is impossible to say whether he was a historical figure. At some point in the late Archaic period Spartan society shifted from a monarchical system to an aristocracy of warriors. The change was probably linked to the rise of hoplite warfare and to the conquest of Messenia, which provided both the basis of helotage and the need for a large force to hold down the conquered people. The Spartiates became a permanently armed master class living off helot labour.

Under the kleros system each full citizen was assigned land worked by helots, and a certain income was needed to pay the dues of the syssitia, the common messes, on which Spartiate status depended. Politically the Spartiates formed the army assembly, which elected the ephors. Boys lived with their mothers until the age of 7 and then entered the agoge, where surviving accounts record athletics, dances and reading and writing rather than weapons drill, but also deliberate hunger that drove the boys to steal. Some young men served in the crypteia, which assassinated helots thought likely to lead revolts.

In battle the Spartiates fought in the phalanx with the aspis, dory, xiphos and kopis, and stood out among Greeks for sophisticated drills: subdivided units with officers, marching in step to flutes, and wheeling and countermarching in formation. Losing one's shield was a mark of shame. The Skiritai served beside them as scouts and light infantry, and their cavalry, the hippeis, was thought unimpressive by contemporaries.

Spartiates who could no longer pay their mess dues probably fell into the Hypomeiones, the inferiors, and the strict qualifications made lost men hard to replace. The decline, known as oliganthropia, shows in the battles of the late 5th and early 4th centuries BCE: 5,000 Spartiates at Plataea, 4,200 at Mantinea, 2,500 at Coronea and only 1,500 at Leuctra. The loss of 300 Spartiates at Mantinea was hard felt, and Sparta never fully recovered from that battle.
spear-thrower: The user holds the spear-thrower in one hand and rests the butt of a dart in its cup, or hooks it on its spur. The dart is much longer than the thrower. An overhand throwing motion, driven by the upper arm and wrist, lets the thrower act as a low-mass extension of the arm, so the force acts on the dart over a longer distance and gives it higher speed. Darts are typically 1.2 to 2.7 m long. Experiments with replicas of Basketmaker spear-throwers found exit velocities of 72 to 108 km/h, and the device is most accurate at 20 m or less.

Designs added thong loops for the fingers, flexible shafts and small stone weights of 60 to 80 grams strapped to the middle, often called bannerstones. Scholars disagree on their purpose: for greater force, for stability, for a quieter swing, or as spindle weights for making string. The woomera, usually made of mulga wood and about 60 cm long, also served to mix ochre, to fend off spears and as a fire-making saw.

Wooden spears are at least 400,000 years old, as the Clacton Spear and the Schöningen spears show. Most stratified European finds of spear-throwers come from the Magdalenian, when elaborate pieces in the form of animals are common; one in the British Museum is carved with a mammoth. During the Ice Age the device gave hunters the power to pierce the thick skin of megafauna. In Europe the bow and arrow supplemented it in the Epi-Paleolithic, since a bow stores the elastic energy in the weapon and not in the projectile. By the Iron Age a strap called the amentum was the standard way of throwing lighter javelins.

In the Americas it may have crossed the Bering Land Bridge with the first settlers and was widespread at European contact. It appears in the art of the Basketmaker, Maya and Moche, and Spearthrower Owl, a ruler from Teotihuacan, is a figure in Maya stelae. The Aztecs opened battles with atlatl darts and then fought hand to hand with the macuahuitl. John Whittaker suggests that the device was a social equalizer, since it needs skill more than muscle, so that women and children could join the hunt.

The spear-thrower survives in Australia, where some Aboriginal people use the woomera for hunting, and among Yup'ik hunters near the mouth of the Yukon River, who call it the nuqaq and use it for seal hunting. The World Atlatl Association was formed in 1987 to promote it as a sport, and throws of almost 260 m have been recorded.
special-administrative-regions-of-china: The provision for special administrative regions entered the Constitution of China in 1982, in anticipation of talks with the United Kingdom over the sovereignty of Hong Kong. Article 31 says that the state may establish special administrative regions when necessary, and that the systems to be instituted in them are to be prescribed by law enacted by the National People's Congress. The principle of one country, two systems was proposed by Deng Xiaoping.

Hong Kong and Macau were transferred to China in 1997 and 1999 under the Sino-British and Sino-Portuguese Joint Declarations, signed in 1984 and 1987. These are binding treaties registered with the United Nations and provide that the regions shall enjoy a high degree of autonomy. The model was also envisioned for an eventual unification with Taiwan: a proposal of 1981, known as Ye's nine points, and Deng Xiaoping's six points of 1983 both offered Taiwan the status of a special administrative region.

A special administrative region is one of four types of province-level division directly affiliated with the Central People's Government. It has the highest degree of autonomy, though the National People's Congress and its Standing Committee remain able to enforce laws for it. Each of the two regions has a codified constitution called the Basic Law, a capitalist economy, its own courts of final appeal and its own multi-party legislature.

The central government is responsible for diplomatic and military affairs. Hong Kong and Macau keep their own legal systems, police forces, customs territories, immigration policies, left-hand traffic, official languages and educational systems. The Hong Kong dollar and the Macanese pataca are their currencies, and the Macanese pataca is pegged to the Hong Kong dollar. They belong to organisations such as the WTO and APEC and send their own teams to events such as the Olympic Games as Hong Kong, China and Macau, China. The People's Liberation Army is garrisoned in both.

The term has had other uses. Between 1912 and 1949, special administrative regions were areas designated by the Beiyang government, most of which the Nationalist government converted into provinces in 1928. The Wolong Special Administrative Region in Sichuan, founded in 1983 with the approval of the State Council, is a nature reserve and not a region under Article 31.
special-region-of-yogyakarta: The Special Region of Yogyakarta lies in southern Java. On the landward side it is surrounded by Central Java Province to the west, north and east, and it has a long coastline on the Indian Ocean to the south. With a land area of 3,170.363 square kilometres, it is the second-smallest province-level unit of Indonesia after Jakarta. Mount Merapi stands immediately north of the city of Yogyakarta and Sleman Regency. It has erupted regularly since 1548 and is the most active volcano in Indonesia. The region also has nine geo-heritage sites, among them pillow lava at Berbah, dunes at Parangtritis Beach and a prehistoric volcano at Nglanggeran.

The Yogyakarta Sultanate was established in 1755 and survived Dutch rule and the 1942 invasion of the Dutch East Indies by Japan in 1942. In August 1945 Sukarno proclaimed Indonesian independence, and by September Sultan Hamengkubuwono IX and Duke Sri Paku Alam VIII had written to him acknowledging the Sultanate as part of the Republic. The Sunanate of Surakarta did the same, and both Javanese kingdoms were given special status. Surakarta lost its status in 1946 after a leftist anti-royalist uprising and was absorbed into Central Java.

During the Indonesian National Revolution (1945–1949) the city of Yogyakarta served as the capital of Indonesia from January 1946 to December 1948, after Jakarta fell to the Dutch. When the Dutch also invaded Yogyakarta, the capital was moved to Bukittinggi in West Sumatra on 19 December 1948. In return for its support, Yogyakarta received its special status in full in 1950, which made it the only region in Indonesia headed by a monarchy. A 6.3-magnitude earthquake struck on 27 May 2006, killing 5,782 people and leaving 600,000 homeless; Bantul Regency suffered most.

The region is co-ruled by the Yogyakarta Sultanate and the Principality of Pakualaman, and it is the only officially recognised diarchy within the government of Indonesia. Under the laws on its status, the governor and vice governor are chosen from the descendants of the ruling family, and until 1988 the reigning Sultan held the post of head of the region automatically. The region has four regencies and one city, and Javanese is its official language alongside Indonesian.

The city is known as a centre of classical Javanese art and culture, such as batik, music and shadow puppetry, and the Sultan's palace, the Kraton, lies at its core. It has more than one hundred institutions of higher education and is the home of Gadjah Mada University, the first state university established in Indonesia.
special-settlements-in-the-soviet-union: Political and administrative exile had existed in Imperial Russia, and the first Soviet decrees on labour camps already spoke of using settlers to colonise remote lands. In 1929 Stalin's government named districts of Western Siberia for the deportation of socially dangerous classes from Belarus, Ukraine and north-western Russia. After the grain crisis of 1928 and forced collectivisation, peasants were deported in large numbers, and a joint decree of 1 February 1930 ordered wide-scale dekulakization. On Nazino Island near Tomsk in 1933 more than 4,000 deportees died or disappeared within thirteen weeks, given only raw flour to live on.

From 1939 the lands annexed under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact were cleared of supposed social enemies; estimates of deported Poles range from 400,000 to 1.9 million, including prisoners of war. On 23 June 1940 Lavrenty Beria ordered Murmansk Oblast cleansed of foreign nationals, and deportations from the Baltic States, Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina followed in May and June 1941. During the war whole peoples of enemy nationality were deported as a precaution, and in 1943–1944 peoples declared guilty of collaboration, among them Balkars, Karachays, Meskhetian Turks and Crimean Bolgars.

Deportations went on after 1945: 35,000 people from Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina in July 1949, Iranians and Assyrians from Georgia and Armenia in 1950, and about 9,400 Jehovah's Witnesses, about 4,000 of them children, to Siberia in Operation North in 1951. Kolkhozniks convicted as parasites under a decree of 2 June 1942, the ukazniks, received eight years of exile.

Archival data for 1 January 1950 counted 2,572,829 settlers, according to an MVD document quoted by Dmitri Volkogonov. The historian J. Otto Pohl has described the special settlements as a form of apartheid. When the system was abolished, most deported peoples could return home, but the Crimean Tatars and Meskhetian Turks were denied the right of return under Khrushchev and Brezhnev and largely remained where they had been sent, held there by the propiska system. The special settlement restriction on members of persecuted religious groups was lifted only in September 1965.
speicherstadt: From 1815 the independent city of Hamburg belonged to the German Confederation but not to the German Customs Union. After the Austro-Prussian War it was obliged to join the North German Federation, but Article 34 of the North German constitution kept Hamburg and the other Hanseatic cities as free ports outside the customs border until they applied for inclusion. Article 34 was carried into the imperial constitution of 1871. Hamburg came under great pressure from Berlin after 1879, when the Customs Union greatly increased its external tariff. In 1881 an agreement was signed under which Hamburg joined the Customs Union with all its territory except a permanent free port district, for which Article 34 still applied.

In 1883 the demolition of the Kehrwieder and Wandrahm area began to clear space, and more than 20,000 people had to be relocated. The Freihafen-Lagerhaus-Gesellschaft, the predecessor of the Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG, managed the construction, which was completed before the start of World War I, and it was also responsible for the later operation.

The Speicherstadt, meaning City of Warehouses, is the largest warehouse district in the world whose buildings stand on timber-pile foundations, in this case oak logs. It was built from 1883 to 1927 in the port of Hamburg as a free zone in which goods could be transferred without paying customs. It is 1.5 kilometres long and interlaced by loading canals, called Fleets in Low German. The warehouses were built with different support structures, but Franz Andreas Meyer gave them a Neo-Gothic red-brick outer layer with small towers, alcoves and glazed terracotta ornaments. They are multi-storey buildings with entrances from both water and land, and one of the oldest, Kaispeicher B, houses the International Maritime Museum.

About half of the buildings were destroyed in the bombing of Operation Gomorrah in World War II, and a conservative rebuilding was finished in 1967. The Hanseatic Trade Center occupies the sites of the completely destroyed structures. The district was listed as a protected heritage site of Hamburg in 1991 and has been part of the HafenCity quarter since 2008. On 5 July 2015 the Speicherstadt and the Kontorhaus District were made a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as an exceptional example of Neo-Gothic and modernist architecture and for its testimony to the development of international maritime trade. It is a major tourist attraction, with museums such as the German Customs Museum and Miniatur Wunderland, while some buildings keep their original use as warehouses.
spessart: The Spessart is a Mittelgebirge, a range of low wooded mountains in the German states of Bavaria and Hesse, bordered by the Vogelsberg, the Rhön and the Odenwald. Its extent can also be described by its rivers: the Main to the south and west, the Kinzig to the north and the Sinn to the north-east. It covers about 2,440 square kilometres, of which 1,710 lie in Bavaria, and its highest point is the Geiersberg at 586 metres.

The name derives from Spechtshardt, from the German Specht, woodpecker, and Hardt, an old word for hilly forest. Its lowest strata are gneiss and mica schist about 1,200 million years old, and most of the Hochspessart is capped by red sandstone up to 400 metres thick, the stone used for many public buildings including Mainz Cathedral.

People have lived in the region since at least the Bronze Age, and hill forts attributed to Celts of the La Tène culture were built there between 500 and 100 BCE. The Roman frontier, the Limes, met the Main at Großkrotzenburg and followed the river south to Miltenberg, so the Spessart proper lay outside the empire, and the Romans kept the northern Vorspessart as an uninhabited buffer zone. The Burgundians came in the late 3rd century and the Allemanni ousted them in the 5th, before the Franks absorbed the Allemanni.

Under the Franks the forests were used for hunting, and in Charlemagne's reign they were a royal hunting preserve. The uplands were settled only after abbeys were founded, among them the Benedictine abbey of Neustadt am Main around 770, which Charlemagne endowed with woodland.

In 974 Emperor Otto II gave much of the former royal preserve to the collegiate church of Aschaffenburg, and in 982 Otto I, Duke of Swabia and Bavaria, left his territories in the area to Mainz. Between the 12th and 15th centuries the Prince-Electors and Archbishops of Mainz and other nobles built hunting lodges and moated castles such as Mespelbrunn, and in the 14th century Mainz set up local officers to supervise hunting, forestry, fishing and the rafting of logs.

About 85 percent of the Hochspessart is covered by forest, mainly oak and beech. The Bavarian Spessart Nature Park, set up in 1961 as the first in Bavaria, covers 171,000 hectares and has the largest continuous mixed forest in Germany; the Hessian park followed in 1962 and covers 72,900 hectares. No cities or large towns lie inside the parks. The Nordspessart has more evergreens because its original tree cover was largely gone by the 15th century, owing to the fuel needs of local glass foundries. Beavers, hunted to extinction in the region, have been re-established since the 1980s.
spetses: Spetses is one of the Saronic Islands. Its municipality has an area of 27 square kilometres and includes the uninhabited islands of Spetsopoula, Falkonera and Velopoula. The town of Spetses is the only large settlement. The name comes from the Greek spétses, spices or herbs, which derives from the Italian and Venetian spezie; the ancient name Pityussa means abounding in pine trees. No private cars are allowed in the town, and visitors come by ferry and hydrofoil from Piraeus.

The island was first occupied in the Mesolithic period, about 8000 BCE, when an isthmus joined it to the mainland of Argolis. The first Hellenic settlement found there, at Saint Marina, dates to the 3rd millennium BCE, and late Mycenaean settlements are known as well. Strabo and Pausanias call the island Pitiousa. A raid by the Goths on the Eastern Roman Empire sent refugees to Spetses, who resettled it around the Old Port. The Venetians, who had ruled the island since 1220, named it Spezia in the 15th century because it lay on a spice trade route.

In the 18th century many Arvanites took refuge there from Ottoman persecution and built the old village at Kastelli. During the Orlov Revolt, a rising in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774, the island's merchant fleet fought the Ottomans, and in 1770 the Turks destroyed its only village. New settlers from the opposite coast of the Peloponnese reoccupied it in 1774, after the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca. Sailing under the Russian flag, they rebuilt a powerful merchant fleet, which prospered especially during the trade embargoes of the Napoleonic Wars.

In the Greek War of Independence Spetses was the first island to raise the flag of revolution, on 3 April 1821 by the old calendar. Its fleet took part in raids on the Turkish coast, in the sieges of Nafplion and Monemvasia and in the naval battles of Samos in 1824 and Kafireas in 1825. It was the home of Laskarina Bouboulina. On 8 September 1822 the combined fleets of Spetses, Hydra and Psara faced an Ottoman fleet trying to supply Nafplion, which fell to the Greeks about two and a half months later.

The island declined as a maritime centre in the 19th century. In 1899 the shipping heir Sotirios Anargyros, a wealthy tobacco merchant returned from the United States, began to transform it, planting pines and building the Poseidonion Hotel, which became a favourite holiday place of wealthy Athenians. The Armáta Festival each September commemorates the battle of 1822. The island served as the basis for the island of Phraxos in John Fowles's novel The Magus of 1965.
spice-trade: Spices such as cinnamon, cassia, cardamom, ginger, pepper, nutmeg, star anise, clove and turmeric were known in antiquity and traded across Asia, northeast Africa and Europe. Peoples of the Indian Ocean and Island Southeast Asia traded spices, obsidian, seashells and gemstones as early as the 10th millennium BCE. The ancient Egyptians traded with the Land of Punt in the 3rd millennium BCE. The first true maritime network in the Indian Ocean was built by Austronesian sailors from Maritime Southeast Asia, who opened routes to South India and Sri Lanka from around 1500 BCE to 600 BCE, carrying cloves and nutmeg from the Maluku Islands.

In the second half of the first millennium BCE the peoples of South and West Arabia, including Ma'in, Qataban, Hadhramaut, Sheba and Himyar, took over the land trade from South Arabia to the Mediterranean. In the late second century BCE the Greeks of Ptolemaic Egypt learned from Indians how to sail directly from Aden to the west coast of India with the monsoon winds.

After the rise of Islam, Radhanite Jewish and Arab merchants conveyed spices to Europe through the Levant, and the trade enriched the Abbasid Caliphate, whose sailors set out from Basra and sold their cargoes in Baghdad. Arab traders dominated the western Indian Ocean and linked to the Maluku and Banda Islands, where nutmeg and mace were found. From the 8th to the 15th century the maritime republics, among them Venice, Genoa and Pisa, held a monopoly on European trade with the Middle East, and spices were among the most expensive goods of the Middle Ages, used in medicine as well as in cooking.

Portugal broke the Venetian hold. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut. Afonso de Albuquerque conquered Malacca in 1511 and sent António de Abreu to Banda in early 1512. On the Spanish side, Ferdinand Magellan's expedition reached the Philippines in 1521 and, after his death, Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the Victoria home in 1522. The Manila Galleon trade, opened in 1571, lasted until 1815. The trade also moved crops, boats, religions and foods. Austronesian sailors introduced bananas, coconuts, sugarcane and sandalwood to southern India and eastern Africa, and Indian merchants took spice mixtures and black pepper to Southeast Asia.
spilberk-castle: Špilberk Castle stands on a hill in Brno, in southern Moravia. Its construction began as early as the first half of the 13th century under the Přemyslid kings and was completed by King Ottokar II of Bohemia. From a major royal castle established about the middle of that century, and the seat of the Moravian margraves in the middle of the 14th century, it was gradually turned into a huge baroque citadel, which was considered the harshest prison in the Austrian Empire and was afterwards converted into barracks.

The town of Brno bought the castle in 1560 and made it a municipal fortress. After the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620 the leading Moravian members of the anti-Habsburg insurrection were imprisoned there for several years. Its bastion fortifications helped Brno withstand Swedish raids in the Thirty Years' War, and the successful defence led to further fortification.

The castle served as a prison alongside its military role. Protestants were the first prisoners, followed by participants in the revolutions of 1848–49. Franz Freiherr von der Trenck was jailed there and died on 4 October 1749. Jean-Baptiste Drouet, who had arrested Louis XVI, and fifteen Hungarian Jacobins led by Ferenc Kazinczy were held there. From 1822 specially built cells for state prisoners in the northern wing held Italian Carbonari, among them the poet Silvio Pellico, who served eight years and made the prison known across Europe with his book My Prisons. The last large group of political prisoners was nearly 200 Polish revolutionaries, mostly from the Kraków Uprising of 1846. Emperor Franz Joseph I dissolved the prison in 1855.

After the last prisoners left three years later, the buildings became barracks for the next hundred years. During the First World War military prisoners and civilian objectors to the Austro-Hungarian regime were held there, and in the first year of the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia several thousand Czech patriots suffered there, some being put to death, while for most it was a station on the way to German prisons and concentration camps. The Czechoslovak army left in 1959, and the following year the castle became the seat of the Brno City Museum.
spinning-jenny: James Hargreaves was born in Oswaldtwistle, near Blackburn, around 1720. Blackburn was a town of about 5,000 people, known for Blackburn greys, cloths with a linen warp and a cotton weft. Cotton yarn production could not keep pace with the textile industry's demand. The flying shuttle of John Kay had doubled the productivity of weavers and so increased their demand for yarn. The shortage of spinning capacity to feed the more efficient looms gave the motive for more productive spinning, and triggered the start of the Industrial Revolution.

Hargreaves developed the machine as a metal frame with eight wooden spindles at one end. A set of eight rovings was attached to a beam on the frame and passed through two horizontal wooden bars that could be clasped together. The spinner drew the bars along the top of the frame with the left hand, extending the thread, and turned a wheel with the right hand, which made all the spindles revolve. When the bars were returned, the thread wound onto the spindle, guided by a pressing wire called a faller. The machine produced coarse thread. Its success was limited because the rovings had to be prepared on a wheel, and that work was held back by the need to card by hand.

Hargreaves kept the machine secret for some time but made a number for his own growing business. The price of yarn fell, which angered the large community of spinners in Blackburn, and they broke into his house and smashed his machines. He fled to Nottingham in 1768 and set up in secret with a joiner named Thomas James. On 12 July 1770 he took out a patent, number 962, for a machine for spinning, drawing and twisting cotton. By then many Lancashire spinners were using copies, and when he threatened legal action the manufacturers offered him £3,000. The case collapsed when it was learned that he had sold several jennies in the past.

The jenny stayed in common use in the cotton and fustian industry until about 1810, was superseded by the spinning mule and was adapted into the Slubbing Billy. The name is often explained by a story that Hargreaves's daughter or wife, called Jenny, knocked over a spinning wheel, and he saw that the spindles could stand upright in a row. Church registers show no daughter or wife of that name, and a more likely explanation is that jenny was short for engine.
spinning-wheel: Thousands of years ago people began using a weighted stick, the spindle, to speed up the twisting of fibres into thread. The spinning wheel automated the twisting, since a larger wheel now drove the spindle, and it improved the finished product through a more consistent speed. Its history is disputed. J. M. Kenoyer speculated that the uniform thread in a clay impression from the Indus Valley points to a wheel, but Mukhtar Ahmed notes that the spinning whorls used there also produce a tight weave.

Dieter Kuhn and Weiji Cheng propose that it began in Zhou dynasty China, in the first millennium BCE. Arnold Pacey and Irfan Habib think it was most likely invented in the Middle East by the early 11th century, and consider early Indian references vague. Others cite a description of its parts by the Kannada poet Remmavve in the 12th century.

The wheel was at first free-moving, turned directly by a hand or foot. Simple treadles were added so that the spinner could keep it turning steadily, and this was the main source of technological progress before the 18th century. The great wheel was good for long-drawn, soft wool but hard to use for the strong smooth yarn needed as warp. In 1533 a citizen of Brunswick is said to have added a treadle, freeing both hands. Leonardo da Vinci drew a flyer, which twists the yarn before winding it onto the spindle, and in the 16th century the treadle wheel with a flyer, the Saxony or flax wheel, was in common use.

The wheel increased the productivity of thread making by a factor of more than ten. The historian Lynn Townsend White Jr. credited it with increasing the supply of rags, which led to cheap paper and so helped the development of printing. According to Mark Elvin, 14th-century Chinese manuals describe an automatic water-powered spinning wheel, but it fell out of use when fibre production shifted from hemp to cotton.

Lewis Paul and John Wyatt patented a roller spinning machine in 1738, and Richard Arkwright adapted it in 1771 as the water frame. The spinning jenny was essentially an adaptation of the wheel. In South Asia the charkha became a political symbol: Mahatma Gandhi made hand spinning part of the swadeshi movement, and a spinning wheel was the main symbol on the flag of the Provisional Government of Free India from 1931.
spis: Spiš lies between the High Tatras and the Dunajec River in the north, the springs of the Váh in the west, the Slovak Ore Mountains and the Hnilec River in the south, and a line from Stará Ľubovňa across the Branisko mountain to Margecany in the east. Its core is formed by the basins of the Hornád and Poprad rivers and the High Tatras. The region has always been heavily forested; in the late 19th century forest covered as much as 42.2 per cent of it.

Its name probably relates to a Slavic word for a cut stick, so that Spiš may mean 'a cut forest', and early Latin documents call it silva Zepus. A Hungarian derivation from szép, 'beautiful', is rejected by Šimon Ondruš as linguistically impossible.

Neanderthal remains have been found at Gánovce and Bešeňová, and Celts were the first later inhabitants. Spiš belonged to Great Moravia and after its dissolution to Poland. The Kingdom of Hungary conquered the southern part at the end of the 11th century, the royal county of Szepes was created in the second half of the 12th century, and by the early 14th century its northern border had stabilised. German settlers were invited from the mid-12th century and founded mining settlements in the south, many of which became towns. Their descendants, the Zipsers, spoke Zipser German, and until World War II Spiš had a large German population.

In 1412, under the Treaty of Lubowla, Sigismund of Luxembourg pawned towns, castles and villages in Spiš to Poland to finance his wars with Venice in Dalmatia. They included Stará Ľubovňa, Podolínec, Spišská Sobota, Poprad and Spišská Nová Ves, and belonged to Poland for 360 years. During the Swedish invasion of Poland the Polish Crown Treasury was kept at Ľubovňa Castle. The Habsburg monarchy occupied the Polish Spiš county in 1769. In 1918 the county became part of Czechoslovakia, confirmed by the Treaty of Trianon in 1920, and in 1993 the bulk of Spiš became part of Slovakia.

Spiš is one of Slovakia's 21 tourist regions but not an administrative one. Since 1996 it has been divided between the Košice and Prešov regions. Its population is about 320,000, and almost half live in towns, the largest being Poprad, Spišská Nová Ves and Kežmarok. A very small part lies in south-eastern Poland, in 14 villages. Many Slovaks, Germans and Rusyns lived there historically. Today there are also Romani settlements and between 40,000 and 48,000 Gorals, who speak a dialect of Polish. Historical sites include Spiš Castle, Spišské Podhradie, Spišská Kapitula, Žehra and Levoča, all listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites, as well as Kežmarok and Stará Ľubovňa Castle.
spiti: Spiti, whose name is usually explained as the middle land, takes in the valley of the Spiti River and side valleys such as the Pin and the Lingti. It is bordered by Tibet to the east, Ladakh to the north, Lahaul to the west, Kullu to the south and Kinnaur to the south-east. The river rises below the K-111 peak and joins the Sutlej at Khab. Lying in the rain shadow of the main Himalayan range, the valley gets about 50 mm of rain a year and is a treeless cold desert with only one growing season, from May to September.

Pre-Buddhist rock art shows people in the valley for nearly 3,000 years. Spiti may have belonged to the western Tibetan kingdom of Zhang Zhung until the mid-7th century. In the 10th century it was part of Ngari Khorsum, founded by Kyide Nyimagon; on his death Zanskar and Spiti went to his youngest son Detsukgon, and for long afterwards Spiti's history was tied to Ladakh's. Local rulers called Nonos governed, autonomous when Ladakh was weak, and paid tribute to Ladakh, Chamba and Kullu. Buddhism likely came with the Second Diffusion into Tibet.

After the Tibet–Ladakh–Mughal War of 1679–1683 Man Singh, Raja of Kullu, set up a loose control, but in the 18th century Spiti passed back to Ladakh. It was under Dogra rule, as part of the Sikh Empire, from 1842, and by the Treaty of Amritsar it was split from Ladakh and placed under direct British administration, later under the Assistant Commissioner of Kullu. After China's annexation of Tibet roads were built, reaching Manali and Shimla by the 1970s, and Spiti became part of Himachal Pradesh in 1966.

Spiti is a sub-division of Lahaul and Spiti district with its headquarters at Kaza, and its lower part, the Hangrang valley, belongs to Kinnaur district; in 2011 the whole valley had 17,104 inhabitants. Its people speak Spiti Bhoti and follow Tibetan Buddhism, with Gelug, Nyingma and Sakya monasteries such as Dhankar and Kungri. Pin Valley National Park and Kibber Wildlife Sanctuary protect its wildlife.
spoleto: Spoleto lies in east-central Umbria, in the province of Perugia, on a foothill of the Apennines. It is 63 kilometres south-east of Perugia and 126 kilometres north of Rome. The town rises in tiers up a hill resting against Monte Luco, which reaches 453 metres at the fortress. In antiquity the territory was fertile, and its wine was particularly esteemed. Monte Luco, covered with holm oaks, was a sacred wood in the Roman period, and from the 5th century hermits fleeing Syria settled there, founding a network of hermitages.

Spoleto was founded by the Umbri in the 10th century BCE and taken by the Etruscans in the 7th century BCE. A Roman colony was founded at Spoletium in 241 BCE, shortly after the First Punic War, and the city was expanded and fortified with polygonal walls. In the 5th century it suffered barbarian invasions connected with Theodoric, Belisarius, Totila and Narses. Faroald I made it the seat of the Duchy of Spoleto, a key Lombard duchy, which included Umbria, Sabina, Picenum as far as Pescara and the lands of the Marrucini, Marsi and Peligni.

In 1155 Frederick Barbarossa ordered Spoleto destroyed, after the duchy refused tribute and the inhabitants acted against his envoy Guido Guerra; the city was captured, burned and destroyed. With the death of Henry VI the line of dukes ended, and he ordered in his testament that the duchy be restored to the Holy See. Pope Innocent III reclaimed it, expelling Conrad of Swabia. In 1319 the Ghibellines of Spoleto, led by Federico of Montefeltro, expelled the Guelphs. Plague struck in 1414 and 1436, and in 1418 Martin V appointed Guido Antonio, count of Urbino, as duke. Later popes, among them Gregory XIII, who in 1577 had the iron mines exploited, kept the territory under papal rule.

The Cathedral of Spoleto, dating to the first half of the 11th century on the site of an earlier church, was destroyed in 1155 and consecrated again in 1198 by Innocent III. The Basilica of San Salvatore, built between the late 4th and early 5th centuries, stands outside the medieval walls. The Rocca albornoziana, begun in 1359 for Pope Innocent VI and named after Cardinal Albornoz, crowns the hill of Sant'Elia. The Ponte delle Torri, a limestone bridge about 230 metres long and 80 metres high, links that hill with Monteluco and was given its present appearance in the mid-14th century.
spratly-islands: The Spratly Islands are an archipelago in the South China Sea, off the coasts of the Philippines, Malaysia and southern Vietnam. They are made up of islands, islets, cays and more than 100 reefs, sometimes grouped in submerged old atolls. They are named after Richard Spratly, a 19th-century British whaling captain who sighted Spratly Island in 1843. The naturally occurring land totals less than 200 hectares, spread over hundreds of square kilometres of sea. The islands are cays, sand islands formed on old degraded and submerged coral reefs. Their northeast part, known as Dangerous Ground, has low islands, sunken reefs and degraded atolls rising abruptly from depths greater than 1,000 metres, which makes navigation hazardous.

Geologically the reefs and banks of biogenic carbonate lie on the crests of submarine ridges formed of uplifted fault blocks. Almost no arable land exists, and very few islands have a permanent supply of drinkable water. Resources include fish, guano, oil and natural gas, and the islands lie near major shipping lanes. In 1939 they were coral islets mostly inhabited by seabirds.

The nearby Tabon Caves on Palawan hold evidence of human presence dating back nearly 50,000 years, and by 2000 BCE Austronesian peoples of the Philippines and Taiwan had established the maritime jade road. Seafarers of the Sa Huỳnh culture, forebears of the Cham people, may have passed through the Spratly Islands on their way to Vietnam between 600 BCE and 3 BCE.

The Song Dynasty work Zhu fan zhi by Zhao Rugua uses names for reefs and sands that some interpret as the Paracels and the Spratly Islands respectively, though different authors read these names differently. A Ming text, Haiyu, uses Wanli Changsha for the Spratly Islands. The Qing continued to include the area on maps compiled between 1724 and 1817 without officially claiming jurisdiction. A European chart of 1758 left the Dangerous Ground largely blank, since it had not been surveyed. In the 19th century Europeans found Chinese fishermen from Hainan staying on the islands for part of each year, and in 1877 the British made the first modern legal claims.

The archipelago is claimed in whole or part by several states. China, Taiwan and Vietnam each claim it, the Philippines and Malaysia claim parts, and Brunei claims an exclusive economic zone in the southeast. Of about 45 islands, cays, reefs and shoals that are occupied, all have structures held by military forces of Malaysia, China, Taiwan, the Philippines and Vietnam. In January 2013 the Philippines began arbitration proceedings against China under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. The surrounding waters hold over 600 coral reefs and 2,927 recorded marine species.
spurius-cassius-vecellinus: Spurius Cassius Vecellinus was three times consul, held two triumphs, and was the first magister equitum and the author of the first agrarian law. According to one tradition his father was still living at the time of his death, which would make it hard to place his birth much before 540 or 535 BCE. He left three sons. The original Cassii are believed to have been patricians, though the later members of the family were all plebeian, and the historian Niebuhr suggested that his sons were expelled from the patricians, or went over to the plebeians because the patricians had shed their father's blood.

Cassius was first consul in 502 BCE with Opiter Verginius Tricostus. Dionysius reports a victory over the Sabines near Cures and a triumph, while Livy says the consuls fought the Aurunci and took Suessa Pometia, events he also reports under 495 BCE. The following year, amid fear of war with the Sabines and the Latins, he became the first magister equitum, and after the victory at Lake Regillus is said to have urged the senate to destroy the Latin towns. In 493 BCE, as consul with Postumus Cominius Auruncus, he ratified the treaty with the Latins known as the Foedus Cassianum. That year he also consecrated the temple of Ceres, Bacchus and Proserpina.

In 486 BCE, consul for the third time with Proculus Verginius Tricostus Rutilus, he marched against the Volsci and Hernici, who sued for peace, and formed a league with the Hernici. By one account the three peoples agreed to divide conquered land equally, and the treaty held for over a hundred years. He then held his second triumph.

Cassius then proposed the first agrarian law, distributing land to the plebs and the Latin allies. His colleague Verginius and the patricians strongly opposed it, and the plebs turned against him, suspecting him of aiming at regal power. In 485 BCE, after he had left office, he was condemned and executed.

Livy gives two versions: a public trial for high treason, after which his house was demolished, or a private trial by his own father, who put him to death and dedicated his property to Ceres. Dionysius says he was hurled from the Tarpeian Rock. Cassius Dio believed him innocent. Pliny the Elder records the destruction of his statue, which is the earliest known case of a Roman honorific monument destroyed in accordance with damnatio memoriae, though the chronology of that record is disputed.
sputnik-1: On 17 December 1954 the Soviet rocket scientist Sergei Korolev proposed a plan for an artificial satellite to the Minister of the Defense Industry, Dimitri Ustinov. In July 1955 the United States announced that it would launch a satellite during the International Geophysical Year, and four days later the Soviet physicist Leonid Sedov said the Soviet Union would do the same. The Politburo approved the proposal on 8 August 1955. The launch vehicle was the R-7, designed as an intercontinental ballistic missile. A much heavier satellite, Object D, was planned first, but the lighter Object PS, which became Sputnik 1, was launched ahead of it.

Sputnik 1 was a polished sphere 58 centimetres across, assembled from two hemispheres sealed with O-rings and joined by 36 bolts, with a mass of 83.6 kilograms. Its chief constructor at OKB-1 was Mikhail Khomyakov. Four whip antennas gave it an almost spherical radiation pattern. It could not be controlled, only observed. A spherical body let scientists work out the density of the upper atmosphere from the satellite's lifetime in orbit, and its radio signals were meant to give data on how radio waves travel through the atmosphere.

It was launched from Tyuratam in the Kazakh SSR on 4 October 1957 at 19:28:34 UTC, which was 5 October at the launch site. Several engines did not fire on time, which nearly aborted the mission, and the satellite entered an orbit with an apogee about 500 kilometres lower than intended. It circled the Earth every 96.20 minutes at a peak speed of about 8 kilometres a second. It transmitted on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz for 22 days until the batteries ran out on 26 October. On 4 January 1958 it burned up on re-entering the atmosphere, after 1,440 orbits.

Radio operators around the world picked up the beeping signal, and the first recording in the United States was made by RCA engineers on Long Island. Groups of observers at 150 stations in Operation Moonwatch looked for the satellite in the sky. What most people actually saw was the much more visible core stage of the rocket. The Soviets did not at once use the launch for propaganda, but later stressed the achievement as a sign of their superiority.

President Dwight Eisenhower was not surprised, having been forewarned of the R-7's capabilities, but he underestimated the reaction of the American public, who were shocked by the launch and by the televised failure of the Vanguard rocket. The anxiety was sometimes called the Sputnik craze, and the launch began the Space Race. Two physicists at Johns Hopkins University, William Guier and George Weiffenbach, used the Doppler effect in Sputnik's signal to fix its position, which led to the TRANSIT navigation system, a forerunner of the Global Positioning System.
sranan-tongo: Sranan Tongo, meaning Surinamese tongue, likely developed from an English-based pidgin, when English colonists in what was then part of the English colony of Guiana brought enslaved Africans to the plantations. The enslaved, who came from various peoples, had no African language in common and developed a pidgin to communicate. After the Dutch takeover in 1667, following the Treaty of Breda, a substantial overlay of Dutch words was adopted, making Dutch a secondary lexifier. There were also additions from Spanish and Portuguese, some dating from an earlier Portuguese occupation of the colony.

The first enslaved Africans probably spoke Gbe or KiKongo languages, and were bilingual for some time. Around 1720 large numbers of Akan people, about 65 percent of those brought, were transported from the Gold Coast to Suriname. Akan further altered a language that had already begun to creolise, causing relexification and giving the creole its own Africanisms. Indigenous peoples also intermarried with enslaved Africans and added cultural influence to Afro-Surinamese culture. When East Indians, Chinese and Javanese were later brought as indentured workers, Sranan Tongo became a lingua franca.

Although many words in its lexicon are English, the lack of contact with English speakers since the 17th century means Sranan Tongo is seldom mutually intelligible with modern English. African influence appears in grammar, morphology and phonology, from Gbe (Fon, Ewe, Aja, Gun, Gen and Xwelak), KiKongo and Akan (Twi and Fante). The Cariban languages, Carib and Arawak, contribute botanical, zoological, musical, culinary and Winti vocabulary.

Remnants of a Portuguese-based period can still be traced in words of Portuguese origin and in the Odos, the proverbs, folklore and stories that Afro-Surinamese people passed down orally through slavery. Many can be traced to specific regions in Central and West Africa.

The first publication in Sranan Tongo came in 1783, when Hendrik Schouten wrote a part Dutch, part Sranan poem, Een huishoudelijke twist. The first important book, by Johannes King, appeared in 1864 and relates his travels for the Moravian Church. Until the middle of the 20th century most written texts used a non-standardised spelling based on Dutch. A movement for the emancipation of Sranan led to a phonology-based orthography, which the Surinamese government adopted on 15 July 1986 in Resolution 4501. Because the language is not taught in schools, many speakers still use a Dutch-like spelling.

The Dutch-based school system repressed Sranan Tongo, which was dismissed with the names Taki Taki and Negerengels, but it gradually became more accepted. The poet Henri Frans de Ziel, known as Trefossa, wrote Suriname's national anthem, whose second verse is sung in Sranan Tongo. About 519,600 people speak it as a first or second language, in Suriname and the Netherlands.
srebrenica: Srebrenica is a small mountain town and municipality in eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Republika Srpska entity. Its name means place or land of silver, the same sense as its old Latin name Argentaria. Illyrians mined silver nearby, and silver was a main reason for the Roman invasion of the area. A Roman settlement called Domavia stood near a mine, and ore was carried along the Via Argentaria to the mints at Salona and Sirmium. Mineral springs, notably the Crni Guber, later supported a spa, which drew tourists in the Yugoslav period and brought the town an annual income of about three million dollars.

In the 13th and 14th centuries the region belonged to the Banate of Bosnia and then the Bosnian Kingdom. The name first appears in 1376, when Srebrenica was already an important trading centre. Merchants of the Republic of Ragusa controlled the silver trade and its export through Dubrovnik, and many German miners settled there in the 14th century. Armed conflicts over the mines were frequent: according to the historian Konstantin Josef Jireček, between 1411 and 1463 the town changed hands several times among Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and the Ottomans.

Under Ottoman rule its economic importance declined, and a Franciscan church was converted into the White Mosque. Austria-Hungary occupied the town in 1878, after the Congress of Berlin, and introduced modern administration, schools and a postal service.

During the Bosnian War, Serb forces occupied the town in April 1992, and Bosniak resistance groups retook it. Refugees from the Drina valley gathered there, and it was besieged. On 16 April 1993 the United Nations declared the enclave a safe area, guarded by a small Dutch unit with no permission to use force. In July 1995 the Army of Republika Srpska under General Ratko Mladić captured it.

Men of fighting age and teenage boys who fell into Bosnian Serb hands were killed in a systematically organised series of summary executions, 8,372 men and boys in all, while women, boys under 12 and men over 65 were taken by bus to Tuzla.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia ruled in 2001 that this was genocide, confirmed on appeal in 2004, and the International Court of Justice upheld the finding in 2007.

Under the 1995 Dayton Agreement Srebrenica was placed in the Republika Srpska. Its population is roughly half Muslim and half Orthodox, and most of the 23 mosques destroyed in the war have been rebuilt. The White Mosque dates to the 17th century, and the Sase Monastery is a Serbian Orthodox monastery dating back to the 13th century. The Church of the Intercession of the Holy Virgin dates to 1903.
sremski-karlovci: Sremski Karlovci stands on the banks of the Danube in the region of Syrmia, in the South Bačka District of Vojvodina, about 75 kilometres from Belgrade. Its name in Serbian is plural. It is known in German as Karlowitz or Carlowitz, in Hungarian as Karlóca and in Turkish as Karlofça. The older Serbian form Karlovci is still used unofficially.

The town was first mentioned in 1308 under the name Karom. The medieval fortress of Karom was built on the ruins of a Roman one, and Hungarian noble families, among them the Báthory and Morović, held it until 1521. In that year the Ottoman commander Bali-beg conquered it, and it remained Ottoman for about 170 years. The Slavic name Karlovci was first recorded in 1532/33. An Ottoman survey of 1545 counted 547 Christian Serb houses, three Orthodox churches and a monastery.

From 16 November 1698 to 26 January 1699 a congress at Karlovci ended hostilities between the Ottoman Empire and the Holy League, a coalition that included the Habsburg monarchy, Poland, Venice and Russia. It produced the Treaty of Karlowitz. It was the first time a round table was used in international politics. Karlovci then passed to the Habsburg monarchy and its Military Frontier, and became the spiritual, political and cultural centre of the Serbs there, with the Serbian Orthodox metropolitan in residence. The first Serbian gymnasium was founded in 1791, and an Orthodox seminary three years later.

At the Serb National Assembly in May 1848 the Serbs declared the union of Syrmia, Banat, Bačka and Baranya into Serbian Vojvodina, with Karlovci as its first capital, and the metropolitan's title was raised to that of Patriarch. The Patriarchate of Karlovci operated until 1920, when the Serbian ecclesiastical provinces were united. From 1921 the patriarch's palace housed the synod of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia.

The municipality consists of the town alone, with 7,872 inhabitants at the census of 2022. The Karlovci Gymnasium is the oldest secondary school in Serbia, and the Saint Arsenije Seminary still operates. The Serbian Patriarch retains the title of Metropolitan of Karlovci.
sri-jayawardenepura-kotte: Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte lies next to the urban area of Colombo, which is Sri Lanka's de facto economic capital. The municipal area is bounded on the west by Colombo, on the south-west by Dehiwala-Mount Lavinia and on the south-east by Maharagama. The older village of Darugama lay at the confluence of two streams, the Diyawanna Oya and the Kolonnawa Oya. It was a naturally secure place that enemies could not easily enter, and in the 13th century a local chieftain, Nissanka Alagakkonara, built a kotte, or fortress, there.

Kotte was a jala durgha, a water fortress, in the shape of a triangle, with the marshes of the Diyawanna Oya and Kolonnawa Oya forming two long sides and a large inner moat dug along the shorter land side. It covered nearly 2.5 square kilometres and was fortified with ramparts of laterite 2.5 metres high and 10.7 metres broad. Alagakkonara held the army of Arya Chakravarthy in front of Kotte, while he defeated the enemy's invasion fleet at Panadura. In 1391, after Prince Sapumal conquered the Kingdom of Jaffna, Kotte was given the epithet Sri Jayawardenepura, meaning resplendent city of growing victory. It remained the capital of the ancient Kingdom of Kotte until the end of the 16th century.

The city had a king's palace with walls of quartz and a golden spire, a three-storeyed temple housing the Buddha's tooth relic, a five-storeyed arama where sixty monks lived under a high priest, and a royal cemetery at Beddagana. The Portuguese arrived on the island in 1505 and were initially welcomed by the king, but they had militaristic and monopolistic intentions and gained control of the city by 1565. Unable to withstand repeated assaults by the neighbouring Kingdom of Sitawaka, they abandoned it and made Colombo their capital. Urbanisation restarted in the 19th century, and the archaeological remains were torn up for building materials, some of them ending up in the Victoria Bridge across the Kelani River.

Sri Lanka designated Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte as its new capital in 1977 to relieve congestion in Colombo. The official move was marked on 29 April 1982 by the inauguration of the new Parliament building, which stands on reclaimed land on an island of 50,000 square metres in a lake formed by dredging the marshlands around the Diyawanna Oya. President J. R. Jayewardene declared it open. The Kotte Urban Council became the Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte Municipal Council in 1997. Traces of the old moat and rampart are still visible in places, and the city is the seat of the Education Ministry and the University of Sri Jayewardenepura at Nugegoda.
sri-lanka: Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean between latitudes 5° and 10° N, separated from the Indian subcontinent by the Gulf of Mannar and the Palk Strait. According to Hindu mythology a land bridge once joined the island to India. It now amounts to a chain of limestone shoals, and legends claim it was passable on foot until 1480 CE, when cyclones deepened the channel. The island consists mostly of flat to rolling coastal plains, with mountains rising only in the south-central part. The highest point is Pidurutalagala at 2,524 metres, and the longest river is the Mahaweli, at 335 kilometres. The coastline is 1,585 kilometres long.

Prehistory on the island goes back 125,000 years and possibly 500,000. In caves such as Pahiyangala, Batadombalena and Belilena archaeologists found the remains of anatomically modern humans, named Balangoda Man. The earliest inhabitants were likely ancestors of the Vedda people. During the protohistoric period, 1000 to 500 BCE, the island was culturally united with southern India and shared its megalithic burials, pottery, iron technology and farming techniques.

According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a Pāḷi chronicle written in the 5th century CE, the original inhabitants were the Yakshas and Nagas, and Sinhalese history traditionally begins in 543 BCE with the arrival of the semi-historical Prince Vijaya, who sailed with 700 followers after being expelled from Vanga, present-day Bengal. Vijaya is the first of about 189 monarchs described in chronicles such as the Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa and Cūḷavaṃsa.

The earliest known Buddhist writings on the island, the Pali Canon, date back to 29 BCE. The island was known to explorers as early as the Anuradhapura period. The Portuguese reached it in 1505 and established a colony in the sixteenth century, the Dutch later controlled the coastal areas, and the British established a colony by the early 19th century. Independence came in 1948 as the Dominion of Ceylon, and the country became a republic in 1972. A civil war between Tamil separatists and the armed forces lasted from 1983 to 2009.

Colombo is the executive and judicial capital and the largest city, and Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte is the legislative capital. The island has been called by many names: Taprobanā by Greek geographers, Sarandīb by Arabs and Persians, and Ceilão by the Portuguese, which became Ceylon in English. Sinhala and Tamil are the official languages. The Sinhalese form about 74% of the population and Sri Lankan Tamils about 12%, with Moors, Indian Tamils, Burghers, Malays and Veddas among smaller communities. Buddhism is the largest religion, and Sinhalese culture, centred in Kandy and Anuradhapura, and Tamil culture, centred in Jaffna, are the two main traditions.
sri-lankan-tamils: Sri Lankan Tamils, also called Ceylon Tamils or Eelam Tamils, are Tamils native to Sri Lanka. They form a majority in the Northern Province and the plurality in the Eastern Province, and are a minority in the rest of the country. According to the 2012 census there were 2,270,924 of them in Sri Lanka, 11.2% of the population. Modern Sri Lankan Tamils descend from residents of the Jaffna kingdom in the north and of the Vanni chieftaincies in the east.

Scholars do not agree about when Tamils first settled on the island. One older theory holds that there were no large Tamil settlements until the 10th century CE, but anthropological and archaeological evidence points to a presence since at least around the 2nd century BCE, when potsherds with early Tamil writing were left from Poonagari in the north to Tissamaharama in the south.

In the 9th and 10th centuries CE, Pandya and Chola incursions ended in the Chola annexation of the island, which lasted until the latter half of the 11th century. Tamil literature on religion, medicine, mathematics and history flourished at the court of the Jaffna kingdom. The Portuguese conquered that kingdom in 1619, and Portuguese and Dutch colonial rule lasted until 1796. Large-scale Protestant missionary activity from 1814 provoked a revival among Hindu Tamils, who built their own schools and temples.

After independence in 1948 relations with the Sinhalese majority were strained. The Sinhala Only Act of 1956 made Sinhala the sole official language, and riots targeting Tamils occurred in 1956, 1958, 1977, 1981 and 1983. The Black July violence of 1983 killed between 1,000 and 3,000 Tamils and led many young people to join militant groups, of which the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam eventually eliminated most. The civil war ended on 18 May 2009 with the government's victory, having killed at least 100,000 people. A United Nations panel found that as many as 40,000 Tamil civilians may have been killed in its last months.

Most Sri Lankan Tamils are Hindus of the Shaiva tradition, with a significant Christian minority, mostly Roman Catholics who converted after the Portuguese conquest. They speak Tamil in dialects that are more conservative than those of India and preserve features of Old and Medieval Tamil. The group is divided into Jaffna or Northern Tamils, Eastern Tamils and Negombo Tamils from the west, and education is highly valued.

The civil war drove more than 800,000 Tamils from their homes within Sri Lanka or abroad, and about one-third of Sri Lankan Tamils now live outside the country, with more than 200,000 legal residents in Canada. For some Tamils in Sri Lanka and the diaspora the tiger of the Tamil Eelam flag has become a symbol of Tamil nationalism.
sri-vaishnavism: The tradition's historical basis lies in the joining of two strands: the Sanskrit traditions of the Vedas and the Agama texts, Pancaratra and Vaikhanasa, and the Tamil devotional songs of the Alvars, composed between the 7th and 10th centuries. Its founding is traditionally attributed to Nathamuni, who developed it in Tamil Nadu after a pilgrimage to Vrindavan in north India. Nathamuni collected the poems of Nammalvar as the Divya Prabandham and set the Alvar songs to Vedic music, teaching his nephews to sing them; the Araiyar tradition of singing and dancing the verses descends from this, and the songs are still sung in Sri Vaishnava temples.

His grandson Yamunacharya, known in the tradition as Alavandar, headed the monastery at Srirangam and linked Alvar devotion and the Pancaratra texts to Vedic ideas in works such as the Siddhitrayam and the Gitarthasangraha. Ramanuja, who never met him, succeeded him there.

Followers hold that Sri is inseparable from Vishnu. Vishnu alone creates, preserves and destroys the universe, while Sri is the kind mother who recommends living beings to him and so helps them towards salvation. Ramanuja's Vishishtadvaita, or qualified non-dualism, holds that souls and Brahman are different, a difference never transcended, yet that souls share the essential nature of Brahman and every soul can reach the bliss of God himself. Unlike Madhvacharya, Ramanuja rejected eternal damnation. Theologians of the tradition hold that the poems of the Alvars contain the essential meaning of the Sanskrit Vedas.

The tradition has been organised around mathas, or monasteries, especially since Ramanuja, whose reforms at Srirangam paralleled the Advaita monasteries of his time. Tradition credits him with founding 700 mathas, though historical evidence suggests several were founded later. Debate over the weight given to the Vedas and to the Prabandham of the Alvars later split the tradition into the Vadakalai, named for Kanchipuram in the north of the Tamil country and following Vedanta Desika, and the Tenkalai, named for Srirangam in the south and following Manavala Mamunigal.

The Tenkalai hold that prapatti, unconditional surrender, is the only means to salvation, while the Vadakalai add karma yoga, jnana yoga and bhakti yoga. The Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam, regarded as the foremost site of the tradition, belongs to the Tenkalai, and its priests descend from the 74 disciples appointed by Ramanuja.
sri-vikrama-rajasinha: Born Kannasamy Nayak, he was a member of the Madurai Nayak dynasty and the nephew of Sri Rajadhi Rajasinha, whom he succeeded in 1798 at the age of eighteen. The Nayak kings were of Telugu origin, practised Shaivite Hinduism and were patrons of Theravada Buddhism; they used Tamil as a court language alongside Sinhala. Queen Upendrama's brother Muthuswamy had a stronger claim to the throne, but the first Adigar, or chief minister, Pilimatalauwa chose the young prince, reportedly planning to seize the crown for himself in time.

Pilimatalauwa worked secretly with the British, who held the coastal provinces, to provoke the king into a war that would give Britain a cause for intervention. On 22 March 1803 the British entered Kandy unopposed after the king had fled; in June the Adigar massacred the British garrison and restored him. Pilimatalauwa's plot to take the throne was later discovered, and, having been pardoned twice before, he was executed.

His nephew and successor Ehelepola Nilame fell under the same suspicion. After a rebellion he instigated was put down he fled to the British, and the king confiscated his lands and ordered the imprisonment and execution of his wife and children. Ehelepola persuaded the British that the king's tyranny justified intervention, and the seizure and torture of British merchants, several of whom died, gave the pretext. The invading force reached Kandy without resistance on 10 February 1815, and the kingdom was ceded on 2 March. The historian Louis Edmund Blaze judged him less a monster of cruelty than a weak tool of scheming chiefs.

Held at Vellore Fort on a small British allowance with his two queens, he died of dropsy on 30 January 1832. Kandy Lake and the Octagon of the Sri Dalada Maligawa, built in 1802 by the royal architect Devendra Mulachari, were made on his instructions. His royal standard, a yellow lion holding a sword on a red ground, is part of the present flag of Sri Lanka, and his tomb near Vellore is the memorial Muthu Mandapam.
srimanta-sankardev: Sankardev was born as Sankaravara into the chief Baro-Bhuyans family at Bordowa in the present-day Nagaon district, in about 1449. The Bhuyans were independent landlords in Assam, and his family were Saktas. His father died of smallpox when he was about seven, and his grandmother Khersuti raised him.

At twelve he entered the school of Mahendra Kandali, who gave him the name Sankardev, and he studied grammar and the Indian scriptures. After leaving school in his late teens he took up his duties as Shiromani Bhuyan. In 1481 he set out on a twelve-year pilgrimage to the major seats of Vaishnavism, including Puri, Mathura, Dwaraka and Rameswaram, and composed his first borgeet in Brajavali at Badrikashram in 1488.

On his return he refused to take back the Shiromaniship. He built a prayer house at Bordowa and received a copy of the Bhagavata Purana from Jagadisa Mishra of Mithila, an event regarded as critical to the development of Ekasarana, which holds Krishna to be the only God. Pressure from the Ahom and Koch kings drove the Bhuyans from their lands, and Sankardev moved east of the Brahmaputra, to Gangmau and then to Dhuwahat, where he won his chief disciple Madhavdev after a debate. Brahmins complained to the Ahom king Suhungmung, but Sankardev convinced the king that he was no threat to the social order.

He later settled in the Koch kingdom, at Patbausi near Barpeta. When Koch king Nara Narayan ordered his arrest for spreading a new religion, the general Chilarai persuaded the king to hear him instead. Sankardev refuted the charges at court and was given freedom to teach. At Chilarai's request he supervised the weaving of the Vrindavani vastra, a long tapestry of Krishna's life at Vrindavan; parts of it survive in London and Paris. He died at Bheladonga in Kochbehar in 1568, having declined the king's wish to be initiated.

Sankardev preached devotion to Krishna through hearing and singing his deeds, in the attitude of a servant of God, and did not worship Radha beside him. He initiated people of all castes and religions, including Muslims, and called on followers to give up Vedic rites. His Kirtana-ghosha, narrative verses for communal singing, remains in many Assamese homes.

He rendered eight books of the Bhagavata Purana into Assamese, wrote one-act plays called Ankia Naat, and composed borgeets, of which 34 of 240 survive. He is credited with originating the Sattriya dance, now a classical dance form of India, and the sattras, the monasteries that carry his teaching on.
srinagar: Srinagar lies in the Kashmir Valley along the banks of the Jhelum River and on the shores of Dal Lake and the Anchar Lake, between the Hari Parbat and Shankaracharya hills. Nine old bridges connect the two parts of the city. The earliest record of the name is in Kalhana's Sanskrit chronicle Rajatarangini, as Śrīnagarī, meaning city of Lakshmi. The name first belonged to an older capital nearby; between the 14th and 19th centuries the city was also called simply Kashmir or Shahr-i-Kashmir.

According to the Rajatarangini, an older capital called Srinagari was built in the valley by an Ashoka whom historians identify with the Mauryan emperor, at what is now Pandrethan. A new capital was built by King Pravarasena of the Gonanda dynasty in the 6th century CE at the base of the Hari Parbat, where modern Srinagar stands. In the 14th century Rinchana, a Buddhist convert to Islam, built the first mosque in Kashmir, and the Sultans after him set their capitals in what is now the old city. Sultan Sikandar built the Khanqah-e-Moula in 1397 and the Jamia Mosque in 1402.

The Mughals annexed Kashmir in 1586. Jahangir, fond of the valley, brought prosperity to the city; the Shalimar and Nishat gardens were built around the Dal Lake in his reign and that of Shah Jahan. The Afghan Durrani Empire took Kashmir in 1753 and the Sikh Empire in 1819. After the 1846 Treaty of Amritsar Srinagar became the capital of the Dogra princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, and in 1872 the Darbar Move shifted the capital to Jammu for six months in winter. Srinagar became the summer capital of the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir in 1952.

Srinagar is the largest city and summer capital of the Indian-administered union territory of Jammu and Kashmir. It is known for gardens, houseboats on Dal Lake and traditional Kashmiri crafts such as the Kashmir shawl, papier-mâché, wood carving and carpet weaving. Its religious buildings include the Khanqah-e-Moula, the Jamia Mosque, the Hazratbal Shrine and the Shankaracharya temple. The University of Kashmir dates from 1948.
srinagar-uttarakhand: Srinagar lies on the left bank of the Alaknanda River at an average height of 560 metres, about 33 km from Pauri, the headquarters of Pauri Garhwal district, and about 104 km by road from Rishikesh, where the plains end and the mountains begin. The town rests on terraces of boulders and sand laid down by the river, above a fractured rock called Pauri Phyllite. Shut in by high mountains, its valley has the hottest summers in the Garhwal Himalaya, with daytime highs above 44 °C between May and July.

The town rose to importance as the capital of the Garhwal Kingdom. King Ajay Pal, who unified the chiefdoms and garhis, the small fortified counties, of the region between 1506 and 1512, founded the kingdom and moved its capital from Chandpur Garhi to Srinagar. After taking Kathmandu, the Gorkhas turned west and attacked Kumaon and Garhwal in 1803, and Raja Pradyumna Shah of Garhwal was defeated and killed in January 1804. When the British defeated the Gorkhas, Srinagar became part of British Garhwal.

The old town, with all its ancient relics, was destroyed when the Gohna Lake dam burst. A Jain temple that stood in the old settlement was lost in a flood of 1894; its images are said to have survived, and a new temple dedicated to Rishabhanatha was built in the relocated town between 1911 and 1924.

Srinagar is a municipal corporation and a cultural and educational centre of central Garhwal, with a large valley bazaar. It is the seat of Hemwati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, founded in 1973 and made a Central University in 2009, and of the National Institute of Technology, Uttarakhand, opened in 2010. The temple of Dhari Devi, a form of Kali revered as a guardian of the Char Dham pilgrimage sites, stands on the Alaknanda between Srinagar and Rudraprayag.
sriranga-iii: Sriranga III was a great-grandson of Aliya Rama Raya. Before his accession he rebelled against his uncle, Venkata III, and with help from the Sultan of Bijapur attacked him at Chandragiri and Vellore in 1638. A second invasion in 1642 was beaten back by Venkata's army, which was also facing Golkonda forces near Madras. When Venkata died in these difficult circumstances, Sriranga, who was with the Bijapur army, deserted it, returned to Vellore and made himself king.

Many of his nobles, among them the Nayaka of Gingee and Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka, the chieftain of Madras, disliked him for his rebellion against the old king, and he struggled to win the consent of the nayakas that his coronation required. At the Raja Mahal of Chandragiri fort he granted agents of the English East India Company the site of Fort St. George at Madras.

In 1645 Tirumala, the nayaka of Madurai, who had tried to kill Sriranga by witchcraft, formed a league against him with the nayakas of Tanjavur and Gingee. Sriranga sent his army against Gingee, and Tirumala urged Golkonda to invade. When Tanjavur sided with Golkonda, Tirumala called in Bijapur, but the plan backfired: the two sultanates agreed to divide the conquests between them. With help from Mysore, Gingee and Tanjore, Sriranga met the Sultanate armies at Virinchipuram, a village on the southern bank of the Palar River just west of Vellore, and was defeated. Left without a kingdom, he lived as a guest of Tirumala in Madurai until 1647, then at Tanjavur, and in 1648, as his allowance there shrank, he moved to Kannaiga territory.

He spent his last years under the protection of one of his vassal chieftains, Shivappa Nayaka of Ikkeri, still hoping to recover Vellore. Kanthirava Narasaraja I of Mysore continued to recognise him as emperor and, angered by Tirumala's treachery, waged destructive wars against Madurai that won Coimbatore and Salem for Mysore. Sriranga died an emperor without an empire, ending over three centuries of Vijayanagara rule. His only daughter married Srivallabha, a descendant of Narasimhacharya.
srirangam: The Kaveri divides at the Upper Anaicut, a dam at the island's western tip: the Kollidam, its first and largest distributary, flows to the north and the Kaveri itself to the south. At the eastern end the Grand Anaicut splits the Kaveri into four streams, one of which joins the Kollidam and closes off the island. The island is about 31 kilometres long and 2.4 kilometres wide, with the town at its centre. The name comes from arangam, the Tamil word for an isle among the branches of a river, with the honorific prefixes Sri and Tiru.

Old Tamil literature calls the place Tiruvarangam or Arangam, and the epic Cilappatikaram describes Vishnu reclining on the thousand-hooded serpent in the temple on the island in the Kaveri. Legend holds that Vibhishana, carrying Vishnu's image to Lanka, set it down on the riverbank, where it refused to move, and that the deity faces south towards Lanka to bless him. Tradition credits the Chola kings Dharmavarcholan and Killivalavan, with the help of Tirumangai Alvar, with the temple's foundations and main buildings.

The theologian Ramanuja made his monastic home at the temple in the 11th century and wrote there his commentaries on the Brahma Sutra setting out Vishishtadvaita. Under the Vijayanagara Empire, Krishnadevaraya treated the town on a par with Tirupati and gave the temple treasure, jewels and lands. The southern gateway tower, the Rajagopuram, was begun under Achyuta Deva Raya and left unfinished for over 400 years, until it was completed and consecrated on 25 March 1987.

Srirangam is a neighbourhood of Tiruchirappalli, and most of the island forms its Srirangam zone. The Ranganathaswamy Temple covers about 631,000 square metres within seven enclosures and has 21 gopurams. The town is the first of the 108 Divya Desams and home to many Sri Vaishnavas, and its economy rests largely on pilgrims, who come in the largest numbers for Vaikunta Ekadashi.
