srirangapatna: Srirangapatna, also spelled Srirangapattana, is a town in Mandya district in the Indian state of Karnataka, on an island in the Kaveri river, near the city of Mandya. It takes its name from the Ranganathaswamy Temple, consecrated around 984 CE. Under British rule it was called Seringapatam. Karighatta, the Black Hill, rises a few kilometres outside the island town, reached by 450 stone steps to a hilltop temple of Vaikunta Srinivasa. The Nimishamba temple, to Parvathi, stands on the bank of the Lokapavani river.

Srirangapatna became the capital of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan. Tipu put aside his show of deference to the Wodeyar Maharaja, whom he in effect held captive, and proclaimed the Khudadad State under his own kingship, though Chamaraja Wodeyar IX was still officially king of Mysore. In his wars against the British, the Kodavas and the Malabar rajas, he rounded up whole communities of Nairs, Kodavas and Mangalorean Catholics and deported them to Srirangapatna, where they were held in bondage until the British defeat of Tipu in 1799 freed them.

The Treaty of Seringapatam, signed on 18 March 1792, ended the Third Anglo-Mysore War. Its signatories included Lord Cornwallis for the British East India Company, representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maratha Empire, and Tipu Sultan.

In 1799 the town was the scene of the last and decisive battle of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, fought between Tipu Sultan and a combined force of 50,000 men provided equally by the Nizam and the East India Company under General George Harris. At the climax Tipu was killed within the fort, betrayed by one of his confidants. The victors plundered the town and ransacked Tipu's palace. In 1809 Lord Harris's House was the scene of a mutiny by Madras Army officers led by Col. Bell against the Governor of Madras, Sir George Barlow.

The fortress in the west of the island is surrounded by double walls, and an obelisk marks where the British broke through; the spot where Tipu fell has a memorial. The ramparts, the Water Gate and the site of the destroyed palace survive, as does Colonel Bailey's Dungeon, where British officers were held. The Garrison Cemetery holds about 307 graves of officers killed in the assault of 1799 and their families. The monuments of the island have been nominated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the application is on the tentative list. The town appears in Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone.
srivijaya: The earliest reference to Srivijaya dates from the 7th century. The Tang dynasty Chinese monk Yijing wrote that he visited it for six months in 671. The earliest known inscription naming it is the Kedukan Bukit inscription, found near Palembang and dated 605 Saka, which corresponds to 682 or 683. It tells of Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa, who set out on a sacred siddhayatra journey with 20,000 troops from Minanga Tamwan to Jambi and Palembang and founded a kadatuan, a kingdom or polity.

The name itself is Sanskrit, meaning something like glorious or shining victory. Early 20th-century scholars thought it was a king's name, until the French historian George Cœdès postulated the empire's existence in 1918. Its history had been forgotten, and Indonesians, even around Palembang, had not heard of it until the 1920s, when Cœdès published his findings in Dutch and Malay newspapers.

The kingdom first had to consolidate its position in south-eastern Sumatra, which consisted of several quasi-independent polities ruled by local chieftains, and many of its forces were sea peoples, the orang laut. During the 7th century Langkasuka on the Malay Peninsula became part of it, and Pan Pan and Tambralinga came under its influence. In the second half of the 8th century its mandala seems to have been ruled by the Sailendra dynasty of Central Java, although it is not known whether the capital moved to Java or Srivijaya became subordinate to it. Between the late 7th and early 11th century it was a hegemon in Southeast Asia and a centre for the expansion of Buddhism.

Rajendra Chola, the Chola king from Tamil Nadu, launched naval raids on its ports in 1025. His fleet sailed with the monsoon winds and took Srivijaya by surprise, first ransacking Palembang and then moving on to other ports, including Kadaram. An inscription of Rajendra says he captured its king, Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman, and plundered treasures such as the jewelled war gate. The kingdom may have disintegrated after 1025, though Chinese sources continued to refer to a polity called Sanfoqi for some centuries, which some historians identify with Jambi after that date.

In its formation the empire had three zones: the capital region around Palembang, the Musi River basin as a source of valuable goods, and rival river-mouth areas, such as the Batang Hari in Jambi, held under its power by raids and conquests. Its main foreign aim was a lucrative trade agreement with China, kept through tribute missions from the Tang to the Song dynasty, and it controlled the Sunda and Malacca straits between India and China. Historians debate whether it was chiefly a sea power or a land-based polity.
ss-kaiser-wilhelm-der-grosse: At a naval review for Queen Victoria's jubilee in 1889, Emperor Wilhelm II saw the size of the British liners, among them White Star's RMS Teutonic, and admired how easily they could be turned into auxiliary cruisers. Norddeutscher Lloyd, one of only two German lines with influence on the North Atlantic, then commissioned AG Vulkan of Stettin to build a superliner named after the emperor's grandfather, William I. She was launched on 4 May 1897 in the presence of the imperial family, with decks strengthened to carry guns in wartime.

The ship was 627.4 ft (191.2 m) long, with a beam of 66.0 ft (20.1 m) and a tonnage of 14,349 GRT, and for a time she was the largest ship in the world. Her four funnels were served by only two uptake shafts, which is why they were unequally spaced, yet passengers came to associate four funnels with size and safety. Two triple expansion engines gave her more than 20 knots. She carried up to 1,506 passengers, and Johann Poppe designed all her Baroque revival interiors, including a domed dining room. In February 1900 she became the first liner with a commercial wireless telegraphy system.

She sailed on her maiden voyage from Bremerhaven by way of Southampton to New York on 19 September 1897. In June 1900 a fire at her quay in Hoboken killed one hundred men, and on 21 November 1906 she collided with RMS Orinoco in Cherbourg harbour, a collision that killed five of her passengers and three of Orinoco's crew. Outclassed by Lusitania and Mauretania, she was rebuilt in 1913 to carry third-class passengers only.

As an auxiliary cruiser under Captain Reymann she sank Tubal Cain, Kaipara and Nyanza after taking their crews aboard, and let two liners go because they carried women and children. While coaling at Río de Oro on 26 August 1914 she was caught by HMS Highflyer. The Germans said Reymann scuttled her when ammunition ran out; the British held that gunfire sank her. Most of her crew were interned in Nova Scotia. Underwater footage of the wreck was taken in 2013.
st-albans: St Albans lies in Hertfordshire, 20 miles (32 km) north-west of London. It takes its name from Alban, the first British saint. In Bede's account, which is the most elaborate, Alban lived at Verulamium in the 3rd or 4th century, when Christians were persecuted. He sheltered a fleeing Christian priest and was converted by his piety. When the authorities came, Alban put on the priest's cloak and gave himself up in the priest's place. He refused to renounce Christianity and was executed. Later legends say that his head rolled downhill and that a well sprang up where it stopped.

An Iron Age settlement called Verlamion stood near the present city, as a centre of the Catuvellauni from about 20 BCE until shortly after the Roman invasion of 43 CE. The Roman city of Verulamium, the second-largest town in Roman Britain after Londinium, was granted the rank of municipium around 50 CE. Boudica of the Iceni sacked and burned it in 61, and a black ash layer dated to 60–65 confirms the Roman record.

By the early 3rd century it covered about 125 acres behind a ditch and wall, and it had a forum, a basilica and a theatre. Roman occupation ended between 400 and 450. Alban's grave outside the walls became a place of pilgrimage, and Germanus of Auxerre visited the church in 429.

The Benedictine Abbey of St Albans was founded by Ulsinus in 793 on the hill east of the Roman town, and the present building was begun in 1077. It was the principal medieval abbey in England, and the first draft of Magna Carta is said to have been drawn up there.

The Clock Tower in the Market Place, built between 1403 and 1412, is the only surviving medieval town belfry in England. Two battles of the Wars of the Roses took place in or near the town: the First Battle of St Albans on 22 May 1455, within the town, and the Second on 17 February 1461, just to the north. The abbey was dissolved in 1539 and became a parish church. Edward VI incorporated the town as a borough in 1553.

The abbey church was made a cathedral in 1877, when Queen Victoria also granted the borough city status, and St Albans remains a cathedral city. Parts of the Roman walls, a hypocaust under a mosaic floor and the theatre of Verulamium can still be seen, and the Verulamium Museum holds finds from the excavations. St Albans School, said to have been founded in 948, educated Matthew Paris and Pope Adrian IV. The railway reached the town in 1858.
st-andrews: St Andrews lies on the east coast of Fife, 16 kilometres south-east of Dundee and 50 kilometres north-east of Edinburgh. It is named after Saint Andrew the Apostle, and the settlement grew to the west of the cathedral, between the Scores to the north and the Kinness Burn to the south. Its earliest recorded name occurs in 747, when an Irish annal noted the death of Tuathalán, abbot of Kinrymonth. The name combines the Old Gaelic cenn, head or peninsula, with Rigmonad, containing the words for king and moor, later rendered in Lowland Scots as King's Muir.

The first settlers on the estuaries of the Tay and the Eden arrived in the Mesolithic, and farmers settled around the modern town about 4,500 BCE. In the Iron Age a fortified enclosure, possibly a hillfort, stood on East Balrymonth hill a mile to the south, and it is the oldest surviving structure in the area. The burgh became the ecclesiastical capital of Scotland, and held that position until the Scottish Reformation. Its cathedral, the largest in Scotland, is now a ruin. The Martyrs Memorial, at the west end of the Scores, honours Patrick Hamilton, George Wishart and other martyrs of the Reformation.

The town was once bounded by gates called ports, of which West Port, rebuilt between 1843 and 1845, and the Sea Yett survive. The Lade Braes Walk follows a medieval mill lade that may have been built before 1144. Fishing declined before the First World War, and the St Andrews Railway link to Leuchars ended in 1969.

St Andrews had a population of 16,460 in 2022, and its economy rests heavily on tourism and education. It is home to the University of St Andrews, the oldest university in Scotland, and is known worldwide as the home of golf. The earliest surviving document, from 1552, records permission from Archbishop Hamilton to play golf on the links beside the water of Eden.

The Royal and Ancient Golf Club of St Andrews was founded in 1754 and until 2004 held legislative authority over the game outside the United States and Mexico. The town bought the Old Course in 1894, and it is the most frequent venue of the Open Championship, staged from 1873. The film Chariots of Fire used West Sands beach for its opening scene.
st-augustine-florida: St. Augustine stands on the Atlantic coast of north-eastern Florida, 40 miles south of downtown Jacksonville, with access to the ocean by the St. Augustine Inlet of the Matanzas River. Before the Spanish arrived in 1565 the area was inhabited by the Timucua, who lived in villages along the St. Johns River, farmed, fished, hunted and traded with neighbouring groups. Their society had hereditary chiefs and organised ceremonies.

Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded the settlement on 8 September 1565 and named it San Agustín, because his ships had first sighted land eleven days earlier on 28 August, the feast day of St. Augustine. The city served as capital of Spanish Florida for over 200 years. On 28 and 29 May 1586, soon after the Anglo-Spanish War began, Sir Francis Drake sacked it. The townspeople evacuated, and after Spanish rearguards killed their sergeant major the English razed the town.

The Treaty of Paris of 1763 ceded Florida to Great Britain, and many Spanish settlers left for Cuba. St. Augustine became a Loyalist haven during the American Revolutionary War. The Adams–Onís Treaty, negotiated in 1819 and ratified in 1821, ceded Florida to the United States, and in 1824 Tallahassee replaced St. Augustine as capital.

In 1883 Henry Flagler, a co-founder of Standard Oil, spent the winter there and decided to make the city a winter resort for wealthy northerners. In 1885 he combined short railroads into the Florida East Coast Railway. In 1963 African Americans seeking to integrate schools and lunch counters were met with arrests, Ku Klux Klan violence and police violence, and homes were firebombed.

St. Augustine is the county seat of St. Johns County and had a population of 14,329 in 2020. It is the oldest continuously inhabited city of European origin in the contiguous United States. Castillo de San Marcos, the city's 17th-century Spanish fort, is a major attraction, and St. George Street, a pedestrian street, has over 30 historic houses and attractions.
st-bartholomews-day-massacre: The Peace of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 8 August 1570 ended three years of civil war between Catholics and Protestants, but intransigent Catholics refused to accept it. The queen mother Catherine de' Medici and her son King Charles IX supported peace and the Huguenot leader Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, who had returned to the king's council in September 1571, because of the kingdom's financial difficulties and the Huguenots' strong defensive position. To cement the peace, Catherine arranged the marriage of her daughter Margaret to the Protestant Henry of Navarre on 18 August 1572. The Pope and Philip II of Spain condemned her policy, and many well-born Protestants gathered in Paris, a violently anti-Huguenot city already strained by poor harvests, higher taxes and rising food prices.

On 22 August Coligny was shot from an upstairs window as he returned from the Louvre, and seriously wounded. The Guise family, the Duke of Alba and Catherine have each been suspected. The king and court visited him, but fears of Huguenot reprisals grew. On the evening of 23 August Catherine met her advisers and then the king, and Charles IX and his mother apparently decided to eliminate the Protestant leaders. The killing began that night, on the eve of the Feast of Saint Bartholomew. Coligny was killed, and the slaughter spread through Paris as mob violence.

Charles sent orders on 24 August to his provincial governors to prevent violence, but from August to October similar massacres took place in twelve other cities, among them Toulouse, Bordeaux, Lyon, Rouen and Orléans. Mack P. Holt notes that all were cities with Catholic majorities and former Protestant minorities. It seems unlikely that orders came from the king. Estimates of the dead vary widely: modern figures for all France run from 5,000 to 30,000.

The massacre was a turning point in the French Wars of Religion. The Huguenot political movement was crippled by the loss of many aristocratic leaders, many rank-and-file members converted, and those who remained became increasingly radicalised. A historian has called it the worst of the century's religious massacres, and it printed on Protestant minds throughout Europe the conviction that Catholicism was a bloody and treacherous religion.
st-donatians-cathedral: Arnulf I, Count of Flanders, built St Donatian's Church, Sint-Donaaskerk in Dutch, around 950 to house the relics of Saint Donatian, which monks from Torhout had brought to Bruges around 870. The church was built in the Romanesque style, with an octagonal main building, a tower and a sixteen-sided ambulatory. It stood on the Burg, one of the main squares of the city, facing the Stadhuis, the city hall, and it was the largest church in Bruges. Count Charles the Good was assassinated inside it on 2 March 1127. The church became a cathedral once the first Bishop of Bruges had been installed.

Canon Joris van der Paele commissioned Jan van Eyck's painting The Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele, dated 1436, as an altarpiece for the church; the panel also depicts Saint Donatian. Van Eyck himself was buried in St Donatian's in 1441.

Jan Provoost's altarpiece Mary in Glory, of 1524, was also made for the church. It was hidden during the Reformation and was found in the walls when the building was demolished. The painting later belonged to the collection of King Willem II, and after his death it was bought for the Hermitage.

The cathedral was destroyed in 1799 by the occupying forces of the French First Republic, in the aftermath of the French Revolution and the dissolution of the Diocese of Bruges. Its site is now occupied by the Crowne Plaza Brugge Hotel. The foundations of the cathedral were uncovered in 1955 and can still be seen in the hotel's cellars.
st-francisville-louisiana: St. Francisville is the parish seat of West Feliciana Parish and part of the Baton Rouge metropolitan area. It was laid out on a narrow ridge above the Mississippi River, which earned it the description "the town two miles long and two yards wide". The town covers about 4.7 square kilometres, all of it land, and was the commercial and cultural centre of the surrounding plantation country.

The town was established on 11 May 1807 by John H. Johnson and was first known as the Villa of St. Francis. Below its bluffs stood Bayou Sara, a settlement founded by French colonists in the early 1790s. It was at one time the largest antebellum Mississippi River port between New Orleans and Memphis, but Natchez overtook it, and repeated floods and fires gradually destroyed it. Nothing of Bayou Sara exists today, though a few of its buildings were hauled up the hill into St. Francisville in the 1920s.

The land changed hands several times before the town was founded. Former French territory east of the Mississippi passed to Great Britain after the Seven Years' War in 1763, and Britain ceded what it called West Florida to Spain in 1783 under the Treaty of Paris. The eastern boundary of the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 remained disputed for years, and Spain kept claiming land east of the river until the Pinckney Treaty settled the matter. The region is now called the Florida Parishes. In 1824, when Feliciana Parish was divided into East and West, St. Francisville became the seat of West Feliciana Parish.

In June 1863 the Confederate officer William Walter Leake arranged the burial of the Union naval officer John E. Hart, who had died aboard his ship during the blockade of the Mississippi. A three-day commemoration each June, called The Day the War Stopped, re-enacts the event. After the Civil War, Jewish emigrants fleeing persecution in Germany settled in the town. They became successful merchants, provided credit when the banks failed and built Victorian houses such as the Wolf-Schlessinger House.

The 2020 census counted 1,557 people in St. Francisville. Community efforts have focused on restoring the town's historic houses, and several restored plantations are open for tours, among them Rosedown Plantation State Historic Site, Audubon State Historic Site, Butler Greenwood Plantation, the Myrtles and the Cottage Plantation. The John James Audubon Bridge, built in 2011, replaced a ferry as the river crossing to New Roads.
st-gallen: St. Gallen lies in the north-east of Switzerland, in a valley about 700 metres above sea level, between Lake Constance and the Appenzell Alps, whose highest peak, the Säntis, reaches 2,502 metres. It is one of the highest cities in Switzerland and receives abundant winter snow. The city is the gate to the Appenzellerland.

The town grew around the Abbey of St Gall, built in the 8th century at the site of a hermitage said, according to legend, to have been founded by the Irish missionary Gallus by the river Steinach in 612. The monastery itself was founded by Saint Othmar around 720. The abbey prospered in the 9th century and became a place of pilgrimage and trade, with a hospital and one of the first monastery schools north of the Alps. By the tenth century a settlement had grown up around it.

From the 12th century the town pushed for independence from the abbey, and in 1180 an imperial reeve not answerable to the abbot was installed. In 1207 King Philip of Swabia granted Abbot Ulrich von Sax the rank of Imperial Prince, making the abbey a regional power. The town became a full member of the Old Swiss Confederation in 1454 and was completely free of the abbot in 1457. In early 1490 four cantons invaded in support of the abbey, and the town accepted a settlement that restricted its power and imposed heavy reparations.

In 1526 the mayor and humanist Joachim von Watt, called Vadian, introduced the Reformation. The town became Protestant while the abbey stayed Catholic, remaining a stronghold in a Protestant city until 1803. After the French invasion of 1798 the abbey and city lost their power and were joined with Appenzell in the Canton of Säntis; after the Act of Mediation, St. Gallen became capital of the canton of St. Gallen.

St. Gallen is the capital of its canton, with 76,213 inhabitants at the end of 2020, and the centre of eastern Switzerland. The Abbey of Saint Gall is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its library holds books from the 9th century. Twenty-eight sites in the city are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance. The University of St. Gallen specialises in business, economics, law and political science.
st-georges-grenada: St. George's is the capital and largest city of Grenada and its main port. It stands on the south-west coast of the island, on a horseshoe-shaped harbour, and is surrounded by a hillside that is the rim of an old volcano crater. The climate is humid and tropical, with a wet season from June to December and a dry season from January to May, which favours the spice crops on which the island's economy rests. Nutmeg is the key crop, followed by cocoa, mace, cloves, vanilla, cinnamon and ginger.

The French colonised the island, then called La Grenade, under Jacques Dyel du Parquet, governor of Martinique, and began with skirmishes that virtually exterminated its native Carib population. In 1666 French colonists built a wooden fortification, Fort Royale, on a promontory overlooking the natural harbour. Work began in 1705 on a star fort on the same site, with four stone bastions, to the design of Jean de Giou de Caylus, chief engineer of the French West Indies, and was completed in 1710. The first settlement, at the eastern edge of the harbour, was named Saint Louis after King Louis IX but suffered from flooding and malaria, so a new town, the Ville de Fort Royal, was built.

When the island passed to Britain the town was renamed Saint George's Town after the patron saint of England, and Fort Royal became Fort George. After the mid-1880s St. George's was the capital of the British Windward Islands. Grenada became independent in 1974, and after a leftist coup in 1983 the island was invaded by US troops. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan damaged some 90 per cent of the island's homes.

Fort George still stands on the promontory west of the harbour, and its buildings are used by the police. The Grenada National Museum occupies French barracks dating from 1704, which later served as a prison and as the island's first hotel; it displays Carib and Arawak artefacts and Josephine Bonaparte's marble bath. The tower of St. George's Cathedral was built in 1818 and St. George's Anglican Church in 1825. York House houses the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Supreme Court.
st-georges-night-uprising: After the Livonian Order conquered Ösel (Saaremaa) in 1261, Northern Crusaders from Germany and Denmark held the whole of Estonia. The new rulers imposed taxes and duties, built manor-houses across the country and suppressed native religious practice, and the Catholic Church added its own economic demands. Danish power in Harria and Vironia had weakened by the 14th century, and the province was split between a pro-Danish party led by Bishop Olaf of Roskilde and a pro-German party led by Marquard Breide. Of the Danish vassals in the Duchy of Estonia, 80 per cent were Germans from Westphalia, 18 per cent Danes and 2 per cent Estonians.

On Saint George's Night, 23 April 1343, a house set alight on a hilltop gave the signal for an attack on the foreigners in Harria. According to the Younger Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, the rebels renounced Christianity, burned the manors and killed the Germans they caught, among them 28 monks of Padise Abbey. The Estonians elected four kings and besieged Reval (Tallinn) with 10,000 men. The uprising spread to Rotalia, where the rebels besieged Hapsal.

The Livonian Master Burchard von Dreileben invited the four kings to talks at Weissenstein on 4 May and then had them and their squires killed. The chronicle blames the envoys, but some historians see a ruse to kill the leaders. The Order won the Battle of Kanavere on 11 May, where the Estonians lost 1,600 men, and the Battle of Sõjamäe on 14 May, where 3,000 were killed. Swedish forces arrived on 18 May, found Reval held by the Order and went home after looting. Reinforcements from Prussia crushed the remaining resistance in Harria.

On Ösel the islanders rose on 24 July 1344 and took the Order's castle at Pöide, then killed its defenders after promising them free passage. The rebellion there ended in 1345 with a conditional surrender.

Weakened Denmark lost Narva in 1345, and in 1346 Valdemar IV sold the Duchy of Estonia to the Teutonic Order for 19,000 marks. Sovereignty passed on 1 November 1346. The remnants of the pre-Christian Estonian nobility in northern Estonia disappeared. Historians still debate the uprising. Some, such as Edgar V. Saks and Uku Masing, argue from contemporary documents that it was not a fight against Christianity but against the Livonian Order. Others dismiss this as biased.
st-johns-antigua-and-barbuda: St. John's lies in the western part of Antigua, around St. John's Harbour, on a gentle slope east of the harbour. It is the main city of the Central Plain region. Before the town was founded, a small group of houses lined the harbour, then known as the Cove. The flat land around it allowed a large network of roads to converge on the city, and its low coastline is prone to flooding.

St. John's was laid out after the French invasion of 1666, because of the strategic position of the harbour, and an act to build a town there was passed in April 1668. On 16 September 1675 the island's legislature, sitting at Old Road, established six places of trade, one of them St. John's, where the island had traditionally had two. By 1689 the town was as large as Falmouth, which it later replaced as the island's dominant city.

The town was largely spared armed conflict. In 1736 a plan by a St. John's resident, Prince Klaas, to turn Antigua into an independent African kingdom was discovered; he was killed and 132 other conspirators were punished. The scare led to the building of barracks on Rat Island in 1741 and in the centre of the town in 1753. A major fire struck in 1768, a hurricane in 1772 damaged its shipping, and another fire in 1782 broke out in one of the most densely populated districts. In 1784 a night watch was established, and building rules required most public buildings to have brick walls and tiled or slate roofs.

St. John's was the seat of government of the British Leeward Islands until the colony was abolished in 1959. The present Government House was built in the early 1800s. In the late 1800s and early 1900s the city had an elected council, which no longer exists.

St. John's is the largest city of Antigua and Barbuda, with a population of 22,219, and houses the Parliament and the other branches of government. Landmarks include the white baroque towers of St. John's Cathedral, Fort James at the harbour entrance, the Museum of Antigua and Barbuda and the Antigua Recreation Ground, the national stadium. Cruise ships dock at Heritage Quay and Redcliffe Quay.
st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador: St. John's lies on the eastern tip of the Avalon Peninsula, on the island of Newfoundland, and is the easternmost city in North America apart from Greenland. The city covers 446.04 square kilometres, more than Montreal, though most of that area is still undeveloped woodland. Its downtown stands to the west and north of St. John's Harbour and the rest of the city spreads out from it. The climate is humid continental, but with smaller seasonal variation than is usual at its latitude, because of the moderating influence of the Gulf Stream.

Fishermen set up seasonal camps at St. John's in the early 1500s. A series of Portuguese expeditions from the Azores took place in the early 16th century, and by 1540 French, Spanish and Portuguese ships crossed the Atlantic every year to fish the waters off the Avalon Peninsula. A Portuguese map of 1519 marks the place as São João.

The origin of the name is disputed. Sebastian Cabot wrote on his map of 1545 that he and his father, John Cabot, sailed into the harbour on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, 24 June, which he dated to 1494 and British and French historians date to 1497; the locations of Cabot's landfalls are themselves disputed. In the Basque Country a common belief holds that Basque fishermen named it after a similar bay at home.

On 24 April 1800 nineteen Irish soldiers of the British garrison mutinied in what is called the United Irish Uprising. They were suspected of belonging to the Society of United Irishmen. The mutiny failed, and the men fled into the countryside and were caught within weeks. Of the seventeen captured, eight were executed, four were released and five were sentenced to transportation. The Great Fire of 1892 destroyed most of the downtown core, and most of the surviving wood-frame buildings date from the rebuilding after it. The city was incorporated in 1888, and from 1898 until 1988 it was the eastern terminus of the Newfoundland Railway.

St. John's is the capital and largest city of the province of Newfoundland and Labrador. It is the eastern end of the Trans-Canada Highway. Its economy has long rested on the sea, first the cod fishery, which collapsed in the 1990s, and then offshore oil and gas. Guglielmo Marconi received the first transatlantic wireless signal at St. John's. Memorial University of Newfoundland and the Rooms, which houses the provincial museum, art gallery and archives, are among its institutions.
st-johns-river: The St. Johns River begins as a network of marshes in Indian River County, west of Vero Beach, and flows north through or beside twelve counties. Its elevation falls by less than 30 feet (9 m) from source to mouth, so the current is very slow, about 0.3 miles an hour, and the river is often described as lazy. Tides pass up the channel and regularly affect water levels as far south as Lake George. Its drainage basin covers 8,840 square miles (22,900 km2).

The river is divided into upper, middle and lower basins. In the middle basin it forms Lake Harney and Lake Monroe, and beyond Lake Monroe it becomes navigable. The Ocklawaha River is its largest tributary. Blue Spring, the largest spring on the St. Johns, is the winter home of West Indian manatees, which are protected in Blue Spring State Park. Between Palatka and Jacksonville the river widens to between one and three miles, and this lower stretch carries most of its shipping.

Humans reached the Florida Peninsula about 12,000 years ago, when the sea was about 350 feet (110 m) lower and the peninsula was twice its present size. Archaic people, the Timucua and others later lived along the river. Juan Ponce de León reached Florida in 1513, but Europeans did not settle the north Atlantic coast until 1562. Early Spanish explorers called the river Rio de Corientes, the River of Currents.

After Florida was annexed to the United States in 1821, violent conflict broke out between settlers and the Seminoles, whose bands often included escaped slaves. A cattle crossing on the river, earlier called Cowford, was renamed Jacksonville after Andrew Jackson, whose campaign of 1818 became the First Seminole War. Steamboats then carried tourists, lumber, cotton and citrus, and until railways arrived they were the only way into the interior. In 1911 the Englishman Nelson Fell began draining the St. Johns Marsh for the Fellsmere Farms Company; floods broke its levees and it went into receivership by 1916.

Drainage works in the 1920s lowered the upper basin, and in 2016 the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers completed a project restoring natural flow to much of it. Fertiliser, septic seepage and stormwater have polluted the river, and algal blooms and fish kills occur regularly between Palatka and Jacksonville. The river was named one of fourteen American Heritage Rivers in 1998.
st-lawrence-river: The St. Lawrence River connects the Great Lakes with the North Atlantic, flowing northeast from Lake Ontario to the Gulf of St. Lawrence through Ontario and Quebec in Canada and New York in the United States. A portion of it forms the Canada–United States border. It runs 1,197 km from the outflow of Lake Ontario, and 3,058 km from its farthest headwater in Minnesota. The estuary begins just below Quebec City, where the river becomes tidal. The river formed when the Champlain Sea drained as the land rebounded after the Last Glacial Maximum. Its islands include the Thousand Islands and the Island of Montreal.

The river was a primary thoroughfare for many Indigenous peoples, among them the Innu, Mohawk, Algonquin and St. Lawrence Iroquoians. The Norse explored the Gulf of St. Lawrence in the 11th century. Jacques Cartier was the first European known to have sailed up the river itself; on his second voyage in 1535 he reached the estuary on the feast day of Saint Lawrence, 10 August, and named the gulf for the saint. Basque whalers and fishermen traded with Indigenous Americans from the early 16th century. Samuel de Champlain recorded the present name on a map in 1604, and the river became the main route for European exploration of the interior.

Control of the river was crucial to British strategy in the Seven Years' War. After capturing Louisbourg in 1758, the British sailed up to Quebec the following year with charts drawn by James Cook, and troops ferried along the river attacked the city at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. The first steamboat on the river, the Accommodation, made its maiden voyage from Montreal to Quebec City in 1809. The Lachine Canal, opened in 1825, first let ships pass the Lachine Rapids.

The St. Lawrence Seaway, a system of canals and locks opened on 26 June 1959 by Elizabeth II and President Dwight D. Eisenhower, now lets ocean-going vessels reach Lake Superior. The river has played a key role in the growth of cities such as Montreal and Quebec City. Its drainage area includes the Great Lakes, the world's largest system of freshwater lakes, and whales, among them the beluga, frequent the estuary and gulf.
st-magnus-cathedral: According to the Orkneyinga saga, Earl Magnus, who ruled jointly with his cousin Håkon from 1105 to 1114, was killed on the island of Egilsay on 16 April 1116 or 1117, when Håkon's cook Lifolf struck him on the head with an axe. Miracles were reported at his grave at Birsay. When the king of Norway granted Magnus's nephew Rögnvald Kali Kolsson the earldom, Rögnvald's father Kol advised him to win over the islanders by promising a stone minster at Kirkwall dedicated to his uncle. Magnus was canonised in 1135, and work began in 1137 under Kol's direction.

The Romanesque work is attributed to English masons who may have worked on Durham Cathedral, and alternates red sandstone from near Kirkwall with yellow sandstone from Eday, sometimes in a chequerboard pattern. In the late 12th and early 13th centuries the building was extended east, and in the late 14th century the west front was joined to it, bringing in the pointed arches of the Gothic style. Rögnvald was killed in 1158 while work was under way. In 1919 a box of bones, including a skull with a wound like an axe blow, was found in a column.

The bishopric passed from the province of York to that of Trondheim in 1152 and stayed nominally under Trondheim until St Andrews became an archbishopric in 1472, after Orkney's annexation by Scotland in 1468. People accused of witchcraft between 1594 and 1708 were held and tried in the cathedral, some in its bottle dungeon, Marwick's Hole. In 1614 government forces meant to destroy it after rebels hid inside, until Bishop James Law intervened. King Haakon IV of Norway was buried there in 1263 until his body could be taken to Bergen. Since the Reformation it has been a Church of Scotland parish church, owned by Orkney Islands Council.
st-marys-church-lubeck: St. Mary's stands on the highest point of Lübeck's old town island, within the Hanseatic merchants' quarter, and served as the main parish church of the citizens and the city council. After 1160 a wooden church was built on the site and first documented in 1170 as a market church. It was replaced at the end of the 12th century by a Romanesque brick church. The sixth pair of pillars in the nave, from around 1200, is a remnant of that building.

The Gothic church was built as a three-aisled basilica with side chapels, an ambulatory with radiating chapels, and vestibules like the arms of a transept. Its design followed the stone cathedrals of France, such as Reims, and of Flanders. The west front has two towers, each over 124 metres high with their weather vanes, and the central nave, 38.5 metres high, has the tallest brick vault in the world.

St. Mary's epitomises north German Brick Gothic and set the standard for about 70 other churches in the Baltic region, among them St. Nicholas in Stralsund and St. Nicholas in Wismar. It is called the mother church of brick Gothic and, with Lübeck city centre, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987. The city had been the de facto capital of the Hanseatic League.

The church was richly endowed by the council, the guilds and families, and at the end of the Middle Ages it had 38 altars and 65 benefices. Surviving medieval works include a bronze font by Hans Apengeter of 1337 and a tabernacle of 1479 made of about a thousand bronze parts. The Antwerp altarpiece of 1518 shows the life of the Virgin Mary in 26 scenes. The church was Lutheran from the Church Order of Johannes Bugenhagen in 1531.

Its musical tradition was shaped by the organists Franz Tunder and his son-in-law Dieterich Buxtehude, who served from 1668 to 1707. In 1705 Johann Sebastian Bach, aged twenty, walked more than 400 kilometres from Arnstadt to hear Buxtehude and stayed nearly three months.

In an air raid by the Royal Air Force on 28 and 29 March 1942 the church was almost completely destroyed by fire, along with about a fifth of the city centre. The great organ, the Danse Macabre organ and works by Bernt Notke were lost. Heat from the fire dislodged plaster and revealed medieval wall paintings. In 1948 Dietrich Fey was given the task of restoring them and hired the painter Lothar Malskat, who invented some of the paintings. This became the largest counterfeit art scandal after the Second World War: Malskat reported it in 1952 and both men received prison sentences in 1954. The church was rebuilt between 1947 and 1959.
st-michaels-church-hildesheim: Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim, who held the see from 996 to 1022, commissioned a Benedictine monastery on a hill linked with the archangel Michael, half a kilometre north of the city walls. Work on the church began in 1010, and Bernward dedicated the unfinished monastery on the feast of St. Michael, 29 September 1022, only weeks before his death. He had been trained in bronze casting, painting and metalwork, and had lived for a time in Rome. His successor, Bishop Godehard, finished the work and moved Bernward's remains to the crypt.

St. Michael's is a double-choir basilica with two tripartite transepts at either end of the nave and a square tower at each crossing, with four narrower towers on the ends of the transepts. The eastern choir had three apses, and the west choir has a single high apse above a cross-vaulted crypt with an ambulatory. The square of the transept crossing is the unit of measure for the whole plan, and alternating columns and piers mark out the squares. Nikolaus Pevsner called it "the earliest surviving example of a truly Romanesque exterior" and its plan a "more thorough metrical system" than any earlier Romanesque building.

The ceiling carries a painting of the Tree of Jesse, the ancestry of Jesus, 27.6 metres long and 8.7 metres wide. It was made around 1130 on more than 1,300 oak planks and heavily restored in 2010. The Bernward Doors, with bronze reliefs of 16 biblical scenes running from Genesis to the New Testament, were probably commissioned after 1008 for this church and now stand in Hildesheim Cathedral.

The church was reconsecrated in 1186 by Bishop Adelog of Dorstedt, after a fire and rebuilding. Around 1542, during the Reformation, Protestants took over most of the church and left little to the monastic community, and it became a shared church, with most of the building Protestant and the crypt Roman Catholic. A British air raid on 22 March 1945 badly damaged it, and reconstruction lasted from 1950 to 1957. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1985, together with the Tree of Jesse and the Bernward Doors.
st-ninians-isle: St Ninian's Isle is a tied island, linked to the south-western coast of the Mainland of Shetland by the largest tombolo in the UK. The tombolo, known locally as an ayre, from the Old Norse for gravel bank, is 500 metres long. In summer it stands above sea level and walkers can cross it. In winter stronger waves strip sand from the beach, so that it is usually covered at high tide, and sometimes throughout the tidal cycle, until the sand returns the following spring. Depending on the definition used, the isle is therefore either an island or a peninsula, with an area of about 72 hectares.

The island's history is far older than Christianity: Neolithic graves have been found within the walls of its chapel, formerly beneath the floor. Like other places in the Northern Isles, the Hebrides and the Faroes, it may have connections with the Culdees or the papar. The ruins of a 12th-century chapel stand near the end of the tombolo, dedicated to Saint Ninian of Galloway, Shetland's patron saint. Excavation also found the remains of an earlier, pre-Norse chapel, which may point to a Culdee presence.

The treasure was found on 4 July 1958 by Douglas Coutts, a local schoolboy helping visiting archaeologists led by Professor A. C. O'Dell of Aberdeen University. It lay under a cross-marked slab in the floor of the early church, in a wooden box. The pieces, not all of which were probably new when they were deposited, are believed to date from about 750 to 825; the hoard was suspected to have been buried to hide it from, or stolen in, a Viking raid.

The last family to live on the island, that of Henry Leask, who was married twice and had 13 children, left it in 1796. The island belongs to the civil parish of Dunrossness on the South Mainland, and the nearest settlement is Bigton. Many seabirds visit it, puffins among them, and several species nest there.
st-olafs-church-tallinn: It is assumed that a church stood on the site before the 12th century, built by Scandinavian merchants and named after the canonised Norwegian king Olav II Haraldsson (995–1030), who is regarded as a patron saint of seafarers. The earliest mention dates from 1267, when Queen Margaret of Denmark granted the parish rights of the church to the Cistercian convent of St. Michael in Reval, the German name of Tallinn. Little is known of the early years of the Gothic building. Records of the 14th and 15th centuries attest to its expansion, and the tower is mentioned in 1364.

The church is a Gothic building and the tallest church in Estonia, about 123.8 metres to the top of its spire, with an observation platform in the tower at 60 metres. A medieval craftsman claimed that it was 84 fathoms tall. One source took this to mean Rhineland fathoms, which would give 159 metres, but he probably meant local fathoms, and the tower in 1590 was probably 115.35 to 125 metres. The tower has been struck by lightning about ten times and the whole church has burned down three times, so that it was reconstructed repeatedly.

A legend says that the citizens wanted the tallest church in the world, but a curse killed whoever finished it. A stranger offered to build it for a large sum and said that the debt would be forgiven if they learned his name. A spy overheard the name Olev in a song sung by the builder's wife, and when the builder was fixing the cross on the tower the citizens shouted, "Olev, the cross is crooked!" He fell, and a toad and a snake came from his mouth. A mural in the church shows this.

The church was Catholic until the 16th-century Reformation, when it became part of the Lutheran tradition. It had a large, mostly German-speaking congregation until 1939. As a result of World War II it had no active congregation, and the Soviet occupation regime handed it to Baptists in 1950. From 1944 until 1991 the Estonian branch of the Soviet KGB, whose headquarters stood nearby, used its spire as a radio tower and surveillance point. The organ was built in 1840–1842 by Friedrich Hermann Lütkemüller with Johann Eberhard Walcker's firm, was renovated in 1914 and has 76 registers.
st-panteleimon-monastery: Saint Panteleimon Monastery is one of the twenty Eastern Orthodox monasteries of Mount Athos, on the south-western side of the peninsula. It is also called Rossikon or New Russik, and it is the Russian monastery there, housing Russian and Ukrainian monks sent by the Russian Orthodox Church. Its liturgies are held in Russian, although every monk on Athos becomes a citizen of Greece.

It was founded by monks from Kievan Rus' in the 11th century and was recognised as a separate monastery in 1169. The original foundation is known as Old Russik. A Russian pilgrim, Isaiah, confirmed that by the end of the 15th century it was Russian.

The monastery prospered in the 16th and 17th centuries, lavishly sponsored by the tsars of Russia and the Serbian dukes of Kratovo, but declined sharply in the 18th century, until only two Russian and two Bulgarian monks remained in 1730. During the Tatar yoke in Russia most of its monks were Greeks and Serbs. It was repeatedly gutted by fire, notably in 1307, when Catalan mercenaries set it alight, and again in 1968.

The present monastery, on a new site nearer the shore, was built in the first two decades of the 19th century with the help of the ruler of Moldo-Wallachia, Skarlatos Kallimachos. The katholikon, dedicated to Saint Panteleimon, was built between 1812 and 1821. Russian monks numbered 1,000 in 1895, 1,446 in 1903 and more than 2,000 by 1913. In that year a theological dispute, Imiaslavie, divided the Russian monks and led to tsarist intervention and the deportation of about 800 of those on the losing side.

After Athos passed to the Kingdom of Greece in 1912, and especially from 1914, the flow of Russian pilgrims and monks was disrupted and then strictly controlled by the Greek government until the collapse of the USSR in 1991. The number of Russian monks on Athos fell from several thousand in the 1900s to 13 in the early 1970s. Greece relaxed its policy in the 1990s and the monastery revived, with about 70 Russian and Ukrainian monks by May 2016.

The monastery has the architecture of a small town, with buildings of many heights and many domes, and is the largest on the peninsula. Its library holds 1,320 Greek manuscripts, 600 Slavonic ones and 25,000 printed books, and it keeps relics such as the head of Saint Panteleimon. It has a daughter community at New Athos in Abkhazia. Notable monks include Silouan the Athonite and Archimandrite Sophrony.
st-pauls-church-frankfurt: The Free City of Frankfurt commissioned Johann Andreas Liebhardt in 1789 to build an oval central church to replace the Barfüßerkirche, which had been demolished in 1786 because of dilapidation. Construction halted during the Napoleonic Wars, and the building was finished between 1829 and 1833 by Johann Friedrich Christian Hess. In the meantime Lutheran services were held at the Old St Nicholas Church. In 1830 the city issued deeds of dotation, by which it kept ownership of nine church buildings in its old centre and left their use to six Lutheran congregations and three Catholic parishes.

Its centralised Protestant design, a Predigtkirche in which everyone could easily hear the speaker, made the church the desired meeting place for the Frankfurt Parliament during the German revolutions of 1848. From 31 March to 3 April 1848 it housed the Vorparlament, which prepared the election of the National Assembly. The Assembly met there for the first time on 18 May 1848 and was therefore called the Paulskirchenparlament. It worked on the first constitution for a united Germany, but the resistance of Prussia, the Austrian Empire and several smaller German states ultimately destroyed the effort.

In May 1849 uprisings tried to force the constitution's implementation and were put down with the help of Prussia. The Paulskirchenparlament was dissolved on 30 May 1849, and after 1852 the building was again used for Lutheran services.

In March 1944 the church was destroyed in the Allied bombing of Frankfurt along with much of the city centre. As a tribute to its symbolism of freedom it was the first structure the city rebuilt after the war, and it reopened on the centennial of the Frankfurt Parliament. Because of financial limits and a new concept of use, the architectural team of Rudolf Schwarz greatly altered the interior: an inserted floor now separates a display room in the basement from the hall above.

The church is no longer used for worship. In 1963 US President John F. Kennedy gave a major speech there, and the building drew public interest again for the 150th anniversary of the German democratic experience in 1998. Its best-known regular event is the annual award of the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade during the Frankfurt Book Fair. With Hambach Castle it is regarded as a symbol of the democratic movement in Germany.
st-peters-basilica: Old St. Peter's Basilica was the fourth-century church begun by the Emperor Constantine the Great between 319 and 333. It had a wide nave, two aisles on each side and an apsidal end, and it was over 103 metres long, with a large colonnaded atrium. It was built over a small shrine believed to mark the burial place of Saint Peter, and it held most of the popes from Peter to the 15th century. By the end of the 15th century, after neglect during the Avignon Papacy, it had fallen into disrepair.

Pope Nicholas V, who reigned from 1447 to 1455, was the first to consider rebuilding, but little was achieved before his death. Pope Julius II then held a competition, and the design of Donato Bramante was chosen: a Greek cross crowned by a dome inspired by the Pantheon. Construction began on 18 April 1506. One method of financing it was granting indulgences in return for contributions, promoted by Albrecht, Archbishop of Mainz and Magdeburg, who appointed the Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel; his salesmanship provoked a scandal and led to the Protestant Reformation.

Michelangelo took over a building site where four enormous piers were rising behind the remaining nave of the old basilica. The dome rises to a total height of 136.57 metres from the floor to the top of the external cross, with an internal diameter of 41.47 metres. On 18 February 1606, under Pope Paul V, the dismantling of the remaining parts of the Constantinian basilica began. Carlo Maderno added the nave and façade, as the Counter-Reformation increasingly saw the Latin cross as the true symbol of Christianity. The basilica was completed on 18 November 1626.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini received the patronage of Pope Urban VIII in 1626 and worked on the basilica for 50 years; his works include the baldachin and the chair of Saint Peter, and he designed St. Peter's Square, built between 1656 and 1667. Catholic tradition holds that the tomb of Saint Peter lies directly below the high altar. The dome greatly influenced church architecture in Western Christendom, from Sant'Andrea della Valle in Rome to Christopher Wren's dome at St Paul's Cathedral in London.
st-rumbolds-cathedral: Construction of the church started shortly after 1200, and it was consecrated in 1312, when part of it had become usable. From 1324 the flying buttresses and a revised choir took on Brabantine Gothic characteristics, distinct from French Gothic. After the city fire of 1342 the Master Mason Jean d'Oisy managed repairs and continued this second phase, and by his death in 1375 it had formed the prototype for that High Gothic style. His successors finished the vaults of the nave by 1437 and those of the choir by 1451.

The tower was erected in the final phase of 1452–1520, financed by pilgrims and later by the city. The church has been a cathedral since 1559, and in the 18th century the sculpted cabbage leaves round each capital were replaced with a double ring of crops.

The tower was designed to reach 600 Mechlinian feet, about 167 metres, and was built on what had been wetlands with foundations only three metres deep. Its upper part was abandoned in the early 16th century for financial reasons, not technical ones. It should have been topped by a 77-metre spire, but only seven metres were built, which gives it its flat-topped shape.

The tower is 97.28 metres high with 514 steps. For centuries it held the city documents, served as a watchtower and sounded the fire alarm. It contains 49 bells, of which the six largest swing. The bourdon Salvator weighs 8 tons and strikes the hours. The nave is about 118 metres long, and the interior has a Baroque high altar and choir by Lucas Faydherbe, paintings by Anthony van Dyck and stained-glass windows.

The tower was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999, as part of the Belfries of Belgium and France site. Few original furnishings survive: forty decorated Gothic altars and all other furniture disappeared during the religious troubles of 1566–1585. The cathedral was spared in the Iconoclasm of 1566, but Mechelen was sacked in the Spanish Fury of 1572 and suffered the English Fury of pillaging by mercenaries in the service of the States General in 1580.

In 2010, 4,165 skeletons were unearthed in excavations of the cemetery before an underground car park was built. In 1985 Pope John Paul II said Mass there, and Jo Haazen, the city's carillon player, heard him say, 'Your tower is not complete.' Saint Rumbold's relics were examined and indicated a death date between 580 and 655, while tradition had claimed 775.
st-stephens-cathedral-passau: Churches have stood on the site since 730. The fire of 1662 destroyed the previous building except for its late Gothic eastern part, which survives in the present church. The new cathedral, a Baroque building about 100 metres long dedicated to Saint Stephen, was completed in 1693. Carlo Lurago drew up its overall plan, Giovanni Battista Carlone designed the interior decoration and Carpoforo Tencalla painted the frescoes. It is the seat of the Catholic Bishop of Passau and the main church of his diocese.

Eight large bells hang in the north and south towers. The largest, the Pummerin of 7,550 kilograms, was cast in 1952 and hangs in the south tower with the Sturmerin of 5,300 kilograms, cast in 1733. The north tower holds the other six, among them the second bourdon, Misericordia, of 6,000 kilograms, and a ninth bell hangs near the sacristy door. Three of the bells strike the clock: the Elfuhrglocken chimes every quarter hour, and the Predigtglocke and the Sturmerin in turn strike the hours.

The cathedral's organ was once the largest in the world. Later instruments, among them the Wanamaker organ in the United States, have surpassed it, but it remains the largest church organ outside the United States. It is in fact several organs of different tonal styles, added to over the years, with 17,774 pipes and 233 registers that can all be played from the five-manual general console in the gallery; parts of it have their own mechanical-action or electric-action consoles, six consoles in all.
st-thomas-church-leipzig: The site held a church at least from the 12th century, and foundations of a Romanesque building have been found in the choir and crossing of the present church. Between 1212 and 1222 the earlier structure became the church of the new St. Thomas college of Augustinian canons, founded by Markgraf Dietrich von Meissen. The college later became the core of the University of Leipzig, founded in 1409.

In 1217 the minnesinger Heinrich von Morungen, on entering the order of canons, bequeathed the church a relic of St. Thomas. The choir was changed to Gothic style in 1355. After silver was discovered in the Ore Mountains brought wealth to Leipzig, the Romanesque nave was demolished and replaced between 1482 and 1496 by the present hall church, which Thilo of Trotha, Bishop of Merseburg, consecrated on 10 April 1496.

The church mainly keeps the character of a late-Gothic hall church, although it was rebuilt over the centuries. It is 76 metres long, its nave 25 metres wide, and its unusually steep roof, pitched at 63 degrees, rises to 45 metres. The tower, first built in 1537 and rebuilt in 1702, is 68 metres high.

The Baroque furnishings Bach knew were mostly removed in a Gothic Revival renovation between 1884 and 1889, which also gave the pulpit and the west portal. The bell Gloriosa, cast in 1477 by Theodericus Reinhard, is the largest and is rung only on solemnities. The church has two organs, a Romantic instrument by Wilhelm Sauer, built from 1884 to 1889, and a Bach organ by Gerald Woehl, built from 1999 to 2000.

After the Reformation the church became Lutheran, and Martin Luther preached there on Pentecost Sunday 1539. Mozart played its organ in 1789, and Richard Wagner was baptized there on 16 August 1813. In the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 the church served as a military hospital. Johann Sebastian Bach, Thomaskantor from 1723, was first buried in the cemetery of the Johanniskirche.

His bones were identified in 1894 by the anatomist Wilhelm His as very probably his, and after the Johanniskirche burned in the raid of 4 December 1943 they were found undamaged in 1949. They were placed in a new grave in the sanctuary of the Thomaskirche on 28 July 1950, the 200th anniversary of his death. The church was listed in the 2000 World Monuments Watch, which brought funds for repairs.
st-vitus-cathedral: The present cathedral is the third church on its site in Prague Castle, all dedicated to Saint Vitus. The first was an early Romanesque rotunda founded by Wenceslaus I, Duke of Bohemia, in 930, after he obtained a relic of the saint's arm from Emperor Henry I. In 1060 Prince Spytihněv II began a larger Romanesque basilica, which incorporated the rotunda's apse housing the tomb of Saint Wenceslaus. The present Gothic building was begun on 21 November 1344, when Prague was raised to an archbishopric and King John of Bohemia laid the foundation stone. Charles IV intended it as a coronation church, a family crypt and a treasury of relics.

The first master builder was Matthias of Arras, a Frenchman summoned from Avignon, who planned a French Gothic basilica but lived to build only the easternmost parts of the choir. After his death in 1352 the 23-year-old Peter Parler took over and developed his own style, with net vaults, varied window tracery and sculpted busts of the royal family, saints and the two master builders. At Parler's death only the choir and parts of the transept were finished. His sons continued, completing the south tower and the Golden Gate, through which kings entered for coronations.

The cathedral is 124 metres long and 60 metres wide, and its main tower is 102.8 metres high. The Chapel of Saint Wenceslaus, built by Peter Parler between 1356 and 1364, has walls decorated with over 1,300 semi-precious stones, and a small door with seven locks leads to the chamber holding the Bohemian crown jewels. Since 1997 the cathedral has been dedicated to Saints Vitus, Wenceslaus and Adalbert.

The Hussite War halted construction, and Hussite iconoclasm damaged the furnishings. A fire in 1541 caused heavy damage. For centuries the cathedral stood half-finished, and a baroque spire was added to the south tower between 1753 and 1775. A society formed in 1844 to complete it, and work began on a new nave in 1870 under Josef Mocker, who designed the west facade, with Kamil Hilbert completing it. Alfons Mucha designed windows in the nave, and by the jubilee of Saint Wenceslaus in 1929 the cathedral was finished, nearly 600 years after it was begun.
st-wendel: The centre of the town was supposedly the farm of a lord named Baso from the Merovingian period, in the late 6th century, so the place was first called Basonevillare, the farm of Baso. In the mid-7th century Bishop Paulus of Verdun bought it, and the area belonged to Verdun for centuries. The hermit Wendelin died near the settlement shortly before. He was highly venerated, an intense pilgrimage developed, and in the 12th century the settlement was renamed St. Wendel. A church was built on the site of today's basilica in the late 9th or early 10th century, and Wendelin's relics were taken there in the 11th century.

In 1326/28 Archbishop Balduin of Luxembourg, prince elector of Trier, bought the castle and village, which soon became a medieval town, and the emperor Ludwig IV granted its city certificate in 1332. A wall was built in 1388, when about 500 people lived there.

The town suffered repeated destruction. A fire in 1591 destroyed a large part of it, requisitions in the Thirty Years' War almost bankrupted it, and in 1677 all but a few buildings were burned down. Only from the middle of the 18th century did it grow again, with a wool and leather industry and a baroque dome on the basilica. From 1798 the canton belonged to the French Saardepartement.

In 1814 Duke Ernst III of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld received the cantons of St. Wendel, Grumbach and Baumholder, about 20,000 people, and called the area the Principality of Lichtenberg from 1816. Dissatisfaction with his rule led to uprisings in 1832, after the Hambach Festival, which were put down with the help of Prussian troops from Saarlouis. In 1834 the duke sold the land to Prussia, and the town became a chief town of an administrative district of Trier with a garrison.

The railway between Bingen and Saarbrücken opened in 1860 and brought a train maintenance works. St. Wendel, Breiten and Alsfassen were united as one town in 1859. After World War II Saarland remained a French protectorate until it rejoined West Germany in 1957, and a French garrison stayed in the town from 1951 to 1999.

St. Wendel lies on the river Blies, 36 kilometres north-east of Saarbrücken, and has about 26,000 residents since a district reform of 1974 joined several surrounding villages to it. Pilgrims still come to the Wendalinus basilica at the beginning of October. The International Sculpture Symposium, begun in 1971 by the local sculptor Leo Kornbrust, produced stone sculptures that since 1979 line 25 kilometres of the Saarland hiking trail from St. Wendel to Lake Bostal. The town's coat of arms uses four lilies from the Scottish royal arms, recalling the legend that Wendelin was a Scottish king's son.
stabat-mater: The Stabat Mater is a Christian hymn of the thirteenth century that portrays the suffering of the Virgin Mary as a mother during the crucifixion of her son Jesus. Its title comes from its first line, Stabat Mater dolorosa, which means the sorrowful mother was standing. Its author may have been the Franciscan friar Jacopone da Todi or Pope Innocent III. The ascription to Jacopone, who lived about 1230 to 1306, has often been made, but it has been strongly challenged by the discovery of the earliest notated copy of the hymn, in a thirteenth-century gradual that belonged to the Dominican nuns of Bologna.

The hymn was well known by the end of the fourteenth century. Georgius Stella wrote of its use in 1388, and in Provence, about 1399, it was used during processions lasting nine days. As a liturgical sequence it was suppressed, along with hundreds of other sequences, by the Council of Trent, and Pope Benedict XIII restored it to the missal in 1727 for the Feast of the Seven Dolours of the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is sung in the liturgy on the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows. An indulgence of 100 days was attributed to each recitation of it.

Many Western composers have set the text to music. Early settings include those of Josquin des Prez, Orlande de Lassus in 1585 and Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina around 1590. Antonio Vivaldi wrote a setting in 1712, Alessandro Scarlatti in 1723 and Giovanni Battista Pergolesi in 1736, and Joseph Haydn followed in 1767. Franz Schubert, Gioacchino Rossini and Antonin Dvořák made settings in the nineteenth century, Giuseppe Verdi in 1897, and Karol Szymanowski, Francis Poulenc and Arvo Pärt in the twentieth. Most settings are in Latin, but Szymanowski's is in Polish, though it may also be sung in Latin.
stabiae: Stabiae lay about 4.5 kilometres southwest of Pompeii and 16 kilometres from Mount Vesuvius, near the modern town of Castellammare di Stabia. The eruption of 79 buried it under tephra to a depth of up to 5 metres, shallower than at some neighbouring sites. Its villas stood on a headland about 50 metres high overlooking the Gulf of Naples, and together they form the largest known concentration of well-preserved, very large elite seaside villas in the Roman world.

A settlement existed by the 7th century BCE. A necropolis found in 1957 on the via Madonna delle Grazie holds over 300 tombs with imported Corinthian, Etruscan, Chalcidian and Attic pottery, and was used from the 7th to the end of the 3rd century BCE, which shows wide commercial contacts. The small port was overshadowed by Pompeii by the 6th century BCE. The town later became an Oscan settlement, and the Samnites seem to have taken it over in the 5th century.

Pliny the Elder recorded that the town was rebuilt after the Social War and became a popular resort for wealthy Romans, with several miles of luxury villas along the headland. The villas that can be visited today date from between Sulla's destruction of Stabiae in 89 BCE and the eruption of 79 CE. The surrounding Ager Stabianus had about 60 farmhouses, some with wine and olive presses.

The ruins were found in 1749 by the engineer Roque Joaquín de Alcubierre, working for Charles VII of Naples. Karl Weber drew plans and in 1759 described part of the town: five paved streets meeting at right angles, a forum, a temple on a podium and a gymnasium. The excavations were reburied, and by 1782 the site had missed its chance of becoming a stop on the Grand Tour.

Excavation resumed in 1950 under Libero d'Orsi. The Villa San Marco, over 11,000 square metres of which about half is excavated, was being renovated when the eruption struck and has frescoes, stucco and mosaics. The Villa Arianna, the oldest of the leisure villas, dates to the 2nd century BCE and is named for a fresco of Dionysus rescuing Ariadne. The Villa del Pastore, at 19,000 square metres, has no domestic rooms, and one hypothesis is that it served as a health spa or infirmary. Many frescoes and objects from the villas are in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples.
stadacona: No archaeological trace of Stadacona has been found, so its exact site remains unknown. It is assumed to have stood near the confluence of the Saint Lawrence and the Saint-Charles River, in what is now the Vieux-Limoilou district of Quebec City. The name Canada comes from the Iroquoian word for town, which Jacques Cartier used for the country around Stadacona and the similar village of Hochelaga and for the Saint Lawrence River, the rivière de Canada.

On his first voyage Cartier met Donnacona, who showed him five scalps taken in a war with the Toudaman, probably the Miꞌkmaq, who had killed 200 of his people at a fort the previous spring. Cartier seized some of the inhabitants, and Donnacona agreed that his sons Taignoagny and Domagaya should go to France for a year. They returned with Cartier on his voyage of 1535–1536, when he recorded their word for a town, Kanata.

The Stadaconans tried to keep Cartier from going upriver to Hochelaga, as they wished to keep their monopoly of the trade in European metal goods with the peoples upstream. During the winter they saved Cartier's crew from scurvy, which had killed a quarter of them, with a broth rich in vitamin C, while more than 50 people of the village died of diseases carried by the Europeans. Cartier then seized Donnacona, his sons and seven others and took them to France, where nine of the ten died; none ever returned.

On a later voyage Cartier found the village abandoned and destroyed, probably by the wars of the Mohawk of the Haudenosaunee confederacy to the south. Samuel de Champlain later chose its location for l'Habitation, the settlement that grew into the city of Québec.
stade: Stade lies in the lower reaches of the Elbe in northern Germany, about 45 km west of Hamburg, and is the seat of the district that bears its name. It is first mentioned in records in 934, and it lies on the German Timber-Frame Road. Settlers first came to the area in about 30,000 BCE.

Swedish and Danish Vikings under Eric the Victorious conquered and looted Stade in the 990s and took many prominent Saxons back as slaves. From 1180 it belonged to the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen. In 1208 King Valdemar II of Denmark conquered it, and in the following years it changed hands several times. On 2 May 1209 Emperor Otto IV granted it important privileges: the burghers were confirmed as personally free and as a political entity under their own law, and property within the town could not be subjected to feudal overlordship.

After Danish attacks ended in 1216, Stade remained part of the Prince-Archbishopric. From the 13th century to the late 17th it was a prominent member of the Hanseatic League, and it was later eclipsed by Hamburg. The Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 turned the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen into the Duchy of Bremen and granted it, with the Principality of Verden, to the Swedish crown. Stade was the capital of the Swedish province, and some buildings the Swedes built are still in use.

Two-thirds of the town were destroyed in a great fire on 26 May 1659 and rebuilt on the same plan. Allied forces held it from 1675 to 1679, and the Treaty of Saint Germain returned it to Sweden. Swedish rule ended in 1712, when Danish troops shelled the town for ten days and destroyed 152 houses, a quarter of the built-up area. It stayed the capital of Bremen-Verden under the Electorate of Hanover and of the Stade region after 1823.

The plague of 1355 and that of 1712 each killed at least 30 to 40 per cent of the city's population. In 1757, after the French invasion of Hanover, the Duke of Cumberland and the Hanoverian government took shelter in Stade. A Jewish community was permitted in 1611, and in 1845 a regional rabbinate served 16 congregations. Stade was untouched by Allied bombing in the Second World War.

The old town has notable buildings such as the St. Cosmae et Damiani and Wilhadi Lutheran churches, the city hall, the Schwedenspeicher and the Zeughaus. The decommissioned Stade Nuclear Power Plant on the Elbe was connected to the grid in 1972 and closed in 2003.
stadthagen: Count Adolf III of Holstein created a new settlement at the foot of the Bückeberg around 1224, after clearing the Dülwald forest, at a site near the Hellweg route. It was first recorded in 1244, as a city and fort, under the name indago comitis, the count's enclosure. In 1287 it became Grevenalveshagen, and it acquired its present name in 1378. The town received its seal in 1320 and the privileges of a town in 1344. Stone fortifications were built around 1400, and coal mining began nearby in 1501 and lasted until 1961.

Count Otto IV introduced the Lutheran confession in 1559. His predecessor Count Adolf XI had commissioned the present castle from the architect Jörg Unkair of Tübingen, built between 1534 and 1538 and regarded as one of the most notable Early Renaissance castles in Lower Saxony. In 1607 Prince Ernst of Schaumburg moved his residence to Bückeburg. In 1609 the count's mausoleum was raised behind the church of St Martini, a domed heptagon with a resurrection group by Adriaen de Vries. A grammar school founded in 1610 became a university in 1620, though it soon moved to Rinteln.

Stadthagen is the capital of the district of Schaumburg in Lower Saxony, about 20 km east of Minden and 40 km west of Hanover, and lies on the German Timber-Frame Road. Parts of the town wall and two towers of the old fortifications survive. After the monarchy ended in 1918 it belonged to the Free State of Schaumburg-Lippe; in 1948 it became the administrative centre of the district of Schaumburg-Lippe and in 1977 of the new district of Schaumburg.
The synagogue built in 1857 was burnt down by the Nazis on 9 November 1938. American troops took the town without resistance on 9 April 1945, so it escaped war damage.
stadtholder: The Dutch word stadhouder means steward, a literal stead holder, and corresponds to the Latin locum tenens. In the Middle Ages feudal lords appointed stadtholders to represent them in their absence. A stadtholder was thus more powerful than a governor, who had limited authority, but he was not a vassal himself and had no title to the land. The Duke of Guelders, for example, appointed one to represent him in Groningen.

In the 15th century the Dukes of Burgundy acquired most of the Low Countries, and most of the duchies, counties and lordships of the Burgundian Netherlands had a stadtholder of their own. In the 16th century the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V became the sole feudal overlord and appointed stadtholders to represent him and his son Philip II. Philip's centralist and absolutist policies strongly diminished their actual power compared with that of the governor-general.

After 1581 the stadtholder no longer represented a lord but became the highest executive official, appointed by the States of each province, although most held appointments from several provinces at once. The stadtholder was commander-in-chief of the armed forces and appointed lower officials, and he sometimes affirmed the members of regent councils or chose burgomasters from a shortlist. In Holland and Zeeland he was also Captain-General of the army and Admiral-General of the fleet. By law he was a mere official, but in the conditions of the Eighty Years War his real powers were sometimes greater, and Maurice of Orange after 1618 ruled as a military dictator.

William the Silent had been appointed stadtholder of Holland in 1572, and his reputation passed to his house. Tension persisted between Orangists and republicans, and after the death of William II in 1650 and of William III in 1702 the regents appointed no stadtholder, in the First and Second Stadtholderless Periods. After the French invasion of 1747 a popular movement forced the regents to accept William IV of Orange, and on 22 November 1747 the office became hereditary in every province.

After William IV died in 1751 his infant son William V was appointed under his mother's regency, whose misgovernment led in 1780 to the Patriot movement. Prince William V suppressed it with Prussian military intervention in 1787. French revolutionary forces and Dutch exiles returned in the winter of 1795, William V fled to England and the office was abolished with the creation of the Batavian Republic. His son William Frederick became sovereign prince in 1813 and king of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1815.

The stadtholderate was also studied abroad. Oliver Ellsworth, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, argued that without its influence the government of the United Provinces would no more move than a ship without wind.
stafa: The early history of Stäfa is closely linked to Einsiedeln Abbey. In 972 King Otto II confirmed in documents the abbey's possessions on the lake, among them Steveia, the later Stäfa. The villages of Kehlhof and Uerikon are politically part of the municipality. The poet Goethe is linked with the town, having once stayed overnight there.

Stäfa is a municipality in the district of Meilen in the canton of Zürich. It lies on the north bank of Lake Zürich in the Pfannenstiel region, near Rapperswil, and has an area of 8.6 square kilometres. Of this, 46.1 per cent is farmland, 18.8 per cent forest and 34 per cent built over. The population was 14,791 at the end of 2020. Most people speak German, with Italian and Albanian the next most common languages at the 2000 census, and in 2000 about half the population was Protestant and just over a quarter Catholic.

Wine production remains important, particularly white wine from Riesling grapes. The daily newspaper Zürichsee-Zeitung is published in Stäfa, and the high-technology companies Sonova, which makes hearing devices, and Sensirion, which makes sensors, are based there. The town has a cultural centre, the Rössli, near the lake shore. Trains of the Zürich S-Bahn line S7 run to Zürich and Rapperswil, taking about 25 minutes to Zürich, and in summer ships of the Zürichsee-Schifffahrtsgesellschaft call at the town; a ferry crosses all year to Wädenswil on the opposite shore.
stafford: Stafford lies about 24 kilometres south of Stoke-on-Trent, 24 kilometres north of Wolverhampton and 39 kilometres north-west of Birmingham. The name means a ford by a staithe, or landing place. The original settlement stood on a near island of gravelly lowland bounded by a loop of the River Sow, a tributary of the Trent, to the south and west and by Sandyford brook to the east, with marsh to the north. Drains were built in the 19th century, but the area is still prone to flooding. Nearby, 4 kilometres south-west of the town, is an Iron Age hill fort at Berry Ring.

In the autumn of 1069 a rebellion against the Norman Conquest led by Eadric the Wild ended in the Battle of Stafford, where Norman forces under Brian of Brittany and William I decisively defeated the Anglo-Welsh rebel army. Two years later another rising, led by Edwin, Earl of Mercia, ended with his assassination, and William the Conqueror divided Edwin's lands among his followers.
