Robert de Tosny, later known as Robert de Stafford, received the manor of Bradley and a third of the king's rents in Stafford, and the estate became the seat of the powerful Stafford family. Stafford was already an ancient borough at the time of the Domesday Book of 1086, and King John confirmed its status by charter in 1206.

The town declined in the Tudor period: in 1540 many houses were in disrepair, and it was still in decay when Elizabeth I visited in 1575. The Ancient High House, believed to be the largest timber-framed town house in England, was built in 1595. When James I visited in 1617 he was said to be so impressed by the Shire Hall and other buildings that he called the town Little London. The playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan represented it in Parliament from 1780.

Shoemaking, recorded from 1476 as a cottage industry, became a mechanised business in the 18th century; William Horton founded a firm in 1767, and by the 1880s there were 39 manufacturers in the town. The industry then declined, and the last shoe factory was demolished. The locomotive firm W. G. Bagnall was set up in 1875, and its Castle Engine Works produced 1,869 locomotives between 1875 and 1962. Stafford was reconstituted as a municipal borough in 1835.

Stafford is the county town of Staffordshire. Staffordshire County Council has its headquarters there, and the Shire Hall, completed in 1798 as a courthouse, is now an art gallery. The Ancient High House is a museum. Izaak Walton, author of The Compleat Angler of 1653, is among the people associated with the town, and the three-looped Stafford knot is the traditional symbol of the county and county town.
staffordshire: Staffordshire is a ceremonial county in the West Midlands of England, bordering Cheshire, Derbyshire, Leicestershire, Warwickshire, Worcestershire, Shropshire and the West Midlands county. It covers 1,713 square kilometres, with Stoke-on-Trent in the north as its largest settlement and Stafford in the centre. The north is hilly, with the southern end of the Pennines and part of the Peak District National Park, and Cannock Chase lies in the south. The River Trent and its tributaries drain most of the county. The village of Flash, at 463 metres, is the highest in Britain.

The county contains Iron Age tumuli and Roman camps. The Angles settled it in the sixth century, and the oldest example of the Stafford knot, the county's symbol, appears on an Anglian cross in the churchyard of Stoke Minster. The county was formed in the early tenth century, when Stafford became the capital of Mercia. In July 2009 the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold ever found in Britain was discovered in a field near Lichfield. The Staffordshire Hoard has been tentatively dated to the 7th or 8th centuries, in the time of the Kingdom of Mercia.

In 1553 Queen Mary made Lichfield a county corporate, which kept it administered separately until 1888. The county industrialised rapidly in the Industrial Revolution, when the North Staffordshire coalfield was exploited and fuelled iron and motor industries in the south. Pottery became its most best-known product, and in 1910 the six towns of the Staffordshire Potteries became the single county borough of Stoke-on-Trent. Hugh Bourne, a native of Stoke-on-Trent, founded Primitive Methodism at a gathering at Mow Cop, and by 1811 he and his brother had founded the first chapel in the Tunstall area.

The historic county included much of the present West Midlands, including Walsall, West Bromwich and Wolverhampton. On 1 April 1974 under the Local Government Act 1972 the Black Country county boroughs and the Aldridge-Brownhills urban district became part of the new metropolitan county of West Midlands. On 1 April 1997 Stoke-on-Trent became a unitary authority independent of Staffordshire.

The county's only cathedral is Lichfield Cathedral, in the city of Lichfield. Burton upon Trent is known for brewing, and Stoke-on-Trent still produces a limited amount of pottery, including the work of Wedgwood and Royal Doulton. Keele University and the University of Staffordshire are in the county. The Trent and Mersey Canal and the other canals of the county form an extensive network, and the West Coast Main Line passes through Stafford.
staffordshire-hoard: The hoard consists of almost 4,600 items and fragments, with 5.1 kg of gold, 1.4 kg of silver and about 3,500 pieces of garnet cloisonné jewellery. It was most likely deposited between 650 and 675 CE, and its objects were probably made in the 6th and 7th centuries, most of them in the 7th. Apart from two or possibly three crosses, the items are military. There are no domestic objects and no women's jewellery, the more usual Anglo-Saxon finds of gold. It includes 66 gold sword hilt collars and 86 sword pommels, the largest number of pommels ever found in one place.

A small gold strip, perhaps from a shield, a sword belt or the arm of a cross, is inscribed on both sides in insular majuscule with a biblical quotation from Numbers 10:35, rendered in the KJV as "Rise up, LORD, and let thine enemies be scattered". The largest cross was folded, and explanations include that it was folded to fit a small space, by pagans with no esteem for it, or by Christians to remove its sacred character before burial.

The hoard was deposited in a remote area just south of the Roman Watling Street, within the kingdom of Mercia. Most of the gold and silver appears to have been deliberately removed from the objects it was attached to, so it does not look like simple loot. Brooks linked its warlike character to the custom of giving war-gear as a death duty to the king, and a parallel in Beowulf describes warriors stripping the pommels of enemy swords. Wall proposed a connection with Peada, briefly king of Mercia in 655–656, and Sharp one with a Viking attack on Lichfield in 875.

Terry Herbert found the first gold with a metal detector on 5 July 2009 in a field near Hammerwich, and 244 gold objects were recovered in five days. The find was announced on 24 September 2009. The coroner declared it treasure, and on 25 November 2009 the Treasure Valuation Committee valued it at £3.285 million. On 23 March 2010 it was announced that the sum had been raised for the Birmingham Museum and Art Gallery and the Potteries Museum & Art Gallery to buy it jointly. A further 91 items were found in the field in 2012. A research project begun that year concluded that Byzantine coins were probably a primary source of the gold and that the garnets were probably recycled from Roman objects.
stalinism: Stalinism developed from Leninism. Its central doctrine was socialism in one country, which Stalin developed from December 1924 and elaborated in his writings of 1925–26, in the factional struggle against Leon Trotsky. Other Bolshevik leaders had seen the revolution of 1917 as the beginning of a world revolution, but it had not spread, and Stalin argued that the socialist state must grow stronger before it could wither away, since counter-revolutionary elements would try to derail the transition to communism.

The word came into use in the mid-1930s, when Lazar Kaganovich reportedly proposed replacing Long Live Leninism with Long Live Stalinism. Stalin dismissed this as excessive and as feeding a cult of personality that might later be turned against him.

At the start of the 1930s Stalin launched what became known as the Great Turn, abandoning the mixed economy of the New Economic Policy for a planned economy, with rapid industrialisation and mass collectivisation of agriculture. A cult of Stalin spread from 1929 to 1953 in architecture, statues and posters, in which he was cast as father, saviour and warrior.

The Great Terror, from September 1936 to December 1938, was the peak of political repression, under Nikolai Yezhov, head of the NKVD. Hundreds of thousands of party officials, military officers, intellectuals and ordinary citizens were sentenced and either executed or sent to the Gulag. The NKVD worked to central quotas. Before, during and after World War II, Stalin also deported whole peoples, among them the Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans and Chechens. It is estimated that nearly 3.3 million people were deported to Siberia and Central Asia between 1941 and 1949.

After Stalin's death on 5 March 1953 and the Khrushchev Thaw, a period of de-Stalinization began in the 1950s and 1960s. Historians disagree about the system's causes and effects. Some, such as Robert Service, blame collectivisation for famines such as the Holodomor, while others disagree. Several international legislatures have called the campaign against the kulaks a genocide, which some historians dispute.

Rival currents of communism judged Stalin differently. Mao Zedong declared that he was 70 per cent good and 30 per cent bad, and Maoists criticised his view that class contradictions ended once socialism was built. In Albania, Enver Hoxha kept his own brand of Stalinism, Hoxhaism, for decades after the Sino-Soviet split, which isolated the country.
stamford-connecticut: Stamford lies in Fairfield County, about 55 km from New York City and roughly halfway between Manhattan and New Haven. It covers about 135 square kilometres, of which about 97 are land, which makes it the largest city in Connecticut by area. Its climate is temperate, with long hot summers and cool to cold winters, and it lies in the transition zone between the colder continental climates to the north and the warmer climates to the south.

The Siwanoy people who lived in the region called the place Rippowam, and the first European settlers used the same name. The present name comes from the town of Stamford in Lincolnshire, England. A deed to the land was signed between Captain Turner of the New Haven Colony and Chief Ponus. By the 18th century one of the town's main industries was trade by water, which its closeness to New York made possible. In 1692 Stamford had a witch trial, smaller and less well known than the one at Salem in the same year; the accusations grew through gossip.

Stamford had 135,470 inhabitants at the census of 2020 and is the second most populous city in Connecticut after Bridgeport. It is part of the New York City metropolitan area and has become a cluster of corporate headquarters, with the largest financial district in the region outside New York City. It is governed by a strong mayor and a Board of Representatives of forty members. Its railway station on the New Haven Line of the Metro-North Railroad is the second busiest on that system.

The Stamford Museum and Nature Center holds works by the sculptor Gutzon Borglum, who lived in the town for a decade. The Palace Theatre opened as a vaudeville house in 1927 and reopened as a nonprofit theatre in 1983, and the Fairfield County Astronomical Society, founded in 1954, runs the Stamford Observatory. UConn Stamford has its main building in a former department store in the downtown.
stamford-lincolnshire: Stamford forms a south-westerly protrusion of Lincolnshire between Rutland to the north and west, Peterborough to the south and Northamptonshire to the south-west. The River Welland was historically the boundary between Lincolnshire and Northamptonshire, and the land south of it was Stamford Baron in Northamptonshire. Much of the town is built on Middle Jurassic Lincolnshire limestone, and the area is known for its limestone and slate quarries. Cream-coloured Collyweston stone slate covers the roofs of many of its stone buildings. The name means stony ford and appears in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle as Steanford in 922 and Stanford in 942.

The Romans built Ermine Street across what is now Burghley Park and forded the Welland to the west of the town. Their own town lay to the north at Great Casterton, and the Anglo-Saxons later chose Stamford as the main town because it stood on a larger river. By the early 1500s the wool and broadcloth industry on which Stamford depended had declined sharply, and in 1548 the town, reduced to about 800 people, merged its eleven parishes into six. After almost 150 years of stagnation the population began to rise again in the second half of the 17th century, with leather and fibre working, wood and stone working as the main activities.

For over 600 years, until 1839, Stamford held a bull run each year on 13 November, St Brice's day. Local tradition says William de Warenne, 5th Earl of Surrey, saw two bulls fighting in the meadow below his castle and a bull ran into the town, and that he enjoyed the chase so much that he gave the meadow to the butchers on condition that they provide a bull each year. Lying on the Great North Road, Stamford hosted several Parliaments in the Middle Ages. In the 19th century the East Coast Main Line, which might have passed through the town, was routed through Peterborough after resistance, and Peterborough grew at Stamford's expense.

Stamford was the first conservation area designated in England and Wales, under the Civic Amenities Act 1967, and more than 600 listed buildings stand in and around it. It has 17th- and 18th-century stone buildings, older timber-framed ones and five medieval parish churches. St Leonard's Priory is the oldest building, legendarily founded by Wilfrid, and keeps Norman pillars and arches of about 1090 and a west front of about 1150. The Stamford Mercury has been published since 1712. The town had 19,701 people at the 2011 census.
stamford-raffles: Thomas Stamford Bingley Raffles was born on 5 July 1781 on board the ship Ann, off Port Morant, Jamaica. His father, Captain Benjamin Raffles, was a ship master in the trade between England and the West Indies, and the end of that trade in 1800 brought the family hardship. In 1795, aged 14, Raffles began work as a clerk for the East India Company in London. In 1804 he married Olivia Mariamne Devenish, a widow ten years older than he. His knowledge of Malay and his ability won him the favour of Lord Minto, governor-general of India, who sent him to Malacca.

In 1811 Raffles took part in a military expedition against the Dutch and French on Java, after France annexed the Kingdom of Holland. Under British rule he ordered several expeditions against local rulers. On 20 June 1812, after rumours that the Yogyakarta Sultanate planned an attack, he led a force of 1,200 against its Royal Palace, which fell in one day and was sacked and burnt. It was the first time a European army had captured an indigenous palace in Javanese history. In 1817 he published The History of Java and was knighted by the Prince Regent, the future George IV.

Raffles arrived at Bencoolen on Sumatra on 19 March 1818 and became its lieutenant-governor three days later. He found a colonial backwater whose only real export was pepper, and he began reforms like those on Java, abolishing slavery and limiting cockfighting. On 29 January 1819 he established a post at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, where there was no Dutch presence, and treated with the Temenggong Abdul Rahman. William Farquhar served as the first Resident of Singapore from 1819 to 1823.

Raffles returned to Singapore in October 1822 and found a bustling trade hub, but judged Farquhar's administration unsatisfactory. A plan drawn up by the engineer Philip Jackson, known as the Raffles Town Plan, segregated the population by race but was considered remarkably scientific. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 gave Singapore to the British and Bencoolen to the Dutch. Raffles returned to England in poor health and died on 5 July 1826, his 45th birthday.

Many Singapore institutions bear his name, and the Rafflesia flower is named after him. Critics characterise him as an imperialist and argue that celebratory narratives overlook the people who lived there before his arrival.
stamp-act-1765: The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) was won at great expense: the British national debt nearly doubled between 1755 and 1764. The Bute ministry decided in early 1763 to keep ten thousand regulars in the American colonies, at about £225,000 a year. One reason was that disbanding the army would put 1,500 well-connected officers out of work, and Britons disliked a standing army at home. Pontiac's War, which began in May 1763, led to the Royal Proclamation of 1763 and gave the troops the added duty of keeping peace between Native Americans and colonists.

Stamp duties had been a successful tax in Great Britain, raising over £100,000 at little cost, because a document without its stamp was void. When the Sugar Act 1764 passed in April, George Grenville made clear that further taxes, including a stamp tax, might follow. Colonial agents, among them Benjamin Franklin, did not expect the intensity of the protest.

Parliament passed the act on 22 March 1765, to take effect on 1 November 1765. It passed the House of Commons by 205 to 49 and the House of Lords unanimously. Stamped paper from London had to be used for legal documents, newspapers, pamphlets, playing cards and many other papers, and the tax had to be paid in British currency, which was scarce, rather than colonial paper money. Attorney licences bore the highest tax, £10, cards were taxed a shilling a pack and dice ten shillings. The revenue was to be spent in America, especially on the troops stationed there.

It was the first internal tax, one based on activities within the colonies, laid directly on them by Parliament. Colonists judged it a graver threat to their rights than the Sugar Act because it reached so much of the colonial economy.

Most colonists held that they could be taxed only with the consent of their own assemblies. A member of Parliament argued that colonists were, like the majority of Britons without a vote, represented virtually, but the Maryland lawyer Daniel Dulany rejected the claim in a widely read pamphlet. The Sons of Liberty organised protests, sometimes hanging effigies, and the stamp distributors were intimidated into resigning, so that the tax was never effectively collected. The Stamp Act Congress met in New York in October 1765, with twenty-seven delegates from nine colonies, and petitioned the King and Parliament.

Grenville was replaced by Lord Rockingham as prime minister on 10 July 1765. British merchants, hurt by colonial non-importation agreements, lobbied for repeal, which Parliament passed on 18 March 1766. It also passed the Declaratory Act, affirming its power to legislate for the colonies in all cases whatsoever. The Sons of Liberty, the committees of correspondence and the congress foreshadowed the opposition to the Townshend Acts and the later Continental Congresses.
stamp-act-congress: After the French and Indian War Parliament sought more revenue from the colonies to meet the cost of stationing troops there. The Sugar and Currency Acts of 1764 raised money through trade duties, but the Stamp Act 1765 was its first attempt at direct taxation: newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, playing cards and dice had to carry a stamp bought from a government agent, from 1 November 1765. In June 1765 the Massachusetts Assembly invited the other colonies to consult together. Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland and South Carolina sent delegates, while the governors of Virginia and Georgia prevented their assemblies from meeting.

The Congress sat from 7 to 25 October 1765 in New York City Hall, now Federal Hall, behind closed doors, and little is known of its debates. It chose Timothy Ruggles of Massachusetts as chairman, narrowly rejecting James Otis, and agreed that each delegation would cast one vote. The delegates spent much time on the difference between internal taxes and the regulation of trade, and on 19 October adopted the Declaration of Rights and Grievances, whose fourteen statements professed loyalty to the Crown and held that only the colonists' own representatives could tax them.

An address to the king, a memorial to the House of Lords and a petition to the House of Commons followed on 22 and 23 October. Connecticut, South Carolina and New York declined to sign, and Ruggles and Robert Ogden of New Jersey refused as well; Ruggles quarrelled with Thomas McKean, challenged him to a duel and left the city.

In London the Lords of Trade called it a general congress appointed without the authority of the Crown, a measure of dangerous tendency. The Commons declined the petition as the work of an unconstitutional assembly, and Lord Dartmouth rejected the one to the Lords. The Rockingham Ministry, rallying merchants whose trade had suffered from colonial boycotts, carried the repeal of the Stamp Act on 18 March 1766, but Parliament passed the Declaratory Act the same day, asserting its power to make laws for the colonies in all cases whatsoever. Historians generally see the Congress as one of the first organised political actions of the American Revolution, though its members did not yet seek independence.
standard-chinese: Chinese has long had considerable dialectal variation, along with prestige dialects and linguae francae. Confucius is thought to have used a dialect known as yayan rather than regional speech, and Han dynasty texts refer to a common language, tongyu. For the educated elite the language was unified in Literary Chinese, a form that was primarily written. During the Ming and Qing dynasties the term Guanhua, official speech, named the lingua franca of the imperial courts. The English word Mandarin comes from the Portuguese mandarim, from the Sanskrit mantrin, minister, and was first used for scholar-officials; the Portuguese then called Guanhua the language of the mandarins.

In the 17th century the state set up orthoepy academies to bring officials' speech to a standard, with little success: as late as the 19th century the emperor had difficulty understanding some of his ministers.

After the Republic of China was established in 1912 a Commission on the Unification of Pronunciation was convened, and a Dictionary of National Pronunciation published in 1919 defined a hybrid pronunciation that matched no existing speech. The commission gradually settled on the prestigious Beijing dialect, and in 1932 its Vocabulary of National Pronunciation for Everyday Use normalised the pronunciation of all characters to it. Standard Chinese is therefore defined by the pronunciation of the Beijing dialect, though it is no longer synonymous with it.

It is an analytic language with almost no inflection, subject-verb-object word order and five phonemic tones, four classic ones and a neutral tone. It is written with characters that mostly represent a morpheme and usually descend from those of Classical Chinese. Words with no classical counterpart were written either with a borrowed character of similar sound, as with zhe, this, or with a newly created compound character.

Standard Chinese is the official lingua franca of the People's Republic of China, one of the six official languages of the United Nations, a national language of Taiwan and one of the four official languages of Singapore, with English, Malay and Tamil. It is called Putonghua, common speech, on the mainland and Guoyu, national language, in Taiwan. The word Guoyu was first used in the late Qing dynasty for Manchu, and its modern sense was borrowed from Japan in the early 20th century. In Taiwan Standard Chinese spread widely after 1949, when the Kuomintang and many refugees arrived from the mainland. In both places it is taught by immersion from elementary school.
standard-of-ur: The Standard of Ur is a Sumerian artefact of the third millennium BCE, now in the British Museum. It comes from the First Dynasty of Ur in the Early Dynastic III period, from the ancient city of Ur in what is now Iraq.

It was found in tomb PG 779, one of the largest royal tombs in the Royal Cemetery at Ur, which is associated with the king Ur-Pabilsag. It lay beside the skeleton of a ritually sacrificed man who may have been its bearer, near a shell cylinder seal with the name e-zi. It is thought to have decorated the outside of a hollow wooden box inlaid with a mosaic of shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli.

The present form is a reconstruction of a best guess: a box 21.59 centimetres wide and 49.53 centimetres long, with end pieces shaped as truncated triangles. Mosaic panels cover each long side, in three registers, and they have been called War and Peace. In the War panel a figure often taken to be a king, though he lacks the usual marks of kingship, stands taller than the rest in the top register, with his head breaking the frame, before his bodyguard and a four-wheeled wagon drawn by equids, facing naked, bound prisoners with bleeding wounds.

Below, soldiers in leather cloaks and helmets give way to a battle scene, and four wagons shown walking, cantering, galloping and rearing carry drivers and warriors over fallen enemies. In the Peace panel the king sits on a carved stool at a banquet, with six seated participants holding cups, a lyrist and a possible singer, while the lower registers show figures leading animals or carrying goods.

Sir Leonard Woolley's excavation of 1927 and 1928 found the Standard in the corner of a chamber of a tomb that robbers had plundered long before. A workman noticed a piece of shell inlay. The wooden frame and the bitumen that held the mosaic had decayed, and the weight of the soil had crushed it, so the excavators filled hollows with plaster or wax and lifted small sections under wax.

Woolley took it for a standard carried on a pole, which gave it its name, but this is now thought unlikely. Other suggestions are the soundbox of a musical instrument and a chest for funds. The two sides may form one narrative, a battle followed by a victory feast. It was consolidated with paraffin in 1928, which caused deterioration, and was dismantled and reassembled in 1973.
stanis-aw-zo-kiewski: Stanisław Żółkiewski was born in the village of Turynka, now in western Ukraine, the son of the voivode of Ruthenia, Stanisław Żółkiewski of the Lubicz coat of arms, and Zofia Lipska. He attended a cathedral school in Lwów, had no higher education and did not travel abroad, but studied history on his own. In 1566 he joined the court of King Sigismund II Augustus as an aide to the royal secretary Jan Zamoyski, and in 1573 he took part in the mission to France to meet the newly elected king Henry III.

Żółkiewski commanded a company of hussars under King Stefan Batory in the Danzig rebellion and fought in his Livonian campaign. On the night of 11 to 12 May 1584 he captured Samuel Zborowski, whose execution caused controversy. At the Battle of Byczyna in 1588 he led the right flank for Sigismund III Vasa and received a knee wound that lamed him for life, and he was made Field Crown Hetman.

He later defeated the Tatars, took part in the Moldavian campaign and defeated the Cossack uprising of Severyn Nalivaiko the year after. He had promised the surrendered Cossack leaders fair treatment, but Nalivaiko was executed in Warsaw and a mob of Polish soldiers massacred the other prisoners, worsening Polish-Cossack relations. In Livonia he fought in the Polish-Swedish War.

In the Polish-Russian War he won the Battle of Klushino in 1610 against combined Russian and Swedish forces, then seized Moscow and captured the tsar Vasiliy Shuisky and his brothers. He backed the election of Władysław as tsar and a union of the two states, but Sigismund rejected his plan, which would have required Władysław to convert to Orthodoxy.

In 1618 he received the office of Grand Crown Hetman, and soon after that of Grand Crown Chancellor. He died on 7 October 1620 during the retreat after the Battle of Cecora against the Ottomans, reportedly refusing to retreat and staying with the rear guard. His head was sent to Constantinople as a trophy, and his widow bought back his body.

Żółkiewski wrote memoirs of the Muscovite war, Początek i progres wojny moskiewskiej, published in 1612 and critical of Sigismund's policies. In 1616 he proposed a larger standing army against the Tatars and Cossacks, but the parliament did not approve it. He was buried in St Lawrence Church in Żółkiew, the town he enlarged. His son Jan raised a monument at the site of his death in 1621, inscribed with a line of Horace. Poland remembers him as a military hero, while Russia's Unity Day marks the surrender of the Polish garrison he had installed in Moscow.
stanislaus-hosius: Hosius was born in Kraków on 5 May 1504, the son of Ulrich Hosse of Pforzheim, and spent his youth in Kraków and Vilnius. At fifteen, already at home in German, Polish and Latin, he entered the University of Kraków, graduating as Bachelor of Arts in 1520. Piotr Tomicki, Bishop of Kraków and Vice-Chancellor of Poland, made him his secretary and paid for his studies at Padua, where Reginald Pole was a fellow student, and at Bologna, where he studied law under Hugo Buoncompagni, the future Pope Gregory XIII.

After taking his doctorate in canon and civil law at Bologna on 8 June 1534, he served in the royal chancery and from 1538 as royal secretary to King Sigismund, who rewarded him with church benefices. He was ordained priest in 1543. Nominated to the see of Chełmno in 1549, which he accepted reluctantly, he was first sent on a mission to King Ferdinand I at Prague and Emperor Charles V at Brussels and Ghent, and was consecrated bishop at Kraków on 23 March 1550. As bishop of Warmia he drew up the Confessio fidei christiana catholica, adopted by the Synod of Piotrków in 1557, and with Marcin Kromer kept Warmia Catholic while neighbouring Ducal Prussia became Protestant.

Pope Pius IV sent him as nuncio to Emperor Ferdinand I in Vienna to prepare the reopening of the Council of Trent and to win over the emperor's son Maximilian, who appeared to have Protestant sympathies. Made cardinal in 1561, he served as legate with Cardinals Puteo and Gonzaga, mediating between factions and raising Polish questions such as the status of the Teutonic Knights.

In December 1563 he left Trent for his diocese to carry out the council's decrees, declining to go to Rome although Cardinal Truchess thought him a candidate for the papacy. He became papal legate to Poland in 1566. The lyceum he founded at Braunsberg became the centre of the Catholic mission among Protestants. He died at Capranica Prenestina, near Rome, on 5 August 1579. A collected edition of his works appeared at Cologne in 1584, and his cause for beatification has been opened.
stanislaw-august-poniatowski: Stanisław Antoni Poniatowski was born on 17 January 1732 at Wołczyn, now Vowchyn in Belarus. He was the fourth son of Count Stanisław Poniatowski, Castellan of Kraków, and Princess Konstancja Czartoryska, and one of eight surviving children. In his twenties he travelled through Berlin, Vienna, the Netherlands, Paris and Britain, where he made friends such as the British diplomat Charles Hanbury Williams, and he sat in the Sejm as a deputy. In 1755, aged 22, he reached the Russian court in Saint Petersburg as a diplomat and became closely involved with the future empress Catherine the Great.

After the death of Augustus III in 1763, Catherine supported Poniatowski, and Russia spent about 2.5 million rubles on his election. The Sejm elected him king on 7 September 1764 with 5,584 votes, and he was crowned in Warsaw on 25 November. Contrary to expectations he tried to reform the Commonwealth, but Prussia, Russia and Austria wished to keep it weak, and conservative nobles saw reform as a threat to their liberties. At the Sejm of 1766 he tried to restrict the liberum veto and failed. The War of the Bar Confederation (1768–1772) led to the First Partition of Poland in 1772.

In the 1780s Poniatowski could not pass even small reforms, because he failed to confederate the sejms and so protect them from the veto. The Great Sejm of 1788–1792 produced the Constitution of 3 May 1791. Conservatives formed the Targowica Confederation, allied with Catherine, and Russian troops entered Poland in 1792. The royal army, of only about 37,000 men, was commanded by his nephew Józef Poniatowski and Tadeusz Kościuszko. After the victory at Zieleńce the king founded the Order of Virtuti Militari. The Second Partition followed in 1793.

Poniatowski did not encourage the Kościuszko Uprising of 1794 but supported it once it began. After its defeat he was told to leave Warsaw and went to Grodno, and he signed his abdication on 25 November 1795, a month after the Third Partition. He ended his life as a captive in Saint Petersburg and died on 12 February 1798.

He remains controversial. Critics blame his lack of resolve against the partitions, while others see a skilful statesman who showed courage in passing the Constitution. He was the most important patron of the arts of the Polish Enlightenment: he founded the National Theatre in Warsaw, remodelled the Royal Castle and built the Łazienki Palace, and he laid the foundation for the Commission of National Education.
stanislaw-leszczynski: Stanisław Leszczyński was born in Lwów (now Lviv) in 1677, the son of Rafał Leszczyński, voivode of Poznań Voivodeship, and Princess Anna Leszczyńska. He married Katarzyna Opalińska, and their daughter Maria became Queen of France as the wife of Louis XV.

In 1697, as Cup-bearer of Poland, he signed the confirmation of the articles of election of Augustus II the Strong. In 1703 he joined the Lithuanian Confederation, which the Sapiehas, with the aid of Sweden, had formed against Augustus.

After a successful Swedish invasion of Poland, Charles XII of Sweden chose Stanisław to replace Augustus II. With a bribing fund and an army corps, the Swedes secured his election on 12 July 1704 by a small assembly of castellans and a few score of noblemen.

He was crowned on 24 September 1705 with a new crown and sceptre supplied by Charles, since Augustus had carried the ancient regalia off to Saxony. His first act was an alliance with Charles against the Russian tsar, and he induced the Cossack hetman Ivan Mazepa to desert Peter the Great. After the Battle of Poltava in 1709 his authority vanished, and he abdicated the crown, though he kept the royal title, in exchange for the principality of Palatine Zweibrücken.

After Charles's death in 1719 he moved to Wissembourg in Alsace, and from 1725 to 1733 he lived at the Château de Chambord. When Augustus II died in 1733, Louis XV supported his claim. Stanisław reached Warsaw on 11 September 1733 disguised as a coachman and was elected the next day, but Russia backed Augustus's son, and the War of the Polish Succession followed. A Russian army besieged him at Danzig. The city capitulated on 30 June 1735 after 135 days, and he escaped in peasant disguise two days earlier.

On 26 January 1736 Stanisław abdicated again. In compensation he was later given the duchies of Lorraine and Bar, which were to revert to France on his death. He held court at the Château de Lunéville, which drew Enlightenment figures such as Madame Émilie du Châtelet. In Nancy in 1750 he founded the Académie de Stanislas and the Bibliothèque municipale, and he argued with Jean-Jacques Rousseau. His Głos wolny wolność ubezpieczający is counted among the important political treatises of the Polish Enlightenment.

He died on 23 February 1766, aged 88, after his silk clothing caught fire from a spark while he slept near the fireplace at Lunéville. His titles passed to Louis XV. Buried first in Nancy, his remains were taken to Poland after the French Revolution and laid in the royal tomb at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków. Nancy's Place Stanislas bears his name.
stanley-falkland-islands: The original capital of the Falkland Islands was Port Louis, in Berkeley Sound. Governor Richard Moody recruited Captains Francis Crozier and James Clark Ross to help find a new capital, and after a survey he chose Port Jackson, renamed Stanley Harbour, which was thought to have a deeper anchorage for visiting ships. Not everyone was pleased, and one inhabitant complained that Moody had chosen one of the worst of the miserable bog holes. Work on the settlement began in 1843, and it became the capital in July 1845. It was named after Lord Stanley, then Secretary of State for War and the Colonies. In 1849 thirty married Chelsea Pensioners were settled there to help defend the islands.

The settlement grew as a deep-water port, specialising at first in ship repairs. Before the construction of the Panama Canal, it was a major repair stop for ships travelling through the Straits of Magellan, since rough waters and storms forced many ships into the harbour. Later it became a base for whaling and sealing in the South Atlantic and Antarctic, and an important coaling station for the Royal Navy, which led ships based there to take part in the Battle of the Falkland Islands in the First World War and the Battle of the River Plate in the Second. Landslides caused by peat cutting destroyed part of the town in 1879 and again in 1886, and killed two people.

Argentine troops occupied Stanley for about ten weeks during the Falklands War in 1982 and renamed it Puerto Argentino, a name many islanders find extremely offensive. The town suffered considerable damage from the occupation and from British naval shelling, which killed three civilians, and the Argentines surrendered without fighting in the town itself. The beaches and land around it were heavily mined.

Stanley is the capital of the Falkland Islands, on a north-facing slope on East Falkland, and is the hub of that island's road network. Government House, built in 1845, is the home of the Governor, and the Anglican Christ Church Cathedral is the southernmost Anglican cathedral in the world. At the 2021 census it had a population of 2,974, about 81 percent of the islands' people.
stans: Stans is one of the oldest settlements in the Nidwalden valley, with the first traces of human settlement dating to the second century BCE. The Roman era left little evidence except some funeral pyres and the Latin root of its name, stagnum, meaning a pool. The Alamanni settled the region in the seventh or eighth century, and the Christian Alamanni built the first church in Stans around 750, which served as parish church for the whole Engelberg Valley until the church of St Peter and Paul replaced it in 1647. The town covers 11.08 square kilometres, its highest point on the Stanserhorn.

Stans was first mentioned in 1124. By 1291, when Unterwalden joined Uri and Schwyz in what became the Swiss Confederation, it was already the capital of Unterwalden below the forest, which became the half canton of Nidwalden. Tradition places a soldier from Stans, Arnold von Winkelried, at the Battle of Sempach in 1386, where he is said to have thrown himself on the Habsburg pikes. It is doubtful that he existed, since the first mention of the act comes over 150 years later, but the legend is firmly kept in Stans, with a monument and a house bearing his name.

After the Burgundian Wars the Confederation was nearly torn apart when the city cantons claimed the larger share of the proceeds. In 1481 the Tagsatzung met in Stans, and the hermit Niklaus von der Flüe sent a message whose contents remain unknown. It calmed tempers and led to the Stanser Verkommnis, under which Fribourg and Solothurn were admitted to the Confederation. In 1713 a fire destroyed two thirds of the town, and the square was rebuilt in 1715 with baroque houses.

In 1798 French troops stormed Stans after Nidwalden refused the constitution of the Helvetic Republic, and Pestalozzi gathered the orphaned children in the Convent of St Klara, until the army needed the building the following year. Stans and Nidwalden joined the Sonderbund in 1845 and took part in the Sonderbund War of 1847. The open-air Landsgemeinde was held there annually until 1997.

Stans is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden, and its official language is German, though the main spoken language is the local Alemannic Swiss German. Its sights include the Dorfplatz with the Winkelried monument of 1865, the Capuchin monastery founded in 1583 by Melchior Lussy, and the Winkelriedhaus, which houses a museum. The Stanserhornbahn, built in 1893, is one of the oldest mountain railways in Switzerland.
stapleton-cotton-1st-viscount-combermere: Cotton was born on 14 November 1773 at Lleweni Hall, Denbighshire, in Wales, the second surviving son of Sir Robert Salusbury Cotton, 5th Baronet, and Frances Cotton, née Stapleton. A lively boy, known to his family as Young Rapid, he was schooled at Audlem near the family estate of Combermere Abbey, then at Westminster School and at Norwood House, a private military academy in Bayswater. In 1790 his father obtained for him a second-lieutenancy in the Royal Welch Fusiliers.

He rose quickly through the ranks. He served at the Siege of Dunkirk in 1793 and the Battle of Beaumont in 1794 during the Flanders Campaign, became a lieutenant colonel in 1794 and went to India in 1796, where he was present at the Siege of Seringapatam in May 1799 and first met Colonel Arthur Wellesley. He then helped suppress Robert Emmet's insurrection in Ireland in 1803 and became a major-general in 1805. He was elected Member of Parliament for Newark in 1806.

In the Peninsular War he first commanded a cavalry brigade, then the whole cavalry, and his splendid dress earned him the nickname Lion d'Or. At Salamanca in July 1812, where he was second-in-command, his charge against Maucune's division led Wellington to exclaim that he had never seen anything so beautiful; at the end of the battle a Portuguese sentry shot him by accident. He was made Baron Combermere in 1814. The command of the cavalry at Waterloo went to Lord Uxbridge, but Cotton took it over when Uxbridge was wounded.

He was Governor of Barbados from 1817 to 1820 and Commander-in-Chief, Ireland, from 1822. After his success at Bharatpur he brought home the 17.75-ton Bhurtpore gun, which long stood outside the Royal Artillery Barracks at Woolwich, and he retired from active service in 1830.

In October 1852 he succeeded Wellington as Constable of the Tower. He died at Colchester House in Clifton on 21 February 1865, aged 91, and was buried at St Margaret's Church, Wrenbury. The people of Cheshire raised a bronze equestrian statue of him at Chester by Carlo, Baron Marochetti, in October 1865. According to the Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slavery, he was compensated after the Slavery Abolition Act 1833 for 420 enslaved people on his estates on Saint Kitts and Nevis, receiving £7,195.
star-catalogue: The earliest known star catalogues were compiled by the Babylonians in the late second millennium BCE, in the Kassite period. Known by their Assyrian-era name Three Stars Each, they listed thirty-six stars on clay tablets, twelve each for Anu, Ea and Enlil. The later Mul.Apin lists descend from them. In Greece, Eudoxus laid down the classical constellations around 370 BCE, and his Phaenomena was rewritten as a poem by Aratus of Soli between 275 and 250 BCE. Hipparchus completed his catalogue in 129 BCE, compared it with that of Timocharis and discovered that stellar longitudes had changed, which gave him the first value of the precession of the equinoxes.

Ptolemy's catalogue in the Almagest listed 1,022 stars and was based almost entirely on Hipparchus. It remained the standard in the Western and Arab worlds for over eight centuries. Al-Sufi updated it in 964 in his Book of Fixed Stars, which gave positions, magnitudes and colours, drawings for each constellation and the first known description of the Andromeda Galaxy. Ulugh Beg redetermined the positions in 1437 in his Zij-i Sultani. Tycho Brahe's catalogue of a thousand stars, in 1598, finally superseded it.
Chinese star names appear on Shang oracle bones, and Sima Qian's Book of Celestial Offices names some 90 constellations. Zhang Heng compiled a catalogue of 124 constellations in 120 CE.

A star catalogue lists stars with their positions and brightness, and many stars are known simply by catalogue numbers. Two historical systems of naming remain in use. Johann Bayer's Uranometria of 1603 gave bright stars a Greek letter and the genitive of the constellation, as in Alpha Centauri. John Flamsteed's Historia coelestis Britannica of 1725 used numbers instead, as in 61 Cygni. A catalogue's completeness is described by its limiting magnitude and its accuracy by the precision of its positions.

Jérôme Lalande's Histoire céleste française of 1801 listed 47,390 stars and was the most complete catalogue of its time. The Bonner Durchmusterung of 1852 to 1859 covered 320,000 stars, and the Henry Draper Catalogue of 1918 to 1924, compiled by Annie Jump Cannon and her colleagues at Harvard, was the first large attempt to catalogue spectral types. The Hipparcos satellite catalogue, published in June 1997, holds 118,218 stars with greatly improved parallaxes, and the first Gaia release of 13 September 2016 gave positions and magnitudes for 1.1 billion stars.
stare-mesto-uherske-hradiste-district: Staré Město, which means old town in Czech, lies in the Zlín Region about 22 kilometres south-west of Zlín. It has about 6,700 inhabitants and forms a conurbation with Uherské Hradiště, from which it is separated by the Morava River. It lies mostly in the flat agricultural landscape of the Lower Morava Valley, with a small western part reaching into the Kyjov Hills, and the Baťa Canal flows through its eastern part. It is a railway junction, and the I/55 road from Olomouc to Uherské Hradiště runs through it.

The area was inhabited in the 9th century, in the era of the Great Moravian Empire, and the site has been identified with Velingrad, one of the empire's two capital cities. After Great Moravia fell, Velingrad lost its importance and became a village with two churches. It is first mentioned in writing in 1141. In 1205 Cistercian monks founded a monastery nearby and named it Velehrad, and the market village of Velingrad became their property. The Great Moravian rotunda was rebuilt in 1250 as the parish Church of Saint Michael the Archangel, and in 1321 the village was renamed Staré Město.

A railway was built in 1841. From 1971 to 1990 the settlement was part of Uherské Hradiště, and from 1990 it was again a separate municipality. It was hit by the 1997 Central European flood and in the same year was promoted to a town.

Staré Město is known for the Great Moravia Monument, built above the foundations of the first Great Moravian building discovered on Czech territory, the church known as Na Valách. It is a museum with displays on the empire and on life in the 9th century. The Church of Saint Michael the Archangel dates from the first half of the 13th century, and its core holds remains of a Great Moravian rotunda. Staré Město is twinned with Sées in France and Tönisvorst in Germany.
starocherkasskaya: Starocherkasskaya is a stanitsa in Aksaysky District, on the right bank of the Don River about 35 kilometres upstream from Rostov-on-Don. Its name means Old Cherkassk. The town grew up on an island of the Don later called Monastyrsky. The site suited a fortress and a military camp, but not a centre of government and trade: in spring the island was flooded, and the crowded wooden town suffered devastating fires.

A Cossack fortress probably stood on the island before 1570, though the chronicles first mention it in 1593. About fifty years later it became the capital of the Don Cossacks, at first an independent entity between Russia, Turkey and Poland, then a vassal of the tsars, and later the Don Voisko Province of the Russian Empire. In its heyday in the 18th century Cherkassk was a busy town with a strong fortress. Stepan Razin, Yermak Timofeyevich, Kondraty Bulavin and Matvei Platov all lived there, and Russian, Ottoman, Crimean and Cossack forces fought hard battles around it.

In 1805 Platov, as ataman of the province, moved the capital to Novocherkassk, a city built for the purpose on a hill about 40 kilometres away. Most of the inhabitants followed, and what remained of the old town became the stanitsa of Starocherkasskaya.

The village is now a museum, a tourist centre and the seat of an Orthodox monastery for men; the writer Michail Aleksandrovich Sholokhov did much to organise the museum. Its more than forty historical sites include the Resurrection Cathedral with its gilded wooden iconostasis and the chains said to have held Stepan Razin, the Transfiguration Church of 1740, the Petropavlovsk Church of 1751, the ataman's estate, the house of Kondraty Bulavin, the ruins of the Annensky fortress of 1730 and the monastery of Our Lady of the Don.
stasys-girenas: Born Stasys Girskis on 4 October 1893 in Vytogala, in the Šilalė district of Lithuania, then part of the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire, he was known in the United States as Stanley T. Girenas. In 1910, aged 17, he emigrated to the United States and settled in Chicago, where he worked as a young man in a printing house.

When the United States entered the First World War in 1917 he enlisted in the United States Army and was trained as a mechanic. After his honourable discharge in 1919 he worked as a cab driver and learned to fly at the same time. He bought a plane in 1925 and, although injured in a crash, kept flying and working in civil aviation. In 1931 he won first prize at the Chicago Air Festival for the best landing of a plane with its engine switched off.

On 15 July 1933 he and Steponas Darius set out from New York City in a Bellanca CH-300 Pacemaker named Lituanica, aiming to fly 7,186 kilometres without landing. They crossed the Atlantic in 37 hours and 11 minutes, but the plane came down at 0:36 Berlin time on 17 July by the village of Kuhdamm, near Soldin, today Pszczelnik in Poland. The official investigation found that difficult weather combined with engine defects had caused the crash. The two men had covered 6,412 kilometres.

Both aviators died in the crash. On 18 May 1934 Lithuania issued a set of six airmail stamps in honour of Captains Girėnas and Darius and their aircraft. In 1957 a granite flagstaff showing the pair in bas-relief was raised in Lithuania Square in Williamsburg, Brooklyn. The asteroid 288961 Stasysgirėnas, discovered by Kazimieras Černis and Justas Zdanavičius in 2004, was named after him in 2017.
state-anthem-of-the-soviet-union: The music was composed by Alexander Alexandrov in 1938 for the Hymn of the Bolshevik Party. Its opening bars came from his earlier piece Life Has Become Better, which was based on a remark by Joseph Stalin at the First All-Union Meeting of the Stakhanovites on 17 November 1935. Alexandrov described the piece as a combination of a march with Russian traditional music, particularly the bylina epic songs. Its chord progressions resemble those of Vasily Kalinnikov's overture Bylina, Epic Poem.

When the Comintern was dissolved in 1943, so that the Soviet Union could keep its alliance with the other Allies, a replacement was needed for The Internationale, which had been the national anthem. A contest in mid to late 1943 drew more than 200 entries, and Stalin personally chose Alexandrov's music, both praising and criticising it. He wanted short words that invoked the coming victory of the Red Army over Germany. His staff called the poets Sergey Mikhalkov and Gabriyel' Arkadyevich Ureklyan to Moscow, and they completed a first draft overnight.

The anthem was first published on 7 November 1943, broadcast on Soviet radio at midnight on 1 January 1944 and officially adopted on 15 March 1944. The words had three stanzas, each followed by a refrain whose second line spoke in turn of friendship, happiness and glory. Stalin and the war against Germany were invoked in the second and third verses. Stalin is reported to have opposed putting his name in the words but to have relented when some Politburo members insisted.

After Stalin's death and the process of de-Stalinization, the lines about him were considered unacceptable, and from 1956 to 1977 the anthem was performed without words. One exception was at the 1976 Canada Cup ice hockey tournament, where the singer Roger Doucet insisted on singing it. In 1977, to coincide with the 60th anniversary of the October Revolution, new words written in 1970 by Mikhalkov were adopted. The varying refrains gave way to one refrain after all stanzas, and the line praising Stalin and the lines on the Great Patriotic War were dropped. A line about the Soviet flag was replaced by one naming the Communist Party as the party of Lenin.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 Russia first adopted the Patriotic Song. In December 2000 the federal legislature approved the Soviet anthem's music again as the national anthem of Russia, with new words by Mikhalkov, who had written both earlier versions. The same music was proposed for an anthem of the State Union of Russia and Belarus, but that was never adopted.
state-counsellor-of-myanmar: The office was created after the National League for Democracy, led by Aung San Suu Kyi, won a landslide victory in the 2015 Myanmar general election. The constitution barred her from becoming President of Myanmar because her late husband, Michael Aris, had been British. The post was designed to let her lead the government despite that bar and to give her a greater role within the Government of Myanmar.

The bill creating the post passed the upper house of the Assembly of the Union on 1 April 2016 and the lower house on 5 April, and President Htin Kyaw signed it on 6 April 2016. The law names Aung San Suu Kyi explicitly and sets out several priorities: the cultivation of a multi-party democratic system, the proper working of a market economy, the establishment of a federal union, and domestic peace and development.

The State Counsellor was the de facto head of government of Myanmar, equivalent to a prime minister. The holder could contact ministries, departments, organisations, associations and individuals in an official capacity while remaining accountable to parliament. Like a prime minister, the State Counsellor could work across every area of government and acted as a link between the executive and the legislature. The term of office was five years, the same as the president's.

The office existed from 2016 to 2021. It was abolished by Aung San Suu Kyi's political adversary, Min Aung Hlaing, the Commander-in-Chief of Defence Services, after he seized power from her in the military coup d'état of 2021, five years after the post had been created to let her lead the government.
state-great-khural: Tögs-Ochiryn Namnansüren became chairman of a State Great Khural in February 1914 and served until his death in April 1919. The first State Great Khural of the Mongolian People's Republic was called in November 1924. It delegated much of its power to an executive committee, the Little Khural, and held nine sessions between November 1924 and February 1949. After electoral reforms in 1951 its sessions were numbered again from one. A new constitution of 1960 renamed it the People's Great Khural, a name sometimes applied in Russian and Mongolian writing to the earlier body as well.

The Democratic Revolution of 1990 led to the first free multi-party election in Mongolia, in July 1990. The new parliament established the State Baga Khural, or State Little Khural, as the lower house, leaving the People's Great Khural as a kind of upper house. The Little Khural had 50 members. From 1990 to 1992 it adopted 27 laws and ratified 17 international treaties.

A new constitution ratified on 13 January 1992 abolished the two chambers and established a single parliament, the State Great Khural, which first convened on 20 July 1992. In the 1992 elections the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party won 70 seats, and Natsagiin Bagabandi became chairman. The first Khural adopted 137 laws. Later parliaments of four years each were led at different times by the Mongolian People's Revolutionary Party, the Democratic Union Coalition, the Democratic Party and the Mongolian People's Party, which won 65 seats in 2016.

The electoral system changed several times. The 2012 election was the first with a mixed system, in which 48 seats were chosen in multi-member constituencies and 28 by closed party list, and electronic voting machines were used for the first time. The 2016 election used single-mandate constituencies for 76 seats. After a constitutional amendment in 2023 the Khural grew to 126 seats, 78 chosen by multiple non-transferable vote and 48 by closed-list proportional representation. The election of June 2024 returned a reduced majority for the Mongolian People's Party.

The Khural meets in the Government Palace in Ulaanbaatar and is elected every four years. Voters must be 18 or older and live in Mongolia, and any person over 25 may stand. Regular sessions run for at least 50 working days every six months, an autumn session beginning on 1 October and a spring session on 5 April. Standing committees of 10 to 19 members meet twice a week, and a coalition with eight or more seats must form a party caucus. Draft laws pass through three stages of discussion in committee and plenary session before the chairman signs them and sends them to the President, who may veto them.
state-of-east-indonesia: The Dutch had grouped the eastern islands of the Indies as the Great East region in 1938; after the Japanese invasion four years later the area was placed under the Imperial Japanese Navy. After the Japanese surrender and the Indonesian declaration of independence in August 1945, Dutch administrators backed by Australian troops returned and kept republicans from setting up an administration. The Malino Conference of 16 to 25 July 1946 planned a federal Indonesia, a principle the Republic accepted in the Linggadjati Agreement of 15 November. The Denpasar Conference founded the State of the Great East on 24 December 1946 and renamed it the State of East Indonesia three days later.

The Balinese nobleman Tjokorda Gde Raka Soekawati, elected at Denpasar, was president for the whole life of the state, appointing prime ministers who led parliamentary cabinets, although much real power stayed with the Dutch East Indies authorities. Opponents joked that its initials NIT stood for negara ikoet toean, the state that goes along with the master. A Provisional Representative Body of the 70 delegates of Denpasar opened on 22 April 1947; a draft constitution passed on 1 March 1949 was never adopted. More than three quarters of the territory belonged to 115 self-governing regions ruled by rajas, whose special status the state was bound to recognise.

In the elections held between September and December 1949, supporters of a unitary Indonesia won almost half the seats. On 17 March 1950 a large demonstration in Makassar demanded union with the Republic, and Justice Minister Soumokil ordered arrests of unitarist supporters. When Jakarta announced it would send troops of the federal army, former colonial soldiers under Andi Aziz seized the city on 5 April and turned the troopships away. Soekawati and his ministers discussed declaring independence but could not muster the two-thirds majority needed, and Aziz was arrested after travelling to Jakarta.

On 21 April Soekawati agreed to dissolve the state if the Republic of Indonesia did the same. The formation of its last cabinet in May 1950 for that purpose set off a rebellion in the largely Christian Moluccas, where the Republic of the South Moluccas was proclaimed. The United States of Indonesia was dissolved on 17 August 1950, and the rebellion in the Moluccas was crushed in November.
state-of-qin: Qin is traditionally dated to 897 BCE and arose from a reconquest of western lands lost to the Xirong. Its position at the western edge of Chinese civilisation allowed an expansion unavailable to its rivals on the North China Plain. According to Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, it traced its origin to Zhuanxu, one of the Five Emperors of ancient times. Its ancestors, the Ying clan, served the Shang as a buffer against the Xirong. Under the Zhou, Feizi so impressed King Xiao of Zhou with his horse breeding that he received a fief in the valley of Qin, in modern Gansu, with its seat at Qinyi. The Ying lived among the Rong tribes, sometimes fighting them and sometimes intermarrying with their kings.

In the Spring and Autumn period Qin dealt mainly with the Rong to the west. Its main contact was its eastern neighbour Jin. When Jin suffered famine in 647 BCE, Duke Mu of Qin sent relief, but Duke Hui of Jin gave none when Qin starved the next year. War followed in 645 BCE, and Duke Mu captured Duke Hui and released him in return for land and an alliance. He then backed Chong'er, who became Duke Wen of Jin, and turned to campaigns against the Rong.

In the early Warring States period Qin was less involved in the Central Plains, apparently through an isolationist policy, and relied on natural defences such as the Hangu Pass. Between 413 and 409 BCE a Wei army under Wu Qi took Qin territory west of the Yellow River. In 362 BCE Qin defeated Wei and Han, and in 361 BCE Duke Xiao invited talented men from other states to assist his reforms. Shang Yang carried out Legalist reforms against conservative opposition, abolishing direct primogeniture, granting commoners citizenship rights, resettling many to raise farm output and imposing strict laws that spared neither nobility nor royalty.

In 247 BCE the 13-year-old Ying Zheng became King of Qin, and he took full power in 238 BCE after eliminating Lü Buwei and Lao Ai. With help from Han Fei, Li Si and Wei Liao he planned the conquest of the other six states, which unified China in 221 BCE.

Qin's unification under Qin Shi Huang in 221 BCE founded the Qin dynasty, which, despite its short duration, influenced later Chinese history greatly. The state before that is called predynastic or proto-Qin. The Wuzi, attributed to Wu Qi, described the Qin people as ferocious by nature, in a treacherous terrain, with strict and impartial decrees and clear rewards and punishments.
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs: The South Slavic peoples of Austria-Hungary were divided among several administrative units. The Austrian Littoral, the Duchy of Carniola and the Kingdom of Dalmatia lay under Austrian jurisdiction, while the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia and Fiume were under Hungarian jurisdiction, and Bosnia and Herzegovina was a condominium. On 30 May 1917 the Yugoslav Club, a group of Croatian and Slovene deputies in the Reichsrat, adopted the May Declaration, which sought the unification of all lands of the monarchy inhabited by Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in one independent entity.

A meeting in Zagreb on 2 and 3 March 1918 produced the Zagreb Resolution, which proclaimed the unity of the three peoples and demanded self-determination. In the summer, people's organizations were formed in Split, Sušak and Ljubljana. The People's Council was established in Zagreb on 5 to 8 October 1918 with 95 representatives, and on 19 October it declared itself the supreme representative body of all South-Slavic peoples in the monarchy.

The state was proclaimed on 29 October 1918. Its first president was the Slovene Anton Korošec, with the Serb Svetozar Pribićević and the Croat Ante Pavelić as vice presidents. It aspired to include all the Austro-Hungarian territories inhabited by Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, but Serbs in Vojvodina formed their own administration under the Serbian National Board in Novi Sad, and Vojvodina joined the Kingdom of Serbia on 25 November 1918. Syrmia had seceded and joined Serbia a day earlier.

Emperor Karl assigned the Austro-Hungarian Navy and its harbours to the National Council, but the Italian navy attacked and dismembered the fleet. The Armistice of Villa Giusti, signed on 4 November 1918, allowed Italy to occupy large parts of the state's territory, and Italian troops held Istria and much of Dalmatia until the Treaty of Rapallo took effect in 1921. The state was never recognised internationally.

In a note of 31 October the National Council told the governments of the United Kingdom, France, Italy and the United States that it intended to form a common state with Serbia and Montenegro. On 23 and 24 November it declared unification, but its instructions were largely ignored by the delegation, which negotiated with Regent Alexander instead. Stjepan Radić's Peasant Party called the move foolish and argued that the Croatian Parliament had never approved it.

On 1 December 1918 Regent Alexander proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, thirty-three days after the state's proclamation. The National Council had ceased to operate and never formally ratified the proclamation.
state-of-the-presidi: The name means state of the garrisons. Duke Cosimo I de' Medici overran the Republic of Siena in 1555, during the last Italian War, with the support of the Emperor Charles V and his son Philip II. On 29 May 1557 Philip settled the question of Piombino by a treaty signed in London with Lord Iacopo VI Appiani, and on 3 July 1557 Siena and its contado were granted to Cosimo in fief, in return for the cancellation of debts owed by Philip and Charles.

The act of infeudation expressly excluded Porto Ercole, Orbetello, Talamone, Monte Argentario and Porto Santo Stefano, a territory of about 287 square kilometres; the islet of Giannutri also belonged to the Presidi. The French, who still held Talamone, failed in an assault on Orbetello in April 1558, and the Spaniards took Talamone by force that September.

The Presidi let Spain watch shipping between Genoa and Naples, and during the Eighty Years' War and the Franco-Spanish War they served as a stopover on the Cammino di Fiandra, the route by which troops from Naples reached the Spanish Netherlands. In 1587 Grand Duke Francesco offered Philip II a million gold pieces for a single one of the places, but the king refused. From 1605 Spain built Fort San Giacomo at Porto Longone on Elba, with barracks for 2,000 men. Orbetello withstood a French siege sent by Mazarin from May to July 1646; the French took Porto Longone that September, and the Spaniards recovered it in 1650.

During the War of the Spanish Succession the Emperor Charles VI took all the Presidi except Porto Longone between 1708 and 1712. The Treaty of Turin of 1733 assigned them to Don Carlos, the future Charles III of Spain, together with Naples and Sicily, and the Peace of Vienna of 18 November 1738 confirmed the change. By the Treaty of Florence of 28 March 1801 King Ferdinand IV of Naples ceded them to the French Republic; the formal cession to Etruria took place on 19 September 1801. After the Congress of Vienna they went to the restored Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

Under Spain the treasury of Naples paid for the Presidi and normally kept five infantry companies there, a third of the Spanish forces deployed by Naples. Three governors commanded the garrisons, an auditor named by the viceroy administered civil and criminal justice, and an inspector oversaw the fortifications, wages and munitions. In the 16th century Tuscan shepherds also brought their flocks to graze the warm coastal pastures in winter.
state-of-vietnam: After the Second World War the Viet Minh led the August Revolution, and Ho Chi Minh declared the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Full-scale war with France began in December 1946. Surviving nationalists who opposed both the communists and French rule rallied behind the exiled Bảo Đại. On 5 June 1948 the Halong Bay Agreements allowed a unified Vietnamese government within the French Union, and a Provisional Central Government was proclaimed under Nguyễn Văn Xuân while Bảo Đại waited for full reunification.

On 20 May 1949 the French National Assembly approved the reunification of Cochinchina with the rest of Vietnam. Bảo Đại brought the Élysée Accords into effect on 14 June 1949, and the first government of the State of Vietnam was proclaimed on 2 July. It had partial autonomy as an associated state of the French Union, and it gained recognition from 34 countries by 1950, among them the United Kingdom and the United States. Its strongest support came from the United States, while the Democratic Republic was backed by China and, from 1950, the Soviet Union.

Roughly 60 per cent of Vietnamese territory was under the Democratic Republic in 1952, but most delta and urban areas with large populations were held by the French and the State of Vietnam. Five groups, known as the Big Five, chose to work with Bảo Đại: the Cao Đài, the Hòa Hảo, the Bình Xuyên, the northern Catholics and the northern Đại Việt Party. Most kept semi-independent territories of their own. A Vietnamese National Army was created under General Nguyễn Văn Hinh, and a national currency was introduced in 1953.

The Matignon Treaty of 4 June 1954 was seen as granting independence from France. Bảo Đại appointed Ngô Đình Diệm to lead the government that month, and on 20 July 1954 the state formally withdrew from the French Union. The Geneva Accords of 21 July divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel. Some 120,000 Viet Minh personnel moved north, while at least 500,000 Catholics and others moved south.

The State of Vietnam and the United States opposed the partition. In July 1955 Diệm announced that the south would not take part in the elections the Geneva Accords specified, since it had not signed them. A referendum on 23 October 1955 chose between Diệm and Bảo Đại. Supporters of Bảo Đại were not allowed to campaign, the official result of 98.2 per cent for Diệm was condemned as fraudulent, and the votes counted exceeded the registered voters by over 380,000. On 26 October 1955 Diệm proclaimed the Republic of Vietnam.
state-protection-authority: The force began in 1945 as the Budapest Department of State Political Police. In 1946 it became the State Defence Department of the Hungarian State Police, the ÁVO, and in 1950 the State Protection Authority. Gábor Péter headed it from 1945 to 1952. László Rajk, the Communist minister of the interior, played a crucial part in organising it, and in 1949 became one of its victims: he was arrested, tried for nationalism and Titoism and executed. On 1 January 1950 the authority was removed from the Ministry of the Interior, made independent and given the Border Guard.

The authority served the Hungarian Working People's Party directly, with little reference to the norms of government, and its actions were not subject to judicial review until the early years after Stalin. It gathered intelligence through a vast network of informants. Secret arrests were followed by periods of torture lasting from 3 to 18 months, after which the public prosecutors and courts were called in to pass sentence.

Prisons and internment camps were placed under its supervision, the most notorious at Recsk, Kistarcsa, Tiszalök and Kazincbarcika. Before 1953 some camps aimed at the eventual death of their inmates through overwork and maltreatment. The first government of Imre Nagy, from 1953 to 1955, greatly improved conditions in the camps and ended these efforts.

In 1953 the authority prepared a show trial meant to prove that Raoul Wallenberg had not been taken to the Soviet Union in 1945 but had been killed by Zionists in Budapest. Leaders of the Jewish community, among them Miksa Domonkos and Lajos Stöckler, and two intended witnesses were seized and tortured. After the death of Stalin the preparations were stopped and the prisoners released in the autumn of 1953. Domonkos died shortly afterwards, mainly from the torture.

On 29 October 1956, during the revolution, the militia of József Dudás stormed the secret police headquarters and massacred the officers inside, and the crowd lynched others. The students' and workers' councils then set up armed patrols to detain members of the authority for their own safety and for later trial. When Soviet forces intervened, its officers carried out brutal reprisals against revolutionaries.

The government of János Kádár, who had himself been tortured by the authority, did not revive it under its old name. Its work passed to a department of the Ministry of the Interior, known as III, which operated with considerably more restraint. Its former headquarters at 60 Andrássy Avenue in Budapest is now a museum, the House of Terror.
state-shinto: Much of its thinking came from Kokugaku, or National Learning, an Edo-period school that sought a pure Japanese Shinto stripped of Buddhist influence. Followers of Hirata Atsutane led a Great Promulgation Campaign from 1868 to 1884 to join nationalism and Shinto through worship of the emperor, but it won little public support, and Fukuzawa Yukichi dismissed it as an insignificant movement. In 1868 the state issued the Kami and Buddhas Separation Order and in 1869 restored the Department of Divinity, stressing the emperor's descent from the Sun Goddess Amaterasu.

A dispute over which kami to honour, between the Ise and Izumo sects, led the Ministry of the Interior to separate state ritual from personal doctrine: Shinto rites became a civic duty, while religious Shinto was left to individual faith. Out of this came the Thirteen Sects of Shinto and the theory that shrines were patriotic, not religious, institutions.

The divine origin of the emperor was taught in schools as historical fact, with ceremonial recitations, rites before his portrait and class trips to shrines. In 1906 the government limited its support to one shrine per village, and Japan's 200,000 shrines had fallen to 120,000 by 1914. Practices without a state function, such as preaching at shrines and funerals, were restricted; priests of Omotokyo were imprisoned in 1921, and from 1931 shrines were pressed to focus on the divinity of Emperor Hirohito. The Institute of Divinities of 1940 widened state control. In occupied Korea almost 400 shrines were built and worship there was mandatory.

Critics at the time included Yanagita Kunio, who disputed the claim that Shinto was not religious. On 1 January 1946 Emperor Shōwa declared that he was not a divinity in human form. Scholars still debate how far the state controlled local shrines and how far people supported emperor worship; Ashizu Uzuhiko, Sakamoto Koremaru and Nitta Hitoshi argue that state funding was never enough to justify speaking of a State Shinto at all. The Yasukuni Shrine, founded in 1869 for the war dead, became contested after several class-A war criminals were enshrined there in a secret ceremony in 1978.
states-general-of-the-netherlands: The States General originated in the 15th century as an assembly of delegates from the provincial states of the Burgundian Netherlands, from about the middle of the century under the dukes of Burgundy. The word staten originally related to the feudal estates of clergy, nobility and commons, and came to mean the body in which they were represented. The first important session met at Bruges on 9 January 1464. After the death of Charles the Bold the States General were convened on 3 February 1477 and forced Mary of Burgundy to grant the Great Privilege, which recognised their right to meet on their own initiative. Their main function was to let the central government discuss matters with the provinces, especially special subsidies.

In 1576 the States General as a whole openly rebelled against the Spanish crown, and in 1579 they split: the southern provinces of the Union of Arras returned to obedience, while the provinces of the Union of Utrecht continued the revolt. In the Act of Abjuration of 1581 the northern States General replaced Philip II as supreme authority. In the Dutch Republic, a confederation, most government functions stayed with the provincial states. Each of the seven provinces had one vote, and from 1593 the States General sat continually until 1795.

Under the Union of Utrecht they were formally sovereign, represented the Republic abroad and made treaties, and their honorific title was Hoogmogende Heren. They also supervised the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch West India Company. The southern States General were dissolved for the last time in 1634 by Philip IV of Spain. The northern body disbanded itself in January 1796. The name was revived in 1814, and after the constitutional revision of 1848 ministers became accountable to the States General, which made the king's role largely ceremonial.

Place names preserve the institution's name: Henry Hudson called Staten Island in New York Staaten Eylandt in 1609, and Abel Tasman first named New Zealand Staten Landt. In 1815 the States General became a Senate and a House of Representatives. Universal male suffrage came in 1917 and women's suffrage in 1919. Today both chambers meet at the Binnenhof in The Hague, the oldest parliament building in the world still in use.
states-of-germany: Federalism has a long tradition in German history. In 1796 the Holy Roman Empire was made up of more than 300 political entities, a number greatly reduced during the Napoleonic Wars, and the Empire was abolished in 1806. The Congress of Vienna created the 39-state German Confederation in 1815. The German Empire of 1871 included 25 states, three of them free cities, plus Alsace-Lorraine, and 65% of its territory and 62% of its population belonged to Prussia. The word Länder dates to the Weimar Constitution of 1919, since the states of the Empire had been called Staaten.

The Federal Republic of Germany consists of sixteen partly sovereign states. Thirteen are area-states, Berlin and Hamburg are city-states, and Bremen, made up of the cities of Bremen and Bremerhaven, is a mixture of the two. Bavaria, Saxony and Thuringia call themselves Freistaat, free state, a title that is merely stylistic. After the war the Allied military governments redrew the internal borders and established new states in all four zones of occupation, none above 30% of population or territory, to prevent any one from dominating as Prussia had. In 1952 Baden, Württemberg-Baden and Württemberg-Hohenzollern merged into Baden-Württemberg, and Saarland joined in 1957.

The individual states formed the Federal Republic in 1949. In East Germany the five states were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 14 administrative districts called Bezirke. They were reconstituted on 3 October 1990 as the five New States, and East and West Berlin joined as one city-state, which gives the present sixteen. In principle the power to make laws lies with the states, and the federation may legislate only where the Basic Law assigns it power, as in foreign and defence policy. The states alone make police law and culture, which includes schools and universities, and they take part in federal legislation through the Bundesrat.
states-of-jersey: Jersey's self-government under Norman law goes back to the guarantee John, King of England, gave the Channel Islands after the division of Normandy in 1204, when the islanders held to the English king against the King of France. The legislature takes its name from the estates from which it was first summoned: the Crown, represented by the Bailiff and Jurats, the Church, represented by the rectors of the parishes, and the people, represented by the connétables. Until 1887 the States had no meeting place of their own and met in the Royal Court on the Royal Square in St Helier.

On 6 November 1856 the States voted to add 14 deputies, to correct the imbalance of population and voting power between St Helier and the country parishes, and the first deputies were elected on 12 January 1857. The first election by secret ballot followed on 1 December 1891. The present chamber, above an extension of the Royal Court, opened in 1887, a sign of the Assembly's growing standing and of Jersey's growing autonomy.
