When Baku fell in mid-September they escaped or were released and sailed to Krasnovodsk, where anti-Bolshevik forces arrested them. They were executed on the night of 20 September 1918 in the Turkmen desert. The British role is disputed: Captain Reginald Teague-Jones later claimed he left before the decision was made. The Soviet government made Shaumian a hero, and Khankendi was renamed Stepanakert and Jalaloghli Stepanavan. In January 2009 Azerbaijan demolished the 26 Commissars Memorial in Baku, which caused an outcry in Armenia.
stephanie-of-milly: Stephanie was one of three children of Philip of Milly and his wife, Isabella, and was named after her Flemish paternal grandmother. Philip held wide lands around Nablus, which in 1161 he exchanged for the Lordship of Transjordan, centred on the strongholds of Montreal and Kerak. When he entered the Order of the Temple in 1166, the lordship passed to Stephanie's sister, Helena, and on Helena's death to Helena's daughter, Beatrice. Stephanie inherited it only when Beatrice too had died, by February 1174.

Her marriage to Humphrey III of Toron, son of the constable Humphrey II, produced two children, Humphrey IV and Isabella. King Amalric then married her to his seneschal and favourite, Miles of Plancy, probably between 24 March and 18 April 1174. After Amalric's death Miles governed in the name of the young Baldwin IV, but he was murdered at Acre in October 1174 in a dispute with Count Raymond III of Tripoli, whom Stephanie believed responsible.

Transjordan lay across the routes between Cairo and Damascus, just as Saladin was extending his rule over Syria, which made Stephanie the most important heiress of the kingdom. Backed by her father-in-law and by the Templars, she stayed a widow for some time and ruled alone. Her husband Raynald of Châtillon, who had returned from Constantinople early in 1176, became a serious threat to Saladin, and the couple sided with Guy of Lusignan in the quarrels among the nobility.

In 1180 Humphrey was engaged to Isabella, half-sister of King Baldwin, and the girl was sent to live at Kerak. During the wedding in October 1183 Saladin besieged the castle. Ernoul, probably informed by the bride's mother, Queen Maria Komnene, tells that Stephanie sent dishes from the feast to Saladin, who then asked which tower the couple occupied so as to spare it. King Baldwin relieved the castle in early December.

After the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187 she held full authority over Kerak and Montreal. Imad al-Din al-Isfahani, who called her virtuous and intelligent, describes her agreeing in tears to give up the castles. The garrisons refused her order to surrender and accused her of siding with the Muslims, so she handed Humphrey back to Saladin and went to Tyre. Saladin, impressed, released him after a few months. Kerak held out until November 1188.
stephen-bathory: Stephen Báthory was born on 27 September 1533 at Somlyó, in a noble Hungarian family. Around 1549–1550 he visited Italy and probably attended lectures at the University of Padua. He then joined the army of Ferdinand I and fought the Turks, and some time after 1553 he was captured by them. When Ferdinand refused to pay his ransom he joined John II Sigismund Zápolya in the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom as a commander and diplomat. After Zápolya's death in 1571 the Transylvanian estates elected him voivode of Transylvania. By 1573 he had defeated Gáspár Bekes, who was supported by the Habsburgs, in the civil war that followed.

The throne of Poland-Lithuania fell vacant in 1572 with the death of Sigismund II Augustus. After Henry III of France left it, an election in 1575 produced two claimants, and a faction around Chancellor Jan Zamoyski secured the election of Báthory, who married Anna Jagiellon and was crowned on 1 May 1576. He first had to win recognition. Lithuania accepted him after he agreed to its conditions, and Danzig, which had supported the Habsburg candidate, was defeated in the field on 17 April 1577 and then agreed to recognise him and pay compensation of 200,000 zlotys.

With Zamoyski he reorganised the courts through the Crown Tribunal of 1578 and the Lithuanian Tribunal of 1581, and he raised infantry from the peasantry. He founded the Academy of Vilnius from a Jesuit college and protected Polish Jews while promoting Catholicism. Against Ivan the Terrible in the Livonian War he took Polotsk in 1579 and Velikiye Luki in 1580, and in 1581 he besieged Pskov. The Truce of Jam Zapolski of 15 January 1582 gave the Commonwealth Polotsk, Veliz and most of Livonia.

In 1584 Báthory allowed Zamoyski to execute Samuel Zborowski for treason and murder, a conflict between the king and the nobility that remained controversial. He was planning another war against Russia when he died on 12 December 1586. He left no legitimate children. He remained interested in Hungarian affairs, never learned Polish, and sponsored works about his own deeds, so that he became a recurring figure in Polish literature.
stephen-count-of-blois: Stephen Henry was the son of Theobald III, count of Blois, and Gersent of Le Mans. He is first mentioned approaching William the Conqueror to ask for the hand of his daughter Adela of Normandy, and he received it. Theobald gave him the administration of Blois and Chartres in 1074, and in 1089, on his father's death, he became count of both. The couple married around 1090 at Chartres, and they had a large family.

Stephen was one of the leaders of the First Crusade, commanding one of its major armies and often writing enthusiastic letters to his wife about its progress. He was present at the Siege of Nicaea, where he wrote that the defenders surrendered out of fear of the siege towers. Either before or at the start of the Siege of Antioch in October 1097 he was chosen as leader of the army, a role that seems not to have gone much beyond presiding over the assemblies of the leaders and handling provisioning and housekeeping for the armies.

On 2 June 1098, the day before Antioch was captured, Stephen withdrew from the siege, leaving his comrades in a difficult position as a superior Turkish army under Kerbogha approached. On the way back to the West he met the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who was marching with an army to help the crusaders, and persuaded him that the expedition was futile. Alexios turned back, which added to the crusaders' suspicion that the Byzantines were not to be trusted and to later conflicts with Byzantium.

Stephen came home with his vows unfulfilled and was in disgrace. Adela pleaded with him to make a second pilgrimage, and he joined the crusade of 1101 with others who had also returned prematurely. He took part in the disastrous campaign in Anatolia to free Bohemond from prison, then sailed from Constantinople to St Simeon and on to Jerusalem, finally fulfilling his vows.

In 1102, already on his way home, King Baldwin of Jerusalem persuaded him to fight the Fatimids at the Second Battle of Ramla. Stephen was taken prisoner and executed, probably at Ascalon on 19 May. His children included William, Count of Sully, Theobald II, Count of Champagne, Stephen, later King of England, and Henry, Bishop of Winchester. His daughter Matilda and her husband Richard d'Avranches, Earl of Chester, drowned in the White Ship disaster on 25 November 1120.
stephen-decatur: Decatur was born on 5 January 1779 at Sinepuxent, in Worcester County, Maryland, where his parents had fled from Philadelphia during the British occupation. His father, Stephen Decatur Sr., was a merchant captain who served as an officer in the navy during the Revolution, and his mother was Ann Pine. The family returned to Philadelphia, where Decatur graduated from the Episcopal Academy. In 1797 he worked for the shipbuilders Gurney and Smith on the frigate United States, and in 1798 he began his naval career as a midshipman aboard that ship under John Barry.

In the First Barbary War Decatur served from 13 May 1801 as first lieutenant of the frigate Essex. For the raid on Tripoli harbour he sailed in the Intrepid with 80 volunteers, and his promotion to captain, dated 16 February 1804, made him at twenty-five the youngest man to hold that rank in the United States Navy. On 8 March 1806 he married Susan Wheeler, daughter of the mayor of Norfolk, Virginia. He supervised the building of gunboats, sat on the court martial that found Commodore James Barron guilty of unpreparedness after the Chesapeake–Leopard affair, and in 1809 patrolled the New England coast in the Chesapeake to enforce the Embargo Act.

In the War of 1812 Decatur's squadron was trapped at New London by a British squadron under Sir Thomas Masterman Hardy from June 1813 until the end of the war. On 20 May 1815 President James Madison gave him command of the frigate Guerriere and a squadron of ten ships for the Mediterranean.

As a member of the Board of Navy Commissioners Decatur settled in Washington, where in 1818 he built a house on Lafayette Square designed by Benjamin Henry Latrobe, the first private residence near the White House. He strongly opposed the reinstatement of Barron, who had returned from Copenhagen, and Barron challenged him to a duel, in which Decatur was killed on 22 March 1820. Congress had awarded him a gold medal on 29 January 1813 for the capture of the Macedonian. Five ships of the United States Navy have been named Decatur, and his house is now a museum of the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
stephen-f-austin: Stephen Fuller Austin was born on 3 November 1793 in south-western Virginia, the son of Moses Austin and Mary Brown Austin. In 1798 the family moved to the lead-mining region of present-day Potosi, Missouri. He was educated in Connecticut and at Transylvania University in Kentucky, from which he graduated in 1810, and at 21 he was elected to the Missouri Territory legislature. Left penniless by the Panic of 1819, he moved to Arkansas Territory and then, in November 1820, to New Orleans to study law.

Moses Austin had obtained a Spanish grant to bring 300 American families to Texas, and after his death in 1821 Stephen, reluctant at first, took it over. He reached San Antonio on 12 August 1821 and learned on the way that Mexico had become independent. In December 1821 the first colonists crossed into the granted territory, and in Mexico City a law of 3 January 1823 approved the grant. By late 1825 he had brought the first 300 families, known as the Old Three Hundred, and he later gained contracts for 900 more. He held civil and military authority over the settlers and helped Mexican troops suppress the Fredonian Rebellion.

Austin was an enslaver who defended and expanded slavery in Texas. In 1826 about 25 percent of the people in his colony were enslaved, and when Article 13 of 1827 freed the children of the enslaved at birth he advised colonists to call the enslaved workingmen or family servants. He wrote that the Karankawa would have to be exterminated and in 1825 ordered them pursued and killed on sight, a policy described as genocidal. Imprisoned in Mexico from January 1834 for pressing the colonists' demands, he was freed under an amnesty in July 1835 and temporarily commanded Texian forces at the siege of Béxar.

Austin ran for president of Texas in 1836, but Sam Houston entered the race on 20 August and won, with 5,119 votes against Austin's 587. Houston appointed Austin the first secretary of state. Austin caught a severe cold and died of pneumonia on 27 December 1836, aged 43. He never married and left his estate to his sister Emily Austin Perry. Houston proclaimed that the Father of Texas was no more. The city of Austin, Austin County, Austin College and Stephen F. Austin State University are named for him.
stephen-i-of-hungary: Stephen was the only son of Grand Prince Géza and his wife Sarolt, who was descended from a prominent family of gyulas. He was given the pagan name Vajk at birth. His birth year is uncertain: later chronicles give 967, 969 and 975, and the late 11th-century and early 12th-century hagiographies, which call him still an adolescent in 997, support 975. His Lesser Legend places his birth at Esztergom. Both his parents were baptised, but Stephen was the first of the family to become a devout Christian. He married Gisela of Bavaria, a member of the Ottonian dynasty.

Géza died in 997, and an assembly at Esztergom declared Stephen grand prince. Succession by a son contradicted the older principle of seniority, under which his relative Koppány, Duke of Somogy, had the stronger claim. Koppány announced his claim, supported mostly by pagans, and Stephen defeated him with the help of foreign knights such as Vecelin, Hont and Pázmány and of native lords. Part of Koppány's quartered body was displayed at Gyulafehérvár, the seat of Gyula the Younger. Stephen was crowned with a crown sent by Pope Sylvester II, on 25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001.

In wars against semi-independent chieftains, including the Black Hungarians and Gyula the Younger, he united the Carpathian Basin. He founded an archbishopric at Esztergom, a bishopric at Kalocsa and other sees, and three Benedictine monasteries, so that the Church in Hungary developed independently of the archbishops of the Holy Roman Empire. His local administration rested on counties organised around fortresses and run by royal officials. Hungary became a route for pilgrims and merchants, and Stephen set up hostels for pilgrims in Constantinople, Jerusalem, Ravenna and Rome.

Relations with Emperor Henry II, Stephen's brother-in-law, were friendly. Under Conrad II they worsened, and in 1030 Conrad's invading army had to withdraw from Hungary; in 1031 Conrad ceded the lands between the rivers Lajta and Fischa.

Stephen's son Emeric died in a hunting accident in 1031, and Stephen survived all his children. According to the Annals of Altaich he named his sister's son, the Venetian Peter Orseolo, as heir, and his cousin Vazul, who had the strongest claim, was blinded. Stephen died on 15 August 1038 and was buried in his basilica at Székesfehérvár. Civil wars followed for decades.

King Ladislaus I initiated his canonisation, and he was canonised in 1083 with Emeric and Bishop Gerard of Csanád. His right hand, the Holy Dexter, became an object of veneration. A work of moral instruction attributed to him, the Admonitions, argues that kingship is bound to the Catholic faith. His feast day, 20 August, is a public holiday in Hungary, State Foundation Day.
stephen-i-of-iberia: Stephen, known in Georgian as Step'anoz I, was the son and successor of Guaram I of Iberia. He reversed his father's pro-Byzantine policy in favour of the Sasanid Empire and, through loyalty to his Sasanid suzerains, reunited Iberia under his rule. He made Tbilisi his capital. His rule over Kartli, as central and eastern Georgia was known, coincided with a crucial moment in the history of Georgia. His turn towards the Sasanid Empire was matched by a turn towards anti-Chalcedonian doctrine, which the catholicos of Iberia officially adopted in 598 or 599. By 608, however, the Georgian Orthodox Church had returned to the Chalcedonian position, and the sister church of Armenia broke communion with it and excommunicated its catholicos Kirion I.

Stephen was the first Georgian ruler to place the initials of his name, in stylised Georgian letters, on the obverse of the Ibero-Sasanid drachmas he minted. On the reverse he replaced the sacred flame of Zoroastrianism with the Cross. The change is read as a political act, pointing less to sympathy for Iran than to an effort to restore the autonomy of eastern Georgia and to strengthen the Christian church.

During the Byzantine–Sasanian War of 602–628 Stephen defended Tbilisi with a Georgian-Sasanian force against the army of the Byzantine emperor Heraclius and its allies. In 627 the Byzantine Empire and the Western Turkic Khaganate invaded Iberia and laid siege to Tbilisi. When the city fell, Stephen was flayed alive, and his office was given to his relative Adarnase I, of the old Chosroid house. The campaign of Heraclius brought about the final victory of the Chalcedonian faith in Iberia.
stephen-ii-duke-of-bavaria: Stephen II was the second son of Emperor Louis IV the Bavarian and his first wife, Beatrice of Silesia, and a member of the Wittelsbach dynasty. During his father's reign he served as vogt of Swabia and Alsace. Louis IV had acquired Brandenburg, Tyrol, Holland and Hainaut for his house and had reunited Bavaria in 1340. On 27 June 1328 Stephen married Elisabetta of Sicily, daughter of King Frederick III of Sicily, and all his children came from this marriage; in 1359 he married Margarete of Nuremberg.

When his father died in 1347, Stephen succeeded as Duke of Bavaria and Count of Holland and Hainaut together with his five brothers. In 1349 the country was divided again, and Stephen ruled Holland and Lower Bavaria-Landshut with his brothers William I and Albert I until 1353, and afterwards Lower Bavaria-Landshut alone. After a reconciliation with Emperor Charles IV he joined the emperor's expedition to Italy in 1354, but the Golden Bull of 1356 caused a new conflict, as only the Palatinate branch and his brother Louis VI the Roman received the electoral dignity. In 1362 he was absolved from excommunication.

When Duke Meinhard, son of his elder brother Louis V the Brandenburger, died in 1363, Stephen succeeded in Upper Bavaria and invaded Tyrol, allying himself with Bernabò Visconti against Rudolf IV, Duke of Austria. After the death of Margarete Maultasch in 1369 he gave up Tyrol to the Habsburgs in the Peace of Schärding for a large payment. His quarrel with Louis VI over Meinhard's inheritance led Louis to make Charles IV his heir, which in the end cost the Wittelsbach dynasty Brandenburg.

Stephen died at Landshut on 13 May 1375 and is buried in the Frauenkirche in Munich. His three sons, Stephen III, Frederick and John II, succeeded him; two of them, Stephen III and Frederick, married daughters of his ally Bernabò Visconti. His daughter Agnes married King James I of Cyprus.
stephen-ii-kotromanic: Stephen was the son of Ban Stephen I Kotromanić and Elizabeth, a sister of King Stefan Vladislav II, and a member of the Kotromanić dynasty. When his father died in 1314, his mother fled with her children into exile in the Republic of Ragusa. Mladen II Šubić, the Croatian ban who then held Bosnia but was unpopular there, decided to install the young Stephen as his vassal, expecting the Bosnians to accept him and hoping to use him against the Bosnian Church.

After the death of the Serbian King Stefan Uroš II Milutin in 1321, Stephen took the lands of Usora and Soli, which he fully incorporated in 1324. He won support by granting privileges to the local nobility, and from 1326 his brother Vladislav Kotromanić shared the rule as Prince of Bosnia, although the real power stayed with Stephen. In 1324 he backed Juraj II Šubić against Prince Ivan Nelipić in Croatia.

The conquest of Hum, made in alliance with Ragusa, gave Bosnia the coast from the mouth of the Neretva to Konavle and brought in areas with a large Orthodox population; he also expanded into Završje, with the fields of Glamoč, Duvno and Livno. The Pope sent the Franciscan Fabian as inquisitor to root out heresy in Bosnia, but the effort failed. After King Charles Robert of Hungary died in 1342, Stephen sought an alliance with the Republic of Venice in order to rule independently, but Venice offered only help in arming him.

Emperor Stefan Dušan of Serbia repeatedly demanded the return of Hum, which Stephen refused. At Christmas 1349 Stephen raided Konavli as far as the Bay of Kotor, razing Trebinje, Gacko and Rudine. In October 1350 Dušan crossed the Drina with 50,000 cavalry and 30,000 infantry. Stephen avoided open battle, blocked the roads with timber and rock and withdrew to forests, mountains and forts, but several of his trusted servants were bribed and abandoned their posts.

After 1352 Stephen called himself Herzeg of Bosnia, after the German title, and married relatives to Count Ulrich of Helfenstein and Count Hermann I of Celje. His daughter Elizabeth was raised for three years at the Hungarian court at the wish of the king's mother, Elizabeth of Poland; Stephen was gravely ill and missed her wedding. He died in September 1353 and was buried in his own foundation, the Franciscan church of Saint Nicholas at Mile near Visoko. His underage nephew Tvrtko succeeded him, with Vladislav governing in his name. In his edicts to Ragusa Stephen called his people Bosnians (Bošnjani).
stephen-king-of-england: Stephen was born in Blois in France, the fourth son of Stephen-Henry, Count of Blois and Chartres, who was killed at the battle of Ramlah while on crusade when Stephen was at most ten years old. His mother, Adela, daughter of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders, was known for her piety and strong personality and shaped his upbringing. Placed in the court of his uncle Henry I of England, he rose in prominence and was granted extensive lands. By his marriage to Matilda of Boulogne in 1125 he gained estates in Kent and Boulogne.

In 1120 Stephen planned to sail on the White Ship from Barfleur but left it at the last moment. The ship sank with the heir to the throne, William Adelin, and nearly all its passengers, which left the succession open to challenge.

When Henry I died in 1135, Stephen crossed the Channel and took the throne with the help of his brother Henry, Bishop of Winchester, arguing that keeping order took priority over his earlier oaths to support the Empress Matilda. In 1138 Robert, Earl of Gloucester, renounced his fealty and declared for Matilda, while Geoffrey of Anjou invaded Normandy and David I of Scotland invaded northern England. Stephen created many new earldoms for loyal supporters, many of them for his advisor Waleran de Beaumont and his family.

Matilda and Robert landed in England on 30 September 1139 with 140 knights. At the Battle of Lincoln on 2 February 1141 Stephen fought on foot, and after his sword broke he used a borrowed battle axe, but he was overwhelmed and taken prisoner. He was freed only after his wife and William of Ypres captured Robert at the Rout of Winchester. By 1147 England had suffered extensively, and the chronicle of the time recorded nothing but disturbance and wickedness and robbery. The royal coinage fragmented, and unauthorised castles multiplied.

Late in his reign Stephen sought to have his son Eustace crowned, but Pope Eugene III refused. In 1153 Henry, the Empress's son, invaded England. The armies met at Wallingford, but neither side's barons wished to fight another pitched battle, and the sudden death of Eustace hastened peace. By the Treaty of Winchester Stephen recognised Henry as his heir, passing over his second son William. He died on 25 October 1154, and Henry II succeeded him. Modern historians have debated whether his personality, external events or weaknesses in the Norman state caused the long civil war.
stephen-of-perm: Stephen was born around 1340 in Ustyug in northern Russia, where the native Komi, also called Zyrians or western Permians, lived beside a minority of Russians. His father was a cathedral cleric, and Stephen mastered reading and writing in Russian early and became a lector. He took his monastic vows in Rostov, where he learned Greek and the trade of a copyist, and befriended Epiphanius the Wise, who later wrote his biography, and Sergius of Radonezh, though he did not become Sergius's disciple.

Around 1370 Stephen began to create an alphabet for the Zyrians, without Russian influence, despite the trilingual heresy current in some Byzantine and Russian circles. He then travelled to the lands along the Vychegda and Vym rivers and began converting the Komi. Where contemporary missionaries imposed Latin or Church Slavonic, he learned the people's language and traditions and devised a distinct writing system, the second oldest for a Uralic language. His destruction of pagan idols, such as holy birches, earned him the anger of some Permians. Pimen, head of the Russian Orthodox Church, created the bishopric of Perm in 1383 and consecrated Stephen as its first bishop. He settled at Ust-Vym and preached in Komi, and most of the Komi were baptised.

The new bishopric threatened Novgorod's control of the region's tribute. In 1385 Archbishop Aleksei of Novgorod sent an army to remove it, but the bishopric, helped by the city of Ustyug, defeated it. In 1386 Stephen visited Novgorod, and the city and its archbishop formally accepted the new situation. Afterwards the tribute went to Moscow, part of a wider shift of the northern fur trade from Novgorod to Moscow.

Stephen died in Moscow on 26 April 1396 and was canonised by the Russian Orthodox Church in 1549. He is called the Enlightener of Perm or the Apostle of the Permians, is regarded as the founder of the Permian written tradition, and is commemorated on 26 April. The historian Serge Aleksandrovich Zenkovsky wrote that he, Epiphanius the Wise, Sergius of Radonezh and the painter Andrei Rublev signified the Russian spiritual and cultural revival of the late 14th and early 15th century. Epiphanius wrote the Life of Stephen of Perm and a Panegyric to him, styling him the creator of Permian letters.
stephen-the-great: Stephen was the son of Bogdan, himself a son of Alexander the Good, Prince of Moldavia, and of Maria Oltea. His birth date is unknown, and historians estimate it between 1433 and 1440. The death of Alexander the Good in 1432 began a succession crisis of more than two decades. Bogdan seized the throne in 1449 with the support of John Hunyadi, and Stephen was styled voivode in his charters as his heir and co-ruler. In 1450 father and son repulsed a Polish invasion. Peter III Aaron murdered Bogdan in October 1451, and Stephen fled to Hungary. He won the throne in 1457 at the Battle of Orbic with the support of his cousin Vlad the Impaler.

Stephen captured the Danube port of Chilia in January 1465 and ordered the Church of the Assumption at Putna in 1466 to commemorate it. After repulsing Matthias Corvinus of Hungary at the Battle of Baia, he stopped paying tribute to the Ottoman sultan in 1473. He then invaded Wallachia to replace Radu the Fair, an Ottoman-installed vassal, with his own protégé, Basarab III Laiotă, and took Bucharest. Each prince he put on the throne was soon forced to pay homage to the sultan. In 1475 he defeated a large Ottoman army at the Battle of Vaslui, and Pope Sixtus IV called him Athleta Christi, Champion of Christ, though promised support never came.

The following year Mehmed II routed Stephen at the Battle of Valea Albă but withdrew from Moldavia for lack of provisions, a failed siege of Neamț and an outbreak of plague. The Ottomans and their Crimean Tatar allies took Chilia and Cetatea Albă in 1484, and Stephen's efforts to recover them failed. From 1486 he again paid a yearly tribute to the Ottomans. He played Poland, Hungary and the Ottomans against each other, and defeated the Polish army of John I Albert at the Battle of the Cosmin Forest in 1497. In 1502 he and his Crimean Tatar allies destroyed the remnants of the Golden Horde at the Battle of Samara River. He acknowledged the loss of his ports to the Ottomans in 1503.

Stephen died on 2 July 1504 after a reign of more than 47 years, during his last years sharing government with his son Bogdan III. He restored old fortresses and built new ones, and from 1487 more than a dozen stone churches were built at his initiative, among them Voroneț in 1488 and Tazlău in 1496 to 1497. They mixed Byzantine and Gothic elements with local tradition and helped form a Moldavian style of architecture. The Romanian Orthodox Church canonised him in 1992, and he is regarded as a national hero in Romania and Moldova.
stephen-tomasevic: Stephen Tomašević was born about 1438 into the Kotromanić dynasty, a son of the Bosnian prince Thomas by a commoner, Vojača. Thomas became king in 1443 and converted from the Bosnian Church to Roman Catholicism about 1445. In 1459 he arranged his son's marriage to Helen, eldest daughter of the late Lazar Branković, Despot of Serbia, who took the name Maria. It was meant to unite Bosnia and the Serbian Despotate against the Ottomans.

Stephen took the Serbian throne at Smederevo on 21 March 1459, but his Catholicism made him unpopular. When Sultan Mehmed II attacked, he surrendered the fortress on 20 June 1459 and fled to Bosnia. Matthias Corvinus of Hungary accused him of selling it for gold, an allegation the sources do not support.

Stephen succeeded his father on 10 July 1461. He made peace with the powerful nobleman Stjepan Vukčić Kosača, and on 17 November 1461 a papal legate crowned him in Jajce with a crown sent from Rome, the last coronation in Bosnia. He corresponded with Pope Pius II, but Western rulers refused help.

By spring 1462 it was known that Mehmed meant to conquer Bosnia. Kosača's quarrel with his son Vladislav Hercegović broke out again, and Vladislav sought help from Mehmed. In June 1462, relying on Matthias, Stephen refused the customary tribute. In the spring of 1463 Mehmed marched into Bosnia with an army of 150,000 men. Bobovac fell within days, and Stephen was pursued to Ključ, where he surrendered on a written promise that no harm would come to him.

Mehmed's mullah, Ali al-Bistami, ruled that the sultan was not bound by a promise made without his knowledge. Stephen was beheaded on 25 May 1463 in a field near Jajce, with his uncle Radivoj, his cousin and two noblemen. His fall ended the Kingdom of Bosnia, which submitted within weeks. His half-siblings were taken to Constantinople and converted to Islam, and his stepmother, Queen Catherine, campaigned unsuccessfully from the Papal States for the kingdom's restoration.
stephen-w-kearny: Stephen Watts Kearny was born on 30 August 1794 in Newark, New Jersey, the fifteenth and youngest child of Philip III and Susanna Watts Kearny; his father, of Irish ancestry, was a wine merchant and landowner in Perth Amboy. He studied for two years at Columbia University and joined the New York militia as an ensign in 1812. In the War of 1812 he was commissioned a first lieutenant in the 13th Infantry. At the Battle of Queenston Heights on 13 October 1812 he and Lieutenant Colonel Winfield Scott led a charge that took the British position, but the militia failed to reinforce them. Wounded and captured, Kearny spent months in captivity, which hardened his prejudice against militias.

After the war he served on the western frontier under General Henry Atkinson, on the Yellowstone Expedition of 1819 and the 1825 expedition that reached the mouth of the Yellowstone River. In 1826 he became the first commander of Jefferson Barracks at St. Louis, and in the late 1820s he married Mary Radford, stepdaughter of William Clark; they had eleven children, six of whom died in childhood. In 1833 he became second in command of the new 1st Dragoon Regiment, from which the U.S. Cavalry later grew, and its colonel in 1836. In 1845 he led the dragoons on a reconnaissance of over 2,000 miles to South Pass and back in 99 days.

In California, after San Pasqual, a force of about 600 men including his dragoons retook Los Angeles on 10 January 1847. Kearny then quarrelled with Commodore Robert F. Stockton over command, since the War Department had set no rule for it, and Stockton made John C. Frémont military governor. Once reinforcements arrived, Kearny took command and had Frémont court-martialed for insubordination.

Kearny was later governor of Veracruz and then of Mexico City, and in September 1848 he received a brevet promotion to major general over the opposition of Senator Thomas Hart Benton, Frémont's father-in-law. He caught yellow fever in Veracruz and died in St. Louis on 31 October 1848, aged 54. The historian Allan Nevins, writing of the quarrel with Frémont, called him "a stern-tempered soldier who made few friends and many enemies". Kearny, Arizona, Kearney, Nebraska, Fort Kearny and Kearny Street in San Francisco are named after him.
steponas-darius: He was born Steponas Jucevičius-Darašius on 8 January 1896 in Rubiškės, in the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire, and emigrated to the United States with his family in 1907. In 1917, after the United States entered World War I, he joined the United States Army and changed his name to Darius. He served as a telephone operator in the 149th Field Artillery Regiment, fought in France, was wounded and received the Purple Heart.

In 1920 he returned to Lithuania and joined the Lithuanian Army, graduating from the War School of Kaunas in 1921, and he took part in the Klaipėda Revolt of 1923. While in Lithuania he completed pilot training and promoted many sports. He played for the Lithuania national football team in its first competitive game, against Estonia on 23 June 1923, and was in the squad for the 1924 Summer Olympics without playing a match.

He initiated the building of the first stadium in Kaunas, later named the S. Darius and S. Girėnas Stadium. As the first to publish booklets on basketball and baseball, he is considered to have brought both sports to Lithuania; he was also the first chairman of the Lithuanian Physical Education Union and a founder of Sporto Žurnalas. In 1927 he returned to the United States to work in civil aviation, forming South Bend Airways with Carl G. Jordan of South Bend, Indiana, before moving to Chicago.

Darius and Stasys Girėnas left New York City on 15 July 1933 in a Bellanca CH-300 Pacemaker, aiming to cover 7,186 kilometres without landing. They crashed at 0:36 am Berlin time on 17 July by the village of Kuhdamm, near Soldin (now Pszczelnik, in Poland), most probably because of bad weather combined with engine problems. They had flown 6,411 kilometres and were 650 kilometres short of Kaunas.

On 18 May 1934 Lithuania issued six airmail stamps in honour of the two captains and the Lituanica. A monument to them stands in Marquette Park in Chicago, a World War II Liberty ship was named SS Stepas Darius, his birth village was renamed Darius, and the asteroid 288960 Steponasdarius, discovered in 2004, bears his name.
stepwell: A stepwell has two parts: a vertical shaft from which water is drawn, and the inclined passages, chambers and steps that give access to it. The galleries and chambers around the shaft were often carved profusely and became cool, quiet retreats in the hot summers. Some stepwells have several storeys, and water could be raised to the first or second floor by a Persian wheel pulled by a bull.

The names vary by region. In Hindi-speaking areas they include baoli, baori and bavadi, in Gujarati and Marwari vav or vavri, and in Kannada kalyani or pushkarani. A related form, the stepped pond, usually stands beside a temple, is open to the sun and is rectangular, whereas a stepwell is dark, more linear and more isolated.

A stepwell may have first appeared in periods of drought to secure access to water. Dholavira has tanks with flights of steps, and the great bath at Mohenjo-daro has steps on opposite sides. Ashoka's Pillar Edict No 7 says that wells were dug and flights of steps built every eight kos along roads, and that this was an old practice of former kings.

One of the earliest bath-like ponds reached by steps lies in the Uperkot caves at Junagadh, dated to the 4th century, and the stepwells at Dhank in Rajkot district are dated to 550-625 CE. The Mata Bhavani stepwell in Gujarat, built in the 11th century, is among the earliest surviving examples and has elaborately ornamented columns, brackets and beams.

Stepwells gave water in a land where fresh water is abundant only in the monsoon. Because they were built without mortar, groundwater filtered through the stone, and at depth the water was less exposed to sun and heat. Most surviving stepwells served for bathing, washing, farming and watering animals, and as places for social gatherings and religious ceremonies. Women, who collected the water, prayed at them and offered gifts to the goddess of the well. Stepwells were also thought to spread disease, since the water attracted insects and animals.

The Mughal emperors encouraged the building of stepwells, while British authorities in the Raj found their hygiene poor and installed pipes and pumps. Babur's garden at Agra, the Aram Bagh, is said to have drawn on stepwells for its reflecting pool. The Stepwell Atlas, begun in 2016, mapped over 2,800 stepwells in India, and some have been restored to their original purpose as water shortages have grown.
stesichorus: Ancient tradition has Stesichorus born at Metauros, modern Gioia Tauro in Calabria, around 630 BCE and dying at Katane, modern Catania, in Sicily around 555 BCE. Some say he came from Himera, which they explain by a later move there from Metauros. He was thought to have been exiled from Pallantium in Arcadia. The Suda says his name was originally Tisias and that he was called Stesichorus because he first established a chorus of singers to the cithara. Its claim that Hesiod was his father is called fantasy by modern writers. Aristotle mentions two public speeches by him, one warning the people of Himera against Phalaris and another warning the people of Locri against presumption.

According to the Suda his works, in the Doric dialect, filled 26 books, each probably a long narrative poem. Titles recorded include Helen, Sack of Troy, Nostoi, Geryoneis, Cerberus, Cycnus, Eriphyle, Europa, Oresteia and Boar-hunters. The Geryoneis, on Heracles' theft of Geryon's cattle, ran to about 1500 lines. Papyri show that he composed in units of three stanzas, strophe, antistrophe and epode, a form later used by Bacchylides and Pindar. His best-known poem is the Palinode, written, according to ancient accounts, after he was blinded for abusing Helen. It absolves her of blame for the Trojan War: in one version she never sailed to Troy, and in another only her image reached Troy while she went to Egypt.

Quintilian wrote that he sustained the weight of epic poetry on his lyre and might have rivalled Homer had he shown restraint, but that he was redundant and diffuse. Many modern scholars hold that his narratives were composed for solo performance with the lyre rather than for choirs.

Stesichorus ranked among the nine lyric poets esteemed by the scholars of Alexandria, yet few fragments survive. David Campbell wrote that time has dealt more harshly with him than with any other major lyric poet. Discoveries on Egyptian papyrus, notably the disputed Lille Stesichorus, confirm his role as a link between Homer's epic narrative and the lyric narrative of Pindar. He influenced the representation of myth in sixth-century art and the development of Athenian drama.
stethoscope: The word comes from the Ancient Greek stêthos, breast, and skopéō, to look. Laennec's wooden tube was similar to the common ear trumpet, a historical form of hearing aid. He called his device the stethoscope, meaning chest scope, and called its use mediate auscultation, because it was listening with a tool intermediate between the body and the physician's ear. Today auscultation means all such listening, mediate or not.

The first flexible stethoscope of any sort may have been a binaural instrument with articulated joints, not very clearly described in 1829. When Golding Bird published his description in 1840 he noted an earlier design that he thought of little use, which he called the snake ear trumpet.

An acoustic stethoscope carries sound from the chest piece through air-filled hollow tubes to the listener's ears. The chest piece usually has two sides, a diaphragm, a plastic disc, and a bell, a hollow cup. The bell transmits low-frequency sounds and the diaphragm higher ones. An electronic stethoscope amplifies body sounds and can record them or transmit them wirelessly. A fetal stethoscope, shaped like a listening trumpet and also known as a Pinard horn after the French obstetrician Adolphe Pinard, is placed against a pregnant woman's abdomen. The stethophone, described by Somerville Scott Alison at the Royal Society in 1858, had two separate bells for comparing sounds from two places.

Cammann also wrote a major treatise on diagnosis by auscultation, which the binaural stethoscope made possible. The medical historian Jacalyn Duffin has argued that the invention helped to redefine disease from a bundle of symptoms to a problem of an anatomical system, even where no symptoms are visible, because before it there were no non-lethal instruments for exploring internal anatomy.

In the early 1960s David Littmann, a Harvard Medical School professor, produced a lighter stethoscope with better acoustics. In 1999 Richard Deslauriers patented the first external noise-reducing stethoscope, the DRG Puretone. The stethoscope has also become a symbol of healthcare professionals.
stevan-supljikac: Stevan Šupljikac was born in Petrinja in 1786. He had a brother, Jovan, who was also a fighter, and a sister, Anka, who later married Gabriel Miletić. He entered the Austrian army in 1805 and later rose to the rank of general. Between 1806 and 1814 he served as an officer of the Imperial French army, and during the Russian Campaign of 1812 he was awarded the Légion d'honneur.

Back in Austrian service from 1814, he commanded the Ogulin regiment in the Banat and Lika and then served as a brigade commander under Joseph Radetzky von Radetz, receiving the Great Cross of the Iron Crown. In 1848 he took part in the suppression of Italian rebels during the Unification of Italy.

In the Revolutions of 1848 the Serbs under Austrian rule demanded the recognition of Serbian as an official language, equality of the Orthodox church with the Catholic, and annual church assemblies. Several thousand Serbs met at the May Assembly in Sremski Karlovci on 1 May 1848, which chose Šupljikac as voivode, the civil and military commander, and elected Josif Rajačić patriarch. They demanded a national unit made up of the Banat, Bačka, Baranja and part of Srem, known together as Vojvodina.

Fighting between Hungarian and Serbian bands began in Vojvodina in June. A large wave of volunteers came from the Principality in June and July, and Stevan Knićanin, elected military commander, arrived on 25 July. While the Hungarians were hostile, Vienna supported the Serbs: the new emperor Franz Joseph approved the establishment of the Serbian Vojvodina with Šupljikac as its duke, its first voivode. On 6 October he became supreme military commander of the Serbian national troops. He died at Pančevo on 15 December 1848 and was buried in the Krušedol Monastery.
steve-biko: Bantu Stephen Biko was born on 18 December 1946 at his grandmother's house in Tarkastad, Cape Province. His family settled in Ginsberg township at King William's Town, where Xhosa, Afrikaans and English were all spoken. His father, a former police officer who worked as a clerk, died in 1950, and the family depended on his mother's wages as a cook. Advised that law was too closely tied to political activism, Biko entered the University of Natal Medical School in 1966 and was soon elected to the Students' Representative Council.

Biko joined the National Union of South African Students but grew frustrated that white liberals dominated it and, in his view, failed to understand the black experience. He became a leading figure in founding the South African Students' Organisation, launched in July 1969, and was elected its first president. Influenced by Frantz Fanon, Malcolm X and the Black Power movement, the organisation adopted Black Consciousness as its ideology.

Biko rejected the government's division of the population into whites and non-whites, which he saw as defining people by an absence. He described blackness as a mental attitude rather than a matter of pigmentation and applied the word to Africans, Coloureds and Indians. He urged black people to free themselves of any sense of inferiority, popularised the slogan "black is beautiful", and hoped for a non-racial South Africa with one person, one vote.

The government came to regard Biko as a subversive threat and banned him in 1973. On 17 August 1977 he broke the order by driving to Cape Town with his friend Peter Jones. On 18 August they were stopped at a police roadblock near Grahamstown and arrested. Biko was beaten to death by state security officers and died on 12 September 1977. More than 20,000 people attended his funeral.

Biko is regarded as the father of Black Consciousness and as the first icon of the anti-apartheid movement. Nelson Mandela called him "the spark that lit a veld fire across South Africa". Peter Gabriel's song "Biko" was a hit in 1980 and was banned in South Africa, and Donald Woods's 1978 biography of him was the basis of the film Cry Freedom. His political legacy remains a matter of contention.
steyr: Celts settled the area from about 600 BCE, and their kingdom of Noricum became part of the Roman Empire in 15 BCE. The Roman Iron Road led from the Erzberg mine along the Enns River to the camp of Lauriacum on the Danube. Slavic settlers who moved in during the 6th century were defeated by Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria, who granted the land to Kremsmünster Abbey in 777.

A fortress above the Steyr River, built by the Traungau counts during the Hungarian invasions, is first mentioned as Styraburg in a deed of 980. From 1055 the castle and the adjacent March of Styria were ruled by the Otakar dynasty, who controlled the iron mining at the Erzberg and made Steyr a centre of courtly culture and Middle High German poetry.

In 1180 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised Margrave Ottokar IV to Duke of Styria, but the line died out in 1192 and under the Georgenberg Pact of 1186 his lands passed to the Babenberg dukes of Austria. Steyr then lost its importance as a residence but remained a centre of ironworking, producing mainly knives and arms.

After the Habsburg king Rudolf I won the Battle on the Marchfeld in 1278, his son King Albert I confirmed the town privileges and market rights in 1287, and the citizens profited from a preferred place in the iron trade of the Holy Roman Empire, above all with Venice. In the 13th and 14th centuries Steyr was a centre of the Waldensian movement, and the Reformation spread quickly there from about 1525.

The iron trade declined during the Thirty Years' War and the Peasants' War of 1626. A fire in 1727 destroyed the medieval Styraburg, which the Baroque Lamberg Castle replaced. The Armistice of Steyr was signed there on 25 December 1800.

Steyr is a statutory city in Upper Austria, where the Steyr and Enns rivers meet beneath Lamberg Castle. The firm of Leopold Werndl, founded in 1830, became a stock company in 1864 and later the Steyr-Werke, which merged with Austro-Daimler and Puch in 1934. The town was heavily bombed in February 1944. Its historic centre around the Stadtplatz was restored after the war, and the Gothic Bummerlhaus is among its best-known buildings.
stilicho: Stilicho was the son of a Vandal cavalry officer and a provincial Roman woman. There is little to suggest that he saw himself as anything but a Roman, and he was probably a Nicene Christian like his patron Theodosius I. The main sources are the panegyrics of the poet Claudian, whom he patronised and who portrays him in a positive light, and, for the years after 404, Zosimus, who drew on one historian hostile to Stilicho and one supportive.

He rose through the army under Theodosius, who sent him in 383 to the court of the Persian king Shapur III at Ctesiphon to negotiate over the partition of Armenia. He then married Serena, the niece of Theodosius, and was promoted to senior commands. After the Battle of the Frigidus Theodosius appointed him guardian of his son Honorius, shortly before the emperor's death in 395.

Honorius became emperor in the West and his brother Arcadius in the East. Stilicho became the de facto commander-in-chief of the western armies and tied himself to the throne by giving Honorius his daughter Maria in marriage in 398 and, after her death, Thermantia in 408. In 395 he led the army into the Balkans against the Goths of Alaric but obeyed an order from Arcadius to send back the eastern troops. He defeated Alaric's forces in Macedonia in 397 and put down the revolt of Gildo in Africa.

In 402 he broke Alaric's siege of Mediolanum, where Honorius was living, and defeated him at the Battle of Pollentia on Easter Sunday, the last victory marked by a triumphal march in Rome. In 406 he surprised and captured the force of Radagaisus at Florentia, executed Radagaisus and enrolled 12,000 of his warriors, selling the rest into slavery.

To defend Italy Stilicho had weakened the Rhine frontier, and on 31 December 406 a coalition of Vandals, Alans and Suevi crossed it and devastated Gaul. His reputation never recovered. He failed to put down the rebellion of Constantine III in Britain. After rumours that he intended to place his son on the throne, the army at Ticinum mutinied on 13 August 408 and killed senior officers. Stilicho retired to Ravenna, did not resist arrest and was executed on 22 August 408. His son Eucherius was killed soon after.

In the disturbances the families of barbarian federates in Italy were massacred, and perhaps 30,000 of these soldiers joined Alaric, who stood before Rome by September 408 and sacked it in August 410. Many historians hold that the removal of Stilicho was the main catalyst of that event.
stip: Štip lies in the eastern part of North Macedonia, where the Lakavica, Ovče Pole and Kočani valleys meet. Two rivers pass through it: the Bregalnica, the second longest in the country, and the Otinja, which divides the city centre. The Isar hill, crowned by an early medieval fortress, dominates the town, which is commonly described as the town under the Isar. The name developed from the ancient Astibos to the Byzantine Stipeon and the modern Štip. The ancient writer Polyaenus records that the Paeonian kings bathed ritually in the river Astibo as a coronation rite.

The capital of the Paeonian royal house was probably in the area of Astibos. In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE the Paeonians lived west of the Axius basin, and two tribes lived along the Astibo: the Derrones, named after their god of healing Darron, and the Laeaeans, who minted heavy coins. The Persian invasion of 480 BCE under Xerxes I weakened them, and they were absorbed into the Macedonian realm before 360 BCE.

A settlement called Estipeon is first mentioned under the emperor Tiberius as an important place in the Roman province of Macedonia and a stop on the road from Stobi to Pautalia. In the 6th century Slavs raided the Balkans and destroyed the Byzantine settlement, and the Slavic tribe of the Sagudates settled the area permanently.

Štip belonged to the Bulgarian Empire until the Byzantine victory at Kleidion in 1014, and it was Byzantine again until Bulgaria was re-established in 1185. From the mid-13th century it changed hands several times. By 1284 the Serbian king Stefan Milutin had conquered the region, and in 1334 a charter of Stefan Dušan gave the Church of the Holy Archangel, built by the protosebastos Hrelja, to the Hilandar monastery. It was annexed in 1385 by the Ottoman Empire and made it the seat of a sanjak; it was held by Austria only in 1689–1690.

In 1912 Bulgaria occupied it in the First Balkan War, but in 1913 all of Vardar Macedonia was annexed by the Kingdom of Serbia, and from 1929 to 1941 Štip belonged to the Vardar Banovina of Yugoslavia.

Štip is the centre of the textile and fashion industry of North Macedonia and has the Goce Delčev University. Its three 14th-century churches date from the time of medieval Serbia: St Michael under the Isar, built in 1332, St John the Baptist, built in 1350, and the Ascension church, built in 1369, which keeps 14th-century frescoes. The Bezisten, a stone Ottoman indoor bazaar, is now an art gallery. The ruins of the ancient city of Bargala lie nearby.
stirling: Stirling lies on the River Forth, 42 km north-east of Glasgow and 60 km north-west of Edinburgh. It stands where the flatter Lowlands meet the slopes of the Highlands along the Highland Boundary Fault, and for this reason it is called the Gateway to the Highlands. To the west and east stretches the Carse of Stirling, one of the flattest and most productive expanses of farmland in Scotland. Control of the lowest crossing point of the Forth brought military advantage in times of unrest and tolls in peacetime. Stirling remained the river's lowest reliable crossing until the Alloa Swing Bridge was built in 1885.

Stirling's oldest catalogued artefact is a stone cist found in 1879, whose bones were radiocarbon dated to between 2152 and 2021 BCE. Prehistoric carvings of cup and ring marks near King's Park date to about 3000 BCE, and Iron Age forts stand on Gillies Hill. David I created Stirling a royal burgh between 1124 and 1127. The name appears as Strivelin in early sources; scholars once thought it Brittonic, but a survey of 2017 derives it from Gaelic srib-linn, a pool in the river. A 9th-century legend says a wolf's howl woke a sentry when Danish invaders attacked, and the wolf became a symbol of the town.

On 29 July 1567 the infant James VI was anointed King of Scots in the Church of the Holy Rude, and he grew up in Stirling, educated by George Buchanan. James III and his queen, Margaret of Denmark, are buried at Cambuskenneth Abbey; the king died at the Battle of Sauchieburn. The Battle of Stirling was fought in the town on 12 September 1648. The earl of Mar failed to take the castle in 1715, and in January 1746 the army of Bonnie Prince Charlie took the town but not the castle, blowing up the church of St Ninians, where it had stored munitions. Only the tower survives.

Stirling is visually dominated by Stirling Castle, once a principal royal stronghold of the Kingdom of Scotland. It was granted city status in 2002 and is the administrative centre of the Stirling council area. The old town below the castle keeps its cobbled streets and buildings such as Mar's Wark and Argyll's Lodging. The University of Stirling opened in 1967. The custom of Walking the Marches, which inspects the town's boundaries each year, is thought to have begun in the 12th century.
stirlingshire: Stirlingshire lies on the Forth-Clyde isthmus, commanding the main overland routes from Glasgow and Edinburgh to central and northern Scotland. It borders Perthshire to the north, Clackmannanshire to the east, West Lothian to the south-east, Lanarkshire to the south and Dunbartonshire to the south and south-west. Its sparsely peopled western arm is dominated by Loch Lomond and the Trossachs, with Ben Lomond, at 974 metres, its highest point. The Campsie Fells, Kilsyth Hills and Gargunnock Hills fill the centre, while the flatter east, opening on the Firth of Forth, holds most of the population.

In 1130 King David I made Stirling, one of the principal royal strongholds of the Kingdom of Scotland, a royal burgh, and the shire itself seems to have been created in his reign, though its origins are obscure. Besides Stirling Bridge and Bannockburn, the county saw King Edward I of England defeat William Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk on 22 July 1298, and the Battle of Sauchieburn on 11 June 1488, where rebel nobles nominally led by the 15-year-old Prince James, Duke of Rothesay, fought the followers of King James III of Scotland.

In 1645 the Covenanter army under General William Baillie formed near Banton to meet the Royalist forces of Montrose at the Battle of Kilsyth on 15 August, a major battle of the Wars of the Three Kingdoms. On 17 January 1746 the Jacobites under Charles Edward Stuart beat a government army under Lieutenant General Henry Hawley at the Battle of Falkirk Muir. The shire's boundary with Dunbartonshire shifted several times, the parishes of Kirkintilloch and Cumbernauld passing between the two counties in the 13th century, in 1504 and again in 1509.

Commissioners of Supply governed the shire from 1667, and an elected county council first met in Stirling on 22 May 1890. The reforms of 1889 took Milngavie, Alva and part of Lecropt from the county and gave it Cambuskenneth and parts of Kippen and Logie. The council's coat of arms, granted in 1890, set the red lion of Scotland on the saltire of St Andrew with caltraps and spur-rowels recalling Bannockburn.

Stirlingshire was abolished for local government in 1975, most of it passing to the Central region and the area around Kilsyth to Strathclyde. Since 1996 its former area has been divided among the council areas of East Dunbartonshire, Falkirk, North Lanarkshire and Stirling. Its pre-1975 boundaries survive as a registration county used in land registration.
stirrup: The stirrup came late in history, since horses were domesticated in about 4000 BCE and the earliest saddle-like equipment, fringed cloths or pads, was used by Assyrian cavalry around 700 BCE. The earliest hard foot support was a toe loop holding the big toe, used in India late in the 2nd century BCE and possibly as early as 500 BCE. Buddhist carvings at Sanchi, Mathura and the Bhaja caves show horsemen with toes slipped under girths, and the archaeologist John Marshall called the Sanchi relief the earliest example of stirrups by some five centuries.

The solid saddle tree allowed the true stirrup to develop, since without it the rider's weight creates pressure points that make the horse's back sore. Some credit the Sarmatians with the first stirrups.

The earliest extant pair of stirrups was found in the tomb of the Northern Yan noble Feng Sufu, who died in 415, made of mulberry wood gilded with bronze and iron plates. Stirrups are mentioned in Chinese texts by the end of the 4th century, and their appearance coincided with the rise of heavily armoured cavalry, which dominated Chinese warfare until the early Tang dynasty. In Japan the earliest stirrups come from 5th-century tombs.

In Europe, stirrups were adopted more widely by the 8th century, but they were rare in western graves: of 704 eighth-century male burials excavated in Germany by 1967, only 13 had them. In Denmark in the 920s to 980s, under the Jelling kings, many leading men were buried with stirrups, bits and spurs. Accounts of the Empire of Mali also mention stirrups and saddles in its cavalry.

The stirrup has been called one of the most significant inventions in the history of warfare before gunpowder, the third step in equipment after the chariot and the saddle. A rider supported by stirrups was less likely to fall and could deliver a blow with the weight and momentum of horse and rider. Some scholars credit it with the birth of feudalism. Others argue that it gives little advantage in shock warfare and mainly lets a rider lean further to either side, so that it was not the reason for the shift from infantry to cavalry. In the Ottoman and Mughal empires the stirrup became a symbol of the ruler's presence.
stjepan-radic: Stjepan Radić was born in Desno Trebarjevo, near Sisak, in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia within Austria-Hungary, the ninth of eleven children. Expelled from his gymnasium in Zagreb, he finished school in Karlovac. In 1888 he visited Bishop Josip Juraj Strossmayer in Đakovo to ask for help with a journey to the Russian Empire, and stayed six weeks at the Monastery of the Caves in Kiev.

He enrolled in law at the University of Zagreb in September 1891. In 1893 he called the Ban of Croatia, Károly Khuen-Héderváry, a "Magyar hussar" and served four months in prison. After students burned the Hungarian tricolour on 16 October 1895, during Emperor Franz Joseph's visit to Zagreb, he was imprisoned again, expelled and barred from every university in the Monarchy. He graduated in 1899 from the École libre des sciences politiques in Paris.

After the First World War Radić opposed merging Croatia with the Kingdom of Serbia without guarantees of Croatian autonomy. On 24 November 1918 he urged delegates not to "rush like geese into fog", and he was the only member of the National Council's central committee to vote against sending a delegation to Belgrade. A resolution he wrote on 8 March 1919 refused to recognise the new kingdom, and he was arrested and held until February 1920.

His party won 50 of 419 seats in the elections of November 1920 and stayed out of parliament, becoming the Croatian Republican Peasant Party. The Vidovdan Constitution passed on 28 June 1921 without it. In March 1923 the party won 70 seats. In 1923 Radić travelled to England, France, Austria and the Soviet Union. After the elections of 1925 his party, renamed the Croatian Peasant Party, struck a power-sharing agreement with the People's Radical Party and recognised the monarchy and the constitution on 27 March 1925. Radić became Minister for Education, resigned in 1926 and in 1927 formed a coalition with Svetozar Pribićević.

On 20 June 1928, in the Assembly, Puniša Račić of the People's Radical Party, a deputy from Montenegro, drew a pistol and shot several opposition deputies, among them Radić, who received a serious stomach wound. He died several weeks later, on 8 August 1928, aged 57. Račić was sentenced to 60 years in prison, reduced at once to 20, and spent most of the term under house arrest in a villa. In January 1929 King Aleksandar abolished the constitution, dissolved parliament and declared a royal dictatorship.

Radić is buried in the Mirogoj Cemetery in Zagreb. His death made him a martyr and an icon for the peasantry and for Croatian patriots, and his image was used by later parties of both left and right. Croatia has awarded the Order of Stjepan Radić since 1995.
stjepan-vukcic-kosaca: Stjepan was the son of Vukac Hranić Kosača, Knez of Drina, and his wife Katarina, whose ancestry is unknown. His father held modest hereditary lands in the Upper Drina region in the east of the Kingdom of Bosnia, around the village of Kosače near Goražde, which still bears the family name. With his father and his uncles Sandalj and Vuk he was admitted to the nobility of the Republic of Ragusa, and a charter of 30 October 1435 granted him and his sons Vladislav and Vlatko citizenship and a palace in Dubrovnik. In 1424 he married Jelena Balšić, daughter of Balša III of Zeta.

Neighbours who expected the new head of the family to be weak eyed his inheritance, but in his first years he joined Murad II's attack on the Serbian Despotate in 1439, took Omiš after an eight-month siege and probably Poljica, pushed the Pavlović family out of Trebinje and Dračevica, and seized Upper Zeta and Bar. After the death of King Tvrtko II in 1443 he opposed the new king, Thomas, and backed his exiled brother Radivoj, the Ottoman candidate, which began years of civil war. Thomas sought peace by marrying Stjepan's daughter Katarina in 1446.

In 1451 Stjepan attacked Ragusa in Konavle and besieged Dubrovnik in the Second Konavle War; the republic declared him a traitor and offered 15,000 ducats to anyone who killed him. A lifelong member of the Bosnian Church, he sheltered at least 40 of its high clergy when King Thomas moved against its followers in 1459. The Saint Sava of his title came from the relics of the Serbian saint kept at Mileševa in his lands. Reconciliation came only under Thomas's son, King Stephen Tomašević.

After the fall of Bosnia in 1463, Mahmud Pasha besieged Blagaj, and Stjepan ceded all his lands north of it for a truce. Old and terminally ill, he dictated his testament at Novi on 21 May 1466, blaming his eldest son Vladislav for bringing the Ottomans into Bosnia, and died the next day. His youngest son became Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha, Grand Vizier to the Sultan. The town of Novi, his winter seat, took his title as Herceg Novi.
stockholm: Stockholm lies on Sweden's east coast at the 59th parallel north, where the freshwater Lake Mälaren flows out into the Baltic Sea. The central parts of the city consist of fourteen islands that continue into the Stockholm archipelago. More than 30% of the city area is waterways and another 30% parks and green spaces. Its position, at the eastern end of the Central Swedish lowland and near the Bergslagen region, reflects the early orientation of Swedish trade toward the Baltic.

The area was settled from the Stone Age, in the 6th millennium BCE. Norse sagas name the location as Agnafit, and Birka, near Stockholm, was one of Sweden's major trade centres in the Viking Age. Numerous runestones were carved in the area because of its importance as a trading hub.

The earliest written mention of the name Stockholm dates from 1252, by which time the mines of Bergslagen had made it an important site in the iron trade. Stock means log in Swedish, though it may also connect to an old German word meaning fortification, and holm means islet, probably the islet of Helgeandsholmen. According to Erik's Chronicle the city was founded by Birger Jarl to protect Sweden from sea invasions by Karelians, after the pillage of Sigtuna on Lake Mälaren in the summer of 1187.

The Old Town, Gamla Stan, was built on the central island next to Helgeandsholmen from the mid-13th century onward. The city rose to prominence through the Baltic trade of the Hanseatic League, developing strong economic and cultural links with Lübeck, Hamburg, Gdańsk, Visby, Tallinn and Riga. Research and higher education in the sciences began in the 18th century. Karolinska Institutet was formalised in 1811 and KTH Royal Institute of Technology was founded in 1827. The city hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics, and the Stockholm Metro opened in 1950.

Stockholm is the capital and most populous city of Sweden. Its municipality had 984,748 inhabitants in 2022, with about 1.6 million in the urban area. It is the seat of the government and the Riksdag, and Stockholm Palace is the official residence of the Swedish monarch. The Vasa Museum is the most visited museum in Scandinavia. The Stockholm region has three World Heritage Sites: Drottningholm Palace, Skogskyrkogården and Birka. The Nobel Prize ceremonies and banquet are held in the city each year.
stockholm-bloodbath: The Bloodbath grew from a conflict between pro-unionists, who favoured the Kalmar Union then dominated by Denmark, and anti-unionists, who supported Swedish independence. Sten Sture the Younger headed the anti-unionists and Archbishop Gustav Trolle the pro-unionists. Christian II intervened to help Trolle, who was besieged at Stäket, but was defeated at Vedila and again at Brännkyrka in 1518. In 1520 he returned with a large army of French, German and Scottish mercenaries.

Sture was mortally wounded at the Battle of Bogesund on 19 January 1520. The Riksdag agreed to do homage to Christian on condition of a full amnesty and rule by Swedish law, but his widow, Lady Kristina, continued to resist in Stockholm and was not defeated at Uppsala until Good Friday, 6 April. After a siege of several months Christian offered terms in which he swore that past acts against him would be forgotten, and the city opened its gates.

On 4 November 1520 Archbishop Trolle anointed Christian in Storkyrkan Cathedral, and Christian took the usual oath to rule through native-born Swedes only. A banquet followed for three days. On the evening of 7 November he summoned Swedish leaders to a private conference at the palace, and at dusk on 8 November Danish soldiers entered the great hall and imprisoned noble guests, all of whom were on Trolle's proscription list.

On 9 November a council headed by Trolle sentenced the proscribed to death as heretics, the main charge being that they had united in a pact to depose Trolle a few years before. At noon the bishops of Skara and Strängnäs were beheaded in the great square, followed by fourteen noblemen, three burgomasters, fourteen town councillors and about twenty common citizens of Stockholm. The executions continued the next day, and the chief executioner, Jörgen Homuth, gave the number of dead as 82. Lady Kristina and many other noblewomen were taken as prisoners to Denmark.

Christian justified the killings in a proclamation as necessary to avoid a papal interdict, but in apologising to the Pope for the beheading of the bishops he blamed his troops for unauthorised acts of vengeance. Gustav Vasa, whose father Erik Johansson was among the victims, travelled to Dalarna to raise a new revolt, and the population rallied to him. They defeated Christian's forces in the Swedish War of Liberation.

The massacre became the catalyst that permanently separated Sweden from Denmark, and in Sweden Christian became known as Kristian Tyrann, Christian the Tyrant. Memory of it fed hostility between the two countries that lasted nearly three hundred years.
stockholms-banco: Johan Palmstruch made two unsuccessful proposals for a banking institution in the 1650s. His third, which added a promise to pay half of the bank's profits to the crown, was accepted, and King Charles X Gustav signed two charters on 30 November 1656, one for an exchange bank and one for a loans bank. The exchange bank opened in July 1657 and took deposits for a fee, paying no interest; account holders could later withdraw cash or write cheques. The loans bank opened at the beginning of 1659 and lent against property. The two were combined as Stockholms Banco, with Palmstruch as general manager.

The bank was modelled, imperfectly, on the older banks of Amsterdam and Hamburg, and it was hoped it would steady Sweden's currency. Sweden then had a copper daler (kopparmynt) and a silver daler (silvermynt). Because a copper daler had to hold as much metal value as a silver one, copper daler were large, heavy, plate-sized coins, and since silver coins were often hoarded, the copper ones were what circulated.

Palmstruch used depositors' money to fund the loans instead of capital from the owners. Deposits were short-term and loans long-term, so the money was not there when depositors asked for it. The problem grew in 1660, when the copper content of the coins was cut by 17 per cent: the old copper daler were now worth more as metal than as coin, and depositors wanted them back.

His answer, from 1661, was the Kreditivsedlar, credit notes in round sums that could be freely passed on and were backed by a promise of later payment in metal. They were far easier to carry than copper plates, and they eased a shortage of coin. The first notes, signed by Palmstruch and the bank's clerks, were for 5, 25, 100 and 1000 copper daler; a second series, the Palmstruchare, followed in 1666 in silver daler. Lending rose fast in 1663, and by that autumn the notes had begun to lose value. From October the bank more and more often had to refuse to redeem them, and the government and Riksdag took over.

Outstanding loans were reduced and the notes exchanged for coin, the liquidation was completed in 1667, and Palmstruch was imprisoned and blamed for the losses. On 17 September 1668 his banking privilege passed to the Riksens Ständers Bank, run by the parliament. Because of the earlier failure, the new bank was not allowed to issue banknotes until the 18th century. It was renamed Sveriges Riksbank in 1866 and is regarded as the oldest surviving central bank in the world.
stoicism: The name derives from the Stoa Poikile, or painted porch, a colonnade decorated with mythic and historical battle scenes on the north side of the Agora in Athens, where Zeno of Citium and his followers gathered near the end of the fourth century BCE. Unlike the Epicureans, Zeno chose to teach in a public space. The philosophy was at first called Zenonism, a name soon dropped, probably because the Stoics did not consider their founders perfectly wise and wished to avoid a cult of personality.

Zeno's ideas developed from those of the Cynics, brought to him by Crates of Thebes, whose founding father, Antisthenes, had been a disciple of Socrates. Zeno also studied under the Megarians. His most influential successor was Chrysippus, who followed Cleanthes as head of the school and moulded what is now called Stoicism. It became the foremost popular philosophy among the educated elite of the Hellenistic world and the Roman Empire.

Stoic philosophy is traditionally divided into logic, physics and ethics. Logic, which included language, grammar, rhetoric and epistemology, was held necessary for understanding ethics. Its smallest unit was the assertible, a proposition that is either true or false. Chrysippus listed five basic argument forms, called indemonstrables, to which all other arguments reduce, and the Stoics studied paradoxes such as the Liar and the Sorites, or Heap. Along with Aristotle's term logic, their propositional logic was one of the two great systems of logic in the classical world.

In physics the universe is a material reasoning substance, logos, with an active part, a primordial fire or intelligent aether, and a passive part, matter. Each human possesses a portion of this divine logos. In ethics the Stoics taught that virtue is the only good and is enough for eudaimonia, a well-lived life, pursued through the four cardinal virtues of prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice. Health, wealth and pleasure are neither good nor bad in themselves. For Chrysippus the passions, such as distress, fear, pleasure and lust, are errors of judgement that the wise person avoids.

Stoic logic was discussed alongside Aristotle's for around five hundred years. In late antiquity the school declined, its logical writings did not survive, and only elements reached the Middle Ages through Boethius and later commentators. Knowledge of Stoic logic as a system was lost until the 20th century, when logicians such as Jan Łukasiewicz and Benson Mates reappraised it. Early Christian writers used concepts such as logos, virtue and conscience, and in the late 16th century Justus Lipsius sought in Neostoicism to join Stoicism and Christianity. Albert Ellis and Aaron T. Beck drew on Stoic ideas in cognitive psychotherapy.
stolac: Stolac is a town in Herzegovina, in the Herzegovina-Neretva Canton of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It stands on the tourist route that links the mountainous hinterland of Bosnia with the coast and Dubrovnik, along the road from Sarajevo through Mostar, Stolac, Ljubinje and Trebinje. Its natural setting, climate and hunting grounds attracted settlers from prehistory, and Illyrians, Romans and Slavs all left remains. It is described as one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the world.

The area has been settled for at least 15,000 years, according to markings in Badanj Cave that experts have dated to between 12,000 and 16,000 BCE. The mainstream view holds that Daorson is 2,500 years old, though some geological studies place the ruins beneath the site at 7,000 years. Three kilometres west of the town lies the Radimlja necropolis of stećak tombstones, dating from the 15th and 16th centuries. They are carved with epitaphs, portraits of the dead, and motifs such as grapevines, hunting scenes and wild animals, and five of them are thought to mark the graves of members of the Hrabren Miloradović Vlach family.

The historic core of Stolac has nine historical layers, from prehistory through the Illyrian-Roman period, the Middle Ages, the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian periods and the first and second Yugoslavia. The town belonged to four empires, the Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian, and to three kingdoms, and its people held to Christianity, Islam and Judaism. During the Yugoslav Wars a number of monuments were demolished by Croat extremists as part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, including the town's four mosques, which dated from the 16th to 18th centuries, and the Orthodox Church of the Holy Assumption of Christ.

In 2003 the Commission to Preserve National Monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina designated Stolac Old Town a National Monument, allowing only research, conservation and restoration. A dispute followed over a series of crosses, the Way of the Cross, built within the old town from the war years onward, which the Commission and the Federation Ministry for Spatial Planning objected to. After the Dayton peace treaty the territory of the 1991 municipality was divided between Stolac and the new municipality of Berkovići in Republika Srpska, where most of the Bosnian Serbs from Stolac now live. A road of 36 kilometres linking Stolac with Neum was completed in 2022.
ston: Ston lies at the south of the isthmus of the Pelješac peninsula, in Dubrovnik-Neretva County. Its position at the gates of the peninsula, surrounded by three seas and protected by four hills, with fresh water and salt water and fertile plains, made it an important political, cultural and ecclesiastical centre. It was first an Illyrian settlement, until the Romans established a colony there in 167 BCE.

In the 6th century a diocese of Sarsenterum was set up for the Zachlumia area, and Ston was spared when the Avars destroyed Sarsenterum. After the arrival of the South Slavs in the 7th century the area formed the principality of Zachlumia, whose rulers acknowledged Byzantine supremacy. The diocese of Ston is first mentioned in 877. In 1120 it became a suffragan of the Archdiocese of Ragusa.

About 1219 Saint Sava of Serbia founded a monastery at Ston as the seat of the Eparchy of Hum. The old town was demolished by an earthquake in 1252, and the Republic of Ragusa later built a new town on the present site. Zachlumia passed in turn to Hungary, the Šubić family, and in 1325 to the medieval Bosnian state.

Ragusa bought Pelješac with Ston from the rulers of Serbia and Bosnia in 1333, in return for the tribute of Ston, and in that year began the planned building of Ston and Little Ston with walls between them to defend the peninsula. The saltworks gave the Republic 15,900 ducats a year. The walls, among the longest in Europe, were shaped over four centuries as weapons developed.

Between 1461 and 1464 the Florentine architect Michelozzo directed work on the Great Wall, which is 1,200 metres long. About half a kilometre fell in the earthquake of 1667. In the 19th century the walls of Little Ston were pulled down to suppress malaria, and stones from the complex were quarried for new buildings.

The 2021 census counted 2,491 people in the municipality, with 500 in the town itself. Restoration of the fortifications resumed after 1945, and the walls were damaged again in the Croatian War of Independence and the earthquake of 1996. Reconstruction of the Great Wall was completed in 2009, and part of the wall is open to visitors. The church of St Michael on the hill is the only one of the early Christian churches of old Ston that still stands.
stone-of-scone: The Stone of Scone is an oblong block of red sandstone, measuring 66 by 43 by 27 centimetres and weighing about 152 kilograms. A cross is roughly incised on one surface, and an iron ring at each end helps with transport. Geologists have found that it is a lower Old Red Sandstone quarried near Scone. Its first recorded use was at the coronation of Alexander III of Scotland in 1249, and it was kept at Scone Abbey, near Perth.

Legends place its origin elsewhere. One story has Fergus, son of Erc, the first King of the Scots, bring it from Ireland to Argyll, and some versions identify it with the Lia Fáil of Tara. Other traditions identify it with the Stone of Jacob, taken from Bethel and carried to Ireland by the prophet Jeremiah.

In 1296, during the First Scottish War of Independence, Edward I of England took the stone to Westminster Abbey as spoils of war. It was fitted into a wooden chair, the Coronation Chair, on which most later English and British sovereigns have been crowned.
