French was the language of diplomacy, and its translation, Sublime Porte, was soon adopted in most other European languages, English among them. It was used not only for the gate but as a metonymy for the Ottoman Empire.

In the 18th century a large Italian-styled office building was built just west of the Topkapı Palace area, on the other side of Alemdar Caddesi. It became the location of the Grand Vizier and many ministries, and from then on this building and the gate leading to its courtyards bore the name Sublime Porte. Colloquially it was also called the Gate of the Pasha. The building was rebuilt after a fire in 1839 and badly damaged by another fire in 1911.

The building housed the office of the Grand Vizier, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of the Interior and the Supreme Council of Judicial Ordinances. Western states used the term in diplomacy because their envoys were received at the porte, the Turkish word for which means gate.

After the Young Turk Revolution and the start of the Second Constitutional Era in 1908, the reformed Imperial Government replaced the functions of the classical Divan-ı Hümayun. In this period the word porte came to refer to the Foreign Ministry, the Grand Vizier's office came to resemble that of a prime minister, and viziers became members of his cabinet as government ministers. The buildings now house the office of the Istanbul governor.
submarine: The word submarine means underwater, and as a noun it is a contraction of submarine boat. A report published in 1562 tells that two Greeks submerged and surfaced several times in the river Tagus near Toledo in the presence of the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, with the flame they carried still alight. In 1578 the English mathematician William Bourne recorded one of the first plans for an underwater navigation vehicle.

Submarines could not enter routine naval service until suitable engines were developed, and the period from 1863 to 1904 was pivotal. The French Plongeur, launched in 1863, was the first submarine not relying on human power, using compressed air. Narcís Monturiol's Ictíneo II, launched in Barcelona in 1864, was the first air-independent, combustion-powered submarine.

The submarine became feasible as a weapon with Robert Whitehead's torpedo of 1866, the first practical self-propelled torpedo. Early submarines used gasoline engines, which gave way to kerosene and then diesel engines, and diesel-electric propulsion became the norm. Submarines were first used widely in the First World War. Before and during the Second World War their primary role was attacking surface ships, and they were particularly effective in sinking Allied transatlantic shipping in both wars and in disrupting Japanese supply routes in the Pacific. They also laid mines, landed and recovered covert agents and special forces, and rescued aircrew during air attacks on islands.

Submarines worked in polar waters early. In 1930 USS O-12 operated under ice near Spitsbergen, and USS Nautilus used an inertial navigation system to reach the North Pole on 3 August 1958. Late in the Second World War, when faster and longer submerged operation became possible, hulls again took the teardrop shape that reduces drag and noise. Civilian uses developed alongside the military ones, including marine science, salvage and exploration. The first tourist submarine entered service in 1964, and by 1997 there were 45 tourist submarines operating.
subotica: Subotica lies in the Pannonian Basin at an altitude of 109 metres, about 10 kilometres from the border with Hungary, and is the northernmost city in Serbia. Lake Palić is near it. Its earliest recorded name is Zabotka or Zabatka, from 1391, which gave the Hungarian name Szabadka. One explanation derives it from a Slavic word for a place with a Saturday market fair, while another links it to a word for free, referring to the colonists settled after the Battle of Zenta.

Subotica probably first became a settlement of note when people from nearby villages destroyed in the Tatar invasions of 1241–42 poured into it. In 1391 it was a tiny town in the Kingdom of Hungary. After Mohács in 1526 the Hungarian population mostly fled north. The Ottomans ruled the city from 1542 to 1686, and by the end little remained of the old town. They encouraged settlers from the Balkans, mostly Orthodox Serbs, and in 1687 about 5,000 Catholic Bunjevci settled in Bačka. In 1743 Subotica gained a civil charter as a market town and was called Sent-Maria.

In 1779 Maria Theresa made it a Free Royal Town and it was renamed Maria-Theresiopolis. Its population doubled twice in the 19th century as Hungarians and Jews settled there alongside the Bunjevci. After 1867 the railway came in 1869, an electric power plant in 1896, and the city acquired its fin de siècle architecture. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Hungarian troops entered on 11 April 1941. Of about 6,000 Jews who had lived there before the war, many were deported, mostly to Auschwitz, and a ghetto was set up in April 1944.

Subotica is the administrative centre of the North Bačka District in the autonomous province of Vojvodina, Serbia, with 88,752 people in the city proper in 2022. It is known for buildings in the Hungarian Secession style, a variant of Art Nouveau. The Synagogue of 1902 and the City Hall of 1908–1910 were both built by Marcell Komor and Dezső Jakab, and the Raichle Palace of 1904 by Ferenc J. Raichle. The Synagogue is the second largest synagogue building in Europe.
subutai: Historians believe Subutai was born in 1175, probably just west of the upper Onon River in what is now Mongolia. An older account makes him a member of the reindeer people and an outsider to steppe horsemanship, but recent scholarship, including Stephen Pow and Jingjing Liao, discounts it. His family had been associated with the family of Temujin, the future Genghis Khan, for generations. His father, Jarchigudai, is said to have supplied food to Temujin and his followers at Lake Baljuna, and his elder brother Jelme was a general and close companion of Temujin.

In 1217 Genghis Khan sent Subutai against the Merkits and the Cuman-Kipchak confederation in what is now central Kazakhstan. Between 1220 and 1223 he and Jebe led about 20,000 men round the Caspian Sea and through the Caucasus. They defeated the Georgian army by luring its knights away from the infantry with a feigned retreat, and at the Kalka River in 1223 his 20,000 men routed a Russian army of 80,000. In 1226 he struck the Tanguts of Xi Xia from the west across mountains and deserts while Genghis invaded by the northern route. After Genghis died in 1227, Ögedei sent him to retrieve a failing campaign against the Jin dynasty.

Under the overall command of Prince Batu, Subutai directed the invasion of Rus' from 1236 to 1240. In 1241 and 1242 he was the actual commander in the field of the attack on central Europe, leading the central column against the Kingdom of Hungary. He routinely coordinated armies operating hundreds of kilometres apart, and his methods relied on feints, encirclement and rapid cavalry charges.

After the kurultai that elected Güyük as khagan, Subutai was placed in charge of a campaign against the Song dynasty in 1246 and 1247, at the age of 71. He returned to Mongolia in 1248 and spent the rest of his life at his home near the Tuul River, dying there at the age of 72. His descendants Uriyangkhadai and Aju served the Great Khans as commanders for the next three decades.

The historian Paul Buell wrote that no Mongol general played a greater role in establishing and maintaining the early Mongol Empire. Western military writers largely ignored his methods until the 20th century. Russian analysis of the Mongol campaigns fed into the deep battle doctrine of the Soviet Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky, and the American theorist John Boyd cited the campaigns of Genghis Khan and Subutai as examples of maneuver warfare.
suceava: Suceava is the seat of Suceava County, in the historical regions of Bukovina and Western Moldavia. It stands in a moderately hilly area in the south-western part of the county and covers both hills, the highest being Zamca Hill, and the meadows of the Suceava river valley. Its position at the crossroads of several trade routes linking Central Europe with Eastern Europe made it a commercial town, and it is a transport hub with Ukraine to the north and Transylvania to the west. The name was explained by the chroniclers Grigore Ureche and Dimitrie Cantemir as coming from the Hungarian Szűcsvár, meaning furriers' castle, although there is no historical or vernacular evidence for this.

The area was inhabited from the Paleolithic period, and traces of a Dacian oppidum of the 2nd century survive. Suceava and the rest of Bukovina were not conquered by the Roman legions and remained among the lands of the free Dacian tribes. Ptolemy places the Celtic-speaking Anartes and Taurisci and the Germanic Bastarnae in the region. After the fall of Rome the population was invaded in turn by Goths, Gepids, Huns, Slavs, Magyars, Pechenegs and Cumans.

From 1388 to 1564 Suceava was the capital of the Principality of Moldavia, and in the Middle Ages it operated under Magdeburg law. Petru Mușat built the Princely House in wood in the late 14th century, and after 1400 Alexander I of Moldavia rebuilt it and added a stone wall and stone buildings. A fire in the second half of the 15th century burned the wooden house. The Seat Fortress and the Șcheia Fortress belonged to the principality's system of fortification.

From 1775 to 1918 Suceava was under the Habsburg monarchy, later the Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary. The Austrian census of 1880 recorded 10,104 inhabitants, of whom 5,862 were Bukovina Germans and 2,652 Romanians. In the interwar period it grew within the enlarged Kingdom of Romania.

Suceava had a population of 84,308 at the 2021 census, having grown from just over 10,000 in the late 1940s to over 100,000 in the early 1990s. The reconstructed Seat Fortress stands on the eastern edge of the city. The Saint John the New Monastery, whose Church of Saint George was built between 1514 and 1522 and served as the metropolitan cathedral of Moldavia until 1677, is one of the Churches of Moldavia inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. An equestrian statue of Stephen the Great, made in 1977, is the tallest in Romania. The Ștefan cel Mare University of Suceava was established in 1990.
sucre: Sucre lies in south-central Bolivia at about 2,790 m above sea level, in the inter-Andean valleys of the Eastern Cordillera, at the foot of the Sica Sica and Churuquella hills. The area marks the boundary between the Amazon basin and the basin of the River Plate, and its climate is mild and dry for the altitude. The city has been known as Charcas, La Plata, Chuquisaca and Sucre, and its white-painted colonial houses earned it the nickname La Ciudad Blanca, the White City.

Before the Spanish arrived the site was an Inca town called Chuquisaca, the provincial capital of the wamani of Charca, which Topa Inka Yupanqui had taken from the Aymara kingdom that held the area. The name possibly comes from Quechua words meaning a heap of silver. In 1538 Hernando Pizarro travelled there with the Emperor Paullu Inca and met Consara, the principal lord of the Charcas, who told him of the silver, gold, copper and tin deposits of the region.

The Spanish city was founded on 30 November 1538 by Pedro Anzures, Marqués de Campo Redondo, as Ciudad de la Plata de la Nueva Toledo. In 1559 Philip II set up the Audiencia of Charcas there, with authority over what is now Paraguay, south-eastern Peru, northern Chile, Argentina and much of Bolivia. It belonged to the Viceroyalty of Peru until 1776, then to the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata. An archbishopric was founded in 1609 and the university of St Francis Xavier in 1624.

On 25 May 1809 the bell of the Basilica of San Francisco was rung to begin the Bolivian independence movement. La Plata was proclaimed provisional capital of Upper Peru in July 1826, and on 12 July 1839 President José Miguel de Velasco named it capital of Bolivia and renamed it for Antonio José de Sucre. After the decline of Potosí's silver industry the seat of government moved to La Paz in 1898.

Sucre is the constitutional capital of Bolivia and the capital of the Chuquisaca Department; the Supreme Court sits there, while La Paz is the seat of government. Its colonial and republican centre, laid out on a grid, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991. Landmarks include the House of Freedom, built in 1621, where the declaration of independence is kept, and the Metropolitan Cathedral, built between 1559 and 1712. Sucre remains the seat of the Roman Catholic Church in Bolivia.
sudak: Sudak lies on the south-east coast of the Crimea, 57 km west of Feodosia and 104 km east of Simferopol. The date and circumstances of its foundation are uncertain. Its first written mention is in the Ravenna Cosmography of the 7th century, and local tradition later placed its foundation in 212 CE, while archaeology supports a foundation in Roman times. It was probably founded by the Alans: its Greek name, Sougdaia, is related to a word meaning pure or holy, or derives from Ossetian.

Under loose Byzantine influence Sougdaia was became the seat of a bishopric, first attested at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. The 8th to 11th centuries are obscure, with signs of decline and probably Khazar suzerainty until the early 11th century. The 11th to 14th centuries were a time of prosperity. The city was a terminus of Black Sea trade on the Silk Road in the 12th and 13th centuries, and the Arab traveller Ibn Battuta compared its harbour with that of Alexandria. Byzantium regained it by the mid-11th century, and it then fell under Cuman control until the 13th century.

The Seljuk Turks besieged the city in about 1222, and the Mongols raided it in 1223 and 1238; in about 1249 it came under the Golden Horde, though it kept considerable autonomy. Its population was then given as 8,300, among them Greeks, Alans, Mongols, Armenians, Latins and Jews.

Venetian and Genoese commercial colonies raised its prosperity in the late 13th century, but Genoese Tana and Kaffa eclipsed it in the early 14th. On 19 July 1365 the Genoese from Kaffa seized it, refortified it and built the citadel still visible today. Gedik Ahmed Pasha took it after a long siege in 1475, and it lost much of its military and commercial importance. Russian troops occupied it in 1771, and it passed to the Russian Empire in 1783; by the census of 1805 it had only 33 inhabitants.

Sudak is a resort best known for its Genoese fortress, the best preserved on the northern shore of the Black Sea. A Russian school of viticulture opened there in 1804. The Orthodox see of Sougdaia, raised to an archbishopric in the 10th century and a metropolitan see between 1275 and 1282, gave its old name Surozh to a diocese of the Russian Orthodox Church, and a Latin Catholic diocese of Soldaia was established under Genoese rule in 1390.
sudan: The modern state of Sudan covers 1,886,068 km2, the third-largest country in Africa by area, with an 853 km coast on the Red Sea. The terrain is generally flat plains broken by mountain ranges, and the highest point is the Deriba Caldera, at 3,042 metres, in the Marrah Mountains. The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum to form the Nile, which flows north through Egypt.

The north and centre are extremely dry, with the Nubian and Bayuda deserts, while the south has grasslands and tropical savanna. The name comes from the Arabic bilad as-sudan, the Land of the Blacks, which was historically applied to the Sahel from Senegal to Northeast Africa; before that the area was known as Nubia.

The oldest evidence is the camp remains at Affad 23, some 50,000 years old, and the war of Jebel Sahaba, around 11500 BCE, is described as the earliest known war in the world. The Kingdom of Kerma flourished from about 2500 to 1500 BCE and in its last phase became a populous empire rivalling Egypt. Egyptian rulers of the New Kingdom then held the region, beginning when Thutmose I occupied Kush and destroyed Kerma. The Kingdom of Kush lasted from about 785 BCE to 350 CE, and after its fall the Nubians formed the Christian kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

Arab nomads settled most of Sudan between the 14th and 15th centuries. From the 16th to the 19th centuries the Funj sultanate dominated the centre and east, while Darfur ruled the west and the Ottomans the east. Egypt conquered the whole country in the 19th century. After the Mahdist Uprising was defeated by a joint Egyptian-British force, Egypt agreed in 1899 under British pressure to share sovereignty with the United Kingdom, and Sudan was in effect governed as a British possession. It became independent on 1 January 1956.

Sudan has known repeated civil war. The first, from 1955 to 1972, was followed by a second between government forces and southern rebels, which led to the independence of South Sudan in 2011. Sharia law applied from 1983 until 2020, when Sudan became a secular state.
sudan-national-museum: The museum was housed in a two-storey building constructed in 1955 on Nile Avenue in Khartoum's al-Mugran area, close to the confluence of the White and the Blue Nile. A major spur to its creation was the mass of artefacts relocated during the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia of 1960–1980. Before 2023 it held an estimated 100,000 objects, from the Paleolithic to the Islamic period, shown in a main hall, a gallery on the first floor, an open-air museum in the garden and a monumental alley outside.

A 4-metre granite statue of the pharaoh Taharqa faced the entrance; it had been broken when the Egyptians of Psamtik II sacked Napata in 591 BCE, buried by Kushite priests, and excavated by George Reisner in 1916. The first floor held the Faras wall paintings, dated between the 9th and the 13th century, and Greek and Coptic epitaphs of Christian Nubia catalogued by Adam Lajtar and Jacques Van der Vliet. In the garden the relocated temples of Aksha, Kumma and others stood around an artificial stream symbolising the Nile.

The museum was the scene of heavy fighting in the Sudanese civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which began in April 2023, and the RSF took it over on 2 June 2023. Most exhibits, among them mummies dating to 2500 BCE, were destroyed, looted or badly damaged. Ikhlas Abdel Latif, head of museums at the National Corporation for Antiquities and Museums (NCAM), said that items had been taken by truck to western Sudan and border areas, and reports said some were sold in South Sudan.

After the RSF was driven from Khartoum in March 2025, the director of NCAM, Ghalia Garelnabi, accused it of destroying 90% of the museum's holdings, looting its archaeological gold collection and deliberately smashing other artifacts. According to The Guardian almost all of the 100,000 objects were looted, leaving only very heavy pieces such as monumental statues and rebuilt temples.

With the support of the Louvre and Durham University, the French Archaeological Unit for Sudanese Antiquities (SFDAS) helped the museum create a virtual site to display the lost artefacts and recreate its exhibits. At the end of 2022 The Guardian had reported on a new generation of Sudanese archaeologists, many of them young women trained at the University of Khartoum, working for NCAM alongside foreign-led research.
suddhodana: The name Śuddhodana means "he who grows pure rice". His father was Sihahanu and his mother Kaccanā, and his earliest predecessor was named as King Maha Sammatha, or the first king of the Kalpa. His chief consort was Maha Maya, with whom he had Siddhartha Gautama, later called Shakyamuni, the Sage of the Shakyas. When Maya died shortly after the birth, her sister Mahapajapati Gotami was raised to chief consort. They had a second son, Nanda, and a daughter, Sundari Nanda, who both later became Buddhist monastics. At the age of 16 Siddhartha married his cousin Yasodharā, niece of Maha Maya and Mahapajapati.

Śuddhodana led the Shakya, who lived in an oligarchic republic with its capital at Kapilavastu. Later accounts of the Buddha's life often call him a king, but modern scholars dispute this and most recent scholarship rejects it. Many hold that the Shakya republic was ruled by a council of the warrior and ministerial class that chose its leader, the rājā, who did not rule autocratically, since questions were debated in the council and decided by consensus.

By the time of Siddhartha's birth the republic had become a vassal of the Kingdom of Kosala, and the rājā took office with the approval of Kosala's king. The earliest Buddhist texts do not describe the family as royal. Later texts may have misread the Pali word rājā, which can mean king, prince, ruler or governor.

According to legend, Śuddhodana tried hard to keep Siddhartha from becoming a śramaṇa, forbidding him to leave the palace and surrounding him with sensual pleasures. At 29 Siddhartha left home after his first journey outside, an episode known as the Great Renunciation.

Śuddhodana grieved at his son's departure and long sought him. Seven years later, when word of his enlightenment arrived, he sent nine emissaries to invite him back, but they joined the sangha after hearing him preach. He then sent Siddhartha's friend Kaludayi, who also became a monk but kept his word and invited the Buddha home. The Buddha returned and preached the dharma to his father. Four years later, hearing that his father was near death, he came again to the palace and preached to him, and Śuddhodana is said to have reached arhatship on his deathbed.
sudebnik-of-1497: The Sudebnik, also called the Sudebnik of Ivan III, replaced the separate legal charters of the Russian principalities with one code for the whole state. Its rules on courts and legal norms bound every part of the country alike, and so strengthened the central authority in Moscow. Historians see it as an important step in the centralisation of the Russian state, the making of all-Russian legislation and the end of feudal fragmentation.

The code grew out of earlier law: the Russkaya Pravda, the Pskov Judicial Charter, princely decrees and customary law, whose rules were brought up to date to meet social and economic change. It was above all a collection of legal procedures.

The Sudebnik set up a single system of judicial bodies across the state, defined what each could hear and to whom it answered, and fixed the fees of the courts. It widened the range of acts treated as crimes, among them sedition, sacrilege and slander, and renewed the distinction between kinds of crime. Proceedings became investigative in character, and the punishments included the death penalty and flogging.

Several articles protected the land of the great owners. The code limited the law of estates, lengthened the period within which claims to princely land could be brought, and imposed flogging for breaking the boundaries of princely, boyar and monastic land, while the same offence against peasant land was punished by a fine. A peasant who wished to leave his lord had to pay a fee, the pozhiloye, and could move only at one time fixed for the whole state, Yuri's Day, 26 November.
sudeten-german-party: The party's forerunners went back to the German Workers' Party founded in 1903 by Sudeten Germans in the Bohemian crown lands of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy, a pan-German and anti-Slav party centred on Eger and Aussig. Renamed the German National Socialist Workers' Party (DNSAP) in 1918, it demanded that the German-settled borderlands join German-Austria rather than Czechoslovakia, and with the German National Party it led the so-called negativism of Sudeten Germans who refused to accept the Czechoslovak state. Both parties dissolved themselves in 1933 to forestall a ban by the Prague government, and the Sudeten German Home Front was founded on 1 October 1933.

Konrad Henlein at first rejected any link with the DNSAP. He favoured the corporative ideas of Othmar Spann and the Austrian model, and until 1937 his speeches stressed loyalty to Czechoslovakia; he later called his contacts with Nazi leaders merely tactical. After Karl Hermann Frank became deputy leader in 1935, the party grew more radical. In the May 1935 election it won 1,249,534 votes, 15.2 per cent, and about 68 per cent of the German vote, while groups within it were increasingly financed from Germany.

After Adolf Hitler declared his intention to separate the Sudetenland, as recorded in the Hossbach Memorandum of November 1937, the party coordinated its policy with Nazi leaders. Henlein first met Hitler on 28 March 1938, the Farmers' League joined the party that month, and at Carlsbad on 24 April the party demanded self-government for the Sudeten Germans and the freedom to choose annexation to Germany. By June 1938 it had over 1.3 million members, and in the communal elections of May 1938 it took 88 per cent of German votes.

After the Munich Agreement, Henlein was made Reichskommissar of the annexed territory on 1 October 1938, and the party was merged into the Nazi Party at a ceremony in Reichenberg (Liberec) on 5 November 1938. Officials such as Reinhard Heydrich distrusted its members, who had to apply individually; about 520,000 were admitted. The mandates of 46 deputies and 22 senators of the party and its Carpathian German ally were annulled on 30 October 1938, and its branches left in Czechoslovakia formed the German People's Group in Czecho-Slovakia.
sudeten-germans: Ethnic Germans moved into the Kingdom of Bohemia from the 11th century, mostly into the border region later called the Sudetenland after the Sudeten Mountains. In the late 12th and 13th centuries the Přemyslid rulers promoted settlement by Germans from Bavaria, Franconia, Upper Saxony and Austria, part of the eastern settlement movement known as Ostsiedlung. The name Sudeten Germans came into use only in the early 20th century, after the fall of Austria-Hungary, and the Nazi regime used it so heavily that many Germans now prefer the older term German Bohemians.

Most Sudeten Germans were Roman Catholics, a legacy of Habsburg rule. Czechs and Germans mixed in many places, but from the second half of the 19th century each built separate cultural, educational, political and economic institutions.

When Austria-Hungary broke up in 1918, Czech politicians insisted on the traditional boundaries of the Bohemian Crown, which put about three million Germans under Czech control. On 29 October 1918 German politicians formed the Province of German Bohemia, with its capital at Reichenberg, but it did not survive.

In 1921 the Germans were 3.2 million of Czechoslovakia's population, about 23.4% of the republic. Many felt that the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye had not been honoured, since minority rights were too few, yet they gradually accepted remaining in the state. In 1926 the first Germans became ministers, among them Robert Mayr-Harting and Franz Spina.

Nationalist sentiment grew after the Depression and Adolf Hitler's appointment as German chancellor in January 1933. On 28 March 1938 Konrad Henlein met Hitler in Berlin and was told to raise demands that the Czechoslovak government could not accept. His party then demanded complete autonomy for the Sudetenland, and Nazi propaganda accused the Czechs of atrocities against Germans. After the Munich Agreement the Sudetenland became part of Germany.

After the Second World War the restored Czechoslovak government expelled most of the German population, believing that its behaviour had been a major cause of the war. From May to August 1945 local authorities ordered "wild" expulsions, which armed volunteers carried out, and in some cases the army took part. Several thousand Germans were murdered, and many more died of hunger and illness as refugees. They went mainly to Germany and Austria. Sudeten German dialects are now practically extinct, and people of Sudeten German descent speak mainly Czech or standard German. Smaller groups had also settled earlier in Chile, Paraguay and Argentina.
sudetenland: The areas later called the Sudetenland never formed a single historical region, and their history is hard to separate from that of Bohemia before nationalism arrived in the 19th century. German settlers were invited into the Bohemian border regions from the second half of the 13th century, especially by the Přemyslid kings Ottokar II and Wenceslaus II, and German speakers remained dominant there through the Hussite Wars. The word Sudeten comes from the Sudeten Mountains. The publicist Franz Jesser in 1902 first applied Sudetenland to all the areas of Bohemia, Moravia and Austrian Silesia with a German-speaking majority, and the term became common in the 1920s.

When Austria-Hungary broke apart in October 1918, German deputies from Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia citing Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points tried to unite their regions with the Republic of German Austria, and four provinces were proclaimed. The Czechs rejected this and demanded the inclusion of the lands inhabited by Germans, which they said had always been part of the Bohemian Crown. The Treaty of Saint-Germain in 1919 confirmed their place in Czechoslovakia. The 1921 census counted 3,123,000 German speakers, 23.4% of the population. The Great Depression hit the region's export industries hard, such as glassmaking and textiles, and the Sudeten German Party of Konrad Henlein gained great popularity.

After the Anschluss of Austria in March 1938, Adolf Hitler made himself the advocate of the Germans in Czechoslovakia. Lord Runciman's mediation failed, and on 15 September Neville Chamberlain agreed with Hitler to the cession, as did Édouard Daladier three days later; no Czechoslovak representative was invited. At Munich on 29 September Hitler, Daladier and Chamberlain, on the proposal of Benito Mussolini, signed the agreement that allowed the immediate occupation of the Sudetenland, which took place between 1 and 10 October 1938. Poland annexed part of the borderland in 1938. Germany invaded the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939. The Sudetenland was divided, and its northern and western parts became the Reichsgau Sudetenland, governed by Henlein.

After the war the Potsdam Conference decided that the Sudeten Germans would have to leave Czechoslovakia, and the overwhelming majority were expelled, about 500,000 of them in the spring and summer of 1945. In 1950 only 159,938 Germans were left of 3,149,820 in 1930. Czechs mostly, and also Slovaks, Greeks and others, resettled the region. The Sudeten German dialects have largely disappeared.
sudetes: The Sudetes are a geomorphological subprovince of the Bohemian Massif shared by the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany. They consist mainly of mountain ranges and are the highest part of the massif, stretching from Dresden in the north-west to Lower Silesia and the city of Ostrava in the east. Their plateaus and subtle summit relief make them more like the mountains of Northern Europe than the Alps. The highest peak is Sněžka, 1,603 m, in the Giant Mountains on the Czech-Polish border. Praděd, 1,491 m, is the highest mountain of Moravia, and Lausche, 793 m, the highest in the German part. The Elbe, Oder, Spree, Morava, Bóbr and Lusatian Neisse all rise here, and national parks protect the highest parts.

The name derives from Sudeti montes, a Latin form of the name Soudeta that the Greco-Roman writer Ptolemy used around 150 CE for a range of mountains in Germania. There is no consensus about which mountains he meant, since he could have intended the Ore Mountains or the Bohemian Forest. The meaning of the name is not known. One derivation gives it as Mountains of Wild Boars, and a better one perhaps from the Latin sudis, spines. The rocks of the range formed during the Variscan orogeny, and the Giant Mountains were the most glaciated part of the Sudetes during the Quaternary glaciations.

By the 12th century the area around the Sudetes was relatively densely settled, and agriculture and settlement expanded further from the 13th century. Most of the settlers were Germans from neighbouring Silesia, who founded villages of the Waldhufendorf type. Deforestation was clearly unsustainable by the 14th century, and by the 15th and 16th centuries farming had reached the inner part of the Table Mountains. Forest destruction peaked in the 16th and 17th centuries, when glasshouses throughout the area demanded firewood. Norway spruce was planted in place of the former broad-leaf trees in the early 19th century, in places as monocultures.

In the 19th century the central Sudetes enjoyed an economic boom, with sandstone quarrying and a tourism industry built on the scenery, although villages had been losing population since the 1880s. After the First World War the name Sudetenland came into use for the areas of the First Czechoslovak Republic with large ethnic German populations. The Sudeten Germans, the German-speaking inhabitants of Czechoslovakia, are named after the mountains. In 1918 the short-lived rump state of German-Austria proclaimed a Province of the Sudetenland in northern Moravia and Austrian Silesia around Opava.
sudirman: Sudirman was born in Purbalingga in the Dutch East Indies and adopted by his uncle, the sub-district head Raden Cokrosunaryo, who gave him the noble title Raden; he was not told until he was eighteen that Cokrosunaryo was not his birth father. Raised in Cilacap, he studied Islam under Kyai Hajji Qahar and was active in Hizboel Wathan, the scouting body of Muhammadiyah. In 1936 he married Alfiah, daughter of a batik merchant, and began teaching at a Muhammadiyah school, becoming its headmaster without a teacher's certificate.

Under the Japanese occupation he joined the Defenders of the Homeland (PETA) in 1944 and commanded a battalion at Kroya. When PETA troops under Kusaeri rebelled on 21 April 1945, he agreed to stop them only if they would not be harmed, and talked them into surrender. He and his men were then interned in Bogor, from which he led a break-out after the proclamation of independence. Back in Banyumas he and Iskaq Tjokrohadisurjo forced the Japanese commander there to hand over his weapons, which made his unit one of the best equipped in the country.

He took part in the talks that produced the Linggadjati Agreement of 15 November 1946, though he opposed it, and helped form the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) on 3 June 1947. When the Dutch launched Operation Product on 21 July 1947, Indonesian lines crumbled quickly. After the Dutch attack on Yogyakarta he burned sensitive papers and left with a small group and his doctor, travelling through Kretek, Wonogiri, Ponorogo and Kediri; near Trenggalek republican soldiers, not recognising him, briefly held his party as suspected spies.

In August 1949 he asked Sukarno to continue the guerrilla war, doubting that the Dutch would keep the Roem-Royen Agreement, and threatened to resign when refused, but stayed so as not to unsettle the republic. On 27 December 1949, the day of Dutch recognition, he was reconfirmed as commander-in-chief. He died in Magelang on 29 January 1950, and thousands lined the streets as his convoy passed to Yogyakarta, where he lies in Semaki Heroes' Cemetery. His 100-kilometre guerrilla route is walked by Indonesian cadets, and he was declared a National Hero on 10 December 1964.
sue-harukata: Sue Harukata was the second son of Sue Okifusa, a senior retainer of the Ōuchi clan, and his childhood name was Goro. The Sue clan, whose name derives from Sue pottery, was related to the Ōuchi and served as shugodai of Suō Province. As a boy he served Ōuchi Yoshitaka, a childhood friend, and after his genpuku he was given the name Takafusa after Yoshitaka. He became head of the Sue clan in 1539, when his father died of illness.

An able retainer, he became known as the Samurai General Without Peer in the Western Provinces. From 1540 to 1542 he led the war against the Amago clan in place of Yoshitaka. After the Ōuchi troops lost heavily in 1542, Yoshitaka's interest in war faded and he turned to cultural pursuits; the civil official Sagara Taketō grew close to him, and Harukata's relationship with his lord declined.

In his coup of 1551 Harukata killed Sagara Taketō and drove Yoshitaka to suicide. The next year he secured control of the clan by making Yoshitaka's adopted son Ōuchi Yoshinaga, born Ōtomo Haruhide and a half-brother of Ōtomo Sōrin, its head, and changed his own name from Takafusa to Harukata to match his new master. His large military expansion that followed caused discontent among the Ōuchi retainers.

In 1554 Yoshimi Masayori of Iwami Province, Yoshitaka's brother-in-law, and Mōri Motonari of Aki Province rose against him, and his retainer Takagawa was defeated by Motonari at the Battle of Oshikibata. Harukata lost the Battle of Itsukushima in 1555 and killed himself after it, on 16 October. His son Nagafusa, attacked by the Mōri, committed seppuku at Wakayama castle, and the Ōuchi clan declined; two years later Motonari annihilated it.
suessa-aurunca: Sessa Aurunca, the ancient Suessa Aurunca, is a town in the province of Caserta in Campania. It lies on the southwest slope of the extinct volcano of Roccamonfina, about 40 kilometres by rail west-northwest of Caserta and 30 kilometres east of Formia, near the river Garigliano. The hill on which it stands is a mass of volcanic tuff.

The area was inhabited by the Aurunci, an Italic people, and Suessa was their chief town. It is sometimes identified with a site more than 600 metres above sea level on the crater of Roccamonfina, where Cyclopean masonry exists, though the enclosed area is too small for more than a detached fort. In 337 BCE, under pressure from the neighbouring Sidicini, the Aurunci abandoned their oldest city in favour of the present site. Between 340 and 315 BCE the Romans decisively defeated them under the consuls Lucius Papirius Cursor and Quintus Publilius Philo.

A Latin colony was founded at Suessa Aurunca in 313 BCE, which marked its full integration into the Roman state. Cicero speaks of it as a place of some importance, and the triumvirs settled some of their veterans there. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Sessa lost much of its population. The Placito of Sessa, issued in March 963, contains one of the first written attestations of the Italian vernacular in an official and legal context. From the 14th century the town was a semi-independent duchy of the Marzano family within the Kingdom of Naples, and in 1466 it returned to direct control of the Neapolitan crown.

A Roman theatre of the 2nd to 1st century BCE, excavated since 2001 and enlarged by Matidia Minor in the 2nd century CE, could hold more than 6,500 spectators. The cathedral, begun in 1103, has a Cosmatesque mosaic pavement, and the ducal castle was built in the 10th century by the Lombard gastald. The Real Ferdinando Bridge over the Garigliano, built in 1832 by the Bourbon Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and designed by Luigi Giura, was the first iron catenary suspension bridge in Italy.
suetonius: Suetonius was probably born about 69 CE, a date deduced from his remark that he was about 57 years after Nero's death. His place of birth is disputed, but most scholars place it at Hippo Regius, a small town in Numidia in modern Algeria. His family was of moderate social position, and his father, Suetonius Laetus, was a tribune of the equestrian order in Legio XIII Gemina. He was educated at Rome at a time when schools of rhetoric flourished.

Suetonius was a close friend of the senator and letter-writer Pliny the Younger, who described him as quiet and studious, a man dedicated to writing. Pliny helped him buy a small property and interceded with the emperor Trajan to grant him the tax immunities given to a father of three, although he was childless. Through Pliny he came into favour with Trajan and Hadrian. Under Trajan he was secretary of studies and director of the imperial archives, and under Hadrian he became the emperor's secretary. The Historia Augusta, an often unreliable collection written more than 150 years later, says that Hadrian dismissed him for acting too informally around the empress Vibia Sabina.

His best-known surviving work is De vita Caesarum, the Twelve Caesars, a collective biography of Julius Caesar, Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian, Titus and Domitian. It was probably written in Hadrian's time and dedicated to his friend Gaius Septicius Clarus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard in 119. Each life follows a set formula, giving appearance, omens, family history and quotations before the history, and the first chapters on Caesar are missing. It contains the earliest accounts of Caesar's epileptic seizures.

Other works dealt with the daily life of Rome, politics, oratory and the lives of writers. His Lives of the Grammarians survives, apparently complete, with 20 brief lives, and five of the sixteen Lives of the Rhetoricians survive. From the Lives of the Poets come the life of Virgil and fragments of the lives of Terence, Horace and Lucan. Many of his books are lost.
suez-canal: Several earlier canals joined the Nile to the Red Sea. According to Herodotus, Necho II (610–595 BCE) began a canal through the Wadi Tumilat between Bubastis and Heroopolis but never finished it, and the only fully functional ancient canal was completed under Darius I (522–486 BCE). The Roman emperor Trajan re-excavated it in the 1st century CE, and after the Arab conquest of 641 Amr ibn al-As ordered it restored to improve links between Egypt and Medina.

After Bartolomeu Dias sailed around southern Africa in 1488, Venice, which had been a leading spice-trading centre, considered digging a waterway between the Red Sea and the Nile. In the 16th century the Ottoman Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha also attempted a canal, but the project was judged too expensive. Napoleon's expedition of 1798 found remnants of an ancient canal, recorded in the Description de l'Égypte.

The Suez Canal is an artificial sea-level waterway 193.3 km long, running from Port Said on the Mediterranean to Port Tewfik at the city of Suez. It was designed by Alois Negrelli without locks, so that seawater flows freely through it, and it opened as a single-lane waterway with passing places in the Ballah Bypass and the Great Bitter Lake. By avoiding the route around Africa it shortens the journey from the Arabian Sea to London by about 8,900 km.

Ferdinand de Lesseps, a French diplomat, obtained concessions from Sa'id Pasha in 1854 and 1856 to create a company to build a canal open to ships of all nations, to be operated by the company for 99 years from its opening. He formed the Compagnie de Suez in 1858 and construction began the following year. The canal opened on 17 November 1869. It had an immediate effect on world trade.

In 1875 Isma'il Pasha, unable to pay his bank debts, sold Egypt's 44 per cent share to the British government for £4,000,000. Under the Convention of Constantinople the canal is open to every vessel, in war as in peace. On 26 July 1956 President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised it and transferred it to the Suez Canal Authority, which led to the Suez Crisis, in which the United Kingdom, France and Israel invaded Egypt's Sinai. Egypt closed the canal at the start of the Six-Day War in 1967, and it stayed closed until 1975.
suez-crisis: The Suez Canal opened in 1869, financed by the French and Egyptian governments, and was operated by the Suez Company, an Egyptian-chartered company. After the Second World War Britain's base on the canal became one of the world's largest military installations and a growing source of tension. On 23 July 1952 the Free Officers movement, led by Muhammad Neguib and Gamal Abdel Nasser, overthrew King Farouk.

On 26 July 1956, in a speech in Alexandria, Nasser announced the nationalisation of the canal, using the name of its builder Ferdinand de Lesseps as the code word for Egyptian forces to seize it. Egypt also closed the canal and the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. French prime minister Guy Mollet was outraged, and the British prime minister Anthony Eden began planning an invasion in July.

Between 22 and 24 October 1956, France, Israel and the United Kingdom reached a secret agreement at Sèvres. Israel would attack Egypt on 29 October; Britain and France would then call on both sides to withdraw from the canal and, if one refused, attack on 31 October. Operation Kadesh began on 29 October, with Israeli aircraft attacking Egyptian positions across the Sinai. Israeli forces advanced quickly and by 3 November were closing on Sharm el-Sheikh.

The Anglo-French ultimatums were sent on 30 October, and bombing began the next day. British paratroopers dropped on El Gamil airfield on 5 November. At first light on 6 November Royal Marines stormed the beaches at Port Said. Eden announced a ceasefire that day without warning France or Israel. Israeli losses were 172 dead and 817 wounded; Egyptian casualties in the Israeli invasion were estimated at 1,000 to 3,000 dead, and about 1,000 Egyptian civilians died.

The United States was dealing at the same time with the Hungarian Revolution, and Eisenhower believed that backing the attack might push the Arab world towards the Soviet Union. The Soviet premier Nikolai Bulganin threatened rocket attacks on Britain, France and Israel; the West did not know that the Soviets lacked the missiles for it. The canal stayed closed from October 1956 to March 1957, and Egypt kept control of it. A United Nations emergency force was set up, and Lester B. Pearson received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957.

Eden resigned on 9 January 1957 after being accused of misleading Parliament, and his successor Harold Macmillan accelerated decolonisation. Historians hold that the crisis showed that Britain and France could no longer act independently of American consent. It strengthened Nasser's standing and, according to some analysts, led France to seek its own nuclear weapons.
suffolk: Suffolk is a county of eastern England, in East Anglia, bordered by Norfolk to the north, the North Sea to the east, Essex to the south and Cambridgeshire to the west. Its coast has several deep estuaries, including those of the Blyth, Deben, Orwell, Stour and Alde, and a large spit at Orford Ness. Inland the landscape is flat and gently undulating, and the county is largely arable farmland; its highest point is Great Wood Hill, at 128 metres.

In 1797 John Frere found flint hand axes in a deposit twelve feet deep at Hoxne and suggested that they belonged to a very remote period, the earliest recognition that hand axes were made by early humans. At the start of the Roman period most of Suffolk was inhabited by the Iceni, with the Trinobantes in parts of the south. The Iceni unsuccessfully revolted under Boudica in 60–61 CE. Anglian settlement followed in the 5th and 6th centuries, and the area was mostly governed by the Kingdom of East Anglia. Sutton Hoo, an elaborate royal ship burial, is probably that of King Rædwald, whose son Sigeberht Christianised East Anglia.

In the medieval period Suffolk became part of the Danelaw after Viking incursions, and the county was formed in the 10th or 11th century. After 1066 castles were built at Framlingham, Clare and Eye, and the abbey at Bury St Edmunds became one of the wealthiest religious institutions in medieval England. King Edmund of East Anglia, after whom Bury is named, was killed by invading Danes in 869. Towns such as Lavenham and Hadleigh prospered from the cloth and wool trade in the 15th and 16th centuries, and during the English Civil War the county was a centre of Puritan and parliamentary strength.

Suffolk is a ceremonial county whose county town and largest settlement is Ipswich. Its other principal towns include Lowestoft, Haverhill and Bury St Edmunds. Felixstowe is a major container port, and Newmarket is the headquarters of British horseracing. The Hoxne Hoard, found in 1992, is the largest assembly of late Roman silver and gold found in Britain, and the Sutton Hoo treasures include a sword of state, a helmet and a lyre.
sugarcane: Sugarcane is a perennial grass of the genus Saccharum, 2 to 7 metres tall, with stout, jointed stalks that store sucrose. It is native to New Guinea. Two centres of domestication are recognised: Saccharum officinarum, bred by Papuans in New Guinea from the native Saccharum robustum beginning around 6,000 years ago, and Saccharum sinense, domesticated by Austronesians in Taiwan and southern China. Both peoples first used it mainly as food for domesticated pigs. Austronesian sailors carried it to Polynesia, Island Melanesia and Madagascar in prehistoric times, and also to India and then to southern China by 500 BCE.

The Persians and Greeks found, in the words of Strabo, that reeds in India yield honey without bees, and they adopted and spread its cultivation. By the eighth century sugar was a luxurious and expensive spice from India, and merchants carried it across the Mediterranean and North Africa. The word sugar derives ultimately from the Sanskrit śárkarā, which became sukkar in Arabic, saccharum in Latin and sucre in Middle French.

From the 18th century plantations were established in the Caribbean, South America, the Indian Ocean and Pacific islands. The demand for labourers to work the crop became a major driver of large migrations: some people accepted indentured servitude, while others were forcibly imported as slaves.

The juice is boiled to make jaggery, a solidified molasses, and syrups. Mills extract raw sugar and refineries purify it. The fibre left after crushing, bagasse, is used as fuel and for paper, and molasses goes into rum, baking and animal feed. Sugarcane reeds are also made into pens, mats, screens and thatch.

Sugarcane is the largest crop in the world by quantity produced, and it supplies about 79 percent of the world's sugar, most of the remainder coming from sugar beet. Commercial varieties are complex hybrids. Its cultivation has left lasting marks on landscapes: clearing for plantations replaced rain forests and wetlands, and heavy irrigation has strained water resources in places such as India and Australia. It is also a source of ethanol, which is used as a fuel in Brazil.
suger: Suger was born about 1081 into a family of minor knights who held land at Chennevières-lès-Louvres, near Saint-Denis. He was given to the abbey of Saint-Denis as an oblate at the age of ten, in 1091, and trained at the priory of Saint-Denis de L'Estrée, where he would first have met the future king Louis VI.

Becoming secretary to Abbot Adam of Saint-Denis in 1106, he took part in the synod at Poitiers that year and later in missions to Rome, and served as provost at Berneval in Normandy and then at Toury.

From 1118 he was deeply involved in royal affairs, welcoming the fleeing Pope Gelasius II to France and later living at the courts of Gelasius and of Calixtus II. On his return in March 1122 he learned that Abbot Adam had died and that the monks had elected him abbot in his absence. Louis VI was at first angry that he had not been consulted but was content with the choice. Until 1127 Suger occupied himself mainly with the temporal affairs of the kingdom, and in the following decade with the reform of Saint-Denis.

He advised the marriage of the future Louis VII to Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1137 and bitterly opposed their later divorce. He opposed the Second Crusade, partly because of problems in France, but a council in February 1147 elected him a regent. After the failure of the crusade he proposed a new one at Laon in 1150, but support collapsed, and the pope advised the king to remain in France. Suger died on 13 January 1151.

Suger's reconstruction of the abbey church began with the west front, which echoes the Roman Arch of Constantine and has three large portals and the earliest known rose window of its kind. After its completion in 1140 he rebuilt the eastern end as a choir suffused with light, using the pointed arch, the ribbed vault, the ambulatory with radiating chapels and flying buttresses that allowed large clerestory windows. It was dedicated on 11 June 1144 in the presence of the king. Later scholars discount the nineteenth-century view that Suger designed it, and see him instead as a bold patron of an unknown master mason.

He wrote an account of the building, the Libellus Alter de Consecratione Ecclesiae Sancti Dionysii, and the unfinished Liber de Rebus in Administratione sua Gestis, as well as a Life of Louis the Fat and an unfinished history of the first year of Louis VII's reign.
sugita-genpaku: Sugita Genpaku was born on 20 October 1733 in the Wakasa-Obama domain, the son of Hosen Sugita, official physician to the lord of Wakasa. His mother died at his birth. From about the age of 17 he studied surgery under Gentetsu Nishi and Confucianism under Saburoemon Miyase. At 25, with his lord's permission, he set up as a physician at Nihonbashidōri in Edo, and fires later forced him to move his practice twice, in 1759 and 1762.

He worked under sakoku, the policy that closed Japan to most of the world and left Nagasaki the only port open to Dutch traders. The eighth shogun, Tokugawa Yoshimune, had begun the systematic study of Dutch in 1740, but Western books remained restricted. In 1768 Genpaku watched the Dutch surgeon Rudolf Bauer treat a patient with gangrene of the tongue, and he knew at second hand of Tōyō Yamawaki's dissection of 1754.

The dissection of 4 March 1771, attended with Maeno Ryōtaku, Hoshū Katsuragawa and Junan Nakagawa, was of an executed woman known as Aocha-Baba. The Dutch atlas they compared with the body, Ontleedkundige Tafelen, went back to a German work by Johann Adam Kulmus of 1734. With only Maeno's vocabulary of some 600 Dutch words, the first Kaitai Shinsho took at least eleven manuscripts and contained errors and omissions, yet it is regarded as a turning point for Western medicine in Japan.

Genpaku taught many students of rangaku, among them Gentaku Otsuki, Shojuro Arai and Genzui Udagawa. Otsuki rewrote the translation of Kaitai Shinsho in 1788. In his Keiei yawa Genpaku argued that apart from the difference between men and women there was no real distinction between human beings, from the emperor to the commoners, a view shared by other Tokugawa physicians but not widely accepted.

In old age Genpaku built a large medical library and spent more time as a physician than as a scholar. Seeking an heir, he took in a young student named Genshin, disowned him for his temper, and later accepted him again as his son and left him his estate. Genpaku died on 1 June 1817. His students formed a generation that brought Western medicine to Japan, and his translations from Dutch were put into Chinese, among the first Western medical texts in that language.
suharto: Suharto was born on 8 June 1921 in the hamlet of Kemusuk, about 15 km west of Yogyakarta, then part of the Dutch East Indies. His Javanese parents, Kertosudiro, a village irrigation official, and Sukirah, divorced early in his life, and he was raised partly by foster relatives and moved between households in Kemusuk and Wuryantoro. Like many Javanese he had only one name; he spelled it Soeharto throughout his life.

He joined the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army in June 1940. After the Dutch surrender to Japan in March 1942 he joined the Yogyakarta police, part of the Japanese-organized security forces. When Sukarno and Hatta declared independence, he joined the newly formed Indonesian army and became a battalion commander in October 1945. In 1950, as a colonel, he led the Garuda Brigade in suppressing the Makassar uprising, and he later rose to major general.

Before dawn on 1 October 1965, six army generals were kidnapped and killed in Jakarta by soldiers of the Presidential Guard and two army divisions. Untung bin Syamsuri announced on the radio that the 30 September Movement had forestalled a coup against Sukarno by CIA-backed generals. The movement made no attempt on Suharto's life, and troops led by Suharto countered it. The army then led a nationwide violent anti-communist purge. In March 1967 the MPRS appointed Suharto acting president, and he was appointed president the following year.

When Suharto took power inflation was running at over 650%. He appointed an economic advisory group that applied free-market policies, and by 1969 prices were stable. His New Order government was centralised and dominated by the military, and Western powers, particularly the United States, backed his anti-communism during the Cold War. Industrialisation and growth of around 7% a year led the People's Consultative Assembly to name him Father of Development in 1982, and in 1986 the FAO awarded him the Ceres Medal for self-sufficiency in rice. In 1975 he ordered the invasion of East Timor, followed by a 23-year occupation.

By the 1990s the regime's authoritarianism and corruption had fuelled discontent. The Asian financial crisis of 1997 brought economic turmoil and protests. On 12 May 1998 security forces killed four demonstrators from Trisakti University, and rioting over the following days killed over 1,000 people, with ethnic Chinese a particular target. Suharto resigned in May 1998. Repeated illness kept him from trial on corruption charges, and he died on 27 January 2008. Indonesians remain divided over his legacy.
suhl: Suhl was first mentioned in a deed of 1318, though the annals of Fulda Abbey name a place called Sulaha at various points between 900 and 1155. Its coat of arms of 1365 shows two hammers, pointing to metal processing as its chief livelihood. The region belonged to the Franconian counts of Henneberg from the 11th century, and Suhl lay on a trade route from Gotha, Erfurt and Arnstadt across the Thuringian Forest. It became a small market town in 1445 and received full municipal rights in 1527. The Reformation was introduced in 1544.

Iron ore mining created the basis for a gunsmith trade, and metalworking boomed in the 16th century. When the Henneberg counts died out in 1583, Suhl passed to the Wettin electors of Saxony, and it stayed a Saxon and later Prussian exclave within Thuringia for nearly 300 years. The boom ended in the Thirty Years' War, when Croat mercenaries under the imperial general Johann Ludwig Hektor von Isolani burnt the city down in 1634. From about 1690 Duke Moritz Wilhelm of Saxe-Zeitz supported its reconstruction as a mining town.

The Congress of Vienna in 1815 gave Suhl to the Prussian Province of Saxony. The railway arrived in 1882, and industrialisation followed. After 1935 armaments production boomed again, and about 10,000 forced labourers worked in the city's arms industry after 1940. The US Army reached Suhl on 3 April 1945 and was replaced by Soviet troops on 1 July.

Metalworking led during the Renaissance to gunsmithing and armouring, and Suhl made cannons throughout the 17th century and after, which many European powers used. J. P. Sauer und Sohn, maker of hunting rifles, shotguns and pistols, was based there for almost 200 years. Other firms included Simson, which made vehicles, the Waffenfabrik August Menz, which produced the small Liliput pistol in the 1920s, and C. G. Haenel.

Suhl lies on the south-western edge of the Thuringian Forest, south-west of Erfurt, and is one of the six urban districts of Thuringia. Its population is about 37,000, down more than 35 per cent from 1988, after the city lost its administrative functions in 1990. The old town was largely demolished in the 1960s and rebuilt in concrete. It has a weapons museum, a vehicle museum devoted to Simson, and the Baroque St Mary's Church of 1753 to 1756.
sui-dynasty: The Sui was founded by Yang Jian, a Northern Zhou general from the military aristocracy of the northwest. His clan, the Yang of Hongnong, claimed Han descent but had intermarried with the Xianbei for generations. He became regent for the child emperor Jing of Northern Zhou, whose stepmother was his own daughter, and then took the throne as Emperor Wen of Sui. He had 59 Zhou princes put to death. He emphasised Han cultural identity, abolished the anti-Han policies of Northern Zhou and reclaimed his Han surname. For the dynasty's name he created a new character, 隋, from the one in his former title of Duke of Sui.

To conquer the south, Emperor Wen assembled thousands of boats on the Yangtze against the navy of the Chen dynasty. The largest had five decks and room for 800 men. In 588 the Sui had 518,000 troops along the river's northern bank, and by 589 they entered Jiankang, where the last Chen emperor surrendered and the city was razed. Wen built granaries to store food and steady prices, and the large agricultural surplus supported a population that reached a peak not passed until the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang. He also began the Grand Canal, first linking Chang'an to the Yellow River, and his diplomacy split the Turkic Khaganate into eastern and western halves.

Emperor Yang came to the throne after his father's death, possibly by murder. He enlarged the Grand Canal enormously and restored Confucian education and the examination system for officials. His armies retook the Hanoi area from Lý Phật Tử in 602 and then met war elephants from Champa. The four expeditions against Goguryeo were vast, one army reportedly taking 30 days to leave its rallying point, and each ended in failure. Heavy taxation and forced labour drove men to break their own limbs to escape conscription, and revolts spread. In 618 Emperor Yang was killed by his advisers of the Yuwen clan, while in the north the aristocrat Li Yuan rose and became Emperor Gaozu of Tang.

The dynasty lasted only 37 years, yet the Tang adopted its political system with little change except at the top. The Grand Canal later carried trade, travellers and culture for centuries. Wen and his empress turned to Buddhism, and in 601 he sent relics of the Buddha to temples across the empire, presenting himself as a Cakravartin king in imitation of Ashoka. Zhiyi founded the Tiantai school during this period. The Sui court also favoured Taoism, and the Confucian thinker Wang Tong wrote the Explanation of the Mean. Historians often compare the Sui with the Qin: each reunified China, reformed and built on a huge scale, and then collapsed quickly.
suintila: Suintila, also written Suinthila or Svinthila, was a son of King Reccared I and his wife Bado and a brother of the general Geila. He was born in about 588. When his older brother Liuva II was deposed in 603 he was spared by the nobility, possibly because of his age, for he was fifteen. Little is known of his life until about 620, when under King Sisebut he fought against the Byzantines, who had re-established themselves on the Iberian Peninsula during the 550s. He was elected king the next year, after the deaths of Sisebut and Sisebut's son Reccared II.

Suintila secured a peace unknown in Hispania since the early 5th century, with no foreign troops on its soil for the next 87 years. Sisebut had retaken Cartagena, Málaga, Sagunto and Assidonia from the Byzantines, and in 624 Suintila finished the work by seizing the Algarve, weakening Byzantine power in the former enclave. According to Isidore of Seville he was the first to rule all of Spain.

Like Liuvigild before him he tried to bring the Basques under his command, which led to the creation of a town named Ologicus, believed to be the later Olite in Navarre, though archaeologists have not confirmed this. Isidore praised his faith, prudence and generosity to the poor, calling him the father of the poor.

Others thought differently. The Chronicle of Fredegar reports that Suintila became hated for trying to make the kingdom hereditary, appointing his son Reccimer as co-regent in 626. In 631 the nobleman Sisenand rebelled in the Ebro valley after obtaining a promise of help from the Frankish king Dagobert I, whose generals Abundancius and Venerandus came to Saragossa and declared Sisenand king of the Goths.

At the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633 the council legitimized Sisenand's seizure of power. Suintila was accused of various iniquities, forced to renounce power, excommunicated, stripped of his possessions and exiled with his family. His death is dated between 633 and 635. In 1858 a farmer's plough uncovered the Treasure of Guarrazar and Torredonjimeno, which included eleven votive crowns, three of them bearing names: Suintila, Recceswinth and Sónnica.
suiyuan: Suiyuan, a name meaning Pacify the Distant Region, was called after a district of its capital, Kweisui (also written Guisui), that had been established under the Qing dynasty. The province covered roughly the area of the present-day prefecture-level cities of Hohhot, Baotou, Wuhai, Ordos and Bayan Nur and parts of Ulanqab, all of them in Inner Mongolia.

In the early 1930s Suiyuan was occupied by the Shanxi warlord Yan Xishan, who mined its iron, reorganised the provincial finances and brought over 4,000 acres of land under cultivation for the first time. Most of the work and settlement was done by Shanxi farmer-soldiers under the direction of retired officers of his army, and one visiting reporter called Suiyuan a "colony" of Shanxi. During the Second Sino-Japanese War the province was the scene of the Suiyuan campaign, and from 1937 to 1945 it formed part of the puppet state of Mengjiang under Japanese rule.

In 1935 the Communist leader Mao Zedong had promised Mongol leaders a unified autonomous administration that would include all the historic Mongol lands within China, in exchange for their support against the Kuomintang. After the Communist victory in 1949, however, the administrators of the territories meant to become Mongolian but with Han Chinese majorities resisted annexation by the new Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Suiyuan, with a population of over 2 million, was the largest of them.

The compromise Mao reached with Suiyuan in 1954 gave the Mongols the administration of the province but laid down that its Han natives were not to be expelled. Uradyn Bulag, a professor at the University of Cambridge, has noted that the Mongols' territorial ambitions towards Suiyuan ironically left them a small minority within their own autonomous region. Its former capital is now Hohhot.
sukaphaa: The chronicles, Ahom and non-Ahom, contradict each other on Sukaphaa's life before he reached Assam. In the account that the historian Phukan (1992) has tried to make consistent, he was the son of Chao Chang-Nyeu, a prince from Mong-Ri Mong-Ram, and Nang-Mong Blak-Kham-Sen of Möng Mao, near present-day Ruili in Yunnan. Born no later than 1189, he was raised by his maternal grandparents and named heir by his uncle Pao Meo Pung, until a son born late to the ruler's queen ended his claim.

Sukaphaa left Möng Mao in 1215 with three queens, two sons and a daughter, chiefs of five dependent Mongs, priests and soldiers, some 9,000 people in all, with 300 horses and two elephants. Following an old route through Myitkyina, Mogaung and the upper Irrawaddy valley, he reached the Nangyang lake in 1227, where he subdued the Nagas with great severity, and came through the Pangsau pass to Namrup in December 1228.

He came as the head of a farming people in search of land rather than as a raider. He avoided densely settled areas and opened new ground, lived among the local tribes, learnt their languages, honoured their rites and married the daughters of Badaucha, the Moran chief, and Thakumatha, the Barahi chief. He urged his soldiers and the Ahom elite to marry locally, and locals who took up Ahom wet-rice farming and statecraft were accepted into the Ahom fold.

His search for a capital took him from Tipam to Mungklang in 1236, Habung in 1240, Ligirigaon in 1244 and Simaluguri in 1246, before he built Charaideo in 1253. With local labour he set up three large farms for sali rice: Barakhowakhat, Engerakhat and Gachikalakhat.

When Sukaphaa died in 1268 his kingdom was bounded by the Brahmaputra in the west, the Disang in the north, the Dikhow in the south and the Naga Hills in the east. The kingdom lasted until 1826. The Borahi and Moran called his people Ha-Cham, a name that later became Assam and Ahom. He is remembered with the honorific Chaolung, great lord, and the Assam Government decreed in 1996 that 2 December be kept as Sukaphaa Divas, or Asom Divas.
sukarno: Sukarno was born Kusno Sosrodihardjo in Surabaya, in the Dutch East Indies, on 6 June 1901. His father was a Muslim Javanese primary school teacher and his mother a Hindu Balinese woman of the Brahmin caste. He studied at Dutch schools, met the nationalist Tjokroaminoto in Surabaya, and obtained an engineering degree in Bandung in 1926. There he began to develop an Indonesian-style socialist self-sufficiency that he called Marhaenism, after a peasant he met who worked his own small plot.

On 4 July 1927 he and his friends founded the Indonesian National Party, and he became its first leader. Arrested on 29 December 1929, he used his trial in 1930 to attack colonialism in speeches titled Indonesia Accuses. He was then sent without trial to internal exile, in 1934 to Ende on Flores and in 1938 to Bengkulu in Sumatra.

The Japanese invasion of January 1942 freed him, and he cooperated with the occupiers in the hope of using them to gain independence. On 1 June 1945 he put forward the five principles known as pancasila to a committee preparing for independence. After Japan's surrender he was pressed by younger nationalists, who briefly kidnapped him on 16 August, and on 17 August 1945 he and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed the independence of Indonesia in front of about 500 people. As president he led the republic through the war with the Dutch, including the second invasion of December 1948, when he allowed himself to be taken prisoner. Dutch recognition came in 1949, and in August 1950 he declared a unitary republic.

In 1959, after unstable years of parliamentary democracy, he reinstated the constitution of 1945 by decree and introduced Guided Democracy; in 1963 he was elected president for life. He had organised the Bandung Conference in 1955, and he placed Indonesia among the leaders of the Non-Aligned Movement. Meanwhile the economy deteriorated, with hyperinflation exceeding 600 per cent a year in 1964–1965.

On 1 October 1965 the 30 September Movement killed six senior army generals, and General Suharto took control. A large anti-communist purge followed, in which between 500,000 and over 1 million people were killed. Sukarno gave up his executive powers on 20 February 1967 and on 12 March was stripped of the title of president for life, while Suharto became acting president. He was held under house arrest, died of kidney failure on 21 June 1970 and was buried in Blitar, East Java. Under Suharto his role was minimised, but after Suharto's fall in 1998 interest in him revived, and he is widely respected as the founding father of Indonesia.
sukbin-choe: Lady Choe was born on 17 December 1670, during the reign of King Hyeonjong, the youngest of three children. Her father was Choe Hyo-won and her mother a lady of the Namyang Hong clan. How she first met King Sukjong is unknown. The best-known telling is in the Sumunrok of Yi Mun-jeong, who wrote that the sleepless king, passing the servants' quarters one night, found a young maid weeping before a memorial table for the deposed Queen Min on her birthday, though no one dared honour her for fear of Queen Jang, and was moved by her loyalty.

Lady Choe openly supported Queen Min against Jang Ok-jeong. In 1694 Sukjong brought Queen Min back and demoted Jang Ok-jeong. When Queen Min died in 1701, one version holds that it was Lady Choe who told the king that sorcery had been used against her. The king found that Jang Ok-jeong had built a shamanist altar in her quarters with effigies bearing the queen's name, and ordered that she and all others involved should die by poisoning. He then passed a law forbidding royal consorts from becoming queen.

The belief that Lady Choe was next in line to be queen has no basis: two consorts of the yangban class, Gwiin Park and Gwiin Kim, were better placed, and her low birth was a major obstacle in a Confucian society ruled by class. Between 1699 and 1702 she was the principal benefactor of Gakhwangjeon Hall in Hwaeomsa Temple. In 1704 the king gave her Ihyeongung, a large complex in the capital, as her residence, and in 1711, when Queen Kim fell ill with smallpox, she sent palace women to look for remedies among the commoners.

She was taken out of the palace while ill in 1716 and died on 9 April 1718, aged 47, at Changuigung, her son's residence. Her tomb, Soryeongwon, lies in Paju in Gyeonggi Province and is designated Historical Site No. 358. When her son became king he set up an altar near the tomb, built memorial halls around it and wrote the texts of its gravestones himself.

The court officials opposed honouring her as his public mother, which would have obliged them to honour her and allowed the king frequent visits to her tomb as royal rites. In 1739 he censured two officials over the protocols for such a visit. Her spirit tablet was enshrined in Chilgung, which houses the tablets of seven royal consorts who bore kings, and she received the posthumous name Hwagyeong, harmonious reverence.
sukkalmah: The title sukkal-mah, great sukkal, first appeared at Girsu in an inscription of Urukagina, with a meaning close to prime minister or grand vizier. It remained in use in the Ur III period at Lagash, where the sukkalmahs reported directly to the king, and in that form it was adopted by the rulers of Elam. Siwe-palar-huppak also called himself likawe rishakki, which may be the Elamite rendering of the title, risha being Elamite for great. The Sukkalmah or Epartid dynasty, c. 1900 to c. 1500 BCE, took its name from the title, though not all its rulers used it.

The creation of the system is generally attributed to Ebarat II, but an inscription of the reign of Idattu I calling Kiten-rakittapi the sukkalmah of Elam suggests an earlier start, with the sukkalmah of Elam subordinate to the king of Anshan. Some rulers held other titles first and are thought to have become sukkalmah later in life. The structure is commonly described as a triumvirate with the sukkalmah as the highest authority, but De Graef proposes at least two sukkalmahs, of Anshan and Susa and of Elam and Shimashki, with several sukkals and governors beneath them, and Potts cautions that a simple triumvirate leaves out the many other offices recorded.

Rulers often called themselves the son of the sister of an earlier ruler, above all of Shilhaha, and at least eleven did so. Some scholars, such as Hinz and Vallat, read this as royal incest, but Potts sees in it an avuncular succession, from uncle to nephew, and De Graef calls the incest theory outdated. Where real descent was impossible, the phrase seems to have claimed legitimacy through a fictitious descent.

In the letters from Mari under Zimri-Lim the sukkalmah of Elam held a prestigious place in international affairs. He mediated between Zimri-Lim and Hammurabi of Babylon over disputed border cities, and while Amorite rulers of their rank addressed one another as brothers, they called the sukkalmah father, denoting superior rank. The scribes of Mari were less sure of the Elamite system, often calling the sukkalmah the sukkal of Elam, and many letters from him give only his title. The numerous cuneiform documents from the period, above all from Susa, make it one of the best documented in Elamite history.
sukkur: Sukkur stands on the western bank of the Indus directly across from the historic city of Rohri, on a small Eocene limestone outcrop that is the most notable land deformation on the vast Indus plains of Sindh and Punjab. This outcrop and a similar one on Bukkar Island are sometimes called the Sukkur Gorge, and have traditionally marked the northern boundary of Sindh. The name comes from the Sindhi sakhar, meaning superior. The climate is a hot desert one, and Sukkur was described as the hottest city in British India.

The region has been inhabited for millennia. The ruins of Lakhan-jo-daro, near an industrial park on the outskirts, date from the Mature Harappan period, between 2600 and 1900 BCE, and cover more than 300 hectares. Old Sukkur was a small village until a military garrison was established in 1839. Date palm groves around it were traditionally believed to have grown from the date stones discarded by Arab invaders in the 8th century. Across the river Rohri was a busy port and a major trading centre for agricultural produce by the 1200s, and a minaret 26 metres high was built at Sukkur's shrine of Mir Masum Shah in 1607.

Modern Sukkur was built under British rule. The garrison was abandoned in 1845, but the town kept growing as a trading centre, and its municipality was constituted in 1862. The Lansdowne Bridge, completed in 1889, was one of the first to cross the Indus. It is made of metal and has two large pylons rather than a series of piers, a cutting-edge design for so wide a span. The Sukkur Barrage, formerly the Lloyd Barrage, was built between 1923 and 1932 under Sir Charlton Harrison to a design by Sir Arnold Musto. It is 1,524 metres long and waters nearly 40,000 square kilometres of farmland through seven canals.

Before Partition in 1947 old Sukkur had about 10,000 residents and New Sukkur about 80,000. About 70 per cent of the population was Hindu in the 1941 census, and only 2 per cent in 1951, after most Hindus left for India, many of them after riots in Karachi on 6 January 1948. Muslim refugees from India settled in the city. The Ayub Bridge was built in 1962 beside the Lansdowne Bridge.

Sukkur is the third largest city in Sindh, with a population of 563,851 in the 2023 census. About three quarters of its people speak Sindhi as a first language. It is a trading and processing centre for the farms of northern Sindh and is known for its dates, and it is the capital of Sukkur Division and Sukkur District.
sulawesi: Sulawesi, also known as Celebes, is one of the four Greater Sunda Islands and the world's 11th-largest island, with an area of 186,064 km2. It lies east of Borneo and west of the Maluku Islands. Its landmass has four peninsulas, separated by the gulfs of Tomini, Tolo and Boni. The interior is rugged and mostly non-volcanic, so the peninsulas have traditionally been remote from each other, with better connections by sea than by road. The name Celebes was given by Portuguese explorers and first recorded in 1512. Sulawesi is part of Wallacea, and many of its animals and plants are found nowhere else.

The oldest evidence of humans on Sulawesi is stone tools made by archaic humans, dated to at least 1.04 million years ago, found at the Calio site in the south-west. Cave paintings at Maros were announced in 2014 to be about 40,000 years old; a hand stencil is 39,900 years old, and a pig in Pettakere Cave has a minimum age of 35,400 years. From the 13th century, access to prestige trade goods and to sources of iron began to change older cultural patterns and allowed ambitious individuals to build larger political units.

The first Europeans to visit were the Portuguese Simão de Abreu in 1523 and Gomes de Sequeira in 1525, sent from the Moluccas in search of gold.
