A Portuguese base in Makassar lasted until 1665, when the Dutch took it. The Dutch had arrived in 1605 and were followed by the English. From 1660 the Dutch fought Gowa, the main Makassar power, and in 1669 Admiral Speelman forced Sultan Hasanuddin to sign the Treaty of Bongaya, which gave trade to the Dutch East India Company. The Bugis ruler Arung Palakka of Bone aided the Dutch and became regional overlord.

Luwu was the first kingdom to adopt Islam, in February 1605, and Gowa-Talloq followed in September; the Gorontalo and Mongondow peoples of the north largely converted in the 19th century. Islam is the majority religion. The island was one province between 1945 and 1960 and is now divided into six provinces: Gorontalo, West Sulawesi, South Sulawesi, Central Sulawesi, Southeast Sulawesi and North Sulawesi. The 2020 census counted 19,896,951 people, and Makassar is the largest city.
sulayhid-dynasty: The Sulayhids, the Banū Ṣulayḥ or Children of Sulayh, came from the Yemeni clan of Banu Salouh, of the al-Hajour tribe of the Hashid. Isma'ili missionaries had worked in Yemen since 881, when Ibn Hawshab and Ali ibn al-Fadl al-Jayshani arrived; Ibn al-Fadl took San'a in 905, but the Yu'firid dynasty overthrew their regime in 916.

The Fatimid mission went on despite that setback. Its da'i in Yemen, Sulayman az-Zawahi, befriended Ali bin Muhammad as-Sulayhi, the son of a respected Sunni chief from Haraz, south-west of San'a, who was nevertheless drawn to the doctrines of the Fatimids. Ali converted to the Isma'ili creed in 1046 and was made khalifa within the da'wa. In 1047 he raised an armed force in Haraz and founded the dynasty.

Ali took Zabid after the Najahid ruler of the Tihama was poisoned in 1060, defeated the Ma'nids of Aden and made them pay tribute in 1062, and in the same year conquered the whole of Yemen and moved north into the Hejaz, for a time appointing the Emirs of Mecca. He held San'a from 1063, after ending his fighting against the Zaidiyyah, and made it his capital. Relatives of the Najahids killed him, in 1067 or 1081.

Under his son al-Mukarram Ahmad the realm shrank, possibly to the area of San'a, until he rescued his captured mother, Asma bint Shihab, and won back much ground. In 1086 he handed government to his wife, Arwa, and died at the fortress of Ashyah in 1091. Arwa, recognised by the Fatimids as suzerain over the Yemeni kings, moved her capital to Jibla in about 1087 and ruled through strong commanders: Saba' bin Ahmad, Al-Mufaddal bin Abi'l-Barakat and Ibn Najib ad-Dawla, who attempted a coup in 1125 and was sent back to Egypt in a wooden cage.

Throughout its existence the dynasty was an enemy of the Zaidi rulers of Yemen. Arwa joined the Taiyabi Ismaili sect, while other Ismaili dynasties such as the Zurayids of Aden, at first Sulayhid tributaries, and the Hamdanids adhered to the Hafizi Ismaili sect. When Arwa died in 1138 no member of the dynasty was left, and the Sulayhid era ended.
sulayman-al-baruni: Al-Baruni was born around 1870 in the Jabal Nafusa, then part of the Ottoman vilayet of Tripolitania, into an influential Berber family of the Ibadi sect. His father, Abd Allah al-Baruni, was a jurist, poet and theologian. From 1887 he studied at the University of Ez-Zitouna in Tunisia, where the reformist Muhammad al-Nakhli, a critic of colonialism and Sufism, influenced him strongly. In 1893 he entered Al-Azhar University for three years, met anti-colonial currents in Egypt and admired the ideas of Mustafa Kamil, and then studied Ibadi theology and literature in the M'zab valley under Muhammad ibn Yusuf Atfayyash.

In Cairo he founded a newspaper and later a printing press. Under Sultan Abdul Hamid II the Ottoman authorities arrested him several times on the charge of planning to restore an Ibadi imamate or emirate in the Jabal Nafusa. After the Young Turk Revolution he was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1908 as the member for the Jabal Gharbi. When the Italo-Turkish War broke out in 1911 he began recruiting Berbers against the invasion, and in late October 1912, after the Ottoman capitulation, he took a leading part at the Congress of Aziziyya.

He then sought an understanding with Italy, hoping for an autonomous Ibadi principality centred on the Jabal Nafusa and Marsa Zuaga, or at least special privileges for the Berbers. After the last Berber resistance was crushed at the Battle of Al-Asaba'a on 23 March 1913 he went into exile in French Tunisia. In October 1916, during the First World War, the Ottoman sultan appointed him governor of Tripolitania, Tunisia and Algeria, territories the Ottomans did not actually control. After joining the leadership of the Tripolitanian Republic in November 1918, he made his peace with Italy when the Fundamental Law was issued in June 1919.

By September 1921 Italian policy had helped bring about a civil war between Berbers and Arabs, and many Berbers blamed al-Baruni. He left in November 1921 for his final exile, travelling to France, Egypt, Turkey and Mecca before settling in Oman. He died on 1 May 1940 while visiting Mumbai with the Sultan of Oman, Said bin Taimur. His daughter, Za'ima bint Sulayman, published some of his papers at Tripoli in 1964, and in 1970 his body was returned to Libya and buried in Tripoli after a national ceremony.
sulaymaniyah: Sulaymaniyah, also called Slemani, is the capital of the Sulaymaniyah Governorate in the east of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. It is surrounded by the Azmar, Goizha and Qaiwan Mountains in the north-east, Baranan Mountain in the south and the Tasluja Hills in the west. Its summers are cooler and its winters rainier than those of most of Iraq's main cities, and snow falls every year or two.

The region was known as Zamwa before the modern city was founded. The earlier capital of the Kurdish Baban principality, which existed from 1649 to 1850, was a territory called Qelaçiwalan, a battleground between the Safavid dynasty and the Ottoman Empire. Ibrahim Pasha Baban became ruler of the emirate in 1783 and began building a new capital. In 1784 he finished a number of palaces for trade, called Qeyserîs, and bazaars that also served as baths, and he invited people from surrounding villages and emirates to settle. Melkendî, which had originally been meant to be the city itself, became one of its quarters. Slemani was the capital of the Baban principality from 1784 to 1850.

According to Jewish tradition, the Baban ruler Sulaiman Baban held that a town was incomplete without Jewish residents, and the Jews of Qaradagh sent the first group of Jewish inhabitants. In the early 1800s refugees from Ardalan, among them the widow of the ruler Xosraw Xanî Erdalan, moved to Slemani, and the ruler himself, who wrote an account of Kurdish history in Persian, was buried there when he died in 1848. The Iraqi Revolt of the early 1920s against British rule of the Mandate for Mesopotamia, led by Shaikh Mahmud, triggered a wave of Jewish emigration. From 1922 to 1924 Slemani was the capital of the Kingdom of Kurdistan, a short-lived unrecognised state declared by Iraqi Kurds after the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.

By 1947, according to Iraqi government documents, the city had 23,475 residents, among them 1,517 Jews, nearly all of whom emigrated to the newly established State of Israel between 1951 and 1952. The population was estimated at 548,747 in 1998.

Slemani was the home of the poets Nalî, Mahwi and Piramerd. The University of Sulaimani opened in 1968 and teaches in Kurdish, Arabic and English; it is the largest university in the Kurdistan Region. The Sulaimani Museum holds Mesopotamian, Kurdish and ancient Persian artefacts, and the city also has an archaeological museum and a museum of modern art.
suleiman-ibn-qutalmish: Suleiman was the son of Qutalmish, who struggled unsuccessfully against his cousin Alp Arslan for the throne of the Great Seljuk Empire. When Qutalmish died in 1064, Suleiman fled with his three brothers into the Taurus Mountains and took refuge with Turkoman tribes living beyond the empire's borders. Alp Arslan answered with a series of punitive expeditions. Of the four brothers only Suleiman and his brother Mansur survived the raids, and Suleiman consolidated his leadership of the Turkomans of the Taurus.

Suleiman founded an independent Seljuk state in Anatolia and ruled as Seljuk sultan of Rum until his death in 1086. The chronicler al-Azimi says he captured Nicaea in 1075. The Great Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I recognised him as ruler of Rum, and the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im sent him an edict and a robe of honour. No record shows him minting coins or having the sermon delivered in his own name, and several sources state his subjection to Malik-Shah, so he was probably still subject to the Great Seljuk Empire.

In 1078 the Byzantine emperor Michael VII asked for his help against Nicephorus Botaneiates, who had challenged him for the throne. Botaneiates persuaded Suleiman and Mansur to join his rebellion with better offers, and after his success their Turkmen were allowed to settle on the Asiatic side of the Bosphorus, near Constantinople. Two years later Suleiman backed another pretender, Nicephorus Melissenus, who opened the gates of Nicaea to the Turkmen. All Bithynia soon fell to Suleiman. In 1084 he captured Antakya from the Byzantine governor Philaretos Brachamios. The Uqaylid Muslim ibn Quraysh demanded tribute, Suleiman refused, and in 1085 he defeated Muslim's army after Turkmen under Cubuk bey defected.

In 1086 Suleiman besieged Aleppo. Its emir offered the city to Tutush I, the Seljuk ruler of Syria, and Suleiman lifted the siege to meet him. At the battle of Ain Salm near Aleppo, his forces fled before Tutush's army under Artuk Bey, and Suleiman was killed. Malik-Shah marched to Antakya, where Suleiman's vizier surrendered the city and Suleiman's son Kilij Arslan I, whom Malik-Shah took to Isfahan as a hostage. After Malik-Shah's death Kilij Arslan re-established the Sultanate of Rum.
suleiman-the-magnificent: Suleiman succeeded his father Selim I on 30 September 1520. His reign was the longest of any Ottoman sultan, and by its end the empire had at least 25 million subjects. He took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, and at Mohács in 1526 he broke the strength of the Kingdom of Hungary, much of which was then incorporated directly into the empire. His defeat at the siege of Vienna in 1529 stopped his advance into Europe. In the east he fought the Shia Safavid Empire of Iran and annexed Iraq, entering Baghdad in 1535.

At sea he appointed Khair ad Din, known to Europeans as Barbarossa, admiral-in-chief to rebuild the fleet. The Ottomans took Aden in 1538, and although they failed against the Portuguese at the siege of Diu that year, they went on to take Yemen. In 1535 Charles V led a Holy League to victory over the Ottomans at Tunis. This and the war against Venice led Suleiman to accept an alliance with Francis I of France against Charles.

Subjects knew him as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, although the epithet is absent from 16th and 17th-century Ottoman sources and may date from the early 18th century. The Sharia lay outside the sultan's power to change, but the Kanuns, covering criminal law, land tenure and taxation, depended on his will. He collected the judgments of the nine sultans before him, removed duplications, chose between contradictory rulings and issued a single code, the kanun-i Osmani, with the help of his chief judicial official Ebussuud Efendi. It lasted more than three hundred years.

His patronage drew artists to the Topkapı Palace, where the Ehl-i Hiref, the Community of the Craftsmen, employed painters, bookbinders and goldsmiths. A payroll register of 1526 lists 40 societies with more than 600 members. The poets Fuzûlî and Bâki worked under him. In 1534 he broke with tradition by marrying Hürrem, a former concubine.

Suleiman died on 6 September 1566, aged 71, on campaign in Hungary, before an Ottoman victory at the siege of Szigetvár. His Grand Vizier Sokollu Mehmed Pasha kept the death secret during the retreat so that Selim II could be enthroned. His body was taken to Istanbul, while his heart and some organs were buried at Turbék, where a mausoleum became a pilgrimage site.

His image as an ideal ruler was built in his own reign, notably by the chancellor Celalzade Mustafa. Later Ottoman writers of advice literature held his reign up as a model and presented departures from it as decline. Western historians long accepted that account, but since the 1980s scholars have overwhelmingly rejected the idea of decline after his death, seeing instead a period of crisis and adaptation.
suleja: Suleja is a city and Local Government Area in Niger State, Nigeria, just north of Abuja, the capital of the country. Its wooded savanna area of about 2,980 square kilometres originally included four small Koro chiefdoms that paid tribute to the Hausa kingdom of Zazzau. The town was first named Abuja, and the name was taken from its then emir, Sulayman Bal, when the new federal capital was named Abuja in 1976, which is why the two places are sometimes confused.

After warriors of the Fulani jihad captured Zaria, the capital of Zazzau, about 1804, Muhamman Makau, the sarkin of Zazzau, led many of the Hausa nobility to the Koro town of Zuba, 10 kilometres to the south. His brother and successor Abu Ja, called Jatau, founded the town of Abuja in 1828, began building its wall a year later and proclaimed himself the first Sarkin Abuja. The emirate withstood attacks from Zaria and remained an independent Hausa refuge.

Trade with the Fulani emirates of Bida and Zaria began under Emir Abu Kwaka, who reigned from 1851 to 1877. When Abuja's leaders disrupted the trade route between Lokoja and Zaria in 1902, the British occupied the town. Alluvial tin mining began under Emir Musa Angulu, who reigned from 1917 to 1944.

In 2011 bomb attacks struck Suleja: ten people were killed on 3 March, and another bomb killed 25 people on 7 April. On 18 January 2025 a tanker carrying about 60,000 litres of petrol overturned at the Dikko junction near Suleja, and residents gathered to collect the spilled fuel. It exploded, killing over 100 people and injuring another 69.

Farming remains the chief occupation, and local trade is mainly in agricultural products. Cotton weaving and dyeing with locally grown indigo, and mat making, are traditional activities, and the town exports Gbari pottery. The Ladi Kwali Pottery Centre was established by Michael Cardew in 1950, and its leading exponent was Ladi Kwali, whose works are displayed internationally. Ancient sculptures of the Nok culture found in Suleja town and in the bed of the Makabolo River have helped to show Nok influence on the Yoruba art of Ife.
suleymaniye-mosque: Suleiman I chose the architect Mimar Sinan to build a mosque in memory of his son, Crown Prince Mehmed, the Şehzade Mosque. Impressed by the result, he asked Sinan to design a mosque for himself. It stands on the Third Hill of Istanbul, on the site of the old Ottoman palace, Eski Saray, which had to be demolished. An inscription gives a foundation date of 1550 and an inauguration date of 1557, though planning began earlier and parts of the complex were not completed until later.

Suleiman's empire covered much of the Islamic world after his father Selim's conquest of the Mamluk Sultanate in 1517, and he promoted reliance on the Shari'a and orthodox Sunni ideology in rivalry with the Shi'a Safavids. The mosque was meant to represent the pre-eminence of the empire, and its design recalls the Hagia Sophia and the Bayezid II Mosque.

The mosque is the largest Ottoman-era mosque in the city. Its prayer hall measures almost 58 by 57 metres, with a central dome 53 metres high and 26.5 metres across, flanked by semi-domes and rows of smaller domes. Sinan hid many load-bearing buttresses in the outer walls, so that the exterior rises to the dome in an almost pyramid-like progression, and he added galleries and corner entrances.

Four minarets stand at the corners of the courtyard, the two taller ones 76 metres high with their caps; their ten balconies are said to reflect that Suleiman was the tenth Ottoman sultan. The interior decoration is restrained, with calligraphy in thuluth script attributed to Hasan Çelebi, and Iznik tiles used only around the mihrab.

The mosque is the centre of a külliye, a religious and charitable complex that included four madrasas, a primary school, a medical school, a hospital, a public kitchen serving the poor, a guesthouse, baths and a school of hadith. Shops along its edges brought in revenue.

Behind the qibla wall are the octagonal mausoleums of Suleiman, built between 1566 and 1568 on the orders of his son Selim II, and of his wife Hürrem Sultan, who died in 1558. The tomb of Sinan stands just outside the complex walls.

The mosque was damaged by fire in 1660 and by an earthquake in 1766 that brought down part of the dome, and the courtyard suffered a fire in the First World War. The painting of the dome dates from a 19th-century restoration by the Fossati brothers. A comprehensive restoration took place between 2007 and 2010. The mosque and its conservation area form one of the four components of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Historic Areas of Istanbul.
sulfuric-acid: The study of vitriols, the hydrated sulfates of various metals from which sulfuric acid can be derived, began in ancient times. The Sumerians had a list of types of vitriol classified by colour, and the Greek physician Dioscorides and the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder discussed its origin and properties. Metallurgical uses are recorded in the Hellenistic alchemical works of Zosimos of Panopolis, and Ibn Sina and Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Watwat included vitriol in their mineral lists. Medieval European alchemists called the acid oil of vitriol because it was prepared by roasting green vitriol in an iron retort.

By the 16th century a method called oleum sulphuris per campanam, oil of sulfur by the bell, was known: it burned sulfur under a glass bell in moist weather. It was very inefficient, since Gesner reported that 5 pounds of sulfur gave less than 1 ounce of acid, and most alchemists, Isaac Newton among them, did not consider it equivalent to oil of vitriol.

Sulfuric acid is a mineral acid of sulfur, oxygen and hydrogen with the formula H2SO4, a colourless, odourless, viscous liquid that mixes with water. Pure sulfuric acid does not occur naturally because it absorbs water vapour readily. The concentrated acid is a strong oxidant with a powerful dehydrating property and is highly corrosive. Dilution releases considerable heat, so the acid is added to water and not the reverse. The permanent clouds of Venus are made of concentrated sulfuric acid.

In 1746 John Roebuck of Birmingham adapted the sulfur method to lead-lined chambers, which were stronger, cheaper and larger than glass vessels. This lead chamber process made industrial production possible and remained the standard for almost two centuries. Refinements by Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and John Glover raised the concentration to 78 percent, but dyes and other processes needed a stronger acid, which in the 18th century could be made only by dry distillation of minerals such as pyrite, at too great an expense for large-scale use.

In 1831 the British vinegar merchant Peregrine Phillips patented the contact process, a far more economical way to make sulfur trioxide and concentrated acid, by which nearly all of it is now made. In the early and mid 19th century vitriol plants stood at Prestonpans in Scotland, in Shropshire and in the Lagan Valley in County Antrim, where it bleached linen faster than the lactic acid of sour milk. Its dominant modern use is in making phosphoric acid for fertilizers.
suliko: Akaki Tsereteli was closely tied to the Georgian national liberation movement, and readers have heard in the poem his wish for an independent Georgian homeland as well as his own search for meaning. The poet and folklorist Eter Tataraidze recorded a story told in the village of Toneti in the Tetritskaro Region: that Akaki dedicated the poem to Suliko Samadashvili of Toneti, the brother of a friend.

In that story Suliko was killed by a wild animal in the forest while on his way to town to buy clothes for his wedding, and his bones were found only after months of searching. When Akaki came to the grave he found Suliko's beloved weeping there, and so changed the first line from a search for a brother's lost grave to a search for a beloved's. Such a folk tale is not historical fact, but it shows how far the poem reached into Georgian lore.

Scholars have read the poem in several ways. Akaki Bakradze saw in its sequence of images, the rose, the nightingale and the star, a vertical ascent in search of God and of the lost paradise from which mankind was exiled. Emzar Kvitaishvili extended the idea, arguing that the search for Suliko as the embodiment of supreme love is a search for God. Others read it as a symbol of an unattainable dream, whether the reconciliation of the self or a person's place in life.

The song was translated into and sung in many languages, among them Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, Romanian, English, German, Basque, Chinese and Hebrew. It has been performed in widely different traditions, from Georgian ensembles such as Mdzlevari and Ensemble Batumi to the Alexandrov Ensemble and the Large Academic Chorus of Mendeleev University.
sulis-minerva: The meaning of the name Sulis has been debated, but an emerging consensus among linguists links it with Old Irish súil, eye or sight; a root related to the Indo-European words for sun has also been proposed, and some researchers have seen her as a solar deity at least before the Romans came. Devotion to her at Bath probably began before the Roman presence, among the local Celtic Dobunni tribe, and eighteen Iron Age Celtic coins found at the lowest levels of the site, documented by Barry Cunliffe in 1988, point the same way. This is one reason Sulis is named first in the joined name.

Of the 17 dedicatory altars and bases found at the temple, 9 name Sulis Minerva by one or both names. Sulis Minerva is one of the few attested pairings of a Celtic goddess with a Roman one, since Celtic goddesses tended to resist such identification.

Worshippers probably came to the goddess for healing, and pewter vessels found in the reservoir may have been used to pour the water over visitors' bodies. Additions to the altar area suggest that sacrifice was a major part of the cult, and the altar fire burned coal rather than wood, brought by slaves who also served at cult meals. Over 12,500 Roman coins were found in the reservoir, with jewellery, gems, bowls and military items. According to Miranda Green, the cult was active until the mid-fourth century CE.

The curse tablets ask the goddess to deny thieves sleep, health or even life until stolen money or clothing is returned. Their local British Latin shows that many came from the native population, and some were written backwards or in alternating lines. Two texts on pewter sheets are in an unknown language that may be Brythonic. The handwriting of the tablets ranges from the second to the fourth century CE.

A gilt bronze head of the goddess, probably from a cult statue that stood beside the spring, was found in 1727; the statue appears to have been deliberately damaged in later antiquity. The temple pediment, found in 1790, has a large Gorgon's head at its centre. A lead tablet found in 1979 gave the phrase dea Sulis, the only example of the name in the nominative case, and settled the scholarly preference for Sulis over the older reading Sul, though the debate continues.
sulla: Lucius Cornelius Sulla was born into a branch of the patrician gens Cornelia, but his family had become impoverished by the time of his birth. An ancestor, Publius Cornelius Rufinus, the last of the family to be consul, had been expelled from the Senate for possessing more than 10 pounds of silver plate, and the family did not reach the highest offices again until Sulla himself. A stepmother of considerable wealth helped his ambitions. He stood for the quaestorship in 108 BCE, after reaching the minimum age of thirty, and was assigned by lot to serve under the consul Gaius Marius in the Jugurthine War.

Sulla came to prominence in the war against the Numidian king Jugurtha, whom he captured after the king was betrayed by his allies, although Marius took the credit. He then served against the Cimbri and Teutons and, as governor of Cilicia from 96 BCE, restored Ariobarzanes to the throne of Cappadocia, after which his troops hailed him imperator. In the Social War against Rome's Italian allies he won the Grass Crown for bravery at Nola.

He was elected consul for 88 BCE. When a deal between Marius and the tribune Publius Sulpicius Rufus transferred the command against Mithridates VI of Pontus from Sulla to Marius, Sulla took command of his army and marched on Rome, the first Roman general to do so. Marius and Sulpicius were driven out. Sulla then crushed the Pontic armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenos in 86 BCE and made a generous peace with Mithridates. Returning to Italy in 83 BCE, he defeated the faction of Marius and Lucius Cornelius Cinna at the Battle of the Colline Gate in 82 BCE.

Sulla published proscription lists naming first about 80 men and then hundreds more, and he had three or four thousand Samnite prisoners killed. He revived the dictatorship, dormant for over a century, under a law that set no time limit, and reformed the constitution to restore the primacy of the Senate and limit the tribunes of the plebs. He then resigned his powers.

Sulla retired to a country villa near Puteoli, where he wrote his memoirs and intervened intermittently in politics, and he died in 78 BCE. Much of his legislation was repealed within a decade, and the powers of the tribunes were restored under Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus. Late republican and early imperial writers described him almost uniformly as a cruel and vengeful tyrant. Cicero reports that Pompey once said, 'If Sulla could, why can't I?', and Sulla is generally seen as the precedent for the marches on Rome by later generals such as Julius Caesar.
sullas-civil-war: After his first march on Rome, Sulla left Italy to fight the First Mithridatic War. In his absence Gaius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Cinna took back the city from Sulla's supporter Gnaeus Octavius; Marius's soldiers killed leading Sullans, some 100 nobles in all, Sulla was declared an exile and his laws annulled. Marius died soon after his election as consul for 86 BCE, leaving Cinna in control. Cinna was later killed in a mutiny at Ancona, and with Mithridates defeated for the moment, Sulla turned back to Italy.

In the spring of 83 BCE Sulla landed in two divisions, at Brundisium and Tarentum. Outlawed nobles joined him, among them Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius and Marcus Licinius Crassus with armies of their own, while Pompey raised three legions in Picenum. Sulla routed the consul Gaius Norbanus at the Battle of Mount Tifata, and the army of the other consul, Scipio Asiaticus, went over to him during negotiations at Capua.

In 82 BCE Sulla defeated Gaius Marius the Younger at Sacriportus, and Marius retreated to Praeneste, where he was besieged. Before Sulla reached Rome the praetor Lucius Junius Brutus Damasippus had Sullan sympathisers killed, among them the Pontifex Maximus Quintus Mucius Scaevola. In the north Metellus and Pompey wore down Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, who finally fled to Sicily. A Samnite and Lucanian army under Pontius Telesinus and Marcus Lamponius then marched on Rome, and at the Colline Gate about 50,000 men are estimated to have died. Some 8,000 prisoners were executed afterwards on Sulla's orders, and Marius took his own life at Praeneste.

Pompey went on to take Sicily, where he had Carbo sentenced to death, and Africa, while Quintus Sertorius was driven from Spain only to return the next year. The proscriptions killed some 1,500 senators and equites and perhaps as many as 9,000 people, many for their property, and the sons and grandsons of the proscribed were barred from office for over 30 years. Sulla stripped the tribunes of most of their powers, doubled the Senate from 300 to 600 members and gave it control of the courts. Near the end of 81 BCE he resigned the dictatorship and was elected consul for 80 BCE.
sullivan-expedition: When the Revolutionary War began, both the British and the Continental Congress sought the allegiance of the Haudenosaunee, or Six Nations. Most Senecas, Cayugas, Onondagas and Mohawks sided with the British, while most Oneidas and Tuscaroras joined the revolutionaries, partly through the influence of the Presbyterian missionary Samuel Kirkland. After the surrender of General John Burgoyne at Saratoga in October 1777, raids from Fort Niagara led by the Loyalist Major John Butler, the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant and the Seneca war chiefs Sayenqueraghta and Cornplanter struck American frontier settlements and Oneida villages. A raid on Cobleskill on 30 May 1778 killed 22 regulars and militia.

The expedition took up more than a third of the Continental Army: four brigades, 4,469 men on paper and just under 4,000 when it set out. Sullivan marched from Easton, Pennsylvania, on 18 June, reached the Wyoming Valley on 23 June and, delayed by supply shortages, moved up the Susquehanna to Tioga, where Fort Sullivan was built. James Clinton's brigade dammed Otsego Lake to float its boats downriver and joined him on 22 August.

On 29 August Sullivan's army of 3,200 met about 600 Loyalists and Seneca, Cayuga and Delaware warriors behind a log breastwork at Newtown on the Chemung River. A flanking march through a morass came too late, and Butler withdrew. The army then burned Catherine's Town, Kanadaseaga and Chenussio, whose 128 houses were destroyed with their fields, and detachments laid waste the Cayuga villages around Cayuga Lake. Colonel Daniel Brodhead led a separate force up the Allegheny from Fort Pitt, and Colonel Peter Gansevoort seized the neutral Mohawk settlement of Tiononderoga. The army abandoned Fort Sullivan on 3 October.

On 21 September there were 5,036 refugees at Fort Niagara, and about 2,600 by 21 November; most of the Seneca and Cayuga who wintered there later settled at Buffalo Creek. The winter of 1780 was bitterly cold, and estimates of the dead vary widely: Jeffrey Ostler counts about 200 killed by military action and up to 1,000 later deaths, Colin Calloway and Alan Taylor several hundred, while Koehler suggests roughly 5,000. Sullivan, his health broken, resigned on 30 November 1779. Monuments marked its centenary in 1879 and its 150th anniversary in 1929, the 35 of 1929 with plaques claiming that Sullivan had forever stopped Indian depredations, a narrative now regarded as false.
sulmona: Sulmona lies in the Valle Peligna, a plain once occupied by a lake that disappeared in prehistoric times. In the province of L'Aquila, it was one of the principal cities of the Paeligni, an Italic tribe. Ovid praises its healthy air and the many permanent streams of clear water in its neighbourhood, and calls it gelidus Sulmo, cold Sulmo, since like the whole district it was extremely cold in winter. The territory was fertile, with grain and wine, and Pliny mentions the care given to the irrigation of the vineyards of one district, the Pagus Fabianus.

Nothing is recorded of Sulmo before the Roman conquest. A tradition alluded to by Ovid and Silius Italicus gave its foundation to Solymus, a Phrygian companion of Aeneas, which is regarded as an etymological fiction. Hannibal ravaged its territory in 211 BCE during the Second Punic War but did not attack the city. According to Florus, Sulla destroyed it as a punishment for loyalty to Gaius Marius, though it is more probable that its lands were confiscated and given to his soldiers. In 49 BCE it was a populous town, and its citizens, favourable to Julius Caesar, opened their gates to his lieutenant M. Antonius. Ovid calls it a small provincial town, one of three municipal towns in the territory of the Paeligni.

Tradition places the beginning of Christianity in Sulmona in the 3rd century. Saint Pamphilus, a convert from Corfinium, was elected bishop of Valva in 682, died in 706 and is the patron saint of the town. Sulmona became a free commune under the Normans, within the Kingdom of Sicily. Under Frederick II an aqueduct was built, and he made it the capital of a large province, with a tribunal and a fair, which it lost to the Angevins. A paper industry began in the 16th century, and an earthquake in 1706 nearly razed the city, which was largely rebuilt in the Baroque style.

Sulmona is the birthplace of Ovid, who is commemorated by a bronze statue on the main road. Surviving medieval buildings include the Church of Santa Maria della Tomba, the Palazzo Annunziata, the aqueduct and the Gothic portal on Corso Ovidio. Campo 78, a prisoner-of-war camp, held Austrian prisoners in the First World War and as many as 3,000 British and Commonwealth soldiers in the Second, until the guards deserted in September 1943.
sultan: The word derives from an Arabic and Semitic root meaning to be hard or strong. The noun sulṭān first designated a kind of moral authority or spiritual power, as opposed to political power, and it is used in this sense several times in the Qur'an. In the early Muslim world ultimate authority was held in theory by the caliph, while local governors bearing the title amir were appointed by him. After the 8th century political fragmentation challenged this arrangement, and in the 9th century some governors became de facto independent and founded dynasties, such as the Aghlabids and Tulunids. Towards the late 10th century the term began to be used for an individual ruler with practically sovereign authority.

The first major figure to clearly grant himself the title was the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud, who reigned from 998 to 1030. The Great Seljuks adopted it soon afterwards, and their early leader Tughril Bey was the first to use the epithet sultan on his coinage. Their power overshadowed that of the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, which led scholars such as Al-Juwayni and Al-Ghazali to argue that legitimate authority derived from the caliph but was delegated to sovereign rulers he recognised.

After the Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, the surviving Abbasid descendants lived in Cairo under Mamluk protection, and the Mamluks styled themselves sultans. In the 16th century the Ottoman Empire conquered the Mamluks, and the jurist Ebüssuûd Mehmet Efendi recognised the Ottoman sultan Suleiman as caliph as well as sultan. In the 19th century Ottoman authorities emphasised this combination, claiming that Selim I received the caliphate in Cairo in 1517. Shi'a rulers did not use it as a sovereign title: the Safavid dynasty of Iran used the Persian title shah.

The Ottomans themselves usually called their ruler padişah, and the formal title combined sultan with khan. By the 16th century the title was carried by men and women of the Ottoman dynasty, and Ottoman princesses and the mother of the reigning sultan bore it after their names. In the Kazakh Khanate a sultan was a prince descended from Genghis Khan. Sultanates stretched from West Africa and the Horn of Africa through India to the Malay world. The monarch of Morocco changed his title from sultan to king in 1957, and Brunei, Malaysia and Oman are the sovereign states that retain the title.
sultan-agung: Born Raden Mas Jatmika and popularly known as Raden Mas Rangsang, he was the son of Anyakrawati, the second monarch of Mataram, and Ratu Mas Adi Dyah Banawati, a daughter of Prince Benawa, the last Sultan of Pajang. He came to the throne at the age of 20, succeeding his half-brother Duke Martapura, who reigned for only one day to fulfil a promise their father had made to Martapura's mother. In 1614 he began the new Karta Palace, about 5 km south-west of the old capital at Kotagede.

His early campaigns against Surabaya and Malang failed, but the indemnity he extracted paid for the conquest of Wirasaba in 1615. Lasem fell in 1616, Pasuruan in 1617 and Tuban, one of the oldest cities of the coast, in 1619. He weakened Surabaya by taking its allies, Sukadana in south-west Kalimantan in 1622 and the island of Madura in 1624, after which he changed his title to Susuhunan Agung. With Surabaya taken, Mataram held all of central and eastern Java except the west end and the mountainous south.

Mataram's economy rested on agriculture, and Agung, openly contemptuous of trade, kept no strong navy; at Batavia the Dutch East India Company's command of the sea proved decisive. He then turned against the Balinese in Balambangan, but could not carry his power to Bali itself. Rebellions in Pati, Tembayat, Sumedang and Ukur followed, and Giri Kedaton was subdued by Pangeran Pekik, a descendant of Sunan Ampel. At home he reformed the tax code, brought the courts closer to Quranic precepts and set adipati over new provinces, a structure the Dutch later kept as the kabupaten.

In 1632 he began his burial place at Imogiri, about 15 kilometres south of Yogyakarta, which remains the resting place of most of the royalty of Yogyakarta and Surakarta. He died in the spring of 1645 and, by his will, was succeeded by his son Raden Mas Sayidin, styled Amangkurat I. His court is credited with developments in the bedhaya dance, gamelan and wayang, though there is almost no historical evidence for such claims. He was declared a National Hero of Indonesia on 3 November 1975, and pilgrimage to his grave is held to be auspicious.
sultan-al-atrash: Sultan al-Atrash was born on 5 March 1891 in al-Qrayya, a village 20 km south of Suwayda and the home of the Al-Atrash family, which had nominally governed the region since 1879. His father Zuqan fought the Ottoman forces of Sami Pasha al-Farouqi near Al-Kefr in 1910 and was captured and executed in 1911. Sultan himself was conscripted into the Ottoman army and served in the Balkans before the First World War.

During the war he made contact with the Arab Revolt in the Hijaz and raised its flag on the citadel of Salkhad. When the Arab forces reached Aqaba he sent a thousand men to join them, and he followed with 300 more at Bosra. His men were the first to enter Damascus, raising the revolt's flag on the government house on 29 September 1918. Emir Faisal, a close friend, gave him the title of Emir and the rank of general.

After France occupied Syria following the Battle of Maysalun on 24 July 1920, Jabal al-Druze became one of five states into which the country was divided. On 7 July 1922 French soldiers seized Adham Khanjar, a Lebanese rebel wanted for an attempt on General Henri Gouraud, at Sultan's house. Sultan attacked a French convoy, the French destroyed his house, and he fled to Jordan, raiding French posts until he was pardoned ten months later.

In 1925 he led the revolt from the Druze Mountain, winning the Battle of al-Kafr on 21 July and the Battle of al-Mazraa on 2 August. France then sent thousands of troops from Morocco and Senegal with modern weapons and regained many cities. Sentenced to death, he escaped to Transjordan, was eventually pardoned and returned in 1937 after the Franco-Syrian Treaty. He later opposed Adib Shishakli, supported the union of Egypt and Syria in 1958 and opposed its end in 1961.

Al-Atrash refused any political office after Syrian independence in 1946 and rejected a French offer of independence for the Druze Mountain, demanding national unity. During the revolt he used the slogan "Religion is for God, the fatherland is for all". He died of a heart attack on 26 March 1982, aged 91, and more than a million people attended his funeral. Statues of him stand in the main squares of the Druze Mountain.
sultan-hasanuddin: Hasanuddin was born in Makassar on 12 January 1631 as I Mallombasi Daeng Mattawang, the second prince of Sultan Malikussaid, the 15th king of Gowa, who died on 15 November 1653. His full name, which included Muhammad Baqir, was given by the kingdom's qadi, Sayyid Syaikh Jalaludin bin Ahmad Bafaqih Al-Aidid, who was also a teacher of Sheikh Yusuf. Gowa was by then the only large kingdom of eastern Indonesia not yet colonised by the Dutch, and its conflict with the Dutch East Indies Company (VOC) had begun as early as 1616 over the company's aim of a monopoly of the spice trade.

Makassar was a cosmopolitan city with nearly 2,000 Portuguese, and European experts helped to modernise its army and navy; the capital was guarded by the fortress of Sombaopu. A VOC blockade of the harbour in 1654–1655 ended in a treaty on 2 February 1656. When Hasanuddin demanded on 27 April 1659 that the company end its attacks on his vassals Seram, Buru and Amblau, a fleet under Johan van Dam captured the fortress of Panakkukkang by a feint against Sombaopu, and a new treaty required Makassar to expel the Portuguese and pay an indemnity.

In 1660 the Bugis of Bone rose under Arung Palakka, and Hasanuddin crushed the rising, reportedly with great cruelty. He then sealed Makassar's coast with a brick wall nearly eleven kilometres long and refused to expel the Portuguese. In 1666 Cornelis Speelman arrived with the flagship Tertholen and twenty other vessels, while Arung Palakka raised the Bugis in rebellion. After the Treaty of Bongaya of 1667 Hasanuddin repudiated the terms within months, and the war resumed.

With an army of 10,000 men raised by Arung Palakka, Speelman attacked Makassar directly, and the siege dragged on until the defences were overcome by sapping on 12 June 1669. The company made Makassar its puppet state, pulled down Sombaopu and built Fort Rotterdam in its place. Hasanuddin died on 12 June 1670. The Dutch called him the Rooster of the East for his aggression in battle, and he was proclaimed a National Hero of Indonesia on 6 November 1973.
sultan-husayn: Soltan Hoseyn was born in 1668 in the royal harem, the eldest son of Shah Solayman and a Circassian woman, and grew up with little experience of the affairs of the country. He read the Quran under Mir Mohammad-Baqer Khatunabadi and preferred Azeri Turkish to Persian. On his deathbed Solayman is reported to have said that the younger son, Soltan Tahmasp, should be chosen for fame and the elder for peace and calm. The succession of the elder was secured by his great-aunt Maryam Begum and by the court eunuchs. He was first enthroned on 7 August 1694, a week after his father's death.

Soltan Hoseyn was nicknamed Darvish and Molla for his piety, and he left much of the government to ministers, above all the Sunni grand vizier Fath-Ali Khan Daghestani, in office from 1715. Clerics were allowed to pursue anti-Sufi measures and action against non-Shi'ites, including the forced conversion of Zoroastrians and the collection of jizya from Jews and Christians, yet he also issued decrees protecting Christians and allowing missionaries to work. The anti-Sunni policies alienated many Sunnis, most of whom lived on the frontiers.

The reign saw growing disorder. A Balochi invasion overwhelmed Kerman in 1699, and in 1703 the Georgian prince Gorgin Khan was made governor of Qandahar, where he came into conflict with the Afghan chief Mirwais Hotak. In 1721 an earthquake destroyed three quarters of Tabriz and killed over 40,000 people. The weight of the abbasi coin was cut from 7.39 g to 5.34 g between 1717 and 1722.

Mirwais's son Mahmud Hotak besieged Isfahan in 1722, and famine forced Soltan Hoseyn to surrender on 21 October 1722. His third son declared himself Tahmasp II at Qazvin in November. In February 1725 Mahmud ordered the other princes killed; Soltan Hoseyn was wounded trying to stop it, but saved two young children. His successor Ashraf Hotak had Soltan Hoseyn beheaded on 9 September 1727, answering an insulting message from the Ottoman commander Ahmad Pasha. Contemporary and later writers have counted his devotion, superstition, pursuit of pleasure and extravagance among the causes of the decline of the Safavid state.
sultan-khalil: Khalil was born in spring 1442, the eldest son of Uzun Hasan by Saljuqshah Begum, a daughter of Kur Muhammad Bayandur. In 1459 he married an unnamed daughter of Suhrab Beg Çemişgezeki. During his father's reign he governed Fars from Shiraz, which the Aq Qoyunlu had taken in 1468. Several manuscripts are dated to his years there, among them a Divan of Ali-Shir Nava'i of 1471, and he is known to have worked on a copy of the Khamsa of Nizami while in Tabriz.

Khalil ruled as sultan from 6 January 1478. Immediately after Uzun Hasan's death he had his younger half-brother Maqsud Beg, a son of Despina Khatun, executed in Tabriz, and after his enthronement he sent his full brothers Ya'qub Beg and Yusuf Beg, with their mother, to Diyar Bakr. Shiraz was given as an appanage to his eldest son, Alvand Mirza. In May 1478 his cousin Murad b. Jahangir rebelled; the revolt was suppressed and Murad was executed by the middle of June.

A more serious rebellion then rose in the west in Ya'qub's name. The two armies met near Khuy, north-west of Tabriz, on 15 July 1478. The battle at first went Khalil's way, but he was cut off from the main body of his army, surrounded and killed, and Ya'qub succeeded him.

His son Alvand died shortly after his father's overthrow; another son, 'Ali Mirza, is also known. An illustrated manuscript of the Diwān of Hidayat, written in Azarbayjani Turkish in 1478, shows Khalil in four miniatures at courtly pursuits such as hawking and receiving audiences, painted in the Turkman style with its small, round-faced figures. A manuscript dedicated to him in Tabriz in the same year is also known.
sultan-kudarat: Kudarat was a direct descendant of Shariff Kabungsuwan, a Malay-Arab noble from Johor who in tradition brought Islam to Mindanao. His name joins the Malay title di-Pertuan, ruler, literally the one who has been made to rule, with Kudarat, from the Arabic qudrat, power, which in Maguindanaon was sometimes pronounced Kurlat. When Sultan Laut Buisan died, custom expected his successor to come from Lanao, but Kudarat lobbied the datus of Maguindanao and Lanao for himself. The displeasure of the Lanao datus led Lanao to break away and form the Lanao sultanates, and about the same time Kudarat made an armistice with the rajas of Buayan to prevent raids.

In 1619–1621 Kudarat allied with the Dutch East India Company, selling it rice and slaves captured from the Visayas, and he played the Dutch and the Spaniards off against each other as both sought access to local ports and the spice trade. When the Spanish expedition of 1637 reached his strongly fortified position at Lamitan, the Spaniards took 8 bronze cannons, 27 lantaka or culverins and 100 muskets, but Kudarat escaped to the mountains and gathered his strength again.

In 1639, when the Spaniards invaded the lands of the Maranaos, he went to confer with the datus of Lake Lanao. A Spanish ambassador recorded his appeal to them not to sell themselves into slavery to toil for foreigners, as he said the Tagalogs and Visayans had. Within months the Spaniards withdrew towards Zamboanga and did not venture into inland Lanao again. By the end of 1639 Kudarat had also reached an understanding with Datu Maputi for a united front against them.

On 25 June 1645 Governor-General Diego Fajardo Chacón signed a treaty with Kudarat that let Spanish missionaries minister to the Christians of Mindanao, allowed a church to be built and opened trade in the sultan's territories. Kudarat died in 1671, aged 89 or 90, at Simuay, now part of the municipality of Sultan Kudarat in Maguindanao del Norte. The Soccsksargen province of Sultan Kudarat is also named after him, and his descendants, who bear the title of datu, take part in local politics.
sultan-said-khan: Sultan Said Khan was a grandson of Yunus Khan, ruler of Moghulistan, and the third son of Akhmad Khan, and a direct descendant of Tughlugh Timur, the first Moghul khan. The Moghuls were turkicized Mongols who had converted to Islam. When the nomadic Uzbeks of Shaybani Khan overran Maverannahr, killing the descendants of Timur and Chagatai Khan, he saved his life by moving east. In May 1514 he marched on Kashgar from Andijan with only 5,000 tribesmen, took the Yangihisar citadel and then the city, and dethroned Mirza Abu Bakr, whose rule had been marked by forced labour of convicts in excavations of ancient cities.

Yarkand, Khotan, Aksu and Uch Turpan soon recognised him, forming the union of six cities called Altishahr; the population's discontent with Abu Bakr and the reluctance of the Dughlat emirs to fight a descendant of Chagatai Khan explain much of his success. In 1516 he made peace with his elder brother Mansur Khan of Turpan, bringing the eastern oasis cities into his state, so that he united the settled lands from Kashgar to Kumul. Kashmir and Bolor paid him tribute. His cousin Mirza Muhammad Haidar wrote that tyranny gave way to law and order under him, with theft punished severely, even by death.

He kept close ties with his cousin Babur. When he raided Badakhshan in 1529 at its people's request and found Babur's son Hindal Mirza holding the Zafar fortress, a council in Agra decided against war, Hindal was recalled and Suleiman Shah was restored as ruler.

With Haidar and a few thousand men he crossed the Karakoram, suffering severe altitude sickness, and devastated the Nubra Valley. In Baltistan he killed and enslaved the Muslim population, possibly because they were Shiites. He is said to have died at Daulat Beg Oldi on his way back to Yarkent, of high-altitude pulmonary edema. A bloody succession brought his son Abdurashid Khan to power, who ruled until 1560.
sultanate-of-gowa: The Nagarakretagama, the poem in praise of King Rajasanagara of Majapahit, lists Makassar among that kingdom's tributaries in 1365. Gowa's first ruler was a queen, Tomanurung Baine, of whom little is known. Under the sixth king, Tonatangka Kopi, the realm was divided between his two sons: Batara Gowa ruled Gowa, and Karaeng Loe ri Sero founded the kingdom of Tallo. The two fought for years until Tallo was defeated. Under Tunipalangga, the tenth king, who reigned from 1512 to 1546, they were joined as twin kingdoms under a treaty called Rua Kareng se're ata, dual kings, single people, and from then on the king of Tallo was also king of Gowa.

The conversion of Gowa-Tallo to Islam is traditionally dated to 22 September 1605, when the 14th king, Karaeng Matowaya, took the name Sultan Alauddin. He ruled from 1591 to 1629, and his conversion is linked with three scholars from Minangkabau: Datuk Ri Bandang, Datuk Ri Tiro and Datuk Ri Pattimang. When neighbouring kingdoms refused the faith, Gowa launched the campaigns known locally as the Islamic wars in 1611, subjugating all of south-western Sulawesi, its rival Bone included, and invading Sumbawa in 1618. Defeated rulers had to profess the shahadah as a sign of submission, though their peoples were not commonly forced to convert.

From 1607 the sultans welcomed all foreign traders, and an English factory was built at Makassar in 1613. Bone rose against Gowa in 1644 and was defeated at Passempe, and a Bugis revolt led by Arung Palakka in 1660 failed. Under the 16th sultan, Hasanuddin, Gowa fought the Dutch East India Company and its Bugis allies. After the war Admiral Cornelis Speelman destroyed the great fortress of Somba Opu and built Fort Rotterdam in its place; Hasanuddin gave up the throne and died on 12 June 1670, and Arung Palakka became sultan of Bone in 1672. The Dutch made war on Gowa again from 1904, and in 1911 it lost its independence and became a regency of the Dutch Indies.

Its rulers bore the title Karaeng Sombayya ri Gowa, the king who is worshipped in Gowa. Gowa's expansion brought order to the many local titles of the small Makassarese polities. Karaeng titles, granted by the ruler, marked high noble rank and were often place names that gave the holder the right to tribute and labour from that community. The chief office was the Tumabicarabutta, regent and chief adviser, a post that by the early 17th century the ruler of Tallo held as a rule; the Tumailalang ministers managed everyday affairs.
sultanate-of-rum: The Sultanate of Rum was a culturally Turco-Persian Sunni Muslim state set up by the Seljuk Turks over conquered Byzantine territory in Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071. Rum was a synonym for the medieval Roman Empire and its peoples, and the Seljuks used it for Anatolia. Its founder was Suleiman ibn Qutulmish, a distant cousin of Alp Arslan, who gained control of Nicaea between 1075 and 1081 and seceded from the Seljuk Empire in 1077. Malikshah recognised the sultanate as a vassal state in 1084. Suleiman died in the Battle of Ain Salm in 1086, and his son Kilij Arslan I re-established the state between 1092 and 1094.

Kilij Arslan I defeated the People's Crusade of 1096, was driven back by the First Crusade and set up his capital at Konya. His son Mesud I held nearly all of central Anatolia by 1156. Kilij Arslan II defeated a Byzantine army under Manuel I Komnenos at the Battle of Myriokephalon in 1176. The sultanate reached its height in the late 12th and early 13th century under Kaykhusraw I, Kaykaus I and Kayqubad I, who took Antalya in 1207 and Sinop in 1214 and made the Empire of Trebizond a vassal. Trade across Anatolia grew along a system of caravanserais, with close ties to the Genoese.

Kaykhusraw II faced a revolt led by the preacher Baba Ishak, and in 1243 the Mongol commander Baiju crushed him at the Battle of Köse Dağ. The Seljuks became vassals of the Mongols, and after 1256 all Anatolia was subject to Möngke Khan. The state split into small beyliks, among them the early Ottoman state. Mesud II, the last of the vassal sultans, was murdered in 1308, and the Karamanids conquered the last lands in 1328. Seljuk coins stayed in use throughout the 14th century, including among the Ottomans.

The sultanate was founded by Oghuz warriors, but a Turco-Persian synthesis defined its intellectual and aesthetic life by the 13th century. The sultans bore Persian names, the administration and courts used Persian, and refugees fleeing the Mongols reinforced Persian culture. The poet Rumi took his name from the state. The population included Greeks, Armenians, Kurds, Turks and Persians, and the Seljuk palaces were staffed with slave-soldiers taken as children from non-Muslim communities, mainly Greeks. The Seljuks of Rum built madrasas, mosques and about a hundred caravanserais, including the Sultan Han of 1229 between Konya and Aksaray.
sultaniyya: Soltaniyeh lies in the Central District of Soltaniyeh County in Zanjan province, about 240 kilometres north-west of Tehran. It is the capital of both the county and the district. Its name refers to the Islamic ruler title sultan and translates loosely as the Regal, a fitting name for a city laid out as a seat of royal power.

The city was built in the 14th century as the capital of the Mongol Ilkhanid rulers of Iran. The traveller Ruy González de Clavijo visited it and reported that it was a hub of silk exportation. The writer William Dalrymple notes that Öljaitü intended Soltaniyeh to be the largest city in the world, but that it died with him and is now a deserted, crumbling spread of ruins.

Soltaniyeh also became the seat of an archdiocese. On 1 April 1318, in response to the progress of the Persian missions of the Dominican and Franciscan orders, Pope John XXII established the archdiocese of Soltania and separated it from the archdiocese of Khanbalik. Its first archbishop was the Dominican Francesco da Perugia. In 1329 the Latin Diocese of Samarcanda became its suffragan for the Chagatai Khanate, at least until Tamerlane swept its see at Samarkand. The archdiocese ceased to have a resident archbishop around 1450 and was then kept as a titular archbishopric, which was itself suppressed in 1926.

UNESCO listed Soltaniyeh as a World Heritage Site in 2005. The city is small. At the census of 2006 it had 5,864 inhabitants, and the census of 2016 counted 7,638. A road runs from Zanjan to Soltaniyeh and continues as far as the Katale khor cave.
sulu-archipelago: The Sulu Archipelago is a chain of islands in the south-western Philippines. It forms the northern limit of the Celebes Sea and the southern limit of the Sulu Sea. Its islands belong to the provinces of Basilan, Sulu and Tawi-Tawi, whose first syllables give it the name Basulta. Basilan, Jolo, Tawi-Tawi and other islands are extinct volcanic cones rising from the southernmost of several small submarine ridges; the chain is not, as is often supposed, the remains of a land bridge between Borneo and the Philippines. The largest municipalities are on Jolo, and the islands are an important migration route for birds.

The archipelago was once part of Majapahit, and the Nagarakretagama mentions it as Solot. It later became part of the Sultanate of Sulu, founded in 1405 by Shari'ful Hashem Syed Abu Bak'r, which also included parts of Borneo, Mindanao and Palawan. Spanish expeditions against Jolo met firm and organised resistance. In 1578 a Spanish mission to Jolo produced a compromise in which the sultan paid tribute in pearls, but the Spanish burned Jolo in 1587, and attacks in 1598, 1628 and 1630 failed. In 1638 Governor Sebastián Hurtado de Corcuera took Jolo with about 80 ships and 2,000 troops, but a garrison there was worn away by raids and was gone by 1645.

Hostilities resumed in the eighteenth century, and Great Britain became a new player after occupying Manila from 1762 to 1764, when it made trading alliances with the sultanate. In 1848 and 1850 Spanish forces under Narciso Claveria and Juan Urbiztondo destroyed the Balangingi strongholds, a powerful ally of the sultanate, and its maritime power began to decline. In 1876 Admiral Jose Malcampo captured Jolo with 9,000 soldiers and established a Spanish settlement, though the Spaniards were never secure there. After the war between Spain and the United States in 1898, the independence movement known as the Moro Rebellion, from 1899 to 1913, continued the resistance against the United States, and the Philippines became independent on 4 July 1946.

The archipelago is the home of the Tausug and of various Sama peoples, including the semi-nomadic Bajau, the Yakan and the Jama Mapun. Tausug is widely spoken as a first and second language, Yakan mainly on Basilan, and many dialects of Sinama from Tawi-Tawi to the coast of Mindanao. Jolo still has short stretches of its Spanish perimeter wall, partly covered by buildings.
sumatra: Sumatra is one of the Sunda Islands and the largest island entirely within Indonesia, about 482,286 square kilometres including adjacent islands. It stretches about 1,790 kilometres along a northwest-southeast axis, with the equator crossing its centre. The Bukit Barisan mountains, with several active volcanoes, form its backbone, while the northeast has large plains of swamps, mangrove forest and river systems. The narrow Strait of Malacca separates it from the Malay Peninsula, and the Sunda Strait, with the Krakatoa archipelago, separates it from Java. The Great Sumatran fault and the Sunda megathrust run along its west coast, so earthquakes and tsunamis are common.

Sumatra has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Its ancient Sanskrit names, Svarṇadvīpa and Svarṇabhūmi, meant the Island of Gold and the Land of Gold, after gold deposits in its highlands. The earliest known mention of the form Sumatra is from 1017, when a local king, Haji Sumatrabhumi, sent an envoy to China. By 692 the Melayu Kingdom had been absorbed by Srivijaya, whose influence declined in the 11th century after a defeat by the Chola Empire of southern India in 1025. By the end of the 12th century Srivijaya had shrunk to a kingdom, and the Palembang area later declined as Srivijaya's heritage was superseded by the economic policy of the Singhasari and Majapahit.

Because it lies close to the Strait of Malacca, Sumatra was the first area of the archipelago to receive Islam, which spread through trade and the formation of kingdoms; in the 13th century the king of the Samudra kingdom converted. Aceh became known in the 16th century as a trading centre for pepper, with trade routes to the Mediterranean via the Red Sea to rival the Portuguese. Under Iskandar Muda, whose reign is called the golden age of Sumatra, it extended its cultural influence to Padang and Johor.

The Dutch Empire gradually took over the princely states. Aceh posed a major obstacle, and the Dutch fought the long and costly Aceh War from 1873 to 1903. Japan invaded Sumatra in 1942, and in 1945 it was one of the eight original provinces of Indonesia.

Sumatra is divided into ten Indonesian provinces and has about 62 million people, with more than 52 spoken languages. Its largest indigenous peoples are the Malays, Minangkabau, Bataks, Acehnese and Lampungs, and its largest city is Medan. Most Sumatrans are Muslims. Three national parks form the Tropical Rainforest Heritage of Sumatra World Heritage Site, and the island is home to the Sumatran tiger, elephant, rhinoceros and orangutan.
sumbawa: Sumbawa lies in the middle of the Lesser Sunda Islands, with Lombok to the west, Flores to the east and Sumba to the south-east. It has an area of 15,448 square kilometres, three times that of Lombok, and with Lombok it forms the province of West Nusa Tenggara. It is bounded by the Alas Strait, the Indian Ocean, the Sape Strait and the Flores Sea, and Saleh Bay almost cuts it in two. On the Sanggar Peninsula stands Mount Tambora, a stratovolcano and the island's highest point.

The island marks a boundary between the islands to the west, influenced by religion and culture from India, and the less influenced region to the east. The name probably derives from the Sanskrit śāmbhawa, relating to Shiva, by way of the local Sambawa and the Portuguese Cumbava.

The 14th-century Nagarakretagama names principalities in eastern Sumbawa, among them Dompu, Bima and Sape, and four in the west were dependencies of the Majapahit Empire of eastern Java. Because of its resources the island was regularly invaded, by Javanese, Balinese and Makassarese and later by the Dutch and Japanese. The Dutch first arrived in 1605 but did not effectively rule Sumbawa until the early 20th century.

The Balinese kingdom of Gelgel ruled part of the west for a short time, and the east and centre were traditionally divided into four sultanates, Sumbawa, Sanggau, Dompo and Bima, with links to the Bugis and Makassar peoples of South Sulawesi. Islam was introduced by the Makassarese.

Sumbawa was known in the East Indies for honey, horses, sappanwood, which gives a red dye, and sandalwood. In the 18th century the Dutch introduced coffee plantations on the slopes of Tambora. Tambora's eruption in 1815 was the most powerful in recorded history, ejecting 180 cubic kilometres of ash and debris. It killed up to 71,000 people, caused the global cooling of the Year Without a Summer in 1816, and apparently destroyed a culture known to archaeologists as the Tambora culture.

Three languages unintelligible to each other were historically spoken: Basa Semawa in the west, Nggahi Mbojo, the language of Bima, in the east, and the language of the Tambora culture, related to neither. After 1815 the kingdoms based at Sumbawa Besar and Bima became the island's two focal points, and the division persists. The island's population was 1,561,461 at the 2020 census. Most people work in agriculture, and the island has the Batu Hijau gold and copper mine, which began commercial operation in 2000.
sumbawa-besar: Sumbawa Besar, officially just Sumbawa, is a town and administrative district on the island of Sumbawa and its second-largest settlement after the city of Bima. Its harbour, Labuhan Sumbawa, is of minor importance; the island's main port, Poto Tano, lies 90 kilometres to the west, with a ferry across the Alas Strait to Labuhan Lombok. The volcano Mount Tambora, whose eruption of 1815 was one of the most powerful in the world, stands 40 kilometres to the northeast, and the waterfall of Air Beling lies in a forest that was once a royal hunting ground.

The sultan's former palace, the Istana Dalam Loka, was built with 99 columns and without a single nail; Sultan Jalaludin III reigned from 1883 to 1893. It was renovated in the 1980s and now serves for cultural events. The town's largest mosque, Masjid Agung Nurul Huda, was built beside the palace. Under Dutch rule a Reformed church was founded around 1900 and still holds services.

In 1932 the Dutch put up the Balai Kuning, a tall administration building in a European half-timbered style, whose foundation stone of 11 February 1932 still carries its Dutch inscription on the northern wall. It now houses weapons and clothing used by former sultans and stands in a park with two cannons of the colonial period. A few other buildings of the Dutch colonial era survive in the town.

Sumbawa Besar is the administrative capital of the Sumbawa Regency in the province of West Nusa Tenggara, with 62,753 inhabitants at the 2020 census. Indonesian is widely spoken beside the Sumbawa language, and some people speak Balinese; a Balinese Hindu temple, Pura Agung Giri Gnatha, stands near the palace. Universitas Samawa was founded in 1998, and Sultan Muhammad Kaharuddin III Airport serves small flights to Mataram on Lombok. The Batu Bulan Dam, built from 1998 to 2003 with financial aid from Japan, irrigates 5,576 hectares.
sumedang: Sumedang, formerly spelled Soemedang, lies about 46 km north-east of Bandung, the provincial capital, and is the capital of Sumedang Regency. The town is made up of two administrative districts, South Sumedang and North Sumedang, with a combined area of 125.32 km2 and a population of 184,293 in mid-2025. It lies just south of the volcanic Mount Tampomas, 1,684 m high, which is usually climbed from Cimalaka District, 7 km from Sumedang.

Near the town lies Cadas Pangeran, a section of the trans-Java postal road built on the order of the Dutch governor Willem Daendels in the first quarter of the 19th century. Its construction required blasting a mountainside, hence the name cadas, Sundanese for mountain rock. It was finished through cooperation between the governor, the regent Kusumadinata, known as pangeran kornel, and the people of Sumedang, though the forced labour caused considerable ill feeling. A statue on the road commemorates the work.

Cut Nyak Dhien of Aceh, honoured as a national heroine of Indonesia, spent her old age in exile in Sumedang after she was captured during the Aceh War at the beginning of the 20th century. Her tomb is near the town.

The Prabu Geusan Ulun museum on Geusan Ulun Road holds a collection of traditional Sundanese weaponry, crown jewels and other finery. The town is known for tahu sumedang, a deep-fried tofu first made under the name tahu bunkeng by Ong Kino, an immigrant from Anxi County in Quanzhou, China, in the early 20th century. The Tahu Bunkeng shop in the town centre is one of the oldest tofu stores in Sumedang.
sumela-monastery: The date of the foundation is not known. The Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism places it around 386 CE, in the reign of the emperor Theodosius I. According to William Miller, two Athenian monks named Barnabas and Sophronios founded it. It became known for an icon of the Theotokos called the Panagia Gorgoepekoos, said to have been painted by the Apostle Luke. The name may come from the Pontic Greek Sou Mela, "on Melas", the name of the mountain, which means "black" in reference to the dark rock, or from the Laz word for the Trinity, Sumela.

The monastery fell into ruin several times and was restored by various emperors; in the 6th century the general Belisarius restored and enlarged it at the request of Justinian. It reached its present form in the 13th century and rose to prominence under the Empire of Trebizond. Alexios III (1349–1390) gave it its most important grants. Legend says that the Theotokos saved the young Alexios from a storm and told him to restore the monastery. A chrysobull of 1365 confirmed its autonomy and hereditary lands, exempted them from all taxes but one biannual tax, and listed 40 serfs by name.

After Mehmed II conquered Trebizond in 1461 the monastery received the sultan's protection, with privileges renewed by his successors. From 1682 it housed the Phrontisterion of Trapezous, a Greek school. It remained active until the end of the Russian occupation of Trabzon in 1918, visited by Christian and Muslim pilgrims. It was abandoned after the population exchange laid down in the Treaty of Lausanne. In 1930 the emigrants founded a new Panagia Sumela monastery near Veria in Macedonia, Greece, and carried some treasures there. The same year fire destroyed the wooden parts of the old monastery, and treasure hunters later damaged it.

The monastery stands at about 1,200 metres on a steep cliff above the Altındere valley, within Altındere National Park. Its Rock Church was built in a cave and is the centre of the complex, which has chapels, kitchens, a guesthouse, a library and a sacred spring; the large building with a balcony, used for cells and guests, dates from 1840. Frescoes from the time of Alexios III line the church wall facing the courtyard, and those of the chapel date from the early 18th century.

Restoration work in 2015–2017 found a hidden tunnel and frescoes of heaven and hell. The site was registered as a first-degree archaeological site in 1972 and placed on UNESCO's Tentative List in 2000. Liturgy was allowed again on 15 August 2010, and it reopened as a museum on 18 May 2019 after closure for rock falls and restoration.
sumer: Most historians have suggested that Sumer was first permanently settled between about 5500 and 3300 BCE by a West Asian people who spoke Sumerian, a language isolate that is neither Semitic nor Indo-European. Other suggestions, that the Sumerians came from the Green Sahara or the Caucasus, are not generally accepted. In their own inscriptions the Sumerians called their land Kengir, the country of the noble lords. The Sumerians were unknown in the early period of modern archaeology. Jules Oppert first published the word Sumer, in a lecture of 17 January 1869, and the first major excavation of a Sumerian city was at Girsu in 1877.

In the late 4th millennium BCE Sumer was divided into many independent city-states, each centred on a temple to its patron deity and ruled by a priestly governor, the ensi, or by a king, the lugal. The first war recorded in any detail, between Lagash and Umma about 2450 BCE, is shown on the Stele of the Vultures. The Akkadian Empire, founded by Sargon of Akkad about 2334 BCE, was the first state to unite larger parts of Mesopotamia. The Third Dynasty of Ur under Ur-Nammu and Shulgi, about 2112 to 2004 BCE, did so again. By then Amorites were founding competing powers in the south, and Babylon united Mesopotamia about 1700 BCE.

Sumerian farmers on the Tigris and Euphrates grew a surplus of grain, which allowed urban life, and the need to manage temple accounts led to writing. The earliest known texts come from Uruk and Jemdet Nasr. Sumerian cuneiform is the oldest deciphered script, or the second oldest after Egyptian hieroglyphs. The Sumerian language continued as a sacred and school language in Babylonia and Assyria for as long as cuneiform was used, as Latin did in medieval Europe. Sumerian mathematics used a sexagesimal place-value system, and the Sumerians were among the first to map the stars into constellations.
sumer-is-icumen-in: The song is the oldest known musical composition in six-part polyphony. It is sometimes called the Reading Rota, because the earliest known copy, written in mensural notation, was found at Reading Abbey, though it was probably not drafted there. The manuscript is now in the British Library, and a copy of it in stone relief stands on the wall of the ruined chapter house of Reading Abbey.

A rota, Latin for wheel, is a kind of round. One singer begins, and a second starts from the beginning when the first reaches a point marked with a red cross. The main verse runs to six phrases over twelve bars, and beneath it two lines marked pes, Latin for foot, two bars each, are sung together over and over. The manuscript gives these instructions itself, in Latin.

The words greet summer with the cuckoo's song, growing seed, a blooming meadow, a ewe bleating for her lamb and a cow lowing for her calf. Some read it as a counterpart to the French reverdie, a poem of spring, but it lacks that genre's usual words of renewal, and Roscow called it the wrong bird, season and language for one unless the meaning is ironic. The phrase bucke uerteþ is disputed: many editors gloss it as a buck-goat passing wind, while Platzer argues the reading is less secure than its supporters imply.

Beneath the English words the manuscript gives a Latin text on the Crucifixion of Jesus, which tells of the heavenly farmer who did not spare his Son and who crowns the redeemed with him on the throne of heaven.

A boys' choir sings the rota at the climax of Benjamin Britten's Spring Symphony, first performed in 1949, and it was performed at the opening ceremony of the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich. The English Singers made the first studio recording in New York around 1927. Little John whistles the tune in the 1938 film The Adventures of Robin Hood, and villagers sing a version by Anthony Shaffer at the climax of The Wicker Man (1973). Ezra Pound parodied it as Ancient Music, which opens with winter in place of summer.
sumerian-king-list: The Sumerian King List, also called the Chronicle of the One Monarchy, is a composition in Sumerian that was likely created and revised to legitimise the claims to power of city-states and kingdoms in southern Mesopotamia in the late third and early second millennium BCE. In contemporary sources it was named after its first word, nam-lugal, kingship. The oldest known version dates from the Ur III period and probably rests on Akkadian source material. It is not a single text but a composition of which versions differ in content, order, names and the lengths of reigns. The best preserved is the Weld-Blundell Prism, from the Old Babylonian period.

Each entry names a city, its kings and their reigns, and records how the city was defeated and kingship taken elsewhere. The Weld-Blundell version opens with eight kings of five cities who reigned 241,200 years in all before the flood swept over the land; this section is missing from some copies. After the flood kingship went to Kish, whose 23 kings are credited with reigns of 1,500 to 300 years. Only Etana, who ascended to heaven, and Enmebaragesi, who made Elam submit, are given any deed.

The list runs through Uruk, Ur and other cities to Sargon of Akkad, named as cup-bearer to Ur-zababa of Kish. After Shar-kali-sharri it asks, Then who was king? Who was not king?, a sign of the chaos at the end of the Akkadian Empire. Gutian kings, the Third Dynasty of Ur and the Isin dynasty of 14 kings follow. Kug-Bau, a tavern keeper, is thought to be the only queen listed.

The first fragment was published in 1906 by Hermann Volrath Hilprecht and the second in 1911 by Jean-Vincent Scheil. During much of the 20th century many scholars treated it as an important source for Early Dynastic Mesopotamia, but recent research holds that it should be used with great caution, if at all, for that period. Only seven pre-Sargonic rulers in it, among them Enmebaragesi, Gilgamesh and Lugal-zage-si, are attested in contemporary inscriptions, and several kings it presents in sequence ruled at the same time. From the Akkadian rulers onward, and especially for Ur III and Isin, it is far more reliable. It influenced later compositions such as the Curse of Akkad, the Assyrian King List and the Babyloniaca of Berossus.
sumerian-language: Sumerian was the language of ancient Sumer, and it is the oldest attested language, dating back to at least 3100 BCE, perhaps earlier. It is a language isolate, unrelated to any other known language, and was spoken exclusively in ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Akkadian, a Semitic language, gradually replaced it as the main spoken language around 2000 BCE, though the exact date is debated. Sumerian continued as a sacred, ceremonial, literary and scientific language in Akkadian-speaking states such as Assyria and Babylonia until the 1st century CE. The history of written Sumerian is divided into periods from the proto-literate period, c. 3100–3000 BCE, through Neo-Sumerian, in which the Ur III period falls, to Old Babylonian Sumerian and later.

The scripts used for Sumerian began as pictographic proto-writing in Mesopotamia around 3300 BCE. By about 2800 BCE some tablets used syllabic elements that clearly indicated Sumerian, and around 2600 BCE cuneiform symbols were developed, made by pressing a wedge-shaped stylus into wet clay. Sumerian is an agglutinative, ergative language with a subject–object–verb word order. Its standard variety was called Emegir, and a sociolect called Emesal appears in some literary texts as the speech of female characters and in cult songs. Attempts to link Sumerian to other languages, including Indo-European, Dravidian and Turkic, have failed, and such proposals enjoy virtually no support among modern linguists.

The cuneiform script was adopted by many regional languages, including Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite, Hurrian and Aramaic, and it inspired the Old Persian alphabet. Sumerian influenced Akkadian greatly, and was influenced by it in turn. After it fell into obscurity, it was rediscovered in the 19th century when Assyriologists began deciphering the inscriptions and excavated tablets. The key came from the Behistun inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite and Akkadian. In 1838 Henry Rawlinson, building on the 1802 work of Georg Friedrich Grotefend, deciphered the Old Persian section, and when he recovered the rest of the text in 1843 he and others gradually translated the Elamite and Akkadian sections.
sumptuary-law: The term comes from the Latin sumptuariae leges. Black's Law Dictionary defines such laws as made "for the purpose of restraining luxury or extravagance, particularly against inordinate expenditures for apparel, food, furniture, or shoes". Societies used them to limit the market for expensive imported goods and so regulate the balance of trade, to make status and privilege easy to see and so stabilise social hierarchies, and to reduce chances for political bribery. They often kept commoners from imitating aristocrats and could be used to stigmatise disfavoured groups.

The 7th-century BCE code of Zaleucus for the Locrians, the first written law code of ancient Greece, barred free-born women from gold jewellery or purple-bordered garments unless they were courtesans. Rome's Twelve Tables forbade extravagant funerals, the censors listed those found guilty of luxurious living in the nota censoria, and at the height of the Empire wearing Tyrian purple without right was treason punishable by death. In China such laws existed from the Qin dynasty onward; the Hongwu Emperor, founder of the Ming dynasty, regulated graves by rank in 1368 and tightened the rules in 1396.

In Japan during the Edo period (1603–1868) every class was bound by strict rules on dress, and in the 18th and 19th centuries these sought to keep the samurai above the chōnin merchants, who had grown far wealthier.
