In Europe, secular laws keeping people dressed according to their station began in the later 13th century, falling hardest on women and the middle classes. England's first comprehensive act came in April 1463, and the Caps Act 1571 made males over six wear woollen caps on Sundays and holidays. In the Massachusetts Bay Colony a rule of 1634 reserved lace and gold or silver thread for the wealthy.

Such laws were frequently ignored. The historian Lorraine Daston called them "an extreme case of rule failure", and Montaigne argued that forbidding turbot and velvet to the people only made everyone more eager for them. Adam Smith thought it "the highest impertinence and presumption" for kings and ministers to restrain private expense. The term later became a pejorative for any control of consumption on moral or health grounds: in 1918 William Howard Taft decried prohibition in the United States as a bad sumptuary law.
sumu-la-el: Sumu-la-El, also written Sumulael or Sumu-la-ilu, was a king of the First Dynasty of Babylon. About 36 of his year names are known. He was a contemporary of Sîn-kāšid of Uruk and of Sūmu-El and Nur-Adad of Larsa. In his time Babylon contested control of the surrounding region with the city-state of Isin.

He subjugated and conquered nearby cities such as Kish, and he is known to have conquered Sippar. During the first half of his reign Marad was an independent kingdom that also controlled Dilbat. His daughter Šallurtum married Sîn-kāšid, the king of Uruk, and economic ties of his reign reached as far north as Tilmen Hoyuk.

Sumu-la-El built a string of fortresses around his territory. His year names record the city wall of Dilbat, the great city wall of Babylon, the walls of Kutha, Anzagar-urgi, Sippar and Habuz, a temple of Adad and a temple of Zababa, the Emeteursag. Other year names mark the destruction of Kish, the defeat of the army of Kazallu, the driving out of Iahzir-el from Kazallu, and the year Sumu-la-El entered Borsippa.

The Old Babylonian levels at the city of Babylon lie below the water table and have not been excavated, so what is known of him comes from other sites, such as Sippar and Marad, which Babylon controlled. A text from Sippar in the time of the later ruler Apil-Sîn records a case in which families kept houses that Sumu-la-El had given them. One of the witnesses was Ayyalatum, a daughter of Sumu-la-El.
sumuabum: Sumu-abum, also written Sūmû-abum, Su-abu or Sūmabum, was an Amorite and is counted as the first king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, also called the Amorite Dynasty. His reign is dated c. 1894–1881 BCE in the middle chronology. It fell in the period after the collapse of the Ur III Empire, when the city-states of Isin and Larsa were the major powers of the region. Babylon was then a minor administrative centre in southern Mesopotamia.

Sumu-abum freed a small area of land that had been ruled by the fellow Amorite city-state of Kazallu, and Babylon lay within it. Neither he nor the three Amorite kings who followed him claims the title King of Babylon, which suggests that the town was still of little importance at the time.

About fourteen year names of Sumu-abum are known. They record the building of the great city wall of Babylon, the temple of Ninisina, the temple Emah of Nanna and the wall of Dilbat, a city 25 kilometres south of Babylon that he controlled. In his third year he claimed to have conquered Elip, a major city of the Manana Dynasty, and another year name says he destroyed or seized Kazallu.

By his tenth year he had gained control of Kish, 12 kilometres east of Babylon, which the Manana dynasty had held for some time. Kish was briefly lost to Larsa and recovered in his thirteenth year. It was no longer a powerful city but kept an outsized symbolic importance, and one year name says that he gave it a city wall reaching heaven. He is also known to have become king of Kisurra, although an alternative view holds that the Sumu-abum who controlled Kisurra was a ruler of the 6th Dynasty of Uruk, before Sîn-kāšid.

The Old Babylonian levels at Babylon lie below the water table and have not been excavated, so what is known of him comes from other sites: Kazallu, Dilbat, Sippar and Kisurra. He should not be confused with Isi-sümü-abum of the same period, who ruled a city not yet identified. A tablet from Sippar, BM 80328, lists rulers of Babylon and names fourteen unknown rulers before Sūmû-abum.
sumy: Sumy was founded in the 1650s by the Cossack Herasym Kondratyev, who came from Stavyshche in the Bila Tserkva Regiment, on the banks of the Psel in the historical region of Sloboda Ukraine. In 1656–1658 a fort and town were built on the site under the Muscovite voivode K. Arsenyev, and from 1658 Sumy was the centre of the Sumy Cossack Regiment. A fortified craftsmen's town added in the 1670s made it the biggest fortress in Sloboda Ukraine. Muscovite troops gathered here for the Crimean campaigns of 1687 and 1689, and from December 1708 to January 1709 the city was the headquarters of Tsar Peter the Great during the Great Northern War.

After the Cossack community was abolished in 1765, the regiment became Sumy Province of the new Sloboda Ukraine Governorate, and the city became its centre. Sumy then stagnated until the 1860s. Paul's Sugar-Refining Factory, founded in 1869 by I. Kharytonenko, and the Sumy Engineering Workshops of 1896, which made equipment for sugar refineries, began its growth into an industrial and trading centre, and the railway station opened in January 1877. During the Russian Revolution of 1905 Sumy was among the areas that set up an independent peasant republic.

Germany occupied Sumy from 10 October 1941 to 2 September 1943, and the city was heavily damaged. In February 1942 about 1,000 Jews were murdered in two large operations, and the Germans ran a prison, a forced labour battalion for Jews and the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 308 there. In 1944 about 30,000 Polish soldiers were stationed in Sumy and trained before rejoining the war.

Sumy is the administrative centre of Sumy Oblast in north-eastern Ukraine, and its census population was 292,139 in 2001. Its oldest building is the Resurrection Church of 1702. The neoclassical cathedral of the Saviour's Transfiguration, of the 18th century, received its 56-metre bell tower in the 1880s. The Sumy Regional Art Museum and the Museum of Local Lore opened in 1920, and the Chekhov Museum occupies the Lintvarev country estate of the 18th and 19th centuries.
sun-bin: Sun Bin, who lived from 382 to 316 BCE, was a Chinese general, strategist and writer of the Warring States period. He is supposed to be a descendant of Sun Tzu. He studied military strategy under the hermit Guiguzi and could recite The Art of War. A fellow student, Pang Juan, became his blood brother, left to become a general of Wei and built a reputation through a few victories. Sun accepted an offer to join him in Wei, and Pang, who found Sun the more talented, grew jealous.

Pang framed Sun for treason, and King Hui of Wei sentenced him to death, then commuted the sentence at Pang's urging. Sun was branded and crippled by the removal of his kneecaps. Pang tried to win him over so that he would write a book on strategy, intending to kill him afterwards. Sun discovered the plan, feigned insanity and escaped with the help of Qi diplomats. He became a retainer of General Tian Ji in Qi, and the king made him chief military adviser after he advised Tian Ji in a horse-race to match his worst horse against the king's best. Sun declined to be a commander because he could not ride a horse.

In 354 BCE a Wei army under Pang besieged Handan, the capital of Zhao. A Qi army led by Tian and Sun attacked the Wei capital Daliang on Sun's principle of besieging Wei to rescue Zhao, and defeated the returning Wei army at the Battle of Guiling. In 342 BCE Qi's army feigned defeat and reduced the number of its cooking stoves, so that the pursuing Wei overestimated Qi's losses. At the Battle of Maling the Qi ambushed the Wei, captured the crown prince of Wei and killed Pang.

Sun wrote the treatise Sun Bin's Art of War, believed lost after the Han dynasty, so that some historians doubted it existed. Fragments were recovered in 1972 from a tomb at Linyi, Shandong, among the Yinqueshan Han Slips, in which 16 chapters have been identified, against 89 attributed to the work in historical texts. Unlike Sun Tzu's Art of War, which advises against siege warfare, it gives advice on attacking besieged cities, reflecting developments in the later Warring States period.
sun-ce: Sun Ce, whose courtesy name was Bofu, was the eldest son of the general Sun Jian. Sun Jian served the warlord Yuan Shu in the campaign against Dong Zhuo, and was killed in an ambush while attacking Liu Biao, governor of Jing Province. Sun Ce brought his father's body to Qu'e for burial, then went to Danyang, where his maternal uncle Wu Jing was governor, and raised a militia of a few hundred men.

In 194 he went to Yuan Shu, who returned Sun Jian's former troops to him. Yuan Shu twice promised him a governorship and each time gave the post to someone else, so Sun Ce asked to lead forces against Liu Yao, who had occupied Qu'e and driven Wu Jing across the Yangtze.

Yuan Shu sent him off with about a thousand troops and a small cavalry force, expecting him to fail. At Liyang Sun Ce raised his strength to more than 5,000, crossed the Yangtze and took Niuzhu in 195. After fighting Liu Yao's allies Ze Rong and Fan Neng, he took Qu'e, and Liu Yao fled south. Strict discipline won him local support. He took Kuaiji, whose governor Wang Lang surrendered. The campaign from Niuzhu to the conquest of the region took less than a year.

In 197 Yuan Shu declared himself emperor, and Sun Ce denounced the act in a letter and broke with him. Cao Cao then recommended him for the title General Who Attacks Rebels and the rank of Marquis of Wu. After Yuan Shu died in 199, Sun Ce captured Wan County and took over his former troops, numbered at 30,000, then defeated Liu Xun and Huang Zu.

In 200, while Cao Cao fought Yuan Shao at Guandu, Sun Ce is said to have planned an attack on Xuchang. On a solo hunting trip he met three former servants of Xu Gong, whom he had had executed, and one shot him in the cheek with an arrow. Accounts of his death differ: the most generally accepted has him dying that night, another has him dying after he angrily struck a table on seeing his scar.

Sun Ce passed his territory to his younger brother Sun Quan, who, on becoming emperor of Eastern Wu, honoured him as Prince Huan of Changsha. The tale that the ghost of the Taoist Gan Ji caused his death comes from Gan Bao's In Search of the Supernatural, a work largely based on legend, and was dramatised in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
sun-dance: The Sun Dance is a ceremony of some Native Americans in the United States and of Indigenous peoples in Canada, primarily of the Plains. Members of otherwise independent bands gather to reaffirm beliefs about the world and the supernatural through rituals of personal and community sacrifice. Common features are dances and songs passed down through generations, a traditional drum, a sacred fire, prayer with a ceremonial pipe and fasting from food and water before the dance. Communities plan for at least a year, one leader or a small group is in charge, and many elders advise. Family and friends stay in the surrounding camp and pray for the dancers.

In many ceremonies, particularly among the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho, dancers are pierced through the skin of the chest or back with skewers attached by thongs to the central pole or to heavy objects such as a bison skull, and they pull until the skin tears free. Not all nations pierce. The Plains Cree Thirst Dance involves fasting from water and strenuous movement around the pole, and among the Shoshoni the dance centres on prolonged fasting.

Practitioners and scholars describe the dance as an offering made for the people rather than as punishment. The Oglala Lakota holy man Black Elk told Joseph Epes Brown that the dancer offers his body and soul for the sake of the people. The dance takes place in a circular lodge around a cottonwood pole, which represents the axis mundi, the centre of the world, and its 28 posts are often read as lunar cycles or cosmic balance. Ruth Underhill called it a rite of renewal, and Ella Cara Deloria, a Dakota scholar, wrote that it signified an offering of one's own body in thanks or petition.

The United States and Canada both passed laws meant to suppress Indigenous cultures and force assimilation, and the Sun Dance was among the banned ceremonies. In Canada, Indian agents interfered with it from 1882 until the 1940s, and an 1895 amendment to the Indian Act outlawed any dance involving wounding of the body. The Plains Cree, Saulteaux and Blackfoot kept holding it, some in secret, some with the agents' permission and some without piercing. Canada dropped the ban on flesh-wounding in 1951, and in 1978 the United States Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act.

The Sun Dance is a living tradition practised each year in many Native communities. Filming a ceremony is forbidden in most Sun Dance cultures. In 1993 the Lakota Summit V, about 500 representatives of 40 peoples and bands, condemned what it called exploitation of Lakota spirituality, and in 2003 the Keeper of the Sacred White Buffalo Calf Pipe asked non-Native people not to approach the altars.
sun-hao: Sun Hao, originally named Sun Pengzu, was born in 242 as the eldest son of Sun He, then crown prince of the founding emperor Sun Quan, and of his concubine Consort He. In 250 Sun Quan, tired of the disputes between his sons, exiled Sun He to Guzhang as a commoner. In 253 the regent Sun Jun had him exiled again to Xindu and forced him to commit suicide; Consort He refused to die with him so that someone would raise his sons.

On 10 December 258 Emperor Sun Xiu made Sun Hao the Marquis of Wucheng. When Sun Xiu died on 3 September 264, the chancellor Puyang Xing and the general Zhang Bu passed over his son Sun Wan, judging that after the fall of the allied state of Shu Han in 263 the people wanted a mature ruler, and on the advice of Wan Yu they enthroned Sun Hao.

He began by reducing taxes, relieving the poor and releasing palace women to marry, but soon turned to cruel punishments, superstition and indulgence. Late in 264 he had Puyang Xing and Zhang Bu executed with their clans, and in 265 he forced Sun Xiu's widow to commit suicide and executed Sun Xiu's two eldest sons. Trusting a prophecy, he moved the capital at great cost from Jianye to Wuchang, returning in 266 after a revolt against his heavy levies, for which he executed his brother Sun Qian.

From 268 he attacked the Jin borders, without success. After the chancellor Lu Kai died in 269, no official dared speak out. In 272 the general Bu Chan, summoned to the capital, defected to Jin, and Sun Hao tried to poison Wan Yu and Liu Ping, after which Wan Yu killed himself. He ignored the general Lu Kang's requests to strengthen the western border, and in 275 had the paralysed minister He Shao tortured to death.

In late 279 Jin attacked in six prongs, while Wang Jun's fleet cleared the river of Wu ships. Sun Hao surrendered in May 280 and was taken to Luoyang, where he presented himself bound and covered in mud. Emperor Sima Yan pardoned him and on 9 July 280 named him Marquis Guiming, the marquis who resigns to his fate. He died early in 284. Historians call him the Later Lord of Wu or the Last Emperor of Wu.
sun-jian: Sun Jian, courtesy name Wentai, was born in Fuchun County, Wu Commandery, around present-day Fuyang in Zhejiang, and was allegedly a descendant of Sun Tzu. No earlier records survive, and even his father's name is unrecorded, though folk tradition gives it as Sun Zhong. As a youth he was a civil official in his home county. At 16 he is said to have driven off a band of pirates dividing their spoils at Qiantang by pointing as if commanding a detachment to surround them. In 172 he became acting major of pro-government militias against Xu Chang's rebellion in Kuaiji Commandery.

After the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out in 184, Sun Jian joined the general Zhu Jun and, at Wan, climbed the city walls alone, so that the rest swarmed in. Appointed Administrator of Changsha Commandery around December 187, he put down a rebellion within a month and was made Marquis of Wucheng.

In 190, after Dong Zhuo seized the capital and set Emperor Xian on the throne, Sun Jian joined Yuan Shu in the coalition of warlords against him, and Yuan Shu appointed him General Who Destroys Barbarians and Inspector of Yu Province. Outnumbered near Liangdong, he escaped by giving his red scarf to Zu Mao, who hung it on a half-burnt pillar and hid, so that the pursuers were fooled. He defeated Dong Zhuo's forces at Yangren, and when Yuan Shu stopped his supplies on a suspicion of ambition he rode overnight to protest his loyalty. When Dong retreated to Chang'an, burning Luoyang, Sun Jian entered the ruins and had the opened tombs of Han emperors resealed.

In 191 Yuan Shu sent Sun Jian against Liu Biao, Governor of Jing Province. He defeated Huang Zu and pursued him to Xiangyang, and while travelling alone he was ambushed by Huang Zu's troops and shot dead with arrows. He was buried at Qu'e and survived by at least five sons and three daughters. His eldest son Sun Ce conquered several territories in Jiangdong, and Sun Ce's younger brother Sun Quan, who succeeded him, established the state of Eastern Wu and honoured his father with the posthumous title Emperor Wulie.
sun-quan: Sun Quan, courtesy name Zhongmou, was born in 182, the second son of Sun Jian, then a low-ranking Han official, and his wife Lady Wu. After Sun Jian's death in 191 the family moved between cities on the lower Yangtze while his elder brother Sun Ce built a warlord regime in the Jiangdong region. When Sun Ce was fatally wounded by assassins in 200, he entrusted the 18-year-old Sun Quan to his faithful officers, among them Zhou Yu, Zhang Zhao, Zhang Hong and Cheng Pu. Some followers thought him too young, and Li Shu, the Administrator of Lujiang, went over to Cao Cao, but Sun Quan defeated him and regained Lujiang.

That winter of 208 Cao Cao came south with an army of about 220,000 men, estimated against Sun's 30,000. Zhang Zhao urged surrender, while Zhou Yu and Lu Su argued that Cao Cao would not tolerate him even if he submitted. Sun Quan chose to fight, allied with Liu Bei, and defeated Cao Cao at the Battle of Red Cliffs. He then took the northern half of Jing Province and Liu Bei the southern half, and the alliance was sealed by the marriage of Sun Quan's younger sister to Liu Bei. In 211 he moved his headquarters to Moling, which he renamed Jianye the next year.

The alliance broke in 219, when Guan Yu besieged Fancheng and Sun Quan attacked him from the rear; Guan Yu was captured and executed, and Jing Province came under Sun's control. After Cao Pi ended the Han dynasty in 220, Sun Quan accepted the title King of Wu, but refused to send his son Sun Deng as a hostage to Luoyang and in November 222 declared himself independent by changing his era name. He formally became emperor in May 229. His early administration was known for its efficiency, and he delegated trust to officers such as Lu Xun and Zhuge Jin.

After the crown prince Sun Deng died in 241, two factions formed around his sons Sun He and Sun Ba. In 250 Sun Quan forced Sun Ba to commit suicide and deposed Sun He, naming his youngest son Sun Liang crown prince, and officials who objected were executed. He died in May 252, aged 70 by East Asian reckoning, and was succeeded by Sun Liang. He had the longest reign among the founders of the Three Kingdoms, and is known posthumously as Emperor Da of Wu.
sun-tzu: Sun Tzu means Master Sun and is an honorific. His birth name is said to have been Sun Wu. The earliest account of his life is a short biography in the Shiji, the Records of the Grand Historian, written around 97 BCE by Sima Qian. It says he was born in Qi, in present-day Shandong, near the end of the Spring and Autumn period. The scholar Victor Mair considers the biography essentially fictional.

According to the Shiji, King Helü of Wu heard of Sun Wu's Art of War, summoned him and asked him to show how he trained soldiers, using the king's harem of 180 concubines. Sun Tzu appointed the two concubines the king favoured most as commanders and gave orders, which they ignored, laughing. Over the king's protests he had the two commanders executed, after which the rest obeyed at once, and the king made Sun Wu a general. He is said to have led Wu to victory over the much larger state of Chu at the Battle of Boju in 506 BCE.

Beginning in the 12th century scholars began to doubt that he existed. Ye Shi noticed that the Zuo Zhuan, which describes the Battle of Boju in far more detail and was written centuries before the Shiji, never mentions Sun Tzu, and the name Sun Wu appears in no text earlier than the Shiji.

The Art of War is a Classical Chinese text in 13 chapters, each devoted to a different set of skills related to warfare, strategy and tactics. It also advocates diplomacy and the cultivation of relations with other states. The earliest parts probably date from at least a century after Sun Tzu, and since the 12th century most scholars have placed the text at the beginning of the Warring States period. Bamboo slips found at Yinque Shan in Shandong in 1972 hold about a third of the chapters of the modern text, with closely matching wording.

The earliest known commentary was written by the warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century CE. Emperor Shenzong of Song formalized the Seven Military Classics in 1080, and the Art of War led that anthology for almost 1,500 years. Lionel Giles completed the first annotated English translation in 1910.
sun-yat-sen: Sun Yat-sen was born on 12 November 1866 in the village of Cuiheng, Xiangshan County, in Guangdong, to Sun Dacheng and Madame Yang. His father owned little land and worked as a tailor in Macau and as a journeyman and porter. At 13 he went to live in Hawaii with his elder brother Sun Mei, who paid for his schooling at the ʻIolani School, where he studied English, mathematics, science and Christianity. His brother, alarmed at his interest in Christianity, sent him back to China in 1883. He graduated from the Hong Kong College of Medicine for Chinese in 1892.

In 1894 Sun wrote a petition on modernising China and travelled to Tianjin to present it to the viceroy Li Hongzhang, who did not receive him. He turned to revolution and founded the Revive China Society in Hawaii. Its First Guangzhou Uprising of 26 October 1895 failed after the plan leaked. In London in 1896 he was detained for 12 days at the Chinese Legation, which planned to smuggle him to China, and was freed through the efforts of James Cantlie, the press and the Foreign Office. Further uprisings also failed, and he raised money among overseas Chinese. His Three Principles of the People were nationalism, democracy and welfare.

After the 1911 revolution representatives meeting in Nanjing elected him provisional president on 29 December 1911. When the Qing emperor abdicated on 12 February 1912, Sun stepped down and Yuan Shikai became provisional president. The Kuomintang was formed on 25 August 1912, and its leader Song Jiaoren was assassinated on 20 March 1913, almost certainly on Yuan's secret order. Sun's Second Revolution failed in July 1913 and he fled to Japan. In 1921 he began a military government in Guangzhou, and he later cooperated with the Chinese Communist Party.

In January 1925 an operation at Peking Union Medical College Hospital found extensive cancer of the liver. Sun died on 12 March 1925, aged 58, and an autopsy gave the primary cancer as that of the gall bladder. After his death the Nationalist government split into rival factions led by Chiang Kai-shek, Wang Jingwei and the Western Hills Group. The Republic of China calls Sun the Father of the Nation, while the People's Republic of China honours him as the Forerunner of the Revolution, and his home county of Xiangshan was renamed Zhongshan in his honour.
sunan-ampel: Sunan Ampel, also named Raden Ahmad Rahmatullah or Sayyid Ali Rahmatullah, was the son of Maulana Malik Ibrahim, known as Sunan Gresik, and a princess of Champa, in present-day central Vietnam, where he was born. He came to Java in 1443, possibly to visit his aunt Dwarawati, another Cham princess, who was married to Kertawijaya, the king of Majapahit. A long genealogy makes him a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, while another theory gives him Chinese ancestry and identifies him as Bong Swi Hoo; the two need not exclude each other.

He married Nyi Gede Manila, daughter of Gan Eng Cu, a Chinese captain at Tuban. Their sons Sunan Bonang and Sunan Drajat became wali songo themselves; their daughter Syarifah married Sunan Ngudung and was the mother of Sunan Kudus; and another daughter became the first wife of Raden Patah and mother of Trenggana, later ruler of the Sultanate of Demak. Sunan Ampel taught both Raden Patah and Sunan Giri.

His preaching is summed up as Moh Limo, the five refusals: to drink alcohol, to gamble, to commit adultery, to use drugs and to steal. It arose in the 15th century, when Majapahit was torn by civil war and troubled by gambling, robbery and rape, and King Dyah Kertawijaya invited him to help improve the conduct of the people.

Local history credits Sunan Ampel with building the Great Mosque of Demak in 1479, though other sources attribute it to Sunan Kalijaga. His mission in Demak was carried on by Raden Zainal Abidin, known as Sunan Demak, his son by his wife Dewi Karimah, whose youngest son, Raden Zakaria, became imam of the Great Mosque. Sunan Ampel died in 1481 and was buried in Surabaya, East Java, within the Ampel Mosque complex.
sunan-giri: Sunan Giri, also called Raden Paku, Joko Samudro and Muhammad Ainul Yakin, was born in 1442 in Blambangan, now Banyuwangi. He was the son of Dewi Sekardadu and Maulana Ishak of Melaka, a brother of Maulana Malik Ibrahim, and was later adopted by Nyai Gede Pinatih, a woman merchant. A traditional story, told in the Sejarah Banten, makes him the son of a Hindu princess who was forced in a crisis to set him adrift on the ocean in a small boat, from which sailors rescued him.

As a young man he studied at the school of Sunan Ampel, whose daughter he later married, alongside his fellow student Raden Patah. He then founded his own school in Sidomukti village in southern Gresik, East Java, and took his name from the place, giri meaning hill. The school was a place of religious study and also a centre of local civic activity and social development. The king of Majapahit granted him authority to extend his political role, and the school grew into what became known as Giri Kedaton; Sunan Giri was also known as Prabu Satmata.

Sunan Giri spread Islam to Lombok, Sulawesi and Maluku. He was a proponent of orthodox Islam and disapproved of innovation. Under its later head Pangeran Singosari, Giri Kedaton, as a centre of religious and political authority, offered persistent resistance to the Dutch VOC and to Amangkurat II, who worked with the Dutch.

Javanese children's games and toys such as Jelungan, Jamuran, lir-ilir and Cublak Suweng are attributed to Sunan Giri. His name is also associated with Gending Asmaradana and Pucung, forms of Javanese poetry that were largely shaped by pre-Islamic Javanese beliefs and traditions but show signs of Islamization.
sunan-gunung-jati: Born Syarif Hidayatullah in 1448, he was the child of Syarif Abdullah Maulana Huda, a Hashemite of the Azhmatkhan branch of the Ba 'Alawi sada, and Nyai Rara Santang, daughter of Prabu Siliwangi, King of Sunda. He could thus claim descent from the Islamic prophet Muhammad on his father's side and from a Hindu Devaraja of the Sunda Kingdom on his mother's. Some say he was born in Pasai, one of the earliest centres of Islam in Southeast Asia, others in Pajajaran, his grandfather's capital.
During fourteen years of travel abroad he studied Islam under venerated scholars in Egypt, probably including leading Sufis, and he is assumed to have made the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina.

Much about his career is uncertain, and the many conflicting stories have led some scholars to conclude that he may be a conflation of more than one historical figure. He is reported to have married a sister of Trenggana, Sultan of Demak, and to have led expeditions for Demak against Sunda. Accounts that identify him with Fatahillah credit him with defeating the Portuguese at Sunda Kelapa and renaming it Jayakarta in 1527, a victory still marked as the founding anniversary of Jakarta.

He was the only one of the Wali Songo to take a sultan's crown, and he used his kingship, backed by his Hashemite and royal descent, to spread Islam along the Pesisir, the north coast of Java. He followed the strict methods of Middle Eastern sheikhs and built roads linking isolated areas. The ruler of Banten later submitted to him, and Banten became a kingdom; in old age he turned to preaching and Pangeran Pasarean became king after him.

He died in Cirebon in 1568 and was buried at Gunung Sembung, Gunung Jati, about 5 km north of the town centre. The walls of the tomb enclosure are set with porcelain plates, which pilgrims replace with new ones; today they are mostly of European or Japanese origin.
sunda-kelapa: Sunda Kalapa, Sundanese for Coconut of Sunda, lies on the estuary of the Ciliwung River, in what is now Penjaringan District of North Jakarta. From the 13th to the 16th century it served the Sunda capital, Pakuan Pajajaran, about 60 km inland up the Ciliwung, on the site of modern Bogor. With Aceh and Makassar it was one of the few ports of the archipelago that kept ties with Europe. Between 1512 and 1515 the Portuguese Tomé Pires described the port of Calapa as the most important and best of all.

Under the agreement of 1522 King Prabu Surawisesa gave the Portuguese free access to the pepper trade in return for help against the rising Sultanate of Demak. Portuguese in his service settled in the port and were the first Christians in what is now Indonesia. Fatahillah, acting for Demak, took the harbour on 22 June 1527, and it later passed to the Banten Sultanate, from which Jan Pieterszoon Coen of the Dutch East India Company seized it in 1619.

The narrow, shallow harbour admitted only small ships, which sailed up the canal to the Kali Besar to load and to be repaired in the VOC and Chinese shipyards opposite Batavia Castle; larger ships anchored at sea. Sandbanks kept building up at its mouth, the Waterkasteel fort was built in 1741, and in the 18th century slaves and horses were used to tow dredges along the canal, at a cost of lives.

In the 19th century the port, known as the Haven Kanaal and as Batavia's Roadstead, was still the only entrance to the city, and cargo and passengers reached it in small shallow steamers called lighters. In 1885, as traffic grew after the opening of the Suez Canal, the government of the Netherlands East Indies decided to build a new port at Tanjung Priok, 9 kilometres to the east.

After Indonesian independence the old port took back the name Sunda Kelapa as the cradle of Jakarta. It is now a minor port, run by the state-owned Indonesia Port Corporation, and is used by pinisi, traditional two-masted wooden sailing ships that carry freight between the islands.
sunda-strait: The strait takes its name from the Sunda Kingdom, which ruled the western part of Java, an area covering present-day West Java, Jakarta, Banten and some of western Central Java, from 669 to around 1579. The name also alludes to the Sundanese people of West Java and Banten.

The strait runs roughly south-west to north-east and is essentially triangular, with two large bays on its northern side. It is very broad and deep at its south-western end, but narrows to a minimum width of 24 km between Cape Tua on Sumatra and Cape Pujat on Java and becomes much shallower, with a minimum depth of only 20 m. Shallows, very strong tidal currents and sandbanks make it notoriously difficult to navigate, and most modern large ships use the Strait of Malacca instead.

For centuries the strait was an important shipping route, above all while the Dutch East India Company used it as the gateway to the Spice Islands of Indonesia, from 1602 to 1799. It is dotted with islands, many volcanic, among them Sangiang, Sebesi, Sebuku, Panaitan and Krakatau.

The 1883 eruption of Krakatau killed tens of thousands of people with tsunamis and pyroclastic flows, and of 3,000 people on nearby Sebesi not one survived. Some land was never resettled and became Ujung Kulon National Park.

The eruption changed the strait's topography, depositing as much as 18 to 21 cubic kilometres of ignimbrite over an area of 1.1 million square kilometres. Anak Krakatau emerged from the shattered remains in 1927.

On 1 March 1942 the Battle of Sunda Strait took place, when the Allied cruisers HMAS Perth and USS Houston met a Japanese landing force near Bantam, and both were sunk. A bridge across the strait has been proposed since the 1960s, and an agreement was signed in April 2012 for a road and rail bridge, but the plan was shelved in November 2014.
sundial: The earliest sundials known from the archaeological record are shadow clocks of about 1500 BCE, from ancient Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy. By 240 BCE Eratosthenes had estimated the circumference of the world using an obelisk and a water well, and a few centuries later Ptolemy had charted the latitude of cities using the angle of the Sun. The people of Kush made sundials through geometry. The Roman writer Vitruvius lists the dials and shadow clocks known in his time in De architectura, and the Tower of the Winds in Athens had both a sundial and a water clock.

A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun. In its narrowest sense it consists of a flat plate, the dial, and a gnomon, which casts a shadow onto the dial. As the Sun appears to move, the shadow aligns with different hour-lines marked on the dial. For accuracy throughout the year the edge of the gnomon that tells the time, called the style, must be parallel to the axis of the Earth's rotation, and its angle from the horizontal equals the latitude. Dials differ in the surface that receives the shadow: equatorial, horizontal, vertical, polar and spherical dials are the main types, and a movable gnomon is used in analemmatic dials.

A canonical sundial indicated the canonical hours of liturgical acts, and religious orders used them from the 7th to the 14th centuries. In 1570 the Italian astronomer Giovanni Padovani published a treatise on sundials, with instructions for making and laying out vertical and horizontal dials, and sundials have been in common use since the 16th century. Portable dials included the shepherd's dial, the ring dial and the card dial; the Venerable Bede gave a table for estimating the time from the length of one's shadow. A sundial does not match clock time without corrections for time zone and for the equation of time, which can reach a quarter of an hour. Sundials often carried mottoes reminding the viewer of the passing of time.
sundiata-keita: Sundiata is known chiefly through the Epic of Sundiata, a semi-historical poem handed down orally by Maninka griots. According to it, he was the son of Naré Maghann Konaté and Sogolon Condé, and he was crippled from childhood until he rose and walked. His half-brother Dankaran Touman and Dankaran's mother, Sassouma Bereté, resented him, and after his father's death Sogolon took her children into exile. They were eventually given asylum in Mema, where its king gave Sundiata a senior position.

When King Soumaoro Kanté of Sosso conquered the Mandinka, messengers found Sundiata in Mema and persuaded him to return. The epic says the king of Mema gave him an army, and that on the plain of Siby he and his allies, among them Tiramakhan Traore, formed a pact of brotherhood. Written accounts by Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun, who travelled to Mali in the following century, give independent evidence that he existed.

At the Battle of Kirina, about 1235, Sundiata and his allies defeated Soumaoro, and he became the first emperor of Mali and the first Mandinka king to take the title Mansa. He set his capital at Niani, near the present border of Mali with Guinea. His generals extended his power: Tiramakhan Traore is credited with conquests in Senegambia, including Kaabu, and with defeating the king of Jolof, while Sundiata himself is credited with Diafunu and Kita.

Mansa Sundiata was not an absolute monarch. The empire was reportedly run like a federation, with each clan holding a chief representative at court, and the Great Gbara Assembly checked the Mansa's power and chose his successor. The Manden Charter and the Kouroukan Fouga, unwritten and altered in retelling, are traced to his reign. Under him Mali began to control trade routes and gold fields, and he is reported to have introduced cotton and weaving.

The generally accepted year of his death is c. 1255. The cause is uncertain: the version now generally accepted is drowning in the Sankarani River, where a shrine bearing his name remains, while Maurice Delafosse reported an arrow during a ceremony and others an assassination. Mandinka tradition forbids disclosing the burial ground of great kings. His sons Mansa Wali Keita, Mansa Ouati Keita and Mansa Khalifa Keita succeeded him, and Mansa Musa was his great-nephew. Scholars disagree on whether he was Muslim: the original epic does not say so, and later Muslim griots added Islamic ancestry to it.
suniti-devi: Suniti Devi was born on 30 September 1864, a daughter of Keshub Chandra Sen of Calcutta and Jagonmohini Sen. She was fourteen when she married. For two years afterwards she stayed in her father's house, since her husband left for London for higher studies immediately after the wedding. She had four sons and three daughters. Two of her sons, Rajendra Narayan and Jitendra Narayan, later became Maharajas of Cooch Behar. Her daughters Sudhira and Pratibha married the brothers Alan and Miles Mander of Wightwick Manor in England, and Sukriti married Jyotsna Nath Ghoshal, a nephew of Rabindranath Tagore.

In 1887, when she attended the Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria with her husband, she was made a Companion of the Order of the Crown of India, the first Indian woman to receive the honour. She was also present at the Delhi Durbar of 1911.

The girls' school that her husband set up in her name in 1881, later called Suniti Academy, was her idea. She gave it annual grants, exempted the pupils from tuition fees and rewarded those who did well. She arranged for palace cars to carry the girls between home and school and, to avoid controversy, ordered the car windows to be curtained. With her sister Sucharu Devi, Maharani of Mayurbhanj, she financed the foundation of the Maharani Girls' High School in Darjeeling in 1908. She was President of the State Council and in 1932 the first President of the All Bengal Women's Union.

She was also an author. Bengal Dacoits and Tigers, a collection of short stories, was published in Calcutta in 1916. The Beautiful Mogul Princesses, published in London in 1918, tells the lives of Mumtaz Mahal, Zebunissa, Nur Jahan and another princess. The Autobiography of an Indian Princess appeared in London in 1921, and her last book, The Life of Princess Yashodara: Wife and Disciple of the Lord Buddha, in 1929. She died suddenly at Ranchi on 10 November 1932. In Cooch Behar the school, Sunity Road and a tank known as the Sunity Tank or Bairagi Dighi are named after her.
sunjong-of-korea: Sunjong, whose personal name was Yi Cheok, was the second son of Emperor Gojong and Empress Myeongseong. In 1876, when he was two, he was proclaimed Crown Prince of Joseon. In 1882 he married a woman of the Yeoheung Min clan, later Empress Sunmyeonghyo, who died on 5 November 1904 after trying to protect her mother-in-law at the assassination of Empress Myeongseong by the Japanese military on 8 October 1895. When his father proclaimed Korea an empire in 1897, Sunjong became Crown Prince of Imperial Korea, and in 1898 he was appointed Field Marshal of the Imperial Korean Army. On 11 December 1906 he married Yun Jeung-sun of the Haepyeong Yun clan, later Empress Sunjeong.

On 19 July 1907 Gojong was deposed under Japanese coercion and Sunjong became emperor, crowned at Don-doek-jeon. His younger half-brother, Prince Imperial Yeong, was named heir. His rule was limited by increasing Japanese intervention, and he was at once forced to accept the Japan–Korea Treaty of 1907, which let the Japanese government supervise Korean administration and appoint Japanese ministers. The Korean army was dismissed on the pretext of a lack of public finance regulations. In 1909 the Japan–Korea Protocol effectively removed Korea's judicial power.

Itō Hirobumi, the Japanese Resident-General, was assassinated by Ahn Jung-geun at Harbin, which was followed by annexation. Pro-Japanese politicians such as Song Byung-jun and Lee Wan-yong helped to arrange the Japan–Korea Annexation Treaty of 29 August 1910, by which Japan abolished the Korean Empire, ending 519 years of the Joseon dynasty. Historians have characterised Sunjong as a powerless puppet of the Japanese.

After the treaty Sunjong and Empress Sunjeong lived virtually imprisoned in Changdeokgung Palace. He was demoted from emperor to king, and Japan allowed him the title King Yi of Changdeok Palace, which could be inherited. He died in April 1926 at Changdeokgung without children and was buried with his two wives at the imperial tomb of Yureung in Namyangju. His state funeral on 10 June 1926 was a catalyst for the June 10th Movement against Japanese rule.
sunni-ali: Sunni Ali, also called Si Ali and Sonni Ali Ber ("the Great"), was the 15th ruler of the Sunni dynasty of Songhai. He was the son of Sonni Muhammad Da'o, who appears in the kinglists of the Tarikh al-Sudan and the Tarikh al-Fattash as the 10th Sonni ruler. His mother came from Fara, an area that was still heavily pagan, and Ali was raised in that setting. As a Sonni he also received an Islamic education, but he practised a syncretic, unorthodox faith.

When Sunni Ali took the throne, the Songhai already controlled the Niger basin from Dendi to Mema. His first major conquest was Timbuktu, held by the Tuareg since the Malian retreat a few decades earlier, whose Timbuktu-koi 'Umar asked for Songhai protection. Sunni Ali followed a repressive policy toward the scholars of Timbuktu, whom he associated with the Tuareg. He built a powerful fleet on the Niger and used it in 1473 to besiege Djenné, which surrendered only after being reduced to starvation.

He tried to dig a canal of hundreds of kilometres from Ras el Ma toward Walata, so that his fleet could be used against that town, but in 1483 he abandoned the project to defeat an invasion by the Mossi. He also conquered the Sanhaja lands called Nunu and the lands of Kunta, and he intended to seize Borgu but could not. He fought the Fulani of Massina and other nomadic peoples raiding within his borders. Gao was his main capital, but he was also based at Kukiya, Kabara and Tindirma, depending on where he campaigned.

Sunni Ali ruled urban Muslims and rural non-Muslims at a time when their traditional coexistence was being challenged. Because he combined African animism with a profession of Islam, some writers describe him as outwardly or nominally Muslim, although he observed the prayers, fasted and gave alms. Toby Green notes that he did not permit the acceptance of Sharī’a in Songhai. The scholars of Timbuktu wrote of him with fury, and al-Maghili said he worshipped idols and venerated trees and stones. Green argues that his relations with the clerics were less brutal than this picture, and funeral stelae from Kukiya cast doubt on the chroniclers, who wrote for the Askias who overthrew his dynasty.

He died on 6 November 1492, in circumstances that are a matter of conjecture. The Tarikh al-Sudan says he drowned while crossing the Niger; oral tradition holds that his sister's son, Askia Muhammad Ture, killed him. His son Sunni Baru was proclaimed king by the army commanders but was challenged by Askia, as he was not seen as a faithful Muslim, and Askia eventually defeated him and took power.
sunno: Sunno was a leader, or dux, of the Franks. His invasion of 388 came while Magnus Maximus, the usurper who held the whole of Roman Gaul, was surrounded in Aquileia by Theodosius I. The raid is known from Gregory of Tours, who cited the now lost work of Sulpicius Alexander. In that account Marcomer, Sunno and Genobaud crossed into the provinces of Germania Inferior and Belgia, broke through the limes, killed many people, laid waste the most fruitful lands and threw the city of Cologne into panic.

The main body of the Franks then went back over the Rhine with their booty, while some stayed in the Belgian woods. The Roman generals Nanninus and Quintinus, hearing the news in Trier, attacked those who remained and killed many of them. Quintinus then crossed the Rhine to punish the Franks in their own country, but his army was surrounded and beaten: some soldiers drowned in the marshes, others were killed, and few made it back.

After the fall of Magnus Maximus, Marcomer and Sunno held a short meeting about the attacks with the Frank Arbogastes, a magister militum of the Roman army. The Franks gave hostages, as was usual, and Arbogastes returned to his winter quarters in Trier. A couple of years later, by then master of the western army, Arbogastes crossed the Rhine into Germania; Marcomer was seen with the Chatti and Ampsivarii, but the two sides did not engage.

The poet Claudian records that the Romans arrested Marcomer and banished him to a villa in Tuscany. Sunno, his brother, crossed the Rhine and tried to make himself leader of Marcomer's band, but he was killed by his own people.

The later Liber Historiae Francorum says that after Sunno's death Marcomer proposed that the Franks should live under one king and put forward his son Pharamond. Modern scholars such as Edward James do not accept this account as historical, since it makes Marcomer a son of the Trojan king Priam and Sunno a son of Antenor.
sunthorn-phu: Sunthorn Phu was born in Bangkok on 26 June 1786, in the reign of King Rama I, four years after the founding of the Rattanakosin Kingdom, in a house behind the royal palace. His father is usually said to have come from Ban Kram in Klaeng district, Rayong province, though some historians now place his family in Phetchaburi. His parents divorced; his father became a monk and his mother a wet nurse in the royal household, where Phu grew up and fell in love with Chan, a lady of the palace related to the royal family. The pair were punished for breaking the social order and pardoned on the king's death.

A journey to visit his father produced Nirat Mueang Klaeng, one of his best-known poems, written for Chan, whom he then married; they had a son, Phat. King Rama II made him court poet and gave him the title Khun, but the marriage ended in divorce, the first of several. Phu drank heavily, and around 1821 he was jailed after a fight; in prison he began Phra Aphai Mani, which he published in instalments over the next twenty years.

Under Rama III he publicly corrected one of the king's poems and lost his title. He spent many years as a monk, writing travel poems such as Nirat Phukhao Thong, on his journey to the Golden Mountain, and Nirat Suphan. Under King Mongkut he became head of the royal scribes of the Front Palace with the rank of Phra. He died in 1855 at a house by the Khlong Chak Phra canal in Taling Chan, Bangkok.

Phra Aphai Mani tells of a prince's adventures in a world where people of all races and religions live together. Its character Sudsakorn inspired The Adventure of Sudsakorn of 1979, the only cel-animated feature of Thai cinema, by Payut Ngaokrachang. His birthday, 26 June, is kept as Sunthorn Phu Day, and a memorial park at Klaeng, opened in 1970, has his statue with figures from his poems.
suo-province: Suō bordered the provinces of Aki, Iwami and Nagato, and was known in short as Bōshū. It was one of the provinces of the San'yōdō circuit, and the Engishiki classed it among the superior countries in importance and the far countries in distance from the imperial capital at Kyoto. Its provincial capital stood in what is now the city of Hōfu, which also holds the Tamanooya Shrine, the province's ichinomiya or chief shrine.

Before the ritsuryō system the area was held by several semi-independent kuni no miyatsuko, among them the lords of Ōshima, Suō, Hakuki, Tsunu and Sawa. These were joined into a province of five counties, and a sixth, Kuga, was split from Kumage in 721. In the Asuka period the mountain fortification of Iwakisan Kōgoishi was built against a feared invasion by Tang China and the Korean kingdom of Silla. Wooden tally strips found at Fujiwara-kyō and Heijō-kyō name the province as Suho, Shuyō and Suō, names used interchangeably in records of the Nara period such as the Nihon Shoki.

The Hōjō clan held the office of shugo in the Kamakura period and were followed by the Ōuchi in the Muromachi period. In the Sengoku period the Mōri supplanted the Ōuchi, and in the Edo period the province formed part of the Chōshū Domain. An early Meiji assessment of the nation's resources counted 295 villages in the province, with a total yield of 548,861 koku.

After the Meiji restoration Suō was divided into six districts and became part of Yamaguchi Prefecture. Its former area is now shared among the cities of Hōfu, Kudamatsu, Iwakuni, Hikari, Yanai and Shūnan, most of the city of Yamaguchi, a portion of Ube, and the districts of Ōshima, Kuga and Kumage.
supayalat: Supayalat was born at the Royal Palace in Mandalay on 13 December 1859, the second of three daughters of King Mindon and Hsinbyumashin, and full sister of Supayagyi and Supayalay. She held the appanages of Tabayin, Manle and later Myadaung, and so was known as the Princess of Myadaung. Her mother grew powerful at court after the death of the chief queen, Setkya Dewi, and planned to marry Thibaw, son of the middle-ranking queen Laungshe Mibaya, to her eldest daughter, but Thibaw declared his love for Supayalat.

At the royal wedding Supayalat pushed in beside her sister to be anointed queen at the same time, against ancient custom. She was 19 and Thibaw 20 when they took the throne, and she is said to have kept him from taking other consorts; she had his secret concubine, Daing Khin Khin, executed though she was pregnant. Supayalat denied any part in the killing of the royal relatives, saying she had been a teenager and that ministers and officials must have organised it. She urged war with the British and mocked the chancellor Kinwun Mingyi U Kaung when he pleaded for peace.

After the Third Anglo-Burmese War the couple left Mandalay Palace on 25 November 1885 in a covered carriage, between lines of British soldiers and weeping subjects, to a steamboat on the Irrawaddy. Some crown jewels vanished, among them a large ruby called Nga Mauk. The family was taken to Madras and in April 1886 to Ratnagiri, where a proper residence, Thibaw Palace, was built only in 1911.

After Thibaw died in 1916 she fought in vain to take his body home, and in 1919 she returned to Rangoon, where she lived under house arrest on a pension. The writer and nationalist Thakin Kodaw Hmaing revered her defiance of colonial rule and founded a committee to protect her. She died of a heart attack in 1925 and was buried at Kandawmin Garden Mausolea. Burmese memory holds her responsible for the kingdom's fall and sees in her the proverb that a woman can bring ruin to a kingdom.
supermarine-spitfire: In 1931 the Air Ministry issued specification F7/30, calling for a modern fighter capable of 250 mph to replace the Gloster Gauntlet biplane. R. J. Mitchell, chief designer at Supermarine Aviation Works, a subsidiary of Vickers-Armstrong from 1928, answered with the Type 224, which first flew in February 1934; the Gloster Gladiator biplane was accepted instead, and Mitchell went on to the design that became the Spitfire.

The public first saw the Spitfire at the RAF Hendon air display on 27 June 1936. Numerous problems delayed production, and the first production aircraft, K9787, left the Woolston, Southampton, line only in mid-1938. Mitchell continued to refine the design until his death from cancer in 1937, after which Joseph Smith became chief designer and oversaw its development.

In 1934 Mitchell's team chose a semi-elliptical wing to meet two conflicting needs: it had to be thin to limit drag, yet thick enough to house the retractable undercarriage, armament and ammunition. The original airframe was designed around a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine of 1,030 hp, and it was strong enough to take more powerful Merlins and, in later marks, Griffon engines of up to 2,340 hp. Because the Merlin had a carburettor, Spitfires could not nose straight down into a dive as the Bf 109E could, and RAF pilots learned to half-roll before diving after an opponent.

The first Mk I entered service with 19 Squadron at RAF Duxford on 4 August 1938. In the Battle of Britain the Hurricane flew more sorties, but the Spitfire captured the public's imagination, helped by the Spitfire Fund run by Lord Beaverbrook, the Minister of Aircraft Production. Its squadrons had a lower attrition rate and higher victory-to-loss ratio, and the usual tactic was to use Spitfires against the escorting Bf 109s while Hurricanes attacked the bombers. Afterwards it became the principal aircraft of RAF Fighter Command and served in the European, Mediterranean, Pacific and South-East Asian theatres.

It flew as interceptor, photo-reconnaissance aircraft, fighter-bomber and trainer into the 1950s, and the Seafire adaptation served the Fleet Air Arm from 1942 until the mid-1950s. On 26 September 1940 bombing destroyed the Woolston and Itchen factories, killing 92 people, and production was dispersed to small sites around Southampton. The Spitfire became a symbol of British resistance, and about 240 are preserved.
suphanburi: Suphan Buri is a town in central Thailand, 101 km north-north-west of Bangkok, on the Tha Chin River, which is known locally as the Suphan River. It stands at an elevation of 11 metres in a low, flat landscape where rice farms cover much of the land. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with a monsoon season from May to October. The town covers parts of Mueang Suphan Buri District, and in 2006 it had a population of 26,656.

Karen Mudar records the moated settlement of Suphanburi as enclosing 366 hectares, one of the three largest on the central plain and one of seven regional centres in her hierarchy. The moat has not been dated on its own. Baker and Pasuk connect the town's beginnings to the decline of U Thong, whose people may have moved some 30 kilometres north-east.

The town stands in a river bend, closed by a rectangular moat measuring 1.9 by 0.7 kilometres, with a forest temple outside the walls and a relic stupa in Angkorian style at the centre. Baker and Pasuk hold that walls and stupa may date to the 12th century. Kilns at Ban Bang Pun, north of the town, made large stoneware jars in the 12th and 13th centuries.

The Siamese historian Damrong Rajanubhab speculated that the city was founded as Suvarnapuri around 1350, when an epidemic plagued U Thong. Ramathibodi I appointed his brother-in-law Khunluang Pha Ngua as governor, and Pha Ngua gave the city its present name before becoming king of Ayutthaya in 1370 as Borommarachathirat I.

Suphanburi remained a frontier town between Siam and the kingdoms of what is now Burma, and several battles were fought nearby until the first half of the 19th century. The most important took place on 18 January 1593 at Nong Sarai, when the Siamese king Naresuan challenged the heir of the Toungoo dynasty to a duel on elephant back. Naresuan killed his rival, the Burmese withdrew, and Ayutthaya regained independence after 29 years of vassalage to Pegu. The provincial coat of arms still recalls the duel.

The municipality took its present form under Mongkut (1851-1868), when the central nucleus was joined to neighbouring settlements. The entrepreneur Banharn Silpa-Archa, a native of the city who was prime minister of Thailand from 1995 to 1996, had many buildings put up there, among them seven schools and a tower 123 metres high. The town is a centre of the Thai music industry and the burial place of the luk thung singer Pumpuang Duangjan. A branch line of 157 kilometres joins it to the southern railway line.
suppiluliuma-i: Šuppiluliuma's origins are unclear. Seal impressions naming him as the son of Tudḫaliya III led most scholars to take him as that king's son, though his first wife Ḫenti is called the daughter of a great king, which has led some to think he was also Tudḫaliya's son-in-law and possibly adopted son. Before he became king he served as adviser and chief military commander. According to the Deeds of Šuppiluliuma, written by his son Muršili II, he helped recover Hittite lands from the Kaška in the north, defeated King Karanni of Azzi-Ḫayaša, and fought the Arzawa confederacy in the west, retaking the city of Tuwanuwa.

Tudḫaliya III's heir, Tudḫaliya the Younger, had sworn oaths of loyalty from Šuppiluliuma and other nobles. He was murdered with some of his brothers by Šuppiluliuma's supporters, and Šuppiluliuma became king. An oracle later named the murder as a cause of the plague that afflicted the Hittite kingdom.

Šuppiluliuma set out to recover Kizzuwatna and Tegarama, which had come under the influence of Mittani. An early attack failed, so he allied with a rival Mittanian royal, Artatama II, and married a Babylonian princess. In the so-called One-Year War he overran Mittani's vassal Išuwa and plundered the capital Waššukanni, then crossed the Euphrates and took Aleppo, Mukiš, Qatna and other Syrian kingdoms. Niqmaddu II of Ugarit accepted his suzerainty, and Kadesh fell after its king Šutatarra gave battle.

In the Six-Year War, fought largely by his son Telipinu, he besieged and captured Carchemish and made his son Piyaššili its vassal king. Telipinu ruled Aleppo, and the two princes served as viceroys in Syria. When Šattiwaza, son of Tušratta, fled Mittani, Šuppiluliuma gave him a daughter in marriage and sent him with a Hittite army to take what remained of his father's kingdom, which became in effect a dependency, later of Assyria as well.

Late in his reign an Egyptian queen, usually identified as Ankhesenamun, asked him for one of his sons as husband and king. He sent Zannanza, who was killed on the way. Šuppiluliuma blamed the Egyptians, attacked Egyptian territory and took captives. Muršili II recorded that these prisoners brought a plague to the Hittite kingdom. The plague lasted at least two decades and is often considered the cause of the deaths of Šuppiluliuma and his eldest son Arnuwanda II. Muršili II blamed the kingdom's misfortune on his father's cruelty, counting the murder of Tudḫaliya the Younger and the attacks on Egypt among its causes.
suppiluliuma-ii: Šuppiluliuma II was a younger son of the Hittite great king Tudḫaliya IV and succeeded his elder brother Arnuwanda III. He made his court and subjects swear oaths of allegiance, advertising his loyalty to his dead brother and his own legitimacy, since Arnuwanda left no heirs. The surviving texts hint at disloyalty and possible challenges from members of the extended royal family. Abroad, an official was sent to rebuke Ibiranu, the vassal king of Ugarit, for failing to show him respect, and Talmi-Teššub of Carchemish was bound by a new treaty and left in charge of Syria.

Two inscriptions in Hieroglyphic Luwian, one at Nişantepe in the Upper City of Hattusa and one in Chamber 2 beside the East Pond, record his wars. They tell of conquests in Wiyanawanda, Tamina, Maša, Lukka and Ikuna in south-western Anatolia, and of the defeat, sack and annexation of Tarḫuntašša, a hostile regime in a city that had once served briefly as the empire's capital. Letters mention urgent grain shipments from Merneptah of Egypt, which suggests a famine in the late 13th century BCE.

A fleet under his command defeated either the Cypriots or a group of Sea Peoples who had settled on Alašiya, the first naval battle recorded in history. Records from Ugarit show that the Hittite king asked it for help against a threat from the west.

He was probably the ruler who abandoned Hattusa. Some scholars hold that he vanished, others that he was killed in the sack of the city. The violent end of Hattusa as the capital is now doubted, and it is suspected that he moved his court elsewhere, perhaps to the south-west. Neither he nor any later ruler returned, and the Hittite Empire disappeared as such. The causes are unclear and may have combined droughts and earthquakes with internal and external strife. Hattusa's remains were burned, and its site was reoccupied by a Phrygian fortress about 500 years later.

He is generally considered the last great king of Hatti, though Zsolt Simon has proposed from a Luwian inscription on a silver bowl that he had a successor, possibly his son Tudḫaliya V. Kuzi-Teššub of Carchemish later took the title of Great King as a descendant of Šuppiluliuma I.
supreme-commander-for-the-allied-powers: The post was created at the start of the United States-led Allied occupation of Japan, on 14 August 1945, and was held by General Douglas MacArthur. It was first styled Supreme Commander of the Allied Powers. SCAP issued directives, called SCAP Directives, to the Japanese government, aiming to suppress what it called militaristic nationalism. In Japan the office was generally called GHQ, since SCAP also meant the occupation's offices, formally General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, with several hundred US civil servants as well as military personnel. Australian, British Empire and New Zealand forces formed the British Commonwealth Occupation Force under it.

SCAP worked through the Japanese government. A land reform, led on the American side by Wolf Ladejinsky, bought about 38 per cent of Japan's cultivated land from landlords between 1947 and 1949 and resold it to the farmers who worked it; by 1950, 89 per cent of agricultural land was owner-operated. By 1947, 48 per cent of the non-agricultural workforce was unionised. SCAP largely abolished the zaibatsu, the financial combines that had dominated industry. Its public health section under Colonel Crawford F. Sams organised food distribution, immunisation and quarantine, which kept outbreaks of smallpox, typhus and cholera among returning refugees localised.

SCAP staff drafted a new constitution within about a week, presented as a wholesale amendment of the Meiji Constitution. It was ratified in November 1946 and took effect on 3 May 1947, abolishing the kazoku peerage. SCAP did not conduct the Tokyo Trials, which belonged to the International Military Tribunal for the Far East. MacArthur shielded the emperor from prosecution, arguing in a cable of February 1946 that trying him would require a million occupation soldiers. The historian Herbert Bix argued this had a lasting and distorting effect on Japanese understanding of the war. MacArthur also declined to prosecute Shirō Ishii and the bacteriological research units in exchange for data on their human experiments.

SCAP's Civil Censorship Detachment banned 31 topics from the media, including criticism of SCAP and the atomic bombings, which stayed taboo until 1952. MacArthur legalised the Japanese Communist Party and released political prisoners; the party won six seats in the 1946 election, the first in which women voted.

President Harry S. Truman relieved MacArthur on 11 April 1951, and General Matthew Ridgway succeeded him. The San Francisco Peace Treaty, signed on 8 September 1951, took effect on 28 April 1952, when Japan again became independent. General Order 10 dissolved GHQ-SCAP that day, and its remaining functions passed to the Far East Command. The United States continued to administer some Japanese islands afterwards; Okinawa stayed under US administration until 1972.
supreme-court-of-canada: The authority to establish a national appeal court dated back to the creation of the Province of Canada in 1840, but the power remained unused. When the British North America Act, 1867 was finalized, section 101 allowed Parliament to create a general court of appeal. Prime Minister John A. Macdonald introduced two bills to establish a supreme court, in 1869 and 1870, but both were withdrawn.

The Liberals under Alexander Mackenzie made a central court of appeal part of their platform in the 1874 federal election, and Minister of Justice Télésphore Fournier introduced the Supreme and Exchequer Court Act, which passed on 8 April 1875 with bipartisan support and created both the Supreme Court and the Exchequer Court.

The court began with six judges and a quorum of four, so that a tied vote meant an appeal was dismissed. In 1927 Parliament added a seventh position and set a mandatory retirement age of 75, and in 1949 the bench reached nine justices. Before 1949 most appointees owed their positions to political patronage.

The appointment of the constitutional law professor Bora Laskin as chief justice in 1973 marked a turning point, and later appointees increasingly came from academic backgrounds or from appellate courts. The Constitution Act, 1982 added the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and greatly broadened judicial review. Beverley McLachlin became the first woman to serve as chief justice in January 2000.

Justices are appointed by the governor general on the advice of the prime minister. By law three of the nine seats go to members of the Quebec bar or bench, because Quebec uses civil law, and by convention the other six are divided among Ontario, the western provinces and the Atlantic provinces.

The court is bijural and bilingual: counsel and judges may use English or French, and since 1970 all judgments have been issued in both languages. Hearings take place only in Ottawa, and the court grants leave to appeal to between 40 and 75 litigants each year. It has sat in a building designed by Ernest Cormier in the Art Deco style, begun in 1939 and in use for hearings by January 1946.
supreme-leader-of-iran: The office rests on the concept of vilayat-e faqih, the Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist, set out by Ruhollah Khomeini in his book Islamic Government. He argued that government must follow the sharia and that a leading Islamic jurist must provide political guardianship, a task that fell to jurists in the absence of the twelfth Imam. Before the revolution, observant Shia Muslims chose their own leading jurist to follow, known as a marja'.

In March 1979, shortly after Khomeini returned from exile and the monarchy was overthrown, a referendum asked 'Islamic Republic, yes or no?', and 98 per cent of those voting said yes. The constitution of 1906 was declared invalid, and a new constitution was ratified by referendum in the first week of December 1979. It combines theocratic and democratic elements, and it created the office. The Deputy Supreme Leader's role was incorporated into the leader's authority in 1985, when Grand Ayatollah Hussein-Ali Montazeri held it.

The constitution calls the holder the Leader, the leader of the Islamic Revolution or the leadership of the Islamic jurist; Supreme Leader is a style of respect. The holder is the head of state, takes precedence over the president, who is head of government, is commander-in-chief of the armed forces and supervises the legislative, judicial and executive branches. The judiciary, state radio and television and bodies such as the Guardian Council and the Expediency Discernment Council are subject to the office, and the holder serves for life.

The Assembly of Experts, elected by voters to eight-year terms from candidates approved by the Guardian Council, is charged under Article 111 with choosing, supervising and dismissing the leader. If the office falls vacant, an interim council of the president, the head of the judiciary and one jurist of the Guardian Council temporarily takes over its duties.

The original constitution required the leader to be a marja'-e taqlid, the highest-ranking cleric in Usuli Twelver Shia law. Shortly before Khomeini's death in 1989 he fell out with his intended successor Montazeri, who had disapproved of the mass executions of political prisoners in 1988. Khomeini chose Ali Khamenei, a lower-ranking cleric, and the constitution was amended so that Islamic scholarship was enough.
suq-al-shuyukh: Suq al-Shuyukh stands among date palm orchards on the right bank of the Euphrates, at the western end of the Hawr al-Hammar lake and wetlands, about 40 km southeast of Nasiriya. The town is the centre of a district of the Dhi Qar Governorate, and the land to the north and west of the lake is given over to the cultivation of dates and rice.

The town was founded in the early 18th century in Ottoman Iraq to serve as the marketplace of the Muntafiq tribal confederation, and the word Shuyukh in its name refers to the members of the clan of the confederation's leader. Toward the end of the 18th century it was described as a small town with a mosque, surrounded by earthen walls. Accounts of the early 1800s put its people at 6,000 families and describe it as a centre of trade with Basra, and even with Bushir and Bombay.

In the 19th century the town was divided into Muslim, Christian, Jewish and Mandaean quarters, as Julius Heinrich Petermann reported after his visit of 1854. The Mandaean quarter, known as Margab or Ṣubbūye, lay on the opposite bank of the Euphrates. Shortly before his visit, around 1853, about 200 of the town's roughly 260 Mandaean families, many of them silversmiths or boat-builders, had moved to al-Amarah because of persecution by the Muntafiq. Petermann estimated the population at 3,000 and met Yahya Bihram, the high priest of the Mandaeans.

Around the end of the 19th century V. Cuinet put the population at about 12,000: some 2,250 Sunnis with two mosques, 8,770 Shi'is with one sanctuary, 200 Jews and 700 Mandaeans. Under Ottoman rule Suq al-Shuyukh became the seat of a kaza in the sanjak of Muntafiq. The town later took part in the Iraqi revolt of 1920 and in the Iraqi Shia revolts of 1935 and 1936.
Suq al-Shuyukh remains a centre of date and rice growing on the edge of the marshes. It has a stadium, the Suq Al-Shuyukh Stadium, and two football clubs, Suq Al-Shuyukh FC and Al-Forat FC.
sur-empire: The Sur dynasty was of Afghan origin and ruled from Sasaram in what is now Bihar. Its founder, Sher Khan, campaigned against the Bengal Sultanate, whose ruler asked Humayun for help. Humayun marched in 1537, besieged Chunar for over six months and in September 1538 occupied Gauda, which the Afghans had stripped of its treasury. Humayun made peace, and when he crossed the Karmanasa River Sher Khan attacked at the Battle of Chausa, where the Mughals lost over 7,000 dead. At Kannauj Humayun's larger army was defeated and he fled to Sindh. On 17 May 1540 Sher Khan was crowned Sher Shah, with the epithet Sultan Adil, "Just King".

Sher Shah captured Delhi, took Lahore in November 1540 and held Multan from 1541, but did not extend his rule beyond the Indus. He put down a revolt in Bengal in March 1541, divided it into 47 smaller units, and ordered Rohtas Fort built to check the Gakhars of the Punjab. In 1542 he took Gwalior and Malwa.

He took Raisen in 1543 after a six-month siege, and a force of his then destroyed the retreating Puran Mall's men, an act the sources present as justice for Muslim families wronged at Chanderi. At Sammel in 1543 he defeated Maldeo Rathore of Marwar, after forged letters made Maldeo suspect his own commanders, though his army suffered thousands of casualties.

Sher Shah was mortally wounded when a cannon burst during the siege of Kalinjar Fort and died on 22 May 1545. His second son Jalal Khan succeeded as Islam Shah and fought rebellious amirs, among them the Niazis under Haibat Khan, who took refuge among the Gakhars.

Civil war followed after his reign. The last stage of the Mughal reconquest was the siege of Mankot, where Sikandar Shah Suri surrendered to Bairam Khan on 25 July 1557 after six months, and entered the service of Akbar.

The empire was divided into iqtas, some under military governors such as Haibat Khan in the Punjab. Iqtas were divided into sarkars and these into parganas, each with a shiqdar for order and a munsif for revenue and civil justice. Village panchayats were left to govern themselves. Sher Shah's silver rupee of 178 grains became the precursor of the modern rupee. He rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with caravanserais, mosques, wells and shade trees, set up a postal service of relay riders and abolished internal customs duties. His criminal law was harsh and made officials answerable for crimes in their districts. Historians differ on his religious policy toward Hindus.
suraj-mal: Suraj Mal was born Sujan Singh on 13 February 1707, the son of Raja Badan Singh and Rani Devki, in a Hindu Jat family of the Sinsinwar clan of Bharatpur. He was trained in war from a young age. His father, who was going blind, handed him power over the state in 1750, and he succeeded him officially as maharaja in 1756. He also built the palace at Deeg, 32 km from Bharatpur, as a summer resort for the rulers of the state.

His first independent decision in external affairs came in November 1745, when Nawab Fateh Ali Khan of Koil asked his help against the Afghan chief Asad Khan, sent by the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah. Suraj Mal sent an army under his son, and the war at Chandaus ended in Asad Khan's death and the defeat of the imperial army. In the succession struggle at Jaipur he backed Ishwari Singh with 10,000 soldiers, and Ishwari Singh won the battle of August 1748.

He fought under Safdar Jang, the rebellious wazir of Oudh, when Safdar Jang attacked Delhi. In 1754 Khanderao Holkar, son of Malhar Rao Holkar, besieged his town of Kumher for the Mughal emperor Alamgir II; Khanderao was killed by a cannonball while inspecting his troops, the siege was lifted and a treaty with the Marathas followed. When the Afghan ruler Durrani came to Delhi and demanded tribute in 1760, Suraj Mal pleaded poverty, and Durrani besieged his fort of Dig on 6 February 1760 before giving up and marching away.

Around March 1756 his troops took Alwar Fort from Madho Singh of Jaipur. His capture of Agra Fort on 12 June 1761 came after a siege of a month and a bribe to its commander. After the Battle of Panipat in 1761 he sent his sons Jawahar Singh and Nahar Singh to conquer Haryana. Besides the garrisons of his forts, he had an army of more than 75,000 infantry and more than 38,000 cavalry.

In the war with the Rohilla Afghans of Najib ud-Daula, an ambush near the Hindon River took his army by surprise, and Suraj Mal was killed on the night of 25 December 1763. His son and successor Jawahar Singh built his large cenotaph at Kusum Sarovar in Govardhan, flanked by those of his wives Hansiya and Kishori, its ceilings painted with scenes of the life of Krishna and of Suraj Mal. His court poet Sudan recorded his life in the Sujan Charitra.
surat: Surat stands on the banks of the Tapti River, known popularly as the Tapi, close to its confluence with the Arabian Sea. The city lies 284 km south of Gandhinagar, the state capital, 265 km south of Ahmedabad and 289 km north of Mumbai. The Gujarati, Hindi and Urdu word surat means countenance. After dams were built on the Tapi its water flow decreased and the original port facilities closed, so the nearest port is now in the Magadalla and Hazira area of the metropolitan region.

The traditional account holds that Surat was built up around 1500 by a wealthy Hindu merchant named Gopi, who asked the king of Gujarat to approve the name Suryapur, city of the sun. The Muslim king is said to have altered it to Surat, after the word surah, the name for the chapters of the Qur'an. Both names appear in sources before 1500, so the town and its name are older than Gopi's time. Before the 1500s the nearby town of Rander was the main commercial centre; it declined because of Portuguese raids, and some of its merchants probably moved to Surat.

Under the Mughal Empire Surat was the most prosperous port of the realm. Despite its wealth it looked like a typical trader's town of mud-and-bamboo tenements and crooked streets, with a few mansions and warehouses along the riverfront and the establishments of Turkish, Armenian, English, French and Dutch traders. England established its first Indian trading factory there in 1612. Shivaji looted the city twice, the first sacking coming in 1664, and his raids scared trade away. Under the British Raj Surat declined, remaining important for textile products but less important as a port.

Surat is the commercial and economic centre of South Gujarat and the administrative capital of the Surat district. The 2011 census gave it a population of 4,467,797. Its diamond trade began in the late 1950s, when the first diamond workshops of Gujarat appeared in Surat and Navsari, and its textile industry is long established. Surat railway station was built in 1860.
surat-thani: Surat Thani is a city in southern Thailand, 651 kilometres south of Bangkok, and the capital of Surat Thani Province. It lies near the mouth of the Tapi River. It is the regional commercial centre, with a seaport dealing in the main products of the province, rubber and coconuts. The city has a tropical monsoon climate with only two seasons, wet and dry. A short dry season lasts from January to April and the wet season from May to December, with the heaviest rains in October and November.

The city was previously known as Bandon, meaning village on higher ground. King Vajiravudh, Rama VI, gave it its present name, meaning city of good people, in 1915. It was given because of the intense devotion of the local people to Buddhism, and it was taken from the Indian city of Surat in Gujarat, on the Indian river Tapi, with which the king was impressed.

On 21 December 1930 Surat Thani became a sanitary district, and on 7 December 1935 it was upgraded to a town with a municipal area of 2.67 square kilometres. The municipality was enlarged to 6.95 square kilometres in 1958 and to 68.97 square kilometres in 1994, and on 4 May 2007 the town was made a city.

The city is mainly known to travellers as the jumping-off point to Ko Samui, Ko Tao and Ko Pha Ngan, and ferries run from the mainland to the islands. The Southern Line of the State Railway of Thailand links the province with Bangkok, with its main station at Phunphin, about 15 kilometres from the city, and Route 401 connects the city to Nakhon Si Thammarat. It has 132,040 inhabitants.

Local festivals include Chak Phra, which celebrates the Buddha's symbolic return to earth at the end of Buddhist Lent with a parade, floats and long-boat races, and a vegetarian festival held every October. Higher education includes the Surat Thani campus of the Prince of Songkla University and Surat Thani Rajabhat University.
