surb-karapet-monastery: The monastery stood in the historic province of Taron, about 30 km north-west of Mush in present-day eastern Turkey, and was also called Innaknian vank, the Monastery of the Nine Springs, and Glakavank after its traditional first father superior, the Syriac archbishop Zenob Glak. By the 20th century it was a walled, fort-like enclosure with a main church of the Holy Cross, a hall on 16 columns, four chapels to the east and an 18th-century three-storey bell tower. From the 12th century it was the seat of the diocese of Taron, and it was regarded as the second most important Armenian monastery after Etchmiadzin.

Tradition holds that Gregory the Illuminator replaced pagan statues on the site with a martyrion for relics he brought from Caesarea; the art historian Christina Maranci links the foundation instead to the monastic movement of Bagratid Armenia in the 940s. It was the burial abbey of the Mamikonian princes of Taron. An earthquake ruined it in the 7th century, fire destroyed a palace and a church in 1058, Persian troops destroyed the Surb Karapet church in the 1750s, and an earthquake in 1784 brought down the main church before a full rebuilding in 1788.

Kurdish bands looted it in 1827. From 1862 Mkrtich Khrimian, its father superior and prelate of Taron, founded a largely secular school and published the journal The Eaglet of Taron there in modern Armenian. The monastery was looted again in 1895 during the Hamidian massacres. During the genocide of 1915 Armenians who had fled to it held out for more than two months; contemporary reports say about five thousand were massacred near its walls, and it was sacked.

In 1916 Russian troops and Armenian volunteers carried about 1,750 manuscripts to Etchmiadzin. The ruins, still visible in the 1970s, were later used as a source of stone by the Kurdish village of Yukarıyongalı built on the site, and in 2001 the historian Robert H. Hewsen found only traces of two chambers of the chapel of Surb Stepanos. A pair of carved walnut doors dated 1212 survives in a private collection.
surena: Surena, or Suren, was a Parthian spahbed, a general or commander, and the leader of the House of Suren. The name is the Greek and Latin form of Sūrēn, which comes from the Avestan sūra, meaning strong or exalted, and Suren remains a common name in Iran and Armenia.

Plutarch, writing about 125 years after the events in his Life of Crassus, called him an extremely distinguished man who ranked next after the king in wealth, birth and honour, and the foremost Parthian of his time in courage and ability. He wrote that Surena's army included many slaves, though the meaning of the words for slaves there is disputed, and he described his painted face and his hair parted in the fashion of the Medes, which belied his manly skill.

In 54 BCE Surena commanded troops of Orodes II at the battle for the city of Seleucia, a contest over the Arsacid succession after Mithridates IV had deposed Orodes, and he was instrumental in restoring Orodes to the throne. He was one of the most powerful men in the Parthian Empire, and he travelled with what one scholar, Gazerani, calls an unmistakably courtly retinue.

In 53 BCE the Romans advanced on the western Parthian vassal territories, and Orodes II sent his cavalry under Surena to meet them. The armies met at Carrhae, at Harrân in present-day Turkey. The superior equipment of the Parthians and their tactic of luring the Romans into the middle of the desert let them defeat the numerically larger force of Marcus Licinius Crassus.

Plutarch speaks of 20,000 Roman dead and 10,000 prisoners. The victory echoed among the peoples of the East but brought the Arsacid dynasty no territory and no decisive shift in the balance of power. Surena was then executed by Orodes II, most likely because the king saw his power and influence as a threat.

The Battle of Carrhae is commonly seen as one of the earliest and most important battles between the Roman and Parthian empires and one of the most crushing defeats in Roman history. Surena died in 53 or 52 BCE. His place in the historical tradition has been described as curiously parallel to that of Rustam in the Shahnameh. The last work of the 17th-century French dramatist Pierre Corneille, a tragedy titled Suréna, is roughly based on his story.
surendra-sai: Surendra Sai was born on 23 January 1809 in the village of Khinda, about 40 km north of Sambalpur, one of the seven children of Dharma Singh. He belonged to the ruling Chauhan clan of Sambalpur State, through the branch descended from Prince Aniruddha Sai, brother of an earlier Maharaja. Only a man could rule Sambalpur, and the childless Maharaj Sai is said to have chosen Surendra Sai as his successor. The British refused the claim, since he sought full independent rule.

When Maharaj Sai died in 1827 the British installed his widow, Rani Mohan Kumari, against the custom that only men ruled. Her land revenue policy alienated the Gond and Binjhal tribal zamindars, and the British replaced her with Narayan Singh, a member of the royal family born of a low caste, again passing over Surendra Sai.

Surendra Sai began resisting the British at the age of 18 in 1827, with the Gond zamindars as his closest allies. In 1840 he was captured with his brother Udyanta Sai and his uncle Balaram Singh, who died in Hazaribagh Jail. When Narayan Singh died without a male heir in 1849, Lord Dalhousie annexed Sambalpur under the Doctrine of Lapse. During the rising of 1857 sepoys freed Surendra Sai after 17 years in prison, and he carried the struggle into the hills, supported by brothers, sons, relatives and zamindars.

The rebellion elsewhere in India had collapsed by the end of 1858, but he fought on. Major Forster, given full military and civil powers, was removed in 1861 after three years without success. His successor, Major Impey, seized the rebels' food stocks and then turned to a policy of conciliation, and Surendra Sai surrendered soon after Sambalpur passed to the new Central Provinces on 30 April 1862.

After Impey's death the administration turned hostile again and arrested Surendra Sai with his relations and followers; he and six companions were held in the Asirgarh hill fort, where he spent 19 years and died in 1884. Many of his associates were executed, and Hatte Singh died in the Cellular Jail in the Andamans. Sambalpur is counted among the last districts outside the princely states that the British occupied. A statue of him was placed at the Parliament of India in 2005, and a university of technology at Burla, a medical college and the Jharsuguda airport bear his name.
surendranagar-district: Surendranagar district lies in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat. It takes its name from its headquarters, which began as Wadhwan Camp, where the British political agent for Wadhwan lived. After the agent left in 1946 the town was renamed after Surendrasinhji Jorawarsinhji (1922 to 1983), then ruler of Wadhwan, though it is still called the Camp locally. When the princely states were merged the district was known as Jhalavad, the land of the Jhala Rajputs, who held many of them. A legend says the name comes from Jhalavun, a Gujarati word meaning to hold, after the mother of Harpaldev's children who held them while fending off a wild elephant.

A Harappan site found at Rangpur in 1931, the first in Gujarat, shows that the Indus Valley civilisation reached Saurashtra, and Late Stone Age tools were found at Sejakpur in 1957-58. The early history is unclear, but the district was probably ruled in turn by the Mauryas, Indo-Greeks, Western Satraps, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Chaulukyas, then the Delhi Sultanate. In 1407 the governors of Gujarat declared independence and the district became part of the Gujarat Sultanate. After 1573 it was part of the Mughal Gujarat Subah, though real control lay with many local rulers and landlords.

In the British period the district held several states. Dhrangadhra, Wadhwan and Limbdi were ruled by Jhala Rajputs, who claimed descent from Harpaldev, a son of Kesar Makwana. Bajana was founded by Malik Haider Khan, a Jat leader driven out of Sindh, and Dasada was ruled by the Multani Maliks. Dhandhalapur passed from the Babarias to the Khadvads in 1790.

The district had a population of 1,756,268 at the 2011 census, and Gujarati was spoken by 98.77 per cent of people. Its salt pans, especially around Kharaghoda, supply a large part of India's salt, and it is a centre of cotton ginning. The Surendranagar Cotton Oil and Oilseeds Association, founded in 1964, was the first cotton futures exchange in India. The Gangavo kund at Dedadara dates to the 11th century, and a legend tells of Ranakdevi, who died by sati on the banks of the Bhogavo near Wadhwan.
suriname: Suriname lies on the Guiana Shield on the northern coast of South America, bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the north, French Guiana to the east, Brazil to the south and Guyana to the west. It is the smallest sovereign country in South America. The northern lowland coast has been cultivated, and most of the people live there. The south is tropical rainforest and sparsely inhabited savanna, covering about 80% of the land. The name may come from an Indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived there at the time of European contact. British settlers wrote it Surinam, which long remained the standard English spelling until the official change to Suriname in January 1978.

Indigenous settlement dates back to about 3,000 BCE. The Lokono were a nomadic coastal people who lived by hunting, foraging and fishing, and the Carib, using superior sailing ships, conquered them. British settlers founded the first European colony at Marshall's Creek on the Suriname River in 1630. Jews, expelled from Spain and Portugal, began to settle from the early 17th century and were granted freedom of religion in 1665. In 1667, in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of Breda, the Dutch kept the plantation colony they had gained from the English, and the English kept New Amsterdam, which they renamed New York.

Under Dutch rule Suriname was a lucrative plantation colony, mostly of sugar, driven by African slave labour. About 300,000 enslaved Africans were taken there from the mid-1600s to the early 1800s. After slavery was abolished in 1863, indentured servants were recruited mostly from British India and the Dutch East Indies. Suriname became a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 and independent on 25 November 1975.

Suriname is a representative democratic republic under the Constitution of 1987. Paramaribo is the capital and largest city, home to nearly half the population. Dutch is the official language, and Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is widely used. No ethnic group forms a majority. The population includes descendants of indentured workers from India, Java and China and of enslaved Africans, among them the Maroons, whose ancestors escaped to the interior. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve, established in 1998, became a World Heritage Site in 2000.
suriname-river: The Suriname River is 480 kilometres long. It rises in the Guiana Highlands on the border between the Wilhelmina Mountains and the Eilerts de Haan Mountains, where it is known as the Gran Rio, and the Upper Suriname begins at the confluence of the Gran Rio and the Pikin Rio near the village of Goddo. The Brokopondo Reservoir, held back by the Afobaka Dam, divides the river into two sections. The lower river passes Berg en Dal, Jodensavanne, Carolina and Domburg before reaching Paramaribo on its left bank. It is joined by the Commewijne at Nieuw-Amsterdam and enters the Atlantic at the sandspit of Braamspunt.

The name Suriname may derive from an indigenous people called the Surinen, who lived in the area at the time of European contact. Early sources spell the river's name in many ways. Lawrence Kemys wrote of a river called Shurinama, and a Dutch fleet in 1598 mentioned the river Surinamo. A Dutch notary in 1617 wrote Surrenant for the river where a Dutch trading post had existed three years earlier, and in 1634 David Pietersz. de Vries wrote of travelling up the Sername river until he met the English colony there.

A Spanish manuscript of 1640 called the river Soronama. In 1653 instructions to a British fleet sailing to meet Lord Willoughby in Barbados used the spelling Surinam, which remained standard in English, and a royal charter of 1663 spoke of the region as called Serrinam also Surrinam.

The Suriname is the country's most important river for trade. Vessels carrying bauxite, aluminium oxide and aluminium leave by it, and nearly all vessels carrying materials vital to the country enter at Braamspunt to unload at the harbours of Paramaribo, Smalkalden and Paranam. During the Second World War the German cargo ship Goslar was scuttled in the river to keep it from Allied hands, and its wreck remains visible. The Jules Wijdenbosch Bridge at Paramaribo opened in 2000 and gives access to the eastern part of the country.
suriyothai: Her given name, Suriyothai, means dawn: it joins Suriya, from the Sanskrit sūrya, sun, with Uthai, from udaya, rising. Somdet Phra and Sri, often written Si, are honorifics. She married Prince Tien, the future King Maha Chakkraphat, while he was regent under King Yodfa. According to the story told of him, the prince entered a monastery to remain faithful to her and to escape the advances of the Queen Mother, Si Sudachan.

She was queen in the early part of Maha Chakkraphat's reign. In 1548, barely six months after his accession, Tabinshwehti, the King of Burma, invaded Siam intending to sack Ayutthaya, in a campaign of the Burmese–Siamese War of 1547 to 1549.

The Burmese met little resistance at the border, found Kanchanaburi deserted, took Uthong and Suphanburi, crossed the Chao Phraya River near Phong Phaeng and camped on the Lumpli Plain north of the capital. Maha Chakkraphat rode out on his chief war elephant to test their strength. The queen, as his Chief Queen, went with him on a smaller elephant together with their young daughter, Princess Boromdhilok. Both wore male military dress of helmet and armour, the queen in the uniform of an Uparaja. Their sons Prince Ramesuan, the heir, and Prince Mahin also rode with the army.

The Siamese met the column of Thado Dhamma Yaza, the Viceroy of Prome. In the single elephant combat of the commanders, the king's elephant panicked and fled. The queen drove her elephant between the king and the pursuing viceroy, who struck her from shoulder to heart with his halberd and mortally wounded her daughter. Her sons drove the viceroy from the field and carried the bodies back to Ayutthaya. Burmese chronicles do not mention any single combat by the Viceroy of Prome.

Her children included Mahin, later King Mahinthrathirat, and Sawatdirat, mother of King Naresuan. The chedi Phra Chedi Sisuriyothai stands at Wat Suanluang Sopsawan, now part of Ayutthaya Historical Park. The Suriyothai Memorial Park at Tung Makham Yong, with a statue of the queen on a war elephant, was founded in 1992 for Queen Sirikit's 60th birthday. The film The Legend of Suriyothai followed in 2001, and S. P. Somtow's ballet-opera Suriyothai in 2013.
surkh-kotal: Surkh Kotal, also called Chashma-i Shir or Sar-i Chashma, lies in the south of the ancient region of Bactria, about 18 kilometres north of Puli Khumri, the capital of Baghlan Province. The name was given by the French team led by Schlumberger and is that of the hills on which the remains stand, not the ancient one. W. B. Henning and J. D. M. Derrett proposed that a word found on fragments at the site, bagolaggo, may be its old name, comparing it with the Old Iranian baga-danaka, temple or sanctuary, and with the name of nearby Baghlan.

Excavated by the Délégation Archéologique Française en Afghanistan until 1966, Surkh Kotal is the main excavated site of the Kushan Empire. It yielded large temples, statues of Kushan rulers, a fire altar and inscriptions that revealed part of the chronology of the early Kushan emperors. The Rabatak inscription, with its evidence on the dynasty's genealogy, was found in the village of Robatak just outside the site.

Only fragments survive of an inscription from the reign of Kanishka, which records that a stronghold and sanctuary were built in four years, with a façade, stairs and a canal lined with stones. The longer inscription known as SK4 tells that the sanctuary was abandoned when the canal ran dry and the gods were taken away, until Nokonzoko, a favourite of the king, came in the 31st era-year, had a well dug and appointed inspectors over the well and the stronghold. A Greek inscription naming Palamedes, apparently the temple's main architect, shows that Hellenistic populations remained in the region in the Kushan era.

Some of the sculptures were moved to the National Museum of Afghanistan in Kabul, and the rest of the site was looted during the Afghan Civil War. The statue of King Kanishka was destroyed by the Taliban in February and March 2001 and later restored by French conservators; it is shown in the museum with the inscriptions and the fire altar.
suro-of-geumgwan-gaya: The founding legend of Geumgwan Gaya was recorded in the 13th-century chronicle Garakguk-gi and cited in the Samguk yusa. It tells that as the nine chiefs and their people, commanded by heaven, performed ancestral rites with dancing and song, a gold bowl wrapped in red cloth came down from heaven holding six eggs. Twelve days later six princes were born from them. Suro, the firstborn, led the others in setting up six states and claimed the leadership of the Gaya confederacy. His posthumous name was Sureung.

According to the legend his wife, Heo Hwang-ok, also called Suriratna, was a princess from a distant country named Ayuta, which the story implies lay in southern India. Their children are said to have included King Geodeung, two sons who took the Heo clan name, seven sons who became Buddhist monks, and two daughters, Princess Yeongan and Lady Jijinnaerye. Historians read the legend as a sign of the early belief that kings descended from heaven; several other Korean kingdoms tell of founders born from eggs, among them Jumong of Goguryeo and Park Hyeokgeose of Silla, and the story has been searched for clues to the little-known customs of Gaya.

Suro is said to have died in 199. King Munmu of Silla, counted as his fifteenth-generation descendant, had his spirit tablet honoured with the Silla kings and ordered ancestral rites for him, according to the Samguk yusa. A tomb attributed to him is still maintained in Gimhae. The Gimhae Kim, Gimhae Heo and Incheon Yi clans all trace their descent to him and did not intermarry until the beginning of the 20th century. Ayodhya and Gimhae became sister cities in 2001, and a memorial park to Suro and Heo Hwang-ok is being built in Ayodhya by the South Korean and Indian governments.
surrender-at-vilagos: Once Russia had joined the war, the combined Austrian and Russian forces were far stronger than the Hungarians, and their defeat was a matter of time. The decisive point came at the Battle of Temesvár, a clear Austrian victory, after which the Hungarians were left to choose between surrender and destruction. On 21 July Count Theodor von Rüdiger and Cavalry Captain Katlaroff brought Görgei, then at Rimaszombat, now Rimavská Sobota in Slovakia, an offer from the Russian General Chruloff that promised full freedom to Hungarian officers and men.

László Batthyány and another officer carried back Görgei's answer: he asked freedom for all Hungarians, not only those who had fought, and said he would gladly accept one of the Russian princes as wearer of the Holy Crown of Hungary.

The terms were signed at Bohus Castle by Görgei and Rüdiger. Görgei hoped to show by surrendering to the Russians that Hungary had been beaten by Russia and not by Austria, but the Russians simply handed the prisoners over to the Austrian authorities. Lajos Kossuth, the political leader of the revolution, left the country on 17 August.

Other troops and fortresses held out for a time and then gave up one after another. General János Damjanich surrendered the fortress of Arad to the Russians on 17 August, and the remnants of the Army of Transylvania laid down their arms at Déva the next day. Munkács fell on 26 August and Pétervárad on 7 September, and General György Klapka surrendered Komárom to Field Marshal Julius Jacob von Haynau on 2 October.

Haynau became Imperial plenipotentiary in Hungary and subdued the country harshly. Despite the Russian Emperor's pleas for clemency, the Austrians sentenced hundreds of soldiers and civilians to death, imprisoned many more and conscripted prisoners into the Austrian Army. On 6 October 1849 they executed twelve Hungarian generals and one colonel at Arad, remembered as the 13 Martyrs of Arad, and on the same day shot Lajos Batthyány, the first Hungarian Prime Minister.
surrender-of-japan: By 1945 Japan had suffered nearly two years of defeats in the South West Pacific, India, the Marianas and the Philippines. After the loss of Saipan in July 1944 General Hideki Tōjō was replaced as prime minister by General Kuniaki Koiso, and after the loss of the Philippines Koiso was replaced by Admiral Kantarō Suzuki. The Allies took Iwo Jima and Okinawa in the first half of 1945, and Okinawa was to be a staging area for the invasion of the Home Islands.

Policy was made by the Supreme Council for the Direction of the War, the so-called Big Six. In the summer Japan's leaders privately asked the Soviet Union, then neutral, to mediate, while the Soviets prepared to attack in Manchuria in fulfilment of promises made at the Tehran and Yalta Conferences. On 26 July the United States, the United Kingdom and China issued the Potsdam Declaration, calling for unconditional surrender.

On 6 August 1945 the United States dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Late on 8 August the Soviet Union declared war, in violation of the Soviet–Japanese Neutrality Pact, and invaded Manchuria soon after midnight. A second atomic bomb fell on Nagasaki on 9 August. The Big Six and the cabinet remained split, and Emperor Hirohito then ordered the council to accept the Potsdam terms. After several more days of negotiations, including a failed coup attempt by army hardliners between 12 and 15 August, he announced the surrender in a recorded radio address on 15 August.

The Emperor gave the public the new and cruel bomb as his reason and told the military that the Soviet entry into the war threatened the empire's foundation. The occupation began on 28 August under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, and the formal ceremony took place on 2 September aboard the battleship USS Missouri, where Japanese officials signed the Instrument of Surrender.

Allied countries marked V-J Day. Isolated Japanese soldiers refused to surrender for months and years afterwards, some into the 1970s. The Soviet Union continued fighting until early September and took the Kuril Islands, but its plan to occupy Hokkaido was frustrated by President Truman's opposition. The state of war formally ended when the Treaty of San Francisco came into force on 28 April 1952, and Japan and the Soviet Union ended theirs with a joint declaration in 1956. The part played by the atomic bombings in the surrender, and the ethics of the two attacks, remain debated.
suruga-province: Suruga was an old province in the central part of today's Shizuoka Prefecture. It bordered Izu, Kai, Sagami, Shinano and Tōtōmi provinces and, to the south, the Pacific Ocean through Suruga Bay. Its short name was Sunshū. It consisted of seven districts: Abe, Fuji, Ihara, Mashizu, Shida, Suntō and Udo, most of them since dissolved or merged.

Suruga was one of the original provinces of Japan, set up in the Nara period under the Taihō Code. Its first capital stood at what is now Numazu, which also had the provincial Kokubun-ji and the Ichinomiya, Mishima Taisha. In a cadastral reform of 680 the districts forming Izu Province were separated from it, and the capital moved to the right bank of the Abe River, in what is now Shizuoka City. Under the Kamakura shogunate the Hōjō clan held it directly, and traffic grew on the Tōkaidō road between Kamakura and Kyoto. From the early Muromachi period through much of the Sengoku period it was under the Imagawa clan, who tried to bring the customs and rituals of the kuge aristocracy to their capital.

After Imagawa Yoshimoto was defeated by Oda Nobunaga at the Battle of Okehazama, Takeda Shingen of Kai took the province, and Tokugawa Ieyasu in turn defeated the Takeda. After the Siege of Odawara in 1590 Toyotomi Hideyoshi forced the Tokugawa to exchange their domains for the Kantō, and gave Sunpu Castle to one of his retainers, Nakamura Kazuichi. After the Battle of Sekigahara Ieyasu recovered his lands and made Sunpu Castle his home after he retired as shōgun.

In the Edo period Suruga prospered on the Tōkaidō, and many post towns grew up. For defence the Tokugawa shogunate forbade bridges on the major rivers, such as the Ōi, which led to towns growing at the river crossings. Sunpu was held directly by the shōgun through the Sunpu jōdai. After the Boshin War the last shōgun, Tokugawa Yoshinobu, returned to Suruga in 1868 to rule the short-lived Shizuoka Domain until the han system was abolished in 1871. Suruga was then merged with Tōtōmi and Izu to form Shizuoka Prefecture, though it continued to exist for some purposes, and treaties of 1894 with the United States and the United Kingdom name it.
suryavarman-i: Suryavarman rose against King Udayadityavarman I, defeating his armies, and then fought a long war with Jayavirahvarman, Udayadityavarman's would-be successor, before his claim to the throne prevailed. His reign lasted some 40 years, much of it spent defending it. Known as the King of the Just Laws, he invited some 4,000 local officials to the royal palace to swear allegiance to him. His palace stood near Angkor Thom, and he was the first Khmer ruler to protect his palace with a wall.

Around 1012 he established diplomatic relations with the Chola dynasty of south India and sent a chariot as a present to Emperor Rajendra Chola I. He seems to have asked the Chola for help against the Tambralinga kingdom, which in turn sought aid from the Srivijaya king Sangrama Vijayatungavarman. The resulting war ended in victory for the Chola and the Khmer and heavy losses for Srivijaya and Tambralinga. His territory reached east into the Mekong basin, and during his reign 47 cities were under Khmer control.

Suryavarman was a Mahayana Buddhist who tolerated the growing Theravada Buddhist presence in his kingdom and allowed his people to continue practising Hinduism. The inscription at Tuol Ta Pec says he knew the principles of the six Vedangas. He probably began building at Preah Khan Kompong Svay and enlarged Banteay Srei, Wat Ek Phnom and Phnom Chisor; his major works were Preah Vihear on Dangrek Mountain and the completion of the Phimeanakas and Ta Keo. He also began the West Baray, the second Angkor reservoir, 8 kilometres long and 2.1 kilometres wide, the largest Khmer reservoir to survive.

Suryavarman died in 1050 and received the posthumous title Nirvanapada, the king who has gone to nirvana, a reference to his Buddhist beliefs. He was succeeded by his sons Udayadityavarman II, who died around 1066, and Harshavarman III, who fought internal rebellions and attacks by the Chams until his death in 1080.
suryavarman-ii: Suryavarman II, whose name begins with a Sanskrit root meaning sun, grew up on a provincial estate at a time of weakening central control in the empire. An inscription names his father as Ksitindraditya and his mother as Narendralakshmi. As a young prince he contended that he had a legitimate claim to the throne. He appears to have dealt with a rival claimant from the line of Harshavarman III, probably Nripatindravarman, and then to have turned on the elderly king Dharanindravarman I, his great uncle; scholars disagree about which of the two an inscription describes him killing.
In 1114 he sent a mission to the Chola emperor Kulothunga Chola I in south India. He was enthroned in 1113, with the Brahmin sage Divakarapandita officiating, and formally crowned in 1119.

During his decades in power the king reunited the empire, and vassals paid him tribute. His large military operations against the Chams and Dai Viet were largely unsuccessful. Vietnamese and Cham sources record three major attacks in Nghe An and Quang Binh provinces. In 1128 he is said to have led 20,000 soldiers against Dai Viet and been defeated, and the next year sent a fleet of more than 700 vessels against its coast.

In 1145 he appears to have invaded Champa, sacked its capital Vijaya and placed a new king, Harideva, on the throne, but Cham forces under Jaya Harivarman I recaptured the capital and killed Harideva. In 1116 he resumed formal relations with China, and in 1128 the emperor conferred high dignities on him as a great vassal of the empire.

He presided over the building of Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu and Shiva, whose five central towers evoke the peaks of Mount Meru. Other temples of his reign include Banteay Samre, Thommanon, Chau Say Tevoda and Beng Mealea. He made Vishnu, rather than Shiva, the focus of court religion, which was unusual among Khmer kings; scholars debate whether this explains why Angkor Wat faces west.

Inscriptions suggest that Suryavarman II died around 1150, possibly during a campaign against Champa, after his troops had been defeated by Vietnamese forces under Tô Hiến Thành. His cousin Dharanindravarman II succeeded him, and a period of weak rule and feuding began. He was given the posthumous name Paramavishnuloka, and Angkor Wat appears to have been completed only after his death. He is the first Khmer king depicted in art, seated on a dais in a bas-relief in the south gallery of Angkor Wat.
susa: Susa lay in the lower Zagros Mountains, about 250 km east of the Tigris, between the Karkheh and Dez rivers. Its name is of Elamite origin and appears in many languages, as Šušan in Elamite, Soûsa in Greek, Shushan in Hebrew and Šuš in New Persian. It appears in the earliest Sumerian records, among the places obedient to Inanna in Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta. Aeschylus set his play The Persians there, and the Book of Esther is set in Shushan.

Calibrated carbon-14 dates place the foundation of a settlement as early as 4200 BCE. Its inhabitants soon built a monumental platform, and a thousand or more graves near its base held ceramic vessels of great artistry. During the Uruk period Susa fell within the Uruk cultural sphere, though Daniel T. Potts argues that it adopted Uruk's writing selectively. From about 3100 BCE tablets appear and Susa became the centre of Elam. Sargon the Great took Susiana into the Akkadian Empire in about 2330 BCE. Around 1175 BCE Shutruk-Nahhunte plundered the stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi and took it to Susa, where archaeologists found it in 1901.

Cyrus the Great captured Susa in 540 or 539 BCE, bringing it under Persian control for the first time. After Alexander the Great invaded, the satrap of Susa surrendered, and in 324 BCE Alexander held a mass wedding of Persians and Macedonians there. Under the Seleucids it was called Seleucia on the Eulaeus. Trajan briefly captured it in 116 CE. Ardashir I conquered and destroyed it in 224 CE but rebuilt it. An Arab army under Abu Musa al-Ash'ari besieged it after taking Tustar in 642.

The ancient centre is unoccupied, and the population lives in the adjacent town of Shush, in Khuzestan province. The first French excavations were made in 1885 and 1886 by Marcel-Auguste and Jane Dieulafoy, who found glazed bricks and column bases from the palace of the Achaemenid kings. A tomb presumed to be that of the prophet Daniel stands in the area. Susa was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2015.
susan-b-anthony: Susan Anthony was born on 15 February 1820 in Adams, Massachusetts, the second of seven children of Daniel Anthony and Lucy Read Anthony, in a Quaker family committed to social equality. She added the middle initial B. in her youth, after her father's sister Susan, who had married a man named Brownell, though she never used that name herself. She collected anti-slavery petitions at the age of 17, and in 1856 she became the New York state agent for the American Anti-Slavery Society.

In 1851 she met Elizabeth Cady Stanton, who became her lifelong friend and co-worker. In 1863 they organised the Women's Loyal National League. It collected nearly 400,000 signatures for the abolition of slavery in the largest petition drive in the nation's history up to that time, with Anthony as chief organiser of some 2,000 petition collectors. After the war they began the weekly newspaper The Revolution in 1868, and in May 1869 they formed the National Woman Suffrage Association. In 1890 their organisation merged with a rival to form the National American Woman Suffrage Association, with Anthony as its key force.

In 1872 she was arrested in Rochester, New York, for voting, and she was convicted in a widely publicised trial; she refused to pay the fine, and the authorities took no further action. In 1878 she and Stanton arranged for Congress to be presented with the amendment later called the Susan B. Anthony Amendment. She travelled extensively, giving as many as 75 to 100 speeches a year, and helped found the International Council of Women, which met in Washington in 1888.

Anthony died at the age of 86 at her home in Rochester on 13 March 1906. At a birthday celebration in Washington a few days earlier she had spoken of her fellow workers and said that with such women, failure is impossible, a phrase that became a watchword of the women's movement. The amendment was ratified as the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920. Her home in Rochester is a National Historic Landmark, and in 1979 she became the first female citizen to be shown on a United States coin.
sushruta: Suśruta, whose name means well heard in Sanskrit, was an ancient Indian physician and surgeon. He was born in Kanyakubja and later moved to Varanasi, where he wrote the Compendium of Suśruta. The printed editions of the work open each chapter with the phrase as Lord Dhanvantari declared, framing it as Dhanvantari's discourse, but the earliest manuscripts omit this and present it as the work of Divodāsa, king of Varanasi.

Scholars now generally accept that several ancient authors contributed to the text, and that several of them used the name Suśruta, which makes misattribution possible. Rao suggested in 1985 that an original layer by an elder Sushruta was later reworked by another Sushruta and by Nāgārjuna, and that the Uttara-tantra was added as a supplement. Modern scholarship places the composition in the first millennium BCE. The surviving text is a composite that may have begun in the last centuries BCE, and it was probably known to Dṛḍhabala, a contributor to the Charaka Samhita in the fourth or fifth century CE.

The Suśrutasaṃhitā has 186 chapters and addresses general medicine, including diet, surgery, nosology, anatomy, developmental biology, therapeutics, toxicology and paediatrics. It is considered a foundational text of Ayurveda. Its chapters on surgery are historically important, but they have wrongly led some to believe that surgery is its main subject. G. D. Singhal called Suśruta the father of plastic surgery on account of its detailed accounts.

The text describes how students were taught. They studied for six years before hands-on training, then practised incisions on vegetables, dead animals or soft or rotting wood, and observed real procedures before operating themselves. Sushruta laid down rules for cleanliness: instruments of iron or copper were to be kept sharp and clean, and the operating room and wards fumigated with the smoke of guggulu, vacha, white mustard, rock salt and neem leaves.

The work describes the reconstruction of a nose with skin from the forehead or cheek, often for criminals punished by amputation. This method was historically known as the Indian method. According to reports in The Gentleman's Magazine of October 1794, Indians still practised Sushruta's surgical methods in the late 18th century.
sushruta-samhita: The text names Sushruta, whose name means 'well heard', as its author, presenting him as narrating the teaching of his guru Divodasa, a physician associated in early Buddhist Jataka stories with Kashi (Varanasi). Hindu tradition holds Sushruta to be a descendant of Dhanvantari, the god of medicine. Modern scholars, following the medical historian Jan Meulenbeld, doubt that a single person wrote it. An older version seems to have consisted of the first five sections, with the long final section, the Uttaratantra, added by a later author, perhaps named Nagarjuna. Like Hippocrates, the name Sushruta is therefore taken to stand for the work of many authors over several centuries.

In its surviving form the work has 186 chapters and describes 1,120 illnesses, 700 medicinal plants, 64 preparations from minerals and 57 from animal sources. It differs from the Charaka Samhita chiefly in its detailed treatment of surgery, surgical instruments and training.

Students were to practise incisions on gourds, cucumbers, squashes, leather bags filled with fluid and the bladders of dead animals, and the text recommends that a student of surgery examine a dead body systematically. It lists 300 bones, where the Charaka tradition counts three hundred and sixty, and describes skin grafts and the reconstruction of a severed nose with a flap of skin from the cheek, among more than fifteen methods.

The oldest surviving manuscript, a palm-leaf copy in the Kaiser Library in Kathmandu, was completed on 13 April 878. More than 230 manuscripts survive, yet printed editions rest on no more than ten percent of them.

Early in the 8th century the work was translated into Arabic at Baghdad, at the instruction of a member of the Barmakid family, and it was also known to the Khmer king Yasovarman I and in Tibetan literature. Dalhana wrote the earliest surviving commentary on the whole text around 1200. The first printed edition appeared at Calcutta in 1835 and 1836, and Kaviraj Kunjalal Bhishagratna published the first complete English translation between 1907 and 1916.
susquehanna-river: The river forms from two main branches. The North Branch, regarded as the main branch, rises at the outlet of Otsego Lake in Cooperstown, New York, and the West Branch rises in western Pennsylvania and joins it near Northumberland. The river drains 71,000 square kilometres, including nearly half of Pennsylvania, and cuts through a succession of water gaps in the Appalachians. It enters the northern end of the Chesapeake Bay at Havre de Grace, Maryland, and provides half of the bay's freshwater inflow. The bay itself lies in the flooded valley of the Susquehanna.

At European contact the lower valley was held by the Susquehannock, first described by John Smith, who explored the upper Chesapeake in 1608. They traded furs with Virginia, New Sweden and New Netherland, fought Maryland until a treaty in 1652, and were attacked by the Haudenosaunee. By the 1670s disease and war had sharply cut their numbers, and a remnant settled on the Conestoga River in the late 1680s. The Haudenosaunee then claimed the valley by conquest and let displaced Lenape, Shawnee, Conoy, Nanticoke and Mahican groups settle at Shamokin and in the Wyoming Valley. In December 1763 the Scots-Irish vigilantes known as the Paxton Boys massacred the remaining Conestoga.

William Penn negotiated with the Haudenosaunee to open land along the Susquehanna, and in the first half of the 18th century thousands of German and Scots-Irish immigrants settled the lower valley. Lancaster County was founded in 1729. In July 1778 Loyalist soldiers and Seneca warriors under Major John Butler destroyed most of the Patriot militia at the Battle of Wyoming, and in 1779 Brigadier General James Clinton and Major General John Sullivan led a campaign down the river and up the Chemung, destroying 40 Seneca and Cayuga villages and winter food stores.

In the early 19th century canals beside the river carried anthracite coal to Atlantic ports, and Harrisburg replaced Lancaster as the state capital in 1812. Railways made the canals unprofitable by the 1850s. Before the Port Deposit Bridge opened in 1818 the river could be crossed only by ferry, so it formed a barrier between the northern and southern states.

The river is about 715 kilometres long and is the longest river on the East Coast of the United States. About 200 bridges cross it, among them the Rockville Bridge at Harrisburg, built in 1902, which is the longest stone masonry arch bridge in the world. The river was designated an American Heritage River in 1997. Floods from Hurricane Agnes in 1972 were among the worst in its recorded history.
susquehannock: In the late 15th and early 16th centuries the Susquehannock lived in scattered hamlets on the North Branch of the Susquehanna River, in what is now Bradford County, Pennsylvania, and Tioga County, New York. In the second half of the 16th century they moved south towards the Chesapeake Bay, possibly because of conflict with the Haudenosaunee, the shorter growing seasons of the Little Ice Age or the pull of trade goods. They absorbed the Shenks Ferry people and built palisaded towns in present-day Lancaster County, one near Washington Boro estimated at about 1,700 people.

From the 1620s they traded beaver pelts for cloth, glass beads, brass kettles, axes and knives, and from the 1630s for muskets. After the Province of Maryland was founded in 1634 and allied with the Piscataway, whom they often raided, relations with the English soured; a Maryland expedition in 1643 failed, and the Susquehannock captured two of its cannon. The Articles of Peace and Friendship followed a Mohawk attack, and in 1660 the treaty became an alliance. Despite a smallpox epidemic in 1661, they withstood a siege by 800 Seneca, Cayuga and Onondaga in May 1663.

In July 1675 Virginians chasing Doeg raiders killed several Susquehannock in Maryland. In September a thousand-man militia under John Washington and Thomas Truman besieged their fort and executed five sachems summoned to a parley; in early November the besieged slipped away by night. Many fled to Virginia, where Nathaniel Bacon's militia hunted them, and in 1677 most of those living among the Lenape joined the Haudenosaunee. At Conestoga Town only seven men, five women and eight children remained by 1763. That December the Paxton Boys killed six there and, two weeks later, the fourteen sheltered in the Lancaster workhouse.

Their society is assumed to have resembled that of other Northern Iroquoian peoples: clan-based, matrilineal and horticultural. Families related through the female line shared bark longhouses up to 80 feet long, inside a double palisade, and a village moved roughly every 25 years as the soil wore out. Maize, beans and squash were the staples, maize soup making up nearly half their calories. Women farmed, ran the household and made shell-tempered pottery, including face pots; men travelled to hunt, trade and raid, and tended fishing weirs for shad and eels. Their language survives mainly in about 100 words recorded by the Swedish missionary Johannes Campanius in the 1640s.
susu-people: The Susu speak Sosoxui, a language of the Soso-Yalunka branch of the Mande languages, closely related to Yalunka and influenced by Mandinka, Soninke and Kpelle. They are believed to have Soninke roots and to be connected with the medieval Sosso Empire. One tradition holds that they were a section of the Soninke who migrated out of Wagadou, at first a clan of blacksmiths. In the twelfth century, as the ancient Ghana Empire declined, they are said to have moved south and founded a capital, Soso, in the mountainous region of Koulikoro. They were once ruled by Sumanguru Kanté and afterwards by the Mali Empire.

In the fifteenth century, as the Mali Empire broke up, the Susu moved west to the Fouta Djallon plateau. Portuguese writers of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, including Valentim Fernandes and Duarte Pacheco Pereira, give some of the earliest written records of the Soso and Yalunka. They describe a kingdom called Jalo Concho, and record that the two peoples were animists with organised caste systems, active in regional trade and at war with the Mané.

In the eighteenth century Fula invaders separated the Susu from the Yalunka. The Fula formed an Islamic state in the Fouta Djallon and, from the 1720s, justified enslaving the non-Islamic by a jihad, according to the historian Ismail Rashid. Under this pressure the Susu converted to Islam in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and moved south and west to the coastal plains, absorbing peoples such as the Nalu, Baga and Landouma.

Their coastal chiefdoms were decentralised. Dubréka was a prominent Susu chiefdom in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, and its ruler Balé Demba concluded a protectorate agreement with French authorities in 1880. Kindia, inland, was another political and commercial centre. When the colonial powers divided the region in the late nineteenth century, the Guinea regions where Susu lived became part of the French empire, while the Sierra Leone regions where Temne was spoken went to the British.

Susu society is patrilineal, and more than 99 per cent of Susu are Muslim. Extended families live close together, and polygyny is practised within Islamic law. Like other Mande peoples, the Susu have castes of artisans, among them smiths, carpenters, musicians, bards, jewellers and leatherworkers. Girls are prepared for adulthood through the Bondo society. Most Susu are farmers, growing rice and millet, and they are also known as traders and blacksmiths. Women make palm oil, and many also trade in garden vegetables. In the Susu language the word for woman is guinea, from which the country's name derives.
sutan-sjahrir: Sutan Sjahrir was born on 5 March 1909 in Padang Panjang, West Sumatra, into a Minangkabau family. His father, Muhammad Rasyad Maharajo Sutan, was chief public prosecutor at the Landraad in Medan, where the family lived, and had six wives. Sjahrir was a half-brother of Rohana Kudus, an advocate of women's education and a journalist. He attended the Europeesche Lagere School and the MULO in Medan and then the Algemene Middelbare School in Bandung, where he directed and acted with a student theatre group and helped found a People's University against illiteracy.

In 1929 he went to the Netherlands on a scholarship and studied at the University of Amsterdam and then law at Leiden University, where he came to value socialist principles. He became briefly secretary of the Perhimpoenan Indonesia, from which he and Mohammad Hatta were expelled in 1931 as communist influence grew.

Sjahrir went ahead to the Dutch East Indies in 1931 to help set up the Indonesian National Party and wrote for its newspaper, Daulat Rajat. The Dutch imprisoned him and Hatta at Cipinang in March 1934 and convicted them in November for nationalist activities. They were exiled to Boven-Digoel in 1935, a year later to Banda and shortly before the Japanese conquest of 1941 to Sukabumi.

Under the Japanese occupation Sjahrir, who was ill with tuberculosis, took little public part. He, Sukarno and Hatta agreed that he would go underground and organise resistance while the other two cooperated with the occupiers. His pamphlet Our Struggle (Perdjoeangan Kita) of 1945 appeared amid the violence of the early Bersiap period and called for understanding of other ethnic groups, against racist outbursts.

Sukarno appointed Sjahrir prime minister in November 1945, at 36 the youngest world leader. He served until June 1947. His non-cooperation with the Japanese made him one of the few Republican leaders acceptable to the Dutch government, and in 1946 he played a crucial role in negotiating the Linggadjati Agreement, which some political adversaries opposed.

He founded the Indonesian Socialist Party in 1948 to oppose the Indonesian Communist Party. It was small but influential in the early years because of its leaders' education, and it did poorly in the 1955 elections. Sukarno banned it in August 1960 for supporting a rebellion in Sumatra and opposing his policies. In 1962 Sjahrir was jailed on alleged conspiracy charges and never tried. He had a stroke in 1965, lost his speech and was sent to Zürich, where he died on 9 April 1966. That day he was named a National Hero of Indonesia. The former Dutch prime minister Professor Schermerhorn called him a noble political warrior.
sutherland: Sutherland is a historic county, registration county and lieutenancy area, stretching from the Atlantic in the west to the Pentland Firth and the North Sea in the east. It is Scotland's fifth-largest county by area but has a smaller population than a medium-sized Lowland town. The west and north coasts have very high sea cliffs and deep sea lochs, and Cape Wrath is the most north-westerly point in Scotland. Ben More Assynt, at 998 metres, is the tallest peak in the county, and in the west isolated sandstone peaks such as Foinaven, Arkle and Suilven rise from Lewisian gneiss.

Much of the area belonged to the Pictish kingdom of Cat, which also included Caithness. In the 9th century it was conquered by Sigurd Eysteinsson, Jarl of Orkney, and the Scottish crown claimed overlordship from Norway in 1098. The Diocese of Caithness was established in the 12th century, and its seat moved to Dornoch Cathedral, begun in 1224. About then an earldom of Sutherland was made from the southern part of the earldom of Orkney and Caithness. A shire called Sutherland was created in 1633, with Dornoch as head burgh, and the county ceased to be used for local government in 1975.

The Sutherland Estate, about two thirds of the county, saw the largest clearances in the Highlands, mostly in 1812, 1814 and 1819-20. In the last of these, 1,068 families, an estimated 5,400 people, were evicted. They were offered resettlement on the coast with work in fishing, but many moved to farms in Caithness or emigrated to Canada, the United States or Australia.

The clearances concentrated Gaelic speakers in the new fishing villages and so prolonged the language there. East Sutherland Gaelic, spoken around Golspie, Brora and Embo, was the last Gaelic dialect commonly spoken on the east coast of Scotland, and its last known native speaker died in 2020.

The population peaked at 25,793 in 1851 and fell to 12,803 by the 2011 census. Four of Scotland's National Scenic Areas lie wholly or partly in the county. The pre-1975 boundaries are still used for land registration. A flag adopted in 2018 shows an overlapping saltire and Nordic cross, for Scottish and Norwegian heritage.
sutlej-river: The Sutlej is a major river of Asia, flowing through China, India and Pakistan, and is the longest of the five major rivers of the Punjab. It is also known as Satadru and is the easternmost tributary of the Indus. It rises on the Tibetan plateau at the lakes of Manasarovar and Rakshastal, on the southern slope of Mount Kailash, about 4,570 metres above sea level, and is fed by snow and glaciers. Under the Tibetan name Langqên Zangbo, meaning Elephant River, it flows west-northwest for about 260 kilometres to the Shipki La pass and enters India in Himachal Pradesh.

It then turns south-west, passes through the Bhakra gorge and the Anandpur Dun, and leaves the hills near Ropar to enter the plains of the Punjab. It meets the Beas near Harike, enters Pakistan, and joins the Chenab to form the Panjnad, which flows into the Indus.

The Sanskrit name was Shutudri, and it was also called Zaradros. In the Mahabharata the sage Vasishtha leapt into it, and it is said to have divided into a hundred streams, so that it became the river of a hundred courses. The upper valley was known as the Garuda Valley to the Zhangzhung, the ancient civilisation of western Tibet, who built a palace called Kyunglung there; they were eventually conquered by the Tibetan Empire.

The river was the main means of transport for the kings of the region, and in the early 18th century it carried deodar timber to Bilaspur, Hamirpur and other places along its banks. It also formed the eastern boundary of the Sikh Empire under Maharajah Ranjit Singh.

Before the 11th century the Sutlej did not join the Indus but flowed into the Hakra or Ghaggar River by one or more old channels. Geological evidence suggests that before about 1700 BCE, and perhaps much earlier, it was an important tributary of the Ghaggar-Hakra, thought by some to be the Sarasvati. Authors put its redirection at various dates, from before 8000 BCE to 2000 BCE.

If the diversion was recent, it may have caused the Ghaggar-Hakra to dry up and Harappan settlements along it to be abandoned, though the Sutlej may have been captured by the Indus thousands of years earlier.

The Sutlej is an antecedent river, one that existed before the Himalayas and cut its way down as they rose. Its waters are allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty and are mostly diverted into irrigation canals such as the Sirhind Canal and the Rajasthan canal. The Bhakra Dam, with 1,325 MW of generating capacity, supplies irrigation to Punjab, Rajasthan and Haryana, and further hydroelectric works stand upstream, including the Nathpa Jhakri and Karcham Wangtoo plants.
sutri: Sutri, in Latin Sutrium, lies in the province of Viterbo, about 50 kilometres from Rome and about 30 kilometres south of Viterbo. It stands on a narrow tuff hill surrounded by ravines, with a narrow neck on the west alone connecting it with the surrounding country. In antiquity it commanded the road into Etruria, the later Via Cassia, and Livy describes it as one of the keys of Etruria, the nearby town of Nepi being the other.

Sutrium came into the hands of Rome after the fall of Veii, and a Latin colony was founded there. It was lost again in 386 BCE, but was recovered and recolonised around 383 BCE. The Etruscans besieged it in 311-310 BCE without taking it, and in 209 BCE it joined Nepi and ten other Latin colonies in refusing further help to Rome in the Second Punic War. It received a colony of veterans under the triumvirs and was a place of some importance under the empire. It was later occupied by the Lombards.

In 728 the Lombard king Liutprand and Pope Gregory II reached an agreement there by which Sutri and some hill towns in Latium were given to the papacy, as a gift to the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. It was the first extension of papal territory beyond the Duchy of Rome. A hoard of jewellery of this period, the Sutri Treasure, was found near the town in the 19th century and is in the British Museum.

The Synod of Sutri was convened at the request of Emperor Henry III to resolve three rival claims to the papacy, and ended in favour of Pope Clement II; Gregory VI abdicated at Sutri on 20 December 1046. In 1433 the condottiero Niccolò Fortebraccio set fire to Sutri, and from then on it declined in favour of Ronciglione.

The modern comune has a few more than 5,000 inhabitants. Its remains draw tourists: a Roman amphitheatre cut in the tuff, of elliptical plan and about 49 by 40 metres, an Etruscan necropolis with dozens of rock-cut tombs, and ancient walls of rectangular tuff blocks. The cathedral is Romanesque in origin but largely modern, keeping a belltower of 1207 and a crypt of the Lombard period. The church of the Madonna del Parto was developed from an Etruscan tomb and, according to some scholars, was a Mithraeum.
sutta-nipata: The Sutta Nipāta is the fifth book of the Khuddaka Nikāya. Robert Chalmers explained sutta as a consecutive thread of teaching, and Hermann Oldenberg took nipata to mean a small collection. It has five sections: the Uraga Vagga (The Chapter on the Serpent, 12 suttas), the Cūḷa Vagga (The Minor Chapter, 14), the Mahā Vagga (The Great Chapter, 12), the Aṭṭhaka Vagga (The Chapter of Octads, 16) and the Pārāyana Vagga (The Chapter on the Way Beyond, 16), with a prologue and an epilogue, 70 suttas and 1149 verses in all. Every sutta is a poem, sometimes mixed with prose.

Several Buddhist legends originate here, such as Asita's prediction at the birth of Siddhartha Gautama in the Nalaka sutta and the meeting of King Bimbisāra with the Buddha. The Khaggavisāṇa or Rhinoceros Sutta seems to reveal an early form of monasticism, stressing an individual quest close to the Indian tradition of sannyasa.

Chalmers held that its materials are not all of equal age but include some of the oldest Buddhist compositions, and Bharat Singh Upadhyaya, Maurice Winternitz and Hajime Nakamura place its poetry at the beginnings of Buddhism; Nakamura holds that the Aṭṭhaka and Pārāyana sections already existed in the Buddha's lifetime. Bhikkhu Bodhi and K. R. Norman agree that it contains much early material, while Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu finds nothing that allows certainty, without ruling it out. The Niddesa, a canonical commentary traditionally attributed to Śāriputra, is regarded as evidence of early composition.

Scholars differ on the unity of the work. Luis Oscar Gómez sees the five sections as a homogeneous whole, while Tilmann Vetter regards it as composite, with suttas of the Aṭṭhaka Vagga coming from ascetic groups older than Siddhartha Gautama, and André Bareau sees no logical order in its sections. A version of the Aṭṭhaka Vagga survives in the Chinese canon, with fragments of a Sanskrit version, and a fairly complete Rhinoceros Sutta was found in 1994 among the Gandhāran Buddhist texts.

The Mettā Sutta, the Ratana Sutta and the Maṅgala Sutta hold an important place in Theravāda ritual: they are recited daily in monasteries and on special occasions, as texts of protection and blessing. English translations include V. Fausbøll's in the Sacred Books of the East (1881), K. R. Norman's The Group of Discourses (1984) and Bhikkhu Bodhi's of 2017.
sutton-hoo: Sutton Hoo lies on the bank of the tidal estuary of the River Deben, opposite the town of Woodbridge, which stands 11 kilometres from the North Sea and below the lowest convenient fording place. The estuary formed a way into East Anglia after the end of Roman rule in Britain. The name derives from Old English, meaning the southern farmstead on a hill shaped like a heel spur.

The land was farmed in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, when timber roundhouses stood there, and again in the Iron Age and Romano-British period, when it was divided into small enclosures. After the Romans withdrew, Angles and Saxons settled in the south-east of Britain, and East Anglia is regarded by many scholars as a region where this settlement was early and dense.

Two Anglo-Saxon cemeteries of the 6th to 7th centuries stand there. They appear as about twenty earth mounds, the tops of which have been flattened by farming. The earliest burials are probably cremations, such as those under Mounds 3 and 4, which held ashes of a man and a horse and of a man, a woman and a horse, with imported objects from the eastern Mediterranean.

Mound 2 held a chamber burial covered by a small ship. Other graves are those of people who died violently, some by hanging and decapitation, thought to have been executed from the 8th and 9th centuries onwards near a gallows that may have stood on Mound 5.

4 metres wide, whose timber had decayed but left its form in the sand. In the chamber lay a crested and masked helmet comparable to those of Vendel and Valsgärde in eastern Sweden, a sword with a gold and garnet pommel, a shield, spears, a gold buckle with a hollow chamber, shoulder-clasps, drinking horns from aurochs, a lyre, silver from the Eastern Roman Empire and textiles.
Scholars believe that Rædwald, the first king of the East Angles, is the most likely person buried in the ship. The finds have prompted comparison with the world of the poem Beowulf.

Edith Pretty, owner of the land, had Basil Brown, a self-taught Suffolk excavator, dig from June 1938, and national scholars took over when the importance of Mound 1 became clear. Further excavations were led by Rupert Bruce-Mitford of the British Museum from 1965 to 1971 and by Martin Carver from 1983 to 1992. The principal finds are in the British Museum, which received the treasure as a gift from Pretty. The site is in the care of the National Trust, whose visitor centre holds replicas and a reconstruction of the burial chamber.
suva: Suva lies around a harbour on a hilly peninsula in the south-east corner of Viti Levu, between Laucala Bay and Suva Harbour, in Rewa Province. The mountains to the north and west catch the south-east trade winds, so conditions are moist all year. The city has a tropical rainforest climate and averages about 3,000 millimetres of rain a year, with no true dry season. Fiji's second governor, Sir Arthur Gordon, is said to have remarked that he had never seen it rain anywhere as it rains in Suva. Although the city is almost surrounded by sea, its coast is lined with mangroves, and a significant part of the centre, including the Parliament buildings, stands on reclaimed mangrove swamp.

In 1868, when Suva was still a small village, the Bauan chieftain Seru Epenisa Cakobau granted 5,000 square kilometres of land to the Australian-based Polynesia Company in exchange for its promise to pay off debts owed to the United States. More than a tenth of that land, 575 square kilometres, was near Suva. The company meant to develop cotton farming, but the land and climate proved unsuitable. Control of the Fiji Islands was ceded to the United Kingdom in 1874.

The colonial authorities moved the capital to Suva from Levuka, on Ovalau, because Levuka's position between a steep mountain and the sea made expansion impractical. Colonel F. E. Pratt of the Royal Engineers, appointed Surveyor-General in 1875, designed the new capital, assisted by W. Stephens and Colonel R. W. Stewart. Suva became a municipality in 1910 under the Municipal Constitution Ordinance of 1909, and its area stayed at one square mile until 1952, when it annexed the Muanikau and Samabula wards. In October of that year it was designated a city, Fiji's first. Later it took in Tamavua and the Cunningham area.

Among its colonial-period landmarks are the Suva City Carnegie Library, built in 1909, and Government House, built in 1882, destroyed by a lightning fire in 1921 and rebuilt in 1928. The government building complex stands on a drained creek bed, with foundations of reinforced concrete pilings driven in from 1935, and was completed in 1939. The Fiji Museum was founded in 1904 and moved to Thurston Gardens in 1954.

Suva is the capital and most populous settlement of Fiji, with 93,874 people at the 2017 census and a metropolitan population of 268,423. Indigenous Fijians and Indo-Fijians form the bulk of its population, alongside Rotumans, Lauans, Europeans, part-Europeans and Chinese. English is the most widely spoken language, with Fijian, Fiji Hindi and others also used. It is the site of the main campus of the University of the South Pacific, and Kings Wharf handles much of Fiji's international shipping. Suva hosted the Pacific Games in 1963, 1979 and 2003.
suwalki: The name derives from the Lithuanian su- (near) and valka (creek, marsh), meaning a place near a small river or swampy area. The Czarna Hańcza river flows through the town, which lies about 30 km from the south-western border of Lithuania, beside the Via Baltica road that links Warsaw with Kaunas, Riga, Tallinn and Helsinki. The Suwałki Landscape Park and Wigry National Park lie nearby. It has among the coldest climates of the larger Polish towns, and is often called the Polish pole of cold.

Yotvingian and Prussian tribes lived in the area from the early Middle Ages. After the Teutonic Order arrived in Yotvingia their lands were conquered and stayed largely depopulated for centuries. In 1667 John II Casimir, Grand Duke of Lithuania and King of Poland, granted the land around the future town to the Camaldolese monks, who built a monastery and church at Wigry. The village is first mentioned in 1688, and two years later it had just two houses.

Growth was fast. By 1700 the village was split into Lesser and Greater Suwałki, on the trade route from Grodno and Merkinė to Königsberg. In 1710 Augustus II the Strong granted it the right to hold fairs and markets, and in 1715 the order's grand master, Ildefons, gave it town rights, dividing it into 300 lots. Augustus II approved the rights on 2 May 1720 and a coat of arms showing Saint Roch and Saint Romuald. After the Partitions of Poland the area passed to Prussia in 1795, and the Wigry monastery was dissolved in 1796. Suwałki then had 1,184 inhabitants, a large part of them Jewish.

After the Congress of Vienna Suwałki belonged to Congress Poland under the Russian Empire, and in 1816 the government of the new Augustów Voivodeship was gradually moved there. It later became capital of the Augustów and then the Suwałki Gubernia. By 1857 it had 11,273 inhabitants, making it the fourth most populous town of Congress Poland. In the Second World War it was annexed to East Prussia as Sudauen. Almost all of its Jewish community of about 7,000 was deported and murdered, and the Germans ran the Stalag I-F camp for Soviet prisoners of war at Krzywólka. The Red Army took the town on 23 October 1944, and most of its historic buildings had survived.

Suwałki is the capital of Suwałki County and had a population of 69,206 in 2021. Its sights include the Saint Alexander Co-Cathedral, Neoclassical Kościuszko street and a cemetery complex holding Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, Jewish and Muslim graves. The poet Maria Konopnicka, author of Rota, is among its notable people, and a museum stands in her childhood home.
suwayda: The city was founded by the Nabataeans as Suada. In the Hellenistic period and under the Roman Empire it was known as Dionysias Soada, after Dionysus, the patron of wine, in a wine-producing region. The name Dionysias replaced the Nabataean one in 149 CE, as Nabataean influence declined and Hellenization accelerated in Coele-Syria. Dionysias belonged to the Roman province of Arabia Petraea and received the rights of a civitas under Commodus, between 180 and 185. Dionysus was worshipped in the same Nabataean temple that had been dedicated to Dushara. In the Byzantine period, under the influence of the Ghassanids, it was a diocese with a suffragan bishop from Bosra, and after the early Muslim conquests it became a titular see.

In 1516 the Ottoman Empire took the area from the Mamluk Sultanate. An Ottoman tax register of 1596 lists the place as Majdal Sawda, with five households and five bachelors, all Muslim. In the late 17th or early 18th century Druze from Mount Lebanon and other parts of Syria migrated in large numbers to the Jabal Hauran, which came to be called Jabal al-Druze, the Druze Mountain. They settled the deserted but defensible ancient villages there, and Suwayda was among the villages settled before 1812. By at least 1860 it was the main Druze settlement of the region. In the 19th century the French statesman and antiquarian William Waddington identified Dionysias as Suwayda.

Suwayda is the capital of the Suwayda Governorate, one of Syria's fourteen governorates, on the border with Jordan. The 2004 census gave it 73,641 inhabitants. It is a Druze-majority city with small Christian, mostly Greek Orthodox, and Sunni Muslim Bedouin minorities. The Bedouin live mainly on its northern and eastern outskirts.

The old part of the city holds ancient remains. Eight decorated columns of the Temple of Dionysus-Dushara still stand, and the Basilica of Saint Sergius dates from the fifth century. An arch of a ruined church, known locally as the Gallows, bears grape motifs. Old Roman houses are still lived in, and a 7th-century mosque from the time of the Rashidun Caliphate is also recorded. Much of the old city awaits excavation, including a Roman aqueduct and a larger Roman theatre.
suwon: Suwon lies in the north of the Gyeonggi plain, in a basin-like terrain among low hills. Gwanggyosan, at 582 metres, is its highest point, and the Yellow Sea coast is not far to the west. The name means water source, and almost all of the names the area has borne since antiquity share that meaning. The present name was given in 1310. The streams that rise on the hills flow south to the Yellow Sea at Asan Bay, and the city has eleven small reservoirs, one of which, Irwang Reservoir, has been designated a world heritage site for irrigation. Four districts make up the city: Jangan, Gwonseon, Paldal and Yeongtong.

Artefacts from the Bronze Age to the early Iron Age have been found in the area. In the Three Kingdoms period it was a territory of the statelet Mosuguk, part of the Mahan confederacy. It came under the influence of Goguryeo in the late 5th century, became part of Unified Silla and then fell to Goryeo after a campaign led by King Taejo. Under Joseon it was made an administrative centre of Gyeonggi Province in 1395. Until the late 18th century Suwon was administered from the foot of Hwasan. In 1796 King Jeongjo moved it to its present site at the foot of Paldalsan and commanded the building of Hwaseong Fortress to protect the new town.

Suwon became a city on 15 August 1949. In the Korean War, on 27 June 1950, United States planes there were attacked by North Korean fighters in the Battle of Suwon Airfield, the first aerial combat of the war. The city fell to the North on 4 July 1950 and changed hands four times in all. An eyewitness account by a US intelligence officer places a massacre of about 1,800 people at Suwon in late June 1950. The provincial headquarters of Gyeonggi began moving there from Seoul in 1964.

Hwaseong Fortress is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Four main gates pierce its walls, and Haenggung Palace stands in the centre. The city once lay entirely within the walls but has long since grown far beyond them. Suwon is traditionally known as the City of Filial Piety. It has about 1.2 million inhabitants and is home to Sungkyunkwan University and Ajou University, and the research and development centre of Samsung Electronics. Three expressways, the national railway and three lines of the Seoul Metropolitan Subway serve it.
suyab: Suyab, also called Ordukent, lay in the Chu river valley some 50 kilometres east of Bishkek and 8 kilometres west-south-west of Tokmok, in present-day Kyrgyzstan. A settlement of Sogdian merchants grew up there along the Silk Road in the 5th or 6th century. Its name comes from the Suyab River, an Iranian name meaning toward the water. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who passed in 629, described a walled city where merchants from many nations gathered, with a cold, windy climate and millet and grapes grown in the soil.

Under Tong Yabghu Qaghan, Suyab was the principal capital of the Western Turkic Khaganate, which also had a summer capital at Navekat. The Sogdians provided economic prosperity and the Göktürks military security. After the khaganate fell, Suyab was absorbed into the Tang dynasty and served as a military outpost between 648 and 719. A Chinese fortress was built in 679 by Wang Fangyi, and Buddhism flourished. According to some accounts the poet Li Bai was born there. The Old Book of Tang says the city had twelve gates on four sides, curved to hide its inhabitants.

Suyab was one of the Four Garrisons of Anxi until 719, when it passed to Suluk of the Türgesh, whom the Tang court named Loyal and Obedient Qaghan. After Suluk was murdered in 738, Tang forces retook it, and it was strategically important in the wars against the Tibetan Empire. The traveller Du Huan found a working Buddhist monastery among its ruins in 751. In 766 it fell to a Karluk ruler allied with the nascent Uyghur Khaganate, and little is recorded after the Chinese left the Four Garrisons in 787. The Hudud al-Alam, completed in 983, lists it as a city of 20,000 inhabitants. It is believed to have been supplanted by Balasagun in the early 11th century and abandoned soon after.

In the 19th century the ruins at Ak-Beshim were wrongly identified with Balasagun, the capital of the Kara-Khitans, and Vasily Bartold supported this after visiting in 1893–1894. Excavations began in 1938, and in the 1950s it was shown that the site had been abandoned in the 11th century, while Balasagun flourished until the 14th. The site covers some 30 hectares and holds Chinese fortifications, Nestorian Christian churches, Zoroastrian ossuaries and Turkic balbals, with many Buddha statues and stelae. There was a 7th-century Nestorian church and cemetery, and probably a 10th-century monastery with frescoes and inscriptions in Sogdian and Uyghur scripts. The ruins were inscribed in 2014 as part of the Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor World Heritage Site.
suzdal: Suzdal lies on the Kamenka, a tributary of the Nerl, 26 kilometres north of the city of Vladimir. Its name is thought to rest on an Old Russian verb meaning to make from clay, and more likely derives from the nickname of a person, perhaps a potter or bricklayer, from which the settlement was named. The region was already populated by Finnic and East Slavic tribes in the 9th and 10th centuries, and Suzdal arose on the site of a settlement of the Meryans. By 1096 it was fortified.

At the turn of the 12th century Grand Prince Vladimir Monomakh arrived with a wave of settlers and about 1102 began a stone cathedral. He made his son Yury Dolgoruky prince of Suzdal, and by Monomakh's death in 1125 the Rostov-Suzdal principality was virtually independent, with Suzdal as capital. Yury promoted the founding of new towns, among them Moscow. In 1157 the capital moved to Vladimir, and Suzdal became part of the Grand Principality of Vladimir. Following the Mongol conquest it became in 1238 the capital of the Principality of Suzdal. The Nativity Cathedral withstood the Mongol siege, though its interior was looted.

In 1341 Suzdal united with Nizhny Novgorod, and in 1350 Konstantin of Suzdal moved his capital to Nizhny Novgorod. Grand Prince Vasily I of Moscow annexed the principality in 1392. In 1445 Tatars sacked the town and set fire to the cathedral, whose upper part collapsed; it was rebuilt in 1528–1530. As political importance faded, Suzdal regained prominence as a religious centre, with building funded by Vasily III and Tsar Ivan IV, and it was the seat of a diocese until the 19th century. In the late 17th and 18th centuries wealthy merchants funded 30 churches. In 1864 local merchants failed to persuade the government to bring the Trans-Siberian Railway through the town, and it went through Vladimir, 35 kilometres away.

Suzdal avoided the industrialisation of the Soviet period, and its buildings from the 13th to the 19th century remain. It has 305 monuments and listed buildings, among them 30 churches, 14 bell towers and five monasteries and convents, and has had federally protected status since 1967. In 1992 the Saviour Monastery of St Euthymius and the Kremlin with the Nativity of the Virgin Cathedral were entered on the UNESCO World Heritage List together with other white monuments of the region. The monastery, founded in 1352, became a prison in 1766 on the orders of Catherine the Great. Suzdal is the smallest of the towns of Russia's Golden Ring, and tourism is its main industry.
suzhou: Suzhou lies in southeastern Jiangsu Province on the Lake Tai Plain, a fertile alluvial basin bordered by Lake Tai to the southwest and the Yangtze River to the north. The terrain is low and flat, crossed by many rivers and lakes, and rivers, lakes and mudflats make up 36.6 percent of the city's land area. The Yangtze River and the Grand Canal cross its northern area. It has been called the Water Capital and the Venice of the East, a comparison the Travels of Marco Polo makes in the 13th century. Along with Hangzhou it is praised in Chinese poetry as paradise on earth.

Suzhou is one of the oldest towns in the Yangtze Basin. In the Spring and Autumn period local Baiyue tribes called the Gou Wu lived in villages on the edges of the hills above the wetlands around Lake Tai. During the Zhou dynasty a settlement known as Gusu, after nearby Mount Gusu, became the capital of the state of Wu. In 514 BCE King Helü of Wu established a new capital nearby, Helü City, which grew into the modern city. It was later known as Wuxian, Wu County, and Wujun, Wu Commandery, and under the Qin as Kuaiji after its greatly enlarged commandery.

The city grew quickly by the Eastern Han dynasty, mostly through emigration from northern China. From the 10th century it was an important economic, cultural and commercial centre, and until Shanghai overtook it in about 1850 it was the largest non-capital city in the world. Silk production has a long history there. From the Song and Yuan dynasties it was one of the centres of silk weaving and dyeing, by the 13th century it was the centre of the profitable silk trade, and in the Ming dynasty its silk was praised as the clothing of the world. Painters and writers of the Ming dynasty came from the city, among them Tang Yin, Wen Zhengming, founder of the Wu School, and the writer Feng Menglong.

Suzhou is a prefecture-level city divided into six urban districts and four county-level cities. Its Classical Gardens, over 60 in number, were added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1997 and 2000. Other landmarks include Tiger Hill, the Yunyan Pagoda built in 961, which leans and is nicknamed the Leaning Tower of China, and the Baodai Bridge, first built in 806, with 53 arches. Kunqu opera originated in the Suzhou region, as did the ballad-singing tradition pingtan. In 1994 China and Singapore signed an agreement to develop the Suzhou Industrial Park, which began on 12 May of that year.
svans: The Svans call themselves Mushwan, a name that probably lies behind the Misimian of the classical authors. In their own language they are the shwanær, and in Georgian they are the svanebi. They are usually identified with the Soanes mentioned by the Greek geographer Strabo, who placed them more or less in the area that Svans still occupy, the region of Svaneti in north-western Georgia.

The Svans were Christianized between the 4th and 6th centuries and are Georgian Orthodox Christians today, although some remnants of pre-Christian belief survive. Saint George, a patron saint of Georgia known locally as Jgëræg, is the most respected saint among them. The medieval painter Tevdore, active in the 11th and 12th centuries, is among the Svans remembered for religious murals and frescoes.

In the Russian Empire and the early Soviet Union, Mingrelians and Svans had their own census grouping. The pre-1930 Soviet census counted the Svans as a separate ethnic group alongside other subgroups of Georgians, and in the 1930s they were classified under the broader category of Georgian.
The Svans speak Svan, an unwritten Kartvelian language, and most are also bilingual in Georgian, the other Kartvelian language of the region. Before the 19th century many Svans knew only Svan.

The Svans have kept many old traditions, including blood revenge, though the custom has declined as law enforcement has taken hold. Their families are small, and the husband is the head of the family. Older women in the family are strongly respected.
